## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION WHICH HAVE SURVIVED FROM THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, BASED UPON THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND MOST CAREFULLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED IN THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ORNAMENTED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS WELL AS WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING ITS SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH NEVERTHELESS POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two ample general indices: one, namely, an index of subjects, through consulting which everything that each of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other, an index of Holy Scripture, through which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each passage of each book of Scripture, and in what places in their works. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS if the following be weighed: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time brought together in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III.** Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Library for the Entire Clergy*, or of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. # [The Complete Works of John of Salisbury]

## Prolegomena

[Col. IX]

# Notice Concerning John of Salisbury

(*New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1146)

[Col. IXA] John was English by nationality, commonly surnamed “of Salisbury” from his native country. Having gone to Paris in 1136, he had as his teachers Peter Abelard, Alberic of Rheims, Gilbert of Poitiers, Robert Pullen, and other men eminent for learning in that age. He spent almost twelve years in the Parisian schools, teaching the children of nobles in order to relieve his poverty. He was intimate with Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, and with his successor, St Thomas. To the former, while still chancellor of Henry II, king of England, he sent his notable work *On the Trifles of Courtiers*, when he was accompanying the king at the siege of Toulouse in 1159. He was also acceptable to the king of England, who employed him in public affairs. For the king sent him to Pope Adrian IV to obtain the privilege of occupying Ireland; he solemnly read this out in the synod at Waterford, and, in the pope’s name, presented the king with a gold ring as a sign of investiture.

[Col. IXB] He was also beloved by and well known to the supreme pontiffs Eugene III and Adrian IV, as is clear from the freedom and confidence with which he dared to lay before this pope many abuses of the Roman Curia. He was likewise secretary and letter-writer to Pope Alexander, who particularly used him in writing against the antipope Octavian and his supporters. Finally, after travelling through Italy and France, which the fame of his name had already filled, he was, chiefly through the support of William, Archbishop of Sens and likewise bishop-elect of Chartres, and with the king’s approval, elected bishop of Chartres—both because of his learning and manner of life, and especially because he had been the companion of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, in exile and other sufferings.

[Col. IXC] After this election, on 22 July 1176, the dean, cantor, and chancellor of the Church of Chartres came to Canterbury, requesting that John be granted to them; the chapter gave him letters dimissory while the bishop was absent. King Louis himself also wrote to John, asking him to give his assent to the election. Thus he was consecrated at Sens on Sunday, 8 August, by Maurice, Bishop of Paris; on the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary he solemnly took possession of his church, which he governed for four years.

Of him the supplement to Sigebert says: “John of Salisbury succeeded in the city of Chartres, an honourable and wise man, who had formerly been clerk of Theobald, bishop of Canterbury, and afterwards of the holy martyr Thomas, successor of that same Theobald.”

[Col. XA] He had also been a clerk of Peter of Celle, as is clear from Book VII, Letter 6, to the Archbishop of Lund: “The Archbishop of Sens became Archbishop of Rheims; Master John of Salisbury, once our clerk, became Bishop of Chartres.” In Book VII, Letters 20 and 21, speaking to the Archbishop of Canterbury concerning John’s election, Peter calls John his foster-child:

“Your predecessor, Archbishop Theobald, of most holy memory, received Master John, now Bishop of Chartres, poor and needy, from our bosom and lap; but, with God’s aid, advanced him by his encouragements to the rank of the great who are on the earth.”

The same Peter of Celle contains seven letters written to John before he became bishop, and several others [Col. XB] from which it becomes known that he was bound to him by a close tie of friendship. John, while in exile, was kindly received into the abbey and afterwards granted many benefits. He declares himself indebted for these, particularly in Letter 85, which begins:

“It is not new that your kindness has procured for me support for my sustenance. It received my poverty in a foreign land in such a way that neither a father’s service nor a mother’s affection seemed lacking to me. It was indeed a great thing to provide for an exile so that among foreign nations I might enjoy the comforts of citizens; but much greater is the care you took for me, that I might not remain forever banished from the sweetness of my native soil, by which the whole human race is held captive. For it is your gift that I have returned [Col. XC] to the land of my birth. It is your gift that I have attained acquaintance, intimacy, and favour with many eminent men. It is your gift that I seem to flourish in my homeland and, by the Lord’s agency, to be preferred to many of my fellow citizens and contemporaries. But why do I recount item by item the titles of your liberality and generosity, when their number and immensity so fill my whole mind that they overflow and exceed the capacity of my entire understanding? From the Lord, indeed, I must have deserved both those benefits alone which I cannot sufficiently recall and whatever I am and can do. I am therefore bound in such a way that no giving of thanks can free me, since your merits absorb all my efforts, especially since your devotion continually binds me to itself by its benefits,” etc.

Having thus become bishop, John gave Abbot B. of Saint-Laumer permission in 1176, the first year of his episcopate, to build an oratory in the village of Moresio. [Col. XIA] In 1177 he confirmed to the canons of St Mary Magdalene at Châteaudun the church of Choue, granted by his predecessors. In the same year, acting in this matter in the pope’s stead, he ratified an agreement made between Simon, Bishop of Meaux, and the abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés. He was also present when the kings of France and England swore that they would undertake service of the Cross. In 1178, called the second year of his episcopate in the cartulary of Saint-Avitus, he adjudged the church of Villamauri to the canons of St Cloud against Walter, archdeacon of Dunois, on 15 September.

He attended the Lateran Council in March 1179, at which, while the Fathers were sitting to frame new decrees, he said, “Far be it that new things should be enacted and that very many old things should be recast and renewed,” etc. [Col. XIB] In the same year he invested the abbot of St Peter with an alms made to the monastery. Delegated by the Apostolic See, he settled disputes between the abbot of St Denis and the canons of St Exuperius at Corbeil in 1180. In the same year, he accepted satisfaction from John, Count of Vendôme, who was preparing for a journey to Jerusalem, for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of St Laumer at Blois; and he absolved him from the bond of excommunication which he had incurred three years before through injuries inflicted upon the monks of Vendôme. Martène publishes two letters of John’s, preventing Peter of Candeio from compelling the monks of Fontaines to celebrate Mass in the church of [Col. XIC] Lauda contrary to the practice of the Cistercian order.

Robert of Torigni, in his Appendix, places John’s death in 1181; others, in 1182. The more common opinion among scholars is that John was taken from the living on 25 October 1180. This is established by the necrology of the monastery of Josaphat, where he was buried; by the chronology of Hugh, monk of Auxerre, his contemporary, who assigns John’s death to the said year; and by William of Nangis, who praises him for wisdom and strength of spirit. The necrology of Josaphat says of John:

“On the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October], the death of Lord John, Bishop of Chartres, a man exceedingly distinguished by Christian principles and excellent morals, whose body lies among us in the chapel of Blessed Mary. Before obtaining the episcopate, he was chaplain of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, when Thomas suffered martyrdom among the English.”

But the necrology of Chartres reads: “[lacuna] The father of blessed memory, our John, formerly secretary to Blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and martyr, afterwards venerable bishop of this church of the most merciful Mother of God, has died: a man of great piety, illumined by the rays of every kind of learning, a shepherd beloved by all in word, life, and morals, excessively harsh only to himself, continually subduing his flesh from feet to neck with a hair-shirt. [Col. XIIA] He freed the bishop’s house from the rent in oats which the provost of Bailliol held in it. He loved this church with the whole affection of his heart and the whole intention of his mind, and adorned it with the splendour of diverse ornaments: an excellent cope, three pallia, a precious episcopal ring, and costly priestly vestments. He bestowed two precious vessels upon the same church: in one of them, as we ourselves saw, he placed the blood of the glorious martyr Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, still dripping; in the other, relics of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian. He also bestowed upon us glorious relics of St Gereon, from the company of virgins at Cologne.

“He also obtained a privilege by which the serfs of the Church of Chartres might, out of need or manifest advantage to the church, be manumitted without obstruction from secular violence of power. It was also added that, if we should at any time be brought before secular or ecclesiastical judges concerning our rights, no one should impose upon us trial by combat, or judgment by glowing iron, or by hot or cold water; but we might prove our rights by two or three lawful witnesses. [Col. XIIB] He also gave this church the following volumes of books: Jerome on Mark, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, the Pauline Epistles, and the Twelve Prophets; his lesser breviary and the Psalms; likewise, *Against Jovinian*, the book *On the Divine Offices*, Hugh’s book, and the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*; the book *On Ecclesiastical or Celestial Hierarchy*; Rabanus, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; also *Paralipomenon*; Augustine *Against the Jews* and *On Eighty-Three Questions*, *On Christian Doctrine*; Origen on Joshua; Valerius; Lactantius; Vegetius; the Chronicle of Sigebert; Lombard’s Psalter; a glossed book of Kings; the *Hierarchy*; Lanfranc, *On the Eucharist against Berengar*; the Histories of John of Tours; the Histories of Eutropius; Isidore’s *Etymologies*; the homilies of Pope Leo; a Benedictional and Collectary; Seneca, *Natural Questions*; Cicero, *On Duties* and *On the Orator*; and, besides these, his own *Polycraticus* and an entire library. The greater part of these were lost through the negligence of time or furtively stolen through the condemned greed of certain persons.

“For the use of the brethren who shall attend his anniversary, he also acquired, in the district of Saint-Pierre-de-la-Vallée, eleven solidi of annual rent at Mongerville, twenty sextaries of [unspecified reading: *oblitarum*] with the appurtenances, a share of the harvest, and other revenues from one and a half *beatae* of land. [Col. XIID] In the parish of Chaufour, the tithe of Charmoy. In the mayoralty of Fisc, the tithe of the freehold estates of Genainville, and many other things.”

This bishop, eloquent in both Greek and Latin, left to posterity the celebrated book *Polycraticus*, divided into eight books, *On the Trifles of Courtiers and the Traces of Philosophers*. Alberic states that the author dedicated it to Theobald, chancellor of King Henry of England, although the preface says nothing about this. Peter of Blois, Letter 22, writing to the same man whom he calls his master, says of this book:

“I read your book *On the Trifles of Courtiers*, and it wonderfully refreshed me; for it contains an excellent pattern of instruction and, through the artful variety of its thoughts, material for inestimable delight.”

Justus Lipsius also praises the *Polycraticus* in connection with Book XII of Tacitus’s *Annals*. [Col. XIIIA] John also composed the life of St Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, under whom he served as notary. He was Thomas’s inseparable companion—indeed, his hand and eye. He attributed so much to Thomas’s merits that, once made bishop, in all charters issued at that time he ascribed his pontifical dignity not to his own merits but to those of the holy martyr.

Among the many letters written to him by Peter of Blois, Letter 70 deserves especially to be read. From it we learn that John was so detached from flesh and blood that he preferred promoting strangers to benefices rather than his nephews, although they were poor and respectable. In the notes to Letter 22 of the same Peter of Blois, who had been John’s pupil, Gussenvillaeus composed an encomium of our John. For his other works, bibliographers should be consulted.

[Col. XIII]

# Literary Notice

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin*, VI, 131.)

[Col. XIIIB] John Petit, or Parvus (“Little” or “Small”)

> [Note: [Col. XIIID] Menage, p. 239, on Laërtius. In the same author, p. 109: “John of Salisbury, or John Paraeus”; read “John Parvus.”]

was called “of Salisbury” from his native place, having been born in the English region of Salisbury, which was also called Severia after the emperor Severus.

> [Note: [Col. XIIID] Refer here to John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus* VIII.19, p. 647: “In the catalogue of emperors, Severus is he from whom my people has its name.”]

Hence, in Leland, chapter 176, he is called John Severianus instead of “of Salisbury.” Letters of Peter of Blois addressed to him survive, and Morsus of Ravenna wrote for him a book on the interpretation of Greek words. For his studies, see Bulaeus, vol. II, *History of the University of Paris*, p. 750 ff. His writings testify to his mastery of both languages, his thorough reading of the best authors, and the brilliance and eloquence of his talent in verse and prose.

A most vigorous defender of papal and priestly authority—or, as he himself calls it, majesty—he was for that reason driven into exile by the king of England. [Col. XIIIC] Yet he also clearly perceived and freely noted the vices and abuses of courts, the clergy, and even the popes themselves. He was intimate with the Archbishops of Canterbury, Theobald and Thomas, and with Popes Eugene III, Adrian IV, and Alexander III. At length, having become Bishop of Chartres in 1172,

> [Note: [Col. XIVD] Peter of Celle greatly exults over this election in Book VII, Letter 8, to William, Archbishop of Rheims. See also Peter of Blois, Letter 114.]

he attended the Lateran Council in 1179 and died in 1182, having Peter of Celle as his successor.

> [Note: [Col. XIVD] The Sammarthani, vol. II of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 491; Oudin, vol. II, p. 1504.]

His writings:

*Polycraticus*, or *On the Trifles of Courtiers and the Traces of Philosophers*, in eight books, addressed to Thomas, then still chancellor of England,

> [Note: [Col. XIVD] Alberic in the *Chronicle*, under the year 1157, p. 329.]

and afterwards Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 to 1171. It is a varied and pleasant work to read, in which Lipsius, on Tacitus XII.63, recognized a patchwork containing many pieces of purple cloth and fragments from a better age. [Col. XIIID] This is also clear from the index of authors, which Fabricius intends to provide more fully and accurately in a new edition of *Bibliotheca Latina*, IV.3.

John himself, in Letter 80 to Peter of Celle, says:

“I have published the book *On the Trifles of Courtiers and the Traces of Philosophers*, which will please or displease me according to your judgment. It is uncultivated, and, by my own decree, asks to be corrected by you, my friends. It was hastening to the illustrious man, chancellor of the king of England; but restrain it unless its progress is expedited. For it is talkative and will scarcely have a friend at court. Yet I should not wish it to make us enemies of courtiers. I ask that you instruct it without delay and return it corrected to the friend awaiting it. Not indeed like that British thief of Canterbury, from whose hands it could not be torn until he had been portrayed all over, perhaps so that, more easily accused, he might be thrust before the eyes of his enemies.”

These books appeared at Paris in 1513, quarto; then at Leiden in 1595, octavo; and Paris in 1610, octavo; and, in more corrected form, with the *Metalogicus* appended, at Leiden in 1639, octavo, and Amsterdam in 1664, octavo. They appeared also with the letters in the Cologne supplement to the *Library of the Fathers* in 1622 and in vol. XXIII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*. [Col. XIVC] An old French translation was in the Menars Library, p. 35: *Polycraticon des traces des philosophes, et des truffes et vanitez de ceux qui suivent les cours des princes*—“*Polycraticon* on the traces of philosophers, and on the mockeries and vanities of those who follow the courts of princes.”

The metrical *Eutheticon*, which Labbe says he has not seen, is that polished admonitory elegiac poem of 306 verses prefixed to the *Polycraticus*, beginning:

> “If you believe me, you will restrain your tongue,” etc.

It concerns Thomas, whom it celebrates in verse 27:

> “Sought out as chancellor for yourself, O kingdom of England,” etc.

Nor is it other than the poem *Against Barbarism*, wrongly attributed to Nigel Wireker by Bale, III.50, and Pits, p. 270, as Jacob Thomasius correctly observed in his dissertation on Nigel, §51 ff. Thomasius also rightly notes in §56 that Pits, pp. 248 and 246, wrongly distinguishes as two different works of John of Salisbury the *Metrical Eutheticon* and the *Eutheticum on the Polycraticus*. It should not be omitted that Andreas Rivinus published at Leipzig in 1655, octavo, the metrical writings of two ancient Bishops of Chartres, Fulbert and John of Salisbury. This *Euthetic* poem appears there with the editor’s notes, and is followed [Col. XVA] by another elegiac poem of 200 verses, *On the Members Conspiring Together*,

> [Note: [Col. XVD] See below, at the end of this volume.]

beginning:

> “The limbs of the human body hold a council.”

John of Salisbury had also expounded in prose the famous fable of Menenius Agrippa in Book VI, chapter 24, of the *Polycraticus*.

The *Metalogicus* consists of four books. From its title, “Mythologicon” was wrongly fabricated in Leland, chapter 176, Bale III.1, and John Pits, p. 248. The first book contains an apology for grammar and philology, and Books II, III, and IV for Peripatetic logic against a certain Cornificius of his own, whom in IV.25 he calls “the accuser of logic, the buffoon of philosophers.” He also mentions him in the preface to the *Polycraticus*, p. 5: “For I too have my Cornificius and [Col. XVB] my Lanuvinus.” These books appeared at Paris in 1610, octavo, in a separate volume, and appended to the *Polycraticus* at Leiden in 1639, octavo. They were written after the *Polycraticus*, which he mentions in Book I, chapters 4 and 10; also after the death of Adrian IV in 1156, but while Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, who died in 1161, was still alive. Both facts are established by the last chapter of Book IV.

The 302 letters which he wrote from 1155 to 1180 were first published from the library of Papirius Masson, together with the Life of Thomas of Canterbury and certain writings of Gerbert, or Sylvester II, and Stephen of Tournai, Paris, 1611, quarto. These are the same letters which, as I said, were reprinted at the end of the *Polycraticus* in the Cologne supplement to the *Library of the Fathers* in 1622 and in vol. XXIII of the Lyons edition. Most of them are also the same as those among the ninety-three letters published by Christian Lupus as letters of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Brussels, 1682, quarto.

Meanwhile, below you have an index of the said 302 letters, of which Stephen Baluze promised a better edition.

> [Note: [Col. XVD] Baluze’s letter to Hieronymus Ambrosius Langenmantel, written at Paris on the Kalends of May [1 May] 1686 and published by W. E. Tentzel in 1692, *Monthly Dialogues*, p. 673: “After finishing the edition of the *Marca Hispanica*, I shall immediately set about the second volume of my Collection of Councils, in which many matters of great importance, nowhere hitherto published, will appear. Meanwhile I shall ensure that the Letters of John of Salisbury, which we have from the edition of Papirius Masson, defiled by countless errors, are brought to better light through the aid of old manuscript exemplars—both those used by Masson himself and others as well.”]

Among them are also the seven historical letters, 128, 159, 167, 195, 214, 234, and 268, which Andreas du Chesne presents corrected from a royal Paris manuscript in vol. IV of *French Affairs*, p. 465 ff.

The *Life of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury*, was published at Paris in 1611, quarto, with Salisbury’s letters. Peter of Blois praises it in Letter 114; in Letter 21 the same author testifies that Salisbury was Thomas’s eye and hand during Thomas’s lifetime. Stephen Langton used it in the *Quadrilogue* prefixed to Thomas’s Letters, as did William Stephanides in the Life of Thomas published by Joseph Sparke in *Writers of English History*,

> [Note: [Col. XVID] *Acta Eruditorum*, 1725, p. 490.]

London, 1723, folio.

The *Life of St Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury*, was abridged from Eadmer for the benefit of Thomas, who wished to offer it to Alexander III and commend Anselm for enrollment among the saints. [Col. XVIA] Henry Wharton published it, with a prefixed index of eighteen chapters, in vol. II of *Anglia Sacra*, pp. 151–176, followed on p. 177 by Alexander III’s bull on Anselm’s canonization, London, 1691, folio.

A *Penitential* is mentioned by Trithemius, chapter 394, Leland, and others; so far as I know, it has not been published. Nor have the following seen the light: the little book *On the Evil End of Tyrants*, which Salisbury states that he composed in *Polycraticus* VIII.20; *On the State of the Roman Curia*; *On Twofold Mathematics*; *On the Music of Love*; *Mirror of Reason*; *Mirror of Folly*, addressed to Nigel Wireker in verse; and *On Nigel’s Mirror: Hermeneuticon*; sermons; poems of various kinds, including the *Entheticus on the Doctrine of the Philosophers*, [Col. XVIB] beginning:

> “Examining the doctrines of the ancients,”

in manuscript in the library of Cambridge University; and the *Rebuke of the Clergy*, or *of Clerics*, from which Flacius quotes in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to Truth*, and John Wolf in vol. I of *Memorable Readings*, p. 456, etc.

A commentary on all the Pauline Epistles is mentioned by Bale III.1 and Pits, p. 249, and is said by Lipenius, Cave, Oudin, and James Long to have been published at Amsterdam in 1646, quarto; I do not recall ever having seen it. A commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians was published at Cambridge in 1627, according to William Crowe. In the Morgenwegan Library there was a folio edition published at Cambridge and bearing the year 1630.

# Preface of J. A. Giles

(*The Complete Works of John of Salisbury, later Bishop of Chartres, now for the first time collected into one body and compared with manuscript codices by J. A. Giles, Doctor of Civil Law and formerly Fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. — Oxford and London, 1848, octavo, 5 volumes.*)

The works of John of Salisbury have never before been collected into a single body, nor have they hitherto been committed to print in England either entire or even in part. Yet John shone in the twelfth century with no ordinary reputation for learning, and his writings readily claim the foremost place among the literary monuments of that age and the following one which time has spared.

John, surnamed of Salisbury, was perhaps so called from his native city; he was born about the year 1120. For he indicates somewhere that in 1138 he was still a young man. [Note: [Col. XIX] See *Polycraticus*, Book II, chapter 10, at the beginning.] From another passage, [Note: [Col. XIX] Epistle 202, at the beginning: “But what is this, that I am altogether—a little man by name, lesser in means, least in merit,” etc.] in which he calls himself *Parvus* (“Little”), some have inferred that his true surname was Petit (“Small”); but this can scarcely be drawn from the ambiguous words.

What we know of John’s life is known from no other source than his own occasional statements. In chapter 10 of Book II of the *Metalogicus* he speaks thus of his studies:

> “When first, still quite a youth, I crossed over into Gaul for the sake of study, in the second year after Henry, the illustrious king of the English, the Lion of Justice, had departed this mortal life, I attached myself to the Peripatetic of the Palatine, who was then a renowned teacher on Mount Sainte-Geneviève and held an authority admired by all. At his feet I received the first rudiments of this art; and, according to the measure of my little talent, I caught with the whole eagerness of my mind whatsoever fell from his lips.
>
> “Then, after his departure—which seemed to me too hasty—I joined Master Alberic, who shone out among the rest as the most celebrated dialectician and was indeed the most vigorous opponent of the Nominalist school. Thus, for almost two full years on the Mount, I studied this art under Alberic and Master Robert of Melun—so called from his distinction in governing schools, which he deserved, though English by birth. Of these, the one, scrupulous in every respect, discovered an occasion for a question everywhere; so that however smooth the level ground, it was not without some obstacle, and, as they say, no rush was for him without a knot. For even there he pointed out what ought to be untied. The other, most ready in reply, never evaded the proposed point for purposes of escape, without either choosing the other side of the contradiction or, after defining the ambiguity of the expression, teaching that there was not merely one answer. The former, therefore, was subtle and copious in questions; the latter clear-sighted, brief, and useful in answers. Had these two qualities together happened to belong to any one person, no equal disputant could certainly have been found in our age.
>
> “For both were of keen intellect and tenacious application; and, as I think, they would have distinguished themselves as great and eminent men in physical studies, if they had built upon a great foundation of literature, if only they had followed the traces of their elders as closely as they applauded their own discoveries. This was so at the time when I adhered to them. For afterward one of them went to Bologna and unlearned what he had taught; indeed, upon returning, he taught others to unlearn it. Whether this was better, let those judge who heard him before and afterward. The other, however, advancing in sacred letters, attained the glory of a loftier philosophy and a more celebrated name.
>
> “Having been trained under these men for two whole years, I became so accustomed to assigning loci, to rules, and to the other elementary rudiments by which childish minds are instructed—and in which the aforesaid teachers were most powerful and most skilful—that I seemed to know all these things as well as my fingernails and fingers. For I had plainly learned [Col. XXI] to think, in youthful frivolity, more highly of my knowledge than it was worth. I seemed to myself a little learned man, because I was ready in matters which I had heard.
>
> “Then, coming back to myself and measuring my strength, in gratitude for the benefits of my teachers I deliberately transferred myself to the grammarian of Conches, and heard him teach for three years. Meanwhile I read much, and I shall never regret the time spent with him. Afterwards I followed Richard, surnamed the Bishop, a man almost unacquainted with no branch of learning, who has more heart than speech, more knowledge than eloquence, more truth than vanity, more virtue than display. With him I reread everything which I had heard from others, and learned certain things I had not heard before, belonging to the quadrivium—in which I had previously heard the Teuton Hardewin to some extent.
>
> “I also reread rhetoric, which I had only slightly heard before from Master Theodoric along with certain others, and consequently understood only a little. But later I received it more fully from Peter Helias. And because I had undertaken to instruct the sons of noblemen who, when I had been deprived of the help of friends and kinsmen, supplied sustenance to my poverty through God’s consolation, I was compelled by the necessity of my office and the insistence of the youths to recall more frequently to memory what I had heard. Hence I formed a closer friendship with Master Adam, a man of the keenest intellect and—whatever others may think—of extensive learning, who devoted himself above all others to Aristotle. Although I did not have him as a teacher, he generously shared his knowledge with me and explained himself to me more openly—something he did for no one, or for few outsiders. For he was thought to suffer from envy.
>
> “Meanwhile I taught William of Soissons the first elements of logic and at length placed him with the teacher already mentioned. He afterwards constructed, as his followers say, an engine for overthrowing the antiquity of logic, constructing unexpected consequences, and destroying the opinions of the ancients. There perhaps he learned that the same thing follows from a contradiction when Aristotle objects: because, if the same thing both is and is not, it does not necessarily follow that the same thing is. Likewise, if something is, it does not necessarily follow that the same thing both is and is not. For nothing follows from a contradiction, and it is impossible for contradiction to follow from anything. Hence even when the engine of this friend pressed upon me, I could not be compelled to believe that from one impossibility all impossibilities result.
>
> “Financial straits, the request of companions, and the counsel of friends drew me away from this, so that I might undertake the office of teacher. I obeyed. Thus, when I returned at the end of three years, I found Master Gilbert and heard him in logic and divinity; but he was taken away too soon. Robert Pullen succeeded him, recommended alike by his life and learning. Then Simon of Poissy received me, a faithful reader but a duller disputant. Yet these two alone were my teachers in theology.
>
> “Thus almost twelve years slipped away while I was occupied with diverse studies. It therefore seemed pleasant to revisit the old companions whom I had left and whom dialectic still held upon the Mount, and to compare with them the former ambiguities, so that by mutual discussion we might measure one another’s progress. They were found to be what they had been, and where they had been. For they seemed not to have advanced a hand’s breadth toward settling their old questions, nor had they added a single little proposition. They pressed with the same goads with which they themselves were pressed. They had advanced in one thing only: they had learned the manner, but did not know moderation; so much so that one might despair of their reform.”

On taking leave of Paris, John went to the monastery of Celle, then ruled by Abbot Peter, called of Celle. By him he was ordained a cleric, and to him he later wrote several letters. [Note: [Col. XXI] See Epistle 85.]

After three years he returned to England and was received among the household of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury. When that pontiff died, he entered the service of his successor, the illustrious Thomas Becket. Thereafter he stood vigorously on Thomas’s side, and, himself an exile, faithfully adhered to him in exile. In 1176 he was elected Bishop of Chartres; and he died on 25 October 1180, after the fourth year of his episcopate.

The works of John of Salisbury, now published complete for the first time, are these:

I. **329 LETTERS.** Among them are several written by Henry II, Archbishop Theobald, and others. [Note: [Col. XXI] In manuscript no. 126 of St John the Baptist’s College, Oxford, which appears to have been written immediately after the death of John of Salisbury and contains only extracts, there occurs the following rubricated title: “Here begins a concise florilegium from the book of letters of Master John of Salisbury, who afterwards became Bishop of Chartres, concerning the cause of blessed Thomas the martyr, carefully excerpted by Guy, prior of Southwick.” This will not be useless to those who wish diligently to copy it, both for its manner of writing, for the elegance of its sentiments, and for explaining the cause of the aforesaid martyr. The aforesaid book of letters was carefully and briefly collected into one body by the aforesaid Master John after the passion of the martyr already mentioned, and was clearly and carefully divided into four volumes. Moreover, in the collection, division, and correction of that book, the aforementioned prior—then a canon of Merton—adhered to the said Master John as an inseparable companion and intimate.]

II. **POLYCRATICUS, or On the Trifles of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers.** It is deservedly regarded as the most outstanding among our author’s philosophical writings. Why John entitled his work *Polycraticus* is unknown to us.

For the etymology of the word teaches us nothing concerning the nature or subject of the work. It consists of eight books, preceded by a metrical preface or prologue called the *Entheticus*. In this John dedicates his book to Thomas Becket, then chancellor and afterwards Archbishop of Canterbury, and writes that almost the whole human race is addicted to those trifles which he censures in his work.

From the Peterborough Chronicles [Note: [Col. XXI] “1156. John of Salisbury wrote his *Polycraticus*.” *Chronicle of England at Peterborough*, ed. J. A. G., London and Oxford, 1844, octavo.] this work appears to have been completed in 1156, although it may have been written at various earlier times and afterwards revised by its author.

It had already appeared more than once from various manuscripts:

1. Folio, without place or year, but apparently Brussels or Cologne, about 1475. At the end is read the poem *On the Conspiring Members*. [Note: [Col. XXI] A copy of this edition is preserved in the library of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris.]

2. Octavo, Lyons, 1513, from the press of Constantin Fradin.

3. Quarto, Paris, in the same year, from the press of Berthold Rembolt.

4. Octavo, Leiden, 1595, from Plantin’s press.

5. In the *Great Library of the Fathers*, folio, Cologne, 1622, vol. XV, p. 338.

6. Octavo, Leiden, 1639, from the press of Jean Maire; this edition also contains the *Metalogicus*.

7. In the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, folio, Lyons, 1677, vol. XXIII, p. 242.

We have carefully collated the printed text with a Cambridge manuscript, through whose assistance it appears much more corrected than before.

III. **METALOGICUS.** It had already appeared two or three times attached to the *Polycraticus*, and separately at Paris from the press of Hardouin [Col. XXIII] Beys, and at Leiden in 1630. We also present the text of this book collated with the Cambridge manuscript just mentioned.

IV. **ON THE SEVEN SETS OF SEVEN.** A scholastic book, a singular philosophical specimen of its age. It is now published for the first time from Harleian manuscript 3969, fol. 206; unfortunately, however, it ends mutilated.

V. **ENTHETICUS, or On the Doctrine of Philosophers.** It bears the same title as the metrical preface prefixed to the *Polycraticus*. The author called it *Entheticus*, perhaps to indicate a lighter labour amid more arduous studies. But this is mere conjecture. To investigate the rationale of titles of this kind belongs rather to a curious than to a learned man. We have again collated the text of this poem—most accurately edited by the distinguished Petersen at Hamburg in 1843, octavo—with both manuscripts now extant: namely Cambridge I.1.2.31, fol. 46, and British Museum 13 D. IV, fol. 109.

VI. The poem **ON THE CONSPIRING MEMBERS.** It appeared, joined to the *Entheticus*, at the end of Fulbert of Chartres’s poem, published by Andreas Rivinus at Leipzig in 1655, octavo. It was later reprinted in Fabricius’s *Library of Medieval and Later Latin*, vol. IV, p. 117, whence we have taken it. Whether a manuscript survives anywhere is unknown to us.

VII. **LIFE OF ANSELM, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.** From the edition of Henry Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, II, 149. [Note: [Col. XXIII] From the letter of Pope Alexander appended to John’s book *On the Life of Anselm* it is clear that Thomas presented the pope, at the Council of Tours in 1163, with a book *On the Life and Miracles of Anselm*, in order to obtain Anselm’s enrollment in the catalogue of saints. John composed the book at Thomas’s command, compiling it almost entire from Eadmer’s books *On the Life of Anselm* and *On His Miracles*, generally using the same words. John’s book was transmitted by a Lambeth manuscript, which has the following note appended at its end: “Written by me, brother and fellow monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, Dom Richard Stone; in the year 1507 this work was completed on 12 December.” When dissension soon arose between the king and Thomas after the Council of Tours, Anselm’s canonization was left unfinished. Pope Alexander VI finally completed it by a bull issued to John, Archbishop of Canterbury, in 1494; it is found in volume II of the *English Councils*, p. 721, and thence in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. XIII, p. 1476. —WHARTON.]

VIII. **LIFE OF ST THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP AND MARTYR OF CANTERBURY.** It has already been published in the collection entitled *Life of St Thomas, Archbishop and Martyr of Canterbury*, 2 vols., octavo, London and Oxford, 1845. [Note: [Col. XXIII] See *Patrology*, vol. CXC.]

A commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians was also formerly published under the name of John of Salisbury (Amsterdam, 1646, quarto; and Cambridge, 1630, folio); but it is not established that he wrote such a work.

A book on ecclesiastical discipline, under the title *Summa poenitentiae* (“Summary of Penance”), is likewise ascribed to our author. The only complete manuscript copy of this work that survives is preserved in the Burgundian Library at Brussels. It is entitled: “The work of John, dean of Salisbury—perhaps John of Oxford—during the time when Thomas Becket was dean of Salisbury.” For our John was never dean at Salisbury.

See Alexander III, Epistle 169, *Patrology*, vol. CC.

[Col. 0001]

# LETTERS OF JOHN OF SALISBURY, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

## LETTER I. TO POPE ADRIAN

[Note: [Col. 0001] Letters 1–22 to Pope Adrian IV, and various others elsewhere, were written by John in the person of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, whose secretary he was.]

[Col. 0001A]

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

A dispute has long been conducted between the monks of Hugh’s abbey and the clergy of Henham. The monks demanded thirty-three shillings from the aforementioned Hugh, asserting that these were owed to them as a pension with which the church of Henham had from ancient times been bound to them. They added that the said H. was bound to pay them by a special agreement, confirmed by a pledge of faith and the testimony of documents. To establish the basis of their claim more firmly, they said that they had received this pension from two predecessors of the aforesaid H., namely William and S., and also from Hugh himself, and were prepared immediately to prove this.

Humphrey, on the other hand, [Col. 0001B] said that his church had from ancient times been free, although the monks had violently extorted an unjust mark from Hugh, his predecessor. He firmly denied having entered into any agreement whatsoever with them to render any pension, maintaining that he had received the church free from the Abbot of Abingdon, without any statement of a burden, and that he had been canonically put into free possession through the bishop’s archdeacon, as is customary; nor had any bond of faith, written instrument, or other obligation arisen by which he might be sued.

He asserted that those from whom the monks said they had received the aforesaid sum were not incumbents of the said church, but hired priests, who had received the church and its lands equipped by the monks so that the amount of the aforesaid pension might be paid. He also produced witnesses prepared to prove this very point. He further relied upon the monks’ own testimony, producing against them the document by which they had persuaded us that the aforementioned Segarius was not incumbent of the said church but its vicar, and a hired one at that. Moreover, he said that his church was so poor that, after episcopal dues and the necessary maintenance of ministers had been deducted, it could scarcely bear the burden of one mark. Nor, he maintained, should it harm him if he had sometimes unwillingly paid something in the name of the church, since the church also enjoys the law applicable to a ward and should receive relief through the benefit of minority.

The monks, [Col. 0002A] however, strove by every means to prove that an agreement had intervened, producing several men who wished to confirm their assertion by testimony. Since he had pleaded the poverty of the church, they promised him twenty shillings annually, free of every charge, provided that he delivered the church to them for a time. Some persons, wishing to settle matters between them, offered forty shillings annually, with every charge deducted, if he would cede the church to them, ready to give suitable sureties for this. Although Humphrey seemed disposed to accept this, he immediately took counsel with his advocate and friends and withdrew, saying that it was unsafe in any way to entrust his property to men who were trying wholly to expel him—especially because they oppressed him so severely that, for fear of the monks, none of his friends or witnesses dared stand by him, and they even compelled his father to come against him. He therefore appealed to your hearing, fixing the day as the feast of the Epiphany.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

By mandate of the Apostolic See, Berengar, bearer of this letter, appeared before us to proceed against Roger of Pichewurda; and, after many allegations by both sides, a settlement was made between them. But lest in the course of time either might have an occasion to raise any suit against the other, we caused the agreement made between them to be confirmed by the religious sanction of an oath. Nevertheless the aforesaid Roger, violating that agreement and the obligation of faith, refused to abide by the settlement. Having been convicted of this in our presence, he incurred the penalty of suspension; afterwards escaping it by a fitting satisfaction which he promised that he would render [lacuna], he again began to evade matters. In order to escape our jurisdiction, he appealed to your presence, fixing the day as the Sunday on which is sung, “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” Therefore, lest he be able to deceive your clemency, let the eminence of your holiness know for certain that he has most plainly acted against faith and his oath.

## LETTER III. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0003A]

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

So that, having learned the entire sequence of the matter, you may be able to judge more fully and clearly concerning the things brought to the ears of your holiness by our islanders, we send to inform your eminence concerning the bearer of this letter, insofar as the fact has become known to us. The bearer of this letter was ordained priest by your venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of York of blessed memory, and for some time exercised his ministry in that order.

It happened, however, that he was in the company of certain laymen who, following headlong rashness, committed a homicide without due deliberation. He was in their company with the man who was afterwards killed, pursuing him not with intent to kill but as a thief who had stolen from him his priestly garments. But his brothers, moving more swiftly in pursuit, overtook the thief with the garment and, in his sight as he followed behind—yet, as he admits, against his will—killed the captured thief. A few days afterwards the archdeacon suspended him from the exercise of his order, since the See of York was then vacant. Nevertheless he presumed to minister in the office of deacon. Your exalted authority will determine what punishment should be inflicted upon him, since he wears the cross as a sign of pilgrimage.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0003C]

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

When a dispute between Master Richard of Lichfield and Osbert of Icco concerning the church of Bradley had been long drawn out in the court of the Bishop of Chester, it was at length transferred by appeal to our hearing. The parties therefore standing opposite each other, the said Richard sought restoration to himself of the aforementioned church, declaring that it belonged, as a chapel, to his own church and that of his predecessors, namely William and Walter, and had been peacefully possessed by them in full right.

To this Elias, Archdeacon of Stafford, came forward, maintaining that this claim did not belong to Richard at all, because Richard possessed a certain prebend in [Col. 0003D] the aforesaid church, which had been given and delivered to him by the Bishop of Chester; he produced the bishop’s charter of donation. He further said that Richard had brought a suit against him concerning another church, seeking to deprive both bishop and archdeacon of synodal dues and certain episcopal revenues. For this reason he appealed to the Apostolic See, fixing the day as the octave of the feast of St Andrew.

Richard, on the contrary, answered that he had renounced in the bishop’s hand the prebend which the archdeacon now challenged, and he himself appealed to your hearing by the same date regarding unlawful agreements, an archdeaconry improperly acquired, and the entry which the archdeacon is said to have gained into the church of Halton through lay hands. Yet the archdeacon produced the bishop’s charter concerning the donation of [Col. 0004A] that church. We have therefore reserved the whole cause for you.

## LETTER V. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

The bearers of this letter, W. and R., stood in our presence. R. complained that W. had rashly expelled him from his church by force and without judicial procedure, through the power of Count Simon, into whose more intimate service R. was said to have been admitted. Not content with this injustice, he afterwards, through accomplices in his rashness, attacked the same priest in the cemetery of another of his churches. His companions drew their swords, bent and made ready their bows, while he himself, holding a spear in his hand, threatened immediate death unless R. at once gave his pledge that he would come before the archdeacon and there renounce the aforesaid church.

Thus constrained by reverence for the oath and fearing the pressure of a powerful adversary, whom he could not escape unless he left the country, he renounced his church in the archdeacon’s hand as he had promised. Alleging these and similar matters concerning the injury inflicted upon him, he sought satisfaction, producing two priests who would testify that violence had been done to him.

R., on the other hand, denied that such violence had occurred. Now relying upon the shield of patrons, now fleeing to legal subtleties, he asked whether the claimant was claiming that church, what action he was bringing, and under what right he requested satisfaction. When we attempted more diligently to investigate the truth of the matter, so that what the law required might afterwards appear more clearly, R. interposed an appeal, to which we must defer, setting the date as the Sunday on which is sung, “As newborn babes”; W. shortened that date to the Purification of the Blessed Virgin.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

Ernald of Devizes laid a complaint before us against the noble Count Roger and his clerk Osbert. He said that the church of [Col. 0004D] Henton had been forcibly taken from him by the count, so that he might install his own Osbert, and taken contrary to every respect for law. Ernald said that he had long possessed it canonically by the authority of our venerable brother J., Bishop of Salisbury; he produced the bishop’s charter, which affirmed the title of his grant. To prove that his possession rested upon every legal formality, he maintained that he had obtained it from the bishop by the consent of a certain knight whom he called the church’s advocate. He therefore sought restoration both of the church and of all that had been taken from him.

At last, after many summonses and threats, we compelled the count, who denied all these matters, to restore the church which Ernald claimed, provided that the count and his O. would be admitted, without frivolous delays and the hindrance of other difficulties, to the question of right. When a day had therefore been appointed for the parties concerning this matter, on that day the said O. and the count’s representatives instituted a proprietary action against the aforementioned E. They said that he was unjustly occupying the church, which he had entered without the consent of the count and of the advocates of that church; contrary to the custom of the whole Church and kingdom of England, contrary to the king’s ordinance and the ancient dignity of all nobles, he had entered it through the hand and violence of a robber who had long deprived the aforesaid count of the whole estate on which the frequently mentioned church stands.

Moreover, the king’s mandate was produced, directing us either to render justice to the count concerning the advowson of his church, or to restore the aforesaid church to O., from which he had been removed after the king’s death contrary to [Col. 0005B] the king’s edict. Ernald replied that he lawfully possessed the church through the bishop, with the advocate’s consent. But that advocate and his other friends, he said, were so intimidated by the count’s power and injuries that none of them dared appear against him in this judgment or kingdom, especially since the count and his O. defended in court not only their own position but themselves with the weight of royal majesty against a poor man whom they had excluded from his church for many years.

For this reason he appealed to your hearing, fixing the day as that on which is sung, “To you have I lifted up” (Psalm CXXII). Osbert, replying that neither the case nor the church was worth so great a lawsuit to him, withdrew from the appeal.

## LETTER VII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0005C]

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

At the request of the noble Rag. of Saint-Valery, we directed our venerable brother Richard, Bishop of London, to render him canonical justice against Count Alberic, from whom he said that sixty marks were owed to him under a pledge of faith. But the bishop, prevented by certain intervening causes from carrying out our mandate, delegated the hearing to the venerable Rad., Dean of London, and Hugh, archdeacon.

When the defendant had been summoned three times at lawful intervals, and the plaintiff, after proving his standing, had fulfilled the claim he advanced, yet the defendant did not make himself available and did not send, as he ought, adequate excuses or representatives, the said plaintiff Rag. urgently requested that the judges, or guides of the law, perform their office. They replied that the bishop had delegated to them the examination of the cause, not its decision, and that therefore they could not proceed without consulting him. The aforesaid Rag. requested that they either proceed, if lawful, or give him open letters reporting the conduct of the matter to the bishop. Since he was not heard in this request, he appealed from them to our hearing.

When, therefore, they appeared before us on the appointed day and the parties set forth the sequence of the matter in the manner aforesaid, the frequently mentioned Rag., saying that he had been deceived by the judges delegated to him, summoned them to the Apostolic See, fixing the day as the octave of Pentecost. [Col. 0006A] They, excusing their innocence, said that the bishop had reserved the decision of the case for his own examination and that they had in no way acted maliciously in the affair, prepared to demonstrate this very point by a bodily oath. But you, to whom the judgment of determination has duly been reserved, will impose the proper end upon the cause.

## LETTER VIII. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

Appearing before us, the Prior of Rumilly sought that the church of Coggeshall, which the monks of Coggeshall had occupied by intrusion, be restored to him by our office. A few days later, the summoned abbot and brethren of the said place appeared before us to answer the prior regarding that church. When the prior renewed his claim, the abbot, after consulting the brethren, replied that they had canonically possessed the said church with the assent of a certain Theobald, who had been Prior in the monastery of Rumilly, the community consenting to and approving the prior’s grant.

They further added that they would have witnesses from among the monks of Rumilly concerning the grant of this church, in return for the pension which, they said, had been agreed between them as payable to Rumilly monastery. In order that they might use their documents and witnesses to demonstrate their innocence, they asked that a term be granted to them. Having obtained this by judgment, they went to Rumilly; when all the brethren had assembled in chapter, [Col. 0006C] they found none of those upon whose testimony they relied. For, when the prior of the place had enjoined all the brethren in virtue of obedience that, as the others departed, only those should remain who had been present at the grant of the frequently mentioned church to the aforesaid abbot and monks, not a single one remained, as we have been told.

When the brethren of the said place saw this, they began to assert that P., W., I., and R. had deliberately been sent by the prior to another monastery, lest they bear testimony to their truth. At last, in the presence of our venerable brother Milo, Bishop of the Morini, they appealed against the aforesaid prior, and there, as we have learned from the testimony of certain abbots, summoned him to the eminence of your Apostolic authority.

## LETTER IX. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

We were unable to settle the case, much and long litigated between the Abbot of Coggeshall and the Prior of Rumilly concerning the church of Coggeshall. For, after many summonses and delays, they came before us, and there each summoned the other to the presence of your Apostolic authority. The Prior of Rumilly appealed against the abbot because he was taking from him the frequently mentioned church and the tithes of parishioners whom they had expelled from their houses and lands; he fixed the date as the octave of Pentecost.

The monks, however, then pleaded their poverty and asserted that they had appealed against the prior in the presence of the Bishop of the Morini to your hearing, making the feast of St Luke the term of their appeal; they renewed the same appeal before us.

## LETTER X. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

Four clerics, brought by appeal from the judgment of our venerable brother the Bishop of London by the Prior of Rumilly, appeared in our presence. The prior complained that they had recently deprived him, without judgment, of a certain chapel belonging to his church of Reia, which he had peacefully and without disturbance possessed for sixty years and more.

To prove this matter [Col. 0007B] he used these arguments: first, that those priests who could reach the memory of this age had possessed both together in the name of Rumilly monastery; then, that each seemed equally to belong to the advowson of the same lord; and that they asserted that the same chapel was situated in the parish of Reia. Finally, that the bodies of those dying who belonged to the chapel were buried by right and custom in the frequently mentioned church.

Against these claims, since they said that the mandate had not been established for them, the clerics required security for ratification from the said prior. The prior maintained that such security ought not to be demanded, since the mandate was established both by letters of the Abbot of Cluny and the community of Rumilly and by the written authority of the Bishop of the Morini. Moreover, they ought to have raised this dilatory exception at the outset in the court of the Bishop of London. Nevertheless, to prevent the aforesaid laymen from prolonging the cause in their accustomed manner, he gave us adequate sureties.

The adversaries, however, relying upon legal subtleties, demanded that a further security be given them: if judgment were rendered in their favour, they said, it would be a trap after our lifetime should the monks attempt to renew the litigation, especially because these same laymen complained that they had repeatedly been harassed with suits and expenses over this very cause by different persons. The prior maintained that it ought to suffice that assurance had been given to the judge.

While they disputed thus, [Col. 0007D] we stated interlocutorily that nothing of this kind had emanated from the Roman Church as far as us, that we did not remember anything of the kind expressed in the Decretals, and that what they demanded was contrary to the custom of the kingdom of England. The aforesaid men therefore, seizing the opportunity, appealed to your hearing, fixing the date as the octave of Pentecost. Since we reserved the whole cause, as was proper, for your majesty to determine, the prior complained that he was greatly burdened: coming repeatedly to us from overseas, he had obtained no justice either through us or through the Bishop of London; he had often been unjustly harassed in this case by Archdeacon Ailward; and now, finally, his justice was being deferred by the intervention of an appeal for almost a year. He appealed to the Apostolic See against the said archdeacon, who, as he declared, supported the laymen and through whom these evils came upon him, fixing the date as the octave of St Martin.

## LETTER XI. TO THE SAME

To Lord Pope ADRIAN.

Alan of N. demanded that, by the authority of our office, the church of which he said he had been unjustly deprived should be restored to him, A., the possessor of the same church, being present; after many citations we had fixed for A. a peremptory day for answering. Alan, however, sought to repel A.’s claim by the exception of res judicata, saying that he had already fallen from possession of the aforesaid church by a judgment of our venerable brother Richard, bishop of London, then archdeacon, a sentence rendered in favour of his predecessor Ernard; and in proof of this he produced letters of the lord bishop attesting the matter. Conversely, A. replied that that judgment, if it had been rendered, could not avail him, since a matter conducted or adjudged between others ought neither to benefit nor injure others. And although he might reasonably have complained of the injustice of the sentence, by which he had been condemned while absent and not contumacious, nevertheless, at some cost to his own case, out of reverence for his bishop, the lord of London—whose sentence, so far as lay with him, he did not then wish to challenge—he abandoned the possessory action and instituted a petitory one. He maintained that the church was his, and that he had been its incumbent from the time of Maurice, bishop of London of good memory; and that in the time of Gilbert, bishop of London of pious memory, he had canonically proved this by the testimony of lawful witnesses, producing several witnesses whom, he said, had been present at that trial. Therefore, when at our command our venerable brethren Roger, archbishop of York, Hilary, bishop of Chichester, Robert, bishop of Lincoln, and other prudent men to whom we had entrusted the matter had examined the witnesses and found them consistent in all points, and we, having heard their testimony, were intending to bring the case to its due conclusion, Ernald forestalled our sentence by lodging an appeal, appointing as its day the Sunday on which is sung *Quasi modo geniti*. We therefore, as was fitting, deferring to the apostolic majesty, reserved the whole cause intact for your Holiness to determine.

## LETTER XII. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

A controversy concerning the church of Presteberia had long been disputed between Richard, clerk, and Ralph Mansel. When our venerable brother Walter, bishop of Coventry, after many citations, was at last preparing to bring it to its proper conclusion, Richard—who sought restoration of the aforesaid church, saying that he had been violently and without judgment deprived of it—was required by the bishop to produce, in the synod of Chester, the proofs in which he said that he abounded against Ralph. Seven witnesses were accordingly produced, who, as we have learned from the testimony of the aforesaid bishop, confirmed on oath that Richard had been canonically instituted in the aforesaid church and expelled without judgment. But through the intervention of the lord king’s prayers, the case received a postponement before sentence was delivered. Richard therefore appealed to our hearing. On the appointed day, both parties appearing before us, Richard renewed his complaint, seeking restoration of the said church and producing three witnesses, who asserted, as they had in the bishop’s court, so also before us, that he had been canonically instituted and expelled without judgment.

To this Ralph replied that what had occurred in the bishop’s presence ought not to harm him, since he too had deserved the postponement, and because, while he was absent, the evidence of the aforesaid Richard had been improperly received by the bishop. When they insisted that we should receive their evidence in his presence and hearing, Ralph alleged, by way of exception, crimes against two of the witnesses: he said that one, a priest, was notorious, accused of homicide and counterfeiting coinage, and implicated in many robberies; and he asserted that the other, Andrew the acolyte, was a murderer. He left the third untouched. He also requested that time be granted him to prove these accusations. We therefore required from him lawful security, lest he should appear to seek delay not for justice but from malice: he was to assure us that he did not request it from a malicious intention or merely to procure a vexatious delay. But when he could obtain from us no period of postponement beyond the canonical and lawful limit which we offered him, he appealed to your presence, appointing as the day the Sunday before the Kalends of April, on which is sung *Ad te levavi* [Psalm 122]. The plaintiff, complaining of the length of time, shortened the term, appointing the day of Pentecost.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

We received the letters of your Holiness with due reverence, containing instructions that, after summoning before us both the lord of London and the chapter of that church, together with Walter the priest, we should, setting appeal aside, bring the controversy between them to a canonical conclusion. The parties therefore being placed opposite one another, Walter alleged that two of the principal men of that church, H., the archdeacon, and Master Alberic, both on behalf of the chapter, had informed him, while another, namely Master A., on behalf of the bishop, had told him that he should be ordained priest, to minister at the altar of St Paul like one of the others. Not only the lord of London but the whole chapter steadfastly denied that they had given such an instruction.

The two men mentioned likewise answered for themselves and denied it, though admitting that of their own initiative they had approached, questioned, and advised Master Walter, as a friend, concerning ordination, telling him to proceed to priestly orders and that this pleased the chapter. Yet they maintained that they had said none of this on behalf of the chapter, nor had promised anything. Then, after consultation upon these matters, with our venerable brethren Robert of Lincoln, William of Norwich, and Hilary of Chichester, bishops, sitting with us, we absolved the bishop of London and his chapter from Walter’s claim, because he produced no proofs against them.

But because the two men named appeared in some fashion liable from their own confession, resorting to the solicited assistance granted to a poor man, we tendered them an oath: they were to declare that they had communicated or promised nothing to Walter on behalf of the bishop and chapter. As they stood ready to swear upon the holy Gospels laid before them, Walter broke out into an appeal against the bishop of London, his dean, the aforesaid Hugh the archdeacon, and Master A.; yet he deferred to the dean’s person, allowing him to pursue this appeal through a proctor, sparing his old age and infirmity. He appointed the octave of St Andrew the Apostle as the day. But because every appeal in this case had been prohibited by authority of the apostolic mandate, we proceeded further; after receiving the oath from the said men, we wholly absolved them.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

We know that your Holiness is occupied with many concerns, as one who alone among men continually watches over the safety of the whole Church of God. One who approaches your ears must therefore bring a brief discourse. Ours indeed is short in words, but extended by the whole force of its feeling, especially because it concerns the benefit of the English Church and the glory of your name.

Our venerable brother Nigel, bishop of Ely, in fulfilling your command concerning the recovery of those things which the tempest of war had wrested from his church, labours to the point of blood and fears nothing, so long as he provides for the church entrusted to him and satisfies your will. All of us who live near him sympathize with his labours, expenses, and sufferings; and all the more because your displeasure against him has not yet ceased, but the apostolic hand remains outstretched against his neck. Yet, that a father’s ear may patiently admit what we think it expedient to say, your command ought not to have been a snare to him. Since he has been found obedient and faithful in carrying it out, he ought to have been strengthened by your aid.

Therefore, if it please you, do what befits a father and the Roman pontiff: let the aforesaid bishop find your help in the tribulation which he seems humbly to endure for executing your command. Restore to him, if you please, your favour, and he will fight more bravely against the enemies of the Church. For he must fight with beasts. Who ever suspended his own athlete in order that he might fight more vigorously? You have ordered the bishop into battle, yet keep his hands bound. We therefore fall at the feet of your majesty and beg that, once the bishop is released, the punishment of due correction may be turned upon those who dare with sacrilegious boldness to retain the goods of the Church against the bishop and ourselves—indeed, what is greater, against apostolic enactments—and that despisers of the apostolic name may be driven by your goads toward the path to which they may more easily and successfully be brought by the bow than by the sword.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

We recently received your Holiness’s command that we should not delay to report to your majesty what, after diligent inquiry, had become known to us concerning the birth and parentage of the venerable Walter, canon of Saint-Ruf. The matter of which you inquire requires no lengthy investigation among us, since it shines by itself so clearly that, in view of the nobility of his ancestors, the distinction of his entire kindred cannot be concealed.

The aforesaid Walter, as we know certainly, was the son of an illustrious knight, born of a noble mother in lawful marriage; and he is connected by close blood relationship with our nobleman W. de Braiose. Moreover, he lived for a long time most honourably in the diocese of Chichester, adorned with the title of his own virtue the distinction he derived from his ancestors, and has always conducted himself among us in every respect without reproach. These facts concerning him are known to us, to our venerable brother the bishop of Chichester, and to the other neighbouring persons, by the public testimony of the whole province.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

In the cause between G., the bearer of this letter, and a certain Gregory, which was brought before us by appeal, proceedings were as follows. Augustine, son and proctor of Gregory, maintained that his master had possessed the church of Beccles and had been despoiled of it without judicial process. He produced as witnesses for his assertion certain laymen and one clerk, whom this man alleged was his enemy.

Conversely, Geoffrey denied that Gregory had possessed it. He said that, after the times of which Augustine spoke, a certain Baldwin had been presented to the aforesaid church by the abbot and convent of St Edmund, before the lord bishop of Norwich in full synod. When the lord of Norwich had carefully investigated whether that church was vacant, the archdeacon, after discussion with the brethren of the chapter, replied that it was vacant, the others testifying in the public hearing; and he thus recalled that Baldwin had been installed, and that he himself had succeeded him, producing sufficiently suitable instruments concerning his entry.

Augustine, however, urgently requested that his witnesses be heard. Geoffrey then complained that Gregory always litigated through a proctor and never made himself available, although he was well and nearby. He added that, if he saw his person, he would show that he was such a man that he could possess neither this church nor any other. He said this as though he wished to bring some accusation. When we demanded that he explain the matter more openly, he appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See against Gregory, saying that there he would state what he did not dare to express in England because Gregory was an officer of the king. He appointed as the day of the appeal the Sunday on which is sung *Quasi modo geniti*.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

A controversy concerning the church of Bolteford had long been disputed between Alexander Malambestia and Roger the priest. At last, when Alexander, by authority of the bishop of Lincoln, had been put into possession of the aforesaid church because of Roger’s contumacy, and sought from Roger restitution of the fruits that had been ordered, Roger appealed to our hearing.

When Roger, in his adversary’s presence, set forth the grounds of appeal, he asserted that he had been wronged by the bishop of Lincoln contrary to legal reason, since he had been despoiled while absent, unheard, and undefended, contumacy having been imputed to him although he had never contumaciously disregarded any summons of a judge. Moreover, he said that, even if he had been contumacious, by the law of statutes and canons and the custom of the holy Roman Church—whose example, as is right, the English Church follows—his possession ought to be restored to him within a year if he appeared and was ready to provide security for standing trial. While he pressed us to receive his security and sought restoration of possession, Alexander appealed to your hearing, appointing the Sunday immediately after the octave of Easter; by the Lord’s mercy you will impose the due conclusion upon the case.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

When a controversy concerning the church of Wakerings was being conducted between the prior of Prittlewell and a certain Robert, through some collusion in order to prejudice Richard de Ambli in respect of that church, Richard de Ambli, who had been its possessor, was absent and had not been cited. Yet by concession of the same prior, while certain clerks of Richard repeatedly protested his absence and objected that he had not been cited, the lord of London nevertheless pronounced judgment for Richard against the prior—who regarded being defeated in this way as a victory.

Then, when Richard de Ambli’s clerks immediately appealed to our presence, the lord of London sought to execute his sentence by sending a certain priest, William. Richard’s clerks did not admit Robert and did not resist violently, as the priest afterward confessed; rather, they repelled the hands of their adversaries with the utmost moderation. Therefore the lord of London, having heard Robert’s complaint that the clerks of Ambli had laid violent hands upon him, declared them excommunicated: namely G. the priest and S. A. Although we believed them guilty of this offence, we repeatedly instructed the lord of London to treat them as not excommunicated, as they had been on the day when appeal was made to us; or at least, after receiving from them an oath that they would obey the law, to absolve them. When he delayed doing so, we received from them an oath that they would submit to ecclesiastical judgment. On the day appointed, the adversaries failing in their proof, and after hearing the accused men’s purgation, we absolved them from the charge laid against them.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

The cause between Master Jordan Fantasma and Master John Joichel, clerks of the lord of Winchester, concerning Winchester, was at length transferred to our hearing. Having heard Master Jordan’s allegations and carefully inspected the documents, we forbade the said John, by your authority and ours, to presume to conduct schools in the aforesaid city against Jordan’s will.

On the following day they appeared before us, each making many allegations against the other. Jordan said that the said John, contrary to the religion of the faith, had usurped the schools from him in that city and inflicted many losses upon him, seeking redress from our office. Conversely, John asserted that by judgment of the synod he had cleared himself of the charge of injury to the faith; and he said that Master Jordan, to whom a like purgation had been awarded because he too had been accused of injury to the faith, had entirely failed. He requested that we compel him either to make the purgation adjudged or to fulfil the agreement which was said to have been confirmed by an oath.

While they thus disputed, John appealed to your hearing, saying that he would show that the aforesaid Jordan had violated the religion of faith and his oath, appointing the Nativity of St John as the day. When Jordan complained of the length of time, since John had postponed the term from the beginning of December until the end of June, John further extended it to the feast of St Michael. We, however, reserving the question of the accusations to your judgment, because Jordan’s right to the schools was established, and after taking counsel with our brethren the bishops of Chichester, Hereford, and Worcester, instructed the lord of Winchester not to allow John further to harass Jordan concerning the schools; and if he found John contemptuous of your authority and ours, to declare him publicly bound by the bond of anathema.

A few days later they returned to our presence, Jordan renewing his old complaint. He said that John, after the prohibition, had usurped the schools and incurred the sentence of anathema. John most firmly denied this, ready immediately to swear upon the holy Gospels that after our prohibition he had ceased from the mastership. Conversely, Jordan said that on the appointed day he would prove by the testimony of lawful witnesses that John had exercised the mastership after the edict. But John refused to accept a day, saying that he was already preparing for the Roman journey; and you, by the Lord’s prompting, will impose the due end upon their disputes.

## LETTER XX. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

In the case between William son of Geoffrey and William, canon of the church of Lichfield, concerning the church of Salawa, which your Holiness had delegated to our venerable brother Walter, bishop of Coventry, an appeal was made to our hearing because William son of Geoffrey regarded the bishop’s court as suspect, as he said, although the bishop was offering him every justice in accordance with your command.

When the said William, his adversary resisting, set forth his action in our presence, William of Lichfield raised against him the objection of jurisdiction, asserting that the appeal made to us was invalid because from a delegated judge it is lawful to appeal only to the delegating authority. The other William therefore immediately appealed to the Apostolic See, appointing the Kalends of May as the day.

## LETTER XXI. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

While a controversy concerning certain parishioners and tithes was being heard between Robert Winegot and William of Sturminster before Adelelm, archdeacon of Dorset, Robert sought their restoration, because they had once been adjudged and resigned to him, which he said he was ready to prove by witnesses.
