The aforesaid William, against whom the claim was brought as possessor, appealed to our hearing.

When both appeared before us, because William, though he had appealed, had come quite unprepared, we remitted the case to their diocesan bishop, our venerable brother Jocelin of Salisbury. After he had sufficiently investigated the matter in his synod and was preparing to pronounce judgment, the aforesaid William appealed a second time. On the day appointed for the appeal both appeared before us to litigate. Robert, continually setting forth his claim to the aforesaid parishioners and tithes, produced three witnesses, priests, ready to swear that they had been present when, by judicial procedure, the parochial right he sought, together with the tithes, had been adjudged to Robert.

After they had been carefully examined and found sufficiently consistent, and when, following the reception of their oaths, we were about to pronounce judgment, with our venerable brethren Hilary of Chichester, Gilbert of Hereford, and Richard of London, bishops, sitting with us, the aforesaid William, without alleging any grievance, appealed for the third time, contrary—as it seemed to us—to the form of law, to the eminence of your consistory, appointing as the term of appeal the Sunday on which is sung *Laetare Jerusalem*. Robert shortened the term, appointing Epiphany.

> **Note:** [Col. 0013] Edition and manuscript: *tertio quam*. I have supplied *contra* by conjecture.

## LETTER XXII. TO THE SAME.

To Pope ADRIAN.

Your Serenity delegated to us for decision the controversy between a certain Robert and Richard de Ambly concerning the church of Wakerings. The parties being placed opposite one another, with our venerable brethren Richard, bishop of London, and Hilary, bishop of Chichester, sitting with us, Robert claimed the said church, which he maintained had been adjudged to him in the court of London.

Conversely, Richard alleged that the judgment had been contrived through some collusion against the monks of Prittlewell; he steadfastly maintained that he, the possessor of the church, had never been cited and that no judgment between himself and Robert had been rendered. This the bishop of London himself openly confessed before all of us. Robert therefore made no reply, but appealed to your hearing, fixing the octave of St Andrew as the day.

## LETTER XXIII. TO ALFRED, BISHOP OF WORCESTER.

> **Note:** [Col. 0015D] Cambridge manuscript: “To the same, the bishop of London R.”

To Alfred, bishop of Worcester.

We cannot sufficiently marvel at your prudence, which, setting aside or despising the counsel of ourselves and our brethren, appears to provoke against itself the displeasure of almost all higher powers. The supreme pontiff, the most serene prince, and the illustrious queen expect from your brotherhood a small concession in which more provision will be made for your honour and safety than for their advantage. Certainly, if any one of them separately requested some great matter, he ought most properly to be heard. Let us and our brethren be silent for the present; yet, if it had pleased you, we ought not to have held the last place in your counsel.

I fear, dearest brother, I fear that your counsellors gave foolish and useless counsel when they sought to be preferred to all of us in your estimation. All jointly advise that, in accordance with the will of the rulers, you should yield to Master Solomon the churches which are said to have entered into the settlement between Geoffrey and William. Was not their will, so praiseworthy, not merely to be accepted but anticipated? They wish to bind to your service a worthy and learned man and, while you fulfil a work of your generosity, to ensure that those things which have proceeded from a bishop’s lips are not made void. In consideration of his learning and character, and by right of an ancient association, he should certainly have been admitted even if no one had requested it.

Is not he unworthy of his brethren’s counsel in his own necessities who so lightly rejects it? Do not the prayers of him who refuses so pious a will of the rulers deserve to be excluded? Not to mention others who nevertheless ought to have great influence with you by merit, the will of the lord pope ought to have been interpreted with fuller kindness. A saying commonly repeated and faithfully accepted is true: the will of the supreme pontiff is a decree. And lest it be thought to prevail only in the establishment of law and the hearing of cases, when that will becomes known it is accustomed to impose on the devotion of those who love him an obligation to act.

But perhaps you will say that Master S. earned this treatment because he stirred the queen’s mind against your innocence. What else is this than to make the queen—who excused him in your hearing—guilty of lying? Since we do not doubt that the will of the lord pope has been made known to you, by this notice we command your brotherhood to fulfil it, forbidding any innovation against it concerning the same churches. We also command you to provide us with the letters which G. the archdeacon brought on this subject. Your discretion knows what awaits him who knows and does not do the Lord’s will.

## LETTER XXIV. TO KING HENRY.

> **Note:** [Col. 0016D] In the person of Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury.

To the King of the English.

As we have learned through the report of your increasingly gracious renown, your strength continually prospers in the Lord, who does not cease to accumulate success upon success, and who amid so great a course of prosperity has granted you knowledge both of yourself and of Him. Indeed, affairs among us enjoy so great a gladness of peace and tranquillity that the happiness of your reign, beyond popular expectation, softens—or wholly absorbs—the storm of war, the public ruin, and the whole succession of earlier evils.

This is the finger of God, who in the hand of His servant, my lord the king, restores golden ages and, by the Lord’s power, has driven away every assault of troubles from the nations and languages committed to you. Yet this great happiness is diminished in one respect: though we long for you, we are for too long deprived of your bodily presence, while we continually abound in the benefits of your majesty and strength. We know what we say, for we speak from abundance of heart and have spent part of our lives in labours and hardships for the safety of your kingdom.

Nevertheless, since the compulsion of love prevents us from being unconcerned for you, we beseech your blessedness—may the Lord extend it to long and happy times—to deign to report to us through the bearer of this letter what concerns you. It is more certain than certain that upon your safety depends the welfare not only of the whole island, which with happy prayers petitions for your health, but also of all the neighbouring nations.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE BISHOP OF DURHAM.

To H., bishop of Durham.

From your report we have grounds to complain of your brotherhood, since under the constitutions of the sacred canons you ought to have notified your fellow bishops that notorious man whom your letter described to us as condemned by anathema by your church because of the atrocity of so great a crime. But although he relied upon letters of our venerable brother the archbishop of York, and although many great men pleaded for him, either wholly concealing or diminishing his fault, we neither granted him communion nor remitted the penalty of his journey. We merely extended the term until the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, changing in no respect the things imposed upon him.

Therefore, since his malice or deception ought not to profit him, we leave him to be dealt with by your brotherhood according to the canonical sanctions, commanding that, in proportion to the guilt of so grave an offence, you punish the crime with such severity that, by the Lord’s working, his sin may be blotted out through penance and others may be terrified from like acts by fear. For, by the Lord’s mercy, we have not wished to be patrons of crimes but avengers, and we are pleased that you preserve zeal for justice among barbarians. We shall ratify whatever you decide according to the Lord against those who persecute Him who was crucified and is still to be worshipped in the Church.

## LETTER XXVI. TO …

I should deserve rebuke, Father, if necessity rather than negligence had not obstructed my efforts to execute your command. Therefore, because since leaving you I could not see Master William, I caused him, after seeing your letters, to be summoned through the lord archbishop to Lord A. in order to obtain a truce. The archbishop laboured in this matter, and I too laboured with associates; yet our labour was not lost upon him. He will therefore come on the day appointed for him and perhaps, if necessary, he who despised our requests will accept them.

We consulted the lord of Chichester about the affair, sounding out his mind—which certainly need not be feared in this matter—because he assured us on oath that, though you inflicted a great injury upon himself, he would have no vengeance taken for himself unless it were so monstrous that it could not be overlooked without loss of honour. For he knows your innocence and the affection you bear toward him. He therefore ordered me to write that he does not disapprove if you carry out the lord pope’s command to the letter. He also knows that you must fulfil it. He likewise instructed your A. to tell you to trust my written message. You perhaps know why it was not fitting for him to write this himself. He wishes the matter kept secret.

On the feast of Mary Magdalene, the appurtenances of the church of Celcra, which belong to your right, will be litigated before the lord archbishop. I advise that on that day one of your people be present, at least a messenger with copies of your title-deeds, so that we may assert your right. If the messengers whom you sent have brought anything concerning Worcester, let it be produced without delay both to him and to the archbishop.

## LETTER XXVII. TO POPE ADRIAN.

To the lord pope ADRIAN.

Immoderate love has given me such boldness that I presume, though I am dust and ashes, to trouble the apostolic majesty on behalf of my own needs and those of my friends. Yet I petition more confidently for those whom, beloved Father, I recognize to be more faithful to you and to the holy Roman Church. Among them is the venerable father, the lord bishop of Norwich, who, as he submits himself to your apostolate with readier and fuller devotion, serves more fruitfully in the English Church.

Yet he is repeatedly afflicted by manifest calumnies and crushed by undue vexations under colour of your mandates, as you may learn from the bishops’ reports. Walchelin the archdeacon, caught in the works of his own hands, strives to outwit your religious authority under the pretext and appearance of restitution, so as to render void not only our command but the justice of the Lord, and to escape the snares of the sacred constitutions and the hands of judges—although it has depended upon himself that he has lacked anything by which he might have obtained restitution.

I pass over the fact that, in redemption of his crime, he promised much, but on returning from the Apostolic See, in contempt of it, committed still more. I come to an affront against you: he ordered an illegitimate child, borne to him on his return from you by his concubine, to be called Adrian after your most sacred name. He left the same woman pregnant; but by a provident arrangement it was settled that, should she perhaps bear a boy, he should be called Beneventum, because his father is travelling there; should she bear a girl, she should be called Adriana. O true friend of the Roman pontiff! He remembers you even in his crimes, and gives his wickedness a name drawn from your goodness, which he mocks with impunity.

This is the man, lord, this is the man who persecutes the holy bishop for no other reason than that the bishop opposes his crimes. When you see a wicked man whose manifest crimes have gone before him to judgment, you will not take a share in wickedness with him, even though he, so far as in him lies, makes you a participant in his infamy. For, though he ought to have returned from you, if not cast down, then at least corrected, the latter deeds of that man have always been worse than the former. I shall say it, Father, I shall say what the report celebrated by every voice agrees in declaring: whoever lets this man go is an enemy of justice and, by consenting to vice, a violator of justice, honour, and chastity. The bishop of Worcester, to whom his case has been entrusted, is slow in executing your command and is shortly to leave the island. Therefore may it please you to appoint in his place whatever lover of justice in England you choose, so that the bishop’s cause may at last receive its due conclusion.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SAME.

To the lord pope ADRIAN.

I should blush to knock so often at the door of your majesty, unless both the sincerity of my devotion and the kindness of your eminence encouraged my shame, and unless the pressing need of those whom I cannot forsake on any grounds compelled me, even unwillingly, to write. I sympathize all the more with the vexations and injuries of the holy brethren who serve the Lord at Merton and illuminate our island with the light of good works, because I know with greater certainty that they abstain from harming everyone and, as is evident to all islanders, serve their neighbours’ welfare with all their strength. They are therefore compelled to flee to your apostolate, that you may extend the hand of mercy to their labours.

Among other matters, the lord of Winchester gave their church of Effingham—given to them by the lord of the manor and confirmed under privilege by your glorious predecessor Eugenius, following the written grant of that same bishop of Winchester—to a publican, almost a layman, the son of a priest who had ministered in that church. This was an injury to the apostolic majesty and an affront to the sacred canons. Likewise, a certain knight, while the bishop looked away, with impunity despoiled their church of Upton of its tithes. But this cannot be remedied unless your command presses the matter, since the power of certain men who undermine justice impedes it and the malice of many grows stronger.

May it please your graciousness kindly to receive the causes and persons of the aforesaid brethren, and to send them back swiftly, because the insolence of those who spend more than this man does at home on the uses of the poor cannot endure a longer delay. Indeed, if you look more closely upon the bearers of this letter, in one of them you may admire a small lodging-place of many great virtues; and though the Spirit commends both to your charity, flesh and blood will secure favour for the other. Let it profit the men of Merton that, while you were at the church of Saint-Ruf, their good repute reached you, and that your graciousness was accustomed to speak with me, your servant.

## LETTER XXIX. TO THE SAME.

To the lord pope ADRIAN.

In the affairs of friends I presume to knock at the ears of your clemency—although perhaps it should suffice me if I deserve to be heard even in my own concerns. Yet you granted this boldness to my timidity when you instructed me to take occasions for writing to you from the business of many persons. Now, since I could not fail the bearer of these letters, William, in his need, I prostrate myself at your feet with as much devotion and earnestness as I can, beseeching your Majesty at last to set a due end to his labours. For now a second time he is being drawn to the Apostolic See by the malice of his adversary—a man swift to appeal, slow to prosecute; no more ignorant of the sacred canons than contemptuous of them; a supporter of the court, a persecutor of the Church. By the backing of secular powers he strives to weaken the strength of Catholic unity. By this novel kind of evasion he instructs our countrymen to appeal simultaneously to the Roman pontiff, the king, and the queen, so that, under cover of reverence for you, he may escape the hands of the bishops and provoke the king’s or queen’s indignation to crush innocence.

## LETTER XXX. TO THE SAME PERSON

To Pope ADRIAN.

The silence which I had imposed upon myself, venerable Father, has been interrupted by the bishop of Ely, who compelled me to report to your Majesty proofs of his devotion. He believes that he can be aided before your eminence by the testimony and intercession of your faithful servants; and, because he showed me—while I was conducting your affairs—the sincerity of his devotion by tangible performance, I earnestly beseech your Serenity to preserve for him intact that favour which he earned from your kindness before the Lord exalted your throne above the heads of the sons of men. The lord of Canterbury makes the same request; with him I deposited one hundred marks sterling, which I had received from the aforesaid bishop for carrying out your command.

The said bishop is indeed ready for your service, but he will be far readier if you extend to him the sweetness of your clemency, mindful of the matters laid upon me when I returned from your Majesty. I entrusted one of those whose care I had undertaken to his protection. Therefore, that your favour towards him may be more secure, please send him letters of the dispensation granted to him. May your fatherhood flourish for ever; and would that it remember well what everyone knows and very few declare in your hearing: that the Roman pontiff cannot long remain pope.

## LETTER XXXI. TO . . . .

Although I had resolved to be silent, the business of the lord pope which I conducted with the lord of Ely compelled me to burden apostolic ears with letters. It is therefore necessary that your diligence should carry out my purpose. For since the affair has been conducted manfully, what has been done will be strengthened by the authority of the law.

As Lord Boso instructed, the lord of Ely delivered to us one hundred marks sterling to fulfil the lord pope’s command; he also sends ten marks in payment for a mark of gold to Lord Boso through the lord of Canterbury and me. Therefore act with Lord B., that he may send the bishop the letters of the dispensation of absolution, as he promised. In this matter he ought not to feel burdened if, having received the gold, he releases the promised words.

Besides this, nothing has happened here, except that peace has been restored between the archbishop of York and the abbot of Gloucester, the archbishop having renounced the lawsuit upon receipt of an income of ninety-four pounds. Moreover, I advise you on this journey to enter into a partnership in grain, even if only for one year; other provisions are expensive in London, whereas Master Rad. has abundance near the waterways. Fifteen thousand herrings are expected after expenses have been deducted.

## LETTER XXXII. TO JOHN, TREASURER OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0021A]

To JOHN, treasurer of Canterbury.

Although I am offended by your silence, yet I address friends even when offended. I address you, indeed, but in a different manner from that which your negligence has deserved. You ought to have been reproved for excessive silence; but the venerable Father Rod., bishop of St Andrews, restrained the spirit of my indignation, desiring that his person and cause should be commended to your diligence. The abbot of Kelso harasses him: prompted by the example of the Acephali, and taking by the path of disobedience—which Christ does not recognize—some image of liberty, he rises to equality with episcopal authority.

The Father of Canterbury commends the bishop’s cause to you, and so do I; and one whom you will not dare to despise commends it—the humble and just one, Christ the Lord is his name. The fault of your silence will be somewhat excused in the bishop’s cause, provided that the preceding fault does not by its continuance become a crime. But if you remain silent longer, do not suppose that you are to be spared: for, if you do not now give words to friends, we shall extort either words or blows.

Nothing has happened here except that the lord of Ely has satisfied Lord Boso’s command, as I have now written for the second time both to him and to you.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF NORWICH

To WILLIAM, bishop of Norwich.

He opens the way to the excesses of many who, by overlooking the errors of his subjects, gives them boldness to sin. But you are said to have sinned gravely, to the injury of the Apostolic See and in contempt of us. After an appeal had been made to us in the case pending between Alexander of Drayton and Ralph the foreigner, you dared, to Alexander’s prejudice and in contempt of our authority, to introduce some innovation.

We therefore command you, under obedience, to appear before us on the next Sunday on which *Sing unto the Lord* is sung, to answer the said Alexander and R., his brother, concerning your disobedience and contempt of the lord pope and of us, and concerning participation in a sacrilegious anathema. Take care also that you are not found guilty—something we by no means desire—of the manifold incontinence with which the report of evil fame has stained your name.

For we shall not be able to leave such grave offences uncorrected, lest we be rebuked more severely for negligence in our office by him with whom, as there is no respect of gifts, so neither is there respect of persons.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO JOHN, TREASURER OF YORK

To JOHN, treasurer of York.

After the departure of Master William and Rad., to whom, with much urgency of entreaty, I entrusted the business of which we spoke, I went to Norwich, and there conducted your affair with the devotion and fidelity required. Through my insistence, therefore, and that of our friends, John the monk and Master N., I obtained from the lord of Norwich what was owed to you, although he complained greatly of you—and perhaps with reason.

For he said that, though he counted you foremost among his friends, you alone failed him at the critical moment of necessity. This occurred when, under peril of his life, he was fighting against his archdeacon amid the greatest danger to his honour and reputation. Troubles pressed upon him from every side: on the one hand apostolic authority, on the other the king’s majesty. On the other side, those who favoured authority threatened his life everywhere; and, what he judged more ruinous, there were the enemies of a man of his own household. Then he implored the help of friends and tested their fidelity; while others assisted him according to their capacity, you alone turned your face away on the day of battle.

When all his people met with refusal from you, at last he himself came in person; yet he was not heard out of respect for his own standing. For you would not delay your meal while you watched the outcome of the imminent battle. Yet the disciple who had denied the Lord with an oath, constrained by love, followed the Lord to see the end. You, however, went to the table while the man to whom you promised the service of love was being led to the cross. For these reasons he believed that you despised the favour of that man to whom, in such great necessity, you would not render aid.

But I dissolved these and his other objections, though they seemed strong to me, as though they were spiders’ threads; and at length persuaded the man to count you among his most faithful and closest friends. For I know that, in accordance with my word, you will devote effort and diligence to ensuring that by your assistance he may be safe from the plots of his enemies.

I handed over to your A. the sixty shillings which I received from him; A. was obliged to dispose of the rasurae (“shavings” or payments so called), if he wished to prevent the outcry of your clerks. Write back whether I did well. Moreover, write how I ought to deal with the lord of Ely: whether I should demand the money by weight or in pure silver. For I received instructions from you, and from no one else.

I have passed over a matter which ought by no means to be omitted, since it concerns very greatly the preservation of your honour and advantage. If the lord of York should attempt to crown the king, or, prompted by rashness, undertake anything else against the Church in our province, do not associate with him, but restrain his attempt; for the avenger of our wrongs is the Lord, the God of Canterbury, the God of vengeances. Yet if our northern see has injured you in any respect, we are ready to make satisfaction, provided only that you are willing to cast in your lot with us in a serious matter.

## LETTER XXXV

By the attestation of the present document we make known to you all that the disputes pending between our venerable brother Richard, bishop of London, and Henry of London have been settled by an amicable agreement in the following manner.

While we were sitting with the venerable men Robert, bishop of Lincoln, William, bishop of Norwich, Gilbert, bishop of Hereford, and Hilary, bishop of Chichester, the same Henry, standing in the midst of the assembly, asserted that the archdeaconry of Colchester and the churches of Fulham and Stubeham belonged to him by right, and that the bishop himself was bound to pay him six pounds annually. He was ready immediately to prove this and to produce witnesses and documents.

It was therefore agreed by both parties, with our authority intervening, that Roger le Brun freely surrendered into the bishop’s hand the church of Fulham, which he held; and the bishop at once granted it to the aforesaid Henry and invested him with it, on this condition: when the said Roger should cease to hold the church of Stubeham, whether by death, voluntarily, or for any reason whatever, Henry should freely receive it as his own; and afterwards he should resign the church of Fulham to the bishop of London who should be in office at the time.

These acts were done with Roger’s willing consent for the sake of peace, in the presence and with the assent of himself, the dean, and the chapter of the church of St Paul in London. Henry consequently entirely renounced the aforesaid disputes and was fully reconciled with the bishop, so that the bishop and his Church are bound to confirm this agreement by their charters. We likewise strengthen it by the authority of the Apostolic See, whose office we exercise, and command that it remain inviolate.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO POPE ALEXANDER

To the most excellent lord and Father A., by God’s grace supreme pontiff, T., humble minister of the holy Church of Canterbury, greeting in the Lord.

Obedient sons carry out the commands of the Apostolic See; those who resist them plainly bring upon themselves the sentence of condemnation. From the beginning of your promotion, sometimes at the risk of our safety and life, we have embraced obedience to the supreme pontiff; and before the charge of disobedience overthrows us, we desire to be deprived of life and light itself.

And you, if it please you to remember, have ready proof of our prompt obedience. For in the time of your predecessors we did not evade shipwreck, exile, nakedness, and dangers of death, as the Church of the Lord knows, for faith in the holy Roman Church; rather, we stood against princes, prepared, if need arose, to offer our own blood for the Church’s security. We have satisfied your creditors and most willingly transferred your burden to our own shoulders.

Now, however, we bear your burden rather than ours; and it is the heavier because, unless you provide for it, it will not merely diminish your authority but, what we fear more, will annul the glory of the Roman pontiff. For, in accordance with your command, we invested Hugh, the bearer of these letters and your faithful servant, with a prebend in the Church of London, the contumacy of the lord of London requiring it. Yet the bishop has decreed to oppose not only our commands but apostolic commands. Therefore, if it please you, preserve your honour and do not permit our face to be put to shame on account of obedience. For he who despises the legate of the Apostolic See appears rather to despise him who sent him. The bearer of these letters will be able to explain more conveniently in person the remaining matters relevant to the present case.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO . . . . Election of an Abbot

The absence or negligence of shepherds inflicts such injury upon churches that what is easily lost in conduct or possessions, or lost in a short time, can scarcely be restored except by great labour, much vigilance, and a long span of time. For armies, plundering, and manifold losses of temporal goods abound; the enemy ravages at home. Indeed, when both the branches and root of its propagation and religious life have been cut off, the roaring lion finds everywhere one exposed for him to devour.

But he who, placed in such peril, does not fear has been tested, rather than awaits testing. The salvation also of those who ought to meet or cure such great diseases is endangered unless they expend all their vigilance in providing for the salvation of their subjects.

Therefore, compassionating your desolation with paternal affection, we have obtained from our lord the king that, according to the institution of the sacred canons, we may set a suitable shepherd over you. The matter requires speed and diligence, since every delay in postponing salvation entails danger, and the state of your church hangs upon such a reckoning that it seems to your religious brethren more fit to be lamented than described. Religion is perishing within; outward goods are being dispersed, plundered, and drained away. There is no one at home to offer help or counsel. The disease has now become inveterate, since for a long time there has been no one willing and able to drive away these evils.

Since at present we cannot be personally present with you, we send to you, through the abbots of Sorensem and Winchcombe, our venerable brothers Gauter., bishop of Coventry, and Alf., bishop of Worcester, your beloved sons.  
[Note: [Col. 0023D] The Cambridge manuscript omits “through S. and W.”]

By virtue of obedience and through apostolic authority, we command you, on the next Sunday after the feast of St John the Baptist, to elect as your abbot, with their counsel, a religious and learned person who has a good testimony from those outside, and who, with the Lord’s help, may be able both to preside and to benefit. If one of the aforesaid brethren should happen to be absent in mind or body, the counsel of the others shall nevertheless prevail among you.

We know that whoever among you seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ will gladly submit to so religious and salutary a counsel. But we wholly invalidate the voice of those who, resisting the Holy Spirit, are found to obstruct, so far as lies in them, their own salvation and that of others, in opposition to the aforesaid brethren sent for this purpose. Nor should any one of you suppose that he has recourse to the lord king, for delay in your salvation will be unwelcome to him who entrusted his authority to you in this matter so that it might not be delayed. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO POPE ADRIAN

To Pope ADRIAN.

Our beloved son R., precentor of the Church of Lincoln, a man commendable for learning and uprightness of conduct, is compelled by urgent necessity to flee to the stone of help, the successor of Peter, and to seek the aid of the Apostolic See, which is accustomed to extend assistance to all in the administration of justice.

Although his case is not wholly clear to us, we trust that it is just; nor do we believe that, knowingly, he has crossed the boundary of equity to another’s injury. We therefore beseech your Majesty kindly to receive his person, if it please you, and to command that his justice be expeditiously administered with your customary kindness. For so great a man, holding such an office, cannot remain long absent without harm to his Church. Whatever you find to have been presumed against him—or rather against the holy Roman Church—your clemency, with the Lord’s help, will restore to a better state.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Pope ALEXANDER.

We venture more safely to commend to the excellence of your holiness those whom we know, illustrious in faith and charity, to be duly formed in life and conduct. May it therefore please the successor of blessed Peter to apply a remedy worthy of apostolic authority to the injuries and vexations of the poor brethren who render devoted service to the Lord in the regular habit in the church of St Osith the Virgin.

That church illumines our whole island with the light of good works and religion, the integrity of its life, and the holiness of its conduct; and it adorns the Church among us with such examples of charity that I ought deservedly to commend it to apostolic Majesty. The bearer of these letters, Abel by name, abbot of that church, worn down by expenses and vexations imposed by our venerable brother Richard, bishop of London, has had to flee to the aid of your mercy.

For he has been summoned by the aforesaid bishop concerning certain churches which had devolved upon his church by the gift of Richard, of good memory, bishop of London, founder of the same church, who served fourth before him in the church of St Paul. Pope Calixtus, who then happily presided over the holy Roman Church, judged worthy of confirmation by his privilege both the charter of the illustrious King Henry I and the confirmation of Rad., archbishop of Canterbury, of blessed and cherished memory, which had been granted to them concerning those churches as evidence of the gift.

Therefore, prostrate at the knees of your Majesty, we earnestly beseech you for the brethren of the said church and together with them: kindly, if it please you, receive their abbot, who has fled to the aid of your mercy; and let them henceforth peacefully possess, with apostolic authority strengthening it, what they have possessed for so long, so that, free to discharge the prayers which they owe for the Roman pontiff, they may attend more freely and devotedly to their own affairs. We have seen and handled with our own hands the charters whose sealed transcripts we send you.

## LETTER XL. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0026A]

To Pope ALEXANDER.

When a dispute was being conducted between the nuns of Gisam and B., archdeacon of Norwich, concerning the church of Nenton, Baldwin, by way of an exception, demanded that restitution be made to him of goods which, he said, had been taken from him by the nuns, before I proceeded to the principal case. In reply, the nuns’ representatives complained that their church had often been very unjustly harassed by Baldwin and that they could not endure his evasions, since no one was able to apprehend him in his own parts. Therefore they appealed against him to the Apostolic See, fixing the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary as the date.

## LETTER XLI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0026B]

To Pope ALEXANDER.

The Church of Thérouanne has always bestowed maternal affection upon those who attack it, though deprived of the holy bishop Milo, its excellent father, and it is known to have provided many consolations of mercy in their necessities. But they repay us with evil and, seeking their own interests, endeavour to tear their mother apart.

Therefore, prostrate at the knees of your Holiness, we beseech you with all the devotion we can: may your grace—which is accustomed to punish the ungrateful and to open the bosom of clemency to those who are worthy and deserving—look mercifully upon the Church of Thérouanne and frustrate the efforts of manifest ambition.

For the apostolic right hand is accustomed to water tender plantations with the benefits of its grace, that they may grow; and to remove every distress of assault so that they do not wither or fail. This, if it please you, you will do with all the greater justice because it is more confidently hoped that our venerable brother Milo, who succeeded St Milo in the episcopal see, will also succeed him in holiness and virtue.

## LETTER XLII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To Pope ALEXANDER.

How highly they esteem me who trust that they can be aided by my prayers before your Majesty! Would that it might happen to me according to their words! And indeed I deal confidently with you, presuming not upon consciousness of my own merits, but upon your kindness, always recalling with joy and exultation the words which proceeded from your lips when at Ferentino you gave me the ark of future things, your own ring, and belt.

From that day, therefore, I have always hoped in these things; through the mercy of the Lord I know your disposition, that I shall not be put to shame. From that time the bearer of these letters has been my friend, although in these days he has adhered to Henry, archbishop of York, of good memory, who persecuted me, as you know; for this I owe him greater thanks.

Great men make supplication to you for him—such men that I should count it great if I were allowed to adore their footsteps. Yet I am certain that, however great they may be, none of them is more faithful or devoted to you than I, your least servant. Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your mercy, I beg you to command that his right be advanced, and not allow him to be torn away, through the wickedness of those who think religious life complete if they prevail in every lawsuit, from the stricter way of life which he has undertaken on the counsel of religious men.

## LETTER XLIII. TO THE ABBOT OF ARROUAISE

To the venerable friends and most beloved brethren in Christ, R., abbot, and the sons of peace who will assemble in the chapter of Arrouaise, T., humble minister of the holy Church of Canterbury, greeting.

New scandals have arisen among you from your order—scandals all the more bitter to the faithful because they were less foreseen and occurred contrary to everyone’s expectation. Jealousy and contention are signs of carnal affection; and the disorderly defence of one’s own rank betrays and convicts ambition. Behold: among your brethren there is not merely rivalry, but now strife; it is now almost turning into battle.

We have often intervened, in order that peace might be restored in the house of the Lord and scandals removed from its midst by agreement or judgment. We have therefore been troubled and have accomplished nothing; indeed, unless God puts forth his hand, their latter condition is daily becoming worse than their former. The abbot of Lilleshall and his brethren do not follow the paths of justice because they stray far from charity and do not know the way of peace. Each party throws blame upon the other; and lest the truth should then become clear, the abbot’s party appears to prevent it.

We therefore beseech your unanimity in the Lord at last to put an end to our labours: either restore peace to the Church, if it can be done while the parties remain in place, or cut down with the axe of justice the root of the tree which bears the bitterest fruits of dissension and quarrels. May your love always flourish, mindful of us in its prayers before the Most High.

## LETTER XLIV. TO THE KING

To the lord king of the English.

This is the true peace of kingdoms and the tranquillity ever to be desired: that the members of the Church should cleave together in faith and love; that princes should show priests the reverence due to them; and that priests should show princes the service of complete fidelity. But if they clash against one another with their own resources, the strength both of secular and ecclesiastical authority will be weakened, because, according to the voice of the Most High, every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste.

We have always, and especially in your time, laboured to bring about and preserve this unity, and have suffered losses of body and possessions so that these powers might be joined in the unity of faith and charity. With the Lord’s help we have made progress thus far; but now we are involved in a graver labour and danger.

For the schism in the Roman Church arouses lovers of novelty and has given great boldness to presumptuous men. Some among us are planning to approach and visit Alexander, others Victor. We do not know which of them has the stronger cause; nor can we restrain and hold back, by your authority, those who fly heedlessly to either one. Nor, while the matter remains uncertain, do we consider it lawful in your kingdom to receive either one without your counsel; nor is it in any way expedient that the Church of the English should be divided after the example of the Roman Church, or furnish the kingdom and priesthood with matter for strife.

Since some bishops and abbots go or send to Rome, what are we to do, who depend more than the rest upon your counsel and are more bound than the rest to the Roman Church? For whatever others may do, by our profession we are obliged to visit it at fixed times. It will be dangerous for us if others, who have received less honour from the Roman Church, anticipate our devotion with the one who is to prevail, whom we do not yet know.

It is said that your Majesty has given some people permission to go there, and particularly those who rejoice at Adrian’s death—he loved you as a mother loves an only son. Some of them, as is widely known, lie in wait for our person or our Church. We therefore beseech your graciousness to provide in this matter for our age and weakness, and, what we desire and pray for more earnestly, for your glory.

For our days will henceforth be few, and at present we are not greatly anxious about them, but about the Church of Canterbury, which God has entrusted to my insignificance and your Majesty. Nothing better becomes your excellence than to preserve it unharmed. For it is the head of your kingdom, the mother in Christ of faith for you and for the whole realm. Whatever is taken from it will disfigure your honour, since the honour of the head can never equally suit the other members. He is imprudent who exposes his head to dangers in order to honour an ignoble part of himself.

On these matters we await and desire your counsel and aid. May your Highness flourish for ever. The bearer of these letters will explain the matter more fully.

## LETTER XLV. TO THE ABBOTS OF WAVERLEY

[Col. 0028D]

To the beloved sons in the Lord, all the abbots sprung from the bosom of the monastery of Waverley, greeting.

We admonished by our letter those brethren who, withdrawing from obedience to their own abbot, listened to the voice of another to whom they were bound by no tie of profession, and with him departed from the congregation and unity of their monastery. Yet, as is said, persisting nonetheless in schism, to the dishonour of your order and the injury of the Cistercian chapter—to which the abbot of Waverley has appealed—they do not cease, in contempt of our official admonition, to follow the same abbot.

We are therefore compelled by the authority of these letters to urge your charity diligently to approach our venerable friend Philip, abbot of La Charité, by whose counsel, it is said, they arm themselves, that he may by no means foster the disobedience of those brethren but allow them to return to their father, who is known to have begotten them in Christ. Likewise command the same brethren by our authority to return and strive to repair the rupture of their mother by the bond of charity, the fruit of obedience, and the unity of the Spirit.

But if, as despisers of our command, they prefer to persist in their schism, we shall hold valid the sentence which their abbot has canonically pronounced against them and, with the Lord’s help, shall cause it to be inviolably observed in the kingdom of England.

## LETTER XLVI. TO HILARY, BISHOP OF CHICHESTER

To HILARY, bishop of Chichester.

Often, most beloved brother, we blamed the delay of your silence and inferred from it that the ardour of your charity had grown cold, since silence seems clothed in the guise of one who does not love. But when the reason for your long silence became known to us from what followed, we knew for certain that pardon was due not so much to the delay as thanks were to be rendered to your affection and concern, on account of your sound counsel.

For none of our brethren or faithful servants who are around you seemed to have such concern for us as to inform us of what is happening concerning the lord king or forewarn us, while ignorant, of events. We therefore confess that we owe you greater thanks, because, though you were silent longer than we wished, you nevertheless afterwards compensated for the delay of your silence with prudent discernment.

And because a more serious crisis seems to have arisen, we earnestly ask you, as a most dear brother and friend, to forewarn us in every particular which you know to be expedient, for we resolved long ago to follow your counsel most closely. This is the way in which you can make your absence fruitful to us: by taking care to promote what is beneficial for our Church. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII

We have received the lord king’s letters, in which he complains that William the abbot and his church of Lilleshall have been badly treated by us. He requests that the case pending between you and the said abbot be concluded by us with a canonical judgment; and, unless you are willing to submit, he will not permit you henceforth to have anything in the said church.

We have, however, persuaded the said abbot to renounce every appeal, provided that you also will renounce appeals and submit to our judgment; and he has already renounced both an appeal made and any to be made, under this condition. Therefore, if you accept this condition, we appoint for you the Sunday on which *The mercy of the Lord* is sung. Then, with the Lord’s help, we shall confirm what you have decreed concerning the abbot if it appears just, and annul it if it is unjust.

For the merits of the cases will become clearer to us, the parties will be able to obtain justice without harassment, and religious observance can be restored in the Church, if the truth is made known through the parties’ assertions. In this way you will be able to retain the king’s favour, which is most necessary; you will lose it altogether if you wish through any wickedness to oppress his church.

If, then, you are willing to be present on the stated day under the prescribed condition, write back to us without delay; or tell us if the condition displeases you. For it is unbecoming either that we should be deceived by friends or that we should deceive friends. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO THE KING

T[heobald] of Canterbury to the king of the English.

Although we are pressed by our own private distresses, we are more afflicted and more severely tormented by public storms. For the hand of the Lord has visited us in our own person, in the scourge of his clemency, and has now raised us somewhat from a long and grave illness. Yet more grievous than every bodily sickness is the storm of discord in our soul, which, by the Lord’s permission, rends the Church and, clashing kingdoms and principalities together, has shaken security and peace from the people of God.

This is our daily affliction, the most just sorrow and most bitter groaning of all good men; and it is made more bitter because, in your absence, we do not know what we ought to hope or fear. Therefore, in your absence, we earnestly beseech your Serenity to deign to inform us, who are anxious, about your condition. If your affairs prosper, we hope in the Lord that we and the Church of God which is among you will prosper. For it stands in unity and, with the Lord’s help, will never adhere to schismatics.

The French Church, as we have learned by trustworthy report, has received Alexander and withdrawn from Octavian. So far as human judgment is concerned, it appears to have adhered to the better and sounder party, since all agree that Alexander’s person is more honourable, prudent, learned, and eloquent, and his cause is declared by all who come from there to be more sincere and just.

Although we have not yet seen a messenger or letter from either of them, we know that all our countrymen, if your assent is present, are more inclined toward Alexander’s party. We have heard, however, that the emperor is attempting to draw you to Octavian’s side. But far be it from you, in so great a danger to the Church, for the love or honour of a man to do anything except what you believe pleasing to the Lord. Nor does it become your Majesty, if it please you, to set over the Church of your kingdom, without its counsel, a man who without election and, as is publicly said, without the grace of God, has dared to occupy so great an honour solely through the emperor’s favour and force.

For almost the whole Roman Church is on Alexander’s side. It is incredible that the other party can prevail through a man who lacks justice and whom the Lord opposes. By frequent report we recall that, in a lowly position, those prevailed whom the French Church received and supported; and that those introduced by German violence met an unhappy end. Thus in our own times Innocent prevailed against Peter, Calixtus against Burdinus, Urban against Wibert, and Paschal against three—Albert, Maginulf, and Theodoric—and likewise many others in the days of our fathers.

May your graciousness therefore provide for us, and may God incline your assent toward that party which rests upon justice and truth and, Christ being propitious, will triumph. And, if it please you, in this great peril of the whole Church of the Lord, you ought to use the counsel of your kingdom, and nothing ought to be decided to its prejudice without the counsel of your clergy.

## LETTER XLIX. TO THE KING’S CHANCELLOR

Cantuar.

We have been burdened more heavily than we can tell you or anyone else, and we have not yet escaped well. Yet we hope to escape safely, because, by the Lord’s prompting, we have resolved to make satisfaction to Him who chastens us and, by present correction, to avert the eternal scourge. And we are the more assured of pardon the more grievously we are afflicted by the present punishment of the body. For the Lord chastens every son whom He receives. We are therefore ready, with a patient and cheerful heart, to receive bitter things from the hand of the Lord, from whom we have so often received sweet things for our use—or misuse. Thus, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

For in life we desire nothing else, although we defer some part of our purpose until we may use the counsel of the lord king and of yourself. Meanwhile we are making provision for our household and our soul; and henceforth, by the Lord’s grace, we shall make more effective provision according to the counsel of religious persons. There is also something which we have conceived both by the counsel of religion and in our own spirit: namely, that before our death we should correct [Col. 0031C] all the evil customs which have arisen in the archbishopric in our time and through us. Accordingly, when we seemed to be at the point of death, among other vows we made to the Lord this one: that we would abolish the custom concerning second aids which our brother the archdeacon had imposed upon the churches; and, releasing and freeing the churches from it, we have forbidden under anathema that it should henceforth be demanded by anyone.

And lest this benefit of ours—or rather, this duty—should later be impaired, we have confirmed it in our written instrument. Had you seen our present distress, you too would welcome whatever you saw done for our salvation; and you would prefer that our soul be delivered rather than acquire money and boundless riches from our sins and damnation. [Col. 0031D] This is why, for the present, we cannot heed you in the matter of this aid without injury to our vow and danger to our salvation. But if God grants us life and health, which we have not yet fully recovered, we hope that the Lord will still provide for you through our hand in such a way that you will not need aids of this kind, and that you will thank the Lord because in your days He has freed His Church from an evil custom. We therefore ask you to accept graciously what we have done, since the whole world would profit us little if we lost our soul.

## LETTER L. Concerning Meriton

Having decided, by command of the lord pope, the case which was being disputed between our beloved brethren, the canons of Meriton, and the monks of Meaux, [Col. 0032A] concerning possession of the place called Acchab. and B., and the damages which the canons complained had been inflicted upon them, we condemned the monks to restore the aforesaid place to the canons and to compensate their damages. When the latter, preserving truth and applying moderation, assessed their total at eighty marks, we intervened between the parties and reduced it to forty marks.

We therefore command your brotherhood, and by the authority of the lord pope enjoin, that you compel the aforesaid monks, with every pretext removed, to restore the said place and the aforesaid money to the aforementioned brethren, lest anyone be able to charge you with negligence in carrying out the apostolic mandate. [Col. 0032B] Nor ought it to avail the monks that they delivered the aforesaid estate, as they confessed to us, to an advocate; for one who fraudulently ceases to possess is condemned as a possessor. Let them therefore restore the place immediately and pay the money before the approaching feast of All Saints. If the lord of the estate opposes you on any pretext, do not delay to restrain him, with due diligence, by ecclesiastical severity.

## LETTER LI. To …

Sometimes a man wounds his own nose or tears out his eye while intending to fortify his face with the saving sign. “What is the point of this?” you ask. I answer the matters about which you wrote to me, [Col. 0032C] though I do not exult over your misfortune. Rather, I marvel and sympathize with a pain all the more bitter because I love both parties more sincerely: one of them, if the complaint is just, has lost both labour and expense; the other is more ruinously dishonoured by the vice of ingratitude. Yet the latter’s loss is far more serious: on one side there is loss of goods; on the other, loss of honour.

But if you are wise, this shifting injury of fortune serves your purposes. For it compensates by knowledge of realities for what it seemed to have taken away through the fault of ungrateful people. Thus it has increased your prudence, since it wished you to be stirred by this spur. Commanders dismiss mercenary soldiers from court if fortune removes the enemy; when he threatens again, they recall them more eagerly. Whoever therefore wishes to enjoy perpetual wages must not withdraw from military service. Yet this is a benefit not only from the commander but from the enemy as well.

Indeed, unless you prefer to overlook it, you sail in harbour; and at your will, although your fortune is slippery, the wind will change and blow, the waters will flow, hail will fall, lightning flashes and thunderclaps will threaten. [Col. 0032D] At these things human minds will be moved and recalled to an awareness of their condition.

## LETTER LII. To the Clergy of the Church of Exeter

### To a people deprived of its shepherd

Although we sympathize with your bereavement in paternal affection, we nevertheless have great consolation for the sorrow thereby conceived, because we trust that your blessed father has passed to the heavenly places and will be able to intercede, with his customary prayers but with greater efficacy, before the Father of mercies both for us and for you. But since the widowhood of a desolate Church cannot be prolonged without danger to souls and loss of property, we ask and exhort your charity in the Lord that you think the same thing, and that with all diligence you avoid every occasion of scandals and schism, walking unanimously in the house of the Lord and preferring the things of Jesus Christ to private advantage.

So that you may proceed, as is fitting, in providing yourselves with a shepherd, we command that, in order to preserve the peace of the Church, you approach the lord king through an honourable embassy sent from your body, [Col. 0033A] offering him your petitions with due devotion, that he grant you freedom canonically to elect a shepherd and provide for the deprivation of the church with the compassion fitting a Christian prince.

## LETTER LIII. To Pope Alexander

### To the lord pope ALEXANDER

Our venerable brother Maurice, bishop of Bangor—slender in resources and possessions, but in our judgment a religious man who fears the Lord—found the Church over which, by the Lord’s appointment, he presides disturbed and defiled by the wickedness of those dwelling in it, being ignorant of the divine law and entirely unaware of canonical institutions. For they are a rude and untamed people, living after a beastly fashion; they despise the word of life and, while professing Christ in name, deny Him in life and morals. [Col. 0033C] Christians among them are sold in customary trade to overseas regions and taken captive by unbelievers.

Despising the law of marriage, they exchange for a price the concubines whom they keep together with wives; and, ignorant of the crime of incest, they are not ashamed to uncover the shamefulness of women related by blood. And, more miserably still, priest as well as people, imbued with the same errors, foster this pestilence and corrupt by their pernicious example those whom they ought to lead back to the path of virtue and truth.

To crown this pestilence, the prince of these barbarians, O., is abusing his maternal uncle’s daughter. Though often admonished both by us and by his bishop, he has, so that he may remain more freely and licentiously in his military following, drawn no small part of the clergy [Col. 0033D] into support of his crimes; and he has stripped the bishop himself of his goods and expelled him from his bishopric, because, inflamed by zeal of charity, the bishop rebuked with such boldness the errors both of the prince and of the people.

The bishop has bound certain contumacious persons, some clergy and some laypeople, by the bond of anathema. But they wander openly and as fugitives to neighbouring bishops in Wales, England, Ireland, and Scotland, and fraudulently receive from them ordinations, chrism, and the other sacraments of the Church. Consequently, the vigour of ecclesiastical discipline in those regions has now grown so faint that a seedbed of heresy and schism is almost springing up there. Therefore, reverend Father, we beseech Your Holiness to arise to aid us and our aforesaid suffragan bishop and, by your open letters sent jointly to the bishops of England, Wales, Ireland, and Scotland, command them to hold valid and firmly observe whatever we, compelled by necessity, shall canonically decree against the Welsh on behalf of the bishop exiled among us. [Col. 0034A]

## LETTER LIV. To the King

### The Archbishop of Canterbury to the King of the English

I judge it superfluous to recount in words with what devoted loyalty I have served you, since the evident deeds of many years bear witness for me, my fidelity has a witness in heaven, and my conscience has one who knows it in the Highest. My flesh is worn away; my limbs are exhausted by both age and labours; and a grave and prolonged illness announces that the end of my days is near at hand.

I had hoped to see your long-desired face before I died, and, in your presence as witness, to commend personally to you those whom God had entrusted to my care in your kingdom. But because I am called sooner to His judgment-seat, before whose tribunal we shall all shortly stand, I address your serenity by this letter, prostrate in heart at the royal feet, before the Lord who judges all things; earnestly beseeching you to deign to hear your faithful servant as he faces death, whose devotion to you has never grown cold. [Col. 0034B]

Hear me, I beseech you, so that God may hear you in your final hour. Hear me for the house of the Lord and for His little ones, whom I leave deprived of human consolation, so that the Most High may protect your house, comfort your little ones and your children’s children for ever. I send to you and to your seed the blessing of the Lord Jesus Christ; and you, if it please you, send the consolation of your majesty to those whom I leave destitute.

I commend to you the holy Church of Canterbury, from whose hand, through my ministry, you received the helm of the kingdom. If it please you, protect it from the assaults of wicked men; and strive to appoint in my place—I who, though unworthy, have hitherto governed it by God’s ordering as best I could and knew—a shepherd who will not seem unworthy of so great a see, who delights in religion, and who may be believed pleasing to the Most High by the merits of his virtues. [Col. 0034D]

Your faithful servant owes you his counsel: behold, before the Lord and all His saints, I give counsel. In this matter seek not what is yours but what is the Lord’s. For I answer to you for this: if you faithfully advance His cause, He Himself will advantageously advance yours. After many troubles, by the Lord’s help, we have restored peace in the Church of Canterbury, advanced the observance of religion, and appointed, according to our conscience, suitable guardians over the order. Before an archbishop is appointed in my place, let your dignity forbid any one of them to be changed by another’s rashness, and restrain those who may devise divisions and new schemes. For we have forbidden this under anathema, and excommunicated those who presume to alter the ordering of the religious community which we have made. [Col. 0035A]

Moreover, I commit to your protection our dependants, clergy and laity, whom we have had as ministers of our own service and often of yours. We ask that you mercifully preserve what we have conferred upon them and do not allow them to be harassed by anyone’s importunity. Let my most merciful lord hear yet one word and gladden my departing soul. The remainder of my movable goods, and those things which, until my death, had seemed to be kept for use because the duration of life was uncertain and the illness prolonged, I have ordered, as God inspired me, to be distributed to the poor after my death. I condemn by the already promulgated anathema those who commit fraud, or who hinder their distribution for the salvation of myself, yourself, and your children. [Col. 0035B]

If it please you, ratify my disposition and confirm it by open letters sent to your officials. For no gold or silver remains, but only provisions and things whose loss would greatly harm the poor, while bringing you no benefit, or only the least.

## LETTER LV. To Walter, Bishop of Rochester

### To WALTER, bishop of Rochester

He gravely offends Christ—whose place has become most pleasant in the unity of brethren—who strives to disturb those things which have been established in His house for peace. We have always loved the peace of the Church of Canterbury; and, by the Lord’s favour, our charitable affection toward our brethren has daily increased, and after our time we desire every source of scandal to be removed from them.

According to our conscience, therefore, we have appointed suitable guardians over the religious community according to their ability, through whose ministry religion has, by the Lord’s grace, flourished now for many years and the administration of external possessions has been managed more commendably than usual. What we have established, we command and enjoin by the authority we exercise to remain unshaken: the priors are to attend to the love and benefit of their subjects, and the subjects are to obey their prelates in all humility and reverence. [Col. 0035D]

We also permanently remove Walter—whom we removed from the priorship through no fault of the church, but because of his own—from the office of prior and subprior and from every prelacy in the community of the Church of Canterbury. Nevertheless, if he is peaceable, we grant him fellowship with the brethren and residence in the Church of Canterbury. If, as a private member, he conducts himself commendably, we do not forbid him to rise to other obediences of our Church or to the governance of another church, provided that he in no way aspire to the priorship, subpriorship, or the other forbidden keys of the community. If ever he aspires to this, we subject to anathema all whom he may have as helpers in this undertaking.

And to you also, Walter, we forbid this, in the name of almighty God and under anathema; and on whatever day you attempt it, we command all our brother bishops and all your parishioners and subjects, by virtue of obedience, [Col. 0036A] not in any way to communicate with you until you cease and make fitting satisfaction. If you devise anything in evasion of this our ordinance, know that you, together with all your accomplices, are subject to the aforesaid sentence.

Do not err, brother—do not; for God is not mocked. Rather, keep peace with your brethren; and may God forgive you what you have sinned against us, though undeserving. May the God of peace and consolation be with you, most beloved brother; and may He cause us, whom the frailty of the human condition now separates, to rejoice continually with Him in eternal blessedness.

## LETTER LVI. To Nigel, Bishop of Ely

### To NIGEL, bishop of Ely

[Col. 0036B] You have consulted us concerning a matter not doubtful, and one which above all ought rather to have been resolved by wise persons than delayed. For there is no deliberation concerning disgraceful things: a delayed rejection of shamefulness presents a certain appearance of dishonourable consent. What could be more disgraceful than, with all authority of the divine law scorned, to rush shamelessly into the Holy of Holies and, driven by avarice, against right and justice, to claim a hereditary right in ecclesiastical property—even in the altar itself?

Who but a profane person could patiently hear, much less request, what the sacred canons so plainly forbid and the authority of both Testaments so expressly condemns? Turn over the canons, for in this matter they speak most extensively, and you will plainly see that the petition of those who seek such things is condemned and that the consent of those who hear such petitioners must be punished with the utmost severity. [Col. 0036C]

No room for dissembling is left to us, since at the Lateran council, at which both we and you, brother bishop, were present, with the lord Innocent presiding, we heard such claims condemned by a promulgated canon. But perhaps royal authority pressures us. It would indeed do so rightly—unless you knew that the Lord must be preferred to man, unless a prince’s religious devotion could be deceived, unless some things had been wrung from him by misrepresentation, as you have already experienced.

The sum of our counsel, therefore, is this: obey the law of the Lord and the sacred canons in accordance with your profession; and whenever such straits press you, judge it safer to fall into the hands of men than into those of the living God. Yet perhaps there is a reason why you have deserved to be troubled about successions of this kind: you have been too prone to unlawful resignations and substitutions in fraud of the canons. [Col. 0036D]

## LETTER LVII. Testament of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury

The laws show favour to the final wishes of those who are dying; and he who obstructively opposes their pious desires calls down upon himself, as it were inhumanely, the wrath of the Lord. Our will is indeed—and, by the Lord’s prompting, will never change—that the remainder of our movable goods, which because of household necessities and the prolonged duration of illness we judged should be kept until the end of life, should pass entirely to the use of the poor, according as the Lord inspired us and as we entrusted to our venerable brother Walter, bishop of Rochester, and to our faithful servants Philip our chancellor, Master Ralph of Lisieux, and John of Salisbury, whom we appointed to administer our alms. [Col. 0037A]

We therefore command what we commanded at the beginning of our disposition, and have enjoined all our servants and faithful men, by the fidelity which they owe us: that they obey these persons and place all our goods at their disposal. We humbly entreat all God’s friends, for the mercy of almighty God, to give them assistance and counsel.

We have condemned by sentence of anathema all who commit fraud in the aforesaid goods of the poor, or hinder the execution of our disposition. And if the king’s officials involve themselves in disturbing our disposition, let them know that they are deprived of communion with the faithful, and, as sacrilegious and excommunicated persons, let them abstain from entering all churches. [Col. 0037B] But upon all helpers of our disposition we confer the blessing of the Lord and our own blessing; we make them participants in the benefits of the holy Church of Canterbury; and we grant them remission of forty days from the penance enjoined upon them.

Furthermore, in the name of almighty God and under anathema, we forbid any official of the lord king rashly to lay hands upon the goods dedicated to the proper uses of the monks of the Church of Canterbury. Rather, let them possess all their goods in the integrity and liberty in which we caused these same goods to be confirmed to them by the privilege of the lord pope and by our own.

Under the same anathema we also forbid every alienation of lands belonging to the archbishop, as well as the felling and damaging of woods, until a successor is appointed in our place—except insofar as the necessary use of the Church requires, or the lord king commands by his own word, or discerning mercy, with moderation, relieves the need of poor persons. [Col. 0037C] Under the same threat, we forbid the clergy of our bishopric to be oppressed by undue exactions and unjust vexations; and we command that all liberties and just customs which they had in the time of William, our predecessor of good memory, be observed for them.

## LETTER LVIII. To Richard, Bishop of London

### To RICHARD, bishop of London

[Col. 0037D] Things which abandon proper order either never, or only rarely, obtain happy outcomes. There is a most correct order in legal causes: examination should precede judgment, and only then should someone be struck by a lawful penalty, when he either cannot defend his innocence or scorns to do so. But you are arranging, if Adelitia of Valognes has a just complaint, to condemn her contrary to lawful order; and, denying her a hearing, you shut off every avenue of defence.

We remember having written to you previously on this matter, directing that, after summoning her at a suitable place and time, you should handle the matter according to canonical order. Whatever ought to be decided against her, we advised and commanded should be confirmed by mature, not hasty, judgment. But she complains that she is being treated more harshly on that account. We do not wish to obstruct a religious purpose; but, with justice leading the way—which goes before the face of the wise—we desire it to be fulfilled without scandal to our office.

We therefore again command your love to proceed lawfully in the aforementioned case, tempering justice with prudence so that those who hear of the zeal you have in the Lord may rejoice that knowledge also has attended you. We command you, therefore, to grant her the hearing due to her, and then let the case attain its proper conclusion according to the Lord. Our brethren will shortly gather with us in London, by the Lord’s help, so that, if in the meantime you choose to apply diligence in executing your office, you may be able more safely to determine this case with their counsel. [Col. 0038A]

## LETTER LIX. To Ranulf de Serris, Concerning the Election of Alexander as Roman Pontiff

### JOHN of Salisbury to his dearest friend Master R. de Serris: greetings, and whatever is better than greetings.

[Col. 0038B] My dear friend, I do not doubt that you share in our distresses, since, although in another manner and differently, we are troubled by no other or different cause. We receive at close quarters, in our own hands, the missiles of raging Fortune; and before our eyes continually lies matter for unceasing toil, pain, and sorrow. Bitter fate grants neither place nor time for joy or rest; scarcely even a slender hope of consolation remains. Yet that hope is from the Lord, since human help is now despaired of.

For my part, distress presses me through the burden of household affairs, debt, and importunate creditors; but grief darkens this anxiety, and the stronger onset of public fear swallows up everything private. You yourself feel what I feel; what I say to you, you yourself, I think, utter in continual reflection; and your attentive mind anticipates the sorrowful word of one seeking speech. For unless you cast off yourself, while you are anxious over the illness of our common lord, you engage, with vigilant and continual care, in our labours and sorrows. As you behold the collisions of the universal Church, at whose breasts we were nourished, weigh their cause, and foresee their dangers, reflection adds pain to pain—a pain which you cannot endure to bear. [Col. 0038D]

Yet in all these matters you are treated more gently, since you are not compelled to weep at every rumour and every moment, and at every complaint of the desolated household; since, having obtained the fortune of a freer condition, you do not fear either exile or the necessity of committing some accursed crime for yourself. For you live under a prince whose memory is held in delight and blessing.

But we fear beyond measure lest the German emperor ensnare us by his deceits and overturn our prince’s serenity. He seems to me to possess so little discernment that the presumption of the Pavia conventicle moves him—unless it be that Alexander’s election, should anyone doubt it, is confirmed even by the testimony of the opposing party. For, to pass over that man’s rashness—he presumed to judge the Roman Church, which is reserved for the judgment of the Lord alone; and summoned by peremptory edict to judgment one who had been excommunicated, as the dishonouring at Besançon of the cardinals indicates; and, by a prejudicial sentence, greeted one man by the name of his former office and dignity, the other by the title of Roman pontiff, revealing to the senators and people the secret counsels of his favour—everything done at Pavia is found contrary both to equity and to the lawful constitutions and enactments of the Fathers. For absent persons were condemned; and in a case not examined—or rather, one not to be examined there, in that way, or by such persons—a sentence was rashly rendered, shamelessly, imprudently, and wickedly. [Col. 0039A]

But perhaps they would rather be called “persons staying away” than “absent persons.” This is plainly the view of those who either do not know or conceal the privilege of the holy Roman Church. Who subjected the universal Church to the judgment of a particular church? Who made Germans judges of the nations? Who bestowed upon brutal and impetuous men this authority, to appoint at their will a ruler over the heads of the children of men? Indeed, their madness has most often attempted this; but, by the Lord’s help, it has so often been overthrown and confounded that it blushed at its own wickedness.

But I know what the German plots. For I was in Rome when blessed Eugenius presided, when, in the first embassy sent at the beginning of his reign, intolerable arrogance and an unguarded tongue revealed the insolence of so great an undertaking. He promised that he would reform the empire of the whole world and subject the world to the city, and that he would easily subdue all things if only the favour of the Roman pontiff were present for this purpose. [Col. 0039C] For this was his aim: that against whomever the emperor drew the material sword after declaring enmity, against that same person the Roman pontiff should wield the spiritual sword.

He has not yet found anyone who would consent to so great an iniquity; and, with Moses himself resisting—that is, with the law of the Lord contradicting him—he has taken to himself a Balaamite pontiff, through whom he might curse the people of the Lord. Thus, a son of curse: through whose designation and expectation, through many successions from the first fathers of the family down to the man for whom it was reserved, both the surname and the name “accursed” have been transmitted. And perhaps, for the purification and testing of the Roman Church, the onslaught of the Germans has been left for ever, like another Canaanite, so that it may always trouble her for her instruction, yet fall when defeated, while she, after triumph, is rendered stronger, more pleasing, and more glorious for the embraces of the Bridegroom. [Col. 0039D]

Thus, to the glory of the Fathers—as the Lateran palace bears witness, where even laypeople read this in invisible paintings—to the glory of the Fathers, schismatics whom secular power has intruded are given to the pontiffs as a footstool; and posterity recalls their memory as a triumph. Judgments ought to be free, and whoever strives to disturb them by force deserves the capital punishment appointed by ancient constitutions. Ecclesiastical judgments, moreover, ought to be entirely free; and by the ordinance of the sacred canons, just as the election of a shepherd in the Church is to be celebrated freely and without nomination by secular power, so that same election is to be examined in the Church by ecclesiastical judges, secular and terrifying persons being removed, according to ecclesiastical rules. Whatever is presumed contrary to this is rendered void. [Col. 0040A]

But this matter was rushed through as though in a camp and under the sword: by threats and terrors the hope of an examination was fraudulently wrung from the simple and fearful, and it was driven forward against right and justice by deceitful, violent, and malicious persons. Yet what was investigated? What was proved? The question was ostensibly both factual and legal: namely, which of the elected men had the canonical or sounder election. Accordingly, the fact was proposed and proved in accordance with the will of the party that makes flesh its arm.

It was proved, I say, that Victor alone was elected by the sounder part of the cardinals, at the request of the people, with the consent and desire of the clergy; that he was solemnly mounted and placed in Peter’s chair, with Roland present and not opposing—indeed consenting—and commanding his own clergy to obey the man whom they saw adorned in the apostolic see with pontifical insignia. This too was proved: that on the twelfth day after Victor’s promotion Roland, having left the city, was first mounted near the Sicilian territory in an obscure place.

Have you not considered the method of proof? For the dean of the basilica of St Peter and two of his brethren swore this in the person of the whole chapter; religious persons and the governors of the Roman clergy also swore it.
