The prefect offered to swear the same in words, as did other citizens; but only the clergy’s oaths were received, because they had handled all these things with their own hands. [Col. 0040C]

Who, even blind, would fail to detect such manifest malice, such open lies? For it is known to almost everyone what importance these “governors,” whom the Council of Pavia magnifies in order to defend its malice, have—especially in the election of a Roman pontiff. Who does not find it incredible that those men handled these matters, as they boast? But grant that they were present at the beginning of the disputes: did they pursue R. for twelve days up to his consecration? Did the chapter of St Peter, in whose name the oath was sworn, see this—or the governors who swore on its behalf? Did the prefect see all these things, though he is an exile and not permitted to enter the city? Indeed, as people commonly say, he is Octavian’s nephew, or, more correctly, a close relative, being his sister’s son.

But other citizens saw everything, so that they could swear safely. Did they go to the Sicilian territory? Clearly, the witnesses who swore all these things in the presence of that sacred council were faithfully examined. But the citizens were deliberately excused from the necessity of swearing, because they certainly would not have sworn. For, even if they did not fear injury to conscience, they feared injury to their reputation among their fellow citizens.

Moreover, what became of the greater number of the sounder party? If they flourished in unimpaired prudence and justice, under what influence did they depart from the truth and justice which they held? Or were they corrupted by that money which the senators confessed they had received from Octavian in order to swear to his promotion? It had been allotted by the people to repair the walls, while many cried out that it must not be put into the purse, because it was the price of blood. [Col. 0041A] Of that great host only three remained—certainly worthy cardinals—concerning whom Germans in a camp might pronounce judgment.

William of Pavia, cardinal of St Peter in Chains, heard all these things and did not deny them in the presence of the council. But what did he assert for Victor? Why was his testimony neglected? He ought to have been questioned: he had sufficient voice, courage, and age to speak for himself. But plainly he was not questioned because he would have denied it; and he knowingly kept silent amid the tumult, seeing the onset of fury and that this presumption prejudices ecclesiastical liberty in no respect.

Yet I learned one thing from his silence: if Victor’s election was so sound, why did the cardinal bishops and all the rest, except these three—whom you indeed knew, but whom the world will henceforth recognize—not attend his consecration? What prevented the Tuscan bishops summoned to it from taking part in the consecration, except consciousness of sacrilege? I wonder that all follow poor Alexander and prefer exile with him from the presence of princes to ruling with the princes of the nations by adhering to his rival. Here are the bishops, here the priests, here the deacons, here is the whole curia; everyone of any rank who is not in exile is here. The sentence of the Council of Pavia does not frighten them; rather, hoping in the Lord and strengthened in the might of His power and in the Holy Spirit, they have hurled a sentence of anathema against the emperor himself and his idol, together with all his worshippers. [Col. 0041C]

I pass to the new and unheard-of subscriptions of the decretal synod, in which counts are admitted in place of bishops because bishops are lacking; in which those men claim for themselves the principal authority of episcopal sees whose election is either nonexistent or rejected. For Reginald, the emperor’s chancellor, acted as archbishop of Cologne, although it is certain that his election was condemned by the Roman pontiff, blessed Adrian. Nor do I see why, since he seeks a bishopric, he has delayed being consecrated by his Victor, unless he fears the ruin that threatens.

Guy, count of Flanders, supplied the place of the archbishop of Ravenna, although not even his son—whose election has been annulled, though he is a good young man—can yet perform the office of archbishop. Who would not find these things ridiculous? It is the spectacle of a theatrical stage rather than the image of a venerable council. [Col. 0041D]

What of the great but false number assembled from kingdoms and provinces, so that these subscribers may more easily drag those ignorant of affairs with them into the precipice? Who would be moved by the decrees of that council, where:

> “… the Fathers sit ready to decree,  
> if he seeks a kingdom, temples, or the throat of the senate,  
> and daughters-in-law destined to suffer unspeakable things.”

(Lucan.)

And whatever more cruelly tyrannical thing can be imagined? Indeed, it went well with the Church in that Caesar, [Col. 0042A] who was present, was ashamed to command more than she herself could endure.

I could write more in reply to what you wrote, but I judge that this is enough to persuade you that, if possible, the lord of Reims should receive Alexander, and that consent, if he thinks it expedient, should conveniently be deferred until that is done. For I believe he is sufficiently persuaded not to acquiesce in worshipping the emperor’s idol. But if danger were threatening, it is most expedient that the matter be postponed for the present. In difficult affairs, precipitancy is dangerous; and delay, which in matters being pressed forward brings danger, frequently provides an opportunity to act. The bishops of Pavia and Piacenza have been solicited sufficiently and beyond measure by the party that trusts in man; but neither of them has consented to the counsel and deeds of the wicked, because they too await the kingdom of the Lord. Yet the emperor is pressing them, so that, strengthened by their example, those farther away may speak the word for truth more boldly, advancing against the wolves and setting themselves as an impregnable wall before the house of Israel. And because I speak to you no otherwise than to myself, I shall openly set forth whatever burns within my breast. You, being nearer and more familiarly acquainted with the face of affairs, will be able to judge each point more fully and faithfully.

If, now that the sides have been strengthened, schismatic fury should press less heavily, so that it may be doubtful in whose hands the authority of the Roman Church resides, nothing seems to me wiser than that the decision of the prior election be deferred until the day when the Lord’s righteous judgment is revealed, [Col. 0042C] because that day alone will render the guilty party defeated. For, as the poet says:

> No hand in war is pure when the judge has been changed.

Human justice, because it does not possess full and clear understanding of the truth of merits, is for the most part overthrown by some cloud of error. But the justice of the Lord is justice for ever. Meanwhile, until He illumines the hidden things of darkness, He must be invoked and asked to show plainly by judgment whom He Himself has chosen to receive the lot of this ministry. Yet if there is nothing that leaves room for question, or permits doubt even in one who, like an Academic, wavers about almost everything—when the new pair of contestants has come forward, by the Lord’s permission, to the astonishment of all beholders: on the one side the whole Church standing firm, on the other only three reed-like scourges, who, while striving to divide unity, provoke divine vengeance against themselves. If you compare person with person: one is learned, modest, humble, a zealot for justice; the other has always embraced vanity alone. If cause with cause: one forced himself in like a thief and robber, by violent hand and contrived deceits, bursting into the bride’s embrace while the bridegroom protested; the other stood back with chaste modesty until he was introduced by the bride. Hence one must fear that delaying the condemnation of so manifest a crime may seem to afford consent to the schism.

Although, as you know, the lord of Canterbury is suffering from a very severe illness, the necessity of this matter nevertheless makes him hasten to London, [Col. 0043A] having summoned the bishops and clergy of the whole realm, so that, when a council of the brethren has been convened, he may tell the lord king, who consults him, what must be done. We feared that the journey would burden him still more; and therefore I detained your Acard for several days, though he was unwilling, so that through his report of what he had seen you might be more fully informed of my lord’s condition. Since he mounted the litter, he seems somewhat strengthened, although he is still grievously afflicted. At times the abscess has rested somewhat, and natural purgation is restored of itself. The bishops of Winchester and Durham, they say, would gladly go over to Octavian’s side if they dared openly to support him as they wished. Conversely, the archbishop of York and our treasurer support Alexander with all their strength; nor are they alone, since this party is accepted by more and better men, [Col. 0043B] though they defend it more vigorously.

## LETTER LX. TO …

Apothecaries are accustomed to mix different ingredients, thus softening the sharpness of pungent substances with milder ones and tempering bitter things with sweet, so that, once they have blended into the taste and efficacy of a new compound, all become sweet, and together are more effective for overthrowing minds than separately. This perhaps occurs more often also because sweeter things are taken more greedily, and excess abandons the boundary of sobriety when the charm of sweetness introduces an enemy against whom there is least guard. Whether you have ever been an apothecary, I do not know; but I am quite certain [Col. 0043C] that in some respect you imitate apothecaries—if indeed you may rightly be said to imitate men whom, in preparing certain compounds, you seem more rightly to surpass. Perhaps for that reason, during the preceding autumn, you bought up various sorts of wine, the purchase and conveyance of which, as I remember you wrote to me, diverted your attention from other business.

But although you disdain the hand of a common apothecary, you will by no means be able to excuse your tongue and pen, which breathe the potency of every powdered drug of the apothecary—though that potency befit a philosopher. Your speech indeed makes you manifest, and the page recently sent to me convicts you even while you conceal yourself. For you display that genius of Lisieux in speech and learning against a friend unskilled in both; you sharpen the tongue of Lisieux, with which I have resolved from the beginning never to join battle; and, like a very powerful orator, now establishing your own points and now demolishing another’s, you forestall for me every avenue of defence. It would indeed be shut off, so that I could not utter a sound, if you fully knew my occupations. But in this respect it goes well with simple persons—men like myself—whom the spirit of prophecy does not always illumine, you wise men. Yet I could readily believe that the men of Lisieux, since they know very much and can say whatever they please, are divine.

Shall I therefore, on whatever grounds, rashly presume to contend with you, who in authority and merit are the equal of the fathers of Lisieux? The lords, the fathers of Lisieux, are not merely men of eloquence, but in some fashion are eloquence itself. For although in many respects they equal the men of Orléans, who are skilled and experienced in many matters, [Col. 0044A] they readily surpass them in this: here men are born and made eloquent—so much so that a native use of eloquence permeates and forms every age and sex. What then shall a little man of impeded tongue answer to so great a torrent of eloquence? Though I cannot resist on equal terms, perhaps, once pardon has been obtained, I may pass without penalty over the points by which you have undeservedly branded me.

You accuse me, then, of long silence. Is it not permitted to keep silent? Indeed, among wise and eloquent men it is also just for one whose tongue is more impeded and whose mind more dull. If such a person speaks or writes more often, will he not, being less suited to these things, uncover or perpetuate his own disgrace? For spoken words pass away, but written words [Col. 0044B] remain. Yet I seem more taciturn than you only to you, since I always answer you when you write, and sometimes write before you are about to write. But perhaps the unlettered appearance of my letters and the bloodless colour of a dry tongue represent one who merely wants to write or speak rather than one who writes or says anything. It is quite right for me to be called tongueless or mute, since, by a similar pattern of language, a badly formed woman is called shapeless, and letters that make the least sound are classed as mute.

You assign another cause to my silence, marking the arrogance of my pride: you say that, from the throne of power which you imagine me to occupy, I disdain to visit a humble friend with some paltry little letter. Whence do you lay this sin upon me? Or which of those with whom I have lived is the author or informer of this accusation? You reproach me with a throne and exercise of power. Yet from however small an experience of time you learned—indeed, I complain only of the briefness of the days during which we have lived together—you learned, I say, that in my lord’s household I do not usurp the first places at table, but willingly and voluntarily yield precedence to many. It is just, indeed, that in so great a father’s house very many should precede me in honours and the exercise of authority, as they do in merits and dignities. “A humble friend,” you say. What else, I ask, is this profession of humility but a crafty display of dignity and rank, an affected concealment of eminence and honour? You added, “with some paltry little letter.” For what other kind than such a one—namely, a foolish one—[Col. 0044D] will an unlearned and rough man send, one who, when observed by some man of Lisieux, will fall silent like another Moeris? Here at least you had your eyes open and judge my powers correctly, since you expect from me nothing but some such little letter.

Then, to convict me of arrogance or negligence, you reproach me with the number of our men who are setting out for Toulouse, as though I knew that all the Toulousans would pass through the city of Lisieux or Bayeux. For I do not know the situation of your cities, nor through which places those were to travel who, by the king’s edict, had to assemble in the city of Poitiers. I certainly did not think that you were to be found there, nor had I heard that you pursued the fortunate expedition otherwise than with prayers. Yet I knew from many reports [Col. 0045A] that the undertaking could not be carried on without the men of Lisieux, because their tongues had become the fires of war, and they themselves, carrying fire and sword in their hands, serve the Lord of hosts. Hence it is clear, clearer than any daylight, that the law ought to be sought from their mouth: for they are guardians of knowledge, and by the authority in which they excel they can and ought to command that peoples gather to them.

Meanwhile I thought that you were resting at home after peace had been settled, not knowing whether any of those departing our borders would see you. For although very many of your people return, no one except William the physician brought me a verbal greeting from you. Yet you saw many returning from my lord’s household and table. You did these things, and I was silent—or rather, you were silent, and I kept silence too. I cannot deny that I gave attention to many travellers; and, to whisper this in your ear, I would more gladly have dismissed some of them carrying letters to you than with the various portions of my household goods, of which the villainy of men on campaign stripped me.

Finally, you say that my genius had to be deprived of both the sweetness of dreams and the festivities of banquets. You know, of course, that nothing else hindered a lover of pleasure. For you take no account of my lord’s business and that of his friends, nor even of the care of my household. Thus, having branded my innocence with the mark of pride, negligence, and pleasure, in your letter you mixed these charges together as though grinding a variegated apothecary’s powder. And because each charge might be bitter, [Col. 0045C] you first rubbed my ears with sweet speech, lest I should understand what you were saying. You cook this mixture with the fire of charity, so that all the things offered may become sweet. Let it therefore be as you wish: I yield to the greater man, and interpret everything well and amicably.

## LETTER LXI. TO KING HENRY

To the lord king of the English:

To entrap royal majesty by devised deceits is akin to sacrilege, especially where fraud procures the indignation of power against innocence, and impiety, labouring to the detriment of salvation and sowing hatred, seeks to extinguish brotherly charity. Though God hates other crimes, this is the one which His soul detests because of its exceptional wickedness. Wicked men, as we have learned with grief, have tried to deceive Your Holiness by delivering to you letters composed in my name. These stated that, placed at the point of extreme difficulty, I regretted the promotion of our venerable brother Roger, archbishop of York, and offered prayers to Your Majesty that, because I was refused the opportunity to repair the fault which I had committed in this matter, you should correct it by the power bestowed upon you by the Lord, when you had received an opportunity to judge justly and execute vengeance among the nations.

Behold, with the Lord as observer and judge, I shall speak in your hearing what is true. I neither wrote these letters, nor wished to write them, nor do I know that they were written by any of my people. They are false; and the forger alone knowingly used them to deceive you and to bring condemnation upon himself. Whoever he may be, he will plainly bear his own judgment and, by the authority of the sacred canons, will fall into the snare of anathema, because the soul of the Lord detests those who do such things as sowers and instigators of discord and division. [Col. 0046A] We therefore beseech Your Serenity, if it please you, to order the authors of such great wickedness seized for punishment, and to have them punished with such severe administration that those who hear of the vengeance may learn, and teach others, that deceits and malice do not please a true and just prince.

## LETTER LXII. TO KING HENRY

To the king of the English:

The virtue of princes shines forth in no clearer indication [Col. 0046B] than when, through their majesty, the people receive peace, the Church tranquillity, and religion an increase pleasing to the Lord. For the throne of a king is firmly strengthened in the one who relies upon the foundations of such great virtues. We repeat these things often in your hearing because it is evident that they are welcome to you; and, as they are more illustrious in practice, so through frequent exercise they are more pleasing to Your Majesty. While your attention is occupied with these matters, your steps shall prosper in the Lord and in the glory of the whole world. For the intercessions of the saints, whose tranquillity you provide for, will obtain this also.

The monastery of St Mary at York perseveres in prayers to the Lord for you. We commend it to you with the greater confidence because, by the testimony of all the provincials, we believe it more worthy of commendation both for the observance of true religion and for its pious devotion toward you and your children. As we have reliably learned, its peace was for a long time disturbed by a certain brother, who at last, driven by his wickedness and instability of conduct, flew away like useless chaff from the Lord’s threshing-floor. He then approached Your Majesty, proving himself hateful to the Lord by not being ashamed to slander the monastery and by attempting to procure, contrary to the Rule of St Benedict, a privilege to commit wrongdoing. Out of reverence for you, the brothers wished to receive him according to the statutes of their Order. But he would not consent to enter unless the monastic order were dissolved by his entry. We therefore beseech Your Excellency kindly to hear the brothers of that religious house [Col. 0046D] and refuse a hearing to the man who strives to hinder brothers who continually pray for you. Further, prostrate at the feet of your mercy, we most earnestly commend to you the cause of the universal Church, praying the Lord for ourselves—and you, for yourself and your Church—that at the emperor’s request you may make no decision by which the fury of schism may gain further strength.

## LETTER LXIII. TO THE SAME

To the king of the English:

The merciful and compassionate Lord, who does not despise the prayers of the poor, has heard the groans of His Church and, through His grace, has restored peace to you, so that you may restore it, as you ought, to your subjects. For it is just [Col. 0047A] that those who have been worn down by your labours should share in consolation, and that those who have exposed their possessions, bodies, and souls at your disposal should be able to breathe again with you, at least for a little while, so that afterwards they may be fitter for your service when need arises.

Moreover, because in your absence there is no hope of peace for our contemporaries, the whole land longs for your presence and prays to the Lord, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, that He may grant you true peace and itself your favour, and that it may please you to remain longer in your realm, for the consolation and benefit of clergy and people. The Most High is accustomed to hear those who pray for you, and we trust that this very petition of the humble is accepted by Him. We therefore beseech Your Majesty [Col. 0047B] to be pleased with what we believe pleases the Lord, and to return to your own people, for whose need and prayers we believe peace has been restored to you on every side by the Lord.

May the devotion of your people move you; may the affection of your children move you, from the sight of whom scarcely the sternest father could restrain his eyes for so long; may conjugal fidelity move you; may the pleasantness of places and abundance of delights move you, which we cannot sufficiently recount. And, lest I pass over my own cause, may my desolation move your mind: because of age and illness I shall not be able to await your longed-for arrival much longer. My bone clings to my skin, my flesh having been consumed; my spirit threatens to depart, yet remains fast in my limbs through longing and hope of your arrival. It waits and hopes, and meanwhile makes a deaf ear to nature calling it and refuses to close the eyes unless your face has first been seen. [Col. 0047C] The sum of my prayers and longing, therefore, is that you return as soon as you can suitably do so.

Further, it is reported that the emperor, through his chancellor, seeks to incline you toward his pope, whatever his cause may be. But, with the Lord protecting your mind, you will prefer God to any human being. You know that: “Cursed is everyone who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jeremiah 17). And indeed, in matters so arduous and perilous, it is safer to defer consent to a later time than to precipitate it prematurely. On this matter and certain others, I should have great need of your counsel—or at least that of my archdeacon—and of a personal conference. [Col. 0047D]

## LETTER LXIV. TO THE SAME

To the king of the English:

The glory of a Christian prince is especially vigorous and advances when he renders pious service to the Lord, from whom all principality comes; and an inheritance of peace, rejoicing, and glory is perpetuated for the one who calms the storms of the labouring Church and provides faithful and fortunate service, so that the rejoicing bride may be able to cling to the desired embraces of the bridegroom. But he provokes against himself the almighty hand of the Most High who does not receive Christ’s shipwreck [Col. 0048A] with a full feeling of compassion, who either causes or neglects the Church’s collisions, and who, abusing the power granted him, fosters by consent the evil which he does not repress or extinguish. For the collision of peoples, the undoubted overthrow of kingdoms, and the fuel of schism are an indication of a rule condemned by the Lord and now on the point of collapse.

Yet we hope in the Father of mercies, the author of consolations, that your throne will be established by perpetual blessing, and that your sons and your sons’ sons will happily inherit the royal seat which you have received from Him and wisely administer. For we have found, with Him favourable, such unity of concord among your subjects that it is established by the most trustworthy and evident indications that their faith is grounded upon the rock of the Church. For when, by your command, the Church of the English had assembled, a question was proposed in the hearing of wise men, concerning which the sincerity of your faith, as was proper, deigned to consult the magnates of your realm. Numerous documents were read on either side, by which either party could support its position—or its error. Then the standard of faith, the rule for action found in the enactments of the Fathers, was brought forward, so that it might become known to all to which cause its character could more fittingly be applied. Thus, with the Father of mercies propitious, matters proceeded so that truth shone out from the parties’ assertions, since witnesses coming forward unexpectedly established among us the cause of truth, and public report proclaimed the abominable deeds [Col. 0048C] of the schismatic.

Accordingly, on the basis of the matters set forth, no judgment was rendered—for it was not permitted—nor was anything decreed to the prejudice of royal majesty—for that ought not to have been done. But what was permitted, what ought to have been done, what Your Majesty’s command required, was done: a counsel was formed, with the Lord as witness and judge, which the faithful prudence of subjects ought to have dictated to a true prince even unasked. Further, so that the first credit, as is just, may be due to you and that the glory of the completed work may be yours, we caused it, as you commanded, to be recorded without any publication in books of conscience, which we ordered to be opened for you by the bearers of this letter, Master Bartholomew the archdeacon and William de Ver, our chaplain. For the said archdeacon took part in all the inquiries and deliberations [Col. 0048D] and examined with us the votes of each and all. Do not doubt that what you receive from him has proceeded from our heart. We commend them to you, earnestly asking that, if it please you, you hold their persons commended to you and graciously receive our petitions, which are in their hands.

## LETTER LXIV. TO THE SAME

> [Note: [Col. 0047] Letters 64 and 65 in the Paris edition, joined with the preceding Letter 64, make one letter out of three; in the Cambridge manuscript they are transmitted separately.]

Love produces confidence, and is accustomed to act more confidently with one whom it ardently loves. But with what affection I have always loved you, I have always judged it more honourable and more useful to show by deeds than by words, [Col. 0049A] although I have never been able to fulfil that affection as I wished. He who knows all things is my witness that the devotion I have had toward you has always exceeded my powers. I therefore hope that Your Majesty too will, in an affection of kindness, condescend to me and my little ones.

Indeed, I remember that I have long since commended all my dependants to you. But now I commend to you above the rest the man who has laboured above the rest in my service and has received least from my hand, though by sincerity of faith and performance of service he has deserved much. I therefore cast myself at the feet of Your Clemency, beseeching with all the devotion I can that you hold him commended to you; may your kindness make up to him for my deficiency, and, when he has lost me, may Your Serenity, if it please you, take my place for him, with kindly affection and the consolation due for a lost father. This is John of Salisbury, whom indeed I would commend to another, if among friends and lords I had anyone more powerful.

## LETTER LXIV. TO THE SAME

My longing will never be satisfied in the flesh unless it is granted me to see your most desired face in the flesh. Then Christ will dismiss His little servant in peace, if, before I depart from the labour of suffering to peace, He grants me to see the anointed of the Lord, the son of peace. May Christ grant me to see His anointed, and then I shall joyfully go to meet approaching death. I wait in this hope, and with repeated sighs say to myself: “Will not my Christ grant me to see him—to me, when I longed for him, He gave the task of anointing His anointed? Shall I not see, before I die, the son of the right hand, bringing relief from labours, bringing relief from dangers?” [Col. 0049C]

I still have at home an incomparable treasure, the treasure of a fatherly blessing, which I reserve for you, if Your Majesty deigns to come to a father in his last extremity. “I have appointed you as head of nations; I have subjected to your feet the sons of your mother.” And still, if you heed the Father’s call, there shall be added to you, from the storehouse of fuller grace, a heaped-up blessing from the dew of heaven above and the richness of the earth. But if you cannot or do not wish to return, I entrust this treasure to the faithfulness of the Church, to be restored to you by her. I have commended you to her, and she commends herself to you as an object of your desire. She is your mother; she is the bride of Christ; she is more glorious and powerful than any principality, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against her. She received from her Christ the power to bring in, without anyone preventing it, those whom she decrees to bring in, and powerfully to cast out from thence whom she chooses. If you wish—indeed, because you wish—to have Christ favourable to you, strive to have favourable to you His bride, which is the Church, whose head He Himself is; for she is the body of the head. Whoever lacks the grace of the Church has the whole creating Trinity opposed to him. [Col. 0049D]

The children of this age urge you to diminish the Church’s authority, so that your royal dignity may be increased. Whoever they are, they certainly attack Your Majesty and incur the Lord’s indignation. He it is who enlarged your boundaries; He it is who advanced your glory. It is altogether unjust if you diminish the glory of your benefactor and Lord; it is worthy of punishment and will without doubt be punished with a most severe punishment—indeed, with the Lord favourable, it will not be punished, because, with Him favourable, it will not happen. The bridegroom of the Church summons you through my mouth; the shepherd of all, Peter, prince of the apostles, summons you, earnestly asking that, if you wish to have them as patrons and helpers of your principality, you should be willing to appoint a shepherd according to the Lord in the Church of Exeter and should strive to rescue it from so great a shipwreck. It was the first of all churches in your realm for which you provided. Let Your Highness, if it please you, consider [Col. 0050B] what has followed from this.

You know whom He excluded from the Church—the One who also cast out the sellers of doves—and far be it that anyone should enter whom Christ has excluded. I make myself Peter’s surety, because the honour you show him will repay you even in this present life with a hundredfold reward. Moreover, if you make a longer delay, I ask that my archdeacon be sent back to me, if this can be done without harm to you.

## LETTER LXV. TO THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

> [Note: [Col. 0049] MS. V: “The same [letter] to all the clergy established throughout England and Scotland.”]

To the venerable brethren the bishops, and to all Christ’s faithful established throughout England, greetings.

As you have heard, the ancient enemy assailed the integrity [Col. 0050C] of the Church and, relying upon all the powers of his deceit and wickedness, sought to tear apart its indissoluble unity. But unfailing mercy is abroad: as it foresees rising storms for the testing of the faithful, so it tempers those same storms when they arise and gain strength, by a saving dispensation for the benefit of the elect, so that those instructed through punishment may, having been proved through repentance, be crowned. Therefore He who allowed His Church to be disturbed by the wickedness of those dwelling in it now begins, its rotten members having been cut away and hope of peace already approaching, to restore its calm. At the head of the Church, in Peter’s seat, He has set an apostolic man, canonically elected and consecrated, approved by all who think rightly and in a Catholic manner.

This is Lord Alexander, whom, with the assent of our princes, the English and French Churches have received as father and shepherd. In full devotion obedient to the holy Roman Church, he condemned Octavian, together with all his supporters, as a manifest schismatic and heretic. Therefore we command and exhort your whole body in the Lord that you obey Lord Alexander as a father and show him in every respect the reverence due to the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0050D]

## LETTER LXVI. TO KING HENRY

From the letters which Your Serenity sent me, it is clear that your prudence has been circumvented by the suggestion of malicious men against my innocence. For those whom you assert to be your parishioners were often summoned by the lord archbishop, through the deans and his other officials; and, when they were always found obstinate in their contumacy, they were finally notified, under threat of anathema, to appear at the synod. They being absent—or rather, obstinately making themselves absent—the officials of the archdeacon through whom they had very often been summoned were present. Since through them the summonses and the contumacious reply of the absentees had been established, I thought the matter ought to be referred for the lord archbishop’s consultation, although the synod advised otherwise. For nearly the whole synod opposed me, and some spoke disparagingly, saying that I was neglecting the justice of the Church of Canterbury and of the lord archbishop in favour of you, who, taking advantage of the time of his illness, had decided unexpectedly to rise against him, enter the boundaries of the Church of Canterbury, and mutilate it of what it had possessed for one hundred years. [Col. 0051B]

All were astonished at the impunity of such persistent audacity. Moreover, five or seven intervening parishes, as they say, of eyewitness certainty demonstrate that the estate in question does not in any way belong to the Church of Chichester. Clerics were also present who complained that violence and cruel injuries had been inflicted upon them; and it was known to all the neighbouring people that our priests administer all divine offices to those same parishioners throughout the year. These matters and very much more were brought before the lord archbishop—and, so far as my part was concerned, against my will—and the outcry from every side became so great that even I incurred some suspicion through delay. I therefore ordered that your contumacious parishioners be subjected to anathema, as the dean and synod advised. On the following day, in the hearing of the others, I notified that dean of this order as it had been imposed. And this is that judgment of mine which Your Discretion has discovered and censured as proceeding from ignorance of the law. [Col. 0051C]

I confess that I am unskilled in speech and learning, and that I am now capable of perceiving whatever you may wish to attack. For who is suited to that? But I do not know whether this proceeded from your prudence: that men who have always been subject to our jurisdiction, conceiving a greater spirit of wisdom, have disdained to appear when summoned by him to whom they were subject, if not by episcopal right, at least by metropolitan right—even if only in order to avail themselves of a plea of forum. I know that this proceeded from profound counsel. Yet I do not allege these things in my own excuse, if you pronounce me guilty, because I would rather seek pardon from you than employ legal arguments and plead the Lord’s command and the necessity of obedience. The remaining matters will be answered separately; but I advise you to see my lord before the council.

## LETTER LXVII. TO …

[Col. 0052A] From your testimony we have learned that the bearer of this letter, having been deserted by the cleric to whom she was joined in marriage, married another man and bore children by him. The cleric, however, while away abroad, was promoted to the priesthood; and on his return, disregarding the wife whom he had married, began to minister in the priestly order. Since it is established both by their own confession and by the lawful testimony of witnesses that she contracted marriage with the cleric, it is plain that she cannot thereafter remain attached to her second husband.

The cleric’s assertion that, when the marriage was contracted, he was a subdeacon—since this cannot be proved—has this consequence: he is to be considered unworthy of the order which he despised and is not to be permitted to minister in that order which, being married, he presumptuously assumed by unlawful usurpation. For it is clear both from many authorities and from the Second Council of Toledo [Col. 0052B] that those who enter the subdiaconate must profess continence. Likewise, it is evident from the Council of Arles that a married man ought not to be admitted to the priesthood unless conversion has first preceded; hence, unless the wife had chosen the continence which he wishes to vow, she would undoubtedly have had to be restored to her former husband, while he, deprived of the exercise of priesthood, would have granted his wife authority over his body according to the holy Apostle.

For blessed Eugenius decided the same in a similar case: a man who had entered the presbyterate after leaving his wife was to be removed from the altar and return to marital duty, until his wife should wish to profess continence. But now, because the cleric vowed continence at ordination, and because the wife accepts and approves her husband’s vow for love of [Col. 0052C] chastity and hope of fruitful penitence, necessity of continence lies upon each of them, and the priest is for the present forbidden to minister. For one who has entered the presbyterate cannot disregard the vow of continence, since, by Pope Martin’s decree, it is taught that this vow is either express or implicit even in the ordination of deacons.

For he says: “If a deacon who is elected has declared that he intends to take a wife and has said that he cannot remain chaste, he is not to be ordained. But if he has kept silent at ordination and has been ordained, and afterward desires marriage, he is to be excluded from ministry and removed from the clergy.”

Leo also agrees with this—Leo, the heavenly trumpet—who forbids carnal marriage to subdeacons and enjoins upon all sacred orders the purest cleanness of chastity. Therefore these two shall be husband and wife forever, even while separated; and, though placed in marriage, they shall remain as though not having marriage, and, restrained by the vow of continence to which they are bound, shall remain perpetually unmarried. If they should perhaps return to the practice of sexual intercourse, they will incur the guilt of a broken vow if with one another, and of adultery if with others.

Nor is the priest’s presumption assisted by the fact that you received from him an oath, merely as an additional precaution, to establish that he had been a subdeacon when the marriage was contracted. He alone asserted this, and afterward, in the presence of the lord bishop of Chichester, as you write, confessed that he had sworn falsely. Thus no credence is to be given either to his assertion or his denial, except that [Col. 0053A] his own confession is sufficient to condemn him against himself. If he was a subdeacon, he must be punished as one who despised his order; if he was not, he must equally be punished as a violator of marital fidelity—indeed, all the more because he appears to have furnished the occasion for the second marriage, if it is proper to call it a marriage.

For, as blessed Augustine says in his book *On Adulterous Marriages*: “If you abstain without your wife’s consent, you grant her licence to fornicate, and her sin will be imputed to your abstinence.” What then, if you abandon her? What if you travel abroad for ten years or more? What if, on returning, you pretend, without your wife’s knowledge, to lead a celibate life, or pass into another’s embraces? Accordingly, almost the entire fault seems to lie with the priest; the woman too was equally inconstant, except insofar as she consented to a second union after learning that her first husband was alive [Col. 0053B]; the second husband’s fault is either none at all or certainly very slight, unless he too perhaps knew of the earlier marriage.

Since, therefore, the apparent second marriage was not a marriage, the latter husband, if he cannot or will not remain continent—which perhaps would be more expedient because of the children—may marry whomsoever he wishes, provided only that it be in the Lord. But the priest, who gave occasion for the separation, is bound to restore the dowry to his wife, especially since, in your presence, by a word of truth—which prevails over every stipulation—he promised before a priest that he would repay her valuation of it. If anything sounder or more useful shall have been revealed by the Lord to your charity, carry it out in accordance with your office. For we have set down this counsel without prejudice [Col. 0053C] to a sounder judgment.

To the bishop of Lincoln:

The priest who is known to have contracted marriage with the bearer of this letter, because he gave occasion for adultery and, having abandoned his wife, usurped the priesthood, must be excluded from the ministry which he presumptuously assumed, since his wife has chosen continence. It is unlawful for a priest to return to the marriage which he despised. For the vow of continence is attached to sacred orders, either expressly or implicitly. Nor does it help the priest that he alone swore that he had been a subdeacon at the time of the marriage, in the presence and at the request of the lord bishop of Worcester, since, when questioned by the bishop of Chichester, he confessed that he had sworn falsely.

Certainly, if as a subdeacon he contracted marriage, he is unworthy because he despised his order and rashly assumed the priesthood; if he was an acolyte, he is likewise unworthy because he despised [Col. 0053D] the priesthood and presumptuously assumed it. Moreover, he who caused the separation is bound to restore the dowry to his wife, especially since he bound himself by oath in the presence of the bishop of Worcester. We therefore command you to compel him to restore what he promised as the valuation of the dowry in the presence of the lord bishop of Worcester, or more, as justice shall require, if his resources suffice for this.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO . . .

Zeal for charity is kindled in prelates whenever they discover in the conduct of their subjects something from which harm to their salvation may threaten them. From the tenor of your letter, however, we trust that you desire the beauty of the house of the Lord and will devote care to that work [Col. 0054A]: that those who bear the vessels of the Lord may be clean under your guardianship, and that those who, through the office laid upon them, ought to consecrate those subject to them to God may themselves be consecrated to the Lord by purity of conduct and innocence of life.

Moreover, your wish to ask our counsel in matters not doubtful is a mark of humility, not evidence of ignorance. For your discernment does not fail to know what the sacred canons decree concerning clerical continence. Pope Siricius, for example, does not allow women of any other sort to reside in clerics’ houses, except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely because of close kinship. From the decrees of Symmachus, the Council of Carthage, and various enactments of Roman pontiffs, it is easy to infer that only those women are to be admitted [Col. 0054B] from whom nature, reverence for character, or an honourable cause—such as compassion in the case of those afflicted or physically infirm—removes every stain of sinister suspicion. And although very many canons have held that a mother, sister, grandmother, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, nieces, household members, and persons connected by first-degree affinity are not to be suspected because of cohabitation, blessed Augustine nevertheless did not permit a cleric to live even with his sister, because women who are not sisters sometimes live with sisters; as the pagan poet says:

> “Fault may be concealed beneath the name of kinship.”

[Col. 0054C] From these principles your discernment will more easily determine how you ought to deal with Renier, whom, as you wrote, was living with a woman who had once been his prostitute, under the guise of paternal service, than we can, since the persons themselves and their reputation are unknown to us. For cohabitation does not necessarily entail fornication: by God’s mercy they may no longer be what they once were, and may erase former errors by subsequent penitence. But if the persons are suspect, they may be compelled to make canonical purgation; and then punishment or absolution will follow when their innocence or guilt has appeared in judgment.

As for the oath which, according to the custom of the Church of Lincoln, is taken by those being ordained, and which you mentioned: we neither condemn what was introduced by fathers who preceded us in that church and were better than we, [Col. 0054D] nor indeed approve it, since it is clear that from it has especially arisen a source of danger and an easy occasion for graver sin. This is not because it is sinful to vow lofty things, but because human weakness “always strives after what is forbidden” (*Ovid, Amores* III.4.17), and embraces what is not allowed even when it burns most bitterly. Thus, when the law was given, sin also entered; and sin became, as the Apostle says, sinful beyond measure, when transgression was added to the prohibition of the given law. Let the authors and supporters of the oath consider what they have done. Would that transgression might cease and chastity be preserved, so that sin may not gain strength through the agreement of offenders and their superiors, nor increase through negligence or malice.

Concerning that priest who, in abusing a prostitute, squanders the Church’s goods, neglects the care of the sanctuary, and has unworthily and dangerously handled the price of our redemption with an unsuitable and improper chalice: [Col. 0055A] we command you to rebuke him with canonical severity, so that in the punishment of one man the errors of many may be corrected. Let it therefore be your most attentive concern to ensure that in all churches entrusted to you, according to their means, not only silver chalices are provided, but vestments and every implement of sacred ministry are repaired so that the Lord may now be served honourably. In this matter spare neither monks nor canons nor any person whatever, but see that the firstfruits of honour are rendered to the Lord from His own goods; and plainly, each person will honour the church committed to him according as he loves the Lord and his own soul.

If, however, the priest of Lincoln is found guilty in judgment of the charge brought against him—namely, that the woman who bore his child died without sharing in confession or communion, and that afterward, in order that she might receive Christian burial, he caused her to be purified in the church—then, in accordance with the statutes of the Fathers, he is to be deprived of the exercise of his order until fitting penitence has shown, so far as human judgment can ascertain, that he has deserved pardon. [Col. 0055B] His chaplain also is to be subject to the same punishment unless he can adequately establish his innocence. Indeed, if purification must be made, this man seems to deserve the heavier burden, since he has proved less worthy of trust in resisting what appeared to be his own confession.

[Col. 0055C] It belongs to Him alone who can raise the dead both to loose and to bind the dead; and He who conferred the exercise of this power upon His disciples on earth reserved in heaven, by the special privilege of divine majesty, this dignity to Himself. But, beloved son in the Lord, conduct yourself in such cases with such painstaking caution that you may not seem to thirst after offenders’ money, but, as befits a shepherd, to seek the salvation of souls. For you know that even secular laws punish most severely, under the Julian law concerning extortion, those who seek sordid gain by doing or failing to do acts required by their office. The canons likewise impose upon all prelates the peril of their order and office if, for a price received or promised, they restore an office forbidden to those subject to them. Therefore, that God may be glorified in your diligence and your ministry honoured, [Col. 0055D] shake your hands free from filth and calumnies, lest the office of judge entrusted to you by the Lord appear to be a kind of trade.

## LETTER LXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF CHESTER

To the lord bishop of Chester.

Those things which more ruinously injure and defile the Church with fouler stains we are bound by our pastoral office to pursue more vigorously and drive more forcibly from God’s house. For our consent to the faults of our subjects also involves us and convicts us before the Lord, unless, when we are able, we endeavour to correct their offences.

We remember that through Alan of Wilnai you sent our letters to the archdeacons, deans, and officials of the Church of Coventry, for [Col. 0056A] uprooting the pestilential root of simoniacal depravity which is said newly to be sprouting in the bishopric of Chichester. For vicars, in order to be admitted to churches, are individually compelled to pay twelve pence, and, having in a sense bought the licence to sanctify the Lord, pay an annual rent to ministers of Satan rather than of the Church. We forbade this practice henceforth under anathema, delivering to Satan their prince those who should further practise this simoniacal wickedness. We commanded the archdeacons and their officials to be content with the ancient customs.

Yet, as the repeated lamentable complaint of the clerics of Derbyshire shows, the said Alan long fraudulently suppressed our command, until he and his accomplices had been able to satisfy their perversity in disposing of [Col. 0056B] the poor’s goods. As though our prohibition had encouraged them toward what was forbidden, at the approaching solemnity of Easter they compelled priests, who could not for sacramental necessity lack holy chrism, to buy it. Every faithful member of the Church knows how contrary this is to the sacred canons; nor could they themselves be ignorant, since it is established that Walter, your bishop of holy memory, condemned among you this sale of chrism and forbade, under anathema, that it should thereafter be sold for a price.

Accordingly, certain persons who came to us reported that they had suffered many grievances from John of Lexovia and his accomplices. Others also complain that, because they appealed to us, he attempted to suspend them from their office. Therefore we command your discernment, by this injunction, to investigate the truth of the matter with the most exact diligence; and, if it is established that Alan fraudulently suppressed our letters, suspend him by our authority from office until he has made fitting satisfaction to you and to the Church of Canterbury. Compel John of Lexovia also, and the officials of the archdeacon of Derby, by your authority, to restore to the clerics what they extorted from them through the corrupt custom mentioned above or through the accursed sale of holy chrism, after we condemned this wickedness. [Col. 0056C]

But if they neglect to obey you in this, suspend them by your authority from entry into church until they restore what they took from the clerics and make satisfaction to us. If they have presumed to suspend anyone after an appeal was made to us, release those persons, and declare that the suspenders themselves have been suspended by us from the thresholds of the church so long as they persist in imposing upon others the sentence of suspension inflicted upon themselves. If they should despise this our authority, we command you to go with our letters to our venerable brother, the bishop of Hereford, and procure the public excommunication of these contemners of the holy Church of Canterbury.

## LETTER LXX. TO THE KING

To the king of the English.

Hearing on every side of the clash of kingdoms, the emergence of new configurations of affairs, and the increasing evils arising from [Col. 0057A] our iniquity, we have conceived a particular anxiety for your welfare, upon which the welfare of so many peoples depends. This anxiety, added to the scourge of the Lord by which, through His grace, we are scourged in body, afflicts our mind day and night. We are therefore compelled to inquire after your condition through a messenger, though, if possible, we should prefer to behold it in person.

We remember having entreated you to permit our archdeacon, who is our only one and first in our counsel, to return to us, since the malice of the time denies us the benefit of your presence. He ought to have come without being summoned, and he would have been chargeable with disobedience before God and men unless your need excused him. But because we have always preferred your will to our own and have resolved to promote it as far as may be permitted, we pardon for your sake the fault which he has committed. [Col. 0057B] We direct him to continue in your service as long as necessity requires, applying all his loyalty and skill to your need; provided, however, that as soon as you can dispense with him, you permit him, if it please you, to return.

For I myself, though the Lord’s mercy has confined me to bed, would most willingly carry your affairs upon my shoulders even at the cost of my temporal life, if peace might be restored to the lands and peoples whom the Lord has entrusted to your rule. I hope, however, that the more willingly I comply, and always have complied, with your will, the more graciously, if it please you, you will yield to my necessity and more readily hear my petitions concerning the return of the chancellor and the advancement of the business of the Church of Exeter [Col. 0057C]. Know certainly that we would by no means ask this unless we believed it pleasing to the Lord and useful and honourable to you. Hear, if you please, what we so earnestly request in this matter; perhaps we shall ask nothing further.

## LETTER LXXI. TO R., ARCHDEACON

To the archdeacon.

You have already often been recalled, though you ought to have returned at the summons of one father, old and infirm. Indeed, you should fear that the Lord will punish your delay if you become deaf to obedience, forgetful of benefits, and contemptuous of the father whom, when infirm, you ought to have carried on your shoulders. You were wholly inexcusable [Col. 0057D] and close to our curse, unless the lord king excused your absence on the pretext of his own necessity.

But because we prefer the public benefit at stake in the lord king’s affairs to private advantage, and have always preferred his will, insofar as it was possible and expedient, to ours, we still endure the prejudice caused by disobedience to our command, but on this condition: that, as soon as you can obtain his permission, you do not delay in returning to us. We grant this for the present both to your need and to his will, fearing the danger to you should you return having offended him. For we fear that, if you incur for us the danger of losing his favour, you may not be able to recover it through us. Our days are short, and it is not sufficiently known what favour we ourselves, or our people, shall thereafter enjoy on our own behalf. [Col. 0058A] For the favour of the dead commonly languishes, and with them the memory of their merits lightly fades away.

Yet we hope—and may our hope disappoint no one!—that charity may grow strong in the hearts of our friends through the Holy Spirit. But take every precaution lest you do anything to frustrate this indulgence, being certain that the justice of the Lord is deceived by no human error. Moreover, we have resolved to test your affection and diligence in advancing our petitions before the lord king concerning the business of the Church of Exeter. We earnestly ask you to pursue these matters so that we may have in them consolation both for your absence and for that of the lord king, and the surest proof of the mutual affection and service promised between us. [Col. 0058B]

We are at such a point that our counsel ought not to be suspect; nor would we dare, especially in ecclesiastical matters, to request anything which we did not believe would please the Lord, benefit the Church and the kingdom, and be expedient in every respect. Certainly, if we were asking a great thing, we trust we would be heard. Write back concerning the king’s will and your own counsel about the monk who styles himself abbot of Boxel.

## LETTER LXXII. TO THE ABBESS OF AMESBURY

Whenever ecclesiastical persons, in contempt of every right, assail ecclesiastical enactments, they deserve punishment all the more severely because they seem in some measure to approach the crime of sacrilege and the sin of apostasy. [Col. 0058C] For the severity of the law is rightly exercised against those who, under the habit of religion and a certain impious veil of piety, attempt with impunity to overthrow justice.

We have often heard that this is your purpose; and, if what is said is true, your impiety is now openly breaking forth. In order to exercise your boldness in injuring the innocent, you rejoice alike over the Roman schism and over our weakness. But the Lord has power to restore serenity to His Church, to relieve [Col. 0059A] our labour according to His good pleasure, and to requite you according to your deserts. We had deferred the penalty of suspension for a time; but, as is said, you cannot longer endure to have the penalty of suspension itself suspended. You strive to overthrow the statutes of the apostolic see, and you provoke the axe which hastens [Col. 0058D] to cut down the root of your foundation.

For it is established that our beloved son Jordan, treasurer of the Church of Salisbury, was confirmed by Pope Adrian in possession of the church of Froila. Yet, as his complaint states, you have presumed, in injury to the apostolic see and to us, violently and with armed force—conduct unbecoming a woman, a nun, or any religious person—to dispossess him. Since we cannot fail him in justice, we command you, by this injunction, either to restore to him without delay the aforesaid church together with everything taken from it, or to appear before us on the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary to answer the allegations. Though by law we could punish your disobedience, we prefer patiently to wait for you quickly to correct your errors and so deserve to escape the impending scourge. Jordan is fortified by apostolic privilege, by your letters, and by sufficient witnesses, as you know and ought to remember: how faithfully and usefully he and his people have often laboured.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO . . .

Fortune begrudges me the successes I desire, and most often impiously resists my devout affection. Long ago the treasure of my heart was placed in your parts; and with you is the abundance of faithful friends which I consider the most precious thing in the world. But if I have been deceived, the error of this shaken yet trusting opinion is still exceedingly welcome. [Col. 0059B] For one’s judgment concerning friends’ character ought always to be holy and reverent; it is the mark of a perverse disposition readily to judge them wrongly. I may rightly also call it an abundance, since, being a friend to many, I trust that I am in turn loved by many.

I trust, I say, not wavering from certain hope, and I know that this hope does not disappoint, because charity does not know the end of disappointment. Even if it sometimes errs through simplicity of conscience, it avoids every disappointment through the merit of assisting grace and perfect virtue. What, then, is sweeter than often to visit such a treasure, whence the soul is gladdened and makes others sharers in its gladness? “Where love is,” it is said, “there is the eye; and where your treasure is, there is your heart.” [Col. 0059C] What, then, is more bitter than to be withheld from the sight of that which either releases the heart or above all else the heart desires, and toward which the eye’s ray is always directed?

This has long been my bitterness—and a most bitter bitterness—that I have not been allowed to see any of my friends among you. Therefore, as my conscience bears witness, to remedy this distress I recently allowed myself to be impelled to descend to a friendly people, though for an unwelcome cause. I came indeed to you, but there my pain was made heavier, increased, and inflamed. For when I had seen your desired face only by night, briefly, and scarcely at all, it was taken from me again all too swiftly by my customary misfortune; so that, as I was departing and desired it all the more, I was not permitted even to see it in the morning to offer a greeting. I sought long, waited long, begged, and [Col. 0059D] importuned many, but there was no one to help. At that time fortune had this power over me. Yet though it is rash to love and greet one who is absent, she neither will nor indeed can prevent it. Farewell; and know that your presence cannot be withdrawn from my mind.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO THE ABBESS OF AMESBURY

Royal authority moves us to vindicate the injury done to the holy Roman Church, and—to say nothing of our own injury—the contempt shown to royal majesty. To prevent our being compelled to do this, we admonished you with paternal gentleness to restore possession of the church of Froila to our beloved son Jordan, treasurer, which is known to have been confirmed to him by the Roman Church while blessed Adrian presided. [Col. 0060A] Yet after the lord king’s edict, in contempt of the Roman Church, you violently and without judicial procedure expelled him, as his repeated complaint declares.

But because you still persist in your contumacy, we command you by this injunction that, in accordance with the queen’s command which you received, you permit the said Jordan to hold the aforesaid church, as he possessed it by apostolic authority during the king’s passage. Otherwise, when you appear before us on the octave of Blessed Mary, we shall not be able to leave unpunished your contempt of the holy Roman Church. And if the lady queen corrects with fitting punishment the offence you committed against the king’s edict, we shall hold it valid; for by the authority of the canons, when rights are thus held in contempt, military force must be used to restrain wickedness. We also forbid, by the authority of the Roman Church and our own, that you presume to alienate the tithes and goods of the church before judicial examination.

## LETTER LXXV. TO THE ABBOT OF LA CELLE

To the abbot of La Celle.

How much effort I have devoted to promoting the business for which you sent to England is known to truth and ought not to be unknown to your discernment. Although I never expected success, because I knew the character of the man who always fights against the Church, depresses rather than [Col. 0060C] exalts venerable places, and, insofar as he is allowed, devotes himself more to destruction than to building up, I nevertheless first pressed him while absent through messenger and letters; then when present before the lord of Canterbury; and finally, when I went down to his district for other reasons, I summoned his friends and household and pressed him sufficiently. I asked that, if he could not be induced to give what he was said to have promised, he should compensate the loss suffered by your church and your humiliation by granting some benefit of consolation.

But what I had foreseen from the beginning became more and more evident the more he was pressed. Having dismissed the count, I pursued the man who had deceived you, and succeeded in obtaining an order that the archbishop of Canterbury bind him with the bond of anathema and [Col. 0060D], through letters sent to the bishops, command his arrest. He has therefore become a fugitive from the face of the Lord, so that he may nowhere be found by His faithful. Perhaps he now lurks about cells and monasteries, presenting himself now as a Cluniac monk, now as a monk of Rheims, or as a monk of whatever profession he pleases. As we have learned from those who saw him, he has already discarded his infamous name and, calling himself “the son of Barathrum, to be erased altogether from the book of the righteous and from every congregation of the faithful,” disowns the name Radulfus Baratri. I also suppose that he who formerly cast off the monk has now thrown away his monastic habit, in which he fears being recognized. Yet, by the Lord’s help, I hope that, although this may take time, he will be caught in the works of his own hands.

The brother who had come with him ought not to be blamed for the outcome of the business, for [Col. 0061A] he omitted nothing within the circumstances but pressed matters diligently enough until, having received the count’s answer in person, he learned that he had laboured in vain. He received this answer at the feast of Saint Remigius. Thereafter, as I remember having written to you, he delayed a little in order to visit friends whom he had not yet seen, and finally returned. If he needs another’s patronage, and if mine has any weight, I ask that you receive him with paternal affection and treat him with the gentleness which you know his character requires. You know better than I whether it is lawful or expedient to ask more. I know well that one who knows you more intimately either does not dare to ask an improper thing, or asks it shamelessly. Therefore I venture more confidently to write this to you than Cicero once wrote to his intimate friend Porcius Cato. [Col. 0061B]

I send you a small gift, all the more confidently because from long experience I have learned that in such matters you consider not so much the value of the gift as the affection of the giver. Yet it is a gift worthy of acceptance, if the significance of the gift is considered together with the giver’s affection. This vessel is certainly a silver salt-cellar bearing gold devices. It is fitting, because you possess an abundance of that salt which, by the precept of the law, is the seasoning of all sacrifices. You also offer to the Lord the tested silver of chaste speech; and golden images of virtues shine for those who behold them in the mirror of word and deed, inviting them, by imitation of those virtues, to become a mirror for others. The very roundness of its shape also suits your perfection.

[Col. 0061C] You know that the signs of sacred things are venerable even in humbler material. But I think that, even if the gift became cheap through its own valuation, its grace nevertheless gains strength because it signifies my charity and your holiness together with wisdom. Since Brother Thomas was alone, I gave him an attendant knight; when he arrives among you, you may retain or send him back as seems best—mounted or on foot, late or soon. I gave the horse to Lord Thomas, but on the condition that he might not sell it in England. Once he has left us, however, he may use or misuse it at his own pleasure as his own—indeed, truly his own. I imposed this condition upon the gift only in order to provide for the recipient’s honour and the traveller’s need.

[Col. 0061D] As to necessary expenses—and perhaps not all voluntary ones—I supplied them willingly. Nor is he under any obligation to his attendant, unless perhaps, by the practice of religion, he is bound to charity and familiarity under the law of common life and fellowship. I am bound to him by agreement, and, with the Lord’s aid, shall satisfy the obligation. Thus his delay or return depends on your judgment; write back through him what you decide.

Furthermore, because Master Hugh’s exposition cannot be found among us, please send it, if you will. I recall that it is with you. Also send me through the same man Boethius’s *On the Trinity*, which is with you, and the books which I deposited with my lord Simon, prior of Provins, since my brother needs them.

## LETTER LXXVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0062A]

To the same abbot of La Celle.

I think that the sincerity of my devotion to you has long been known, so that you ought not to believe every spirit concerning it. I say this lest, if Brother Thomas has presumed to instil anything untoward in your ears, you give him credence; for there is a matter between him and me, concerning which I do not fear to submit to your judgment, or that of any discerning person. That you may examine it more readily, I shall disclose the matter briefly. Very few days having passed after he arrived among us, it became manifest to all that his labour had been lost, and your effort and expense as well. Then he stayed with us and in our vicinity for several days, and [Col. 0062B] began for a while to comport himself more lightly than was fitting, though only in speech and gesture (for nothing criminal can be alleged against him). Many wise and foolish people gather about us, so that nowhere can error or prudence more easily be detected. Thus, as the man’s sobriety and self-restraint pleased us, so the frivolity of his speech and gesture, and the instability of his counsels, displeased us. For he was easily and excessively stirred, although at times he also readily laid aside his anger; and because association with courtiers and the tumult of the populace never, or rarely, advances simpler minds toward religion, I deliberately wished him, while he stayed with us, to spend time about monasteries and houses of canons with which I was familiar.

Meanwhile, I advised him to visit those kinsmen [Col. 0062C] whom he wished to see, but on the condition that he should by no means give them hope of his return. For I have learned in many affairs that, though it is dangerous for a monk to move alone amid a secular crowd, among our people it is most dangerous. Therefore I sent to you the boy through whom I thanked you for the bread, also asking for drink—for, as you know, I am no more an eater than a drinker—that he might bring back your counsel concerning his delay or return. While he delayed, and I saw that this was advantageous, I admonished Brother Thomas to return. It was indeed unwelcome to him; yet I did not desist, but pressed all the more because I saw many people anxious that he should be retained—people who had seen him only briefly and, as happens, while passing through. Some of them also pressed me on the matter. I was therefore the more moved [Col. 0062D] and took greater pains that he should return. Deliberately I withheld expenses, rejected his plans, and, as it were, spurred him on to return.

This was most unwelcome to him because he had determined and arranged to spend the festivities of his birthday among relatives, friends, and acquaintances, in common places wholly devoid of reverence. I preferred to expose myself to his indignation rather than assent to a dangerous plan. For the brother is gentle and, I believe, well-intentioned, but still too simple to be safely entrusted to his own direction amid popular crowds. Apart from levity, I find either nothing or very little to blame in him—except that there is hardly anyone, or no one at all, in whom he does not find something to criticize; and I think this arises from the fuel of his innate levity. I saw [Col. 0063A] that one of two dangers threatened me: either I should risk losing his favour, or I should deserve to lose yours. I acknowledge my fault: I deliberated, indeed, for more than a month; but at last, gathering courage, I steadfastly set myself against his indignation, lest I endanger the loyalty which I owe you. Thus I compelled him to return, and this too is my fault. At length he reluctantly yielded to my counsel; but I am grateful that he yielded at last, even unwillingly. Hence the causes of ill-will; hence the seedbed of detraction; hence the blackening of all my dutiful service.

You have at times sent us Brother Thomas of Norwich, Brother William, and some others. All complied in this matter, nor did any of them regret complying with my counsel. This man alone for some time preferred his own judgment to mine [Col. 0063B], but at last he yielded. Judge whether I have done wrong. And because the brother is simple and, I believe, in no way malicious, I ask that you hold him dear and employ him, for he is useful: just as he ought by no means to be left to himself in public places, so he is necessary in your service. Perhaps he will bear a different testimony about himself; but nothing compels me to lie. You too used to believe me. Nor have I yet forfeited that confidence: the faithful witness of my conscience and my word is in heaven, He who punishes every lie and rewards with a friend’s recompense the truth dear to Him.

The bearer of this letter has been accustomed to love me less since I compelled him to return, suspecting that he had influenced me—so much so that I scarcely compelled him to cross the sea. But your love compelled me to this [Col. 0063C], for I owe it whatever I am and can do—indeed, whatever I shall be and can do, and whatever further I may yet be able to do. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO …

I congratulate Your Grace, which, while seeking, as is believed, the advancement of my friends, has won my service. Yet, just as I cannot but approve the affection of your charity, so I cannot but disapprove the counsel of your simplicity. For the office into which you wish to thrust that friend of yours is suited neither to his purpose nor to his age, and certainly not to his welfare. The circumstances both of time and place, together with many other considerations, oppose your desire. No one can [Col. 0063D] serve two masters; hence it is clear that one cannot both usefully watch over the advancement of the brethren and serve the attendants of the court for favour.

Does not this man invoke royal authority at every point in defence of wrongdoing—if I may not say crimes? Thus the king’s authority obstructs one who acts well and protects ecclesiastical liberty among you; but the authority of the Lord’s law everywhere cries out against one who acts ill. Who can suitably make an old man, stationed in the corner of a consular office, travel about the province and swiftly address, at a moment’s notice, the articles of newly arising difficulty? It has always been foreign to the man’s purpose to investigate others’ lives for gain, to lie in wait for neighbours’ actions, to make friends and acquaintances—known and unknown alike—into defendants, and to despoil them so as to please another or profit himself. But henceforth, with the Lord’s aid, it shall be utterly foreign to him.

I write this not to injure anyone. Rather, I portray Satan’s instrument, which we sometimes see lurking beneath the cloak of this office—lurking, I say; or rather, raging and rioting. For the name is honourable and useful, and was accordingly instituted by the holy Fathers; but beneath the covering of piety and proper office rages shameless action, blind ambition, impious cruelty, conspicuous greed, and filthy, impudent gain. What is more filthy, shameless, or wicked than an old priest turned informer? Will he make so great a sacrifice of reputation and conscience in order to please the court’s attendants? Or how will he serve if he displeases them? In short, he will have either them or you as enemies, though neither is advantageous to him or his people. Spare your friend, then [Col. 0064B], and do not procure for him the enmity of many—and, what we chiefly fear, of the Lord.

Know moreover that the lord archbishop wholly rejects your petition and will not permit any friend to become such a dean—that is, an informer against his fellow-citizens.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO THE CHANCELLOR OF ENGLAND

In accordance with the command of your affection, I had drafted my lord’s letters to the lord king and to you under such authority as would notify you of the urgent necessity of returning, unless you preferred to incur the crime of disobedience and, together with the penalty of anathema, suffer the loss of the possessions which you hold from the Church of Canterbury. But in response to unexpected royal requests, presented to my lord through Hugh of Doura, accompanied by blandishments and promises, I was compelled—under the pressing command of my lord—to moderate this severity and make some allowance for public necessity.

For if what those returning say is true—and would that it is true—the king and the entire court depend so greatly upon your counsel that no hope of peace is at hand unless your prudence foreshadows it. Hence my lord at times began to wonder why the lord king and you had sometimes made and written contrary requests concerning the hastening or postponement of your return, when common report has it that you are one heart and one soul, or that the compelling impulse of friendly intimacy makes it necessary for you to will and not will the same things [Col. 0064D]. He also at times asked whether there might be collusion in this affair. And I seem to foresee what truth contains and, in a fashion, to behold as present the condition of one absent and labouring.

When therefore I was compelled to condemn the letters already drafted, I began to waver whether it were preferable to hold the messenger back rather than send him. But because, having already obtained the leave which we had contrived beforehand, he was about to depart, I finally resolved to test your disposition, and I took care to send to you and to the king letters as urgent as I could make them, though they grant something to the royal will. Our lord presents through you and through his own letters requests to the royal majesty, and trusts that he will be heard if you take pains to advance them. I do not remember that he has ever asked anything more earnestly [Col. 0065A].
