They are honourable requests, such as it is just to grant; and their rejection will bring him not merely shame, but above all a loss of confidence in the favour which he has always striven to deserve.

His request is that he obtain the king’s assent and authority for the promotion in the Church of Exeter of Master B[artholomew], archdeacon of Exeter, an honourable and learned man for whom he dares to stand surety. He often says to his intimates—though only to those with whom it is permissible to share the matter—that he does not possess much favour with the lord king if he suffers rejection in the case of an honourable and learned man, when he formerly heard that Robert, son of Harding, an unlearned and useless man, was to be promoted, unless that assent had been impeded by the canons of Exeter and others who fear the Lord [Col. 0065B]. For the lord king wrote on this matter, and certain persons even dared to solicit the archbishop himself while he lay sick in bed. Therefore he asks that there be granted to him what can canonically be done, whereas something contrary to the canons was long ago allowed to a wealthy man.

It is reported among us that the lord king granted you the revenues of three vacant bishoprics to secure your release, but he nonetheless trusts in your support in this matter. There is much that you may allege in this regard, and I do not doubt your goodwill, if you choose to exert yourself for him. Your effectiveness is known, and what you have done at Lincoln, York, and in many other places is concealed from none of us. Leave the soul of your father joyful through the granting of his petition, and have his prayers heard—he who, as he himself writes to the lord king in his letter, will ask nothing further. He has put his words in the messenger’s mouth and instructed him to speak and do in all matters whatever you direct him.

Know, however, that if you postpone the result of the petition until the arrival of the lord king, he will take the very delay to mean that it is sought for his death. Enough on these matters, especially for a wise man. For the rest: for myself and Master William of Slidis, your clerk, two writs of the lord king concerning the administration of justice are needed, in accordance with the form of the petitions which I send you. Farewell, and have copied whatever seems fit. But know this: it is necessary for you by every means to return before our lord’s departure, even if you must cross the sea immediately [Col. 0065D]. Farewell again and always. The Lord knows that the man for whom the lord archbishop is interceding is wholly ignorant of this entire matter.

## LETTER LXXIX. Form for an Election

From the report of the noble Richard, Count of Devon, and Alan de Furnellis, who assert that they were present at the arrangements made by your late prior R., of holy memory, while he was at the point of death, we have recently learned that the aforesaid friend of God, when you asked him which brother he would wish to succeed him if he should depart this life, named Brother Richard expressly, urging—and, with the pious modesty that characterized him, commanding under the guise of advice—that you should all obey his will [Col. 0066A].

The command of the holy Father ought indeed to have been observed, especially one dictated by a man filled with God’s Spirit when he was passing from the prison-house of the flesh to Christ. But now, as we have sorrowfully learned anew from those who come among us, after the holy man’s death Satan has sought you, so that through Peter of Taunton and his brother William he might sift you in the sieve of levity and, casting down the walls around you, divide and scatter the unity which the holy Father had founded among you. Clearly, whoever contrives this, so far as lies in them, drives Christ out from your midst. For His dwelling is made in the peace of holiness and righteousness, without which no one shall see the Lord.

Therefore, commanding your whole community by virtue of obedience [Col. 0066B], we direct that you faithfully obey in all things pertaining to the Lord the aforementioned brother whom the departing Father wished to set over you, until, with the Lord’s aid, we are able to appoint a pastor in the Church of Exeter, to which the guardianship of your house has been entrusted by a double right, spiritual and temporal. We command this to be observed in the meantime without prejudice to that pastor’s rights. Against those who presume to oppose the arrangement of the aforesaid prior, we command canonical severity to be exercised; and we shall ratify whatever sentence the aforesaid Richard, named by the prior, may pronounce against Peter and William, or any of their accomplices, should they have any.

## LETTER LXXX. TO …

[Col. 0066C] The bearer of this letter, a native of London, as he says, investigated his lineage with care and could not find his birthplace this side of the farther Cornwall. This friend of ours, if his statements are true, has been despoiled by one of your deans and injured in a manner far different from what should be done to a citizen of London. The lord king had ordered that, after summoning the dean and his accomplices, the lord archbishop should examine this case; but because he places the greatest confidence in your prudence and justice, he entrusts it to you, that, when faced with a more powerful adversary, you may consider the Lord in the poor man, if he rests his case on truth. Otherwise the archbishop is pressed, by royal command, to render justice to our fellow citizen, not without vexation to the dean.

It is a serious matter, although dean and archdeacon make sport of the spoils of the poor. Why should they not? Others’ sorrow turns to their joy, whose hands contain iniquities and whose left hands are either filled with gifts or gape after them. These monsters among men have no right hands. For as some are ambidextrous in the exercise of virtue, so these men are shown by greed and rapine to be “two-left-handed” (*ambilaevi*). This against the rage of archdeacons, on behalf of our poor fellow citizen, whom the hidden recess of farther Cornwall brought forth beside the Tower of London.

As regards the condition of our house, it is the same as it was, and a little more cheerful. For that fear which the Bishop of Rochester and our Ranulf had instilled in you proved groundless: they had serious business, indeed business to which they had especially hastened with eagerness. They had been summoned to receive a hundred marks and something more [Col. 0067A]. Yet one of them regretted that his watchfulness and effort had been mocked, because he received nothing; for the other

> “Carried off every vote and blended the useful with the sweet.”
>
> —Horace, *Ars Poetica* 343

Now let me see whether the spirit of prophecy flourishes in you, so that you may answer without hesitation which of the two had his affair turn out as he wished. If you lack this gift, consult our young man, who, whenever he comes to me, leaves me as much more learned as he is thinner. For it is expedient that what I say be hidden from his eyes, lest, if he should detect a collision of three vowels, I be compelled to pay the penalty for an ugly sound and an irregular word. In vain could I plead the licences of authors in my defence against a young man who sets grammatical law before me [Col. 0067B] and diligently attends to grammar’s rules.

But if our elder brother reveals this secret to the younger one so that he may exact the penalty, then look after my case and say that I did not set out to dispute grammar with a young grammarian, but to plead, in whatever words I can, the cause of a London friend from Cornwall. And if danger threatens either alternative, I consider it better to win the case at the expense of grammar than, to speak grammatically, to suffer the loss of the case. For when two former advocates, now, as they say, shepherds of souls and bishops—namely, the bishop of Lisieux and the bishop of Chichester—proceeded by different paths, and the man of Lisieux preferred that the case should suffer loss rather than his wording, the man now at Chichester yielded to him a painted tongue but, through diligent attention to the facts, snatched away the glory of triumph [Col. 0067C]. I cannot imitate either, but I think the footsteps of one of them should be preferred.

Let us therefore do what is to be done, and keep the cause of our poor fellow citizen commended to you. That you may do so more diligently, I have given him the slippers which our friend Jordan, subprior of Lewes, had sent to you. I have filled a page of words with sheets, because it was pleasant to speak into a friend’s ear and because the matter that ought to be reported to you was not new. Farewell; and announce to our brethren that they may fare well—extending the designation of brotherhood so that it applies not only to the master and the sinner, but also to the son of Remfred and others

> [Note: [Col. 0067] The passage is corrupt, and not even the manuscripts seem able to remedy it. Once this has been noted, let it suffice for all.]

who are united to us in the brotherhood of charity; so [Col. 0067D] also that both the person meant and the thing meant may be understood. Farewell again and always.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO THE ABBOT OF LA CELLE

The excellence of friends determines that all things should be shared between them, and the judgment of discretion excludes from friendship’s sanctuary those who claim affections as private possessions for themselves in preference to their friends. For who doubts that things should be shared by those whose soul is one, if the truth of their profession is maintained in love’s fidelity? For love is what unites souls in the bond of charity and, as Chalcidius says, makes one soul out of many by the wonderful bond of grace; and, as Plato maintains, the same spirit presides over the bodies of many true lovers. Although it is one for the offices of innate or kindred virtue, it sometimes grows stronger in individuals or is hindered according to the quality of their bodies.

When, therefore, I professed myself your friend, I willingly acknowledge a sharing of goods and souls, except for the sorrow I have conceived because of the long and uncertain illness of my lord and father. I wish all to be the more aware of this misery in proportion as they are dearer in faith and charity. Let this sorrow meanwhile, since it must be so, be mine; for it is not advantageous that it be yours. But let everything else, so far as it concerns me, be ours—as long as it is expedient and lawful, even if it displeases you—and let all things be held in common under the guidance of honour [Col. 0068B].

For I do not aspire to things that admit no partnership, dissolve it, or oppose it; things which, against the protest of arithmetic and physics—indeed while nature herself is astonished—divide an indivisible unity. Far be it from me to provide a cause why, in pursuing and avoiding, we should not have the same will and the same refusal. Rather, I would gladly strive that in the Lord we may be one heart and one soul. Yes, in this way lower things share in higher; and the sun, though most bright and pure, does not disdain to recognize as akin the rivers, the clouds, and the filthy earth, insofar as they receive its heat and vigour.

All things subsist by mutual aids; heavy things are in turn tempered by light. Indeed, the universe proceeds thus because the same spirit of unanimity inwardly nourishes so great a harmony of discordant things and discord of harmonious things, and disposes the parts of the worldly body, like limbs, to accord with one another through a kind of reciprocal service [Col. 0068C]. Thus in the human body the limbs serve one another, and the offices of individuals are assigned to common uses. Some are farther away, others nearer, according to the body’s size; yet all are united in the achievement of its health. They have diverse impulses, but if you consider the service of health, all converge upon one end. Still, all are not equal: lower things serve higher. The foot that moves in mud does not aspire to the dignity of the head; nor does the head raised toward heaven despise the foot that moves in mud. Thus we too, if it does not displease you, are reckoned with you and among yours.

For my part, I shall put forward what I have ready, if only your seriousness deigns to admit trifles. You, then, repay trifles with serious things; for I too learned in Apulia that gold is exchanged for tow.

I have published a book, *On the Trifles of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers*, which will please or displease me according to your judgment. It is unpolished and, by my own command, asks to be corrected by you, my friends. It was hastening to the illustrious chancellor of the king of England, but restrain it unless its progress be favourable. For it is talkative [Col. 0069A] and will scarcely have a friend at court. Yet I should not wish it to make me an enemy of courtiers. I ask that you instruct it without delay and return it, corrected, to the friend who awaits it.

Not, indeed, like that British thief at Canterbury, from whose hand it could not be torn before he had been painted all over, perhaps so that, more easily accused, he might be thrust before the eyes of enemies. I had heard that this was a Greek custom, but did not know that it was British.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO THE SAME

As I wrote this, the salutation placed before it made the secretary laugh. When I asked the reason, he warned me, a ridiculous sender of greetings, to speak more prudently and not mingle bitter and tasteless things with sweet ones. For, he says, just as you accept the offered “greeting” (*salutem*), so you reject what follows, “and himself” (*et se ipsum*). Perhaps because it is bitter, perhaps because it is tasteless—especially in your own house, where sweeter things abound. But what have I to do with this? To alter the address seemed disgraceful, but to send it without examination seemed rash.

Moreover, it was uncertain to whom this inquiry should be entrusted. If I investigate it myself, although lenient, I may be suspect to you; if I entrust it to an accuser, I remember that an accuser’s mouth does not speak truth. If I entrust it to you, my rival will not agree, saying that you cannot render an impartial verdict, since you are either a new enemy or a friend through long-standing intimacy. Private feeling does not produce an uncorrupted judgment.

After much deliberation, therefore, I at last resolved to choose the court of your household, where, in your absence but with Walter of Calne present—though he too may be charged with deceit—the case may be more familiarly argued. I do not fear the helpers of the opposing side; and though Mandrogerus grunt, Trimalchio pine away, Bromius laugh, and the assembly of Mercurial clients take my advocate from me, even with Corydon as patron I do not evade examination before this venerable tribunal. I would not formerly have declined your judgment, since you once thought me lovable—and truly:

> “I was then, as was said, worthy to be loved.”
>
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* V.89

But that I now decline it must be imputed to you, who, regarding the person’s outward appearance, have preferred a new love to an old friendship. As for me, I am what I was; I possess more than the two of us possessed at Provins. I sing no worse than usual and, unlike many men of Salisbury, though they are excellent singers:

> “Nor am I so uncomely: once I saw myself on the shore  
> (at Pisa),  
> when the sea stood still in quiet winds.”
>
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* II.25

I shall rehearse and unfold the rest more fully in the ear and presence of the judge, before whom I shall stand or fall. And, having written freely as a friend with his judgment dictating, no one shall hear an appeal from whatever judgment I may form of “himself.” Yet by every means I shall take care to summon the weighty opposing party before they burden you [Col. 0070A]. However great the commotion, it shall never by my purpose be carried to an outsider’s ears. If Walter cannot be present, I shall readily agree that he be absent with you—unless he would rather perform the role of a supporter.

Receive, then, the greeting and myself, and write back what you wish; provided that you either accept less of what is offered or that, while you are absent, my devotion submit to the judgment of the chosen court.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF LINCOLN

To Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln.

The welfare of the whole Church is endangered if the vessel over which Peter presides is entrusted to impure hands. We know that the Church is the ship of the outstanding Fisherman; we do not doubt that the Roman pontiff is the vicar of the prince of the Apostles, who governs, corrects, and directs the entire Church as a helmsman governs a ship by its rudder, through the regulation of his seal. Corruption of this seal, therefore, endangers the universal Church, since by the mark of one seal the mouths of any pontiffs may be unbound and bound, every offence pass unpunished, and innocence be condemned.

Accordingly, those who dare attempt this must be punished as public enemies and, so far as lies in them, overthrowers of the whole Church. One of these lurks among you: A. s. of Grimelinche. Having committed forgery in apostolic documents and compounded the crime by perjury, he has deserved to be bound by the bond of anathema. We therefore command that you publicly announce him excommunicated and, if he can be apprehended, have him brought to us as a manifest perjurer and forger [Col. 0070C]. And lest you doubt that he committed forgery, we have ordered a copy of the lord pope’s letters to be sent to you; he and the priest Jordan swore that he possessed them sealed with bulls.

## LETTER LXXXIV

The Church of Holy Trinity, London, proceeding against Martin of Waltham, demanded that certain tithes belonging to the church of Welcumeston, which Ralph Rotundus had offered on the day that the said church was consecrated, in the presence and with the approval of the bishop of London, be restored to it. It said that it had been despoiled of them without judgment, and maintained that its right was all the clearer because many persons in the neighbourhood knew that the canons of Holy Trinity had recovered these tithes from Martin’s predecessor and from the church of Waltham.

When this case had long been conducted in the court of the Church of London, it was transferred by appeal to your hearing. At last Martin, who had obtained several postponements for various reasons, after the oath against calumny had been given on both sides, and this by the consent and request of the parties, was assigned a final day—although Martin denied this. When the canons wished on that day to establish their claim, the said M. raised dilatory exceptions. He said that something was wanting on the canons’ part because, after furnishing sureties [Col. 0071A], he had bound himself to preserve the aforesaid tithes until the decision of the suit; and, because he was not permitted to alienate them, he alleged that he had suffered prejudice.

In reply, the canons steadfastly asserted that they had extracted no obligation from Martin, nor had anyone done so in their name. The man who had accepted the sureties from Martin said that he had received them neither in the canons’ name nor by their mandate, as he was prepared to swear; rather, because he saw that the tithes were disputed, he wished in this respect to protect himself, lest they perhaps be reclaimed from him if he had imprudently paid them to an unjust claimant. He also released Martin and his sureties from the obligation of the suretyship. Therefore, when it was pronounced in interlocutory judgment that this exception was wholly insufficient to delay the case, and Martin was required to proceed, he appealed to your hearing for Quasimodo Sunday.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO PETER, ABBOT OF LA CELLE

To the lord abbot of La Celle.

It is nothing new that your kindness has procured me the support of food, receiving my poverty in a foreign land so that neither a father’s gift nor a mother’s affection seemed lacking to me. It was great indeed thus to provide for an exile that, among foreign nations, I should enjoy the advantages of citizens; but far greater is the fact that your diligence has provided that I should not remain for ever exiled from the sweetness of my native soil, by which the entire human race is held captive. For it is your gift that I have returned to the land of my birth; your gift that I have obtained the acquaintance, friendship, and favour of powerful men; your gift that I seem to flourish in my homeland and, with the Lord’s aid, to be preferred to many fellow citizens and contemporaries.

But why do I enumerate in detail the titles of your liberality and munificence, when their number and immensity so fill my whole mind that they overflow and surpass the capacity of my entire understanding? Indeed, even those benefits which I am unable to remember should have earned for you all that I am and can do. I am therefore bound in such a way that no thanksgiving can release me, since your merits absorb all my efforts—especially as your devotion binds me to itself by continual benefits. For your generosity provides me with daily bread; and you who were accustomed to feed me, a poor man, with temporal nourishment now refresh me, though otherwise abundant, as it were with the delights of eternal life.

Certainly, whoever does not find this food sweet suffers from the tasteless sickness of a foolish palate and needs I know not what bread:

> “… now he prefers honeyed cakes,  
> and, like a runaway priest, refuses sacrificial loaves.”
>
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.10.10

For who would not be refreshed by such abundance of breads, when no king has seen more delicate fare upon his table? Who has ever assembled more varieties of most delicious bread? They give satiety without disgust, and a sweet hunger without deficiency or starvation; and, by the marvellous grace of their seasoning, they raise those whom earthly dwelling weighs down to a happy ascent toward things above [Col. 0072A]. Therefore I do not presume to lay a correcting hand upon them, because I find nothing in them to correct. I would devour them with such avidity that not even a crumb, however thin, of the substance of their meanings or the form of their words should escape me. For, with the Lord’s help, I shall swallow crumbs and crusts.

But your experience knows that man does not live by bread alone, and that continual drinking has made Englishmen notable among foreign nations. I therefore judge it right that you should give drink to one whom you have excellently fed, and that, having set bread before him, you should also offer a cup. I am now thirsty, and I, a devourer of breads, may be choked in dryness unless your clemency provides me with wine. This is more readily available to you than *coelia*, which among our people common usage calls *cervisia*—ale. Yet I drink both, and shrink from nothing that can intoxicate. But because you have an abundance of it—as testified by that old friend of mine who never “leapt forth to the arts except after drinking,” and who composed verses exceeding Virgil’s in their number of syllables and feet—I ask before all other intoxicants for that which may cheer one strengthened by bread.

Moreover, among others the vineyard of Lord Soreth is better known to you, and I do not doubt that every implement necessary for its use is in your possession. You have built there too a winepress [Col. 0072C], through whose service wine is frequently pressed for you: for the conversion of sinners, the delight of devotion, the welfare of the brethren, and the benefit of all hearers. Now it reddens in the cup of Passion; now it whitens in the holiness and purity of chastity; now it burns with charity; now it gives forth fragrance through the cheerfulness of honourable conduct. At times it is refined, so that it may benefit the delicate; now it is full-bodied, so that it may profit the more unformed and ignorant. There are also those differences too numerous to list, any one of which I would prefer to Falernian, Panormitan, or Greek wine—the wine with which the Sicilian chancellor used to make me drink to the destruction and ruin of my health.

I ask, therefore, that you grant me from it an abundance—or mercy—sufficient, however, for an Englishman and a drinker. Otherwise I may brand you with the mark of treachery and charge you with fraud: you have crammed me with bread but withhold the drink by which it can be digested. This is surely the custom of the French, who often dismiss those whom they invite to table sober, but never dry. So far for that.

I remember having written to you on another occasion how that worthless apostate Ralph acted with you and with Brother Thomas; but afterwards the same Ralph was publicly excommunicated for this and ordered to be seized if he could be found. Brother Thomas, in my presence and with me interpreting, delivered your letter to Count Hugh, but achieved nothing, because the count said that he knew nothing of the entire affair. Brother Thomas has remained with us and around us until now and will return when you command [Col. 0073A]. But because he has not yet seen any of his kinsmen, he will visit them before returning, if you permit it.

For my part, I have found a servant and prescribe what is to be done. In addition, I ask that you keep our Thomas, who laboured long with you and for you, as I know, in your favourable regard, so that he, and other Englishmen too, may find—so far as propriety permits—that my prayers have benefited them. Relieve James also with some consolation, if possible. For I confidently stand surety for him: he keeps the cloister unwillingly and, as he wrote to me, he believes this of those who glory in despising obediences, as a wolf submits.

> [Note: [Col. 0073] Should the reading perhaps be *credite* (“believe”)? Or perhaps the punctuation between *credit* (“he believes”) and *his* (“these/those”) should be removed.]

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO …

[Col. 0073B]

The demand of humanity requires that a lover of truth bear witness to truth, especially where truth is in peril. Therefore we have taken care to convey to your knowledge the case of the bearer of these letters, insofar as it was heard in our court, according to the account of it that, upon careful inquiry, could be found in our records; you are bound to bring it to conclusion by apostolic mandate. It is established, therefore, that, under pressure of a mandate from Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, we absolved the said H. of Hameledona from every obligation which had been extorted from him and by which he appeared to be bound to your venerable brother, the bishop of Winchester. In order that the grounds of this absolution may be more plainly made known to your discretion, we have ordered the apostolic letters to be copied for you. Thus it was written to the lord bishop of Winchester concerning H., clerk of Hameledona:

“We remember that, at the representation of your clerk Osbert, we wrote to your brotherhood. Subsequently, however, that same Osbert was refuted and convicted in our presence of lying and false representation, since the aforesaid H. was neither found nor captured with his companions, nor with stolen goods. Therefore, although as human beings we may sometimes be deceived, we neither wish nor ought to permit Henry himself to be unjustly treated or condemned on the strength of our letters. Accordingly, by these present letters we order and command you, putting aside every pretext and delay, wholly to absolve the same H., restoring in full everything whatsoever that may perhaps have been taken from him by you, and to permit him to depart freely. If you neglect to carry this into effect, we shall not be able to allow your neglect to go unpunished.”

And the same pope wrote to us as follows, as you will be able to learn from the copy of our letters:

“To our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin that he wholly absolve H. of Hameledona and permit him to depart freely. If he neglects to carry this into effect, by the authority of these present letters we command you strictly, in our stead, to compel that same our brother to absolve and release Henry.” [Col. 0074A]

We therefore, obedient as was fitting to the apostolic command with ready devotion, arranged that the oft-mentioned Henry should be both absolved from the extorted obligation and freed from the custody in which he had been held; and we enjoined upon our aforesaid brother of Winchester, in accordance with the form of the apostolic injunction, that he should not delay to restore to him in full all that had been taken. These things were done before us. You, who have received the mandate, will, by God’s help, make the remaining arrangements beneficially.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO POPE ALEXANDER

The case between Roger, priest of Guiga, and the abbess of Berkinges had been litigated before the venerable bishop of London, our brother, for longer than was proper. When the casting of his definitive judgment was imminent, the abbess—against whom an action was brought for the unlawful usurpation of certain parishioners and tithes said to belong to the church of Guiga—appealed to our court. Accordingly, after many delays which the abbess had obtained on various grounds, when a peremptory day had been fixed for the parties and the opposing side, sufficiently furnished with witnesses, wished to establish its claim, she, frightened by empty fear and led astray by imprudent counsel, declined our jurisdiction by appeal.

We, however, yielding as was fitting to the Apostolic See, suspended ourselves from the determination and cognizance of the matter until judgment in this cause should issue from your see, or authority to judge should be delegated to whomsoever it pleased. Meanwhile your predecessor of pious memory, Lord Adrian, was taken from our midst; and while the Saviour of the faithful was being invoked by prayers, the storm of schism grew violent and conflict between kingdoms arose. God permitted His Church to be troubled, and, as though an obstacle of unbelievers—may God disperse it—had been placed between us, a kind of chaos was established between you and us, so that no one could pass from one side to the other without great danger.

The time therefore elapsed within which the appellant ought, as promised, to have pursued her appeal; so much so that both plaintiff and defendant seemed wholly to have abandoned prosecution of the case. Then, about the beginning of the following year, the aforesaid Roger came before us with letters from the lord king, renounced the appeal he had made, and, out of reverence for the royal mandate, requested justice for himself.

At length, after one and another appeal, the abbess was cited by a third peremptory edict. She sent proctors and attempted to excuse her absence; but, as it seemed, she alleged insufficient grounds. Since she had been forbidden, she could obtain no further delay and appealed to your court, fixing the Sunday on which is sung *Quasi modo geniti* (“As newborn infants”), declaring that she had long been unjustly harassed by her adversary; that he had no right in the matters he sought to extort by vexatious litigation; and that she relied against him upon prescription through the passage of a very long time. [Col. 0075A]

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO HILARY, BISHOP OF CHICHESTER

The excesses of evildoers can most fittingly be restrained by those who know the merits of the parties more intimately and who have received from the Lord the power to correct. You will therefore decide more appropriately the controversy between Reginald and Pag., since truth cannot be hidden from you and the duty of administering justice between them necessarily rests upon your judgment and good faith by reason of your office.

That disputes belonging to your court flow to us is evidence of defect or dissimulation; nor should anyone believe that there is a defect either of authority or of prudence, since the Lord has bestowed both upon you. Take pains, therefore, lest the will to fulfil justice should deservedly appear lacking. If you dissemble, you persist equally to your own loss and ours: our labour is increased, and the reputation for strength which you have acquired is diminished, which is not expedient for you.

For we owe it to you, if we may speak more freely with a friend, that Edward and Helias have troubled us for a long time; and, to answer you in your own words, concerning what you wrote to me about the aforesaid persons, I write back concerning R. and P.: namely, let justice answer each according to his own case. But if either is otherwise discovered in manifest guilt of disobedience or of another crime, let him be punished with a manifest punishment, so that the rest may fear and remember why judicial authority has been established among them. Your prudence also knows that some matters shine with so clear a light of fact that they need no hearing, but punishment or reward alone. [Col. 0075C]

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO POPE ALEXANDER

We ought to support the assertions of parties with faithful testimony when cases depart from us and fly to the apostolic majesty. Therefore we take care to convey to your knowledge the course of the controversy between Richard of Anestia and Mabilia of Francheville, long litigated in our court, as far as the issues that arose could be collected.

The aforesaid Richard, being kinsman and nephew of William of Saccavilla—since common usage calls a sister’s son a nephew—brought a claim of inheritance in order to obtain his uncle’s property. The said Mabilia, William’s daughter, opposed him in the secular court where the matter was being heard, asserting that a daughter was to be preferred to a nephew in a paternal inheritance. Richard answered that she had no hereditary right, because she had not been born of a lawful marriage but begotten in an adulterous union.

Since, therefore, a question of marriage was at issue, which is invalidated or validated under ecclesiastical rules, the court of the Catholic prince, the most serene Henry II, king of the English, decreed that the cause should be returned to ecclesiastical examination, where the marriage question might receive its due conclusion under the law of the canons, which the clergy know and the common people do not. We accordingly fixed a day for the parties by royal command; and at last, after delays which Mabilia had obtained for various reasons, Richard renewed his claim.

To establish his case more clearly and demonstrate that his adversary was illegitimate, he asserted that his uncle William had contracted marriage with a certain Albreda of Tresgoro, and that, after abandoning her contrary to the fidelity owed in marriage, he had taken Adelicia, daughter of Humphrey the viscount, and had by her begotten Mabilia and other illegitimate children. He further asserted that, when William had taken Adelicia as an additional wife, Albreda, whom he had married first, publicly asserted for herself in the very wedding her right under the marriage bond and, by ecclesiastical authority, forbade the said Adelicia to enter into unlawful embraces with her husband. [Col. 0076B]

Moreover, since Albreda could not be heard there because of the crowd and her husband’s obstinacy, she approached the bishop of Winchester, then legate of the Apostolic See. As that bishop testified in his letters, she finally obtained by his judgment that her husband, after abandoning the adulteress, should be restored to her. He further asserted that the judgment of the bishop of Winchester had been confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See, because the said bishop, while the dispute was pending before him, had consulted it and, as they said, had received a written opinion from Lord Innocent, your predecessor of holy memory, in these words. We have never received the originals, but only the lord bishop of Winchester’s letters concerning this matter:

“Concerning what you asked about the sacrament of marriage, I answer briefly. The woman whom, you said, had been given to him in marriage by her father and, after being so given, entrusted again to her father until he should bring her into his own house on the appointed day—I say that, lawful consent having intervened, she became his wife immediately upon consenting by voluntary agreement to be his wife. For a future act was not being promised, but a present act was being confirmed. Therefore whatever was afterwards done with another woman, whether in intercourse or in the begetting of offspring, is so much the more blameworthy as the first union is more truly a marriage. For while the first remains in force, the more that is committed in the second, the greater the guilt.” [Col. 0076D]

Therefore, since a divorce had been pronounced on the basis of an apostolic writing and the judgment had not been challenged by any legal remedy within ten years or more, the marriage joined by the legate was to be regarded as the valid marriage, and the union condemned by the Apostolic See as adulterous. Further, it was no longer in question whether their union had been a marriage, since this was clear from a matter adjudicated, from the divorce pronounced, and from the fact that, after putting aside the adulteress, he remained united to his first wife until the last days of his life.

He said that he had an abundance of witnesses on all these points, so that no one could doubt either the earlier contracted marriage, the challenge to the subsequent cohabitation, or the divorce canonically pronounced. And, although he advanced many arguments for himself, he chiefly insisted upon the point of res judicata and upon the judgment which he said had been delivered in the London synod, where the divorce had been pronounced against Mabilia’s mother by the bishop of Winchester, then legate and vicar of the Church of London. He also produced witnesses whom he asserted had attended that synod and the divorce.

Since children begotten from condemned and unlawful intercourse, or from unrestrained lust, are wholly excluded from every benefit of inheritance; since neither civil law nor statute recognizes them; and since the force of the canons rejects them so thoroughly that it does not even decree them maintenance, but in some fashion accepts the legal deprivation imposed upon them—he maintained that Mabilia herself, as evidence of her father’s crime, must be excluded from all hope of inheritance.

In reply, Mabilia, to repel her kinsman’s accusation, asserted that her parents, William and Adelicia, had been lawfully joined and had contracted not a clandestine but a solemn marriage in the face of the Church. She did not, however, greatly deny that her father William had made an agreement of betrothal to marry Albreda with Albreda’s father before he married Adelicia, Mabilia’s mother; but she denied that it had proceeded to marriage. Rather, because marriage must be free in its making and dissolution by the consent of the parties, she said that both parties had released the agreement of betrothal. She sought to prove this because witnesses appeared ready to prove that money which William had received from Albreda’s father had been repaid to him. They further asserted that Albreda and her father had released William and his father from every obligation that had arisen from the intended marriage; and that Albreda’s father had attended the wedding of William and Adelicia as a guest and had been the readiest approver of this marriage. [Col. 0077C]

Both the laws of princes and the decrees of pontiffs show that a betrothed woman is not a wife, since a betrothed girl may choose a monastery even if the man objects, as Eusebius declares; and the laws, Gregory testifying, impose no penalty upon a betrothed woman if she enters a community of women. Further, a marriage is not perfect which bodily union does not confirm and complete, although it takes its beginning from the first pledge of betrothal. If, therefore, things begun prejudice things perfected, it is altogether unjust that an agreement of betrothal should be said to have prejudiced a true marriage.

For Pope Evaristus, after setting forth the form of contracting marriage and the sacred marriage rite in the Church, added:

“Know that marriages are lawful when they have been completed in this manner; but unions undertaken otherwise are, without doubt, not marriages but adulteries, debaucheries, cohabitations, or fornications rather than lawful marriages, unless the parties’ own will has given support and lawful vows are present.”

But William, after dissolving the earlier agreement, as he was permitted to do, contracted a lawful marriage, and never gave consent to leave the woman to whom he had been lawfully joined. The divorce alleged by the opposing party either had never occurred at all, or had not been lawfully pronounced.

For when justice, after the death of the king who loved peace, had gone into exile from the realm, and, amid the growing madness of those rejoicing in novelties, all were incited to every kind of action, she asserted that her mother Adelicia had not been separated from her husband by any right, but had been violently shut out and expelled from her husband’s house through the contrivance of Geoffrey, archdeacon of London. Having received a price, he sought to condemn her without defence, without a hearing, indeed without even a citation in the matter, relying upon the authority of the bishop of Winchester, who, she asserted, had himself been corrupted by bribes, though he did not yet hold the office of legate. [Col. 0078A]

She sought to establish this on the ground that Adelicia, when excluded by her husband, had approached the holy man Alberic, legate of the Apostolic See in England, seeking justice for the injury inflicted upon her by her husband and the archdeacon. From the chronology, it is clear that the bishop of Winchester first received the office of legate after the departure of the bishop of Ostia already mentioned by us.

Thereafter, when the said bishop of Winchester presided in the London synod in order to perform the office of the vacant see, Adelicia publicly produced the legatine mandate which she had obtained and sought redress for the wrongs she had suffered from the archdeacon and her husband. Yet the weight of injustice and bribes received had so depressed the mind of this judge that he could not be raised to do justice, even by the command of his lord and legate.

It was further established that no earlier marriage had been contracted between William and Albreda, since it was only then, when through the fraud of the said archdeacon and bishop of Winchester the wife was cast out by her husband, that even the solemnity of betrothal in the Church and the nuptial rite before the people were solemnly celebrated between them. Witnesses for this matter were then present.

Therefore, she said, the judgment by which an absent woman was condemned had been null either in fact or in law: she was not contumacious, but had not been cited in the case; and it is established that a judgment pronounced contrary to the solemn order of judicial proceedings has no force. She also repeatedly argued from the privilege of persons and ignorance of law: parents might be permitted to be ignorant by reason either of the belt of knighthood or the weakness of their sex; and what preceded the beginning of marriage had no force of marriage, since it was not confirmed into a marriage bond by authority of laws and canons, and ancient custom among us had hitherto not recognized it in the consummation of marriage. [Col. 0078D]

Moreover, her father, when near death, was said openly to have repented that he had acquiesced in the fraud of the said archdeacon in expelling his wife, as Gilbert, venerable abbot of Colchester, testified in his letters—though not sealed, but supported by witnesses—and as other religious persons who were present testified. But whatever had been done between the parents, she asserted, ought not to harm her or the children, because the archdeacon and bishop of Winchester had pronounced nothing against the children. Rather, whenever they were challenged on this point, they had declared, as several witnesses testified, that they had pronounced nothing against the children of the marriage which they nevertheless sought to invalidate.

Accordingly, as she asserted, the illustrious Count Theobald of Blois, a prince indeed devoted to justice and most expert in the law of the Cismontane region, to whom the bishop of Winchester himself had referred the children’s case because the matter belonged to him by feudal right, summoned the leading bishops of Gaul. Taking their counsel and that of other wise men, having heard the case after the father’s death, he recognized the children as legitimate heirs and held that whatever crafty fraud had procured to their prejudice ought not to harm them. [Col. 0079A]

She said that she possessed an abundance of witnesses in all these matters and produced them on many points. But Richard, insisting on res judicata, could not be moved from the position that the judgment must stand, since it had not been challenged by any legal remedy, not merely after the ten legal days had elapsed but during a full twenty years. He also produced witnesses by whom he sought to show that he had been appointed heir by his uncle William and that the others had been disinherited as illegitimate.

Nor, he said, could privilege of persons avail them, since no one may be ignorant of his own act. Although William, Mabilia’s father, had been a knight, he should not have been ignorant of what he did when he received Albreda as wife—not by a contract promising something future, but by a present contract of marriage. Since consent makes marriage, whatever had been undertaken in violation of the legitimately preceding consent did not dissolve the inseparable bond of the earlier marriage. If carnal intercourse and offspring conceived from it afterwards arose contrary to the fidelity of marriage, this did not invalidate the first union, but established the guilt of the subsequent cohabitation.

It is therefore clear that whatever he did, he either knew or ought to have known. Nor should it aid his children if, by reason of military privilege, he believed himself permitted with impunity to mock the pledged fidelity of persons acting rightly. Perhaps, if a maternal inheritance were sought, provision could be made for the children in this respect, because their mother might have had no wrongful conscience in contracting marriage. But because the dispute concerns paternal succession, the father’s deceit does not aid the children at all.

The clemency of the laws sometimes spares those convicted of ignorance who are separated from one another by reason of kinship, and frees their children from disgrace and loss of inheritance when the authority of the Church joins those whom ignorance had kept apart. But the severity of laws and canons is exercised against those who knowingly unite incestuously or unlawfully, while both divine and human law forbid it. [Col. 0079D]

Against this, Mabilia’s party advanced many arguments from reason and law. It used many examples, saying that it would be impossible, or very difficult, for the children of the king of the Franks and others whom they named to be disinherited because a divorce had been lawfully pronounced between their parents. Yet Mabilia’s party did not admit that a divorce had been lawfully pronounced between her parents. It also said that the laws incline more readily toward absolution, especially of the innocent, whom it is unjust to condemn for another’s sin.

It sought to show that the separation had not been carried out by the bishop of Winchester in the London synod because, before that synod—summoned at London by the said bishop alone—was held, Adelicia, as many present testified, had been ordered removed by the aforesaid archdeacon in the chapter of Colchester without a preceding judgment, unheard and undefended. And, what was more serious, he himself then expelled from her husband’s home a wife wholly ignorant of this entire controversy. [Col. 0080A]

When Adelicia approached the bishop of Winchester in the said London synod, she did nothing except lament the injury inflicted upon her by the archdeacon and seek justice pursuant to the mandate which Lord Alberic, legate of the Apostolic See, had issued to the bishop of Winchester. As she sought to prove, no other word was there exchanged with her than that she lodged her complaint before a deaf judge.

She also complained that the same bishop of Winchester intended to employ to her detriment the advice of Lord Innocent, when in the aforementioned letters of Lord Innocent nothing was expressed concerning her parents, but only concerning certain persons, she knew not whom, improperly joined. Her parents, she maintained, had by no means so come together. If the said bishop had represented to the lord pope that they had done so, the guilt of false representation and the crime of another’s lie ought not to harm her.

In short, just as Richard chiefly relied upon his uncle’s appointment of him as heir in bringing his inheritance claim, and upon the judgment of the bishop of Winchester to prove what he called condemned adultery, so conversely Mabilia chiefly relied upon her father’s last will and the judgment of Count Theobald. She promised to establish both by witnesses. Further, unless the party wholly departed from the author’s position, she declared that she ought to receive relief through the length of time, ignorance of law, the number of children, and the authority of the Church, which had joined that marriage.

For in a more difficult case the divine Marcus and Lucius answered more leniently, writing thus to Flavia Tertulla through Mensorem, a freedman:

“We are moved both by the long time during which, through ignorance of law, you remained in marriage with your uncle, by the fact that you were placed in that marriage by your grandmother, and by the number of children. Therefore, since all these circumstances concur, we confirm the status of the children begotten in your marriage, which was contracted forty years ago, as though they had been lawfully conceived.”

If, therefore, secular princes show such clemency that, for the children’s sake, they even spare incest, what boldness will Christian pontiffs display if they condemn with unheard-of severity those whom the womb of the Church has brought forth as lawfully conceived?

When these arguments had been advanced on both sides and, at last, almost at the end of two years, a peremptory day had been fixed for the production of the parties’ proofs—after delays which the parties had earned, though more frequently the defendant, since she excused herself because of childbirth or another illness, or because of her husband’s absence, which was regarded as just—she also sent persons to excuse her absence on grounds of illness. Richard appealed to your court, fixing the Sunday on which is sung *Laetare Jerusalem* (“Rejoice, Jerusalem”), and declared himself aggrieved because he had been harassed by delays for almost two years and deceived by the woman’s evasions so that he could not obtain justice.

## LETTER XC. TO BARTHOLOMEW, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER

[Col. 0081A]

To Master B., archdeacon of Exeter: greeting, and the grace of the Spirit who orders all things toward good.

May the Lord be with you, dearest of friends, and establish you in the solidity of virtues, so that you may neither be broken by reed-like weakness nor be tossed by every breeze of the same instability. The Lord of hosts is strong and mighty; He also orders all things gently and will mightily crush beneath His feet those who resist His ordering. What He has determined concerning you, He determines without you. In the Acts of the Apostles, according to the judgment of Gamaliel, the newborn Church was committed to God’s decision; at His nod all things are weakened or strengthened.

Commit your cause therefore to Him, for under His protection it cannot be endangered. Do not be faint-hearted in Him, for it was said to the body of little ones: “Cast thy care upon the Lord, and He shall nourish thee.” For adults no longer need a nurse’s food, but the protection of preservation. Let it therefore be your desire and your prayer that the Lord’s will may be fulfilled not only concerning you, but also by you. If He is for us, who is against us? His word will not be void, even if, often to the glory of Him who orders all things, it is fulfilled amid the resistance of evil men.

From the beginning strong and powerful men stood against Him, possessing the wisdom of this age and famous for the bestowal of favour, stirring up war; but the Lord cast them down and divided their tongues, because He saw contradiction flowing from wickedness in the city which prefigured the Church. [Col. 0081C]

Do not therefore fear if on the opposing side there is, against God whom I trust you serve, a mouth like a blazing torch; for on the side of Him who rises and speaks from the eternal counsel on high, the word is brighter, more abundant, and more effectual. Nor be troubled if the grace of God is sometimes attacked by a shadowy favour, for that favour which seeks its own interests will vanish. Though it rejoices for an hour in borrowed light, it will utterly fail and grow dark when justice is turned into judgment.

If anyone relies upon Ulpian alone—or rather upon the opinion of Ulpian—by the Lord’s favour he will be taught; nor, through his own spirit, will he prove wicked against Him who humbles the proud and exalts the humble. Individuals speak according to their own judgment, but with one alone rests the universal and necessary interpretation of the laws and canons, of all divine and human law, and of everything established from the beginning.

I call Him as witness—though, willing or unwilling, I shall have Him as judge—that, according to the conscience of my mind, you were neither the author of this proposal nor its advocate, indeed not even privy to it. And so that you may rest more securely in the divine calling: whether the archbishop wrote to the lord king concerning this matter or did not write, I know that the king did not receive letters concerning it.

He was indeed solicited on behalf of Harding’s son—would that he were an episcopal man!—but neither when Simon urged him nor when Gehazi-like men pressed him could he be induced to bring spiritual harm upon himself for another’s advantage. Thus Harding’s son was rebuffed, at present indeed by word rather than writing; yet in such a manner that hope of another benefice remained unharmed for him. But whether you feast or not, whether you die or live, he will never, with our king as the author, be bishop. Indeed, as is believed, neither will he be so by the Lord’s will, because he has always striven against the Lord and, to the extent of his own power or that of his associates, has disturbed all the churches.

Master W., the archdeacon, consulted me through his companion Boson, and he will diligently submit to the divine ordering, with such associates as he can enlist. So will R. of Limesheia. Indeed, if your rivals could in any manner impede your election—which nevertheless, by God’s help, they will not—they would accomplish nothing they wished. One has already been provided who will be imposed upon the stiff-necked and upon those whom they cannot endure. [Col. 0082A]

The proposal concerning you pleases the Roman Church, the lord king, the metropolitan, the fellow bishops, and all who have heard it, except those whom ambition, greed, impurity, or envy has blinded. If they perhaps appear in the sight of good men while persisting in their malice, God will confound them, lest He Himself be confounded by them through the frustration of His purpose.

I had kept silent and concealed my joy, because, if it were possible, I wished you to be called by the Lord without knowing it beforehand. But now, because He has judged otherwise and has made His servant Bartholomew privy to His counsel through many signs, I give the counsel I gave before: do not anticipate the one who is to invite you; do not despise the one who invites you. If he says, “Come up higher,” obey his command; but if not, remain, for as long as he pleases, in the calling in which you were called. For you will obey if commanded to come down.

There is one thing I advise for winning favour, if it is lacking: make yourself better—not that you should pretend to be so. If you displease through hatred of virtue, do not make yourself pleasing to many to whom virtue itself is displeasing, unless you bring it about that virtue itself becomes pleasing. Yet do all things at the right time, remembering Him who became all things to all people in order to gain all. Correction ought not to be begun precipitately or abruptly.

I know it is superfluous to warn you not to make any bargain concerning your promotion, for you are wholly known to me. Nor should you be troubled concerning the transfer of the archdeaconry to Harding’s son, for it is an empty rumour that often disturbs many people. Before you are bishop, it will not be given to another by anyone’s authority; once you are bishop, it will be yours to give to whom you wish. You may perhaps hear requests meanwhile or afterwards, but whether you grant them will depend on your own decision, not another’s.

If you tremble where there is no fear, He whose minister, by God’s help, you are to be will rebuke you in the words with which He rebuked: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?” (Matthew 14). In short, your counsel rests in large measure with the lord archbishop, so that he may be able to advise you. Without him you will do nothing in this matter. Whatever the sons of Belial may do, you and the sons of peace will come on the appointed day of summons, as prescribed to you.

Let Master B., son of Reinfred—a sinner, my little brother—and all our people, indeed God’s people, come with the rest or before the rest. Let the prior of Plympton and the abbot of Tavistock come also, if indeed they understand peace. And if you can avert the indignation of your rivals without disgrace to conscience or reputation, do so. For what concern is there about fickle people? I do not care for you unless you take especial care for your character. Farewell with my brothers and the others whose welfare we ought to desire. Our household, whose welfare you desire, sends you this greeting. [Col. 0083A]

## LETTER XCI. TO …

I offer such thanks as I can to your high rank and fidelity, which have deigned to refresh me, across so many expanses of land and sea, with the comfort of your letter. While Fortune’s cruelty raged violently against us both, I greatly shuddered; but since its force has subsided, peace having been restored to you, I seem, if not to feel, then at least, by God’s help and through your efforts, to foresee a gentler breeze for myself.

If, through the demands of my sins, my hope should—God forbid—prove false, I shall with strong and cheerful spirit submit my body to the scourge of divine providence, confident that no adversity will harm me if I withdraw my neck from the yoke of sin. Moreover, the testimony of an innocent conscience relieves the straits of my mind; it fears the judgment of Him alone before whose tribunal rich and poor will shortly assemble and all children of men will be compelled to render account for themselves.

But why should I defend my innocence, when your holiness knows it more fully and clearly? As the will is in heaven, so let it be done. He is twice an exile who is an exile at home; and those wandering abroad are sometimes not forsaken by the grace of predestined blessedness. [Col. 0083C]

## LETTER XCII. TO THE MONKS OF N.

To the monks of N.

The command issued by the Holy Spirit through His apostle subjects every soul to higher powers; whoever resists it is proved to oppose the divine ordering. Obedience is the virtue by which human things are joined to divine things, earthly to heavenly. Those who despise it, so far as lies in them, divide the unity of the Church and break apart the bond of the Spirit which consists in the bond of peace.

We therefore cannot sufficiently wonder at your brotherhood, which by God’s mercy has professed the rule of a stricter life and attained a rank of most eminent religious observance, because you have hitherto despised the mandate of the lord pope and ours. For when, by apostolic command, we had repeatedly admonished you with paternal diligence as was fitting—perhaps more often than was fitting—to restore to Paridi, archdeacon of Rochester, the tithes of the church of Rochester, as justice requires, we achieved nothing by repeated commands. Nor did any signs of submission or humility, in word or deed, appear to us.

Since, therefore, although we can sometimes bear an injury to ourselves with equanimity, we neither can nor ought to overlook contempt of the lord pope, we command and enjoin you: putting aside every pretext and delay, restore the aforesaid tithes to the said archdeacon according to the apostolic mandate; abstain from divine offices, according to the ordinances of the Fathers, until you have fulfilled the mandate of the lord pope and ours; and let none of you presume to enter the church while, through the crime of disobedience, you commit the sin of divination and idolatry. [Col. 0084A]

## LETTER XCIII. TO THE BISHOP OF NORWICH

To the bishop of Norwich.

Our beloved sons R[ichard] of Drayton and his brother A. have tearfully represented to us in their complaint that, contrary to the sacred canons and to our authority, they have been unjustly treated by our son R., archdeacon of Norwich, and that their appeal, once lodged, could not avail them before that same archdeacon. They further add [Col. 0084B] that, after an appeal had been made to us, your fraternity, under the pretext of a royal command and by a semblance of judicial procedure, attempted to deprive the aforesaid A. of the advowson of the church of St Andrew of Ringet, in order that it might be transferred to the stranger R[ad.]. Accordingly, that same R[ad.], with sacrilegious boldness, with the assent and indeed the patronage of R., the archdeacon, presumed to take the aforesaid church from the said Richard, who lawfully possessed it by our judgment and that of the brethren present.

Since they were prepared to establish these matters before us by witnesses and documents, we could not but be moved. Nevertheless, that we may more fully learn the merits of the entire case from the parties’ assertions, we have thought fit to grant the parties the postponement requested by your belovedness, while annulling everything [Col. 0084C] undertaken after the appeal. For although we can sometimes bear injuries to our own person with equanimity, we cannot—and ought not—dissemble an injury to the holy Church of Canterbury and contempt of the Apostolic See, whose office we exercise.

Therefore, by authority of this kind, command the aforesaid archdeacon to appear before us on the Sunday on which *Cantante Domino* is sung, to answer the aforementioned brothers R[ichard] and A. concerning their losses and injuries. Send R. of Passu, the archdeacon’s son-in-law, to the Apostolic See as excommunicated for disobedience, contempt of the lord pope and of us, and participation in sacrilege, since, at the devil’s prompting, he killed a priest. [Col. 0084D] Let the archdeacon know what awaits him if he has dared to associate with the aforesaid sacrilegious man while the Church abstains from communion with him. We command that you cause the church of Ringet, together with the full restoration of what has been taken, to be restored to the aforesaid R[ichard]. But if the stranger Rad. scorns to obey our and your commands, do not delay to exercise upon him the severity of ecclesiastical discipline. If, however, he believes that he has any legal claim against Richard, he may afterwards obtain it, with impartial equity, wherever it is just.

## LETTER XCIV. TO MASTER GEOFFREY

To his friend and kinsman Master G..., John of Salisbury [Col. 0085A] sends greetings, and whatever may be more delightful than greeting.

Although I have often received letters from you—yet less often than I should wish—none has arrived more welcome than those which, under the authority of our domestic instruction, imposed upon me the necessity of truth. For I rejoice that from the treasure of your learning there has at last been communicated to me also the example of integrity which you had kept in reserve for yourselves. By these and similar examples I may indeed be encouraged toward brave deeds and, with the Lord’s aid, ascend to higher things, if he stretches out to me the hand of his propitiation—he who gives a glorious end only to those works of which he remembers himself to be the beginning.

And although the memory of that man of ours, whoever he was, is pleasant, and his opinion seems plausible, yet, I think, there is a means by which one may offer consolation to his grief. It is indeed a great thing to be distinguished by the burdens of honours; but without doubt it is greater to merit those same honours by the titles of virtues. Therefore he who has attained the merit of virtue, even though abundance of possessions or the pomp of rank does not accompany it, ought nevertheless to be content with the good bestowed, lest, if he murmurs under the goad of an impatient conscience as though he had suffered an injustice, he may by the vice of ingratitude appear thereby to have made himself unworthy of what he seemed to possess. And would that, if we do not attain the reward of learning, we might at least not be deprived of it through our own desert!

I do not, however, say this because I mean to depart from the instruction of our old master, whom, God willing, I have resolved to obey with all the vigilance of mind and body. In fearing weakness of spirit and fearing the apprehensions of suspicion, [Col. 0085C] you act prudently indeed and as a friend. For I am neither greater than Pompey or the man who conquered him, nor wiser than Augustus, nor more eloquent than Cicero or Curio; and the well-known course of history has taught you how greatly the breath of suspicion injured them. I pass over the fact that faint-heartedness broke the Maccabaean victor more often than the courage of the nations did. Hence it is clear that I cannot withstand their assault unless he meanwhile sustains me who protects man from faintness of spirit and from tempest. But in his strength I shall not fear what man may inflict from without or the flesh murmur within.

Moreover, however swift a horse may be, when the spur ceases it becomes slower; and, as someone says:

> [Col. 0085D]  
> “Ease corrupts the mind,  
> And waters become foul unless they are stirred.”

So too my mind, sluggish through its own fault—if I may not say by nature—will not cast off its inborn indolence unless it is more frequently roused by the goads of exhortation. It will therefore be for your industry and diligence to shake the torpor of my sleepiness more often, so that one whom his own virtue does not kindle to act well may at least be kindled by another’s. Above all, I shall recognize the proof of true friendship if you restore me to myself in such a way that my faults are not spared and that you take more careful measures henceforth to kill them before my face, lest I continue to displease others most in that respect in which I do not know how to displease even myself.

## LETTER XCV. TO JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

[Col. 0086A]

To Joscelin, bishop of Salisbury.

The brethren of the Hospital, under a certain novel and unheard-of title of humanity, level manifestly false accusations in order to make private alms: they seize in order to distribute; they placate the Most High from another’s property; and, to the insult of the apostles, they usurp the office of binding and loosing, usurp the keys of the Church, and abuse the generosity of bishops. Churches which they have once occupied they withdraw from the authority of bishops, though they seek the bishops’ power or authority if they wish to summon any of the provincials. But if they themselves are summoned by another, episcopal authority vanishes, since they assert that they have no court except that of Rome or Jerusalem. [Col. 0086B]

I have therefore resolved to advise and beseech your highness not to indulge their malice, which they exercise against the bearer of this letter, your clerk and priest, since their cause seems more likely to injure your Church than this individual. For every church which you grant them, you will take away from yourselves and your successors.

## LETTER XCVI. TO PETER, ABBOT OF CELLES. [A.D. 1160]

To the abbot of Celles.

The bearer of this letter brought me letters from your blessedness, but they kept holiday during the very solemnities of Easter. I therefore received the complaints of your rebuke seriously, and with the same disposition in which I knew them to have been written—except that I believe the affection of charity to be more sincere in a purer soul. For if I should contend with you about these matters through the vice of arrogance and ingratitude, I stand condemned by domestic proof, apart from the reputation which is made illustrious by the clear and enduring titles of virtues. By the grace of the Lord and by yours, I am what I am, if indeed I am anything; and through the benefit of your instruction I hope always to become better.

I had indeed written to you concerning my coming, which I believed would take place for the reasons set forth below. But that I changed or delayed my decision was not due to my own fickleness but to the counsel of my friends. I therefore judge this either no fault or a slight one, since even the Most High changes his purpose, though his counsel remains for ever. [Col. 0086D] For I could not alone avoid the snares of fortune, since all things under the sun are tossed in the vain gamble of a slippery lot. The flow of time, the movement of affairs, the darkness of minds, and the instability of spirits whirl Fortune’s axle with such swiftness that it is plainly easy to see that not only her wheel, but the whole mass of the world, is changeable.

But lest I seem vainly to accuse not so much myself as the condition of things, judge after learning the cause. Consider then for a little the state in which I stand. Since last year, the serene lord king of the English has been stirred to grave indignation against me by the zeal of my rivals. If you ask the cause, my crimes are the profession of liberty and the defence of truth. [Col. 0087A] The searcher of hearts is my witness—whom my whole worthless and pernicious life has always offended too much—that, as regards the lord king, I know in my conscience no other fault. As you heard, I had intended to approach him to clear my innocence; but through his intimates I learned that I was in no way to be admitted in the absence of the lord of Canterbury, and that through him grace might be restored to me. Moreover, the lord king’s return was promised us every day.

What, then, was I to do? To leave the island seemed to bear the appearance of flight; to avoid meeting my accusers would be to profess a guilty conscience; not to await the prince’s presence would make my head liable under the laws for treason. In short, the testimony of an innocent conscience, the authority of the Roman pontiff, the counsels of prudent men, and the entreaties of friends at last persuaded me to await the examination of the case at home, if possible, where its conclusion might come more easily at less expense and with a richer abundance of friends. But, as you write, I ought to have reported this. I had entrusted this task to your faithful friends and mine, the venerable men John, treasurer of York, and Master William. I delayed sending a messenger of my own because the outcome of the brief, as it seemed, though great shipwreck was still uncertain, and because I preferred to announce good news rather than sad. I therefore kept your courier with me for several days awaiting the arrival of the illustrious queen of the English and the king’s most renowned chancellor, [Col. 0087C] who, through the Lord’s mercy, told me that the storm had subsided for me. Yet the Lord is able, through your prayers and those of his Church for which I suffer, to turn it, however great it is, into a breeze and bring my innocence to the haven of desired peace. So much on this matter.

When you find a trustworthy messenger, please send me the letters of blessed Bernard. I also ask that you have collected for me certain flowers of his words, and of your own, and of the cantor of Troyes, and of any others like them—yet in such a manner that the delight of the flowers does not destroy or diminish the usefulness of the fruit. I shall certainly, with God as author, visit you in my own person or through a personal messenger before autumn is over. [Col. 0087D] For the generosity you showed to my brother, I return such thanks as I can, since I cannot return those which I owe. Greet most warmly in my name our dearest T., your provost; greet also those who love you and know me, whom, though the brevity of paper cannot, the breadth of my mind nevertheless embraces.

## LETTER XCVII. TO THE SAME. [A.D. 1157]

When your messenger arrived, the expedition of our most serene lord, the king of the English—who had set out to subdue the Britons of the Alps and Sub-Alps—kept us occupied with the affairs of the whole kingdom, but especially anxious concerning the guardianship of the illustrious queen of the English and the lord king’s children, who [Col. 0088A] have been entrusted to the fidelity of the lord of Canterbury, from whose side I do not depart. Thus I could not visit your eminence so quickly, even by my messenger.

But what sorrow and grief your messenger brought to my soul, I knowingly and prudently leave unspoken, lest, if I add my own pain to the pain of your wounds, you be swallowed up in deeper sadness. A wounded mind is ordinarily made raw rather than comforted by the recollection—still more by the inundation—of sad things. It is indeed pleasant to remember evils, but when they have passed; only then is it pleasing to have been cast down, when you have prevailed more strongly. It is likewise pleasant to have been miserable, but only to one now rejoicing in happiness. Yes, yes: the memory of misfortune is welcome, but when one triumphs over Fortune’s injury. Who looks with cheerful eyes upon the ruin of his own house? Who willingly watches his dwelling blaze or smoke?

Therefore, my dearest friend, let us turn our minds for a little from the memory of such great grief, turning toward him who does not allow his faithful people to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but makes an outcome from temptation, so that all things cooperate for good. For the rod of sinners does not remain upon the lot of the righteous; and whatever departs from iniquity, whether it assumes the guise of prosperity or adversity, nonetheless advances toward salvation and strives toward glory. [Col. 0088B] For faith’s merit grows from the difficulty of circumstances, and more glorious is the triumph preceded by continuous labour, the undertaking of dangers, and unceasing patience. If anyone trusts in himself, he fails in that wherein he trusts; if in the Lord, he does not fail therein. “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 14); but the apostle, moved by his spirit, can do all things in him. What man of strength and high spirit would not gladly embrace this?

> You, do not yield to evils, but go forth more boldly against them,  
> So far as your fortune permits you.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid* VI.95.)

What then of him whom the Word of the Father summons to brave deeds and encourages amid the tribulation and pain of evils, saying: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16)?

The Lord wished to spread abroad his own name and the glory of his martyr [Note: [Col. 0087D] In manuscript N there is a marginal note: “Of St Aigulf.”] among foreign nations, [Col. 0088D] so that he who lay hidden, as it were, under the bushel of the Church of Sens might answer forth among the nations and amid a multitude of peoples. Perhaps he permitted the fire to touch only their buildings, so that, tested as it were by the benefit of fire, when they are rebuilt through the Lord’s aid, they may appear not only cleaner but also more beautiful.

But when it pleases you to concern yourselves with the Church of the English, make every effort, with careful solicitude, to choose prudent and honourable men for this task, whose sins may not bring the blush of shame upon your innocence. Let them indeed come equipped with letters of recommendation from your princes—not because the matter could not otherwise be completed, but because an undertaking supported by the authority of great men is more easily and more successfully advanced. The lord of Canterbury promises goodwill; the Lord will provide the result. What shall I say of myself, who am wholly yours and theirs?

Henceforth I thank your generosity for the letters of blessed Bernard, repeating my former request that you have copied for me such flowers of his words as you can find, and that whatever of this sort is ready among you be brought by our messengers. Moreover, you promised me relics of blessed Aigulf, for which I cannot sufficiently rejoice; but although your favour is enough for me, I ask, if possible, that you send me by the same persons relics of blessed Savina, Memorius, Frodobert, and the others by whose bread I have been nourished. Whatever you decide to send should be delivered to the messengers under your seal and made authentic by the accompanying text of your letters.

## LETTER XCVIII. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER. [A.D. 1157]

To Henry, bishop of Winchester. [Note: [Col. 0089] “In the name of Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury.”]

Although we might previously have been ignorant of how many and how great evils the absence of a shepherd brings upon the churches of Christ, we have been able to learn it from the loss caused by your journey alone. It is now two years since famine began in your land: not, indeed, a famine of provisions, by the abundance of which the people are turned away from the worship of the Lord and, grown fat, sleek, and bloated, often kick against him; but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. For the little children asked for bread, and there was no one [Col. 0089C] to break it for them.

If therefore we approach one of the neighbours in order to borrow merely the three loaves of the Gospel for your household, we immediately encounter the difficulties of creditors: he opposes such an abundance of excuses that, though his children are at rest in bed, scarcely anyone rises at our importunity and opens even out of regard for us. But if pressing necessity drives us to take refuge with a stranger or traveller, we fear lest he offer us a serpent instead of a fish, or a scorpion instead of an egg. Moreover, your sheep either do not hear, or hear too little, the voice of strangers. Why say more? No account can suffice to tell the Lord’s loss which daily occurs in possessions and morals.
