Hear therefore, dearest brother in the Lord, the lament of the hungry; hear the voices of crying infants; hear the voice of the bride who languishes for love and wastes away in longing for you. [Col. 0089D] Hear at last the voice of the bridegroom, who set you over his household so that you might give it food in due season. Return, then, to your church, and illuminate the whole island with the rays of your wisdom and virtue. Let not losses of possessions move you, when dangers to souls concern you. Without doubt it is more fitting and more just that you devote the watchfulness of your care to the churches entrusted to you than to others. The lord king has assured us of your safety; and, except for two whom he expressly excludes, you will be able to bring whomever you wish into his favour. We shall rejoice at your return and gladly offer whatever aid or counsel we can. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX. TO THE SAME. [A.D. 1157]

When the crisis of temptation presses upon our friends, we have believed that we should show them that course of counsel which seems preferable to others by the appearance of honour or the fruit of usefulness. And although the mind of one in doubt refuses obedience to sound advice, charity’s urgency does not rest until it draws the reluctant friend, even against his will, toward good. Thus we, reverend and most beloved brother in the Lord, advised your fraternity to return to your own place, wholly believing that nothing could better serve your honour or the usefulness of your Church.

For, to pass over the rest, which would be long to recount, the ruin of morals is certainly far more lamentable than that of money. Nor should loss of temporal things be grieved where damage to eternal things is incurred. Of two griefs affecting the same mind, the greater darkens the other. Far be it, moreover, that anyone should dare suspect of your prudence that the basest of things—wealth, that is—moves your mind where souls are in danger. Far be it that envy should insult you with its old proverb:

> “What you bewail, that you loved.”

Choose one of two things: do you want the hazard of litigation or peace? If you prefer the uncertainty of a lawsuit, observe that nothing is more disgraceful than to be conquered by one’s own weapons [Col. 0090C] and, as it were, cut down by one’s own sword. If peace, return—and there is peace. But you are afraid, and indeed where there is no cause for fear. For it has never entered the mind of our most serene lord king to stain the innocence of his life, the integrity of his reputation, and the glory of his kingdom with so great a reproach as to lay his hand, for any cause whatsoever, upon the Lord’s anointed, or to suffer any insult to be inflicted upon him by anyone.

Indeed, he was greatly troubled because you thought it necessary to seek a safe-conduct, since he has never harmed anyone who came to him, however great the hostilities that had arisen. What then were you afraid of when he recalled you by his own voice and by the voices and letters of us all? But the command of the lord pope and the need of your Cluniacs keep you. Yet the lord pope himself will rejoice at your return, unwilling that that command should prejudice your welfare; and you do not doubt that your person is more bound to the churches of Winchester and Glastonbury than to Cluny. You undertook the governance of those churches after being released by the Cluniacs. On what grounds, then, did you turn aside from these to those? Is it fair that, while these are hungry, the others should be fed with their bread? This is the complaint not only of the lord king but of almost everyone. Whether it is just, you must see.

Moreover, from your absence the king complains that in the needs of the realm he is deprived of your counsel and assistance, whereas, at the Lord’s command, the things that are Caesar’s ought to be rendered to Caesar. Hence very many urged him to act more harshly against all your people and to lay hands upon the property of the Church, even upon its inmost treasures. Yet he restrains his hands despite the crowd’s incitement and awaits your arrival in whatever manner he can. If, however, by this provocation you expose the Church and all your people to royal indignation, it is to be feared that evils greater than those feared will come, and that you, who do not wish to avoid the foreseen stings, will afterwards feel sharper ones. We therefore pray and, in the power of charity, advise that you return. Once we hear that you are at Boulogne, we shall meet you on our very shore, arranging for you to reach the lord king with honour and for so great labours to receive a happy conclusion.

## LETTER C. TO POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0091B]

To Pope Alexander.

At the command of your holiness we summoned into our presence the venerable man G., abbot of Westminster, to answer the monks of Malvern concerning the charges which they had advanced against him before you. In the hearing of the case, however, it became manifest to us from the testimony of the venerable men Gilbert, bishop of Hereford; Hamelin, abbot of Gloucester; and Reginald, abbot of Pershore, that the monks of Malvern had deserved worse than they suffered, through their fault of stubbornness and their offence of disobedience—an offence which blessed Benedict teaches should be punished more sharply than others in monasteries, and which the whole Catholic faith and all ecclesiastical discipline detest [Col. 0091C] as the crime of idolatry.

At last, brought to their senses by their abbot, whom they had gravely injured through many wrongs and vexations, they adopted sounder counsel. Falling at his feet, they sought pardon and promised satisfaction; and, after restoring the privilege which they had obtained from the royal majesty by a corrupt suggestion, they were, through our intervention and that of the venerable men present—G., bishop of Rochester, and Silvester, abbot of St Augustine’s—received into his favour, and peace was thus restored. Since it is evident that the cell of Malvern has from the beginning been wholly subject by right to the Church of Westminster, we offer prayers to your excellency, asking that you do not permit it, contrary to the custom of all monasteries, to be deprived of its right, and that you mercifully hear the just petitions of the abbot, from whom we hope for better things.

## LETTER CI. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER. [A.D. 1157]

To Theobald, bishop of Winchester.

We rejoice greatly at your safety, of which we have learned from your messengers; but at that integrity of spirit which does not feel losses of possessions, we give thanks to the Most High, giver of all good things. The trial arising from loss of property had indeed been grave, had it not fallen upon a strong mind; but that strength will shine forth more clearly if, tested by the fire of tribulation, it returns to the fold which, through the shepherd’s absence, lies open to the bites of those who lie in wait.

Nor, beloved brother, is there now any reason why you should fear, since the king himself desires your coming and promises peace and complete security. So that you may not be able to doubt it for any reason, we have received that security into our own hand, giving you a safe-conduct from the sea to the king; we shall arrange accommodation for you and, if necessary, your return. If therefore you love your Church, if you love your soul—indeed, because you love both—do not delay to return when the opportunity has been given, lest, God forbid, as we have often said, the latter circumstances of your condition always become worse than the former. For the indignation of authority established by God will be doubled if it perceives that the grace it has offered is despised.

## LETTER CII. TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Pope Alexander.

[Col. 0092B] Receiving your holiness’s command with due reverence, we have satisfied your creditors, always ready to obey apostolic commands, but readier than ever in the time of your apostolate. For by the Lord’s mercy neither prison nor sword, nor any persecution if one be more severe, will separate us from faith in the Roman Church or from the service of obedience—especially since we see reigning on Peter’s throne him from whom we expect consolation in our sufferings.

Many things, indeed, almost unbearable, we willingly endure for the house of the Lord when it is fitting that this be done; and certainly things greater than it is expedient to commit to writing. We hope, however, with the Lord’s aid, soon to explain them more conveniently to you in person, since the report is celebrated with almost universal agreement that you are coming down into the regions of Gaul. We therefore beseech your majesty, if it please you, to deign to give us advance notice of your arrival, so that we may meet your fatherhood more promptly as is fitting and may sooner rejoice in the much-desired sight and conversation of your blessedness.

Meanwhile, sweetest Father, we ask to be visited often with the comfort of your writings and the benefit of an apostolic greeting, lest the delay of our dutiful longing appear to signify, if not to us then at least to others, contempt for our service, a failure of your favour, or forgetfulness of our former friendship. And because our hearts are continually stirred with unwearying concern over the affliction of our mother, the holy Roman Church, while the mouths of unbelieving sons are opened wide, reproaching us with the labour of the head because of our languor, it is expedient that you order us to be informed by letters—letters which we may show among our people to confirm the faithful—of your own condition and that of the holy Roman Church, and whether the storm is yet abating in the world or any brightness of the peace to come shines forth from somewhere.

A severe illness, demanded by my sins, brought me in the past summer to the gates of death. After I had already made my will and distributed all my possessions down to scant livelihood, the merciful hand of the Almighty withdrew me, so that I might be permitted a little longer to bewail the sins I had committed in this city. For henceforth my days are few. Yet, that my soul may depart more joyfully from the prison-house of the flesh, to give thanks before the sight of the Most High for its benefactors, I lie wholly prostrate with all the intention of my mind at the feet of your clemency, begging that you restore to my Church the profession of the abbot of St Augustine’s which all my predecessors possessed, but which is now, by your pleasure, withheld from me, the last and least of all.

For this is the one pain that consumes my body, tears at my inmost soul, and causes this wound beneath my breast to grow so strong that your clemency may patiently hear me: I grieve and am sorrowful that last winter not even one small petition of mine could be granted, whereas the monks of St Augustine’s obtained against me a multitude of letters. Those letters—the only ones our messengers brought to you for us in that affair—I have, God as witness, trusted to no one thus far for inspection, out of reverence and honour for you, which I always desire to preserve unharmed. Whenever it pleases them, I am dragged, at your command and unwillingly, before the tribunal of my suffragans.

## LETTER CIII. TO R., THE CHANCELLOR

To R., chancellor.

I offer your fatherhood as many thanks as I can, since I cannot render as many as I owe, for the honour and benefits always shown by you to me and mine, and especially because you alone among the many to whom my devotion has at times become known took care to instruct me by your letters, carried in the hands of my messengers, while giving consolation.

Accordingly, acquiescing in your counsel and having summoned those whom it was necessary to summon, I proceeded in word as you instructed me, not intending to depart from apostolic commands even in the least, not even for temporal life. Let the Roman Church see what it especially wants or what is expedient: for its sake, if necessary, I am ready to go both to prison and to death. Whoever says otherwise of me in the hearing of the Roman Church speaks from his own resources, because he speaks a lie. The performance of past deeds is proof of future ones. For the third time I have already exposed myself to dangers, indeed to death, for apostolic commands. Shall I, an old man at the end of my journey and life, exchange the eternal reward of long labour and constant obedience for any deceitful promise of the present time? May the whole world perish before me rather than I perish for it before my God.

I say this because I hear that certain of my lords the cardinals have become hostile to me otherwise than is expedient for me and my Church, or than I have deserved in my conscience. If I have offended them—which I do not recall—I shall most willingly make satisfaction with the humility due to lords and fathers. If I have not offended, I beseech them by the mercy of the Lord and his just judgment to remove the stings of their conceived indignation and restore their favour to me, who henceforth deserve it well. Since my messengers are received less than well by some, I desire this petition—if I dare make such a request—to be presented to my lords the cardinals through your hand, and to receive their replies through your letters.

[Col. 0094A] [Note: [Col. 0093] The Cambridge manuscript attaches this paragraph to the end of the following letter.] It is commonly reported that the lord pope is approaching the borders of Gaul. Therefore, that we may meet him and you more promptly, please give me notice through the bearer of this letter, with dispatch. May your fatherhood live and prosper, remembering me in its prayers.

## LETTER CIV. TO THE CARDINALS

To John Scor. and John Paul, cardinals.

Having embraced obedience from my earliest age, I have preferred nothing to it since then, for its sake having abandoned all things from the beginning. When it pleased him who called me to set his servant, though unworthy, over the Church of Canterbury, I thereafter thought nothing more important than to submit myself with complete devotion to the holy Roman Church and to render it, according to my ability, service always most ready. It will be my pleasure and glory to present my devotion to the Apostolic See each year, or more often.

Yet I am astonished and deeply grieved that the indignation of certain of my lords the cardinals has flamed against me without merit on my part. I am conscious of no fault whatever; but if I have sinned, let them receive me, humbly making satisfaction, into favour. If I have not sinned, then through mercy and the just judgment of the Lord let them receive with brotherly charity one who will always deserve well hereafter; and, ceasing persecution, let them not decline the offices of our service. Let this petition of ours be advanced through your hands, because the presence of our messengers has been received less well by some. The petition of sincere love is confident.

## LETTER CV. TO CARDINAL BOSO

[Col. 0094C]

To Boso, chancellor.

For the honour and benefits often conferred by you upon me and mine, I thank your goodness, praying that the affection of your charity toward me may not grow cold, since the devotion of my service does not rest. But because friends ought to open their hearts to one another, I shall briefly disclose what most torments my soul.

Since I was promoted to the episcopate, I have endeavoured with all my strength to serve the holy Roman Church, believing that through love and observance of justice and continual displays of devotion I could obtain its favour. Yet the contrary has occurred. For although no ill desert proceeds from my conscience, certain of my lords the cardinals, as I hear from some, persecute me severely. I judge this to be especially true because they favour my detractors and support my adversaries. Let it therefore be your concern that, if I have deserved this through my fault, they not reject one who repents with the fruits of due satisfaction. But if, as I believe, I have not deserved it, let them remove the troubles of this bitter hostility out of regard for mercy and the just judgment of God, and not reject from themselves the service of our devotion.

Moreover, what wounds my mind with a still graver grief is that the lord pope, who did not admit my petitions last winter, granted my adversaries—and especially the monks of St Augustine’s—bundles of letters [Col. 0095A] with which they might overwhelm my old age. He granted me letters to the abbot of St Augustine’s concerning the making of a profession which, if I may speak without offence to him, would not have been honourable to the pope, would have disgraced me, and would have brought contempt upon the abbot. For he wrote weakly, directing that the profession be made. But for a long time the cardinals, on the contrary, had instructed the abbot by letters to appeal. Who does not see that letters sent on both sides invited the hazard of a two-sided contest? He likewise ordered that, at the monks’ pleasure, I should come to the court at London to litigate. Why say more? I, who have so many and such great friends in the Roman Church, was not heard in the slightest matter; those monks were heard in everything. I lay these things before your ears with sorrow in heart and speech, so that you may endeavour at some time to prevent similar things. Henceforth, we have satisfied your creditors, receiving nothing from the money of St Bertin.

## LETTER CVI. TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Pope Alexander.

We informed you by letters sent through your Herbert of our situation and that of the Church here; but he either betrayed them through malice, lost them through negligence, or fraudulently pretended that they had been lost. For, after being dismissed by you, he waited with the chancellor of the king of the English for more than a month against your prohibition, and then, having sent a messenger back to England with letters of the aforesaid chancellor, he requested that we send him letters like the former ones, which he said had been taken from him, to carry to you more faithfully. Since he proved too little faithful on the first occasion, we prefer to send our own messenger rather than be deceived a second time through another’s. You may deal with your messenger as you please and, if it seems good, instruct him to conduct your affairs more cautiously and faithfully.

Moreover, the monks of Saint Augustine are plotting to take from us the churches situated on their estates; and because they have found favour in the eyes of the Church of Rome, if you decide that anything is to be left for our welfare or that of our church, do not henceforth admit their petitions to our detriment. Furthermore, know that everyone is free to appeal. You may be assured of this from the fact that some, fleeing to you, have escaped by this remedy alone. Consider how you should proceed [Col. 0095D] with them, and, if any honour is owed to us in their cases, reserve it as you see fit.

## LETTER CVII. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

The archdeacon of Norwich, a man conspicuous for malice, deceitfulness, and skill in lying, shook our realm last summer with his rumours and grievously stirred up the magnates of the kingdom against your faithful servants—indeed, against the Church of God—commonly declaring that he had been sent by you into England, in the bishopric of Norwich, to receive seven hundred marks from William, count of Warenne, son of King Stephen, which the aforesaid count was bound to pay you [Col. 0096A] for hearing his petitions against the king. Under this pretext of excuse, so that he might not be brought before the court in accordance with your command, he repeatedly obtained delays from the lord bishop of Norwich, and long postponed the case pending between himself and Master William, clerk of the lord of Canterbury, concerning the church of Alveston. Yet, by virtue of your letters, justice so requiring, he was defeated and deprived of the aforesaid church in the presence of the Church of Norwich, through the attendance of the bishop to whom you had entrusted the case, without recourse to appeal, within the prescribed term for its conclusion. If, therefore, he attempts to revive an unjust cause, it is not fitting for your goodness to admit his prayers—or rather, his deceptions—but instead to punish him for having falsely claimed, or foolishly boasted, that he was your agent and manager of your affairs. [Col. 0096B] For his boasting sounded badly in everyone's ears.

## LETTER CVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER. (A.D. 1159.)

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

I might be accused of rashness and arrogance for presuming so often to knock at your ears, if the kindness of a Father did not encourage my timidity, and the duty of brotherly charity excuse my boldness. Persuaded, therefore, by the sweetness of your compassion and compelled by the need of an honourable and learned poor man, I fall with my whole heart at the feet of your majesty and offer such prayers as I may to your clemency: kindly receive the bearer of this letter, and do not permit the violence of the archbishop of Sens to take from him his case and the support of his livelihood. [Col. 0096C] If you please, you will hear from the man himself what impedes his justice. Moreover, the precentor of Sens, by his honourable character, his learning, and his special devotion to you, deserves to be heard insofar as equity allows.

Now I return to myself. When it pleases your excellency, repay the bishop of Lisieux for having stirred up against me, your servant, such indignation in our most serene lord king that it is unsafe for me to remain in England, while leaving it is either impossible or exceedingly difficult. Our elders are safe from the abbot of Reading, although he has deceived you together with his Thomas. We shall scarcely be able to wring anything out for the use of our R. Osbert, archdeacon of York, [Col. 0096D] failed in his purgation. Do not believe anyone who tells you otherwise.

## LETTER CIX. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Andrew, clerk of Lenham, complained in our presence that his church of Lenham had been unjustly despoiled of certain tithes, asking that justice be done him against G., priest of Wichelemera, who had occupied them, and against a certain knight Richard, lord of the estate, who supports the occupier. When at last a peremptory day had been fixed for the parties, and the aforesaid Andrew was present, the opposing party, by evasion, resorted to frivolous delays. When the rule of law denied them these, the aforesaid [Col. 0097A] knight said that he had been forbidden by his lord, the noble William, brother of the king, to enter upon the case concerning the tithes in question during William's absence. The aforesaid priest likewise, seeing the knight whose protection he relied upon yield, answered that he would not litigate.

Accordingly, when the plaintiff, having produced the suitable witnesses in which he was well supplied, had urgently obtained from us admission of his proof, and when, after receiving it, we were about to pronounce judgment in his favour upon the advice of the synod, the aforesaid priest appealed to your hearing, setting a day: “As newborn infants.” You, therefore, shall impose the due end upon the case as God inspires you.

## LETTER CX. TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0097B] To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

We had conceived great joy, sweetest Father, hoping, as report had it, that we might this side of the Alps be refreshed by the consolation of your presence. Yet our harp has been turned to mourning and our joy has passed into sorrow, since we learned for certain that the city, begrudging your blessed presence to those on this side of the Alps, preferred to be made illustrious by the glory of your name. Since, therefore, we cannot visit the height of your apostolic office as we desire, we shall again, by envoys sent with speed, supply the customary duty of visitation insofar as we can. May it please your condescension to suspend, until their arrival, the case of the monks of Saint-Bertin, that of Osbert, archdeacon of York, and any matters affecting us and the realm of England; for [Col. 0097C] they will inform your discernment more fully about all these things, and, after hearing them, you will proceed more safely and advantageously in each matter, the Lord being favourable.

## LETTER CXI. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Contrary to expectation and hope, your letters, the receipt of which is usually pleasant, brought us sorrow. For while we awaited your arrival in Gaul with the greatest longing, we learned that you had returned to the city—would that it were beneficially!—and thus the joy of our hope was disappointed. Moreover, our petitions had no effect because, as you wrote, your secretaries may perhaps have lost our letters. But, mitigating as far as we can the bitterness of both misfortunes, we are dispatching with all speed to the Apostolic See envoys who may visit you on our behalf and repair the loss of the letters. We ask that you cause the case of the monks of Saint-Bertin, that of Osbert, archdeacon of York, and whatever matters concern us or the kingdom of England, to be deferred until their arrival. [Col. 0097D] For after hearing them, with God as author, you will settle each matter more beneficially.

## LETTER CXII. TO ARNULF.

To his dearest friend ERNULF, JOHN, his own, greeting and the service of true affection.

I know that the lord chancellor, hindered by the tumult of pressing business, the various occupations of court, and domestic needs, cannot attend to advancing his friends’ petitions unless another urges him. Trusting, therefore, in your intimacy with him, I ask that, having examined the letters which I send him, you encourage him to restore to me the favour of the lord king, and let me know your advice in a return letter. Please write back carefully how the lord king receives the petitions of the lord pope, the bishop of Canterbury, and his own chancellor. It is far more honourable to forewarn a friend truthfully than to deceive him falsely. Missiles, too, wound less when foreseen.

## LETTER CXIII. TO THE KING’S CHANCELLOR. [A.D. 1159.]

[Col. 0098B] To the king’s chancellor.

Among the many grievous injuries inflicted upon me by raging Fortune, I bear nothing more painfully than that, deprived of the consolation of friends, I find no one to share my cares or participate in my grief. From what you see and hear, and from what long experience has taught you, you can easily understand, without the judgment of my own complaint, on what throw of the dice my lot is cast. Yet, that I may disclose it briefly: since our companions returned from you, they have made our common lord their own by promises and rumours, almost to my exclusion—except when burdens must be borne.

> I do not indeed begrudge it; rather, I marvel.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* I.11

If, therefore, my devotion, however slight, has any weight with your excellency; if there remains any memory of our old familiarity; if the assaults of Fortune have not overthrown faith in a friendship tested and proved: act so that the unmerited indignation conceived against me by our most serene lord the king may be softened, and that, at his discretion, I may clear my innocence, or, if I have incurred his displeasure in any matter, may be permitted to regain his favour by suitable satisfaction. Then I may more honourably and freely withdraw myself from so much anxiety, labour, suspicion, and danger—either through the favour of letters or through engagement in another pursuit. [Col. 0098C] For now, if anything is done well, it is credited to others; if anything badly, to me. There is no evil in the city that I am not said to do. My absence may perhaps most conveniently excuse me [Col. 0098D] and enable you more easily to incline his mind.

I send to your affection the lord pope’s letters in my favour; please arrange for them to be returned to me. The messenger of the lord bishop of Ely brought them to me, unasked and without a reply. The lord of Canterbury supports this petition of the lord pope in his own letters.

Moreover, you ordered me to have care of your affairs: I gladly obey, even where my care is of no avail. Our lord has ordered that aid be withdrawn from you in respect of your own churches. Others resisting me, I have stretched out my arms against the torrent in vain. But write to him yourself on these matters. I fear to write you more about the state of the island and the members of the court, since, through the envy of Fortune, some of my letters [Col. 0099A] fall among robbers, others suffer shipwreck, and others, to my loss, shamelessly thrust themselves before the eyes of princes. Yet write back what I ought to do in these and other matters.

## LETTER CXIV. TO MATTHEW, PRECENTOR OF SENS. [A.D. 1159.]

To MATTHEW, precentor of Sens.

I am astonished, my friend, and grieved, if the lord pope has withdrawn the benefit of his indulgence and ordered you to undergo the judgment of men who may rightly be suspect to you and who cannot be summoned except with supreme and almost insuperable difficulty. Although I hesitate for a while, I cannot be persuaded that the sinister hand of the opposing party has prevailed against the right hand of the Roman pontiff. Yet I remember that, under the light burden of words from the imperial majesty, the integrity of the Virgin was oppressed and almost overthrown by the fraudulent incursion of the men of Sens. Rome ought to have regarded the men of Sens as suspect—even when bearing gifts. But perhaps the prince’s chamberlains and assessors, and the most diligent investigators of the sacred palace, deceived religion under the appearance of administering justice and judged that the Gauls should be admitted while they were being squeezed dry.

I do not begrudge their success; rather, I sympathize with your injury and that of the lord precentor, all the more because I can less readily remedy these evils. For the state of affairs among you is unknown to me. Because I am absent, I cannot fully investigate the strength of the case or examine the issues that arise without the parties’ assertions; and therefore [Col. 0099C] in a matter uncertain I cannot offer you definite advice. This will be far more advantageously supplied to you, God being its author, by your natural and cultivated prudence, the faithful diligence of friends, and the sought-after instruction of wise men.

Nevertheless, without prejudice to advice, you should diligently solicit the intervention of the bishop of Auxerre, so that he may admit the lord pope’s petitions made for you; and through him and others carefully investigate the hidden counsel of the opposing party, so that from this you may prepare your case more readily and successfully. If he scorns the petitions, you will draw him, as it were unwillingly, before judges, especially if apostolic letters do not compel you to submit to the judgment of others. Do not, however, believe your adversaries’ assertions in this matter unless they produce the prince’s letters patent. If you can obtain execution of the apostolic mandate from your judges, you will be content. Otherwise, if you plan to proceed to the lord pope, your friends will furnish an honourable reason for the journey—friends whom the nature of the facts and the calculation of the case will instruct more fully by visible evidence. [Col. 0099D] I too will not fail you in whatever I can do. From the bearer of this letter you will receive the letters which, on my behalf, you are to deliver to the lord pope, wishing good to you and to the brethren of the lord precentor—and, would that we might obtain it! If the result does not follow the intention, do not blame the spirit of an old friend, but Fortune.

## LETTER CXV. TO PETER, ABBOT OF LA CELLE. [A.D. 1159.]

To the abbot of La Celle.

I gladly seized an opportunity of writing to you [Col. 0100A] when I saw here a man whom I believed would return to you. Having therefore graciously received the messenger of your greeting, I made an arrangement with him for conveying my greeting to you, after taking security, since the man was unknown to me. I describe in part the things concerning me—and would that I could write happier news! Since returning from the Roman Church, Fortune has heaped upon me so many troubles of her bitterness that I think I had previously endured almost nothing in the way of adversity.

Perhaps you wonder and are astonished what could have so greatly disturbed me. I shall reveal this to you briefly and in your ear. The whole indignation of our most serene lord, our most powerful lord king, our invincible prince, has blazed against me. If you ask the reason: perhaps I supported him more than was just, pressed his advancement beyond what was fitting, longing with all my heart for this—that I might see him, whom I believed exalted through Fortune’s envy, reigning by divine mercy upon the throne of the fathers and declaring law among peoples and nations. [Col. 0100B] Thus perhaps the Lord decreed to punish the impatience of my desire. Whatever is sought impatiently brings the stings of grief either through its flight or its attainment.

Yet I am not accused of this fault; rather, a matter wholly beyond my powers—and one for which its magnitude may excuse my smallness—is charged against my innocence. I alone in the kingdom am said to diminish royal majesty. When they describe more closely the deed alleged against me, they twist these things onto my head: whatever person invokes the Roman name among us, they lay to my charge. Whatever shadow of liberty the English Church dares to claim for itself in holding elections or examining ecclesiastical cases, is imputed to me, as though I alone instructed the lord of Canterbury and the other bishops what they ought to do. [Col. 0100C] For these reasons I am utterly shaken; indeed, under this pressure, exile is thought to threaten me. I shall endure it for justice’s sake, if necessary, not merely with equanimity but even with joy. Therefore I expect to leave England before the Kalends of January, having taken your advice, to remain in Gaul and then proceed from there to the Roman Church.

Meanwhile, I give your goodness all the thanks I can for the honour and generosity you showed to my brother; and I ask that on my behalf you convey thanks to the abbot of Boullecourt for visiting my brother. After the prior of Cantumerle has privately read this letter, take care that it does not pass before the eyes and ears of many people. [Col. 0100D]

## LETTER CXVI. TO THOMAS, PROVOST OF LA CELLE.

To THOMAS, provost of La Celle.

Having examined the letters which I send to the lord of La Celle, your prudence will be able partly to infer my circumstances. As for what especially concerns you, know that your friend P. is healthy and well, and enjoys great prosperity. As for the man whom, at your request, we commended to the lord chancellor of the king, the treasurer of York and I recently saw him healthy [Col. 0101A] and in good condition, although he cannot be entirely free from the king’s exactions.

## LETTER CXVII. TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

The case pending between Suanus and Baldwin, priests, concerning the church of Chiltedic, was brought from the tribunal of our venerable brother Richard, bishop of London, to our hearing by the aid of an appeal. The said Suanus therefore sought restoration of the aforesaid church to himself, complaining that he had been unjustly deprived of it without judgment, after, as he said, violently expelling his vicar. Baldwin, raising a dilatory objection, replied that he could not lawfully be sued concerning the aforesaid church [Col. 0101B] until the goods of that church, which he said had been taken from him by the force and fraud of the aforesaid Suanus, were restored. Nevertheless, he was ready to answer on the principal matter if Suanus cleared himself by an oath tendered to him.

Suanus, however, was unwilling either to undergo the risk of the oath or to tender it back, maintaining that his claim could not be removed by any obstacle of exception through the judgment of the lord bishop of London. When the opposing party admitted this, saying that it had appealed for the reason that on one day it had received from the same bishop of London, together with this judgment, two other perverse judgments, Suanus appealed to your presence, setting the Octave of the Apostles as the day, although we were ready to render complete justice to both parties.

## LETTER CXVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER.

[Col. 0101C]

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

The compassion of brotherly charity warns us to entreat your majesty on behalf of our venerable brother William, bishop of Norwich, that you command a due end to be put to the vexations and injuries which Wachelin, archdeacon, incessantly inflicts upon him. We have taken care to make known to your sincerity how necessary this is, prompted by hatred of injustice and abhorrence of scandal rather than by any regard for persons.

For it happened recently in London, when we were holding an assembly, that the aforesaid bishop, constrained by certain necessities, approached our venerable brother the bishop of London—namely, the man to whom, [Col. 0101D] together with the bishop of Worcester, you had delegated cognizance of the accusation brought against Wachelin—with a most pitiable petition. He asked that, at least on that day, which had then been set as the third peremptory day, after many vexations of himself and of many good men, the bishop admit his proofs: that he had restored to the aforesaid archdeacon what had been taken from him in accordance with the form of your mandate, or had rendered justice, unless in every respect the fault lay with Wachelin himself.

He brought forward a multitude of religious men—abbots, archdeacons, priors, and clerks—intending to prove by their testimony what he had alleged. Very many other men of unimpaired reputation also came forward. Out of love for justice and to shame iniquity, they said they were ready to prove that they had heard the aforesaid [Col. 0102A] archdeacon, after the bishop had offered remission of all the restitutions he demanded and, in addition, sixty marks of silver from his own resources, on the condition that the same bishop obtain absolution for him from his crimes, reject the bishop’s offer—partly because he could not grant it, and partly lest he appear to have received the marks as the price of redeeming such great crimes.

Since all alike, clergy and laity, were scandalized beyond measure by these things, the lord bishop of London could neither conceal nor wished to conceal that the aforesaid proofs had then been offered for the third time, whereas Wachelin had appeared at none of the three peremptory citations. He added that, without the bishop of Worcester, to whom cognizance of the case had been jointly delegated and who was absent, he could not and ought not decide anything on the appointed day. [Col. 0102B] It is therefore for your discernment, if you please, to counter promptly the evasions in which the aforesaid archdeacon puts his trust, and to bring relief through the remedy of peace to the bishop, who has been afflicted by vexations for so long.

## LETTER CXIX. TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Jordan, prior of Acre, initiated proceedings against Osbert, priest, concerning the church of Trichestana, saying that he possessed the aforesaid church, which he had entered without the prior’s consent, without another patron, without the solemn order of law and the custom of the realm, and despite the unwillingness and protest of the parishioners. Osbert replied that he had canonically entered the same [Col. 0102C] church, Count Warenne, the patron, presenting him and William, archdeacon of Norwich, acting in the place of Everard, bishop of Norwich of good memory, inducting him and granting him the aforesaid church with all its rights. He added that he had proved this by the statements of lawful witnesses in the presence of our venerable brother William, bishop of Norwich, as the bishop testified in letters sent to us.

Nevertheless, he maintained that he ought not to be compelled to establish the author or title of his possession, since a defendant retains possession, even if he proves nothing, unless the claimant proves what he alleges. Accordingly, when our venerable brother the bishop of Chichester pressed the prior to establish his claim if he wished to proceed in the case, the aforesaid priest appealed to your hearing, setting the day as the Sunday on which is sung: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.”

## LETTER CXX. TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Our venerable brother Robert, bishop of Bath, restored the church of Cerda to our beloved son, your faithful servant William Cumin, in accordance with the command of your mercy, by which you had ordered that it be restored to him, appeal set aside, if it were clear that he had made full satisfaction to the church of Durham. Now a certain clerk named A. is said to be going to the Apostolic See in order to invalidate this benefit of your clemency. Therefore we offer to your [Col. 0103A] majesty such prayers as we can for W., beseeching you faithfully to preserve what your goodness has deigned mercifully to confer upon him, and mercifully to hear him in his just petitions.

## LETTER CXXI. TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Among all that your goodness has done, nothing is more welcome to the lord king of England than the mercy which you extended to your faithful servant William Cumin. A certain brother named A. of Cerda strives to nullify this, would that he had a better life and a more unimpaired reputation! He desires that your majesty should be subject to fickleness and inconsistency—far be it! It would have been better, Father, never to hear the man crying out than gratuitously to dispossess one restored, and cast down without fault one lawfully in possession. [Col. 0103B] May it therefore please your condescension justly to preserve what you mercifully bestowed, and mercifully hear him in his just petitions.

Moreover, the bishop of Lisieux is a hammer of iniquity for crushing the Church of God. He has heaped upon me, a poor man, such royal indignation that the king himself has declared to the lord of Canterbury and his chancellor that I have diminished the royal majesty and must therefore be excluded from the number of friends and faithful servants. Even after hearing the letters in which your kindness excused my innocence, that faulty and lying man dared to say: “The lord pope wrote what he wished; therefore I report to the lord [Col. 0103C] king what I know to be true.” Let your compassion therefore provide for me and endeavour to restore the king’s favour.

## LETTER CXXII. TO THE SAME.

To the lord pope.

A clerk from the household of William, archbishop of York of good memory, named Symphorianus, accused Osbert, archdeacon of York, in the presence of King Stephen and the bishops and barons of England at a notable assembly, of the crime of poisoning. He said that the aforesaid archbishop had been killed by poison administered to him by the archdeacon at the Lord’s table, and promised firmly to prove this by red-hot iron, boiling water, single combat, or another judgment. [Col. 0103D] Osbert, however, most steadfastly denied the crime and replied that, by the privilege of his rank and order, he was subject not to lay judgment but only to ecclesiastical judgment, to which he was ready in every respect to submit.

Accordingly, when both parties had furnished sureties in the king’s hand for pursuing the suit according to the custom of our people, the dispute was postponed until the Octave of Epiphany. The king claimed, though we and our brethren protested and resisted, that the case belonged to his court because of the atrocity of the crime and because it had begun in his presence.

Meanwhile our most serene lord King Henry succeeded King Stephen. From his hands, only with the greatest difficulty, with a strong hand, and amid the indignation of the king and all the magnates, we recalled the aforesaid case to ecclesiastical examination. [Col. 0104A] As, owing to numerous intervening delays, the question had necessarily been prolonged, and the accuser—namely S.—could not complete the accusation according to the subtleties of laws and canons, we examined the sacred canons and, on the advice of our venerable brethren Richard, bishop of London; Hilary, bishop of Chichester; Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury; Robert, bishop of Exeter; and other wise men present, because the report was spread throughout the whole island, imposed upon the aforesaid archdeacon a purgation by the hands of three archdeacons, with four other deacons joining him. We set a day for the performance of that purgation.

As that day approached, the said archdeacon came to us, declaring that he preferred to establish his innocence before the Roman Church, to which the report had perhaps reached. He placed himself and all his affairs under your protection and, by apostolic authority, prohibited anyone from determining anything to his injury. He also added that at the Octave of Epiphany he would present himself before your sight. Therefore, as was fitting, deferring to the apostolic majesty, we reserved the determination of the affair for your holiness. [Col. 0104B]

## LETTER CXXIII. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Divine providence set your excellency over the head of all the Churches so that, once vices have been driven out from the house of the Lord, virtue may take pleasant increase, and the perfected completeness of your majesty may supply what is imperfect in all humanity. The case pending between our beloved brethren Rad., of Durham, and the monks of the Church of Canterbury recently escaped from our hands to apostolic examination by the aid of an appeal. Its nature is as follows.

The said Rad. sought through our office the restoration of revenues of seventy pounds which he had held in the church of Dover, or repayment to him of an equivalent compensation from other revenues. He said that they were bound to this by an oath which Auricus the chamberlain, in the name and by command of the convent, had sworn when [Col. 0104D] Rad. gave way for the monks to enter the church of Dover. He promised to prove this too by lawful witnesses. The prior and monks, however, said that his claim was empty, since they had always satisfied him under the aforesaid agreement by the assigned revenue. They added that they were ready to submit to an accounting in order to make up, at the decision of a good man, whatever might further be due to him.

Rad. replied that he would not litigate these matters except before your hearing, summoning the prior and monks before your tribunal concerning the oath sworn, and the prior specifically, together with his brother Hugh, concerning contempt of you: for, in that parish, enjoying the protection of your patronage, they had built a chapel against the reverence due to law and despite my opposition. He therefore fixed the day as Palm Sunday. [Col. 0105A]

## LETTER CXXIV. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

He who presumes to deceive, by any colouring of falsehood, the Holy Spirit dwelling in you—as is deserved by your virtues, granted by succession, and privileged by your see—calls down upon himself a sentence of death, as Ananias testifies; especially when a lying petitioner labours to the detriment of right and the injury of another. Now the bearer of this letter, Nicholas, was despoiled, while absent, unheard, and unsummoned, by our venerable brother David, bishop of St Davids, of the archdeaconry which he canonically held, contrary to every reverence of law. This occurred through letters which a certain Jordan, perhaps unknown to you, obtained from your clemency by false prayers, not without the astonishment of the whole English Church. [Col. 0105B]

This is he, best Father, this is the man publicly perjured, stained with the public infamy of an earlier accusation of homicide, whom your holy predecessor Eugenius deprived of ecclesiastical office and benefice for the crime of forgery committed in apostolic letters. Cast down by that sentence, he hid in remote corners among unknown peoples until he learned that the aforesaid father had been removed from human affairs. We therefore beseech your majesty that, considering the justice and pitiable poverty of the bearer of this letter, you mercifully correct what has been enormously done against him; and, after restoring him, command the case to be tried through lawful procedures on its own merits—if, indeed, you determine that your predecessor’s sentence should be set aside and that a man already condemned is owed an action rather than a penalty. [Col. 0105C]

## LETTER CXXV. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Since all the faithful enjoy the protection of the holy Roman Church, those whose desires justice supports, and who advance their neighbours’ virtues by the encouragement of holy conduct, flee with greater confidence in need to the bosom of its mercy. We have learned from the testimony of public report that the brethren who serve the Lord with the utmost devotion at Tewkesbury are such men. Therefore we offer to your majesty prayers as sincere as they are confident on their behalf, beseeching with all the devotion we can that you fulfil their just desires, so that, gladdened by the easy and happy outcome of their affairs, they may strive more earnestly to obtain from the Most High for you the successes of both lives.

Among other things, a certain knight is attempting to take from them a church which they have held unchallenged for forty years, under pretext of an advowson, which laymen among us most perniciously claim against the Church of God. [Col. 0105D] They are dragged on that account before the Apostolic See, as though they could there suffer the burden of injuries, where rights originate. But, with the Lord as author, following in the footsteps of your holy predecessors, you will so curb one man’s rashness that others, instructed by his example, will never dare to aspire to similar acts. [Col. 0106A]

## LETTER CXXVI. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

In accordance with the command of your holiness, we carefully admonished the nobleman Hugh of Dover to restore to the monks of Saint-Bertin the church of Chilleham. They complained that it belonged, as they said, to the right of their monastery and had been violently taken from them without judgment. He promised that he would obey apostolic commands and the law in every respect with the greatest devotion; but he charged that the petitions which the monks had submitted to you were false in many particulars.

First, he asserted that the aforesaid church did not belong to the monastery’s right, since they had never possessed it with the consent of himself or any of his predecessors; especially since the status of a church cannot be changed or subjected to servitude without the founder’s consent—much less against his opposition. [Col. 0106B] Next, he said that the monks had never possessed it in their own name, but in that of a certain Odo, whom that most notorious tyrant and most grievous persecutor of our church, William of Ypres, had somehow procured to be put in possession after the lord of the estate had been disinherited.

He further asserted that, by the fraud of collusion, the monks had assigned fixed revenues to the said Odo so that he might cede the aforesaid church to them; that this too was publicly known; and that thus, through simony, they had held whatever possession of the church they had, while our venerable brother Roger, now archbishop of York but then archdeacon of Canterbury, prohibited this very thing by apostolic authority. Finally, he said that when the aforesaid tyrant was expelled from the kingdom of England, the abbot and monks of Saint-Bertin who had been present renounced forever the suit and possession which they had held, so that they might be allowed, God permitting, to carry off the fruits of the aforesaid church. [Col. 0106C] He promised to prove all these things more than sufficiently.

Moreover, he said that he had already sent envoys to your majesty to expose there the monks’ fraud and malice; nonetheless, he was prepared to demonstrate his innocence and justice at our hearing. When, therefore, wishing as was proper to ascertain the truth of the petitions, we set the monks a day, they replied that they would not submit to the case unless they were restored without examination. We, therefore, being unwilling to proceed to the prejudice of the matter and the subversion of law, await your command, prepared to obey you in all things and in every respect. [Col. 0106D]

## LETTER CXXVII. TO THE SAME.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER.

Although we put our words in the mouths of our messengers—men whose honour and fidelity rightly require that they be believed—we have nevertheless taken care to inform your fatherhood by letter how proceedings took place in our presence in the case of the monks of Saint-Bertin concerning the church of Chilleham. The nobleman Hugh of Dover, [Col. 0107A] warned by us at your command to restore the aforesaid church, together with everything taken from it, to the monks who complained that they had been violently despoiled by him, replied that no right to restitution belonged to them, since those who had never been instituted could not have been deprived.

He said that he had held the property of the said church, from which they seemed to derive their claim, not in his own name but in another’s—namely, that of a certain Odo, whom we ourselves know to have possessed the church in question. But whether Odo renounced it or transferred it to another, we wholly do not know. We also know for certain that our archdeacon, who is now Archbishop of York, after an appeal had been lodged, forbade the monks to involve themselves in the goods of that church. Nevertheless, [Col. 0107B] because the times were evil, and that notorious tyrant and most grievous persecutor of our Church, William of Ypres—whom the said Odo supported—was threatening us, we had to dissemble when, disregarding the appeal, the monks began to handle Odo’s property in William’s patrimony under William’s name, Odo thus providing for his own future.

Moreover, even if it were established that the monks had possessed it in their own name, he excluded their claim by saying that they had renounced both possession and litigation when he permitted them to carry away the revenues of the church, offering to prove this most fully. When therefore the knight pressed the monks either to establish their claim or to allow proof of his defence, the monks, [Col. 0107C] declining the contest, demanded that they be restored without examination of the case.

To this the knight replied that your majesty had not ordered them to be instituted, but restored; and that, from the word “restoration,” together with the other matters contained in your sacred rescript, full examination of the case had been entrusted to us. Since, as he said, they had misled your religious disposition by a false representation, they were unwilling to proceed to proof. He said that he would report everything for your consideration, and would obey you in all things as Father and lord.

But as time went on, before his messenger reached you, you repeated your command that the knight be compelled. We therefore, showing due reverence and obedience to your commands, although the knight always offered himself to justice [Col. 0107D] and, conversely, the monks avoided the outcome of judgment, sequestrated the church with all its appurtenances, even at our own peril. We retain it in our own hands until both the truth of the matter is made more fully known to you and your will is made more fully known to us.

If they have produced to you a charter drawn up in our name, know that it was extorted from us by the force and fear of the aforesaid tyrant—if we may confess our own weakness. Nor should your majesty be unaware that your devoted servant John, treasurer of York, whom the monks assert to have occupied the often-mentioned church through a lay hand, never stretched out his hand toward it or involved himself in its case in any way, except that he faithfully stood by an old friend, whom he could not abandon in need without dishonour and enormous loss to his friends. [Col. 0108A]

We therefore beseech your graciousness to command whatever shall please you in this matter with such moderation that, if the monks have any right, they may obtain it in such a way that we do not incur the indignation of the lord king and the persecution of all the magnates who have been scandalized by this affair. We pray that you will cheer your faithful servant, your beloved son John, treasurer of York—whose happiness you have somewhat disturbed through the malicious allegation of the monks—with the benefit of due consolation.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF NORWICH (A.D. 1156)

To the Bishop of Norwich.

[Col. 0108B] We have received our messengers returning from the lord king safely. They promise, at the king’s arrival, the desired fulfilment of our requests. For in all things he will acquiesce in the archbishop’s counsel, and with the whole intention of his mind will devote himself more zealously to the honour and advantage of the Church.

In the meantime, however, he cannot remit the scutage or refrain from certain exactions, because the reconciliation with his brother, badly patched up, has come together in vain; indeed it has been most ruinously torn apart because the brother would not renounce to the lord king the whole paternal inheritance—particularly the land whose possession a stronger force had taken from him—although he was prepared both to surrender his fortresses to the king and to give hostages, in order to recover the land which he had received as his father’s gift.

He has therefore gone [Col. 0108C] to the king of France, relying on Count Theobald’s aid; he is stirring up the French to our harm and trying to expose their throats to our wealth, forces, and power. Perhaps he is acting so that fortune may thereby deserve still more grievously to give the king and people of France into our hands, with justice’s favour. We shall fulfil in him the measure of our fathers, if only we choose to be content with their lot. Yet what fortune promises us if Vernon is restored is indeed greater.

The French, on Count Theobald’s advice, have deprived us of the hoped-for conference. The lord king, returning from Anjou and Poitou, will send men to us to manage affairs in their entirety and, by exercising judicial administration entrusted to them, compensate in his absence for the losses inflicted upon him.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0108D]

To Lord Pope Alexander.

The members have their life from the head, and from the holy Roman Church, by the Lord’s authorship, comes the salvation of all Churches. Therefore all must have recourse to you when a crisis of necessity presses which they cannot resolve for themselves.

We have here a difficult case between our venerable brother Michael, Bishop of Llandaff, and Robert, son of his predecessor, which, unless apostolic authority intervenes, we do not believe will reach an end in our lifetime. We have long been harassed by it, but could by no form of correction restrain the recklessness of the aforesaid Robert, so that his latest deeds, as [Col. 0109A] they were reported to us, were always worse than the former. Not to speak of bodily uncleanness, very many persons brought us reports of his arsons, robberies, and various kinds of crimes.

As often as, with much care and labour, we restored peace between him and his opponents, so often peace was torn apart by him and withdrew after being restored. At last, excommunicated by his bishop, he approached your majesty; but whether he deserved the favour of your absolution, we do not know. He nevertheless brought apostolic letters commanding our venerable brother the Bishop of Worcester to render him and certain of his accomplices justice against the Bishop of Llandaff and his archdeacon Ralph.

Then, after a few days had passed, his opponents brought us letters of your blessedness commanding that [Col. 0109B] the case be brought to its proper conclusion without evasion by appeal, notwithstanding the rescript which Robert had obtained from your gentleness through surreptitious means. When the parties were therefore summoned into our presence in accordance with the apostolic command, Robert’s opponents raised many crimes against his claims by way of defence. Among these they also charged him with the crime of lèse-majesté, saying that he had committed forgery in the letters of yours which he produced.

To you indeed, and to the brethren who were present, we presented the discrepancy and the letters, which he appeared deliberately to have made, as wholly suspect and therefore, in our judgment, to be referred to the examination of your highness. He, however, firmly said that he had received the case from you and acknowledged the Roman pontiff as author of everything [Col. 0109C] contained in the letters.

Accordingly, after taking counsel with our brethren and receiving from him a sworn assurance that he would abide by your command, we send the same letters to you through your beloved son Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff. We ask that you hear him in his just petitions and look with the eyes of your mercy upon the miseries of the Church of Llandaff which he will set forth to you. Moreover, if it please you, write back to us what punishment ought to be inflicted upon corruptors of your letters. For it is difficult to await the counsel of your majesty in every individual case of this kind that arises.

## LETTER CXXX. TO AN ABBESS

[Col. 0109D]

We can no longer conceal the manifold and grave offences of your negligence, even if for the moment they are so called, since your misdeeds have reached the ears of the Roman pontiff and provoke the indignation of the holy Roman Church against your innocence.

We have often warned you to abstain by every means from the notorious intimacy and cohabitation of Hugh, the official, which is an offence and scandal to all connected with your religious house, since by the Lord’s command even a foot or an eye must for such a reason be cast away. Thus far we have borne your contempt, however we could; but we still grieve over the danger to your soul and reputation, and indeed we shall cause you grief without delay unless you change your life for the better and strive by swift correction to restore the reputation of your house. [Col. 0110A]

For we have received the apostolic command and rebukes, which instruct us that we must not spare you if we spare you further in your errors. Therefore, commanding you in the power of obedience, we order you to remove the aforesaid Hugh from the familiarity and society of your household within seven days of receiving this letter, and not permit him to conduct the administration of your church. Otherwise, if you presume to act contrary to this, know that you stand condemned by the authority of the lord pope. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXI. TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Lord Pope Alexander.

That you may more conveniently judge concerning matters which pass from us to the examination of your majesty, [Col. 0110B] the sequence of events must faithfully be communicated to your holiness.

A controversy of this kind was pending before us between Philip of Danthehela and Reginald of Ledescumba. Osmund of Salisbury possessed, in the name of the said Philip, the churches of Renebera, Lidescumba, and Falesleia. The said Reginald, however, possessed the churches of Lidecumba and Falesleia in the name of the aforesaid agent, namely Osmund, paying him an annual pension.

When the said Osmund, weighed down by sickness, lawfully entered the religious order of regular brethren, he summoned Philip, who possessed them, to resign his property to him. The agent’s accounts having therefore been settled, Philip peacefully entered the church of Renteberia. But when he went on [Col. 0110C] to Lidecumba and Falesleia, he was by no means admitted by the aforesaid Reginald.

When judicial assistance was sought to repel the violence, and Philip appeared to be about to be put in possession, Reginald, who had already entered into possession, appealed to our hearing. On the appointed day, the parties appearing before us, Philip, sufficiently supported by witnesses, instruments, and charters of the Bishop of Salisbury and of Amesbury monastery, said that the churches of Lidecumba and Falesleia were his and that he had possessed them through Osmund.

Reginald replied that he had long possessed them peacefully as his own, but that he had come insufficiently prepared, although he had abundant documents and witnesses available. We therefore thought fit to grant him about four months—[the text appears to read *quorum*, perhaps *quatuor*]—in which he might sufficiently prepare his case. When that period had almost elapsed, the oft-mentioned Reginald appeared before us, saying that he regarded our court with suspicion and lacked witnesses and documents because the aforesaid Philip was our household member and kinsman, and was consequently formidable to many persons.

We, however, were prepared to compel any witnesses he had to bear testimony to the truth, or to delegate the case to another bishop in whom they had greater confidence, so that our authority might not seem in any respect harmful to him. Nevertheless, appealing on that very account to your hearing, he fixed the feast of Saint Andrew for examination of the case. We therefore, yielding to your honour as was both your wish and our duty, send the case to you, asking only that, preserving justice for both sides, you order the case to be decided by others [Col. 0111A] in such a way that every occasion for suspicion and the necessity of labour are removed from us.

## LETTER CXXXII. TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Lord Pope Alexander.

Richard of Ambly asserts that he possesses the church of Wacheringerii in the name of certain monks, to whose right it is known to belong. A certain Ralph claimed it from the aforesaid monks before the Bishop of London, while Richard of Ambly was neither present nor summoned.

Nevertheless, as the bishop’s messengers afterwards showed us, moved by the confession of the opponents and by certain documents, the bishop adjudged the said church to Ralph—perhaps with the monks’ consent—[Col. 0111B] although two clerks of Richard of Ambly were present, one of whom asserted that he was Richard’s business representative. Both publicly protested that Richard, being absent and unsummoned, ought in no way to be condemned. They therefore appealed from the judgment of the lord Bishop of London to our hearing.

On the appointed day Richard and Ralph appeared, with monks supporting them. After the case had been long debated, the said Ralph produced two documents which we had retained, because one was marked by the defect of manifest deformity and the other was charged with falsity. Nevertheless Ralph repeated his demand for the church adjudged to him.

But because the prior of the monks was absent, who could have informed us more carefully about the case, and because we also wished to ascertain more fully [Col. 0112A] the truth about the documents, the case seemed to require adjournment to another day. Therefore the aforesaid Ralph, alleging that the case on appeal ought not to be suspended, appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See, fixing the Sunday on which is sung: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.”

## LETTER CXXXIII. TO THOMAS, PROVOST OF CELLES

To Thomas, provost of Celles.

We formerly received a command from Pope Eugenius of blessed memory to decide the case between the monks of Crowland and a certain Haldon concerning the church of Sutterton and certain tithes. Accordingly, carrying out that command and conducting careful inquiry into the aforesaid matter, we adjudged the church to the monks [Col. 0112B] with full restitution of what had been taken; restitution amounting in value to fifteen marks was proved by the oath of suitable witnesses.

When the monks frequently demanded restitution and the same tithes before the lord Bishop of Lincoln, Haldon at last appealed to our hearing. When both parties stood before us, Haldon began to reopen the case, long since decided, concerning the church of Sutterton. But while the monks persisted in their claim, demanding the fifteen marks adjudged to them together with certain tithes, Haldon, asserting that he ought not to answer concerning these matters, appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See, fixing the Sunday on which is sung: “As newly born.”

[Col. 0111] Thus far are the letters which John wrote while he was still in England; there follow letters which he wrote after the year of the Lord 1164, when he was in exile in France together with Saint Thomas.

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0111C]

To the venerable Father and dearest lord Thomas, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury: his own John of Salisbury sends greeting and happy success according to his wishes.

Since I reached the lands on this side of the sea, I seemed to have felt the mildness of a gentler breeze; and with joy I marvelled, amid the swelling storms of tempests, at the abundance of things everywhere and at the peace and gladness of the peoples. When I left the ship, the servants of the Count of Guînes, by his command and through the agency of Ernulf his nephew, received me honourably; and, displaying to me and mine the count’s house and land out of reverence for you, they conducted us, free from every customary burden, almost as far as Saint-Omer.

When [Col. 0111D] I had arrived there, through the agency of a certain monk Marsilius, who was accustomed to reside at Chilleham and Truleigh, I was received most honourably in the house of Saint-Bertin. I clearly understood that that church is devoted to the honour of the Church of Canterbury and to yours. If it please you, return thanks both to the count and to the monks when an opportunity is offered.

From there, when I came to Arras, I heard that Count Philip was at the castle of Écluses, from which the tyrant of Ypres had been driven out after so long a siege. I therefore turned aside thither; [Col. 0112C] and, the Lord mercifully prospering my journey in all things, not far from the public road I met the man I sought. For, in the manner of rich men, whom this sort of frivolous pastime delights, he was amusing himself with the birds of the air, roaming about rivers, pools, marshes, and bubbling springs.

He rejoiced to have found someone from whom he could faithfully hear of the condition of England; and I rejoiced still more because God had offered him to me, so that I could carry out your commission without much loss of time on the road. He asked many questions about the king and magnates, but I restrained my reply, so that conscience might not reproach me with falsehood nor anyone accuse my recklessness in matters touching the king.

On hearing of your troubles, he sympathized with you and promises assistance. He will procure ships if your need [Col. 0112D] requires this, provided that he himself is properly warned beforehand. But if the storm should drive you to this course, send in advance either Philip, your buyer, or another trustworthy agent, who can use the count’s authority and make such arrangements with sailors and carriers as circumstances require. Leaving the count in this way, I came to Noyon the following day.

By I know not what report of swift and restless rumour, the calamity of the English and the affliction of the Churches had been spread abroad wherever I came, so that there I heard many things alleged to have happened in the assembly at London and Winchester [Col. 0113A] which I had never heard in England. Indeed, as commonly happens, most things were reported greater and worse than the truth. I carefully concealed all these matters which flew about on people’s lips; yet no one fully believed one who dissembled prosperity, nor one who concealed adversity.

And, remarkably, on the day when I was at Noyon, the Count of Soissons set forth to the dean all the articles of the London—whether I should call it a little council or a little un-council, I do not know—so consecutively as though he had personally been present at everything, not only at what occurred in the palace but also at what was said most secretly by this man or that in the private chamber. I could scarcely believe that the French had not there had prudent spies, either among their own people or among ours.

The dean of Noyon, a man of wholly unimpaired fidelity, heard of your oppression with no little grief. He is preparing to join you, not merely to place all that he possesses at your disposal, but, if necessary, to give himself for the Church of Canterbury. He had decided to go to the curia; but because he is uncertain and anxious about your situation, he waits at home until he is more certainly informed.

There I learned from some people as certain that the King of France was at Laon and that the lord of Reims was awaiting a conference near him. I therefore intended to approach them. But because of the wars waged by the Count of Rosières and certain other magnates against the lord of Reims, I abandoned that plan and turned my journey toward Paris.

There, seeing an abundance of provisions, the joy of the people, the reverence of the clergy, the majesty and glory of the whole Church, [Col. 0113C] and the varied occupations of philosophers, I marvelled—as at that ladder of Jacob whose summit touched heaven and which was the way of angels ascending and descending—and, compelled by the impulse of a happy pilgrimage, I confessed: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28).

That poetic line also came to mind:

> Happy the exile to whom this place is granted.

After a few days spent in hiring lodging and arranging my small baggage, I approached the King of France and set forth your case to him in order. In brief: he sympathizes, promises aid, and declared that he had written to the lord pope on your behalf; he will write again if necessary and will do what he can by personal speech.

When I greeted him on behalf of his daughter, whom I had lately seen in good health when I took leave from the lord queen, [Col. 0113D] he answered that it would be most pleasing to him if she had already been received by the angels into paradise. When I added that this would one day happen through God’s mercy, but that first she would bring joy to many peoples, the king replied: “That indeed is possible to God; but it is much more likely that she will become the cause of many evils. Yet may what a father’s mind forebodes be far from her! For,” he said, “I scarcely hope that any good can come from her.” [Col. 0114A]

The French both fear and hate our king; yet, as far as they are concerned, he can sleep in calm and deep slumber.

Since I could not approach the Archbishop of Reims, I sent my letters to the abbot of Saint-Remi, who is most friendly to me, that he might in this matter discharge my office. Moreover, it seems advisable to me that, through some monk of Boxley or another trustworthy messenger, you send your letters with some small gift to the lord of Reims and establish a friendship with him. For, whatever he may be personally, he is powerful in the kingdom of France and has great influence in the Roman Church, both through the king and through the eminence of his own church.

I have not yet gone up to the Roman Church, avoiding, as far as I can, any plausible suspicion being conceived against me. This itself, as I learned from the letters of the lord of Poitiers, has become sufficiently known to the lord pope and the curia. Upon receiving your letters, I immediately wrote to Lord Henry and William of Pavia, and explained sufficiently how greatly the actions undertaken against you, if they proceed, tend toward the ruin of the Roman Church. [Col. 0114B]

I deferred going there because nothing was certain concerning the crossing of the Abbot of Saint Augustine or the Bishop of Lisieux. If they come to the curia, we shall quickly be informed through Master Henry, who resides there.

But what we can then do for you, I do not clearly see. Many things are against you, few for you. For great men will come, lavish in the expenditure of money, [Col. 0114C] which Rome has never despised.

> [Note: [Col. 0113D] Understand this of certain courtiers who perform various offices concerning ecclesiastical affairs. As men, they may sometimes be infected by insane greed; this is not to say that the successor of blessed Peter or his chair of incorruptible holiness suffers any impairment. Yet John of Salisbury, indulging too greatly in zeal for the cause which he had undertaken, scarcely seems, while writing this and what follows, to have remembered the reverence due to the supreme pontiff. EDITION OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.]

They will be supported not only by their own authority but by that of the lord king, whom the curia will dare to offend in no matter. Moreover, they will be fortified by privileges of the Roman Church, which in such cases has never, or seldom, deferred to any bishop whatsoever. In this case the lord pope has always opposed us and still does not cease to reproach what Adrian, a lover of the Church of Canterbury, did for us—Adrian, whose mother is tortured among you by cold and hunger.

We are humble, poor, unprotected: shall we be able to give the Romans words? But they long ago heard their comic poet’s warning not to buy hope at a price.

But you write that, finally, if no other way is open, we should promise two hundred marks. Yet certainly the opposing party, before it is defeated, will give three hundred or [Col. 0114D] four hundred:

> Nor, if you contend with gifts, will Iollas yield.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* II.55)

And I answer for the Romans that, out of love for the lord king and respect for his messengers, they would rather receive more than hope for less. What serves your cause is that you suffer for the liberty of the Church; but the king’s advocates and your rivals, diminishing the honour of our cause, will endeavour to attribute this more to rashness than to liberty.

And, that they may more readily be believed, they will give the lord pope—for “my ear has now caught the faint whisper of this rumour” (Job 4)—hope of coming to England. They will say that the royal son’s coronation has been deferred so that he may be consecrated by apostolic hand; and you should know that the Romans are ready for this. For some already taunt us, saying that the lord pope will come to the Church of Canterbury to remove your lampstand and sit there for some time. Yet I do not believe that the lord pope has yet conceived this plan. For, as I hear, he has much favour for your steadfastness.

But one thing I know without doubt: if the Bishop of Lisieux comes, he will not hesitate to assert anything. He is known to me, and in such matters I have experienced his deceits. Who doubts concerning the abbot? Afterwards the Bishop of Poitiers wrote to me [Col. 0115B] that he had been unable to obtain anything against the Abbot of Saint Augustine, though he had exerted the utmost effort.
