Yet, God being our author, we shall go there because you so command, and we shall test what we can do. But if it is in vain, it must not be imputed to us, for, as the moral poet says:

> It does not always lie within the physician’s power that the sick man be relieved;  
> sometimes the disease is stronger than learned skill.  
> (Ovid, *Epistulae ex Ponto* I.3.17)

## LETTER CXXXV. TO GUY, BISHOP OF CHÂLONS

To Guy, Bishop of Châlons.

I give thanks to your fatherhood, which deigned to anticipate me with the grace of consolation offered. Your kindness has indeed encouraged me all the more greatly to your service because your generosity has become more reliably known, not only through the report of your friend, the Abbot of Saint-Remi, but through the very performance of the deed.

It would be praiseworthy among men and of great merit before God to receive in the arms of mercy a pilgrim who comes; but it is far more glorious and without doubt more worthy of reward to invite into participation in one’s goods an exile—indeed, one exiled for the Lord and for the liberty of the Church. What then shall I answer to my lord? But assuredly the Most High will answer your charity, he who rewards in his chosen ones not only deeds of the hands but also good will with abundant recompense.

He, most serene Father, he will open over you the eyes of his mercy because you have kept open eyes toward me. [Col. 0115D] As soon as I can be free to do so, I shall gladly come to you, if it should ever be divinely granted to me that I may be able to comply with your will.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF SAINT-AMAND

A crisis of necessity tests the fidelity of friends and proves what affection moves each person toward another. We, who long ago devoted our whole mind to your service and, by the Lord’s aid, preserve that devotion inviolate, are oppressed by a grave and burdensome necessity. We hope and ask that it may be relieved by your favour, in which we place the greatest confidence.

For, what may perhaps surprise you, we are condemned to exile and in it are continually troubled and tortured by distress. A certain cleric, always most friendly to us, whose prosperity and adversity alike have for many years been our own, a man more approved by all the more he is known for learning and uprightness of character, lives here among us as an exile from England; and we are exiles in our own home with him. [Col. 0116A]

For he bears the anger of the King of England, not through any fault of his own, as our own conscience and his bear witness, but because he served his lord, the Archbishop of Canterbury, as he ought. He is Master John of Salisbury, possessing good testimony in lands on this side of the sea and beyond it.

Therefore, that you may remove from us the distress of exile both personal and impending, we earnestly beseech your affection to reconcile him to the King of England through the intervention both of the Count of Flanders and of yourself. Procure for him, as you judge expedient, open letters of the king under which he may safely return and peacefully enjoy his possessions. Know for certain that in no matter could you earn greater obligation from us; nor should you conceal the fact, since it is well known to many that this power has been granted you, if only the will is present.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO MILO, BISHOP OF THE MORINI

To the lord Bishop of Thérouanne.

Trial proves fidelity, and the mind’s affection is most faithfully made known through deeds. Since the whole Church of Canterbury—indeed, the Church of the English—has experienced your fidelity and rightly proclaims your charity proved, because you were the first of all to receive the shipwreck of our Father and lord, and with fatherly care [Col. 0116C] received his exiles, placing your goods at their disposal and even sharing them with them according to their wish, beyond your means yet not beyond a spirit nobly generous in freedom.

I am nevertheless more particularly bound to thank you spiritually, since in my kinsman Master Richard you received me spiritually and bestowed the consolation of abundant compassion. Since I cannot respond to so great a kindness as fittingly as I should wish, I desire that what you have done and do for them may be repaid to you by the Lord, who is mighty and may give and pour into the bosoms of benefactors a good measure, pressed together, running over, and overflowing.

For my part, I gladly devote all that I can to your service, giving thanks to God if in his mercy he grants [Col. 0116D] that I may be of service to you in some way.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY (A.D. 1165)

When I lately urged and encouraged the lord pope, and more earnestly explained to him the way which I thought I understood for restoring peace to himself and to us, he replied that he had conceived hope of peace from the emperor’s words, which he had then sent through the Abbot of Saint Mary of the Vow. The emperor promised that the King of England could easily be induced to do whatever the lord pope wished, if the pope himself would unite the kings in alliance, as had long been requested.

Since the lord pope is disposed to this and the King of France easily inclined, he seemed confident of a conference between himself and the kings; he had already summoned the King [Col. 0117A] of France to spend the feast of the Purification with him. Leaving that place, I met the king near Paris and spoke with him long. Although he sympathized with you and your exiles and condemned the harshness of the lord king, he seemed to speak of your cause with less warmth than he had been accustomed to show.

When I tried more insistently to encourage him, he replied that he certainly held your person in great affection and approved your cause, but feared that if, at his urging, Pope Alexander did something which would admit the King of England, the Roman Church would thereafter charge him with having lost so great a friend solely because of him. He repeated this reason often.

Reflecting intently upon this, I turned it over in my mind and measured what we can hope for when the King of England is present, setting forward much in his own favour and much against you, and, in his accustomed manner, moving pliant and unstable minds now by threats, now by promises, now by varied agreements. This is especially so since he has won over the king’s butler and, more importantly, Count Robert, whose wife, kinswoman of my abbot, lately sent the king in England three hundred ells of Reims cloth, together with other small gifts, for making shirts. She is a prudent woman and, besides the gifts which she and her husband frequently receive, hopes that the king will provide for their many children through marriages to noble persons. The Archbishop of Reims, moreover, loves Count Robert [Col. 0117C] and his children most tenderly. I therefore fear that fortune will easily shake off friends of this kind when the time comes.

Accordingly, my counsel, desire, and chief petition are that you turn your whole mind to the Lord and to the aid of prayers. For as it is written in Proverbs: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; if anyone takes refuge in it, he is delivered from every distress” (Prov. 18). Meanwhile postpone all other occupations as far as you can, because, however very necessary they may seem, what I urge is to be preferred, since it is more necessary.

Laws and canons are indeed useful; but believe me, for now there will be need of this:

> This time does not call for such spectacles.  
> [Col. 0117D] (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.37)

For they awaken not so much devotion as curiosity. Do you not recall that in the people’s distress, as it is written, “Between the porch and the altar the priests and ministers shall weep, saying: Spare, O Lord, spare thy people” (Joel 2)? “I was exercised,” says the Prophet, “and I swept my spirit, seeking God with my hands in the day of tribulation” (Ps. 76). Thus he teaches that spiritual exercise and the cleansing examination of conscience turn away the scourge and obtain God’s mercy.

Who rises from reading laws, or even canons, with a contrite heart? I say more: scholarly exercise sometimes increases knowledge unto pride, but kindles devotion rarely or never. I would rather that you ruminated upon the Psalms and pondered the moral books of blessed Gregory [Col. 0118A] than philosophized in the scholastic manner. It is more beneficial to discuss moral life with some spiritual person whose example may kindle you than to inspect and debate contentious questions of secular learning.

God knows with what intention and devotion I make these recommendations. You will receive them as you please. But if you do these things, God will be your helper, so that there will be no need to fear what man may devise. He knows that, in the present distress, we ought, in my opinion, to place hope in no mortal person. Yet I have heard that the King of France has urged the lord pope on your behalf and has thanked the people of Pontigny.

I have heard that you wrote to the Archbishop of Rheims, asking him to have your goods conveyed through Flanders in his own name, as though they were to become his. If this is true, I am greatly astonished. Moreover, it is said that Brother Hugh of Saint-Benedict has returned from England, as have certain others who were acting as envoys of our king to the lord pope and the king of the Franks; but I wish to know what they brought back. It is also reported that an earthquake recently occurred in England, about Canterbury, London, and Winchester; but I have no assurance of its truth. Likewise, it is said that the bishops in whose dioceses your churches lie are now exercising jurisdiction in them, because your clergy, stunned with fear, do not dare to utter a word. Yet, if this is true, I am surprised—unless it be because I can readily believe that they gladly wish to creep in by any means whatever, so that one day they may say that they have possessed them. For, as I hear, Sefrid, Bishop of Chichester, when the Church of Canterbury was vacant, thus occupied those churches concerning which his successor now disputes. And although it is incredible that they should do this, it nevertheless seems good to me that you should make provision for yourselves with the lord pope, obtaining his letters patent, so that whatever may have been usurped against the Church of Canterbury during this storm may not harm it in the future. But you hear more often and more certainly what is happening in England. Therefore I beg you to inform me, through the bearer of this letter, concerning your own condition and that of the court, and whether the abbot whom the lord pope sent into England has yet returned. Moreover, do not forget the affair at Lyons, concerning which you approached Lord Henry of Pisa.

Farewell; and recall how untiring your predecessor was in the service of God on the very day on which he died. May all your people fare well. My abbot greets you, as does the Bishop of Châlons, with whom I spoke so that he might receive one of your clerics. He readily agrees, asking only that you send some worthy man. Nevertheless, he will receive whomever you send. But whenever you dispatch anyone, instruct him to behave modestly, because the people of this kingdom are modest.

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO HENRY, ELECTED BISHOP OF BAYEUX (A.D. 1165)

To Lord HENRY, bishop-elect of Bayeux.

It is no small rashness if anyone strives to render void the counsel of the Lord: though His sentence may change, His disposition is always fulfilled. Accordingly, neither the harshness of raging fortune nor its flattering blandishment makes a well-ordered mind forgetful of itself, so that it hopes for stability except from grace, or fears downfall except from consciousness of evil deserts. Therefore let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall; and let him whom the world persecutes cry out to the Lord, by whose mercy he will be delivered if, having turned back, he cries out confidently. For insofar as one despairs of grace, by that very fact one becomes undeserving of grace. For who has hoped in the Lord and been abandoned?

That you may be assured of these things, you can read them no more clearly in the books of the Fathers than behold them with the faith of your own eyes in the course of your life. For I too see this when I recall the years of your youth and your advancement: although storms of adversity frequently assailed you, your progress has continually prospered in the Lord. Perhaps your holy father, worthy of so great an offspring, foresaw this in the Holy Spirit, like another Jacob. He embraced you before the rest as his own Joseph, known to him, in the budding growth of virtues which he saw in you; and almost to the envy of your brothers he bestowed himself wholly upon one whom he knew to have been chosen beforehand by the Lord and destined to be sent forward, for the salvation of others, through good report and ill report, through prosperity and adversity, into the favor of princes.

For you have tasted this cup for the Lord and the Church, for your father and your brothers; and even without thirst, wormwood and vinegar have been offered you by those who mix and present the cup to us—and would that it were the cup of salvation! You have tasted it, I say; and may it henceforth be withdrawn, so that, according to your desire, you may cleave to the Lord more familiarly and peacefully—if indeed this is expedient for you and for the Lord’s Church. These things, as one conscious of your course, since we have grown together from long ago, I have recounted, rejoicing at your promotion and giving God, the author of that promotion, such thanks as I can; although I sympathize with my own misfortune—or rather with the misfortune and irreparable loss of your whole church. For I have learned from a moral philosopher that to grieve deeply at one’s own disadvantages belongs not to a friend but to a self-lover.

But what will that Church of Salisbury do—once noble and glorious beyond others, but now, what I cannot say without tears, lowly and cast down among the daughters of Jerusalem—bereft of so great a father? Who will extend a right hand to a shipwrecked bishop? Who will console the clergy? For I seem to hear from there the voices of grieving clergy and people, crying with one voice: “Why, Father, do you leave us, or to whom do you leave us desolate?” Certainly, among those whom rumor has put forward to succeed you, scarcely anyone appears worthy to sit at your footstool; indeed, no one. Even if liberty were present, no one now appears to me more suitable than if, with the sun removed from the world, one were to seek among those now living for someone to take his place. Yet the Lord is able to raise up children of Abraham from stones.

But now I return from the public grief to my own particular cause. In what balance my position hangs since you departed England, I wholly do not know. Meanwhile, there was firmer hope, as I have often written before. I do not deny that I have kept the faith due to the Church and Archbishop of Canterbury; but I am prepared to show from my conscience that I have in no way acted against the honor or advantage due to the king; or, if I have erred anywhere, to make fitting satisfaction, as justice directs, to the king and lord, if it please him. Nor is there anything that I could do consistently with the integrity of my reputation and conscience which I would not willingly do to recover his peace and favor. May it therefore please your dignity to instruct me in this matter for the honor of God, and, through the Empress and others as seems more advantageous, procure peace for me on equitable terms—that is, without disgrace.

## LETTER CXL. TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY (A.D. 1165)

[Col. 0120B]

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, from JOHN of Salisbury.

From the report of the bearer of this letter and the letters which my friends have sent me from England, you will be able to perceive the condition of the Church in the kingdom. I also send you a letter which the Bishop of Bayeux sent me through my messenger, whom I had dispatched to him so that through him I might be informed concerning the condition of my brother and our affairs. For the king had entrusted to him our revenues which we held in the diocese of Salisbury. Those which we held in other churches he entrusted partly to the Bishop of London and partly to others; and they employ such diligence that neither my brother nor I, nor anyone in our name, can receive anything from them. As those who return from those regions report, our property is being entirely wasted, so that neither the churches nor the houses are repaired. On this matter I have written both to the Bishop of London himself and to the bishops of Hereford, Worcester, and Chichester, and to the Archdeacon of Poitiers. The Bishop of Chichester, however, complains that he has fallen from the lord king’s favor, and adds these words: “Because the Bishop of London alone is regarded in his own name.” None of the others has answered me. Yet I await at least empty words from my old friends when my messenger returns.

Concerning Kent, however, I have heard nothing. Nevertheless, after my servant returned from you, I heard that the King of Scots had written to you and had obtained your peace from the king. But I could not put faith in these reports: first, because I hear that the king of Scots did not come to our king; and secondly, because I see that an affair begun so sharply cannot easily be settled by letters without a miracle. Furthermore, it is said that the Count of Flanders, at the request of the Empress and the queen, sent great men to the king to negotiate your peace, and that they have returned. But what they reported I do not know. In addition, certain members of your household, as I hear, have returned to you from the Welsh expedition. Therefore I beg you to write back to me concerning the messenger whom the king of Scots sent to you, the envoys of the Count of Flanders sent to the king, what you have heard of the lord king and the Welsh, and whether anything concerning the lord pope has become known to you since he came to Montpellier.

I desire to hear favorable news of him, especially because a great many of those among whom I live prophesy adverse things concerning him. They say that the Pisans, Genoese, and even the men of Arles have put to sea at the command of the German tyrant, to lay snares for him and practise piracy, so that no one at all may sail on that sea without their safe-conduct. They add that he wishes to force into the Church of Mainz that man who is not a Christian but an Antichrist, his apostate, who succeeded Reginald in the office of chancellor, in persecution of the Church, in the collision and slaughter of peoples, and in the overthrow of cities. For, they say, he earned this favor with him because he subjected all Tuscany to the Germans, and Campania also, so that nothing has been left to the Romans outside the city walls, neither fields nor olive groves nor vineyards. Hence, as they report, the enclosed people, as though afflicted by famine, obtained by many prayers and by payment of money a truce until the feast of Saint Michael; then, unless the lord pope comes and assists in the meantime, they will receive Guy of Crema and swear allegiance to the Germans.

And, lest I omit anything, they assert that certain German prophetesses have uttered prophecies which may further inflame German fury and encourage the schismatics. Yet God is surely able to crush the pride of Moab, which exalts itself mightily against the Lord. Its arrogance is greater than its strength. Therefore, amid so great a storm of affairs, I judge that nothing is more salutary than to flee to the mercy of Christ, who, although crucified again, is not killed, but will cause His crucifiers to be crucified more bitterly in vengeance for the Dove. And He is already crucifying them in part, calling against them pestilence and the sword and His other angels, through whom He punishes more gloriously those who glory savagely against Him. If the patrons of the holy Church of Canterbury are present to you—whose remembrance must continually be maintained—then, God being the author, this storm will beneficially be calmed, and we shall happily sail into the desired harbor. Nor do I doubt that we have them propitious, if we set our hearts upon our ways and so conduct ourselves in the exercise of the divine law that we endeavor no less to do it than to hear it. For, as a certain wise man says: “Experience of things is the teacher of understanding.” Farewell.

## LETTER CXLI. TO BARTHOLOMEW OF EXETER (A.D. 1165)

To the Lord Bishop of Exeter.

Since the lord pope’s departure, nothing worthy of report has arisen among us; nor is anything certain known of the emperor’s court. Therefore I refrain from reporting what is called public news and attend to my own affairs. The Archdeacon of Poitiers promised me, as I have already written, that he would work for my reconciliation; but he has not replied how far he has succeeded. I have now again pressed him by letter, and also the Bishop of London, who is said to possess the king’s favor beyond the others, as the bearer of this letter will be able to tell you.

But if anything concerning my peace has been discussed in your presence, I beg that you and others work to secure it on such terms as bring neither the stain of treachery nor the mark of disgrace upon me; otherwise I prefer perpetual exile. For if I were required to renounce my archbishop—a thing which no one of his people has yet done, nor anyone in all England—far be it from me to be the first or the last to consent to such disgrace! I have indeed kept due faith with my venerable archbishop; but, consistently with the king’s honor, if anyone says that I have acted against him, and if I cannot excuse this, I am prepared to make amends, as justice directs, to his honor and good pleasure.

For the Searcher of hearts and Judge of words and deeds knows that I have rebuked the lord archbishop more frequently and more sharply than any mortal concerning those matters in which, from the beginning, he seemed, with a somewhat ill-considered zeal, to provoke the lord king and his supporters to bitterness, although much had to be dealt with according to place, time, and persons. Yet I firmly believe that by the Lord’s mercy my righteousness will answer for me at least tomorrow, and that this exile has been of great benefit to the Lord of Canterbury in learning and character, and somewhat to myself also, so that I may give thanks for the divine ordering. I would not indeed promise that I would no longer serve the Archbishop of Canterbury; and yet God is my witness that henceforth I shall, in accordance with your purpose, be a courtier. But if the Lord opens for me a way of return, write back, if you please, whether I ought to return with provisions and all my baggage. For if that is so, more horses will be necessary, and more things which are presently lacking.

## LETTER CXLII. TO MASTER HUMPHREY BOVI (A.D. 1165)

To Master HUMPHREY BOVI.

The admonitions of Scripture teach that counsel must be sought from a wise man, that the loyalty of friends must be tested in straits, and that the degree of affection one bears toward another is examined by a point of necessity. And since I have less doubt of your wisdom—which you have acquired both through abundance of learning and experience of affairs, and, what is foremost, have received through grace—than I do of that charity which your nature and virtue, proved to me in many ways, promise, I do not distrust it in you. Therefore, seeking counsel from you at this crisis of my need, I earnestly ask that through the messenger whom I have sent to the lord of Bayeux you write to me concerning my situation: what, preserving honor, without which I judge nothing expedient, will seem most expedient.

That you may be more fully informed for giving counsel, my case is this. I have kept the faith due to the Church and Archbishop of Canterbury, and have faithfully stood by him, both in England and beyond the sea, where justice and moderation seemed to be present. But wherever he seemed either to depart from justice or to exceed due measure, I resisted him to his face. God, my conscience, my friends, and companions who have associated with us are witnesses to this. In all these matters I have deliberately done nothing against the honor or advantage due to the lord king, as I am prepared to show if justice so dictates and if it is free and safe to do so; or, if I should be found guilty in any respect, I shall make fitting satisfaction willingly and wholeheartedly.

This year my peace was discussed, and the king granted that I might return if, touching the holy things, I would swear that while beyond the sea I had not acted against his honor or advantage. I referred this to the lord pope, and he replied that the king and court would interpret as against the king’s honor anything which he knew I had done against his will; and he advised me not to return on that condition, but to wait until the king’s anger had cooled somewhat. Then certain persons urged me to give an assurance that I would henceforth assist the archbishop in nothing, so that I might thus return to the king’s favor. But although I am not bound to the archbishop by fidelity arising from homage or oath, nor by any obligation of fealty—for I owe him nothing but the obedience owed by subjects to every bishop—I nevertheless thought it dishonorable to disown my lord and renounce obedience, something no one in the whole kingdom has yet done. I therefore did not think that this condition should be accepted. In other respects, I would willingly do whatever I could with a clear conscience and unstained reputation.

When I set these things before the Lord of Rouen, in whom I place great trust, he steadfastly promised me assistance. May it therefore please you to write me your counsel concerning these matters. Know for certain that I have resolved that henceforth I shall not be a courtier. The Lord of Canterbury himself knows this well: I have withdrawn from his companionship, but I do not withdraw either my fidelity or my affection.

## LETTER CXLIII. TO HENRY, COUNT OF CHAMPAGNE (A.D. 1165–66)

To Count HENRY.

That I, an outlaw and exile, address so great a majesty—one occupied with public concerns—and have dared, especially in an uncultivated style and with an enfeebled manner of expression, to recall you even for a moment to the pursuits of philosophers, might be ascribed to rashness, unless contemplation of your surpassing goodness demanded it of my smallness, and unless the authority of your command not so much invited as compelled me to write. In all things that can be done in the Lord, I desire to obey that command with all my heart, gladly and willingly.

And indeed I acknowledge myself indebted to you, because it is certain both to me and to many others that in your land I have received advancement in many good things; and that, under your blessed father, whose memory is in blessing—for the whole Church of saints recounts his almsgiving and celebrates the praises of his many virtues—I flourished in France, under his patronage, beyond all my contemporaries, while I was still rather young. And by grace going before me, without which no progress in good can exist, I attained that from which, afterward, next to God, both knowledge of worthy men and worldly prosperity came to me. In my own country I abounded in these beyond my fellow-countrymen, as is publicly known. I can readily persuade myself that, as is credible, it was gained by the merits of so great a father that he left an heir who, though he himself was most excellent, would surpass him in cultivation of virtue and magnificence of works.

But why do I say that he left an heir, when he left all his children such that each of them, by the merit of his worth, seems not so much to represent the image of the departed excellent count as to be like a king? Yet, according to the ordinance of the Most High, double goods have rested upon the firstborn; and he who preceded his brothers in time surpasses them twice over, both in the abundance of his possessions and in the splendor of exceptional virtues. Among these, two shine above the rest: conspicuous generosity, which the whole world proclaims, and outstanding humility. I happily experience the latter, for the refreshment of my exile’s distresses, in the questions drawn from sacred letters which you have set before me.

When Alberic of Rheims—called “of the Gate of Venus,” which is commonly called Valais—proposed these questions to me in your name, with several learned men present, I confess, my lord, that I was astonished and could not believe the questioner, until he brought forward the venerable man, your most faithful and devoted Abbot of Saint-Remi. The abbot both set forth the questions themselves and, with much insistence in prayer, requested answers to them for love of you and of himself, confidently asserting that in life nothing is more pleasant to you than to converse with learned men and about learning. He added familiarly in my ear that you very often incur the displeasure of the unlearned multitude for this reason: they cannot call you back from the exercise of study and plunge you, according to their own wish, into storms of business and tumult. For they think all time is wasted which is not spent either in courtly trifles, in the abyss of turbulent malice, or in the whirlwinds of lawsuits. They do not know that philosophy is satisfied with few judges and disdains to entrust the purity of its office to popular judgment.

Accordingly, to oblige you, I was pleased to take up the questions proposed and answer them, taking account of the time and unavoidable necessities—if not as fully as I might wish, at least as circumstances permit. The questions were: what number of books I believe there to be in the Old and New Testaments, and who their authors are; what Jerome, in his letter to the presbyter Paulinus, says concerning a table of the sun seen in the sand by Apollonius the philosopher while pursuing letters; likewise, what he says in that same letter about Virgilian cento poems and Homeric centos; and finally, where it is written, and what is meant by, the saying read and commonly used by many: “Things which are not are more godlike than things which are.”

This too was added to the request: that, setting aside every excuse, I should carefully and promptly explain all these matters in a paper to be sent to you, supported by the foundations of reasons and the testimonies of authorities. How difficult—indeed, rather, impossible—this is, your prudence readily perceives. Our age marvels at and venerates your most acute intellect, your tongue ready for uttering all things, and your most capacious and retentive memory. For, as Apuleius says in *On the God of Socrates*, no one attains the praise of speed and thoroughness at once; nor can the weighty subject-matter of great books ever be compressed into one and the same paper, however diligent one may be.

Concerning the first two questions, namely the number of the books and their authors, Cassiodorus composed an elegant book. But since my own faith is scrutinized in this matter, I think it makes little difference whether I or others believe one thing or another. For whether this is believed in one way or another, no loss of salvation follows. And to dispute more sharply over something which neither harms nor benefits, or in which either alternative makes little difference—is this not the same as wrangling bitterly among friends about goat’s wool? Therefore I think that a person attacks the faith more by obstinately determining a matter which is uncertain than by abstaining from a rash definition and leaving uncertain what he sees the Fathers disagree about and cannot fully investigate.

Nevertheless, opinion can and ought to incline more readily toward one side, so that what seems right to all, or to most, or to the best-known and most eminent, or to each approved master within the limits of his own competence, may more easily be admitted—unless a manifest or more probable reason, in matters subject to reason, teaches that the opposite is true. I added “in matters subject to reason” on account of those articles which altogether transcend reason, in which the Church chose to be foolish, that in the foolishness of faith it might apprehend Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, rather than, along with the philosophers of the nations—who, professing themselves wise, became fools and were made vain in their thoughts, so as to be given over to a reprobate mind—be deprived of God’s wisdom and power through a proud profession of wisdom.

Since therefore I read diverse and manifold opinions of the Fathers concerning the number of books, I follow Jerome, doctor of the Catholic Church, whom I judge most trustworthy in laying the foundation of the literal sense. Just as there are twenty-two letters of the Hebrews, so I hold without hesitation that there are twenty-two books of the Old Testament, arranged in three distinct orders.

The first order contains the Pentateuch, namely the five books of Moses, divided in this manner according to the variety of their mysteries, although their historical subject matter is continuous: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, the Book of Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

The second order contains the prophecies and is completed by eight books. Why these are called prophecies above the rest, when some of them seem to recount bare history, while others which weave prophecy, such as Daniel and the Book of Psalms, are not counted among prophetic works, is neither part of the question proposed nor something which the present limitation of time or paper permits me to explain; nor does the bearer’s urgency allow it. Among these are counted Joshua; the Book of Judges, to which Ruth is joined because the history narrated occurred in the days of the Judges; likewise Samuel, which is contained in the first two books of Kings; and *Malachim*, which is completed in the following two, and is followed, each in a separate volume, by Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Book of the Twelve Prophets.

The third order contains Job, the Psalter, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Daniel, Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther. Thus the total of the books of the Old Testament is twenty-two, although some count the Book of Ruth and the Lamentations of Jeremiah among the Hagiographa, so that the whole total is extended to twenty-four. These matters are found in the prologue to the Book of Kings, which blessed Jerome calls the “helmeted prologue” of all the Scriptures which flowed from the Hebrew source through him to the understanding of Latin readers.

But the Book of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and the Shepherd, as the same Father affirms, are not reckoned in the Canon; nor is the Book of Maccabees, which is divided into two volumes, the first of which has the flavor of Hebrew speech and the second Greek, as the style itself proves. As for the work entitled *The Shepherd*, I do not know whether it exists anywhere; but it is certain that Jerome and Bede testify that they saw and read it.

To these are added eight volumes of the New Testament: the Gospel of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; the fifteen Epistles of Paul, contained in one volume—although the received and almost universally common opinion is that there are only fourteen, ten to churches and four to persons—provided that the Epistle to the Hebrews is to be numbered among Paul’s epistles. Jerome, the teacher of teachers, seems to establish this in its preface, dissolving the arguments of those who contended that it was not Paul’s. The fifteenth, moreover, is that written to the Church of the Laodiceans. Though, as Jerome says, it is rejected by all, it was nevertheless written by the Apostle. This opinion is not presumed from the judgment of others but strengthened by the Apostle’s own testimony. For he mentions it in the Epistle to the Colossians in these words: “When this epistle has been read among you, see that it is read also in the Church of the Laodiceans, and that you yourselves read the one from Laodicea” [Colossians 4].

There follow the seven Catholic Epistles in one volume, then the Acts of the Apostles in another, and finally the Apocalypse. This number of books admitted into the canon of sacred Scripture is a renowned and unquestioned tradition in the Church. These books possess such authority among all that they leave sound minds no room for contradiction or doubt, because they were written by the finger of God. Rightly and deservedly, therefore, one is guarded against and condemned as reprobate who, in ordinary intercourse of conduct and speech—especially in the forum of the faithful—does not freely and publicly accept the silver of this divine utterance, tested by the fire of the Holy Spirit, purified from every earthly dross and stain, and purified sevenfold. Faith may therefore safely rest upon these books and upon those which receive from them a proved and due foundation; for one who dares to oppose them is an unbeliever and a heretic.

Opinions vary concerning the authors of the books, although the prevailing view in the Church is that they were written by those named in the titles of the individual books. In Book VI, chapter 2, of the *Etymologies*, Isidore explains, borrowing from Jerome, the source of letters, both the reasons for the names given to the books and their authors. Rabanus too, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, which some call *On the Sacraments*, and Cassiodorus, in the book *On the Instruction of Divine Letters*, treat more fully of what pertains to this subject. Cassiodorus indeed discusses not only the canonical Scriptures and their authors, but also, in his customary elegant style, describes by whom they are expounded.

Moreover, whenever individual Fathers undertook to expound a book, they customarily prefaced their treatises, as reason required, with matters concerning its author and subject, purpose and occasion, title, and whatever else might prepare hearers and readers for easier understanding of the work that followed. They did this with consideration for place, time, and those to whom their speech was directed, so that, after the pattern of evangelical teaching, they might distribute to the Lord’s household its measure of saving food at the proper time. “For,” as Palladius says, “a great part of prudence is to measure, with considered judgment, the person who writes.”

Therefore I deliberately suspend my style from carrying out the received opinion, being about to proceed to other matters, unless perhaps your graciousness commands that I pursue this also more carefully. Meanwhile let your discernment know for certain that Philo, mentioned by Jerome in chapter eleven of *On Illustrious Men*, disagrees with others in the book entitled *Why Certain Names Have Been Changed in the Scriptures*. Theophilus of Alexandria follows him in his *Chronicles*, as does Epiphanius, Bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, in his book *On Illustrious Men*; Theodore, who translated their books from Greek into Latin in an urbane style, attests this as well. For he says that Gamaliel too—at whose feet the Apostle boasts that he learned the Law—and the public assertion of the Hebrews, who understand more correctly the letter of the Law, agree with Philo’s opinion.

But lest I extend my discourse when I must hasten to the remaining matters, I shall set out their opinion. It is this: Moses wrote the Pentateuch, although there is no agreement about the end of Deuteronomy, where his death is treated. Some assert that this small part too was written by Moses himself with prophetic certainty, as were the passage on the creation of the world which he placed at the beginning, and the predictions concerning the future which he uttered in the blessings of the patriarchs. Others say that it was added by Joshua; others, by Ezra.

Joshua wrote the book named after him. Samuel wrote *Sophithim*, that is, Judges; likewise the Book of Ruth; and part of the Book of Kings named after him. David supplied the remainder; but at last Jeremiah wrote *Malachim*, that is, the latter two Books of Kings. The same man published his own book together with the Lamentations. The received opinion does not conflict with all this.

Hezekiah and the wise men whom he had associated with himself in a school of virtues and letters during the fifteen years by which God had extended his life, devoting himself thereafter to divine things, gathered into one volume the prophecies of Isaiah. Isaiah appears, from his own words, to have proclaimed them among the people rather than written them. Nor is it contrary that he was commanded to write in a great book with the pen of a man, because that book had already been written and was large; and, as they say, it did not concern the gathering of his prophecies, which had been taken down by hearers and arranged by the aforesaid king. The same men also compiled the Proverbs, previously spoken by Solomon and, however the matter may stand, silently taken down by listeners and circulated by common use. Hence in those same Proverbs occur the words: “These also are the proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, transferred.” They are said to have “transferred” them because, as it were, they conveyed them from place to place—from common use and perhaps from the private papers of individuals—into the Canon of Scripture by public authority.

This tradition is further confirmed by what is written in III Kings, chapter 6: “Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs numbered five thousand; and he discoursed from the cedar of Lebanon even unto the hyssop,” etc. For he is believed rather to have spoken these things than to have written them. Some refer his songs to the Song of Songs, and his discourse on natural things, proceeding from the greatest to the least, to the significance of those matters which Ecclesiastes proclaims to the hearing of the whole world. But of these elsewhere.

For Ecclesiasticus also, and the Song of Songs, are said to have been added to the canon of Scripture by Hezekiah, king of Jerusalem, and his fellow pupils; though Solomon’s authority was put forward, since they regarded him as the originator in composing these works and, as it were, the herald of public usefulness. Yet whether this has been said against common opinion only, or against the truth, let him decide who knows.

Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, with fifteen men assisting them, most faithfully compiled the oracles of Ezekiel for the Synagogue. For Ezekiel himself preached the visions and impressed them upon the memories of his hearers; he did not wish to write them in an unclean land, lest he profane holy things, but commanded that they be written in the land of the Lord. To this suspension [of writing] the Psalm alludes, saying: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments,” etc. (Psalm 136 [137]). And from this opinion the common view does not dissent, as Isidore testifies.

The same prophets wrote Daniel. For Daniel too refrained from writing, both for the reason given in Ezekiel and because public duties hindered him. The same three prophets and their fellow pupils also wrote the Book of Esther, which common opinion maintains was compiled by Ezra, and likewise the book of the Twelve Prophets, which the populace holds to have been compiled by the Twelve Prophets themselves. The aforesaid Philo, together with his followers named above, praises these same three prophets as authors of this book and of the preceding ones, as has been said.

[Col. 0129A] Since the visions of each of them were brief, it seemed sufficient to the prophets to publish them by preaching and thus entrust them to other writers, especially since some of them are believed to have been ignorant of letters, being countrymen and shepherds, or occupied in other offices.

David composed the Book of Psalms, sometimes employing the services of the men whose names are affixed in the titles of certain psalms. There were ten such men. Although they composed some psalms—which the common opinion reported by Isidore does not deny—nevertheless all the psalms are called David’s, because he bestowed his authority upon them. This accords with what Justinian teaches in the Code: “We make all merits our own to which we impart our authority, because all authority is imparted to them from us.” For one who improves a work without subtlety is more praiseworthy than the one who first devises it.

Ezra composed the book which bears his own name, and Chronicles, down to his own days. The remainder was written by the most learned and faithful members of the Synagogue which rebuilt the Temple at Jerusalem.

According to these writers Moses wrote Job; common opinion ventures to decide nothing concerning this, though it seems more inclined to the view that blessed Job himself, after overcoming his trials, wrote his own book. Concerning Tobit, Judith, and the Book of Maccabees, which have not been received into the canon, neither common opinion teaches by what authors they were written, nor do Philo’s followers mention them; nevertheless, because they build up faith and religion, they have been devoutly admitted.

[Col. 0129C] Philo composed the Book of Wisdom, and is called a pseudographer—not because he wrote badly, but because he entitled it badly. For it is entitled *The Wisdom of Solomon*, though it was not issued by Solomon; but because of the style which it assumes and the elegance of morals which it likewise portrays, it is called Solomon’s.

Ecclesiasticus was written by Jesus son of Sirach; he too, by similarity of style and morals, is called Solomon’s. Conversely, by common Latin usage, certain passages are said to be from the Book of Wisdom which are unquestionably found not there but in Proverbs. Thus in the Church the pericope from Proverbs beginning, “Who shall find a valiant woman?” (Proverbs 31), bears the title “Wisdom.”

This is enough concerning the number and authors of the books of the Old Testament, in which the authors just mentioned differ in part from common opinion. The number and authors of the books of the New Testament are certain, and there is scarcely any matter of dispute. Each Evangelist issued his own volume. Paul composed his Epistles, although some suspect that the Epistle to the Hebrews was written by Barnabas or Clement. The Catholic Epistles were written by those whose names they bear. There is, however, a question concerning the final two Epistles of John. Luke is recognized as having written the Acts of the Apostles in a style as faithful and salutary as it is sweet. Some suppose that the Apocalypse was written by John the Apostle; others, by a certain most holy Ephesian priest named John, as blessed Jerome, father of men of letters, reports. [Col. 0130A] But the Apostle prevails in the belief of the Church.

Let these remarks for the present suffice concerning the number and authors of the books of the New Testament. Whoever wishes to know their contents should read blessed Jerome’s letter to Paulinus concerning the divine books; for, to speak from my own experience, nowhere will he find it better or more plainly set forth.

But what concern is it, most serene lord, to examine these and other opinions in investigating authors, when it is agreed that the one author of all Holy Scripture is the Holy Spirit? Blessed Gregory, in the *Morals*, most truly and elegantly says that, since the Holy Spirit is agreed to be the author of the book of blessed Job which he was expounding, to inquire afterward who wrote the book is like questioning, when the writer is known, what pen was used to write it.

Therefore do not make much of knowing who the authors of the Scriptures are, but of understanding them truly—indeed, certainly, of fulfilling them devoutly and faithfully. For “not the hearers of the law,” as the Apostle says, “are righteous before the Lord, but the doers” (Romans 2). It is best to occupy oneself with these books, because, as Truth itself declares through its most faithful instrument: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” Thus, for an intelligent man leisure without letters is death, and the burial of a living person.

I proceed to the third question: What is the table of the sun in the sand, which Apollonius, the most diligent investigator of truth and pursuer of letters, saw in the sand—a table most famous among the Gymnosophists? I asked everyone in France who seemed to hold primacy in the Scriptures; but because pagan history was unknown to them, I do not greatly blame them for being unable to teach what they had not learned. Some, however, exposed their ignorance more shamelessly, persuading me by their foolish answer only of this: that they had learned from the teachers whom they had hired for a long time and at great expense to know nothing.

[Col. 0130C] This history, which Jerome—so richly endowed with truth and learning—touches upon in the passages mentioned above, is found in Valerius Maximus, Book III, chapter 1, under the heading “On Moderation.” As he relates, fishermen in the region of Miletus were drawing a net when a certain man purchased a cast of the net. When at last a golden Delphic table of great weight had been drawn out, a dispute arose: the fishermen asserted that they had sold him a catch of fish, while he, on the contrary, said that he had bought merely the fortune of the cast.

When the case had been heard, the people of the city, because of the novelty and magnitude of the affair, judged that it should be referred for consultation to the Delphic Apollo. When consulted, Apollo replied that it should be given to the man who surpassed all others in wisdom; otherwise it would be unpleasant and harmful to its recipient.

Accordingly, since Thales of Miletus was held, in the judgment of those who heard the case, to be the wisest among the Seven whom Greece then celebrated above all others, they notified him to take possession of the aforesaid table. Having heard the terms of the consultation and Apollo’s response, he declared with prudent humility that not he but Bias of Priene had been designated by Apollo’s oracle. Bias too was approached in the same manner, and similarly transferred the entitlement to Pittacus of Mytilene.

[Col. 0131A] Meanwhile the table lay in the sand; and because of the novelty of the event, the moderation of the sages, and the fact that no one among the people dared seize the gold which the wisest men so earnestly declined, report, the herald of such things, spread this occurrence far and wide—not so much wonderful as astonishing.

Thus the table became exceedingly famous, as the offer of it passed in this manner to each of the Seven Sages, until it came to Solon. He bestowed both the title of supreme wisdom and the offered gift upon Apollo, in whom the sun is worshipped, because he beholds all things and because his fiery power penetrates the universe so that nothing can be hidden from him. Hence it was called the table of the sun, which Apollonius saw lying in the sand while he pursued learning.

There remain still two of the five questions proposed to be resolved; but I lack time and leisure to answer them. If it shall seem good to your graciousness, I shall gladly undertake them, and shall count it among my successes if it is granted me from heaven to be of service in any way to your honor and wishes.

> The rustic loves the farmer, the soldier one who wages fierce wars,  
> The sailor the helmsman of the uncertain ship.  
> —Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* II.561

[Col. 0131C] And will not possessors of learning love a prince who cultivates philosophy and embraces and fosters the honorable studies of men of letters? I do not deny that an unlearned prince can sometimes be advantageous to the commonwealth; but, if matters proceed rightly, neither of the two will ever attain equality with learned men, or will attain it only rarely. For, as your Vegetius says, there is no one who ought to know either more things or better things than a prince, whose knowledge can benefit all his subjects.

Nor do I doubt that different people will judge differently concerning what has been written here. But I have attained my purpose if this letter pleases you. For just as it has no ground for pleasing by its own elegance, so, because of its writer’s devotion, it has no ground for deserving displeasure. [Col. 0131D] Nor do I fear the judgment of those who pronounce a rash verdict before they have heard the matter, because I remember Scripture saying: “He who answers before he hears shows himself to be foolish and worthy of confusion” (Proverbs 18).

Is not that kind of men known to you also, of whom Solomon’s proverb speaks, asserting that the fool pays no attention to the words of the prudent man unless he says what is already turning in his own heart? At last I shall believe, most glorious count, that the devotion of my smallness has not been despised, if your eminence—may the Almighty bless and preserve it for long ages—shall deign to entrust me with any task within my powers, since I shall faithfully obey your commands in all things.

## LETTER CXLIV. TO MASTER GEOFFREY OF SAINT EDMUND. (A.D. 1166)

[Col. 0132A]

JOHN TO GEOFFREY OF SAINT EDMUND.

When, at the Easter festival, I had gone to Angers to the king for the sake of restoring peace, I caused him, before he received the Lord’s body, to be approached more earnestly by the abbot of Saint Victor at Paris and other religious men concerning the peace of R., your son. I also enlisted other friends, in whose loyalty I had conceived fuller hope at court. For I had previously solicited on this matter that excellent man, worthy of my reverence for his merits, Master Walter of Lille, and through him other Fathers whose loyalty seemed to me more sincere.

But the king answered more kindly, both because of reverence for God and for those who interceded. Yet, when he heard that the affair concerned the lordship of Saint Edmund, he summoned William of Hastings, through whom he investigated the truth, so that nothing might be represented to him by deception. William, so far as he could and dared, gave a favorable account of your case. The king therefore ordered the boy to be sent to him, so that he might receive in person the letters of the remission granted him and carry them back to all the officials of the kingdom, so that his peace might be established.

Accordingly, as the Lord pleased and our need required, I sent the boy back in haste to Master Walter of Lille. May the founder of Christ’s Church reward the loyalty and charity which he has shown us. For faith in and love of Christ, as our consciences bear witness, we gladly endure—as needs must—losses, injuries, insults, and exile, being certain that the Lord is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but will bring from this very trial an increase of salvation and a cleansing of our past life.

[Col. 0132C] I speak of myself and certain others whom I know to rejoice in this tribulation, so that they may meditate frequently and say to Him: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart,” etc. (Psalm 93 [94]). For by God’s grace we suffer, not as adulterers or murderers, not as incendiaries or sacrilegious persons, but as Christians.

The world regards our faith as madness and calls constancy in faith obstinacy; it brands the profession of truth with both the mark and name of vanity; it tries to dishonor the practice of religion by calling it hypocrisy, superstition, or some other falsehood. But the Prince of the Apostles thinks otherwise and teaches the contrary: “For this,” he says, “is grace before the Lord, because you were called by Christ to this end, that you might follow his footsteps.” And again: “If you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you shall be blessed” (I Peter 2).

My beloved, soon the Judge and arbiter of consciences will come—He who will render to each according to his deserts—and then, whatever the world now chatters, it will be made manifest with what intention each person has lived. Meanwhile, I beg you to secure the aid of your prayers and those of the holy persons whom you know, that, if I am on a trackless way—which I do not believe—Christ, the way of the righteous, may lead me back to the path; and that, if I am on the way, he may lead me through prosperity or adversity, as shall please him, unto life.

[Col. 0133A] If you see Master Walter, return to him through yourself and through such friends as you can muster every possible thanks, especially through Count Geoffrey, whom he loves. If you have the means, receive him and cause others to receive him as an angel of the Lord, for he too, I believe, is God’s minister and, so far as is permitted at court, consoles Christ’s members in many ways. From the helpers whom the boy finds, he will be able in part to judge what my situation is. Attribute it to fortune, not to me, that I could not show him more generous kindness. Would that henceforth he may find better friends! I did him good insofar as circumstances permitted.

I hear that Master Walter is being bound by oath neither to receive letters nor messengers from exiles. From this it is clear what a wretched necessity hangs over good men, who are not permitted to fulfill the commands of the Lord’s law—that is, the duties of charity.

## LETTER CXLV. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1166)

BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER, FROM JOHN OF SALISBURY.

Although, according to the custom of those writing to friends, this letter does not display a wish for your welfare, nothing is more earnest in my wishes and prayers than that your paths may continually prosper in the Lord. For no lack or change of affection has suspended the greeting owed to my lord and father, [Col. 0133C] but a prudent ordering of duties and the controlling principle of all things rightly done. The reason for this reserve is manifest enough that it need not be alleged at all, or may be stated in a few words.

For they say that all things are full of the king’s snares, so that good men can have no safe exchange either in conversation or in writing. Wickedness is plotting I know not what trifling thing against innocence; and, driven by the goad of a conscience that continually pricks and burns it, it suspects everyone and everything. It does so justly and deservedly, since there ought to be no peace for the wicked while justice attacks and overcomes its enemies. Indeed, what the wicked fears shall come upon him, and the righteous shall be delivered from distress, because the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

For a moment malice rages like a storm against the Church, and the wicked seem to prevail against the Lord. But Christ, whom they persecute, will soon answer them according to their deserts, so that the scale of vengeance will seem to outweigh them; and those whom he powerfully punishes he will seem not so much to weigh in the balance of equity as to overwhelm by the greatness of the burden. [Col. 0133D] This is not because he inflicts an injury, but because he will impose an immeasurable and unmoderated punishment upon those who sin without measure or restraint. Let no one suppose that I prophesy of events far off, although the authority and truth of a divine oracle endure perpetually; for it is plain that judgment has already in some measure begun—indeed, that the sentence is already being put into execution.

Did not the German tyrant, whose name’s renown recently struck terror into the world, nearly subdue neighboring kingdoms and shake even the Greek Empire with fear, so that by sending embassies he seemed to offer surrender rather than alliance? But behold: by the Lord’s working he is feared less, and the prince who formerly terrified both near and far by a mere nod cannot restrain his own Germans from wrongdoing. He who by a word alone formerly imposed peace and wars upon nations at his pleasure now rejoices at truces sought and obtained from his own people and among his own people.

[Col. 0134A] For, as he himself complains, since he came to Laon in order to separate the king of the Franks and the Gallican Church from the faith and pervert them to his own heresy, that they might worship his idol, his successes have fallen away; and Fortune, which had exalted him, has begun to fluctuate toward his abasement. The hope of the faithful is that, for God’s honor, he will soon be brought down still further, until Christ, whose bride he persecutes, utterly crushes him beneath his feet.

And is not judgment already being exercised among you against the torturers of the Church? Consider how great the king of the English was when he seemed small in his own eyes. He maintained before God’s Church at least an appearance of faith and reverence, and you plainly saw that none of his undertakings failed. His arrow did not turn backward, his shield did not yield in battle, and his spear was not turned aside. He crouched over his prey like a lion, so that no one dared rouse him. By sight alone he terrified his enemies; neighbors bowed themselves in service; distant princes sought his friendship. He was revered by his own people, honored by foreigners, praised by all, loved by good men, but most of all by the clergy, who honored him beyond their power, venerated him with all their strength, and loved him with one purpose more than the love of women.

[Col. 0134C] Why say more? In the judgment of men, he enjoyed an abundance of every desirable thing, free from fear and anxiety, except such as will or impulse—not necessity or reason—brought upon him. But to what end did he bring all these gifts of God, if he remains in this state without repentance and satisfaction?

To pass over the injuries which he had previously inflicted upon individual churches, as was thought, through ignorance or under pretext of his own right: when preparing to attack Toulouse by war, contrary to ancient custom and due liberty, he ordered all churches to contribute, according to the will of himself and his satraps, to a tax. Nor did he allow churches even to be treated as equal to nobles in this contribution—or rather, this exaction, as improper as it was unjust. For churches were assessed more harshly, as though unworthy of their possessions or honor.

But what result did this vast sum of money, acquired by such exactions and injuries, bring him? Was it not cast into a pierced sack, so as to profit the enemy who received it and to be not merely useless but harmful to the one who poured it out? Did not his fortune begin to retreat from that day, and the abundance of his successes wither away?

[Col. 0135A] But someone will say that this imposition of the tax and vexation of the churches must be charged wholly against his chancellor, who now either holds the archbishopric, as I believe, or strives to obtain it, as his rivals allege; for he then urged the king in every matter according to his pleasure and introduced this evil, along with many others.

Although I know this to be false, since I know that he then gave not authority to lust but compliance to necessity, nevertheless, because I do not doubt that he was a minister of iniquity, I judge most justly that he should be punished in such a way that he is punished especially by the author whom, in such matters, he preferred to the Lord, the author of all good things; and that the man whom he held and praised as the author of his perversity may in turn become his punishment. For the saying of Wisdom is celebrated in the hearts and mouths of the wise: “By the things through which a man sins, by these also he is punished” (Wisdom 11).

Thus Cain, the first murderer, was slain; Canaan, who imposed servitude upon others, was condemned to perpetual servitude; Pharaoh was drowned with his power in the waters in which he had drowned innocent Hebrews. Very many examples of this kind are evident. But let it be so: he is now doing penance; he recognizes and confesses his fault; and, if at one time he attacked the Church with Saul, he is now ready with Paul to lay down even his life for it.

[Col. 0135B] Who then will deny that judgment has already begun from the house of the Lord, when the princes of the people are already hanging upon gibbets in the sun, so that God’s justice may be revealed in the sight of the nations? For are not these two princes of the people—the one who dispenses spiritual things, the other who administers temporal things? Is not the law of this dispensation and ministry committed to be handled by their hands?

These are the two cherubim by whose wings the law and the mercy-seat are overshadowed, facing one another but with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat. For they ought so to delight one another by mutual regard that they continually behold and venerate the law of God in the ark of their breast; nor ought they, for their own advantage, admit one another’s regard for any other cause by which they might deserve to forfeit God’s propitiation. For it is not permitted to turn one’s face from the mercy-seat.

If, therefore, God finds perversity in these his angels and punishes it, who doubts that the causes of their subjects are already being heard before the Most High, or have already been heard? Let anyone turn the eyes of his mind around and consider how many and what sort of adversaries the Lord has raised up against him since he lifted up his heel against the Lord by oppressing the Church. He will plainly marvel and, if wise, reverence the judgment of the Lord, who chose not emperors, kings, or princes of nations to tame him, but the remotest of men—the Britons, first the Nivicollini, and afterward those whom he stirred to resistance and open contest, who had been accustomed to worship the traces of his feet.

[Col. 0135D] And this was done so that no flesh might glory, but that the name of the Lord might be blessed for ever. Thus, to punish Solomon’s ingratitude when he departed from the Lord, God raised up not so much princes as robbers, slaves, and outcasts.

Let no one suppose that his condition will henceforth prosper unless, by repentance and the Lord’s favor, he returns and adopts more merciful counsel. For, as the prophet says: “In our days and regions there have been found foolish princes of Zoan, who have given foolish counsel to their king” (Isaiah 19). Anxieties burn him on every side, but the war which he wages against Christ and the Church burdens him still more, and seems to him an inextricable labyrinth and an accursed toil.

Having recently summoned to the conference at Chinon his magnates and intimates, who are known to possess both skill and experience in evil designs, and who are wise in devising and doing evil, he inquired most earnestly—with promises, threats, and very many adjurations—what counsel he should use against the Church. He complained most bitterly of the Archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 0136B] not without many groans and sighs; and, as those who were then present afterward reported, he wept, saying that the same Archbishop of Canterbury would take from him body and soul alike. At length he said that all were traitors who, with effort and diligence, would not free him from the harassment of one man.

At this the lord of Rouen grew somewhat angry and rebuked him—though, in his customary spirit of mildness, less severely than God’s cause required—saying that the severity and authority of the pontiff, who was languishing from illness, had been employed in the cause of reason and faith. The king’s grief was the more acute because of the fear which he had conceived from letters sent to him and to his mother by the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury. A copy of them is being sent to you. There was indeed fear, and deservedly, lest a sentence of interdict upon his land and anathema upon his person should very soon be pronounced by the authority and command of the Supreme Pontiff.

When they were thus oppressed by these anxieties, the Bishop of Lisieux said that there was one remedy: to impede the imminent sentence by the obstacle of an appeal. And so, I do not know by what means—unless because truth, when debated, prevails more strongly, and justice, the more it is shaken, the more it gains strength—while the king attempts through ancestral customs to annul the right of appeals, he confirms it all the more, since he himself is compelled to fly for refuge to an appeal for his own head.

[Col. 0136C] Therefore the Bishops of Lisieux and Sées left that council from the presence of their lord and king, hastening to the oft-mentioned Archbishop of Canterbury, in order, by entering an appeal, to suspend his sentence until the Octave of Easter. The Archbishop of Rouen went with them too, not, he says, to appeal, but to negotiate the peace which he desired.

Our archbishop, however, being on the point of pronouncing sentence, had set out for the city of Soissons, in order that he might commend his struggle in prayer to the blessed Virgin, whose memorial is celebrated there, to blessed Drausius, to whom those about to fight flee, and to blessed Gregory, founder of the English Church, who rests in the same city. Blessed Drausius is a most glorious confessor, who, as the Franks and Lotharingians believe, makes invincible those champions who spend the night at his shrine; hence in such necessity people flee to him even from Burgundy and Italy. Thus Robert of Montfort also spent the night at his shrine when he was about to fight Henry of Essex.

[Col. 0137A] Accordingly, by the Lord’s ordering, the anxiety of the royal bishops was frustrated. When they came to Pontigny, they did not find the archbishop whom they wished to appeal against; disappointed in their purpose, they returned complaining that they had spent their resources, labored, and accomplished nothing.

After our archbishop had spent three nights at the memorials of the aforesaid saints, on the day following Ascension he was hastening toward Vézelay, intending there on Pentecost to pronounce a sentence of anathema against the king and his men. But by divine direction it happened that, while he was in the church at Reginensis [place-name uncertain], on the Friday preceding the aforesaid solemnity, he was informed most certainly and truthfully that the king of the English was suffering from a very grave illness. Thus he had been unable to attend the conference with the king of the Franks, which he had sought with great desire and great gifts; instead, he had sent Richard of Poitou and Richard of Humaz as his excusers, who wished to establish the reason for his absence by oath.

When this was made known to the archbishop by a messenger of the king of the Franks, he postponed pronouncing sentence against the king, as your John had previously advised him, urging him not to hasten toward repentance. But he publicly declared John of Oxford excommunicated and excommunicated him by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, in his own words, because [Col. 0137C] he had fallen into condemned heresy by swearing a sacrilegious oath to the emperor, had communicated with the schismatic of Cologne, and, contrary to the command of the lord pope, had usurped the deanery of the Church of Salisbury.

He alleged these reasons from the pulpit in the hearing of all who had assembled at Vézelay from diverse nations for the feast day. There also, on various just grounds alleged, he excommunicated Richard, Archdeacon of Poitou; Richard de Lucy; Jocelin de Baillol; Ranulf de Broc; Hugh of Saint-Clair; and Thomas son of Bernard; and all who should thereafter lay hands upon the possessions and goods of the Church of Canterbury in order to misuse them or impede their use by those to whose needs they had been assigned.

As for the king, whom he had previously summoned through letters and messengers to make satisfaction according to the Church’s rule and custom, he invited him, in a public summons, to bear the fruit of repentance, threatening shortly to pronounce a sentence of anathema against him unless he came to his senses and made satisfaction for such great assaults against the Church. Yet he will do this only unwillingly; and I know none of his household who is inclined toward the issuing of such a sentence.

[Col. 0137D] Moreover, he publicly condemned that document which contains the wicked practices of the persecutors of the Church, which they call ancestral customs, binding by the bond of anathema all who thereafter use the authority of that document. In particular, by the counsel of the Roman Church, these articles were first condemned:

- That a bishop may not excommunicate anyone who holds from the king without the king’s permission.
- That a bishop may not restrain any of his parishioners for perjury or breach of faith.
- That clerics be drawn before secular courts.
- That laymen, whether king or another, deal with cases concerning churches or tithes.
- That no appeal be made on any matter to the Apostolic See unless permission has been obtained from the king and his officials.
- That an archbishop, bishop, or other persons may not come when summoned by the lord pope without the king’s permission.

And likewise other provisions of this sort, which are found contrary to the divine laws and the constitutions of the holy Fathers.

He absolved all bishops from the promise they had made, contrary to ecclesiastical institution, to observe that document. He also announced this by his letters to the archbishops and bishops, as the Roman Church had advised him.

[Col. 0138B] These are the things which the archbishop has done in the meantime. And the king—as I do not doubt has come to your knowledge—sent the good man Master Walter of Lille to England with letters from the conference at Chinon, in order to forewarn the islanders concerning the appeal allegedly made, to have the ports and crossings guarded more carefully, and to suspend the clergy from obedience, although no appeal has yet been made and the archbishop can easily be found.

I do not doubt that this scheme displeases the aforesaid Master Walter, as do all things undertaken against the Church of God, because he fears the Lord. The king has also summoned to himself the lord of Cîteaux and others by whose prudence he believes the malice of his counsel can be armed against the Lord. But indeed, if they were wise, they would spare themselves and their own in this cause, because:

> This punishment shall return upon its own head.  
> —Ovid, *Art of Love* I.340

Henceforth the lord pope prospers in the city. Cremona, together with eight other cities, is reliably said to be rebelling against the German. The Bishop of Tusculum and Cardinal Humbald have died. William, king of Sicily, has also died; his sons succeeded him, one in the kingdom and the other in the duchy of Apulia. In his last days he caused sixty thousand florins to be delivered to John of Naples for the use of the lord pope. His son, who succeeded him in the kingdom, sent an equal sum.

[Col. 0138D] The king of the Franks supports the Archbishop of Canterbury in every matter and reveres him more than a brother. But the developments at the English court, where changes in affairs are frequent, are, I think, better known to you than to us.

May your fatherhood flourish and prosper in the Lord, and endeavor to commend us to the prayers of the saints, that they may console us in all our tribulation. We shall return when it pleases Him who set us apart for exile, and for whose sake, insofar as it pleases him, we have resolved with most ready will to remain in exile and suffer whatever adversities he commands; and he will strengthen our weakness to endure them. May he, by his grace, grant perseverance in patience—he who has granted to unworthy persons the will to suffer for him!

[Col. 0139A] May the Church and all your household, according to my wish and prayer, fare well; and likewise all who, by the benefit of their intercessions, share in our necessity.

## LETTER CXLVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1166)

To the Lord Bishop of Poitiers.

Although among us Fortune—the parent of novelties—and Rumour—the nurse and spreader of both true and false reports—have produced nothing worth reporting or requiring notification to you, a sad rumour has nevertheless imposed upon me the necessity of writing. Since the departure of our good lord, and would that he might always be blessed, I have heard or seen nothing at all sadder than this—God and my conscience bear witness to my words—although my own lot has been exposed to every danger and tossed by unceasing storms from the day when divine providence took from us our father and lord. For our companions who are staying at Paris recently wrote to me that they had learned from certain tale-bearers that an illness had forced you to take to your bed—an illness brought on neither by nature nor by the ordinary human mishap that commonly occurs, but by the malice of poisoners who, at whose instigation I do not know, mixed poison for you and for a certain religious man. It was also said that this religious man has already died from that cause. Since, therefore, I had heard long ago of the hostility of certain persons living with you, knew the cruelty of others, and remembered the bold ambition of some, I was afraid, and am afraid, and until the truth itself has been more certainly established, shall be excessively afraid lest the devil and his angels, who now rage almost at will against the Church, have been allowed thus far to vent their fury upon the good.

Previously I had feared that the fortress of the Church might be taken from you; that wicked men might proscribe you from your possessions; that those who make what is lawful equal to whatever pleases them might compel you also to share exile with the children and faithful members of the Church. But behold: of two fears concerning the same lord and friend, the greater darkens and wholly swallows the other, so that I receive this as though a sword passed through my soul, my shoulder fell from its joint, and my arm with its bones were crushed. My spirit shall have no rest until the truth is more certainly known. May it therefore please your graciousness to inform me with all speed of what concerns you, while I languish in desire for certainty; and if you yourselves—may it never be so!—cannot attend to this request of mine, I earnestly beg that the Master of the Schools carry it out with every care and haste.

## LETTER CXLVII. TO MASTER RAYMOND. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master RAYMOND.

A most bitter rumour has wounded and grievously afflicted my soul, nor shall there be rest until I can be informed by your letters concerning those things which I most fear. For my Parisian companions wrote to me that those seeking the life of the lord Bishop of Poitiers, employing I know not whose agency and an ineffectual and wholly detestable art, administered poison to him. A certain religious prior, who had shared in the poisoned cup, has already died from it; and the bishop, they say, has fallen ill. I therefore feared, and fear beyond measure, because I have heard of the hostility of certain persons, and that a bishop of Poitiers was recently killed by poison. Whether this report speaks truthfully is uncertain; but the cruelty of others is so great that it escapes neither neighbours nor those far away.
