And it is known to all how headlong and bold, and ignorant of the fear of the Lord, blind ambition is; thus very many grounds for fear rather than confidence seem to concur.

I therefore beg you to write, with all haste, most carefully concerning what is happening about you; and, if he is not hindered by illness—may that be far from him!—to persuade the lord bishop to write himself whatever it may then be appropriate to write. I had intended to ask that both he and you write about what was done at the conference of Chinon, and afterwards, for us and against us; and what seems to you concerning the matter which has so exiled me that I did not receive peace with the others under the oath and conditions offered. But since then I have not seen your letters; and the greater cause which now compels me to write has swallowed up all concerns of that kind. Yet if, as may the Lord grant, matters are rightly proceeding with the lord bishop—I mean in respect of his safety—I shall then most gladly receive an answer concerning this as well.

Moreover, because this anxiety does not leave my mind, if—may the Lord avert it!—the lord bishop should happen to be so ill, exert every effort, as a wise and prudent man, that in such peril he may show himself a Christian and, if necessary, await death as a priest of Christ; and, having set his house in order, patiently receive the gift of nature which cannot be avoided. Yet I trust in the Lord Jesus Christ that he who gave him wisdom to pass through temporal goods will grant him at the completion of his course the grace that, as his life has shone among those who eat at his table, so his death may also benefit all who are dying as an example. No one will offer a more faithful proof of devotion and faith than one who takes pains and care to advance, by exhortations to virtue and the notable examples of good works—and above all at the end of the road—those whom he loved as fellow-exiles in the flesh and pilgrims in the Lord; and to pursue and urge on those departing and ascending to Christ, as it were with the arms of a twofold charity.

But if, through the mercy of God, matters concerning you proceed more joyfully, I earnestly ask that you endeavour by every means to induce our translator in this matter: that he translate and revise in his own manner what remains of the work on the *Hierarchy*, of which he has translated one book; for what he has already sent forth greatly pleases those who have seen it in France. I had intended to write more, but haste does not permit it.

## LETTER CXLVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0141A]

To the lord Bishop of Poitiers.

To the Father of mercies, who raised you from grave illness for his own honour, the benefit of the Church, and the consolation of our shipwreck, I give manifold and every kind of thanks; then to your graciousness, which, constantly and effectively caring for me, has softened by the comfort of its letter the distress of my fear and grief conceived over your illness. But since afterwards I have received no information either about your complete recovery or about the promised and hoped-for peace, I judged that the bearer of this letter should be sent to you. Through him I beg with my whole heart that you write back more carefully concerning each matter which you know should be communicated to me.

Indeed, I desire your peace exceedingly; nor do I see what means you can employ in this case for recovering or preserving the rights of your Church, except those supplied to you by the Church itself and her children, or those which, by common law, avail the other churches—especially since a man of foreign birth, reared and educated among foreign peoples, cannot adequately be taught the special customs of Aquitaine and its unheard-of rights. Therefore, since you have omitted, and omit, nothing among the available means, if the cause of the Church is endangered because her children dissemble or betray it, this must not be imputed to your negligence. For who, unless he were of unsound mind, reckless, or an enemy, would advise you, without the support of arguments and resources, to presume alone and vainly to raise your arms against a torrent that drags and overturns everything behind it?

For the approved form of peace presents the appearance of equity; and in truth, if the matter is conducted on both sides in the making of the agreement with simple sincerity of faith, it contains complete equity—unless perhaps, during the peace of your predecessors, some custom had been usurped by one side against the Lord. For no lapse of time and no agreement of contracting parties can make that which is knowingly presumed against God’s commands be done lawfully, much less justly; indeed, can make it not a criminal act.

Yet I mistrust both the unfaithfulness of your people, of which I hear, and the terrible and malicious power of the opposing party, which many experience; so that I cannot easily believe that anyone dares resist its will. Perhaps he exercised hostilities against your archdeacon, whose ability he feared and whose intimacy with you he suspected, so that, once reconciled with him, he might not dare thereafter to utter a word against him; nor might others, frightened by his example—or rather by ours—especially because he presents himself as one who wishes to appear without fear of God or reverence for men. Yet God is able to raise up and direct your cause—indeed, his own cause—in your hands. And he who, by the Lord’s command, granted Israel, hastening toward the promised land, favour with its enemies, can either appease your Egyptians or utterly overthrow them.

[Col. 0142A]

One thing I know: the righteous man shall at last be delivered from distress, and the wicked shall be given in his stead. I rejoice that his peace and favour have been fully restored to you. But I fear—may it be far otherwise!—that, in the manner of a man known to all, this restoration of peace and favour may be feigned and short-lived. This is the more so because it is notorious everywhere that he follows the counsel of locusts, whose power is only in their tongues and tails. If it is short-lived, it is certain that it was feigned, especially so that he might thereby extort an obligation of fidelity; and, unless I am mistaken, he thinks that something is thereby to come within his power to which Christian faith does not permit a Christian to bind himself: namely, that henceforth you should withdraw the offices of due charity from those whom he has decided to hate, and should attack, at least by counsel and assistance, all whom he has called his enemies. And if, constrained by the religion of Christian faith, you conduct yourself otherwise toward him, he will try, as he is accustomed, to brand you in the ears of the nations, even as old friends, with the mark of faith not kept.

His locusts too will cry out for him; and he cherishes frogs in the mud, which with the unclean breath of their mouths encrust every purity, and by the deceit of oaths turn anyone black into white. These are limbs of flesh joined to one another, where scale clings to scale so that not even a breath can pass between them. They may think whatever they please; and, so that those who are in filth may become filthier still, they cloak the unchastity of their minds with the buffoonery of their gestures and the foul speech of their mouths. For nothing is permissible to a Christian—much less to a priest—under the pretext of fidelity where charity, the life of faith and the thing made manifest by the testimony of works, is endangered. For faith without works is dead.

That formula, however, by which he wishes security to be given to himself and his heirs against all mortals—how highly he values it is clear from the letters of the German tyrant, which he sent to Count Henry and which I would have sent you had they not slipped from my possession; I have sent them to the lord of Canterbury. For when John of Oxford, in the king’s name, was about to swear an alliance with the German tyrant and promised by oath the aid of assistance and counsel against all men, except the king of France alone, the German said through his interpreter—as distinguished, numerous, and religious men of our country, I mean the province of Rheims, who were present, testify:

> “Roland, the enemy of the Church and Empire, is indeed a mortal man, and so are all his cardinals; and none of them is the king of France. Therefore I understand, and do not wish it to be understood, that any of them is excepted in this confederation of myself and the king of England. If you understand otherwise, publicly declare it.”

To this John replied: “We and our lord understand it as you do, and under this understanding we give the oaths on behalf of our king.”

Why say more? Thereafter proceedings were taken against the Lord and the Church, in accordance with that confederation. You will see this even more fully from letters recently sent to me from Cologne, a copy of which I send you. In them the king seeks safe-conduct for his messengers who are going to Rome against the Archbishop of Canterbury, and thereby his devotion to the Roman Church will readily become known.

[Col. 0143A]

But the wicked shall be caught in their own snares, and he who prepares a pit for his brother shall fall into it first. Yet blessed is he who, amid such great snares of the great harlot and the assault of the beast, can preserve both conscience and reputation: the one for the Lord, the other for his neighbour, both for himself. For when anyone is justly accused of harming either, I do not at all see from where he may draw consolation unless he redeem by virtue what he has lost.

Accordingly, in answer to the final point of your letter, I earnestly beg you, by the ineffable charity of the Lord, that if you judge that my peace should be negotiated, whether through your archdeacon or another—which indeed I desire—you secure it in such a form as cannot damage my reputation—or rather, conscience, which keeps reputation intact. For what would it profit to gain the whole world and to risk these things? And if you see me—may God avert it!—inclined toward anything shameful, which in men such as I often happens through weakness but always through fault, I beg you, raise me with your right hand. By “shameful,” moreover, I understand whatever is deliberately presumed against the Lord.

Although both the straitness of my resources and the cooling charity of my friends seem to press hard upon my brother, who shares exile with me from necessity, and upon me, nevertheless, the Lord urging:

> “I do not yet yield to evils, but shall go forward more boldly against them,  
> wherever my fortune permits me.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.95

I know that, on your counsel, I shall accept no condition which bears even the appearance of dishonour. Meanwhile the Lord will provide, as he has done until now, whatever may be necessary. In the account of giving and receiving, I am indebted to very few, but above all to my abbot and to you, and almost to you alone.

## LETTER CXLIX. JOHN SARRACENUS TO MASTER JOHN OF SALISBURY. (A.D. 1167.)

Since I perceived that your integrity of judgment takes delight in the books of blessed Dionysius, I have translated for your charity his book *On the Angelic Hierarchy*. Yet I confess that I have been unable to express in Latin the refinements of diction of this most learned and eloquent man. For among the Greeks there are certain compounds by which things are elegantly and precisely signified; but among the Latins the same things are designated by two or more words, inelegantly, imprecisely, and sometimes inadequately. For the commendation of a person or another thing, articles are beautifully repeated among them, and through the same articles many clauses are connected with one another with great polish. I say nothing of the remarkable construction of participles and of infinitives joined with articles. Such refinements could not be found among the Latins.

For it happens that if words are translated in the order in which they stand, they are either understood only with difficulty or seem to make a different sense. Therefore, where I judged it suitable, I preserved the order of the words; but elsewhere I changed the order for easier understanding. Where I found no Latin words equivalent to the Greek ones, or discovered that an expression departed from Latin idiom, I either distorted the Greek words or expressed, in Latin words, what I could and as I could from the author’s meaning. Frequently, where I put two or three Latin words for one Greek word, I joined them together as though they were one—not because I wished them to be a single word, but so that the meaning might be fuller and it might appear how much elegance this treatise loses through the poverty of Latin expression.

This book contributes very greatly to the understanding of all the divine Scriptures in which the deeds or sayings of angels are discussed. For it includes all divine spirits under three hierarchies; it divides each hierarchy into three orders and discusses each of them most profoundly. It also raises certain questions concerning angels and supplies their solutions. Finally, it explains the meanings of figures assigned in the sacred Scriptures. It will be for your discernment to compare this translation of mine with the translation of John Scotus. And if perhaps I shall seem to you to have translated it more suitably than he did, you may obtain for me the opportunity to translate also the book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.

## LETTER CL. TO THE ABBOT OF ST EDMUND’S. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0144C]

To the Abbot of Saint Edmund’s.

I ought not to be unconcerned about your condition, which may God make prosperous, since I keep constantly in mind the merits of your integrity. For charity neither slips away through neglect, nor is stolen by deceit, nor violently shaken out, because it is more firmly founded by Christ and in Christ in the minds of the elect. The malice of the times deprives you of my service, but no one can take away my will. No violence can accomplish that end, and every effort of all deceit shall be frustrated, he mercifully granting success who in the free goodness of charity gave the beginning.

It will therefore be for your graciousness to uphold with your prayers, and those of the holy persons who are with you, the shipwreck of the Church and the cares and labours of Christ’s exiles, so that he who has exposed us to temptation and granted us the will to suffer for him may grant perseverance in patience. For this, as Peter says (1 Peter 2), is grace: that we may at least in some measure share in the sufferings of Christ and the saints, certain that those who suffer with him shall also reign with him. Was the clergy established merely to eat, drink, snore, await death, and inflame hell with varied incentives to lust? At this the prudence of the flesh laughs; it mocks in the voices of the faithless Jews and curses him who hangs on the tree with Christ. Yet meanwhile, according to Deborah’s prophecy: “The Lord devises new wars; he himself overthrows the gates of the enemies” (Judges 5).

## LETTER CLI. TO NICHOLAS OF MONT-SAINT-HILAIRE. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0145A]

To NICHOLAS of Mont-Saint-H[ilaire].

Your brotherhood knows how patiently we have borne the losses, injuries, and insults inflicted upon us and ours by our most beloved lord, the illustrious king of England. But he, abusing our patience, has broken out into injuries against his most holy mother: I mean the bride of the Crucified One. He has not feared to enslave her, for whose liberation the Son of God and Lord chose to be condemned to a most shameful death. We warned him often with a father’s affection; we pleaded with him by the fidelity owed to the Lord; we rebuked him with a shepherd’s authority. But in our person he likewise despised his faithful father and shepherd; and, lest anything further be withheld from the truth—what is more dangerous to the Church and more destructive to himself—he spat upon Christ whose person we bear.

Let these things be considered empty and let him despise them as usual, if the Son of God does not say to the shepherds of the Church: “He who despises you despises me,” and “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2). Our concern proceeded further: for the peace of the Church, the supreme pontiff offered devout prayers, but was not heard; he made exhortations and found a deaf hearer; he added rebukes, which were despised; at length the apostolic trumpet sounded threats, yet even thus neither faith nor religion could be roused.

And lest we omit anything among the available measures, the king of France, who is his friend and lord, applied every effort and diligence; but even he, despite the respect owed him, was not granted a hearing. We came to his conference; but we were not admitted even to his presence, nor did he allow mention to be made of your name or of God’s cause. Afterwards we sent him honourable men as messengers and open letters, as was fitting, in which both the justice of the Church and the substance of our petition were set forth; but our labour and theirs, so far as he was concerned, came to nothing. We had followed the pledge of the Empress, as you know and as he ought not to be ignorant; but he has utterly deceived us.

Since, therefore, this patience of ours is harmful to God’s Church, yet more harmful to him whose later actions become daily worse than the former, and most harmful to us, who shall have to render account before the tribunal of the Bridegroom not only for our own deeds but also for his blood and for the affliction of his bride: know for certain, and inform the Empress, that shortly—indeed, very shortly—while life accompanies us and the Lord gives the impulse, we shall draw against his person and land the sword of the Holy Spirit, sharper in penetration than any two-edged sword, so that it may be ruin to hardened flesh and salvation to a spirit asleep—indeed, almost extinguished.

Persuade our lady, therefore, henceforth to hold us excused in a matter which we may no longer voluntarily overlook; and let her know for certain that, if her son should return to life and accept his mother’s counsel by hearing the Lord’s voice, she will find us ready for the honour of God and for her will. Meanwhile let us together mourn, with one and the same affection, her dying son, whose salvation and honour, God being witness, we alike desire and desire with a like longing. We speak these things amid pain, tears, sobs, and sighs, as though our own entrails were drawn from the enclosure of our breast by bitterness and seared by the burning of a cautery. God knows this; and we ought no longer to exercise impious pity to his injury, preferring on earth mother, father, and sister to the Lord. There is no sorrow like this sorrow; but the charity of God, and the welfare and honour of him whose cause is being attended to, compel us to endure these things with a strong mind.

Farewell. Greet and stir up our brethren, that they may obtain for us the spirit of counsel and fortitude, praying for the lord king that the spirit of knowledge and truth may be with him, so that his peace may be restored in the Lord to God’s Church and to us.

## LETTER CLII. TO WILLIAM AND ODO, PRIORS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1166.)

To the priors of the holy Church of Canterbury, JOHN OF SALISBURY.

Your discernment can and should remember how great a reverence must be shown to Fathers, and how much kindness the holy Church of Canterbury has bestowed upon its archbishops. Although I do not dare to compare him who now presides over us with his predecessors, who shine in our Church by miracles, nevertheless I do not think the cause he defends is inferior. For it is the same cause, since in each case the struggle has been for the liberty and salvation of the Church.

I hope in the Lord, because the Roman Church gives many indications encouraging confidence, that the pilgrimage and labour of our Father will prevail for the restoration of the Church of Canterbury and the complete re-establishment of the dignities and privileges which it enjoyed under the presidency of blessed Lanfranc. But let this be said in your hearing: it is fitting for you too to bring every assistance within your strength—indeed, almost beyond your strength—to your Father’s shipwreck, and to earn his favour by benefits, so that when, with God’s help, he has prevailed, he may and ought to remember you favourably.

For is it not indecent and disgraceful if strangers assist a bishop exiled for justice’s sake, while the children—for whom (the text has *cujus*; read *quibus*) he stores up honour and glory—refuse to share his necessities? Did you not offer him in chapter everything, even the shrines of the saints, so that he might obtain these things for you? Therefore, because for this cause he is indebted to the Roman Church in a modest sum of money, he himself petitions and I, your faithful servant, advise that you assist him in this necessity, lest the lord pope repent of his favour and you be ashamed and grieved forever at your inhumanity. Let the examples of strangers encourage you: they withdraw from their own uses and necessities—even things obtained by the labour of their hands—in order to give them to your exiles.

## LETTER CLIII. TO MASTER R., OF REDON. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0147A]

1. To R. of Redon.

It is long, most loving of friends, since I have wished to be informed of your condition and that of my other old friends; and I desire it all the more ardently because it has happened more rarely that I receive news of you, either about you or from you. Yet I sometimes hear something about you, through the kindness of intermediaries; but I have never heard anything from you. I do not clearly see why this occurs, unless I conjecture that, since the days are evil and you are a prudent man, you have kept silent out of a certain caution.

But, to confess my weakness in your hearing and reveal my folly to a friend, I have never been able to maintain such caution as would prevent me from wishing to share in my friends’ opportunities and to exercise concern for them according to my capacity. Since, therefore, I have often written to you and you have never written, my ever more inflamed concern can no longer be restrained from seeking by a personal messenger what is your condition and that of our old friends. Do not suppose that by “old” I mean “grown old,” persons in whom charity has grown cold; for I have neither thought nor said that they have suffered any loss of charity. For who am I, that I should judge another’s servant, who stands or falls to his own Lord? But he shall stand, God being the author of it.

And for my part charity is serviceable, ignorant of every evil, strong as death, and reveals its sincerity through many enduring signs. It has a testimony continually greater than John: both works and the fruits of works bear witness to it. If you have leisure and permission, and care to do so, you may learn from the bearer of this letter, whom I sent for this purpose, about my condition and that of the others; and he will explain to you how you may make me more fully informed about yours. Know, however, that I have permission and leisure for this, and am concerned with whole-hearted devotion that I may gladly obey your commands and those of yours, if in your pilgrimage you deign to enjoin anything upon me. It will count for me as a great gift if, by your command, I happen to be occupied in some service of yours. Dare then, friend—dare to ask or command something of a friend who offers himself and all that is his with his whole heart.

## LETTER CLIV. TO ROBERT, PRIOR OF MERTON. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0147D]

To ROBERT, Prior of Merton.

Where human counsel fails, one necessarily has recourse to divine counsel; and this, I think, is obtained by no way more easily or happily than when the friends of God seek to obtain by prayers what the fault of those needing assistance has forfeited. I am indeed an exile and an outlaw; and, so far as human judgment is concerned, I see no just cause for either punishment, although before the Lord I know myself to have deserved harsher things. Perhaps, through the claims of my sins, it has happened that I am struck with these and harsher scourges, yet do not know the cause of the blow. God’s judgments are all the more to be feared because they proceed from a more hidden justice and a more secret reason.

The punishment is twofold when the punishment itself is felt and its cause is unknown. Yet if it is the divine mercy that wishes me to suffer for justice’s sake, I receive it most gratefully, certain that he has judged it right to bless his friends in this way, because through many tribulations one enters the kingdom. I confess that I have kept faith with God’s Church and faithfully obeyed my archbishop, as I ought; nor, God being the author of it, shall I ever repent of fidelity or obedience maintained. I hope, moreover, that your archbishop too, following the footsteps of the Fathers on the straight path, proceeds by the way of God’s commandments toward life.

Therefore I beseech your fatherhood, your lords, and your brethren, with all the devotion I can, to commend our struggle to the Lord in prayer: so that, if we are off the road, we may be brought back to the way; if we are on the way, as indeed we believe, we may make progress and be led to life. For we need nothing else except that our cause may please the Lord.

## LETTER CLV. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER. (A.D. 1166.)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to BALDWIN, Archdeacon of Exeter.

Although I have been indebted to your affection from long ago, the concern of your integrity, not so much frequent as unceasing, renders my devotion ever more strictly bound to you each day. For whom would untiring and unfailing fidelity not win favour in adversity? Whose heart is not kindled and inflamed amid dangers and the furnace of trials by charity that is incorruptible, active, and surpassing?

What I commend in you I have greatly experienced in my own case, but experience even more in that of my brother. For I regard his lot as harsher than mine, except that mine and his are shared from the heart, and thus our condition is the same. Yet he is more heavily exiled who is exiled at home. Just as it is glorious to flourish in one’s own city and pleasant to be honoured in one’s native land, so it is grievous to be needy or held cheap among one’s own people. For it is less shameful to beg among strangers.

This adversity is of no small—indeed, of great—use to both of us: through it we come to know ourselves, and the world becomes known to us, more faithfully and intimately. At last we learn what we had heard for a long time and what was written many ages ago: “He who does not appear as a friend in prosperity does not lie hidden as an enemy in adversity.” Therefore, most beloved friend, amid the storm of this tempest each person has cast off the mask he wore, wiped away deceptive cosmetics, and revealed his own face with countenance uncovered.

Accordingly, because we see the face of your faith and charity in your apparent tribulation unchanged indeed, but certainly clearer and more illustrious, we approve it all the more rightly and deservedly. We desire, with frequent sighs and the greatest longing, that we may make a fitting return; and meanwhile we return it in affection. God, who is charity, shall beyond doubt make an effective return to our charity, so that, as he promised, he may pour into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, and overflowing.

I have written to the lord bishop concerning the state in which your cause stands, and from this matters concerning us will become more fully known to us. I therefore beg you to aid our pilgrimage by your prayers and those of the holy persons who are with you: that our faith may not fail, nor may we do anything to swell the storm of this tempest, by which the Lord is offended; but that he may do what is his—to provide, together with temptation, also the way of escape. Indeed, he has already begun: he has given us devotion to suffer for justice’s sake and softened the bitterness of exile; for it is now lighter than it was on the first day. Did we lack anything? Do we not now have more acquaintances and friends, who have demonstrated by the performance of services and benefits the love which they profess? Thus they bring a testimony greater than John to prove their love: for the works they themselves do bear witness concerning them.

## LETTER CLVI. TO RICHARD, HIS BROTHER. (A.D. 1166.)

To R., his brother.

I have written very little to you, because you will learn my situation both from the letters sent to the lord bishop and from the bearer’s own voice. When anything worthy of report emerges, I shall not delay to notify you. Meanwhile, carefully ascertain the counsel and intention of the lord bishop and of Master Baldwin, the archdeacon, and the disposition of the other friends, so that from these matters, with the Lord’s help, you may either write back or carry out whatever seems most expedient.

Do not be disturbed about my exile, but remember that we brought nothing into this world, nor indeed shall we carry anything out. May God vindicate the cause, for I too trust that it is just; because my condition is not only bearable but pleasant to me, especially when I look to the cause. I do not deny that I have deserved more bitter things, but those things are not alleged against me by my persecutor: rather, sin is punished. I gratefully receive the scourge of my purification. If patience is tested, I hope it will lead to a crown; if I am afflicted so that pride may be crushed, I know that devout humility ascends to glory.

It is certain that every scourge benefits the patient sufferer, making the mind more ready to despise the world and practise virtues. But if the spur of a harsher hell hardens the mind, it is the opinion of brutish men that merits must be weighed by outcomes, although the righteous are made a mockery and an image of reproach for the wicked. But wait a little, and [lacuna]; even their visitation; and meanwhile there is no peace for the wicked. By God’s most just judgment, persecutors of justice clash against one another, are cast down, broken, and perish. But even sleeping, the righteous man shall triumph over his enemies all the more gloriously because more innocently. Who has hoped in the Lord and been abandoned? Search will be made from the beginning of time, but not even on the last day will such a person be found.

## LETTER CLVII. TO ROGER OF SIDEBERIA. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0150A]

To ROGER of Sideberia, J. sends greetings, and wishes that you may happily attain the desired fruit of blessing before everyone else, with no obstacle or annoyance from one flying ahead, running ahead, or hindering you.

I hope, most beloved friend, that my desire in this matter will easily be fulfilled, unless perhaps Richard of Sideberia, with youthful eagerness, snatches the palm from your diligence. But if this has entered his mind, may God grant him such matter for joy and delight that necessity may remove from him the obligation of rendering what youthful rashness was attempting to snatch from you. Yet if in this or any other matter he imitates his father in something that may seem to involve fault, let us who are more advanced in age and rank, and those like us, correct him in a spirit of gentleness, considering whether we too may at some time have been tempted.

Should not indulgence be granted to a boy if he bends once in the night, when even the righteous falls seven times in the day? What if he had entered a path on which no other had gone? If the mother no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world, why should the father henceforth feel the pangs of one giving birth? Let him therefore be punished only so far that he is not allowed to call out our “bless you” until the appointed day, unless pardon has been obtained—provided, however, that he shares in the fruit of the blessing.

For the rest, I thank you for the honour and love which you show to me and to my brother. For what is done to him I consider done to me, so much so that I regard my own sides as warmed in him by the fleeces of your sheep.

### Letter CLVIII. To Alfred de Cerda. (A.D. 1166.)

To ALFRED de Cerda.

I am bound to render fuller thanks to your affection in proportion as you have shown the more sincere and ardent charity in compassionating my exile, especially since no merits of mine preceded it, though the will to deserve it has always been present. And because at present I cannot answer your merits in kind, meanwhile I devote myself, with the readiest will, to your service, and, God being the author of it, shall one day give effect to this ready devotion. God, moreover, will undoubtedly reward the service of your charity; and although He has deprived us of the means of recompensing you, He whose hand is neither poor, nor miserly, nor powerless will render to your kindness what befits Him, pouring into your bosom, in abundant mercy, a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.

### Letter CLIX. To Robert, Son of Aegidia. (A.D. 1166.)

To ROBERT, son of Aegidia.

I must begin by giving thanks, unless I wish to stain both conscience and reputation with the fault of ingratitude. For you have deserved this in many ways, [Col. 0151A] much indeed in my own person, but especially in that of our little brother, whose necessities you are said to share, bearing them as your own and encouraging others to share them. For you know the saying of the Apostle Peter: “If anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify the Lord” (1 Peter IV); for this is grace in His sight. And you are certain, I think, that this little brother of ours does not suffer as a murderer, thief, reviler, or coveter of other men’s goods; and this too, as I hear, you make known to others, for our consolation, indeed, but for the glory and salvation of those who render him offices of humanity.

My affection therefore gives you the greatest thanks for the present, while the resources of an exile permit nothing more; yet, God being the author of it, I shall one day show them in deed [Col. 0151B] most fully. I pray that you may laudably persevere in the kindness you have begun toward my brother, because whatever is withdrawn from your means will be supplied to you by the recompender of all good things. Farewell.

### Letter CLX. To Master Gauf. of St Edmund. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master GAUFRID of St Edmund.

I pray you, most reverend sir, to provide the protection of my innocence against—or before—those among whom, God being witness, I am endangered without cause, and among whom I had trusted that I myself could secure the most effective protection, nor indeed do I yet despair, if only the truth becomes known to our friends and lords. The matter is this. It has been represented to the Bishop of Norwich and to Master Nicholas that from Sens I wrote letters to Benedict of Bedigeham against their honour, advantage, peace, and security—letters which I could not have written without injury to conscience and the stigma of a traitor. My brother sent me a copy of them, and I send it on to you.

I call upon the Lord as judge and witness over my soul that I neither wrote those letters nor know in my conscience who wrote them. I say more, testifying under the same adjuration: they were neither conceived nor written by my command, manner of direction, knowledge, will, or ratification. I shall say still more: so may God restore me to the land of my birth and grant me to enjoy the sight and conversation [Col. 0151D] of you and my other friends, as I never in my life remember having sent to the aforesaid Benedict either these letters or any others, as I speak from the most certain knowledge of my conscience. I add that, whenever I could, I opposed Benedict with all my strength on Nicholas’s behalf.

But perhaps Benedict himself proclaimed me as the author of the letters. Ought his word to have been believed—he who, just as he strove to deprive me, his adversary, of the favour of my friends, so desired to withdraw my service from them? Certainly he craftily deceived his credulous enemies, so that a false author of the letters might be accused and the true one not guarded against, and thus, unsuspected, might injure them more effectively. Yet if my accuser, Benedict or another, wishes to charge me, let him come forward and accuse me openly; and unless I defend my innocence, [Col. 0152A] I concede without contradiction that I ought to be punished with a traitor’s penalty.

But if my innocence is made clear, I ask that my old friends and lords do not withdraw their due favour from an innocent man. If, however, my accuser prefers to slander me in silence rather than accuse me openly, I pray that, after such purgation as may please my lords has been accepted, I may be held acquitted. Nor do I say this because I expect temporal profit from them. For now, through thirty months of exile, Christ’s generosity has been enough for me—He who feeds the birds of heaven and clothes the lilies of the fields.

You ask, therefore: what do you seek? Surely that which will benefit them more than me: their former and due charity in the Lord. For, Christ being the author of it, I shall love them as long as I live, whether they wish it or not. And if they refuse to love one who loves them, tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me, if the Lord sees anything upon the mountain. But, as I hear, my Nicholas says that the style is mine. I plainly do not believe it to be mine; and the Lord is my witness that I grieve more that his firmness admitted so readily the suspicion of so great a falsehood than I do for the loss I have endured for many days. For an occasion to depart from a friend, especially at such a time, was not to be lightly embraced. I, with the Searcher of hearts delivering me, shall easily escape. And would that he himself, for the rashness of his judgment against an innocent friend, may not easily incur the stain of disgrace.

### Letter CLXI. To Master Nicholas. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0152C]

To Master NICHOLAS.

For a long time I have withheld my pen from the frequent letters which I was accustomed to send you; but my affection burns all the more. For excessive grief often restrains tears that seek to flow, and so tortures the mind more severely, shut up in the narrow confines of a wounded heart, the longer liberty to emerge, pour itself forth, and come into the light is denied it.

Nor do I say this as one driven by the force of an overwhelming storm. For, under philosophy’s teaching, I have learned that, just as violent impulse manages everything badly, so its force cannot endure long: driven by a suddenly rising whirlwind, it throws all things into confusion at once, but vanishes in a moment—indeed, it commonly fails before it has time to languish. Since therefore [Col. 0152D] the form of this world passes away like a shadow and, in a moment of storm, vanishes like smoke in the sight of philosophers—and this is even more firmly established by the faith of Christians—how can anything in prosperity or adversity seem lasting to the wise? And what is momentary—whose philosophic mind can it cast down or exalt?

I am therefore persuaded to bear with composure what I cannot avoid; and where my conscience does not reproach me, to rejoice in tribulations and in the plundering of my goods, giving thanks to divine providence. Yet, although grief does not consume me over the injuries and losses inflicted upon me, I am troubled because I am not permitted to see my friends; because the welcome conversation of the well-disposed is withheld; because the occasion and means of doing what duty requires of me are denied. [Col. 0153A] Over these things, I say, I am troubled—troubled, I say, over these things. But I am troubled far more over the affliction of the Church; and amid the disturbance of my friends, which I hear of almost every day, my whole heart is shaken.

Yet no cause of sorrow is stronger or more violent than this: that the force of this storm has shaken charity, as the testimony of deeds proves, out of the minds of certain persons in whom I trusted and who seemed to be of some account. This, dearest friend, is what I lament in your ears, since I consider you unlike them: I see the finest colour changed, and the silver of faithful men turned into dross. Perhaps you ask whence I infer this. To that I answer: I do not infer it; I prove it from the fact that, although I had many friends while I stood in prosperity, [Col. 0153B] scarcely one or two have been found who are willing or dare to greet me when, as they believe, I am in adversity. Nevertheless, if the hope of greeting me would bring them harm, I prefer, provided charity itself is not endangered, that they refrain from dangerous acts rather than endanger themselves on my account.

But perhaps receiving my letters is a crime; and thus I may be restrained from writing. Yet, God being the author of it, no one can prevent me from loving my friends—even those less affectionate toward me, or wholly hostile. But enough of this.

Furthermore, I ask that you keep my brother in your care. Although he has not obtained the full favour which he never deserved, he has at least obtained the king’s peace; and I ask you to commend him to my lord, the Bishop of Norwich. And because he would not dare to repay me the three marks due at the present feast of St John, I pray that he transfer them, under whatever designation he chooses, to my brother; for whatever good he does to him, I shall receive more gratefully than if it had been shown to me in my own person.

### Letter CLXII. To Henry, Bishop-elect of Bayeux. (A.D. 1166.)

To Lord HENRY, bishop-elect of Bayeux.

Whether I ought rather to rejoice or grieve over this thing which the Lord has done concerning us is nearly uncertain even to me after long reflection. For when I consider your advancement, proceeding especially from your good merits, [Col. 0153D] I rejoice in the divine dispensation and in the virtues which, from your earliest years, I embraced as growing and flourishing in you, as in another patriarch Jacob; and I strengthened them by the aid of continual prayer and daily blessing, that they might know no failure at all.

But when, from the other side, Salisbury Church—once illustrious, now as though bereaved of its sun—comes before my mind, and the clergy meet me sorrowfully and repeat in tearful voice: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver” (4 Kings II), “why do you leave us, or to whom do you leave us desolate?”—and multiply many more words in this fashion, easier to conceive than to write—I cannot keep back tears, but mourn with those who mourn; and, sharing the grief of my mother, Salisbury Church, [Col. 0154A] I hesitate. When I think of a successor, a crowd of competitors comes rushing forward; but if there is one whom my mind imagines likely to surpass the rest, when he is compared with his predecessor he is regarded just as if Phaethon were usurping his father’s chariot. Whose breast, then, is so iron that it can restrain its tears?

Indeed, the joy conceived at your promotion would be swallowed up by sorrow arising from the Church’s desolation, unless the pagan poet reminded my mind that “to be distressed by one’s own misfortunes rather than by a friend’s is the part not of a friend, but of a man who loves himself.” Thus consoled in mind, I submit and give thanks to God, who alone is powerful and has chosen, by your splendour, to illuminate another realm also for His glory. Yet because you are now departing from our regions, I earnestly pray you, before your departure, always and everywhere to strive to restore peace to me [Col. 0154B] and to my brother. For the Lord knows that I do not believe I have deserved this indignation. Consider therefore, Father, if you please, on what reckoning you leave your friends.

### Letter CLXIII. To Robert, Prior of Merton. (A.D. 1166.)

To the Prior of Merton.

I give you thanks because, as I have learned from your letters and from the reports of very many persons, you are concerned for me; and I hope that through God’s mercy your concern will benefit me. I believe it has already benefited me, and I ascribe to your prayers and those of my friends the fact that every day of my pilgrimage has gone well for me. And because I count myself yours always and everywhere, I earnestly pray [Col. 0154C] that you intercede for me with the Lord: that He may not allow me to be tempted beyond what I can bear, but may grant me an issue with the temptation; that, when and how He sees fit—if indeed this be His will—He may restore me to the land of my birth without loss of conscience or reputation; and that He may soften the settled indignation of the lord king, who, with the Lord and my conscience as witnesses, has long persecuted me without cause and still persecutes me.

May God spare him and not allow the storm of this tempest to shake charity out of my heart. Yet I trust that the Bishop of London and the Archdeacon of Poitiers will, if they see an opportunity, act for my peace. Nor do I despair of Richard de Luci. I therefore ask that you too, if you see an opportunity, urge these men on my behalf, provided that you do not think it harmful to your church. But if it is not safe to approach men, I ask that you pray to the Lord more devoutly, that He may direct my steps in His paths. For He is able, in every place, to make a homeland for me, and beneficially to compensate abroad whatever is taken away at home.

### Letter CLXIV. To Richard, Archdeacon of Poitiers. (A.D. 1166.)

To RICHARD, Archdeacon of Poitiers.

Your discernment may remember in what hope I left you, when your sincerity cheered me by showing me a certain way toward reconciliation and peace. Since I do not yet know how far the promise of your fidelity [Col. 0155A] has proved effective, I ask that you now release me from this uncertainty of doubt—me whom you have so far caused, through uncertain hope, to drift not without grave loss of time and resources—so that henceforth I may always be yours and your friends’.

For if it is safe for me to return, I am ready to make fitting satisfaction to the lord king wherever I cannot establish my innocence. Perhaps military disturbances have until now hindered you from considering this matter, or a domestic enemy—one with whom, if it is so decreed, I shall never have peace. For he did not harm me before he promised faith, friendship, and great advancement. But now I beseech you to tell me how far I ought to hope and what course I ought to follow, if a different one is now acceptable from that which was previously shown. And if I must return in any way, provide that I may pass safely through Kent; and remember the threats and the matter which I explained to you at Paris.

### Letter CLXV. To Richard, His Brother. (A.D. 1166.)

To RICHARD, his brother.

If I withheld affection or prayers from my greeting to you, I should seem deservedly to have shut myself out from the joys of my own salvation, which cannot exist without yours. Therefore, when this page does not offer you the customary greeting of those who write to friends, this does not arise from any lack of charity or from an impulse of faint-heartedness, but from reflection on your need. Therefore, that my longing for you may be satisfied, may the Most High greet you with a share in that salvation [Col. 0155C] with which the Virgin Mother—whose mind I do not doubt was and is most undefiled—desired with most sincere charity that her Son should be greeted.

Perhaps you marvel with the people, and grieve with my friends, that I have not accepted the peace which is said to have been offered to me by the most serene king of England, especially since learned men and better men have not merely accepted it but eagerly seized it. But remember that it was offered to me on the condition on which Nahash—whose name means “serpent”—the prince of the children of Ammon, “the straitener and oppresser,” or “people of sorrow,” wished to receive into alliance the inhabitants of Jabesh, “the dried-up place,” in Gilead: namely, with the sting of testimony. For Scripture says: “I will make a covenant with you if I put out all your right eyes and make you a reproach to all the children and borders of Israel” (1 Kings XI).

For I could have received what, as I think, is taken from me unjustly, had I been willing to set eternal things aside for a time and bind the freedom of the spirit with a harmful and certainly most dangerous oath. Each person abounds in his own understanding. I do not doubt that my right eye is occupied in contemplation of heavenly things, faith in the unseen, and hope of things to come; while the left is inclined toward transient and temporal things that flow away in a moment. They were admitted more kindly and, God being the author of it, may be saved in the sincerity of their faith. I, as circumstances required, could not give the demanded security without damage to salvation and reputation.

Therefore, turning to the Lord, I hope [Col. 0156A] that tomorrow salvation too will be mine, when the sun has grown hot—the sun that will reveal the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts, each person’s own righteousness or wrong answering for him. Although in this week of days Nahash presses me with his Ammonites—that is, the people of sorrow and the children of Gehenna—Christ will shortly come and console His chosen ones, in whom He now suffers for a moment. Therefore be comforted, my beloved, my beloved, be comforted. If you pass by but a little while, their place will not be found, because the wicked will vanish like smoke.

If meanwhile this expectation distresses you, it lies within your discretion and the bishop’s counsel for you to come aside to me, away from the face of the oppressor. If this is pleasing, I shall receive you as you come with the most sincere arms of charity; I shall have you not only as a sharer in all my goods but also, so far as you yourself allow it, as guardian and instructor both of myself and mine—and, if you can bear the word, as a father in affection. You will learn the rest from my other letters, and you need not hesitate to share yours with me, as you do habitually.

The king of France and the Gallican Church show much humanity to our fellow-exiles. Would that you may not find your fellow citizens and the household of the pledged faith more inhuman! But if necessity presses you, although your brothers are present, you will find no one more humane than me, for no bond is stronger than blood, nor, I think, than charity. Greet your friends, and urge the holy persons to share your necessities by relieving them with their intercessions. May the Most High always grant you happy success according to your desires.

### Letter CLXVI. To Nicholas de Sigillo.

[Col. 0156C]

To NICHOLAS de Sigillo.

There was, as I remember, a class of men who in the Church of God are designated by the name of archdeacons, for whom your discernment used to complain that every way of salvation was shut off. For, as you were accustomed to say, they love gifts, pursue recompense, are prone to injuries, delight in false accusations, eat and drink the sins of the people, and live by plunder, so that no guest is safe from another guest. Those among them who are most excellent ought certainly to keep the law of the Lord, but do not do so. Your compassionate pity used to lament these and similar things concerning the most wretched condition of men.

But good men and your friends must give thanks [Col. 0156D] to God and to the Bishop of Lincoln, who has opened your eyes and taught you the way by which this class of men may not only attain salvation, adorned with an innumerable crown of the saved, but may also win the higher aureole which marks out, just as it does those crowned by martyrdom and flourishing in virginity, those radiant in the office of preaching. This has indeed been done by the Lord, who opened the eyes of your blindness and, after truth was disclosed in the case of archdeacons, made you change your destructive opinion.

Although archdeacons may rightly rejoice at being acquitted by your judgment, I believe that I conceived no less joy than they at your promotion, because wherever I may be, I have devoted myself with the readiest will to your honour and service in whatever matters the judgment of your discernment should deem fit to prescribe. It would indeed be like a great gift if you wished to impose upon me something within my powers and thus in some measure test the affection of an exile.

Furthermore, the bearer of this letter has long remained in my and our brother’s service and has been found faithful in every respect. [Col. 0157A] He possesses skill in writing and experience in many useful matters. If, for love of you, it should please you to retain him in your service and employ his service, it would be most pleasing to us, because we cannot presently provide for him as we would wish. We trust, however, that with you his work and diligence will earn such favour that he will need no recommendation from us or others.

### Letter CLXVII. To Robert, Son of Aegidia. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0157B]

To ROBERT, son of Aegidia.

Besides the remembrance of you which brotherly affection calls forth in me, the token sent me by you—an outstanding sign of faith and devotion—very often gives my mind both cause and occasion to rejoice with you and to converse with you. For the material of the gift itself, if we examine its properties more carefully, plainly indicates what chiefly rules in the mind of its sender, provided that Archdeacon B[aldwin], R[oger] de Sideberia, and your little brother do not disagree.

For gold, incorruptible, abundant in extension, diminished neither by fire nor by blows, and uncontaminable, since it admits no rust and therefore preserves other metals too—does it not signify incorruptible faith, generous and expansive charity, constancy in adversity, and moderation, the preserver of virtues, in prosperity? For such, as you know better, is the nature of gold, made known by physical nature herself as teacher. Hence prudent men who wish to preserve their money from corruption mix silver with gold, so that through partnership with gold the silver may be preserved free from rust.

The roundness of the shape is a sign of perfection, teaching that the sender is perfected in the virtues mentioned. The gemlike brightness is an image of shining prudence and knowledge. And what of the heavenly colour itself? Does it not most fittingly indicate the end toward which the sender’s mind chiefly tends in its actions? The very name of the stone denotes beauty of word and deed. For *hyacinth* (*jacynthus*), if we consider the origin of the word in relation to the grace of its form, is interpreted “entirely a flower” or “universally flowering.” For *ja* conveys “universal,” and *cynthus* is rendered “flower.”

And lest faith waver at this crisis of the time, or reason be seduced by human persuasions, the inscription too confirms faith and enlightens reason. For, cleansing reason from error, it sends it to Christ; and lest a Christian’s faith fail from weakness amid tribulations and pressures, it ascribes victory to Christ. By these two words, faith is purified from weakness and reason from error. And because victory is the end of battle, and a crown the fruit [Col. 0158A] of victory, it consequently attributes kingship to Christ, teaching that those who have endured with Christ the hazards of contests and labours will reign with Him, while His adversaries, when justice is turned into judgment, will be crushed in a twofold crushing and confusion.

For the king’s honour loves judgment, and his eyes see because he loves equity. For where love is, there is the eye. And this, as it seems to me, is the meaning of the two enclosed devices; the third repeats Christ’s name and is silent about the dignity of empire, by a design, I think, intended both to fix the mind of the recipient upon Christ, victor over his persecutors and King of kings, and to bind it inseparably to Him; and to show that today there is no emperor who belongs to Christ. For the schismatic, striving by force, fraud, and the stain of heretics to divide indivisible unity, corrupt integrity, violate chastity, and, so far as lies in him, overthrow the Lord’s ordering and nullify the promises of truth, contrives to take the Roman empire away from Christ.

It follows, therefore, that Christ’s name is to be erased from the empire. But, as the inscription of your gift teaches, Christ’s name alone remains forever; the honour of one who presumptuously claims empire and glories in the false name of glory has been emptied, and He who is before the ages will surely humble him. All these matters, and more which I pass over in pursuit of brevity, I have contemplated in the ring, recognizing brotherly charity in the gift and being beneficially and variously instructed toward virtue by its qualities.

Is not such a man therefore to be loved and honoured by every right and desert? Indeed, it is always permitted to love him, nor can this be forbidden; and I do so ceaselessly and intensely, intending, when opportunity permits, gratefully to render love its due homage. Meanwhile I give such thanks as I can, earnestly asking that you keep our little brother commended to your care and show as much diligence as you can toward those connected with us.

### Letter CLXVIII. To Richard, Archdeacon of Poitiers. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master RAYMOND, Chancellor of the Church of Poitiers.

My servant, returning from you—for which I give innumerable thanks to your sincerity—brought letters displaying many signs [Col. 0158D] of faith and charity. They seem composed in such a spirit that every word, and almost every letter-stroke, faithfully declares that it has proceeded to a friend from the rich substance of most sincere affection.

But because those letters, like the written communication of my lord bishop, contained several heads of business that could increase the anxiety of one who loves—namely, that his full recovery, not yet attained, was hoped for; that there had been an agreement about restoring peace between him and the king; that my reconciliation had been mentioned; and other such matters in which you acted as a friend—I have sent the bearer of this letter to you, asking that through his intervention you make me more certain, by your letters if you please, concerning the matters aforesaid and all else affecting your own situation [Col. 0159A] or that of the public.

In obedience to your counsel, I deliberately sent a man unknown to you or known to few, who has proved faithful to me and mine in all things. He has been charged to conduct before the lord bishop the business of Master Walter, clerk of the lord Archbishop of Rheims, for the recovery of books which that Walter had entrusted to Master Peter Elias. I spoke with you about these at Angers and gave you a memorandum. You may therefore treat him as a servant of the household of the Archbishop of Rheims, as circumstances require; but the constant spur of anxiety in my soul, denying me rest until I learn something more certain about the foregoing matters, requires that he be sent back quickly.

But if, as I most greatly desire, peace has been restored and completed for the lord bishop, as was hoped, to the honour of God and the Church, may it please you to inform me more carefully by return letters how the election of the sworn men proceeded and at what point the matter has come to stand. For what I feared—indeed, what I fear—in every article of the offered terms will be clear from the letters which I sent to the lord bishop. Yet I do not think anyone wise who advises against peace that can be made in the Lord and, before the winter day, does not detract from honour. May peace be made, if only in our days, with safety of conscience and integrity of reputation; but may it be neither pretended nor momentary. Neither of these defects, however, is in you: one depends on the adversary, the other on the Lord.

[Col. 0159C] How the man with whom you are conducting this business is accustomed to reward his friends and those who negotiate with him, when they do not comply in all his wishes, even at the cost of reputation and conscience, is evident from many examples. Hence I judge it far more dangerous than heedless people suppose ever to sacrifice conscience and honour to his promises. Once harmed, they cannot easily be repaired. For wounds inflicted in either are almost fatal—though “almost” should be understood as said rather from weakness of flesh than from the judgment of reason. By reason’s judgment they are more ruinous than wounds which dissolve the union of body and soul, as the pagan poet says, and still more as a Christian ought to say:

> Believe it the greatest crime to prefer life to honour,  
> And for the sake of living to lose the reasons for living.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VIII.83

Therefore, with my whole heart I beg that, if my peace is being negotiated, a form may be provided in which neither God nor honour is offended—honour which, I do not dare say I myself, but God has preserved intact for me hitherto, and which may likewise remain unharmed among men hereafter. If such a form can be found, I shall give thanks to the Lord, to you, and to all who have laboured toward it.

If oaths are under discussion, my lord bishop knows with what scrupulous reverence I am bound in such matters. Could I then swear under that prescribed formula of words—or rather, that proscription [Col. 0160A] of salvation—which, as I hear, is required and given by others, where it is not permitted to make mention of preserving either the Lord, the law, or one’s order? And who offers an oath to observe reprobate customs and unknown laws, or laws contrary to the law of the Lord, except one alien from the faith and a despiser of all sacraments?

I should indeed regard as excessively rash, and wholly headlong—casting himself into a thousand snares of condemnation—anyone who bound himself by an oath to observe the sacred canons or, certainly, to keep the Gospel itself, unless perhaps one is greater who, conscious of his own weakness and a witness to our humility, confesses that “in many things we all offend.” If the past is at issue, I do not deny that I rendered to the Archbishop of Canterbury, as to my lord and father, due and devoted service. Would that I had rendered it more effectively; and, with the Lord’s favour, may I never for any advantage or loss be brought to stain my life—and indeed the memory of my name and lineage before God and men—by abjuring or denying my lord, whoever he may be.

Moreover, as I have learned from many persons, unless I do these and the things already stated, the restoration of peace to me is either impossible or extremely difficult. Let the vigilance of the lord bishop and yours therefore serve this end: if my reconciliation is being negotiated, let unjust and dangerous conditions be removed. In all matters that can be done without danger to salvation and reputation, I shall follow the lord bishop’s counsel, and yours insofar as it does not differ from his. Yet I would not wish to set out for court to make peace unless I knew its form to some extent beforehand.

For the narrowness of my means, and the business of letters—which provides me alike consolation and support—does not allow me either to make great expenditures or to remain away long. My resources are more slender than usual, while my burdens do not diminish. Assistance grows scarcer, though it was most rare from the outset. On my journey toward Angers and to the Easter meetings of the kings, I spent thirteen pounds and lost two while travelling on horseback; to say nothing of the labours, inconveniences, and weariness of courts—and, what grieves me most, all proved fruitless. For both labour and expense were lost; nor, if it could be avoided, would I wish to undergo the humble loss of my affairs [Col. 0160D] and resources.

My condition will become known to you in part through the messenger. It is almost what it was. I do not despair of the cause of Canterbury, because he, doing penance for what he has done at court, does not despair of the Lord and, I think, does not make flesh his arm. I believe that the Lord still delays the final remedy because he is not yet deprived of every human aid.

Master Gerard summons me to go to Cologne while preserving faith with the Roman Church; but, through the merciful Jesus, for no gain shall I take a share with schismatics in schism for the overthrow of the house of the Lord. Yet I do not at all consider Gerard himself a schismatic, because evident proofs of his faith appear in his letters. I send a copy of his reply to the lord bishop, [Col. 0161A] suppressing the author’s name lest its publication harm him or others.

I do not doubt that you would pity me if you knew in what anxiety my mind is placed. Yet, God being witness, although I dwell among hard-hearted people, I am concerned not so much for myself as for my friends. For, as regards myself, the exchange of letters would suffice, were I not pressed also by others whose needs I must share. If you do not know, Belgica Secunda, now called the land of Rheims, is named in ancient histories the province of the Hard-hearted (*Duricordii*), although, in consideration of certain persons, it might also be called the province of the Soft-hearted (*Mollicordii*). For no one who approaches more intimately could plausibly accuse the archbishop and his people of hard-heartedness.

But who, I ask, among our own people and old friends is not proved to belong to the race of the Hard-hearted? I shall say what perhaps you will not believe, yet is certainly true. The son of Master Gaufred was my fellow-exile for eight months; but when my messenger from the Bishop of Norwich and the Abbot of St Edmund’s called upon him, he could not obtain even a single little letter for me. Yet the Lord knows that I asked nothing of any of them; and I count it a kindness that, from the beginning of my banishment, I have not yet had to suffer the shame of rejection.

From these things and what precedes, reason’s path is plain. But I should pour myself wholly into a letter from affection, unless modesty and the multitude of occupations, from which I have stolen this little time, compelled me merely to say from my heart: Farewell!

### Letter CLXIX. To Master John Sarracenus. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0161C]

To Master JOHN Sarracenus.

The letter of your affection, for which, so long as I live, I must hold and render you thanks, breathes alike the philosopher and the Christian; and by many manifest tokens declares that it has proceeded from an abundant treasury of virtues and learning. Nor was an orator lacking to forge and compose it, who most effectively persuaded what philosophical reason and the profession of the Christian religion suggested. For the diction, fitted by grace for persuasion, was vigorous [Col. 0161D] and so took hold and prevailed with me that henceforth I should be ashamed, should it happen through weakness to mention the bitterness of exile, and utterly ashamed to have mentioned it.

For although the fourth year of my exile and the third of my proscription is now passing, I am day by day less shaken or moved by the storm of fortune and my losses, knowing assuredly that what the enemy so easily tore away was never among my true goods. Perhaps I should more rightly call him a friend: he opened my eyes, dazzled by the fantastic mockeries of fortune; having shaken off the trifles of court life and the allurements of pleasures, he impelled me into the path of virtue and joined me to the company of philosophers. Therefore, far freer than when I was burdened with worldly household goods and the little packs of chance possessions, I experience, in a happy condition—indeed, I may say poverty—[Col. 0162A] what philosophy teaches:

> “Every land is a homeland to the brave.” (Ovid)

This serves to raise the spirit amid adversity; and for the Christian the whole world is exile while he is a pilgrim away from the Lord, so that he may never be exalted by prosperity.

Let complaints, then, about the mockeries of fortune cease. For the rest, insofar as we can, let us not cease from philosophical inquiries; let us pardon our persecutors, perhaps not knowing what they do; and the prelates of churches—not yours, but ours, I mean—who, as Cicero reproaches Gaius Cassius in his letter to that same Cassius, long ago took leave of virtue and their duty, and have no dealings with them, softened as they are by riches and the allurements of pleasures. [Col. 0162B]

I await from your kindness the translation of the remainder of the *Hierarchy*, so that through your service blessed Dionysius may become more fully known to his French people, to your eternal glory. Would that a place might be granted me at your feet, so that, like Mary sitting beside Christ’s feet—Christ whom I trust dwells in your heart—I might receive from your mouth the words of heavenly oracle and the maxims of true philosophy. But my desire is obstructed by the anger of the king of England. May He who directs the hearts of kings grant him understanding, if it please Him, that he may know the things of God.

Meanwhile, prostrate at the knees of your graciousness, I knock in supplication by prayers and letters, asking that your sincerity may deem me worthy of a hearing concerning the explanation of the translation of blessed Dionysius. Recently I encountered in the book of blessed Ambrose, *On the Incarnation [Col. 0162C] of the Word*, an obstacle which none of our masters can remove, since they lack Greek. These are Ambrose’s words that raise the question:

> “The Latin translator rendered *ousia* as *substantia* [substance]. But when the *ousia* of the Lord is spoken of, what else does it signify except that the Lord always is? This the very letters express, although *ousia* is divinely said as *aei ousa*, that is, ‘always being’; it is called *ousia* with the order of one letter changed for sound, suitability, and elegance of expression. Therefore *ousia* signifies that the Lord always is.”

Ambrose indeed draws this conclusion; but the reasoning of the inference is clearer to you and to Greeks, whereas to me and those like me it is rather clouded.

Hilary, moreover, in his book *On the Synods*, reasons similarly concerning *essentia* [essence], as Ambrose does concerning *ousia*—perhaps because *essentia* and *ousia* are the same. Hilary’s words are these:

> “Essence is a thing which either is, or is that from which things are, and subsists in that which remains. It can be called the essence, nature, genus, and substance of each thing; but it is properly called essence because it always is. For that reason it is also substance, because a thing which is must necessarily subsist in itself. But whatever subsists undoubtedly remains in genus, or nature, or substance. Therefore, when we say that essence signifies nature, genus, or substance, we understand that it subsists as always being in all these.”

Hilary’s reflection in these words is exceedingly subtle and difficult [Col. 0163A] to understand; but I suppose it is clearer to those skilled in Greek. For the most holy Father and most learned doctor says of blessed Hilary that “he rises in the Gallic buskin, is adorned with Greek flowers, and is far removed from the reading of simple brethren.” Elsewhere, however, he commands that Hilary and Athanasius be read “with an unoffended foot,” that is, without stumbling.

If among the Greeks these terms so often pressed here—essence, nature, genus, substance—have a clearly expressed distinction, I think it is very much in everyone’s interest for it to be explained. Hence I do not doubt that it will contribute to your merit and glory, and profit unto life, if you open to one knocking at the door of the Scriptures and break for the use of the multitude the loaves entrusted to you by Christ, so that through your care the crowds may be refreshed. [Col. 0163B] Good Jesus has such compassion on them upon the road of this pilgrimage that He wishes to give Himself to them daily as food. Will not reproach be made to teachers because “the little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them”?

## LETTER CLXX. TO ENGELBERT, PRIOR OF THE VALLEY OF SAINT PETER. (A.D. 1166)

To ENGELBERT, prior of the Valley of Saint Peter.

Sudden changes of circumstance are accustomed to bring troubles; and those who have sought honours, when they bear the burdens attached to them, commonly fail and regret having attained their desire. Rightly so: for if they are reprobate, a just punishment pursues their iniquities; if predestined to life, pious correction consumes the excess of conceived ambition, and laborious exercise either extinguishes or restrains the pleasures attached to honours.

I can readily believe that you too have conceived some anxiety from such sudden changes, but from other causes, very different and almost contrary. For who could suspect that you were urged by any spur of ambition to seek honours, to desire the soft comforts of pleasure, or to pursue the winds of popular opinion in worldly pride? You have despised all these as dung, that you might gain Christ alone. He will restore to you not the momentary and dishonourable honours which you exchanged for precious poverty, but eternal honours in heaven, surpassing with incomparable majesty the purple of emperors. There soft and effeminate pleasure will have no access, where spiritual strength will fill the flesh, remaining in the truth of its nature, [Col. 0163D] and angelic exultation will delight it. There the proclamations of your praise will not depend upon the judgment of liars; holy angels will endlessly proclaim the magnificence of your virtues.

These things, beloved, ought to be established for you not so much by my words as by Holy Scripture, if you persevere in what you have begun. Perseverance alone attains the fruit of every virtue. Nor must you long sweat in this labor, if you measure rightly what is to come: the glorious reward of your labours hangs before your eyes, and your Rewarder stands at the doors.

Therefore, if any troubles come upon you because of the priorate imposed upon you, and from the care of souls and bodies [Col. 0164A] laid upon your shoulders, weak and feeble as they seem to you for so great a burden, endure them patiently. Cry to Him, for He is near. Cast upon His shoulders, with pious confidence, whatever seems unbearable to you: He carried back the lost sheep and bore on the wood the burdens of the whole human race, when “his government was upon his shoulder.” He Himself will lift you up, for He is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will make the temptation itself your advancement.

## LETTER CLXXI. TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1166)

I think that the cause of my exile is known to you from the account of the prior of Mont-Dieu and from my own; yet, that it may be clearer to you, I shall set it forth briefly. I stood by the lord of Canterbury and the Church as best I could; yet, as I dare safely declare with conscience as witness, I did not deliberately offend the lord king of England unjustly. Yet he has proscribed both me and my brother, together with our possessions, and I suffer exile.

I have neither wealth, friends, nor arms with which I may attack so great a prince or repel the injuries which, according to his pleasure, he inflicts upon me and mine. Therefore I must flee to the protection of you and the other saints, that by your intercessions the Lord may remove this scourge from His Church and from us, or turn it to the uses of our salvation; and may not allow us, amid this storm and tempest, to commit anything against Him, but direct [Col. 0164C] our steps in His good pleasure.

We awaited peace, and behold, an even graver disturbance now assails the Church—so great that human assistance seems vain for bringing relief. Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your holiness and of your brethren, with all devotion of heart I most earnestly beg you to pity us, at least as friends of the Lord and of the Church of Canterbury, and by your prayers to lighten the exile of me, my brother, and those exiled with us. We now despair of human aid.

I also entreat you more particularly to intercede with the Lord for the king of England, that God may recall him from this oppression of the Church; and that the merciful Lord, who alone can cure this disease, may either convert or crush the persecutors [Col. 0164D] of the Church.

## LETTER CLXXII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT MEDARD. (A.D. 1166)

To the abbot of Saint Medard.

The cause of Christ needs no great recommendation, especially among you, who desire, through the service of pious devotion and the interceding merits of saints, to be more happily commended to Christ. Who doubts that the cause of the holy poor men of the Valley of Saint Peter is Christ’s cause? Who does not know that Christ Himself is grieved by their grief and consoled by their consolation—unless he is ignorant of the evangelical prophecy from whose truth Christ will pronounce judgment, for the condemnation of the wicked and the salvation and glorification of the elect? [Col. 0165A]

And since, as we hear, your piety has compassion for the brethren mentioned and your humanity gladly aids them, we offer immense thanks to your charity with them and for them. When you command, and circumstance and time require, we shall render such acts of thanksgiving as we can, assured that Christ, whom you now console in His members, will return what is due in the mercy of His word, pouring into your bosoms a measure pressed down and overflowing.

We pray and beseech with all the supplication we can offer that you hold their prior, L., your most dear foster-son, dear; that you grant him and his brethren aid and counsel wherever they need your protection; and that, as befits so great a father [Col. 0165B] and a church of such nobility, you spare the poor men’s embarrassment by anticipating their requests when appropriate, enlarge your glory, and soothe your conscience. And since some of your brethren are said to trouble them, which is expedient neither for your honour nor for your advantage, we earnestly ask that you restore peace to them and restrain your brethren from disturbing them.

Whatever you do for them, if we say that it has been done for us, whatever is said will be true. Yet that will be too little to express your merit, since whatever good or evil is shown to these men in either condition is directed personally to Christ.

## LETTER CLXXIII. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF NORWICH. (A.D. 1166)

To the lord bishop of Norwich.

I know, Father, that you have been accustomed to love your faithful servants with sincere charity, and to receive and reward their devotion and service according to ability and merit. Therefore, because I have always shown myself faithful and devoted to you, I hope that you will have compassion on me both for the integrity of the cause and for affection toward my person.

Accordingly, I earnestly commend to your fatherhood my brother, who has been proscribed from his goods more by another’s will than by any fault of his own.
