I would not commend him to you, except because he enjoys the peace of the lord king, although he has not yet obtained full favour. Since payment of my revenues has been forbidden, so that I cannot demand three marks from the present feast of Saint John, I ask that you cause three marks, under whatever designation you please—whether as a loan or otherwise—to be given to him, if it please you. This cannot be charged against me if assistance is given to a man who is innocent and possesses the peace of the lord king. [Col. 0165D]

## LETTER CLXXIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1166)

To the lord bishop of Poitiers.

I believe it has come to your knowledge that Gir., archdeacon of Paris, is a very great friend of mine and especially close to me by his own merits and those of his people. He wishes and hopes, through my prayers to you, to secure advancement for one of his servants, named Jordan. [Col. 0166A] The abbot of Saint-Maixent, he says, owes him money and treats him less than amicably, so that he distrusts the debtor’s good faith unless your fatherhood makes him faithful, even against his will.

Therefore I earnestly ask that you so further the servant’s justice that you make the aforesaid archdeacon, for whose consideration I make this request, beholden to you and yours; and that his servant, through your diligent intervention, may, if possible, obtain without difficulty or delay what is established to be due to him.

## LETTER CLXXV. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1166)

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, JOHN of Salisbury: greetings, and strength in Him who “scatters the counsels of nations, frustrates the designs of the wicked, and overthrows powers.” [Col. 0166B]

I recently received letters from your fatherhood commanding me to write back what seemed to me proper after examining the letters of the lord of Salisbury, John of Oxford, Master Hervé, and Lord Nicholas. But the boy delivered neither John’s letter nor Master Hervé’s letter, which I had greatly desired; yet John’s mind is easily discerned from your letters and those of the bishop and chapter of Salisbury. I do not know what the bishop-elect of Chartres has informed you, since his letter contains nothing other than that you should trust Vincent.

Thus my instruction lacked what I most desired and what is most worthy to be known: namely, how your affairs have prospered in Master Hervé’s hands, and what aid the Apostolic See—on whose account we suffer—has decreed to grant to the shipwreck of the English Church. For from this it will be necessary to frame prudent counsel: so that, in accordance with the Gospel parable, one intending to build a tower may sit down and calculate the expense, and one about to engage a king may count his forces at home, lest sudden and unconsidered presumption in some great undertaking or display be shamefully exposed to ridicule or ruin. [Col. 0166C]

I do not say this because I think the Roman Church should be made the foundation of our hope, but Him alone upon whom it too is founded, and in whom every work faithfully rooted is strengthened unto fruit and perfected in glory. Let Him be the foundation in our consciences; then man will assuredly not prevail, and we need not fear either the threats of tyrants, the snares of those who think carnally, the treachery of traitors, the weakness of a judge, or the greed and inconstancy of those who seek in all things what belongs to the flesh, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture most faithfully teaches:

> “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous flees to it and is delivered from every distress.” (Prov. 18)

Since, therefore, you seek the counsel of my smallness, I advise now, as always, that we cast all and our entire hope upon Him who can rescue us from the tribulations that have found us in excess. In order that He may will this justly and mercifully, let us, warned by Haggai, set our hearts upon our ways; let us produce fruits worthy [Col. 0167A] of repentance; and let us receive with joy from the hand of the Lord the cup of this saving bitterness. Abusing His gifts through the deadly sweetness of prosperity, we have so often rejoiced to our destruction.

For this is the grace of Him who knows how to bless His friends in such a way that, tested through many tribulations, He brings them purer, brighter, and stronger into the kingdom. Let us survey the whole course of the ages: whom do we find from the beginning among the elect to have passed from delights to delights? Whom do we read to have flourished and exulted here with the world, and now to rejoice and reign with Christ in the abundance of fruits, unless his mind had been wounded in itself by repentance, strengthened by patience, softened and raised by hope, and by the proofs of holy conduct?

According to the circumstances set before us, I think nothing is more advisable than that, following the counsel of Nicholas, whom I trust to possess the Spirit of the Lord, you write to the empress, the archbishop, and the bishops of Normandy that you always have been and are ready to obey the law according to the judgment of the canons, and to return to your see and receive what is yours and what belongs to your people, provided security be arranged for you and them and the Church be restored to that liberty in which it stood before the storm of this iniquity shook it. I judge that the letter should be written all the more modestly, and the conditions required, because I seem to myself more certain that the hearts of those opposing the Lord’s Church are so hardened that they will accept no condition whatever except one that overthrows the Church’s liberty and destroys your honour and that of us all. [Col. 0167C] Yet the writing will be useful insofar as it may serve as testimony for you against the hostile bishops and make your moderation, which is highly expedient, known to all.

But if, which I do not hope, they offer these terms to the king and he accepts the conditions up to the provision of security, I do not think that you ought to be too scrupulous over that word, provided the empress and archbishop intervene and the king publicly declares and orders by open writing that you and yours are to be secure. For what if God has decreed to exercise you by this anxiety, so that you live in the midst of those lying in wait and are surrounded by those seeking to take your life? Did not the prophet Gad, in a similar case, advise and compel David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, to return into Judah, so that the plots of enemies might advance his exercises in virtue and the marks of his merits might shine forth more clearly? [Col. 0167D]

But perhaps someone will censure the rashness of this counsel, which exposes your head to hostile swords, and say that it is more advantageous and prudent to wait until you have completed repentance, because the consciousness of sins has not yet made you fit for martyrdom. To this I reply: no one is unfit except one unwilling to suffer for faith and works of faith—whether child or adult, Jew or Gentile, Christian or unbeliever, man or woman; it makes no difference. For whoever suffers for righteousness is a martyr, that is, a witness to righteousness and defender of Christ’s cause. But why say this? I know, as my mind forebodes, that the king will not prevail so far that discussion of security becomes necessary; and that that most steadfast pillar of the temple says that whatever you do springs from pride or anger.

This opinion must be met by showing moderation in deeds and words, as well as gesture and dress; though this avails little before the Lord unless it proceeds from the hidden place of conscience. [Col. 0168A]

Concerning the affair of Salisbury, I recall what I heard from you, on the part of the bishop and church, about the intrusion of the dean and the circumvention by bishops who led the bishop and Church by their counsel into transgressing the apostolic command. If, as law provides, no one’s own fraud will protect him before men, much less will it protect him before the Lord, who will destroy lying lips and reject the wisdom of the wise. And as has been reported to me from the city, and as I remember writing to you, the lord pope has now confirmed your sentence—or rather vindicated his own injury.

I shall not conceal what I think of the bishops’ appeal. Because they are unwilling to be free, I fear their slavery may be perpetuated—and justly. For when the year of remission had come, that is, the year of grace calling the Church to liberty, after six years in which they had been afflicted as though in mud and brick, they preferred, because some of them had taken wives to whom they are bound by affection, others had amassed many yokes of oxen, others were storing money without knowing for whom it would be gathered, and others had given themselves to other pleasures—I say, oppressed by the yoke of the vices pleasing to themselves, they preferred to be kept in their old slavery and to have their ears pierced with the awl of perpetual servitude, because they profess obedience to the servile customs of corrupt practices, rather than to wish to escape into the liberty of the Spirit. [Col. 0168C]

Do you not recall that the two tribes and a half, possessing many cattle and very great holdings, did not receive their inheritance in the midst of their brethren—that is, in the common land, namely the land of promise—but, before crossing the Jordan, remained within the borders of the Amorites? Does not kind Jesus interpret this in the Gospel, declaring through a figure of speech that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye [Col. 0168D] of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven?

Those who had been slow to cross the Jordan later set up an altar of contradiction and scandal; just as our bishops, under the pretext of law, endeavour to evade the form and force of justice. But Jesus, conqueror of the nations, will recall them too to unity and the worship of piety by sending an embassy—that is, to the profession of the law and the observance of justice—so that they may think, speak, and do what is right before God; and, armed with the exhortation of Moses, that is, the divine law, may go before their brethren until Christ’s inheritance, namely the Church, is freed from enemies’ hands and, after splendid triumphs over vices, is established in the land.

If meanwhile the bishop of Hereford, whom many seemed to expect would deliver Israel, calls you disturbers of the Church because of your contempt for the world and your learning—of which he is believed by the ignorant, or by those ignorant of him, to have an abundance—he and his accomplices may be answered with the words of Elijah, similarly rebuked, who said to Ahab:

> “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, because you have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and followed the Baals.” (3 Kings 18)

I do not mean that you, to whom I commend moderation, should answer the bishops thus with your own mouth; rather, let their own consciences, or some religious person rebuking them because they are worshippers of Jezebel, say it to them. Jezebel is interpreted “cohabitant,” which is the name of a harlot, or “vain flux”; for, in the manner of harlots who pursue banquets and taverns, they first expose themselves to luxury and afterward to every disgrace, pursuing only things that flow away, so that with those things they themselves may flow away and vanish together in a moment with their vanities. [Col. 0169B]

What, then, can you modestly reply to these rebukers—or rather slanderers—of yours? Surely what the most modest and holy David threw in Abner’s teeth, whose name is interpreted “my father’s lamp,” when the drowsy guard exposed Saul, sleeping in the camp, to his enemies; so that, as proof of negligence, they took and carried away the king’s spear and cup of water from beside his head.

Therefore let it be said to the bishop of Hereford, since he is, as they say, guardian of his Saul, and to the bishop of London, who is known to have received this guardianship from the supreme pontiff when he moved from his own see to another. Let it be said, I say, to them both:

> “Are you not a man? And who is like you in Israel? Why have you not guarded your lord the king? As the Lord lives, you are sons of death, because you have not guarded your lord, the Lord’s anointed.” (1 Kings 26)

For where are the spear of the king, signifying the straightness of justice, and the cup of water, that vessel of the pure law, which had been by his head for the refreshing of the flesh and strengthening of the spirit in his thirst? [Col. 0169C]

But they will immediately answer your faithfulness, watchfulness, and rebuke with Abner’s words:

> “Who are you, that you cry out and disturb the king?” (1 Kings 26 [printed: 27])

As though they said: Allow our king to sleep with us in contempt of the commandments and persecution of the saints, so that, while he rests, we may lead and bring him onward in contempt of the divine law to the sleep of death.

Yet you who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give Him no silence; but carry out what the Apostle says:

> “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, in season and out of season.” (2 Tim. 4)

That is, with every timely importunity. Under the pretext of appeal, however, all of them will henceforth protect themselves, ready to incur any disobedience while awaiting either the death of the lord pope, which they desire, or yours, or some other event that may support their malice. For from communion with what excommunicated king has anyone ever withdrawn? Have not the bishops and nearly all the clergy always stood with him against the Lord and against His Christ?

Yet I believe there are among the bishops some who steadfastly persevere with us—indeed, with the Lord and His Church—in desires and prayers, although in body and outward speech they share much with the enemies and persecutors of the Church. Thus Jonathan was bodily with his father Saul, but in all the sincerity of his heart was exiled with David. Thus David sent back Hushai the Archite, hastening with him into exile, to the company of the parricidal son, preferring that he remain usefully among enemies with his friends Zadok and Abiathar the priests rather than share exile uselessly with him. I do not doubt that certain bishops favour the justice of the Lord and you, and likewise the greater part of the clergy, although they conceal it from necessity or faintheartedness. For who would suppose that all the stars suffer eclipse together? [Col. 0170A]

To draw my hand in at last: the counsel you seek from me exceeds the powers of my little talent. Nor will I ever hasten counsel that you pronounce a sentence of anathema against your lord the king, or a sentence of interdict against the innocent of the realm. What I told you at the castle of Thierry remains fixed in my mind, and I do not depart from that judgment. You may remember what it was, because you held the same view.

But I add this: concerning these matters and others that have emerged subsequently, consult the lord bishop of Poitiers; examine the opinions of other wise men; and, if meanwhile the Lord restores him, have Hervé’s counsel. Before all things, devote yourselves to prayer and to the other exercises of Christian warfare; commend your struggle to the Lord through the intercession of the saints; [Col. 0170C] and then proceed to whatever it is that the Holy Spirit shall teach through His instruments—I mean the wise and faithful—and that your cause requires. I believe that you yourselves also possess the Spirit of the Lord, because He who gave zeal without merit is to be believed, at the critical point of necessity, to supply counsel to one who merits it well.

Therefore I do not advise you, as our common father and lord used to say, to put into a little boot (*caligula*) the counsel which the Lord has inspired in your heart, and to prefer the opinions of others who are less watchful in your cause.

After the feast of blessed Peter, God willing, I intend to come to you at once; then many things which a page cannot [Col. 0170D] adequately explain may become clear through mutual discussion. What you have done at Vézelay has for many days been known to the archbishop and Church of Reims, and I do not think it worthwhile to repeat what is already public.

If he has been offended by the Templars, I think the matter should be overlooked; for I am accustomed to abort an offence with the same ease with which I conceive it. And since you as yet owe him nothing, I do not advise making yourselves beholden to him in such matters. Besides, if supplication is made to him, he will magnify the injury; if it is overlooked, even an injury that preceded may be effaced by overlooking it. The easiest road to reconciliation will be for him to be won by some small gift. Yet I see that the Templars are received graciously in his court and that their affairs are conveniently dispatched.

He himself has gone to Clairvaux, summoned, as they say, by the greater part of the convent for the destruction of the abbot. Fromundus, who had arranged this journey for him, died on the day before the Ides of July and was buried in the monastery of Saint Remigius. [Col. 0171A]

## LETTER CLXXVI. TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1166)

To the lord of Canterbury, JOHN of Salisbury.

Although it is certain that bishops inclined to disobedience, and shepherds feeding themselves, who through love of ease and luxury and through impious fear of temporal losses hesitate to declare their impiety, propose henceforth to defend themselves by the pretext of an appeal lodged against all your commands—and even apostolic ordinances, insofar as these displease them—unto every overthrow of law and each separate injury to churches, saying, “Good, good!” [Col. 0171B] nevertheless I think it expedient that you immediately summon, if possible, some of your suffragans—either to hear the lord pope’s command, to confer with you on the state of the Church of Canterbury, or for some other reason for summoning them, should a more convenient one occur to you and those with you.

Since they have already appealed, which perhaps has already been reported to the lord pope, and obey their king in everything, I do not see why their conference—or even the king’s—ought henceforth to be avoided. For I believe that fear of the labour they must undergo, the expenses they dread, the pressure of approaching dangers, and uncertainty about the outcome of the case will make them work more diligently for the peace of the Church and your reconciliation; for I do not think one of them can be found who would not dislike having to suffer the losses of so many and such great inconveniences.

And if they cross the sea, perhaps through the empress’s mediation the Church’s peace will be restored; or, with the Lord’s favour, your cause will be left in a better position. For, they say, the time is at hand when the Eagle of the broken treaty, according to Merlin’s prophecy, will gild the bridle that is given to its boar, or is now being forged in the Armorican peninsula. [Col. 0171C] For, as I have learned for certain after writing my earlier letter, he suffered a grave loss in the approach to Fougères, which friends of the French still lament among us: some were captured, others wounded, while thirsting for pure silver they strove to appear more valiant than the rest.

I had heard this before at the court of the most Christian king of France, at Laon, where I was honourably and respectfully received by him; but I did not readily believe rumour-mongers, although Count Robert’s inability to conceal the sorrow he had conceived from it gave some credence to my uncertainty. They also say that the hungry besiege the well-fed, and the needy those rich in every kind of possession, and that the besieged man is much safer than the besieger.

For Ralph, as they report, has fortified his castle very well and devastated whatever provisions he could find in the surrounding region. Nor is it permissible to advance farther afield without great bodies of troops going ahead, because the aforesaid Ralph, having a force of chosen knights, fences their paths with very sharp thorns and urges their horses with goads so that their riders fall backward, and, as they say, makes frequent incursions into the army itself. [Col. 0172A] They add that he has entered into a mutual alliance with the most powerful nobles of Brittany, except Count Eudo.

Will not this solitary wild boar—or boar close to being solitary—that feeds upon and tramples the vineyard of the Lord, thus be restrained and bridled? I myself interpret the prophecy in this way, awaiting the Eagle’s gilding of these troubles by whatever contrivance, unless our Alexander, Merlin’s kinsman and a more prudent interpreter of his oracles, thinks otherwise. So much for this.

For the rest, you will do me a great favour if you convey my greetings in my name to the lord of Lyons, whom I hear is with you and whom I greatly desire to see, and if you write carefully concerning your affairs. [Col. 0172B]

## LETTER CLXXVII. TO THE TREASURER OF REIMS. (A.D. 1166)

To the treasurer of Reims.

I would rather, if it could be done with advantage to us both, enjoy the desired conversation with you than commit to a little sheet matters which it is right that I should say and expedient that you should hear more fully. A letter speaks only what has been entrusted to it, and cannot conveniently expand upon matters that friends might profitably lay before one another. Yet both the pressure of numerous unavoidable affairs and some slight infirmity of body prevent this desire of mine, so that what it would have been better to say must be written. Let then my lord and friend remember that, as the orator says: “To be deceived once is unfortunate, a second time foolish, a third time disgraceful.”

I regret that it has happened that I must call to your mind that you were once deceived, to your disadvantage, in the matter of the matricular office; a second time, to your error, in the resignation of the Paris prebend; and that henceforth you should not assent to every spirit, so as to be disgracefully deceived in arranging the sub-treasurership. Your fellow-canon Laurence is indeed a worthy man, to whom the lord archbishop has resolved to give it, and he would be worthy of a greater honour, if he were called by the Lord and cleansed of the fault of ambition. But is it to your advantage and honour that you choose your lord’s associate for service in your own office—or rather suffer him to be forced upon you—so that he will owe to another, rather than to you, the office which he performs? Do you wish to be sub-treasurer under the treasurer? Is it not better that you should be the guardian of your own officers than that another guardian should be appointed over you and them, to your inconvenience?

For the future, consider what you do. Out of the loyalty and affection which I bear toward you, and out of reverence for our venerable and pious father, blessed Samson, I set this before you—I see that you have been shaken in many respects—that you may remember yourself and us, who have always been faithful to you; lest, God forbid, it may plausibly be said that we suffer from the vice of ingratitude. When you return, we shall not be displeased if you arrange your office in a manner becoming to your honour and not unbecoming to ours. For in matters conducive to your honour, you shall have us, so far as we can, as helpers in whatever pleases you. Loyalty invites this, affection urges it, but that Samson compels it, whose memory is blessed.

## LETTER CLXXVIII. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1166.)

To the lord bishop of Exeter.

A double reason has now moved me to write: first, that contrary to custom I might not permit anyone, departing for you with my knowledge, to leave without letters; second, that I might comply with friends whose wishes it is proper to satisfy. They wished the bearer of this letter, who claims Devon as his native country—although one may believe that he drew his origin from your more remote fellow-countrymen near the Mount of the Blessed Archangel in the Armorican peninsula—to be commended to your fatherhood through the service of one so small as myself, since he is said to have lived commendably and without reproach for years in the district of Rheims.

Therefore, to satisfy them, I offer to your kindness prayers as sincere as they are confident. For long ago both experience and common report have made it certain to me, as to many others, that your discretion is not ignorant of the rule established among friends, both by the persuasion of equity and by the decree of philosophers. That rule is, as you know better, that honourableness should govern requests, and that friends should be heard only in those matters in which it is not opposed. Reason prescribes that unlawful things should neither be requested nor done because of friendship.

Since, therefore, for my friends’ sake I have undertaken to commend a friend to a father and lord, I pray that, for the Lord’s sake and at the intervention of my prayers, you may hear him, should he request it, in such matters as your discernment judges expedient both for his need and for your honour. And if it should happen that he returns to us with your approval, he will be able to inform me concerning your circumstances and those of our friends, at least from public report conveyed in letters.

Of my own circumstances I write more sparingly at present, not because I wish anything concerning me to be concealed from you, but because I recall that I recently reported everything most fully through Fulk. For whatever the letter lacked, I thought would be supplied by the service and diligence of a more substantial messenger.

As regards public affairs, the following have since been widely reported on the testimony of many Englishmen: namely, that all the bishops met by the king’s command and, in order that the sentence pronounced by the lord pope might not take effect, appealed against their archbishop. He, for their salvation and for the liberty of the Church, permits his resources to be seized by plunderers, exposes his fortune to dangers, his reputation to mockery, and, if circumstances require, does not shrink, fear, blush, or hesitate to offer his head to hostile swords.

Two clerks recently came to him, as I have been reliably told by one who was then at Pontigny, publishing these matters and appealing: one on behalf of the lord of Salisbury, the other on behalf of his dean, who wholly denies that he gave any oath to the emperor or shared in anything with Reginald of Cologne, the schismatic. The latter also confessed that he was a familiar clerk at the table of Master John of Oxford, who is the king’s clerk; and he said that he bore a word from the king to the archbishop, appealing on the king’s behalf and in his name and by his command, as he said, to a hearing before Pope Alexander; and through him he appealed, appointing as the day the feast on which is sung, “I am the good shepherd” (John XI [sic]).

The archbishop replied to him in these words: “Since you are unknown to us, possess neither a mandate nor letters from the king, and through communion with your lord John of Oxford—who is known to be excommunicated—you yourself are excommunicated by letters of the lord pope, you cannot perform the office of an appellant. But we shall execute the apostolic command and, with the Lord’s help, fulfil it.”

Wishing to know his disposition toward the man of Salisbury, I sent a special messenger to him, to investigate his mind more closely. The whole of France, however, wonders at this action of the bishops, saying that they ought to have met to deliberate concerning the safety of their king, whom they see daily shaken, as though he were the emperor, on account of schism, and on account of the clergy and Church which he crushes. They ought also to have been concerned for the liberation of the Church and for peace, and to have taken pains and care to restore peace to the clergy—not to expose themselves and their possessions to expense, labour, and danger, and, disfiguring their own reputation, thereafter subject the Church to servitude.

All who hear it are likewise astonished at a remarkable matter, if indeed it is true: namely, that the bishop of Hereford, a man reputed learned and a despiser of the world, attacks his own archbishop and consecrator, calling him a disturber of affairs because he vindicates the Church’s liberty. Did not the overseers of the children of Israel similarly cast blame upon Moses and Aaron, executors of the divine law, because they were scourged by the taskmasters after being denied the straw due to them by right? Was it not reproached against the ministers of the Lord that they had made the names of the overseers stink before the king and his servants? Yet they, though complainers and murmurers, followed Moses. Would that those who now complain and murmur might follow the law of the Lord. If they do, they will approach the king on one side and the archbishop on the other; whomever they find at fault, they will openly rebuke; and they will stand apart, nor by consent to or concealment of another’s wrongdoing will they pollute themselves by contact with uncleanness.

## LETTER CLXXIX. TO HIS BROTHER RICHARD. (A.D. 1166.)

To his brother Richard.

My sweetest of all mortals, I should plainly seem unjust toward you if, during my exile, I wrote to anyone while saying nothing to you, whom, together with the Lord and our beloved mother, I do not doubt to be more concerned than any other mortal about my condition. Even if matter or occasion for writing is sometimes lacking, I think this very fact ought to be written to you: that occasion and material for writing have been lacking.

What I wrote to the lord bishop will likewise be made known to you; and you may present to his sincerity what has been written to you. For I wish you to comply with him in all things which concern you, and to prefer his counsel to mine: both because he is wiser than we are and because I trust that he possesses a fuller grace of the Lord; and because, as he has always loved us with sincere charity, so he surpasses us in merits as well as in authority.

What ought to have been written to him, had not the brevity of a failing page prevented it, I wish to be urged upon him in my name; and may the Holy Spirit persuade him, who does not permit those hoping in him, in a crisis of necessity, to be deprived of the consolation of counsel. It is this: that in this conflict of authority and right he should proceed with such moderation—law going before, grace leading, and reason assisting—that he may neither seem guilty of rashness against the authority which God ordained, nor, through fear of authority or love of fleeting possessions, consent to wrongdoing for the oppression of the Church and destruction of both present and future generations, and thus be judged not merely a deserter of his office and betrayer of his profession, but an opponent of justice.

But perhaps you will say that it is easier for me, as for anyone, to prescribe what should be done than to carry out what has been prescribed. Thus the book to be devoured becomes sweet in the prophet’s mouth, but when passed into his inward parts it becomes bitter. The orator likewise teaches in his art of speaking that it is very easy to deliver precepts concerning an art and to speak about it, but very difficult to act according to the art—that is, to observe the commands one has prescribed. Yet nowhere is this more difficult than in the art of living. For this is the art of arts, and surpasses all others incomparably in difficulty as in usefulness.

You will add too that saying of our comic poet:

> “When we are well, we give sound advice to the sick.”  
> (Terence, *Andria* II. i)

“But if you were here, you would think otherwise.” To this I shall reply that, though I neither know nor perhaps seek to preserve that golden mean which I prescribe, I shall nevertheless freely imitate the lyric poet:

> “…performing the office of a whetstone,  
> which can make iron sharp, though itself incapable of cutting.”  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica*, 304)

I do not entertain this concern because I have conceived any sinister suspicion—God knows it—concerning so great and sincere a father; but because charity cannot but be anxious amid dangers to a friend. I know the persistence of very powerful persecutors and the weakness of the Church, although the lord pope is now greatly recovering and being strengthened in the Lord. I know also, on one hand, the faint-heartedness of certain bishops and, on the other, the envy of others. Thus there is nothing I fear more than that his innocence may be endangered among false brethren and among those who seemed to be something, pre-eminent through the authority of rank and through the pretence of learning and religious habit.

For even Moses and Aaron, leaders in Israel both by office and merit, fell at the waters of contradiction under the pressure of the multitude, and so deserved to be denied entrance to the land of promise. Among us, however, report has spread that the English bishops have already met repeatedly to deliberate and decide what must be done. But what, I ask, will they truly decide except that they are troubled and afraid, and both beyond measure? What will they decide except what they have preferred—to yield shamefully rather than vigorously repel injustice? What will they truly decide except that iniquity should rule, while they neither announce to sinners their life nor show them the Lord’s way?

I do not say this because I wish or advise him to “stretch out his arms against the torrent,” or to set himself imprudently against the multitude and expose his church to dangers and miseries. Rather, let him imitate what we read that good men did: Hushai the Archite, who, by using moderation, strove to defeat Ahithophel’s counsel and military plan; and who dealt all the more faithfully with Absalom because he deprived him of material for sin and barred the occasion for parricide. Do you suppose those faithful who make the paths of sin easy for the lord king and zealously seek his success in things undertaken against the Lord’s justice? Which seems more faithful to you: one who, at the nod of a misguided man, supplies occasions of guilt, or one who drives away destructive pleasures? Let each think what he wishes.

I shall never count that man faithful to his lord and friend who so obeys the latter’s pleasure as to bring loss of salvation and life—unless perhaps you think Doeg the Edomite faithful to Saul: Doeg, who killed the priests of the Lord with the sword by which Saul was to pierce himself. Or unless Ahithophel was necessary to Absalom, at whose advice he openly committed incest with his father’s wife and was preparing to commit parricide.

It is said—and would that it were false!—that the lord bishop of London and that friend of mine, the bishop of Chichester, are arming the ministers of iniquity against the Church, thirst for the blood of the archbishop of Canterbury, and labour to ensure that no return may ever be open to him. Are they afraid lest savagery be softened? Or, in Cicero’s phrase, “lest Caesar’s spear grow cold or his sword grow blunt”? [Note: Col. 0175D; *Epistulae ad familiares* IX.10.] But I think this is a fable, as do not many others. For such great priests are too wise to do evil, especially since they know that, if iniquity prevails,

> “That punishment will return upon its own head.”  
> (Ovid, *Ars Amatoria* I.340)

They cannot be ignorant how fire, issuing from the bramble when it was raised to kingship, devours the cedars of Lebanon.

Farewell, and dutifully greet those whom you know should be greeted, but greet our mother with especial affection. Obtain for us the help of prayers, that the Lord may not permit us to stray from his path; but that, according to his good pleasure, whether through prosperity or adversity, after the affections of the flesh and all vices have been conquered, he may lead and draw us to that place from which, being exiles, we may in him and in ourselves despise lower things and have compassion on the wretched, who are now uselessly occupied with plundering the little burdens of the Church and of ourselves.

## LETTER CLXXX. TO MASTER RADULFUS NIGER. (A.D. 1166.)

Master Radulfus Niger, from John of Salisbury.

The excuse by which you have sought to clear yourself of the long duration of your silence, being plausible, I consider proved and accepted. I know that your affection lacked no diligence, but that fortune did not stand by that diligence. Your diligence is all the clearer because, after a delay so long and unpleasant to me, the attentiveness of your charity set in order for my instruction all that, in your judgment, may either harm or benefit you. Although I had learned some of these things earlier through others, no one has treated all and each of them so particularly.

Everything which you heard was true [variant: “good”], although I do not doubt that very much of it was false. What else can I do without loss of salvation except what reason prescribes on the testimony of conscience and the inexorable necessity of my office itself compels? When I came to the lord king’s court, offering with all humility whatever satisfaction the law permitted or his will might indicate to me, provided my honour remained intact, was I not excluded from the form of peace then offered and conveyed to Master Philip? What was I further to do? Were the possessions violently and cruelly taken from me for the law of the Lord—this I safely protest before the Lord, who, whether the world wills it or not, shall judge this cause—to be redeemed at so shameful a price that I should swear to observe customs condemned by the law of God and renounce all obedience to my archbishop?

These things might suffice for the overthrow of my faith; yet they went further, to matters which even adversaries could more honourably have kept silent than expressed. I do not impute these things to the king, but to those who said that they knew his mind more fully and who, as they boasted, were interpreters of his will. For he himself, in my hearing, said nothing unworthy either of my honour or of his; and I can blame him only in this: that, when I demanded an answer, complaining of the loss of property and time, he so turned aside the conversation as to make it wholly useless both to his majesty and honour and to my necessity.

Therefore, knowingly and deliberately, because of the pressure of circumstances, I withdrew from him in order to safeguard my innocence, necessity, and good name—indeed, the Lord’s cause as well. Yet, God willing, I shall return if ever, as I hope, a straight path of peace appears to me consistent with unimpaired conscience and reputation. Otherwise may merciful Jesus first inflict temporal death upon me rather than allow me knowingly to offend him in recovering peace or the favour of man.

But you raise many difficulties. First, that the English Church, turned into a crooked bow, lifts up its heel against the Lord, and that the bishops under the pretext of appeal strive to colour their malice and render void the sentence issued by judgment of the apostolic see. Yet surely, if the Lord is with us—or rather, because in his mercy he is with us, who suffer and are proscribed for his sake, because in this cause we have resolved in conscience to serve him unto death—more are with us than with them. It is now certain that labour and grief await the bishops, unless, accepting wiser counsel, they swiftly endeavour to restore the peace of the Church which they undertook not to betray but to guard.

The king trusts in the emperor and in the capture of the lord pope, which the prophets of Baal foretell to him, seeing falsehood and speaking folly because they do not speak from the Lord. But remember that Ahab too was deceived in this way and, while hoping for victory, fell beneath the swords of his enemies. Meanwhile let the wise hear Cato:

> “Do not place your hope in another’s death,”

especially in that of an innocent man and of the Lord, whose day to anticipate even by a wish is akin to parricide. But with the Lord’s aid the lord pope prospers; and, since Alban was recently captured, as is entirely certain, his steps have been enlarged. Conversely, may God daily hedge with thorns the paths of the German tyrant and his heresiarchs; may their strength be diminished and their authority vanish—something they cannot conceal. What you heard concerning the Sicilian is said to be utterly false by the soldiers of Rheims, who were in his pay for a full year and returned the day before yesterday.

That those whom the lord of Canterbury declared excommunicated are not avoided harms not so much him as those who communicate with them. Let them see with what conscience they communicate; and let those excommunicated see with what innocence they deny or excuse the offences laid to their charge. I know that I was neither present at the pronouncement of the sentence nor was it issued on my advice or from my conscience. Nor yet, the Lord bearing witness, do I know some of those who have been marked, nor, so far as I remember, have I seen them.

I shall certainly try, as you advise, to incline the archbishop in favour of the archdeacon of Poitiers, provided you understand that my effort can advance the Church’s peace. Otherwise it would be shameful and disgraceful to circumvent a father and lord. But you know that, though we have pursued this since last year, not once has a single word been answered us by the archdeacon. As for your journey, I do not know what counsel to give; I would unreservedly advise against it, except that I do not see how you can refrain from sharing with the excommunicated. For that they have deserved the sentence is somewhat clear to you, but far more fully clear to them on the testimony of conscience.

Let the soul of the Lord detest him who sows discord among brethren. What then of him who, with an Edomite henchman, persecutes priests, sets fire to the town of the Lord’s tabernacle, and rages against the Levitical order with the sword of a ruler? In this matter, therefore, consult your conscience and employ some religious and discerning arbiter; and, when you have poured out your heart in his presence, follow what the Lord inspires.

If, however, at the urging of friends you should go to court, persuade the archdeacon whom you love—and whom I also, so far as the sincerity of charity permits, venerate and embrace with my whole heart—that, as the Prophet warns, he should turn the eyes of his mind toward his own ways and those of his lord, lay his heart upon them, and no longer offer him soft things, hoping in the uncertainty of riches and in the various blandishments of fortune that seduces. Let him remember that those at the summit are not granted to stand long, and that the heart is exalted before ruin. For however much he dissimulates, he knows that the sentence of his shepherd, whether just or unjust, must be feared.

Why say more? If Lot can be in Sodom, Joseph in Pharaoh’s court, Hushai in Absalom’s conversations and counsels, Obadiah in Ahab’s service and Jezebel’s society, and Daniel in Babylon, you may safely go there, both for yourself and for those whom you persuade to preserve innocence and behold equity; for there are remnants for the peaceable man. And though the unjust perish together, salvation for the righteous is expected from the Lord, who is faithful in his promises and does not permit his elect to be tempted beyond their power, but makes all things work together for their good. May the Lord direct your journey and your actions.

## LETTER CLXXXI. TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master Radulfus Niger.

Your loyalty and devotion have a testimony greater than John’s: they shine not through the noise of words but through the showing forth of works. For Jesus, the Truth—would that we were his imitators as we are his professed followers—prefers the testimony of works to John’s testimony. He does not condemn the latter as reprobate, but judges the former, through its evident soundness, to be preferred. For each person’s works bear testimony concerning him. A tree is assessed not by its height and strength, nor by the number and beauty of its branches, nor by the abundance and density of its foliage, but by the usefulness of its fruits.

Since you have omitted nothing that lay within your power, and the fruits of your loyalty and devotion have plainly appeared—if not as you wished, yet according to the time, and with hope for more—why does your discourse proceed to arguments intended to establish your charity? If you seek to commend it to the faithful, you are doing what has already been done; if to the faithless, it accomplishes nothing. Yet there is one person, and uniquely one, to whom I desire it commended, not so much by the ornament of arguments and phantasms of expression as by sincerity of charity, the continence of life, and the earnest persistence of affectionate prayer.

I think it was from these grounds that you answered our friend Hugh as you did: an answer which, though to persons inexperienced in affairs it may seem to bring loss, undoubtedly brings profit to conscience and salvation. I therefore congratulate you on your studies, recognizing from clear signs that, in that talkative and windy city—to use a phrase current among the scholars—you seek not so much the loci of useless argument as those of virtues. For one who believes that arguments have many loci and seats, but virtues none, may indeed be talkative and vain, but he is certainly not a dialectician—indeed, not even a philosopher.

To pass, however, from generalities to particulars: I praise your refusal, while the archdeacon of Poitiers is excommunicated, to enter into any association with him whatsoever, no matter what is offered you. You have preferred the Lord to man and eternal things to temporal. Yet, speaking without prejudice to a truer judgment and preserving reverence for the canons, I think a distinction should be admitted in participation with excommunicated persons. Whoever shares in their malice condemns himself as well to the bond of anathema. But in the four matters where special caution seems required—namely, the kiss, table fellowship, prayer, and greeting—a manifold distinction, I think, must be observed both among persons and circumstances.

Those professing perfection avoid these things differently from the imperfect; those pressed by necessity differently from those who are free. For a perfect person never communicates with any excommunicate, not even in exchange of words, without declaring to him the fault for which he must be avoided—how much more, then, in food, church, and the like? Thus Elisha, questioned concerning the outcome of the expedition by the king of Judah and King Joram of Israel, whom he knew to be an idolater, answered:

> “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, if I did not reverence the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not even have attended to you or looked upon you.”  
> (IV Kings [2 Kings] III)

Behold: because the prophet stood at the grade of perfection, he revealed the secret of the divine will necessary to the inquiry only out of reverence for another, having first declared, as was proper, the idolater’s fault. But Naaman the Syrian, although healed of leprosy and acknowledging and confessing the true Lord, had attained no grade of perfection. Carrying away with him from the holy land a load of earth for two mules, he obtained from the same Elisha permission to attend his lord’s worship, as the necessity of his office compelled, without forfeiting God’s grace. For he said:

> “When my lord enters the temple of Rimmon to worship, and leans upon my hand, if I worship with him in the same place, I pray that the Lord may forgive his servant in this matter.”  
> (IV Kings [2 Kings] V)

And Elisha said: “Go in peace” (*ibid.*).

It is clear from this how far reverence for public authority sometimes constrains the imperfect. From these examples I venture to advise you that, if the aforementioned archdeacon wishes to have your company, you should approach him to discover how far you may be able to help him, and should privately and intimately declare to him what faith requires: that he remember that he is a Christian; fear the sentence by which he is bound; and above all mortals fear him who can cast body and soul into Gehenna. Would that, with the king and with this man as with all other excommunicated persons, there were men who feared the Lord and would stand familiarly and kindly before their faces and call them back from their impieties. But if he ceases to summon you because you are a Christian, Christ, whom he hates in you, can most easily and most happily compensate for this loss—unless your merits prevent it. For the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, who protects them in time of tribulation.

## LETTER CLXXXII. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1166.)

To the lord Thomas of Canterbury.

Nearly everything which your graciousness communicated to me I had heard through spreading report, but it became more certain by the authority of your name. I therefore reported it in my letters to the lord of Poitiers, not as certain but as heard, adding what I had heard concerning the condition of England, and earnestly asking him to give you counsel on these matters.

When I was afterward made more certain through your letters, I immediately conferred concerning your affair with your friends, of whose sincerity I have no doubt, Master Philip being included; yet I showed no one copies of the letters sent to you. Although, as you had directed, I met our friends separately—namely, the abbot of Saint-Remi, Master Fulk, and Master Radulfus—they all nevertheless agreed not only in the same judgment but almost in the same words.

In short, none of them was found to oppose the counsel of the lord pope; and all unanimously approve the advice given you by Nicholas, the hospitaller of Rouen, although they have heard nothing either of his letter or his counsel. The urgency of the time, the condition of the Roman Church, the necessity of the English realm, and the danger not only to your see but to the churches and souls entrusted to you must be considered. If you can either meet or help these dangers, you ought scarcely to value your own life so highly that, for the salvation of that life itself and the liberation of the shipwrecked Church, you should not enter into conversation with persecutors and try what merciful Jesus may deign to accomplish through your humility. For after the glory of his Ascension he declared, as authentic writings record, that he is still prepared to die for the humble and to endure the shame of the cross—especially because those who persecuted you, and Christ in you, are said to have fallen somewhat from the king’s favour and to be in such a condition that they are now weary of my life. Whether this is true I do not know; but the report is public among us. Whether it is so or not, it is more certain than certain that Christ will unquestionably triumph and will render to each person not only according to his deeds, but will also grant to a will brought to completion the crown of a perfect work.

The counsel of your most accomplished friends, from whom Master Philip and I do not differ, is this: if the empress summons you, go to her safely under the escort of the archbishop of Rouen. If you hear anything good there, give thanks to the Lord, and so proceed in all things that your moderation may be known to all. But if, God forbid, the result is otherwise, return with honour and safety when the aforesaid archbishop returns to the land of your exile.

Concerning the clerks to take with you, they advise that you take not a multitude but a few prudent and discerning men—if indeed you have such men—upon whose counsel you may rely if necessary, and through the pretext of those who are absent may conveniently obtain a delay if necessity requires it. As for me, I do not thrust myself into this undertaking, but neither do I refuse, if you decide that I shall share your journey, labour, and fortune. For, with the Lord’s help, I am ready for all such contingencies, for the loyalty due to the Church and to you. Yet if you wish me to meet you, give me enough advance notice that I may conveniently arrive at the place and day which you appoint. For:

> “…there shall be no delay on my part.”  
> (Virgil)

Although I have many duties at home presently necessary, both because of the pressing demands of my abbot and because of the presence of Gir., the archdeacon, I cannot fail their wishes any more than I can yours.

## LETTER CLXXXIII. TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1166.)

To Thomas of Canterbury, from John of Salisbury.

Reading more closely the letter which, for your consolation and for the relief of the Church, after the long exile and proscription of you and all your people, the sons of the Church of Canterbury—your brethren and fellow bishops—recently sent to you their father, I could infer nothing more plausible from examining it than that it had been dictated by the counsel of Ahithophel, whom it is credible returned from hell for the ruin of the faithful, and written by the hand of Doeg the Edomite, still thirsting for the blood of priests and seeking and insatiably pursuing the life of Christ, who lives in the faith and charity of the elect.

For they so pervert everything that it is plain to anyone with even slight understanding that their intention is far from common opinion. Yet it is far more distant from truth. All their flatteries and elaborate colouring aim at this: that, under the pretext of an appeal, the little town of the priests, Nob—whose name means “barking” and signifies the vigilant watchfulness of the Church’s shepherds—may appear rightfully to be overthrown, so that after this conspiracy none of them may dare to keep watch in the Lord’s flock and, through the duty of preaching, repel the fury of threatening wolves.

Solomon says in Proverbs that “the end of a discourse is better than its beginning” (Ecclesiastes VII); but assuredly the end of this letter is worse than its beginning. At its opening they wish you health and profess obedience—would that both were sincere—so that, contrary to the Lord’s prohibition, they may not speak good things to their neighbour while evil is in their hearts. Soon afterward they attach bitter stories—yet ones for which thanks ought to be given to God—false stories, which a captive is accustomed to hear from pirates “with throat stretched out,” [i.e. at swordpoint]. By these they justify the cause of the wicked and call good evil and evil good, so that by the consequence of their reasoning they seem at last to infer: “He who resists Caesar is guilty of death.”

Did not Judas the traitor, prefigured by Ahithophel—leaving an example of betrayal and parricide not only to the Jews in Christ’s death but also to our scribes and Pharisees—approach Christ in this manner, honouring the Lord and Master with a humble greeting and saying, “Hail, Rabbi” (Matthew XXVI), to him whom he betrayed both by word and by kiss? Then, with soldiers’ swords and clubs, on which these men relied, after the disciples had been put to flight and scattered, he dragged him before the chief priests, so that there he might be accused and convicted by false witnesses of nullifying the laws of his fathers and forefathers and of attacking Caesar’s laws. For, after taking account of Caesar’s claim, he taught that the Lord’s own image ought to be rendered to the Lord, and thus he appeared guilty of impiety because he spoke against, protested against, indeed resisted, iniquity.

They say these things; but with what conscience, let the Lord see and judge. We do not say that the lord king has never sinned; rather, we confidently say and proclaim that he is always ready to make satisfaction to the Lord. Has not the face of a harlot been made theirs, and their brow harder than adamant, so that they are not ashamed confidently, as they say, to proclaim the innocence of a man whose malice and iniquities the Christian world knows, proclaims, and detests? The bishops of London and Hereford, it is said, met with him, and he offered himself to them, as they say, for every act of justice. Is not the bishop of London that man who first in England tore asunder the Church’s unity—something all know—and who, drawn by ambition for the archbishopric, as very many suspect, was above all the chief tinder and instigator of this whole discord? [Col. 0183C] Does not the very style convict him of having represented in this letter Ahithophel and Doeg, whose spirit fills him, communicating such things as he could invent from his own spirit—a spirit which, as experience of events proves, is inferior to neither of theirs in such matters? For his speech itself makes him manifest. Nor do I care about the lies which he dared insert concerning your arrival, because I heard and saw the matter in person. He alone did not welcome the announcement of your election, though he had aspired, above all others—as many indications made clear and still make clear—to be brought into your see. Yet he did not dare speak against it for long, others reproving his ambition [Col. 0183D] and shamelessness. Whatever was in his mind—the Lord judges this from the conscience—he was among the first to elect you, and he applauded the election when made more than almost all the rest.

What shall I say of the bishop of Hereford, except that for some time, though not greatly, he nevertheless stood as the shadow of some reputation before it became known what he was? Now, under the pretext that he is learned, as those ignorant of letters believe, the impious wish to advance either him or their own unholy campaign, so that whatever a learned bishop, ancient in days, approves may seem consonant with reason. Therefore to answer these two men, or to acquiesce in their judgment, is wholly to adopt the judgment of the Londoner—as though Bibulus were counted together with Caesar. You remember, indeed, the classical writers:

> [Col. 0184A] Nothing has lately been done by Bibulus, but by Caesar.
>
> For I recall nothing done while Bibulus was consul.  
> (Suetonius, *Caesar*, 19.)

With what shamelessness, moreover, did they say—and, lest their words vanish into the winds, write—what all know to be false: that “the king,” whom no one doubts to be most impatient, “is pleased when he is corrected, and considers obedience sweet when he is admonished to correct himself if he has offended against the Lord.” “If he has offended,” they say—as though it were doubtful to them that he has offended against the Lord: he who attacks the Church’s liberty, prefers inherited perversities to the Gospel of Christ and to the ordinances of the Fathers; and, not to speak of you and of the clergy whom he unjustly proscribed, who compelled wretched women and innocent little children in cradles, stripped of every comfort, [Col. 0184B] to go into exile—not so much by a cruel sentence as by madness; who revived and strengthened the fury of schism when it was now almost lulled to rest, and, reawakening the storm which had already greatly subsided, has, so far as lay in him, sunk the apostolic ship together with Christ—and indeed is still sinking it.

What, I ask, do those men count as criminal, who boast that this is innocence? Or do these facts need proofs—facts which the world has acknowledged, which the Church unceasingly feels in its sufferings and torments, and which daily experience makes clearer than light? But if he considers correction sweet obedience, it is plain that those who permit their lord—whose service has claimed their body and soul—to err so monstrously are guilty of deeper faithlessness.

Indeed, that prophetic saying is fulfilled in them today: “Your prophets, O Israel, are like foxes in the desert” (Ezek. XIII), when those who hold the place of prophets in the Church weave manifold snares of deceit for the Church’s overthrow: first offering sweet words of greeting, professing devoted obedience, and promising aid and counsel; so that, passing through little clouds of arguments and abusing lawful words to the injury of the law, they may finally cry: “He is guilty of death; crucify, crucify him! Do not keep this man for us, but Barabbas!” (Luke XXIII).

See what salvation they desire for their father; with what devotion of faith they fulfil the obedience due to him; with what diligence they wish peace between kingdom and priesthood to be restored. I do not doubt that these things have been said superabundantly both to you and to all [Col. 0184D] who understand the cause and history of our proscription; yet, contemplating the mass of their impiety and deceit, shamelessness and falsehood, I truly could restrain neither mind nor pen. For:

> If nature refuses, indignation makes verse.  
> (Juvenal, I.79.)

—against the malice and shamelessness of men in whom:

> Every vice has reached its utmost height,  
> (ibid., 147)

so that scarcely anything can be added to their wickedness—or even devised by posterity, however subtle and ingenious in discovering evils. But why do I linger over these matters? [Col. 0185A] May God repay them; and assuredly, unless truth itself—an impossibility—be changed into falsehood, He will abundantly repay those who commit and foster this wickedness.

You, however, as it seemed to me, replied most wisely and elegantly both to their letter and to their malice; and you dissolved their long-devised and laboriously wrought subtleties, like spiders’ little nets, by the strongest arguments. Although your letter is somewhat long, it nevertheless contains only what is necessary. Yet I should have wished you to press more carefully one point which is both true and well known: namely, to show the patience with which you long remained silent, and the care which you devoted to restoring peace—repeatedly recalling the king with every humility through letters and messengers of the lord pope; through your own representatives; through his mother, whom he ought to have believed; through bishops beyond and on this side of the sea; through the brethren of the Temple and the Hospital; through the king and nobles of the realm of France; and finally by approaching in person for a conference with him and enduring a rebuff.

Moreover, since our bishops write and confidently proclaim that he is ready for every act of justice and due satisfaction, and willing also to give satisfaction if reason requires it, it seems advisable to me and to certain other friends of yours that you summon the bishops—specifically those who signed the letter, the bishop of Salisbury who complains of unjust suspension, the bishop of Worcester, who is the beginning of your generation in the Lord, and any others [Col. 0185C] whose presence you consider useful—and test whether their testimony, proclamation, and written statement are trustworthy. Summoned under the authority of obedience, perhaps they will not come, although no appeal ever protects disobedience. Yet your cause will be clearer if their falsehood and malice are exposed.

I do not, however, suppose that all the bishops—or likewise all the persons established in the dioceses, whom a deceptive superscription encloses—consent to this malice. For it is certain, or at least seems probable, that in so great a church of eighteen bishoprics there are still those ten for whose sake the Lord presently spares the island, lest it be utterly destroyed along with its sisters, whose luxury and impiety it imitates. Although some are more silent than is right, and conceal matters from whatever motive, I nevertheless believe that among the bishops there are some, and among the clergy many persons, who in purity of faith and conscience of good works hope for and await the kingdom of God. Thus Joseph was found faithful in Pharaoh’s house; righteous Lot remained in Sodom; Hushai served usefully in Absalom’s counsels; Daniel presided innocently in Babylon; and Obadiah, amid Ahab and Jezebel’s company, concealed with grief what he could not correct. By beneficially sustaining the Lord’s prophets who hid in the courts, he won, through long endurance, the mercy of God and the grace of prophecy.

Accordingly, I think it expedient that, if the chasm fixed between us and our homeland permits, you send this letter of yours to each bishop and to the more eminent churches, so that you may strengthen the faith of those who waver [Col. 0186A] and stir the affection of all; and that by frequent letters you urge each bishop, in a spirit of gentleness and mildness, to return to his heart and remember his condition. In all things, moreover, take care that nothing of yours presents an appearance of arrogance or excess.

Further, I have heard from those who say that they knew the bishop of Hereford rather intimately that, while he was engaged in the schools, he was greedy for praise and as great a lover of glory as he seemed a despiser of money. It is therefore thought that nothing could move him more than if schoolmasters and religious men—such as the prior of Saint-Victor and the like, whom he had known in France—were to awaken and encourage by their letters the zeal of one who was hoped would redeem Israel, [Col. 0186B] so that he may now show himself to be the bishop whom he used to depict in the schools, repelling from himself the vices which he criticized in others, and redeeming his lost reputation.

The same advice is offered regarding the bishop of Worcester. Yet I do not hope well of either of them or of the king of France; I presume, more than is proper, that, like other things, this will have been said merely into the ear when the moment of supreme necessity comes. Nor do I place much confidence in the Roman Church, whose habits and necessities have become known to us. Certainly the lord pope is a holy and just man, and he has, as many say, Lord Albert as an imitator; but his necessities are so many and so great, and the greed and wickedness of the Romans so great, that he sometimes uses the latitude of his power and, by dispensation, arranges what is said to be expedient for the commonwealth, although it is not expedient for religion.

I therefore fear that the day of appeal must be awaited; and when it comes, that those who love gifts will follow the rewards. I fear the narrowness of the time and our circumstances, and those of others. It is decreed by our adversaries—indeed, Christ’s and the Church’s—that they shall wound and pierce us with our own spoils. If meanwhile they are given vexation for understanding, perhaps fear of toil and expense will make them more inclined to restore peace, for themselves and for us. For this very thing nourishes their malice and audacity: while we alone bear the burden, they have hitherto rested in their wealth and pleasures. And because human help fails us, let us flee with the whole attention of our minds to the Lord, that He may deliver us from present and imminent evils, and that His truth may surround us with the shield of His compassion.

## LETTER CLXXXIV. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1167.)

To Lord BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Exeter, JOHN of Salisbury.

There would indeed be much to write, but shortage of time and the tumult of necessary occupations compel me to touch upon matters rather than expound them. Recently, by the Lord’s help, I received my brother, who greatly congratulates your kindness and generosity. He has made me, beyond the great devotion I already had toward you, far more devoted [Col. 0187A] and more indebted.

At his arrival I received a letter from a most intimate friend, who wished to warn me—and, if possible, you through me—that the king, through Jocelin de Balliol and certain other ministers of his graciousness, had ordered that you and the lord bishop of Worcester be treated and handled in every respect as the kingdom’s mortal enemies and enemies of the public welfare. Would that my fear were empty! But whatever bishops may have written of him to the pope in their letters of appeal, whatever they proclaim of his mercy and mildness, justice and affability, reverence for the priesthood—nothing is so impious against God or inhuman toward men that Frenchmen and Latins will not readily believe it of him. Therefore all who hear are greatly astonished and appalled: with what conscience, what shamelessness, what face did you dare to assert, write, and confirm with the seals of episcopal authority the innocence of a man whose injustices are everyone’s tale, whose treacheries and violences the world has known? How did the venerable assembly of so many and such great Fathers bear false witness for malice to the overthrow of justice?

For these are the words of your document on behalf of the king, whose cause your secretary endeavors to justify: “The king promises all justice and is ready to fulfil it in deeds; and he considers obedience sweet when he is admonished to correct himself if he has offended against God; nor is he only prepared to make satisfaction, but also, if the law requires it, to give security for satisfaction.” A little later it adds: “He submits himself to the judgment of the Church in matters belonging to the Church, withdrawing himself not even in the least, but bending his neck beneath Christ’s yoke.” [Col. 0187C] And slightly above: “We do not say that the lord king has never sinned, but we say and confidently proclaim that he is always ready to make satisfaction to the Lord.”

“Oh,” they say, “what sound, what holy preaching from England’s bishops! What sincere and incorrupt testimony for the liberty of the Church! How true is the assertion of priests who proclaim what a mime or actor could not utter without loss of shame!” If your London scribe—and those who agree with him—desires the faith which he does not possess, they must depart from the Latin world, lest whenever they proclaim these things:

> Why should the hoarse neighborhood cry out against the foreigner?  
> (Horace.)

And lest that wise and eloquent clerk should give such testimony against the Church for ancestral customs—or rather ancestral corruptions—and against the people as well, he inserted in your document: “The king, established by the Lord, provides in every respect for the peace of his subjects; and in order to preserve it, he desires and demands that the dignities due and rendered to kings before him be rendered to himself by the churches and peoples entrusted to him.”

What does the Gallican Church say on hearing this? “So,” it says, “may the Lord and the words of the Gospel assist those from whom and for whom these things were written.” Perhaps he provides peace for all—but from afar, because in his presence he throws everything into disorder. The bishops say—or perhaps, more truthfully, the bishop says—that there is peace; and everyone, on the contrary, cries out that there is no peace but the bitterest bitterness.

[Col. 0188A] But if he demands only customs that are due, as your Demosthenes asserts, he ought certainly to have been content with those not hostile to divine laws, not opposed to good morals, not dishonoring the priesthood, not endangering souls, and not undermining the freedom of mother Church—from whose hand he received the sword in order to defend her and repel injuries—but all things contrary to her wishes. This his document testifies, condemned by the authority of the holy Fathers and by the utterance of the supreme pontiff, as do the daily complaints of clergy and people. I fear that the bishops themselves may be forced to depart from their written statements, retract what they preach, justify the cause they now condemn, and condemn the cause they now justify.

Their attestation was composed in the name of all, but fortified only by the seals of three bishops: namely, the chief of the synagogue (archisynagogus) of London; my lord and friend, whom I spare for the present, the bishop of Winchester; and the bishop of Hereford, equally powerful in learning and eloquence, indeed an old schoolman but a novice bishop. Their authority would take precedence if it did not concur with the opinion of iniquity; yet the written attestation of manifest falsehood, convicted by the document itself and the protection of seals, prejudices both. Meanwhile, the others enclosed by the document’s superscription are accused more mildly, because it can scarcely be believed that so many wise men assembled, so many religious men conferred to deceive divine law and the canons, [Col. 0188C] and wrote for the Church’s destruction that from which iniquity might everywhere grow strong and prevail, while justice was oppressed. But, as I hear, all of them lent their authority to the document. If they saw it beforehand, it was most impious to bear witness to such great wickedness; if they did not see it, it was most foolish to lend authority to another’s iniquity by affixing their own seals.

But why do I prolong my discourse upon a manifest matter, when necessity requires more to be said? For that document, even if your people cease their efforts, will nevertheless be carried to the Roman pontiff through the diligence of our side. He knows from many indications the character of the man whom you justify, and he will easily discover [Col. 0188D] with what sincerity this attestation of the bishops was framed; and what was the intention of your scribe, who, because, by the Lord’s otherwise ordering, he could not become what he sought—the archbishop of Canterbury—has been made chief of the synagogue (archisynagogus) in the English Church by the consent, counsel, and authority of those who persecute Christ.

The lord king recently wrote to him through his archdeacon Ralph de Diceto that he entrusts his whole kingdom and the cause between himself and the Church to that man’s discretion, as to a father and most faithful friend; and he commands that his officials obey him in all things and everywhere. Therefore, if any burden comes upon you, your church, or the lord bishop of Worcester, have him summoned so that he may admonish the king on your behalf and that of God’s Church—he who, as he testified in that famous letter of his now circulating through provinces and kingdoms, [Col. 0189A] “considers obedience sweet when he is admonished to correct himself if he has offended against the Lord.”

For whoever sins against his neighbor also sins against the Lord; and whoever dishonors the Church, Christ’s bride, dishonors the bridegroom, Christ. For they are one body, indeed one spirit; and, what is more, through the sharing of grace they are in some manner one God, since by a wondrous exchange she imparts to the Lord those things which belong to flesh by original nature, in order to receive from Him the fullness of the divine nature, and, through a kind of participation, to abound and overflow wholly from Him with the oil of gladness.

By “original nature” I mean this, lest the inveterate habit of misuse be considered nature, according to which we are all by nature children of wrath—not because we were created in it, but because we degenerated into it. For, as the orator says, habit is a second nature, from which it is most difficult to be torn away. Yet I do not think the chief of the synagogue (archisynagogus) should be summoned because I greatly hope that you can profit by his patronage, but so that truth may shine forth more fully and that no one may further trust in words of falsehood, which the Holy Spirit forbids through the prophet.

To state my judgment briefly: either Scripture, which cannot be broken, is deceptive and false, and God’s truth degenerates from itself; or the wicked will be caught in their own snares, and he who prepares a pit for his brother will himself fall into it first. Christ, I call upon You Yourself; [Col. 0189C] You who are unfailing truth, I appeal to You, intending, if reason permits, to refute Your falsehood on the last day of judgment—unless a man is judged by the same judgment by which he judges, and receives a measure corresponding to his measure.

Certainly it is the Spirit of Wisdom who speaks: “By the things through which a man sinned, by those things he will also be punished” (Wisdom XI). Cain, the first murderer, was slain. Pharaoh, while he planned drowning for others, was drowned. Adoni-bezek likewise experienced this law of requital. Ham, while he desired to impose slavery upon others, was condemned to perpetual slavery. So too Judas the traitor, who arranged for the Lord to be hanged, is known to have ended his life by the noose of hanging. In every nation and age, if anyone observes the history of divine providence, he will plainly recognize a certain conformity between guilt and punishment always to exist.

We too experience what I say: conscious of our faults, we acknowledge the just scourge, awaiting—but not desiring—that soon the rod of correction may be turned back upon our torturers and adversaries. For we would rather that our adversaries should come to their senses and return as sons than that they should be tormented as slaves by what threatens them. For a race of this sort is corrected only by punishments. Ezekiel writes—and it is true—that such as the counsellor is, such also is his prophet; and even now a lying spirit goes forth from the Lord’s presence to be in the mouth of all the prophets of Ahab and of similar kings. Thus the king of the English also, as those who heard the appeals of the chief of the synagogue (archisynagogus) say, has bishops conformed to himself, who, as is written of others, [Col. 0190A] “trained their tongue to speak falsehood” and “labored to act wickedly”; he incites others to overthrow, and others overthrow him by their incitements. From the reply sent to you, you may infer what a glorious, catholic, and pious letter he recently sent to the schismatic of Cologne, so that it may be apparent to all how true is the preaching about your king’s piety and justice, uttered with such confidence.

Recently there also came to him, on behalf of the lord of Montferrand, vain deceivers: namely, the abbot of Cluny and the bishop-elect of Hippo. They requested one of the king’s daughters for the marquis’s son, steadfastly promising that they would cause the archbishop of Canterbury to be deposed if they obtained the daughter sought. Under this hope the king sent his envoys with them: namely John Cumin, R. de Tamewurda, and John of Oxford, against whom sentence of deposition from his deanery has been pronounced and confirmed by the authority and written decree of the supreme pontiff.

That decree is held by the archbishop of Canterbury, primate of England and legate of the apostolic see. The lord pope judged valid and confirmed the sentence which he pronounced against the plunderers of Canterbury Church and the king’s counsellors, and ordered it observed by bishops both on this side of the sea and beyond it. For to him the legation was granted and the primacy of all England confirmed. He wrote concerning these things to the bishop of London and to all of you, and I believe that the same bishop of London has already received the letters concerning the legation, to be shown to all of you.
