[Col. 0190C] Moreover, the aforesaid archbishop and legate, by apostolic authority, excommunicated and ordered excommunicated all who guard the ports in order to hinder appellants or persons appealed, or those proceeding out of pious devotion to the thresholds of the apostles, or to himself who holds and exercises apostolic authority. He also commanded all bishops to have this sentence published throughout their dioceses.

Although he believes that the appeal made against him by the bishops is of no force, nevertheless those who think it has some force—namely, the king, bishops, and magnates, making the prudence of the flesh their arm—ought to have permitted everything belonging to the archbishop to remain in the same condition, because nothing ought to be changed while an appeal is pending. Yet afterwards, by the king’s command, William the chaplain and other clerics—to say nothing of laymen—were seized; and after Church possessions were taken away, they were treated atrociously. Therefore the archbishop reported to the lord pope that the king himself had incurred the canonical penalty and was excommunicated by his act—unless perhaps the Apostolic See judges ecclesiastical laws to be comparable to civil laws, which, as Anacharsis the Scythian says, are like spider-webs: they hold flies, but let larger flying creatures pass through.

The pope had commanded the archbishops of Bourges, Rouen, Tours, Bordeaux, and York to observe, and to cause to be observed in their provinces, [Col. 0191A] whatever sentence the archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, should pronounce against the malefactors of Canterbury Church and his own adversaries. He added, however, in those letters that he did not command him to excommunicate the king’s person, but neither did he forbid it, because the archbishop ought not to deprive him of his authority, especially since the same king abuses the Church’s patience in many matters.

He also commanded under anathema that all who, by the king’s order, had received the revenues of the archbishop’s clerics should restore to those from whom they were taken all goods intact; for a king engaged in the cause of a robber can confer authority on no one. I argued strongly with the archbishop of Canterbury that these letters should not proceed, but the counsel of others prevailed, advising that while the lord pope survives—whose death the king is known to desire—the archbishop should use the privilege granted him and its benefits, especially since the king’s inhumanity and savagery grow ever harsher in response to his patience.

Moreover, if these commands reach you, do not fear any danger among yourselves on account of what has been taken from us. Whatever may be done with our property at your pleasure, we shall, by the Lord’s help, hold it ratified and welcome. Since you retain the benefices and rights, we do not greatly value the loss of movable goods, provided that it benefits you. We have excused your innocence before the lord archbishop of Canterbury, and it has been sufficiently excused; do not believe anyone who persuades you otherwise. He is anxious beforehand and fears dangers for you, so that he would rather you went into exile with others for the Lord than be uselessly and shamefully worn down by the world.

[Col. 0191C] Weigh both sides, and from his counsel and ours always follow the better course: that is, what, when it becomes known to you, will be more pleasing to the Lord. If even that is doubtful or hidden, faith must be followed, because whatever is not from faith is sin.

He therefore sends you letters of summons by apostolic authority, commanding, under the force of obedience and at peril of your order, that within forty days of receiving them, putting aside every excuse and delay, you come to him to hear the lord pope’s command and deliberate upon the needs of the Church. But if you see it to be advantageous, use the command; otherwise receive it with the issuer’s consent as though no command had been given. For we have not prepared a snare for you, as negligent care prepared one for a certain member of his household. Rather, we instructed the boy to deliver the letters to Master Baldwin the archdeacon or to our brother Robert, son of Aegidia; afterwards, if you wish to receive or see them, let it be according to your pleasure.

Know this for certain: unless the king restores William the chaplain, sentence of anathema will be pronounced upon his head; nor henceforth will he be spared in any respect if he presumes to attempt such acts.

## LETTER CLXXXV. TO MASTER GERARD PUCELLE. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0192A]

To Master GERARD PUCELLE.

That I answer your affection slowly and write seldom, although I have now received your letters for the second time, is caused by the rarity of travellers, the distance between places, and the difficulty of routes unknown to our countrymen. Yet affection burns all the more fervently; the tongue is more impatiently silent in proportion as charity, inflamed for the display of services, is unable to come forth publicly, and intercourse of speech is denied the power, in the pleasant and customary manner of friends, to convey into each other’s hearts the reciprocal judgments of our minds.

There is nevertheless some benefit in this hardship: through the bodies’ absence, the integrity of minds grows stronger; and love’s patience, wounding the mind, advances toward the gain of virtue through the cost of its pain and the exercise of its own discipline, and is strengthened by the habitual separation for endurance of hardships. Yet I should prefer—even if it were beneficial—to lack the experience of this impatience, while we might dwell together, enjoy reciprocal conversations, be instructed by counsel, and be guarded and strengthened for every contingency through mutual services.

But since divine providence has determined otherwise, let us obey His will with ready devotion. Though we may escape His sentence, we cannot alter His counsel: for to those who love Him all things work together for good, and by saving dispensation He provides that all things serve the purpose [Col. 0192C] of wisdom.

You have laid your affairs before me; I thank you, and very greatly. You sought my counsel through the agency of Master Ralph. I answer with what I desire and what I hope from the Lord’s mercy: that even without my effort God will provide what is salutary for you; and would that, through the service of my smallness, He might deign to grant your brotherhood what may contribute to your honor, serve your interests, and advance your salvation.

I shall therefore state what I think, so that I may withhold nothing from truth in conscience, dealing with you in that faith and devotion with which I have learned to deal with a friend, and with which I have been accustomed to please my lords. Know, then, that opinions about your departure were varied: many blamed, few excused, the course which you took. For the multitude did not know what purpose you had, what necessity pressed you, to what extent the Roman pontiff had granted you leave, or what benefit might come to the Church from the dispensation of this counsel of yours.

They do indeed see the crime of schism, the malice of those to whom you went, the danger of sharing with those justly and lawfully excommunicated; and, seeing you mingle with the condemned, they suppose that you also consent to their error. I, who know your cause and intention more intimately than certain others do, agree with the multitude in part, but disagree in a great part. For they judge rightly concerning the condemnation of schism, since from the beginning of the law it is plain how great the malice of this crime is: Holy Scripture records that the first schismatics, Korah, Dathan, [Col. 0193A] and Abiram, together with their followers, were consumed by a death unprecedented among men. Association with them is most dangerous unless one’s life and speech make one’s dissent from their crime evident.

Therefore, in the Book of Numbers—for I speak to one who knows and teaches the law—Moses, excluding the Dathanites and Abiramites from the assembly of the faithful, says: “Depart from the tents of wicked men, and touch none of the things belonging to them, lest you be involved in their sins” (Num. XVI). Nor is guilt redeemed even by the sacrifices of such men, as is clear from that chapter of the Law in which Korah, offering incense, is destroyed by the blaze of divine fire.

Yet bodily association does not imperil salvation for those who dissent from the wicked in piety and rebuke the errors of others both by the dissimilarity of their deeds [Col. 0193B] and by the censure of their words. Thus in Fourth Kings Elisha detests the Israelite king’s idolatry and does not withhold from him the oracle of prophecy, but openly declares who he is and what he will suffer by merit, without speaking any proverb. Thus he pays respect to authority; thus, out of reverence for one man, he answers another, so that religion suffers no loss but zeal expresses charity. For he says: “What have I to do with you, king of Israel? Go to the prophets of your father and your mother. As the Lord lives, in whose presence I stand, if I were not ashamed before the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not even have regarded you or looked upon you” (IV Kings III).

But participation in their sacrifices is extremely dangerous and, in my judgment, not without harm to salvation, as is more fully clear, as you know, from reading the canons. For Naaman the Syrian, cured of leprosy through Elisha’s ministry, does not dare take part in the public prayers of his lord, the king of Syria, unless leave has been obtained; unless he brings to the idol from the Holy Land a load borne by two mules, on which he may stand and sit; unless prophetic prayers cleanse him of this transgression. He says: “When my lord enters the temple of Rimmon to worship, and, while he leans on my hand, I worship the true God in that same place, pray, I beseech you, that the Lord forgive Your servant in this matter” (IV Kings V).

If, therefore, a gentile ignorant of the Law feared so greatly, how greatly ought a Christian philosopher, a doctor of the Law, to fear? But one who among such people is an advocate of truth, a worshipper of justice, and a herald of divine judgment [Col. 0193D] is not polluted by contact with others. Thus Lot pleases the Lord in Sodom; Joseph in Pharaoh’s house; Moses among the Ethiopians; Hushai in Absalom’s counsels; Obadiah amid Ahab and Jezebel’s company; and Daniel is guided and loved by the Lord in Babylon.

My counsel and desire, therefore, is that among schismatics and heretics you preach faith and peace, with such wisdom and moderation as may benefit the Church, for whose advantage and safety perhaps the Lord has sent your person among these barbarians. The Apostle became all things to all men, that he might gain all; through ill repute and good repute, and by every opportunity he can, he proclaims Christ. So you too: if you can, proclaim Christ before the emperor; because you can, proclaim him before the man of Cologne. For [Col. 0194A] it is not the case that they can excuse their error by a fraudulent cleverness of words: their own conscience rebukes them; yours gives you an evil answer concerning them—not, I say, with respect to your own dispensation, but with respect to their rashness. The earth cries out against them, and it is awaited that heaven will shortly reveal their iniquity. Although it has not yet been wholly revealed, their power has nevertheless already begun to be weakened and emptied, and their arrogance vanishes into smoke. For who among the children of men was like Frederick, before from a prince he was turned into a tyrant, and from a Catholic emperor became a schismatic and a heretic? I do not say that he introduces error into the articles of faith, so that right belief may be prevented; but that he does not allow truth to proceed in the integrity of ecclesiastical order. He has torn the priesthood asunder against the Lord, and from the Lord he feels the rending of the empire.

So likewise the king of the English, who had struck terror into neighboring princes: ever since he raised his heel against the Church and attempted to subject her to slavery, he is assailed by unarmed men, so that he is compelled to implore the aid of adjacent nations; and, swelling against the Lord, he immediately experienced manifest losses of his own strength and that of his followers. He still contrives very many things, as you have written; but assuredly either the Holy Spirit—something which not even an irreligious man believes—is deceptive and false, or “his deceit shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown” (Ps. 7). For the wicked are caught in their own snares, and he who prepares a pit [Col. 0194C] for his brother falls into it first. Do you not remember Scripture saying: “The evil man always seeks quarrels, but a cruel angel shall be sent against him” (Prov. 17)?

I sent your letters to the lord of Canterbury; but because I could not keep your messenger beyond the feast of Saint Remigius, I had not yet received his reply. It is certainly the case that he has very great thanks for your service, and that, by the Lord’s help, he will render them when a fitting time is received. But let this concerning his position be firmly known to us: what he has acquired in virtues and letters is of greater worth than what the king’s wickedness and that of those malignantly opposed to him has wrested from him. His primacy has been newly confirmed, and the archbishop of York has been ordered to acknowledge him [Col. 0194D] as his primate by rendering obedience. He is likewise legate of all England, except the bishopric of York; this is for the time being withdrawn from our jurisdiction because the archbishop of York is legate of Scotland. Nor is it the custom of the Roman Church, during a granted legation, to subject the Church of any legate to another legate by reason of that legation; yet neither does it withdraw it if it is subject by another right.

Our king seeks for William of Pavia and another cardinal to be sent as legates, hoping that they will decide this cause in accordance with his own will. Yet, in order that his will may prevail, he has procured many great wrongs and acts of plunder. It would therefore seem advantageous to me if, should it be possible, you induced the man of Cologne, under the appearance of counsel and friendship, to set the king [Col. 0195A] before his own face and show him the difficulties in his case. For by what right, reason, law, or canon can the archbishop of Canterbury be compelled to enter upon the case after he has been despoiled following an appeal? Must not everything first be restored to him, peace fully re-established, and the other requirements prescribed in this matter by the canons when carefully examined? More than ten thousand marks have indeed afterwards been taken from him and his people; and without their restoration he cannot by any right be compelled to answer, even if anything were due to those who persecute him.

Here a broad field for address lies open to your discernment: if possible, since you know the arguments better, persuade him through the man of Cologne to desist from wrongs and plundering, and not multiply exceptions advantageous to his opponents against his own claim. The bishop of Chichester recently attempted precisely this, telling the king that he would help the archbishop of Canterbury more than any man could. When the king asked how, he replied: “Because by frequent, repeated, many, and great wrongs which you have declared just, you have stifled his cause—and whatever justice you had; and you provide him also with counsel and assistance: either the best clerics, or among the best clerics, whom you had in your land, whom you compel to share his exile and do not allow to return.” [Col. 0195B] The king was moved by this and declared his anxiety with sighs, but the violence of his conceived indignation did not permit him to come to his senses.

Furthermore, since you once had the king of France as a friend, and do not know what the day to come [Col. 0195C] will bring forth, I should advise that you either appease him by some means, if he has been offended by your departure, or attract him still more by small gifts, if he remains in the old friendship. Yet there is nothing by which you can reconcile him so thoroughly—and the whole Gallican Church, indeed even the Roman Church—to yourselves, as if they hear that you, as befits a philosopher, indeed a Christian learned in both laws, render to truth the testimony you owe, and prefer neither the wealth of Croesus nor any delights to integrity. For if an ethical philosopher and pagan commendably said, in praise of letters, that

> [lacuna]  
> The mind of a greedy poet is not rashly [so disposed],

will not a philosopher, a teacher of integrity, a herald of the Gospel, be ashamed if he is weighed down by worldly possessions—he whom a pagan poet despised? Yet I hope in the Lord that he will give your devotion an opportunity so that, whether in counsels and inquiries or otherwise, as he knows to be expedient, you may, without harm to yourselves, speak for truth in the ears of princes, for your salvation and theirs; and the spirit of your Father will further it.

Nor should you be delayed if you see something blameworthy in the Roman Church, remembering that the faithful are commanded in the Gospel not to imitate the deeds of those seated in Moses’ chair, but to fulfill their teaching by their works. Farewell; and keep remembrance of me, who is always mindful of you, as befits a friend.

## LETTER CLXXXVI. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND’S. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0196A]

To the Abbot of Saint Edmund’s, JOHN OF SALISBURY.

I remember that Cicero wrote in his letter to Marcellus that, in the judgment of a wise man, it matters greatly to whom one is obliged; and that the mind of an honorable man is weighed down whenever either narrowness of means or a crisis of time makes him debtor to one whom the principle of honor or the title of character forbids him to respect and love. This, I think, was said both elegantly and truly: if it is faithfully heeded, it neither withdraws the bond of charity from those joined to us by nature, nor, under the pretext of natural association, allies in conduct those who differ through participation in error.

[Col. 0196B] It goes well, then, with those who, in the matter of benefits given and received, are obliged only to honorable men. Of these, to speak from the testimony of conscience, I am one: divine indignation has not allowed me, amid the long storm of this tempest rising from the North against the Church, to become debtor to many men on account of generosity shown to me or mine. Yet formerly I had won many by services and benefits. For the fourth year of my exile and the third of my proscription are now under way, and I can call to mind only few and slight memorials of the loyalty of a few friends.

For very many seem to have fallen into the opinion of Photinus, who says:

[Col. 0196C]

> Praised loyalty pays the penalty when it supports those  
> Whom Fortune crushes. Follow fate and the gods;  
> Honor the fortunate, flee the wretched. As far as the stars are from earth,  
> As flame is from sea, so far is expediency from what is right.  
> No loyalty ever chose wretched friends.

This is indeed the wisdom of the flesh, undoubtedly hostile to the Lord: deceitful, full of disgrace, mother and nurse of vices. Philosophy, the parent and nourisher of virtues and the regulator of duties, condemns and detests it on the truest and most learned grounds, not only of believers but also of pagans. For it lays down that expediency and honor mutually delimit one another in their teaching, so that the name of the one admits nothing which does not also require the rationale of the other. The pages of both Testaments affirm this; the teachers of mother Church proclaim it with one [Col. 0196D] harmonious voice: things dishonorable and shameful bring loss of salvation and can by no reasoning be useful. “For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world and suffers loss to his soul?”

But at this utterance commonplace friends stop their ears: those who wish to be bound by benefits, not to bind themselves; who put on and lay aside a shadowy loyalty—for they have no true one—at Fortune’s discretion; who, in order to live however they please, reject the grounds of right living, which reside in virtue alone. I speak from experience, and I am indebted to few; and I am bound to these by a correspondingly closer bond, since the sincerity of their loyalty shines forth more manifestly from clear indications. But among these your merits have given you a pre-eminent place with us; indeed, if they are examined strictly, I should rightly and deservedly call it the first. For they are many and great, and, as the things from which they shine forth are often more necessary—since their use is frequent, indeed daily—they continually compel gratitude toward the giver to increase. Nothing has fallen from my memory. I give thanks for everything, singly and collectively, counting as granted me by your generosity also those things which, on the report of my messenger and the testimony of your letters, you wished and commanded to be supplied for my needs.

[Col. 0197A] For by some hidden dispensation of counsel, my friend and companion Master G. did not obey your command, withholding or postponing the aid which your affection had decreed should be provided for the need of myself and my people. I cannot readily believe that he did this, beyond my desert and against everyone’s expectation, in order to harm me; rather, by some arrangement whose reason I do not know, he suspended your benefit. But no one will suspend the affection of my devotion toward you or my thanksgiving.

I rejoice, moreover, that when bishops, under the pretext of an appeal, sought to prolong the sickness of the Church—which, by the Lord’s help, will shortly recover—you have, as I hear, avoided their snares by an elegant shortcut of truth and justice. Thus you neither set a share of wickedness with the unjust nor leave anything which may rightly be charged against you before provincial governors. They have written and preach that the king considers it “a sweet service when he is admonished to correct himself if he has sinned against the Lord.” Are they so blinded [Col. 0197C] that they doubt that he sins through this persecution of the Church and the proscription of innocent little children and women—to say nothing of others? Or are they so reprobate that they are unwilling to remind a lord who endures, indeed listens kindly, and gives thanks to his reprovers, of what he desires: that he may make satisfaction to the Lord? May the soul of the righteous not enter into their counsel, whose fury is accursed because it is stubborn, whose indignation is hard, since they seek only that what it has long wickedly pleased them to do may be permitted longer with impunity. But he who hopes in the Lord shall not be confounded; and those who feared the Lord before the powers of the world shall lack no good thing. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVII. TO NICHOLAS OF MONT-ROUEN. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0197D]

To Master NICHOLAS of Mont-Rouen.

That I write to you rather seldom has various causes, which need not be recounted: partly because more than one is known to you, partly because it is not expedient to make the others public. But now I could restrain neither hand nor mind from writing, when, upon the arrival of our brother, I learned from the evidence of your generosity what affection you bear toward me and mine. I therefore give your affection as much thanks as I can for the kindness shown to him through the hand of R. of Luneseia, hoping, by the Lord’s help, one day to render thanks worthy of it.

I value greatly what you have done, and all the more greatly because it is plain that loyalty among men is now, according to the prophecy of the Gospel, more precious. Especially is this so since we were born in an age and nation in which scarcely anyone keeps faith with his faith without loss [Col. 0198A] to it. For faith despised is the most certain proof of faith; and he who does not make void, at the discretion of worldly power, the faith promised to the Lord is convicted of unfaithfulness. If you do not believe me, have faith in the works, which, as Jesus says—Jesus whom they crucify anew—bear a testimony in conduct more certain and greater than John’s.

Nevertheless, things go well with our countrymen, and Jesus is treated there more gently—if indeed the testimony is true which the chief priests recently issued in their so-called appeal documents, preaching and writing, and, to give their assertion greater authority, sealing the open document with many seals: that the lord king “considers it a sweet service when he is admonished to correct himself if he has sinned against God,” being most willing to make satisfaction according to the rule of justice. “If he has sinned,” say men inexperienced in evils, men for whom it is not yet certain that he has sinned in any respect against the Lord, or failed to purge his sin by fitting satisfaction.

I say that things go well with them if truth underlies their preaching and testimony. But what if they lie alike, as the lord pope says and the Roman Church has learned, in the document sent there? Henceforth, my beloved, they have no reason to complain: by that sweet service of correction which they proclaim, they will be able to obtain from the king whatever is just and good. Henceforth no one should pity them, who with such ease can change any storm [Col. 0198C] into a gentle breeze.

But we have a wholly different mind, for we experience something different. Would that their preaching might be fulfilled in us! Meanwhile we prefer to endure patiently the plundering of our goods and await him who takes away iniquity from Jacob and ungodliness from Israel, rather than set a share of iniquity with those who have gathered against the Lord and conspired against his Church, or prefer the little blossoms of temporal goods to the divine law. But let this be the end of both little page and word, so that wherever I may be, you may know that I am yours. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVIII. TO MASTER GEOFFREY. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master GEOFFREY.

[Col. 0198D] At my messenger’s return I expected to be refreshed, amid the injuries of raging Fortune, by the consolation of your letters as counsel and help. But by what arrangement, contrary to your custom and against my hope, you withheld them from a friend long exiled and proscribed for the sake of faith, is uncertain. For I cannot readily be persuaded either that you withheld your pen from writing or that you suspended the abbot’s command—which was made known to me from his letter to you—in order to inconvenience me; rather, it was through necessity and an arrangement that brings neither a stain upon loyalty nor dishonors the service of friendship. Far be it from me to think ill so quickly of a friend!

But one thing I hear: that you have lately become entangled in so many and such great affairs, useful to you and yours, that you can not only not write to friends [Col. 0199A] but cannot easily read or hear their letters. Hence I write to you more sparingly, and only about matters to which, if it is in your heart, you may readily reply. Yet even if you are altogether silent, I hold you excused everywhere and in all things, as Cicero writes of a friend in his Letter to Tiro: supposing, whenever you have ceased from an office, that opportunity—not inclination—has failed you.

This is what you can easily do, since, by the Lord’s help, opportunity will not be denied to one who wishes. Greet all your household. If perhaps you ask what is happening in France, know that there the Lord is worshipped—he who has not newly died; nor has he become a monk, nor renounced his possessions, so that he no longer has anything with which to feed his exiles. If you ask concerning me, I answer briefly that, through the Lord’s favor,

> There is a good supply of books and of grain laid in for the year.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.18.109.)

The Lord will provide the rest: he does not desert those who hope in him, nor reserve any good thing for those who abandon faith and simulate faith, but stores up wrath for persecutors on the day of his anger.

## LETTER CLXXXIX. TO MASTER GIRARD PUCELLE. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master GIRARD PUCELLE.

I recently received from you a letter full of devotion and learning. The more diligently I reread it, the more bitterly I lament that the consolation of your company has been taken from us. Yet, although the entire letter deserves very much alike through its elegance and through its affection and reverence for your name, what pleases me above all is what you wisely—and, I hope, truthfully—stated at the end of your letter: that, after weighing the tenor of my letters, you had said, done, and written whatever ought to be said, written, and done.

[Col. 0199C] I could never persuade myself that, in so great a peril to salvation, you would omit anything that circumstances required; that, accepting a sordid exchange of perishable riches for your soul, you would wish not merely to lose the name of philosopher but—what is far more ruinous—to cast away a Christian conscience. Far be this, far be it, most beloved, from your discernment and integrity: that for temporal gain you should set your portion with schismatics or rashly and shamelessly seize anything from the anathema of Jericho which might turn to the ruin and destruction of the camp of the Lord of hosts.

And indeed, to agree with your judgment—rather, with the authority of the Catholic Church—while grains are mixed with chaff and good people with evil, and Jesus labors in fulfilling Moses’ commands and advancing the dispensation of predestining grace, there is an accursed thing (*anathema*) in the midst of Israel, through which many perish; and those predestined are crowned more gloriously after their triumphs. Hence Peter’s ship, as though the Lord were asleep, is often battered by various waves; but because it trusts in Christ as its passenger, it always sails into the harbor of salvation.

[Col. 0200A] Nor do you doubt that even in your midst—I mean the Church of Cologne—the accursed thing does not so much lie hidden, as though it had any reverence for God or shame before men, as rage and run madly against God and the unity of the Church. This is especially so since it has now become known almost to the whole world how great a despiser of the Church, how great an instigator and author of schism, from the moment he was able, has been that presumptuous man of the Church of Cologne, the greatest beast among the locusts, whose power is in their tongues and tails.

For the schism was failing; your tyrant was going to restore peace to the Church, unless Cologne were still inciting him against the Church, so that with one purpose they strive to extinguish not so much the life of the supreme pontiff as the dignity of Peter, saying: “Let us bind the just man, for he is useless to us; we do not wish the knowledge of God’s ways; we know no king but Caesar” (Wisdom 2). For, as they say, they have departed for Italy with the purpose of intruding the heresiarch of Crema into Peter’s see and either seizing, expelling, or killing Christ’s vicar.

Yet unceasing prayer is made by the Church to God for him, so that he need not fear beyond measure the two tails of smoking firebrands, Frederick and Reginald, who, making flesh their arm, do not cease to blaspheme holy Israel. Certainly where human assistance fails, divine aid comes to the Church’s necessities.

[Col. 0200C] Let no one defend his error by a fraudulent excuse of words; let none applaud his own pleasures. For God is not mocked: he does not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor follow the hearing of the ears, but will judge the world in equity; and, condemning the ungodly on behalf of the meek, he punishes the more powerful more powerfully, and is perverse with the perverse. Therefore I ask more earnestly that you more insistently do what you are doing—by speaking, writing, and acting in whatever way the wisdom bestowed on you by the Lord has shown you pertains to the undoing of the schism—so that conscience may be safer before God and your reputation may be fully strengthened before your neighbor.

For the rest, to speak from conscience, you have conceived an unjust suspicion concerning the archbishop of Canterbury and his people, because, so far as I could judge, you ought to have complete confidence in charity both toward him and toward them. Therefore do not attribute to them the king of France’s anger, but to yourselves, since, as he complains, you departed without his knowledge when he was scarcely two leagues from your route. He was all the more moved because, though he had held you as most intimate, you passed on as though to the enemies of the French kingdom—specifically to the schismatic of Cologne, who not only persecutes God’s Church but, as he has heard, habitually calls the king himself a petty king with insolent buffoonery of speech. Yet, if you have it at heart, I do not doubt that the kindness of the most Christian prince will be placable toward you.

## LETTER CXC. TO MASTER WALTER OF LILLE. (A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0201A]

To Master WALTER of Lille.

The diligence of your humanity and your most ready display of generosity had certainly deserved that I should gladly seize every opportunity of serving you or yours; and, if I could do so in no other way, should at least declare, in a greeting, the sincerity of my devotion. For, when I carefully consider all the circumstances, there is none of our people to whom I remember myself more indebted. My silence would therefore deservedly have been blamed, unless it were justified by the support of many plausible reasons—reasons which I could rightly bring forward to an accuser, if it were not clear that between you and us a great abyss has been fixed, so that it is impossible for us, and difficult for you, to travel or send to friends.

An enemy has done this, and does not cease to scatter the seed of tares in Idumea; he labors with unremitting insistence to tear the angels, the rulers of churches, away from the praise of God. They are like foxes in the wilderness, the prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing. These are the men who have attempted to overthrow their most dear lord, their great prince, inflaming his gentleness with the gall of malice and extinguishing the edge of reason with poisoned counsels. May God snatch him from their hands and subject him to himself, so that his rule may be pleasing to God, peaceful, and pleasant to its bearer, [Col. 0201C] and may be happy and fruitful for the churches of which he is patron and for the peoples.

I certainly know that, if he returns to his heart, he will appease his Lord, the bridegroom of the Church, by fitting satisfaction, and withdraw the sword of his power from the blood of the innocent, so that God may be gracious to him and not require that blood from him and his house. If he despises God’s exiles and proscribed people because they are poor, let him remember that Christ is the patron of such people. To avenge the blood of poor Naboth, God destroyed the house of Ahab and Jezebel. Because Saul, on the advice and urging of Doeg the Idumean, keeper of the mules, attacked the priests with the sword of royal power—which had been entrusted to the king for the protection of the priesthood—and destroyed Nob, their village, he provoked against himself the sword of God. By the agency of the Philistines, both he and his house were irreparably destroyed, leaving to his line a hereditary title, which is read as having been affixed to a gibbet at the request of the Gibeonites—whose people Doeg, minister of royal indignation, had afflicted among the priests.

[Col. 0201D] And God still regards the prayer of the humble and does not despise their petitions (Ps. 101). Led by this hope, the poor proscribed people pray—and, by the help of the God for whom they suffer, will continually pray—that the most serene lord king may produce fitting fruits of repentance and turn aside the threatening wrath.

Meanwhile we endure the Lord’s dispensation with equanimity, certain that nothing can harm us if we are zealous for good—that is, for the divine law. For we do not suffer as criminals, as is publicly known, except to those [Col. 0202A] who labor not to understand the things of God; rather, we are afflicted as Christians. And in this, most beloved, we rejoice to have you as our companion: not, God forbid, insulting your rejection, but rejoicing in your virtue.

For you too have proved your loyalty, and despised the loss of temporal things, while pursuing integrity and satisfying charity. What, my beloved, do you marvel at? Why do you mutter? Why do you strive to obscure the lamp? Your offence has become known to the world; all deliver one judgment concerning you. And, lest I delay you further: you have fulfilled the Gospel’s ideal of the man who lays down his life for his brother, when you preferred to be condemned for justice rather than another man—whose obedience seemed worthy to be reckoned a virtue—to be accused of an offence, if he confessed the truth. Yet he too, as the common saying goes, did not dare to profess loyalty and obedience; nor did you, which I gladly embrace, deign to deny the title of loyalty and obedience.

Since, therefore, the virtue of loyalty has freely been punished in you—or rather proved by men—will not the faithlessness of transgressors and the iniquity of slanderers be condemned before God? God is my witness that I grieve because the seal of Christ the King has been taken away. But before the same judge I confess that I prefer you to remain in this condition rather than redeem it through faithlessness or through any stain of disgrace. Let, then, your consolation now be the testimony of an innocent conscience—O friend of God, who have been mine for many days—which is the consolation both of me and of those exiled with me; nothing in life can be more pleasant than this.

[Col. 0202C]

> [lacuna] before this judge no guilty person is acquitted,  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* XIII.3.)

It is this that produces—or, more truly, continually nourishes—the undying worm and unquenchable fire. This offspring belongs not to conscience but to guilt; may God always keep it far from you. If you ask about me, the trade in books supports me, sound and safe, while I await the Lord’s mercy in an abundance of what nature requires or the habits of those with whom I live. My brother rejoices with me, ready for every service to you in the Lord. Since at present we can do nothing else, we offer the gift of greeting and devotion: through you, bidding farewell to those whom you know should be greeted, and specifically [Col. 0202D] to the clerks of the court, who are neither excommunicated by name nor through participation with excommunicated persons.

## LETTER CXCI. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1166.)

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, JOHN OF SALISBURY.

I had resolved not to write to your fatherhood, because an exchange of letters from you has been denied me. Yet, considering the prudence of your circumspection, I approve more highly the wisdom of your consideration in not writing than a certain quasi-friendly dispensation in writing. For sons are to be invited to filial services by deeds rather than writing, by realities rather than words, by benefits rather than sweet speech. Indeed, according to secular laws, sons should be won over by paternal services, not bound by compulsory agreements.

But when I saw the letters which you sent to the king of England and to your suffragans, I rejoiced with great joy at your fervor and righteous zeal for God’s Church, with which you burn: that at least in this perilous time someone is found who does not hesitate, like blessed Peter, to draw the sword in Christ’s name against the servants of wickedness, enemies of truth, and persecutors of the Christian name, for the injuries of the Church and for Christ’s members, whom he redeemed with his own glorious blood. I praise your zeal and purpose; I praise the censure of your severity and discernment which you exercise against depraved [Col. 0203B] conduct. But I observe what is written: “When the head is sick, the other members become weak.” I observe your suffragans, who failed on the day of battle; indeed, they raised the neck of disobedience and set themselves up as adversaries. What then will he do alone who has neither one to raise him up nor a fellow-worker? Yet if the Lord is for us, no one will prevail against you. He himself will reject the unjust thoughts and schemes of the bishops of England and scatter the counsels of the prince.

The king of England has written to the lord of Cologne that Henry of Pisa and William of Pavia will come into France to make fresh exactions, so as to scrape together and collect from every quarter the means by which Pope Alexander may be maintained in the city. One, as you know, is frivolous and changeable; the other deceitful and fraudulent; both greedy and avaricious. Gifts will therefore easily blind them and bend them to every injustice. On hearing of their detestable arrival, I at once began to fear greatly that their presence would do much harm to your cause, and that they might not blush to purchase the king of England’s favor with your blood and that of your people.

[Col. 0203C] I therefore advise that, through the king of France and the Cistercians, they be forestalled in this matter in such a way that, even if they wish to do so, they cannot act perversely in it. Nevertheless, trust in your justice, and let good faith sustain you with certain hope. For Alexander indisputably holds his position. The son of the Sicilian, confirmed in his father’s kingdom, will stand by him at every nod. And God’s vengeance is plainly raging among the princes of Germany. Many princes have now conspired against the duke of Saxony, though the emperor endeavors to make peace. The man of Cologne also joins the opposing party, withdrawing from the alliance he had made with the duke.

Moreover, when the man of Cologne had assembled soldiers and was equipped to go into Italy, he was seized by a double tertian fever; it troubles him so severely that it is nearly certain he cannot go before winter. During this illness he promised me that, if he himself does not go to Italy—whether the emperor goes or does not go—he will entrust himself to the counsel of the Cistercians, the king of France, and you, concerning making peace with Pope Alexander. He proposes to arrange matters so that in some manner [Col. 0204A] he may be compelled by his clergy to do it. I write this to you in confidence, as to father and lord, so that it may remain concealed with you until we see whether the matter will have any effect. If I am freed from my debts, I shall return even if you do not summon me. In the meantime, if I understand that I am needed by you in anything, I shall always be ready to return. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCII. TO MASTER RALPH OF LISIEUX. (A.D. 1166.)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to Master RALPH of Lisieux.

Your letter brought me consolation and desolation alike, unless reflection upon him [Col. 0204B] who comforts us in every tribulation had very easily and swiftly driven away the stings of desolation. For, by God’s favor, we sail in harbor; and he, who does not know how to fail those who hope in him, supplies us, above and beyond our merits, with enough and—with words I do not utter without fear of divine judgment—with necessities in abundance. For, if merits are examined in return, we are unworthy to suffer for justice, since, as you know, the kingdom of heaven belongs to such persons. God and conscience bear witness that, though the world may think otherwise, we have forfeited it by many great sins.

Yet he gives us boldness to hope: he who, as chooser of the lowly and weak, has permitted us to be defenders of ecclesiastical liberty, champions of justice, and witnesses to the law which declares that, so long as that law remains vigorous, a believer ought not to fear exile or proscription for its sake. You know all the points of our cause; you know the wording of the oaths exacted from us, so that there is no need to linger in explaining this matter more carefully.

But perhaps you will say that the formula of the oath formerly proposed will be altered, and that no one will be compelled to swear to the words of condemned customs. The exacter of the oath will be content if the words of loyalty to be kept toward him are simply and absolutely supplied—provided, however, that this is not added: “that faith toward the Church and obedience to the prelates shall remain inviolate.” For, they say, he neither wishes nor has wished to prejudice these things. Yet no such oath is required.

But if it ought not to prejudice them, why is it forbidden to mention an observance necessary to salvation? If it does prejudice them, with what conscience will it be rendered by a believer? You say: “It is the counsel of wise men, both for the good of peace and to avoid every suspicion, and to obtain means for action, that each person may be able to be serviceable to necessary friends.” Shall the Father of mercies, who has comforted us and comforts us in every tribulation—indeed, does not allow us even to know tribulation—be abandoned for the favor of friends and frivolous intimates who deserted us in adversity?

Others advise us to swear; but he gives counsel not to swear. Whom do you think should be believed? I, certainly, believe the counsel of God, incarnate and dead for me, to be more trustworthy and wholesome; and I shall not doubt that the man who judges his own counsel preferable has a brazen face. Therefore, to pass over the other greater causes of exile and proscription, which are known to you: because I believed Christ, who dissuades from oaths, I have been proscribed. Whoever does not believe him will be proscribed far more dangerously. For in his threats and promises alike he is faithful.

Nor do I say that every oath, even though it proceeds from evil, is unlawful. For it sometimes admits of pardon; but there is absolutely no place for pardon unless some consideration obtains forgiveness for the fault that arises. I pass over this point, leaving it rather for God to examine and for the consciences of individuals, lest, if I should express anything too subtly as reason suggests, I seem to have poured out my spirit in reproach against others—perhaps innocent persons—who have taken oaths [Col. 0205B]. For I prefer to restrain my pen with the rein of moderation rather than heap up articles of the divine law which, though correctly stated, sometimes serve only to overthrow their hearers. I therefore pass on to those matters for which you have supplied the occasion, praying and beseeching that your faith may not fail, and that you may not believe the spirit of those who, following their own Neptune, hasten through his agency to Pluto and go down alive into hell. Let them meanwhile say whatever they please; let them boast in their vanity that they have prevailed against the Christ of the Lord: their destruction stands at the door. Their joy lasts but an instant, and their glory is fire, dung, and worm. By what road this comes about, you will shortly know, God being favourable; and their ears [Col. 0205C] will ring with the hissing and outcry of the faithful, to whom Christ’s poor have been an object of hissing and mockery. Nor doubt—unless perhaps you are persuaded that mortals are not destined to die—that those who seem, by the deceit of silence and the craft of fear, to have escaped the snares they deserved will be brought under the sentence of anathema.

Remember to persuade our friends—if indeed any are ours rather than Fortune’s—not to weep over us. And would that they need not weep over themselves. For the Most High deals with us, though wielding the rod, as a most gracious father is accustomed to deal with his dearest children. Yet I sympathize with you, who have found less security in harbour than in shipwreck. But if God grants you even a little patience—which I declare to you with unhesitating [Col. 0205D] faith—the shipwrecked persons of whom men despair will very quickly be able and willing to help. Stand, therefore, in the condition in which you were called by the Lord; and, at least insofar as you can do so without danger, be a defender of the divine law. What I say is sufficiently human, on account of the weakness of our flesh. For that no one can be saved unless he sets observance of the law above every danger is attested by the blessed Apostle and the entire assembly of the perfect. I have written to the man on whose behalf you are concerned; and I think that through the bearer of this letter you will learn from him more certainly about his condition, which, God being favourable, is good. Greet our friends most earnestly; I trust that their names, as though copied from a page, are impressed upon the mind of the bearer through multiplied prayers [Col. 0206A].

## LETTER CXCIII. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER

[Note: [Col. 0205D] The Paris edition has the superscription: “To the Lord of Exeter”; Lupus: “To Bartholomew, archdeacon of Exeter”; [Col. 0206D] but Bartholomew was certainly then bishop of Exeter.]  
(A.D. 1166.)

**To Baldwin, archdeacon of Exeter.**

Long suspended in expectation and fevered by the impatience of desire, we awaited the arrival of our messenger, hoping that at his return we should be refreshed by the diligence of our friends, or at least by the comfort of letters. Yet the contrary occurred, since he brought back not one iota or tittle. Nor do we say this because we wish to accuse our friends of failure in charity or negligence; we infer that they are afflicted all the more bitterly because they dare the less to lament their distresses. For they are restrained [Col. 0206B] by cruel chastisement, like children whom the severity of their teachers compels to force back into the bosom of their eyes, and into the hidden sources of their spring, the tears drawn forth by the violence of grief and wrung out by blows.

We measured the dangers of our situation, the malice of the times, the weakness of the Church, the fury of the persecutor; yet we hoped meanwhile that iniquity, clinging to its talent of lead, cannot long remain on high, and that the Amorite is more swiftly and violently dashed down and thrust into the depths of the earth when its completed wickedness breaks forth on high. We therefore sympathize with our friends and groan over the desolation of the Church in the kingdom of the English. And we wonder how the zeal of so many religious and learned men has vanished [Col. 0206C], when scarcely one or two watchmen appear who dare, in accordance with the prophetic warning, to announce to the wicked man from the mouth of the Lord his wickedness. Thus the wicked go down alive into hell in the presence of the watchmen, so that their blood may justly and deservedly be demanded of the watchmen because they were silent. But why do we say that they are to be punished for silence? Certainly, some among them are those who, seeing a thief, run with him; indeed, they are his forerunning guides and teachers, who hurl him into thefts and robberies, and assign themselves a share with the wicked in every token of iniquity. Foremost among them is your archisynagogue; and those who seemed first clothed in gold and to be pillars of the Church have embraced dung. The Lord had given them silver and gold, and, as He Himself complains through the prophet, “They made Baal from it,” while they fear man more than God and worship and serve the creature rather than the Creator. This, as the blessed Apostle teaches, is the most exact and certain definition of idolatry. For whatever each person worships above all else, he makes his god: one, enslaved to lust, prefers Venus; another, seeking gifts and rewards, and sometimes falling into frauds and robberies, worships Laverna; another, puffed up by wind, dwells in the land of Moab amid Babylonian arrogance; another, following gluttony, puts on Epicurus’ pig. For what is written of such persons—that their god is their belly [Col. 0207A], and their glory ends in shame—may by a probable extension of interpretation be applied also to other vices. Hence Truth teaches in the Gospel that God and Mammon cannot both be served (Matt. VI), and that whoever desires to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God. The Teacher of the Gentiles proclaims and cries out: “If I were still pleasing men, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. I); and those who please men “have been put to shame, because God has rejected them” (Ps. LII). Yet the archisynagogue and his accomplices unquestionably hold another opinion: by a fraudulent interpretation of words they twist the law according to their own pleasure, not according to the author’s meaning. They refuse to conform their understanding to it, but strive in every way to make whatever they choose appear consistent even with divine law. For he says that one ought not to contend [Col. 0207B] for the liberty of the Church. But, deceitful and false hypocrisy, where are you going? What heresies and schisms are you devising? Was not the people called from the beginning of the nascent law into God’s liberty? And was not Egypt afflicted with intolerable plagues because it claimed, according to ancient and inherited custom, a Church held in servitude for nearly three hundred years? Did not the Maccabean martyrs laudably and religiously lay down their most holy souls for the liberty of their brethren? Did not David strike down the Philistine with stones gathered from the stream into a shepherd’s bag, in order to free the ranks of the Lord of hosts from the yoke of undeserved servitude and the reproach of religion? But why put forward a few small examples? Almost the whole Scripture [Col. 0207C] arranged in historical narratives is filled with memorials of illustrious men of this kind.

There are two causes which men defend with the greatest devotion and set above their own lives: one is liberty; the other faith and religion. Yet that which concerns faith is held to be more excellent and is unquestionably more just—so much so that even men of a profane religion hold this firmly. For Ahab, who is certainly known to have been reprobate, exposed without hesitation to the king of Syria, who wished to reduce him to servitude, silver and gold, male and female servants, every sort of household equipment, wife, sons, daughters, and finally himself; yet for the divine law alone he did not fear to enter into conflict. For when that king wished to search the house in order to plunder the law, Ahab opposed him and won the victory [Col. 0207D]. For although otherwise reprobate, in this matter he honoured the Lord. For what cause, then, is religious contention made, if not for preserving God’s law? Surely this law forbids iniquity and commands the shepherds of the Church to punish every disobedience. But perhaps the archisynagogue knows an iniquity which God does not forbid, or which He does not wish to be rebuked by the Church’s shepherds and, if possible, committed to punishment. Moses and the Teacher of the Gentiles certainly did not know such an iniquity. Yet he alleges that John rebuked Herod in a spirit of gentleness, declaring it unlawful for him to abuse the wife of his living brother. In saying this, he plainly seeks comfort not so much for ignorance as for cowardice, since it is certain that John there did not act as a pontiff, upon whom correction of offences would rest [Col. 0208A], but as a herald of the word, whose office was solely the proclamation of things to be done and the rebuke of vices. Eli indeed corrected his sons, but with a father’s affection and gentleness rather than with a pontiff’s severity and authority. Therefore every article of the divine law must be defended; authorities must be opposed; and whatever attacks charity, which is the fulfilment of the law, must be overthrown with all one’s strength. Yet God decreed, as is read in Numbers, that the Levitical tribe, as a figure of the priesthood, should be exempt from public duties and subject only to the dispositions of the high priest. Abiathar also, who had resisted the Holy Spirit in David’s disposition, was removed from the priesthood but escaped the sentence of death because he had borne the ark; protected by the privilege of his former office, he awaited his destined day [Col. 0208B]. If the clergy do not succeed to the privileges of the Levitical tribe, then the Apostle is vain and all interpreters of Scripture are deceivers. From this it ought to be clear to everyone that the cause of those who fight for the Church’s liberty is altogether just, and that they hold God’s law more precious than their fortunes—indeed, than their own lives. But perhaps someone will say: “What has this to do with the case of your Archbishop of Canterbury, who yielded in the Church’s cause at Clarendon and in the monetary suit; conscious of injustice in his legal position and distrustful of his own devices, he confessed in some fashion—indeed, plainly—his own injustice by an imprudent and shameless evasion, and justified the opposing party.” Let it be granted that he yielded. May God be merciful to the bishops who induced him to do so [Col. 0208C], and to the deceivers who led him out, though his fear was just, immediate, and such as might have overcome the most steadfast man. His letter is being sent to you, in which he gives some account in his own defence; but since he sinned, repented, confessed, and deserved absolution from the lord pope after the case had been examined, he obtained that the Church of the English should be absolved from illicit and extorted obligations. Why, then, do those who imitated, as they say, the sinner not imitate him as penitent, confessing, and making satisfaction? Do they prefer to remain in filth rather than rise, be cleansed, and be restored to their former standing? But, it is objected, he feared the monetary suit. This is indeed false; rather, he feared the iniquity of the judges, who had condemned him by an unjust judgment [Col. 0208D] and were prepared to decide whatever pleased the tyrant. And God spared the shame of our age in this respect: the tyrant was ashamed to command more than they were prepared to perform. All were Balaamites, devising what art might curse and condemn the cause which the Lord had blessed. They urged that evils be done in order that good might result, and that pernicious dispensations of possessions and divine right be admitted to soften the madness of the persecutor. What was certain was called into doubt, so that the comic saying revolved in almost everyone’s mind:

> What I know, I do not know.

For who did not know that the king released his chancellor from every administrative duty and obligation in order that he might govern the Church of Canterbury? Who is ignorant [Col. 0209A] with what insistence he obtained a pallium for him from the Apostolic See? What he afterwards promised in order that the ancestral “customs,” as they call them—though they are in truth abuses—might be admitted, is known to very many. Yet the archbishop, through the malice of the accuser and through the iniquity, simplicity, or dispensation of the judges, though he had not come there for this purpose, was pressed to litigate and give security, although he possessed a very great immovable estate; he could scarcely obtain even a day’s respite for deliberation, and that only because of a most severe illness. Previously they had nevertheless condemned him by an unjust judgment, which the Apostolic See, after examining the case, revoked. We possess the privilege recording that revocation. Could he not, then, and ought he not to have regarded the judges with suspicion? But perhaps it will be said that they had to pronounce judgment not according to their own conscience but according to the parties’ allegations, since even the Lord did not condemn Judas, though He knew him to be a traitor, and spared the woman caught in adultery when no accuser came forward. It was also said for our instruction: “I judge as I hear.” But there “hearing” is put for understanding, so that a judge may decide according to the reasonable movement of his own mind, using now assertions, now presumptions, in order that a righteous and innocent person may never be condemned against conscience, even if the multitude seems to stand with the opposing side. For it is written: “You shall not kill the innocent and righteous, for I oppose the wicked” (Exod. XXIII). And elsewhere: “You shall not follow a multitude to do evil, nor acquiesce in the judgment of the greater number in a court case so as to depart from the way” (ibid.) [Col. 0209C]. But if a judge pronounces judgment against conscience, especially to the prejudice of an innocent person, he sins most grievously, because, as the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV). Solomon, using a conjectural argument in the case of the harlots, condemned the false accuser. Daniel, in rescuing Susanna, disclosed the wickedness of the priests through presumptions. If the judges in the case of the Lord of Canterbury had possessed due vigour, exercised the diligence prescribed by law, consulted the Scriptures in giving judgment, and not deferred to power beyond measure and right, one might perhaps plausibly blame him who declined their judgment. But where fury had claimed everything [Col. 0209D], what place could reason or law have had? The Christ of the Lord was brought before the governor: “The chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees assembled against Him” (Matt. XXVII). And this governor was certainly more savage than he under whom Christ was condemned. Pilate, by seeking out occasions, laboured that Christ might escape the accusation; this man, however, devoted effort and diligence to ensuring that Christ, though innocent, should be accused and condemned. Pilate, lest Christ should be punished under his judgment, sent Him on to Herod, where Christ at least escaped with contempt and was sent back clothed in a white garment. Here every effort was made that Christ might in no way escape. Let any man who loves truth, who dares before God and will have to render an account of this testimony in the strict judgment, declare—if he dares—that the archbishop was not there maliciously handled by the accuser [Col. 0210A] and his accomplices, deceitfully or weakly handled by the judges, and contemptibly and shamefully handled with respect to the Church’s dignity; and that, after receiving fitting security, he will return to judgment. Let an upright and discerning man say this, then, and he will easily obtain assent to his counsel. Nor is it believable that even your archisynagogue thinks otherwise, although he is not ashamed to preach the contrary. But may he and all his followers enjoy sound teeth to the degree that their conscience answers them that the archbishop was there treated justly and to the honour of God and the Church; and may all who agree with the archisynagogue be weighed in a like balance.

Since, therefore, the archbishop had once received an unjust judgment, and saw a worse one impending through the malice of the persecutor [Col. 0210B] and the weakness of the judges, he declined the judgment, transferring the case to the hearing of him who has been appointed by the Lord as judge of all the faithful; and he went to the place to which decision of all priestly causes has been specially entrusted. This rests not on the law of emperors or canons, but on the authority of God Himself, who says through Moses: “If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous for you, between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and leprosy, and so forth, go up to the place which the Lord shall choose, to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge who presides at that time; and you shall do whatever he tells you, and follow the sentence of the priests. But the man who acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest and the decree of the judge who ministers to the Lord at that time, that man shall die; and you shall remove evil from Israel” (Deut. XVII) [Col. 0210C]. Observe that it excepts neither cause nor person from the judgment of priests, although priests decide sometimes in person and sometimes through the Church’s vicars and ministers. Was it not said to Jeremiah, in the person of the priests, as the Church’s teachers faithfully hand down: “Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, scatter, build, and plant” (Jer. I)? What sin, then, did the Lord of Canterbury commit if he appealed, provided for his own safety, and spared the bishops, who would otherwise have had wrongly to pronounce a second judgment to his condemnation and disgrace, or to undergo the intolerable loss of royal indignation?

How the opposing party, which itself also instituted an appeal [Col. 0210D], has prosecuted its case; with what moderation and sincerity it has dealt both with the Church and with its opponent—God knows and will judge, and it cannot be unknown to you. A man may deceive himself and weave snares for his own soul; but God is not mocked. Two years have now elapsed—the period, namely, which assists appellants—and when it had expired judgment was pronounced on behalf of the Lord of Canterbury, although execution in certain matters is still delayed by dispensation. It is now plain to all who fear God that the archbishop and his people have been unjustly outlawed. By what right were the clergy’s revenues confiscated? With what patience on the bishops’ part are the Church and the goods of Christ’s altar exposed at will to the Church’s persecutors? What justice outlawed innocent persons without distinction of profession or rank, age or sex? Who ever with such savagery tore apart the bond of marriage? Yet the bishops give the man who does this testimony to innocence and justice, so that, to their own shame and destruction, they are not ashamed to say and write that the king “considers obedience sweet when he is advised to correct himself if he has sinned against God.” Therefore, either in their judgment he does not sin; or they faithlessly withhold from him the welcome and due service; or they openly lie to their own destruction, because “a lying mouth kills the soul.” There is no one who dares tell him what is beneficial both for the hearer and the speaker. There is no one who says with Moses: “Let the people of the Lord depart with all that belongs to them, that they may sacrifice to Him in the wilderness” (Exod. V). There is no one who obtains for the clergy, living under Moses and Aaron—that is, occupied in the worship of the law and the rite of divine sacrifice—leave for a journey of three days [Col. 0211B]. Indeed, it is believable that, if Moses and Aaron were now present at the door of him whose innocence is preached, either they would have no access at all, or a hearing would be denied them, or they would suffer punishments—or at least insults—which they did not suffer there. For there are no lack of Jannes and Mambres to resist the Holy Spirit. Ahithophel has left many heirs in counsel, who make foolish the minds of princes and set forth and prefer against God poisoned counsel. For what else do they now persecute in the Archbishop of Canterbury except that he has dared in the presence of kings to proclaim God’s justice, defend the law, and defend the Church’s liberty? Certainly, while he was a magnificent trifler at court, while he seemed a despiser of law and clergy, while he pursued clownish follies with the more powerful, he was thought great, eminent, and welcome to all, and everyone individually and collectively proclaimed him alone most worthy of the highest pontificate. But after he was raised to the pontificate, mindful of his condition and profession, he wished to present a priest in his own person and chose the word of God as his teacher rather than the people. Thus he became their enemy by speaking truth and correcting life, so that these too might fill up the measure of their fathers, who for a like cause persecuted prophets and apostles; and some of them still persecute Christ’s martyrs—that is, witnesses of truth and justice. What did Ahab and Jezebel persecute in Elijah [Col. 0211D]? Surely the oracle of religion, testimony to faith, profession of justice, destruction of idolatry, remedy for vices, abolition of crimes. Paul and Peter would have escaped Nero’s sword—indeed, would not even have incurred enmities—had they not preached against men’s pleasures and errors. For no one persecuted in anyone what he was or was called as Elijah; no one punished anyone because he was Peter or Paul. And John would have been safe before Herod if he had not said: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark VI). For no one has reached such tyranny as to persecute nature. But it is a frequent maxim, made public by many examples, that

> Truth begets hatred.  
> —Terence, *Andria* I.1.41.

[Col. 0212A] Therefore those who persecute the Archbishop of Canterbury in this matter do not persecute what Thomas is—Londoner by birth, cleric by profession, priest in rank, bishop in dignity—but because he declares to the people of God their crimes and calls the princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah to hear and obey God’s law. What, then, do they persecute? Certainly the spirit of apostles and prophets, the spirit of justice and truth, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and beyond doubt the Holy Spirit. For they abominate, recoil from, and punish what the Holy Spirit taught through prophets and apostles. And if Paul or John himself were bodily present and taught what he wrote, he would either be tortured with punishments or at least told: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways, because you are opposed to us” (Job XXI) [Col. 0212B]. God spoke once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time; nor does He raise the dead to instruct the living. Since Moses and the prophets are present in the Church, that they may be heard and teach the people, and so that the party condemned by the word of the Lord according to the judgment of Moses and the prophets may yield victory to the other party, let the ephod be brought forth, where there is revelation of truth and judgment, and let each person be answered according to his works. The Archbishop of Canterbury and his followers do not shrink from this procedure; rather, they wish and pray that their judgment may proceed from the face of God’s word—that is, divine law—and that the eyes of the Lord may declare equity. If he requires anything contrary to God’s law, if the customs demanded against the Church rest upon God’s word [Col. 0212C], he will gladly yield and will willingly make satisfaction for the opposition and harassment of the other party. But if his cause rests upon God’s word, if apostles and prophets stand with him, no one will by God’s grace tear him or his people from this faith.

For this is the most just cause of exile for a Christian, for which he ought to lay down not merely his property but also his life. Now only the iniquity of the customs and the equity of divine law contend against one another; and there is no mention of the monetary case, which was then merely pretended and in truth did not exist. Against this, wickedness invents and devises many things and labours in the skin of a little fox; but iniquity lies to itself, not observing—or feigning not to observe—how sweet the bread of lies is to a man, though afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel [Col. 0212D]. Yet there is one thing which all ought to wonder at—indeed, to grieve over: namely, that those for whose liberty the Canterbury exiles have devoted themselves to every danger insult those exiles. The latter are pressed in the winepress for the common liberty; and who has stood beside them? They strive that the Lord’s inheritance may be freed from servitude, while those who ought to have been led into liberty return in desire to the fleshpots and garlic of Egypt. They are indeed more pitiable than all nations: if they are outlawed here, afflicted, and counted with the wicked; if they do not await consolation from the Lord; if conscience does not answer the exiles according to their deserts; if in persecutions they do not have Christ as their cause. Carnal prudence mocks them, measuring deserts by outcomes; but God consoles them in their tribulation. In the end He will answer both those who flatter the world and place cushions beneath heads of every age and pillows under every arm, communicating with the excommunicated, making mockery of the Church’s keys, and thinking that God’s law is nothing but words [Col. 0213A]. Meanwhile we give thanks to God in all His gifts, especially because He has deemed us worthy to be joined to the number of those who suffer persecution for justice. We have received sweet things from the Lord’s hand, and have often abused them to our own destruction. Why, then, should we not also receive bitter things from Him with equanimity as medicine for the advancement of our salvation? Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s, so that friends ought only to be asked to relieve the straits of our exile by their prayers: that our faith may not fail, but that He may mercifully work through our affliction salvation for us and peace and liberty for the Church.

## LETTER CXCIV. TO NICHOLAS OF MONT-ROUEN

(A.D. 1166.)

**John of Salisbury to Nicholas of Mont-Rouen.**

He rightly incurs the mark of ingratitude whom remembrance of benefits does not kindle to earn love and service. And indeed the fuller gratitude is owed when benefits, proceeding solely from the rich vein of innate liberality, have more abundantly and frequently preceded neither merit nor a deserving recipient [Col. 0213C]. But whence, my beloved friend, beloved by every right and desert, may I answer your kindness with a return worthy of your generosity? I am in exile, outlawed, exposed to poverty; I am more oppressed by the misfortunes of my fellow-exiles than by my own, and I count nothing alien to myself among the sufferings which the Church of God endures in her afflictions. Yet in all these things I find God favourable to me, whose gift it is that I willingly undergo exile for justice, joyfully receive, if necessary, the plundering of my possessions for the faith, neither fear hardships nor blush at the disgrace of poverty, being a disciple and teacher of poor Christ; and I am certain on the oracle of Truth itself that our sorrow shall be turned into joy. For He is faithful and will not permit His little ones and orphans [Col. 0213D] to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear, but for His glory will make the trial of the humble redound to their profit. But meanwhile, sweetest of friends, how can I answer your generosity? I cannot pass it over in silence, for I speak from repeated experience of it. My people have so often felt its benefits whenever opportunity was given them to enjoy the comfort of your charity. Therefore, for what I can presently do, I give you most abundant thanks with devotion, confidently expecting that He to whom you have lent, at interest, the money of benefactions in your persons will repay your compassion with abundant mercy.

For this alone is an honourable kind of lending at interest, and the page of Truth, which condemns usury and all avarice, not only absolves it but rewards it with a hundredfold recompense [Col. 0214A]. Solomon too testifies to this in Proverbs: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him his return” (Prov. XIX)—temporally, insofar as may be expedient, but with fullest recompense in eternal life. If divine favour would satisfy my desires to this extent, that by His authority and through my ministry He might repay my benefactors in kind, I should think that I had almost wholly attained the sum of my temporal wishes. But I do not clearly see what to think about our peace. Some maintain that it is being more hopelessly delayed because the Lord King prospers in his ways; others, on the contrary, say that peace would not displease him if an honourable form of reconciliation presented itself. I would sooner believe the latter, because [Col. 0214B] a prudent man ought to distrust this very ease and abundance of success; and, conscious of his ways, he cannot be secure if by wronging the Church and Christ’s poor he has made God his enemy. Yet, God being favourable, he will not do what ought to obscure the glory of his rule, nor presume against God on the ease—or rather the deceitfulness—of success, if he remembers how deceitful a horse is for salvation. Asahel, as the history relates, outstripped stags in speed and surpassed roe-deer in swiftness of running; but because he indulged his agility too greatly, as he pursued a fleeing enemy, he compelled him to inflict the fatal blow at the very moment when he had intended to evade death by flight. Christ sometimes flees from the face of a persecutor; but woe to the impenitent man upon whom, provoked, He casts a grim eye! Greet the courtly associates who have not been excommunicated.

## LETTER CXCV. TO MASTER WALTER OF THE ISLE

(A.D. 1166.)

**To Master Walter of the Isle.**

The long duration of my silence might rightly seem proof of an idle friend or of negligence, unless this suspicion were cleared away by probable causes—which may God remove. It is not expedient to allege them at present, because they are as burdensome to me as they are evident to you and known to the world. Would that the gulf established between us might be dissolved and peace restored between kingdom and priesthood, so that, if an opportunity for travel opens, we may render each other the offices of charity which are in the Lord [Col. 0214D]. For I have not forgotten how, through your merits, I am bound to you as to a master and lord. And you, although as yet my merits toward you do not exist, ought to love me as a Christian and a friend. Yet I should not rashly say that he lacks grounds of desert whom ardent affection serves in loving, and whose will, ready for service, desires nothing more eagerly than that God may prepare an opportunity by which he may satisfy the wishes or needs of his friend. For God accepts a devout will as a work accomplished, and rewards each person according to the quality and quantity of his affection. I wait and hope from the Lord that means will be given also to my devotion, and that, through God’s agency, our storm will shortly pass into calm more easily and happily than is believed [Col. 0215A]. Yet let this be received as spoken from the certainty of faith rather than of knowledge, because we know God faithful in His promises, who then most gloriously supplies His help to those suffering for His sake when human help has wholly ceased. Meanwhile the Lord tests whether we love Him; even if He delays, He must be endured with equanimity, because, whatever seems to us otherwise, He will undoubtedly come and will not delay.
