Hence I confidently say that He will shortly help, since I know for certain that in human affairs nothing is but momentary, that the glory of the world vanishes like smoke, and that the end of the wicked is fire and worm. And indeed the remnant of the wicked shall perish, while the salvation of the righteous must undoubtedly be awaited from the Lord [Col. 0215B]. Though the wicked man be exalted above the cedars of Lebanon, if you pass on a little, you will plainly understand that, even when he seemed to flourish, he already was not, and his place was no more. Carnal prudence laughs at this; but God is not mocked. Meanwhile, according to Solomon, He prepares scourges for mockers and hard hammers for the backs and necks of despisers. Yet as regards human opinion, it is easier for you to see the condition in which we stand and what, by the decree of the courtiers, we ought to fear or hope. But we shall hope, for we are ready for every humiliation, provided conscience remains unharmed and we do not derogate from divine law or from honour, once lost, when it is better to die than to live. We reject no condition of peace, being certain [Col. 0215C] that it is better to fall into the hands of men than to abandon God’s law or incur the stain of disgrace. Yet we do not presume to swear observance of the Gospel, mindful of our weakness, so that it may be clear how rash it is to swear to rejected customs. But I wonder beyond measure that the Archdeacon of Canterbury, whether in person or through another, does not labour for peace, though he knows that God and Mammon cannot both be served. Farewell. My brother R. greets you and your household with you. We send greetings to the clerics of the chapel, who have neither been excommunicated by name nor through participation with others. Remember us in your prayers, as we remember you.

## LETTER CXCVI. TO MASTER RALPH OF BEAUMONT

(A.D. 1166.)

[Col. 0215D]

**John of Salisbury to Master Ralph of Beaumont.**
The title of true piety shines forth in no better way than when it mercifully aids those who are deprived of human consolation, and whom a world ungrateful toward God persecutes without cause. I therefore congratulate you on having attained this, rejoicing that, contrary to the expectation of many—indeed, of almost everyone—you practise works of piety, not, I say, by the aid of secular philosophy, but by the spark of the Holy Spirit, at once kindling and enlightening your mind toward true wisdom. And, as I learned from the report of the bearer of this letter, among the opponents of charity you have dared—as befits a true [Col. 0216A] Christian—to remember the brotherhood which is in the Lord.

But whence comes this in you, my Ralph, especially when those who seemed to be pillars of the Church tremble, and the giants who ought to bear the world consent more readily to be submerged by a flood of waters than to groan? The Lord has commanded His clouds not to rain upon those regions; yet you have not feared, in those same regions, to bring forth, under the dripping of divine grace, the fruits of mercy and the works of the Saviour. I had certainly believed you possessed the words of one philosophizing, but not the spirit; yet now I recall that you are in some measure a disciple of the great Aristippus, who bore every condition of fortune with equanimity and philosophized even amid trifles—pleasant to all and burdensome to none. When once asked what philosophy had conferred upon him, he is said to have replied: “That I might converse fearlessly with all men.”

Henceforth I judge that I may place more secure confidence in you, since you do not despair of Christ’s kingdom. In this hope I ask that, as you have begun, you remember to assist the bearer of this letter in his times of need, for the contemplation of God and His service; being assured that, if letters pleased him in our company as much as birds and courtly trifles please you in yours, I would most gladly furnish him with everything necessary. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCVII. TO MASTER GERARD PUCELLE. (A.D. 1166.)

To Master GERARD PUCELLE.

Although your affection has not enjoined it upon me, nevertheless, having found an opportunity, I could no more restrain my pen from writing than I can restrain the fervour of my spirit—especially toward friends and in the vindication of justice. And perhaps I would write more concerning the condition of our own Church, I mean that of England, were it not that I think our common father, the Lord of Canterbury, has written to you more fully on these matters.

Proceeding to other things, I give thanks above all to God, who, beyond and contrary to my deserts, has granted me consolation in every tribulation, has turned all the snares of my adversaries to His glory and to the advancement of my lowliness. For how highly ought I to value the exercise of letters, the transactions of virtue, and the experience of purpose among those who rightly philosophize, [Col. 0216D] who suffer innocently, and who suffer in the defence of faith and justice?

I also congratulate you on your lot, having heard that, among the enemies of the Church, by the Lord’s enabling, you have found favour: so that you both abound in temporal resources for the work to be done, and possess a certain authority arising from letters and virtues, such that among barbarians whatever your discernment dictates is held sacred. But what I esteem most highly is that you have hated the assembly of the wicked; and that, as I hear, you speak publicly against schismatics, in the power of the Holy Spirit and in complete freedom of conscience, for the faith, and write the truth. For indeed, “Where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom” [2 Cor. 3].

Nothing is more becoming to a philosopher than the profession of truth, the cultivation of justice, contempt for the world, and, when necessary, love of poverty. We read that philosophers freely despised and cast aside riches as hindrances to virtue. But that any one of them should have placed truth above deeds even among the pagans has hitherto been unheard of. For the whole force of pagan ethical precepts consists in this: that they restrain and subject to reason the passions of bodily affections, which they cannot wholly extinguish. But if this be divinely granted to anyone—for nature is powerless to achieve it—there is no doubt that he walks in the path of right philosophy unto life, so that he may see good days eternally; and insofar as each person advances in this, so far does he approach true philosophy.

Therefore, since I trust that you have the purpose of one rightly philosophizing, I ask, urge, and counsel you in every way to endeavour to recall those who stray from schism, that they may prefer Christ to man and not permit themselves, through fear of the emperor or the deception of the schismatic of Cologne, to be separated from Christ’s body. Perhaps indeed the Lord has sent you to these barbarians for the salvation of many. Nor do I think this matter should be approached with quarrels, but brought to completion by happy moderation—especially by a wise man, who remembers that the moderation of wisdom disposes all things gently from end to end.

Otherwise, I do not think that one ought to communicate even in the least degree with the obstinate, remembering him whose figure you bear, Zerubbabel—whose name is interpreted “prince” or “Master of Babylon”—who would not permit the enemies of Judah and Benjamin to contribute anything whatsoever, even toward rebuilding the house of the Lord with the children of the captivity. Thus much on these matters.

[Col. 0217C] For the rest, I renew my former request: please send me something from the relics of kings and virgins, together with your letters authenticating them. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER. (A.D. 1167.)

To the lord ALEXANDER, pope.

If we cry from exile to the father for whom we continually cry to the Lord, for whose faith and honour we have always cried out against the persecutors of the Church and, God granting, shall cry out while life remains our companion, your fatherhood ought not to wonder. The force of grief and the bitterness of an urgent and most distressing necessity wring out this cry because of the unforeseen change in circumstances.

We cry, therefore, to Peter’s successor, the Vicar of the Crucified One. Would that our cry might enter your ears, so that, at the calamity of the Church and the afflictions and groans of its children, a father’s heart might be stirred to compassion. Although our miseries, multiplied by recent injury, have exceeded number and grown beyond measure, yet, God is witness, we grieve more bitterly and groan more deeply over the diminishing of your glory and the darkening of the Roman Church’s reputation than over our own losses, wrongs, and oppressions.

It is right, Father, it is right to utter true words, especially before one who is a lover and patron of truth, and through whose ministry the Holy Spirit condemns every fabrication of falsehood. The prophet held excused the widow who complained too impatiently, because her soul was bitter at the recent death of her son. And what complaint can we make patiently amid so many deaths, prisons, chains, scourges, insults, terrors, and the distresses of hunger, thirst, nakedness, and manifold calamity? If pardon is due to righteous bitterness, whose complaint ought to be heard more patiently? With whose groans ought greater sympathy to be felt? Whose prayers ought the Roman pontiff to hear more kindly than those of the exiles of Canterbury, known to have been proscribed for defending the liberty of the Church and establishing the privileges of the apostolic see?

Would that, Father, your ears were open to the mouths of the king and nobles of France! Would that you heard how the enemies of the Church insult you, and how nearly everyone reviles you! And if what is proclaimed at the street-corners is true, I do not see how your majesty can plausibly be excused.

I pass over the fact that that notable oath-taker received from your hand, as though for a service well performed, a deanery and the care of many souls: a man of tested religious devotion and cheerful reputation, who had not learned the ecclesiastical rite even in a single month. But was he to be exempted from the jurisdiction of every bishop, so that—as his supporters boast—he might by apostolic authority rage against his subjects while no remedy of appeal was reserved to them? Was he to be exalted by such great privileges that, at his arrival, after summoning by your authority the bishops and clergy of England, he should order [Col. 0218C] that they obey neither the Archbishop of Canterbury nor a summons to appear before him; and that those lawfully excommunicated, while persisting in sacrilege, should be absolved without satisfaction or any guarantee?

I do not presume to set my mouth against heaven. I confess—and it is true—that all things are lawful to the Roman pontiff; but only those things which by divine law have been granted to ecclesiastical power. Let him be permitted to establish new laws and abolish old ones, provided that he cannot alter those which derive a perpetual cause from the word of God in the Gospel or the Law. I would venture to say that not even Peter himself could absolve one persisting in crime and in the will to sin; nor did he receive keys by which he might open the gate of the kingdom to the impenitent. Whence, then, was this man given such power?

It is further said that, by a new privilege, the king of England has been withdrawn from the jurisdiction of all bishops. If he has indeed obtained this, then behold: authority has been granted him to make the lawful equal to whatever he pleases. Yet I would not readily believe that all these things have been so easily obtained against God’s Church. But I can say confidently that, before these reports were spread among us, we had come into harbour after long shipwreck; and we have been cast back into the deep by those who returned in triumph from the apostolic see.

No one can in any way be persuaded that the legates said to be coming, to procure the wishes of the lord king, can restore our condition to the state in which it stood when this report shook every heart. Yet it is doubtful whether they wish to do so—if it be doubtful—since we have heard from many that one of them assented to the lord king to our ruin, or rather to the loss and dishonour of the Church, and worked, so far as he could, for our destruction. To send him, therefore, as our adversaries boast, is nothing other than to administer to us the cup of suffering and death. If he intends this, may God hedge the path of his approach and coming with thorns, so that they may fall headlong into the pit which they prepared for the innocent.

Those who glory against us, and still more against you, add to our troubles that you have prolonged our exile by a year in order that the king of England might meanwhile be joined in alliance with you. But remember Ben-hadad’s treaty, which became a scandal to the king of Israel and ruin to the people, because he refused to inflict upon the enemy of public religion the vengeance divinely ordained. Without doubt, if you had held firm a little while, this king too would already have been forced to surrender, to place himself in your hands, and the Church under him would enjoy its due liberty.

But who can be secure of a single year of life? Do you not know that all who hate the Church’s liberty, whether allied with the schismatic emperor or not, desire the end of your life—which may God extend through many years? It is clear, then, how dangerous this delay is: through it boldness grows increasingly insolent, and a sadder, harsher condition for the Church is maliciously awaited. Evils must not be done that goods may result; nor can that dispensation be salutary through which the audacity of sacrilegious men is prolonged.

I have exceeded measure and given too little thought to who speaks to whom; but I could by no means restrain the rush of my wounded mind, seeing that, on the occasion of this report, our adversaries—indeed yours—grow more cruel, while the generosity of our benefactors cools or is entirely extinguished, except in the king of France and a few others. They sympathize with us more deeply, yet, what grieves us most, complain about you. May it therefore please your compassion to offer some consolation to your people of Canterbury and to restore the glory of your name, by restraining the enemies of the Church and repaying those who have deceived you according to their deserts.

Know one thing for certain: if the king once suffers a rebuff in any petition whatever, the fruit, as far as he is concerned, of all your services will be nullified. Yet he must suffer a rebuff, since in his requests he knows no moderation.

## LETTER CXCIX. TO MASTER GERARD PUCELLE. (A.D. 1167.)

To Master GERARD PUCELLE.

Although I recently wrote to you what seemed proper to write at the time, I nevertheless think it characteristic of a friendship grown torpid that intercourse in words should cease between intimates, especially when an opportunity for communication presents itself from any occasion. For the well-known proverb says: “Lovers and slavish minds never lack complaints.” As greatly as silence in religious professions is commended as advancing the worship of justice, so greatly is it certainly shown to weaken and produce a defect in love.

The spur of charity therefore moved me, through the God-given opportunity offered by the bearer, to inquire by letter whether anything has recently changed in your situation for better or worse; and whether you have received any certain news about the emperor’s expedition and about your man of Cologne. May God convert them, if they are predestined; and, once they have produced fitting fruits of repentance and been established in the unity of the Church, may He grant them pardon, cleanse them, introduce them, and bring them to life. Otherwise, may the Most High—the merciful and compassionate Lord—break the rod of His wrath, which strikes peoples in indignation and chastises the Church with cruel correction.

I cannot write anything new about my own condition, because nothing concerning me has changed. But I who was yours when you departed will, by God’s enabling, be yours wherever I may be and wherever you reside. Nor do I doubt that, if circumstances require it, your diligent care intends to be serviceable to me in my needs.

We can be more mutually helpful if we ourselves take greater care to serve philosophy, to whose profession we have long devoted effort: that is, if we are executors of its commands rather than discussers of empty words. For the truth of philosophy seeks, attends to, and attains realities—not words. You have long known that knowledge concerned only with discourse has never pleased me. For not hearers of the word, nor heralds, are just before the Lord, but doers; and the surest proof of true philosophy is when someone blunts the impulses of the flesh by the barrier of virtue and repels every assault of fortune.

We are, my friend, in the Lord’s furnace; let us philosophize there through patience, with Him as author. For a man’s teaching is known through patience. Further, if you please, communicate to me some news of what you find in the plundered libraries. If nothing else occurs that our countrymen lack, at least you have there the visions and oracles of that blessed and most celebrated Hildegard, whom I esteem and revere especially because Pope Eugenius embraced her with a special affection of charity and personal intimacy. Examine carefully also, and write back, whether anything has been revealed to her concerning the end of this schism. For in the days of blessed Eugenius she foretold that he would have peace and favour in the city only in his last days.

I pray you most earnestly to protect the interests of Saint Remigius among you as you would protect my own soul.

## LETTER CC. TO WALTER, BISHOP OF ALBANO. (A.D. 1167.)

The same to GALTER, Bishop of Albano.

What gives me great confidence to venture freely with you is that he whose memory is blessed—our most holy father Adrian, father to us both—who planted you as a most steadfast pillar, as we hope, in the holy Roman Church, loved me with a special grace of charity beyond other countrymen, and regarded the reverses of my fortune as to be counted among the events of his own lot. This affection of his toward me became known in the meantime to us mutually and to a few others. But unless fate had prematurely snatched him away from our midst—as the Christian world will now read—it would already have become known throughout the world.

Therefore I judge that I may have safer and greater confidence in your affection in Christ, believing that, as that most blessed man chose you beforehand as successor to his office, so—indeed even more—he sought to have you as heir of his charity. With that confidence with which I used to address him, I address you also; for as I had devoted my service to him with full and sincere affection, so too I am ready to serve your honour and glory with all that is in my power.

But I do not see how either your honour or that of the Roman Church can endure, nor the unity of Christ’s body be preserved, if you show favouritism toward persons and gifts; if, with you as judges, the innocent perish and—as Gaul recently saw and lamented—the unrepentant criminal is absolved; if tyranny is allowed to plunder and trample God’s Church; if powerful and open iniquity openly triumphs over justice in your consistory; if, with your consent or connivance, clerics are given up as victims like sheep for slaughter; if usurped abuses, through your silence and inaction, gain the force of laws to be maintained.

For this is why the wretched people of Canterbury are exiled and proscribed: because they dare to speak for the Church’s liberty; because they assert the privilege of the apostolic see; because they proclaim that the canonical ordinances of the holy Fathers must be preferred to the traditions of the ungodly. Review, if you please, the little book of detestable abominations, and you will plainly see that our adversaries—indeed yours and those of the whole Church of God—have turned their backs upon the sanctuary of the Lord, and strive not merely to profane the law, but to overthrow it.

If you judge that they should be forgiven because they are powerful while we are weak, because they are wealthy while we are poor; if you measure dangerous times and dread evil days, so as to suppose that justice should be dispensed with because of wickedness: do you believe that by this path you can please God, so that He may grant better times, enlarge and strengthen you, and diminish and weaken your adversaries? Is this the Lord’s way? Where is the Law? Where are the prophets? Where is Christ’s Gospel? Where are the decrees and examples of the saints? The Law is certainly eternal and cannot be dissolved: for “with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged”; and “by the things through which one sins, by those things one shall be punished.”

But perhaps lowly men seem unworthy that such great rulers should be troubled on their account, whereas the rigour of justice ought to be exercised for others of equal power. Yet this is not the distinction made by the apostles, but that of the subtle philosopher Thrasymachus, who defined justice as consisting in what most benefits the person with the greatest power. By contrast, sound philosophers defined it as the virtue that most benefits the person with the least power; for it rescues the poor from the powerful and assigns rewards according to merits, not persons.

If the king is deemed innocent because crimes are committed by the ministry of others, though by his authority, then David too may not be charged with Uriah’s blood, because Uriah was killed not by David himself but by the sword of the sons of Ammon. Likewise Ahab and Jezebel will not pay for the blood of innocent Naboth because, we read, he was killed by judicial fraud; but blood is required from both these kings only when it is that of poor and innocent persons, and battles undertaken under the authority of laws are not imputed to them.

Is it not debated in your consistories, as handed down by rule, that ratification is equivalent to command? And do we not make all things our own to which we lend our authority? From your own law, therefore, I infer that if you lend your authority, if by failing to enforce justice you ratify what is dared against the Church, you incur before God and men the guilt of this whole wickedness.

I have thought these matters should be communicated to you more confidentially as to a father and lord, that you may not consent to iniquity, but may free your soul before God and men. Moreover, since the Church of Rheims is said to be going to the curia, I pray that through the lord pope and others you may obtain from the archbishop and canons the deanery for Master Ralph. Discussion of his election has already taken place; and I do not believe that there is among them anyone more learned, more honourable in conduct, or more generous toward Christ’s poor. Farewell.

## LETTER CCI. TO CARDINAL ALBERT. (A.D. 1167.)

[Col. 0222C]

The same to Cardinal ALBERT.

A friend of truth gladly hears truth, and the salvation of one to whom the enticement of deceitful flattery is more pleasing than the wholesome harshness of truth is to be despaired of. Therefore I write more boldly to you, whom I do not doubt to be a lover of truth, thinking that you will not dislike what you know will benefit God’s Church. For I know that it is your desire, if granted from heaven, to follow the footsteps of him who laid down his life for her deliverance.

The Church is crushed under the power of the king of England and oppressed by such slavery that even to have mentioned liberty seems to be a crime of lèse-majesté. Moreover, the pontiffs and Pharisees of our own time gathered, at the arrival of that notable oath-taker John, in council; and there they devised how to destroy the Christ of the Lord, absolve unrepentant excommunicates, nullify the ordinances of divine law and the canons, and commit and protect the crime of disobedience without incurring blame.

The Archbishop of Canterbury and his fellow-exiles feel this, having been proscribed from all their goods because they dare to speak for the liberty of the Church. Some consolation had been hoped for from the arrival of the cardinals; but behold, the horns of the tyrants grow still more cruel because they see that he who has done and is doing all these things is stroked, not bitten. Yet the Church deservedly places confidence in the other legate, who is believed to be guided by the Spirit of God. And would that the other might henceforth prefer truth to the king’s power and favour, which he has sought.

If he does so, he will demand from no bishop either confirmation, toleration, or connivance regarding the king’s customs—customs openly contrary to God’s law, destructive of the privilege of the apostolic see, and transferring to the will of the prince every right and authority concerning what must be done in God’s Church. If the pastoral office may be exercised only at the prince’s nod, crimes will certainly not be punished, the savagery of tyrants will not be rebuked, and the Church will not in fact long endure. Therefore, whoever advises priests to be silent and to connive at the usurpation of such great abuses, I do not doubt is a heretic and a forerunner of Antichrist—unless he is personally Antichrist himself.

“Cry aloud,” says the Spirit through the prophet; “do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes” [Isa. 58]. And the Apostle, in whom Christ speaks, says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” [1 Tim. 4]; and, ready to punish every disobedience, he declares an anathema even upon an angel from heaven if that angel should rise against Christ and teach contrary to the truth of the Gospel. Yet a petty man dares to advise and counsel a priest to be silent and overlook Christ’s injury, doing evil that good may result! Is not the blood of a perishing wicked man required from the hand of the priest who keeps silence, so that he too dies for his silence?

Moses is described as having raised, not lowered, his hands, so that Amalek might be overthrown. The ark of God is not recorded as having been captured except when the priest, through his father’s perverse gentleness, chose merely to rebuke his sons rather than use the severity and authority of a pontiff. Ahab too, though reprobate, possessed more zeal for God’s law than some priests of our age. Having exposed gold, silver, varied furnishings, children, and wives to the king of Syria as the price of peace, he nevertheless refused the search of houses, in order to preserve the books of divine law which the enemy king above all desired to remove. Therefore zeal for the law, God being its author, brought Ahab consolation and victory. Peter found the waters firm beneath his feet while walking upon the foundation of faith; but he began to sink when he feared the blast of the rising wind.

But why turn to the examples of the Fathers? Is it not to be believed that the lord pope—may the Lord make his life most excellent and long for the consolation of the poor—by the zeal for justice which he has always possessed, deserved that Frederick, enemy of the faith, should be crushed before him and that God’s wrath should destroy Frederick’s camp? He had already seemed to triumph over the city, the world, and the universal Church. Yet in this, as I firmly believe, you were aided more by the prayers of Christ’s poor than by your counsels or the strength of the Romans.

I would also boldly say that, by His miracle and apart from human counsel, He rescued you from the lion’s jaws, so that henceforth you may always have such confidence in God—the founder and guardian of the Church, and likewise your deliverer—that neither the threats of opponents nor the deceits of flatterers draw you from the straight path, nor lead you to believe that one may dispense with the law against a king. For He who cast Frederick down before you will surely subject other tyrants to you, if you persist in His commands, or overthrow them entirely.

May your holiness, before whom there is no respect of persons, therefore restrain that lord who tramples the English Church by pressing words of truth and power upon the lord pope and your brethren. For if the Roman Church wills it and does not distrust the Lord, she will easily subdue him—but not, indeed, through the ministry of these legates, unless they take another course. For that king puts great confidence in one of them, whom he requested by name.

Many wise and religious persons do not think it safe, in such a place and crisis, for the Church’s cause to be tried under a judge who, at Pavia, present among relatives, friends, and acquaintances, and at least silent—for others suspect otherwise—heard and saw so great a prejudice inflicted upon the Roman Church, of which he is a member, and the cause of the faith publicly condemned. Nor is it believed that he has now become more sincere in faith, more fervent in charity, or more constant in virtue, clothed with new strength from on high, so that he cannot be bent by gifts, fear, or the favour of the man who has always used him as patron in this cause.

Indeed, the Church would already have prevailed unless that oath-taking dean had succeeded through his help and counsel. Would that there had never been that ring, which, as a sign of the Church’s confusion and his own triumph, he continually displays before all who see it. Would that the lord pope had never made another’s sin his own; and that he had not himself, though supreme in authority over all, installed the intruder whom he had justly deposed for God’s glory; nor made guardian of souls one who has been a persecutor of the Church and still savours nothing but the flesh.

## LETTER CCII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1167.)

To the lord JOHN, Bishop of Poitiers, J. S.

The diligence of your generosity earns, not merely through frequent but through continual and enduring benefits, that I should be bound to you in thanksgiving not frequently, but perpetually. I am bound indeed, and shall remain bound forever. And the more of sincere affection—the only thing I can presently render—I repay, the more fully and closely, I do not doubt, I become obligated.

For in the contract of charity it unquestionably holds, and holds especially, that what has been received is always returned, and that unless returned it is in no way possessed. Yet how small a thing is it that I profess my entire self—that is, a man small in name, lesser in resources, least in merit—to be owed to you. For this entire self is little in proportion to your deserts.

But when, in accounting with me for your bestowed benefit, displayed kindness, and lavish generosity, you have contracted a bond through religious affection, you have bound to yourself also Him whole and entire who will repay into your bosom, a hundredfold, a good measure pressed down and running over. Him whole and entire, I say; and I confidently say whole and entire, for He yields no share to another. Though He grants special uses of grace to individual elect persons, His gift of Himself remains whole—neither divided nor distributed in portions—because He is wholly present to each, or wholly slips away. He certainly owes Himself wholly for me and will without doubt render Himself wholly, since He is faithful in His promise and most generous in recompense.

You have followed and continue to follow His faithfulness, remembering that He is bound by command and promise, particularly because He has given workers of mercy the public safeguard of the Gospel, which He deigned to confirm with the mark of His cross and distinguish with His own blood. This therefore shall be the abundant recompense of your compassion: this, the divine reward for your shown kindness, and the eternal return for temporal expenditure.

And certainly, as is just, I value highly material assistance; but I value still more the consolations of right counsel, which I receive from you without cease, and the aids to true life—memorials, I would call them, and instruments of wisdom.

I have, therefore, a twofold reason for often writing to you: first, to satisfy my concern by investigating your condition, which I fear may be endangered; secondly, to be instructed by your prudence how I ought to fortify myself against fortune’s various changes. Please therefore deign to write back concerning how you have proceeded with the lord king in the matter of peace; what has been done at the court of Poitiers, where it is credible that “foxes have found holes and birds of heaven nests,” while the little one whose birth was celebrated almost lacked a place to lay his head.

For Ralph de Faia’s spirit is thought to have prevailed there, so that both prophets and heralds of the palace were made drunk by his deceits and rashness. Indeed, it is an old proverb, one which the Emperor Vespasian patiently endured as said of himself: “A fox can change its coat, but not its disposition.” Those who have written on the natures of animals also report that this species is never tamed at any time. And Offellus says:

> He who ploughs furrows for a fox must needs vary them.

But I trust that grace has preserved you, if not unshaken, at least unharmed. “For the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” [Prov. 1]. I also pray that, having weighed what the envoys of the king of England are said to have obtained from the apostolic see, you write back how the Lord of Canterbury and I ought to conduct ourselves both toward the Canterbury Church and toward the king or the legates.

For, if rumours and the boasts of adversaries are to be believed, the king feared or was ashamed to ask for more than Rome was willing to allow. Yet I hope that the lord pope has reserved some consolation for our side—indeed, for his own and that of God’s Church. Otherwise, why does he occupy the earth? But far be it from us to believe so unfavourable a thing concerning him as our adversaries perversely boast.

But if the legates come with such authority that there can be no appeal from them, what do you advise? For the Pavia man has hitherto kept before his eyes in this cause the king’s wealth, not fear of God or the Church’s honour. “For where his love is, there is his eye.” The other man, however, is of good reputation, though Roman and a cardinal. If we avoid their tribunal, it is to be feared that the reputation of our cause will suffer with the king and the Gallican Church. If we accept them, though they are suspect, we must fear that they will overthrow our justice. They will make a dispensation concerning us, so as to compensate the Church’s loss out of their own purses. For whatever peace they may seem to have made, they will attribute it to their own titles and triumphs.

What is owed us above all is restoration of what has been taken away, of our sees, and the re-establishment of security. But perhaps they will order us to be satisfied with guarantees alone until the whole lawsuit is decided—a condition that no one except a madman would accept in entering litigation. I have judged it necessary to repeat this at the end so that it may adhere more faithfully to your memory.

## LETTER CCIII. TO MASTER SILVESTER, TREASURER OF LISIEUX. (A.D. 1167.)

[Col. 0226B]

To Master SILVESTER, Treasurer of Lisieux, JOHN OF SALISBURY.

Having heard, dearest friend, of your peace, I rejoiced for a friend as was fitting; but more pleasing to me than every advantage is steadfastness in honour, and the joyful possession of a reputation purer even to the envy of former friends. You were the first, and are still the only one, to provide a pattern of perseverance for those labouring with the Church in the Christian struggle. By God’s grace, the example of good fortune that has gone before in you will henceforth benefit the rest by raising hope, defending liberty, and advancing virtue.

Yet I consider it more fortunate that, through love of possessions and the ease and rashness of swearing, you did not make void your first faith, than that you have attained the advantages of temporal goods in accordance with your friends’ wishes and your own deserts. I say, indeed, in accordance with your deserts, though it is certain beyond all certainty that far greater, more splendid, and more illustrious things are owed to your merits. These will without doubt be rendered by Him who has deceived none of His creditors from the beginning, and who pours into the bosoms of those who deserve it a measure pressed down and running over.

It is thus plain in you that God “resists those who boast vainly, but gives grace to the humble” [1 Pet. 5]; and, according to the Apostle, “he who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing always deceives himself, and sometimes others also” [Gal. 6].

Because, therefore, by God’s favor you have escaped shipwreck, remember to bring such aid as you can to those still sailing on the deep, and shipwrecked with Peter, and to assist the struggle of Christ—now by the support of your prayers, now by the consolation of your letters. For these are the things—so far as concerns myself—which we most need. Through God’s mercy I indeed abound in temporal resources, so that I seem rather to bear the appearance of one flourishing in his native land than of an exile and outlaw. The most Christian king of the French displays royal magnificence toward the lord of Canterbury at Sens, in the church of Blessed Columba; and in all things reveres and honors him as it befits Christ’s anointed to be honored by a Christian king. To this most faithful prince, as he himself declares, the days seem few and the expenses small in comparison with the greatness of the love which he expends upon the service of Christ’s priest and apostolic man. Moreover, God repays his faith—of which he modestly acknowledges himself unworthy—with a fitting recompense: He, whose gift it is that, dwelling among enemies without bloodshed or disturbance, he both prospers in all things and, what he counts greatest, is loved and honored by his subjects. Thus Obed-edom, when he received the ark of the Lord, experienced the fruit of divine blessing in the fruitfulness of his maidservants and the multiplication of his flocks and all his possessions. And Huldah, through receiving the same ark, when the pious Ahaz had cast it out from the temple of the Lord, obtained in the silence of pontiffs and priests the grace of prophecy. So the most Christian king, having received the Roman Church into his kingdom, received from his wife, by the Lord’s agency, a son of faith and heir to the kingdom—a son whom, had he been granted the choice of all things desirable, he would have asked for. Now, however, because of the humanity shown to the English Church, he confidently awaits a new grace, which the Lord will grant according to His will.

The lord pope has lately consoled the archbishop of Canterbury by word and letter; and would that it became known to all by what agreements and guarantees that notable oath-taker obtained the things of which the adversaries of the Church boast. Yet if the agreements are fulfilled, ample provision has been made for us through restoration of what was taken away, peace, and security. For the present these matters are kept silent through the necessity of obedience; but there is hope that everything will shortly be disclosed, because, as we have learned for certain, the coming of the legates which had been expected has been delayed—or entirely prevented—once the oath-taker’s fraud was discovered. Write back, insofar as it may be lawful, whatever you judge advantageous for the Church and for us in Christ’s struggle; and know that, wherever I may be, I am most devoted to you.

## LETTER CCIV. TO MILO, BISHOP OF THE MORINI. (A.D. 1167)

To Lord MILO, bishop of the Morini.

The title of your sincerity shines more brightly in charity, since it is established more certainly by the report of the bearer of this letter: amid the storms of chance events and the varied tempests of affairs, by which the urgency of your office is incessantly shaken and sharply buffeted, yet without the overthrow of virtue, you are able to bear concern for your friends and make their burdens your own through the exercise of brotherly love. For thus the Apostle burns with those who are scandalized, shares the weakness of weak brethren, and through compassion becomes all things to all in Christ, while, after the pattern of a purer ethical and more perfect philosophy, he counts nothing human foreign to himself.

There is laid up for you, Father, this crown of mercy, which the merciful and compassionate Lord will render to you on that day. Meanwhile He consoles us, His exiles and outcasts, through the ministry of His saints, who share our necessities for His sake, in all our tribulation. For the most Christian king of the French, receiving our father the archbishop of Canterbury into the arms of charity, displays toward him royal magnificence in the church of Blessed Columba at Sens, and treats him in every respect as Christ’s anointed ought to be treated by a Christian king. I cannot otherwise express the affection which the most Christian prince shows toward a shipwrecked priest.

We, the priest’s household, though proscribed in our possessions, are enrolled among the faithful who, by suffering for justice, have honored their ministry; scattered as exiles throughout the kingdom of the French. Yet everywhere He is present with us who feeds the birds of heaven and clothes the lilies of the fields. We hope, however, that this same Father of ours and Lord of all will shortly turn our storm into a gentle breeze, although the enemies of the Church boast that a greater shipwreck threatens us.

For they lie in saying that the Roman Church has turned against us into a crooked bow, and that the lord pope has assented to all the king of England’s requests. They infer this because our excommunicated persons were absolved at the arrival of John of Oxford, who, as though he had successfully transacted the affair at the emperor’s court, where the schism was confirmed, carried back from the lord pope’s hand the deanery of the church of Salisbury. But anyone who recalls more carefully what was done at Rome will plainly see that the Roman pontiff, even though outmaneuvered, most faithfully advanced the Church’s cause and ours.

For the said John was at last absolved, after giving the customary oath, as he publicly swore likewise that he had done nothing in the aforesaid assembly of schismatics against the faith of the Church or the honor and advantage of the lord pope—and would that he had not sworn falsely! Afterwards he presented letters of recommendation and petition on the king’s behalf, in which it was inserted that he should be believed in all things just as the king himself. Then, fortified by such great authority, he submitted to the lord pope’s judgment the dispute between the king and archbishop concerning the evil customs, so that they might be confirmed or annulled at his will and peace restored in every respect to the archbishop in accordance with the form of his mandate. Confirming this also by oath, he obtained the pope’s promise to send legates for this purpose. Their journey, they say, has been suspended after the oath-taker’s fraud was discovered.

## LETTER CCV. TO WILLIAM, SUBPRIOR OF CHRIST CHURCH, CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1167)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to WILLIAM, subprior of Christ Church, Canterbury.

[Col. 0228D] You recently spoke to me in parables, saying that your riches—or rather, those of the Church—had newly been made public, and you earnestly begged me not to betray them, lest they be carried away into Babylon. But if they have been made public, I wonder why they have not reached the father who devotes himself for the safety and liberty of his mother’s children, and who has now for three years been exposed to hardships, before the bestowal of such liberality. If they have been made public, we too ought to have belonged to the people of those who receive a share. If you acknowledge him as father, where is your love for him? If you have received him as lord, where is the reverent fear that is due? If you declare yourselves brothers and friends of those in exile, why do the duties of humanity and the consolations of due charity fail?

But perhaps, in order to render your father a more welcome service, you wait until he is in still greater need. Meanwhile, delighting the eyes of an unskilled multitude with empty paintings, you suppose that what is more foolishly squandered on shows and on the seductive curiosities of the eyes will be expended for public uses. Surely:

> This is not the time that such spectacles demand for themselves.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.37

And that satirical passage seems capable of being aptly turned against you—I know to whom and of whom I speak:

> Unhappy Numitor has nothing to send to a friend,  
> Nothing to give Quintilla; yet he did not lack  
> Wherewith to buy a lion to be fed on much flesh.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VII.75

Nor do I say this because the remark applies to all, but to those whom you unquestionably know: they could have avoided transgression, yet transgressed; they could have done good, yet did not. The Searcher of hearts knows that I have sorrow and continual pain in my heart because, while we sleep amid peril of life, strangers alone bring help to our shipwreck.

Yet, to add to my grief, it is said that in so great a necessity you rendered the father one service: you maintained diligent guard lest by any chance he escape, because, having slipped from the executioners’ hands, he had fled to the protection of our patrons. But you plead fear. Certainly God is not mocked. Yet you fear one to whom the authority to punish sins in bodies has been entrusted for a moment; why do you not fear Him who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna? Awake, therefore, and remember Obadiah, Ahab’s steward, who fed a hundred prophets hidden in caves during Jezebel’s persecution. Whatever you do on either side, beyond doubt the Most High will pour back into your laps a good and overflowing measure.

Nor will your colleague of Bath hinder this—would that he be submerged among the companies he deserves and has earned, cast into the *rutefolium* [uncertain term], of which Petronius speaks as a punishment for offenders, or buried in the salt-pit of the Aedui. To return to your parable: know that the names of the books are buried with me. I did receive the seal in your name, but your Britonellus took it from me; I shall suspect this was done by your agreement unless you restore what was taken.

## LETTER CCVI. TO O. OF FAVERSHAM. (A.D. 1167)

O. of Faversham to me.

It belongs to one out of his mind, not to one who loves, to care only for himself and his own affairs, and to regard the concerns of others as alien. As the comic poet testifies, charity regards nothing human as foreign to itself; through rejoicing it attends those who rightly rejoice, and through compassion it groans with those in sorrow. Yet it dispenses its affections in a most ordered manner, so that all may be in the Lord; and it exercises the offices of humanity toward individuals, more or less, according to the law of nature and the grace that gives them form.

Though it extends the benefits of a broader grace to all, it is especially enlarged toward the household of faith. In its judgment, anyone who does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household—whom nature commends to his affection and fellowship in faith commends to his piety—has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. I have no doubt whatever that you hold this view; therefore I confidently intercede for your nephew Adam, who, in the manner of scholars, lives, endures, and rules in the pursuit of letters. I am sure that, just as you will not ungratefully forget the honor of his father’s office and merits toward you, so you will not delay to provide him with timely and due assistance in his needs.

But if, for the reasons set out above—which you surely weigh prudently—my prayers can carry any weight, I rise wholly to prayer and test their efficacy, casting myself at your knees in complete devotion. If you inquire about me, I gratefully embrace my condition as the gift of divine grace, often reflecting how suspect uninterrupted worldly prosperity has appeared to all who think rightly, and how certain an indication of love it is that the faults of erring children are purged through scourges.

## LETTER CCVII. TO ROBERT OF FAVERSHAM, ARCHDEACON. (A.D. 1167)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to ROBERT of Faversham, archdeacon.

He is inhuman and incurs the stain and reproach of extreme impiety who is not afflicted by a father’s affliction, especially where proofs of a father’s kindness toward his son shine clearer than light. For, according to the Lord’s judgment, the whole people of the Canaanites were condemned to perpetual servitude because their father Ham, from whom they derived both lineage and name, acted inhumanely toward his parent. From the wrongdoing of that impious progenitor the entire posterity incurred a penalty; and in receiving the hateful yoke of slavery it supplied to all a salutary example of impiety to be avoided.

Indeed, I should consider myself worse than any Canaanite if I did not suffer with the Father in his hardship, if his scourges did not wound my soul more deeply than the pain of my own wounds. My conscience bears witness to this; God, the Searcher and Judge of conscience, bears witness—He who perhaps sooner than is believed will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts. Even now we stand before His tribunal and await Him as judge in our cause; in His sight it would be foolish and rash, by lying, to lose the reward of all our labor and life, insofar as we suffer anything beneficially or do anything rightly.

I have labored, therefore—as He knows—with the lord of Canterbury, using now soothing words, now harsher ones, and every kind of speech; but my labor, to my sorrow, has come to nothing. What obstacles he opposes to our prayers and persuasions would be lengthy, and almost superfluous, to recount, since Master Gilbert, whose fidelity to you I do not doubt, has heard everything most fully from his own mouth.

Yet I call God to witness upon my soul that, to speak my mind, the archbishop sincerely loves the bishop and desires provision for his welfare and security. But he insists that one who has given others an example of disobedience and unlawful presumption should himself furnish others an example of wholesome and necessary obedience. If he permits himself to be persuaded by the authority of Scripture, the counsel of friends, and the command of the lord pope, he will find the archbishop—whom perhaps he now fears more than is right—a most merciful Father and far more ready to forgive than to avenge.

You can and ought to remember what the Apostolic See has lately written on this subject to the lord bishop of Coutances; for it has either reached, or ought to have reached, your knowledge. You also know what consolation your dean has brought me; or, if you do not know, would that all he did at Rome, both in this cause and in others, became known not only to you but to the whole world. If we were yet permitted to publish these things, it would readily become known what was done: concerning the customs over which the kingdom and priesthood contend; concerning the archbishop’s peace and the Church’s liberty; concerning complete restoration and security for all the exiles; and also what he swore, and by what guarantee he confirmed the agreements.

For the present we are silent because the command requires it, while the fulfillment of the promises is hoped for and awaited. But nothing is covered that shall not be revealed—and this, by God’s agency, shortly. For near is the day of destruction for those who will be found in falsehood, and the times of recompense and vengeance hasten to be at hand.

But if my counsel is meanwhile sought, behold: before God, whom I invoke as witness to this word at the final judgment, I answer with complete freedom of spirit, and with the faith promised and owed to him as a father, what I judge ought to be done in every grave uncertainty. Namely, first of all we should seek and follow what divine law has prescribed on the matter. If it states nothing definite, recourse should be had to the canons and examples of the saints. If there too nothing definite occurs, finally let the minds and counsels of the wise be examined in the fear of the Lord; and let those, whether many or few, be preferred to the rest who set God’s honor before every advantage.

For no one proceeds safely who neglects the law of God, which is the surest pattern of life for all; and one who refuses to imitate the footsteps of the Fathers cannot enter into the fellowship of the kingdom which they enjoy. Joshua also and the elders of Israel incurred blame in the covenant with the Gibeonites because, as Scripture testifies, having taken their provisions, they did not ask the mouth of the Lord. But what is signified by “mouth” except the word of the Lord, which He has spoken once, so that it need not be repeated? The meaning of this word in the law is clear and plain: obedience is better than sacrifices; rebellion is the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry.

Christ proclaimed this by command and example, becoming obedient unto death and teaching the limits to which the virtue of obedience should extend. Obedience must be rendered not only to the loss of temporal things and bodily torments, but unto death itself; and if one falters in a certain necessity, the virtue of obedience does not attain the palm. Wiser friends may perhaps give better counsel, but, God being witness, I know none more fitting at present. For by the grace of my Lord Jesus Christ I am persuaded, and I desire all my friends to be persuaded, that:

> I believe it the greatest wickedness to prefer life to honor,  
> And, for the sake of living, to lose the reasons for living.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VIII.83

## LETTER CCVIII. TO RICHARD DE BOHUN, BISHOP OF COUTANCES. (A.D. 1167)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to RICHARD de Bohun, bishop of Coutances.

My spirit is troubled, as is wholly right, over the affliction of my lord, the bishop of Salisbury; and the more gravely because it sees no easy end to this labor. The Searcher and Judge of all knows how diligently I have acted with the lord of Canterbury to induce him to release him. But success failed my labor for various reasons, which I judge superfluous to recount, because your faithful Master Gilbert heard most of them from the archbishop’s own mouth.

To pass over much, the archbishop is chiefly moved by the fact that the lord of Salisbury has given others an example of disobedience and still supports the bishop of London and others who seek his life to take it away. He adds that the bishop wrote to him defiantly and, under the pretext of a frivolous appeal, tried to disguise the crime of disobedience. Nor afterwards did he repent of his presumption and renounce the appeal; instead, with an inconsistency of word and deed, concealing the wrong of the appeal by which he protects himself, he places an obstacle before the one correcting him, yet asks mercy with a feigned reverence of humility.

Nothing else can therefore be obtained from him except this: that he receive with fatherly kindness a bishop who withdraws from the appeal, publicly acknowledges his fault, and is obedient henceforth; and thereafter treat him in all things as a most beloved son. As for the archbishop’s gentleness, if the bishop is persuaded of this—which you know to be necessary—I have no doubt at all.

You know what the lord pope has lately written to you about this, and what remedy the dean has brought from the Apostolic See for this cause. If his promises take effect, however, and the terms confirmed by oath are fulfilled in good faith, the archbishop and his people will shortly be reconciled, and peace between kingdom and priesthood will be restored with honor to the Church. Meanwhile, as may have become known to you, the necessity of a command binds us to silence regarding what was done at Rome. But when the good faith or bad faith of the agreements has been established, it will be lawful to disclose everything.

Since the lord of Salisbury and Reginald the archdeacon urge me in this matter, asking that I write back to them or to you what I discover, I earnestly ask that you arrange for the said archdeacon to receive the letter I send him, and that, by God’s agency, you provide a fortunate conclusion to the case.

## LETTER CCIX. TO MASTER HUMFRID OF BONI. (A.D. 1167)

To Master HUMFRID of Boni.

Friend, I have no cause to complain about the character of my condition, because God’s mercy makes all human machinations work together for my good. For almost everything succeeds temporally, and there is hope that this very thing which appears to be affliction, as it awakens the understanding, will likewise produce the advancement of true salvation.

Yet it troubles me somewhat that certain friends are more bitterly concerned about my condition and, in the manner of carnal men, are often—indeed almost always—shaken by vain terror, acting rashly rather than wisely and as truly loving friends should. They fear “graver dangers than the real ones”; giving little heed to what truly helps or harms, they tremble where there is no fear. For they do not carefully weigh the loss of conscience or reputation; and so long as the shadow of virtue remains in human opinion and they avoid foolishly babbling detractors, they care little what each person deserves according to the test of sound reason. Many such people value appearing good more highly than being good.

Others lament the withdrawal of the temporal assistance that the Lord had supplied them through me. But reason, consulted at the request of both sorts, replies that neither the management of household goods nor a father’s burial may recall one who has begun to follow Christ in the Church’s struggle. With God as author, it is my settled purpose to follow, insofar as He grants it, the rule of honor, and not to sell the soul’s salvation in the traffic of the world for the price of any temporal good whatsoever.

May He Himself teach the way, lead me along the path of virtue, and bring me into the fellowship of those who suffer for justice. Yet I desire, if it can be done without compromising honor, to be reconciled and to minister, in the churches to which I am attached, for God’s honor and my friends’ consolation. Therefore I beseech your affection not to consider it burdensome to ascertain through the bishop of Bayeux and your other friends what is expedient and fitting, and to write back to me as safely as may be, offering me your counsel. For counsel belongs to those things which, by the law of humanity, ought to be denied to no one: it does not profit when suppressed, does not increase by being held tightly, and is not diminished by being given out; rather, the more widely it is made public, the more brightly it shines.

## LETTER CCX. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF BAYEUX. (A.D. 1167)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to HENRY, bishop of Bayeux.

Father, I hear and rejoice that all things prosper with you according to your merits. While it was permitted, you honored the name and rank of deans; now, by the brilliance of your virtues, you adorn the office of bishop in a foreign land, to the envy of many. This is so much more wholesome for conscience and more glorious for reputation as the shepherd of the sheep—or one who strives to honor his ministry in the Church of God—is rarer amid so great a pomp, number, and merely nominal distinction of priests.

For, as God long ago complained through the prophet: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ and those who held the law did not know justice” (Jeremiah 2). Thus it is right that your eminence should be honored and loved even by those who, because our sins require it, seem now to hold the priesthood in contempt and strive to nullify the law of God, which cannot be annulled. Although the Egyptians detest shepherds of sheep, and the Samaritans of our time do not associate with those who publicly confess the word of God, Joseph nevertheless found favor in Egypt, Daniel shone among the Assyrians, and the distinction of his merits made Elijah illustrious even during Ahab’s reign.

It is therefore no wonder if virtue finds its place with a Christian prince and his officers, and if the man known to be filled with divine grace is loved by men. Thus the ointment descended from Christ, the head, onto the beard of the Church and thence flows down to the hem of the garment, so that, according to the decree of divine dispensation and the grace of merits, it may moisten each of the elect.

Would that we too, dearest lord, might receive something from this abundance of yours, and that the Church in its struggle might benefit from the favor you have found in the king’s sight. It is unnecessary to repeat what our condition is, since you know fully both our cause and the undeserved punishment. But it is worth both effort and prayer to obtain from you counsel wholesome for conscience and honorable for reputation. Though, by God’s favor, I have temporal resources not merely for necessity but for splendor, I am nevertheless ready, insofar as conscience may remain whole and reputation honorable, to earn the king’s favor according to your counsel. For I promise nothing against God; or, if I should ever attempt it, may His mercy thwart my efforts. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXI. TO RICHARD, ARCHDEACON OF COUTANCES. (A.D. 1167)

To Master RICHARD, archdeacon of the bishop of Coutances.

[Col. 0234D] The violence of public authority has outlawed me without cause, as the Most High knows and, I think, you know. Yet, for which I cannot sufficiently give thanks, God has so directed my ways and works that I have learned by experience that those who fear Him lack nothing; nor have I known any fellow exile whose condition ought to be merely tolerable rather than pleasant.

The Lord, however—and I say this not without fear—treats me more gently than the rest and consoles me with a richer abundance of temporal goods, perhaps judging me unworthy to suffer any adversity for His sake. For no sound-minded person doubts that an abundance of success ought to be viewed with suspicion, since the world, like deceitful men, flatters with continuous favor only those whom it betrays, as if it cried aloud to hostile powers lying in wait: “Whomever I have kissed and embraced as a friend for long, he belongs among the reprobate; torture him.”

Hence Anselm, that teacher renowned with the everlasting glory of eminent teachers, as I have received it from his own people, used to say that he regarded nothing more suspiciously than the fact that God had rebuked him with no adversity throughout his whole life. For where God shows Himself a father, He reproves and chastises every son. He knows our frailty, whether we stand or fall; and would that we always stand through His agency. He dispenses prosperity or adversity to each person with salutary moderation, according as He knows either to be advantageous to the elect.

From Him, therefore, I hope and await the outcome of this path, accepting, with His favor, whatever He gives. I shall write more and more certain things when they become known. Meanwhile I desire to be informed about your condition—may God make it excellent—and earnestly ask that this may be made known to me more faithfully through your returning letter. If you can discover some basis for my peace without loss to conscience and reputation, I shall receive it gladly; and, insofar as it is lawful and honorable, I will willingly comply even with my adversaries—may God grant them fruits of repentance worthy of life. Otherwise, it is not my intention, for the melons of the Egyptians and other such things, to incur even the slightest loss of honor. May the gracious Jesus, who has granted the desire for virtue, grant perseverance also; for without Him nothing is rightly begun or ended.

For the rest, I renew a request made long ago: please have the books of Aristotle that you possess copied for me, and also the notes on Mark; though at my own expense, I ask you on no account to economize in this matter. I also repeat my request that, wherever the works of Aristotle are more difficult, you have explanatory notes made, because I regard the translator with some suspicion: although, as I have often heard, he was otherwise eloquent, he was nevertheless insufficiently trained in grammar.

## LETTER CCXII. TO RALPH, PRIOR OF WORCESTER. (A.D. 1167)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to RALPH, prior of Worcester.

An abundance of waters cannot extinguish charity, and the affection of sincere love customarily reveals itself by clear signs. The long duration of my silence might therefore rightly seem blameworthy, were it not excused by the necessity of exile, the distance of places, the scarcity of travellers between them, the difficulty of communication, and the diligence of plotters—pernicious to themselves and hateful to God, but serviceable nevertheless to the Church.

I call the rage of persecutors serviceable indeed to those predestined for life, for whom all things work together for good. While the wicked man is proud, the poor man is set on fire; while malice rages more madly, those in the Lord’s furnace are more fully purified or tested. But now, because an opportunity divinely granted has been given me to send the desired greeting, I have gladly seized the occasion and earnestly ask that, through your office, the whole Church of Worcester may be greeted more diligently in my name. I pray that you may keep me in remembrance, and cause me to be remembered in its prayers, and commend the Church’s struggle to the Lord in earnest prayers.

For, as to temporal matters and bodily consolation—not merely for necessity but for delight—we exiles experience Christ’s promise to be entirely true: from the time we placed the protection of our cause in Him alone, nothing reasonably desirable for the present time has been lacking to us. And, for which we should be more grateful to the Most High, in this season we have received nothing from our household or old intimates; rather, our friends and neighbors have stood against us, making their arm flesh and darkness light.

To say nothing of others, a fourth year of my exile is now passing, and in the account of giving and receiving I have so far been indebted to no one that I could not repay all alike by assigning them a most impoverished debtor for payment. Yet I say this not to reproach the ingratitude of old friends, but to magnify God’s grace, which, contrary to and beyond my merits, has consoled both me and His little ones who are with me in all our tribulation. But that this consoling grace may continue favorable to us, I desire to be assisted by your prayers and those of the saints.

The archbishop of Canterbury, like another Jonah, has voluntarily undergone shipwreck out of charity so that the Church may be delivered. Under the Lord’s guidance, he has found among strangers the favor he had earned among his own people; and, having experienced the devotion of his sons, he serves the English Church at his own expense. Know for certain that through God’s mercy you will shortly and openly see what, I believe, your soul desires: namely, the persecutors of the Church either converted or crushed.

But I must pass over the other matters pertaining to this point, lest I become a transgressor of obedience by making public the agreements and guarantees through which those who persecute the Church claim that concessions, prejudicial to the lord of Canterbury and his people, have been obtained from the lord pope. This, however, I may say freely, and it is true: if the agreements are fulfilled, the cause of the archbishop of Canterbury and of the whole Church could not have been conducted more advantageously.

## LETTER CCXIII. TO MASTER SIMON LUPELLUS. (A.D. 1167)

JOHN OF SALISBURY to Master SIMON LUPELLUS.

It is the mark of a conscience lacking confidence in a friend to wrap requests, at a time of need, in indirect phrasing, and to discharge the office of a petitioner by artifice rather than trust. Therefore, dearest friend, relying on the confidence in your affection which I have conceived over many days, I proceed with still greater confidence: setting aside every covering of circumlocution, I earnestly ask that you advance the bearer of this letter with the lord of Worcester, and wherever you know it advantageous, as you would advance me myself. For whatever I learn has been shown to him out of regard for me, I shall accept as though it had been shown personally to me.

What my condition is, and that of the others engaged in the Church’s struggle, you will learn in some degree from his report, should you wish to hear it. I hope that you too desire to see the day of the Lord: that the Church may regain strength; that God’s law may be strengthened before the nations and the envious; and that the emblem of faith and public authority may so shine on the heads of kings that horns may no longer be given to the sinner.

This would easily come about, were the common report true: “Those who held the law did not know justice” (Jeremiah 2), and “from the priests and prophets of Israel pollution has gone out over all the earth.” Yet, by God’s agency, the Consoler of the faithful will shortly come, and for the elect’s sake will command the winds and sea, so that the momentary sorrow of the mourning Church may be turned into everlasting joy.

If it were lawful to set forth the obligations and guarantees by which the concessions said to have been granted by the Apostolic See to the king’s envoys, to the prejudice of the archbishop of Canterbury, were obtained, I would gladly do so. But without specifying each provision, let this be certain: it was inserted in the agreements that they contain the complete indemnity and absolute security of the aforesaid archbishop and his people, and that they advance the liberty of the whole Church.

Yet it is wondrous in everyone’s eyes, and worthy of every astonishment, that the bishops of the province have not met even once to treat of the Church’s peace and to approach the king even once—a king whose innocence they establish by the public testimony of their whole body, and whose patience they praise so highly that he counts it a sweet service whenever he is admonished to correct, should he perhaps have offended against the Lord. Indeed, either, with God’s favor, they will bring him back to the way, or sooner than is believed they will necessarily be beaten by the lord pope or by the king, whose anger they now fear more than is right, while they seem to neglect—indeed, to kill—his soul. You, being wise, I think know why I have written these things to you. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXIV. TO ADAM, ABBOT OF EVESHAM. (A.D. 1167)

To ADAM, abbot of Evesham.

Beyond the affection which we formed for one another from the beginning of our mutual acquaintance, a further friendship has been established between us by the right of our shared fellowship: so that each ought to receive the other’s fortune into the reckoning of both our lots as though it were his own. For the affection born of common studies has been fostered in exile by likeness of character, and by the exchange between us of a familiarity not so much frequent as constant and unbroken. We might therefore rightly complain of this long mutual silence, were not the distance of places, the rarity of travellers passing between us, and the difficulty—or rather impossibility—of meeting to excuse the reproach of undue silence. For, as the proverbial saying has it, speechless affection puts on the appearance of one who does not love.

Therefore I, as is right, have taken care to offer to my superior and lord such dutiful service of diligent reverence as I could and as I always owe; and to inquire more carefully and diligently into what is done concerning you, your church, and your people, so that I may rejoice at what is rightly done, and, if I discover anything—may it never be so!—troubling to you, may share your suffering in mutual affection. Let it therefore please your belovedness to write back concerning our condition; and, should my diligence be able to be of service to you in any matter, prescribe and command, assured that I shall obey your wishes to the limit of my ability.

Moreover, I pray and entreat you, in the faith and love of God, to love in the Lord my dearest N., your brother and the companion of our exile, and to honour him with the gift of your friendship. Henceforth treat him, for the sake of my prayers, in such a way that he may find them to carry some weight with you. If you care to hear of my condition, know that during this fourth year of my exile the Lord has so tempered matters to my weakness that, as time advances, more abundant success accompanies my affliction and fuller mercy consoles me. Food and clothing are available to my household in abundance; in exile I have an increasing supply of sweet and useful friends; and, as the fidelity of old intimates for the most part fades away, the affection of new ones is more firmly established. In the account of what is given and received, none of my fellow-countrymen binds me to himself; rather, through the ministry of strangers, He alone makes me entirely indebted to Himself—He who feeds the birds of the air and clothes lilies and springing flowers with incomparable beauty.

Let this not be understood as an accusation against friends who have grown cold, but so that the Father of the poor, who is in heaven, may be glorified [Col. 0238C], and who does not allow His elect to be tested beyond what they can bear. I therefore ask and more earnestly beg that you have my exile and the shipwreck of the suffering Church more diligently commended to the Lord by your prayers and those of the holy persons with you. The bearer of this letter can explain what concerns the Lord of Canterbury, where, by the Lord’s agency, affairs are proceeding more prosperously than you may believe; for I have instructed him to communicate everything to your fidelity.

## LETTER CCXV. TO R., ABBOT OF PERSHORE. (A.D. 1167)

To R., Abbot of Pershore.

[Col. 0238D] One who does not share even in a friend’s wish for salvation is far from charity; and one is convicted of not loving who, when an opportunity for conversation is offered, does not refresh his lover even with a word of greeting. For words are not usually lacking even to those who love with the tongue and only in pretence—who neither retain the gift of fidelity and the duty of charity in their affections nor put them into practice in deed and truth.

Mindful, therefore, of the friendship formed between us, I instructed the bearer of this letter, who is endeavouring to visit his native soil, to greet you in my name and diligently inquire concerning your condition—which may God make most excellent—so that, having heard through him the character of your circumstances, I may, as is right, sympathize with the pressures borne by a friend, which may the Father of mercies keep far from your house; or rejoice in your successes, which I desire to be multiplied [Col. 0239A] and made perpetual. You too may learn through him of my condition and that of my fellow exiles—if indeed this concern occupies any of my old friends—and may truly hear, with God as author, favourable news of the present, and hope with us for most favourable things in the near future.

For unless the agreements made with the lord pope concerning the liberty and restoration of the Church, and the peace and security of the Archbishop of Canterbury and his people—agreements confirmed by guarantees which it is not presently fitting to specify—are faithfully fulfilled, then, by God’s grace, those who hate Zion will very soon be confounded and ashamed: those who, along with the Scribes and Pharisees, strive by deceitful verbal cunning to justify their own malice. For from the words of the lord king’s envoys, who did not conceal themselves at the curia, it has been plainly discovered with what sincerity dealings are conducted with the Church of God; and that those who seemed to be pillars of the Church, corrupted by the melons and garlics of Egypt, prefer slavery and the Church’s toil in mud and brick to setting out on a journey of three days into true liberty, there to sacrifice to the Lord the abominations of Egypt.

I pray you earnestly to remember me in your prayers, and to commend our exile to the prayers of the holy persons who are with you.

## LETTER CCXVI. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY. (A.D. 1167)

To Lord Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury, John of Salisbury.

Having received the letters of my most dear friend Reginald the archdeacon, I pressed the Lord of Canterbury more urgently concerning your reconciliation, as I had often done before; and, as formerly when Master Gilbert was present, I gave every effort and attention to satisfying your request. But he remains such as he was found at first: not indeed, as I testify before God in conscience, steadfast in an intention of hatred toward you, but lest horns be given to the sinner, and lest by this act boldness in disobedience gain strength.

For if you return to obedience, I do not doubt that you will immediately find him a most merciful father. In this matter he is supported both by the counsel of the friends whom he has in the Roman Church and by the wise men of the Gallican Church, who feel his persecution as bitterly as their own. Nor is there one of them who advises him to revoke his sentence while you remain disobedient and wish to excuse your offence under the pretext of appeal. For he has received both your letters of appeal and others in the bishops’ name, although he has accepted neither appeal, as is clear to us from his reply.

But, as he says, you have neither yet withdrawn nor ever written to him renouncing the appeals, although this must be done by open letters if you expect mercy from him. He has sent your letters of appeal to the lord pope; and would that what the bishops testified in their own letters concerning the innocence and justice of the lord king were true: that he, as they say, considers obedience sweet whenever he is admonished to correct anything in which he may have offended against the Lord [Col. 0240A]. If his kindness is so great, why do they not meet with him, so that he may spare both the Church of God and himself? If it is not so, why did they testify to it in open letters at the peril of their souls? The archbishop urges these points, and has not resolved to yield to those who resist and openly thirst for his blood against the Church and against himself.

But if you withdraw from the company of persecutors and return by rendering obedience, he will be readier to grant pardon and exercise every mercy than you will be to make entreaties; and this, as you yourselves see, ought indeed to be done—nay, must be done. For you know what the lord pope wrote back to your brother, the Bishop of Constance, and also what comfort your dean brought you from the Apostolic See.
