[Col. 0240B] For the archbishop is not unaware of his undertakings and progress: he recently received, through his envoys, apostolic consolation together with bundles of many letters.

The aforesaid dean too, if he thinks it fitting, may remember the agreements which he made and the guarantees which he gave to the lord pope. Had he afterwards moderated himself somewhat from injuries against his archbishop and lord, perhaps he would have provided more advantageously for himself in future. Yet, from the very matter in which the archbishop appears to have been prejudiced, provision has been made for him contrary to the intention of those conducting affairs; and the absolution of those whom he had excommunicated makes clear how dangerously they had previously been communing with them.

Nevertheless, concerning that absolution and other matters touching this case, we are constrained by the necessity of an injunction to silence until a fixed day, when it will be known whether the lord pope has been informed of the agreements which he accepted in the Church’s cause, or has been deceived. Meanwhile I can advise nothing other than what divine law prescribes: that one must obey God rather than men. Sacrifices are never accepted from one who withholds obedience; nor does he proceed safely who sets the will of worldly power before the duty of his office.

I speak this to you as to a Father and lord before God, whom I invoke as witness upon my soul at the strict judgment: for, if a way of sounder counsel lay open to me, I would disclose it to you with most ready devotion. And if you see anything in which I can serve you, command freely, assured that I shall fulfil your wishes to the limit of my ability. I believe that you have received the letters which I sent to the Bishop of Constance and to my most dear friend the archdeacon, so that there is no need to write more at present.

## LETTER CCXVII. TO ROGER, BISHOP OF WORCESTER. (A.D. 1167)

To Lord Roger, Bishop of Worcester.

Confidence sends forth secure petitions and does not fear rejection of a just request from a friend who is always ready for that friend’s service. What is more just than that a faithful person should encourage his lord to perform offices of charity, and that the lord, to the benefit of his own salvation, should fulfil the wishes of a friend who asks? I think it fitting for your holiness in life, and becoming for your nobility in glory, that in contemplation of divine mercy you should share in the needs of Christ’s little ones [Col. 0241A], and, wherever reason permits, should satisfy the charity which is in Christ by their consolation or advancement; and that you should be true to your lineage, which is known to have raised more of its little ones than the world, though it lies in evil, can yet cast down.

The bearer of this letter is one of Christ’s little ones; and he is also one of your little ones with me. Since divine providence has given you the opportunity, you can, as the saying goes, without blood or sweat, without loss of resources, and with an increase to your reputation and conscience, aid his needs in accordance with the prayers of the lord archbishop. That you may do so, I add the prayers of my littleness to the prayers of so great a majesty; whatever benefit or honour your goodness confers upon him will be counted as bestowed upon me.

Nor have I forgotten the consolation which I received at Sens from a word of your generosity; nor shall I allow you to forget it when either more pressing necessity urges, or modest shame, overcome by the urgency of necessity—which I have not yet found inexorable—yields. But above all I ask, advise, and counsel you in the fidelity of true friendship to remember, in the Church’s cause, what is owed to conscience before God and to reputation before men; and not to trust in the reed of Egypt, which both gives help to no one and pierces the limbs of him who leans upon it. By the display of your deeds show false and vain, so far as concerns you, him who, excusing the malice exercised against the Church, habitually alleges against those who accuse him: “My own nation and the chief priests handed her over to me.”

I address a priest of Christ, a shepherd of the Church, a bishop of souls, son of an illustrious count who would have been worthy to be numbered among kings, had he not, through the title of magnificent virtue, deserved to see kings in the second rank while established on the summit of liberty, and to be held forever the father of kings whom he advanced by adoption. I do not therefore fear that I have cast words into the wind, or that it is perilous for me to have spoken truth in ears of such holiness. Yet I do not fear the snares of those who lie in wait because of truth—would that I had devoted my whole life to truth and spent my soul in its defence!

[Col. 0241D] He is on a pathless track, Father, who thinks governing the Church means lordship over the clergy and arrogance toward the people; draining the purses of Christ’s poor in order to indulge the enemies of the Crucified—actors, mimes, and other plagues of that sort; pleasing worldly powers so that, through the ruinous and shameful patience of Christ’s shepherds, the Church may be trampled underfoot; seeking one’s own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ; lying idle with the Lord’s talent; and failing to employ, by the commerce of care and labour, the interest accruing upon the virtues.

Soon the Shepherd of shepherds will come, and He will demand a strict account from you and us. Then the memory of the just will be with praises, and the name of the wicked will rot. But lest I seem to prophesy at excessive length, you will very soon, through God’s mercy, see the Church rise again, so that those who have hitherto betrayed her will either weep with Peter unto pardon [Col. 0242A], or hang themselves with a noose like Judas.

## LETTER CCXVIII. TO WILLIAM THE BRITON, SUBPRIOR OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1167)

To William the Briton, Subprior of Kent.

By the Lord’s agency, the condition of the universal Church is flourishing anew; the assault of the schismatics has been frustrated, and the pride of Moab is weakened day by day. Aar has not now been laid waste by night, as in the beginning; rather, it has been undermined at noon, and its walls have been utterly thrown down, so that the exultation of Moab, necessarily yielding to Peter, may henceforth cease.

Thus there is hope in the Lord that, as the priests’ trumpets sound, Jericho too will soon fall; and that Jesus, the triumphant conqueror, will obtain the kingdom purchased by His own blood, while Christ—the Bridegroom and guardian of the Church—will peacefully possess what is His by right [Col. 0242B]. For after the Roman pontiff had long awaited the German tyrant patiently, that he might thereby be provoked to repentance, the schismatic abused his patience and continually added sins to sins, until error turned into madness. Therefore Peter’s vicar, appointed by the Lord over nations and kingdoms, released from their allegiance to him the Italians and all who were bound to him by an oath sworn on account of the Empire and kingdom. With such good fortune and speed he shook nearly all Italy free from the face of the raging tyrant then present, that the latter seems to retain there nothing except torturers, whom he sometimes escapes, and the continual punishment of distresses which he cannot escape.

He also took from him royal dignity and condemned him by anathema; and by God’s authority forbade him henceforth to have any strength in military engagements, to gain victory over any Christian, or to enjoy rest and peace anywhere, until he should produce fruits worthy of repentance. In this he followed the example of his predecessor Gregory VII, who in our own era deposed and by a similar sentence condemned at a Roman council the Emperor Henry for overthrowing the Church’s privileges. That sentence indeed took effect; and the Lord Himself appears to have confirmed this sentence pronounced in defence of Peter’s privilege.

When the Italians heard this, they abandoned him, rebuilt Milan, expelled the schismatics, restored the Catholic bishops [Col. 0242D], and unanimously adhered to the Apostolic See. But why do I recount well-known things? Certainly common report everywhere celebrates this almost with a herald’s voice. I do not think anyone doubts it, unless perhaps it is unknown to those alone who at this time are exiles in their own home.

Since, therefore, a ray of serenity has now shone from the East through Christ, and the Church’s safety is restored in its head, there remains the most certain hope of faith that the ointment flowing from the head into the apostolic beard will descend upon the head and hem of the English Church. And he who strives to drive the prophet out of Israel, unless perhaps he comes to his senses, will receive the divine sentence, as Amos says to him:

> Your wife will commit fornication in the city; your sons and daughters will fall by the sword; your land will be measured out with a line; you will die in a polluted land; and your people will go into captivity away from their land.  
> *(Amos 7)*

[Col. 0243A] This is the punishment of those who resist the word of God and of powers which endeavour to close the mouths of priests. Then surely laughter will be mingled with pain, mourning will take possession of joy’s end, and it will be bitter to have shared food, drink, and friendly conversation with excommunicated persons. Will the followers of Balaam—bishops, priests, the princes of Tahpanhes, and diviners—be able by their counsels to save the Midianites when the sword of the Lord pursues them? Will cardinals or legates be of use if they are followers of Balaam on the day of the Lord? Certainly, if Balaam himself is present, he will either bless the tents of Jacob, which now seem proscribed and exiled in the wilderness, or, falling beneath the sword of God’s word, will find the Holy Spirit to be his adversary. He will perceive that, just as the harvests and crops of the Philistines, so too the tails of the foxes that set fires are consumed by flame.

I have said these things beforehand lest any friend make flesh his arm and, by sharing with the excommunicated, draw upon himself the two-edged sword. Yet it is reported—something which I cannot recall without pain and tears—that the holy Church of Canterbury has incurred anathema by association with that notorious excommunicate, Ranulf de Broc; and that, despising God’s law and worshipping Melchom, it sent to the king the letters which the lord pope had sent it in support of the archbishop, so as to evade obedience and exclude the works of mercy which were due.

I therefore earnestly pray, advise, and exhort with all the insistence I can: if the reports are false and the church is still free from anathema, let it henceforth take care, for its own sake, that such a thing cannot plausibly be alleged of it. But if it has fallen under anathema, let it return through repentance, lest it which has hitherto been distinguished among Western churches for religion should henceforth be distinguished also for crime. If these words seem somewhat harshly framed, I know that I speak neither to a devil nor to the schismatic of Bath, but to a friend of truth and faith, and, through him, to one who has charity toward Christ’s Church. Whether the world wishes it or not, God knows that I sincerely love the Church of Canterbury, and I cannot keep silent when danger threatens it. For, as the prophet says: “The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord has spoken; who will not prophesy?” *(Amos 3.)*

[Col. 0243D] Furthermore, if you have heard of the summons of the Lord of Canterbury, do not unwillingly leave your church on that account, unless another cause compels you to depart. For I know—and would that you knew—what I have obtained for you from him. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXIX. TO POPE ALEXANDER—A STATEMENT OF THE CASE WRITTEN FOR LORD POPE ALEXANDER ON BEHALF OF CANTERBURY

To Lord Pope Alexander, John of Salisbury.

Father, our soul is in bitterness, so that the force of grief may, I greatly fear in your presence, strip words of moderation, and patience, beneath the weight of miseries, may be wholly unable to restrain complaints. Some among us, dying for the defence of justice, seek from God and the Church vengeance for innocent blood [Col. 0244A]; others undergo various punishments; all are exiles and have long been proscribed, so that we may thereby be compelled to prefer the wicked traditions of men to the law of God and the ordinances of the Fathers. Yet the faithful have one remedy in tribulation: to knock at the ears of Majesty with prayers and unfold the innermost secrets of the whole mind, that they may thus move the Father’s mercy and obtain consolation in misery.

Whenever the children of Israel employed this remedy, they are recorded as having been delivered from their needs and distresses. They resorted to the tabernacle of the covenant, where the Holy of Holies were preserved—that is, God’s commandments, which surpass all ordinances of righteousness. In their times of need they approached Moses and Aaron, the holy ones of the Lord. And to whom are the miserable people of Canterbury, who must flee to mediators between God and themselves, to resort except to the Roman Church, where the guardianship of divine law and the primacy of the whole priesthood flourish? For if she resolves, after God, to save us, we shall immediately be delivered. If you raise your hands, Amalek will be overthrown; and He who made you a god to Pharaoh will cast down before your face all the Church’s adversaries.

Would that he who glories that he has been pledged by the apostolic hand with ring, honour, and benefice had not deceived your prudence by his oaths and promises, nor weakened the firmness of your uplifted hands. For the Church was already sailing in harbour when he returned in triumph, procured the absolution of unrepentant sacrilegious persons, and, by suspending the authority of the Lord of Canterbury until the arrival of the legates—of whom he was the forerunner—gave the Church’s persecutors added boldness to sin [Col. 0244C]. For previously more persons obeyed the archbishop; but since then, so far as I can remember, none, or very few indeed, have done so. For hope had been given to his rivals that he was to be deposed by the legates; that, stripped of his possessions without their restoration, he must undergo judgment; and that the legates were coming with such fullness of power that, by abolishing what now stands, they could enact new laws.

People were inclined to believe this, seeing the advocate’s ring and honour; and because, when the bishops were called together at his arrival, the unrepentant excommunicated persons of the Lord of Canterbury were absolved and his sentences nullified. They were absolved in fact, I say. Certainly they are still bound in the sight of the Lord, who never absolves unrepentant criminals. Their lack of repentance is clear: although able to do so, they neither make satisfaction nor restore anything of what they have taken. Indeed, if an object taken can be restored and is not restored, repentance is not performed but feigned. These assertions are empty if they do not still occupy the possessions of the Church of Canterbury, if an obol of all the many and great things taken has been restored to any of us—except to those who went back and, after taking an oath, confirmed that they must live according to the king’s law.

Yet that action, which was not an absolution but a mockery of law, ought not be imputed to your holiness, since it was not so much performed as perpetrated in fraud of your command. For you had permitted that, if any of them happened to be ill and in imminent danger of death, he should then at last be absolved, after swearing according to the custom of the Church that he would obey your command. By this your dignity intended to provide for God’s Church and for us. But by the patronage of deceit they obtained absolution, pretending to be in danger of death because, by command of the lord king, they faced the necessity of crossing the sea.

Therefore, since the one who absolved them had neither ordinary jurisdiction nor observed the form prescribed by you, I believe—unless you judge otherwise—that the absolution conferred has no legal force, and that those invaders of the Church remain under the former sentence. For those who, deceiving you and scandalizing the Gallican and English Churches, sinned against the Holy Spirit will, by God’s inspiration and with your justice cooperating, answer for their deserts [Col. 0245B]; and this will happen shortly, as the Most Christian King and his kingdom trust concerning you.

For he rejoices in the things said to him and more fully disclosed at the arrival of the worldly-minded men: namely, that the boasting is vain of those who threatened the ruin of the Archbishop of Canterbury—or rather, of the English Church. For if the archbishop were deposed on this account, who would thereafter dare utter a word? If the king obtained by your authority either confirmation or toleration of the customs which he seeks, what prince would henceforth fear to demand anything against the Church? I know one thing: without violating his profession and injuring divine law, not merely a bishop but not even a Christian can observe them. Nor can I sufficiently wonder in what frame of mind one priest dared suggest to another that, after the example of the Sicilians or Hungarians, he should show tolerance toward such grave perversities. Far be this counsel from the holiness of your pontificate, and far be it that such presumption of perversities, remaining unpunished in your days, should be carried forward into later ages as precedent.

Yet the people do not believe that the legates whom you have sent are fit to restrain the king’s savagery. For the same king has always used the patronage of one of them and places great confidence in him; the other, though he may have good will, cannot bring it into effect for various reasons. Indeed, to speak what I think, I do not believe anyone fit for this task. Who could expect the fruit of a legation in his own country, where no convenient opportunity lies within his power for either litigant or judge to say anything against him?

The prudent people of either realm do not believe that the man whom the king requested from your holiness by name is now either purer in faith, more fervent in charity, or more steadfast in virtue than he was at Pavia among relatives, friends, and acquaintances, where he kept silence while he saw the cause of faith condemned by the heretics who had assembled, and a most grievous injury inflicted upon the Apostolic See through the strengthened agreement of the schismatics.

But blessed be God, who, having had mercy upon the Church, crushed before your face that Frederick, detestable for all ages, author of the schism; teaching that the acceptable year of the Lord and the time of visitation have now come. Thus you who see God’s sword drawn against the heads of tyrants should wield Peter’s sword against them, and know that you have been established as God’s fellow-workers in exterminating those who endeavour to extinguish God’s word so as to establish the wicked traditions of men. In this way you will consecrate your hands to the Lord in the destruction of the idol; Levi will be restored to rejoice in the Father’s blessing; and your priesthood, more than that of Phinehas, will be rendered glorious throughout all ages. May your fatherhood prosper and remember Christ’s poor for good.

## LETTER CCXX. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1167)

To Lord Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Having examined the letters which you resolved to send to Lord William of Pavia, although I do not dare judge the writer’s intention, I cannot approve their style [Col. 0246B]. For it does not appear to speak humility or to have proceeded from the mind of one who has heard the Apostle exhort Christ’s disciples: “Let your gentleness be known to all; the Lord is near” *(Philippians 4).* If the individual points of your letter and of his own article are compared, your response will seem to have proceeded more from bitterness and resentment of spirit than from sincerity of charity.

What, after all, did he write that you should say—leaving aside insults and taunts, that is, open bites and figurative ones—that he offered you poison in the middle of your letter? Did it seem right to you that a cardinal priest, indeed a legate of the Apostolic See, should be branded with suspicions at the very first greeting, gratuitously provoked against the lord pope’s counsel, and dishonoured with abuse contrary to the reverence due the Roman Church? Indeed, I do not think even the lord pope’s courier should have been addressed in that manner. If he sends back his own letter and yours to the lord pope, the testimony of your writing will appear to have justified the king’s case and proved your own contumacy.

Let it be granted that William was, and still is, an enemy. I think this should be concealed until his evil deeds come to light, since it is certain from your envoys’ report that the lord pope likewise advised this. Yet I do not say that, before you have tested and proved a man’s fidelity by good works, you should consent to receive him as judge. But neither do I advise rejecting him too hastily, although I have no doubt that the trial has been postponed because restitution, which cannot presently occur, has not been made.

[Col. 0246D] I thought we should meanwhile hold our ground here and win over the cardinals as far as this can be done without compromising conscience and reputation; and wait upon the Lord for iniquity, the assault on truth, and failure to fulfil promises to be exposed on the opposing side. If he said that he was sent to settle the disputes as he judged expedient for the Church of God, in what has he injured you? Cannot they be settled by the kindness of a composition as well as by a judicial sentence? If he exhorted you to avoid, as far as lies within you, those things which usually produce causes for a more extensive quarrel, I do not see what wrong he committed, since the wisest and most devoted friends give precisely this counsel, urging you to direct your efforts more diligently toward peace insofar as the honour of the Church and of your person allows.

He should therefore, in my view, have been asked to specify the things which he says should be avoided; to deal with the lord king concerning the restoration of you and your people and the Church’s liberty; and to write back to you how far he has progressed. For you and your people lack the resources to travel to meet him, and it is unsafe for any of your party to enter the boundaries of the king of England. May the Angel of great counsel instruct you; and may the Holy Spirit be in the mouth and heart of those whom you send. If the legate fulfils what he promised at the end of his letter, I think that many thanks should be rendered to him. If the Bishop of London and your archdeacon receive from the Lord what they deserve, let them attribute it to themselves; but consider whether your sentence will have force if no citation has preceded it. Would that, as it deserves, so it might obtain effect in law and fact.

## LETTER CCXXI. TO WILLIAM OF PAVIA. (A.D. 1167)

[Col. 0247B]

To William of Pavia.

We have learned from public report that you and Lord Otto, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, at the request of our illustrious lord the King of the English, have come into the regions of Aquitaine by command of the lord pope, so that, by God’s agency, if this can be done, you may restore to the English Church its due liberty and renew peace and concord between the lord king and the Archbishop of Canterbury.

We have also heard from great and venerable men that our aforesaid lord king has such confidence in your friendship that he has resolved to comply with your counsel in all things. Greatly encouraged by this, I have judged it proper to seek your counsel and assistance, ready to obey you in all things, provided the integrity of my conscience and the honour of my person are preserved. For I trust in the Lord that partiality toward persons and gifts will not have such weight with you that you do anything by which the Church is harmed, scandal generated in the world, or the brightness of your name darkened [Col. 0247C]. Such are the deeds of those who either do not know the law or do not fear the Lord of the law. But you are not such a one: the Lord has so approved your faith and prudence that He has placed you, at the head of the world, as an eminent lamp upon the golden lampstand of seven lamps, that those who enter may see the light.

Accordingly, the eyes of all are directed upon you; and many fear that Lucifer, tested anew, may be extinguished and fall, apprehensive that the intimacy which, it is said, you have lately formed with the king may give you an occasion of sin. And indeed:

> Every vice of the mind bears within itself a crime so much more conspicuous  
> as the man who sins is held to be greater.  
> *(Juvenal, Satire VIII.140.)*

Yet for the present I hope that this intimacy between you and the lord king, so suspect to many, will prove fruitful for the Church, necessary for us, salutary for him, and glorious for you. For if he listens to you in what necessity of law requires and what he cannot avoid without loss of his salvation [Col. 0248A], without doubt he will repent, confess his fault, and, humbly making satisfaction to the Church, restore to us all peace and liberty together with what has been taken, in its entirety; and he will utterly root fraternal hatred out of his heart. Otherwise, who can rescue him from the snare of death?

Certainly I know—for it is beyond doubt true and also well known—that not even Peter himself received from the Lord the power to absolve the unrepentant. And it is beyond doubt clear that, if a thing taken away can be restored and is not restored, repentance is not being done but feigned. Where the authority of the Prince of the Apostles is restrained, I could by no reasoning believe that the power of any human being can prevail. I admit, and it is true, that very great deference is due to the lord king, as to a most glorious [Col. 0248B] prince; but only so that God is not offended in the slightest degree. Otherwise, under any pretext of advantage whatever, to prefer the creature to the Creator is a form of idolatry, as the blessed Apostle teaches.

For evils must not be done in order that good may result; nor may anyone dispense against a command of the Lord which has perpetual force in the Law or the Gospel. But, that you may more conveniently make provision for me, so that the cry of the poor may enter your ears: the fourth year of my exile has passed, although I have often offered the lord king, both in person and through others, that, although—with conscience as my witness—I have not deserved his wrath, yet, in order to recover his favour, I would willingly do whatever pleased him, with my conscience safe and my good name intact. Certain mediators have negotiated with me [Col. 0248C] that I should withdraw from loyalty and service to the lord of Canterbury, swear allegiance to the king, and swear to observe the customs of the realm. Since I can neither do this nor wish to do it, because it is contrary to conscience and honour, I am an outlawed exile, and I shall gladly remain in exile while it pleases God.

For shall I, breaking the obligation of obedience in the Church’s peril and in God’s cause, abandon my Father and lord, and swear to customs which the sacred canons reject and which the lord pope, with the counsel of his brethren at Sens, condemned—while you yourselves, I think, were listening? Certainly I would not swear observance even of the canons or of the Gospel itself, because, as the Apostle laments, “we all offend in many things.” And it is a lesser evil simply [Col. 0248D] to transgress than to heap perjury upon transgression. I know, however, that no one will have you as authors either of perjury, disobedience, or any disgraceful act whatever.

But because I fear that you may be wearied by my verbosity, I make an end with these words, beseeching you to strive to end the misery of the Church, which has suffered shipwreck for so long, and to repel the injuries continually inflicted upon us. May my lord always prosper, and have mercy upon Christ’s outlaws. For I intercede on behalf of all my fellow-exiles; and, if consolation is not afforded to me, I shall nevertheless count as bestowed upon myself whatever I learn has been afforded through you to Christ’s other outlaws.

## LETTER CCXXII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1167.)

[Col. 0249A]

To Lord JOHN, bishop of Poitiers, J. [John], greetings.

The clashes of kingdoms, great earthquakes, and the issue of impending dangers compelled me to lay aside my pen for a long time and await more convenient occasions for writing. For the tumults of war, raging through almost the whole summer, prevented letter-carriers from passing through; and the uprising which arose in the city of Rheims so disturbed the province that it was scarcely safe to enter or leave the city. For the citizens, having conspired with the counsel of clerics and the aid of knights, rose against the archbishop, who wished to impose certain new, unlawful, and intolerable services [Col. 0249B] upon the city. Occupying church towers and stronger houses, and driving the archbishop’s officers and friends from the city, they inflicted many injuries upon him.

At first, indeed, they had shown him every humility, being prepared, as many testify, to pay two thousand pounds into his treasury, provided that he treated them according to law and allowed them to live under the laws which the city had continuously used since the time of Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks. They had even approached the Most Christian King, but could not soften the archbishop’s severity even through him. They therefore fled to Count Henry and, on his advice, yielded to the king, whom the archbishop had brought in so that he might crush the city by his force. The king, grieving but nevertheless satisfying his brother’s will, [Col. 0249C] caused about fifty houses to be demolished and departed.

On the third day the citizens returned and, in vengeance for their demolished houses, utterly destroyed the homes of the knights who favoured the archbishop—namely, his lord’s deputy, and another who had held the prefecture in the city. Moved by this, the archbishop invoked the aid of the Count of Flanders and brought him with a thousand knights to Rheims, so that the citizens might perish by the sword or be cast into chains to be ransomed and tortured. But, foreseeing the count’s arrival, they again withdrew, so completely emptying the city that the Flemings, exhausted by hunger, could scarcely endure a stay of one day and night. Since the archbishop did not doubt that the citizens would return to their homes when the Flemings withdrew, [Col. 0249D] he made peace with them through his brother Count Robert, without the Flemings’ knowledge, receiving four hundred and fifty pounds in compensation for losses—which, not to mention the many injuries and insults, had increased fourfold—and granting that henceforth they should use their ancient laws.

Thus, having made a costly and ignominious peace with the citizens, he still carries on hostilities with the clergy and harasses the churches that submit themselves to the law. Such are matters among us.

Furthermore, we have learned that legates have come into your regions; but it is still uncertain what we ought to hope or fear from them. This, however, is entirely certain: the lord of Canterbury has resolved not to submit to the judgment of the Cardinal of the Chains, moved, I think, by many and just suspicions, because he has hitherto proved his manifest [Col. 0250A] adversary. But whether it is expedient to set out to him the grounds for so manifest a suspicion is not sufficiently clear. For the archbishop, as I hear, has already written back to him—contrary to my advice and that of certain others—that he will not submit himself to his judgment and is not bound to do so; and he has amassed many points by which he may have exasperated the man’s mind. I thought rather that he ought to be softened by gentler words and retained in friendship until his actions prove him to be an adversary.

He will gladly receive, through the hands of the legates, a peace consistent with the honour of God’s Church and his own. But whether he will attend their conferences unless what has been taken away is restored, so that he may maintain himself and his people, I have not yet discovered. It is more certain than certain that, unless a settlement is made through them, [Col. 0250B] he will enter into no proceedings without restitution, since the injury and violence done to him are known even to the bleary-eyed and barbers. Nor will he send any of his people until security for going and returning is arranged for travellers.

And since the reckoning of our condition seems to have been changed somewhat by their arrival, I earnestly beg you to write back to me through the bearer of this letter, explaining how I ought to conduct myself without harm to conscience and reputation. For if the matter concerns the oaths which the lord king is accustomed to require of us, I pray my God mercifully to grant me death before I stain conscience and reputation with such oaths.

## LETTER CCXXIII. TO MASTER RAYMOND. (A.D. 1167.)

[Col. 0250C]

To Master RAYMOND.

What compelled me to be silent for so long, and in what condition I have been, you will readily learn from the letters sent to the lord of Poitiers. Therefore, proceeding to the remaining matters of my necessity, I earnestly beg that, after carefully considering my situation in all the circumstances of persons, cause, and time, you will be pleased to write what seems especially advisable—observing in your choice of counsel that honour must always take precedence over expediency.

And, if it seems good to the lord bishop, to you, and to Master Laurence that a safe opportunity to approach the legates should be obtained for me and Christ’s other exiles, I desire it to be obtained for us; yet only on condition that, before I approach them, I may be informed by the counsel of the lord bishop, yourself, and Master Laurence—if he has returned from England—concerning the business to be undertaken. There is conflicting report: some assert that the cardinals will labour faithfully for the Church of God; others say that they have resolved to sell off the Church’s liberty and nullify the justice of our cause for money, which nevertheless may not be put into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.

It was therefore for your diligence to write back what you have ascertained concerning their counsel and the condition of the lord king and the court, and more faithfully to report what is being done concerning the lord bishop and yourselves. I also beg you to send me whatever Master John has written in reply to my requests; or, if he has not yet replied, make an effort that he may reply. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXIV. TO MASTER LAURENCE. (A.D. 1167.)

To Master LAURENCE.

From the examination of your letter I have gladly learned that you will attach yourself to Lord William of Pavia in the exercise of his legation; nor do I doubt that his familiar friendship can be serviceable and useful to you and us. And because it is better known to you than to any of us on what footing our cause stands as regards your countrymen, I earnestly beg that, having considered what I wrote to the lord bishop and the master of the schools, you will write back through the bearer of this letter whatever you believe advantageous to our cause.

It is said that legates of this kind are accustomed to receive no one into the closer familiarity of their household unless he has given them sworn security concerning the loyalty to be shown, the faith to be kept, and the concealment of secrets. On this point I desire your affection to be forewarned, should anything of the kind be demanded: bind yourself, if the matter requires it, only to human service, so that the conscience of innocence may suffer no loss. And although they strive thus to conceal their secrets, I would not readily believe it, unless they intend—so far as ancient custom permits Romans—to practise works of darkness, especially since they know that all eyes are fixed upon them. For, if reports must be believed, one of them has proposed to the king of England to sell the Church’s liberty and the blood of innocent exiles and outlaws for the Lord. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXV. TO PETER THE SCRIBE. (A.D. 1167.)

J. [John], greetings to PETER the scribe.

The rarity of travellers deprives us of the mutual consolation of letters, and the chaos established by the Lord between us, as our deserts demand, denies safe passage to those who travel between us. Yet, although the opportunity for conversation is taken away, the affection of mutual love is not impeded. Rather, in the manner of lovers, the more fear and the hands of those who restrain them torment their inflamed minds, the more abundantly and ardently charity receives increase.

If therefore I may not see you and the other friends, if we are not permitted to serve one another by mutual offices, we are certainly permitted to love and to help by prayers and petitions. For charity, as has been said, cannot be restrained, because “wherever the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3). We are not permitted to hold and defend ecclesiastical liberty; yet we are certainly permitted to cry out and bear witness to the commands of divine law. It is permitted, for the word of God—which, having assumed flesh, exposed itself to death for us—to expose not only our possessions and the perishable household goods of this world, but our souls also.

May that Spirit, the founder of good minds, grant us perseverance in this affection, He who bestowed upon us the will for that affection itself. There is indeed hope that peace will soon be restored through the work and diligence [Col. 0252A] of the cardinals sent for this purpose—unless perhaps peace is delayed because the lord of Canterbury will consent to no terms unless the Church of England enjoys its due liberty. By “due,” however, I do not refer to the times of any Henry, but to the lawful ordinances of the Word of God; for by his profession he ought not to be Henrician, but Christian.

But perhaps you will object: “If this is his determination, why did he flee?” Why did he expose the Church, for which he had known beforehand that priests ought to lay down their lives, to so many and such great perils, if he resolved to subordinate the laws of princes and ancestral customs of the realm to divine ordinances? Why, at Clarendon, did he swear to the words of reprobate customs, which are utterly contrary to divine laws and the customs of the holy Fathers? Why does he not present himself, so that before kings and princes he may speak God’s law without fear? For all the nations ask these questions.

His flight has as its author Christ and Christ’s Apostle, who, let down in a basket, escaped the hands of his persecutors, knowing that it is the person, not the cause, of the persecutor that must be fled from one city to another. For he saw that kings and princes had assembled against the Lord and against His Christ. Therefore he rises up to the Roman pontiff, to whom he had appealed, so that by his protection he might more powerfully aid the shipwrecked Church, which, as is said, the chief priests in England were especially submerging. This was not to expose the Church, but to labour for its deliverance. [Col. 0252C] Unless you think that he too abandons a ship who boards a small boat in order to draw it into harbour.

I cannot excuse the promise at Clarendon, to which he was driven by the counsel of the bishops, because it certainly ought not to have been made. But confession washes away the offence: he was solemnly given penance by the supreme pontiff, who, before many hearers, condemned those perverse customs by apostolic authority. Following thereafter the authority of the lord pope, he subjected some of those customs, with their observers, to anathema, as the Catholic Church is known to have done in many councils.

If he does not put himself in the way of those seeking his life when a more suitable and safer course lies open, he acts rightly, supported by the example of prophets and apostles; for David, Elijah, Peter, and Paul are recorded as having done the same. To expose oneself to certain and manifest dangers when an opportunity of escape lies open in the Lord is to put God to the test.

But God, who has already begun to comfort His Church in its head, will through His mercy strengthen its members also. He who compelled the German tyrant, leader of the schismatics, to depart in confusion from the city, will Himself by His grace lead back and guide the lord king of England into the right path, so that henceforth he may not consent to evil counsellors. And, if astrologers are to be believed—though I do not consider them greatly worth hearing—this year is said, from the configuration of the constellations, to be remarkable: in it the counsels of kings will change, wars will multiply throughout the world, the land will seethe with uprisings, those under Mercury will be brought low, but at the end of the year they will be raised up.

I nevertheless consider these vain dreams, although they seem to have spoken truth in part. For the emperor’s counsellors have died: Reginald, archbishop of Cologne; the intruder at Mainz; the bishops of Liège and Regensburg; and several other schismatic leaders. Wars and uprisings rage everywhere; those under Mercury have been so depressed that France, the gentlest and most civilized of all nations, has driven away foreign scholars. There is also an indication of revelation in the fact that the uprising at Rheims has been pacified and the siege of the city lifted. For, as they say, these two cities show one another such brotherhood that they are subject to the same fates and, suffering together, rejoice together. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXVI. TO MASTER GIRARD PUELLA. (A.D. 1167.)

[Col. 0253B] JOHN OF SALISBURY to Master GIRARD.

The urgency of the bearer and the writer’s lack of time constrain my words, but they cannot restrain or constrict the affection of one desirous of writing. More ought now to be written in view of the times; but the mind of a wise man is accustomed to infer much from little.

Therefore, that you may first know our condition—which you desire to be as favourable as possible—know that the lord of Canterbury and his fellow-exiles are acceptable first to the Most Christian King and then to the leading men of all France, as their reception in fact shows; and they await from the Lord, as is hoped, the speedy coming of peace for the Church. For the cardinals sent for this purpose are labouring to bring it about, saying that, if by no other means they can restrain the little foxes of the Philistines, they will burn their tails, and the fields now sprouting toward harvest, with torches kindled and to be kindled, as correction and example to all flesh and every generation.

But why do I recall their words? By their fruits we shall know them. Do not, beloved friend, find it burdensome to write back to us about matters concerning you. Meanwhile, in assisting the shipwrecked Church—or rather, now recovering by God’s aid—expend the talent entrusted to you. For perhaps the Lord has sent you into that barbarian land for the salvation of many, so that, when the head of schism has been crushed, the Church of Cologne may through your industry return to Catholic unity.

For the emperor, like a brand snatched from the fire, departed the city in confusion; and although the stench of corpses from the camp rose into his nostrils, when the Lord stretched out His hand against him, he has not yet chosen to recognize and confess his error. Let your spirit therefore be raised up, because Christ conquers, reigns, and rules; and, remembering His poor, He more mightily torments mighty wicked men. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1167.) Words of the lord of Canterbury with the legates between Gisors and Trie.

A friend to a friend.

Since I do not doubt that you are concerned about the Church’s condition and the outcome of the legation which has been obtained, I have judged that the following should be set down for your consolation and that of others who fear God, with concise brevity.

Know, therefore, that the lord of Canterbury and several of his fellow-exiles went, on the octave of Saint Martin, to meet the legates in conference between Gisors and Trie. When the latter had advanced much concerning the charity of the lord pope and his concern for us—which he exercises so attentively regarding their labours and the hazards of the journey—concerning the greatness of the prince and the Church’s need, the evil of the times, the love and benefits by which the lord king had anticipated the archbishop of Canterbury, and the honour always shown him by the king, they added also the complaints and injuries by which the king alleges that he has been harmed by Canterbury. Among other accusations, they charged him with having stirred up against the king a war by the king of France, seeking advice on how they might appease [Col. 0254B] so great an indignation. They knew that no remedy could be applied to such great dangers without much humility, moderation, and demonstration of honour.

In all humility and gentleness of spirit, after rendering due thanks to the lord pope and to them, the archbishop of Canterbury answered each point, refuting the king’s complaints with true and plausible arguments and openly setting forth the Church’s injuries and intolerable losses. Since they required humility and the rendering of honour from him, he replied that he would show every humility and all the honour and reverence that he could: saving the honour of God, the liberty of the Church, the honour of his own person, and the Church’s possessions. If they thought anything ought to be added, removed, or changed, he asked them to give him counsel, being resolved to comply, provided the condition of his profession and order was preserved.

When they said that they had come not to take counsel from him but to counsel him and attempt a way of reconciliation, the archbishop was again asked whether, in the legates’ presence, he would promise to observe the customs which kings had used in the time of his predecessors, and thus, with all complaints silenced, return into the king’s favour and receive his see, administration, and peace for himself and his people. To this the archbishop replied: “None of my predecessors had been compelled by any king to make this profession; and I shall never, with God as my author, promise to observe customs which openly oppose God’s law, overthrow the privilege of the Apostolic See, and destroy the liberty of the Church”—customs which the lord pope condemned at Sens in their presence and that of many others, and which he himself afterward, following the lord pope’s authority, subjected, together with some of their observers, to anathema, as the Catholic Church is known to have done in many councils.

He was again asked whether, if not confirmation, he would at least promise dissimulation and toleration; or whether, with no mention of the customs made by either side, he would receive his see and peace. The archbishop replied that there is a proverb of our nation: “He who keeps silent displays the spirit of one confessing.” Since the king seemed to him to possess the customs and to compel the Church unjustly and violently to observe them, if the conflict ceased upon obtaining silence under the legates’ authority, he would immediately seem, both to himself and to others, to have prevailed in this cause. He added that he would rather remain perpetually exiled and outlawed and, if God so ordained, die in defence of justice, than enter into this peace to the injury of his salvation and the prejudice of ecclesiastical liberty.

For God is He who forbids priests to be silent in such a cause and has prepared hell for those who dissemble, where there will be no dissimulation of punishment. The document containing those abominations was read, and the cardinals were asked whether Christians might lawfully observe such things, much less pastors dissemble over them.

They proceeded to another question, asking whether he would abide by their judgment in the matters at issue between himself and the king. He answered that he was confident in the integrity of his cause, and that, when he and his people, who had long been deprived of everything, had been fully restored in all things, he would gladly submit to the law, taking account of the cases, matters, and time. He could neither nor would evade undergoing the judgment of him or them whose judgment the lord pope should decree that he ought to accept—where, when, and how he ought. Meanwhile, he and his people could not be compelled into litigation, nor could their poverty sustain it; they lacked even food, unless they lived at the expense of the Most Christian King of France.

He did not wish at the outset to evade judgment, even though he might with the greatest justice regard one of them as suspect, lest he seem to vindicate the king’s cause; nor did he wish to involve himself in litigation before being restored in all things, so that he might sufficiently prepare his case and, relying on God’s grace, fear no wealthy adversary.

Proceeding from this, they asked whether he would answer before them as judges the bishops who had appealed against him, since they were present. The archbishop, mindful of the letters by which that rather dubious—or rather null—appeal had been presented to him, framed, as is there asserted, in the name of all the suffragan bishops, abbots, and persons of the realm dwelling in the province of Canterbury; knowing that these men had not assembled at Rouen, that a great many were ignorant of this appeal, and that many who knew of it disliked it, as being, so far as its authors could make it so, more an evasion of justice than an appeal, replied similarly that he had received no command of the lord pope on this matter; when he received one, he would deliberate and answer and do what reason dictated.

Furthermore, neither his own poverty nor that of his people was adequate to the costs of travel and litigation; nor could he endure the burdens of the Most Christian King’s clemency to the point that the king’s generosity—which had decreed most humanely to console exiled bishops—should be compelled often and for a long time to maintain him and his fellow-exiles in other people’s houses. For where provisions are abundant, expenses are more easily provided.

The following day, when the Most Christian King admitted the legates to a conference, he cleared the lord of Canterbury’s innocence under the solemnity of an oath, testifying that Canterbury had always advised him to preserve peace with the honour of both kings intact and so that the people on each side might enjoy their due tranquillity. The archbishop asked the legates to give some counsel to the Church and, if he erred anywhere, to show him a more upright way. They approved his zeal in the Lord and sympathized with him, but said nothing that should alter his resolution.

Thus, having exchanged blessings, they departed; and it has been decided—and, with God as author, shall remain decided—that we shall stand within these boundaries until the Church recovers strength and her persecutors either are converted or perish. She asked for you, and does not cease to ask, that your faith may not fail; and you, whenever opportunity occurs, having turned toward them, strengthen your brethren. Show these things to those to whom you have been sent: raise up the fallen, strengthen those who stand, so that they may be firm. For the Church has more patrons and defenders than assailants. He who laid down His life for her deliverance will not abandon her in tribulation. The champions of the holy cause, for which they did not fear to give their blood, will not desert it. The host of all heavenly powers defends it; and the Majesty which crushes Satan beneath His feet will, through Satan’s members—the ministers of wickedness—quickly, easily, and happily triumph, as are the faithful’s hope and the Fathers’ promise.

## LETTER CCXXVIII. TO THE SAME. (December, A.D. 1167.)

[Col. 0256C]

To JOHN, bishop of Poitiers, J. [John], greetings.

I consider it superfluous to explain the reasons for the altered address, since it is evident, especially to a wise man, that the evil of the times and the vigilance of those who lie in wait compel writing contrary to custom and reason. Necessity must therefore be indulged if honour is not accorded; nor should one have reason to suspect injury when the manifest reasoning of an approved cause supports it. Where rashness seems to have brought loss to the office of friendship, charity, pressed by the spur of necessity, gains increase. For the fires of a furnace are increased if they are prevented from bursting into flame.

And, as an author speaking from experience is to be believed:

> The more it is covered, the more fiercely the hidden fire burns.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.64

And just as fire is always in motion and cannot endure rest, so charity, ignorant of idleness and continually active, always reveals itself by some sign. If it does not cultivate by services, if it does not make opportunities available, if it is forbidden to serve useful ends, it nevertheless cannot at all be prevented from helping by prayers, serving by desires, and procuring by petitions what is necessary and expedient. Let the service of charity, therefore, excuse whatever the boldness of my address may seem to have presumed at its opening.

And because I remember having promised to communicate news arising among us, I have taken care, with all speed, to report the few developments which have occurred since I last wrote to you through the servant of Master Reginald.

You learned through the service of the said servant what was done at the conference between the cardinals and the lord of Canterbury between Gisors and Trie. When they had departed from one another, the cardinals found the king so disturbed that he openly complained that he had been betrayed by the lord pope and threatened to withdraw from him unless justice were done to him concerning the archbishop of Canterbury. Then, after many consultations back and forth, the king consulting now the nobles, now bishops and abbots, now his household, now both cardinals together, now one without the other, he finally offered himself to justice. He said that he was ready in every respect to abide by their judgment and command concerning all complaints at issue between himself and the lord of Canterbury, adding that at the beginning he would provide every security, both sworn and by sureties—and a still greater one if the cardinals wished—so that not one iota or tittle of their words should pass unobserved, provided that they rendered him what is due to the least man: namely, justice.

When the cardinals answered that they had received authority not to judge Canterbury but to effect a settlement, the king asked and obtained from them that they should write to the lord pope concerning this humility of his and the integrity of his cause, as they had learned it from wise and religious men: the archbishop of York; the bishops of London, Chichester, and Worcester, who were beyond the sea; and, on this side of the sea, the bishops of Rouen, Lisieux, and Bayeux.

Afterward the bishop of London came forward and, after vomiting forth much venom against his archbishop, offered his own cause and that of the other bishops who had appealed against the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury. He urged, in the name of the realm and priesthood, that it be heard and concluded. The legates likewise said that they could not compel Canterbury and that he did not wish to litigate. Thereupon the bishop and the others present broke out, in the name of the realm and priesthood, into an appeal. They forbade Canterbury to introduce any innovation against either party, placing both under the lord pope’s protection until the day of appeal, which they postponed for a further year, namely to the feast of Saint Martin.

The bishop of London, however, set out special causes for himself, attacking the liberties of the churches which the archbishop of Canterbury possesses within that bishop’s diocese. Having done this, the cardinals sent two messengers to Canterbury. On the next day after the feast of Saint Lucy they presented him letters containing, in part, an account of these events, and forbidding the archbishop, on behalf of the lord pope and the legates, to do anything against this appeal before the lord pope was approached.

The bishops also sent two messengers, Walter, cantor of Salisbury, and Master Jocelin, chancellor of Chichester, to announce the appeal which had been made and renew it before the archbishop. But the archbishop did not admit the bishops’ messengers to a conference, because among them was a messenger of the bishop of London whom the archbishop held excommunicated and had denounced to the cardinals; and because they had communicated with his excommunicates, even though, for the deception of the apostolic mandate, they seemed to less prudent persons to have been absolved.

For this was the final and sole indulgence granted by the lord pope: if they were in danger of death, they might be absolved after first swearing that, if they recovered, they would abide by the lord pope’s command. But they pretended that they were in danger of death because, by the lord king’s command, they now had to cross the sea and now proceed into Wales. They obtained absolution from a Welsh bishop, wholly or almost wholly ignorant of either law—namely, the bishop of Llandaff—who had received the monastery of Abingdon, as more profitable, from the king’s hand in exchange for his bishopric.

And lest there be doubt concerning the lord pope’s command, the archbishop sent apostolic letters to the legates, strictly ordering them to restore those thus absolved to the former sentence of excommunication unless they restored in full the possessions of the archbishop and his people and everything taken away; no obstacle of appeal was to impede this apostolic mandate. They had also previously received other letters, commanding them to take pains that peace should be restored between the kings in such a way that neither could complain of the other; and forbidding them to enter England or involve themselves in the affairs of the realm unless full peace had first been restored to the archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0258C] When the bishops had appealed in their own name and that of the realm, a clerk of Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury, appealed on behalf of his lord. One of the monks of Canterbury also appealed—not, however, sent for this by his brethren, but to implore the king’s clemency so that that wicked Ranulf de Broc might not lay hands on the monks’ possessions after the prior’s death.

The archbishop wrote back to the cardinals that he knew, and they did not fail to know, how far he was bound to obey them; and that, with God as author, he would do what he knew to be expedient for God’s Church. He also entrusted to their messengers and his own several matters to be explained verbally, rebuking the cardinals on many points for just and evident reasons. He earnestly asked them, moreover, in accordance with the lord pope’s command, either to compel his excommunicates to make satisfaction or restore them to the sentence of anathema. Nor could it previously have been believed that Pavia’s eloquence could overthrow his colleague’s fidelity, unless it were now bent, by reed-like lightness and hollowness, toward the breeze—not a breeze that presses upon it, but one that threatens, producing a sound rather than inflicting a blow or stroke.

Perhaps, as had hitherto been believed, the man’s spirit is willing; but it has been discovered that the flesh is weak. For concerning William, what was believed from the beginning now shines forth more clearly: as great-souled and faithful as he was found in the cause of the Roman Church before Frederick at Pavia, so great and such a man will be found in the cause of the English Church, if this may be said, when Henry presides or sits beside him. From this the lord of Canterbury has been persuaded that he must on no account submit himself to the judgment of these cardinals, or of others who await the fruit of a legation in the land of the king of England.

For the rest, a peace between the kings is being discussed. The king of England and Count Henry contend to see whether one may surpass the other in cunning in this affair; but because their conception has as yet produced nothing worth reporting, I thought the execution of this subject should be deferred to another time.

The archbishop of Lyons received his church and city with the honour and rejoicing of all on the feast of Saint Martin. On the same day Frederick, the most exalted emperor, having engaged the Milanese and lost twenty-five knights, was put to flight. The lord pope, having received with gifts and honour the messengers who had gone to Constantinople, and likewise the legates of the king of Sicily, prospers in the Lord’s ways, remaining at Benevento. When more things worthy of being known have become known, I shall not be reluctant, God propitious, to write them to you. Farewell, now and always.

## LETTER CCXXIX. TO MASTER RAYMOND, CHANCELLOR OF THE CHURCH OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1167.)

To Master Raymond, chancellor of the Church of Poitiers, John: greetings, and success according to your desire.

If the form of the old greeting is changed, let this be imputed not to presumption but to those who persecute faith, hinder the office of charity, and lay snares for truth. The men of Canterbury hoped that, at the coming of the cardinals, they would receive consolation for their toil and suffering [Col. 0259C]; but, I fear, in vain. For, to speak my own judgment: one of them fears man more than is fitting; the other does not fear the Lord. Thus, as is said, they have hitherto proceeded in the Lord’s cause as though the former, when summoned before the king, had brought with him the Tullian prison to confine truth; and the latter, to fetter the rights of laws and canons, the chains of Peter. Such is the judgment of the French concerning them. You will learn the matter more fully from the letter which I wrote at greater length to my John. One thing I know: their arrival has taken peace away from certain friends of yours, brought them labor and anxiety, and drained the resources of men who—would that they had not done so in vain! Furthermore, whenever it is convenient [Col. 0259D], urge Saracen that he satisfy my request and send me the books of blessed Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* and *On the Divine Names*, which, as I learned from blessed Dionysius, he has recently translated. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXX. JOHN SARACEN TO MASTER JOHN OF SALISBURY. (A.D. 1167.)

After translating the *Angelic Hierarchy*, I postponed translating the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, because I did not know your wish concerning its translation. I feared that I might seem both excessively approving of my own work and, contrary to Solomon, an unwelcome frequenter of my friend’s threshold. Nevertheless, the master of the schools moved me to translate it; he assured me that you approved the translation of that hierarchy which I had made [Col. 0260A], and requested this one. In this hierarchy I followed the same method of translating as I used in the heavenly hierarchy, except that I have not everywhere joined together several Latin expressions set down for one Greek word, and that in some places I have followed the sense rather than the words. Someone may, however, object: why has it pleased the Latin Church to alter certain things which that most holy man, taught by the apostles, is known to have handed down—or rather, to have reported as handed down by his predecessors, and to have shown the reasons why they were handed down?

## LETTER CCXXXI. TO JOHN OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1167.)

To John, bishop of Poitiers.

[Col. 0260B] Your counsel has been followed insofar as our strength allowed: a message has been sent to the lord pope with letters from the Most Christian King and the leading men of France. The name of cardinal has fallen into contempt among the French, because they have been found to be Balaamites so far as was possible, and worthy to fall with their Midianites by the sword of Moses. For they make alive souls that do not live, and, coveting the gifts of the Moabites, seek to entangle the people of God in curse and disgrace. Nor did they fear to lie in the letters which they sent against the Archbishop of Canterbury to the lord pope, as became known to many who were present at their conference. The aforesaid men of Canterbury heard and fully understood the reply made to them by the archbishop—a reply which these Balaamites nevertheless tried [Col. 0260C] to poison by perverse interpretation and to overthrow sheer truth by the deceitfulness of their insinuations.

For the Most Christian King had sworn that the said Archbishop of Canterbury was not only not an instigator of discord between the kings, but a reconciler of concord and, so far as he could, a helper and fellow-worker for peace among those who sought it most earnestly. They ought to have believed the king when he swore, unless it be that, measuring others by their own habits, they have faith in neither God nor men wherever the hope of deceitful money shines forth. Indeed, no one is astonished at the one man, whose fidelity toward God and the Church ought to have been known from the day when, at the Pavia council of heretics, where Octavian was received as arch-heretic, he sat silently beside Frederick; and several think [Col. 0260D] that he gave explicit consent. Is it not worn smooth as a proverb: “Silence imitates assent”? Yet he will defend himself by a rule of law—even though he is a despiser of divine law—that one who is silent does not necessarily consent; but it is nevertheless true that he does not deny. Thus, beneath the protection of a fine-sounding phrase and festive rhetoric, he will cloak his perfidy before many people.

Moreover, a French proverb is applied in mockery to him: he fits coverings for the shameful parts of the body, though his private parts and buttocks are exposed. Otto’s reputation, however, had seemed brighter; therefore many are astonished and pity him because he so readily departed from the Lord’s way. Nor would their astonishment suffice, were it not well known that character is shaped by company: “He who touches pitch is defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13); and “the grape, when it sees a grape, takes its discoloration from the grape” (Horace, *Epistles* II.20) [Col. 0261A]. The rest has been entrusted to the bearer of this letter. It will be for your diligence to write back, whenever occasion requires, what you judge expedient. It is useful to know the schemes and counsels of the Balaamites; what the Moabites are plotting against the Church; and whether there is anyone who extends his hand to Israel. But let this be most certain: the Archbishop of Canterbury gave no cause for the quarrel between the King of England and the Count of Flanders. By God’s grace, this will soon become known to very many.

## LETTER CCXXXII. TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1167.)

To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, John of Salisbury.

[Col. 0261B] Neither the earlier nor the later draft of the letter which you have decided to send to Lord William pleases me, because they seem too full of suspicions and to abound beyond measure in biting witticisms. I fear that our rashness may justify both him and others hostile to us. Therefore, as I was about to send the bearer of this letter to Poitiers, I ordered him to pass through your presence, so that both my opinion might become known to you and you might, if you please, send something through him to the lord bishop of Poitiers.

For myself, I have chosen a different form, especially for approaching the cardinals, which would not suit the eminence of your person, but which I nevertheless judge more similar to what is fitting. Yet let it be understood as selected only if it seems good to your judgment that it should proceed—your judgment, I say, because I do not wish [Col. 0261C] my foolish thought and the barrenness of my tongue to be exposed to the laughter of your household and to the injury of my reputation. I should not object, however, if, through men compassionate toward my error, it were privately made known to Lombard and Alexander. One is my prince; the other is a brother or friend of our order.

I sent the letters on this condition: that, if they please you, they should proceed to the bishop of Poitiers; and, if he judges it expedient, should pass on to the cardinals—after altering beforehand anything which he may decide ought to be altered. Otherwise, let them be given to the fire in your house or in his.

## LETTER CCXXXIII. TO NICHOLAS OF MONT-ROUEN. (A.D. 1167–1168.)

To Nicholas of Mont-Rouen, John of Salisbury.

[Col. 0261D] The Lord scatters nations that desire wars, and those who remove themselves from God’s peace will undoubtedly perish. What persecutor of the Church is recorded to have escaped the avenging right hand of God, who punishes the mighty more mightily? Therefore our lord, the King of England—whom may God make most excellent, if he is within His good pleasure—and his heirs have much to fear, though I do not say it without pain: lest their kingdom be divided and the power by which they misuse authority against the Church be weakened.

For though vengeance is delayed for the correction and testing of sons, whom the merciful Father chastens that He may crown them, it is not removed. After the patience of the saints [Col. 0262A], however, it will blaze more bitterly against the ungodly. Why, I ask, does a man so wise, endowed by the Lord with such great virtues, the amplest power, and almost every good thing, not return to his heart? Why can he, conqueror of so many and such great cities, not subdue this intemperance? Why, in persecuting the Church—the uniquely beloved bride—does he provoke the wrath of Him who takes away the spirit of princes and treads down by His own power the necks of the exalted?

Surely, if he were wise, he would turn the stings of his indignation against those who surround and mislead him, driving him toward not counsel but a precipice. At least, he should imitate the king of Babylon, lest he be found more cruel than that king: after Daniel had been cast and shut up in the lions’ den by their advice, that king threw into it those who had counseled him, so that the guilty counselors received the punishment which he had intended for the innocent man [Col. 0262B]. And if historical examples do not move him, Frederick, the former Augustus, can instruct him: Frederick has fallen wretchedly, yet pitiable to no one, from the summit of the Roman Empire into poverty and dishonor because of his persecution of the Church—to the glory of Him who alone transfers kingdoms and empires according to His will, raises up whom He wishes, and casts down powers.

He would not punish his counselors who had led him astray; but God’s finger exercised glorious vengeance upon them. Will the King of England be the last to offer God the fruit of repentance—he whom God has exalted above other princes? The Archbishop of Santiago, long exiled, was recalled long ago by his own king. The King of the Danes, having recalled his own archbishop, acts in accordance with his counsel in all things, restrains his enemies, and honors him as a father. The Archbishop of Lyons has recovered his see and restored his province to Catholic unity. The cities of Italy, having expelled schismatics in Frederick’s presence, have received Catholic bishops. God is witness: unless the lord king recalls his own archbishop, I fear what may be said of him, and shrink from saying it [Col. 0262C]. But if he recalls him and restores peace to God’s Church, I confidently hope that the grace of the prosperous outcomes of former times will flourish again around him and his house through the prayers of the Church.

Why say more? One course of counsel lies open: let him exclude wicked counselors and enemies of the Church, and endeavor to placate the God whom he has offended, since he cannot reign or rule happily against God’s will. God has endured him hitherto in great patience; but unless he takes care, He will soon speak against his excess as a woman in labor.

## LETTER CCXXXIV. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF NORWICH, WHOM HE CALLED GODWIN. (A.D. 1168.)

To his dearest friend Godwin, son of Eadwine the priest, his soldier Godric: greetings, and faithful perseverance unto the crown.

The honor of the military belt with which you adorned me, when I was hurrying to the thresholds of the apostles and you were returning from there, in the city of Sens—which Brennus, leader of the Senones, is said to have built to lodge his invalids—more often compels me to remember you in affection and joy than I use the sword which was bestowed upon me [Col. 0263A]:

> Would that this weapon perish in rust.  
> (Horace.)

And also:

> He who slays us, I cry, would do better not to touch us;  
> he will weep, and be sung throughout the whole renowned world.  
> (Same author.)

This is brought about by Him who has already stretched out His hand in retribution, and who has mercifully made Frederick, the enemy of Christians, a former Augustus for His own glory. Against him and his fellow-thieves I have now served as an exile for five years, not knowing whether any friends have been left to me in our homeland or whether all have fallen into death. For I fear that none are anywhere, since they are found nowhere—men who, when they are struck, have neither voice nor feeling. If even one had survived, it is likely that he would at least inquire after those who were dying.

> . . . . . Does Godric live and breathe  
> the air of heaven, or lie beneath the pitiless shades?  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* I.550.)

Therefore I have thought it necessary earnestly to entreat your affection, whose fidelity, tested as in a furnace, gleams more brightly than gold and is more precious than every topaz, that you carefully inquire concerning their condition, if indeed any remain; and, if any of them still live but are ill, procure for them the medicine which you know to be suitable for their diseases. So that, at least by hearing that they live—even though not that they are well, which no one can persuade me to believe—we may receive, through your intervention, some consolation [Col. 0263C] for this great exile and laborious warfare, in which we fight with beasts for our country’s freedom; for you used to know them.

Act vigorously, then, in what you have begun; rejoice and hope in the things said to us, because, with God as author, we shall soon receive our pay and cast the public enemy into chains, or he will cease his persecution of the homeland by surrendering to the Prince who lives and deservedly rules over the whole earth. We have shut Frederick up within Pavia and hold him under siege. We have restored bishops expelled by schismatics to their sees; and when the head of the ungodly has been crushed, the limbs joined to it by flesh will easily be dissolved.

Do not, therefore, be moved from your understanding—that is, from right understanding—whether by spirit, speech, or letter [Col. 0263D] allegedly sent by an apostolic authority, as though God’s wrath were imminent, abandoning the righteous in tribulation while granting glory and triumph to the ungodly who persist in wickedness. You will shortly see God’s glory and the fulfillment of the promises to the Fathers, which an unbeliever does not deserve to receive. For the man who, when Sennacherib was threatening Jerusalem, heard the prophet’s oracle and distrusted it, refusing to believe that the city would be relieved and exalted by so swift a deliverance, by abundance of provisions, and by the glory of victory, was killed at the city gate when crowds of the faithful rushed to the great works of the divine promise.

If you hear that I am serving in Italy under an altered name, do not be astonished; attribute it to yourself, who gave me the military belt in Italy. Farewell. Care for the lethargic. And if the threefold flesh should lie in ambush against you or happen openly to attack you [Col. 0264A], strive, with the Muses’ aid invoked, to soothe it, or to tame it with the club of Hercules. The pleasant soldiery of the camps of faith, worthy to be embraced for its merits, greets you. I shall not object, provided that you judge it safe, if you show this letter of your soldier to those to whom you are sent.

## LETTER CCXXXV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS, AND MASTER RAYMOND, CHANCELLOR. (A.D. 1168.)

To his lords and friends Perpetual and Felix, Cyril: greetings and the peace which the world cannot give.

Those like yourselves, acquainted with the divine writings, cannot fail to know that the meaning of the whole discourse is often disclosed by the significance of wish-names [Col. 0264B]. May Felix rejoice in perpetuity and Perpetual in felicity; and, for the consolation which they have given to Christ’s poor, may the Lord console and glorify them in the council of the righteous and the congregation.

Indeed, consolation would be necessary, if what you have heard is true—but rather for a public than for a private cause:

> Who could wish to watch the stars and the world falling,  
> and himself be free from fear . . . free from sorrow, free from anxiety?

Not because anything that happens can in itself make sad the righteous man who is confident as a lion, but because, at nature’s prompting and under virtue’s compelling goad, he so sympathizes and rejoices with his neighbor that he counts nothing human alien to himself. “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11) [Col. 0264C]. Certainly, no one: for all are in labor until Christ is reformed or formed in them.

Surely I would not believe that anyone could see the Church wounded in her head, her shepherd struck, crushed, and destroyed, so that Christ’s sheep are scattered and perish, without sorrow. Stupid, or wholly no member of Christ’s body, is the person who is not moved to sympathy by the bitterness of so great an affliction. The Stoics commend *apatheia*, which Latin calls insensibility; but their opinion has been rejected by the surest reason and by the virtue of those who philosophize more rightly, and—what is most powerful—by the commands and examples of Holy Scripture.
