When the Lord saw that the city entrusted with custody and dispensation of the law was ruled by the traditions of scribes and Pharisees, who sought their own interests rather than the Lord’s; that they laid on men’s shoulders burdens heavier and impossible to bear, which they themselves would not touch with a finger; that they sat in Moses’ seat, speaking according to the law but living against it—He wept over it, because He saw that, as its deserts required, it would soon fall [Col. 0264D]. He therefore gave the faithful an example to do likewise, because the scribes and Pharisees of our own time provoke a like scourge. This, indeed, can be, and is, a just cause of grief.

Yet things are going well with those for whose shipwreck you are anxious, because those who have been cast from the arm of man into the bosom of God’s mercy cannot perish. Their liberation, therefore—as undoubting faith persuades us to hope—is close at hand, because they have been entrusted to the help of Him who rescues the poor from the mighty and the poor man who has no helper. Certainly, my dearest friends, this is expedient for various reasons: first, so that they may be bound to God alone and, once freed, Christ’s poor may serve more devotedly; and also so that the greedy and arrogant men whom you know may not possess material for plundering and boasting to their own ruin and that of others, and, swelling up against the Lord and trampling upon the Church of God when she has been freed by God’s benefit, may say: “Our hand is high, and not the Lord has done all these things” [Col. 0265A].

For whoever doubts that the Church is to be freed and Christ’s promises fulfilled is faithless and unworthy to be counted by the Christian name. Therefore fear nothing less than that the son should burst out in anger at his father’s scourge; the servant, under correction, murmur against his teaching master; the pupil be angry at being received; or the sick man resist the cautery or incision of his physician. What if the physician cuts or burns for a time the hand that has long been withered for good works, in order to make it permanently stronger? He who reads that Cyril—whose name means “the weak hand”—was healed by Christ does not wonder at this. For He is the one who strikes and heals; and, what is greater, who kills in order to give life.

Suppose that a delay has been granted to the king—but not until a fixed day, for that too is not asserted. Since it is hoped for, the state of the cause can easily, with the Lord as author, be restored to a better reckoning. Indeed, I do not doubt that it will be restored, though I do not presume this from man, but from Him whose majesty is provoked by such frequent and evident injuries [Col. 0265C]. “For the prosperity of fools will destroy them.”

As for your addition that that man, God’s chosen one but, as is believed, rejected, could have obtained a blessing from the lord pope if he had been willing to remove his beard: it is ridiculous, unless he set such value upon his beard that he believed of himself what is recorded of Samson, that his strength and might consisted in his hair. But, as public report and the evidence of living witnesses make known, his strength is in his loins, and his power in wickedness, deceit, and audacity in lying. The Lord will catch the wise in their own craftiness and, to the glory of His name, will advance His cause, not through those from whom hope was expected, but by whatever miracle He chooses. For, as it is written: “The Lord chose new wars; He himself overthrows the gates of the enemies” (Judges 5) [Col. 0265D]. Gnats defeated Pharaoh; a widow defeated Holofernes; and infantrymen are said, before others, to have defeated the most powerful king of Syria.

The Count of Flanders is working to restore the Church’s peace, hoping that he can more easily reconcile the kings if he has the lord of Canterbury as his helper. He has already treated with the King of England, on whose behalf he is believed to be especially concerned; he has invited the Archbishop of Canterbury a second time to a conference; and he has now obtained that the archbishop will go to the monastery of Tours, to speak with him there when the kings next confer. He is working for the king himself and the archbishop to meet and to negotiate their peace with one another in person. Would that you, or some of our friends [Col. 0266A], were present at the said conference and could there be more certainly informed concerning what is worth knowing.

Let these matters go no further from you than a third person. Let nothing be made known to the cardinals about this affair of the lord of Canterbury: neither that he is coming for the conference nor that his efforts are so necessary for the kings’ reconciliation. When his envoys have returned—which we hope will happen soon—we shall not hesitate to report their news to you. For Cyril is believed, and promised, to be healed upon their return.

Furthermore, know that we have heard for certain that Henry, duke of Saxony, was defeated in a pitched battle by the Archbishop of Magdeburg, the Bishop of Halberstadt, and Margrave Albert. Seven hundred knights fell on the duke’s side, and twenty-two counts were taken or killed [Col. 0266B]; while so few fell or were captured on the bishops’ side that no one complains of the loss. The emperor tried to restore peace to the duke, but they do not agree, especially since under the pretext of war they may separate themselves from association with the schismatics. By God’s will the emperor has become, for the most part, hated and despised by the Germans and Alamanni. To the emperor’s disgrace, the Lombards are building a city near Pavia, at a castle called Roboretum; they call it Alexandria, in honor of Pope Alexander and for the ruin of the Pavians.

## LETTER CCXXXVI. TO ROBERT, SON OF GILLES. (A.D. 1168.)

To Robert, son of Gilles.

[Col. 0266C] The bond of charity is closer than that of blood; and where kinship of spirit is severed, flesh joined to flesh profits nothing. Thus it happens that among brothers one is more truly a brother than another, because, by conformity of character and the increase of affection, true kinship receives its own growth. For the kinship which is merely of flesh belongs no more to human beings than to beasts. Since beasts lack reason and are ignorant of virtue, they do not remember what evils they are; they forget lawful affections; and the more advanced their age, the further they depart from nature and follow the useless appetites of the flesh.

I speak as one who has experienced this to one who has experienced it: abandoned by flesh and blood, I found true kinship among strangers. Since, therefore, you are joined to me by blood [Col. 0266D]—as your very face proves—and surpass others in charity, as the gilded hyacinth proves daily among many other signs, whom should I prefer to you? For I know that you too prefer very few to me, unless perhaps my little nephew has so transferred into himself his father’s affection that he has left nothing of charity, or less than usual, for his uncle. But surely I cannot be persuaded of this. Nor do I doubt that a most ample place for me is reserved in your heart.

Yet you have assigned me the best and most delightful place in your house, after the one which the chest will occupy—the chest containing kinds of things very useful for every medicine. If they were exhausted or diminished during the past summer, do not be troubled, because they grow again in the same gardens where you used to gather them. And if their roots have sunk [Col. 0267A] deep into the ground, dig more deeply for them, because their scent is most sweet and their use most great: every day and hour they bring consolation and profit. Perhaps this is the tree of singular knowledge and unique wisdom, lovely to behold and sweet to eat, which was forbidden to our fathers but granted to their contemporaries. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXVII. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1168.)

To the lord of Canterbury, when Reginald was at Rome.

No one now wonders that Romans deceive their friends, because it is exceedingly famous and known to all that among them:

> The more each man pours money from his own chest,  
> the more faith he has; and, often with a crooked mind,  
> in laws and canons, he who is stronger in payment  
> is stronger in right.  
> [Col. 0267B]

If duplicity is found there, therefore, nothing unexpected has happened, since it is common for divine law to suffer loss where greed invents a need for dispensation; although reason never introduces the overthrow of equity and the mockery of integrity. Yet, for which I give thanks to God and the lord pope, I judge that matters are still being handled well for us: amid so many thunders of threats, so many flatteries of promises, and the contrivances of the Balaamites—who, by suborned and carefully devised lies, have erected their manifold deceit from the East to Sicily—he has not been wholly broken [Col. 0267C]. Rather, as I think, he tries to evade their art by art, to break the onset of madness by reason, and to turn it aside by wisdom.

Yet I shall sing his praises at the end, as he deserves; nor shall I rejoice in the beginnings of a virtue begun, unless perseverance in good deeds brings the end to triumph. In the meantime, everything should be interpreted in the better sense, especially the deeds of the Father and Lord, which cannot be shown to lie within the perversity of guilt.

In this case, I think, it is the king and the man for whom he intercedes who have been deceived rather than you, since in the letters sent to you, after counsel and prayers, the whole matter is entrusted to the judgment of your discretion. And since he still offers you prayers for the release of the lord of Salisbury, it is clear [Col. 0267D] that he either did not know the cardinals’ decision or did not think it should be regarded as binding. Although I believe that the bishop will not use these letters before his envoys return—either because this arrangement will displease the king or because he wishes to be more fully informed by the archdeacon’s counsel—yet, if he does use them, I confidently believe that you will await the return of your envoys and, God willing, hear from them what you can do or what is expedient.

Furthermore, you know that I have long been indebted to the lord of Salisbury; and God knows how deeply I sympathize with his misfortune. Therefore, as I have always done and, with God as author, shall do, I beg with all devotion that you have mercy upon him insofar as you can without compromising the honor of the Church and your own honor [Col. 0268A]. You will never hear other counsel from me. When those who have gone to Rome from both sides return, I trust that our cause will become clearer and, by God’s favor, be restored to a better state. I pray that, as soon as they return, you will let me know what report they have brought.

## LETTER CCXXXVIII. TO MASTER GERARD PUCELLE. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Master Gerard Pucelle.

I grieve, dearest master, and grieve greatly, that I see your severity toward the lord of Canterbury disturbed, to speak my mind, more than is right; for I do not think that he has deserved such indignation from your sincerity [Col. 0268B]. Nor do I say this—“As the Lord lives” (Judges 8)—in order to ensnare your charity, which may God preserve unharmed, but so that friends may be bound more firmly to one another through the assertion of truth, lest from a slight suspicion, God forbid, one should be lost to the other. You know who said: “He who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3).

As for the allegation that some of his people have detracted from your honor before the Most Christian King, let one thing be clear to you—if it is clear, I do not know. But this is most certain to me: I have often heard him excuse your departure, both before the king and before others, and intercede repeatedly on your behalf. Therefore I cannot believe that any of his people has detracted from you with his knowledge. For if he did not know it and does not approve it, it is true, or at least probable, that he did not consent.

He does indeed have among his fellow-exiles some perhaps less prudent men in the king’s court, who may have spoken some incautious word against you or another, perhaps so that they might become more acceptable to those whom they thought would be pleased by what they said [Col. 0268C]. God is my witness that I neither saw nor heard them commit what is charged against them, and I still wholly do not know who they are—if, indeed, there are any such persons.

But I do not doubt that the said king was angered for three reasons. The first is that, after receiving much favor and intimacy from him, when you were passing near the place where he was staying, you turned aside and departed from the kingdom in which so many benefits had been bestowed upon you from childhood, where your name had become famous, without even greeting him. The second is that you went over to schismatics—I do not call you a schismatic—and that, though by your reputation for virtue and learning you ought to have raised up and strengthened the weaker, you gave everyone an example tending to common harm. For they are less afraid to communicate with schismatics when they see so great a man kept in their fellowship, a man who, from the many necessities of his condition, cannot while he remains in it refrain from their prayer, table, kiss, or the other things known in religion as signs of communion [Col. 0268D]. And what makes this accusation weigh most heavily with the king is that he says you adhered to that schismatic who was the maker, instigator, and standard-bearer of the whole schism, and was condemned by name by the Apostolic See.

The third reason—which I too, whatever others may say, think the greatest—is that you turned aside to the Germans, who, as he has been persuaded, would gladly rise against his kingdom if they could and dared. And that they can and dare, they proclaim in great words; they swell with threats; and those who are even within his kingdom—indeed, who sit at ease in a chair while living in Paris—find fault with him, as you know, because he lives civilly among his own people, because he does not assume tyranny in barbarian fashion, and because he does not always go surrounded by armed guards, like one who fears for his head. He knows the manners of that people; I think he has often complained about them even to you. Yet the lord of Canterbury pleaded, in my presence, and at last obtained that, insofar as lies with him, your recall should be permitted [Col. 0269A].

As for your assertion that he sent the lord pope a copy of your letters, I do not deny it: they were communicated to him in good faith and with our support as well. But he did not procure this to your disadvantage, as He who searches hearts knows. Rather, he was endeavoring to advance his own cause and to improve your standing with the lord pope. He wished the pope to know that your faith and devotion are with the Church of God and the Apostolic See, although, by dispensation and in order that those who have turned away might more readily be converted by your efforts to God’s honor and the benefit of Catholic truth, you dwell among them for a time. If some of the envoys were less diligent in securing your recall, their negligence should not be imputed to the sender [Col. 0269B]. For the mandate is certain, and the envoys’ diligence was hoped for.

Nor do I doubt that the lord pope is satisfied concerning this, since he is certainly known to have replied that he would never recall anyone—not even the greatest patriarch—if something of this kind had occurred. But let whoever wishes return, and let him return as he ought. And if your pupil, Master Richard, my kinsman, who died while returning, had returned, we should have been more certain on this point.

As to the report that he conveyed to the lord pope remarkable news, allegedly received from you, concerning the state of the Empire: I reply that he conveyed what he received, but not from you; nor did he write to the pope that he had received it from you. For the condition of the Empire becomes known more fully through others. Nor is it surprising [Col. 0269C] that so great a matter cannot be concealed.

But after the interception of those letters and Master Richard’s death, when he spoke of this matter with the cardinals, they advised him not to presume to recall you without the counsel and will of the lord pope. Rather, they urged him to consider that the lord of Reims and all his suffragans, summoned for this purpose, had not dared to receive the Bishop of Cambrai into communion even when he repented with tears, before the lord pope had been consulted. Yet, as they replied, your case is very different. He had entered into the error of the schismatics; you have not consented to error in the midst of schism. He was a bishop and seemed to have subverted Catholics; you, holding private status, are trying to recall schismatics to unity [Col. 0270A].

The lord of Canterbury therefore sent again to the Roman Church, charging his envoys, in my presence, to strive earnestly to obtain your recall from the lord pope. I myself composed the letter from the knowledge of Master Ralph Niger. I asked him to write you an orderly account of this affair. It is certain that our envoys have reached the curia and have long conducted a major dispute there against the envoys of the lord King of England; but, of all seven, not one had returned by the Sunday after Ascension most recently past.

I do not write the outcome of their dispute, because it is still unknown, except that I hear from those returning from the Apostolic See that they prospered in the case and prevailed over the king’s envoys. But to what extent is uncertain. For I do not know whether they return having obtained what they desired and their requests having been fulfilled, or whether the entire sum of their success is that the king’s envoys return ingloriously with the affair unsettled [Col. 0270B].

I recently saw your messenger at the conference of kings held near Meudon, where peace was being negotiated. You had several supporters among the English, but I could not discover what they obtained on your behalf. I saw another of your people in Paris; and your friend Lord G . . ., enclosed at Saint-Hilaire, knows how I wrote to the lord of Canterbury for your recall, since he inspected the letter. It would have been most welcome to me had it reached your knowledge. But when the envoys return, by God’s favor—as is believed likely to happen soon—we shall be more certain concerning both our affair and yours.

Therefore, if you please, your moderation should not be irrevocably angered [Col. 0270C], nor ought you to set so hasty a date for your departure, because it is neither ours nor yours to prescribe a time or a limit of endurance to divine mercy. Rather, it is right that we all, Christ’s poor and exiles, should learn from what you read that the priests learned from Judith the widow: to possess our souls in the strength of patience, to wait in devotion, and in silence for God’s salvation. Thus, upon those who wait, consoling grace will come unexpectedly; and when Holofernes’ head has been cut off, the children of Israel will rejoice in the peace long desired.

Nor do I dissuade you, if your mind is so disposed, from making peace with the lord king of England—a peace which, you say, is being offered to you almost on terms of your own choosing. Yet I pray that the form of it may be preserved which, when the advantage of circumstances arises, prejudices neither your reputation nor your safety. Indeed, terms of peace have been offered to most of us; but an oath is demanded from all, which, I think, cannot be observed without harm to religion. For how will fidelity remain unharmed if subjects are not permitted to obey their pastors and prelates in matters belonging to God? Although the offence of disobedience is not expressly stated in the undertaking, it is uncertain what lies in the mind of the person demanding it. One thing I know: no one will be able to retain the lord king’s favour who, amid this storm, maintains obedience to the Archbishop of Canterbury or is believed to have fellowship of charity with him. But you are among his sheep and, as I think, received him from the Lord as your pastor first, or among the first.

See therefore, dearest brother, and take care to walk cautiously, lest disturbance—which has always been foreign to the philosopher’s gravity—gain dominion over your mind; lest, driven by it, you commit something for which repentance will afterwards come too late. Rather have recourse to the weapons of prayer and almsgiving, that God may lead you, with the other righteous, through straight paths and make you walk in his ways—he who makes all things work together for good to those who love him. He will deliver you, whose name is a most strong tower; and the outcome will be joyful if it has such and so great a guide.

Peace between the kings is being discussed and is still thought likely to result. Meanwhile our world is silent. Thus I write no news, except that the Earl of Leicester has fallen asleep in the Lord [Col. 0271B]. Earl Patrick has been killed by the rebellious Poitevins. The lord-elect of Chartres has been chosen Archbishop of Sens. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXIX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1168.)

John of Salisbury to JOHN, Bishop of Poitiers.

After I had written my earlier letter, these fresh reports came to our knowledge. Such fruit was produced by the lord pope’s letters sent to the king of England: Master Gerard, returning from Cologne, passed over to the king of England without either seeing or greeting his lord of Canterbury—the man who had made him a clerk and conferred upon him his first ecclesiastical benefice [Col. 0271C]. He did homage to the king and took the oath which the others took; and he adheres to the court, chosen, as they say, as a champion against Christ’s poor and exiles.

The abbot of St Augustine’s told Lord Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, that he and his companions had said or done nothing at court except by the cardinals’ instruction; and that John of Naples and John of Saints John and Paul had caused the threats which you heard had been made to be made. He also said that the Bishop of Porto aided the king’s envoys in obtaining letters. The king himself also told the Bishop of Worcester that he and all the other bishops were exempt from the authority of the lord of Canterbury. He ordered them [Col. 0271D] not to fear any threats, because he now had the lord pope and all the cardinals in his purse.

So greatly does he boast that he says openly that he has at last obtained the privilege of his grandfather, who in his own land was king, apostolic legate, patriarch, emperor, and everything he wished. And, as regards the Roman Church, what he says is almost credible. For what more could Octavian, or the heresiarch of Cremona, have granted him? What else could their cardinals have done than those aforesaid lords, who sharpened the tongues of the English and made them spew out fire and poison, so that they might terrify the lord pope and bend him to their will?

These things will be written in the annals of the Roman Church. And surely, God willing, writers will not be lacking to record that, at the request and under the threats [Col. 0272A] of the king of England—whose intolerable excesses he had endured for so long—the pope, disregarding the order of reason and law, deprived of the authority of his office, as though he were a criminal, the herald of truth, defender of liberty, preacher of justice for the Lord’s cause, now in exile for nearly four years with an innumerable multitude of innocents. Not because they deserved it, indeed, but because it pleased the tyrant.

Yet by open letters, which are in our possession, he had granted him full legal use of the authority of his office. In these he expressly declared that he “neither gave a command to excommunicate the king himself nor forbade it.” Good God, what novelty has occurred? The Holy Spirit says in his law: “Cry aloud; do not cease” (Isa. 58). And behold, some spirit, I know not what spirit, going out from the City into the world, says to preachers: “Be silent; do not cry aloud.” The Apostle commands, when instructing a bishop: “Fulfil your ministry” (2 Tim. 4). And behold, the apostolic lord commands: “Desist from the ministry of your office.”

But perhaps he supposes that he can soften the man through patience. Has he not tested this in the Archbishop of Canterbury, who, now deprived of his see for nearly four years, finds himself exposed to the winds of both the Apostolic See’s slackness and that tyrant’s oppression? Let the lord pope, I beg, take thought for his conscience; take thought also for the reputation, honour, and safety of the Church. And you should report these matters to him more diligently, and persuade the lord cardinals to remember God’s judgment, which Christ’s poor continually invoke against all enemies of the Church’s liberty.

## LETTER CCXL. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER. (A.D. 1168.)

John of Salisbury to Master BALDWIN, Archdeacon of Exeter.

Where serious matters are at stake, it is inappropriate to multiply trifles; and it is unbecoming—after the manner of deceitful physicians—when necessity demands one thing, to give needy friends words instead of deeds. You have long known that I am the less pleased by the view of your nominalist friends because, consisting wholly in words, it has not embraced the usefulness of things, whereas it is an unquestioned truth among the wise [Col. 0272D] that philosophy seeks things, not words.

Therefore, to deal with you more briefly in the manner of my realist friends, you will gather from the letters sent to our Benedict the position in which the cause of the priesthood and of the kingdom stands. But I thought it necessary to write to you particularly about what meanwhile wounds my soul more grievously and, I think, will burn your heart more bitterly—if the report, widely spread in many ears, concerning our Bishop of Worcester is true.

For it is said that he acted both unwisely and shamelessly in the case of his archbishop and consecrator, attempting in the presence of bishops and others to prove from it that the cause of the lord of Canterbury did not rest upon the integrity of justice and did not seek the Church’s liberty, but only his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ; because he refuses to yield on the condition that the king grant the Church its due liberty for ever [Col. 0273A]. It is also said that he added, mockingly, that he was ready to resign his own bishopric on the same compact.

This, they say, pleased not even those who heard this display of his purity: both because of the person speaking, whom they loved and had thought more sound in judgment and will; because it would be ruinous as a precedent; and because this kindness of the lord king could easily be revoked and the Church forced back into its former, indeed into a worse, slavery. For who thereafter would dare to cry out for liberty? Who would revive a cause in which and for which he remembered that so great a bishop had fallen?

Another path to liberty must therefore be sought; he may communicate another counsel to his friends. And, if he wishes to test in himself whether he can thus redeem the liberty of his Church and bishopric, he may do so; for, as I have learned from the men of Canterbury, the archbishop will not acquiesce in this counsel, nor allow himself to be deceived by any promise, so as either to exchange his bishopric, as some are contriving [Col. 0273B], or to desist from the pursuit of his right, or to make peace while the customs over which the controversy arose remain in force.

I transcribed these things for you so that, if you see an opportunity, you may persuade our aforesaid lord and friend not to neglect clearing himself of this suspicion, if the matter is important to him. For all who heard this report with me felt pity for his former life and reputation. The Archbishop of Canterbury, however, stopped those who were recounting it, saying that rumours ought not to be believed, especially when the allegation was so unworthy of so great a man. I know, nevertheless, that he was somewhat moved; but, being a prudent man, he adapted himself to the occasion.

You will see from the reply to the lord pope’s letters why, after many threats, the archbishop declared the Bishop of London excommunicated; and why he continues to regard as excommunicated those whom the Bishop of St Asaph, imprudently deceived, absolved, until they satisfy the lord pope’s command. And because the cardinals themselves are known to have exceeded the bounds of their commission, he will henceforth pay less heed to their counsel. For they received no authority to judge him unless he should consent. That I wished the Bishop of Worcester to be forewarned proceeds from the abundance [Col. 0273D] of charity; and whenever it is opportune I shall gladly labour for his honour.

## LETTER CCXLI. TO THE CONVENT OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1168.)

To the whole body of saints who serve the Lord in the holy Church of Canterbury, the first see of the Britains: their fellow servant and least brother, greeting, and obedience pleasing to God, to be preferred before all sacrifices.

From where, my most beloved lords and sweetest brothers, shall I begin? From where shall a sad spirit, dismayed by another’s error, take the beginning of its speech? To what point will the address of a wretched soul, languishing with grief, proceed? Until now, your negligence—if I may use a most restrained term, fitting for lords—could be excused. But behold: if one follows popular opinion, lukewarmness has turned into hatred; negligence has passed into contempt; charity’s feigned show has burst forth into deceit and proves itself, by evident facts, to be treachery [Col. 0274A]. So I say, if popular opinion prevails. But by what arguments can it hereafter be refuted?

Certainly, fleshly wisdom, which presumes deceit, always advances to an outcome contrary to its intention; and from the very source from which profits of pleasure were hoped, losses arise to every advantage and intention. Thus the Jews, lest they lose their place and lest the priests lose authority over the nation, laid snares for Christ; and, falling into the pit they made, they lost both place and nation when the Romans came. So also you, if what the populace cries is true—for I could not easily believe that such blindness had befallen so great watchfulness and concern—you, I say, sent to the king so that, when your prior had died, he might appoint another in his place in a matter not belonging to him.

What else, I ask, did Israel do when Moses was absent, demanding from Aaron that he make gods to go before them in the wilderness after the fashion of the nations, and extorting a bull’s head as a deity, breathing incense to an idol as majesty? But just as that idol was crushed when Moses returned, so whatever idol may be given you will be crushed when the Lord’s law regains strength and justice returns to the Church [Col. 0274C]. It was ground into powder and scattered into the liquid which the people were to drink, so that they might be compelled thus to expel what they had worshipped. And whoever he may be, being the work of flesh rather than God—if he is treated well, at least—he will be turned from head into tail and will become an abomination to those who fear God. But if badly, no place for him will be found in the land of the saints, which he is known to have profaned.

But how did it happen that you, first among all the churches of the whole kingdom, believed that a prior must be sought from the prince? Was it perhaps this precaution: that the archbishop might henceforth be unable to claim anything for himself in the appointment of the prior? Not so, brothers, not so. Rather, you should have feared losing your ancient right when you proceed to a profane misuse and forfeit your own privilege by seizing another’s. Would that you had not furnished an example of this ruin, abandoning the rule of blessed Benedict, turning your backs upon the law, and neglecting the constitutions by which the holy Fathers taught Christians how they must live [Col. 0274D].

By what reasons, however, can the widespread and notorious report be removed? Your prior died; you sent to the king. No mention of the archbishop was made among you. Wisely indeed: so that the king, to whom fools believe the rights of the priesthood belong, might absolve the dead brother’s soul. Otherwise, no reason appears why anyone should receive the care of souls from his hand—much less the care of yours, who by merit of learning, religion, and dignity stand at the head of the kingdom, appointed by the Lord in the first see of the Britains, so that through you the whole island may be illuminated both by the word of teaching and by the example of holy conduct [Col. 0275A].

That wise and religious brother also—I do not remember his name—having taken counsel with the chief priests and others whom I deliberately leave unnamed, most zealously ensured that your innocence, if indeed you possess any, could not be excused through the diligence of a friend. In the name of the whole convent, he framed an appeal against the archbishop and declared him an enemy of the Church, as though he had injured you in anything or it were established that he had conceived any intention of harming you. The man used prudent counsel who preferred to have as an enemy the father and lord whom you should have had as a friend.

Many present mocked the man and pursued him with curses wherever they felt there was safe freedom of speech, saying that nothing surprising had occurred, because the monks of Canterbury have always possessed, as though by inheritance, this trait: to hate their archbishops. And, to support their statement, they say: “They twice drove Anselm into exile for justice’s sake, though they never gave him any comfort. They despised Ralph; they hated William; they laid snares for Theobald; and now, behold, they gratuitously and insatiably persecute Thomas” [Col. 0275B].

What friend of the Church, much less one nurtured by her, could hear these things sung abroad by the uncircumcised in the streets of Ashkelon and at the crossroads of Gath without pain? Who among Christ’s faithful could restrain tears? God is my witness that I do not believe that this brother, whoever he may be, acted in this madness of presumption with the convent’s counsel [Col. 0275C]. Yet others cannot easily be persuaded of this if you ratify what has been done; if you do not punish that presumptuous man with severe correction; if you stand by with counsel or assistance those who seek your father’s life in order to take it away.

Otherwise, you will seem to have commanded, and to agree with, those who say: “We have no king but Caesar; crucify, crucify the bishop,” who dared stand for the Church’s liberty and maintained that God’s law must be preferred to human traditions. You do not know what the coming day will bring; and from the lord pope’s letters you will infer how great is the danger in which those whom the archbishop excommunicated, together with all their accomplices, have been placed. Nor are they safe through the evasion of appeal, since the supreme pontiff excludes appeals and has already commanded the legates to restore to the former sentence those who seemed to have been absolved, unless they make satisfaction at once [Col. 0275D]. The archbishop, moreover, has declared to the cardinals that the Bishop of London and several others are excommunicated, and has supplied reasons which would take too long to enumerate.

You would sometimes receive more letters, and from more persons, were it not that you report to the king, as if they were enemies, the warnings which your friends send you for your protection. Farewell, most beloved brothers and lords; and labour more earnestly, so that your friends—who are few—may be able to succeed in defending your innocence.

## LETTER CCXLII. TO ROBERT, ARCHDEACON OF SURREY. (A.D. 1168.)

John of Salisbury to ROBERT, Archdeacon of Surrey.

Nothing is more hateful before God and men than the vice of ingratitude. I should rightly seem branded with its mark if my tongue were silent in giving thanks whenever, after benefits received, an opportunity for communication is afforded. Therefore, rendering such thanks as I can and as many as circumstances permit, I venture confidently to entrust you to him who repays deserts, who rewards all good things with a generous and abundant hand and leaves no evil unpunished [Col. 0276A]. This, meanwhile, is our consolation; this is the unceasing hope of those who fear the Lord. For who has hoped in him and been forsaken? Let anyone invent such a case if he wishes, for it cannot be found in the whole course of the sacred Scriptures; nor will the Ancient of Days be found a liar, he who promised that he would do the will of those who fear him.

We have received the earnest of this promise; we now experience the faithfulness of him who promises and feel the loving concern of him who comforts us in every tribulation. The fifth year of my exile is passing, and behold, though no consolation had previously been lacking to me, this is an added abundance: the Church’s liberty seems to stand at the door and has already set its foot, in part, upon the island. For, as the cardinal-envoys attest, the king has renounced certain very evil customs which he had previously been accustomed to assert, abjuring them and their authors by oath. He agrees that appeal to the Apostolic See shall be free, that clerics shall not be drawn before secular courts, and certain other things—would that he proved these in deed as he confirms them in speech [Col. 0276C].

The cardinals have no authority over the archbishop; and, by apostolic letters which they have recently received, they have been ordered neither to enter England nor to involve themselves in episcopal consecrations or other affairs of the realm unless full peace has first been restored to the Archbishop of Canterbury. Others also have been commanded, with every appeal set aside, to restore to the former sentence the lord of Canterbury’s excommunicates who seemed to have been absolved, unless they make satisfaction immediately, restoring to him and his people the possessions of the churches and everything they received from them. The Bishop of London has been reported to the cardinals and to the lord pope as excommunicated, for reasons too long to recount [Col. 0276D].

If you wish, these things will become known through you to the lord bishop. I write to him less directly for this reason: lest, under the pretext of a letter, my need should seem to have sought an occasion for begging. Therefore, amid the pressures of this exile, I have never thought it proper to write to suspicious persons who imagine that expressions of need always tend toward gain and relief of distress; I write only to those whom I think will not interpret the speech of a friend as shameless begging. But I ask that he be greeted in my name, to whom I owe much; and, God granting, I shall give thanks for the sincerity of charity which he keeps for me in his heart and, when necessary, will show in deed. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXLIII. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1168.)

John of Salisbury to BALDWIN, Archdeacon of Exeter.

If the comic poet considers nothing human alien to himself, I do not doubt that you care what outcome awaits the cause of God and the labour of friends who suffer for the Church’s liberty or fear the dangers threatening them. Your kindness, gracious by its own merit to all good men, has long been made known to me by many proofs; but, to speak from conscience, it is sweeter to no mortal than to me [Col. 0277A].

You may learn what was done in the conference between the lord of Canterbury and the cardinals, and likewise how the bishops who crossed the sea against the archbishop appealed again, both from the reports of many persons and, more faithfully, I think, from the letters of which copies are sent to you. For I have formed an intimacy with the lord of Canterbury and his fellow exiles, as with friends, so that, should need arise, I may assist them more conveniently. Neither he nor they think their secrets should be hidden from me; by God’s favour I shall keep them faithfully concealed, and shall give aid when my friends’ circumstances require it in such a way that those who rely upon the integrity of my faith suffer no loss. This is what the rule governing the discharge of duties prescribes; this is certainly pleasing to all the men of Canterbury.

Many of them are your friends and, by right of their old association, put confidence in you as in a brother [Col. 0277C]. They therefore acknowledge themselves bound to those dear to you, and desire that provision be made for them, for your sake, as for themselves. For whoever is helpful to their friends is helpful also to them. Therefore, although the Bishop of Exeter—who cannot be troubled without burden to you—has been found neither a friend nor of service in any respect to the archbishop or any of his party, nevertheless, because he is your friend by right, I grieve that the perversity of certain almost execrable men has laid snares for him. May God protect him; and you, guided by grace, be diligent to offer counsel, as you obtain it from the Father of lights, through alms, persistence in prayer, and careful deliberation.

For unless God prevents it, he will offend either the archbishop, with injury to his conscience, or the king and his cardinals [Col. 0277D]. He will receive, if he has not already received, letters of the legates ordering him to absolve the lord of Canterbury’s excommunicates, although the legates have no authority at all to give such an order and have been forbidden by apostolic letters to enter England or involve themselves in the affairs of the realm unless full peace is first restored to the archbishop. By another command they are ordered, without delay and with every appeal set aside, to restore the aforesaid excommunicates to the sentence of excommunication unless they make satisfaction, as you may see from the letters of which I send you a copy.

The Cardinal of Pavia has recently absolved the Archdeacon of Poitiers. From this it is clear how void was the absolution granted to them by the Bishop of Wales [Col. 0278A], and how dangerously communion with them has consequently been maintained. If therefore the Bishop of Exeter absolves them, since it is plain that they are unrepentant, he will first offend God and then grievously provoke the archbishop. But if he does not absolve them, he will seem to have incurred the king’s and his cardinals’ indignation. For they will say: “Behold, it is now openly apparent that he wholly favours the archbishop; that he does not love the lord king’s honour; that he despises the authority of the Apostolic See.”

If the cardinals had been prudent, if they had feared the Lord, if they had not made flesh their arm, they could have reflected upon what they had undertaken by their commission, what the wording of the apostolic letters was, and what was expedient for the Church; and they would have abstained altogether from commands of this kind. Or if they had resolved to prefer man to God [Col. 0278B], why did they not impose this office upon one of those who was present and hastening home? For the Bishops of London, Salisbury, Chichester, and Worcester sat with them; yet, as is said, they thrust this burden upon the shoulders of the Bishop of Exeter—though it is more particularly imposed upon the Bishop of Worcester. If what is said is true, he has spoken against his archbishop more than befits a man of such moderation. But let the bishops be accused.

The Lord knows those who are his, and the truth will be made manifest on that day. Meanwhile, the guilty person will not acquit himself as his own judge; and he who prepares a pit for his brother will fall into it first. What then shall your Bishop of Exeter, and mine for love of you, do amid these snares? If you possess counsel, or any of your friends who rejoice in him possesses it, use it. Otherwise, meanwhile acquiesce in what has been said without prejudice to better counsel. For I know that the Bishop of Exeter gladly listens to you.

If they come to be absolved, let him examine the tenor of the commission, demand repentance, and exact confession. If the form of the commission does not prevent it, let him require a lawful guarantee concerning satisfaction [Col. 0278C]. Let him also display the apostolic letters by which they must necessarily be restored to the former sentence if they delay to make satisfaction. Let him offer admonitions and explain diligently what dangers threaten. If their absolution fails through their own fault, his position is safe. But if they refuse to repent and nevertheless press more importunately for absolution, let this be answered in all charity and moderation: that such a form of absolution is contrary to evangelical and apostolic teaching and, from ancient times, cannot be exercised by bishops without higher authority; so that the matter may be referred to the cardinals for consultation.

Let it also be said to them that absolution will not profit them for salvation unless repentance, confession, and satisfaction according to their means come first. For the legates will never be so shameless as to judge the unrepentant fit to be absolved. But if they repent and publicly promise amendment, perhaps they may be absolved—even though a guarantee cannot be exacted from them and is not included in the commission—so that the king’s and cardinals’ indignation may be averted; for it may be presumed that the commissioners intended this safeguard. But whenever they are present, let there be everywhere and publicly a protest asserting divine law [Col. 0279A].

Nevertheless, I know that the archbishop will be displeased if they are absolved at the command of men who presume to command bishops not by authority received but through the audacity of rashness, and who have no authority over them. And he will rightly be displeased. But because I and your other friends among the men of Canterbury have earned much favour with the archbishop, though he may be hurt, I trust that he will be appeased and will wholly forgive us in his heart if, in this necessity, he sees anything presumed against him.

Had I seen the wording of the commission, the way of counsel would be clearer. I therefore earnestly ask you not to delay sending me the letters themselves, if they have already been delivered. Nor should it slip your memory that in the letters which John of Oxford brought, the lord pope commanded that, if the excommunicated persons were in danger of death [Col. 0279B], they should then be absolved after taking an oath that, if they recovered, they would obey the apostolic command. The same condition of oath is inserted in the letters by which the cardinals are ordered to restore them to the sentence of anathema unless they make immediate satisfaction. I send you a copy of the later letters, so that their ruling may be made public and may protect those in need.

For one who fears God will be moved to dare less toward his own death. But if that friend of yours manages to untie this knot by some means, I fear a harsher snare. For I fear that the chief priests who have taken counsel how they may kill the Lord’s Christ and destroy the Church’s liberty, after summoning the king’s officials, will wish to induce or compel your Bishop of Exeter [Col. 0279C] to subscribe to the appeal made on the counsel of the king and his cardinals, in the name of the realm and priesthood, and to support the proceeding by the testimony of his letters. Perhaps, by the king’s authority, they will command him, by the allegiance he owes the king and by his love for the honour of the realm and priesthood, to undertake the case with the other envoys and prosecute it in his own person.

If he does either of these things, I firmly believe that he will offend God and know that he will perhaps offend the archbishop irreparably. For he was one of the archbishop’s opponents at Northampton with the other appellants. Again, he stood with those appealing a second time, and these acts were treated as though they had never occurred. But if now, for the third time, unburdened by ratification, he turns upon himself the malice of others, he will seem with them to thirst for his father’s blood and will wound his own conscience more deeply than the Church’s cause or the person of him whose ruin is sought [Col. 0279D].

But if he does not do it, his past services will not prevent him from being publicly proclaimed an enemy of the realm and priesthood. And even if he does all these things, I fear the same outcome. Such is that man’s nature that whoever, for any reason, passes over or delays carrying out any one command whatsoever forfeits with him the benefit of every service. Yet such is the moderation of his requests and the sobriety of his commands that it is sometimes necessary to resist him.

The sum of my counsel, therefore, is that, with diligence and entire care of mind, your friend should always, as far as possible, be retained as a friend without harm to religion. But if a crisis comes in which necessity compels him either to offend that man or to sin, God must be preferred, so that the conscience may remain whole [Col. 0280A]. Evils must not be done so that goods may result; nor should the anger of majesty be appeased through offences, so that it may turn against or crush its faithful people’s enemies. If he is for us, who is against us?

Accordingly, if they demand ratification or ask for a subscription, it seems to me, with due respect to better counsel, that a delay may be requested until the bishop has consulted his Church and the religious men of his diocese. For it does not seem a mark of great prudence for a man without complaint to plunge himself into other people’s disputes. And while a witness may attest what he has seen and heard, what can one testify who was not present at the business and hears only the enemies of one party, seeking their own interests rather than God’s [Col. 0280B]? Those who were absent from the appellants may use the same argument, especially since they neither ordered an appeal nor knew of it. They may, I say, if there are any in so great a kingdom who dare to profess the truth they have conceived in their minds.

The Bishop of London fears for his own head and therefore seeks companions in his madness, so that what he has presumed may remain unpunished because so many have joined in it. But if they press more urgently, let the matter, if possible, be deferred to consultation with the cardinals. Nevertheless, the king’s wish need not be denied insofar as his justice appears; a letter may be written for him, and the lord pope may be entreated to restore peace to the Church, preserve the king’s honour, and advance justice, as the Holy Spirit may teach. But if they demand more specific acts, whatever is specified against conscience and honour will have neither appearance nor beauty, and certainly no happy outcome [Col. 0280C].

It is indeed not expedient to undertake the prosecution of this cause; but one who is compelled may perhaps rejoice in the delay by which he may seek what is necessary and put his household in order. Perhaps, under that pretext, resources may be gathered and spent more acceptably before God. In accepting the legation itself, however, every defect and impediment of the cause must be formally protested, so that conscience may remain uninjured and a bitter outcome may not afterwards be imputed to him.

Perhaps a new security by oath will be demanded for the more diligent execution of the commands; but I do not see how it can be given without disgrace. I believe nothing more useful than delay, if it can be obtained [Col. 0280D], because, with the Lord’s help, meanwhile either peace will be restored, or the lord pope or the cardinals will adopt another policy, or the whole form of the business will have to be changed. Would that the dangers feared are graver than the reality, and that anxiety has imposed varied fears on one who loves.

If the Bishops of Chichester and Worcester give their attention and diligence, as I think they can, I shall give less credence to rumours concerning how your Bishop of Exeter is to be extricated. Otherwise they will be thought to have contrived their brother’s danger because they refused to prevent it. But hold this certain: the archbishop does not regard as valid certain absolutions performed by the cardinals, and he has informed them of this. Yet, deferring to the Apostolic See, he did not wish publicly to accuse them, especially since they promise speedily to correct what they are known, having been deceived, rashly to have undertaken [Col. 0281A]. The cardinals asked the archbishop not to declare the Bishop of London or others excommunicated while there was hope of peace; at that time he agreed.

## LETTER CCXLIV. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER. (A.D. 1168, May.)

John of Salisbury to BALDWIN, Archdeacon of Exeter.

After I returned safely, by God’s grace, from Saint-Gilles about the middle of Lent, I resolved, dearest friend, to forewarn your charity concerning what was being done in France and Italy. [Col. 0281B] For I know that it is sometimes expedient, and often pleasant, to know beforehand the movements of the times and, from those things which by divine nod precede human minds, to contemplate, as it were, the sequence of destinies. But because peace between the kings was under negotiation, and Frederick—the former Augustus, broken by the crime and obstinacy of schism—was pretending that he wished to return to Catholic unity, I deferred my purpose until the outcome of such great affairs should become more fully known.

For when the German tyrant perceived that he was deprived of military protection, that the cities of Italy were preparing to rush upon him, that at Pavia he was by no means safe because of the rash act of his followers, who had blinded a certain nobleman of Pavia, and that the count of Maurienne had barred every route of escape because of injuries inflicted upon him—so that he seemed unable by any means [Col. 0281C] to evade the forces of the Lombards—he relied upon the assistance of the count of Biandrate and the marquis of Montferrat, and withdrew into the marquis’s territory, leaving thirty Lombard hostages with the lord of Biandrate. He distributed among the castles of the marquis for custody other hostages whom he had received; and, because the Lombards were pursuing him with an army assembled to the number of twenty thousand soldiers and intended to besiege him, he himself fled from castle to castle with the aforesaid count and marquis, lurking as if in the shadow of death. Thus, as worthy men of full faith and authority who were present say, he scarcely dared, for two or three days, to spend the night in the same lodging.

This misery of the tyrant—or rather, this glory of God and consolation of the Church—was witnessed on our side by the canons of Noyon and the envoys of Count Henry; and on your side by the representatives of the illustrious king of England, who had gone there for various reasons. The men of Noyon were seeking to bring back their archdeacon Boniface, marquis of Italy, whom they had elected bishop: an honourable man and Catholic throughout the entire storm of schism. Count Henry was investigating the condition of the Empire. The king of England’s envoys, however, gave oaths concerning a marriage to be contracted between the son of the aforesaid marquis and the sister of the king of Scotland; and they discharged an embassy to the often-mentioned tyrant—in the opinion of many—in order that, thus displaying the resources and friendship of the Empire, they might frighten the French. But this cunning is turning wholly to the opposite result. [Col. 0282A] For the French are all the more encouraged when they see their enemies, almost desolate—indeed desperate—seeking borrowed assistance and imploring as patrons those who need a defender.

While, therefore, the emperor was in such straits and despaired altogether of escape, he entered into negotiations with religious men whom it was known were faithful to the lord pope, pretending that he would make peace with the Church of God. There is in a Carthusian house [Note: [Col. 0281D] Paris edition: “Canterbury.”] a very devout man, formerly most intimate with the emperor, who had long ago withdrawn from him because of the burden of schism upon his conscience and felt very great compassion for him. This man therefore approached him in tears, asserting that he knew for certain that [Col. 0282B] he would have no peace unless he restored peace to God’s Church. He pressed the matter and obtained that the emperor should summon by his letters the Carthusian prior, the Cistercian abbot, and the bishop of Pavia, whom he had expelled, and promise to abide by their counsel in all things—provided only that they would take upon themselves the risk of the oath which they had caused to be made against Pope Alexander.

All who heard these words rejoiced, and the Lombards already began to act more mildly, hoping that the man had been converted. Meanwhile the aforesaid marquis negotiated with his kinsman, the count of Maurienne, that he might permit the emperor to leave, promising him not only restoration of what had been taken away, but mountains of gold and the perpetual favour of the Empire, with honour and glory.

The religious men whom he had summoned set out, except the Cistercian abbot, who was detained by a serious illness and sent in his place Lord Geoffrey of Auxerre, formerly abbot of Clairvaux. He sent ahead a certain brother to ascertain from the tyrant where and when he wished to hold conference with them. But the tyrant, having heard of their arrival and letters, and now certain of his own escape after obtaining a truce, answered that they would come in vain for this purpose unless they openly brought with them an angel from heaven, or came endowed with power to perform miracles, so that they could cleanse lepers and raise the dead. Thus they returned home. The Carthusian convert himself, who had conducted the embassy, told me this.

[Col. 0282D] The emperor, having collected the hostages whom he had dispersed, hastened to depart. He came to Saint Ambrose with about thirty knights in his company. Leaving thence hastily in the morning, he hanged, near Susa on the height of a certain mountain, a noble hostage of Brescia, accusing him of having known of the conspiracy of the Italians and—what was more—of being the contriver of the assembled army that was expelling him from Italy. He took the other hostages with him into Susa.

But the citizens and inhabitants of the place had the gates shut and armed guards posted; they took the hostages from the tyrant, saying that destruction and extermination threatened them from the other cities if they allowed their neighbours and friends, most noble men of Italy, to be carried off in this manner to Germany for execution—especially since he had still in Italy hanged a powerful and high-born man, while a way of escape lay open to himself and his followers at pleasure. [Col. 0283A] They took such great care to keep the hostages that they permitted no one who spoke Italian to leave.

The emperor, however, put on the dress of a servant and, pretending that he was arranging lodging for some great man, went out at night with five other servants, glad that fate had granted him the chance to lose Italy, which he had deserved to retain at so great a cost. Passing thence through Chrysopolis, he threw Burgundy into turmoil by threatening its magnates. Proceeding onward, he found Germany and Saxony disturbed beyond measure, and perceived his brother to be more hostile than all the rest, though very many opposed him.

After his departure, moreover, the Lombards destroyed Biandrate, having extracted the hostages left there and killed almost all the Germans whom the emperor had left to guard the castle. They gave ten of the noblest and wealthiest Germans, as consolation for her husband, to the wife of the man of Brescia whom, as related above, he had hanged near Susa, so that she might, as she pleased, either hang them, subject them to perpetual slavery, or accept a ransom. Thereafter they are said to have inflicted much damage upon the marquis; and now there is a report that they are besieging Pavia. It is certain that the people of Pavia have already sent messengers into Germany to the emperor, declaring that unless he returns and brings help, [Col. 0283C] they can by no means hold out against the cities much longer.

The heresiarch of Cremona is at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, where the Romans permit him to remain after making an agreement for the restoration of their captives; yet, they say, they would not allow him to depart. The bishop of Albano is acting in the lord pope’s stead in the city. If the Lombards capture Pavia, there is hope that Guido of Cremona will be captured, and that not only all the Romans but all Tuscany will attack the schismatics. It is still uncertain whether the lord pope will heed the Lombards’ prayers by transferring himself to them, though this is believed likely.

He is still prospering at Benevento, where the envoys of the king of England and of the lord of Canterbury [Col. 0283D] met in his presence. Both, indeed, were received kindly and honourably; but, as the justice of the royal party was weaker, so its pomp and display of riches were greater. When they could not overthrow the lord pope by flattery and promises, they turned to threats, falsely asserting that their king would sooner follow the errors of Noradin and enter into fellowship with a profane religion than allow Thomas to remain bishop any longer in the Church of Canterbury.

But the man of God could neither be shaken by terror nor seduced by blandishments. Setting before them two ways, one of life and the other of death, he answered that they could easily, as they had begun, by despising the grace and patience of God, choose the way of those who perish; but that he himself, with the Lord’s favour, would not depart from the straight way. Their spirit therefore soon subsided. Seeing that they could not advance by this path against justice, they sent messengers to Sicily, bearing letters of their king with which they had come, so that through the help of the king and queen of Sicily they might obtain something from the lord pope against the Church.

But the most Christian king of the French, foreseeing this craftiness of evil men, commended the cause of the Church and of the lord of Canterbury to the bishop-elect of Palermo as his own. What outcome either embassy has had is still unknown.

Meanwhile messengers arrived from the legates whom the king of England had obtained, by no means silent. For whatever one of them had sung, another chanted in the curia; yet it is not certain what they will report to their masters. At the request of the king and the legates, with many intercessors employed, [Col. 0284B] the lord pope was petitioned on behalf of the bishop of Salisbury. At length it was obtained that the supreme pontiff should remit to him his injury and offence, and should write to the lord of Canterbury, asking and counselling him to forgive the bishop his injury; and that he should release him from the sentence of suspension and receive him into favour and affection, provided that he gave sufficient security in his own person concerning satisfaction, or sent two of the greater clergy of his church, excluding the dean, who should swear that the bishop had instructed them—and had not afterwards countermanded them—to take this oath, by which they would swear in the bishop’s name and stead that he would make satisfaction to the archbishop for contumacy and injury.

From this it may probably be inferred that the lord pope either did not know of, or did not think ought to be ratified, the sentence of the legates by which they had already absolved the said bishop. The same bishop had earlier obtained letters almost similar, which nevertheless burdened neither him nor his people with any oath; but he has not yet used them, either because they displeased the king or because they were deemed less effective. What verdict each side would carry away was not yet known when the bearer of the aforesaid letters returned; but the lord pope wrote back to the most Christian king that he would not fail God’s Church and his Canterbury, so long as justice accompanying his cause enabled him to support it.

Let us now turn to the conferences of our kings. The illustrious men Henry, count of Champagne, and Philip, count of Flanders, promoted the king of England’s cause at the conference of Soissons before the most Christian king; and finally, according to the prayers of the said king of England, agreement was reached upon this form of peace. [Col. 0284D] The king of England was to return to the homage of the king of France and, having publicly and bodily given faith before all, profess that he would serve him as his lord for the duchy of Normandy, as his predecessors, the dukes, had customarily served the kings of France.

He was bound to cede the counties of Anjou and Maine, together with the allegiance of the magnates belonging to those honours, to his son Lord Henry, who was to render homage and fealty to the king of France for them against all men, owing nothing to his father or brothers except what the principle of merit or nature required. The king of France was to grant the duchy of Aquitaine on a similar condition to Richard, son of the king of England, giving him his daughter in marriage, but without a dowry; she was nevertheless to receive, at her parent’s pleasure, a marriage-gift. No mention was made of Toulouse. Knights captured on either side were to be released, and thus the peace and concord of the kings confirmed.

But when the king of England, having attained his wish, heard that Count Henry was coming to him in order that this arrangement for making peace might be confirmed, he instructed him not to proceed. Setting out for Poitou, he intended to take the castle of Lusignan from the magnates who had agreed to rebuild and fortify it. The matter he was negotiating with the French he entrusted for settlement in his own stead to the archbishop of Rouen, Richard de Humaz, [Col. 0285B] and Richard de Lucy. Our Frenchmen do not value their oaths, made against their lord’s will, at an obol.

Accordingly the king of France, believing himself deceived by the deceit of the other party, went indignantly to Bourges. There he received oaths and hostages from the magnates of Poitou that they would make no peace with the king of England without his counsel and consent, and he promised them mutual assistance. By the oath of his brother Peter, Count Stephen, and William, knight of Chartres, he confirmed that he himself would make no peace unless they made peace, and unless what had been taken from them were restored.

The king of England therefore again, and more earnestly, acted through the aforesaid counts of Champagne and Flanders to obtain a conference with the other king and to restore the peace in accordance with the form upon which they had agreed. In the Octave of Easter he indeed obtained a conference with the French magnates, but was not granted sight of the king’s face until he had given security that he would restore peace to the men of Poitou and to all who had adhered to the king, together with everything taken from them, intact—except that he was not bound, any more than the Poitevins were bound to him, to raise the dead or rebuild houses that had been burned. [Col. 0285C]

He gave this assurance by bodily faith, and promised that he would faithfully observe the other articles of the peace arranged at Soissons. The same security was given in like manner by his magnates. The magnates of France bound themselves to him by faith that the king of France, if the agreements set out above were observed toward him and his people, would keep the stated condition of peace, except that he did not consent to give his daughter in marriage to Richard, the intended duke of Aquitaine. This was expressly said concerning Toulouse: if Richard should seek justice from the count of Saint-Gilles, the king would hear the case by judgment of his court.

When these matters had been reported in order to the king of France, he consented to speak with the king of England on the Sunday next after Ascension and make peace according to the aforesaid conditions. But afterwards the Poitevins complained to him that, while words of concord were being negotiated, the king of England was attacking them with an army sent against them. They had nevertheless assembled an army and killed its commander, Count Patrick, though unwillingly. [Col. 0286A] The king of France was greatly moved by this, but whether it can prevent the peace I do not know, although he regrets having consented in this way.

Moreover, he had been somewhat influenced by consideration of the devotion which he believed the king of England had conceived. For when the same king, in order to restore peace for himself, was more diligently soliciting the French, whose friendship he trusted, and had learned that the bishop-elect of Chartres was more intimate with the most Christian king than any other, because he is believed to surpass the other magnates in fear of the Lord and works of wisdom, he came to him and earnestly begged him to reconcile him to his lord. With him and for him, if it pleased him, he said that he was ready to set out for Egypt.

The bishop-elect, a most prudent man, wishing the hidden meaning of the words to be opened more deeply, said: “Is what you say true: do you wish to go to Jerusalem with him?” The king answered: “I have never done anything more willingly, if it please my lord and he allows me to arrange my household and provide for my children.” The man of Chartres, although he suspected deceit, reported this to the king of France. [Col. 0286B] He replied that it was shameful to be deceived so often, and that he would in no way believe that the king had spoken sincerely before he saw his shoulder marked with the cross. For since he had promised this before and confirmed it with a security by which, even if he had committed an offence, no faithful man is bound, and since he had appeared a violator of his professed religion, the king said that it was foolish to put trust in his bare word. Yet thereafter he was more inclined to make peace.

But now, on hearing that while making this promise he was attacking the Poitevins, he was so disturbed that through his envoys he notified him that he would not come to the conference unless he gave the Poitevins safe passage and hostages, guaranteeing that neither he nor his men would injure them in going, staying, or returning. It is also certain that, if he can withdraw from the conditions without loss of honour, he will gladly seize the opportunity afforded by the time.

There are also those who think that the king of England can in no way endure so great an indignity as to be compelled to restore peace and castles, with the other things taken away, to men who killed his magnates and opposed his honour and will with such obstinacy. For he is accustomed to be wicked, especially when an injury inflames the impulse of an impatient spirit. Others, because he is a crafty man and sees himself in a narrow place, think that for the moment he will employ his accustomed art of pretence and concealment, and when he has obtained an opportunity will seek the desired vengeance upon his enemies. [Col. 0286D]

But whatever the kings may do, it is not believed that the Poitevins will make peace with him, because they despair of finding good faith in a man by whom, they complain, even when innocent they have been injured contrary to faith. Yet it is superfluous to rehearse differing opinions when the event of affairs will shortly disclose the truth itself. When it becomes known, I shall not be slow, God being my author, to inform you as soon as I can, reporting most carefully whatever I judge worthy of report, both concerning the kings’ agreements and concerning the condition of the lord pope and the cause of the English Church.

Do you in return write to me concerning your own condition and that of our friends; keep, and cause the holy to keep, a remembrance of me and mine before God for good.

## LETTER CCXLV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1168)

To JOHN, bishop of Poitiers, J. S.

Benefits are often bestowed upon unwilling persons, and charity is accustomed to call back one who is hastening to his own destruction. Would that the king of England might experience this to his salvation! For we are his debtors, and each of us, if it were possible, owes him, for many reasons too lengthy to enumerate, the most diligent provision of what pertains to salvation and honour, and must recall him, however much he resists, from those things that bring the loss of salvation. [Col. 0287B]

For who would not grieve to see so great a prince, so necessary to God’s Church, placed upon such a cast of fortune that, driven by the counsel of reprobate men, he seems to be rushing headlong in his entirety toward the overthrow of himself and his children—may God avert it! Since he began to harass God’s Church and proscribe the innocent—which I can neither say nor remember without pain and groaning—God immediately stirred enemies against him on every side, and such affliction that it can scarcely be quieted in our lifetime. This place is all too conspicuous, open on every side from the farthest bounds of the Britains to the remotest limits of Gaul. Therefore it is neither proper nor expedient to linger longer over it.

That famous schismatic Frederick, while raging more maliciously and cruelly against the Church, became a former Augustus and was brought to such a point that he now wished he had lost Italy, which he cannot retain. I fear lest the aforesaid king, walking in his paths, meet a like end—may God prevent it! It is indeed remarkable that none of the religious warn him that such great dangers are imminent. What are those men of Grandmont doing now, whom he was accustomed so greatly to love and venerate? Where now are the faith and fervour in the Lord of Fontevraud? [Col. 0287C]

Certainly I trust that if he restores peace to the Church and departs from the evil way, God will be propitious to him and will transfer the impending dangers away from his house. For Ahab also, because he reverenced the face of the Lord, escaped the scourges of the divine threat. I also remember what is written in Proverbs: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will make even his enemies turn to peace” (Prov. 16).

If, therefore, you judge it expedient, I earnestly beg you to arrange that those holy men of Grandmont, or others whom he is accustomed to hear more favourably, should set him before his own face, warning him to return to his heart and turn aside from Frederick’s tracks, lest, when the Lord is angry, he should have in ruin as his forerunner the tyrant whom he had as his predecessor in guilt. Nor should they desist if he hardens himself against prayers or grows angry at admonitions. Rather, let them remember that saying of Cato:

> And when you warn a man, and he himself is unwilling to be warned,  
> If he is dear to you, do not desist from what you have begun.

[Col. 0288A] But if he is wise, he will listen to them and make peace in person with the lord of Canterbury, without the mediation of the Roman pontiff, the king of France, the work of cardinals, or anyone apart from him who is in the midst wherever two or three are gathered in his name. This cannot be accomplished, however, unless they speak personally and mutually pledge faith to one another concerning themselves. For I know that if either could trust the other, they themselves would devise and enter upon the best possible form of concord.

Indeed, the king could, as I most certainly think, place complete confidence in the archbishop, because he is a religious man and seeks only to do that which advances God’s glory and contributes to the king’s salvation. Returning recently from Saint-Gilles, I passed safely through that place itself and rejoiced to find both him and his fellow exiles safe and occupied in divine exercises. He was awaiting the return of his messengers from the Apostolic See; but since it is uncertain how far they have succeeded, I do not know what should be written about him.

My brother sends you a small gift recently sent to him. In it, if you please, measure rather the devotion of the sender than the value or usefulness of the gift. What I should write concerning the affairs being conducted between the kings, I do not know, since it is still uncertain what the envoys of the king of England, who run so frequently to Count Henry, can obtain. For the count is advancing the cause of the other king before the king of France.

[Col. 0288C] Lord William of Pavia was present at the appointment of the bishop-elect of Chartres, a man indeed of great promise, most illustrious reputation, great authority, and much influence in the kingdom of France. After the king of France, he is the one who gives singular patronage, counsel, and help to the lord of Canterbury and his men. He desires to be on familiar terms with you; and would that, with God’s favour, you may someday enter more fully into friendship! For, to speak my true judgment, there is no one in the clergy of France who surpasses him in prudence and eloquence.

## LETTER CCXLVI. TO MASTER LOMBARD. (A.D. 1168, June)

The same to Master LOMBARD.

Mindful of the obligation contracted between us, I shall relate as briefly as I can [Col. 0288D] what was done at the conference of the kings, and what advantage the lord of Canterbury gained there. As you know, the count had drawn him into Flanders by command of the king of England.

As the kings approached the places appointed for the conference, Eudo, count of the Bretons, and Roland of Dinan lodged many grave complaints against the king of England before the most Christian king. Eudo in particular lamented that the king had made pregnant, as a traitor, as an adulterer, as one guilty of incest, his virgin daughter, whom he had given him as a hostage for peace. For the king and Eudo’s wife were born of two sisters.

The Poitevins—namely the men of Angoulême—the count of La Marche, the viscount of Thouars, Robert of Sillé, Geoffrey of Lusignan, Aimeric of Rancon, [Col. 0289A] and the abbot of Charroux demanded that compensation be made to them for the losses which the king of England and his men had inflicted upon them after the truce. The abbot said that his monastery belonged by right to the king of France from the time of Charlemagne, who had founded it.

After many disputes held on both sides, the king of England promised that he would restore what had been taken from the Poitevins, but not at all to the monastery, because it belonged to himself and the lord pope.
