At last, however, he said that, not for the right of the king of France but for the love of God, of the count of Flanders, and of Lord William the cardinal, he would restore to the abbot whatever of his own property the abbot had possessed.

But when the king of France heard that a cardinal was present in the counsel of the king of England, he was moved, saying that he had not deserved such treatment from the Roman Church—that a cardinal, as he had always done hitherto, should support his enemies—and that on this occasion he would receive nothing for love of the count or the cardinal, but only for his own right, if the king of England wished it. When the latter refused, the king of France formally summoned him, by the faith to which he had bound himself, to come to the river where, by agreement, the conference ought to have been held. He had remained for two days at a distance of two leagues from it, but did not comply.

[Col. 0289B] The king of France, having waited almost until evening, crossed the river. Sitting on the other side, he washed his hands and drank before all men, declaring that he had fulfilled the pledged agreement. He then dismissed the count of Flanders and the other magnates, while he himself waited there with a few men until twilight.

He had sent messengers to the other king to summon him to make satisfaction for violated faith. On hearing this, the king of England kept the messengers with him and came armed to the river with a multitude of mailed and helmeted knights. He did not allow the messengers to go ahead and warn the king. Seeing this, the French took up arms; but night prevented them from meeting, and so the king of England returned.

Counts Robert, the king’s brother, and Stephen, Count Henry’s brother, pursued him. He begged them very earnestly to persuade the king not to compel him to seek refuge with the enemies of the kingdom of France, displaying much humility in words. The following day he sent his messengers to Chartres, that they might incline the king to peace, [Col. 0289D] or formally summon the count of Flanders, by the faith by which he had bound himself, to come into the submission of the king of England.

But the king of France denied that he would make peace with him until he had made satisfaction to them and to the kingdom for having rushed against him armed, and almost by night, in that manner; yet he had been unable to move a single Frenchman from his position. He added that he was ready to show, either on the frontier or in the court of the count of Flanders, that he had released both the count himself and the others who had intervened on his behalf from their obligation.

The envoys of the king of England replied in turn that their king would show in the court of the emperor, or of the kings—namely the king of Navarre or of Aragon, to whom he intended to give his daughters—that he had kept faith, while the count of Flanders and the other French mediators had violated it. A truce was meanwhile requested, but not granted. Thus each returned home.

Bretons, Poitevins, and envoys of the king of Scotland and of the kings of Wales attended this conference, promising assistance and offering hostages to the king of France; they departed bound by obligation, as did likewise the magnates of Gascony.

After the kings’ conference had ended, so that it might not remain hidden how the king of England had triumphed over the lord pope and the Roman Church, and so that the lord of Canterbury might become “the reproach of men and the rejection of the people,” together with all his followers, he had the lord pope’s letters copied—the letters by which he had given him impunity to sin—and sent to the churches and persons of both kingdoms. [Col. 0290B] He also boasted that he had such friends in the curia that they would frustrate all the efforts of the archbishop of Canterbury, and were so diligent in advancing his business that the archbishop could neither submit a single petition nor obtain anything without its being sent to the king through those friends.

We know their names, whose counsel he employs, and what they recently did in the curia, so that the cause of God and Christ’s poor might be sold at a cheap price. Nor was there much in their exchanges. Those ounces of gold would never have been given by which men were induced to fall—men who ought to have been pillars of the Church. The king was so elated by his triumph that in his household it cannot be kept silent which cardinals received nothing of that pestilential and infamous gold, and which arranged for more to be distributed to some and less to others according as they had more or less deserved in the overthrow of justice.

The messenger of Lord John of Naples, as the king of France was not unaware, passed from the king’s camp, while we were at Montmirail, to the king of England and certain other persecutors of the Church. The religious men who stand with the king of England, when they heard the aforesaid letters, were deeply grieved and cursed John of Naples and John of Saints John and Paul, who were said to have deceived the lord pope. Master Geoffrey of Poitiers, clerk of Lord William the cardinal, did not consent to the counsel and acts of the king’s envoys, because he too awaits the kingdom of God. [Col. 0290D] But he openly declared that they were perjurers and condemned by anathema, because they had sworn that the lord pope’s command would remain secret; and the lord pope had enjoined upon them, by virtue of obedience and under anathema, that it be concealed.

But they, to make us contemptible to all and to withdraw the consolations of friends despairing, as it were, of our peace, proclaim with their king the triumphs of their wickedness and glory in the confusion of the Church. Would that the ears of the cardinals were turned toward the mouths of the French, among whom this saying has become proverbial because of the affair: “The princes of the Church are faithless companions of thieves.” For they permit and confer authority upon the persecutors of the Church to shake, despoil, and plunder the patrimony of the Crucified One, so that they may share in wicked gain.

Would that you could hear the most Christian king, whom I fear can no longer be prevented from contracting, at the emperor’s request, a marriage between their children. Count Henry is procuring this and hopes to obtain his desire. Henceforth, I beg you, let your industry and diligence be shown, and let the lord pope do what belongs to a just judge. Let him absolve the innocent man, who has been bound without precedent, and condemn the wicked man, who offers himself to the whole world as an example of persecuting the Church. Act also so that the archbishop of York may be commanded to render obedience and submission to the Church of Canterbury, long broken by so many and such great oppressions.

## LETTER CCXLVII. TO WILLIAM THE BRETON, SUBPRIOR OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1168)

To his BRITON, the least of his friends, greetings, and the saving fulfilment in the future of what God has prescribed.

Hearing that the frequency of my letters was troublesome to you, I laid aside my pen for a long time and had resolved no longer to disturb your peace with reports of news. But since I have learned, both from the account of my Osbert and from the testimony of the bearer of this letter, that I had been misled by a false suggestion, behold, I change my purpose. Henceforth, when occasion permits, I shall write, but with such moderation that I ought not through excessive frequency of writing to become troublesome.

For no such uncontrollable itch for writing drives me that I cannot restrain a worthless pen, but must thrust upon unwilling ears what a weary listener might justly suspect had poured forth from a leaky breast. You, however, according as you receive writings that proceed from charity, will either restrain my style within whatever bounds of moderation you wish, or, by the incentives of faith and friendship, compel the affection of one who loves—even if not loved—to break forth into words. For, as the true and common proverb has it: “The proof of love is the exhibition of a deed.”

But I fear that through this present letter there may happen to me what I was guarding against: that, in speaking truth to friends suffering from delicacy of hearing, I may risk the loss of those same friends:

> For what need is there to gnaw tender  
> Little ears with a biting blade?  
> *(Persius 1.121; idem 2.30; Lucretius 4.595.)*

[Col. 0291D] Yet I shall say what duty requires, although success may be snatched from virtue not so much by fortune as by the deception of opinion which overturns reason. I have often warned you, and it ought not to have slipped from your memory, that you should make effort and use diligence so that the Church of Canterbury, both out of regard for God and from consideration of its own honour, might give some consolation to its father, living in exile for the justice and liberty of the Church. Events show that I have cast words to the winds, and, if the assertion of many is to be believed, your prayers have turned to the opposite outcome.

Whenever a command from the lord pope is directed to your church, whenever the archbishop’s welfare is discussed among you, word immediately runs to that excommunicated man who lies upon the Church; a report is dispatched to the king; the Apostolic See is accused; and under the pretext of public authority an occasion for impiety—and, as it were, a necessity for wrongdoing—is contrived. Was not Ralph of Arundel banished for this reason: because, in chapter, with only the Church’s own true-born sons present—its, as it were, inmost heart and entrails—he dared to present apostolic letters to the English Church? “Even the law of the heathen,” he says, “is that children should support their parents, or be put in chains.” And this, indeed, as you know better, is confirmed by the authority of both Testaments. It follows that, since you have a father in need, you owe him support; or else God owes you chains. For what sound-minded persons could believe that men look upon their father’s exile, proscription, and poverty for so righteous a cause without the duty of compassion—or rather, as many say, actually laugh at them? Yet his heart, at which many marvel, has not been alienated from you; rather, through weapons, through fires, and through the perils of the last extremity of life, he heaps up for you treasures of salvation, honour, and glory. By God’s aid, the mother of the Britons shall soon triumph gloriously in Christ, more gloriously than ever in former days.

Was Ralph alone faithful to the lord pope and devoted to the archbishop? Did the chief of the provinces, in the passion of his Christ, cry: “We have no father of souls and shepherd but Caesar”? Therefore, I beseech you, my dear friend: while there is time, redeem the delay, and persuade the brethren who are to be partners in consolations to share their father’s hardships, lest they eventually repent and be ashamed that, through inhumanity, they alone withdrew from the common tribulation that is in Christ. By God’s aid we are sailing in harbour, and after sorrowful Sabbaths a happy day shines forth. Read the replies sent to you; attend to words which it is not yet permitted to make public, some of which it is lawful to communicate only to you and to Odo alone, even under the strict assurance of religious obligation. Having heard these things, use counsel; and do not suppose that I am asking anything for myself. I give thanks to God, who has willed that I should be bound almost to Himself alone in the matter of giving and receiving. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXLVIII. TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1168.)

To WILLIAM, subprior of Canterbury.

[Col. 0292D] You maintain—as I infer from the letter which you sent to Master Ralph—that my rebuke or invective can easily be refuted, because the deed which I criticized did not occur in the manner in which it had been represented. Would that I had erred in reporting the deed rather than the Church in committing it. You may therefore be plausibly excused, provided that your innocence shines more clearly from the merits of your deeds than from the persuasive words of human wisdom. Meanwhile, the archbishop will regard you as excused, unless your own works accuse you.

For I know, so far as a human being may judge of another, that he loves the advancement and honour of your whole community, and would embrace each individual among you with greater affection, were there not some among you who inflame his serenity against [Col. 0293A] others by malicious suggestions. For this purpose they employ certain triflers, who sometimes gain access so that they may pour into his ears the poison of their own or another’s malice. He himself, however, very often despises such things; and if at times he cannot help being moved, it is only for an hour. May God forgive them and direct them to better pursuits.

Since, therefore—I do not doubt that it arises from envy—they persecute you more than the others, preserve your innocence, and act openly in those matters which you have conducted in the prior’s stead, so that, through the testimony of your brethren, your integrity may prevail against your rivals. But you are now newly accused of having caused a certain church to be granted and its charter confirmed by the Church to an excommunicated man, namely the nephew of Ranulf de Broc, whom no one doubts has been condemned under anathema. And know that Lord William the cardinal confessed to me that he had not ordered any of your excommunicates to be absolved unless they had first relinquished the possessions of churches, sworn according to the Church’s custom to restore what had been taken away, and rendered fitting satisfaction.

Those who disparage you also allege that you have seized the treasures of the deceased prior and promise to relax the order more than is right and customary. Yet in all these matters the archbishop’s mind has not yet turned away from you, for he awaits the testimony of your works. I shall defend your interests and those of the Church, so far as God grants me power, as my own; indeed, as the Searcher of hearts knows, I have devoted—and am ready to devote—greater effort to them. I could not obtain from him permission to entrust anything of his office to the bishop of Rochester [Col. 0293C] or to anyone else. And if anyone interferes, he will not endure it patiently. Farewell after Odo, and greet our friends; remember me profitably through Jerome’s letters.

## LETTER CCXLIX. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to BALDWIN, archdeacon.

Although my insignificance is unequal to offering thanks worthy of you, I should injure my reputation if my silence led people to suppose that I had forgotten your benefits or lacked the will to repay them in the offices of friendship. Where, therefore, the means are withheld from the will, it is fitting that a will enriched with affection and gratitude should supply the duty which restricted means cannot perform. For if it is true—as no one doubts it is true, because we have experienced it so often—that the proverb deserves belief:

> We ever strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> —Ovid, *Amores* 3.4.17

then it may plausibly be inferred that the more I am forbidden and kept away from friends, the more eagerly and ardently I am stirred to repay friendship’s services. If you do not believe me, consult lovers; and, if you wish to be perfectly instructed, learn at last what I think you have hitherto failed to know. Women will teach you most faithfully how great are the flames of forbidden love. And if you still desire more perfect instruction, the priests entrusted to your charge will be able to teach you.

Accordingly, with a devotion which cannot be restrained, I offer the fullest thanks, certain that He who rewards a cup of cold water with eternal recompense will here also render you a hundredfold according to the Gospel’s promise, and in the world to come will crown the merits of your piety. There is indeed hope that the storm which has so long battered the Church will soon grow calm. Those who troubled her from the north and west now seem to be summoned before the judgment of Him who punishes the mighty mightily and takes away the spirit of princes. Those who had been banished from Italy have already returned. The schismatic “ex-emperor” has been shamefully and dishonourably harassed, driven out, and excluded by the Lombards; in his passage he disturbed Burgundy, and he found all Germany in turmoil, so that the well-earned precipice now seems to threaten him.

What then remains to be expected from the Lord, except that his own supports likewise perish, and that those whom he had as accomplices in error may have as companions in ruin? For even the game called *rithmachia* indicates this: whenever a pyramid is captured and removed, its sides collapse. Do not the powers of this world and every great household resemble such pyramids, where the members, like parts of a body, rally around their head—those who swelled in reliance upon his power against the Lord and raged against Christ’s poor? Surely heaven and earth shall pass away, but not the words of the Lord. Therefore he who is now a plunderer will himself become plunder; he who judges without mercy shall be condemned without mercy; with the perverse, God too shall act perversely; and by the very things through which a person sinned, by those things he shall also be punished. To those who suffer for justice, the consolation of true blessedness will be given. This is more probable than that heaven and earth should pass away, because the principle of equity is more plainly evident; but it is not more true, because both are God’s decree and an article of unbroken faith. Farewell.

## LETTER CCL. TO ROBERT, SON OF GILLES. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to ROBERT, son of Giles.

Brother, great is that which the priestly prerogative demands; but it is God’s grace that is accustomed to bestow the greatest gifts. Without it human frailty can do nothing, and through it any weakness is strengthened for achievements however great, so that, where necessity or usefulness demands, the lame may leap like a stag and the tongue of the mute become eloquent. [Col. 0294D] Cast yourself wholly upon that grace, then, and labour the more earnestly to make progress in it. For as it is accustomed to anticipate those in need, so it is accustomed to abandon the negligent.

Brother, there is no loss more ruinous than for anyone to fall from grace; and, as you know, no loss is more disgraceful than one incurred through negligence. All moral philosophers, both ours and the pagans’, endeavour to shake off negligence. Thus Cato, who is absorbed from one’s earliest marrow so that he may adhere more firmly to the mind, said to his son: “Guard your own property.” And Solomon commanded us to imitate the ant, which gathers in summer what it may live on in winter. What, however, is more truly ours than grace—that is, God’s gift? For *grace* (*gratia*) is so called as though it were “freely given” (*gratis data*).

Its most bitter assailant is negligence, which a kind of demon often instils into householders and which is cast out only by prayer and fasting. Once you have resolved against it, you will be able to fast; but you will pray without ceasing—not, indeed, using the words of the wise men of this world, who almost say:

> Fair Laverna,  
> Grant that I may deceive; grant that I may seem holy and just.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* 1.16.60

but using the Gospel words with which the Son addressed the Father: “I pray not for the world, but for those whom Thou hast given me” [John 17:9], and other words suitable to this cause. Yet the Apostle speaks and teaches, brotherly love, as the most excellent way of all. The remembrance of brethren in exile convinces you that you must walk in it. And when brotherly love is commended, sisterly love, I think, is not excluded. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLI. TO RANULF OF ARUNDEL. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to RANULF of Arundel, monk of Canterbury.

The reason why I have not written to you until now is, if you please to consider it, complete and twofold. First, I did not know whether your reverence would be pleased to receive the writings of one so insignificant as I, since I had been proscribed by the violence of public authority and was regarded by most people, for the Lord’s cause, as I was styled by heretical schismatics and excommunicates. There are lovers of temporal things whom neither age nor sex, neither the title of profession nor rank of order, neither eminence of dignity nor condition of fortune, neither the impulse of nature, which rules almost all created things, nor distinction of dress or quality of clothing exempts, save only the clear evidence of their merits; and they so fear the powers that be that, unless they have obtained leave from them, they dare not have intercourse even with a single word, not even the word “greeting.” Yet the word of God is a communion of salvation; and they do not dare to profess it before men, but presume publicly and confidently to attack it.

Second, although I was confident that you, like others whom I had deserved to have affection for me, loved my person because I had always loved the Church of Canterbury and, as many know, patiently benefited it in many ways, I did not know what you thought of the cause undertaken, nor whether you wished to stand by it in purpose and favour, with the crowds and chief priests who persecute the Christ of the Lord, or to await with us—I mean the children of the Catholic Church—the kingdom of God. But once I learned of your integrity through those whose fidelity to me in the Lord had been tested, I did not delay to greet you, ready to have with you, as you may decide, fellowship of word and service. For I have learned from the Apostle that the word of the Lord is not bound. Certainly neither is charity, since it is strong as death; and wherever it is not feigned but true, it cannot be restrained from rendering service. It knows no sluggish idleness, and proves that its true substance lies not in word or tongue but in deed and truth.

Your charity toward the Church is plainly evident from the fact that you have defended it earnestly and effectively, omitting nothing which the nature of the case permitted from the circumstances at hand. But that Manerius of yours—perhaps aptly so named because, falling in the morning, he hastens toward a precipice—will not be held excused either by us or by posterity. Having ranged through woods and clearings, rising at earliest dawn, he conducted the courtier’s hunt against an innocent father and lord, though the latter had not yet been clothed in a stag’s skin or, by divine ordinance, exposed to prey. He might mockingly turn against himself the poet’s words:

> I am Actaeon: recognize your master.  
> —Ovid

And against hunters of this sort he might turn the Gospel reproach which Christ hurled against the Jews: “Many good works have I done among you from my Father; for which of these do you wish to kill me?” Yet he has his church—and henceforth will have it excused—if the outcome of events confirms the credibility of your letter. For a tree is known by its fruit, and each person’s works bear witness to them more powerfully than John.

Nevertheless, there are among you persons holding the doctrine of Balaam, accomplices of excommunicates and authors of error. Because of them it is rightly to be feared—may God avert it—that the whole Church may contract a stain and a blemish upon its reputation. For, as you know, slanderers do not say, “This or that man did it,” but “The monks of Canterbury,” or “a Canterbury monk,” do it. Such is the story now current in the regions on this side of the sea concerning the aforesaid Manerius, whose name has become famous from a criminal charge, though he could not have earned fame by virtue. If the accusation is falsely made against him, let him accuse not me but the cardinals, who wrote concerning his appeal. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLII. TO RICHARD, PRIOR OF DOVER. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to RICHARD, prior of Dover.

The face of heaven is becoming clear in the east; the head of schism is being crushed in the north; its sickly members wither, its sides ache, and its scales are loosened so that breath may pass through them. In the west, too, the sun of justice now casts forth its rays; hence peace for the Church is hoped for soon, so that we may pay our friends the thanks that are due.

And indeed, most beloved friend, I profess myself your debtor, ready to serve you wherever and whenever I can. [Col. 0296D] Therefore, if the thing itself seems lacking in generosity, remember that through it you have a servant at hand, according to the established maxim: “To receive a benefit is to sell one’s liberty.” But why say that I alone am your servant, when by this law you hold both me and mine, who pass among you, bound in obligation? It will be helpful to remember these things when he, by God’s aid, has won the Church’s liberty—he who now, to our present and everlasting disgrace, treads the winepress alone and finds scarcely a companion from among his own people, that is, the English Church.

## LETTER CCLIII. TO ROBERT, VICE-ARCHDEACON OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to ROBERT, vice-archdeacon of Canterbury.

It is the judgment of a most learned man that words should be understood according to the meaning in which they are spoken, not according to the meaning they produce. If you follow that principle, you will interpret mine as proceeding from charity. For if I became foolish in speaking, charity compelled me. I could have kept silence, since I was neither addressed by word, invited to service, nor provoked by injuries—except that I saw danger threatening you, whom I love.

For the lord of Canterbury brings many charges against you, asserting that they are just: namely, that you are said to presume greatly both against his own churches and his men; that you openly associate with his excommunicates, though you ought to have been an executor of the law; that, where clerics are compelled to redemption, you give consent or connive; and, more seriously still, that you share not so much in the profit as in the crime. For those who persist without repentance in crime and in the will to sin have not been absolved. Neither cardinal nor pope can grant this.

You would have felt the barbs of his indignation, had not one of your friends intervened with advice. If I learn that these words have been received by you with displeasure, I shall henceforth be silent about you before him, and about him before you.

> Do not suppose that long hands belong only to kings.  
> —Ovid

For bishops’ hands are longer still. The lord of Canterbury fights for his own liberty, indeed, but also for yours and that of the whole Church. To persecute him for such a cause is the crime of idolatry. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLIV. TO MASTER LAURENCE. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Master LAURENCE.

For your dear and splendid gift, which you sent me through our mutual friend, the master of the schools, I thank your generosity, wishing that I may someday be able to respond to it as my heart desires. And I hope that, through God’s grace, an opportunity will soon be given to us to serve one another. For the head of schism is now being crushed, and the members which clung to it—indeed, which have rotted in its own dung—must likewise perish. The more wildly they rage, the sooner and more closely do they show their ruin to be impending. When a disease reaches its height, it hastens toward its decline; and if the physician is skilled, once the cause is known he cures it more easily.

Moreover, the physician of the Church, who heals our infirmities and cures wounds now with cautery, now with fomentations, has mixed a draught which shall be given to the sons of Babylon, so that they may become drunk and fall, and allow the vessels of the captivity to return to the worship of their God. Do not be troubled unto desolation if the assault of the public sickness now afflicts Poitou. For diseases often grow more acute when health is near.

But I shall be troubled if the lord of Poitiers, in response to anyone’s entreaties, drives the nail again into the eye, pierces the side with an irreversible arrow, and binds the feet in fetters, should he once by any benefit of God be set free. Would that he remembered that it is unfortunate to be deceived once, foolish twice, disgraceful three times. For Phoebus too regretted granting even to his son a gift asked without a name—though repentance came late, after he had unwittingly surrendered his own heaven to be burned. If Eritius is removed from his seat, let him seek where he may sit more softly. Let him not seek a blind eye when he ought to have cured one that was bleared. It is better that he should grant you the archdeaconry than give it to someone ignorant of law and hostile to religion. If you are with him, you will be able, as I think, to guard against this. Farewell, you and all yours.

## LETTER CCLV. TO MASTER OSBERT OF FAVERSHAM. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Master OSBERT of Faversham.

The bearer of this letter is your fosterling. If you delay to help him, you will incur the mark of ingratitude among men and perhaps will not be excusable before God. Nor is it necessary now to weave a history of the benefits which his father conferred upon you, for, if you are of sound mind, they will never fall from your memory.

I had heard that surgeons were rather harsh and inhuman. But I thought that another kind of physicians—gentle and mild—devoted themselves to humanity; not, I mean, the humanity by which human beings are carnally begotten, but that by which the sick are treated more gently, by which they sympathize with the infirm, and by which people are accustomed to assist those in great need. Philosophers define humanity as the virtue consisting in an affection of compassion, a gift which, above other virtues and above other animals, humankind has received from its parents—namely, grace and nature.

If I myself were to ask something of you, even if it were considerable, I believe you would grant it. Therefore, I beg you, do something for this man which will give him cause to rejoice in you and me; and I shall count it as a personal kindness to myself and repay it to you with multiplied gratitude. Nor would I burden you with such urgent requests unless, from what I have previously seen, I trusted that you would usefully devote your labour and resources. He has certain matters to conduct on my instruction, which he will communicate to you. I pray that you assist him in carrying them out, so that they may be accomplished more conveniently. And if you see that your own presence is needed in any respect, be present for the business, so far as it may safely be done. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLVI. TO WALTER, BISHOP OF ROCHESTER. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to WALTER, bishop of Rochester.

How faithfully and devotedly I served my lord, your brother, until the end—and after the end—of his mortal life, you may remember, if you think it worthy, and the world knows. From the blessing which, as he was departing, he bestowed upon me as the travelling provision of my journey and the passage-money of this world, I trust that success has come to me in the exile and proscription in which I found myself.

For, when he was almost dying, lest I attribute to him anything fictitious which the Searcher and Judge of hearts now knows, he endeavoured to console me. He exhorted me to persevere, as I seemed to have begun, in the cultivation of honour and virtue; and, laying his hand upon my head, he gave me his blessing and ordered me to have confidence, promising that, if I persevered, the blessing would benefit me to such a degree [Col. 0299A] that God’s grace would never fail in my needs. But I, as though secure in an inheritance bestowed on me, and trusting in the merits of so great a father, still hope—and shall continually hope—that, as I have deserved, I have him as my patron with God, and that therefore His grace will not fail me.

Accordingly, I acknowledge myself so bound to you and yours that I ought to assist you in all matters in so far as your honour and mine require. For I am bound to provide for your honour and advantage and to ward off disadvantages. And since this is my present reason for writing, if you think it expedient, put faith in me, as is just. For in the fidelity which I owe your brother, I speak to you faithfully from my conscience and for your advantage.

Your lord and father is in exile and proscribed for the Church’s liberty and God’s cause, burdened with many fellow-exiles. If you assist him, you will free your conscience; and when it is permissible to disclose the deeds of each person, you will advance your reputation and provide for yourselves and yours hereafter. But perhaps you fear the king, or plead poverty and the burdens of your household. Certainly God must be preferred to man. And you incur many expenses without the knowledge of the king and his people—indeed, even of your own household. For I do not know what to think of a bishop whose right hand is not stretched out to the poor without the left hand knowing, and all of whose works are celebrated by popular acclaim. If poverty presses you, poorer men indeed assist friends who are in need. If you wish provision to be made for yours when they burden you, take care that some friend may be preserved for them after your days.

By God’s grace the Church is sailing in harbour. It will be quite unworthy and shameful for posterity to remember that, while the disciples laboured at the oars, you gave no help to Christ’s ship. I say this not because, God being my witness, I seek anything to be distributed to myself, since by God’s grace I have abundance; but in order to counsel you and perform the duty of charity owed to you. Let each interpret this as he wishes; but my witness is in heaven, and my conscience on high. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CCLVII. TO MASTER RALPH OF LISIEUX. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Master RALPH of Lisieux.

For benefits which I cannot recount and am not free to disclose, I owe you thanks, dearest brother; and, if the Lord is gracious, I shall repay them to you or yours in due time. For I have not forgotten our former fellowship, the devotion I received in prosperity, or the blessing you bestowed in adversity. The Most High will indeed give you blessing for blessing; it is His accustomed way to bestow glory in return for His grace and to reckon the gifts of His mercy, in those who deserve it, toward their crown.

There is no one who does not make use of His free gifts. Very many abuse grace which has anticipated them; many follow grace going before them; but the small number of the elect, at the end of their labour, happily attain what they faithfully desired and are crowned at the journey’s end. For only those who persevere to the end shall attain the prize of the heavenly calling.

Therefore, beloved friend, persevere in what you have begun. You are blessed of the Lord and a priest of Christ—indeed, a Christ among the sons of the patriarchs who were appointed upon Mount Gerizim to bless. Carry out what you were ordained to do: bless often, but especially the household of faith; comfort scattered Israel; have mercy on the poor; share the necessities of those in exile. And, as you learned from the Apostle, fulfil your ministry. He in whom you trust will bring every difficulty, however great, to a successful end: He who substituted a ram for Abraham when he was offering his son as a sacrificial victim.

## LETTER CCLVIII. TO WILLIAM OF NORTHALLA. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to WILLIAM of Northall.

It is the habit of a sober character that, when clamour grows, a serious man restrains both silence and speech: he neither wishes to shout with the noisy nor to chatter back at babblers. But amid the flashes and lightning of thunder, when a whirlwind’s storm breaks upon one, it is madness to recite a story; an untimely narrative resembles music played in jest at a funeral mourning. Although I have loved you, and still love you, above almost all the companions with whom we served in the court, I nevertheless judged that my pen should be restrained while the storm intensified. Now that the tempest is subsiding, it has been released to speak in greeting and congratulation.

For the Church has been made serene in the east; and the Spirit has now told the north wind to withdraw from your land, yielding place to the south wind, which may bring forth the flowers of virtues and bring works of charity to fruit. Meanwhile, concerned for you and for many others, I have decided through the bearer of this letter to ascertain what is being done with you. He can also inform you more fully about my condition, which by God’s aid is good; and through him you may communicate to me whatever you please.

I would add some words for your benefit, but I fear that, under the pretext of another’s advancement, I might seem to be seeking private gain. For I consider that nothing is to be demanded from friends except charity. Through God’s grace and that of old friends, I have sufficient abundance; and I hear the Apostle urging: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another.” The lord of Canterbury labours not for himself but for others, because his advancement will be God’s glory, the Church’s triumph, and the liberation of the entire clergy. He serves the public good, but still at his own expense—indeed, to the shame of our countrymen, at the expense of a foreign nation.

## LETTER CCLIX. TO RALPH OF WINGHAM. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to RALPH of Wingham.

The Lord has granted you, dearest brother, as I hear, to exercise the priesthood. Would that you may deserve praise in His name. There is hope, indeed, that the grace which conferred the beginning of so great a good will also grant its increase, and that Christ will not allow the plant of so great an expectation to wither—He who is accustomed to cultivate and water the garden enclosed by the protection of His defence.

Before your promotion you were industrious among your fellow-countrymen and contemporaries; and it is to be presumed from God’s mercy that, as the Apostle says, His anointing will teach you concerning all things expedient. Everything done under the instruction of charity is expedient, because all things work together for good to those who love God, and bring joy to the mind. For charity gives every person’s free choice such rein that one may without blame do what one pleases. As this is my reason for speaking, so, I pray, if you judge it advantageous, let it be your reason for accepting counsel.

Your lord and father, exiled and proscribed for the Church’s liberty, has long laboured at the oars with Peter and the other disciples. Now, by God’s grace, as the storm subsides and the assistance of faith strengthens him, he seems to walk upon the waters and draw near to harbour. If you give him help and take hold of him as one cast, as it were, upon the shore, you will usefully provide a rope for yourself and yours. What you cannot do personally, you may perhaps do through another; and thus the reward for another’s merit will be reckoned to you.

If you have grown lukewarm, you need not employ a public excuse by pleading fear: first, because by the Lord’s aid you are not held under suspicion; secondly, because, wherever you choose, expenses may lawfully and easily be incurred without any spy being present. If the will is there, I know that you do not lack resourcefulness. And, as the Lord lives, I do not say this in order to make a profit for myself, since God’s grace supplies my necessities and I have not yet entered into an account of debt and receipt with our countrymen. I say it in order to fulfil the office of brotherly charity. For it is better to cultivate friends than to bind oneself into servitude by benefits received. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLX. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to HENRY, bishop of Winchester.

Your magnificence is accustomed to share in the needs of the saints; with provident eyes you look in every direction in order to choose those worthy of beneficence, refresh the hungry, and comfort Christ’s poor according to what you find expedient for each. For you do not, in the manner of this age’s triflers, pour out your wealth upon actors, mimes, and such monstrous specimens of humanity in order to purchase fame and prolong your name. Rather, you place it more wisely and beneficially among those who fear and invoke the Lord’s name, who will receive friends into eternal dwellings.

Since, then, the entire Church of the saints recounts and approves your alms, will your generosity not look also upon Christ’s exiles, who suffer exile for justice’s sake and defend the Church’s liberty? I do not say this for my own sake—God knows it—for the Lord’s grace has supplied me with necessities in abundance, as I complete my fifth year in exile; and it has always been far from my purpose, and hateful to me, to beg under any pretext. For a thing once purchased is acquired more conveniently in the market of saleable goods, since, as the philosopher testifies, it is bought twice when it is begged for.

But the lord of Canterbury moves me: burdened with many fellow-exiles, he serves at his own expense and at that of a foreign nation—to the shame of the English Church and our countrymen—for the public cause of the entire clergy. He seeks not merely an immunity for himself, which he could have obtained very easily; rather, he vindicates liberty for all. For when, by God’s aid, he has won what is hoped shortly to come about, even the least member of the clergy will triumph over the Church’s adversaries.

Yet I know who has given him help, and I offer whatever thanks I can, certain that a hundredfold reward will be repaid to him a hundredfold. When Peter’s fellow disciples, who now seem to be sailing in harbour, rejoice in the desired station of the shore and are invited to dine with Christ, then, as is just, a glorious seat will be prepared for him among—and above—the others at that joyful banquet, because he helped the Church’s children labouring at the oars. For with what face will those appear then, or what will they say, who contributed no aid to the struggling ship? It is certain that the Church will sail through; and then, according to each person’s deserts, there will be glory or shame both for those who persecuted her and for those who abandoned her.

## LETTER CCLXI. TO MASTER RALPH OF LISIEUX. (A.D. 1168.)

His GRATIANUS to his BENEDICT, greeting and blessing from the Lord.

Because the bearer of this letter is more fully known to you, I have omitted from the page many matters worthy of report and entrusted them to his loyalty [Col. 0302C] for more confidential communication to you. But since we are both concerned about the public condition of Church and kingdom, I shall touch briefly upon each. First, then, you should know that the heresiarch of Cremona—fit to be burned—is shut up in the tower of Stephen Theobald; he does not dare to emerge and fears, even unto death, the change of senators who are to assume the government of the city on the Kalends of November. For the senators of the present year, in order to rescue their captives from the emperor’s prison, received Guy of Cremona at Saint Peter’s and, in the Trastevere district, furnished him security under oath. Yet they were never able to subject Rome to him, and, I think, did not wish to do so.

The new senators, however, [Col. 0302D] will swear fealty to Pope Alexander and, as is believed—with God as author—will put an end to the schism. This has long been negotiated and confirmed by many oaths. The cardinals are returning after being recalled, penitently and not without shame; they complain that, in deference to the king’s will, they pressed down the cause of the Church too far. One of them, namely the man of Pavia, supported him in everything; the other also acted more weakly than befitted a man of such great expectation and hope. Hence it is certain that those letters of which the king boasts, restraining the authority of the lord of Canterbury until he should return to the king’s favor, were obtained by this device.

The aforesaid man of Pavia knew that the lord of Canterbury had obtained from the Apostolic See permission to pronounce a sentence of anathema against the king personally and of interdict against the kingdom [Col. 0303A], unless within the term stated in the letters the king restored in full what had been taken from the churches and made fitting satisfaction. He therefore wrote to the lord pope, tearfully beseeching him to deal more gently with the king, lest that same king—as he had already planned, if harsher measures were taken against him—cast both himself and his colleague Lord Otto into chains and prison, to the everlasting disgrace and reproach of the Roman Church, where they would live a wretched and short life harsher than death itself. Having persuaded the pope that the king would do this, he obtained, for the king’s consolation and as it were for his own and his companion’s liberation, so that they might depart more readily, that apostolic rescript which has wounded the minds of both you and all the faithful. But [Col. 0303B] he could not obtain the withdrawal of the letters in which the lord pope reminds the king that certain hope and assurance of peace had been given him both by the pope’s letters and by the promises of the envoys, on condition that such honor should be shown to the oft-mentioned king.

A request was made that this delay be extended for a year; but the petitions were refused, the pope himself telling the envoys that he would shortly revoke this indulgence unless the king quickly made peace with the archbishop. Indeed, it has already been revoked, unless satisfaction is made by a specified day. From that point the archbishop is free to proceed by the force of the letters which, as we said above, he had obtained. This is why the cardinals hastened more eagerly [Col. 0303C] to escape from the king’s hands. The messenger will supply what should rather be said than written, so that, once you have seen everything, you may decide how you can proceed with the greatest caution. If anything further should arise that prejudices what has already been settled, I shall not delay, God favoring, to communicate it to you.

Peace between the kings was lately hoped for and negotiated, but the king has relapsed into such opposition that it now seems almost impossible, although neither wishes for war. They would certainly have met many days ago had not the king of England, after arrangements had been made and settled, always attempted to add some new demand. Thus it nearly happens that, however much he tries to advance, the affair moves toward an outcome contrary to his purpose: he becomes retrograde in his dealings, who strives, beyond what is fair and good, to be not so much an initiator as an over-thrower of agreement and even of law. When it is permitted—which, with the Lord’s aid, will indeed happen shortly—I shall send you [Col. 0303D] the rescripts of the apostolic constitution, adding whatever meanwhile may occur that deserves reporting.

I had passed over what I think least of all ought to be passed over: namely, that Lord Otto, a few days before leaving the king, met with him more earnestly to urge him to restore peace with the archbishop. The king replied that, for love of the lord pope and the cardinals, he would allow the archbishop to return peacefully to his see and to dispose of the Church and his own affairs. And because disputes concerning the customs had been prolonged, he said that he and his children would be content only with those customs which his predecessors were proved to have possessed, [Col. 0304A] upon the oath of one hundred men from England, one hundred from Normandy, one hundred from Anjou, and from his other lands. But if this condition of peace displeased the archbishop, he said that he was ready to abide by the judgment of three bishops of England and three from this side of the sea, namely, those of Rouen, Bayeux, and Le Mans. If even this should not suffice, he will abide by the judgment of the lord pope, provided that his children are not disinherited. For during his lifetime he will readily bear it if the lord pope rejects whatever customs he wishes.

He was asked what he would do, concerning restitution, for the archbishop and his people, since restitution is demanded and owed by him. He replied: nothing, swearing by many elaborate oaths that everything he had received from them he had expended solely upon churches and even upon the poor. [Col. 0304B] But let Apella the Jew believe that, not I. The cardinal added that, unless he adopted another course and dealt more gently with the Church of God, God and His Church would demand everything from him more strictly and more swiftly than he believed. And so, having taken leave, he departed from him. Afterwards William of Pavia met him in much the same manner, but the seed of his word fell upon sand. On their return, passing through the most Christian king of France, they were restored to his favor through agreements which the bearer of this letter will communicate to you. The men of Poitou act courageously and are strengthened, devastating everything far and wide around them.

## LETTER CCLXII. TO THE SAME PERSON. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0304C]

To B., archdeacon of Exeter, J. sends greetings.

Your diligent generosity, most beloved Baldwin, through the assiduity of your merits ensures that I always encounter matter for writing which consists in giving thanks. Continuous benefits require perpetual thanks; and the offering of devotion, which cannot be retained by practice, ought to be inseparably joined to the recipient’s memory. This is what I can do for the present, while awaiting and confidently hoping from the Lord that the peace of the Church will be restored sooner than its adversaries can suppose, and that we may perform toward one another the due and long-desired interchange of service.

Do not be troubled by the letters which the Church’s rivals boast [Col. 0304D] that they have obtained from the Apostolic See against it; for, God favoring, you will shortly hear what was being done, and your heart will rejoice. The Comforter of mourners will come; and those whom He finds obstinate He will crush by the power of His majesty, and the sword of the dove will be unsheathed against the necks of contumacy. But perhaps you will say: “This man prophesies for distant times and speaks from his own heart what he desires, not from the Spirit of God.” To this I reply: if I speak falsely, that spirit was sent to me from the Apostolic See—the spirit which has fixed the day of vengeance and has already bent its bow to strike down the lion and the dragon.

Yet we have a firmer hope in the word of the Lord, which cannot fail to be fulfilled; for to Him differing weights and differing measures are an abomination, and therefore each must necessarily be recompensed according to merit. Frederick, who went before [Col. 0305A] in guilt, goes before also in toil and pain—would that he may not do so in ruin.

## LETTER CCLXIII. TO MASTER RALPH OF LISIEUX. (A.D. 1168.)

To his dearest friend and companion Master Ralph of Lisieux, J. sends greetings and the prudent direction of foresight toward the future.

You have learned from the Apostle that faith is the substance of things hoped for; and it is clear that one does not differ from the error of the heathen who relies only upon present things. Hence those who hope only here, while boasting of the Christian name, are more wretched than Jews and heathens. The works of mercy separate you from their fellowship [Col. 0305B]: through faith, in hope of eternal recompense, and for love of our Lord Jesus Christ, you do not cease to exercise them toward His members. The Churches of the saints tell of your alms; orphans and widows, with other poor and desolate persons, rejoice before the angels that they are relieved by the services and benefits of your kindness.

I have rejoiced when such things are reported to me, confident that by this way you go forward without stumbling and hasten toward the house of the Lord. There the holy angels, lovers of the poor, will joyfully receive you; and, crowned with the diadem of the kingdom, will crown you among the elect in the preordained order of blessedness, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. Therefore, my beloved, bravely continue what you have begun; hasten through the strength of perseverance toward triumph [Col. 0305C]; by a fortunate exchange purchase eternal things for temporal ones. Lay up riches in that place which neither rust nor moth reaches. Be kind and merciful to all, but especially beneficent toward those of the household of faith: toward those who suffer for righteousness; who have despised all their possessions for the word of God; who preferred to expose themselves, for Christ’s word, to poverty, perils, disgrace, and the reproaches of flatterers who follow the world and fortune, rather than reign in the counsel of the ungodly, sit with princes, and flourish above the fortunate of the earth.

To those toward whom you are bound by just and long-standing affection or by obligation, do not delay to respond more kindly, more promptly, and more fruitfully, after the fashion of those who, while alleging the evil of the times and the harshness of authority in order to excuse their own avarice [Col. 0305D], accuse God—the author of times and ordainer of powers, who makes all things work together for good to those who love Him. Remember instead:

> … delay has harmed those who are ready:
>
> He who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow.  
> (Ovid, *Remedia Amoris* 94.)

Nourished in philosophy and advanced in the law of Christ, you will meditate upon and do this. For only

> The rustic waits until the river has flowed away; but it  
> flows on, and will flow on, rolling through all time.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.42.)

The remaining matters have been entrusted to the bearer of this letter. If you believe and comply with him, you will more promptly fulfill what you represented to me through Adam, co-heir with you in the apostolic succession.

## LETTER CCLXIV. TO ROBERT OF LIMESIA. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0306A]

The same writer to Robert of Limesia.

Truth is without disguise, and friendship knows how to speak only with face uncovered. Therefore, speaking truthfully to a friend, I ask you to guide the way of the bearer of this letter and further his affair, since it is a pious one. I have been asked to write to the lord of Winchester and to intercede for another—a thing I have always been ashamed, and am ashamed, to do for myself. Indeed, I thank God that He has so mercifully provided for my need that I have no need to beg and am not indebted to many people. I owe anything at all to few of our countrymen, except the charity which a Christian cannot fail to owe to all. [Col. 0306B]

But the lord of Canterbury, an exile and outlaw for defending the liberty of the Church and clergy, serves everyone, though still at his own expense, and is burdened with many fellow-exiles. Since your lord assists others, I do not know where he can place his alms more fittingly and honorably. Therefore make every effort to ensure that he gives him help.

## LETTER CCLXV. TO ROBERT, ARCHDEACON OF SURREY. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to Robert, archdeacon of Surrey.

Reason lays down this law among friends: that nothing but honorable things should be asked from one another; and, if dishonorable things are requested, they should not be granted. But where honor supports the requests of friends and there is means [Col. 0306C] to grant them, consent should be given without difficulty; and the annoyance of having to demand should, if possible, be forestalled by fulfillment of the wish. I desire this rule to be observed between us, who profess friendship; and if I transgress against it, I would rather be corrected than heard. I also wish to be compelled if, when opportunity is given, I have been sluggish in discharging the offices of friendship.

Therefore, because the requests which I addressed to the lord of Winchester rest upon what is honorable, I ask that your diligence promote them. I ask not for myself but for another, to whom I intercede as one more deeply indebted. I have always been ashamed to pray for myself, although I have always had the most ready will to transact the affairs of friends. The lord of Canterbury, [Col. 0306D] unless he is sustained to some extent by the generosity of the most Christian king of the French, still serves at his own expense, an exile and outlaw for the Church’s liberty; and throughout the English Church he finds very few helpers. He pleads not a private cause, but a common one. The prosperity of all is his consolation. He could have made peace for himself and his followers if he had been willing to expose the clergy to the persecutors of the Church.

I do not see where the lord of Winchester can lay up treasure more profitably, among all the alms that he distributes to churches and the poor, than by giving whatever he thinks fit to Christ’s outlaws, who have exposed themselves and their possessions for righteousness and endure for the Church’s liberty. This is especially so since he sees his father and his son, who bears the burdens of many, to have suffered such shipwreck for God’s law. [Col. 0307A] I call him father because he presides over him by metropolitan right; and son because he received from his hand the gift of consecration. For he gave himself to him as a son, whom he above all desired to have as father when he chose him for that office; consequently he suffers the stings of envy from some of his brethren.

Does he not owe more to this man by a manifold right than he owed to William, the archbishop of York of good memory? William, deposed by sentence of the Apostolic See and even with the indignation of the Roman pontiff, he maintained in his household—to the everlasting glory of his liberality and magnificence—despite the grief and detraction of many, until he was restored through the mercy of another pope. Where has the distinction of such nobility gone? The good or evil done to us by our countrymen [Col. 0307B]—even if the present age dare not utter a word—future ages will sing of forever. Nor, under the pretext of just fear, can anyone color the failure of brotherly charity, because actions done openly appear to be full of danger. They can be done secretly with greater advantage to conscience and will entail no loss of property. The method is well known to anyone who is not so supine as to make no expenditure, I know not how, either without the king’s knowledge or without the knowledge of informers.

## LETTER CCLXVI. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF NORWICH. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to William, bishop of Norwich.

[Col. 0307C] Necessity, not contempt, causes the interruption of the service which I profess that I owe you. For my will is ready to obey, should you decide to accept my service. But perhaps you make allowance for the time and think that, while fury is in full course, it should be yielded to rather than resisted. Nor do I disapprove a counsel governed by prudent reason, so that it looks to utility without abandoning honor.

Yet, by God’s grace, it will shortly come to pass that this accommodation will not be needed, because the storm has now subsided and the peace of the Church seems to be at the doors. With God as author, what I say will soon become more fully known. Peter and his fellow disciples have labored at the oars; among them is the lord of Canterbury, who, still serving at his own expense or at that of a foreign people [Col. 0307D], serves the welfare of the whole English Church. For when he prevails, it will redound to the glory of God. The Church will attain triumph, the clergy freedom, and the people consolation. And indeed, then—as also at the Last Judgment—it will not displease anyone to rejoice in the testimony of conscience that he brought aid to the shipwrecked Church.

Against this, perhaps, fear of public authority and the snares of persecutors will be alleged. But surely there is no one who, without their knowledge, cannot make an expenditure whenever he wishes. And, God bearing witness, I say this not for my own advantage, but in order to forewarn my lord and discharge the office of charity owed.

## LETTER CCLXVII. TO JOHN, PRIOR OF NORWICH. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0308A]

The same writer to John, prior of Norwich.

The condition of outlaws is hard, yet not so much to their own loss as to the detriment of their friends. For they can scarcely greet anyone without that person immediately suspecting that commerce is being conducted under the pretext of affection and respect, and that officious persons are gaping for profit. Lest you think this to be my purpose, dearest friend, I earnestly ask you to understand that, God favoring, I abound in necessities sufficient even for honor and distinction. Therefore I seek not what is yours but you—provided you have not fallen from grace and still retain charity. Even if you have fallen away, I shall nonetheless seek you, desiring charity to be restored in you—indeed, desiring you [Col. 0308B] in that charity without which you can be nothing but misshapen; for I can love even those who do not love me. I do not count you among them, but express my feeling even if you should be such a person.

I shall count it a favor if you make me more certain of your condition. And if you care for mine, the fifth year of my exile under the lord of Canterbury is happily being completed. He still serves, at his own expense or at that of a foreign people, for the liberty of the Church, and finds no faithfulness in Israel. All his friends have despised him; many persecute him and the Church amid their straits—and this is the graver matter. For there is a proverb of Wisdom: “A friend is not known in prosperity, and an enemy will not be hidden in adversity” (Ecclus. 12). This everlasting disgrace awaits our countrymen, though I cannot say it without pain.

Nor do I say this in order that the fidelity rendered to the king [Col. 0308C] should be injured by anyone, unless perhaps it was given contrary to faith. For fidelity is sometimes demanded and rendered in such a way that it is better to repent than, with charity lost under the pretext of loyalty, to imperil fidelity itself. Truth, because it is straight, has no corners; and he who covers himself with falsehood alone is naked: Adam the outlaw learned this. Fear is not just when it leads one to despise the divine command. There is scarcely, or rather no one, who does not have some secret unknown to the king and who cannot make all expenditures without informers’ knowledge. Since these things proceeded from charity, it is fitting to interpret them from charity.

## LETTER CCLXVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0308D]

John of Salisbury to John, bishop of Poitiers.

Your discernment perhaps wonders that the lord of Canterbury rejected the proposed conference with the king of England, which your diligence had secured, when he had previously more than once come to confer with him unasked; and, what is more, had been rejected to the insult of Christ and subjected to various injuries. He was indeed desirous of his own peace, but far more desirous of the Church’s liberation; and he earnestly desired the king’s welfare and glory and the security of his children. For these reasons he exposed himself and his followers to abuse, insults, and diverse dangers—not to mention labor and expense—so long as reason suggested that peace might be restored by the path of humility.

[Col. 0309A] But after he recognized from many clear indications that the king increasingly abused the lord pope’s patience, that inhumanity grew out of humility, and that insolence arose and spread from the gentleness shown him, he judged that he must follow another path—and would that it be the happier one—especially since he plainly perceived that both you and he himself were being dealt with wholly deceitfully. Thus:

> The pipe sings sweetly while it tricks the wary bird.

For while the hope of peace is promised, the destruction of the Church is sought by an embassy dispatched to the Apostolic See. The archbishop is invited to a conference so that he may not beware the snares of those who seek his life to take it away. For arrows which are not foreseen strike more swiftly and wound more grievously.

[Col. 0309B] Where, I ask, is the truth of Scripture if the man who prepares a pit for everyone does not at some time fall into it himself? Who is faithful and true if Truth is deceptive and false, when it promises those who lie the deserved fruits of reward in the same measure—pressed down, heaped up, and overflowing? Are not differing weights in a man’s hand an abomination before God? Shall there then be differing weights in God’s hand, so that He judges unjustly between poor and rich? Far be this from Him who judges the world in equity; who did not spare even the angels; who punishes the mighty mightily; who takes away the spirit of princes; who makes His despisers ignoble. May He judge His own cause, and either convert or crush [Col. 0309C] the oppressors of the Church. May He deliver His poor, for the glory of His name, as He knows to be expedient for them, and rescue them from the face of the threatening sword, lest the nations at any time say, “Where is their God?” (Psalm 113).

The God of the people of Canterbury is patient indeed, but beyond doubt also a most faithful rewarder. There is hope, moreover, that He will not delay vengeance long but will threaten shortly. Unless the persecutor of the Church turns aside the blow through repentance and satisfaction, he will be struck beyond remedy and will become an example for ages.

## LETTER CCLXIX. TO NICHOLAS DE MONT ROUEN. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to his Nicholas.

[Col. 0309D]

> If you count well the times which we lovers count,  
> our complaint has not come before its proper day.

Do not suppose that I wish to complain of you, whose loyalty and devotion I have proved by many evidences. Rather, I complain to you because I perceive that my friends have suffered a most grievous loss, all the more grave because, hindered by stupor, they scarcely perceive their scarcely reparable loss. The philosophers of the gentiles proclaim true friendship—whose beginning faithfully preserves a perfect end, as you learned both from Cicero’s *Laelius* and, more faithfully, from experience of virtue itself—to be something to be valued above life, because without it life is as joyless as it is hateful to God and men.

I believe this friendship to be nothing other than charity, without which, as the Catholic faith teaches, no one will enjoy God. I grieve that friends have fallen away from it [Col. 0310A], so that scarcely anyone does not profess himself bound either to flesh and blood, to his possessions, or explicitly by a pledge to public authority, in a matter that cannot be observed without impairing charity. If anyone contends that such an obligation is lawful, I do not doubt that he is a heretic, and I declare that he must be avoided, even though the world protest.

I have experienced these pledges: my sixth year of exile is now approaching, and, what is greater, the lord of Canterbury and his fellow-exiles are completing their fourth. As he labors for the public welfare, he still serves, at his own expense or at that of a foreign people, for the liberty of the Church, for the blood of the clergy, and for the consolation of the people; and there is no one who looks to him. In the English Church there is no one to help Peter and his fellow disciples laboring at the oars. But you will say: “They fear informers,” as though, when the will is present, they could make no expenditures [Col. 0310B] without the informers’ knowledge. A pledge has been given to authority; certainly the obligation does not bind. They fear the king—probably indeed, and more than God. For when one commands and the other forbids, or conversely, it is plain whom they obey.

Perhaps an oath of purgation will be demanded; it cannot be rendered without loss to conscience and reputation. It is more expedient to allege a subtle reverence and the privilege of the clergy, who are exempt from such oaths. “But,” you say, “we are not dealt with according to law or reason but with fury.” Must one then rage with madmen, rejecting law and despising reason?

[Col. 0310C] But, with God as author, the peace of the Church seems to be at the doors. I do not see with what face, once it is at peace, those will dare to appear who, seeing its peril and repeatedly called upon, gave no help to its shipwreck. Would that even now my lord and the other friends extend to it a helping hand, lest they later repent when they see Christ’s disciples, who have been sailing, rejoicing on the shore, while they themselves are invited to breakfast with them. Do not think I say this in order that anything may be given to me, who, through God’s grace and that of those with whom I have been associated from youth, flourish and abound; rather, with God as witness, I desire to satisfy charity. Concerned for your condition and that of my friends, I have sent this messenger, whose trustworthiness has been proved to me. If you think fit, you may inquire of him about my condition and communicate to him securely whatever you please.

## LETTER CCLXX. TO GERARD, CELLARER OF NORWICH. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0310D]

The same writer to Gerard, cellarer of Norwich.

I gladly hear, most beloved friend, that you desire and hope for an honorable peace for the Church, and do not cast your lot of agreement with the impious, while you too await the kingdom of God. Thus, in addition to the affection I formerly acquired for you by your merit, my charity toward you has been doubled, ready to serve your capacities and needs according to my strength and to obey your commands. Nor indeed do I doubt that I shall have an opportunity; for divine grace, above and contrary to my merits, and apart from the assistance of friends, has provided me even in exile with necessities sufficient for me to be usefully serviceable to lords and friends. He who began will also bring it to completion. For as He anticipates the desires of the righteous, so, with Him as author, what the impious fears comes upon him.

By His gift the archbishop also, who alone struggles for the salvation of the whole English Church, will be able to provide his friends with the consolation owed to them [Col. 0311A], because the peace of the Church is being restored: the head of schism is crushed, and its supporting sides are collapsing into ruin. Therefore pray, and urge your brethren, because Christ has now awakened.

## LETTER CCLXXI. TO WALKELIN, ARCHDEACON OF NORWICH. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to Walkelin, archdeacon of Norwich.

The most learned and eloquent man lays down the rule that the meaning of words must be drawn from the occasions of speaking [Col. 0311B]. If you observe this rule in my discourse, you will not suppose that I have said anything for the sake of profit, since I lack both need and desire to beg. Yet after an exile of five years, it is sweet, so far as can be done, to exchange welcome conversation with friends unseen for a long time and to discover what their condition is. For I am ready to take upon myself the lot of their fortune, and I desire an opportunity of serving them.

Nor do I doubt, through God’s grace, that an opportunity will shortly be offered, since I seem to see the peace of the Church hastening forward, and the lord of Canterbury and Peter’s fellow disciples—who have sweated in steering the ship amid the storm of this shipwreck—now almost visibly arriving at the desired harbor. For the limbs that raged with the head of schism [Col. 0311C] are perishing; once that head is cut off, the whole body must die. We have seen, we have seen the man who used to be like a lion in his house, overthrowing his household and oppressing those subject to him, seek hiding places and be shaken with such terror that he was scarcely safe in his secluded corners.

Would that you had seen that emperor—that emperor who had been the terror of the whole world—fleeing from Italy with everlasting disgrace, so that he who had mocked the Catholics’ labors amid his successes and fury might now seek safety or ruin. Who, then, can keep silent about the praise of God conceived within? For He is the one who alone performs great wonders; who consoles us in all our tribulation, lest through benefits received we become bound to men; He alone is owed what we have: that we live [Col. 0311D], abound, and now are more honored in exile than formerly in our homeland.

## LETTER CCLXXII. TO MASTER NIGEL. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to Master Nigel.

Distance between places does not prejudice faith, and the title of friendship shines more brightly in adversity. Although I have now been an exile for five years and, what the persecutors of the Church believed would be more grievous to me, an outlaw, I am moved not so much by my own loss as because, in this moment of necessity, scarcely any of our countrymen bring aid to the shipwrecked Church. For though she seemed in peace to have many sons and friends—men distinguished by learning and conspicuous for the merits of their virtues [Col. 0312A]—“a thousand fell at her side and ten thousand at her right hand”; and those who were clothed in saffron have embraced dung.

But now, through God’s grace, the force of the whirlwind has been weakened and Peter’s ship is entering the desired harbor. I have taken care to make this known to you because I do not doubt that you will rejoice with the Church’s joys, especially since in the Church’s peace you will receive back friends who, with the Lord as author, will be able to advance your honor and advantage. For the lord of Canterbury, who fights for the liberty of all, has assumed the character of a man who desires continually to serve the Church’s honor.

## LETTER CCLXXIII. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF ST EDMUND’S. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0312B]

The same writer to Hugh, abbot of Saint Edmund’s.

The reason why the form of address varies in the salutation is obvious: because, under the pressure of a time of storm, names must either be suppressed or fictitious names used. Yet reverence for persons is not diminished if titles of dignity are omitted, nor is charity prejudiced by a restricted freedom to serve. For often and in many cases that poetic saying holds true:

> What is allowed is unwelcome; what is forbidden burns more fiercely.  
> (Ovid.)

It would indeed have been a great consolation to me if I were permitted to be of service in any way through my attentiveness toward friends. And, as I must become obliged by benefits, so I would have opportunities to oblige others. Yet there is scarcely anyone except you to whom I am bound in the account [Col. 0312C] of giving and receiving, since all seek under the pretext of empty fear a consolation for their ingratitude. Thus I am closely bound to you, since you have so often anticipated me, beyond my merits, with blessings of sweetness.

Behold, the sixth year of my exile stands at the door, and I have proved burdensome to none of those who, while I flourished in my homeland, were my intimates or debtors. Through God’s grace, necessity has not yet compelled me to descend to entreaties, because Christ supplies me through old friends with all things, not only for necessity but also for honor and magnificence. Indeed, it is not through our merits that He sustains so many fellow-exiles and outlaws in a foreign land, but because He spares and provides for His Church.

For the lord of Canterbury promotes the public welfare [Col. 0312D], fights for God’s cause, vindicates the clergy’s honor, and protects the Church’s freedom. Yet he still serves at his own expense—or, to the disgrace of our countrymen and as a cause of condemnation, a people whom he has not known serves him out of compassion—while the chief princes of the priests thirst for his blood. The bearer of this letter will report most fully what the condition of the Church is and what the situation of the kings is; you may communicate to him in complete security whatever you please.

## LETTER CCLXXIV. TO AZO, A MONK. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to Azo, monk.

Affection is demonstrated by its effect, and often a good word surpasses a great gift in graciousness. [Col. 0313A] What then shall I say, who, shut off from my friends by the barrier of the storm, cannot serve them and am not free even to communicate with them in words? Shall I write? But an unfamiliar bearer rarely travels between us. Shall I send my own man? But snares are laid for my people, and no one willingly throws himself into foreseen danger. Therefore, amid these difficulties, I write more rarely and less often; yet certainly I love no less—indeed, I may more easily and truly say, more.

For, conscious of human weakness, we are more often tempted by forbidden things. But with God as author the storm which has battered the Church is now subsiding and, as we trust in Him, will altogether vanish shortly. Meanwhile it is my purpose, grace going before me, to serve as a fellow-soldier with the lord of Canterbury for God’s cause and the Church’s freedom. Although he serves the public welfare, he still serves at his own expense [Col. 0313B]—or, what is shameful to our countrymen, at that of a foreign people. Would that you had provided him even some small comfort—God knows that I speak more for your advantage than for his. For myself, I ask nothing except that you send me the Quintilian which I requested, copied and corrected.

## LETTER CCLXXV. TO WILLIAM OF DOVER. (A.D. 1168.)

The same writer to William of Dover.

Experience is the most trustworthy mother of knowledge; and in every discipline, what appears so to the practitioner is probable. The precepts of every art are indeed easy to understand, but not so easy to put into practice. Yet the precepts of ethics—that is, those concerned with cultivating the duties of the virtues—are more difficult still. [Col. 0313C] But among them all charity holds the first place; and I should confidently and rightly say that it is nothing other than true friendship. By its own majesty, and also by its rarity, it surpasses every object desirable on earth. From my earliest years I have devoted myself to it, and believed that I had won many persons by acts of service, hoping that they would return my affection in kind.

Thus constancy in loving and serving has produced a habit; and, once turned into habit, it compels me always to love, even those who do not love me. Yet I do not presume that I am established in charity, which is the summit of religion, though my soul thirsts for it. But I do confess that there is in me a certain disposition of goodwill [Col. 0313D] by which, as we read, even some pagans made themselves pleasing to those with whom they lived. And this, although it does not possess the firmness of a root, is nevertheless charity in kind of nature and in its intended end—especially in a Christian.

Moreover, throughout the whole five years of my exile, scarcely anyone has been found who has returned affection in kind to me; and therefore the greater gratitude is due to what is rare.
