But in whose ear ought I to lay this complaint, if not yours? For you are known to cherish a sweet affection toward your companions, and to have established it in the Lord upon the roots of faith. Nor, as God and my conscience know, have I lodged this complaint against my friends in order to gain something, since God supplies me abundantly with what I need; but because it seemed pleasant to lay before one to whom you can speak of everything as if speaking with yourself the ingratitude of others. This alone is asked at the close [Col. 0314A] of this letter: that we may alike devote ourselves to the growth of charity, and that you may always and everywhere regard me as your own.

## LETTER CCLXXVI. TO GEOFFREY. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to his Geoffrey.

Our common Lord has sufficiently shown me that your innocence is excused—unless indeed I had first believed that it needed excuse. For what use is an excuse where one does not believe that guilt preceded it? Nor did the man whom you think an informer attempt to make me suspect anything unfavourable concerning your affection.

This alone I hold against you: that you believed me so easily corruptible—indeed, already corrupted. For is not a person corrupt [Col. 0314B] when the assault of a suggestion shakes his charity? Or, if you know it, explain what corruption can be greater than the tearing away of charity. Certainly no member equally necessary is found either among the members of the soul or among those of the body.

Yet this fault of yours too is capable of pardon, because zeal seems to have begotten it, fear to have nurtured it, and anxiety—the inseparable companion of love—to have strengthened it. So Peter too was alarmed where there was no cause for fear, and tried to hinder the mystery of human salvation, when carnal affection endeavoured to hold the Lord back from it. I am not so foolish as not to weigh your necessities, feel your straits, and measure the discretion by which one must accommodate oneself to the time, passing through ill repute and good repute, while preserving the root of faith and virtue. If [Col. 0314C] you are silent, if you do not write, you avoid snares by prudence. For it is fitting that prudence, the moderator of duties, should regulate a wise man’s acts and words. But no force can restrain the movement of the mind. Nor can many waters prevail to extinguish charity.

Moved by this, I have sent the bearer of this letter, that he may bring news of our friends and make them more fully acquainted with my circumstances. For I am well and cheerful, if they are likewise. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXVII. TO WILLIAM, PRIOR OF MERTON. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to William, prior of Merton.

When I heard of your promotion, I rejoiced, seeing that the man was appointed in place of my lord and friend whom, for the honour [Col. 0314D] of God and the benefit of the brethren, I judged no one in the whole Church should surpass. How dearly I love the Church is known only to Him who gave me the power to love; and my conscience bears such testimony as it can. Nor do I doubt that, by God’s grace, you will succeed to the charity of him whose seat you have succeeded to, or that with you I shall retain the place which I was accustomed to hold with him.

To speak my heart openly: he counted me among his dearest friends, and although few or many had preceded me in merit, I preceded them in favour. For I cannot boast of merits; and if I wished to do so, I should seem—and should be—a fool. Therefore my entire boast is nothing but the divine mercy and the merit of others: I mean good men, by whose help, after God and through God, I am in small measure [Col. 0315A] what I am. It is their merit that, above and against my merits, the Lord raised me from the dungheap and set me upright, though I am dust and ashes. And now, though an outlaw among a foreign people and in a foreign land, He has bestowed goods upon me in abundance and honour.

But since my merits answer me ill and I fear a fall, I need the aid of your prayers, which I entreat more earnestly, and those of others who fear the Lord. This, indeed, is the sum of my petitions. The bearer of this letter is known to you. If it pleases you, go with him to the lord of Winchester, so that his affair may be advanced; if you cannot, send a trustworthy and wise man.

## LETTER CCLXXVIII. TO THE SAME MAN AND ALL THE BRETHREN. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0315B] The same to the same and all the brethren.

Whenever we offer prayers to you, we do not draw them from our merits but from your kindness, which has long held us dear freely and has sought to aid us in many matters. For the abundance and honour in temporal things that have come to us exiles and outlaws, we trust, result from your prayers and merits. For what have we deserved but scourges and tormentors? Yet He who comforts us in all our tribulation knows most fully—as we say from conscience—that we did not deserve this from the man who persecutes us, although from God we deserved worse things. Perhaps the Lord commanded him to harm us; and, if so, may He smell the sacrifice.

[Col. 0315C] Therefore, prostrate in spirit, we most earnestly entreat you to obtain by your prayers from the Lord that He may remember us for good. For He who knows us to be His workmanship knows what is expedient for His workmanship. This alone we ask, declaring in the charity which is God that you must not even think of bringing us aid out of your temporal resources. Let the cause of the Church and of the lord of Canterbury also be commended to you with greater diligence, because he, fighting for the liberty of the Church at his own expense and by his own labours, serves the benefit of all.

## LETTER CCLXXIX. TO JOHN OF TILEBERY. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to John of Tilebery.

[Col. 0315D] On hearing of your recovery and of the greeting with which your affection judged me worthy to be honoured, I rejoiced, returning in thought to happier times, when both the Church of God enjoyed its due peace and we enjoyed the most delightful companionship under an excellent lord. There meditation upon philosophy, the practice of law, mutual exchange of services, discussion of letters, and useful and pleasant disputation drove away tedium and shortened the delays of time, so that time for action almost always seemed too short.

But as I say this, I seem already to see the friend to whom my speech is directed. For it is the philosopher’s part to be angered by words unworthy of hearing, and, out of charity, to pity me as sick, wandering, or pretending to be one or the other. For I fear that praise of the past may seem an accusation of the present, and that [Col. 0316A] I, as a lover of this prosperity which appears to be adversity but is not, may seem overcome by its stings.

But if it were so, I should have wandered in vain, through the Spirit who moves, raises, and halts the prophetical wheels cohering and joined together with the fathers and sons of the prophets, through Chaldea, Canaan, and Egypt; I should have traversed the desert in vain or crossed the mountains of Samaria; and after the Babylonian captivity I should have returned without cause to the house of the Lord. I do not mean that house made by hands, which, after a shadowy cleansing through the blood of goats and calves, was irreparably destroyed and overthrown by the ministry of the Romans; but that house into which the Apostle brings and leads me to drink from the four rivers of Paradise, teaching me to despise all the world’s furnishings as dung, in order that I may gain Christ alone, in whom are all the treasures [Col. 0316B] of things desirable.

Indeed, to turn to your pagans: not only the Stoics, but the Epicureans too, and all schools of philosophers preach contempt for worldly things. Even if they reasonably judge that such things should be used as necessity of condition and time requires, if grieving for those who sleep belongs only to those who have no hope, is it not shameful for a Christian—especially one professing philosophy—to waste away over the loss of temporal things?

Yet it is not, to use the language of fools who accuse or defend Fortune, that I should blame her: for the grace of God meets the wickedness of my opponents in my consolation in such a way that, through God’s mercy, the former benefits of friends [Col. 0316C] seem to me—if one should perhaps come to reckoning—to have given me more than has been taken away. Moreover, this very storm has now, by God’s favour, subsided, and the peace of the Church seems to stand at the doors. Meanwhile, feed our sheep, not beside but within the shepherds’ tents. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXX. TO NICHOLAS, SHERIFF OF ESSEX. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Nicholas, sheriff of Essex.

Whoever does not know that *comites* (“counts”) are so called from participation in companionship is ignorant of the elementary letters which liberal education usually teaches first. For just as other bishops are summoned by the supreme pontiff to share his pastoral care, in order to wield the spiritual sword, so counts are admitted by the prince into fellowship in the material sword, as certain bishops of worldly law.

And indeed, those who discharge this office in the palace by authority of law are palatine counts; those in provinces are provincial counts. Yet both bear the sword—not, certainly, to carry out the butcheries of ancient tyrants, but to obey the divine law and, by its standard, serve the public good, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. You therefore, because you act in the place of provincial officers, as the title indicates from your locality and name, may you so perform what the prince requires that He may not be offended who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible to the kings of the earth; whose bride is the Church; and who so punishes the despisers and evildoers against His priesthood as though they had attacked the apple of [Col. 0317A] His eye.

May the Giver of wisdom grant you what a wise man wishes for himself. I am indebted to you, and for the affection which you have toward me and mine I give whatever thanks I can, confident that the Most High, the most gracious Rewarder, will repay adequate thanks. By God’s authorship my condition is pleasant; but I desire to be informed about yours and that of our friends, and you may safely communicate to the bearer of this letter whatever you please. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXXI. TO PETER THE SCRIBE. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Peter the scribe.

The zeal which you have in the Lord has been known to me for many years, so that I know you cannot fail to be moved by the condition of the Church. For:

> Who could wish to watch the stars and the world falling,  
> yet himself be free from anxiety?

Especially if charity compels him to regard nothing human as alien to himself. Such indeed was lately the appearance of the world, when from north and west it had burst into east and south, apparently about to cast down the greater part of the stars. But in Italy the Holy Spirit blew and crushed the head of schism, so that its sides now waste away and its limbs die with it. For there is no physician or enchanter who can snatch them from the hand of the Lord.

[Col. 0317B] The hope of the faithful, therefore, is that the same Spirit will shortly descend upon England too, to make that Church serene; and many indications of His coming are disclosed. Everywhere Peter’s fellow disciples, long harassed in the service of sailing, seem to themselves to be reaching harbour and rejoicing in the desired shelter of the shore, invited to dine with Christ. But because nothing is hastened enough for a longing soul, I seem already to see what answer you have ready on your lips. For I know the promptness of your discernment. You will say, then: “Whence comes this confidence—or rather presumption? By what arguments do you prove what you prophesy? How do you show that the promises are to be fulfilled?”

> Anyone can be rich in promises.

“Have you not deserved harder scourges from the Lord?” To this I answer: “Wait a little, and you will see the glory of God; then the arguments will be made public, and you will not wonder that we believed. Remember that, when Israel was besieged in Samaria and no hope of escape appeared to the besieged, the unbelieving man, who would not believe the prophet’s declaration that on the next day a measure of fine flour, or two measures of barley, would be sold for one stater at the gate of Samaria, did indeed see it, [Col. 0317C] but through unbelief was deprived of the benefit; for, trampled by the crowd, he died.”

“But,” you say, “are you also a prophet?” Certainly not; nor a son of a prophet. Still, nothing prevents an exile in the shepherds’ wilderness from plucking dried fruit with them. I do not presume on merits, but on the mercy of Him who does not allow the faithful to be tempted beyond what they can bear. We deserved harsher things, but His mercy toward the penitent is accustomed to forestall judgment.

One thing, however, astonishes me beyond measure: that there are some among the clergy who, after the manner of the Jews, have conspired with the chief priests [Col. 0318A] for the destruction of him who alone labours, exiled and outlawed, set up like a target for the arrow, in order to rescue them from the tribulation and distress of evils. For the lord of Canterbury seeks the common benefit of all; he fights for the liberty of the Church; he fights with beasts thirsting for the blood of the priesthood. He has valued his own blood and that of all his kin less than the cause of God, since he has boldly dared to uphold God’s law for the overthrow of fabricated or ingrained corrupt practices. Until now he has served at the expense of his own supporters and strangers. And in the English Church, who is his helper? There is more to communicate to your affection, but it is reserved for its proper time.

## LETTER CCLXXXII. TO THURSTAN OF ACOLT. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0318B]

The same to Thurstan of Acolt.

There are many things, my friend, which ought to perpetuate our charity and strongly urge upon us the diligence of services, without which the virtue of friendship cannot endure. First, the familiarity formed by living together; next, the bonds of association entered upon when for a long time we served under the same lords; finally, the fact that the man greater than all praise by the titles of his merits, Lord John of Poitiers, wishes us to love one another and to strive to anticipate one another in reciprocal services. For I do not doubt that he will diminish his favour toward a man whom he sees negligent in warding off a friend’s troubles.

In view of these reasons [Col. 0318C] I have at last judged that I ought to write to you. This will certainly be more expedient for you and yours than for me. For I neither covet nor demand anything for myself from your possessions, though I do not need them; rather, I urge you to look to yourself. You know that the lord of Canterbury, who is your father and lord by many titles, strives, at his own expense and that of foreign people, and at gravest peril to himself and all his followers, to free the Church of God from servitude; and that he scarcely finds faithfulness in any of his own adherents. Therefore, if you are wise, provide for yourself even now while it is possible; redeem your delay; share in his necessities, that you may be able to share in consolation.

Otherwise, I fear that the association which you are said to have had, and still have, with those whom he has excommunicated will prove harmful to you. Nor should you fear the king alone, since ecclesiastical powers can both help and harm. [Col. 0318D] I have said this to you in secret as to a friend, especially since I have repeatedly been commanded by the aforesaid lord of Poitiers to warn you beforehand if any adversity threatens. If the will is present, the means will not fail you. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXXIII. TO BALDWIN OF VAL-D’ARRY. (A.D. 1168.)

The same to Baldwin of Val-D’Arry.

Anyone who hears you speak or write can remember the office which you first exercised in the court, when, under King Stephen and with the aforesaid Richard, you were still serving as an almost boy. You used to be of keen intelligence and readier than all your contemporaries for every service to everyone, before you immersed yourself in the crowds of grammarians. Therefore what you say partly smells of your old training and partly of modern learning. Hence, although you cannot change your old skin, letters nevertheless make you mad.

But as you formerly used to know, a sane man seems mad to the insane, lamps seem doubled to the drunk, and it often happens that men think men to be beasts and do not remember either themselves or their own affairs. Yet this should not be imputed to you and men like you, upon whom both nature and ancestral custom impose drunkenness, so that even when fasting they cannot be sober. For you are Thebans in your habits. Thus Agave sacrifices her son for a calf, and among you each man sacrifices himself and his possessions to Bacchus. Yet Ceres and [Col. 0319B] Bacchus are at strife. But in the beer which prevails, reigns, commands, and is supreme among you, Ceres prevails; and it sharpens the wits of your people, so that you believe our France to be the homeland of wethers and the French to be wethers.

I do not know how this came into your mind, unless through the cause just mentioned, or because you and your people fear our horns—that is, the horns of the French—and take us Frenchmen for drunkards, as though a lame man mocked one who walks straight, or an Ethiopian a white man. But these and similar things are permitted to your people—indeed, are becoming. For the rest, if you are not yet drunk, press the Breton, seasonably and unseasonably, concerning the letters of blessed Jerome; and give the bearer of this letter whatever aid you can, while preserving proprietary rights. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXXIV. TO MASTER ODO. (A.D. 1168.)

[Col. 0319C]

The same to Master Odo.

Nothing more bitter could have been added to the sum of my exile and outlawry than the loss of the consolation of letters. With grace preceding, letters cleanse the mind from vices, illuminate it with knowledge of truth, kindle charity, and through their exercise establish and strengthen virtues. So long as I was permitted to devote myself to these things under your wings, and, by the benefit of your teaching, to contemplate the wheel within the wheel with the Prophet—indeed, with the sons of the prophets—and to hear from your mouth what the Spirit says to the Churches, the anger of the king of the English, though it took much from me without cause, nevertheless seemed to have brought me a great gain. [Col. 0319D] The loss seemed fruitful, the injury pleasant, and the wrong welcome.

But when I was torn away from your feet, then for the first time I experienced and felt the stings of loss and injury. Nor was I alone in this, since the loss is common to almost all scholars—not because there are lacking men who profess the office of speaking, but because there are lacking men who teach. For masters are many, but workers few. While most of them sit in the chariot of the Ethiopian eunuch, chewing over the law, proclaiming mysteries, and painting the appearance of the word of God with elaborate little flowers of speech, one may justly say: “Do you think you understand what you are reading?” Once more the saying of compassion has come true: “The tongue of the nursing child clung to the roof of his mouth in thirst; the little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations 4).

[Col. 0320A] I am one of these. To whom shall I go but to him who is accustomed to break bread for his disciples, so that it may be digested and pass into the nourishment of knowledge and character? For I have learned that others set before us loaves whole and hard, by which hearers can more easily be choked than refreshed.

I ask, therefore, if it please you, that you deign to write back to me in what book is found the gloss, issued under Augustine’s name, which says that the Jews celebrated the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh month, and so on. According to Master Peter, it is placed three times in the Psalter and once in the Epistles. I do not ask this merely because it says there that the seventh year of the seventh decade is called the Jubilee. For it is established how that point is usually explained. But it is certain that the Jews never celebrated a Jubilee—that is, the fiftieth year.

[Col. 0320B] Or, if anyone believes this, let him say when. For he can be refuted by arguments, and I know that it is not read in the Old Testament. Those who related the smallest matters would certainly not have kept silent about it. And if any commentator says it, perhaps it must be understood in this sense: that they are said to have done what they were bound to do by the necessity of the command. For it is a very common manner of speech in Scripture for something to be stated simply which a faithful understanding cannot accept without some distinction. This is known to students of law and proved by common usage. Thus something is said to exist *de iure* (“by right”), although it is known that the contrary exists *de facto* (“in fact”); and one person is said to possess the same thing by right, another in fact.

I speak to one who knows the law, who has been trained and practised in examining utterances and weighing the force of words. If anyone celebrated a Passover more splendidly; if anyone constructed a pool or built an aqueduct; if anyone did something brave; or, conversely, spared one who cursed him or showed mercy to an offending servant—authors’ diligence transmits it to posterity. Is it then probable or believable that they could have kept silent about the solemnity of the Jubilee? Where, I ask, is a sale found annulled? Where is an inheritance restored? Where is there a general emancipation of slaves? Where is a murderer exiled from a city of refuge found to have returned to his homeland after the death of the high priest? Where, or when, did the land celebrate Sabbaths proclaimed for it?

Certainly Jeremiah testifies that their fathers did not observe even the seventh year. And when, in Zedekiah’s time, at the prophet’s threat, they bound themselves before the Lord to observe those solemnities [Col. 0320C] and confirmed the undertaking by oath, they indeed emancipated male and female slaves in word, but immediately recalled them into slavery. Who, therefore, especially since Scripture does not teach it, can believe that they carried out the lawful rites of the Jubilee? Nor after the captivity under Ezra and Nehemiah does the canon of Scripture teach that they undertook this task, although it relates more carefully the things that were done. Rather, through the prophets the Lord frequently threatens that He will give the land its lawful Sabbaths which the disobedient people withheld from it. It is certain concerning the Maccabees that, occupied with so many wars, they could not have devoted themselves to such rest and solemn observances. From then until Christ, complete silence continues. Under the Roman emperors, moreover, ignorance and contempt of the divine law grew strong.

With all the devotion I can muster, I therefore beg that, if you possess any exposition of Jeremiah on Mark, you will communicate it to me; or, if you do not have one, compose it yourself, because it is a holy work and, with God’s help, will be most welcome both to churches and schools. Nor will an opportunity for writing be lacking, if the Lord inspires the will.

## LETTER CCLXXXV. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1169.)

The same to Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter.

Fortune alternates the turns of affairs and now casts down, now raises up, the condition of mortals. Yet it would be truer and more accurate to say that He who rules the winds and sea, according to the deserts of human beings, permits seditions to arise in the worldly polity—that is, the commonwealth of those living in this age—and sometimes stirs them up as storms, while at other times He restrains them by the mercy of His good pleasure.

[Col. 0321B] By this dispensation of His it recently came about that the illustrious king of England, although he had often solemnly and publicly sworn that so long as he lived he would never again enter the homage of the most Christian king, accepted sounder counsel and changed his purpose. On the approaching feast of Epiphany, at Montmirail in the district of Chartres, he came as a suppliant to the aforesaid king, placing himself, his children, lands, forces, and treasures at his disposal. He committed everything to his judgment, so that he might use or misuse all things as he pleased, retain or take away, give to whom and as much as he wished at will, with no condition whatsoever inserted or added.

He had also previously made secret engagements to the same king through intermediaries; but none of them is so hidden that, as we believe, it will not shortly be made public. The most gentle prince therefore received him kindly, giving thanks to God, who had softened his heart, and to the man who, accepting sound counsel, sought with due humility a peace beneficial to the Church and peoples. Thus he returned into his homage, giving bodily oath that he would keep faith against all men with him as his lord—to whom he had rendered homage and fealty before obtaining his kingdom—and would give him the aid and service [Col. 0321C] which the duke of Normandy ought to give the king of France.

Then they gave one another hands and kisses. The king of France restored the Bretons and Poitevins to the English king, after first receiving security from him that he would restore to them the castles and lands taken away from them at the beginning of this dispute and would keep the peace, compensation being mutually accepted for killings and burnings. The following day he brought forward his sons Henry and Richard. The former rendered homage and fealty to the king of France for the counties of Anjou and Maine; for the king himself remains in the homage of Count Theobald concerning Tours. The latter, after likewise giving fealty [Col. 0322A] and homage, received the county of Poitou.

The chief arrangers of this peace were Count Theobald and Brother Bernard of Grandmont, who were the first, together with the kings, to know of the secret undertaking mentioned above. In this distribution of honours the French believed that their kingdom had been very greatly secured, especially because they recalled with sharper pain that Henry, son of the king of England, had rendered homage to the king of France for everything when his betrothal to that king’s daughter had been contracted.

A few days earlier, the king of England had received, through the most holy man, the prior of Mont-Dieu, and the already mentioned Bernard of Grandmont, the pope’s admonitory letters concerning the archbishop of Canterbury. I send you a copy of them. He had given hope that peace would be approved, if only the lord of Canterbury would show before men an appearance of humility. He had persuaded religious men that he intended to establish the archbishop, after the lord and prince, in every honour and liberty of the Church throughout the kingdom. Accordingly, summoned by their counsel from the most Christian king, the archbishop attended this conference with his fellow-exiles; and in all humility, bending his knees, he approached his king’s feet before everyone, using these words:

> “Have mercy on me, my lord, for I place myself in God and in you, for the honour of God and of yourself.”

[Col. 0322B] But the king, who had promised peace to the Church, feared that his own peace might be disturbed. Elated by his new successes, he broke into insults against the suppliant, and by the shamelessness of his speech earned the reputation of being, whereas earlier he had been less truthful, now also uncouth among the French. And, in order to justify before the most holy king and the other princes a cause which all knew to be unjust, he concluded his insults and fictions as follows:

> “I ask nothing else, my lord king, and you holy men and princes who are present, of the archbishop, except that he should observe for me the customs which his five nearest predecessors—some of whom are saints and shine with miracles—observed for my predecessors; and which he himself promised, and should likewise pledge to me before you, as priest and bishop, without evil intent. For this is the sole cause of discord between him and me: that he breaks them and, at [Note: After the word *apud* the Paris edition omits what follows and reads: “of ecclesiastical liberty,” etc. … [Col. 0322D] down to the word *impressa* (“imposed”), which material occurs at the end of Letter 192.] Vézelay, a place of great renown, on the distinguished day of a great solemnity, excommunicated some of them together with those who observe them?”

He seemed to all to be asking a just and moderate thing, so much so that the devout prince, the archbishops, bishops, and great men present, and even the pope’s own envoys, urged the archbishop simply and absolutely to place himself at the king’s will concerning the customs and every matter. The archbishop replied that he was ready, for the sake of the king’s peace and favour, to observe the customs and to do whatever he could in accordance with [Col. 0323A] the king’s will, saving the honour of God and his own order.

But the king’s clerks who stood by him and, as was believed, feared that the peace of the Church might be restored, whenever they heard “the honour of God” or “saving his order” appended to the terms, said that sophistry lay under the words and that nothing except an absolute promise ought to be accepted. The king therefore said: “I shall never accept these words, lest the archbishop alone should appear to wish to preserve the honour of God, and not I, who desire it to be preserved still more.”

When the lord of Canterbury replied that, by homage and fealty rendered long before, he owed the king his life, limbs, and earthly honour, saving his own order, and would promise nothing further, the king departed angrily, peace unmade. The Carthusians and Grandmontines followed him; the pope had sent them either to restore peace or to deliver the admonitory letters, of which a copy is sent to you. But the king prevailed upon them with soothing flatteries, promising that he would act upon their counsel in a matter to which the entreaties of the princes present could not have persuaded him, lest the peace seem compelled.

[Col. 0323B] He therefore urged them to induce the archbishop to swear the words concerning the customs. For if anything in them should appear harsh or intolerable, he was prepared to correct it according to the counsel of religious men whom he intended to summon for this purpose, once he had gained the archbishop’s assent. He also boasted, affirming upon the sanctity of an oath, that in the whole world there was no Church with so great liberty or enjoying such great peace, and no clergy possessing such honour as those in his land—although the clerics were most impure and atrocious, being for the most part sacrilegious persons, adulterers, robbers, thieves, ravishers of virgins, arsonists, and murderers. For every accusation he produced his own men, clerics and laymen, as witnesses to his assertion.

Deceived by this hope of peace, the religious men therefore postponed delivering the admonitory letters until another conference. They approached the archbishop to persuade him to accommodate himself to the king—that is, simply to profess observance of the customs which the king had resolved to weaken or abolish. The king had also added that it ought to suffice him if he were as his predecessors had been: “For we are not better than our fathers.”

[Col. 0323C] The archbishop replied that none of his predecessors had been compelled or required to make a profession of the customs, except blessed Anselm, who had repeatedly gone into exile on account of the same cause. Nor should fathers be imitated in their evils, when they grieved that they had committed things requiring repentance. They are saints precisely because they repented that they had sinned in matters in which they would not wish successors or contemporaries to imitate them.

For Moses is not to be imitated in distrust; David in betrayal and adultery; the Apostle in betrayal; Peter in perjury; Paul in the zeal of folly; Martin in communion with the excommunicated; nor the patriarch in incest or parricide; nor the archangel, who rose in the morning, in the crime of apostasy. The sins of elders were written down [Col. 0324A] so that they might be avoided, not to impose upon successors a necessity of imitation. For the word of God is the pattern of life, not a company of those who wink at sin. Hence the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4); otherwise, he judged that no one should be imitated beyond the pattern of Christ.

When they heard this, the religious men departed beating their breasts because, in a public hearing, they had urged anything further. The most holy king also, moved to repentance, begged forgiveness because, following the opinion of religious men, he had advised that the honour of God and the saving of ecclesiastical order be left unmentioned.

And because the lord of Canterbury could not be intimidated by his enemies, the bishop of Poitiers was sent after him as far as Étampes, urging him, for the good of peace—which, from the promises he had heard, he confidently hoped for—to submit the entire matter to the king’s arbitration. But he, often deceived by blandishments of this kind, and knowing that it is the act of an unwary shepherd to entrust a sheep to a wolf, promised, saving God’s honour, order, the Church’s integrity, and liberty, that he would do everything for love of the king, but would promise nothing prejudicial to the divine law. Returning to the king, the bishop of Poitiers, to soften his disposition, set the matter out more gently, asserting that the archbishop of Canterbury committed himself and his cause to the king’s judgment above that of all mortals, asking that he, as a Christian prince, should provide for the Church’s integrity and for his person. The king gladly embraced these words and promised to do both, appointing for the archbishop a day of conference fifteen days after the second meeting. [Col. 0324B–C]

Meanwhile the king, knowing through Brother Bernard what was contained in the lord pope’s threatening letters, and perceiving that authority had been restored and conferred upon the archbishop to proceed against him, his land, and the persons of the realm, planned secretly to send envoys to the Apostolic See and repeatedly to delude the aforesaid man of Canterbury with hopes of reconciliation. The bishop of Poitiers himself, however, was also deceived, and invited the lord of Canterbury to Tours for a conference with the king, writing words by which he seemed to himself to have broken the man’s firmness. The king’s object was, by a pretence of mildness, to deceive the friends of the aforesaid man of Canterbury, lest through any one of them the petitions which he intended to present at a meeting with the other king should be dispatched; and also to outwit the unprepared Roman pontiff more easily by hastening his embassy. [Col. 0324C–D] Accordingly the lord of Canterbury wrote to the bishop of Poitiers that he would not come to the council at Tours, reproaching him because, without his mandate or knowledge, he had committed the Church’s cause to the judgment of a man striving to overthrow ecclesiastical liberty and who had so often deceived negotiators by vain hope.

At the second conference of the kings, after long refusing and swearing that he would not receive the apostolic letters, he at last, admonished by his own people, requested and received the aforesaid threatening letters from the religious men who had been sent for this purpose. It would take long to recount how many answers he gave, how diverse and mutually contradictory; by his changeableness he seemed deservedly to surpass Proteus himself. [Col. 0325A] But the sum of the affair, after many consultations, finally settled upon this: suppressing the name of the customs, he said that he had not driven the man of Canterbury from the kingdom; rather, if he would do what his predecessors had done, and promise this simply and in good faith, he might return and have peace in the land and the king’s favour, if he sought to merit it.

But the reply was that the archbishop would enter into no obligation, especially none devised as a trap, except with God’s honour and his own order preserved; he would, however, do what he ought, adding the service of his whole devotion. And although the name of the customs was unspoken, it is plain that they were demanded under that formula of words by which the king asked of him what he said had been done by his predecessors. The archbishop maintained that he could in no way profess observance of the customs: first, because it would be a pernicious precedent to introduce a new form into the Church; secondly, because it was established that the lord pope had condemned them in large part as hostile to the divine law, and had absolved him at Sens from the promise of them which had been extorted. [Col. 0325B]

Moreover, if, in accordance with the apostolic command, the lord king restored the peace and favour of the Church and restored to him and his people what had been taken away, he said that he was prepared to return and to do whatever the archbishop of Canterbury owed to his king, prince, and lord. Otherwise, henceforth he would use his authority and right against the evildoers of the Church and against his own enemies and those of his people. The king, pressed by the insistence of religious and great men, replied that he would shortly summon the bishops of England, whose counsel he had chiefly used in this case thus far; and he asked that his replies not be written to the lord pope. But because, as has been said, those replies did not agree with one another, the religious men in turn asked him to write in open letters what, out of reverence for, at the prayers of, and at the command of the lord pope, he would do; and they promised that afterwards they would write what was necessary. Struck by this request, he left them in indignation. Yet, drawing Brother Bernard aside, he said that he would go quickly to Grandmont and obey the will and command of the master who presided over the brethren there. Meanwhile the bishops would come from England, and then, with God’s aid, peace would be restored together. [Col. 0325C]

[Col. 0325D] This he told Brother Bernard; but in truth he was awaiting the envoys whom he had sent to Rome. Nevertheless the religious men advised the archbishop to spare the king’s person and land until it should be ascertained what fruit that conference with the Grandmontines would bear. Yet this is certain, as I have received it beyond doubt: the archbishop will meanwhile strike some of his evildoers with due severity. The messenger, whom I beg may be sent back to me with all speed, will supply the rest.

The kings, having mutually sworn to one another on each side, have formed a league against all men, with the reservation on each side that Richard, son of the king of England, is to marry without dowry the daughter of the king of the French. Publication of the secret obligation which I mentioned above has been deferred until the end of the following year, lest, if what is being negotiated should become known beforehand, it might more easily be impeded. The German tyrant, by the advice of the prudent men of his party, has summoned the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, intending, it is believed, to negotiate peace with the Church with them and through them. [Col. 0326A]

## LETTER CCLXXXVI. TO SIMON, PRIOR OF MONT-DIEU, AND ENGELBERT OF THE VALLEY OF ST PETER.  
*(A.D. 1169, January)*

To his venerable lords and friends, the prior of Mont-Dieu and the prior of the Valley of St Peter: John of Salisbury sends greetings, and prosperity in God’s cause.

Your discretion may remember that the lord of Canterbury was never pleased that you should delay carrying out the terms of the apostolic mandate. Yet he yielded to Brother Bernard, who promised happier results if the king were granted time for deliberation until another conference. [Col. 0326B] For he promised that the man’s fierceness would meanwhile be changed into gentleness. But behold: from letters which I have lately received, it is clearer than daylight that the mission of the lord bishop of Poitiers was arranged to deceive both the Church and ourselves. Would that the delay itself had not involved deceit; for the event will show this. While we await the promised gentleness, he busily considers how to overthrow God’s honour and subvert the whole liberty of the Church.

Why should he not do so? He had tested our strength and, by his iniquity, had not, I say, deserved—for that would be false—but had stolen the favour of all. And he who alone, at this critical point of such difficulty, dared to assert God’s honour was made an object of derision and hissing to all, and departed as though spat upon by everyone. [Col. 0326C] Could not iniquity, armed with counsels and favour, henceforth easily hope for victory?

As you advised, I urged the lord of Rheims to write to Brother Bernard; but he did not agree, saying that his letters would be of no use because he believed Bernard favoured the opposing party. It is common for those proclaimed to possess nothing to desire exceedingly either wealth or glory. The lord of Canterbury does not wish me or any of his people to be present at the conference, except Master Lombard, subdeacon of the Roman Church, whom you will find in the household of the lord of Sens.

May the Lord lead you there in the spirit and power of Elijah, [Col. 0326D] and direct and strengthen in your hands, with the zeal you possess, the sword of Phinehas. Do not fear the countenance or the multitude of men, for those who are with us are more and stronger than those who are with them. The archbishop of Rheims writes to the lord pope on behalf of our cause, directing that his letters be drawn up according to my judgment; he also promises to stand by us in our necessities as long as the matter requires.

Act courageously, I beg you, most beloved lords; and compensate for the danger of delay by diligent and faithful execution, so that through you it may become known that whatever beyond what he has offered is demanded from the man of Canterbury is not merely an excess of authority but proof of sheer and unmistakable bad faith. Hence, as you know, certain people use the pretext of your holiness to excuse their mistaken counsel; but now let it be clear, by your profession of truth and freedom of spirit, that you never consented to their error. For where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom (2 Cor. 3); and without doubt the truth will set you free.

May your holiness always prosper and flourish in the Lord, remembering us continually before God and, so far as is expedient to integrity, before men.

## LETTER CCLXXXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS.  
*(A.D. 1169)*

To John, bishop of Poitiers, J. S.

Great among us is the expectation of those awaiting what the conference between the illustrious king of England and the holy men of Grandmont will bring forth. Would that, in accordance with the renown which they have suddenly acquired in the Church of God, they may strive to procure peace for the Church. [Col. 0327B] For they are believed to have so deserved and received from the Lord the talent of princes’ favour that the administration of kingdoms, insofar as they permit, is committed to their judgment. Indeed, rumour proclaims that the counsels and deeds of kings are in their hands.

Since therefore I do not doubt that you love these same holy men, and trust that you are their intimate friend, I beg you with all the urgency I can: by the grace divinely bestowed upon you, encourage them with every diligence, so that in the conference which they are to have with the aforesaid king—if indeed it has not already been held—they may provide for ecclesiastical peace. Before God, that peace will be far more advantageous to the king himself than to those who gladly have exposed themselves and all that is theirs for Christ. For whether they live or die, they belong to the Lord; and in proportion to the multitude of labours and sorrows by which for a little while they are chastened, they await his consolations in abundant mercy. [Col. 0327C]

What, unless he repents, can the king expect from the just Judge, whose will is omnipotence, when he persecutes and tortures the innocent without cause? Or what fruit of repentance will there be unless, with a contrite and humbled heart, he confesses his fault, makes amends for the injury, repairs the losses as far as his means permit, and resolves in future to avoid like acts? But if the holy men mentioned, overcome by hope or fear, keep silent about what must be said to so great a lord and so sincere a friend, who will henceforth stand before his face? Who will turn away from his house the sword of the Lord, who punishes the powerful more powerfully, tortures them, and takes away the breath of princes? [Col. 0327D]

See what He has done to the German tyrant, whom, as public report has it among us, gout has struck in the feet like that statue which Nebuchadnezzar saw in a dream, so that he cannot walk unless supported by the aid of attendants. And indeed there is hope that a great downfall will soon become manifest, and that he will yield glory—even unwillingly—to Christ, whom he persecutes in his members while he seeks to overthrow the Church’s liberty.

What good, moreover, will the journey to Jerusalem which the kings have planned accomplish, if peace is not first restored to the Church? For when, in our age, very many and very great princes undertook a similar pilgrimage, the most miserable outcome of the affair, grievous to the Church, taught that offerings made to God from plunder and injuries do not please him: the thankless labour of their service turned wholly to an outcome contrary to its purpose. [Col. 0328A] His own people mourn inconsolably for the count of Nevers, who took the same journey and endured like things; they believe that neither Parthian arrows nor Syrian swords extinguished him ingloriously, so that the glorious death of a brave man might offer some consolation, but rather the tears of widows, the groans of the poor, and the complaints of churches.

Although the necessity of that expedition has been postponed for the pledged term of two years, time is short if it is to be begun or completed for God’s honour and the salvation of those who depart. For the French proverb says: “While the fool sleeps, the creditor’s deadline hastens. The fool sleeps, but interest does not sleep.”

But why do I trouble you in this matter, when you bear this concern continually and beyond your strength? Only because I know that you have so great an affection for so great a prince and so good a lord that you desire his safety and honour as your own—as indeed I do also. [Col. 0328B]

For he is a man greater than all praise, if only he paid greater reverence, as he ought, to the Church of God; dealt more moderately with those who enter into negotiations with him; restrained tongue and mind by some rational consideration rather than by the impulse of anger or the desire to repress another; and kept his speech within the measure of royal dignity. Otherwise he is endowed with so many and such great gifts of nature and grace alike that no prince in the world, as I would more readily believe—or very few, as I would say without hesitation—could be found his equal.

Yet I fear that your loyalty and service may have harmed you with him, because you could not obtain from the archbishop of Canterbury the conference which you desired for the king’s honour. Therefore I earnestly beg you to inform me what result that matter had, and what concerns you and your people. [Col. 0328C] In the affair which the bearer of this letter will explain to you, let your diligence proceed as you judge most expedient. Of those who have gone to Rome I as yet have nothing certain; but when matters requiring report become known, they shall be conveyed to you as opportunity granted by God permits and my care can arrange.

## LETTER CCLXXXVIII. TO HUGH OF GHENT.  
*(A.D. 1169)*

The same to Hugh of Ghent.

My mind gives birth to the thanks that are due. But, as the prophet says, “She who is in labour has no strength” (4 Kings 19). [Col. 0328D] For the bitterness of persecution has until now suspended the effect of devotion; yet no force can or could restrain its affection from yearning to burst forth in the birth of rejoicing.

Indeed, by God’s favour, Christ’s cause and that of his Church have now been brought to such a point that henceforth they cannot be endangered, because the leaders of the schism have failed, and the hammer of the English Church, caught in his own works, can henceforth find no support upon which to lean. Matters had reached the extreme point, at which circumstances are known to be perilous, when he, seeing that by soliciting both the curia and the schismatics—Frederick, namely, and his accomplices—he could make no progress against the Lord and against His Christ, sent an embassy and defected to the cities of Italy. [Col. 0329A] He promised the Milanese three thousand marks and the strongest repair of their walls, if, with the other cities whom he sought to corrupt, they would obtain from the lord pope and the Roman Church the deposition or transfer of the archbishop of Canterbury. For the same cause he had promised the Cremonese two thousand marks, the Parmenese one thousand, and the Bolognese the same amount.

To the lord pope he offered to free him, by payment of money, from the exactions of all Romans and to add ten thousand marks; he also granted that the pope might appoint pastors at his pleasure both in the Church of Canterbury and in other English churches left vacant. But because his many promises undermined his credibility and manifest iniquity lay in his requests, he was repulsed; and what he could not obtain by himself he tried to extort by the power of the Sicilian king. [Col. 0329B] But the latter too was not heard, though the bishop of Syracuse and Count Robert of Bassonville laboured with all their strength toward this end through repeated intercessors, notwithstanding his standing, power, and favour, which is very great in the Roman Church.

The king’s envoys were therefore dismissed without attaining their wish, having secured only this: that the lord pope should send envoys to procure peace—namely Gratian, a subdeacon, and Master Vivian, archdeacon of Orvieto, who ordinarily serves as advocate in the curia. Beforehand, however, he bound them by the sacred obligation of an oath to the prescribed terms of peace, that they should not exceed the limits laid down. He also added instructions that they should refrain from the king’s expenses unless the Church’s peace had been obtained, and that they should make no delay beyond the day assigned. [Col. 0329C]

The form of peace communicated to the archbishop contains nothing dishonourable, nothing unbecoming to the Church or to his person, nor does it diminish his authority in any respect; rather, with every pretext and appeal set aside, he may freely exercise ecclesiastical severity against the king himself, the kingdom, and the persons of the realm, as he recognizes to be expedient for himself and the Church of God. Yet the advice of his friends, and of prudent friends, is that while terms of peace are being negotiated he should act more gently and overlook many things; afterwards, if—God forbid!—peace should not result, he is to overthrow the persecutors of the Church more severely, as though recovering his strength. [Col. 0329D]

Therefore hope, my dear friend, and do not be disturbed by whatever you hear meanwhile, for God has placed the cause in safety. Perhaps you will hear of “the pride of Moab”; but remember that “his pride is greater than his strength.” For sinners in Zion are terrified; fear has taken possession of hypocrites. Unless they turn back from their perversity, they shall be driven out and unable to stand; for already the axe is laid to their root, and the angel holds the winnowing fan in his hand to separate the grain from the chaff.

The aforesaid envoys have departed for the king, but what they have found with him has not yet been made known to us. This, however, is certain: the king has bound himself by word and writing [Col. 0330A] to execute the counsel and command of the lord pope, and his written undertaking is in hand. If he should draw back from it, he will easily be convicted. But not even so has the Church thought him to be trusted before he strengthens the credit of his words by the testimony of deeds.

The archbishop, greeted by you, warmly and affectionately returns your greeting, offering himself to your love and honour with most ready devotion.

## LETTER CCLXXXIX. TO THE COMMUNITY OF CANTERBURY.  
*(A.D. 1169)*

The same to the community of Canterbury.

I grieve, beloved brethren, and grieve deeply over what has been reported to me about your brotherhood: that there are schisms among you, so that you do not think or speak alike in the Lord. For, as those say who are believed to have examined your way of life more intimately and understood it more keenly, one of you says, “I belong to the king”; another, “I belong to Ranulf”; another, “I shall follow fortune and cleave to the victors.” [Col. 0330B] Amid all this, it is exceedingly rare, if indeed there is any such person, for one mindful of his profession to remember that he has an archbishop whom he ought to obey; to speak the word of God with confidence; or publicly to declare that one must obey God rather than men (Acts 5).

I wonder—if what is said is true, and would that it proved false!—that you are so quickly transferred from the Lord’s way to another Gospel, which overthrows the authority of the Catholic Church, grants communion of the faithful to those who, by their deserving, have been handed over to Satan, and teaches men to take a share in wickedness for the sake of pleasure or gain with robbers, thieves, fornicators, and simoniacs. [Col. 0330C] This is believed to have happened because there are some within your body who trouble you, and others outside who, led by blind ambition, seek to rule over you and ensnare your innocence by flattering promises and ingenious deceptions, drawing you away from conformity with your order.

But unless you are so dull-minded as to surpass the most brutish animals in stupidity, you can see more clearly than daylight to what end their schemes are directed. For behold, the bishop of London has publicly declared, not without grief to the faithful, that he owes no obedience to the first see of the Britains, namely the Church of Canterbury; and that he will have the metropolitan chair transferred to the place where he pretends—indeed, not to say lies—it ought to be: namely, to the Church of London, where he boasts that an *archflamen* sat while the religion of Jupiter was worshipped. [Col. 0330D]

Perhaps the prudent and religious man intends to restore the worship of Jupiter, so that if he cannot otherwise become an archbishop, he may at least obtain the name and title of *archflamen*. Yet he relies upon Merlin’s oracle. Merlin, filled, I know not with what spirit, is said to have foretold before the coming of blessed Augustine, apostle of the English, that the Christian religion would be destroyed and then restored when London’s dignity should adorn Dorobernia [Canterbury]. But because the Merlinesque philosopher knew the flimsy authority of his prophet, he is also said to have resorted to more substantial supports, trusting in the power of the prince, the weakness of the Church, the avarice of the Romans, your faintheartedness, the archbishop’s poverty, and the abundance of his own wealth. [Col. 0331A] By these things, in his vanity, he believes that he will prevail against the wisdom and justice of God.

What then will you say and do in response? Do you fear your aforesaid patrons—or rather, to speak more truly, the enemies of piety and faith—so greatly that you will give place to one who seeks to slaughter your mother with such parricidal impiety? Is it not here that not only the Church’s resources must be spent, but blood itself shed, in order to resist him and preserve the Church’s authority? I beg your holiness to be ashamed that until now you have shown no humane consolation to your Father in exile and proscription; you have bestowed either nothing or—what you know better—the very least, although nearly the whole Latin world manifestly recognizes that God’s justice and the liberty of the Church are the cause of his exile and proscription.

For five years now, then, I do not say that he has despoiled other churches, because they have freely and willingly shared in his necessities and tribulations; rather, he has received from them support for the service of your peace, liberty, honour, and glory. [Col. 0331B] I write this not to accuse your stinginess or inhumanity, for perhaps you were occupied, but to admonish you as dearest brethren: let your faith at last revive and flourish in works of charity, so that, when the peace which we hope will shortly be restored has been established, you may not be ashamed, but may receive in joy and exultation the fruit of charity shown, with manifold interest.

For the fullness of time has come, so that Satan may no longer rage with such fury in the Church; and your Father has received authority from the Lord, so that he may

> Spare the submissive and subdue the proud.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid VI.854)*

Would that my eyes might see you distinguished before others by your merit in the consolation of the saints who suffer with us. Would that, in our return, we might embrace you as partners in our joy by a closer bond of charity. Would that your diligence now sowed among your needy brethren in their barrenness, and especially in the heart of your Father, what afterward you may reap in joy. [Col. 0331C] You know who said: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessing will also reap from blessing” (2 Cor. 9). What then, you ask? Along with temporal grace, eternal life.

But perhaps you are excessively afraid of the threats of those who lay snares and threaten labours and pains, so that you do not dare, as the time demands and the Church’s need calls for, to sow in tears. Yet surely almost only those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Nothing has been lacking to you thus far: divine grace has supplied wealth and peace while others laboured amid want and hardship for the Church’s defence. Now at last, if it please you and seem good to your discretion, prove by the performance of deeds the compassion of charity which you have continually professed in words toward the tribulation of your brethren.

Not indeed so that relief may be theirs and tribulation yours, but in equality: that at the present time your abundance may supply, if not your brothers’ poverty, as it ought, at least your Father’s need. [Col. 0332A] Otherwise injustice will be manifest where no equality of mutual balancing is found. For of those who dwell in unity in the house of the Lord it is written: “He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack.” Have you alone in the Lord’s camp lost the lawful *gomer*? If the gift reserved contrary to the Lord’s prohibition—the heavenly gift, the bread and food of angels—rots and breeds worms, what rot and worms will that rottenness gather which, though the Lord forbids it, is kept to the detriment of charity, amid the hunger and nakedness of brethren? Not indeed that they may be hungry or naked, but because, unless charity in you is more fully stirred by grace, you have exposed them to hunger, nakedness, and every danger.

Let these and like considerations be turned over in your minds and discussed in your conversations. Set your hearts upon your ways: upon the cause and journeys of your Father, and upon the ways of his adversaries. Consider what outcome, under God’s inspection and judgment, can come from these things. [Col. 0332B] Yet let there not be one counsellor of Ranulf, another of Jannes, another of Jambres, another of Ahithophel and such magicians; instead, let each examine his own conscience and consult the law of God.

Now, enlightened by reason leading the way through grace, you will call to mind that mercy is the fullness of virtues; and, departing from your former ways, you will show mercy to him who, by God’s favour, may soon answer it with the horn of his word and mightily afflict those who afflict him. May the spirit of counsel be with you and guide your hearts, that you may remember yourselves for good.

For charity has drawn this from my heart and lips, before God who sees, witnesses, and judges, for my sweetest and most reverend brethren: so that hereafter it may not be imputed to me before God—whom I call upon as witness and judge of these things—if they disdain to hear me offering salutary counsel. [Col. 0332C]

## LETTER CCXC. TO WILLIAM, SUBPRIOR OF CANTERBURY.  
*(A.D. 1169)*

To William, subprior of Canterbury.

Although our common Father and lord has learned through the master-teaching of charity both to abound and to suffer need, and everywhere and in all circumstances in which he finds himself to be sufficient for Christ, I nevertheless rejoice on your account that at last your charity has somehow revived and, by the evidence of its deed—though late and at first modest—has appeared, proving that faith, which, as you know, is dead without works according to James’s testimony (chapter 2), lives at least faintly. [Col. 0332D]

He himself has until now suffered no poverty, or only an honourable one, since God tempers the scourges and mercifully softens men’s persecutions so that they may be bearable to the faithful. But he was tested for a time, so that he might know himself more fully, be more clearly known to the world, and in the narrowness of such great tribulation more manifestly test the faith of his friends.

He has now passed through fire and water. He neither blushed nor feared to raise and bear before resistant and hostile kings and governors the banner of faith and justice. Neither prayer nor price, neither threats nor flattery nor tortures could break or bend him so that he should keep silent about the Lord’s name or suffer even the slightest loss to His honour. [Col. 0333A] Was he not told, almost in these very words, though with a different purpose: “Allow me to diminish the divine honour, destroy the Church’s liberty, and make you grow into a great nation, provided that you allow the ancestral customs to proceed and do not set before or against them the reverence due to the divine commands”?

But this vessel of election, speaking faith confidently, said: “Either you will destroy me, or this presumption of yours, hostile to God, will be destroyed; for I cannot serve both you, plotting such things, and Him.” Therefore, by a favourable divine nod, it has come about that he who despised himself for God’s honour has received from the Lord full and glorious authority by which he may crush his adversaries.

Observe, I beg you, how the bishops and others who attacked him are failing; and, persisting in what you have at last begun, convert and strengthen your brethren. Show yourself a son to your Father, for after God and through God the Church’s safety is placed in his hands. Do not delay to do good when you can; but if their safety cannot otherwise be secured, take something from the brethren, whether unknowingly or unwillingly, so that their welfare and freedom from loss may be provided for on the day of obstruction. [Col. 0333B] By God’s aid you are sailing in harbour; through the bearer of this letter you will learn what you ought to do.

## LETTER CCXCI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS.  
*(A.D. 1169)*

To John, bishop of Poitiers.

[Col. 0333C] I rejoice, if the reports of rumour deserve belief, that the king of England has recalled you from the threshold of your intended journey, so that you may see the progress and outcome of the business which he conducts with the man of Canterbury—or rather, against the Church. Would that he may yield to your counsel and that of prudent men. And indeed, if Gratian, as he is now said to have begun, acts courageously, the king will at last yield to sound counsel, even unwillingly.

Yet many hope that the son of grace—whose name corresponds to the fact—and the worthy nephew of blessed Eugenius, will proceed rightly toward the truth of the Gospel, the glory of apostolic majesty, and the integrity and peace of the suffering Church. For he knows beyond doubt that, if he proceeds by this path, he will merit eternal glory before God and men. And because he finds few upon whom he can confidently rely, I beg you to raise and strengthen his constancy in the Lord. [Col. 0333D]

By God’s favour the king is well able to pay; and it is established that sins cannot be forgiven to the unrepentant. But if a thing taken away is not restored when it can be restored, repentance is not performed but feigned. What will absolution confer upon excommunicated persons unless they make satisfaction for injuries and plunder, and for so manifest a crime of disobedience? Crimes rendered most evident by their public character have gravely scandalized the whole Church; and things committed in the light ought not to be abolished in darkness, especially since there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed, nor anything that shall not be proclaimed in streets and upon rooftops. [Col. 0334A]

If they are absolved without an oath, there will be a grave presumption against the public form and to the injury of the Church. Unless a proper undertaking to make restitution is given, a pernicious example will be left to princes and tyrants both contemporary and future. If the king succeeds in having the preservation of the kingdom’s dignities inserted into the agreements, he has prevailed in securing the customs merely by changing their name and has eliminated all authority of the Roman Church from England. But far be it that any of these things should happen! I am certain that the lord of Canterbury would choose perpetual exile rather than have the Church injured for the sake of the king’s peace and the privilege of the Apostolic See overthrown.

Therefore urge Lord Gratian to be on his guard in all things, [Col. 0334B] and especially on these points, lest—may God avert it—

> Hearts lying hidden beneath the fox deceive him.  
> *(Horace, Ars Poetica 437)*

For, unless I am mistaken, he may now have learned that a deceitful tongue loves words of haste. “The Wise Man says: ‘There is never any safety in sleeping beside a neighbouring serpent.’” And in Satan’s seat it is certain that ostriches and scorpions dwell with those who hold the doctrine of Balaam. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXCII. TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER.  
*(A.D. 1169)*

To Baldwin, archdeacon of Exeter, John of Salisbury.

[Col. 0334C]

> Neglecting his own affairs, he busies himself with those of others.  
> *(Horace, Satires II.3.19)*
Quasi with the men of Canterbury or with their rivals I had any familiar intercourse, I recently went to Vézelay on the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene, meeting there the envoys of the lord pope, ostensibly in order to learn what the Canterbury party ought to fear or hope. For this affair alone, it is thought, occupies the tongues and ears of both realms so far as concerns the clergy, and certainly to a great extent the people as well. But I truly wished to see my namesake—and, more than that, my compatriot and in some sense brother—Gratian, of whom you may remember that you were appointed instructor at Ferentino by Pope Eugenius of holy memory. Him I may confidently call a brother, with whom I share the bonds of faith and fellowship; and although one city did not give birth to us, there is no doubt that we have one fatherland: he recalls to mind that fatherland of the brave, indivisible for us, which Carmentis revealed.

Received kindly and respectfully by him and his companion Vivian, I learned more particularly that the lord pope and the Roman Church are very strongly favourable to the Canterbury party. Indeed, unless the king now makes peace with the lord of Canterbury in accordance with the pope’s counsel, they intend to notify him that not only will he be handed over into the archbishop’s hands, but the Roman pontiff himself will lay his hand heavily upon him.

As for your assertion that many wonder by what legal procedure the archbishop of Canterbury excommunicated bishops and others who had not been convicted of crime or contumacy, nor confessed, nor even been cited once—what is more serious, after an appeal—this would indeed be astonishing if the complaint rested on truth. But it is otherwise. Their deeds not only came before judgment, but themselves called forth, as it were, a sluggish and tardy condemnation; and not only will they, when necessary, be convicted by men, but heaven and earth cry out against them. Consequently, the protection of appeal has rightly been withdrawn from them by the Roman pontiff; and full authority has been conferred upon the archbishop against the king himself, the realm, and persons of the realm, to punish every act of disobedience, to restrain the Church’s evildoers, and to restrain his own [opponents]. Thus he proceeds fortified by the counsel of the Apostolic See; and, having recently received his own envoys and letters from the lord pope, he has been assured that the measures he has decreed will not be changed.

Yet the archbishop is ready to absolve those excommunicated persons, according to the teaching of the Fathers and the rule of the Church, if they repent with fruit worthy of repentance. But if—God forbid—they judge that they must persist in the contumacy they have begun, he will proceed further while life remains; nor will he put the sword of the Spirit back into its sheath before the land has been cleansed of such abominations. For the blade must be drawn seven times into infected dust that has caked upon it, so that Syria may be crushed.

As for the boast, so they say, of Reginald the archdeacon, that these envoys of the lord pope will annul every undertaking and act of the archbishop by apostolic authority: they themselves flatly deny it, declaring under oath that they will deliberately do nothing to the archbishop’s disadvantage. Nor indeed can they do so; rather, by every means permitted to them according to God, they will promote his welfare and the honour of the Church. A prescribed form has been given them, whose limits they will not dare to exceed, because they are bound to this by oath. Indeed, they have been ordered, unless peace is restored, to abstain altogether from the king’s gifts, so that they may not even be permitted to receive expenses from him.

Let others say what they please; meanwhile, my hope for peace is greater than it was before. For in illnesses one must reach the climax through an increase of pains, so that, when nature gains strength and corruption is purged away, health and soundness may be restored. And although some boast that they have been absolved by the lord pope, you may know with the utmost certainty that he has absolved none of them. For he did not yet know that they were bound; but later, when this sentence now under discussion became known to him while [the envoys] were travelling, Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff, was sent back to the lord pope to urge him to absolve the excommunicated. But he is not believed likely to succeed. For, to say nothing of other matters, the lord of Meaux, a man greater in authority and stronger in right, will oppose him with all his powers.

Before long, God willing, it will be heard what either party, or both, accomplish. Nor can the secrets of the envoys, who have now reached as far as Auxerre, remain hidden for long. For the outcome of their mission is at the door, since they have now almost come to those whose affair is being conducted. The matter cannot remain long in suspense.

And because you are concerned for your Exeter man—and because he is yours—I approve for the present what he has done in withdrawing from communion with the excommunicated. For it is beyond doubt that the faithful ought to avoid such persons until their absolution has been established. One ought to obey God rather than men. Yet this very often, especially in such circumstances, does not happen without danger, because it is through many tribulations that one enters the kingdom of God. This, my dear friend, is the path of the righteous; this is the cleansing of vices, the furnace of virtues, placing the elect between hammer and anvil. But the Lord delivers them from all these things, and glorifies those who have been tested with a more splendid crown.

If he obtains permission—though I do not think he will—to cross the sea, I fear he will be compelled to appeal, not according to his own judgment, but according to that of his extortioner. For if everything does not proceed at the latter’s pleasure, his impatience will be inflamed: for him nothing is enough without the overthrow of others. If it does proceed thus, justice will be abandoned; and, what is worse and more shameful than anything else, God will be offended. If, as I think more likely, he is forbidden to cross the sea, I fear that he will be unable to stand alone, assailed by so many snares, provoked by so many injuries, and exposed to every tormentor. For perhaps this too will be inserted among the royal commands.

Still, lower ministers of Satan may be endured more mildly—if anything can be mild amid tortures—than that man when present, who, because sins demand it, has received from the Lord a greater power to harm. Therefore I judge it more advisable that, as long as he can escape through administrative byways which in no way obstruct justice, he should patiently endure for the present to dwell with the sons of Kedar, awaiting counsel and consolation from the Lord. But should the king return, and he be more harshly pressed to pass into the company of the wicked, let him raise a voice worthy of a bishop in the spirit of freedom; and, before he harms the condition of the Church, let him take such an honourable cause as God will provide and depart from the midst of Babylon, lest, by touching what is unclean, he receive of her plagues—breaking the rope, if it cannot otherwise be untied—lest, at peril of conscience and with the stigma of infamy, he be compelled to break saving charity.

> [Note: After *otherwise*, the Paris edition omits the remainder and reads “the archdeacon,” etc., as far as “has been permitted”; these words occur at the end of Letter 295.]

Meanwhile, since so many distresses threaten on every side, I advise that, as far as he can, he provide for himself from his resources, above all placing his hope in works of mercy and in the prayers of the saints. Thus, as I desire him to read if he has not yet read it, the great Basil delivered himself and his people from Julian’s jaws. God surely looks down from on high; he will not allow his chosen ones to be tempted beyond their strength, but will make the very trial yield a joyful and glorious result.

[Col. 0337A] But, to lessen your anxiety in some measure, Frederick the German tyrant is believed, God favouring it, to be about to make peace with the Church. He asks that the lord pope receive as emperor his second-born son, whom he has caused to be elected king, and command that he be consecrated by Catholic bishops, on condition that he obey the Apostolic See. Yet Frederick stipulates that in his own person he shall not be compelled to receive any apostolic [legate] unless he wishes, apart from Peter and the others who are in heaven. In these terms he could readily be heard, if he did not insert into the agreement that those ordained and consecrated by schismatic heresiarchs should remain in their ranks and dignities.

The dispute still rests upon this point; but from certain signs each party is believed to be prepared to yield to the other in some part of its request. This will become more fully known when the negotiators in this matter, the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, return from the Roman Church, as is hoped shortly. The bearer of this letter will relate a few matters more privately. I ask you to ensure that care is taken of him until he recovers; and I wish my brother too to be attentive to him insofar as medical treatment is concerned. When matters worthy of report emerge, they will, God favouring, be conveyed to your knowledge with all speed. Farewell; and remember your people before God.

## LETTER CCXCIII. TO THE SAME PERSON. (A.D. 1170.)

To Baldwin, archdeacon of Exeter, J. S.

[Col. 0337C] I send you the letters which the envoys of the lord of Canterbury recently sent him from the curia. From them you may be more cautious, so as not readily to acquiesce in every spirit. For supporters of each party say many things against the other, and each party strives to induce as many people as it can, by whatever means it has power to use, to accept its own side. Both seek the favour of the Apostolic See; and, in my judgment, those who have deserved or obtained it least boast the more loudly that their wishes have been fulfilled. They trumpet that they have obtained this and that; but I know that no wise person will believe them, especially regarding those matters which seem to have been extracted from the opposite party, unless they produce authentic original documents.

One thing I know; and though the world protests, I assert it without doubt and freely: whoever clings to Christ will not repent in the end. The joy of the wicked is momentary and like a point: shortly moths will be spread beneath them, and worms will be their covering. But the Lord will console his chosen ones, and will not allow a double tribulation to afflict them. All hope for the peace of the universal Church, and nearly all desire it. I would think that none should be excepted except those whom the consciousness of their crimes torments, convicting them that they have deserved the sentence of their own condemnation.

For the emperor himself, now stripped of his august dignity, has openly discovered that he cannot return to imperial rank unless he makes peace with the Church. Nor does he now refuse to enter into an agreement with the Italians on fair terms. The consuls of the cities, summoned together with his envoys, are in the curia weighing and framing the articles of the peace to be made, and arranging guarantees that will be binding in the future. The lord of Sens awaits the outcome of this matter, though he is believed and hoped to be keeping the Easter solemnity at home. With him, if life permits, the representatives of the Church of Canterbury will return, having written to their lord that their requests had been heard more kindly than they had hoped, although earlier they had seemed absolutely certain of the faithfulness and constancy of the lord pope.
