The king’s envoys had preceded them: Ragin, archdeacon of Salisbury; Master Richard Barre; and Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff. Yet by no insistence could they bring it about that the lord pope should dismiss them other than confounded before he had received his own Gratian. At Gratian’s arrival their horns were checked and blunted, while the Church’s cause, as truth was more fully disclosed, grew stronger and stronger. For the conspiracy which was being forced into being in England, in imitation of a schism, will serve the advances of the Church against which it was devised.

Other envoys then followed on the king’s side: Giles, archdeacon of Rouen, John, archdeacon of Sées, and that notorious oath-bound dean of Salisbury. They withdrew the demands of the earlier envoys and said that the lord king committed entirely to the lord pope’s judgment both the cause being litigated between himself and the archbishop of Canterbury and the terms by which peace between them was to be restored. They produced sealed letters of the king himself on this point. Receiving this more graciously, the lord pope wrote congratulatory letters to the king, a copy of which I send you.

Meanwhile, the king was discussing with the other king, through the mediation of the archbishop of Tyre, the taking up of the cross. He had persuaded him, with guarantees interposed—which ought not be expressed out of respect for the person concerned—that from the coming Easter he would prepare himself for setting out within a year. Under this pretext he had the Most Christian prince as his helper in settling his boundaries, until the collusion made with Hervé of Montmirail gave reasonable grounds for suspicion of him; he became still more suspect because he sought to prevent the conference and agreement between the king of the Franks and the count of Flanders.

Nevertheless, to establish more plausibly his devotion to taking up the cross, he negotiated peace with the Church through great and religious men and through members of his household, as you will see from their letters. In this affair he used the office of the lord of Tyre. Before archbishops, bishops, abbots, and many nobles assembled, he first gave God—and, as the saying goes, his Christianity—as hostage; then he made his uncle, the king of Jerusalem, and all who were assembled sureties that, sincerely and faithfully, he had remitted to the archbishop of Canterbury every complaint, anger, and rancour of mind, and to all his people, requesting them to return, to receive all that was theirs in peace and safety. He demanded nothing except that the archbishop should render him what is due to a king, and that he in return should render the archbishop what a king owes an archbishop.

He sent the abbot of Cîteaux, Brother Geoffrey Fulcher, master of the Temple, and Geoffrey of Auxerre to Sens, so that they might bring the said archbishop of Canterbury to him, together with the bishop of Sées, on these terms. But when the archbishop, trusting their word, had come to Pontoise, the lord archbishop of Rouen warned him not to proceed, because the king was about to cross into England with all speed, peace not having been made. The king had taken back two of his envoys, Master Richard Barre and the archdeacon of Llandaff; on their return peace was obstructed, through the plotting, they say, of Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury, to whom God will one day answer according to his deserts.

At that time it was bruited about that the king’s envoys had obtained absolution for the bishop of London and all the others, and that the archbishop’s power to punish the king, his land, or persons of the kingdom had been taken away. But these lies were immediately exposed when letters from the lord pope arrived, even before the bishop of London set out for the curia. He would doubtless have spared himself labour and expense if, as some men falsely claimed, he could have been absolved without so much difficulty.

A widespread report says that the aforesaid archdeacon of Canterbury persuaded the king to cross into England in order to torture the bishops and clergy who refused to swear against the lord pope and their mother, the Church of Canterbury. Fear and distress are on every side, imposed by the necessity of avoiding them. It is far better to fall into the hands of men than to abandon the law of God. The latter always brings hell; the former is the way to a crown and makes glory everlasting. For blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness: those whom conflict purifies, proves, and makes illustrious are crowned without end by the end of the conflict.

But Satan rages more fiercely when he sees his destruction drawing near; and that part of winter is the more grim which precedes the beauty of approaching spring. Review histories, examine the deeds of tyrants, and you will plainly find that the Church has always been enlarged amid afflictions, and that the more atrocious persecution was, the sooner it subsided. The king, moreover, has been unequivocally informed by friends as well as by other envoys who preceded these men in order to forewarn him, that unless he makes peace with the Church promptly, in the manner which the lord pope prescribed at his request—and before the Kalends of May—there can thereafter be no grounds for delay in exercising ecclesiastical severity upon his person, his lands on this side of the sea, and his lands beyond the sea.

I think that this gave rise to the present exasperation—may God quickly restrain it as he knows to be expedient for the Church—since those who hate peace continually supply causes, feeding the fuel of heat and conflagration. They know that they will become a detestable example of schism and apostasy, branded with everlasting infamy. The bearer of this letter, if you see fit to admit him, will supply more details. When those whose arrival is shortly hoped for have returned, I shall not be reluctant, God favouring, to write to you what has emerged. And may it happen that I soon receive news of your condition, which may God fill with prosperity.

## LETTER CCXCIV. TO ROBERT THE SACRISTAN. (A.D. 1170.)

[Col. 0340A]

The same to Robert the sacristan.

Your messenger carefully explained the devotion you have toward me, and, as far as words could do so, bound me not a little to return thanks. For when my old friends have utterly abandoned and despised me through so long a time of exile, those who at least share kind words in this tempest with the proscribed—those whom others have despised—especially when they lack the means to console them by deeds, seem to cultivate friendship as far as they can and to deserve further favour. For reason weighs the expenditure not only of possessions but also of dispositions.

[Col. 0340B] It judges the scale filled with solid charity to outweigh the other; but that which offers the lightness of things and displays shadowy images of feigned affection hangs in the air. Therefore persevere in what you have faithfully begun. Bring into the light, whenever occasion offers, by a continual showing of charity, the devotion which you owe to your Father and to the Church in distress, so that both God and the archbishop himself may answer you in the recompense of a word according to your merits. This is hoped, God favouring, to happen shortly, because among us it is believed that the peace of the Church cannot long be delayed.

It is also believed that this peace will come for God’s honour and the Church’s benefit, not, as some have falsely alleged, to the confusion of the lord of Canterbury and of those who have resolved, if necessary, to lay down their lives for justice. Nor should you grieve if the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Nevers come to England. It is entirely certain that, while they can do much for the Church, they can do nothing whatever against it, against the lord of Canterbury, or against his people. Nor do we believe that they wish to harm them; rather, they will labour with all their strength for an honourable and beneficial peace.

I have written this lest I seem to have despised the message of your envoys. Wherever an opportunity exists, I am ready in the Lord for your service. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXCV. TO MASTER GIRARD. (A.D. 1170.)

[Col. 0340D] The same to Master Girard.

My lord the archbishop took it badly that you, who possess the key of knowledge and are continually engaged in the law of the Lord which you publicly teach—so that, having utterly rejected worldly disciplines, you profess the sacred cause of truth and justice alone—have presumed, to pernicious example and to the injury of your conscience and no small stain upon your reputation, to communicate with the archdeacon of Canterbury, whom you do not doubt has been solemnly excommunicated. Such a fault would scarcely be readily excused even in a less learned man, much less in one whose teaching and life alike ought to be an example of virtue to his hearers.

But since it is more credible that you sinned through human weakness than through perversity of malice, serious though what you have done is, I reply by my lord’s command to the contents of your letter. I also send a copy of the letter which he transmitted in his own defence to the lord bishop of Sées, who had warned him to meet him at Paris at an unspecified time. But, as you know, he cannot so suddenly prepare horses, expenses, or companions scattered throughout the kingdom for such frequent and fruitless journeys. Those wise men who summon him so readily ought also to have considered this beforehand.

You, however, were more careful in fixing a definite day for him with only one day intervening, so that, travelling under a safe-conduct, he might meet the bishop of Sées and the archdeacon of Canterbury. Yet you know better how far your words and letters bind the bishop. He himself remembers how he was recently deceived by that bishop’s letters and by the counsel of others, so that he summoned companions and uselessly incurred various expenses. For he had equipped himself for the journey and wearied many people, when public report informed him that the bishop had returned to Normandy—uncertain whether he was thought worthy of warning by letter or messenger.

Perhaps the Church’s business is so lowly that it should be treated only incidentally and by the way, touched upon by those passing through rather than completed. But whoever despises persons who have been grievously injured should remember that the cause is Christ’s: he restrains the swelling of the sea and governs the reins of powers at his will. He is the patron of the Church of Canterbury, and he will inspire the king’s mind to moderate the licence divinely granted him. May he not further afflict the Church which, beyond enough and beyond all right and measure, has been gratuitously afflicted, and which, like a loving mother, promoted, nourished, and protected both him and his predecessors.

For he is wiser than to procure the loss of his salvation and the ruin of his son. Nor are we ignorant of what his envoys have sought or obtained from the Apostolic See. Let threats cease, since, through God’s mercy, the Church sails in harbour; nor must those who, amid such bitterness of exile, have so openly experienced God’s mercy depart from the public road which Christ has shown.

You promise kisses and embraces if we comply with the man; and he who is the model of Christians heard from the tempter: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matthew IV). Let him judge his own cause and bring the lord king to pardon. Moved by the counsels of evil men, the king has forgotten too much the inborn kindness which he was accustomed to possess; and, because he has yielded too strongly to the Church’s enemies, he has taken on the appearance of an enemy. I do not doubt that he himself was displeased with himself while doing these things; but, as though unwilling, he was driven by the cries of fools and drawn by the cords of the wicked.

You add that the lord of Canterbury should meet the bishop and archdeacon named above, as though he were about to receive—much less merely meet—the man whom he himself condemned by solemn anathema, and whose sentence the Apostolic See has confirmed. Certainly he finds it strange that the said bishop of Sées and other venerable prelates of churches communicate with that man before absolution, knowing that they will have to answer for this in a strict judgment; perhaps it will not be forgotten in the Church that is to come.

Yet it is most certain that the lord of Canterbury will receive and comfort with paternal kindness both the bishop of London and the previously named archdeacon, once they show themselves to be sons; and he will embrace with arms of sincere charity all excommunicated persons whom it is lawful to absolve, when they enter upon the path of faith.

> [Note: In place of “the archdeacon,” etc., to the end of the letter, the Paris edition has “at his side,” etc., which occur near the end of Letter 300.]

Why say more? Provided that the Church’s position is not harmed, there is nothing which he is not prepared to do at the lord king’s will, if he experiences his favour fully restored to himself and his people. But in the future conduct your affairs more cautiously. Having sought absolution more diligently, avoid more carefully communion with the excommunicated, unless you wish to be excluded from the Church sooner and to receive with them a share in the anathema. Certainly your former downfall ought to have made you more cautious; recovery from a subsequent one will be more difficult if—God forbid—prudence, so often instructed by warnings and dangers, does not turn away from the cause. I shall share the wished-for greeting with you when I can.

## LETTER CCXCVI. TO THE CONVENT OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1170.)

To the most beloved brothers and dearest friends gathered in the holy Church of Canterbury, who cherish devout unity: John of Salisbury, least of the exiles, wishes that they may always walk happily before God’s face.

It is fitting, most beloved friends, that I should rejoice in your advances, be anxious in your dangers, sympathize with your losses and injuries, and, as far as a Christian may, perhaps be dismayed should failure—God forbid—threaten. For it is too little merely to mourn, when we recall that the righteous have acted piously even at the downfall of enemies, since the extinction of charity bears witness to the setting of the Holy Spirit. Its funeral must not be followed with perfunctory tears, groaning, or momentary pain, but life must be more urgently restored through repentance and the fruit of good works.

Nor should it disturb you that the Holy Spirit, who is undoubtedly immortal and the blessed life of the righteous, is said in some persons to perish, when you hear Paul saying: “Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies.” And would that you had heard effectively what the wise man recalls: not hearers of the word but doers are righteous before God. Let these words not be thought spoken to disparage all of you, because the Holy Spirit is witness that they have been uttered rather from charity—indeed from him alone who is charity—than to injure any Christian.

Nevertheless, I think some among you ought rightly and deservedly to be reproved for injury done to the Spirit and for the destruction of brotherly charity: not that they may perish, but that they may be salutarily put to shame. Let each man turn over and reread the book of his own conscience. In doubtful matters, if any exist, let him seek an interpreter and invoke the Holy Spirit, who teaches knowledge to humankind and reveals hidden truth, so that under his teaching this may become known to him more faithfully and intimately. Then, I think, he will clearly and fully discover what has come to him from charity kindled or inflamed, from charity lukewarm or relaxed, and from charity extinguished, driven away, and lost.

Yet far be it that anyone among you has committed the unforgivable sin through blasphemy, obstinacy, despair, or impenitence. For though charity has been weakened and broken in its branches, there is still hope that it remains in the root and, watered and soaked by the rains of heavenly grace, can flourish anew and bear fruits of true compassion and justice—if the soul sets its heart upon its ways, if it repents, confesses its fault, and, making satisfaction according to its ability, redeems what it has done.

But perhaps you will say: “Who are you, or what is your father’s house in Israel, that you rebuke religious men, especially those placed at the hinge of the churches of Britain? Or what have we done, by which you prove charity to be extinguished or relaxed?” I answer for myself what I have already said: I am the least among Christ’s exiles; and, speaking from conscience, zeal for the house of God has long made me an exiled outlaw, lest I spare another’s judgment or error. To confess my own folly, I cannot bear the scandals of brothers with patient mind and without distress of conscience.

Is it not permitted to me, especially when the Apostle teaches, to lament my own burning anguish over scandals? Is it not permitted to invite those who are sick with me, with whom I am made weak, that together we may run to the physician? Surely every disciple of Christ, even the least, is free, when he inspires him, to bear witness to the truth; and whoever is of God hears that truth not merely patiently but gladly. Hear then with patient mind what I judge to be your fault: namely, the loss of charity. When, I ask, it has been shown, do not cloak it in the empty foliage of words; instead let it be cleansed away by deed and truth.

Nearly six years have passed since your Father, an exile and outlaw for justice, has been pressed by many great distresses, burdened with many fellow-exiles of Christ—poor persons of both sexes and every age. What, during so long a time, have you bestowed upon him or upon those in exile with him? I do not think this has so completely slipped from your memory. Where, I ask, meanwhile were charity, love, and filial affection? For, as the Holy Spirit says through his instrument, the proof of love is the performance of a deed; and by the same author it is established that love cannot be idle.

But you plead the forces of public authority, the snares of its attendants, and the rightful fear that you might lose your place and nation. Truly the power of royal authority is great—and would that it may always be great in the Lord—but it is not so great that it could restrain all your expenditures. Truth knows where those who were able have repeatedly made such expenditures, whatever anyone may deny; and perhaps even before the Day of the Lord this will at some time be revealed, at least in part.

I say without doubt that Christ will never punish, nor people blame, you if you had withdrawn something from your necessities, much less from your luxuries, to be given to Christ’s poor, exiled for justice and the liberty of the Church—unless someone believes that at the final judgment God will glorify those clothed in double garments, who feast splendidly every day. Satan laid many snares against a vowed disposition of piety through the service of armed retainers, but the faithfulness and diligence of some persons, though few, escaped them. I infer that you could have done this more easily, if any attempt had been made. Would that your piety could at least have been proved by the testimony of some act!

It remains for Christ’s apostle to answer you concerning fear: “This fear is not in charity.” The Jews, lest they lose place and nation, as you recall, killed Christ; and thereby deservedly lost the very place and nation which they most wished to avoid losing. For almost whenever God is deliberately offended for some purpose, the matter turns out contrary to what is desired. Yet if those long-awaited persons had repented, they could have retained the primacy of place and nation; but, when they were hardened, it was given to a nation bearing its fruit.

Therefore, most beloved friends, since there is still a time for propitiation and merit, hasten to pardon through fruits worthy of repentance. Anticipate the judge’s face in confession; redeem delay through diligent satisfaction; raise up fallen charity. An easy and glorious opportunity for making satisfaction and redeeming your reputation is offered you, if what is said among us is true. The lord king, they say, intends, to the injury of your Church, to anoint and consecrate his son as king by the hand of the archbishop of York or another bishop. The lord pope forbids this by a repeated command, and his prohibitory letters are in the kingdom.

If others fail to deliver them and they come to you, I beg that some among you be clothed with power from on high so as to deliver them. On God’s and the supreme pontiff’s authority, forbid it, interposing an appeal as well if necessary, lest so great a prejudice be inflicted upon the holy Church of Canterbury—especially since the lord of Canterbury, whose business this is, is prepared to carry it out. Likewise, if anyone suppresses the letters in fraud of the Church so that they cannot reach you, do not delay, trusting in divine mercy, to interpose prohibition and appeal to repel the impending injury. By the authority of the Apostolic See command all the suffragans of your Church to withdraw their presence from this act and under no pretext whatever to participate in prejudice to their mother Church.

If this is presumed while you remain silent, who hereafter could be persuaded that zeal has not perished and charity has not been extinguished? Thus there is no one among you who does not make momentary life more precious than the salvation of his Church and the crown of righteousness. For your possessions are not now sought from you; rather, you are asked to show yourselves worshippers of God and sons of the Church. Proceeding in this strength, you will redeem your offences, and such conspicuous charity will cover the multitude of sins that went before.

Yet for those who, by Christ’s inspiration, have taken up the armour of zeal, clothed with righteousness as a breastplate and sure judgment as a helmet, faithful God will be leader and guardian. He will not allow them to be tempted beyond their strength, but will transform the dangers now seen to threaten into true peace, complete security, and everlasting glory. For the lord king, whatever people may say, if he remembers that he is the Lord’s anointed, and considers the duty of his office, the nobility of his lineage, and the excellence of his spirit, will not merely refrain from inflicting injury upon those who ask what is just, but will restrain others from inflicting it. For he knows that the king’s honour loves judgment.

I seem to see many among you who desire the crown of this splendid merit, each saying with the prophet in the Church’s hearing: “Here am I; send me,” striving to snatch before the others the title by which the community’s reputation will be restored and the Church’s privilege perpetuated in lasting force.

## LETTER CCXCVII. TO THOMAS, BISHOP OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1170, mid-June.)

To Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, J. of Salisbury, from Chartres.

The counsel of the Archbishop of Sens and our own is that, unless something better occurs to you, the more urgent letters which you have in your possession concerning the enforcement of justice should, if peace is not made, be shown more quickly to the archbishops of Rouen and Tours: at least so that the enemy may hear and be afraid. Moreover, he desires that his own letters be returned to the archbishops of Auch and Bordeaux, since this may benefit the cause and weaken the persecutor’s strength if it is heard in Gascony that his land is to be placed under an interdict. For access to the Archbishop of Bourges, whatever happens concerning the wars, is always reasonably hoped to be easier.

And remember how much danger and misfortune delay in delivering the *conventionales* [letters relating to the agreement] to the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, and likewise the prohibitory letters to the Archbishop of York and the overseas bishops, brought upon itself. Nor should you say that what has happened to you was not foretold; rather, say that, in the manner of all augurs, your subtlety was deceived by prophecies that did not come from the Spirit. Would that the sickness of this deception were not incurable; but unless relief or consolation be given from heaven, none presents itself. And rightly so, I think, since we presumptuously undertook, by vain imaginings of another’s mind, to unfold the hidden places of the human heart, of which God alone is judge. What, I ask, is more rash, or more injurious toward God, who claims this as the prerogative of His unique eminence? For the saying that to know oneself is the highest wisdom—even by Apollo’s oracle—is so celebrated among philosophers that none of the ancients dared dispute it. From heaven, as they say, descended Γνῶθι σεαυτόν, that is, “Know yourself.” Since here human understanding fails and angelic understanding does not reach so far, the wisdom of God alone does not conjecture men’s counsels and thoughts through fanciful imagination, but knows them completely as they are. Let us therefore henceforth renounce prophecies, because in this matter misfortunes have struck us too severely. Let Him who formed hearts examine them; let us investigate what is in our own house.

## LETTER CCXCVIII. TO MASTER HEREBERT. (A.D. 1170.)

John of Salisbury to Master Herebert.

Your letter breathes charity, and your zealous care has deserved thanks which I am presently unable to return. But He who is mighty will repay them, He who inspired grace in your heart so that it might offer comfort to the desolate and bear testimony to the truth of Christ’s confessors. Indeed, for us—if I may frame the wishes of fellow-exiles in the plural—there is joy and exultation when we see the pillars of the Church immovable against the assaults of the wicked, who are attempting to transfer us to another gospel: when we see them preferring the sincerity of faith to favour and power, and openly proving that human traditions must be subjected to the divine law.

For those who pursue fugitives most relentlessly yield very readily to those who resist; and, like wolves detected in advance, they inflict no harm upon those who approach if their deceit is revealed by the faithful and exposed by the light. For what gave horns to the sinner from the beginning, except that all turned to flight and vanished from the face of the oppressor, while there was no one to help the Church in her distress against those things which were presumed under the pretext of established law and ancient—or newly to be made ancient—customs? But assuredly those who then, above all others, desired to please men—indeed, men in a frenzy—were confounded, caught in the works of their own hands; and, with divine mercy going before and helping, they shall be still more confounded, because God rejects them while they conduct themselves in this way under the appearance of religion.

But the salvation of the elect seems to stand at the doors; and, God willing, your eyes and the eyes of others who have resolved to obey God rather than men will soon behold their glory. Therefore I congratulate my lord the Bishop of Winchester with all the cheerfulness of spirit I can command: when summoned by the judges and elders of the land, he gave an answer worthy of Christ, and issued a reply befitting his age, profession, honour, and lineage; and, so far as his strength permitted, as he is believed to have done, he encouraged his fellow priests. For they too commendably eluded the snares of those lying in wait. If summoned on another occasion, they will speak the word of faith and truth with confidence, plainly teaching that the lord king, hitherto misled by pernicious counsel, has been led into a trackless place and not into the way; and they will urge—would that they may persuade him!—to return to the way, outside which he cannot be saved nor long enjoy a ruler’s glory, unless he makes peace with the Church of God.

Nor should the empty boasting of those who claim that the lord pope has absolved the men whom the archbishop excommunicated disturb you. They seek from this some comfort for their misery, because he is said to have delegated their case to them with a blessing, and this after they had been condemned by anathema. For ignorance excuses the lord pope, to whom it had not yet become known that a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against them. Yet neither entreaty nor payment could induce him to exempt any one of them from the hand of the Lord of Canterbury, without striking them, according to the measure of their guilt, with the severity of punishment.

But let your affection hold this as certain: my lord of Canterbury has chosen to die in exile rather than return without the Church’s liberation; nor, with God’s help, will he make peace unless it is beneficial to posterity and honourable alike for those now living and those to come. But if the persecutors of the Church resolve to persist in wickedness, he, since he has received full authority, will proceed further and, in administering justice against God’s enemies, will spare no one. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXCIX. TO WILLIAM THE SUBPRIOR AND OTHER MEMBERS OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1170, October.)

To his dearest friends and brothers William, subprior, Robert, sacristan, and the others charged with the care of the holy Church of Canterbury: their own John, greetings, and the prudence to direct your foresight toward the future.

At last the merciful and compassionate Lord has heard your prayers and the wishes of the faithful for His own honour, as appears from many sure indications, restoring peace to the English Church and recalling your father from exile. Would that your ears had been at the mouth of the lord king when, at the recent conference of kings held between the castle of Blois and Amboise, he dismissed the lord archbishop so that he might promptly receive leave from the French, by whom he was being detained, and return to him with all speed, thereafter to cross into England.

Accordingly, as agreed, God willing, he will take leave of Sens on the feast of All Saints, intending and having agreed to return to his own country; and as soon as he can he will make Canterbury, the city of the saints, illustrious by his return. Therefore, if you wish henceforth to provide for the honour and safety of your Church, meet your father, and do not delay to send across the sea whatever faith, friendship, devotion, or counsel you possess, so that he may thereby discharge his burden and remain perpetually indebted to you. Redeem even now the delay, lest perhaps it bring upon you the unavoidable danger of loss of property and reputation.

I find in the *History of Recent Events* that your predecessors were the first to meet Father Anselm when he returned from exile. Will you be degenerate, so as to give no comfort, or only the least—and not such as becomes you—to your returning father and brothers? Far be this forever from Canterbury, the chief see of the Britains, that it should transmit to posterity so foul, inhuman, undevout, and undisciplined an example of our time! Grief and anguish of heart, sympathizing with you and fearing lest, through the faintheartedness and avarice of some—may God avert it!—the Church of God incur everlasting reproach, do not permit me to write everything which the occasion and subject suggest. But, I think, enough has been said to those who fear God, are wise, and love honour. Let it therefore suffice that I have so far warned my friends. Nor do I doubt that those who love will receive the fruit of charity, while upon the deaf—as the old proverb says—beans are beaten. Farewell; remember yours and ours in charity.

## LETTER CCC. TO PETER, ABBOT OF SAINT-RÉMI. (A.D. 1170, December.)

The same to Peter, Abbot of Saint-Rémi.

My delay could most rightly be blamed, if necessity did not itself excuse it. For from the moment I first set foot in England I ought to have sent a messenger through whom your affection might be informed of the condition of your former pupils. But because, at my very disembarkation, a new and astonishing state of affairs met me, I could not inform another while conflicting reports and people’s words left me uncertain.

For three days before I landed, all the goods of the Lord of Canterbury and his people had been inventoried, and his stewards had been removed from administration; and by public proclamation in the ports, under threat of exile and outlawry, it had been forbidden that any of our party, should he wish to leave England, be carried across. Yet the most gracious officials of the lord king, by excessively provident caution and ruinous vigilance toward us, had taken care that the archbishop and his people, returning from exile, should find absolutely nothing, or very little, besides empty houses mostly consumed, demolished granaries, and bare threshing-floors—this, forsooth, as consolation for their long exile and amends for the sacrilege committed.

And although our peace had been restored to us on the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene, and our most serene lord king had by patent letters ordered his son, the new king, that everything be restored in full to the archbishop and his people, as it had been three months before they left England, nevertheless all revenues that could be collected up to Christmas were ordered to be taken in his name. Several possessions and churches which, by the very law and terms of the agreement, ought to have been restored to the Church of Canterbury are still occupied by courtiers under the authority of public power. Among others, I myself have been deprived of one church which paid forty marks annually to my predecessor.

It happened that I landed three days before the Octaves of Saint Martin; and during those Octaves a synod of Canterbury was to be held, at which I had to act in the place of the absent archbishop. Therefore, although contrary to expectation, to favourable opinion, and to the good promises of the lord king, I found everything so disturbed that everyone despaired of our peace and of the archbishop’s return, and although I found myself as though imprisoned, I set out for Canterbury with a cheerful face and steadfast mind. There I was received by clergy and people with great honour, as though I were an angel of the Lord; the faithful already hoped better things from my arrival, because they were persuaded that the archbishop would by no means have sent me ahead unless he himself were shortly to follow.

After the synod had been held, I went on to the new king and was received rather humanely, although his fellow guardians displayed some fear, suspecting that peace had not been made with us simply, but that the roots of resentment, openly remitted, still clung more firmly. Though I clearly perceived this from various signs, I acted as if I thought everything proceeding according to my wish. From there I hastened aside on my journey to my mother, whom I found now weakened by illness for a second year and henceforth joyfully awaiting the day of the Lord. Since she has seen me, I earnestly ask that she be commended to your prayers and those of the saints with whom you dwell. For she had received an answer from the Spirit that she would not see death until she saw me and my brother return from exile.

[Col. 0349B] Meanwhile those old friends of the Lord of Canterbury and champions of ecclesiastical liberty—the Lord of York, the Bishop of London, and their accomplices—entered into counsel with the publicans. They sent an embassy to the lord king urging that he should not allow the aforesaid Lord of Canterbury to return to England until he renounced the office of legate, returned to him all the letters which he had obtained from the Apostolic See, and promised to preserve inviolate the rights of the kingdom—so that, under the pretext of this guarantee, he might be bound to observe the customs. For they said that his return would be damaging and disgraceful to the lord king unless these things came first.

They had also arranged that six persons should be summoned for each vacant church, to whom the decision of the community concerning the choice of a pastor might be entrusted, so that elections might be carried out, removed from the Church into another realm and into the palace, at the king’s pleasure. There, if Canterbury objected, out of reverence for the canons and in fulfilment of his office, he would offend the royal majesty; if he consented, he would be guilty before God and convicted of infringing ecclesiastical constitutions.

The often-mentioned Lord of Canterbury had come to Rouen at the lord king’s command, to be released there, as promised, from the obligation of his creditors and sent honourably back to his native land. But his expectation deceived him. John of Oxford brought letters from the lord king, asking and urging him to return without delay to his Church and to enjoy the escort and assistance of the aforesaid John on the journey. The archbishop obeyed; and on the return journey he learned through friends of the devices of his rivals. They had already set out in the morning and were awaiting a favourable wind, while our archbishop waited similarly on the opposite shore.

When he learned of their crossing and their plots, he frustrated their efforts as best he could. He sent apostolic letters to the Archbishop of York, by which he and the Bishop of Durham were suspended from episcopal office for their usurpation of the new king’s coronation. The messenger also delivered others to the bishops of London and Salisbury, by which they were recalled into the sentence of anathema, and all bishops who had attended the aforesaid coronation were suspended.

Having done this, a more favourable breeze from Flanders brought the lord archbishop safely by sea into England. When he came to the harbour called Sandwich, the king’s retainers met him. Guards had been posted along the shore, it is believed, in order to harm him, and armed men raised a clamour; but the aforesaid John of Oxford restrained them and compelled them to lay down their weapons—not, as is thought, so much from favour toward our party as lest their rashness brand the lord king and his children with the stigma of treason. Nevertheless, they demanded that the foreigners who had come with the archbishop swear an oath to keep faith with the king and kingdom. No foreigner appeared except Simon, Archdeacon of Sens, who would readily have been induced to take the oath had the archbishop permitted it. But the archbishop, fearing the harmful example, replied that it was wholly contrary to good custom that guests and pilgrims should be compelled, by unheard-of barbarity, to take such oaths. Perhaps the retainers would have used force, had not the popular tumult checked them; for they feared the attack of the people, who rejoiced so greatly at receiving their shepherd as though Christ Himself had descended from heaven among men.

When on the following day he had reached Canterbury, messengers came to him from the other archbishop and bishops who had been suspended, appealing to the Apostolic See, although they knew beyond doubt that the supreme pontiff had barred every possibility of appeal. From another side came officials of the lord king, asking in his name and declaring by public authority that the archbishop should relax the sentence pronounced against the Archbishop of York and the other bishops, unless he wished to be declared a public enemy of king and kingdom, as one who was trying to take the crown from the new king.

To this the archbishop replied that he was in no way attacking royal dignity, but rather would, to the extent of his ability, increase its strength, wealth, and glory in Christ. Yet this could not by any means be obtained without his pursuing the justice of his Church against the presumptuous bishops. As they pressed him, he added more strongly that, for the honour of the lord king, although it was dangerous to him and exceeded his powers—because an inferior judge cannot relax the sentence of a superior—he was prepared to absolve two bishops, provided that he first received from them, according to the Church’s custom, an oath that they would obey the commands of the lord pope who had bound them.

But the officials would not allow this to be done, saying that such an oath ought not to be required of bishops because it attacked the customs of the realm. The archbishop replied that, when they had previously solicited the lord pope in every way to absolve them from the bond of anathema into which they had been bound by the authority of the Church of Canterbury alone, they could not be absolved except after taking the oath. If this was necessary to dissolve the sentence of one bishop, which is far weaker than an edict of the supreme pontiff, it is clearer than light that an apostolic sentence ought not to be dissolved without it, especially by an inferior judge.

These and similar arguments moved the bishops; and, as has been reliably reported, they would have fled to the archbishop’s mercy had not the often-mentioned Archbishop of York misled them, counselling them not to do anything without consulting the king, whom they had had as patron in all their actions.

Therefore, while they hurried indignantly to the lord king, our archbishop set out for the new king. But when he had reached London, the young king declared to him that he should proceed no farther and should not enter his cities or castles, but should withdraw with his people within the bounds of his own Church. His people were ordered not to leave the borders of the kingdom nor appear in public, but, as they loved themselves, to beware for their own safety.

When this proclamation had been made, the archbishop withdrew with his people to Canterbury; and there, amid great danger, we await the salvation of God [Note: [Col. 0351D] Paris edition: “with Christ”]. No other way of consolation or safety lies open to us except that, through your prayers and those of the saints, we may escape the snares of those who thirst for our blood and seek either to tear us wholly from the earth or more conspicuously to destroy us in it.

Although the persecution is most severe and few visitors among the rich or eminent come to the archbishop, he nevertheless renders justice with pontifical gravity to all who come to him, entirely setting aside respect of persons and gifts. My brother, having gone to our Bishop of Exeter, whom I have not yet been allowed to visit, remains close at his side [Note: [Col. 0351D] For “remains close at his side,” etc. … the Paris edition has “cannot, breaking,” etc.; these words occur near the end of Letter 292.], in great fear and continual anxiety. It would be long, and I fear it might cause weariness, if I began to recount all our troubles; but what the letter lacks will be supplied by the bearer’s account.

Let it therefore be, if you please, an object of your compassion to urge the holy prior and the friends of Christ at Mont-Dieu and the valley of Saint Peter, the abbots of Saints Nicasius and Crispin, and your other holy friends, to intercede for us before the Most High, so that by their merits we who are endangered by our own people may be delivered in a saving manner. I can scarcely recall to mind without groaning, sighs, and tears our dearest brothers and lords who continually serve most blessed Remigius, remembering that I once dwelt as happily as in paradise while I enjoyed their presence and experienced the image of that charity which is hoped for in eternal life. I ask you to urge them more diligently to remember their former pupils in their prayers. As soon as God grants favourable events, I shall not delay, through the service of letters sent in haste, to communicate them to you, Christ being gracious. May your holiness always flourish and be strong; may the prosperity of the whole Church advance in every good thing; and, if you please, keep the poor priest of Saint Cosmas commended to you.

## LETTER CCCI. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1170.)

The same to Bartholomew, Bishop of Exeter.

The Church is in a narrow place, and troubles press her from every side because of the dissension between kingdom and priesthood. For she defends the liberty which the king seeks to destroy; and if she wished to cease from defending her position and acquiesce in the commands of tyrants, she would immediately incur the indignation of the Apostolic See. But because it is far more tolerable to fall into the hands of men than to abandon the law of God, I judge it most dutiful and prudent not only to expose one’s possessions and the gifts of deceptive fortune for the protection of liberty and paternal laws, after the example of the saints, but also one’s very body. However it may now be worn down by any scourges or tortured by any executions of tyrants, Christ—whether persecutors wish it or not—will restore it on that day more beautiful and more powerful, according to the merits that have gone before, since it is now beneficially offered up or laid down for His faith and obedience.

But even if the rage of tyrants should grow to such a point:

> Easy is the loss of a tomb for him who is covered by heaven and has no urn.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* II.646

Counsel has a place only in doubtful matters; and what the divine law prescribes as to be done ought not to be doubtful. For not even the least of God’s commands—if indeed anything is small, which I can scarcely believe—is to be abandoned for temporal life, much less for worldly goods, vain ease, or counsel. The least commands, when kept, gain life and often merit the glory of martyrdom; but when neglected through the sin of disobedience and contempt, they bring inward death.

The Lord forbids the killing of a captured bird together with its young, adding that the reward for observing this command is that you may live a long time. You will not easily find this added to other commandments except where He commands that father and mother be honoured. Thus He attached the same great reward to what seems least, to teach that diligent observance even of the least thing merits life. Is it not written that “he who despises small things shall fall little by little” (*Ecclesiasticus* 19), and that “he who is faithful in little shall be set over much”? Nor do I say this because all receive this saying, or because I diligently observe the least things; for I often and grievously offend in great and greatest matters.

Indeed, obedience is the greatest commandment, and without its more diligent keeping no one who has advanced can attain salvation. “Obedience is better than sacrifices.” For to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse acquiescence like the crime of idolatry. And that you may be strengthened more firmly for the virtue of obedience, the authority of the lord pope supports you, as you have from the letter which he recently wrote to the Bishop of Worcester. The bishop had asked whether he should rather return to his bishopric and comply with the king’s will, or stand by the Lord of Canterbury for the liberty of the Church and defence of the divine law, while he courageously bears in himself and his people dangers beyond all that can be said. A copy of the letter is appended below. May the Lord make you an executor of His will and grant you such strength and perseverance of faith that you may successfully strengthen brothers of your own age and those to come in the fear of the Lord and the practice of justice.

## LETTER CCCII. TO THE COMMUNITY OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1170.)

The same to the community of Canterbury.

If you please to remember, I have repeatedly admonished your charity that you should faithfully—as was fitting—stand by your father and lord, who has prolonged into a sixth year the struggle for the Church’s liberty which necessity has so far imposed upon him; and that you should share the needs of those who have endured for the word of the Lord the bitterness of exile, the injuries of outlawry, the reproaches of detractors, and the harassment—indeed, I might say the rages—of persecutors. And would that you had listened, or may still listen, to one counselling what is saving and honourable, lest—God forbid!—you repent too late of your unbelief and hardness.

For hitherto, like Cassandra among the Trojans, always proclaiming truth, I seem mad to you; and unbelievers say: “This man prophesies from his own heart. To draw the simpler into partnership in his error and misfortune, he terrifies them with vain oracles; now he threatens adverse events to those of sound judgment, now he promises prosperity to those who comply.” But behold: Peter’s sword has been mightily drawn against the necks of the enemies of the Church, and, unless Malchus avoids the blow, it will cut off his right ear. You know what Malchus means in the Latin tongue; for I speak to those who know, hold, love, and embrace the law.

It was not believed that the Bishop of London and the other authors of schism and inciters of it would be struck by the sword of anathema; but the Church has now rejected and excluded them from her body. It was not believed that the Roman pontiff would approve their condemnation; but that the sentence is ratified is evident from the fact that envoys were sent from the Apostolic See to absolve them, after an oath had been sworn according to the Church’s custom, on the condition that the king make peace with the Church as the lord pope had prescribed. In hope of this peace, the Archdeacon of Canterbury and others who were overseas were absolved after the precaution of an oath had been given. And because peace did not follow before the feast of Saint Michael, as had been agreed, they were restored, according to the agreement, to the same sentence of anathema. It is therefore plain how dangerous is participation with them: in fact, those excommunicated were men who ought to have been absolved.

It remains for punishment to proceed further, because the inheritance of the Lord cannot be delivered from the hand of enemies except by a strong hand. In this conflict the Lord will openly recognize those who are His, and those who value the pots of Egypt more highly than the heavenly bread—that is, the word of God which gives life to the world. Whoever these may be, they shall receive the lot of their condemnation with those whom the earth swallowed alive. For he who shares in others’ sins shall share in their death.

Come out, therefore, I pray you, from their midst; set your hearts upon your ways. And you who have hitherto been, for the most part—though I say it in shame and pain—stepchildren, pass at last even now into the inheritance of sons: share your father’s necessities, perform fruits of repentance and obedience, and drive infamy from the Church. Unless, God forbid, you take precautions, it will be perpetuated forever through the hardness you deserve. The lord pope had admonished this—indeed, had commanded it—yet even he was not heard for reverence of his office. Will you also, after the manner of unbelievers, say to Christ suffering once more for the Church: “We have no pontiff or pope but Caesar”? Do you so fear him who, having received power from God, can torment bodies but cannot destroy them, that you despise Him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna?

He surely commanded that prelates be obeyed, that children honour their parents and meet their needs with most ready charity. Indeed, whoever does not comfort, from the resources given him, a brother placed in tribulation is convicted of lacking this charity. For the outward performance of a deed most forcefully proves the disposition of the mind. May your holiness always prosper; and in the matters of which I have warned you, consult the word of God rather than your neighbours.

## LETTER CCCIII. TO WILLIAM, SUBPRIOR OF CANTERBURY. (A.D. 1170.)

To his Briton, his own J., greetings and godly foresight toward the future.

From the things written to your whole community you may gather what you ought to do. Nor should you offer, as hitherto, frivolous excuses, for the time has come when your Church must suffer or suffer with others. For if she shares the needs of her father, she will soon flourish again amid the consolations which, God willing, we confidently hope for. Indeed, I do not think that for a hundred years there has been a time when she could so easily breathe again in order to restore all her ancient privileges, if she were willing to stand manfully and effectively by her father in his concern for these matters, and share the necessary expenses.

But somehow you wish to reign without burden and care, although it is certain that:

> Great things are attained only by the utmost labour.

In these matters the industry of this poor and outlawed man has already advanced so far, by God’s grace, that I do not doubt that his predecessor, if the opportunity had been given, would have spent two thousand marks in acquiring them. It is said that you alienated the candlesticks for vain uses, perhaps not without consciousness of sacrilege; and yet you are so miserly when the needs of the Church and the restoration of its honours are at issue. Stir up your brothers concerning this; and if they are foolish through contempt, remember to provide for the Church and for yourself. If the Bishop of London sets out for the court, ensure, as you have been instructed, that two monks are adequately prepared to meet him when they are summoned.

## LETTER CCCIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (A.D. 1171.)

The same to John, Bishop of Poitiers.

Unexpectedly, and while I was travelling, it recently became known to me, by God’s gracious favour, that the bearer of this letter was going to pass through your region. Rejoicing, therefore, I gladly seized this divinely supplied opportunity of writing to a friend, believing that great comfort in my long affliction was given me in being permitted to lament the mass of my troubles in safe ears. But where shall a beginning be found? For abundant and overflowing material produces a poverty of speech; and unless wickedness had risen to its height in our own time, such matters would surpass belief.

Shall I lament public troubles or private ones? But the world has recognized the general afflictions. Each person’s own misery burns him more sharply—unless perhaps some follower of Christ is so inflamed with charity that he takes upon himself the burdens of all and burns at his neighbours’ scandals. Since I do not doubt that you have been reliably informed of the passion of the glorious martyr Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, who illumines not only his own Church but both provinces of the English with many and very great miracles, I did not think it proper to dwell longer on it, especially since the time for writing is short and, as I think, the matter is now known and spread through almost the whole Latin world by the reports of many persons.

Yet in so great a gift of divine providence I did not think it ought to be passed over in silence—what all marvel at to the glory of God and His martyr: namely, that all circumstances converge in the bishop’s contest so as to make the title of the sufferer illustrious forever, reveal the impiety of the persecutors, and stain their name with everlasting reproach. For if it please one to consider and weigh the persons on either side, here appears a religious archbishop, primate of the Britains, legate of the Apostolic See, an entirely incorruptible judge—for he accepted neither persons nor gifts—a defender of ecclesiastical liberty, and, like a tower raised in Jerusalem facing Damascus, a hammer of the ungodly but a comforter of the poor and sorrowful.

Let one who knows consider who comes forth on the opposite side. And if the cause makes a martyr—as no person of sound judgment doubts—what cause could be more just or holier than his? For in love of Christ he despised wealth and all worldly glory, the affection of friends and of his whole kindred; he underwent exile and exposed himself and all his people to dangers and poverty. For the preservation of his God’s law and the abolition of the abuses of ancient tyrants, he fought even unto death. Nor, after he had once fallen, caught by the deceit of those lying in wait, could he be induced to enter into any obligation or to promise any of the things demanded of him without adding in every case that God’s honour and the Church’s integrity must remain unimpaired.

Nor did he endure adversity only for a little while or, believing only temporarily, withdraw at the moment of trial; but he prolonged exile and the bitterest proscription into a seventh year. With such strength of constancy he walked the royal road and followed the footsteps of Christ and apostolic men that his unconquered spirit could neither be broken by the onset of raging fortune nor softened by flattery.

But observe also where he was immolated: certainly in the Church, which is the head of the realm and mother of all the others in Christ; before the altar, amid fellow-priests and the hands of religious men whom the tumult of armed executioners had brought together for a spectacle astonishing and pitiable. [Col. 0356B] He, therefore, who long before had presented himself as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; who had continually crucified his flesh, with its vices and desires, by prayers, vigils, fasts, and the use of a harsher hair-shirt; whose back, as his intimate holy companions knew, he was accustomed, like a child of Christ, to expose to scourges; who was accustomed to offer Christ’s body and blood at the altar—prostrate before the altar, he offered up his own blood, poured out by the hands of the wicked.

Nor was it permitted to Satan’s ministers, at the sacrifice of the disciple and servant, what had been permitted to their forerunners at the crucifixion of the Master and Lord. For Christ, lest the city be defiled and the Sabbath polluted, though condemned beforehand by an unjust judgment, was granted whatever opportunity he had of pleading for himself; and, led out from the city, he was crucified outside the gate, [Col. 0356C] indeed through the agency of Gentiles who did not know the Lord and by authority of the public power, being accused by those whose law he seemed to have assailed, while a disciple—the son of perdition—procured the treachery of betrayal. But this man was slain not only in the city but within the church; not at an unholy time but on the day consecrated by the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity. And in every respect it was fitting that the feast-day of his birth, he who had lived innocently and most holily, should, to God’s glory, follow the Nativity—the feast of the Holy Innocents.

Indeed, as is believed, disciples who became traitors procured his death, and chief priests planned it: surpassing Annas and Caiaphas, Pilate and Herod, by as much in wickedness as they more carefully took precautions that he should not be [Col. 0356D] brought to judgment, confronted by accusers, appear before the governor, or escape sacrilegious hands by the privilege of a sacred place, or of time, rank, office, restored peace, and an assurance that had been given—not the hands of Gentiles or enemies, but of those who professed God’s law and the loyalty of friends.

Yet by the marvelous dispensation of almighty God, who orders all things wisely and for salvation, it came about that he who allowed these things to be done so wickedly, shamelessly, and rashly did not allow them to be hidden. Thus even here is fulfilled in time what Truth declared: that nothing is hidden which shall not be revealed. For what is commonly reported concerning Judas, the standard-bearer of traitors, in the well-known saying ought by equal right to be applied also to his accomplices, [Col. 0357A] since the judgment upon like matters is acknowledged to be the same: that it may be clear to all Christians by faith that heaven shall reveal their iniquity and earth shall rise up against them. For which of the faithful would dare doubt that God will either convert or crush the authors and perpetrators of so great a sacrilege?

But the martyr of Christ, who was to suffer in the church, as has been said, before Christ’s altar, when he heard himself being sought, met the soldiers who had come for this purpose, while they shouted amid a crowd of clergy and monks, “Where is the archbishop?” He met them from the steps which he had ascended for the most part, with an undaunted expression, saying, “Here I am. What do you want?” One of the death-dealing soldiers said to him in a spirit of fury: “That you may die at once, for it is impossible that you should live any longer.” [Col. 0357B]

The archbishop replied with no less steadfastness of speech than of soul—for, as I may confidently say without prejudice to all martyrs, none of them seems to have been more steadfast in suffering than he:

> “I am ready to die for God, and for the vindication of justice and the liberty of the Church. But if you seek my head, I forbid you, on behalf of almighty God and under anathema, to harm in any respect any other person, monk, cleric, or layman, great or small. Let them be free from punishment, as they were free from the cause; for it is to me, not to them, that it must be imputed if any of them embraced the cause of the suffering Church. I gladly embrace death, provided that through the shedding of my blood the Church obtains peace [Col. 0357C] and liberty.”

Who appears more fervent in charity than he? While offering himself to persecutors for the law of God, his sole concern was that his neighbours should not be harmed in any way. Do not his words seem to express Christ in his Passion, saying, “If you seek me, let these go their way”? (John 18.)

Having said this, and seeing the executioners with drawn swords, he bowed his head in the manner of one praying, uttering these final words: “To God, to holy Mary, to the patron saints of this church, and to blessed Dionysius, I commend myself and the cause of the Church.”

Who can recount the rest without sighs, sobs, and tears? Piety does not permit us to pursue in detail the acts which those most savage executioners committed, despising the fear of God and forgetful alike of faith and of all humanity. [Col. 0357D] For it did not suffice them to profane the church with the blood and killing of a priest, and to violate that most sacred day, unless, after cutting off the crown of his head which the anointing of holy chrism had consecrated to God, they also—horrible even to relate—with their deadly swords cast out the brains of one already dead and most cruelly scattered them over the pavement with blood and bones. They were more brutal than Christ’s crucifiers, who did not think it right to break the legs of him whom they saw had died, as they did those still alive.

Yet amid all these torments, the martyr—of unconquered spirit and marvelous constancy—uttered no word, gave no cry, made no groan, and raised neither arm nor garment against the assailant; but with wonderful courage he kept motionless, until all was completed, the bowed head which he had exposed to the swords. [Col. 0358A] At last, falling to the ground with body straight, he moved neither foot nor hand.

The executioners, no less greedy than cruel, then returned, to the injury both of royal authority and divine majesty, to the church palace. Seizing with insatiable greed and astounding audacity all the furnishings and whatever could be found in the chests or packs of the archbishop and his household—gold, silver, garments, various ornaments, books, charters, other writings of every kind, and horses—they divided the spoil among themselves as they pleased, becoming imitators of those who divided Christ’s garments among themselves, though in some measure surpassing them in wickedness. And so that human favour might be withdrawn from the pontiff now crowned through martyrdom, [Col. 0358B] all writings which the sacrilegious robber had stolen were sent to the king in Normandy.

But by God’s will it came about that, the more human rashness strove to obscure the glory of that most valiant champion, the more the Lord made it shine by the manifestation of his power and the clear signs of miracles. When the impious men who hated him insatiably saw this, they forbade anyone, in the name of public authority, to presume to publish the miracles that were occurring. Yet in vain does anyone desire to darken what God has purposed to glorify. The more assiduously the wicked appeared to conceal the miracles, the more widely they spread. Man sees the face; God alone searches the reins and hearts.

For when the blessed martyr’s body was to be committed to burial and was clothed, according to custom, in pontifical vestments, it was discovered—something known to very few of his intimate companions—that he was wrapped in a hair-shirt full of lice and worms. [Col. 0358C] His very inner breeches, down to the knees, were found to be of hair-cloth, something previously unheard of among our people. Only his outer clothing conformed to that of others, according to the saying of the wise man: “Let your outward appearance suit the people; let everything within be different.”

Who could describe the groans and floods of tears shed by the holy company present when such hidden religious devotion was revealed? Yet even in all this the rage of the persecutors did not rest. They said that the body of a traitor ought not to be buried among holy pontiffs, [Col. 0358D] but should be cast into a filthy marsh or hung upon a gibbet. Therefore the holy men present, fearing violence against themselves, buried him in a marble sarcophagus in the crypt, before Satan’s agents summoned to commit sacrileges could assemble, before the altar of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Augustine, apostle of the English.

There, to the glory of almighty God, many great miracles occur through him, as crowds of people gather, that in others they may see and in themselves feel the power and mercy of him who is always wonderful and glorious in his saints. For at the place of his Passion, where he lay overnight before the high altar awaiting burial, and where he was finally buried, paralytics are healed, the blind see, the deaf hear, [Col. 0359A] the dumb speak, the lame walk, those afflicted with fever recover, the possessed are freed from demons, and the sick are healed of various diseases; blasphemers possessed by demons are put to shame. These things and many more—too numerous to recount—are wrought by him who alone is blessed above all for ever, and who chose beforehand to make partners in his glory those whom, for the truth of faith, zeal for justice, courage in confession, and persevering unconquered constancy, he would make triumphant over the enemies of truth and faith. Certainly I should never have dared write these things had eyewitness testimony not made me utterly certain concerning them.

It remains, therefore, that your learning should instruct our littleness whether, without the authority of the Roman pontiff, it is safe in the solemnities of Mass and other [Col. 0359B] public prayers to invoke him in the catalogue of martyrs as a patron of salvation; or whether we are still bound to offer intercessory prayers for him, whom God has glorified by such great signs of miracles, as for another deceased person. For it is feared that such insistence in prayer may seem an injury to the blessed martyr and, after the display of so many signs, that devotion not yet confident may bear the appearance of unbelief.

The Roman pontiff would already have been consulted about this, except that the opportunity to cross over has been so completely barred to everyone that no one is allowed aboard a ship unless he first produces the king’s letters. Meanwhile, however, it seems more prudent to us to conform to the Lord’s will and to venerate as a martyr, whether we sing or weep, the man whom he himself deigns to honour as a martyr. [Col. 0359C] For in almost every part of the world God, without waiting for the authority of any human being, has been able and accustomed to glorify whom he wills. This cannot be doubtful to a wise person who examines the various Scriptures more carefully by diligent inquiry.

## LETTER CCCV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. (A.D. 1171)

To the lord of Sens, from those wretches who were once men of Canterbury.

Your eyes saw our struggle, which we endured with the glorious martyr—eyes which a generosity both innate and advanced and perfected by heavenly grace opened to behold the calamities of the English Church. In aid of Christ’s poor, you bore for her the burden of the day and the heat, [Col. 0359D] and, while it was permitted, you guarded like the apple of your eye the champion fighting against the wicked for God’s law. May God reward your faith and diligence, by which you procured peace for us; for you omitted nothing among the possibilities, so that our misfortunes ought to be imputed to you. For the terms of the solemnly concluded peace appeared useful and honourable to all, when, at that most celebrated assembly, the greatest and wisest princes of so many kings had gathered. Peace therefore having been restored, the kingdoms rejoiced.

But what the members of the devil were then doing the outcome of events showed—if indeed those who committed so great a crime, reserving vengeance to themselves in insult to God, are to be believed to have reached their own end. [Col. 0360A] Far be it that that terrible being, who takes away the spirit of princes and strikes those known to have committed unheard-of crimes with a conspicuous—and indeed miraculous—vengeance, should yield this glory of his to another! For the holy pontiff, as you were informed by a trustworthy account in other letters, passed from the miseries of this world to the Lord by glorious martyrdom, that he may now sit with princes and judge those who oppressed him and attempted to destroy Christ’s inheritance.

For Christ, whether the persecutor will or not, is God above all, blessed for ever; yet the presumptuousness of exalted, momentary power—as you often heard with grief—contrived to prefer its own honour and the abuses of former tyrants, established by perpetual laws, to God’s honour. [Col. 0360B] And lest anyone dare speak against it or even mutter, some of us were captured and thrown into prison, others proscribed, others condemned to exile, while others, for whom divine mercy provided more graciously, secured their safety by flight, lest they suffer or see the misery of their brethren, the trampling-down of the saints, and, if I may say so with his leave, the dishonour of Christ.

Opposite sit blasphemers who, under the name and honour of the priesthood, persecute the priesthood: flattering princes, vindicating the cause of the Church’s persecutors, rejoicing in the worst things—namely, that they have stood with the powers against the Lord and against his Christ. His blood, though shed through the agency of soldiers, cries from the earth to the Lord more loudly [Col. 0360C] than the blood of righteous Abel, whom his own brother killed.

Their head is that man of York, whom you saw and heard openly persecuting the archbishop in the court, and who was unworthy even to utter his name with the sacrilegious mouth by which he procured the martyr’s death. Yet that thoroughly corrupt and lying man, as is clear from his letter, calls him Pharaoh even now, though the martyr shines with unheard-of miracles. But we are not troubled if a monstrous criminal does not honour the martyr, for, as his manifest deeds prove, he certainly does not fear God.

It is said, nevertheless, that he is preparing to go to the court in order to clear the stain of his foul life, as though he were a man who had done justice and not abandoned the judgment of his God. And in order that his purgation might not be impeded, he has procured [Col. 0360D] that none of our people may cross the sea without obtaining the lord king’s permission. This cannot be obtained unless security is given that no complaint shall be made against the martyr’s persecutors. What, then, are unhappy men zealous for the law to do, when they see justice oppressed and every means of redress denied them?

But surely the word of God is not bound; you have freedom, a mouth open to the Roman Church, and the truth is very well known. For you knew the martyr during his life, you knew his cause, and you knew us who shared his exile. You also knew this Caiaphas of our time, who, under the guise of a complainant, persuaded men that it was expedient that one should die or be captured lest the whole nation perish.

You were in England with your uncle, the lord of Winchester, when this same Caiaphas—then an arch-devil, now Caiaphas—caused that Walter, a youth whose very handsome appearance had induced him to take excessive pleasure in an infamous sexual liaison, should be blinded. Walter had become rough-haired and was vomiting forth in a more impudent tongue the insults which he had endured to nature’s dishonour. [Col. 0361A] Afterwards the same arch-devil, having corrupted the judges who handled secular affairs, forced him to be hanged for denouncing the crime.

Thus that man, no less kindly than chaste, accepted the affection of his dove. Thus he rewarded the long-displayed service of his former lover: first he inflicted sexual violation on the wretched man; then, upon one yet more wretched because he regretted consenting to such filthy uncleanness, he inflicted castration and the tearing out of his eyes; and at last he caused the most miserable man, because he proclaimed his sufferings as best he could by crying out, to be strangled while hanging from the gibbet. [Col. 0361B]

We do not invent these things, but have sought to call them back to your memory—if indeed they could have slipped from it—for they have sunk more deeply into our breast, as though engraved with a diamond point, through the repeated accounts of many great and trustworthy men. For to this day this sad history is sung repeatedly to the shame of the Church and the contempt of God.

But perhaps someone will ask how he endured so great and so manifest an outrage with impunity, especially when blessed Eugenius was then administering the supreme pontificate. Indeed, as we undoubtedly believe, he would by no means have escaped had it not been through the agency of blessed Thomas. Through the venerable men Hilary, bishop of Chichester, and John, bishop of Worcester, Thomas obtained the acceptance of his purgation by Theobald of Canterbury, archbishop of blessed memory. [Col. 0361C]

Then, perceiving that the Roman Church was angered because the purgation had been made secretly—in a chapter of monks rather than in a solemn assembly—he looked after his own position and travelled to Rome, to that most notorious broker whom your soul always hated: Gregory, cardinal of Saint Angelo. Through him, amid a multitude of gifts scattered about the curia, he obtained permission to return justified to his own house. By what dispensation of God he was reserved for the commission of greater crimes is uncertain, as the present day testifies: the Church is stained purple with the blood of an innocent man, while God, who compassionately spared this wicked man with brotherly charity because he was his fellow-courtier, awaiting the fruit of a better life, withheld the punishment he deserved. [Col. 0361D]

## LETTER CCCVI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. (A.D. 1171)

To the venerable lord and most dear father WILLIAM, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, his own JOHN sends greeting and the service of most ready devotion.

Although the English Church still suffers vast desolation in many respects, its sorrow has now for the most part turned into joy, and its mourning has been transformed, by a wholly happy and joyful change, into songs. [Col. 0362A] For miracles unheard of have now become so frequent at the martyr’s memorial that, if other unprecedented events occurred there, they would scarcely be thought worthy of being ascribed to his miracles. For as his noble spirit strove in every state of life to excel while others connived, so now—if I may say so without prejudice to other saints—he surpasses in the working of miracles all those of whom I have read or heard.

I can readily believe that this has happened so that the merciful Lord might awaken a faith in many parts of our world which was not so much asleep as almost wholly extinguished; raise hope; strengthen charity; and stop the mouths of the wicked, who disparaged the holy man in his lifetime and, out of hatred for his person, persecuted Christ’s cause. For who henceforth will doubt the true and faithful teaching of Christ, when he rewards with such blessedness a man known to us who adhered to his words? Who, unless demoniac, will say that a cause is unjust when it crowns its patron with so great a glory? [Col. 0362B]

Many doubt whether the cause of the lord pope, in which we stand, rested upon justice; but the glorious martyr acquits it of the charge of schism. For if he had been a supporter of schism, he would never shine with so many miracles. He was indeed a man of such prudence that in so great a peril to souls he could not easily have been overthrown by any error.

I would therefore wonder exceedingly why the lord pope has not ordered him received in the catalogue of martyrs, except that I recall reading in ecclesiastical history that Pilate, having sent a report, consulted the emperor Tiberius whether Christ, who had done so many and such great deeds and was worshipped by many as God, ought to be worshipped as God. [Col. 0362C] The senate, consulted by the emperor, replied that he ought indeed to have been worshipped as God, except that the provincials had presumed to do this without the senate’s authority.

And indeed this response was made by divine appointment, lest Christ’s divinity, whose name was to be preached among Jews and Gentiles, should appear subject to earthly authority, and lest unbelievers might call it begged for from men. Whether they wish it or not, they are compelled to hear that the Lord reigns: let the peoples rage, and let the earth rejoice upon which Christ’s Church is founded.

Thus I think it happened by divine appointment that this martyr’s glory is exalted neither by a pontiff’s decree nor by a prince’s edict, but chiefly flourishes through Christ, [Col. 0362D] whose honour he strove to extend while he lived and whose honour he always asserted would remain intact. And will Christ not repay him? Far be it that Truth should be false in its promises! We read in the Acts of the Apostles that certain persons not yet baptized received the Holy Spirit without apostolic authorization. But did the apostolic senate therefore invalidate this? Certainly, where God is the author, a higher authority is sought in vain. If anyone desires to render void the glory of this great martyr, whoever he may be, let him, before we believe him, work greater or at least similar miracles. Otherwise he is thought to sin against the Holy Spirit, whose works he does not fear to disparage.

## LETTER CCCVII. TO ARCHBISHOP ROGER AND THE OTHER YORK MEN. (A.D. 1171)

[Col. 0363A]
