ROGER, by God’s grace archbishop of York and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother H., by God’s grace bishop of Durham, and to his beloved sons R., dean, and William, cantor, and to the whole chapter of York; and to all canons of Saint Mary of Southwell and Saint Wilfrid of Ripon; and to the abbots, priors, clergy, and all the people established throughout the province of York: greeting and grace.

Your belovedness does not ignore how much I have suffered at this time for the dignity of our church, when so much envy was permitted to be directed against me [Col. 0363B] that scarcely any place was left for truth. It is characteristic of all wicked people, whenever they can find an opportunity, to brand with curses those whom they envy and to wound the innocent with the poisoned darts of words. Those who long ago lay in ambush for me have done this.

At first, indeed, they prepared a noose of suspension, by which the lord pope, following their false allegations more than the course of law, bound me. Then, lest I might be released by any means, adding iniquity to iniquity, they sought from one quarter the writings of eminent men by every artifice, as they had been instructed for many years; from another they suborned crowds of foreigners and persons who had never seen me, that by lying about matters of which they knew nothing they might in every way burden my reputation before the supreme pontiff and the Roman curia. [Col. 0363C]

I was absent; and those few who were at the curia on my behalf could scarcely withstand so great a multitude, pressed by such elaborate lies. Especially since certain persons religious only in outward dress, seeing the others prosper in their wickedness, ran with them; and, casting aside the fear of God, they said many things to overthrow the dignity of our Church, together with their prostitutes whom they had brought with them, lest any sex should be absent from my persecution.

All these, assembled in one, proposed in their hearts to imitate the giants: from very large stones, as it were, and many lies they built a wall, filling not only houses but streets with pretended sighs and groans, with howling by day and night. [Col. 0363D] They plastered that same wall, as though with an indissoluble cement, defying nature, with feigned tears, hoping thus to be able to shut heaven and consign truth to perpetual imprisonment.

> [Note: At Col. 0363D the Paris edition reads *volumine* (“volume”) for *bitumine* (“cement”).]

Why say more? Their Pharaoh—the spiritual Pharaoh whose members they are—seemed to proceed in such an escort wearing a crown; while I, assigned to the miserable servitude of a basket, looked for human help, and there was none. For my flesh having wasted away, my bone clung to my skin. Therefore I lifted my eyes to heaven, and in the anguish of my spirit cried to God; and through the interceding merits and prayers of you all he heard me [Col. 0364A] for his own honour. With the hammer of his innate goodness he broke down and reduced to nothing the aforesaid wall; the Babylonians fled; and he brought forth the truth that had been kept shut up, wiped away the filth of its prison, and commanded it to go freely out into public.

As soon as truth was restored to its liberty, it swiftly flew to me. In the presence of Lords R., archbishop of Rouen, and those whom the bishop of Amiens had delegated, to whom the lord pope had entrusted my case, and also of the bishop of Évreux and many religious men—abbots as well as priors—it stood at my right hand, clearer than light. The aforesaid archbishop and the religious men sent by the lord of Amiens, beholding its grave and shining countenance, rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. Without delay, [Col. 0364B] according to the form prescribed to them by the lord pope, they immediately absolved me from the suspicion in which I was held, while all present blessed the Lord who humbles the proud, catches the wise in their own cunning, frees those who presume upon his mercy, and brings the bound out in strength. To him be glory now and through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

God willing, I shall come to you shortly, so that my joy may be fulfilled in you; for I desire beyond expression to see you. May the blessing of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit descend upon you who pray for us.

These things were done on the Monday after the Sunday on which is sung “Rejoice” (*Gaudete*), the feast-day of Saint Lucy, at Aumale.

## LETTER CCCVIII. OF KING HENRY TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER. (A.D. 1171)

[Col. 0364C]

HENRY, king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, to B., bishop of Exeter, greeting.

Know that I have granted my peace to all who left England on account of Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury; and I grant them all their possessions as fully as they held them when they left England for that cause, together with the benefices which the same archbishop afterwards conferred upon them. Therefore cause them to come safely, and let them hold their possessions securely and in peace, saving the fealty which they shall render to me.

Witnesses: Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury; [Col. 0364D] Richard, archdeacon of Poitiers; Richard de Hum.; Const.; Bac. de Luci; Reginald de Courtenay. At Cloec.

## LETTER CCCIX. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1171)

HENRY, king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, to B., bishop of Exeter, his dear and faithful servant, greeting.

Know that by God’s grace I made landfall in Normandy after a prosperous voyage, and found my whole land on this side of the sea established, by God’s ordering, in the greatest peace and tranquillity. I found my men and faithful subjects, as was fitting, filled with abundant [Col. 0365A] joy at my arrival.

I then went to the lord legates. Although at first I found them severe and, as it seemed, wholly incapable of being moved, nevertheless, contrary to everyone’s expectation and each person’s opinion, peace at last followed and was restored between us, to the honour of God and the Church, and to my own honour and that of my realm, as will more fully become known to you from what follows.

These are the terms that I promised, at their urging, to observe: namely, from the coming feast of Pentecost for one year, I shall give so much money that, at the discretion of the brethren of the Temple, two hundred knights may be maintained for a year for the defence of the land of Jerusalem. Appeals to the lord pope shall also be permitted freely, provided that persons whom I regard as suspect swear, before leaving the realm, that on that journey [Col. 0365B] they will not pursue anything harmful to me or dishonourable to my realm. I shall abandon the customs introduced in my time against the churches of my land—customs which I consider either few or none. I shall wholly restore any possessions of the Church of Canterbury that have been taken away, as it held them one year before the archbishop left England.

Moreover, I shall restore my peace and their possessions to clergy and laypeople of either sex who have been deprived on account of the aforesaid archbishop. And this, on the lord pope’s behalf, they have imposed upon me to observe for the remission of all my sins.

I would have returned to England immediately after peace was restored, except that the lord legates are to hold a conference at Caen on the Tuesday next after the Ascension of the Lord. When [Col. 0365C] I have returned, do not fail to meet me at once.

## LETTER CCCX. OF BARTHOLOMEW OF EXETER AND ROGER OF WORCESTER TO POPE ALEXANDER. (A.D. 1171)

To the most holy lord and most dear father A., by God’s grace supreme pontiff, B., bishop of Exeter, R., called bishop of Worcester, and C., called abbot of Faversham, greeting and every duty of obedience with the utmost devotion.

We have received the mandate of your Apostleship that, proceeding together to the monastery of Saint Augustine of Canterbury, we should investigate diligently whether the reports that had reached you were true: namely, concerning the squandering of the Church’s goods and the enormities of C., the elect; the dissolution of discipline; the overthrow of good customs; and other evils said to have arisen, through the said elect’s negligence or malice, from the complaint of the convent. We were also to strive by every means to restore the monastery itself, for God’s honour, to its former condition. You further commanded us, under strict injunction, that if it became clear to us that the Church’s condition could not be restored without the removal of the elect and certain monks, we should not delay in removing both the elect and those monks by your authority, all excuse and appeal set aside, laying aside fear and favour altogether; and that, with God’s help, we should substitute honest and useful persons in their place, so that through the improved condition of the reformed monastery both your care and ours might be commended before God and men. You also sent mandatory letters to the often-mentioned elect, ordering him to obey our judgment—though we had no jurisdiction over him except by your delegation—all excuse and appeal removed.

When your letters had been presented to him in the chapter of the brethren, he finally ordered the cantor to open and read them; but before they had been completely read, he said that he and his affairs stood under your protection, and that he appealed to your hearing against those who had determined to act on the letters. This afterwards became known to us through the properly sworn testimony of witnesses and the account of the convent, namely of fifty-two monks. Later, having returned to himself, he heard your entire command in full in the assembly of the brethren.

Public report agreed so closely with what had been brought to your attention that no one in the province doubted that the greatness of the elect’s excesses—indeed, we might say, of his crimes—outweighed the monks’ complaint. Almost everyone found it astonishing that you had turned your eyes so late toward the ruin and tears of your house—eyes which you owe to the whole world. Therefore, on receiving your letters, we spared neither our labour nor our expense; but, ready to obey, and setting aside fear as you commanded, we came on the day appointed by us for the parties to the monastery.

And indeed, as was established by the solemn oath of the greater and sounder part of the convent, we learned that the often-mentioned elect, in evasion of your command and to the destruction of the monastery, had chosen flight, taking away ornaments, books, and no small sum of money, intending deliberately to seek out some power which he might set against God and the Apostolic See. We therefore exerted ourselves all the more diligently to seek the truth, since the testimony of many established more certainly that, before taking flight, he had said in the hearing of many that he did not hold the abbey from the Roman pontiff, but only the care of a few souls, for whom he did not care; and that he was unconcerned about temporal goods, since the Roman pontiff could not take away estates which he held from another.

We found such a wasting of property that our generation and that of those who connive at it may deservedly despair of repairing it. It is grievous for those who have seen it to inspect the Church’s collapse and desolation: the cloister and workshops open to rain and wind, and the buildings in ruins. It is torture to pious ears to hear the calamities of the Church’s tenants which the lust and rapacity of that elect—or rather, of that man rejected by God—have caused. He has made many enormous alienations of estates, all the less tolerable because he has been found to have sold Christ’s patrimony in a most disgraceful bargain to the patrons of his uncleanness and procurers of his shameful conduct. He took the Church’s seal from the brethren so that he might, as he pleased, ratify the alienations he had wrongly made. The money for which, in the Church’s name, he gave security to Jewish and Christian moneylenders has grown to an immense amount, wholly unbearable for the monastery.

He is so seditious that, because the convent refused to endorse the disposal of goods which he was planning, he surrounded it with a military siege, as is commonly known, and tried to starve it into submission. Hospitality, which had once flourished in that house, perished in his days. Religious observance, so far as he and his household were concerned, passed into ruin. He made the cloister like a public highway for his young men and servants, whom he had gathered about him in his own—that is, military—fashion, to the grief and protest of those trained in a more religious manner. He openly received money for admitting persons as monks, and admitted no one as a monk unless, in utter contempt of your decrees and those of the Fathers, he first filled his own hand with filth. From one such person he received seventy marks, as cannot be denied; and he spent them more outrageously than it is fitting now to relate.

What the faithful contributed in his days for the fabric of the church and its repairs amounted to a very great sum; but, disregarding the Church’s need, he expended it all upon wicked uses. They complained that the honourable customs of the house, laudably established and observed by the Fathers, had for the most part been abolished through him; nor was there anyone able to deny it. The great and venerable community of monks has been enormously diminished. We fear to offend the ears of your Holiness if we report concerning his incontinence what is, as the saying goes, known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers; but, whatever shame may hinder us, we cannot be silent concerning matters which, if kept silent, bring destruction upon good morals, scandal upon religion, and reproach upon the Apostolic See, to which this house is said especially to belong.

Perhaps our lips will be defiled by speaking of these things, because they concern matter excessively defiled; but, God being gracious, the live coal which the seraph will send you from the altar will cleanse them—especially since this is not our assertion, but that of the people, which no one dares resist unless he does not fear to be thought false and deceitful among our countrymen. That elect—or rather, that stallion—flows continually with seed, in the manner condemned by Leviticus, and neighs after women; so shameless that he does not consider lust pleasurable unless he has made it public. He commits incest alike with mothers and their daughters; nor does he fear or blush openly to violate the sanctity of marriages. He equates the practice of fornication with necessity. He is so prolific that in a few years such offspring have grown up around him that he surpasses the line of the patriarchs.

Among those who testified to his shamefulness—of whom there was a great abundance—a most religious priest, of whose integrity no one doubts, told us that in one village alone and its surrounding places he fathered seventeen bastards. It would be long, and unspeakable for us, to tell what he poured forth elsewhere. And that our tongue may at last turn away from describing this filth: God and His Spirit, who presides over our soul, know that we have never heard of so many foul deeds in a man bearing the name or habit of religion, nor perceived such a stench issuing forth. The entire convent stood unanimously against him, as did the clergy and people of the region.

Since therefore we plainly saw that matters could not be amended without his removal, and since we were constrained by your command—which directed us, if this were so, to remove him, all excuse and appeal set aside—we relied upon God’s and your authority, laid aside fear and favour, and removed him. We absolved the brethren from obedience to him and the laity from subjection to him; and we decreed that henceforth the approved institutions of the elders should be observed inviolably, your authority being preserved in all things. It will therefore be a work worthy of God and your Apostleship to confirm what has been done, lest the pestilential tree, once uprooted, strike its roots again in your garden and bear poisonous fruit to the disgrace of the Apostolic See and the reproach of religion.

When the sentence had been pronounced, all the brethren asked us for pardon and absolution because they had communicated with the elect’s servants—namely G., the marshal, and certain others—who, leaving his table with other assassins, shed the blood of the most glorious martyr Saint Thomas and then returned to him. They did so unwillingly; but since they did not dare resist their lord, whom they revered as abbot and feared as a member of the king’s household, when he openly communicated with those same men, we considered their contrition of heart and the circumstances of necessity. Trusting in your mercy, we imposed upon them a light penance in support of your Church and granted such absolution as was meanwhile permitted, asking you, if it please you, to prescribe what further ought to be imposed upon them. For the Church’s need and the martyr’s merit urgently demand that both the assassins who shed precious blood and their accomplices and supporters be punished more severely, so that their punishment may terrify others. But let your Serenity know beyond doubt that in our regions whoever lends assistance to restoring him will be deemed an enemy of God and a destroyer of the Church.

## LETTER CCCXI. TO THE SAME PERSON. (A.D. 1173.)

To the lord pope, JOHN.

From the ends of the earth the English Church cries to you, that you may lessen the straits of that afflicted Church which, above all others in the western lands, was founded and established in the blood of martyrs, and grew and expanded through the various contests of confessors; and that you may order its elect, whom through the diligent action of your legates it at last obtained, to receive consecration and exercise the fullness of authority. Bishops and abbots ask this; clergy and people ask it, and it is not lawful for the support of my smallness to be absent from their wishes and voices.

Indeed, my mother Church of Canterbury has lucidly set forth to you in her letter the form of its election, fortified by the assent and testimony both of bishops and of those elected to govern vacant churches. Men so great and such men have likewise reported the merits of the elect himself that every sinister suspicion may be far removed both from the elect and from the election. Since, then, the election is canonical and the elect worthy of every acceptance, perhaps the consecration of so great a Father has been delayed for no other reason than that he may shine more brilliantly and exercise greater strength when he receives confirmation from your Holiness.

I fear to speak further in the ears of your Majesty, especially since a humbler style diminishes the excellence of the subject, and my inadequate mind and defeated tongue fail to lay bare [Note: Col. 0369D, Paris edition: “to reproach.”] the merits of the cause undertaken, which are evident in themselves. May the Holy Spirit instruct your compassion to advance the prayers of the faithful as the Church’s interest requires, and may you add by promptness what prayer does not presume to request. If my pen, most serene Father, has gone too far, let this be ascribed to necessity, which knows no confinement by laws, not to the man. For our distresses are multiplied beyond number. May your Holiness ever prosper and flourish.

## LETTER CCCXII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. (A.D. 1173.)

[Col. 0369B]

To the venerable lord and most dear Father WILLIAM, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, his JOHN of Salisbury: greetings, and success ever happy in attaining what is to be desired.

Unless the members adhere to the head, the body’s health cannot endure; and rightly is anyone accused as a public enemy who opposes the Church’s advancement. Since, therefore, I am known to be a member, though a small one, of the holy Church of Canterbury, I must offer you such support as I can in our common cause and pursue with all diligence that toward which the efforts of the greater part are manifestly directed.

Your Holiness has indeed always stood by that Church in its troubles; and while the titles of your merits cooperated, the glorious martyr happily completed his contest, and the clergy breathe again in long-desired consolation. For when our lord the king of England had granted the aforesaid Church, as he made known through his officials to the bishops and clergy, free power to elect an archbishop for itself, at last, with the concurrence of the wishes of those living in the greater church and of the others, they canonically united in choosing a man for whom, divine grace leading the way, learning will avail for teaching, life will serve as an example, elegance of character will earn the favour of those who live with him, and eloquence will wholesomely dispense God’s word.

There is, indeed, undoubted hope that the most holy patron, whom he has always loved and honoured, will come to his aid in his needs; and that he whom the martyr seemed to have chosen and called as successor to labour will determine to advance to a share in consolation and glory. He is the venerable Ric., formerly prior of the Church of Dover. Falling at the knees of your Holiness on his behalf, I beseech with all possible devotion that your Excellency may graciously extend to him the right hand of favour and the help of counsel, and may relieve with desired comfort the labours and distresses of the Church which you have drawn from shipwreck into harbour.

This will come about only if your graciousness obtains that the elect, after receiving the gift of consecration, may enjoy fullness of authority, so that he may render God the service due to Him and give aid to those in need. Most serene and sweetest Father, I have all the more need to ask this because, to my great danger, certain persons have dared to lie that I ought to have hindered his consecration before you and through you. God knows this to be utterly false, as do the integrity of your conscience and of mine. May it therefore please your Holiness, since in this matter you know my innocence, in view of divine mercy, to excuse it when it is best, so that God may protect you and yours from every danger.

## LETTER CCCXIII. TO ALBERT AND THEODWIN, CARDINALS. (A.D. 1173.)

To the reverend lords and Fathers most dear in Christ, A. and T., priests of the Holy Roman Church and legates of the Apostolic See, J. of Salisbury, servant of their Holinesses: greetings, and the service of ready devotion and reverence.

By divine grace leading the way and with your cooperation, the hope of consolation has dawned upon the Church, and at last in the sees vacant among us it has been lawfully possible to ordain suitable shepherds. Thus the Church of Winchester chose as its father and shepherd a man whom, as the faithful hope, the Lord had beforehand chosen for this very purpose: a man in large measure such as Paul commands a bishop to be ordained. He is Richard, most devoted son of the Roman Church, formerly Archdeacon of Poitiers, whose alms comfort the churches of the saints, whose resources aid the needy, whose power is the support of justice and the destruction of iniquity.

He is prudent in counsel, discerning in action, restrained in speech; and, I think, you yourselves may at some time have experienced his ability and disposition. He is believed to have turned with his whole mind so completely toward God that he despises all his possessions for the Lord’s law and is ready, at a moment of need, to offer himself as a sacrifice to God. His election was first celebrated in the episcopal see, solemnly approved in an assembly of bishops, and the king’s assent confirmed both the election and the approval. May it please your Holinesses to complete what has been so laudably begun through you, and, using due deliberation, to provide how he may, after receiving fullness of authority, fulfill the office of his divine calling. For, God being favourable, he will be a most firm pillar in the house of the Lord and will very strongly support the needs both of his own and of other churches.

## LETTER CCCXIV. TO HUMBALD, BISHOP OF OSTIA. (A.D. 1173.)

To the venerable lord and most dear Father HU., by God’s grace Bishop of Ostia, J. of Salisbury: greetings and the services of complete devotion.

I should fear to address so great a majesty, were I not supported by your kindness and encouraged by the recollection of that true love which, almost above that of other mortals, you bore toward the holy confessor then, now the glorious martyr, with whom divine mercy caused me to share exile for the Church’s liberty. Strengthened by this confidence, I venture earnestly to commend to your Holiness a man unquestionably worthy of commendation: Ric., Elect of Winchester, whose resources assist the needy and console churches, and whose power is the destruction of iniquity and the support of justice.

He loves your friend, the glorious martyr of Christ, with such affection that he has made himself the martyr’s servant, so that he may comfort in their needs the pupils who flock to him in large numbers and strive, to the extent of his powers, to imitate him. Therefore, falling at the feet of your Holiness, I earnestly pray in my own name and that of those who shared exile with us that your favour may so advance his affairs as though you saw him labouring over Saint Thomas’s affairs. For he too has most devoutly consecrated all that he has—indeed, himself—to the most glorious martyr, whom he has chosen as patron.

## LETTER CCCXV. TO GRATIAN, NOTARY. (A.D. 1173.)

To Lord GRATIAN, JOHN. [Note: Col. 0371D, Paris edition: “The same writer to Gratian, notary of the lord pope.”]

The world has recognized Christ’s truth in you, beyond the rest who were sent in Saint Thomas’s affair; and this gives me confidence to venture safely to commend to your affection those known to be devoted to the aforesaid martyr. One of these, and one to be counted among the first, is the venerable R., Elect of Winchester, formerly Archdeacon of Poitiers: father of orphans and comforter of mourners, supporter of ecclesiastical liberty, cultivator of justice, and adversary of iniquity, as far as the times permit—indeed, beyond that, so that the attacks of evil men are inflamed against him as he often contends for the Lord, not without danger.

He is a man devoted to the Apostolic See, and one whose friendship may serve your honour. He wishes, indeed, that his diligence may be of service to you in some matter, and will regard it as a great gift if your affection chooses to impose anything upon him. Since, therefore, under God he has been called beneficially to the governance of the Church and to the consolation of many, falling at the knees of your charity I beseech with whatever urgency I can that you may hold both his person and his cause in special recommendation, and advance his affairs as you know the needs of the English Church ought to be expedited. For, as is beyond doubt hoped, he has devoted himself wholly to Christ’s service, ready even to sacrifice his own life for the Church. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXVI. FROM BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER, TO POPE ALEXANDER. (A.D. 1173.)

To the lord pope, the Bishop of Exeter.

[Col. 0372A] “The most holy Roman Church,” etc. See among the various letters to Alexander, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.

## LETTER CCCXVII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1173.)

To Pope ALEXANDER, BARTHOLOMEW, Bishop of Exeter.

“Strength comes to the members from the head,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCXVIII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1173.)

To the most excellent lord and most dear Father A., by God’s grace Supreme Pontiff, B., Bishop of Exeter: greetings.

“To your Apostleship,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCXIX. FROM THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF CANTERBURY TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1173.)

[Col. 0372B]

To the lord pope, the Prior of Canterbury and the convent.

“We commend them to you with greater confidence,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCXX. FROM ODO, PRIOR, AND THE CONVENT OF CANTERBURY TO POPE ALEXANDER. (A.D. 1173.)

To the lord pope, ODO, Prior, and the convent of Canterbury.

“The calamities which our Church,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCXXI. TO CARDINAL BOSO. (A.D. 1173.)

To the venerable lord and most dear Father BOSO, by God’s grace priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, his JOHN of Salisbury: greetings and the service of ready devotion.

The affection which your love has always shown to the people of Canterbury since the days of Lord Lucius gives me great confidence to intervene with you, so that I may confidently lay before your goodness what I do not doubt is expedient both for our need and for your salvation. You remember above all others, because above all others you have learned the affairs of the Roman Church, how the Church of Canterbury has almost beyond all churches in the world always shown faith and devotion to the Apostolic See. You recall how Theobald, Archbishop of the same Church of Canterbury, of blessed memory—your friend and intimate—endured hardships in defending the Church’s right and the constitutions of the Apostolic See; and how that Church has always had either martyrs or outstanding confessors as archbishops.

Since, therefore, I do not doubt that the Church’s cause is fully commended to you, I most devoutly offer to your Fatherhood such prayers as are permitted to a son and servant, asking that you may embrace in such affection and protect with such diligence our elect—worthy, as is hoped, successor to such great predecessors, and, God being favourable, most devoted to you at all times—as you have been accustomed to cherish the earlier archbishops; for in service to you he will not, according to his ability, be found inferior to his predecessors.

## LETTER CCCXXII. TO PETER, ABBOT OF SAINT REMIGIUS. (A.D. 1173–1174.)

[Col. 0373A]

To PETER, Abbot of Saint Remigius, his sole lord, his JOHN of Salisbury: greetings and prosperity in both lives.

There is no need to give reasons for prolonged silence, since intercourse between lands has for a long time now been cut off, and persons travelling from nation to nation cannot pass without danger to safety and life. Those regarded as suspect must take more careful precaution lest, on some plausible pretext, they incur the anger of public authority. For when each person fears what he has deserved, he more readily grows inflamed against the person whom he has injured more unjustly and cruelly. For, as someone says with considerable elegance and truth:

> Rumour arising from what is old will make men fear what is to come.  
> Tomorrow shameful things may happen, just as they did yesterday.

Since the Most High—patient indeed, but without doubt a just requiter—raised His right hand in repayment and His hand took hold of judgment, very many fear that the anger of powers clashing with one another may turn into fury; and they withdraw from the assault until justice is transformed into judgment, and through the conversion or contrition of the wicked the Lord’s counsel becomes known. Meanwhile we await God’s salvation in silence, holding certain that the patience of the poor will not perish forever. Now, indeed, it is especially necessary; now there is need of arms, now of a heart made firm in the Lord.

For alarms and reports of wars are heard everywhere. Conflagrations multiply, and those who ought to attack enemies turn to plunder. Nor is the boiling pot kindled for the destruction of peoples only from the north: it is kindled from the four winds of heaven. For from this generation is now demanded not only the blood of the son of Barachiah, shed not long ago more than once between temple and altar, but also the blood of others who for the same cause suffered losses, mockeries, and beatings; who were outlawed, imprisoned, and sent into exile; and who, having passed to the Lord from almost the entire Latin world, seek the due vengeance for their sufferings—vengeance worthy of God and beneficial to the Church.

In these things the righteous rejoice, seeing vengeance consonant with justice serve God’s glory, indeed washing their hands in the blood of sinners. This is a brief account of what is publicly reported among us, where he alone is safe whom madness drives or whom the Holy Spirit makes a despiser of all temporal things. For outside stands the sword, within is fear: citizen and enemy are almost assessed alike. Our lot, however, is comparable to that of those living together, except that, sailing more dangerously between Scylla and Charybdis, we are more graciously consoled by God’s more manifest propitiation, above and against our deserts. For, in order to make us more beholden to Him, He displays dangers close at hand that have not been attempted, and often repels more strongly and at a greater distance dangers rushing upon us with greater force; so that we may deservedly say: “Whoever, whether the world wishes it or not, does not love the Lord Jesus, blessed above all things, let him be anathema.”

But your possessions in our regions are exposed to many dangers. Our powerful men all around have turned into wolves, driven by the shameless gluttony of the belly to despise laws and authorities. Had the laborious and effective diligence of the man to whom you entrusted the estate not intervened, it would by now be cultivated by no inhabitant, or by very few. I remember having written to you on another occasion what condition he found it in, and I do not think it has escaped your memory.

Since I could not go there in person, I sent a diligent investigator from among our household; and, rejoicing at the manifest improvement in its condition reported through him, I did so because matters had now been put in such order that, if the Lord granted peace, they could suffice for those ministering there and laudably show due humility to guests, according to the place’s means. The brethren living there have earned the favour both of the bishop and his officials, and of their neighbours; and henceforth, with God’s favour and their own industry, they might have been enlarged by the support of friends, had an approaching storm not thwarted their efforts.

Yet although the neighbouring custodians of fortresses often extort much from them, they are nevertheless earnestly concerned, to the extent of their ability, to keep faith with God and their lord Saint Remigius and to obey all your commands. Brother Absalon wished, at our return, to cross over to us; but because of the imminent dangers, acting upon my advice and that of my brother, he returned to the house, which was threatened with desolation if he were absent. He deposited the established rent in the hand of your Richard, so that you may receive it from him if God perhaps grants a more convenient opportunity for travel.

Because wickedness has grown so strong that, as necessity requires, the brethren who are in your house must range through castles after robbers and plunderers, so that sometimes neither of them is found at home, it would seem to us—if it pleased you and appeared right to your counsel—highly expedient that, even with some reduction in the pension, you should send some respectable brother, suited to the monastery’s needs, who could be a comfort to them, answer arrivals in the others’ absence, and by his presence testify that the place is consecrated to the Lord under the title of a religious house. For if a larger number of religious persons appears there, the inhabitants will undoubtedly show greater reverence for the Lord, and the insolence of evildoers will more easily be restrained.

## LETTER CCCXXIII. FROM KING LOUIS TO JOHN OF SALISBURY, ELECTED BISHOP OF CHARTRES. (A.D. 1176.)

LOUIS, by God’s grace King of the French, to his most dear friend Master JOHN of Salisbury, Elect of Chartres: greetings with sincere affection.

We consider it pleasing and acceptable that the chapter of Chartres, by the counsel of the lord Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and, as we believe, rather by divine inspiration, has solemnly and canonically elected you as shepherd and lord by unanimous wish and consent—both on account of the blessed martyr Thomas, whose friendship you were worthy to attain through your merits, and in consideration of your character and learning. Accordingly, we earnestly advise and ask your discernment that, giving gracious assent to the election made of you, you may hasten to satisfy, by the presence of your person, the calling of so great a Church, so solemn and so praiseworthy. Let not our desire, and that of the Archbishop of Sens, who has laboured faithfully and effectively to bring this matter to completion, be delayed longer; nor let the hope of the Church of Chartres be tormented by more protracted delay. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXXIV. FROM THE CHAPTER OF CHARTRES TO THE SAME. (A.D. 1176.)

[Col. 0375B]

To its venerable lord and Father, JOHN, by God’s grace Elect of Chartres: greetings in the undertaking of pastoral care unto salvation.

“What is born of flesh is flesh; and what is born of spirit is spirit.” Hence our soul magnifies the Lord and our spirit has rejoiced in God, because it was not flesh and blood that revealed you, elected as our shepherd, to us, but our Father who is in heaven, visiting us as the Dayspring from on high. Indeed, only the Spirit of unity could have brought together such discordant human wishes and so many diverse inclinations of mind, so that it is undoubtedly clear that he whom the Spirit revealed has been sent from heaven.

We believe that joy has been brought to the heavenly court because the Church of the Blessed Virgin, conceiving through the Holy Spirit, has brought forth a shepherd beloved by God and men. Therefore the Church of Chartres, with the acclamation of all its wishes, asks for the one it has desired, and without delay reaches toward the beloved and elect whom it now longs for as a bride longing for her bridegroom: “Let him kiss me,” it says, “with the kiss of his mouth” (*Song of Songs* 1). May Christ’s love urge him whom the embraces of the king’s daughter desire, and may he who is chosen as Christ’s son-in-law to propagate the children of God be pierced by saving goads. Let him blush to enter the kingdom of heaven alone, to whom the glorious splendour of divine offspring is promised; and let him who is believed to have deserved a golden crown, by the labour of his glorious office, merit the eternal one.

We therefore send to you distinguished persons from our chapter—namely, the dean, cantor, and chancellor—to offer you the mind of our whole body, to petition for your person, and to announce to us by living voice the desire for your coming.

## LETTER CCCXXV. TO PHILIP, DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF SAINT MARTIN. (A.D. 1176.)

JOHN, by divine favour and the merits of Saint Thomas humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PHILIP, dean of Blessed Martin, and to the whole chapter in the Lord: greetings.

We do not believe that your whole body is unaware that the lord pope has committed to us for hearing, and for settlement by due judgment, all contradiction and appeal set aside, the controversy between the men of Châteauneuf of Saint Martin and R., the noble treasurer of your Church, concerning certain oaths or a pledge of faith which the said men are alleged to have made secretly among themselves, to the detriment of the right of the said Church.

Accordingly, proceeding in accordance with the Apostolic mandate and upon the counsel of religious and prudent men, and having learned the truth of the matter through sufficient witnesses beyond every objection, we have pronounced, by the Apostolic authority exercised by us in this matter, sentence of excommunication against the said men, both because of their manifest contumacy and because the infamy of the said conspiracy was proved by witnesses. We bound by name in the bond of excommunication those whom we heard to be the leaders of the faction; against all the rest who are accomplices in the same conspiracy we pronounced a general sentence of excommunication, not by name but upon all alike.

We therefore transmit to you in our letter the names of those excommunicated by name: Reginald Meschini; Peter of Montbruis; Nicholas Engelard; Peter Aubert; Pagan Gastinelli; John Ermerard; Ralph of Fulchis; Ralph Thomas; Gilo Baldwin; Peter Aimeri; Gilo Thomas; Gilo Senoret; Bartholomew of Loches; Peter of Savonnières; Hardouin Pelliparius; Peter Chivitton; Reginald Goslan; Juguelmus the Shoemaker; Hameric Epuliard; Sancio Emenard; Geoffrey of Cormery; Bartholomew Fromaud; Jocelin Pelliparius; Herbert of Chartres; Bartholomew Attatei; and Thomas of Amboise.

Accordingly, by Apostolic authority we command your whole body to announce by name as excommunicated those whom we have excommunicated by name; to promulgate generally against all the general excommunication which we have pronounced upon the remaining accomplices of the aforesaid conspiracy; and to cause the aforesaid excommunicated persons, both those named and those included generally, to be frequently and solemnly denounced in your church by the priests of the lesser altars, or else compel them to cease from divine offices.

## LETTER CCCXXVI. LETTER OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, CONCERNING THE ABSOLUTION OF JOHN, COUNT OF VENDÔME, FROM THE BOND OF EXCOMMUNICATION WITH WHICH JOHN HAD BOUND HIM. (A.D. 1180.)

[Col. 0376D]

JOHN, by divine favour and the merits of Saint Thomas humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to all whom these letters shall reach: greetings in the Lord.

You should know that, when we came to the Church of Chartres, we bound the nobleman John, Count of Vendôme, with the bond of excommunication on account of the injuries, damages, and exactions which he had repeatedly inflicted upon the church of the Most Holy Trinity of Vendôme, and kept him bound for more than three years. But as time went on, he approached our venerable father Peter, cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church with the title of St. Chrysogonus and legate of the apostolic see; and, having given sworn security that he would make satisfaction for the injuries and wrongs done to the aforesaid church, he deserved absolution, the illustrious king of the English being present and interceding for him, with what remained due in law being left for us to carry out. Yet when summoned, the count did not stand by the security he had given, saying that he had not sworn in this form; and therefore he was restored by us to his former sentence, which Pope Alexander III confirmed. At last, since the lord king of the English grieved that he had lain so long under excommunication, he added the royal hand, compelling him to obtain release from the sentence of excommunication by rendering justice. Then the count came to us, apparently penitent and contrite in heart; and, having made adequate satisfaction for the injuries, he was absolved at the prayers of the lord king of the English and of the abbot and brethren of the aforesaid church, after giving sworn security that thereafter he would lay hands neither upon that church nor upon its men or possessions, unless he could establish some right at law. And so that this might be known to posterity and provision made for the immunity from loss of the church already mentioned, we caused it to be confirmed by the testimony both of our writing and of our seal.

Done publicly, in the year of Grace 1180.

## LETTER CCCXXVII. LETTERS OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, CONCERNING SATISFACTION MADE TO THE MONASTERY OF ST. LAUNOMAR OF BLOIS FOR DAMAGES AND INJURIES INFLICTED UPON IT BY JOHN, COUNT OF VENDÔME. (A.D. 1180.)

[Col. 0377C]

JOHN, by divine favour and through the merits of St. Thomas the martyr, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to all whom these present letters shall reach, greeting in the Lord.

You should know that the illustrious man John of Vendôme was for a long time bound by us under a sentence of excommunication, likewise confirmed by Pope Alexander III, because of certain unjust customary exactions which he claimed contrary to justice in the villages of St. Launomar of Blois, situated in the district of Vendôme. For he asserted there his right of lodging, tallage, forced labour-service, oat-render, and jurisdiction over bloodshed and theft. All these, when he was setting out for Jerusalem, he renounced before us and many venerable men at Blois for ever, so that he might deserve absolution from the bond of anathema by which he was held. He also established and solemnly confirmed that, should any one of his heirs or successors presume to harass or trouble the monks or men of St. Launomar concerning the exaction of the aforesaid dues, he should be compelled by ecclesiastical censure to pay sixty marks of silver to the said monks. And lest a dispute thus settled might be raised anew either by himself or by his heirs, at his own request I decreed that the terms of peace entered into, committed to this present document, should be strengthened by the protection of my seal.

Done at Blois, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1180.

## LETTER CCCXXVIII. TO PETER OF CANDEIO.

He warns him not to compel the monks of Fontaines to celebrate contrary to the rule of their order in the church of Landa. (D. MARTEN., *Ampliss. Collect.*, I, 601, from the manuscript of St. Mary of Fontaines.)

[Col. 0378B]

JOHN, by divine favour and through the merits of blessed Thomas, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PETER of Candeio, greeting.

Every alms-deed is so much the more acceptable to God and profitable to its giver as, through his own care, it is more fitting and useful to its recipient. Therefore, having regard for your advantage, we counsel and admonish you in the Lord not to compel the monks of Fontaines to celebrate Mass in your church at Landa contrary to the rule of the Cistercian Order. Let the divine office which the monks have appointed to celebrate in that abbey for the salvation of yourself, your predecessors, and your successors suffice for your devotion. [Col. 0378C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXXIX. TO BARTHOLOMEW, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS.

On the same subject. (Ibid.)

To the venerable lord and most dear father B., by the grace of God Archbishop of Tours and legate of the apostolic see, JOHN, by divine favour and through the merits of St. Thomas, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting and continual success according to your prayers.

It is incumbent upon rulers of the Church to love religious men more earnestly, to foster them from their own resources, and to drive injuries far away from them. Therefore we earnestly entreat the compassionate devotion of your lordship that you may persuade Peter of Candeio that the fruit of mercy is so much more abundant as he to whom it is shown is known to benefit more greatly. Counsel him, therefore, and admonish him in the Lord not to compel the monks of Fontaines to celebrate Mass in the church of Landa contrary to the rule of the Cistercian Order, since the aforesaid monks in that abbey for his salvation and that of his predecessors . . . .

[Col. 0379]

# JOHN OF SALISBURY’S *POLYCRATICUS*, OR *ON THE TRIFLES OF COURTIERS AND THE FOOTPRINTS OF PHILOSOPHERS*

## THE ENTHETICUS TO THE *POLYCRATICUS* BEGINS

### The author to his work

[Col. 0379A]

If you will trust me, restrain your tongue,  
and let not your foot enter the thresholds of court: stay home.

Remember cautiously to avoid men’s gaze,  
and, little book, seal up the notes entrusted to you.

Let all things be suspect to you, because you are called  
a public enemy and guilty of treason.

Perhaps consuming fire and a savage sword are being prepared for you;  
or an enemy will overwhelm you with polluted water.

Yet when you go out, let a cloak cover your face,  
and let dust and wind disfigure your skin.

Let your right hand carry a staff, and let your wallet press upon your back;  
let worn caps cover your brow, and a rough shoe your foot.

Let your gait, attire, and bearing be those of a traveller;  
let no tongue sound but barbarous speech.

[Col. 0379B]

Say that you were born among the people of Poitou,  
for they are permitted to speak with freer tongue.

Seek above all the security of hospitality, that you may be  
safe from the snares which each man prepares for you.

Beware fools, men too wise, and little men,  
and those whom a babbling tongue makes conspicuous.

If anyone loves truth, let him be your most welcome host;  
but beware one delighted by empty glory.

By right of patronage cultivate the man who is willing,  
who knows, and who is able, to be your protector everywhere.

Therefore seek the light of the clergy, the glory of the English nation,  
the king’s right hand, the image of goodness.

The chancellor of the English realm, once sought,  
must be the first to be approached with anxious mind.

[Col. 0379C]

He is the one who cancels the unjust laws of the realm  
and gives force to the just commands of a pious prince.

Whatever harms the people or is hostile to good morals—  
whatever it is—ceases to be harmful through him.

He always prefers public advantage to private gain;  
and what he gives to many, he counts as his own treasure.

What he gives, he possesses; what he possesses, he gives to the worthy;  
and in return he scatters wealth, yet scattered wealth increases.

As a man’s virtue lies in his soul, so beauty lies in grace of form;  
each makes him admirable to nations everywhere.

Should a Samian contend with him in keenness of mind,  
[Col. 0380A] Plato would be unlearned and Varro foolish.

If Curius contended in speech, he would be defeated by him;  
if Quintilian contended, he too would be defeated.

To know this man’s house is no difficult matter: for anyone,  
without seeking a guide, a well-worn path lies open.

The house is known to all; unknown to vice alone, it shines.  
From it rich and poor alike receive light.

It stands open to the wretched; that house stands open also to the happy;  
there every stranger rejoices in his father.

Once the door has been opened to you, run  
toward the chamber of your lord.

Wait until the crowd that seethes in court has flowed away  
and your lord’s weary limbs must be refreshed in bed.

Approach; change your face; let your wallet shake out its trifles;  
let the traveller now go abroad as a traveller.

[Col. 0380B]

Yet do not reveal what might burn your prince’s eyes—  
the one from whom all your life and safety come.

If your appearance displeases him, whence will favour come?  
Right and favour alike rest in his judgement.

What he forbids is a crime; what he commands is just;  
laws rise and fall according to his pleasure.

By that virtue alone which pleases him, you alone will please him;  
if it is lacking in you, all else will harm you.

He honours laws, establishes peace, and founds tranquillity;  
with mind and hand he subdues proud enemies.

But whether laws summon him or the sword flashes against enemies,  
he does only holy deeds and approves only holy things.

Set beside him whatever leaders and mighty men you please:  
[Col. 0380C] at this sight the greatest throng of leaders will be mere common people.

If you see kings, what are they beside him but a rustic crowd?  
And well indeed, if they can be called a rustic crowd.

By displaying a portion of yourself, you will discover  
what favour or honour awaits the whole.

If he likes this, perhaps you may reveal yourself entirely;  
but if it displeases him, conceal the rest beneath your cloak.

Let words of greeting come first; then, pleasantly,  
offer your services and request hospitality.

You will not be a burdensome guest, nor formidable in drink or food;  
an inexpensive garment will suffice you.

[Col. 0381A]

You are not burdened with horses, nor do you demand trappings for horses;  
no great multitude of servants presses upon you.

Even a house alone will suffice, and the sight of your patron,  
and enjoyment of his conversation and counsel.

What the court can do, what the people hope, where the realm’s strength lies—  
one house alone can teach you.

If he shows you his unveiled face, and his nets  
do not merely graze your sight,

then what distinguishes the wise from the foolish, the rich from the poor,  
the happy from the wretched? If you are wise, see: you perceive it.

If he is cheerful, perhaps he will gladly expose  
his eyes and ears to your trifles.

Scatter your trifles, therefore, lest they breed boredom,  
which is exceedingly hostile to happy circumstances.

If he orders you to pursue trifles, trifle decorously:  
[Col. 0381B] for through trifles he will think serious business is being done.

So join serious matters to useful amusements  
that no stern hand need be feared by you.

If he orders you to be silent, be more silent than a statue;  
do not redeem with signs the words denied you.

When he has had enough, or when weightier affairs summon him,  
let a hired mouth be given leave to depart.

Go quickly and return, lest those whose trifles  
you dared criticize inflict weapons and prepare death.

As you depart, utter one secret into his ear:  
whatever others do, remember yourself.

All flesh is hay, the flower of hay, the glory of flesh;  
this is nothing: what can be less than nothing?

Think Fortune’s gifts are seeds of vices, smeared with birdlime:  
they are nourishment for crimes and the road to death.

[Col. 0381C]

They are snares, they are ambushes, they are poisons of death,  
which those who worship the blind goddess will not escape.

What Fortune has given, and what she will give, is another’s;  
when she wishes, she will take it all away from you.

Nets foreseen cannot harm winged creatures;  
whatever you see, regard as nets of the mind.

Everything you see is a net, drawing a man bound  
through every evil toward wretched death.

Perhaps he will ask: “Whence comes this boldness of yours?”  
Say without fear: “He who does all things safely acts safely.”

He acts safely in all things whom neither hope nor fear afflicts,  
to whom no evils are pleasing: he acts safely in all things.

On returning, use Spanish or Gascon speech,  
but let there nevertheless be more gravity in your words.

[Col. 0381D]

Put on the language, put on the garments, of that people,  
while the rule of morals and faith remains unharmed.

Let a bronze cross hang from your shoulders; let your hair be dark,  
your locks shaggy, your beard insufficiently trimmed.

Let your countenance be grave, your brow and eyes modest,  
your hands innocent; let your clothing be poor.

So long as you are hired, you will travel more safely,  
and every road will be suitable for your feet.

But if this fails you, prolong your day’s journeys,  
and let the public highway contain your steps.

Turn aside nowhere, lest someone harm you as you go  
and your babbling tongue pay the penalty for its trifles.

Every place, if you do not know it, is utterly full of trifles;  
their whole host is hostile to you.

Trifles reign in the Church and in the prince’s court;  
[Col. 0382A] they reign in the cloister and in the bishop’s house.

The clergy are engaged in trifles; the soldier’s practice is in trifles;  
young men are in trifles, and the entire crowd of old men.

The peasant is in trifles, both sexes are in trifles;  
slave and free, rich and poor, are among them.

Quickly make your way, travelling with a prudent passport  
to the sea, by which the Morini seek our shores.

At length, when late night brings you beneath a roof,  
be sober and grave if you are to prosper.

You must pass among a people exceedingly broad, fond of drink, and talkative—  
a people to whom, unless you accommodate yourself, you will be an enemy.

Small disputes arise, followed by great quarrels,  
fruitful in wounds and bringing death.

But because this people loves and reveres virtue,  
[Col. 0382B] if you are believed to live well, you will be safe.

Not only will you be safe; you will be worthy of the highest honour,  
and do freely whatever you please.

Happy Kent bore you; Kent has nurtured you,  
illustrious mother of kings and bishops.

Here your resting-place and the end of your labours are due to you;  
she prepares rest for you, she prepares a home.

Seek the chief see of the English, or of the Britons;  
if you prefer to call it the Britons’ see, no one forbids it.

It is unworthy that a brief time should prolong a dispute;  
long periods are not fitting for a brief dispute.

When the matter is agreed, let there be no battle over a name;  
let goat’s wool not foster contention for long.

Call it whatever you wish, provided it is the head of the Britons,  
which an angel gleaming from the citadel points out to you.

[Col. 0382C]

You will ask, “Who is this angel, or what is this house?”  
For a novel form of things commonly stirs one to inquire.

This is that house which first received Christ,  
from which the whole island received faith.

The whole island received faith and proclaims, extols, hears,  
honours, and loves the parent of its faith.

If perhaps you know the giver of great counsel,  
this angel will not be unknown to you.

The angel from his watchtower surveys the whole world;  
he bears up and covers the body with wings.

Thus from his watchtower he sees, thus he protects all things with wings,  
so that the enemy has no right within his world.

He foretells storms and fair weather;  
he moderates the rage of winds and sea.

[Col. 0382D]

Lest anything be able to do harm, he does not sleep: night and day  
he stands, because he causes his subjects to stand on every side.

Drawing nearer, you will hasten to Christ’s court,  
that you may earn pardon for your sins.

There the vows of your completed labour will be discharged;  
here you will offer tears, groans, and pious incense.

The whole choir of brethren will receive you returning;  
joyfully they will sing praises for your safety.

Whatever you possess that may please them, give freely;  
give to each whatever will be useful.

If you can, endeavour to offer salvation to Odo;  
and let the Briton receive the cross at your arrival.

Here at last you may recount the perils of your fate  
and all the successes of the journey accomplished.

Say what a sheep hidden beneath a fox is, or a fox beneath a lamb;  
[Col. 0383A] what an ass does in a lion’s skin.

What a lion does while it serves, what an ass does while it reigns;  
tell of a sparrow’s acts in the form of a dove.

What timid leopards and fleeing hares do,  
and what hope is to be held concerning a converted wolf.

What the creeping tortoise prepares, the burdened beetle,  
and why a great wind falls from a light rain-cloud.

But because no one can please everyone by virtue,  
let it suffice that you have pleased a few good men.

If perhaps your trifles are scorned by a judge,  
let neither his hand be unjust nor your tongue insolent.

Let free votes be granted to all: let one call you good,  
and another call you bad.

If the place is free, why should the tongue not be free?  
No one is sufficiently firm whom a light breeze moves.

[Col. 0383B]

What will swords do if a light breeze makes you bleed?  
Words are not blows: do you fear words?

Let the clamour of tongues not pass through a solid ear;  
that ear is far too foolish which an empty sound burns.

Others may exercise their tongues; let your ear obey you.  
The tongue is indeed useful, but not more useful than the ear.

Their mind is in their tongue; let your heart be in your ear.  
Let their mouth be open and your ear open.

The assault of speech is broken by the barrier of virtue,  
and an unhealthy mind perishes through the tongue’s goad.

No one but a vain man rejoices in false honour;  
a conscience aware of guilt is disturbed by evil words.

Let your brow be harder than diamond; let your skin be burned by fire,  
lest blush mark your face at words.

Yet let it be full of that shame which becomes one  
[Col. 0383C] who fears the foul mark of vice.

Say: who holds the reins of another’s tongue?  
There is scarcely one who can restrain his own.

It often slips because it moves in wetness;  
often, falling, it contracts stain and disgrace.

Among the talkative and those who scatter grand words,  
be slow of speech and speak few words.

While others sharpen their tongues, let your ear be trained,  
and be deafer than the ear of the Dulichian oarsman.

Let not the rash tongue of a speaker have such power  
as to break the enclosures of your breast.

If you are patient, words will never harm you,  
nor will anyone disturb your peace.

No one will shake the peace that patience gives;  
[Col. 0383D] though unarmed, it nevertheless crushes weapons.

Let others use their tongues; if you are wise, use the powers of your mind:  
great glory comes from being tongueless.

For patience shows what a man’s learning is  
and with unarmed hand restrains wicked wars.

Who can endure that armed thing which alone triumphs unarmed  
and alone is accustomed to conquer the armed hand?

A patient man is better than a strong one;  
the triumph of a city is said to be less than that of the mind—and is less.

Despise the bad, revere the good, forgive one wishing to injure you:  
no revenge is more pleasing to good men.

No vengeance better befits a strong man than this;  
[Col. 0384A] it ought always to attend princely men.

When fiery law flourishes in their hands, it punishes while it pities;  
while it wishes men to be faithful, it makes them so.

Unjust power, while raging, provokes crime  
and does not permit its subjects to be pious.

No one knowingly harms a man whom he believes a friend;  
a most trustworthy rule: whoever is to be loved, let him love.

This customarily joins hearts divided among men;  
it can reconcile a human being to God.

With this as guide, take the road: none will harm you as you go,  
and you will safely enter all hands.

Yet that hand is to be feared which handles base  
filth, which stains bronze with its colour.

It is not to be avoided because it is polluted and pollutes,  
but because money carries savage poisons—

[Col. 0384B]

poisons that produce perpetual hunger and thirst,  
a wretched life, and every kind of death.

No hand stained with rust will be fit for books;  
nor can money-filled hearts be free for books.

It is not the same thing to approve money and books;  
your flock, Epicurus, persecutes books.

When the fire of avarice burns the hay of flesh,  
it rises and builds an everlasting furnace.

Though the hand of the Almighty can do all things,  
it cannot satisfy the poverty of an avaricious mind.

The hand of the Almighty cannot satisfy the avaricious man:  
tell me, who can do what that hand cannot?

Is not he sufficiently wretched whom not even God himself  
is sufficient to make happy? Who can be more wretched?

Money-seekers and little book-men cannot be together;  
[Col. 0384C] believe me, one house cannot contain both.

Therefore beware these wretches, and expect from them only sorrow:  
for who but a fool would cultivate a wretched man?

It is a most ancient, a most true saying,  
taught by the fathers, by Ennius and by Cato:

“Let him seize both what he has and what he lacks, though every friend fails him;  
yet another’s property will be his ruin.”

He will always abound who knows how to use possessions;  
a mind ignorant of their use is always in want.

A rich man may possess little and a poor man very much;  
the rich man does not know want, nor the needy man wealth.

He who desires much has no friend, and he is not  
his own friend to whom another’s possessions please too much.

If the covetous man is an enemy, beware him as an enemy;  
[Col. 0384D] if he is a friend, strive to be all the more cautious of him.

Does he swear? Trust him less. Does he not swear? Do not trust him.  
Whether he swears or does not swear, beware an enemy as an enemy.

Flee also those whom consuming envy so makes enemies of the fortunate  
that no virtue can bend them.

Perhaps you may appease the miser with gifts;  
to make the envious cease from harming you, be wretched.

The envious mind rejoices in another’s wretched lot  
and counts every neighbouring advantage a loss.

And unless you were in haste, I would warn you of more;  
you can scarcely endure a few words: yet hold fast even these.

# JOHN OF SALISBURY’S *POLYCRATICUS*, OR *ON THE TRIFLES OF COURTIERS AND THE FOOTPRINTS OF PHILOSOPHERS*

[Col. 0385]

## BOOK I

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0385A]

Among the many pleasant fruits of letters, the most pleasant is this: setting aside all intervening distance of place and time, they make friends present to one another and do not allow matters worthy of knowledge to be obliterated by their situation. For the arts would have perished, laws would have vanished, the duties of faith and of religion as a whole would have collapsed, and even the use of correct speech would have failed, had divine mercy not provided mortals with the use of letters as a remedy for human weakness. The examples of our ancestors, which are incentives and nourishments of virtue, would correct or preserve no one at all, unless the pious care of writers and diligence, triumphant over idleness, had transmitted them to posterity.

For brevity of life, dullness of perception, the numbness of negligence, and useless occupation permit us to know very little; and forgetfulness—the deceiver of knowledge, an enemy and ever-faithless stepmother to memory—constantly shakes these things out and tears them from the mind. Who would know Alexanders or Caesars, who would admire Stoics or Peripatetics, unless literary monuments made them illustrious? Who would imitate the footsteps of apostles and prophets, which ought to be embraced, unless divine writings had consecrated them for posterity? Triumphal arches bring glory to illustrious men only when an engraved inscription teaches why they stand and whose they are. The observer at last recognizes the liberator of his country and founder of peace when an inscription identifies Constantine, the conqueror whom our Britain bore. No one ever shone with enduring glory except through his own writing or that of another. After a short time, the glory of an ass and that of any emperor are the same, except insofar as the memory of one or the other is prolonged through writers’ service.

[Col. 0385B]

How many and how great kings do you suppose there have been of whom there is nowhere speech or thought? Nothing, therefore, is wiser for seekers of glory than to earn above all the favour of educated men and writers. Great deeds are done for them uselessly, destined to be covered in perpetual darkness unless they shine by the light of letters. Whatever favour or praise is gathered from elsewhere is as though Echo, whom you hear of in fables, received theatrical applause: it ends when it begins.

Moreover, in sorrow consolation, in labour refreshment, in poverty delight, and in riches and pleasures moderation are most faithfully borrowed from letters. For the mind is redeemed from vices and refreshed with a certain sweet and marvellous delight, even amid adversity, when it directs the sharpness of its mind to reading or writing useful things. You will find no occupation in human affairs more delightful or more useful—unless perhaps devotion divinely pierced by compunction persists in prayerful converse with God, or, with the heart enlarged through charity, conceives God in the mind and handles His mighty acts within itself as it were by the hand of meditation. Believe one who has experienced it: compared with these pursuits, all worldly sweets become bitter, and more so in proportion as each person’s perception is sounder and his reason flourishes in the keener power of purer judgement.

[Col. 0386A]

Do not wonder, therefore, why I do not climb some rung of the ladder which now alone knows ascent, in accordance with whatever advice you have given me. Why do I not thrust myself into greater courts? I shall answer you even with the saying of Isocrates, who, when friends asked why he did not engage in public business, replied: “What this place knows, I do not know; what I know, this place does not know.” For I despise what those courtiers seek, and they despise what I seek. Wonder rather why I do not cut or break the rope, if it cannot otherwise be untied, which has held me so long in the talons of courtiers and still holds me subject to such great servitude.

For it now wearies and disgusts me that for almost twelve years I have trifled away my life, though I was educated quite differently and, as it were, nourished at the breasts of a more sacred philosophy; it would have been fitting, once weaned, for me to pass to the company of philosophers rather than to the associations of triflers. I perceive that you too are in the same condition—except that, being more upright and prudent, if you do what is expedient, you always stand unmoved on the foundation of solid virtue; you are not tossed by reed-like fickleness, nor do you pursue soft delights, but you rule that vanity which rules the world.

[Col. 0386B]

Accordingly, while different provinces, heaping up proclamations of praise deserved by your merits, raise for you something like a triumphal arch, I, a common man with the shrill pipe of uncultivated speech, have cast this book in your honour like a little stone into the heap of your praises. I know that, as it has nothing by which to please through antiquity, so it cannot displease through the devotion of its writer. In part it contains courtly trifles, and concerns itself especially with those things by which it is most pressed. In part it follows the footprints of philosophers, leaving to the wise person’s judgement what in each case should be avoided or pursued.

And because, if it was not to injure anyone, it was necessary to address one in whom nothing frivolous could be charged, I resolved to address you, the most refined of the men of our age, and to describe the matters which seem blameworthy in men like myself. For when reader or hearer recognizes his own follies, he will recall the ethical saying: “With the name changed, the tale is told of you,” especially because everyone knows how constantly you are occupied with serious affairs. Thus, while Seneca teaches others, he admonishes his Lucilius. Jerome writes to Oceanus and Pammachius and commonly rebukes the excesses of others.

[Col. 0387A]

Whoever complains of the follies of one who flatters should measure the work by its occasion and, as befits a wise person, judge spoken words from the circumstances of speaking. If anything sounds too harsh to anyone, let him know that nothing has been said against himself, but against me and men like me who wish to be corrected with me, or against those who, fallen into their doom, bear every rebuke with equanimity. For I know that no Achilles is grievously wounded; and the present age is corrected while the past is reproved according to its merits. Thus Horace, while correcting, allows even slaves to use December freedom.

[Col. 0387C]

> The crafty Flaccus touches every vice with a laughing friend,  
> and, once admitted, plays about the heart.

Whatever pertinent things from various authors entered my mind as I compared them or found them helpful, I took care to insert, sometimes leaving the authors’ names unspoken: first, because I knew that most of them were completely familiar to you, as one practised in letters; and secondly, that the ignorant might be more strongly kindled toward constant reading. If in these matters anything stands too far from the truth of faith, I trust that pardon is owed me, since I do not promise that everything written here is true, but that, whether true or false, it serves the uses of readers.

For I am not so witless as to maintain as true that a tortoise once spoke to winged birds, or that “a country mouse received the town mouse beneath a poor roof” (HORACE, *Satires* II.6.8), and the like. But I do not doubt that these inventions serve our instruction. These very things which I commonly employ are also another’s, except insofar as whatever has been well said anywhere I make my own; now for brevity, now for authority and trustworthiness, I express it in my own words or in others’ words.

[Col. 0387D]

And because I have once begun to reveal the secrets of my mind, I shall disclose my arrogance more fully. Therefore I reckon as my clients all who meet me philosophizing in word or deed; and, what is greater, I claim them for slavery to myself—to such an extent that in their writings they expose themselves for me to the tongues of detractors. For I dare authors too. I have not seen that Alexander or Caesar, nor heard Socrates, Zeno, Plato, or Aristotle disputing; yet I have related very many things about them and other persons equally unknown, for the benefit of readers.

Yet, lest I seem to delight in dispute, I yield; I confess that I have employed serviceable falsehoods. And if my rival will not otherwise rest, since I too have my Cornificius and Lanuvium, I agree that I am guilty of falsehood, knowing it is written that every man is a liar—so much so that our Lanuvium has not received even a huge breast, a swollen belly, a puffy and ruddy face, a saucy and tasteless tongue, readier to gnaw away the morals of others than correct his own. Who he is, unless he abstains from insults, I shall say, and he will plainly recognize that being long-established confers neither full nor unimpaired authority.

[Col. 0388A]

Let him nevertheless come forward and publish; let him refute my falsehood by reason or authority, and I shall not refuse correction even at an enemy’s voice. Indeed, I shall count as a friend the one who corrects my error. But if an author is found anywhere to say otherwise than I have written, it will not therefore be established that I lied; for in matters of military stratagem I have followed historians who frequently disagree with one another, and in philosophical questions, arguing academically, I have pursued such probable views as presented themselves, in proportion to reason.

Nor am I ashamed of the Academic profession, for in matters doubtful to a wise person I do not depart from its footsteps. Although this school seems to cast darkness upon all things, none is more faithful in examining truth, and, according to Cicero, who turned to it in old age, none is more suited to progress. Therefore, in what has been said incidentally concerning providence, fate, freedom of choice, and similar matters, you should know me rather as an Academic than as a rash asserter of doubtful things.

[Col. 0388B]

I have also at times used testimonies of Scripture to make a thought easier to explain, but in such a way that nothing is found contrary to faith or good morals—as though the same unchangeable truth had produced both modern and ancient opinions. For indeed:

> . . . . . . . . their faces are not all the same,  
> yet not different, as befits sisters.  
> (OVID, *Metamorphoses* II.13.)

[Col. 0388D]

But I reserve everything for your judgement, so that greater and more just glory for correction may be owed to you than for writing to me. The unevenness of the volumes must be attributed to the varied occupations by which I have been so distracted at court that I could scarcely sometimes write anything. Yet while you were besieging Toulouse, I undertook these matters and for a little while withdrew myself from courtly trifles, pondering that leisure without letters is death and the burial of a living man.

If anyone, together with Lanuvium, slanders unknown authors as invented, let him accuse the revived Africanus of Plato dreaming of Cicero, and philosophers celebrating Saturnalia; or let him indulge authors and our inventions if they serve public usefulness. Moreover, with all the devotion I can muster, I beg reader and hearer to deign to commend me in their prayers to the Father of mercies, and to strive to obtain pardon for my errors, which have multiplied beyond number. For I too hope to share in the portion of all who fear the Lord; and, in heart and voice, I pray in return for those who forgive, that almighty and merciful God may cleanse our deeds and thoughts, and that, lest we be swept away by the errors of vices, the Angel of Great Counsel may deign to illumine our minds by His Spirit.

## CHAPTER I. What most harms the fortunate.

Among all things which are accustomed to harm princely men, I judge nothing more destructive than this: the enticement of flattering Fortune withdraws from them the sight of truth, while the world heaps up its riches and delights, by which it in turn nourishes and inflames the itching of pampered senses. Thus the mind, caught by the manifold deceit of allurements, falls away from its inward good in a certain alienation from itself and wanders through outward falsehoods among diverse desires.

[Col. 0389B]

For prosperity, the stepmother of virtue, so applauds her fortunate darlings that she harms them; and with unhappy success so attends the fortunate upon their road that in the end she works destruction. From the beginning she offers sweet things to her guests; once they are drunk, she mixes in deadly poison. And what is worse: the more brightly she shines in her own appearance, the denser a darkness she pours into astonished eyes.

Therefore, as the darkness of errors grows strong, truth vanishes; once the root of virtues has been cut down, the crop of vices springs up; the light of reason is extinguished; and the whole human being is borne headlong in a miserable fall. Thus a rational creature becomes brutish; thus the image of the Creator is deformed into a beast through a certain likeness of conduct; thus a human being degenerates from the dignity of his condition, made like vanity because he swelled with the honour bestowed on him and through that swelling lost understanding.

[Col. 0389C]

For who is more unworthy than the person who scorns to have knowledge of himself? He squanders, to the detriment of life and in contempt of its author, the time given with a sparing hand as the measure for life’s use—and time alone cannot be restored—as though it were to be demanded back with usurious increase and penalty. What is more brutish than the person who, through a failure of reason and the impulse of desire, leaves his own affairs and attends to those of others, and is continually occupied not only with others’ business but with others’ leisure? What is more beastlike than the person who, abandoning his duty, rises in the middle of the night, so that, relying on the keen scent of dogs, the skill of hunters, the zeal of companions-in-arms, and the service of little slaves, he may, at the cost of time and reputation, possessions and labour, fight beasts from night until night?

## CHAPTER II. What is improper in occupations.

Foreign, strictly speaking, is whatever the reasoning of nature or of duty does not prescribe—although sometimes “foreign” is rightly said of what would more rightly always have belonged to no one. What belongs to nature belongs equally to all; what belongs to duty belongs properly to each individual. Thus one thing proceeds from duty, another from nature, though the force of nature is owed by duty. Indeed, it is a form of parricide to attack the rights of nature, and like sacrilege to annul the laws of one’s parent [Col. 0390A] and fail to render due honour to the mother of all.
