Yet what reason admits on honourable grounds is not simply foreign. If perhaps a restrained pleasure or an advantage is present, and no one is harmed—for this does not conflict with duty or nature—then it is otherwise; but if it attacks either, it is immediately and simply foreign, and altogether unlawful. To meddle with such a thing is always either error or crime.

## CHAPTER III. The distribution of duties according to the political constitution of the ancients.

The philosophers of the gentiles, who shaped by precepts and customs the justice called political, through which the commonwealth of humankind properly stands and flourishes, wished every person to be content with his own affairs and pursuits, [Col. 0390B] prescribing their own places and occupations respectively to townsmen and suburban residents, and likewise to farmers and country dwellers. The concern of individuals served the common advantage of all. Each received, according to merit, the fruit of nature, labour, and industry. No one appropriated what belonged to another, while in all remained an undivided affection of charity.

The foremost and central place of the city was assigned to the Areopagus, from which, by an appropriate arrangement suited to the requirement of each duty, the rights of offices might be distributed among the several professions, as it were little streams of health and life. Among these, moreover, the art of hunting is scarcely permitted to be taken up even by suburban residents, since hunters, together with farmers and the other inhabitants of the countryside, are kept farther away from cities and the society of the nobler classes. For it is altogether unjust that nobler [Col. 0390C] minds should be dishonoured by inferior pursuits, and that those whom lofty and weightier duties await should be occupied by pleasures or vanities. Hence, they judged that hunting, if practised lawfully, was an art or duty; but, if otherwise, it was frivolity or wrongdoing, and they punished by edict those who pursued it contrary to their duty.

## CHAPTER IV. On hunting, its originators and kinds, and its lawful and unlawful practice.

The Thebans, if we follow the authority of history, were the first to decree that it should be shared by all. And since that people—foul with parricides, detestable for incest, notorious for remarkable deceit, marked by perjuries—is suspect to all, it first assembled the precepts of this art, or rather this mischief, [Col. 0390D] and later transmitted them to a soft, unwarlike, fickle, and shameless nation—I mean the Phrygians.

The Athenians and Lacedaemonians, peoples of graver character, mocked them, veiling the deeds of history and the secrets of nature and conduct beneath various coverings of fiction, yet so as to derive usefulness from the warning of evils, or pleasure from the charm of poetry. Thus they relate that the Trojan hunter Ganymede was carried aloft by an eagle to serve cups, from which he passed to unlawful and unnatural embraces. Elegant indeed is the fiction: frivolity can be borne away by a bird, and pleasure, ignorant of sobriety, is not ashamed to prostitute itself to whatever lust.

A Theban leader, when he saw the nakedness of her whom he had always worshipped in the woods, drew back his inclination from error; but under human perception he was astonished to find himself transformed into a beast. Made like a stag, he tried by voice and countenance to drive away his household dogs; yet, through the vice of evil habit, at the loss of all that he possessed, he was exposed to their bites. Perhaps they set a goddess over hunters because by this softness or wickedness they wished to bring infamy upon their gods. Venus bewails Adonis, slain by a boar’s tusks, she who always has commerce with hunting or with the strong.

When Vergil jested about the welcome of lofty Carthage, he did not know how to bring together the desires of lovers unless, through the opportunity of hunting and the straying of their companions, he opened to them the recesses of the woods. Thus perhaps this pursuit, since it hates the light because of its consciousness of shame, prefers woodland hiding-places; whereas the joys of lawful love prefer the solemn torches of their own daylight.

Whom among illustrious men will you give me who clung passionately to this pleasure?

> Though victorious Hercules fixed the bronze-footed hind,  
> Or appeased the groves of Erymanthus.  
> (Vergil, *Aeneid* VI.803)

He provided not for his own pleasure but for the public good. Meleager may have slain the Calydonian boar; he did not soothe his mind with pleasure, but freed his country from an enemy. The founder of the Roman race may have struck down the bodies of stags; he sought not the consolation of empty pleasure but the means of survival for himself and his companions. The actions of individuals take their character from their outcome and purpose; for a deed is becoming if an honourable cause preceded it.

Yet what man ever assembled an army of men and dogs to fight beasts, not so much by his own strength as by that of others? Why not? Perhaps so great an apparatus will take as its prey some unfortunate little beast, a timid hare. But if the hunters’ labour shines forth in a more distinguished quarry—perhaps a stag or boar—there is unbearable applause: the hunters exult; the head of the quarry and certain ceremonial spoils are borne before the triumphers, as though the king of Cappadocia had been captured. Thus you may see horn-blowers and pipers proclaiming the glory of victory. For them a captured woman commands mournful silence; or perhaps, if the quarry is nobler, it is brought down rather by the treachery than the strength of those surrounding it. If a roe deer or hare falls, it is judged unworthy of triumphal glory.

Moreover, from the eighth degree of Capricorn until Gemini, the rejoicing of pipers and horn-blowers is silent, [Col. 0391D] unless a wolf or a more terrible enemy—perhaps a lion, tiger, or leopard—comes as prey. This, indeed, is a rare glory among our people, God be favourable, although the whole length of the year is occupied with the varied pursuits of hunters. The Albanians in Asia possess dogs stronger than lions; by the prowess of their dogs and the skill of their nation they ravage lions as though they were feeble little beasts. Among those dogs no wild animal is stronger or more spirited. Hercules, after defeating three-bodied Geryon, transported them from Italy into Asia, leaving them, as it were by inheritance, the strength by which they overthrow lions.

Besides, their butchery requires an art and itself becomes an art; it has its own craftsman:

> A hand-reader with a flying knife.  
> (Juvenal V.120)

Now remarkable with a drawn dagger, now with a blunted sword—if by chance you attend their ceremonies. Take care, however, not to offend Mars by any word you speak; for you will either be beaten or condemned as ignorant of every good thing if you do not know their fictions.

These are in our times the liberal pursuits of noblemen; these are the first elements of virtue; this is the road which by a short path leads the fortunate to the summit of blessedness, where our ancestors taught that one must climb only by the steps of laborious virtue. The Gauls mock the Aemilians and Ligurians, saying that they make wills, summon the neighbourhood, and call for the protection of arms if a tortoise threatens their fields and must be attacked. This arises from the fact that no chance occurrence in any contest ever finds them unprepared.

How, then, do our own escape the marks of ridicule, when with greater commotion, more anxious concern, and more lavish expense they think a formal war must be declared upon beasts? Yet they treat more gently those with whom the human race wages just enmities, compelled by those creatures’ malice. Wolf, fox, bear, and every more harmful wild beast—[Note: [Col. 0391D] Paris edition: “better known.”]—rests at the slaughter of others, and is unafraid in the presence of hunters to practise its accustomed malice.

Hannibal is said to have killed a Roman who, by his command, had struck an elephant in single combat, declaring him unworthy of life because he could have been compelled to fight beasts. More truly, however, Hannibal did not wish, from envy, that a captive should be made illustrious by the glory of an unheard-of triumph, nor that the beasts by whose strength he had struck terror into nations should be disgraced. How then is he worthy of life who knows nothing else in life except, from zeal for vanity, to rage against beasts?

Those, however, are pleased by that kind of hunting in which birds pursue birds—if indeed you count this sort of bird-catching as attached to hunting. They are afflicted by a milder madness, yet by no lesser frivolity. Hunting, whether on land or in the air, is the more solid and the more profitable in proportion as it is [so]. They cite from ancient histories Ulysses as the originator of their occupation: after Troy had been destroyed, he first brought armed birds into Greece, arousing them, to the sweet and pleasing astonishment of spectators, for the destruction of their kindred race.

These men defend themselves by a great judge:

> Who saw the manners and cities of many men.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica*)

His foresight could be overthrown by no snares; no enemy escaped his little nets unharmed; and his unarmed warfare advanced the glory of the Greeks further than an armed multitude of a thousand ships. Yet he himself praises Circe as the originator of this exercise. She is said to have altered human minds by songs and drinks, because by the art of words and the attractiveness of things she enticed human minds and transformed them, made conformable to her own will, to whatever purposes she desired.

Thus the poisons of suspect pleasure were offered to the Greeks; but when the prudent Ithacan had tasted them, he refused to drink, lest he be forced to live shamefully and mindlessly under a prostitute mistress. Yet because wisdom knows the use of all things, the prudent man provided, when his labours and wanderings were ended and chaste Penelope and the affection of Telemachus did not recognize him returning, how he might compensate Greece for the losses of his companions, who had borne the cost of so great an exile.

Wonderful was the loyalty of the dog. Alone in that great household, not even the passage of twenty years took from him the memory of his master, so that he did not greet him upon his return—unless, through the praise of that dog, further favour accrued to hunters’ dogs. Yet he commanded that his Telemachus should remain untouched by this new pursuit, saying that the consolations of this new pleasure had been brought only for those who, having lost their parents, felt the losses of the Trojan war. Hence I infer that an art is unprofitable when so great a man took pains to exclude it from his only son.

You too may infer with me as much from the fact that the inferior sex has the advantage in the hunting of birds. In this you might accuse nature, unless you knew that inferior things are always readier for plunder. For it is empty and exceedingly laborious, and never repays the losses of its expenses through the benefit of success.

Many, indeed, practise hunting so that under this pretext they may spend less: they avoid crowds by being less often at home and more often at another’s table, while they roam woods, glades, and lakes, clothed in cheaper garments and content with more frugal food, consoling their companions and servants—whom the starvation of fasting wastes, the torments of nakedness afflict, and immoderate labour exhaust—with the semblance of pleasure, or rather vanity.

Finally, Athens was first captured at the very time when its people decided that the edict prohibiting hunting should be rescinded and that the art of both kinds of hunting should publicly be admitted together with its practice. The Mantuan poet is said to have asked Marcellus, when he was devoting himself too vigorously to the devastation of birds, whether he would prefer a bird to be trained to catch birds or a fly to be trained for the extermination of flies. When Marcellus referred the question to his uncle Augustus, he chose, on Augustus’s advice, that there should be a fly that might drive flies from Naples [Note: [Col. 0393D] Paris edition: “Aeneapolis.”] and free the city from an incurable pestilence. The choice was fulfilled; hence it is clear [Col. 0393D] that the advantage of many is to be preferred to the private pleasure of any individual.

In the cave of the half-man Chiron—if the Greeks are to be believed in everything—Achilles was educated in the melodies of the lyre and cithara, and was then led away to the woods. Becoming accustomed to the slaughter of beasts, killings, and a foul way of life, he cast away reverence for nature and fear of death. What of the fact that Bacchus had the same man as tutor? Surely those who devote themselves to such pursuits or idleness are half-wild; having cast aside the better part of their humanity, they are made, in conduct, like monsters. For from frivolity they are drawn into wantonness, from wantonness into pleasure, and, once hardened, into disgraceful deeds and every sort of unlawful act.

Rest is sought after labours; the fuel of cheerfulness is more pleasing if hardships have preceded; those things which have been most emptied are replenished more eagerly. All hunters still smell of the training of the Centaurs. Rarely is any one of them modest or serious, rarely self-controlled, and, I think, never sober. For in Chiron’s house they had what they might learn these things from. One is indeed warned to beware of the Centaurs’ guest, from whom no one returns without a scar.

But if faith is withheld from histories which poets have discoloured with their fictions, then surely one must believe that history which, because it was written by God’s finger, has obtained irrefutable authority among all nations. Nimrod, therefore, is first set forth as a mighty hunter against the Lord. You do not doubt that he was reprobate, since the whole multitude of learned teachers condemns him. He is reported to have burst into such madness of pride that he did not fear to violate the rights of nature: those who shared his condition and race, whom nature had created freeborn, he consigned to slavery.

Thus the summit of tyranny, beginning with a hunter in contempt of the Creator, found no other originator than one who had learned contempt for the Lord in the slaughter of beasts and the wallowing in blood. For he began to be mighty upon the earth. Thus it is written: “Because he did not wait to receive power from the Lord.” The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and he spread out into the land of Shinar, where, although the whole earth was of one language and the same speech, the tower of Babel was raised to heaven, having bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar, without a rock in its foundation. Built upon that rock’s unique solidity, every building grows strong in the Lord.

But wicked rashness, cut off from unity, cut down the unity of languages and was the first to deserve confusion, because it preferred to glory in itself rather than in God. From this arose the proverb: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” Perhaps this was because his pride was so great that not even the recent punishment of the Flood could instruct him not to be proud in the Lord’s sight and arrogantly appropriate for himself the obedience owed by a human being to the Lord—although it is certain that the Flood preceded the confusion of languages.

Babylon, indeed, makes all flesh drunk from a golden cup and builds camps against the Jerusalem above; without doubt they shall perish, and whoever serves as a soldier in them is condemned by the perpetual curse of the saints.

Esau too practised hunting and deserved to be defrauded of his father’s blessing. In the woods he gathered hunger, so that, longing for lentils in an immoderate heat, he sold the prerogative of the firstborn for a paltry and contemptible price. He passed down to his descendants the yoke of hereditary servitude, so that they might submit their necks to the dominion of the younger brother who stayed at home. His hands bristled with thick hair; nor could one who was wild in character be smooth to the touch. He had left at home the refinement of costly clothing, because through continual hunting he had cast off the garment of virtue. He thirsted for his brother’s blood, and he was not afraid—having first been placated by gifts—to worship him whom he knew had been set above him by divine grace through his father’s blessing.

They boast that the originator of aerial hunting was a Maccabee, who, they believe, lived free from this pleasure because he was occupied with greater matters. For he waged wars excellently, restored freedom to his brothers, established laws, renewed rites, enriched the holy places, adorned with golden crowns the façade of the Temple—from which he believed victory came to him—and into none of his deeds crept

> Pleasure, born for itself, claiming its share.

At last, poured out in battle for the safety of his brothers, he left his kinsmen heirs to a lawful war.

From the first age, to which nature prescribed the law of reason, look at the patriarchs; after the giving of the Law, pass on to the leaders; proceed to the judges; advance to the kings; run through the succession of the prophets; investigate the duties and occupations of the faithful people: whom in the sequence of the Old Testament do you find to have practised hunting? Surely the Edomites, Ishmaelites, and nations that did not know the Lord.

“Where,” asks the prophet—or, if you prefer, the prophet’s secretary, provided it is in the Spirit—“are those who play with the birds of heaven?” (Baruch 3:17). As though by an unspoken subordinate clause he pronounces that those whose life is play have vanished with their birds, and he records that they have descended to the underworld. Ask your fathers and they will tell you; ask your elders and they will say that nowhere have they read of a holy hunter.

But if you flatter yourself with the name “hunters” from the prophetic promise by which the Lord declares that he will send hunters to hunt the erring from shady and lofty places, understand that the beast-like life is rebuked, not the vanity of hunters commended. Nor should Placidus—or Eustace, indeed an eminent martyr, whom you assert from pious though non-canonical writing to have been visited by the Lord while hunting—excessively charm you, unless perhaps you praise the fury of the Church’s persecutors because Paul was thereby called to apostleship and became among others an outstanding preacher of the Gospel.

But suppose there were illustrious men, perhaps Alexanders or Caesars, devoted to hunting: were they philosophers or any of the wise among the people? Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Soranus, or Archytas of Tarentum, who emptied not merely one city but the whole world of its wonders, drawing all admiration to himself by wisdom and virtue? To return to our own, who excel both in the truth of doctrine, the example of virtue, and the authority of faith: what Augustines, Jeromes, Lawrences, Vincents—what man at all from the whole assembly of the Fathers—was stirred by the madness of this vexation?

We are also instructed by the mournful examples of our own times to restrain ourselves from this kind of restlessness. For while our nobles hunted, divine indignation struck them with true and various miracles, and those who, while permitted, had lived beastially often found a beast-like end to their lives. Nor did the hand of the Lord spare kings themselves; against their wickedness it exacted fitting and glorious vengeance. Certainly their names and examples are not withheld through a lack of them, unless perhaps through the lack caused by abundance, but lest by reopening recent wounds we more severely ulcerate minds still wounded with immoderate grief. For very many of the examples are domestic.

Some have burst under the impulse of this vanity into such madness that, forgetting their condition, they became enemies of nature, despisers of divine judgement, and subjected the image of God to elaborate tortures in vengeance for beasts. They did not fear to destroy a human being for a little beast, though the Only-Begotten redeemed that human being by his blood. Things that are wild by nature and become the property of whoever takes them, human rashness dares, under the Lord’s gaze, to claim for itself; and it establishes the same legal right over all such creatures wherever they are, as though it had enclosed the whole world within the boundary of its own preserve.

And, more astonishingly, setting traps for birds, weaving snares, enticing them by calls or pipe, and taking them by any kind of ambush often becomes a crime by edict, punished either by confiscation of property or by loss of limbs and life. You had heard that the birds of heaven and fishes of the sea are common property; but these, wherever they fly, belong to the treasury when hunting demands them. Keep back your hand; abstain from them, lest you too fall as prey to hunters under the penalty for injured majesty.

Farmers are shut out from their fallow fields while beasts are free to roam. To enlarge the animals’ pasture, arable estates are taken from farmers, planted estates from cultivators, common pastures from cattle and sheep keepers, and beehives are excluded from flowering lands; scarcely even the bees themselves are permitted to use their natural freedom. Good God! Though all their power cannot drive away the gadfly and the other pests that harass not wild beasts but the luxuries of the mighty, even the gnat, armed to avenge humankind, rightly exerts the stings of its sharpness against beasts.

Thus, if you live here, year after year you are compelled either to ransom or abandon your crops. Choose which you prefer under the exceedingly equitable law of the Quirites: in either case loss of property or livelihood threatens. If any hunter passes through your lands, promptly and reverently lay before him whatever you have at home; and whatever is not at home but your neighbour possesses, buy for his use, lest under the licence of an edict he take it from you even against your will, and lest, for irreverence and contempt, you be compelled to answer a charge of injured majesty before the centuria or the court of a governor or proconsul, or perhaps before a council. For the patrimony of the treasury is enlarged whenever a household incurs expense from another’s goods.

Yet lest my pen seem to attack hunting and other courtly trifles from hatred rather than judgement, I readily and gladly agree that it should be counted among indifferent things—except that, by an immoderate assault of pleasure, it shakes the manly mind and overturns the foundation of reason. Still, it will not for that reason always be blameworthy, since wine, which intoxicates, throws the blame of overthrow back upon the drinker, and an old man often displays a childish mind not so much through age as through his own fault.

Hunting, therefore, can be useful and honourable, but according to place, time, measure, person, and cause. For the person gives grace to a pursuit when he adheres to his own duty and does not seize another’s. Nothing is more fitting for anyone than what is most suited to his own duty. The moral philosopher has admirably said, in describing the proprieties of particular persons: “That best befits each person which is most his own.” What, then, have you and I to do with the profession of hunter? It is most shameful for anyone, having neglected his own concerns, to be more zealously occupied with those of another.

What has a man who shines with the insignia of public authority to do with a private and perhaps rustic pursuit? Let the people follow their leader; let the teacher sow instruction; let the judge restrain offenders and reward diligent people with the favour of authority; let private persons occupy themselves with lesser things; let freeborn persons be assigned to more honourable tasks, servile condition to more base ones:

> For what is shameful for the good Seius and Titius  
> Will suit Crispinus.

Thus, since one body has many members, they do not all serve the same action, but each has its own functions. Therefore, if you do not yield your own duty to the hunter, why do you usurp his? Would you not think it unworthy if a hunter aspired to kingship or the priesthood? Yet it is more unworthy if you fall from either height into the butchery or filth of a hunter. For the inborn love of the good always seeks ascent; conversely, the fuel of vice by its own motion inclines toward descent.

A cause too can make an act honourable if it rests on necessity, is strong in usefulness, or shines in rectitude, since the whole substance of a work may take its character from the disposition of the mind. “For your disposition,” says the wise man, “gives your work its name.” Esau set out to hunt without blame at the command of his holy father, both to satisfy his father’s hunger and to obtain the promised blessing by the merit of devoted obedience. If hunting could not be practised without fault, so great a patriarch would never have sent his son to do it—the son whom he intended, through the grace of blessing, to establish as the head of nations.

But perhaps delay brought danger upon him, because through evil habit and immoderate love he lingered too long in a lawful work, though beyond what was lawful. Yet no guilt attaches to one who, pressed by the spur of necessity, is compelled by the practice of a pursuit not condemned to sustain life. Those who avoid the inertia of idleness, prepare their limbs for affairs to be undertaken by becoming accustomed to labour, and avoid the vicious heaviness of the body—while preserving in all things the dignity of their person—do not suffer the stings of just rebuke. For a work becomes a crime not from itself but from its cause.

Nor does any display of virtue shine forth when pleasure furnishes its origin; for pleasure is the stepmother of virtue. I do not mean the pleasure produced by peace, patience, kindness, longsuffering, and joy in the Holy Spirit; but that pleasure which is the companion of feasts, drinking bouts, banquets, musical performances and games, painstakingly elaborate adornments, fornications, and various impurities. It effeminates even graver minds and, in a kind of mockery of nature, makes men softer and more corrupt than women.

The time for hunting likewise lessens its guilt or commends the action. Time here means, as is found in many places, an opportunity for things to be done. Hunting therefore becomes untimely either through the observance of religion, [Col. 0398A] through the nature of things, or through a duty that ought neither to be omitted nor postponed to other occupations. But enough on these matters, because my purpose is not to give instruction in hunting but to trifle about courtly trifles.

One must also consider place: hunting should lawfully be practised on one’s own land, or on common or public land, provided no injury is inflicted upon fellow-participants and the place is not exempt from such disturbances by its public character or sacred reverence. For whoever bursts into another’s property in rash usurpation is caught in the snares of the law for punishment.

The praiseworthy measure is that it be undertaken prudently with moderation, and, if possible, usefully, so that you comply with the comedian’s command: “Nothing in excess.” For:

> The wise man will bear the name of madman, the just man that of unjust,  
> If he seek even virtue itself beyond what is enough.

Nothing, moreover, is uglier than to open one’s mouth to the laughter of onlookers by devoting oneself more eagerly to an art one does not know, not with the purpose of learning, as though you affected wit in a language you do not know.

There are persons who are permanently excluded not merely from this pursuit but from certain others, namely lighter and pleasure-loving pursuits: those established in holy orders and those who bear the highest public offices. What in others would have been a lighter fault often becomes a crime in these. Indeed, things that dissolve contracts already made are always graver than those that prevent contracts from being made. Further, by the force and truth of the canons, hunting not only closes advancement to its dependants but removes even the rank of the highest priesthood from one who has already obtained it.

Themistocles is reported to have said many fine things, among them: “Magistrates must be kept away from games and all lighter pursuits, lest the commonwealth seem to be playing and, abandoning its seriousness, proclaim its own failure. Yet if they happen to be occupied with greater matters—which is rare—they are permitted, during the years of youth, by reason of their age to take something away from gravity and be gentler with themselves, provided that as maturity advances they compensate for it by service to the public good.” So he spoke. “Would that our people listened, so that at least in more advanced age they might prefer the serious interests of the commonwealth to their trifles!”

For then the whole body of the commonwealth will flourish in the integrity of its strength; then it will be adorned with the appearance of the finest composition and assume the beauty of elegant loveliness, if:

> Let each thing fittingly keep the place allotted to it.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 92)

That is, if there is not confusion but distribution of duties. This is so if we follow nature, the best guide to life. But now craftsmen promise what belongs to physicians, and physicians handle craftsmen’s work (Horace, *Epistles* II.1.116); and the duty of governing borrows from hunters, humbler occupations, or even evil practices, while the rashness or ignorance of private persons dares to intrude into public offices.

## CHAPTER V. On dice-playing, its use and abuse.

But behold: as the clamour of hunters goes out, other trifles, though quieter, make their own noise. The proverb is well worn: “He who chases hares wastes words.” But if you look more carefully at others, they waste their very lives, wholly spent in foolishness, factions, or crimes. Does not the gambler seem foolish to you—the man who lives, or rather perishes, by the favour of dice and makes every cast the ruler of his fortune? Is an art suited to reason one in which a person is more unstudious the more studious he is?

Attalus of Asia, if gentile histories are believed, is said to have invented this wanton amusement of gaming, a pursuit somewhat diverted from the study of numbers. For whereas earlier men approved only that exercise which advanced the investigation of truth and the liberal disciplines, or trained one in the practice of right living, he, by an ingenious but unfruitful invention, did not temper the severity of the old exercise but softened it, while many still remained in their former seriousness.

For the abacus has not yet fallen from Greek hands, nor the art of calculation, nor the game in which complete victory consists in having, at the announced count, formed on the opponent’s squares a perfect and greatest harmony. But when, in the same game, an harmonic, arithmetic, or geometric mean of three terms arises, the victory is half-complete. Any kind of dice-game, though it may fall short of triumphal glory, attests either the player’s luck or his skill in the art.

It is pleasant and profitable to know the contests of numbers: which are exposed to capture, and by what arrangement some are safer in the camps, unaware of all dangers unless they are surrounded and captured by enemies. We read that Ptolemy, Alexander, Caesar, Cato, and even the Samian tempered their more serious tasks by the pleasure of this contest, so that even in play they might do something which would make them more fit for philosophical work.

Dice-playing, however, after the destruction of the kingdom of Asia, migrated to the Greeks among the spoils of a ruined city, and not under one form only. Hence came the die, the counter, the board, *urio* or the Dardanian battle, *tricolus*, *senio*, *monarchus*, little circles, *taliorchus*, and “fox”—arts which it is more useful to unlearn than to teach. For who would not blush if he owed the favour of his fortune, not to virtue, but to little dice? Who would not resent having the cunning of a dice-box preferred to his own prudence? Is not the practice of any art sufficiently condemned when the more learned a person is in it, the more wicked he becomes?

Every gambler is such a person. Dice-playing is the mother of lies and perjuries. From desire for another’s property, he squanders his own; having no reverence for his estate, once he has poured it away he gradually slips into thefts and robberies. Some, however, prefer the game in which Ulysses is said to have played, because it seems in some measure to sharpen the intellect’s edge by much reflection. But for that very reason it seems to me more ruinous: nothing is more unhappy than to labour most over the thing in which one makes the least progress. It is the useless importunity of one who asks, by which useless things are acquired; and diligence in seeking is empty when finding will bring no advantage. The movement and agitation of mind that is vainly scattered there might therefore be applied to finer and better matters.

The authority of him who, teaching the whole world in his son, declares that it must be shunned by all, wholly banishes dice-playing from the region of moral conduct. For by it people are armed for lawsuits, fall into enmities, and sink into wretched, though not pitiable, poverty. If you ask who authored this prohibition, recognize him who

> Believed himself born not for himself but for the whole world.

Yet in some form it is at times lawfully permitted, if, without fault, it lightens the burden of grave anxieties and, without loss of virtue, brings a pleasant interruption of joys. Every permission is strengthened by the support of moderation, while the use of solid virtue is disfigured by intemperance. The governing principle of every permission is prior consideration of place, time, measure, person, and cause; this either commends the face of all affairs by becoming grace or condemns it by the reproach of ugliness.

Thus in every case the greatest account must be taken of persons, since nature, condition, and fortune clothe every human being with their respective roles, from which each person must infer what suits him. Propriety comes from nowhere else. Chilon the Lacedaemonian, sent to Corinth to establish an alliance, found the leaders and elders of the people playing dice. He therefore returned with the business unfinished, saying that he would not stain the glory of the Spartans—whose virtue was conspicuous in the building of Byzantium—with the disgrace of being said to have made an alliance with gamblers.

Likewise, in reproach of childish frivolity, golden dice were given to King Demetrius by the king of the Parthians. By that gift a senile adolescence was judged deserving of dishonour, since it did not at all fear to commit trivial acts amid the majesty of royal rule.

But now the wisdom of noblemen is displayed if they know hunting, if they have been trained more damnably in dice-playing, if they have broken the strength of nature with the articulations of an effeminate voice, if, forgetful of virtue, they forget through musical modes and instruments why they were born. Yet this ruin flows from parents to children. For what will a son do except what he sees his father doing?

> If ruinous dice delight the old man, his heir too,  
> Still wearing the boy’s bulla, plays and moves the same pieces with a small dice-box.  
> (Juvenal XIV.4)

A tender age, indeed, should have been kept more carefully from lusts and from pleasure, the parent of vices; and greater care should have been taken that elders did nothing too freely in their presence, because, as the same satirist says:

> Domestic examples of vice corrupt us  
> More powerfully and more swiftly, especially when great…

“When they enter the minds of their authors.” (Id., ibid., 33.) Indeed, when Eleazar was being urged, in order to redeem his life, to transgress against the law of the Lord, he set before them the danger of his example, saying: “Who am I, Eleazar, ninety years old, that I should pass over to the life of foreigners and lead astray devout young men?” Thus degenerate heirs are born to their elders—men who dishonour the male sex by womanish softness.

## Chapter VI. On music, instruments, modes, and their benefit

[Col. 0401A]

Yet no one should disparage music as associated with the trifles of courtiers, although very many frivolous persons try to recommend themselves by means of it. For it is a liberal discipline; and whether it praises Pythagoras, Moses, or Tubal, the father of those who play the lyre, as the author of its origin, it has a noble birth. By the power of its virtue, the variety of its kinds, and the numbers that serve it, it embraces the entire discordant and dissonant multitude of all things which exist and are spoken of, reconciling them by the proportions proper to it—that is, by a certain equitable law amid inequality.

For by it heavenly things are harmonized, and earthly and human things governed. It trains and forms character; and, by a marvellous workmanship of nature, clothes the substance of articulated and inarticulate voice alike in melodic patterns and in the colours of rhythms and metres, adorning it with a certain elegance of cultivation. The holy Fathers have exalted it with many proclamations of praise, so that it needs no supporting testimony from us. Finally, through its power the violence of evil spirits is restrained, and music also diminishes their power over those subject to them. For when an evil spirit seized Saul, David played the lyre in his hand until the spirit ceased from afflicting the king.

But, lest the spirit which lies hidden in the letter be revealed too soon, it is altogether fitting that the soul should grow gentle through the affinity of its kind and unlearn every estrangement, since the harmony of its origin and the secrets of its better nature properly resound in it. The opinion—or judgment—of very many is that it is composed of musical consonances. For Plato, prince of all philosophy (if the Aristotelians will allow it), having imagined the soul as made from divisible and indivisible substance, and as formed by the same nature both alike and differently, believed that it could not subsist unless it united, by *hemioliai*, *epitritai*, and *epogdoi*, the discord of the limits which had flowed out on either side from unity through manifold division.

When account is taken of *limmata* and commas, even under the expression of a few terms it is shown that however great the distance between things that oppose one another, their harmony is closely joined through fellowship of kindred nature. Hence, by a certain hidden channel of nature and secret passages, the soul runs through all things in the vigour of its vitality; and, conformed to every nature and substance, it modulates in each the efficacy of reason, sensation, and life, according to the decree of divine dispensation.

[Col. 0401D]

Thus it dispenses nourishment to all things and flourishes in each by its own purity, unless it is weighed down by the heaviness of bodily mass or the tranquillity of the spirit is shaken by the storms of external things. When that assault comes, what can be more salutary than for the soul, so to speak, to be recalled to itself from the crushing pressure of disturbances by the voices proper to its own nature?

Finally, what can be more akin to our spirit than voice? Though it is formed here, it fills the hearing of many people round about by a passage as easy as it is invisible and ineffable; by its force it penetrates the whole density of bodies; and, as if by a certain touch, moves the mind, now casting it down, now raising it up, according to its will. Certainly, even if voice is not spirit in any respect, it is most certainly a kind of vehicle of spirit. At one time it bears a human spirit, at another a divine one, and at another a Pythian one.

When it has been more elegantly coloured by its modes, it captures even sterner minds by its own charm, drives away sadness through the grace of an induced cheerfulness, and powerfully wipes away whatever dust, whirlwind, or mist had clung to the very thoughts. Therefore, for the formation of character and for carrying souls, by the exultation of virtue, into the worship of the Lord, the holy Fathers judged that not only human harmony but also instrumental modes should be devoted to the Lord, when they enlarged the splendour of the Temple.

[Col. 0402A]

And if the authority of the Church militant seems slight to you, that triumphant Church will not be silent in proclaiming music’s praises: the son of thunder saw its elders and showed them to you, and their voices were like the voices of lyre-players playing their lyres. But if you have not yet heard them, hear the rejoicing king, who wishes you to share his kingdom and his rejoicing. For he says: “Take a psalm; give the tambourine, the pleasant psaltery with the lyre” (Psalm 80).

“To what end?” you ask. “That you may praise the Lord with tambourine and dance, with strings and organ” (Psalm 150). This is either music’s sole use or its chief use. The Phrygian mode, however, and all the other enticements of corruption, have no place in sound instruction; rather, they reveal the wickedness of the person who misuses them.

Thus this praiseworthy discipline grieves and groans that it is disfigured by another’s vice, and that a harlot’s face has been put upon that which was accustomed to kindle even manly minds to virtue. Among serious men, erotic songs of herdsmen once counted as a crime; now it is considered praiseworthy if you see more serious men making erotic songs resound—songs which they themselves more elegantly call foolish ditties. Even religious worship itself is defiled, when before the sight of the Lord, in the innermost sanctuary itself, men endeavour, through the luxurious indulgence of a wanton voice and a certain display of themselves, to soften feeble souls by womanish modes, divisions of notes, and phrases.

[Col. 0402C]

When you hear the excessively soft modulations of leaders and respondents, singers and antiphonal singers, those singing between verses and those singing against them, you would think them the harmonies of Sirens, not of men; and you will marvel at the facility of their voices, whose modes neither the nightingale nor the parrot, nor anything more sonorous, can equal. So great is their ease in ascending and descending; so great the division or doubling of notes, the repetition of phrases, and the binding together of each individual one; thus are high and very high tones blended with low and moderately low tones, that the authority of the ears’ judgment is almost taken away, and the mind, softened by the charm of such sweetness, is unable to assess the merits of the singers.

When these things exceed measure, they can arouse itching of the loins more readily than devotion of mind. But when limited by the rule of moderation, they free the mind from cares, banish temporal anxiety, and, by a certain share in gladness and repose and by friendly exultation in God, carry human minds into fellowship with the angels.

[Col. 0403A]

But whence do you possess this rule of moderation? “My lips,” he says, “shall rejoice when I sing to you.” If therefore your mouth gives musical expression to the Lord’s praise from the abundance of your heart; if you sing with the spirit and with the mind; if, finally, you sing wisely, then even without understanding the articulated voice, you possess the most correct rule of modesty. You delight the ears of the Most High not so much by the jubilation of voice as of mind, and prudently turn away his indignation.

But he who expresses an inclination toward pleasure or vanity, who prostitutes the grace of voice to his desires, who makes music the dependent client of seductions, does not know the song of the Lord, though he makes merry with Babylonian modes in a foreign land. Such modes, I know not by what means, please the more, unless it is because

> We always strive for what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> (OVID, *Amores* III.iv.17.)

And stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant. Indeed, by decree of philosophers, the Phrygian mode has long since been banished from the court of Greece, as have the other modes by which one descends into wantonness and corruption.

Do you not recall how the mothers and daughters-in-law of the Ciconians poured out all their indignation upon Orpheus, who had made men effeminate by his modes, even to the envy of the Fates? Yet he had bent the shades below, softened the hardness of Dis, and won his Eurydice by the charm of his voice, though under an unhappy condition. From this point, the trade of such men usually does not await a happy ending, perhaps because

[Col. 0403C]

> Base gain has no good outcome.  
> (OVID.)

Whatever softens minds and overthrows character is adopted on every side by our age, although it itself already abounds in vices beyond measure. If you see any of those who are most devoted to these things who is serious, restrained, and chaste, remember to number him among the brave men of our time. For such a bird is rare.

Accordingly, a certain venerable man, father of about seven hundred nuns, prescribed this law for his monasteries: that all their songs should be stripped of the modes of all melodic performance and that they should be content with a delivery that signifies only the psalms and praises. Softness akin to pleasure was, indeed, suspect to that holy man, since pleasure is the parent of lust.

What of the fact that this same thing sharpens the evil of daily banquets, as though poisons could not harm unless they were made poisonous? Is it not madness to add straw to fire, oil to a furnace, or poison to a serpent? Though the vices of things may be covered by a veil of words, where the substance is the same there is certainly no difference. What the Greeks call *coepulatio* or *compotatio*—feasting or drinking together—we call banquets by a more respectable name. Surely an assembly of banqueters sounds more venerable than an assembly of those feasting or drinking together.

[Col. 0403D]

Do not banquets rage sufficiently of themselves unless they are excited by songs? Does not the Lord condemn this very thing when he says: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness, and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine. Lyre and harp, tambourine and flute, and wine are at your banquets; but you do not regard the work of the Lord or consider the works of his hands” (Isaiah 5)?

Moreover, the king of Babylon saw the hand writing upon the wall only at a banquet: “Mane, thekel, phares”—“numbered, weighed, divided” (Daniel 5), by which the kingdom is declared numbered, weighed, and divided. For by divine judgment he is judged unworthy of rule who exposes the vessels of the Lord—that is, human bodies—to the pleasures of vain delight and opens the bridegroom’s chamber to the impurities of an evil spirit.

> Argus had a head encircled by a hundred lights.  
> (OVID, *Metamorphoses* I.626.)

All of these were not so much put to sleep as extinguished by the pleasure of a single pipe. Who then are you, that you trust yourself to be more watchful?

## Chapter VII. On the difference between Augustus and Nero

When Augustus was playing the tambourine at dinner, a certain soldier insultingly said: “Do you see how that catamite governs the world with his finger?” Stung by the bitterness of this remark, Augustus restrained mouth, hands, and mind from such frivolity for the rest of his life; and he always remained grateful to the one who reproached him.

But Nero was altogether different: the foulest not merely of emperors but of men. He is said to have been so captivated by the sweetness of his voice that he abstained not only from apples and harmful foods, but, to preserve it, frequently purged himself by enema and vomiting, and, on physicians’ orders, repeatedly and for long periods bore a leaden plate upon his belly while lying on his back.

[Col. 0404C]

He so delighted in singing that, even when an earthquake shook the theatre, he would not leave once he had begun until he finished what he had started. Nor was anyone allowed to leave while he sang. Hence many, weary of listening, had themselves carried out as though dead. He did not address even soldiers unless another person pronounced the words for him; nor did he do anything, seriously or in jest, unless a vocal trainer stood by to urge him to spare his vocal organs.

He was also so passionately devoted to instruments that he begrudged others skill in them, and publicly delighted to be called the foremost lyre-player. Hence the saying:

> Born noble under a lyre-playing prince—  
> what will this be to us except a game?

Amid so vast a burden of empire, he hated every form of seriousness. Persecuting philosophy as an enemy of imperial majesty and fearing superior talents, he subjected himself to the counsels of actors, whose shameful profession he himself did not blush to practise.

Hence:

> What nobles do not give, an actor will give.

Although he was most avaricious of all men—so much so that he entrusted no office to anyone without pursuing him with the words, “You know what I need,” or adding, “He who presides over all needs all”—nevertheless he did not hesitate to lavish infinite sums upon actors and mimes. According as each pleased him, he decked them out with titles of the highest rank, calling some patricians and others senators, and adorning them with the designations of *illustres* and *spectabiles*.

## Chapter VIII. On actors, mimes, and conjurers

[Col. 0405A]

Even now some partly imitate him, though no one deserves to be implicated in his foulness, since many prostitute their favour to actors and mimes and, in displaying their wickedness, incur expenses of a blind and contemptible magnificence—expenses more pitiable than admirable. That age, however, if I may for the moment put it so, had more respectable actors—if anything which every free person judges unworthy can in any fashion be respectable.

Yet I do not assert that an actor behaves shamefully in his art, although it is unquestionably shameful to be an actor. There were actors who, by bodily gesture, verbal art, and modulation of voice, presented before the public gaze histories either done or invented. You find such performers in Plautus and Menander, and the art of our Terence is made known through them. But when comic and tragic drama departed and frivolity occupied everything, their dependents—that is, comedians and tragedians—were driven out. You will generally find them, however, only in servile status.

What their function was is made clear by the teaching of poetry:

> Poets wish either to benefit or delight,  
> or to say things at once pleasant and suited to life.  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, 33.)

[Col. 0405C]

But our age, having fallen into tales and every kind of emptiness, prostitutes not only ears and heart to vanity, but soothes its indolence by the pleasure of eyes and ears, rises to luxury, and seeks everywhere stimulants for vice. Does not the lazy man cultivate idleness and invite sleep by the sweetness of instruments, the melodies of voices, the merriment of singers, the charm of storytellers—or, what is more shameful, by drunkenness or surfeit?

Flaccus taught a more elegant art:

> Anointed three times, they swim across the Tiber—  
> men who have need of deep sleep.  
> (HORACE.)

The preacher also says: “Sleep is sweet to the labourer, whether he eats little or much.” For exercise produces and nourishes the grace of rest, which is destroyed by continued idleness and by a certain stagnant decay of its own inertia. Every idle person is indeed in desires, since idleness is an enemy to the soul and banishes every pursuit of virtue from its dwelling-place.

The moralist cries:

> Do you see how idleness corrupts the inactive body,  
> and how waters become foul unless they are stirred?

“What?” you ask. Listen. You will learn if you trust the same writer:

[Col. 0405D]

> Why Aegisthus became an adulterer is asked.  
> The reason is ready: he was idle.  
> (OVID, *Remedies for Love*, 161.)

Therefore the counsel of a most learned man is that the enemy should always find you occupied, so that against his varied temptations you may oppose the shields of your occupations as successfully as wisely.

> The disgraceful Siren,  
> idleness, must be avoided, says the moralist.  
> (OVID.)

Yet actors prolong it among us. For when minds are emptied of occupation, weariness creeps in; and they could not endure themselves unless they were soothed by the consolation of some pleasure. Thus spectacles and endless apprenticeships in vanity have been admitted, so that those wholly unable to be idle may be occupied more perniciously. It would have been better to be idle than shamefully occupied.

Hence come mimes, *salii* or Salian dancers, buffoons, Aemilians, gladiators, wrestlers, *gignadii*, conjurers, and many sorcerers; and the entire stage of jongleurs comes forward. Their error has prevailed so far that even those who thrust upon the sight of all the obscenity of their private parts—an obscenity at which even a Cynic would blush to look—are not excluded from eminent households.

[Col. 0406B]

And, more astonishing still, they are not even expelled when, making a tumult, they repeatedly foul the air below with a loud noise and shamefully reveal what is enclosed more shamefully still. Does a man seem wise to you who opens his eyes or ears to such things?

Yet who would not gladly watch and laugh when the art of a conjurer, drenched in his own urine, is destroyed, and the eyes whose sight his wickedness had obscured recover their power of seeing? It is indeed pleasant, and not inconsistent with propriety, for a good man sometimes to be refreshed by restrained cheerfulness; but it is disgraceful for seriousness frequently to be dissolved by such wantonness.

A man’s eyes should also be kept away from such spectacles, especially the obscene ones, lest their incontinence confess the immodesty of his mind as well. Pericles, reproving his colleague Sophocles while he was praetor, rightly said: “It is fitting for Sophocles the praetor to have not only restrained hands, but restrained eyes.”

“Turn away,” says the man to whom much was permitted concerning royal majesty, “my eyes, lest they behold vanity”; knowing, indeed, to be true what another laments: “My eye has plundered my soul.” Nevertheless, the mind of a wise man discerns what is useful or fitting in individual cases, and does not reject fables, narratives, or any spectacles whatever, provided they offer an instrument of virtue or honourable usefulness.

[Col. 0406C]

You do not doubt that, by the authority of the Fathers, the grace of sacred communion is barred to actors and mimes while they persist in wickedness. From this you infer what hangs over their supporters, if you remember that perpetrators and those who consent are punished with an equal penalty. “Those who give to actors,” he says, “why do they give?” They foster in them precisely that in which they are most wicked. Surely, can one who fosters wickedness be good? But though the wickedness of all these people is hateful, the wickedness of those who do less harm is more tolerable.

## Chapter IX. Why conjuring is called *praestigium*, and who was its inventor

The holy Fathers long ago ordered that those who practise more harmful conjuring, magical arts, and the various branches of condemned astrology should be removed from the court, since they knew that all these arts—or rather, evil practices—flow from a deadly familiarity between demons and men. They often utter truth solely in order to deceive; and the Lord, protecting the faithful soul from them, says: “If they tell you something and it comes to pass, do not believe them” [Deuteronomy 13:1–3].

Mercury is said to have invented *praestigium* (“illusion”), so called because it dazzles the sharpness of the eyes. He was most skilled among magicians, so that he made whatever things he wished invisible or, as it seemed, changed them into other forms. For in every case mathematics marks the source of its teaching. But divine mathematics, when you lengthen the penultimate syllable, refers fictions to magic; and magic has very many and diverse kinds.

## Chapter X. Who magicians are, and why they are so called

Magicians are so called because of the greatness of their evil deeds. With the Lord’s permission, they shake the elements, remove things’ appearances, often foretell future events, disturb human minds, send dreams, and kill men solely by the force of an incantation—a fact not unknown even to our Lucan. For he says:

[Col. 0407B]

> No mind polluted by the foulness of a draught of poison  
> perishes when bewitched.

And lest their authority seem slight to you, you know that Jannes and Mambres were Pharaoh’s magicians. Egypt, indeed, is the mother of superstitions and evil practices of this kind. You know, I say, that they not only resisted Moses but contended with him in signs and wonders, although later they were compelled, even against their will, to confess the finger of God in Moses’ signs.

## Chapter XI. On the kinds of magic

Varro, the most inquisitive of philosophers, derived four kinds of divination from the elements: namely pyromancy, aeromancy, hydromancy, and geomancy. You will see many kinds springing from these heads, whether divination is carried out by art or frenzy. By way of example, I shall set down at least a few of their names.

## Chapter XII. Who enchanters, diviners, haruspices, physicians, image-workers, imagers, interpreters, palm-readers, mirror-diviners, astrologers, diviners by leaps, lot-casters, and augurs are

Enchanters are those who practise an art through words. *Arioli* are those who offer prayers at impious altars or accursed sacrifices; upon their necks lies the hand of the Lord, as the prophet says: “You shall not suffer *arioli* and magicians to live” (Exodus 22).

Haruspices are observers of hours, prescribing what ought expediently to be done at what hour. The Apostle condemned their error when he said: “I fear lest I have laboured among you in vain; for you observe days and years, months and seasons” (Galatians 4), whereas success in an undertaking ought to be expected not from time but from the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0407D]

Haruspicy also consists in inspection of entrails, an art said to have been invented by a certain Tages. Hence Lucan (*Civil War*, book I):

> Put no faith in entrails; their inventor, Tages,  
> invented these things.

By “entrails” are meant all things covered by the outer surface of skin. From this it is clear that those are haruspices who prophesy from animal bones or blood, whether they foretell future things or pronounce upon present or past things. For prophecy is the utterance of hidden matters with knowledge of truth; and it is evident that prophecy concerns not only future things, but present and past things as well.

If blood is used, however, this approaches necromancy, so called because it is wholly occupied with inquiry of the dead. Its apparent function is to raise the dead in order to interpret truth. But this is the deception of mocking demons and the delusion of human unbelief.

Pythians are those filled by a Pythian spirit. This spirit is more frequently active in virgins, in order to deceive more effectively—as though integrity of mind or body pleased the most unclean spirit.

[Col. 0408A]

*Vultivoli* are those who, to alter human affections, fashion in a soft material—perhaps wax or clay—the likenesses of those whom they seek to corrupt. Virgil mentions this delusion in the *Pharmaceutria* (*Eclogues* VIII.80):

> As this clay hardens and this wax melts  
> in one and the same fire, so may Daphnis in our love.

Naso also says in the *Heroides*:

> She curses those who are absent, fashions waxen images,  
> and drives fine needles into the wretched liver.

Yet the malice of these people, even when it causes great harm, is undone by an easy device: namely, if those under suspicion, when confronted by someone, deny their crime; or, if they confess, are compelled to revoke their evil work.

*Imaginarii* are those who commit the images they make, as it were, into the possession of presiding spirits, so as to be instructed by them concerning doubtful matters. Sacred Scripture convicts them of being idolaters and condemns them by the judgment of divine majesty.

[Col. 0408C]

Interpreters are those who claim, by a certain art, the interpretation of dreams. Palm-readers are those who foretell hidden matters from inspection of hands. Mirror-diviners are so called because, divining in polished and shining objects—such as bright swords, basins, cups, and various kinds of mirrors—they satisfy inquisitive consultations. Joseph is described as having practised, or rather feigned, this art when he accused his brothers of stealing the cup in which he was accustomed to divine.

Astrologers, though the designation generally includes all such practitioners, are those who infer future events from the position of the stars, the arrangement of the firmament, and the motion of the planets, as in this passage:

> Either the Fate that clings to truth holds our lives suspended  
> in an equal balance, or the hour that bore us was faithful.  
> The harmony made between two divides us under Gemini;  
> together we break heavy Saturn by our Jupiter.  
> I know not what star it is, but certainly some star governs you for me.  
> (PERSIUS, V.48.)

This is as though the courses and conjunctions of stars with one another clearly supplied some origin of necessity to things that arise from freedom of choice. Those called genethliacs, who attend to *geneses*, that is, natal hours, imitate the same error. Hence the satirist:

> Your birth-hour is known to astrologers.  
> (JUVENAL, XIV.248.)

They are also called horoscopes. Hence again:

[Col. 0409A]

> … under Gemini, Varo,  
> you bring forth by your horoscope.  
> (PERSIUS, VI.18.)

This science flourished, and perhaps it was permitted to practise it to some extent, until a star from heaven announced that God had been born and, by a new and unheard-of guidance, brought the Magi—who were not rejected, but the first fruits of faith—to worship him. From that time onward it was wholly forbidden.

Diviners by leaps are those who assert that something prosperous or adverse will occur from a leap of the limbs or an unexpected bodily movement. Lot-casters are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion and by a superstitious observance, promise the outcomes of events. Of this kind are the lots of apostles and prophets and of those dividing lots, the inspection of the tablet called Pythagorean, and the observation of any chance occurrence as a sign concerning the matter in question.

Augury, which consists in observing birds, is said to have been invented by the Phrygians; it is conveyed by voice or flight. According to their tradition, “flight” applies both to wings and feet; for *vola* is the inner part of the palm or sole. Hence in the sixth book of Maro, doves are described as “flying” when they are walking. For it pertains to a man’s good fortune if walking doves, provided that they are travelling in search of food, go before him.

## Chapter XIII. On all the various kinds

[Col. 0409B]

A Roman consul, sent on campaign, obtained no favourable omen by augury. He therefore ordered that pigeons weakened by hunger be carried ahead and wheat grains scattered in the road by which he was to go, so that he might at least relieve the harshness of the omen by theirs. Since they abstained too carefully from food, he ordered them thrown into the river so that they might at least drink. Drowned in the river, they taught that the consul would be drowned with his army. And this was indeed the outcome.

Bees brought honey to the lips of Plato when he was an infant, foretelling the singular sweetness of his eloquence. Hiero, later the highest magistrate of Sicily, earned his position by merit. His father, a most noble man, had exposed him because, born of a slave-woman, he seemed a disgrace to the family and, as it were, a shameful stain on illustrious blood. But bees, gathering honey around the little child, who lacked human aid, nourished him for many days. Thus, when haruspices declared that a kingdom was foreshadowed, he was acknowledged by his father, taken back, and carefully educated.

[Col. 0409D]

Ants heaped grains of wheat into the cradle of the infant Midas, signifying that he would be very rich. Hence poets invented that things became golden at his touch. When the apex fell from the head of the priest Sulpicius, it took away his priesthood; the cry of a shrew, heard by Marcus Fabius, took away his prefecture.

If you trust Iberian trifles in every respect, and at the beginning of your work find that a garment has been gnawed by shrews, refrain from what you have begun. If, as you go out, you tread upon the threshold or stumble on the road, hold back your foot. If, while preparing to act, you suffer some loss, defer what you have begun, lest you either fail entirely in your purpose or accomplish it uselessly. Wait until, with a better omen, you seize a favourable hour for your business. For all things signify something.

When you set out, birds which they call ominous will foretell hidden future events for you. Perhaps you ask which these are. They are, of course, birds which poets assert were transformed from human nature into bird-form. Listen carefully to what the crow says, and by no means disregard its position, whether perched or flying. It matters greatly whether it is on the right or left, in what position it looks toward the elbow of the traveller, whether it is talkative, noisy, or wholly silent, whether it goes before or follows, waits for the traveller’s approach, or flees; and pay careful attention to where it departs.

For Virgil says (*Eclogues* IX.14):

[Col. 0410A]

> Had not a crow on the left, from a hollow oak, warned me  
> when I was about to encounter these new quarrels,  
> neither your Moeris here nor Menalcas himself would still be alive.

Yet in this he seems to have offended against the art, because the crow which he declares the preserver of life is ignorant of the omens of great events—unless perhaps in it an extraordinary portent occurs contrary to nature, such as the following: when the hated emperor’s death, a good and desired event, was imminent, a crow from the Tarpeian Rock uttered in Greek through the city: “It will be well.” An augur, interpreting this, explained it thus:

> The crow that lately perched upon Tarpeia’s summit  
> could not say “It is well”; it said, “It will be.”

But you will pardon a most learned man for portraying rustic simplicity, or because the life of poor people seems a slight matter to the rich, who maintain that the human race was instituted to serve a few.

[Col. 0410B]

The raven, too, which you will observe with no less care, foretells events of greater importance and everywhere takes precedence over the crow. The swan, moreover, is in augury a bird most welcome to sailors, since as one native to waters it has, by a certain domestic familiarity, foreknowledge of their secrets.

Do you not know that in Maro

> … twelve joyful swans in the air

announced, by Venus’s prophecy, the return of Aeneas’s fleet? Their joy promises the grace of happy outcomes not only to sailors but to all travellers, unless it is overcome by the arrival of a stronger bird.

For the eagle is like the king of birds—unless one excepts the *alarion*, which is perhaps the most powerful kind of eagle by the royal majesty it possesses over all birds; if the *alarion* speaks in opposition, it annuls the omen. In Statius, the Greek army could have been strengthened by the omen of birds. But, behold, a stronger flock arriving through the empty air, interpreted by Amphiaraus, disclosed the destruction of the Greeks as well.

Although an eagle is surpassed by the strength of certain birds, in foretelling truth none is more powerful. It flies higher than all birds and is never excluded from Jupiter’s secret counsel. Since it is said to possess eyesight so sharp that from the highest sky it sees little fish at the bottom of the sea and fixes its gaze upon the sun itself—which no other living creature may do—it derives, through subtlety of perception and through Jupiter’s favour, knowledge of the truth of things and their mysteries. Who would call false an interpreter known to share in Jupiter’s counsels?

[Col. 0411A]

When the Locrians fought against the Crotoniates, an eagle flying overhead while the battle was fought is said to have brought victory, when men few in number destroyed an innumerable host. This, however, is written to have been confirmed by a stronger sign: two young men, taller in stature and more handsome in form, dressed in white, went before the Locrians on either side—Castor and Pollux, according to the common opinion. Omens of this kind are stronger when doubled.

When Hiero, mentioned above, entered upon his first wars, an eagle unexpectedly settled on the shield of the advancing man, signifying that he would be a king ready of hand. On the day Alexander was born, two eagles of auspicious flight sat throughout the day above the roof of his father’s house, bearing an omen of his double empire over Europe and Asia.

Vultures signify difficulty, harshness, and rapacity, as you find in the account of the city’s foundation. The phoenix promises an outcome of singular felicity, as when New Rome, after a phoenix had been seen, was founded under better auspices. A painted bird gave its name to the city of Poitiers, foreshadowing by colour and voice the fickleness of its people. The heron is an omen of arduous undertakings. Since the stork is a bird of concord, it finds concord or makes concord.

[Col. 0411B]

The crane always brings what is expedient; hence the old verb *gruere*, from which comes *congruere*, “to agree,” which is beneficial; and, by contrast, *ingruere*, “to attack,” which is harmful. Hence:

> … twice rain falls upon the vines.  
> (VIRGIL.)

Yet do not hold lesser birds in contempt. The talkative magpie, as it does in many matters, makes you more cautious concerning the reception of guests. If the bird commonly called *albanellus*, flying past the road, is carried from the left to the right, do not doubt the cheerfulness of the lodging you will receive; if the opposite occurs, you will expect the opposite result.

Domestic birds also are not without this art, since the crowing of a cock advances the hope, journey, or work of one who is beginning. When Tiberius was to be born, Livia, seeking an omen, warmed an egg taken from a hen, now in her own hands and now in those of her maidservants, until a cock with a remarkable comb hatched from it; and augurs therefore declared that the boy to be born would reign.

The owl, screech-owl, and night-owl always bring unfavourable omens. Yet the night-owl, because it is not blinded by the darkness of night, signifies the vigilance of a diligent person—as in the portent in which a night-owl is said to have settled on the spear of Hiero when he first advanced to war, signifying that he would be most diligent.

[Col. 0411D]

Dido perceived an ill-omened owl while she was joined with Aeneas. If a hawk, or anything of that kind, performs its accustomed robbery before the eyes of a departing traveller, rapacity will threaten during the journey. Alluding to this in jest, Naso says:

> We hate the hawk because it always lives in arms.

The *regulus* itself, also called *bitriscus*, does not disdain sometimes to foretell true things. Even tiny birds, by their arrival or departure, signify that a household will now diminish or now increase. The calmer the flight of any bird, the more praiseworthy it is. Hence Melampus, renowned as an augur, complains, inferring the destruction of the Greeks from their flight:

[Col. 0412A]

> … Do you see how no bird  
> makes a tranquil course?

You will also seek the outcome of your journeys from beasts. You will fear meeting a hare—if only it escapes. It is undoubtedly far more convenient on the table than on the road. You will rejoice when a wolf meets you: for it is a messenger of good, although it is accustomed to harm, by sight alone, the person whom it first sees, depriving him of speech. As in the passage:

Even Moeris’s voice itself now fails him: the wolves saw Moeris first. (VIRGIL, *Eclogues* IX.53.)

Hiero of Sicily, devoted to literary study, was practising writing among boys of his own age when a wolf, suddenly seen amid the crowd of children, snatched away his writing-tablet—an unprecedented kind of portent, confirming the man’s future success. [Col. 0412B] Why say more? No one will deny the wolf’s efficacy who does not doubt that the Roman race was nourished on a she-wolf’s milk. Hence, for the most part, whatever is sweeter in them still retains a lupine flavour; and they kept faith with one another in the earliest days, as they had learned it from their wolf-mother; and by a certain same law of nature this flowed down to their descendants.

You will gladly meet sheep on your way, provided you avoid a goat; alluding to this, the poet says:

> Beware of encountering a goat: he strikes with his horn.  
> (ID., ibid., 29.)

You will meet oxen threshing, though more willingly oxen ploughing. Nor should it displease you if they have blocked the road, because the delay in travel will be compensated by the benefit of hospitality. The mule is unlucky, the ass useless—though they are most useful for carrying burdens. A horse is sometimes favourable; but [Col. 0412C] nothing about it is more useful than its service for human needs. Yet it signifies quarrels and battle. Sometimes, however, this is softened by its colour and appearance. Thus in Virgil, when white horses are seen as Italy comes into view, aged Anchises cries:

> War, ah war, you bring, land of our welcome!  
> (ID., *Aeneid* III.539.)

A stag, a roe-deer, a wild boar, a wild ass, and other creatures of this sort, I would rather have you set before someone dining than put in a traveller’s path. When Aeneas struck down stags equal in number to his ships, he courageously turned a portent that seemed adverse to the good fortune of himself and his companions.

The swift-footed dog is very convenient; if the Hebrew tradition is true, even the angel who accompanied Tobias [Col. 0412D] did not disdain its company. Moreover, Cyrus, exposed in the woods by the crime of his grandfather in order that he might perish, attained the Persian kingdom through the teats of a little bitch. The locust, although it has little power, nevertheless hinders travellers’ wishes; perhaps it is so called because it makes those walking stand still in one place. Conversely, the cicada advances the traveller’s step and makes the departure of initiates pleasant. The spider, when it draws down its thread from above, seems to bring hope of money to come. A toad encountered on the road announces future success, though to me it is unpleasant even in appearance alone.

Yet no omen is more powerful or effective than this; among mortal things you will never find anything that expresses truth more plainly. Further, if you diligently practise the art, you will observe with the whole attention of your mind a person’s condition, natural endowments, position, bearing, bodily movement, and the character of speech. They say that meeting a priest or another religious person is unlucky. I too think it ruinous to oppose not only priests but wise men. It is also better to meet a race of slaves than those endowed with supreme power. Believe also that a woman who walks with her head uncovered is unlucky—unless, as Pliny records, she is a public woman, or a prostitute exposed to the lust of many. Nor is it expedient to meet a woman who, having removed her veil, is not ashamed to disfigure her head. From the things first heard at the beginning of any undertaking, you will foreknow what is to follow.

> Hence God, leaning upon the staff which he held in his right hand,  
> said: “Omens are usually present at beginnings.”  
>
> We weigh heard voices with a fearful ear.  
>
> [Col. 0413B] And the augur consults the first bird seen.  
> (OVID, *Fasti* I.177.)

For these are indeed forewarnings of future events. Petilius, a Roman consul, was besieging a fortress in Sicily named *Letum* (“Death”). When his soldiers were arming for battle, he said, “Today I shall take Death.” And so it happened by chance: he himself was killed that same day. Another consul, when the senate appointed him to overthrow the king of Persia, asked why his daughter, whom he met weeping at the doorway of the house, was crying. She replied that “Persa had died”—for that was the name of a puppy which had happened to die. He set out on the campaign but did not find triumph, because the Persian king died at the time when the consul’s daughter was weeping for her lost puppy.

Omens are often also drawn from the elements themselves or from [Col. 0413C] the state of the weather. Dew, or a gentle rain, softens the harshness of fortune. For dewy and lightly rainy weather, and clear air, when they readily attend the beginning of an undertaking, are believed to make its progress fortunate. When Fortune, which had long looked with an envious eye upon the Phrygian exiles, at last looked more kindly upon them as if from a watchtower of favour,

> A dark-blue shower stood above his head.  
> (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* III.133.)

Venus, preparing hospitality with Dido for her shipwrecked son, covered him in a hollow cloud as she introduced him, accompanied by faithful Achates, into the queen’s favour.

Thunder also has various meanings. If it brings any damage from lightning, it is unlucky. Hence:

> Often, had my mind not been perverse,  
> I remember that oaks struck from heaven foretold this evil to us.  
> (VIRGIL, *Eclogues* I.16.)

In such cases one also considers whether the bolt came down by a single course, or scattered its fires abroad through a manifold rupture of the air. The latter is certainly always sadder. When Gaius Caesar threatened his native land with civil war, neither ancient histories suffice to tell how lightning-filled the air was, how many fiery whirlwinds it contained, or how many beams it sent forth.

> [lacuna] And then  
> unknown stars were seen by dark nights.

But if the storm is without lightning, and thunders on the left, it is believed to announce the favour of the gods. When Aeneas heard Jupiter thundering [Col. 0414A] on the left, he judged, after sacrifices had been offered, that Jupiter was favourable to him.

But however these matters stand, the inborn fear of human beings may be lessened by this: no one will feel lightning’s stroke if, before it, he hears the sound of thunder or sees the flash.
