In stormier weather the emperor Tiberius wore a crown of laurel on his head, because this kind of foliage is said not to be touched by lightning. Indeed, he always feared thunder exceedingly and intensely.

Yet there is something which without doubt makes a person far safer: that he keep the faith of the Cross in his breast, bear the righteousness of faith upon his head, and with an innocent hand trace the saving sign of faith upon his forehead—always keeping in mind him who, dispelling every worldly fear from his worshippers, says: “Do not fear the signs of heaven, [Col. 0414B] which the nations fear, for I, the Lord your God, am with you” (Jeremiah X). Some write that these words, whether heard or spoken during thunder, have also averted the harm of lightning.

But nothing so completely shakes a person amid threatening signs as a mind conscious of its own wrongdoing, which fears at every point that punishment for its crimes will be demanded. Hence the moralist says of the guilty:

> These are the people who tremble and grow pale at every flash of lightning.  
> (JUVENAL, XIII.223.)

Conversely, the righteous person is confident like a lion. And again: “Whatever happens to him will not make the righteous person sad” (Proverbs XII). A fiery flash, if it does no harm by burning, brings the glory of fame. Nor, because it does not burn, is it not fiery—if Plato is to be accepted on this point. [Col. 0414C] “There are,” he says, “in my opinion, two powers of fire: one consuming and destructive; the other soothing, with harmless light.” He maintains that the latter produces sight and chiefly exerts its power in the upper regions.

When Ascanius, enduring with his father the perils of their fated exile, was illuminated by fire from heaven, as though his head had been set alight, it declared that good fortune in exile was due to him and that he himself would become the founder of a great nation. At the very birth of Alexander of Macedon and of Octavian Augustus, the brightness of fire was miraculously displayed. A wind following an expedition as it sets out makes its hope of success fortunate; when standards are borne against enemies, the testimony of the air declares that the standards will triumph. But if they threaten one’s homeland, they inspire a most justified fear.

The earth itself also knows mysteries, but more often bears grave omens, because, founded upon its stability, it prefers rest to motion. Therefore, when its rumbling is heard, it grieves with bitter events and, by the sadness of its voice, declares the affection with which it suffers alongside its children. For it is the great and loving mother of all. This earth had tried to keep the Phoenician woman from the embrace of her guest; but because Venus, the broker of hospitality, had already prevailed, touched inwardly by grief of heart, it groaned, since groaning serves it instead of lamentation. Whenever it trembles, it foresees something to be feared by its children—unless perhaps it is labouring in childbirth. Then indeed it either miscarries altogether or bears an unprofitable offspring, because, very often, when

> [Col. 0415A] Mountains labour in childbirth, a ridiculous mouse comes forth.  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry* 139.)

These are the matters to which you see very many people devote all their vigilance.

> [Col. 0416A] The remaining matters of this kind are so numerous  
> that they could weary talkative Fabius.  
> (ID., *Satires* I.1.14.)

Whatever house undertakes them, I think it cannot be saved even by salvation itself.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0415]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0415A]

Everything yields to the use of the wise person and provides material for the exercise of virtue, whatever may be said or done. For even leisure is business to such a person; and while, by the balance of reason, he weighs the powers of all things, by prudent ordering he lays hold, with a kind of hand of virtue, of whatever advances blessedness. Thus you give a twofold proof, by a most compelling argument, of your divine wisdom: you proceed uprightly in your own actions, and you philosophize amid the trifles of others.

Let our trifles therefore go forth cheerfully, since your serenity commands them to appear in public, so that they may introduce diviners, astrologers, and certain other triflers. For you who have given them the boldness to go forth will also grant them the confidence of security. Let what follows therefore be joined to what precedes; and if anything faulty or unattractive appears in either, let the prudence of your kindness correct it.

## CHAPTER I. Omens are empty, and things answer each person according to that person’s faith.

[Col. 0415C]

There is a rustic proverb, perhaps Offellus’s: “Whoever believes dreams and auguries will never be secure.” I consider the saying both utterly true and entirely trustworthy. What difference does it make to the outcome of events if someone sneezes once or more often? What if he yawns? What, finally, if he makes a sound from whatever source? These things, however, for reasons known to natural philosophers, bear in some measure upon the person in whom they occur, even though they cannot impede or advance another person’s affairs. The same is true of empty charms and certain superstitious ligatures, which the whole school of physicians condemns, although some customarily call even these “physical” by a rather exalted name.

For they call “physical” that whose most hidden rationale is such that it cannot be understood by human sense. Nothing exists or happens whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and explanation; and, as another says, “Nothing happens on earth without a cause.” It is thus plain that nothing escapes the hand of nature, the artificer. Consequently, it appears that all things belong to natural philosophy.

Whatever the precise character of these matters, I firmly believe that only those things are not to be rejected which proceed from faith and are referred to the glory of almighty God. For I know it is written: “Whatever you do in deed or word, do all in the name of the Lord,” in whom alone the way of humankind prospers. Thus the whole company of saints has gone before us. Guthbert, a standard-bearer of our people, placed the Gospel of John from the Law of the Lord upon sick persons, and they were healed. A garment of blessed Stephen, laid upon a dead person, raised him. The Apostles’ Creed healed a demoniac upon whom it was worn. The Lord’s Prayer, spoken in faith over herbs when they were gathered or administered, very often produced the desired effect of healing. [Col. 0416B] Blessed Benedict broke a deadly vessel with the sign of the Cross, as though he had thrown a stone at it in place of the sign. Chapters of the Gospel, carried, heard, or recited, are found to have benefited very many people. These things, and things like them, are not only lawful but most useful.

The others, however, are not so much to be despised as fled from. For it is certain that all things work together for good for those who love God; but God permits unbelievers, the reprobate, and even those wavering in faith to be subjected to many delusions. Yet all omens have only as much power as the faith of the recipient permits.

Thus Julius Caesar could be deterred from no undertaking by any augury or superstition. Once, when he was sailing to Africa, he stumbled as he disembarked from the ship. Turning the omen to a better sense, he said, “I hold you, Africa,” and he possessed it. Furthermore, on the night which was his last upon earth, his wife Calpurnia saw him lying in her lap covered in many wounds. Though she begged him to stay away from the senate-house on the following day, she did not prevail, lest he seem during his lifetime to have acted timidly under any omen. At the destruction of the Massilians, he was the first to dare cut down a grove held sacred to the gods, proving himself remote from every superstition.

Blessed Mark also, setting out for Alexandria in order to preach the Gospel, broke his sandal when he stepped ashore from the ship; giving thanks, he declared that his journey would be unhindered. If a person is called back while travelling, he should not therefore abandon anything begun in the Lord’s name—unless perhaps he is persuaded that every recall is ominous by the example of the raven, which lost the beauty of its colour because, recalled by the crow, it preferred to go onward rather than remain. An unguarded mind is deceived by these trifles, but a faithful one never assents to them.

## CHAPTER II. The indications of natural things are not to be wholly despised.

Although I maintain that all omens are empty and that faith ought not to be placed in auguries, I do not therefore annul the credibility and usefulness of signs granted by divine ordering for the instruction of creation. God instructs his creation in many and various ways: now by the voices of the elements, now by indications of sensible or insensible things; and, as he knows expedient for the elect, he reveals what is to come.

Certain preceding signs foretell future storms or fair weather, so that the human being, born for labour, may regulate activities accordingly. By familiar observations farmers and sailors infer what ought to be done at each time, measuring the character of coming weather by what has gone before. In this matter I do not think that birds, of which the preceding discussion spoke, are deprived of their mother Nature’s beneficence. The diver, kingfishers, and swan frequently disclose Nature’s secrets.

When, around midwinter, you see kingfishers building nests and brooding their eggs, do not doubt that there will be fifteen days of most welcome calm. Sailors regularly observe them with special care, and these are called halcyon days, when scarcely even a light breath of wind is felt. You may plausibly suppose that Nature has granted these days to them for rearing their young. But when you see the bodies of water-birds diving more eagerly into the waters, expect rain. When you hear the crow’s morning cry, it calls for rain.

> I do not believe this is because they possess divine intelligence  
> or a greater knowledge of events by fate.  
> (VIRGIL, *Georgics* I.416.)

Rather, because they more quickly feel within themselves the movements lingering in the air, and from these conceive cheerfulness or [Col. 0417C] sadness. Nor is this surprising, since even the heavier bodies of animals are very often affected by outward movements and, by a certain secret counsel of nature, conform to the elements as necessity requires.

The science of physicians of nature grasps by sufficiently plausible rules what benefits or harms will threaten animal bodies if seasons return either at their proper time or out of season. It also recognizes from preceding signs a future condition of health, sickness, or what they call *neutrality*, and even the fatal outcome itself; and sometimes, if its practitioners know the causes, they treat such conditions most effectively. But if, to use their own word, they do not know the causes, how do they cure? Certainly not through the benefit of their art, but through chance. Their judgment, drawn from knowledge of signs, although difficult, is often entirely true.

Calm weather and the various forms of storms and tempests are also revealed by many signs, which the disk of the moon, as though from a watchtower, indicates. A reddish colour shows winds, a bluish one rain; a mixture of both indicates clouds and raging storms. A cheerful rising of the moon promises calm to ships by the expression it bears, particularly if it is the fourth rising; for this is the surest authority—provided it is neither red with blunt horns nor darkened by moisture poured over it. For then:

> Both that entire day, and those which will arise from it,  
> will be free from wind and rain until the completed month.

The bright sun also matters: whether it rejoices in even rays or reddens behind an intervening cloud; whether it shines with its usual brightness, is fiery because winds press upon it, is pale with snow, or is spotted because rain is imminent. The air, the sea itself, and the size and appearance of clouds provide very much instruction. Birds and fish also disclose most certain signs of what is to come—signs which Virgil and Lucan grasp with divine genius, and which Varro likewise sets out in his nautical books while instructing anxious sailors.

## CHAPTER III. Some signs are universal and others particular; and what the doubling of the sun signifies.

Whatever signs occur naturally in the sun and moon are most certain and confirmed by the testimony of many authors. “Who would dare call the sun false?” Therefore, whenever the sun seems doubled in the sky, let the world below expect a flood of waters. Although the phenomenon seems almost miraculous because of its rarity, it is nevertheless a work of nature, which does not actually double the sun but creates a cloud very like it; this is called a *parhelion*. A parhelion is a cloud closely resembling the sun: a sign common to many, though not universal.

For some signs are particular and others universal. Particular signs affect individuals; universal signs affect many persons or all. Both kinds are said to arise sometimes from the elements by the Creator’s ordering, sometimes from the nature of things, and sometimes from the malice of demons who, with the Lord’s permission, mock human beings. But which signs do so, how, and for what reason: this is a difficult judgment, frequently uncertain, and often too profound to be resolved by human beings. Nevertheless, books are full of such things through the more unrestrained vanity of astrologers.

Aeneas claims that, with his goddess-mother showing the way, he followed the fates given to him, because at his departure Lucifer—who is also Venus—appeared to him as he sought an omen, until he reached Italy.

Human curiosity fits the various eclipses of the sun and the moon’s labours to the outcomes of events.

## CHAPTER IV. On the signs which preceded the most recent destruction of Jerusalem.

An old history—so called because its author is unknown and it recounts old matters—reports that, as the destruction of Jerusalem approached, an eclipse of the moon continued for twelve successive nights, even in the most distant places. Perhaps it signified the overthrow of Jewish unbelief and superstitious error, which very fittingly occurred when Christ shone upon the world through the apostles’ preaching. For it is written: “The fool changes like the moon, but the wise person remains with the sun” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII).

Very many other things also occurred, as divine judgment threatened the unbelievers. If I began to recount them one by one as the authors have arranged them, these things alone would require their own time and leisure. Yet, following Josephus, I shall run through a few in concise language, because they serve to strengthen our faith and to blunt the Jews’ stubborn unbelief.

For forty continuous years after the crime had been committed, punishment for the impious was deferred. During those years all the apostles—and especially James, called the Lord’s brother, appointed bishop in Jerusalem—unceasingly warned the people about their committed impiety and deadly deed, in case they might repent of what they had done; in case they might weep for their crime and restrain the avenging flames of punishment through the freedom of tears. For by his patience God showed them that he sought their repentance, since God does not desire so much the death of a sinner as that the sinner turn and live.

The divine majesty still strove to soften the hardness of their minds by signs and prodigies sent from heaven, displaying terrors and a threatening right hand rather than inflicting them. In these matters the authority of the aforementioned historian will be sufficient, as in established facts. Let us therefore reread what Josephus himself recorded about these things in the sixth book of his histories:

> “But certain most evil men and deceivers, uttering false prophecies, persuaded the unhappy [Col. 0419B] people not to believe the plain signs and evidences of divine wrath and indignation, which openly foretold the coming destruction both of the city and of the nation. Rather, as though possessed and mad, and as people who possessed neither eyes nor souls within themselves, they despised all that was announced from heaven.
>
> “For a brilliant star, altogether resembling a sword, was seen to hang over the city; and besides it, a comet seemed to burn with destructive flames throughout an entire year. Before the time of destruction and war, when the people were assembling for the festival, on the eighth day of the month Xanthicus, which is April, at the ninth hour of the night, so great a brilliance of light surrounded the altar and the Temple that everyone thought the brightest day had come; and it lasted for half an hour. To the unlearned and ignorant this seemed favourable; but the teachers of the Law and all reputable persons understood that the portent was destructive.
>
> “At the same festival, a heifer brought forward for sacrifice and standing by the altars gave birth to a lamb in the very hands of the attendants. Also, the gate of the inner sanctuary which faced east—though plated with solid bronze and of such immense weight that scarcely twenty men could shut it by a supreme effort, though also secured with iron bars and bolts, and held fast by locks set high above—suddenly, at the sixth hour of the night, on the twenty-first day of the month, was seen to open of its own accord.
>
> “And after the festival day had passed, some days later, on the twenty-first day of the month Artemisius, called May among us, a prodigious and almost unbelievable sight appeared. It would truly have been thought false had the testimony of the eyes not been confirmed by the ensuing disaster. For near sunset, chariots and four-horse chariots were seen throughout the whole region in the air, and companies of armed men mingling with the clouds, while cities were surrounded by unexpected battle-lines.
>
> “Again, on another festival day, called Pentecost, the priests entered the Temple by night to perform their customary ministrations. First they perceived certain movements and noises; then they heard sudden voices saying, ‘Let us depart from here; let us depart from these dwelling places.’
>
> “A further and more terrible thing is added. A certain Jesus, son of Ananias, a common and rustic man, four years before the war, while the city remained in peace and abundance, suddenly began to cry out on the feast-day of Tabernacles: [Col. 0420A] ‘A voice from the east; a voice from the west; a voice from the four winds; a voice over Jerusalem and the Temple; a voice over bridegrooms and brides; a voice over the people.’ Day and night without ceasing, as he went about all the streets, he shouted this. At length certain leading men of the people, as though indignant at an ill-omened prophecy, seized the man and subjected him to many beatings. But he said nothing at all for himself and did not even entreat those standing round him; instead, with the same obstinacy and shouting, he repeated the same cries.
>
> “Then the leaders, understanding that the man’s impulse was, as it was, from a divine power, brought him before the Roman governor. There, torn with whips to the very bones, he poured forth neither prayers nor tears; but uttering the same cry miserably and with a kind of wail, he pronounced it at almost every blow, adding also this: ‘Woe, woe to Jerusalem!’”

The same historian also relates another event, performed by a greater miracle. He says that an oracle had been found in the sacred writings which indicated that at that same time a man would arise from their region who would gain dominion over the whole world. The same historian supposes that the oracle’s prediction pointed to Vespasian. But Vespasian ruled no nations except those which seemed subject to Roman rule. Therefore these responses are more rightly referred to Christ, to whom the Father said:

> Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance,  
> and the ends of the earth as your possession.  
> (Psalm II.)

And of whom, at that same time, it was said through his apostles:

> Their sound went out into all the earth,  
> and their words to the ends of the world.  
> (Psalm XVIII.)

## CHAPTER V. How great was the calamity of those under siege, what end befell their obstinate wickedness, and what mercy Titus showed.

But lest so many and such great signs preceding God’s indignation against the Jews’ impenitence appear to have been only tokens of a moderate chastisement or a passing wrath, let a brief account [Col. 0420D] run through the intolerable calamity, the irreparable destruction, and the unheard-of servitude—unknown to all preceding ages—of a rejected and blinded nation. Whoever wishes to know more fully by how many evils the whole multitude was then afflicted; how the very land of Judaea was devastated by war, famine, fire, and slaughter; how many countless thousands of people—fathers together with wives and little children—were killed without number and without distinction; what sieges there were of different cities; how great the desolation of Jerusalem itself, that magnificent and most celebrated city; how great the carnage of various deaths; what was the course of the wars in each of these particulars; how, in accordance with what the prophets had said, the abomination of desolation was set up in that temple once so famous as God’s temple; and how, in the end, fire ravaged everything and flame consumed it—let such a person read again the history of Josephus.

We, however, shall take from it only those matters which [Col. 0421A] suffice for the exposition of the work we have undertaken. There he relates that people from all Judaea had gathered at Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, as though compelled by some deadly hand. He says that they numbered three hundred thousand, by the just judgment of God: this time of vengeance having been chosen so that, since in the days of Passover they had violated Christ, the Lord and Saviour, with bloody hands and sacrilegious cries, on those very days the whole multitude, shut up as if in one prison, might receive the destruction of the deadly punishment it deserved.

I shall pass over the things inflicted upon them by slaughter with the sword or by the other engines of war, and shall set forth only what they endured through the starvation of dreadful famine, in the words of the historian mentioned above, so that those who read may understand [Col. 0421B] how great a sin it is to dare anything against Christ, and with how grievous punishments such daring is expiated. Come then: let the fifth book of Josephus’s *Histories* be brought forward, from which their entire mournful tragedy may be known.

> “For the wealthy,” he says, “to remain or to perish was one and the same thing. For if they remained in the city, they were killed when an accusation was brought against them on account of their property, as though they were intending to defect. The necessity of famine heightened the arrogance of the factions, and hunger and recklessness increased together. There was absolutely no grain anywhere in public supply; but the city’s brigands burst in and searched houses, and if they found anything, they punished the owners as persons who had deceived them; but if [Col. 0421C] they found nothing, they nevertheless tortured them as though they had hidden it more secretly and carefully. They took as proof that people possessed food the very fact that they were still alive and seemed to be standing on their feet: they must surely already have perished, unless they were concealing food somewhere. If, however, they saw people wasted away with emaciation, they spared them, thinking it superfluous to kill those whom famine would consume shortly afterwards.

> “Yet many in secret purchased one measure—if wealthy, of wheat; if poorer, of barley—with all their property; and, shutting themselves in the innermost rooms of their houses, some ate the grain without even making it into bread, while others cooked it only as necessity or fear allowed. No one waited for a table [Col. 0421D] to be laid; rather, snatching their own food half-burned from the fire, they devoured it as though it were stolen. The sight of that wretched food was pitiable: all the stronger persons seized and carried off whatever they found, while for the weak nothing remained except mourning and tears. And although famine surpasses every bitterness of suffering, nothing so destroys and overturns as shame. For whatever, when circumstances are sound, is deemed worthy of shame is despised in this necessity. Thus wives snatched food from their husbands’ hands, children from their parents’, and—what was more wretched still—mothers snatched food from the hands and mouths of little children. And while their sweetest children wasted away in their hands and before their eyes, no one spared even to take the meagre supports of life from their very teeth.

> “But not even those wretched persons who took the smallest morsels of food escaped notice. A brigand was immediately at hand; as soon as he saw anyone’s doors shut, he took this as proof that those within were eating; and, violently forcing open the doors, he rushed in headlong and, as one might say, squeezing their very throats, made them bring back up whatever they had already swallowed. Old men were beaten if they attempted to hold on to food; women were dragged by their loose hair when they tried to conceal something which happened to have been discovered in their hands. There was no reverence for old age, no pity for little children; but they dashed to the ground little children clinging to a tiny fragment of bread, suspended from the very thing to which they clung. Against a person who had forestalled the robbers by eating food, they raged more cruelly [Col. 0422B] and devised dreadful tortures, blocking the unhappy victims’ natural passages of excretion; against others they drove sharp stakes into those same private parts. I shudder in recounting what was done. They pressed the miserable wretches to provide a single loaf or a cup of meal after this. For the torturers themselves did not suffer hunger. In some sense it would have been more tolerable if they appeared to do these things under compulsion of starvation. But, whether to lay up food for themselves for the future or to strengthen their cruelty through practice, they also met and robbed those who had perhaps secretly broken through the enemy’s guard-posts to gather herbs, though these people rejoiced that they had escaped the hands of the enemy, taking away whatever they had brought.

> “When they begged, invoking upon themselves the dreadful [Col. 0422C] name of God, that the robbers might grant them at least some part of what they had sought at the risk of death, they gave absolutely nothing. Indeed, it counted as a kindness if one who had been seized was allowed to get away alive.”

After this he adds the following:

> “For the Jews, with departure from the city, every hope of salvation was at the same time shut out; and the increasing severity of famine devastated homes, households, and the nation alike. Thus in the inner rooms lay scattered the corpses of women and little children, while in the streets were the bodies of unhappy old men, consumed more by hunger than by age. Young men and everyone of more vigorous age wandered about the streets and passages like so many phantoms, collapsing wherever hunger stole away their steps. The multitude of the dead, [Col. 0422D] and the weakness of their strength, did not allow people to bury the corpses of their dead relatives; at the same time each person feared for the uncertainty of his own life. Thus some gave up their souls over those whom they were burying; many, while accompanying funerals, breathed their last before the grave was reached. And just as no customary lamentation or mourning was offered to the dead, because famine had claimed all this for itself, so the dryness of starvation left no one even the moisture of tears. A profound silence besieged the city, and a night full of death had covered everything.

> “More grievous than all these evils were the brigands alone, who thought it lawful not even to spare tombs from plunder or corpses from stripping, seeking not so much booty as adding crime to mockery, and testing the edge of their swords [Col. 0423A] by cutting up corpses. Sometimes they also put their blades to use on persons still breathing; and when others, half-dead, saw this, they held out suppliant hands, asking that the crime might be turned upon themselves also as an act of kindness, so that they might more swiftly be released from the torments of hunger. Yet, by a new kind of cruelty, when asked they refused the death which they inflicted voluntarily. Nevertheless, each of the dying turned his eyes with groaning toward the Temple—not grieving for his own death, but for the impunity of the brigands whom they were leaving alive. At first, because of the intolerable stench, they had ordered the dead to be buried at public expense. But when the multitude of the dying began to exceed every expense, they threw the corpses down from the wall.

> “When Titus, making the circuit, saw the valleys filled with the corpses of the dead, and the native soil being watered with the putrefaction of human bodies, he groaned deeply and, raising his hands to heaven, called God to witness that this had not happened through his fault, but that he endured these things unwillingly.” [Col. 0423B]

And a little later Josephus again continues with words of this sort:

> “I shall not hesitate,” he says, “to state what I think. I believe that, even if the Roman arms had for a little while ceased against the impious citizens, the city would have paid the penalty either by an opening of the earth, by a flood of waters, or by Sodomite fires and bolts of lightning hurled from heaven; for it had produced this present generation of men, much more unhappy than those who suffered those things and more wicked, for whose sake the entire nation together deserved to be destroyed.”

But in the sixth book he writes the following concerning the same matters:

> “The number of those throughout the whole city who were perishing from starvation by famine,” he says, “was countless, and their misery cannot be described. For in every house, whenever any food was found, wars and murders immediately arose among those dear to one another, even among parents and children, as they struggled to snatch food from one another not only from their hands but even from their very throats. Nor was trust placed even in the dead: while they were already exhaling their spirit, the brigands searched them, lest perhaps someone might have hidden some food in his bosom. Others, gaping from hunger, were carried here and there like rabid dogs and, as if driven by some madness, [Col. 0423D] burst into the same houses again and again within a moment of time.

> “Yet necessity turned everything into food, even things which custom had not allowed even dumb animals to eat. At last they did not refrain even from straps, belts, or their very shoes. Stripping off the coverings of shields, they put them into their mouths to chew. Some even ate stalks of old hay; and a very tiny quantity gathered from refuse was sold for four drachmas.”

## CHAPTER VI. On Mary, who, pressed by hunger, ate her son

> “But what need is there to explain through such details the weight of that famine [Col. 0424A], when a crime was committed there which no report has ever recorded among Greeks or barbarians—horrible to tell, incredible to hear? I myself would gladly have passed over so monstrous a crime in silence, lest anyone think that I was recounting prodigies, had I not had many men of our own time as witnesses of the crime committed. Moreover, I would not think that I was doing any service to my native country by withholding the accounts of the deeds it endured.

> “A certain woman from those who lived beyond the channel of the Jordan, named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, from the village of Hebezobra [Note: [Col. 0423D] Paris edition: Vethezobra.], which is interpreted ‘House of Hyssop,’ noble in birth and wealth, was found at Jerusalem with the rest of the multitude that had gathered there and shared with all the common fate of the siege. The tyrants had seized her remaining [Col. 0424B] possessions, which she had brought from her home into the city. Whatever remnants of her great wealth remained, by which she might have maintained a most scanty daily subsistence, the agents of the brigands kept seizing in their repeated raids.

> “Because of this, the woman, as though mad, was exhausted by a vast indignation, so that at times she provoked the brigands, with curses and insults, to kill her. But since no one, whether angered or moved with pity, killed her, and if she had sought food it was sought by others as well, while there was no longer any possibility of finding it anywhere, and dreadful hunger was pressing upon her very entrails and marrow; since starvation was now driving her into madness, hunger and anger—the worst counsellors—armed her against the very laws [Col. 0424C] of nature. For she had a little son at her breast. Holding him before her eyes, she said:

> “‘O son more wretched than your wretched mother, for whom shall I preserve you amid war, famine, and the plundering of brigands? Even if life could be hoped for, we are oppressed by the yoke of Roman slavery; but now famine has forestalled even slavery itself. The brigands press us more grievously than both. Come now, my child: be food for your mother, fury for the brigands, and a tale for the ages—the one thing lacking from the calamities of the Jews.’

> “Having said this, she immediately cut her son’s throat. Then she placed him over a fire and roasted him; she consumed one half by eating it, while covering and reserving the other half. And behold, the brigands at once burst in. Catching the smell of roasted flesh, they threatened her with death unless she showed them without delay the food which they had perceived was prepared [Col. 0424D]. Then she said: ‘Indeed, I have kept the best portion for you’; and immediately she uncovered the remaining limbs of the child.

> “At once a great horror seized them, and their hearts, cruel though they were, froze; their voices were choked in their throats. But she, with a savage expression and more savage even than the brigands themselves, said: ‘He is my son; he is my child; and the deed is mine. Eat: for I, who bore him, ate first. Do not make yourselves either more devout than a mother or more tender than a woman. But if piety prevails over you and you abhor my food, I who have already fed on such things will feed on them again.’ After this, terrified and trembling, they departed—those who [Col. 0425A] had left this one food alone, out of all her possessions, to the miserable mother.

> “The whole city was immediately filled with the report of the abominable crime; and each person, bringing before his eyes the deed that had been done, shuddered as though he himself had done it. All whom the necessity of hunger pressed hastened more eagerly toward death, calling blessed those who had been allowed to die before they were defiled by hearing of such evils.”

Such is Josephus’s account.

## CHAPTER VII. On the number of captives, those killed, and those destroyed by famine

What end such a great calamity reached I shall add very briefly on the authority of the same writer. For the historian mentioned above, gathering the total number [Col. 0425B] of those destroyed by hunger, thirst, or the sword, set it at eleven hundred thousand. The remaining rebels, assassins, and brigands, he states, perished after the destruction of the city by wounds inflicted upon one another. Those young men distinguished by bodily beauty and height, he says, were selected and reserved for the triumph. The rest, who were over seventeen years of age, were bound and assigned to labour in the mines of Egypt or scattered throughout the other provinces. Some were handed over for gladiatorial games; others, to the beasts. Those found to be over seventeen years old were ordered to be sold into slavery throughout different provinces; their number reached as many as ninety thousand.

All these things took place in the second [Col. 0425C] year of Vespasian’s reign, in accordance with what our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself had foretold, since he saw as present the things that were to occur. Thus, according to the truth of the Gospels, when he saw the city, he wept over it and spoke these words as though in its hearing: “If only you too had known, indeed on this day, the things that make for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, encircle you, hem you in on every side, and cast you to the ground, and your children within you” (Luke 19). In this manner many thunderclaps of divine threat resounded publicly in ears hardened until the blood of the righteous—and also of that singular and only Righteous One—unjustly shed by the impious, was required by God’s just judgment. Therefore they were worn down by blows, laid low in wars, and cut off from their ancestral seats by the whirlwind of divine indignation; so that in the most glorious city not one stone remained upon another. The tribulation of the hardened people, harder than any stone, was so great as had not been from the beginning of nations until that day [Col. 0425D].

## CHAPTER VIII. On the migration of the faithful, whom Christ preserved at Pella during that crisis

The Church which had gathered at Jerusalem was divinely commanded to cross the Jordan to a certain town named Pella. Thus, when God’s worshippers had been removed from the city, there might be room for the heavenly vengeance that was to be exercised upon the sacrilegious city and nation [Col. 0426A]. Eusebius of Caesarea explains this more fully in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

## CHAPTER IX. The testimony borne by Josephus to Christ

And indeed they most justly suffered all these things, having dared to stretch out sacrilegious hands against the Son of God, when the testimonies of the Scriptures and the power of his wondrous works made it plain that Christ himself was God. Thus Josephus says:

> “At the same time there was Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man. For he was a doer of wondrous works and a teacher of people who gladly receive what is true; and he drew to himself many Jews and also many from among the Gentiles.” This was the Christ. When, at the accusation of the leading men of our [Col. 0426B] nation, Pilate had decreed that he should be crucified, those who had loved him from the beginning did not abandon him. He appeared to them alive again on the third day, as the prophets divinely inspired had foretold both these and countless other future miracles concerning him. And to this day the name and race of Christians, who are named after him, endure.

## CHAPTER X. On Vespasian, who is recorded to have healed a lame man and a blind man

Vespasian also, the devastator of Judaea and father of Titus, the most pious destroyer of Jerusalem, was, as some writers have held, raised up by God’s finger through signs of miracles in order to execute vengeance among the nations. For when he was not yet emperor, [Col. 0426C] a certain commoner deprived of sight, and likewise another man lame and disabled in one leg, came together to him as he sat on the tribunal, asking relief for their infirmities. They said that it had been shown to them in a dream that the blind man’s eyes would be restored if Vespasian looked upon them, and the lame man’s leg strengthened if he would deign to touch it with his heel. At the entreaties of his friends, though unwilling, he attempted both actions, and success was not lacking. His accession to empire, too, and the deaths of Vitellius and Otho, who had succeeded the foul Nero, were announced beforehand by many heavenly signs, some of them astonishing.

## CHAPTER XI. Signs are those things which occur contrary to nature

No one who faithfully remembers the Gospel promise doubts that events worthy of such astonishment are generally signs, since it is written: “There shall be signs in sun and moon and stars,” etc. (Luke 21). Yet the things foretold here, without prejudice to a better opinion, I judge to be those which occur contrary to nature: such as the darkening of the sun at the Lord’s Passion, the rending of the veil, the splitting of rocks, the opening of tombs, and the rising of the bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep [Col. 0426D]. For it could not have been a natural eclipse, which happens through the interposition of the moon’s body, since it is certain that the moon was in its fourteenth day the day before—unless perhaps someone should borrow consolation for his unbelief from Jewish perfidy, asserting with them that Venus was then opposite the sun in the ecliptic line. Venus is indeed large and, as astrologers teach, alone among the five planets casts a shadow by night like the moon. But since neither reason nor authority nor faith approves this, it is rejected as futile. For if Venus’s body is so luminous, how could it produce such great darkness?

Dionysius the Areopagite writes in his letter to Polycarp that he and many other philosophers then saw the moon fall upon the sun. And this was contrary to nature, for it was not the time of conjunction. When Paul later preached to him, this gave occasion for his conversion. I know, however, that many have spoken differently about this; but I prefer Dionysius to them all, because he wrote what he saw, whereas the others follow their own opinions.

Signs are often not only universal but also general, as was the case when, at the death of God, darkness came over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth (Matthew [Col. 0427B] 27). What is particular in them, or less universal, is compensated by the continuity of time in its effect upon the human race. For that death unveiled Moses’ face to all, split perpetual hardness, and introduced the firstfruits of resurrection into everlasting joy.

The things likewise said to precede the Day of Judgment during fifteen days—if indeed they are to occur, since they have no foundation in canonical Scripture—will by no means be subject to the laws of nature; provided that here, as in many places, by “nature” we mean the customary course of things, or the hidden causes of events for which an explanation can be given.

## CHAPTER XII. That, according to Plato, nothing occurs contrary to nature, since he calls nature the will of God

[Col. 0427C] But if we follow Plato, who declares that nature is God’s will, certainly none of these things occurs contrary to nature, since God has done whatever he willed. In explaining the causes of things, Plato maintains that the end of all things is divine goodness. “He is best,” he says. Now all envy is far removed from what is best. Accordingly, he willed that all things should be made like himself, insofar as the nature of each was capable of blessedness. And if anyone should maintain that this will of God is the most certain origin of things, I should agree that he thinks rightly.

Indeed, the wisdom and goodness of God, which gives origin to all things, is most rightly called nature. Nothing at all happens contrary to it, because nothing frustrates God’s ordering or deprives of their effect the causes which have stood from eternity in the mind of him who made the heavens by understanding [Col. 0427D]. Therefore things contain seminal causes of events and original rational principles, which at their predetermined time proceed into their effects. They are wonderful, not because they have no causes, but because their causes are most hidden.

Thus moisture is drawn up from the earth’s innermost recesses by the roots of trees or vines through a certain appetitive power; then, through a certain natural distribution, it is spread through the parts of the plants. When it has advanced through its own digestion, it swells into shoots; what it does not need for its own support it sends into leaves and fruits. When these ripen, they foam into must, and so, through intervals of time and habitual process, they bring forth wines. But if by God’s hidden ordering moisture that has been digested [Col. 0428A] and ripened through certain channels of nature is unexpectedly turned into wine without any interval of time, it is indeed a miracle, because the depth of divine providence transcends our understanding.

“But,” as the Wise Man says, “let the cloudy error of ignorance fall away; then certainly miracles will cease to seem miraculous.” Yet I do not weaken faith in, or the authority of, God’s miracles; rather, with full humility I reverence and admire the depth of the riches of his wisdom and knowledge, knowing that what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings. For it belongs to human weakness to err in many things, just as it belongs to angelic or divine perfection never to think otherwise than things are.

## CHAPTER XIII. That God deigns to forewarn his creature by signs

This also belongs to divine mercy: by the indication of his signs, he sometimes fortifies our ignorance beforehand. When a comet appears, public assemblies are believed to be imminent. Do you not know the comet

> changing kingdoms upon earth?  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.529)

Whoever has touched even slightly upon the histories of public affairs knows what signs occurred when Italy’s destruction was impending. Historical volumes written about memorable events are full of prodigies and portents. Nor can you doubt that many signs of faith and power occurred under Elijah and Elisha. The Ninevites also repented at the preaching of Jonah by the indications of signs. For unbelief is challenged by the arguments of signs, and tender faith is strengthened by the same. Hence: “What sign do you show us?” [Col. 0428C] (John 2); and: “Jews demand signs, Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1).

## CHAPTER XIV. What a sign is, and concerning dreams

Here signs are understood as whatever, by any indication, intimates God’s will to a human being. A sign is that which presents itself to the senses and presents something besides itself to the mind. Yet some signs present nothing to any bodily sense, but frequently bring truth or falsehood before the mind through the image of some thing, or without the difficulty of an intermediary. For signs are sometimes true and sometimes false.

Who does not know the varied meanings of dreams, confirmed both by experience and by the authority of the ancients? In dreams, because there is sleep [Col. 0428D], the animal powers—that is, the senses, which are called bodily though they belong to the soul—rest; but the natural powers are active. It happens meanwhile that the mind, relieved of bodily exertion, returns more freely into itself and contemplates truth now through figures and riddles, now more freely in an immediate aspect.

This was not unknown to the poet who, depicting the gates of sleep, imagined one of ivory and the other of horn. Horn is penetrable by sight, which does not often err; ivory, denser by nature, cannot be penetrated by the sharpness of vision even when scraped to the utmost thinness. The former is more like true vision, the latter like teeth. Hence true dreams, hence false dreams:

> The spirits send false dreams up to the sky.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.897)

## CHAPTER XV. On the kinds, causes, figures, and meanings of dreams

[Col. 0429A]

There are many kinds of dreams, manifold causes, varied figures, and meanings. A dream may be an *insomnium*, a phantom, a dream properly so called, an oracle, or a vision. Now *insomnia* arise most commonly from drunkenness, surfeit, various bodily conditions and disturbances of the emotions, and the remnants of thoughts. Thus troubled lovers’ minds are never without *insomnia*. Maro wisely indicates this:

> Sister Anna, what dreams terrify me in my suspense?  
> Great is the man’s excellence that returns again and again to my mind,  
> great the honour of his lineage; his features and words cling fixed in my breast,  
> nor does this care grant peaceful rest to my limbs.  
> [Col. 0429B] (Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.3)

Such dreams likewise do not pass over the experience of the sorrowful or joyful, those tormented by the distress of fear, or those inflamed by the heat of excessive desire.

A phantom occurs when there appear unknown forms of things which differ from nature in quality, size, manner, or number of parts: for example, if “neither foot nor head corresponds to a single form,” while

> [lacuna] a beautiful woman above ends in a black fish.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 3)

Physicians teach that such appearances arise from infirmity of mind and body, and they attend more to their causes than to any meanings derived from them. [Col. 0429C] In this class they think that the *ephialtes* [nightmare] should also be counted: a condition in which someone, under various pressures in a kind of half-waking state, but rather in disturbed sleep, imagines himself awake when he is asleep and thinks that someone is weighing him down. All such things need the treatment of physicians rather than our discussion, especially since nothing true appears in them except that the experiences are very real and very distressing.

A dream properly so called, although its name is generic, is reckoned a distinct species. It conveys images of things under certain coverings, and it is chiefly in these that the discipline of interpreters of dreams is exercised. Such a dream is sometimes one’s own, sometimes another’s, sometimes shared; at times it is public or general. In all these cases the character of persons, things, and times is observed with the greatest care. For, as Nestor says, a dream should be believed concerning the public condition of a king or of someone who holds office, whether by an actual circumstance or by a prediction closely connected with the circumstance; or when a sign of public fortune has been shown to many people, as is written to have been revealed to several Roman citizens, according to some, through the Sibyl’s interpretation of the mystery of the Incarnation.

Indeed, as interpreter, instructed and inspired by the Spirit, she disclosed mysteries not only of the Incarnation, but also of the Passion, the Ascension after the Resurrection, and the Second Coming, as you will plainly find in the Sibylline verses. Their beginning, as it is found in the writings of many Fathers, is this:

> A sign of judgment: the earth shall be drenched with sweat.

But if the initial capital letters of the individual verses are joined in order, this is found expressed, to confound the perfidy of the Jews: **Jesus Christ, God, Saviour** (*Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεὸς Σωτήρ*), except that in the Latin language the proper character of the Greek letters could not be fully preserved. You will find the verses themselves, I think, in blessed Augustine’s *City of God*.

The chief point and whole intention of this mystical vision, therefore, is that Jesus, whom it prefigured, is without doubt the Son of the living God, true man, judge of all, eternal king, rewarder of those who hope in him, author of life, and, by grace, giver of eternal blessedness. The phrase “by an actual circumstance or by a closely connected prediction” was used because an office-holder is understood sometimes as present and sometimes as future. Thus the destruction of Numantia was made known to the younger Africanus while he was still almost [Col. 0430B] a soldier.

When autumn is mature or abrupt, dreams more often prove vain. For when the leaves of trees fall, the vanity of dreams prevails. Virgil too seems to have understood this in the book in which he investigates the mysteries of all philosophy, when he adorned the underworld’s falling leaves with varied dreams. Differences of places likewise admit different figures of sleep, so that some places are richer than others now in these dreams, now in those. A marshy or deserted place is more fertile in fantastic images than a high or populous one.

A matter is also revealed sometimes more clearly and sometimes more obscurely: now it presents itself directly to the mind, now it is disclosed by another who gives information. But when it pours itself in by immediate light, it is a vision, because it appears to be set before the eyes in its own complete and true form. Such was the case when Cassandra recognized, though she had never seen him at all, the man by whom Alexander was to be killed after drinking poison, because sleep had represented him to her.

But one kind of vision is clearer, when the thing appears in a plain image; another requires deeper understanding, when an added array of figures obscures the matter—as when Caesar crossed the Rubicon and brought war upon his native land, in order to signify the terror of the citizens who were to be oppressed through injury inflicted by a fellow citizen,
Source/review notes: The draft supplied a long continuation of Lucan and subsequent prose not present in the source; this has been removed.

A vast image appeared to the leader: the likeness of his trembling fatherland, warning its leader not to attack his fellow citizens with civil arms. For the image of the public empire was an indication of the public terror and of the city laid low beneath Caesar’s name. [Col. 0430D] But if anyone believes that no such image of the empire ever truly existed, appearing in this manner, he will be assured by the testimony of histories. For when the rulers of the city judged that its majesty ought to be honoured in a visible form, they took pains, through refined workmanship, to make in bronze a female figure holding the world in her right hand. When this had been completed in an excellent form, with graceful proportions, fitting arrangement of its parts, limbs appropriate to it, and all things harmoniously corresponding with one another, so that by its entire appearance it demanded not so much the scrutiny as the admiration of the people, certain persons complained that only its lower legs were unequal to bearing so great a mass. The craftsman answered that they were entirely sufficient—until a virgin should give birth—firmly believing a virgin’s childbirth impossible. This was fulfilled when Christ was born [Col. 0431A]: the statue fell and was broken, because human dominion contracts when divine dominion expands.

But when a matter is made clear in sleep by another being who announces it, provided that the person of the announcer is honourable and venerable in the hearer’s eyes, it falls under the kind of oracles. “For an oracle,” as someone has said, “is the divine will proclaimed through the mouth of a human being.” Under the designation “human being” is included whatever appears in human form—whether it is a human, an angel, God, or any other creature. The person of any such being is honourable and venerable either by nature, as a parent; by rank, as a lord; by character, as a religious person; by fortune or office, as a magistrate; or by religion, as God, an angel, or a human consecrated by sacred rites and divine ceremonies. From this it is clear that, if not simply speaking, then in a certain respect even persons who are not merely honourable but detestable may be included under the name of venerable persons by the art of interpretation. [Col. 0431B]

For just as men of the Catholic religion render devout veneration to the true God and to those things made sacred by His gift, so people of heretical and superstitious religion render to fictitious divinities—or rather to real demons—and to their execrable rites, not a reverence properly due, for none is due, but the most shameful servitude. This is gathered more fully from the books of the pagans. Aeneas, directed by oracles, found the Italy promised to and sought by him; and there, not so much by the will of gods as of demons, he established his dwelling and sowed the seed of the Roman race in the garden that pleased them. What else does his father Anchises do in dreams? What Jupiter? What Apollo? What the others, too numerous to recount? [Col. 0431C]

Accordingly, if from that seed there arises a poisoned race—impious toward God, cruel toward human beings, intent upon persecuting the saints, rare in faith, habitually treacherous, slavish in character, kingly in arrogance, foul in avarice, distinguished by its lusts, swollen with pride, intolerable in every kind of wickedness—this ought not to be ascribed to miracles, since their author was a murderer from the beginning and, falling away from truth, fixed death in the world by the dart of envy. Those who are of that father, therefore, though unable to fill up his measure, nevertheless commonly imitate his wickedness. Yet in that garden certain plants, which by apostolic watering bear the fruit of virtue, are known to have been planted by the hand of the Lord.

But if anyone reviews the whole history from the foundation of the city, [Col. 0431D] he will find that they laboured beyond other nations in ambition and avarice, and shook the whole world with various seditions and disasters. They themselves also suffered the very frequent losses caused by their tyranny and seditions, so that scarcely any of their rulers reached the end of life under nature’s guidance. Thus the following satirical lines apply to them most fittingly:

> Few kings descend to Ceres’ son-in-law  
> Without slaughter and bloodshed, and few tyrants by a dry death.

In the canonical Scriptures also there are very many oracles: for example, when Joseph is repeatedly instructed in dreams by an angel; when the Magi are forbidden not to return to Herod; when Peter is taught by the sheet full of creeping creatures that the fullness of the Gentiles is to be gathered in. And when Constantine had been visited by the apostles, the standard of the cross was raised in the citadel of the empire; peace was restored to the churches; and the majesty of the world, through the public voice of secretaries, advocates, and judges, proclaimed aloud that every victory, kingdom, and empire belongs to Christ. [Col. 0432A]

But since the first two kinds are wholly vain, while in the last the truth as it were confronts the mind in visible form, we shall pursue more carefully the middle kind, which spreads a veil of figures over the body, as it were, of truth.

## Chapter XVI. Certain general observations on the meanings of dreams and of other figurative things

For the interpretation of dreams, as well as the disclosure of riddles and figures, one must diligently attend to the meaning of things. This is so much more manifold than the meaning of words as nature’s works exceed the works of an artist who imitates nature. [Col. 0432B] If a word has three or four meanings, it is immediately called *polysēmos* (πολύσημος), that is, “of many meanings.” But every thing bears as many meanings as it has resemblances to other things—provided always that the greater is never a sign of the lesser. For signs are always lesser things.

Thus any substance signifies a human being, because it has something in common with all things. This is clear both in Peter’s figure of creeping creatures and in many passages of Scripture. Further, the more explicit the resemblance, the more kindred and familiar is the signification. Resemblance is either substantial, arising from genus or species; accidental, arising from quantity, quality, or various forms of accidents; or imitative, as when someone conforms to another by any activity or movement of work. In this last way a creature can resemble the Creator, though they share no substantial or accidental feature. An effect also conforms to its cause; and conversely, a cause—provided it is the lesser—may be called like its effect.

Moreover, like things have the same judgment and the same sign. Since signs are often identical, the interpreter’s art is shown especially in this: that under the identity of signs he distinguishes, by cautious discernment, the diversity of things. These are general principles. The particular principles belonging to individual cases are more extensive. Yet it should not be passed over that the power of signs is harsher or gentler according to the character of persons. The handling of money, for instance, foretells a happy outcome to some and a sad one to others. Thus, from unseen causes, Venus’s unexpected appearance more often brings bitterness of fortune. Hence the words of Hypsipyle, mourning the dead Archemorus:

> . . . Never without punishment, through the shadows,  
> Has Venus appeared to me in my astonishment.

For if Venus appears, stirred by remnants of thought or by the impulses of Ceres or Bacchus, she will more properly be assigned to the vanity of dreams—things which the discipline of interpreters despises as vain, in accordance with the saying of the wise man:

> Do not heed dreams; for what the human mind desires,  
> While awake it hopes for, and in sleep sees that very thing.

Yet sometimes [Col. 0432D] the traces of truth must be followed through the antithesis of things. Thus, when ruin threatened the great Pompey, sleep prophesied the opposite of what was seen, setting before the eyes of the doomed leader the city’s joy, the acclamations of a dancing people, and the applause of his theatre, as though the whole empire had been successfully administered. [Col. 0433A]

A thing shameful and obscene on the surface sometimes conceals the substance of a most honourable truth. When Gaius Caesar was young, he dreamed that he violated his mother’s bedchamber. Alarmed by the shamefulness of the dream, he referred the matter to astrologers; they replied that the whole earth was to be subjected to his rule. Thus the hope of a great-souled man was raised toward the seizure of empire.

Finally, to judge by the outward appearance of the deed, who was more just than Uriah? Who more wicked or cruel than David, whom Bathsheba’s beauty invited to treachery, [Col. 0433B] murder, and adultery? Yet all these things produce the opposite meaning, since Uriah represents the devil, David Christ, and Bathsheba the Church, disfigured by the stain of sins. Nevertheless, it is a frequent and almost regular rule that interpretation proceeds from like things to like things.

But it is certain that this division of visions induced by sleep is not made by opposites. For the same experience may partly be a vision, from another source an oracle, and, because of the figures of things, may be classed with dreams; indeed, it may at times possess all their kinds. This is clear to students of Scripture. The vision of Scipio Africanus; the Apocalypse of the apostle; the oracles of Daniel and Ezekiel; the dreams of Pharaoh and Joseph—all establish what has been said.

Truth also dawns more frequently upon some persons, namely those whose mind is well ordered; others are more frequently enveloped in error. [Col. 0433C] When Caesar Augustus was about to fight Antony, he was suffering from a severe illness. In sleep he received an instruction to be present at the battle on the following day, when victory would result. Accordingly, he obeyed, was carried to battle in a litter, and won.

Socrates saw, from the altar of Venus which stood in the Academy, a swan offered to him: it stretched its neck to heaven, touched the stars with its beak, penetrated the region called the Aplane and went beyond the sight of all, singing with such fullness and joy of voice that it delighted the whole world. On the following day Aristides brought his little son Plato from the Academy to Socrates, to be trained in letters and morals. Seeing him, Socrates, discerning the powers of his mind from the disposition of his [Col. 0433D] body, said: “This is the swan which Academic Venus has consecrated to our Apollo.” Plato, setting out for Egypt in pursuit of the learning he sought, saw in a dream that he was captured by pirates on the journey and sold. And this happened while he was travelling.

## Chapter XVII. That the art of conjecture is not to be followed

But while we set forth these teachings of the interpreters, I fear that we may deservedly appear not so much to be pursuing the art of conjecture—which is either no art at all or an empty one—as to be sleeping. Whoever follows the vanity of dreams is little awake in the law of God; and while he impairs faith, he sleeps most perilously. Truth has indeed gone far from him, nor can he grasp it as easily as he can remove an *urionem* [a term uncertain] or cure, with a point, a cataract-like affliction while he gropes at noon with clouded eyes. [Col. 0434A]

Although this drowsiness of unbelief ought to be roused by the goads of faith, and the illusion should be assailed as an evil rather than as an art, nevertheless we do not block the paths or close off the ways of the dispensation of divine grace, so that the Spirit may blow where He wills and pour truth into subject minds according to His own choice. Yet anyone who binds his credulity to the significations of dreams plainly departs both from the sincerity of faith and from the path of reason.

If a speech is uttered ambiguously and has many meanings, would not anyone who, without examining the possible senses, stubbornly persuaded himself of something on its basis rightly seem insufficiently learned? Certainly, as has been said, [Col. 0434B] the meaning of all things is manifold and varied. A careful distinction among manifold meanings must be maintained, lest, while you follow one too eagerly, you fall more grievously into another. Therefore the book of dream-interpretation which bears Daniel’s name is plainly deprived of the strength of authority and truth, since it confines individual things to individual meanings. There is no need to discuss these matters more fully, since the whole such tradition is foolish and the wandering book of interpreters circulates shamelessly in the hands of the curious.

Daniel indeed possessed the grace of interpreting visions and dreams, which the Lord inspired in him. But far be it from us to suppose that the holy man reduced this vanity to an art, since he knew that the Law of Moses prohibited any of the faithful from following dreams. [Col. 0434C] He knew, certainly, that Satan’s attendant transforms himself into an angel of light for the overthrow of human beings, and that visitations are made through evil angels.

Joseph also attained the rule of Egypt by the grace of interpretation. His brothers, out of envy at his dreams, had sold him to the Ishmaelites and made him subject to slavery; but the finger of the Lord, in a mystery no less delightful than salutary, revealed the meaning of future events that had presented themselves to the sleeping king, and by a kind of vehicle of dreams raised Joseph from the filth of prison to the summit of royal honour. Thus he became not only free from a slave, but first among nobles and magnates, surpassed by the king only in the single matter of the royal throne.

[Col. 0434D] If this could have occurred through the artifice of human wisdom, I should believe that one of Joseph’s predecessors had attained it before him, or that the holy man, full of pious feeling, had readily left behind to his brothers and sons—if not to the human race in common, which would have been equitable—the knowledge of attaining it. Moreover, Moses, trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, either did not know this art or despised it, since, abhorring it as an error of impiety, he took care to extirpate it from the people of God.

Furthermore, holy Daniel learned the disciplines and wisdom of the Chaldeans. The holy man would certainly not have done this if he had believed that instruction in the disciplines of the pagans was to be counted as sin. He had companions in learning whom he rejoiced to have as partners in God’s law and justice. [Col. 0435A] For Ananias, Azarias, and Misael learned together whatever a Chaldean could teach; together they abstained from the royal table and its delicacies, as God inspired them; having received vegetables, they were refreshed together; they were content with the same stipends of their service; they served the king together.

But behold: a privilege which no human could confer was given individually to Daniel—that he might bring the riddles of dreams into light and, with the Lord dictating, scatter the shadows of figures. To make the intimacy of divine grace shine forth more evidently, he discovered what the king, lying on his bed, had been thinking; and, joining the vision to the king’s meditation, he wisely explained the mystery of salvation, which a shadow had obscured and which was fulfilled, or is to be fulfilled, at the end of the ages. Do interpreters of dreams commonly examine thoughts as well, empty shadows, unfold coverings, and illuminate the darkness of figures? If anyone enjoys an equal privilege of grace, [Col. 0435B] let him approach Daniel and Joseph, and rejoice with them in the Lord. But whoever is not illumined by the Spirit of truth trusts vainly in the sleepy art, since every art has its origin in nature and its development in practice and reason.

In these matters reason suffers such a failure that it often has no idea at all where to turn or what to judge. Since this happens frequently, it is very easily gathered from a few examples. A certain anxious man—his name has slipped from my memory, though I retain Augustine, a great authority, as the narrator—urgently asked another person, who knew the matter, to explain to him a doubtful point. The other delayed the petitioner’s desire with promises; and, while one man’s urgency [Col. 0435C] was mocked by the other’s cleverness, it happened that on the same night both dreamed. One dreamed that he explained the matter sought to the petitioner; the other that it was very carefully explained to him by a more learned man.

When the shadow of sleep vanished, the latter marvelled that he had attained, without a teacher’s help and without any effort of his own, the knowledge which he had long sought. Then, when as usual he approached the more learned man to demand fulfillment of the promise, the latter said: “What you asked for has already happened, since I came to teach you that night.” Who can explain the cause of this occurrence except by saying that good or evil spirits, according to the deserts of human beings, either instruct them or deceive them?

For, as Jerome relates, mother Church Catholic knows how, when he had been snatched up before the tribunal of God the Judge because he clung too strongly to the books of the pagans, he was compelled there to profess that he would thereafter not merely not read pagan books, but not even possess them. [Col. 0435D] Before making the profession, when he called himself a Christian, the Judge reproachfully objected that he was not Christ’s but Cicero’s man—a “Ciceronian.” Yet I would not rashly say that this ought to be called a dream, since the same most truthful and prudent doctor confirms, even with the solemnity of an oath, that it was not the shadow of a dream, but that the matter was truly enacted with him when the Lord visited him. To provide full proof of his assertion, when he awoke he showed upon his body the bruising of the blows on his skin and the scars of wounds.

But although these things are done by spirits around human beings, the faithful soul rejects no image of a thing that leaves innocence unharmed. If, however, it supplies material for vices—perhaps inflaming lust, or introducing avarice, or an appetite for domination, or anything of that kind tending to the soul’s overthrow—then without doubt either the flesh or an evil spirit sends it. In some persons, through sins that deserve it and with the Lord’s permission, such a spirit rages with so great a license of wickedness that they most wretchedly and falsely believe that what they suffer in spirit happens in their bodies.

Such is the claim that a certain “night-woman,” whether Herodias or the mistress who presides over the night, summons assemblies and gatherings by night; that various banquets are celebrated; that kinds of service are performed in diverse occupations; that now these persons are dragged off to punishment according to their deserts, and now those are raised to glory. [Col. 0436A] Moreover, they claim that infants [Col. 0436B] are exposed to lamiae (child-devouring female demons); sometimes they are torn to pieces and their fragments, swallowed by ravenous gullets, are heaped in their bellies; and sometimes, through the pity of the presiding woman, they are cast out again and restored to their cradles.

Who, even if blind, would fail to see in this the wickedness of mocking demons? This is evident also from the fact that such things happen to weak women and to simpler men, weaker in faith. But if any person suffering this illusion is firmly confronted by someone with certain proofs, the demon is immediately overcome or retreats. As the saying goes, once a person is reproved in the light, the works of darkness cease. The most effective cure for this plague is to embrace faith, withdraw the mind’s hearing from these lies, and in no way look back toward such vanities and false insanities. [Col. 0436C]

## Chapter XVIII. On the foundation of astrology, the exercise of the senses, the powers of the soul, the progress of reason, and the efficacy of the liberal disciplines

Would that the error of astrologers could be removed from more excellent minds as easily as the demons of these illusions grow quiet in the presence of true faith and a sound conscience. Yet they err more dangerously precisely because they seem to ground their error in the solidity of nature and the strength of reason. For it seems rash to transgress universally against the law of nature, and foolish to dissent gratuitously from that which reason has persuaded us. Thus they begin from truths, in order that, advancing longer through truths, they may plunge both themselves and their followers into the snare and pit of falsehood. [Col. 0436D]

They therefore set down as a kind of foundation for their doctrine the probable *mathesis*—the word shortened with the next-to-last syllable brief—which nature introduces, reason approves, and experience of usefulness confirms. From this, through the slippery course of their opinions and under a kind of appearance of reason, they fall most perniciously into the condemned *mathesis*, pronounced with the next-to-last syllable lengthened.

For first they examine the things created by nature and investigate them in many ways, asking now how they consist of their parts, now how they consist of matter and form. To do this more easily, they weigh the powers of the senses and measure the effectiveness of understanding. Since the dullness of the senses does not go beyond the nature of bodily things, they gradually rise to subtler matters with the help of the other faculties.

Sight examines only colours, quantities, and figures, and only in a body that is present. Sound alone reaches hearing. Taste judges flavours. The power of smell is wholly occupied with odours. Touch distinguishes what is hard or soft, smooth or rough, heavy or light, hot or cold, moist or dry. [Col. 0437A] It is sometimes an examiner of shape and aware of quantity and weight. It also perceives pain and pleasure. It is spread throughout almost all parts of the sentient body and clings so closely to the soul that, when it departs, the whole life of the body seems to depart.

But if you inquire into the aforesaid properties of absent bodies, [Col. 0437B] imagination can present them to you by drawing a resemblance from those things which sense has known; and it will be more faithful in proportion as the resemblance is more exact. Hence Tityrus in Virgil (*Eclogues* I.20) complains that his imagination went wrong because it did not attain the resemblance:

> Meliboeus, foolishly I thought the city called Rome  
> Like this city of ours, whither we shepherds often  
> Drive the tender offspring of our sheep.  
> But Rome has raised her head among other cities  
> As cypresses are wont to rise among pliant viburnums.

But if resemblance has represented the thing more familiarly, imagination is faithful and true, such as Andromache employs in Virgil:

> O you, the one image left to me of my Astyanax!  
> Such were his eyes, such his hands, such his face;  
> And now he would be growing to youth of equal age with you.  
> (*Aeneid* III.489)

[Col. 0437C] But if one must turn aside to incorporeal things, reason and understanding are needed, since these cannot be comprehended without intelligence, nor can there be a true judgment about them without reason. Thus, when the others fail, understanding exerts its powers and, as though placed in the citadel of the soul, embraces all lower things, since higher things cannot be comprehended by lower ones. Sometimes it contemplates things as they are, sometimes otherwise; sometimes simply, sometimes in combination; sometimes it joins things distinct, sometimes pulls apart and separates things conjoined.

Understanding proceeds simply when it contemplates some individual thing, conceiving, for example, a human being or a horse. But when it successively embraces several things, it is subject to composition—for example, when the mind grasps the thought that a white human being or horse is running. It joins disjoined things, as if it should [Col. 0437D]

> Join a horse’s neck to a human head,  
> . . . adding feathers from every side in varied forms,

so that, according to the poet,

> . . . a beautiful woman above  
> Ends shamefully in a black fish.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry* III)

Poets convey such things in words to their hearers when they describe a goat-stag, a centaur, or a chimera. Understanding separates things conjoined when, for example, it retains form without matter, though form cannot exist at all without matter, except the form of being and the forms adhering to it—the forms of forms—from which flow those forms that are in matter and make a body.

When understanding considers things in composition otherwise than they are, because it is empty and falls away from the truth of things, it inclines to the error of opinion; and if it asserts that something is, while willing it not to be, it is opinion in the full sense. [Col. 0438A] But although it considers things otherwise than they are, if it separates what is simply conjoined, its conception will not be empty. This produces the most direct road to the whole inquiry of wisdom. For this is the instrument of all philosophy: it sharpens the mind with wonderful subtlety and distinguishes individual things from one another by the property of their nature.

Remove the abstracting intellect, and the workshop of the liberal arts will perish, since none of them can properly be possessed or taught without its operation. Thus it approaches matter without form, just as it approaches form without matter. What it is insufficiently powerful to retain by its proper capacity, it sometimes comprehends through a kind of deficiency of its own: as darkness is seen by not seeing, and silence is heard by not hearing.
