Behold, there is no human being who is not white, black, or a participant in an intermediate colour; nor can there be a human being who is not immediately some particular human being, since to be something and to be numerically one are the same. Nevertheless, understanding apprehends “human being” in such a way that its gaze descends to no individual human, beholding in general what can exist only individually. For diversity in speaking and signifying, as also in understanding, exceeds in its plurality the modes of subsisting; and the human being, who can exist only individually, is enclosed within the universal conception of the mind. [Col. 0438B]

Reason therefore defines what understanding conceives: a rational mortal animal. [Col. 0438C] No one rightly wise doubts that this definition applies only to individual subjects. Accordingly, while reason collects the likenesses and unlikenesses of things, examines more deeply the agreements of things that differ and the differences of things that agree, investigates more diligently what each thing has in common with more things and with fewer, and contemplates more keenly what must belong to individual things and what cannot be absent from them, it finds within itself many states of things—some universal, others singular.

Defining and dividing these in many ways according to its choice, it directs the gaze of the mind into the inner secrets of nature itself, so that nothing natural is wholly hidden from its eyes. First it looks more keenly at substance, which underlies everything. In it the hand of nature is proved to be an artist, when it clothes substance with various properties and forms as though with its own garments, and gives it forms perceptible by the senses, so that it may be more suitably comprehended by the human intellect.

Whatever sense perceives and is subject to forms is singular and primary substance. But that without which primary substance can neither exist nor be understood is substantial to it, and is often called secondary substance. What is present to substance but can be absent while substance remains is counted among accidents. A thing is singular if there is only one; universal if it is common to many, though not by nature, yet by conformity. [Col. 0438D] This perhaps may be found more easily in the understanding than in the nature of things. In understanding it is plainly possible to find genera and species, differences, properties, and accidents, which are called universals; whereas in the actuality of things to seek the substance of universals yields little fruit and infinite labour, while in the mind they are found usefully and with the greatest ease.

For if someone mentally considers the substantial resemblance of things differing only in number, he grasps a species. If, however, an agreement among things differing even in species presents itself to the mind, the breadth of a genus spreads through the mind. Finally, when understanding perceives the conformity of things which nature has made alike substantially or accidentally, it is moved by a comprehension of universals. But when it considers the differences among like things, it comes more familiarly close to the works of nature—which are singulars—in proportion as it does so more exactly. If it considers substance clothed in its properties, it does not depart from nature’s condition. [Col. 0439B]

But if, with species removed, it strips substance, as it were, of the garment of forms, it exercises its acuteness and contemplates more freely and faithfully what things are in themselves and in relation to others. It then examines and distinguishes separately substance, quantity, relation, quality, position, being, place, time, possession, action, and passion. [Col. 0439A] Though these cannot exist separately, they can nevertheless be investigated separately. This inquiry is most useful for the compendium of all philosophy, because it investigates the nature of magnitude and multitude, the two things which encompass and embrace the whole world.

Is abstracting understanding idle or useless when it does these things—understanding by which the soul climbs through the stages of honourable arts to the throne of completed philosophy? [Col. 0439C] It divides multitude, which in its power grows infinitely, just as magnitude conversely decreases infinitely, by a twofold division. It considers multitude now simply and in itself, now in relation to another; it assigns the one to arithmetic and rightly reserves the other for music. It likewise divides magnitude into two kinds: one immovable, which it subjects to geometers; the other mobile, assigned to those who profess knowledge of the stars and heavens.

In these four kinds consists the whole of *mathesis*, that is, the doctrinal discipline; and through these four boundaries of philosophy it attains the perfection of worldly wisdom. The first step is to derive the power of numbers from arithmetic. The second is to draw [Col. 0439D] the grace of proportions from music. The third is to obtain knowledge of measures from geometry. The fourth and final step attains the true position of the stars and investigates the power of heavenly things.

Among those who profess knowledge of the stars, some fall through the error of opinion into fables—Hyginus is found among these. Others are content with imagination alone, leaving judgment about truth to the more learned, and considering it enough if they retain a likeness of truth. One or another astrology admits both groups as professors of its learning. There are others who, in their profession of the stars, attend to truth and are satisfied if they accurately attain the true position and motion of the stars and the theory of the signs.

## Chapter XIX. On the difference between doctrinal mathematics and condemned *mathesis*, on the teaching of astrologers, and on their errors

[Col. 0440A]

But since it is probable that heavenly things possess some power, because even on earth nothing is believed to be produced which does not receive some good effect from the hand of God the Maker, the more curious investigate the power of the heavens and endeavour, by the rules of their astronomy, to account for every individual thing that occurs in the sublunary sphere.

Astronomy is a noble and glorious science if it restrains its following within the bounds of moderation. But if it exceeds them by more unrestrained vanity, it is not so much a form of philosophy as a snare of impiety. Many things are common to doctrinal *mathesis* and divinatory *mathesis*. Yet when divination exceeds the measure of sobriety, differing wholly in its end, it does not instruct but unteaches its professor.

For both divide the zones, mark out the parallels, and give each its own oblique zodiac; both encompass nearly the whole sphere with colures; both measure the course of the planets; both make the Aplane exempt from all error; both draw an axis from the Arctic Pole to the Antarctic; both divide the signs into degrees and points; both preserve the proportion of rising and setting signs and stars. [Col. 0440B] Both likewise agree with natural philosophers in holding that the tenuity of subtle bodies is not scattered into some fixed paths and confined spaces of circles. They also commonly assert that the sun is the source of heat, and they assign the increase and decrease of moisture—because sense proves it—to the moon’s motion, along with many other matters of this kind. [Col. 0440C]

But the *mathesis* that promises a judgment of future events, drawing its origin from the elements of philosophy as stated above, proceeds further. By the rashness of its arrogance it breaks into the prerogative of Him who numbers the stars, and who alone knows their names, signs, powers, courses, places, and times. Yet this is exactly what the astrologer promises himself through the benefit of his astronomy. And they stray farther from the knowledge of truth in proportion as they more proudly attempt to force their way into it.

Thus, examining the nature of the signs according to what they happened to know, while they wavered among similar stars, they call some masculine and others feminine; and perhaps they would have multiplied by offspring, had they not been separated in place and unable to meet in intercourse. They carefully investigate the designs of the planets, because they regard them too as governors of the world; and they say that these designs may easily be discovered from their disposition, movement, application of one to another, and dances among the stars. [Col. 0440D]

Saturn, then, because he is cold and old, is heavy and harmful; from nature he contracts wickedness, and from age ill temper. Thus he is hostile to everyone and scarcely spares even his own pupils. Jupiter succeeds him, by contrast propitious and health-giving, and so benevolent toward all that he harms none subject to him through either his father’s wickedness or his mother’s fierceness—unless perhaps he too has become stationary, retrograde, or suffers a miserable combustion, to the detriment of the world subject to him. [Col. 0441A]

Mars, fierce and naturally untamed, persecutes everyone except his own pupils. Yet he is sometimes softened by Jupiter’s or Venus’s approach, because Venus also is propitious and kindly. Mercury is such as neighbouring planets permit him to be, since he too has a changeable nature and attaches himself to the more powerful. Hence many judge him to be the leader of eloquence, because eloquence joined to wisdom benefits greatly, but joined to wickedness harms greatly.

Lucan, though he did not teach this doctrine, nevertheless touched upon this school of error when describing Rome’s fear and foretelling, by the necessary arguments of astrology, that civil war would inevitably come with Caesar’s approach. For the most learned poet—if he ought to be called a poet, since in his truthful narration of events he approaches historians more closely—indicates that the wickedness of him who alone sat upon the throne of his own domicile would be fulfilled beyond dispute. [Col. 0441B]

Although the maker examines the counsels of the Fates and the mind of the stars, he has not yet conveyed complete knowledge even of the bodies that are visible. For throughout the whole house of astrologers, the question has not yet been resolved whether the stars are composed of the elements or of the fifth essence introduced by Aristotle. As for the objections made to them by boys—whether the stars are soft or hard, and similar questions—they disdain even to hear them, although I have seen certain celebrated men, wise in their own judgment, labour most miserably over such matters.

Nevertheless they explain, and establish by their arguments, what the Fates deliberate and what effect the detected will of the stars will obtain in the sublunary sphere. [Col. 0441C] And perhaps the judgment of the deity is ineffective unless an astrologer pronounces it. Thus he says:

> What kind of disaster, O gods above, by what plague are you preparing...

Cruelty?

The final days of many have converged into one: if the baleful star of Saturn, cold in the highest heaven, had kindled its black fires, Aquarius would have poured out the rains of Deucalion, and the whole earth would have lain hidden beneath the spreading sea.

If now, Phoebus, you were oppressing the savage Nemean Lion with your rays, fires would stream throughout the whole world, and the sky, kindled by your chariot, would blaze.

Those fires are at rest. But you, who ignite threatening Scorpio with his flaming tail and burn his claws—what vast thing are you preparing, Gradivus [Mars]? For gentle Jupiter is oppressed in the west and possesses Venus’s health-giving star; swift Cyllenian Mercury is motionless, and Mars alone possesses the sky. Why have the constellations forsaken their courses and been borne darkly through the world?

[Col. 0441D] Why does the sword-bearing side of Orion shine too brightly?

The madness of war is imminent, and the power of the sword will confound every law by force; virtue will be the name given to unspeakable crime, and this will continue for many years. (Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.649.)

See how, from the character of the planets, the position of the signs, and the concurrence of causes, the outcome of an unavoidable war follows with such clarity. For it belongs especially to the doctrine of this art to establish the natural or causal domicile of the planets. All of them, indeed, except the sun and moon—which alone are content with one apiece—enjoy two domiciles, namely a natural and an accidental one. The natural domicile of each is that in which it had the beginning of its creation—if indeed natal astrologers agree that they were created by the Lord.

Cancer, then, is the moon’s domicile; Leo, the sun’s; Virgo, Mercury’s; Libra, Venus’s; Scorpio, Mars’s; Sagittarius, Jupiter’s; Capricorn, Saturn’s—and this naturally. Accidentally, however, Aquarius falls to Saturn, Pisces to Jupiter, Aries to Mars, Taurus to Venus, and Gemini falls to Mercury’s lot. The moon, however, is useful; God created it, together with the other stars, whatever those people may chatter, to rule the night. What shall I say of the sun, which is the leader, prince, and governor of the other lights? Despite the objections of all these planetary theorists, I do not fear to affirm that it is good and necessary: for everyone sees that it illuminates the day, moderates the world, divides the seasons of the year, brings about the succession of things, and does many other things too lengthy to recount now.

But although the causes of many benefits reside in it and in the other heavenly bodies, there is nevertheless one first cause of them and of everything rightly ordered: the cause which made the world by the power of its own majesty; which formed and established it by the force and immensity of its wisdom; and which was moved solely by goodness to confer upon it both substance and form.

Yet mathematicians, or planetary astrologers, while striving to extend the power of their profession, fall most ruinously into the lies of error and impiety. Nor does the rule of any art remain uninjured unless it is kept within the compass proper to its own kind, especially since, according to the wise man, something is often found outside the rule. Every rule is adapted to some class of things; if it is transferred to another, it immediately runs against a truth exposed to falsehood.

If, therefore, mathematicians were content with the limit of probable *mathesis*, that is, doctrinal learning, they could attain the true positions of the stars; from their signs, by sober instruction, foresee the character of the seasons according to their natural occurrence; and gather the most delightful fruit of their inquiry. But when they broaden their phylacteries and enlarge their fringes—when they attribute too much power to constellations and planets, assigning them some authority over actions—they break out into an insult against the Creator. And because they do not regard with sobriety the heavenly things with which they deal, they are fools, according to the Apostle.

See into what an abyss of error they fall from the very heavens themselves. They ascribe everything to their constellations. Consider whether this does not wrong him who made heaven and earth and all things in them. Next, the constellation imposes necessity upon things in such a way as to destroy freedom of choice. Consider with yourself whether this too is right.

Finally, some have come to such madness that they say an image can be formed by a human being from various positions of the stars; if it is fashioned at intervals of time and with a certain proportional order observed in the constellation, then at the stars’ nod it will receive the spirit of life and disclose the hidden secrets of truth to those who consult it. Although it sometimes commands things that are honourable or right—for example, to wish to preserve oneself in a pure place, or, when something is sought, to invoke God alone with prayers and offerings—it is most certain that this is a deception of evil spirits. In order to be guarded against less carefully, such a spirit often appears to bring precepts of innocence or justice.

No believer is ignorant that this is a form of idolatry. Astrologers, however, ascend much more conveniently into heaven: in the manner of the Academics, they defend as their rightful position whatever seems probable to them. Thus some of them maintain, by a certain irrational impulse, that the planets strive against the Aplane [the sphere of fixed stars]; others, following Aristotle, profess that those same planets are carried along with the firmament. Yet, according to the testimony of Mineius, neither view is found contrary to the rules of astrology.

But natal astrologers, while applying themselves too strongly to divination from knowledge of heavenly things, have lost the knowledge both of the heavenly bodies themselves and of God. Those among them nevertheless seem to excuse their error more conveniently who, with Plotinus, do not take the authority of actions away from the Creator, but assert that a law was established by him once and all at once—a law which no effort ever renders void, since everything he ordained will come to pass as he foresaw. Perhaps Papinius understood this when he said:

A grave and immutable weight begins from on high;
the words of the holy ones have force, and deeds follow the utterance.  
(Statius, *Thebaid* I.212.)

Therefore a power proper to each creature has been bestowed on it by God. Among such creatures the heavenly bodies ought not to hold the lowest place, nor should those more worthy than others possess the least power. Accordingly, he conferred upon them as much as he willed; and although he retained for himself the sovereignty of action, he at least commanded the signs to obey them. Hence, though they do not often perform the works denoted by the signs, nevertheless, with God as author, they render their ministries.

Perhaps this is the source of the saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Psalm 18). Nor is it surprising, since birds also, and very many other creatures, by God’s ordinance and nature’s benefit, anticipate certain future events by signs. If therefore heavenly bodies are signs of things that are undoubtedly to come necessarily, because an immutable ordinance has arranged them, what prevents those things foretold by indications of the heavens from being known by a human being and communicated from one person to another? For signs were given to human beings for instruction, not to those who are aware of the secrets of heavenly things and need no signs.

## Chapter XX. That God’s providence does not destroy the nature of things; that the sequence of things does not alter providence; and that free choice remains alongside providence

[Col. 0443D] These arguments which they advance are plausible; nevertheless, poison lies hidden here beneath honey. Under a pretext of humility and reverence for God, they impose upon things a certain fateful necessity, fearing perhaps that his ordinance may be rendered void unless necessity accompanies the event of things.

Moreover, they invade the prerogative of the divine majesty, claiming the knowledge by which they foresee times and seasons—things which, according to the Son’s testimony, are reserved to the Father’s power. Indeed, they are hidden from the eyes even of those to whom the Son of God disclosed everything that he had heard from the Father.

Then they raise human minds through the swelling of pride or cast them down through the faint-heartedness of despair: they promise long life or worldly prosperity to those needing to be humbled; or, conversely, threaten imminent fates or worldly adversities to those needing encouragement. Certainly they are forbidden to remove the upper millstone of fear or the lower one of hope, between which the faithful soul is ground on the threshing-floor of the world. Yet they remove them, both to the ruin of themselves and their dependents and in contempt of the one who forbids it.

But just as the sequence of things does not alter God’s providence, so the eternal disposition does not destroy the nature of things. For a human being was not unable not to sin because God foreknew that he would sin; nor was the Lord ignorant that he would sin because he was able not to sin. Nor was God unaware that he was able not to die because he was to die through the desert of sin. Nor was he bound to die because the Lord foresaw this.

Thus he was made, in a sense, immortal, though undoubtedly destined to die; and sin brought in death, which the condition of nature had not introduced. From that immortality in which he could not die he would have been transferred to that immortality in which he could not be able to die, had the fault of disobedience not cut off the path of justice and temporarily barred access to so great a glory.

Thus, endowed with the sheer freedom of choice, he could sin and could refrain from sin. No violence of disposition, no compulsion of the fates, no stimulus of his condition, and as yet no defect of nature pressed him toward the fault which, as an unquestionable parent, drove the person who had almost fallen of his own accord into death. But because in injustice he let loose the reins of free choice, he lies so oppressed and buried in it that, by God’s just judgment, because he then refused to abstain from sin when he could, now he cannot abstain even when he wishes.

Yet free choice remains active in him in this alone: that he is sufficient of himself for the work of iniquity, though he rises toward the good only when grace has preceded and aided him. Thus, abandoning justice through himself, he was transferred into the kingdom of sin and death, so that, pressed beneath the yoke of slavery, he is subject to the necessity of sinning and dying. Nevertheless, this necessity is introduced not by a sequence of fates but by the desert of transgression. Otherwise no justice could condemn a human being, since blame would be turned back not upon him but upon its author.

Things, therefore, are possible which will never occur; for if, because they will not occur, they could not happen, they would by no means be called possible. A naval battle, for example, can occur and can also fail to occur; yet one of the two is definitely and determinately true and foreknown.

## Chapter XXI. Whether things unknown can be known by God; that the mutability of things must in no way be attributed to him; that knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, providence, and predestination are the same; that truths are infinite, so that their number cannot be increased or diminished; and that providence imposes no necessity on things

[Col. 0444D] But now the horns of another difficulty arise, and wherever I turn I seem entangled in error. For if things which are not and will not be can exist, then surely God too can know what he does not know, or something can occur without his knowing it. A naval battle which will not occur can, just as it can be fought, be known by those who fight it. Can that which can both exist and be known by a human being not be known by God?

If, then, God can know what he does not know, he can also fail to know what he knows; for there can be no knowledge of contraries at once, since one of them is always exposed to falsehood because it lacks the substance of truth. And there is no knowledge of falsehoods. How, then, is knowledge immutable if things can depart from it and accede to it—if it can be ignorant of what it does not know or know what it does not know?

But if we admit that it is variable, then, despite James’s protest, there is in God variation and a shadow due to change; and he ceases to be the Father of lights if what he foreknew slips away. Even the error of the Gentiles concerning their supposed gods—rather demons—did not deign to admit this. They denied that the Stygian marsh was passable to the gods, saying that it was to be revered by all and was everywhere forbidden to be crossed by heavenly beings. For forgetfulness does not befall the minds of celestial beings. Shall faith, then, receive concerning God what even perfidy recoils from?

Yet everyone agrees that God knows that this will not happen, although many do not admit that he can know, or can fail to know, that it will happen, lest they seem to brand him with mutability or impotence. But let it be granted that God, since many admit this, can—provided, if it is possible, you do not err in proposition or conjunction—know what he does not know. No one thereby proves him mutable, since nothing departs from or accedes to his knowledge, because only that comes to be true in the nature of things which he fixed from the beginning in the point of his stability.

Yet once this is admitted, the most exact care must be taken lest the affinity among verbal moods introduced by Apollonius introduce anything of unbelief or falsehood. This very possibility of occurring is rightly attributed not to the instability of him who is unmoved, but to the capacity of things which can be changed without nature resisting. Thus the complete integrity of God’s knowledge remains altogether unmoved; and if any variation belongs anywhere, it is the mutability of the things known rather than of the knower.

For although the things embraced by God’s knowledge are subject to mutability, that knowledge itself knows no alternations. In one single, indivisible act of vision it encloses and contains the totality of all things which can be spoken or conceived by any sense. It does so so motionlessly that it comprehends things located without place, things beginning without a beginning, things ceasing without an end, things fluctuating without alteration, and temporal things without change or delay, all in the same uniform way; thus past things do not pass away from it, nor future things come to it.

This is not surprising in the state of eternity, except that whatever is there is wonderful; for even our own motionless sight in some measure comprehends the motion and swift course of mutable things. The intellect also contemplates a great thing without extending or contracting itself for a small thing. It needs no place to contain things in places, nor intervals of space to comprehend things separated by distance. In this it follows the Father of lights, though not with equal steps, since the former is subject to many motions, while the latter is subject to none at all.

But although the vision of divine simplicity encloses innumerable things, the substance of the one who foreknows is only one and indivisible, and is essentially one with him, since for him to be is the same as to be wise. Otherwise, let whoever can imagine who joined together these different things; and the first cause of all things would not be such a cause, since it would require the assistance of a joining in order to exist.

The knowledge of a creature, however, is of a very different condition. For spirit and soul do not have being and knowing as the same thing. The soul is disposed toward knowledge of things; when that knowledge has taken root so that, growing strong from the first movement of affection, it cannot be uprooted either at all or without injury to nature, it gives the soul its form by its habit and makes it knowing. This habit, then, is most properly called knowledge, although the things subject to knowledge are sometimes also denoted by the name “knowledge.” Hence, by reciprocal borrowing of names, what belongs to one passes to the other. Thus knowledge too is called manifold, although multiplicity belongs rather to things than to knowledge.

If, therefore, the immensity and simplicity of God’s wisdom are considered, it is one, simple, and indivisible. If the multitude of things subject to it is considered, it is manifold and multiform. Likewise, if you consider the substance of the one who wills or is able—the substance by which he wills or is able—there is one will and one power. If you consider the things he wills and is able to do, there is an infinite number of all things, according to the prophetic saying: “Great is the Lord, and great is his power; and there is no number to his wisdom” (Psalm 147). Likewise: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 111). And: “Who shall declare the powers of the Lord?” (Psalm 106).

This thing, uniform and varied, although ignorant of all variation, is nevertheless called by various names, for various reasons. It is called knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, providence, and predestination. Knowledge concerns things existing; foreknowledge, future things; disposition, things to be done; providence, things to be governed; and predestination, things to be saved.

Predestination is the eternal preparation of grace, through which each person is called to life, as the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified” (Romans 8). And another says: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36).

Therefore, that the knowledge of God, which knows no end, may by a kind of reverent boldness find an end even in speech: God’s knowledge is the true comprehension and complete knowledge of all things that are, were, and will be. For he knows all truths, and only truths; he deigns to acknowledge no falsehood, though he judges and condemns it. His knowledge is therefore necessarily infinite, since it embraces all truths. These assuredly have no number—or their number is so infinite that it finds no end except in God’s wisdom, which alone knows how great it is.

Therefore none of the things he knows vanishes, because they are true, and all things disposed by him are present. Moreover, for things that are to come, truth is their beginning and cause. For the Psalmist says, “The beginning of your words is truth” (Psalm 119); and they will unfailingly come to pass. Heaven and earth will nevertheless pass away, because this too belongs to the words of truth: then, when the deformity of the world has been purged, a new heaven and a new earth will be made anew.

Let each person think what faith in God or reason persuades him. Without prejudice to a better opinion, I judge truths to be infinite in every respect: since in all things that are and are not, it is necessary from the beginning either that they be or that they not be; and, of contradictory alternatives, one is always necessarily true. Thus the number of truths has grown—or rather has come into being—at once and all together in such immense abundance that it can neither be diminished nor increased, and remains altogether infinite forever, except to the infinite wisdom of God.

God’s knowledge, therefore, is unfailing: nothing escapes it, and it admits no increase, since it comprehends all these things. The ancients, however, chose to call the plan of those things which God eternally disposed in wisdom—that is, in the only-begotten Word, creating all things there at once—and which he afterwards brings forth successively into action, conducting each thing according to its foreseen order from generation, by which it begins to exist, through the lot by which it seems to fluctuate among accidents, to corruption, which as it were cuts the thread of existence and thrusts it back into non-being, “the Fates” or “the Parcae.” They did so because the ordinances of God’s providence spare no one from being consigned to their effect, and receive the firmness of their execution from the Word of God, by whom he eternally spoke all things and they were made.

Hence the Stoic believes all things necessary, fearing that immutable knowledge might be rendered void. Epicurus, on the contrary, judges that nothing which happens is disposed by a rational providence, lest providence impose necessity upon mutable things. Thus they err alike, since one subjects everything to chance and the other to necessity.

The disposition of mutable things is therefore immutable; the immutable state of eternal providence contains the course of all mutable things. But because providence itself cannot be moved from the state of its eternity, it frees the sequence of contingent things from every bond of necessity. Although the inaccessible light of God’s wisdom incomparably surpasses the darkness of human knowledge, there is nevertheless one respect in which the eye of our darkness is in some measure equal to its brightness. Just as what I see impending will not occur by any necessity simply because it is seen, so too what God’s eye contemplates need not occur necessarily.

I know that a stone or an arrow which I have hurled into the clouds will, by the demand of nature, fall back to the earth, toward which all weights are borne by their own inclination. Yet it need not simply fall back to the earth, nor need it fall back because I know that it will. It can fall back and can fail to fall back. One of these two, however, though not necessary, is true: namely, what I know will occur. For if it will not occur, then, though it may be thought that it will, it is not known; for what is not is the object not of knowledge but of opinion.

Besides, even if it can fail to be, nothing prevents there being knowledge, which concerns not only necessary things but all existing things—unless perhaps you, with the Stoics, regard existing things as to be reckoned among necessary things. So too, everything which God foreknew will undoubtedly be fulfilled. Yet all such things remain contingent and can also fail to occur. Indeed, with respect to making things occur which we foreknow will occur with him, our sight constrains them no more than his does, although all things derive from his disposition their form of subsistence insofar as they are good. Otherwise they do not bear the image of a form of existence but display, through the defect of their deformity, the lack of that form.

Foreknowledge, then, is not the cause of things occurring; nor is the occurrence of things the cause of foreknowledge. Otherwise the motion of temporal things would be the cause of eternal providence, or streams of evils would flow from the most pure fountain of goodness. God, however, is the author of good things only.

The popular objection in the *Topics*—that, if something is foreknown, it will necessarily occur—is supported by no strength of truth, unless someone attributes modality to the proposition concerning things entirely free from all necessity, so that the truth of the statement rests upon necessity of consequence rather than necessity of the consequent.

Nor will you compel me, although I admit that the nature of disposed things is mutable, to call the knowledge of the disposer mutable on that account. For, according to the hidden meaning of truth itself—I mean John, the son of thunder—it is established by faith that, however great the instability of the things subject to him, “what was made in him was life,” through whom all things were made. Therefore his disposition flourishes and lives in such security of its own stability that no motion of things can shake it and no mutability of time or chance can overthrow it.

## Chapter XXII. That an impossibility does not follow from a possibility; and that the Most High knows what necessarily follows from what, since he alone can do all things

[Col. 0448C] Yet you press on, saying: unless something which God foresaw—for example, that a stone would fall back to the earth—should occur, then the disposition which comprehended it under a certain signification is mistaken. Since, therefore, the stone can fail to fall back, you compel me to choose between two alternatives, neither of which is commonly approved: either to admit that providence can be deceived, which faith abhors; or to agree, absurdly, that by a valid consequence an impossibility follows from a possibility.

I am indeed hemmed in on every side: on this side, lest I diminish the divine majesty; on that, lest I contradict the shouts of many and the opinion which has now persuaded almost everyone. But because it is better to fall into human tongues than to act impiously toward God, if I cannot avoid both, I prefer to seem absurd rather than faithless.

For not everyone has yet been persuaded that an impossibility does not follow from a possibility. Some admit this; but whether they are right, let them see and judge. Yet no wise person agrees that falsehood follows from truth. The true, indeed, follows from the false as well as from the true; but from truth only truth follows. From the possible and the impossible, moreover, something possible sometimes follows; but not every impossibility follows from any impossibility whatever—unless those people have persuaded you otherwise, whose system entails that, if all their claims are true, every impossibility follows from one impossibility and every falsehood from any falsehood.

If you had established that falsehood follows from truth, I would rightly and in the judgment of everyone complain that I had been led away from the path of truth. Yet I am not so pressed by these importunities that I shall strive, by my own rashness, to defend what is unthinkable merely because I find companions in error. With the Academics, if no other path is open, I prefer to doubt each matter rather than, through the destructive pretence of knowledge, rashly define what is unknown or hidden—especially on a point where almost the whole world will oppose my assertion.

I listen to the Academics all the more willingly because they take nothing away from the things I know and make me more cautious in many matters, being supported by the authority of great men. For even in his old age there passed over to them the man in whom our Latin tongue alone found everything with which elegantly to oppose or surpass arrogant Greece: I mean Cicero, the author of Roman eloquence. His book entitled *On the Nature of the Gods* teaches that he turned aside to them, as it were, at the end of life.

Let the Stoics put forward their extraordinary propositions, which they call paradoxes—true, splendid, and admirable propositions. We, proceeding with “thick Minerva,” as the saying goes, approve none of those things which seem false to all people, to most people, or to the wiser individuals in their particular field. Even if Cicero himself or Aristotle were to derive an impossibility from a possibility, I do not think assent is due; I would instead suppose, plausibly, that I myself had been deceived by some cloud of error.

Therefore I escape your traps by saying that providence cannot be deceived, while the thing foreseen can nevertheless fail to occur. But I know what you are accustomed to infer: “Then it is possible that it was not foreseen.” “Let it be so,” I say. “How will you proceed further?” “Then,” you say, “against the protest of philosophy, what is can fail to be, what was can fail to have been, and things already past can be recalled so that they were not.”

Certainly I do not confine God’s infinite power within the laws of my petty learning and petty reasoning, nor do I impose a limit upon what has none. I know that he can do all things. Yet I clearly see that you argue fallaciously. First, because you circumscribe the immensity of divine majesty by the measure of human smallness, and distinguish the immutable state of eternity by the image of slipping things and the changing variety of successive times. But, from what has already been said, it ought to be understood that the situation here differs greatly from that among created things: no movement whatever touches the state of eternity, whereas every creature is changed by the accession or departure of accidents.

When a human being foresees some future thing, a certain motion immediately comes upon the mind, so that the soul, by a kind of application of itself, prefigures within itself the image of another future action; and then it sometimes stores that image, as though in the archives of memory, and sometimes unfolds and turns it over as though in a mirror of native purity. It is easier for this motion to be wholly absent from the soul than for the soul to adhere to it in continual contemplation. This motion, indeed, either is providence, or produces providence, or is connected with it by some kinship.

But when the outcome of the future action frustrates the preceding motion and the image conceived from it, the agitation of the mind is empty and vanishes like a dream-shadow, without a body of truth. Yet because the motion truly existed in the soul, it cannot fail to have existed in the soul; and the soul moved by the agitation of motion cannot fail to have been moved.

[Col. 0450A] The state of divine simplicity, however, is of an altogether different condition. As stated above, in one simple and indivisible act of vision it contemplates all things that are, have been, and will be; and it is moved by no passing of mutable things. Rather, beholding all things within itself once and all together, it remains unchangeable:

> Remaining stable, it grants that all things be moved.

Although words of past or future time are sometimes applied to God, this indicates not that anything thereby departs from or comes to him but, where anything is said properly, the mutability of the things subject to him. Thus, when we hear that he foreknew something, we do not at all understand that his knowledge has passed away in a flow of time. Rather, if we follow the nature of the words, we understand that a time preceded in which it is rightly believed that he had knowledge of that which was going to be.

Accordingly, it is certain that from eternity he foresaw all things—not because time, by its motion, takes anything away from his vision, but because his vision, belonging to one who is by nature prior to all time, always comprehends all things. Therefore his providence is not deceived in its disposition, because the execution of the work always accompanies it. Nor can he be deceived, since nothing can be hidden from his eyes by the mutability of things, the flight of time, or changeability.

Human planning, however, can be deceived and is deceived, because the thing whose image a person has prefigured within himself either does not occur at all in the course of time or appears publicly in a different form. Yet not everything enclosed under the signification of a past-tense verb must be counted among past things.

If I profess that I have lived while the Palatine Peripatetic was flourishing, I do not thereby confess that my life has slipped away or is past. Or if, while Eugenius presided, I dissented from the Arians, I did not depart from the integrity of that faith and confession on account of the past tense. Rather, because at one time it was true to say, “I now live; I think thus,” I fittingly and truly confess afterwards that I then lived and thought thus, without thereby confessing that either my life or my thought has passed away.

I know, however, who said that we err in this: that we do not look ahead to death. A great part of it has already passed; death possesses whatever portion of life lies behind us. But surely, if life had slipped away from him once for all, he either would not say this at all or would say it as one restored to life.

It is therefore not necessary that everything signified by a past-tense word has passed away. Although many are predestined, predestination has not thereby passed away because they have been chosen. And although they can be not predestined, something which is past can be recalled so that it did not pass away.

For the designation “predestination,” in whatever grammatical case of the word you use it, so far as its own force is concerned, signifies the future rather than the past; and it indicates that the person of whom it is said is to be saved, unless he has already ceased to be one who is to be saved. It is, as the saying goes, a fertile word, and always contains within itself the meaning of another verb. It does not, therefore, introduce any motion of the predestined person, but declares that, for the person to be saved, the original grace of God who disposes things opens the gate of salvation and the door of mercy, so that as time proceeds he can be saved—indeed, he will be saved—although he can also fail to be saved.

Nor should you raise against me that saying of your Aristotle: that what was, because it was, necessarily was, and that what is, because it is, necessarily is—so as to infer that statements having a past-tense copula are either definitely true or definitely and necessarily false. This objection will not help you at all, since Aristotle’s own words raise a question and provide no, or only slight, support for deciding the point.

For statements which join to the past the force of a contingent future overturn the integrity of the rule: for example, “Yesterday it was true that you would read tomorrow,” or “Plato at some time knew that you would sleep.” In these statements, the certainty of the past tense wavers because of the attached future. For while you can fail to sleep, Plato can have failed to know this—not because the movement which existed in his soul can fail to have existed, but because what was knowledge can, through the mutability of things and the slipperiness of time, be reduced to opinion, if indeed there can be any knowledge of contingent future things, though there is an undoubted opinion that plausibly imitates knowledge.

Likewise, what we said was true yesterday can fail to have been true—not because a past thing is recalled, since no thing has passed away in this respect, but because a future thing is awaited, hanging upon the hazards of fortune in order to be.

Then you yourself may have foreseen some good which perhaps will be good in the future, yet may not be good; and likewise you may be said not to have foreseen it as good—not because you can fail to have foreseen what you did foresee, but because what you foresaw may not be good. [Col. 0451C] Likewise, you may have promised or stipulated something advantageously, and you may be said not to have promised or stipulated it advantageously; yet what you did promise or stipulate, you cannot fail to have promised or stipulated. Furthermore, you entered before the man following you into Sempronius’s estate; and if you preceded another, someone else either followed, follows, or will follow you. Therefore, since the occurrence of the consequent may be nullified, the truth of the antecedent also may be weakened, so that you who had gone before may be able not to have gone before. Yet you cannot fail to have entered where you did enter; nor can what has been done be counted among things undone, nor can what has passed be recalled so that it may not have been.

For in all these things which have passed—whether conceived in the mind, expressed in words, or completed in action—they cannot, and will not, thereafter be able not to have been; although, while their nature had not yet fixed a certain outcome, they could have failed to be such as they were going to be. Within the compass of such things are enclosed all those designated by the term “imminent,” whatever their kind, although that term is more commonly applied by nature to quantity, relation, or any of the other categories. What wonder, then, if He who can do all things can also be said not to have foreseen what He foresaw, since faith establishes that things foreseen may fail to occur and things not foreseen may occur, although they cannot occur apart from the gaze of providence?

For Isaiah says: “If you are willing to walk in my commandments and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land. [Col. 0452A] But if you are unwilling and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you, because the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1). Behold, free choice is preserved here: by saying “if you are willing” and “if you are unwilling,” he promises punishment or reward to all in either direction, not from an irrevocable judgment or fate of God, but according to the merit of each person. A condition of meriting placed in the will would certainly be useless if the necessity of acting or not acting were bound by the chains of providence or fate.

If this is insufficient for contentious persons, could not the Son, according to evangelical testimony, during his Passion have asked his Father to provide him with more than twelve legions of angels, though it is clear afterward that not this, but its opposite—that which happened—had been foreseen? Nor should it trouble a keener mind if, in examining so great a majesty, examples fail us and arguments are not abundant, since reason removes wonder, and the adducing of examples excludes uniqueness. But He, wonderful in ineffable uniqueness and unique in wondrous immensity, surpasses every understanding, not only of human beings but of angels.

I know indeed that the investigator of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory, and that, by the decree of the Most High, the beast which touches the mountain is to be stoned. Hence what is set forward in such matters is said with the disposition of an inquirer, without prejudice to better views, rather than with rash contentiousness, as though establishing something against the truth. Nor do I profess to know why He rejected this man and chose another, except that with the Fathers [Col. 0452C] I judge that in the former case the hidden justice of God must be revered, and in the latter the manifest mercy of grace embraced.

For he who was caught up into the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter, did not so much discuss as marvel at this difficult question; with humble confession he revered “the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” and declared his judgments incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable. He who rejoices that the uncertain and hidden things of God’s wisdom have been made manifest to him affirms that God’s works are magnified above human understanding; and, while he searches all things, he recognizes the thoughts of the Most High as exceedingly deep. This truth accords with what holy Solomon proclaims in Ecclesiastes to the hearing of the faithful:

“There is a man who by day and by night does not take sleep with his eyes; and I understood that, of all God’s works, man can discover no reason for those things which are under the sun. And the more he labours in seeking, the less he will find; even if a wise man says that he knows, he will not be able to discover it” (Eccles. 8).

If, then, the reason of things under the sun cannot be discovered, who will fully give an account of things above the sun? “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 2), or “who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. 40). It is therefore certain that reason must be sought in all things with zeal for truth, yet with a pious intention recognizing its own weakness and making progress through all things by persuading itself faithfully to honour the divine majesty and constantly to embrace the abyss of unfailing mercy.

Finally, philosophers have laid down that [Col. 0453A] predicates remain such as their subjects permit, and that the force and property of all predicaments are bounded by natural limits; but when one ascends to the summit of theology, this same force is altered, as though stripped of its native colour and strength. Certainly the force of words fails, and mortal understanding itself gives way where the immensity of the divine majesty is examined. In natural matters, namely those which increase or diminish the number of things, it holds that what has been cannot fail to have been, or that what has passed cannot fail to have passed; provided, however, that what was true—namely, that he would perhaps read—may nevertheless be able not to have been true.

What is past, therefore, cannot be recalled so that it may not have been; and likewise that which hangs upon the hazards of fortune, while by the facility of its nature it awaits the outcome of either possibility, is subject to no necessity of occurring. Thus perhaps, when the effect of providence is not fulfilled, what was going to occur and may also fail to occur may likewise not have been foreseen. Yet, as has been said, by the boldness of inquiry I do not diminish omnipotence or prescribe any measure to its immensity. But with many I hold this: whatever God has foreseen will occur; and if it does not occur, he did not foresee it. Hence at least this conclusion is probable: if it can fail to occur, it can also have failed to be foreseen.

For truth itself knows what truly follows from what, and the primal Reason fully and perfectly weighs the connection of arguments. Ancient Academy grants the human race [Col. 0453C] this liberty: that whatever seems probable to anyone, that person may defend by right. A Palatine Peripatetic of our own time used to oppose all these conditions: where the conception of the antecedent does not include an understanding of the consequent, or where the destruction of the consequent is not set down as the contrary of the antecedent; for all wish to maintain a necessary consequence, although some are content with probability alone, though it be great.

For as a more evident opinion accompanies knowledge because of its clarity, so individual propositions, the more probable they are, present a more trustworthy image of necessary propositions. And lest you suppose that I drift upon the slippery tide of mere opinion, I bring forward the great Augustine as the authority by whom I am defended. Explaining the Gospel passage where the Saviour speaks of the many dwelling-places [Col. 0453D] in the Father’s house, he says: “‘If it were otherwise, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you’ (John 14): that is, if they had not been predestined, I would have said, ‘I shall go and predestine [them].’” He applies the diversity of dwelling-places prepared in the heavenly Father’s house to divine predestination, which, according to the good pleasure of the disposer, produces for those to be saved diverse charisms of graces and gifts.

Since so great a Father adopted this sense of interpretation as to say, “If they had not been predestined, I would have told you: I shall go and predestine [them],” it is credible that while the outcome of things remains contingent, if it please the Almighty, those not yet predestined may be predestined to life, and those already written in the book of life may, by merits demanding it, be blotted out by Him. Hence perhaps: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68). Likewise: “Either forgive them this offence, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written” (Exod. 32).

“He who is born of God,” says the Evangelist, “does not sin, because heavenly generation preserves him” (1 John 5). Heavenly generation is, of course, eternal predestination, and all its children enter into life, though it may be possible for those same persons, by the merit of transgression, to stray from righteousness, which is the way of life. If you do not believe me, hear even him whom, if an angel from heaven contradicted him, would be condemned by a most fitting anathema. “Father,” he says, “of those whom you gave me, I lost none; but keep them” (John 13). Did he not, I ask, already lose those who had gone back? Did he not in a certain manner already lose Judas? But surely the Son had not accepted him in the secret counsel, nor had the Father given to the Son to be preserved among those enrolled, the one who had not been predestined to life.

But if the others were preordained, if they could not fall, why does the Son intercede for them with such earnestness? Therefore they were to be saved; and yet, while they were pilgrims away from the Lord, they could merit death, not being constrained to life by any necessity of predestination. One boasts that nothing will separate him from the love of Christ, yet he chastises his body and reduces it to slavery, lest after preaching to others he himself should be found reprobate. In the Apocalypse, too, the angels of the churches are warned now [Col. 0454C] to repent and perform their first works, lest their lampstand be moved; now to hold their place, lest they yield it to another. Why so, if things that were to come could not be changed?

Nor was this opinion unknown to pagan philosophers, who say that the sequence of fates is immovable, not because it cannot be moved, but because it never in fact happens to be moved. Hence:

> Pharsalia could have departed from the midst of its fates.

And likewise the poetic line which the old man of Chartres used more frequently in the straits of fortune:

> The fates will find a way, etc.

But things that have passed and have been completed by the subsequent effect of the ordering cannot, by nature, fail to have been; though I would not dare assert anything in either direction [Col. 0454D] to the injury of Him who orders all things. Yet the most learned of doctors—I mean Jerome—says: “I shall speak boldly: although God can do all things, yet he cannot restore a virgin after her fall.” He can nevertheless crown one who has been corrupted afterward.

Indeed, as the same interpreter explains, the Apostle’s definition of a virgin is that she be “a virgin holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7). But undoubtedly God can both sanctify the soul by virtues and restore corrupted flesh, so that the whole substance of one who had fallen may seem to have been raised again. But if, using an oratorical trope, he meant that things which have been cannot fail to have been, there was no need to resort to a fallen virgin, since the same statement—or error—could have been found in every past event. I deliberately distinguish a statement from an error, [Col. 0455A] because a statement ought always to convey truth. Thus in holy Job you find: “Who is this who enfolds statements in unskilled words?” (Job 38).

But perhaps there is some degree of virginity which it is impossible for any corrupted woman to attain. Moreover, what is called “possible” sometimes refers to the facility inherent in individual things, either by the reckoning of fortune or by the suitability of an arrangement; sometimes it looks to the nature of things themselves; and sometimes it is turned toward the source of all things, the divine majesty, from which comes all power—not only the authority of persons, but the power of all things that can be seen or conceived. Hence Solomon’s saying: “All power is from the Lord God” (Wis. 6). Against this I shall never raise any insolence, [Col. 0455B] certain that it alone can cast both soul and body into Gehenna.

## Chapter XXIII. The objection of the new Stoic

There remains for you the question of that Stoic of yours, whom I saw lingering for a long time in Apulia, so that, after many vigils, long fasts, countless labours and sweats, at the cost of so great an unhappy and useless exile, he might carry back to Gaul Virgil’s bones rather than his meaning. This Louis asked whether you could do something which you are by no means going to do. When you conceded this, he offered you a thousand gold pieces if you would bring it about. If perhaps you rejected them, he ordered that they be multiplied for you by whatever sum you liked, so that you might do what can easily be done. At last he burst into an impudent and shameless [Col. 0455C] laugh, not understanding or scorning the force of the conjunction of opposites; and before those standing by he pointed at you with his finger as ridiculous, because you had despised so much money freely offered.

You heap together very many arguments of this kind. Yet I am not driven by these goads to believe that all things are necessary because they are known, or that no contingent things are known because they are not necessary. Indeed, compared with him I seem to myself a modest little scholar among the Peripatetics, since in the *Attic Nights* he confessed, under pressure from this difficulty, that he did not know that he was not a cicada.

## Chapter XXIV. That mathematicians are rash in presuming to subject future indifferent events to their judgment

Those men also, although we disagree in many respects, admit with me [Col. 0455D] that they do not know everything—those with whom the stars converse and who, as it were, draw truth out from the very bosom of the heavens. The most moderate among them neither promise effects to things from the stars nor bind them to necessity by a law of disposition; but because events are to come and are announced by definite signs, they are not ashamed to predict them.

But if the order of future things can change, it is rash to determine by a certain judgment a thing uncertain by its nature. If, however, it cannot change, what is the use of investigating with such curiosity what no diligence can avert? Perhaps, though it may be otherwise, the thing is not uncertain, and an unquestionable reasoning from signs excuses the rashness of judgment. For although it is possible for the thing to be otherwise, manifest signs announce that it will nevertheless happen thus. “It is not my concern,” says the secretary of the stars, “whether it can be otherwise, since I do not doubt that the thing in question will occur thus.”

But what is this certainty of signs? Surely the often deceptive experience of events, difficult judgment, and the varied and manifold meaning of the signs themselves. Variety, moreover, introduces ambiguity; and in ambiguous matters every determination is dangerous. But let it be that signs are uniform: whence is that single meaning known, or what testifies that it is false? “Nature,” you say? Is it that which consists in things, or that which consists in the divine will? I do not gainsay the divine will, for I know that “he has done whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113). If it has become known to you, well and good. You may indeed see light in that light and bring forth unquestionable truths from the book [Col. 0456B] which is sealed to others but open to you, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden; a book which I had heard it permitted to no one to open except the Lamb who was slain and by his own power destroyed death.

No longer, then, marvel with the Apostle at the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, since his judgments are comprehensible to you, his ways traceable under the guidance of the stars, and the deep abyss of his judgments fordable for you. But if you rely on that nature which consists in things—that is, in the usual course of events—you vainly flatter yourself about intimacy with the stars, since many things depart from the customary course of events and strike human senses with greater wonder precisely because they appear not merely unfamiliar but contrary to nature itself: for example, when an eclipse of the sun occurs at the full moon, or when the moon suffers an eclipse of its light around conjunction, around the full moon, or beyond it.

For he who gave the stars their law, who controls the courses of time by the bridle of his will, who fits the moments of things to their times, can, whenever and however he wills, produce an unprecedented effect—while nature wonders—or a rare one, from concurrent causes which had been accustomed to produce otherwise. “For who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. 40), or who will say to him, “Why do you do so?” (Job 11). Surely he is the Lord: he will do whatever is pleasing in his own eyes. Therefore He alone who has ordered all things can fit times to the arrangement and vary the moments of things with the times; and though according to the measure of his good pleasure he has granted creatures knowledge of many things, the Trinity has reserved this uniquely for itself.

He knows when and how long anything will occur, and He dispenses the divisions of time through whom time itself was made. He also paints times by the motion and variation of things, as by certain colours; He binds the revolving wheel of time by a sort of yoked connection of the things that hold it together; and, to present to understanding a thing incomprehensible, He wonderfully gives time form, as it were, by the properties of things themselves. “It is not yours,” says the word of the Most High, “to know the times” (Acts 1): that is, to know fully when and for how long he will do anything, or the moments, so that you may comprehend the modes and variations of things to come. Behold why it is rash to subject future events to a certain judgment. For they are placed [Col. 0457A] in the Father’s power, not under a necessity of occurring. Things placed in power can be so and can be otherwise; but things under necessity must be so.

## Chapter XXV. That an argument from its sign is not necessary; concerning Hezekiah, Ahab, and the Ninevites; and that things signified can change

“But perhaps,” you say, “Truth, speaking to those close to her, says, ‘It is not yours,’ so that she may reserve so great a prerogative for outsiders—namely, mathematicians.” Let it be so, if only a faithful mind is satisfied. But how great, as has been said, is this certainty of signs? Surely, when

> … the signs of their course  
> Have abandoned their own paths,  
> > (Lucan, *Pharsalia* 1.664)

something new is believed to be impending. I do not contend so far as to believe that great events are never preceded by any indications, since I have learned that the Lord gave the sun, moon, the elements themselves, and their adornment a power of signifying. But that there is an art by which someone can answer truly concerning all future matters put to him—or whether there is such an art at all—has either not yet become known to human beings or does not exist; this, on the authority and reasoning of many, is my conviction.

If I cannot persuade you, because you endlessly raise against me those things you say about providence and fate, and because examples from various histories which you offer oppose me, I have nevertheless persuaded myself not to acquiesce in this vanity. [Col. 0457C] I do not believe that signs and the things signified have such a connection that one necessarily follows from the other. Hear why I believe this, unless courtly trifles detain you.

King Hezekiah fell mortally ill. Do you not believe that the king of Judah found a physician who, from indications of urine, pulse, and many prognostic signs, discerned the severity of the illness? Then perhaps he received in his own body the answer that he would die, having been brought so low that he no longer hoped to live. Finally, the Holy Spirit announced that death stood at the doors. What surer sign do you seek? What, leaving other considerations aside, is certain if you doubt the testimony of the Holy Spirit? Will you deny that Isaiah said: “You shall die in spirit and shall not live” (Isa. 38)? Yet he lived [Col. 0457D] and did not die; fifteen years were added to him through the mercy of Him who has placed the outcome of future things in his own power.

And perhaps the mercy of God, who threatened him, swallowed up the death intended by the failure of nature and of vital powers, because through repentance he had died to sin. Ahab also, that most impious king, when with Jezebel—joined to him not so much in marriage as in cruelty—he had possessed the vineyard through the blood of holy Naboth, awaited the death that was impending, the Lord having announced it. If you do not believe that God himself announced it, hear Elijah. For he says: “Thus says the Lord: You have killed and taken possession” (3 Kings 21). Likewise: “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, there they shall lick [Col. 0458A] your blood, and dogs shall eat Jezebel before the walls of Jezreel” (ibid.).

When Ahab heard this, he tore his garments, put sackcloth upon his flesh, fasted, and slept in sackcloth. And the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: “Because Ahab has reverenced my face, I will not bring the evil in his days” (ibid.). Behold, the punishment owed to Ahab is deferred to his descendants because he repented, while Jezebel, persisting in crime, is condemned by present judgment. One and the same sentence exposed the blood of Ahab and Jezebel to dogs; and yet it is changed in part and remains unmoved in part, because the Author of times so disposes all things.

So too the Ninevites, freed from imminent destruction, changed the Lord’s sentence by undertaking repentance at Jonah’s preaching, by decree of their king and princes. Does the judgment of Jupiter and Mars seem to you truer and more reliable than the judgment of the Creator? Certainly you will not follow Plautus’s advice if you attribute this power to the planets. For when the Sycophant asked Mandrogerus whether the planets that turn the whole by their numbers should be propitiated, Mandrogerus replied that they were neither easy to see with our sight nor approachable in speech, adding that they roll atoms in their mouths, count stars, and cannot change themselves alone.

Thus he introduces the necessity of outcomes from the arrangement of the stars so as elegantly to mock, with sufficiently urbane wit, those who strain their sight in contemplating things that escape sight and address those who disdain to speak. And since they roll atoms in their mouths, one must fear that if an atom should by chance obstruct an astrologer, he may stumble while receiving the pronouncement of the heavenly bodies. Let their authority, then, be eminent, while that of the Creator remains stable and unshaken. Whatever your Mars or Jupiter may suggest to you, God is true; and when you believe them more than God, you are a most ruinous liar.

Indeed, the stars are false in his sight, and even in his angels he finds perversity. Yet, to confess the truth, the stars do not lie to you; you yourself do. Blame yourself for being deceived. For who compels you to think falsely? Has God persuaded you that what you conjecture from preceding signs will come to pass is unchangeable? Or are you deceived because the whistling potter—or this world—says:

> [Col. 0458D] … Through the ages nothing wanders without law,  
> And the stars revolve with no uncertain motion.  
> Or, if fates are in motion, is ripe destruction prepared  
> For the city and the human race?

And the same poet states more plainly:

> … And what profit is there in seeking an end from the gods above?  
> Peace comes with its master: lead on, Rome, the continuous chain  
> Of evils, and draw out slaughter through many ages,  
> Now made free only by civil war.

But surely your many gods could not avert the future war, because they are many—or rather, none. Yet the one God and Lord of all could have done this. For he knows how to change his sentence if you put an end to wrongdoing through his favour. Thus Nebuchadnezzar, redeeming sins by almsgiving and iniquities by mercies toward the poor on Daniel’s counsel, escaped for a time the Lord’s impending sentence, until, glorying in the court of Babylon, he said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I myself have built as a royal house, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my name?” (Dan. 4). Thus by this boastful utterance he called back upon himself the sentence of God which he had already begun to escape.

## Chapter XXVI. That God’s sentence can be moved; that God’s counsel is unchangeable; that God’s will is the first cause of all; and that astrology is a path to damnation

Since, then, the sentence of the unchangeable God can be moved, will the pronouncement of wandering and erring stars remain immovable? Yet, however his sentence may be moved, the counsel of the Lord remains forever. And what sign of God’s counsel and will is surer [Col. 0459B] than a divine command or prohibition? Does he not rightly appear to will what he commands? Certainly he commanded the patriarch to sacrifice the only-begotten son of promise. Did the patriarch rightly obey the one commanding? Indeed, entirely rightly, because a command is the surest indication of that will which is the first cause of all things and is never deprived of its effect.

It is so truly first that, if one asks why something is so, the most proper answer is: “Because he so willed,” he who “has done whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113). But if one asks why he willed it, the question is foolish, because a cause is sought for the first cause, namely will, which has absolutely no cause. It is commonly said—and truly—that it is in a prince’s power to judge more leniently than the laws, since the person who enacted a law has the power to derogate from or repeal it. Will the author of heaven, then, not dare contradict the law which your potter imposes upon heaven?

It is proper and lawful for the prince alone to consider an interpretation standing between law and equity. Where one rule of law advises one thing and equity, concerned with the public advantage, another, the prince’s interpretation must be sought; this is general and necessary. Where there is doubt about the written text and the judgment, the intention of the author must be sought. Who, then, made you the interpreter of heavenly things? How do you know what is expedient? With what rashness do you ascribe another’s works to your own—indeed, to God’s—stars? For I grasp that exceedingly subtle argument of yours:

> [Col. 0459D] You who set threatening Scorpio’s tail ablaze  
> And scorch its claws,  
> What so great a thing are you preparing, Gradivus?  
> > (Lucan, *Pharsalia* 1.658)

But the father of lies, who taught you to attribute this to heavenly things, deals deceitfully with you: after staining the creature with these marks, he thereby defames the Creator of the creature itself. Finally, to suspend the poor souls deceived by fraud upon the swelling pride produced by a prediction of inevitable future events, or to cast them down into the abyss of despair, is madness. This is the fruit of their astrology which horoscope-readers bring forth; even more errant than their planets, as they depart from the knowledge of piety through long investigation of signs, they descend alive into hell with him who rose like the morning Lucifer, [Col. 0460A] and make others partners in their ruin.

But when such things are put before you or urged against you, what do you do? You laugh, indeed, and indulge too much in your hooked nostrils; you hold the simplicity of faith in derision, and flee to the bosom of providence, plunging yourself wholly into its unsearchable abyss like another Antaeus. You have made inaccessible light your refuge, and from there attack the plainness of faith, as if the fountain of truth were a stronghold of error.

But let it be: I cannot silence this old complaint about providence, nor am I sufficient to untie the knots of all questions. For who is so wise as to satisfy every question of any ignoramus, much less yours? Plato, finally, the chief of all ancient philosophy, could not explain some trivial question of sailors—as the story goes, though it would more truly be said of Homer. When he was mocked by them more shamelessly and persistently, being a man of modest disposition, he breathed his last and died, as though pierced by the poisoned dart of humiliation. For he was ashamed that, as though in reproach to the whole Academy, they had cast it in the face of the chief philosopher of Greece that he was ignorant even of the smallest matters.

Flavianus asserts in the book entitled *On the Traces of the Philosophers* that the followers of Xenophon, moved by envy against Plato’s glory, shamelessly invented this story. Yet very many maintain that he voluntarily gave up his soul because of the mystery of number, once he had completed that year of life produced by multiplying nine by itself, since thereafter nothing comes to humanity except labour and pain. I confess that I know few things and, together with many people, am ignorant of very many; yet I do not cast aside the gift of life, like Homer overcome by shame.

If, then, I am unable to settle the dispute between providence and free will, or reconcile the incompatibility of fate with the facility of nature, is this for that reason less true? Just as in civil law the defendant is very often more favourably situated, so in philosophical investigations there are certain cases in which the plaintiff’s side generally seems stronger. I judge this to arise from our deficiency. For understanding fails concerning the first principles of things. Among these I think it wholly fitting to count the scrutiny of providence, the investigation of matter, and many articles of our faith. While you destroy the difficulty of one complaint regarding providence, [Col. 0460D] like a hydra with its head cut off, the heads of many questions grow in its place.

If we proceed into the forest of matter, we at once experience the state of dreamers, situated between some substance and no substance. When the origin of the soul is questioned, understanding sets before us the theory of propagation. Finally, how will you avoid Arius’s snares unless by the strength of faith, when you admit a Trinity of persons in the divine substance? Or how will you escape Sabellius’s hands unless by the reasoning of faith, when you admit one simple and indivisible substance of divinity? Yet these things are no less true because they may be attacked by many questions.

And although the wisdom of God has made itself visible to us in the mystery of the Incarnation, it has not made itself so palpable to our understanding [Col. 0461A] that we can range through it in every direction, knowing what is the length, breadth, height, and depth of all things. If, however, the path of astrologers were altogether praiseworthy, great Augustine would not have so greatly repented of having inclined to their consultations. Moreover, that most holy doctor Gregory, who watered and drenched the whole Church with the honeyed rain of his preaching, not only ordered astrology to depart from the court, but, as has been handed down by elders, consigned to the fire the writings, tested by reading,

> Whatever the Palatine Apollo held.  
> > (Horace, *Epistles* 1.3.17)

Among these were the principal writings which seemed to reveal to human beings the mind of heavenly things and the oracles of those above. Why say more? Is it not enough that the catholic and universal Church detests this vanity [Col. 0461B] and punishes with lawful penalties those who presume to practise it further? But lest we seem not so much to persecute as to follow the error of the planetarians, let the discourse now proceed to the remaining matters. Those who serve this curiosity can no more be truthful than they can be humble and temperate—like men who seek the chief places at banquets and feast splendidly every day. Finally, I have heard of very many of them and known many, but I recall no one who persisted long in this error upon whom the hand of the Lord did not inflict fitting vengeance.

## Chapter XXVII. On haruspices, chiromancers, practitioners of Pythonic divination, and Saul’s downfall
What am I to say of necromancers, whose impiety, [Col. 0461C] by God’s ordering, has now everywhere become contemptible in itself, except that those deserve death who try to borrow knowledge from death?
