As for bird-watchers, augurs, diviners from the leaping of victims, soothsayers, pythonists, haruspices, and the rest—whose enumeration, because of their multitude, would be tedious—it is superfluous to weave a longer discourse, since none of them now comes forth into the light, but, if any such person exists, practises works of darkness in hiding. Yet some of them must be touched upon to a certain extent for definite reasons. And, though they conceal themselves, haruspices still survive, to their own harm. These have already been described as divining partly from the entrails of animals. Under the name of *exta* are reckoned all things covered by the outermost layer of skin. Hence it is evident that those who prophesy from the shoulder-blades [Col. 0461D] of rams, or from the bones of any animals whatever, are to be numbered among them.

Palmists likewise boast that they know the truths hidden in the wrinkles of hands. Since their error rests on no reasoning, there is no need to assail it by arguments—although reason itself defeats them precisely because they fail in reason. Yet there is one thing which I ask of you most attentively, if you will listen to me patiently. What do these triflers—whom, I do not doubt, you know—produce when they are consulted about uncertain matters? When a royal expedition was to be led against the Nivicollinian Britons, of what did the consulted haruspex forewarn you? Although the hidden truth should not have been sought from him, since a fabricator of lies was more to be believed in his watchman’s service than as an interpreter of hidden [Col. 0462A] truth. For when someone is commonly branded as a liar, it is customary to say that he is more lying than any watchman or sentinel. Likewise, what did the employed and consulted hand-diviner contribute? For at that juncture both, whoever performed this office, were consulted. You indeed, a few days later, lost, without having been forewarned, as it were the morning star of your house. I deliberately pass over the rest, which you know better, since these men have deserved by their vanity never again to be consulted.

Consulting pythonists is all the more ruinous because the deceit of malignant spirits is clearer in them; whether they lie or not, they always intend to do harm. They deceive sometimes from a desire to deceive, sometimes because they themselves are deceived through the error of their blindness; yet they work unceasingly to seem fully aware of future things. Hence they strive to cloud their oracles by ambiguity of words, so that, when found to be liars or deceivers, they may seek by some covering of rationality to defend their deception. Thus they do not cease to deceive until they hurl their hearers into ruin.

For whom since the beginning of the world have the answers of seers benefited? Croesus, or Pyrrhus, or anyone among those before or after them? The Theban leader, while hoping for victory from an oracle, is pierced by his brother’s sword. Yet his grandfather Laius seemed to promise him success in war. For what else did the following signify, after many evasions:

> “Is victory certain for Thebes?”

But lest, when the leader was slain, he should be accused of falsehood, the oracle added, in order to cover its deception with the ambiguous semblance of truth and thus preserve [Col. 0462C] its malice:

> “Alas for me: the father conquered through swords.”

Thus, while he is invited to parricide as though secure in the counsel of fate, he is drawn by the snare of impiety to his destruction. The desire of his parricidal father is also fulfilled, when the impious brothers—upon whom he had invoked the wish that the bonds of their kinship should be torn apart by the sword—perish by mutual wounds and fall beneath alternating blades.

Croesus trusts that, if he crosses the Halys, great kingdoms will be subjected to him on the authority of the oracles. But when events turn out otherwise, deceitful Apollo clears himself of the charge of lying by the equivocation of a single little word. And Pyrrhus? Having defeated the Romans, whom he had often routed in battle by courage, he promises himself empire by Phoebus’s favour; but, irretrievably overthrown, he turned the blame upon himself because he had interpreted the ambiguity of the oracle to his disadvantage.

Let us turn to better-known histories. When the single and unparalleled storm of civil war shook the world, Appius, instructed by Phoebus, sought rest in the Euboean recess and found death. Lucan gives the celebrated oracle:

> “You escape the mighty threats  
> Of wars, Roman, untouched by so great a crisis,  
> And alone shall possess repose in a middle valley  
> Of Euboea’s coast.”

But lest oracles alone, rather than histories, should bear the mark of falsehood, let canonical history—upon which unshaken faith rests—be examined. Saul, transformed from prince into tyrant, was abandoned by the Lord because his sins required it; and, while the hostile hand prevailed against the people of the Lord under his leadership, he anxiously sought an outcome amid his shattered fortunes. He consulted the Lord, and He did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by priests, nor by prophets.

Samuel had nevertheless announced this to him beforehand: that the Lord regretted having made him king because he had not fulfilled the word of the Lord. Persuaded by greed, he had spared King Agag, the fattest man, and the choice flocks of sheep and herds, and garments, and rams, and everything that was beautiful in the people’s eyes. But whatever was worthless and rejected, they destroyed at the Lord’s command. And since victory belongs to no commander except from the hand of the Lord of hosts, Saul, giving no glory to the author of good things, applauded before the people his own strength for the gift bestowed upon him. Thus it is written:

> “The word of the Lord came to Samuel: ‘I regret that I have made Saul king, because he has forsaken me and has not fulfilled my words by action.’ Samuel was distressed, and cried to the Lord all night. And when he rose in the night to go to Saul, Samuel was told in the morning that Saul had come to Carmel, had erected for himself a triumphal arch, and, returning, had gone down to Gilgal” (1 Kings 15).

Then, at Samuel’s rebukes, he preferred to excuse the crime of disobedience under a pretext of religion rather than erase it by repentance—the second plank left to the sinner after shipwreck. For he said:

> “Indeed, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord and travelled on the way upon which the Lord sent me; I brought Agag king of Amalek, and destroyed Amalek. But the people took from the spoil sheep and oxen, the first portions of what had been slain, in order to sacrifice to the Lord their God at Gilgal” (ibid.).

See how he excuses himself, and either diminishes whatever guilt there is or transfers it to the people. Samuel therefore said:

> “Does the Lord desire holocausts and victims, rather than obedience to the voice of the Lord? For obedience is better than victims, and listening than offering the fat of rams. Since resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you from being king” (ibid.).

I judge that the same thing happens to all who, established in high position, go after their own desires and, while pretending to exercise principality and lordship, inflict their arrogance upon their subjects—equating what they please with what is lawful, as though their necks were not subjected to the yoke of divine law and as though they were under no obligation to fulfil God’s justice. But could even so great a thunderclap of divine threat soften the hardness (*σκληρότης*) of his hardened breast, or the pride which had taken yet deeper root in Saul’s heart through the iniquity of tyranny? By no means. For Saul said to Samuel:

> “I have sinned, because I have transgressed the word of the Lord and your words, fearing the people and obeying their voice. But now, I pray, bear my sin, and return with me, that I may worship the Lord.”

And Samuel said:

> “I shall not return, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel” [Col. 0464A] (ibid.).

Do you see how difficult it is to cure wickedness, once it has grown together with the nourishment of pride, by words and exhortation? “I have sinned,” he says, “fearing the people and obeying their voice.” Does he not confess the fault in such a way as to entangle others—who, had he been a ruler, ought to have been released—rather than free himself?

Had he heard that Moses acted thus when God’s wrath raged against the people and the Lord said to him, “Let me alone, that my fury may be kindled against the people, and that I may destroy them and make you grow into a great nation” (Exodus 32)? What then did that leader, and faithful prince, established by the Lord in His favour, do? “Either forgive them this offence,” he said, “or blot me out of your book” (ibid.). But did he seek his own glory amid such an affection of charity? That most gentle ruler, pious father, eloquent speaker, mighty in deed and word, leader foremost in the righteousness of God’s commandments, said:

> “The Egyptians will say: ‘The Lord cleverly led them out of Egypt in order to strike them down in the wilderness.’”

Thus, even at the cost of his own loss, he preferred the Lord’s glory and the deliverance of the people whose leadership he administered.

Likewise, when David’s fault had provoked the Lord to anger and the people, subject to the chief fault, bore the penalty, he saw the angel of God striking the people. He poured forth prayers from the depths of his heart and added:

> “It is I who sinned; I acted wickedly. What have these sheep done?” (2 Kings 24).

Truly a king and a just ruler, worthy to break the anger of the Most High: when he set himself before God, who was scourging the people, he removed the scourge of His indignation. For no excuse bends Him except when a person is accused by his own judgment. Nothing moves Him to pardon except when the guilty person lays bare his fault without disguise. Nothing calls mercy forth except when a mind kindled by charity is crushed within itself. Nothing persuades Him to be propitiated except when the mind extends the hand of action in satisfaction. For if anyone confesses his fault, confession is useless unless he hastens toward pardon with the intention of making satisfaction.

“I have sinned,” Judas said, “by betraying innocent blood” (Matthew 27). His confession was indeed wholly true, but useless, because he ran rather to the noose he had deserved than to the fountain of mercy which he had spurned and closed against himself by the hardness [Col. 0464D] of his obstinacy. He repented of having done what he had done, but not with that affection of devotion capable of softening the stone of help. For driven by repentance, he hanged himself with a noose. Thus he ended his life by a punishment he deserved; but because he did not correct his wickedness, he obtained no pardon for himself by any remedy of salvation. So it is written that even in hell there is the sting of repentance, though there is no correction of a perverse will.

Thus Saul undoubtedly tries to place his sin upon other shoulders; and while pretending that he wishes to be freed from punishment through Samuel’s prayers, he entangles himself more grievously, wraps himself in stronger snares, and binds himself by an irreversible sentence of condemnation. For the text continues:

> “Samuel turned to depart. But Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it was torn. Samuel said to him: ‘The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbour, who is better than you. Moreover, the triumphant one in Israel will not spare, nor will He be moved by repentance; for He is not a man, that He should repent.’ But Saul said: ‘I have sinned. Yet now honour me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may worship the Lord your God’” (1 Kings 15).

See the madness of such self-exaltation. He hears that he has been cast down by the Lord, and yet strives to reign as though against the Lord’s will. He does not doubt that the kingdom has been given to one better than himself; nevertheless, stripped of royal glory by an irrevocable sentence, he deceitfully usurps it. He falls, therefore, while striving to ascend where he is forbidden, and becomes worse than himself while wishing, despite the Lord’s opposition, to be preferred to one better. He confesses the fault, indeed, but disdains to bear the punishment. This is what he means by saying, “I have sinned, but now honour me”: as though he said, “Though I have deserved to be despised, justly cast down because of the guilt of my crime, the haughtiness of my pride, and the wickedness of a tyrant, let your patience make me glorious in the sight of those who do not know the counsel of the Lord. Return with me, therefore, so that, exalted by your attendance, attended by so great a retinue and such venerable authority, I may worship the Lord your God—whom I no longer dare call mine, since I departed from Him through disobedience and still withdraw through obstinacy.”

Indeed, his spirit had swelled so greatly that he somehow presumed to prefer himself not merely to man but even to God Himself by the audacity of his own impiety. The one whom the Lord had preferred, the more abundantly endowed with grace he saw him to be, the more keenly did Saul lay secret snares for him, practising hostilities as open as they were unjust. And the more manifestly the Lord exalted him, the more greedily Saul hastened not so much to cast him down as to extinguish him. He set himself in direct opposition to God Himself, striving to steal or tear away from Him the rights of kingdoms.

It was therefore fitting that the Spirit of the Lord should not remain in one who had made his heart not merely a dwelling-place but a foundation of such great wickedness. Accordingly, an evil spirit from the Lord harassed him; and from that time the strength of his kingdom began to ebb away and decline daily, the welfare of the people to waver, and the more frequent, greater, and more conspicuous victories of the enemy to break more powerfully the courage of both king and people. Yet Saul kept the man whose kingdom the Lord had established as though banished from his territory.

What counsel, then, did he finally adopt? Certainly not to hand over the kingdom to one better than himself, nor to submit to the divine disposition made known to him, nor to practise fruitful repentance for his former life. Rather, having raised the heel of his pride against the Lord, he led the people into battle on the mountains of Gilboa, where he was to be punished and slain. He ought indeed to die upon a mountain, since he regarded nothing lofty except himself. Therefore, since Truth itself had forsaken him, the false and wicked prince fled to the fountain of falsehood. He said to his servants:

> “Seek for me a woman who has a python-spirit, that I may go to her and inquire through her” (1 Kings 28).

What else would a pagan and faithless man have said? Is it not the same as saying:

> “If I cannot bend the gods above, I shall move Acheron”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.312),

or, in words more faithful to his sense and with madder faithlessness: “If God withdraws from me knowledge of the truth, I shall nevertheless learn it through the father of lies, against God’s will; and, whether He wills it or not, I shall investigate the secret of His counsel through hostile powers”?

His servants said to him:

> “There is a woman at Endor who has a python-spirit” (ibid.).

He was unworthy of counsel from a man, since despair had broken him so completely that, in order to preserve for himself against God’s omnipotence the kingdom which the Lord was taking away, he begged assistance even from weak and feeblest creatures. He changed his clothing, put on other garments, and went himself, with two men, and they came to the woman at night.

All this was fittingly done, because the Holy Spirit is just even among the perverse. He who had undertaken the accursed journey in order to serve demons rather than God ought to be stripped of royal attire. He who had cast away the garment of innocence and exchanged the clothing of righteousness ought not to be adorned with garments of honour and glory. He surely went after him who did not stand in truth, and two men went with him—men unnamed and unnameable, who could follow a king into such faithlessness without faith resisting. The king is fittingly attended by a company of two, as he withdrew from supreme and true unity. They came to the woman at night: an apt time indeed to deliberate with the prince of darkness about the death of kings, the slaughter of the people, and public mourning.

So Solomon is said to have received wisdom by night, though, seduced and corrupted by the love of women, he was to depart from the Lord. Peter likewise, deprived of the warmth of faith and warming himself by coals at night, fell into faithlessness and made it notorious by the crime of perjury. The other disciples also, overwhelmed by fear, fled in the nighttime.

Saul said to the woman—for the pythonic spirit more frequently fills women:

> “Divine for me by the python-spirit, and raise up for me whomever I shall name to you” (ibid.).

Read the books, turn over the histories, search every corner of Scripture: you will hardly ever find divination in a good sense. Hence Scripture calls the rejected prophets diviners rather than prophets, such as the prophets of Ahab, who, with the Lord’s permission and as their merits required, deceived him by various mockeries. Thus, according to the word of the Lord, a lying spirit went out and became present in the mouths of all Ahab’s prophets, promising prosperity to Ahab as he was about to go up to Ramoth-gilead. Only Micaiah the Morasthite protested. Knowing the divine counsel, he forewarned Israel, which he had seen scattered on the mountains; he was struck for the judgment of truth which he loved by the man who, having taken up iron horns, said:

> “With these horns, O king, you shall scatter Syria” (3 Kings 22).

Moreover, divination was scarcely ever performed without a gift, since it is practised in the spirit of greed and wickedness. Therefore the Holy Spirit reproaches Jerusalem when it is about to fall:

> “Your rulers judged for gifts, your priests taught for payment, and your prophets divined for money; yet they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils will not come upon us.’ Therefore the Lord says: ‘Zion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become like a watchman’s hut in an orchard’” (Micah 3).

Those, therefore, who divined for money, though they vaunt the name of prophets, are often liars, always flawed, and strangers to the power and truth of prophecy.

“By the python-spirit,” he says—as if to say: “Since the Spirit of the Lord has departed, let at least the pythonic spirit protect me.” “And raise up for me whomever I shall name to you.” Deceit surely drives deceit onward. The king, given over to a reprobate mind, had persuaded himself that the python-spirit was the president of knowledge, foreknower of future things, privy to hidden counsel, and interpreter of truth. He also persuaded himself that it possessed such great [Col. 0467B] power that it could raise even the dead, and such great kindness that it would comply with its intimates even in a matter so rare and difficult. Doubtless the song of the faithful soul had slipped from his memory, or was held by him uselessly:

> “The Lord kills and makes alive; He brings down to hell and brings back; He makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and raises up.”

And Saul had seen fulfilled in himself what follows:

> “He raises the needy from the dust, that he may sit with princes and possess a throne of glory” (1 Kings 2).

He who does these things is, beyond doubt, the Lord of knowledges.

The woman said to him:

> “Behold, you know how much Saul has done, and how he has eradicated magicians and soothsayers from the land. Why then do you lay a snare for my life, that I may be killed?”

And Saul swore to her by the Lord, saying:

> “As the Lord lives, no evil shall happen to you on account of this matter” (1 Kings 28).

It is true that whoever wallows in filth becomes filthier still; and one abandoned by grace always has his last state worse than his first. Thus the pythoness, conscious of her sacrilege, is frightened; and the authority established by the Lord to root out sacrileges—otherwise timid when the affairs of the people and the wars of its lord are being conducted—gives boldness to idolaters and lends royal authority to sacrilege.

“The soothsayers and magicians,” the Lord says, “you shall not suffer to live” (Exodus 22). But the man to whom God’s word is addressed, and who bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, not only grants safety to such persons but confirms the peace he has promised by the religious solemnity of an oath. Thus it happens that he learns in his own danger how tangled are the sinews of Leviathan’s testicles, when he has laid for himself a snare of his own act from which he cannot escape without loss of salvation. A tight embrace and a horned syllogism now threaten him: if the pythoness is spared, the Lord’s command is violated, since He commands that such sorceries be eradicated from the land; if she is not spared, the sanctity of the oath is violated. Wherever the impious man turns, he is caught in his own works.

The woman said:

> “Whom shall I raise for you?”

He said:

> “Samuel” (1 Kings 28).

At every time there is one faith: that God exists, and that He is at once just and good, rewarding those who hope in Him and fully answering all according to their merits—before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. No right-minded wise person has ever doubted this. Without it, no one has ever entered into salvation. But one who errs in small matters gradually slips into greater ones. Thus this man, first negligent, then disobedient, afterward stubborn, then obstinate, finally fell into such blindness that he did not even keep this article of faith intact. For he did not believe God altogether just, imagining that malignant spirits were granted power even over saints after their departure from this life. He knew that holy Samuel had not obeyed pythonic powers while living, nor had entered into any intercourse of familiarity with them. Yet he now hoped and requested that Samuel should be raised at the command of the python-spirit. He wished the dead man to be compelled to do what he could not be induced to do while alive. For Samuel had refused while living to tell the king anything except what the Lord inspired him to reveal.

When the woman heard Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice and said to Saul:

> “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul” (ibid.).

She believed herself deceived, and, even after the oath had been given, endangered by the knowledge and presence of the ruler. The king said to her:

> “Do not be afraid. What did you see?”

The woman said to Saul:

> “I saw gods ascending from the earth” (ibid.).

The pythoness’s answer might have deterred even a man of slight faith from his undertaking. For she introduces a plurality of gods and indicates that their dwelling is below the earth and in darkness. Saul said:

> “What is his appearance?”

She said:

> “An old man is coming up, and he is clothed in a cloak.”

Saul therefore understood that it was Samuel; and he bowed with his face to the ground and worshipped [Col. 0468C] (ibid.). He carefully investigates the appearance of the one who appeared, perhaps deceived by the error of the Gentiles, believing that each person in the underworld retained the same appearance of clothing and occupations by which they had been distinguished while alive. Hence the saying:

> “Whatever delight they had in chariots  
> And arms while living, whatever care in feeding  
> Their gleaming horses, follows them when they are laid beneath the earth.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.654)

But could the glory of a holy man not have been brighter, or his living appearance changed after death? Scripture wisely and faithfully does not say that Samuel was raised by the power of the python-spirit, but prudently expresses the blindness of the impious mind. It says:

> “Having heard the man’s appearance and clothing, Saul understood that it was Samuel.”

He understood it while deceived; and this is proved by what follows: “He bowed and worshipped.” For had it been Samuel, he would by no means have allowed himself to be worshipped by a man, since he had believed and taught according to the Law that one God and Lord alone is to be worshipped. Moreover, holy souls are exempt from the power of malignant spirits. Finally, he would not have encouraged the error of the deceived man, as the following words show that he did.

“Samuel” said to Saul:

> “Why have you disturbed me, that I should be raised?” (ibid.)

This is the fraud of malignant spirits: what they do freely and prescribe for people to do, they carefully conceal, so that they may seem to do it unwillingly. They pretend to be compelled and feign that they have been drawn forth by the force of exorcisms. And, lest people take precautions against them, they compose exorcisms allegedly framed in the name of the Lord, or in the faith of the Trinity, or in the power of the Incarnation and Passion; they hand these over to people, obey those who practise them, until they involve them with themselves in the crime of sacrilege and the punishment of damnation. Sometimes they transform themselves into angels of light, command only honourable things, prohibit unlawful ones, promote purity, and provide useful services, so that, appearing good and favourable, they may be admitted more familiarly, heard more kindly, loved more closely, and more readily obeyed. They also assume the appearance of venerable persons so that greater and readier reverence may be paid to them.

Saul said:

> “I am greatly distressed. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has departed from me and would not answer me, neither by the hand of prophets nor by dreams. Therefore I have called you, that you may show me what I should do” (ibid.).

That is, he openly says: “I have been cast headlong into the abyss of despair. Men attack me, God abandons me, and I flee to you, who are truly enemies to both, so that you may instruct me, as a teacher instructs a pupil, what I ought to do in such anguish.”

Although he believed the speaker to be Samuel, in truth it was an angel of Satan. Nor could ignorance assist him, since no one may be ignorant that a creature which seeks to be worshipped is faithless and of perverse will. He also knew that it was unlawful to consult soothsayers and magicians or to trouble a python-spirit concerning future things. If ignorance of the person excuses him, fools will be in a better condition than the learned, and the perverse than the upright.

“Samuel”—not, indeed, the true Samuel, but a shadowy and counterfeit one, such as the impious and reprobate consulter deserved—said:

> “Why do you ask me, when the Lord has departed from you and passed over to your rival?” (ibid.)

The beginning of the answer accords with faith and suits reason. What can a creature contribute to one whom God has forsaken and from whom He takes away his spoils? But little by little the enemy and foe of faith turns toward what is his own, mixing falsehood with truth and clouding the faith of truth with lies. For it follows:

> “The Lord will do to you as He spoke by my hand, and He will tear your kingdom from your hand and give it to your neighbour David, because you did not obey the voice of the Lord nor execute the wrath of His fury against Amalek. Therefore the Lord has done to you today what you suffer; and the Lord will also give Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines. But tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The Lord will also give the camp of Israel into the hand of the Philistines” (ibid.).

The faithless spirit correctly set forth the outcome of the battle; yet he deceitfully entrapped the faithless and unhappy soul in the snares of words. He confirms the error of the one who has gone astray and promises rest after death to the unrepentant. For when he says that the Lord will fulfil what He spoke “by my hand,” he undoubtedly pretends to be Samuel, through whom the Lord had spoken the things he now announces to Saul. But when he adds, “Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me,” he states something true, but deceitfully. For on the following day Saul, laying violent hands upon himself in despair, was to pass into hell and have his portion with the one whose path he had followed through greed, pride, and obstinacy of mind.

But the spirit falsely flatters him by suggesting hope of rest, while by manner and words he falsely represents himself as Samuel. Samuel, it is certain, had been granted by the Lord a dwelling-place of rest among those who call upon His name. What, then, did the answers of Saul’s Samuel—or rather, of his python-spirit—profit him? Had he not been forewarned, perhaps he might have hoped for better things, and at least have waited while pierced by another’s sword. But, rendered more certain by the vanity of the oracle, he fell upon his own sword. At the end, while seeking his own glory—how he might die more bravely in battle—he feared the breath of words; and, by the counsel of a weak and prostrate [Col. 0470B] mind, he chose death both of body and soul.

Let the nations glory in their strength; let their authors say whatever they think while they proclaim the titles of their heroes and extol the courage of great men. Let Cato drink poison at the prompting of those authors; let Vulteius arm the hands and minds of his companions for voluntary death; let Cleopatra send the incurable poison of asps through her breasts to her heart; let Lucretia condemn another’s unchastity by the shedding of her own blood. I do not judge that, in any predicament whatever, a person is permitted by his own authority to inflict death upon himself—not even where chastity is in danger. Though that teacher of teachers, to whom I scarcely dare compare anyone in the sanctuary of letters, seems to make an exception for this case. Such death is entirely the death of the desperate—of those who, though alive in body, have already died beforehand by the death of the mind and have ceased to live in spirit. It is surely the death not of the living, but of those already dead.

Review the succession of faithless kings—Jeroboam, Ahab, Jezebel, Nebuchadnezzar, Sennacherib, and others whose errors I cannot sufficiently recount. What profit did they gain from their seers, who saw for them false and foolish things and did not uncover their iniquity in order to summon them to repentance? All of them surely vanished after the prince of vanity; and while they seek to know what is unlawful, or to know in an unlawful manner, they were reduced to emptiness and nothingness. I have joined the kings of Israel to the faithless, because whereas some kings of Judah were good and others bad, all the kings of Israel proved reprobate.

“Leave God’s secrets and the inquiry into what heaven is,” says Cato, because what God has destined and decreed concerning you He can accomplish without your anxious concern. The moral philosopher speaks excellently:

> “Believe that every day which has dawned for you is your last;  
> The welcome hour you do not hope for will come besides.”  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.iv.13)

But truth is everywhere consistent with itself and never departs from itself, even when uttered from the dwelling-place of falsehood. Nor is purity, so long as it flourishes in its own integrity, defiled by the proximity of any filth. Truth itself commands that death not be feared and directs us to be prepared at every hour to receive it, so that, the less we presume upon length of life, the more eagerly we may run upward through the degrees of virtue in the cultivation of honourableness. Death is indeed a necessary gift to a nature now corrupted; for corruption is the origin of death. Remove corruption; pursue the integrity of purity and virtue: you have already entered the way of immortality and grasped a certain ark of your divinity. Have you grasped it, I say, or received it? But, to speak more faithfully, you have both received and grasped it. “For it is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy” (Romans 16).

Who knows when He will come—late, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning? For, as that man says: “Nothing is more certain than death; nothing more uncertain than its hour.” Death must not be feared as an evil; rather, as the end of evils, when it comes it must be welcomed gratefully. There is one thing to be fled with all the powers of mind and body. What is it, you ask? Shamefulness, and every form of dishonour. These make death not the end of evils, but the bond between evils that precede and those that follow.

To flee this, neither the oracles of seers nor consultation of a python-spirit is necessary: the reason given to us gives more faithful and useful counsel. In the extreme distress of Libya, Cato disdained to consult Jupiter Ammon, believing reason sufficient to persuade him that liberty must be preserved and that not only the yoke of Caesar’s dominion, but every mark of shamefulness, must be avoided. He erred, however, in casting away the gift of life by his own authority—an act forbidden, as is clear, not only by the ordinances of the faithful, but by the laws of nations and the decrees of the wisest men.

The foremost figures of ancient philosophy, Pythagoras and Plotinus, are not so much authors of this prohibition as its heralds, declaring wholly unlawful for any person serving in military duty to leave the garrison and post entrusted to him without the command of his commander or ruler. They use a thoroughly elegant example, because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). But what if the oracles of seers or the answers of a python-spirit command the contrary? Without doubt they must not be obeyed, because no one ought to trust anyone at the risk of innocence.

If you do not believe me, consider Numa, ruler of the Romans, almost the most innocent of men after Titus, if you please. When invited to homicide and asked for a head for sacrifices, he decided that an onion should be cut, turning even the will of a perverse deity toward innocence. When the god added that it required a human being, he promised to offer hairs. And when the unclean spirit thirsted for blood, he answered that a fish should be sacrificed. Thus, because his reason could not be circumvented so that he might be drawn into guilt, he was declared by the testimony of unclean spirits to be most worthy of conversation with the gods.

Nor should anyone defend his own error under the pretext of exorcisms. Such rites were instituted to diminish the demons’ power and to break up the intercourse of familiarity they have with human beings; and they lack efficacy of their own unless they prevail through the finger of God. But the Holy Spirit of discipline flees what is counterfeit, and disdains that a body subjected to sins should be His dwelling-place. Whatever of this kind is done is counterfeit and phantasmal, and does not know the substance of truth. It may indeed seem present when invoked by prayers and offerings, and, as the requested results follow, the sacrilegious desire of a deceived soul is fulfilled. But it is absent so completely that, having withdrawn its protection, it permits those driven by such great faithlessness to be drawn to hell through various deceits of demons.

For the Church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, has forbidden by public proclamation that the Holy Spirit be invited to such wicked acts. Therefore, when the grace of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the Church are withdrawn from disapproved exorcisms, those who do not so much use them as misuse them sin against the Spirit; and when He departs, they strive to retain for themselves His power and efficacy.

## Chapter XXVIII. On diviners by mirrors; on the fact that malignant spirits sometimes foreknow future events; on subtlety of nature, long experience of time, and revelation by higher powers; on the fact that they often deceive, whether deceiving or deceived; and on the certain evils that follow mirror-diviners

Mirror-diviners flatter themselves in vain because they sacrifice nothing, injure no one, more often help by detecting thefts, cleanse the world of sorceries, and seek only a useful or necessary truth. “Not so the wicked, not so” (Ps. 1). “He who does not gather with me,” he says, “scatters; and he who is not with me is against me” (Matt. 12). While the wicked practise these things forbidden by the Lord [Col. 0472C], what else do they do but raise their heel against him who forbids them?

Certainly, he sacrifices far too much who, having cast out the Holy Spirit, prostitutes his mind to idolatry. He sacrifices far too much who summons the polluted ears of demons with a voice consecrated to the Lord. He sacrifices far too much who adapts the movement of his body to the performance of detestable sacrilege. What has he retained for the Creator who has offered mind, tongue, and body to demons? Has he not wronged truth, who sought its integrity amid such corruption?

Clearly no one is excused in such matters through ignorance. For all alike know, or ought to know, that this disgrace to faith has been condemned by the reproach of anathema. The man enrolled in sacred service is certainly not exempt here; nor the child by reason of age, the woman [Col. 0472D] by weakness of sex, or the peasant by his agricultural work, through which he watches over public usefulness. For although, where property is lost, ignorance of the law may bring them relief, in the overthrow of faith there is no remedy from ignorance. The principle prevails that he who does not know shall himself be disregarded; that the fool, guilty in his ignorance, shall be instructed by punishment; and that he who refused to understand so as to do good shall wisely be punished.

For who could have learned, in order to abstain without labour from so great a labour, while laboriously learning how to err laboriously and perniciously? Can one rest in the faith without labour, who is able, by mental anxiety and bodily exercise, to depart from the faith? Whoever submits to these trifles has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever; and although he confesses God in words, he contradicts him by perverse deeds. Nor is it easier [Col. 0473A] for such a person to be faithful than for a judge to be incorruptible who loves gifts and pursues rewards.

Moreover, the matter that troubles simpler minds—that hidden future things cannot be disclosed through such consultation unless by the hand of him in whose power are times and seasons—does not create a knot of difficulty. For though there is one judge of future things, who is both God and Lord of all, they nevertheless sometimes become known to human beings from signs. Why then is it surprising if spirits sometimes foreknow matters concerning which they are instructed in many respects by subtlety of nature, by longer experience of time, and by revelation from higher powers?

If, then, spirits weighed down by the mass of a body—spirits whom the earthy garment of flesh retards, whose acuity the corruption of disturbed sense blunts—infer from preceding events or from indications of any things whatsoever what is to come, what prevents spirits freed from every bond of body, whom no harmful mass retards, from measuring beforehand the outcome of events that are imminent or that will follow over very long periods? But one who was, as it were, born yesterday and will die after a few days gathers like from like in the intervening time and reasons from causes then known to him towards the future. Could not one who is not merely ancient but ancient in days, created from the beginning full of wisdom and beautiful in perfection, do this more easily? Who is so dull and extraordinarily slow that, through so long a course of time, he would not rise at least in some degree to conjecture what is to come?

Furthermore, favourable powers, which continually serve the Lord in the worship of charity [Col. 0473C] and devotion to obedience, can indeed reveal hidden things to such persons, and are sometimes believed to do so. Yet what the reprobate think or foretell is not immediately true; rather, they sometimes hasten to announce what they suspect or fear, so as to appear privy to secrets. Such was the prediction of the demons presiding in the temples of Egypt, when the Lord was about to be born, concerning the desolation of those temples and their own departure. Hence that saying in Trismegistus concerning the destruction of idolatrous religion: “Egypt, Egypt,” he says, “the time will come when only tales of your religion shall remain.”

And they often pretend to do willingly what they do of necessity and under compulsion, as though indignant with those human beings toward whom they feign hostility [Col. 0473D].

They also often lie, whether deceiving or deceived. Yet even if they announce only truths, they must nevertheless either be restrained or avoided. Hence in Deuteronomy:

> “If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and predicts a sign or wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow strange gods, whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ do not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer; for the Lord your God is testing you, that it may be made manifest whether you love him or not” (Deut. 13).

From this it is clearly understood that, even if the things said by diviners apart from God come to pass, they are not to be received in such a way that what they command is done or what they worship [Col. 0474A] is worshipped.

Nor did the Apostle in the Acts of the Apostles spare the unclean spirit merely because, in the ventriloquist woman, it bore true witness to the apostles and their preaching. Nothing is more salutary against this pest than wholly withdrawing one’s ear from such vanity.

I thank God, who even in my tenderer age set the shield of his good pleasure against these snares of the malignant enemy. For when, as a boy, I had been entrusted to a priest in order to learn the Psalms, and that priest happened to practise mirror-magic, it occurred that he enlisted me and another boy, somewhat older, for the sacrilege of mirror-divination. After certain spells had first been performed, we sat at his feet so that whatever he sought might be revealed by our indication in nails smeared with some sacred—I know not what—oil or chrism, or in the polished and smoothed surface [Col. 0474B] of a basin.

Thus, when the aforesaid names were uttered—names which, although I was a little boy, seemed through their very horror to be those of demons—and the preliminary adjurations were made, which, by God’s doing, I do not know, my companion judged that he saw certain images, though thin and cloudy. I, however, was so blind to this that nothing appeared to me except the nails or the basin and the other things I had known before.

Thereafter I was judged useless for such practices; and, as though I obstructed these sacrileges, I was forbidden to approach such things. Whenever they decided to practise this business, I was excluded as though I were an impediment to the whole art of divination. Thus the Lord showed me favour at that age.

When I had advanced a little in years, I came to abhor this crime more and more; and my horror was strengthened all the more because, although I then knew many mirror-diviners, I saw every one of them, before death, deprived of the benefit of sight either by natural failure or by an enemy’s hand. I pass over the other misfortunes by which, before my eyes, they were either struck down or afflicted by the Lord. Two were excepted: namely, the priest whom I mentioned above, and a certain deacon. Seeing the plague of mirror-diviners, they escaped—one to the bosom of a community of canons, the other to the harbour of a Cluniac cell—both marked by sacred vestments. Yet I pitied those same men because afterward, beyond the rest, they endured many adversities in their congregations.

Certainly, if the concurrence of arguments and the authority of the Catholic mother Church did not suffice to overthrow this error [Col. 0474D], examples of its evils are enough to eradicate it. But just as no one can drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons, or serve two masters, God and Mammon (Matt. 6), so no one attains both the grace of God and the practice of this wickedness.

But why, behold, do I pursue point by point, as though with an awl, this teaching hostile to faith and morals, when I might suffice to pierce it through, blade to hilt, with the sword of the Spirit? Let it then be struck once by the mighty hand and arm of him who, in order to drown the Egyptians, “divided the Red Sea into divisions,” and there will be no need for a second blow. For there is none who can snatch anything from his hand.

Let Moses therefore draw the sword, strike down the Egyptian abominations, and hide them so that they may not appear [Col. 0475A] before the faithful, in the sand of their barrenness. Let him speak the word; let him pronounce the sentence condemning the errors which we have long laboured to drive from your house. For the word is a two-edged sword, living and effective, more penetrating than every two-edged blade, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning thoughts. Senseless is he who does not fear when this sword hangs over him. And behold, it hangs before the face of the Church, in the sight of all. Indeed, it is directed against all. For it says:

> “When you enter the land which the Lord your God will give you, beware lest you wish to imitate the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you one who causes his son or daughter to pass through fire, or one who consults soothsayers, observes dreams or omens; let there be neither sorcerer nor enchanter, nor one who consults Pythons or diviners and seeks truth from the dead. For the Lord abominates all these things, and because of such crimes he will destroy them at your entrance. You shall be perfect and without blemish with the Lord your God. Those nations whose land you shall possess listen to augurs and diviners; but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God” (Deut. 18).

Who, then, can doubt that these are crimes, and the destruction not merely of bodily health but of faith, when prophetic speech—or rather the speech of the Holy Spirit—eradicates them with such care? They are abominations, as the Lord declares; yet a human being thinks himself above other human beings once he has acquired their discipline. Nations were destroyed for crimes of this kind [Col. 0475C], and human rashness trusts that it will be exalted through them.

## Chapter XXIX. On physicians, theorists, and practitioners

It is nevertheless permissible to consult someone about future things, provided either that he has the spirit of prophecy, or that, taught by natural science, he has learned from natural signs what happens in animal bodies; or that he infers the character of an approaching season from indications supplied by experience. Yet no one should give ear to the latter in such a way as to prejudice faith or religion.

Nor should the former be heard except in what they speak from the Lord; and that never attacks religion, because truth cannot be contrary to truth, nor good to good. Physicians, however, when they attribute too much authority to nature [Col. 0475D], often offend against the author of nature by opposing faith.

I do not accuse all of error, although I have heard very many disputing otherwise than faith maintains concerning the soul, its powers and operations, the growth and diminution of the body, its resurrection, the creation of things, and even God himself. Sometimes they speak of God himself as though earth-born Giants were trying the stars, and, in a vain effort with Enceladus, desired to earn the imposition upon themselves of the fiery burden of Etna. Yet in these matters they can easily slip, because however great the powers of their intellect may be, they stop short of the depth of the difficulty involved [Col. 0476A].

But when the intellect fails and reason, which is the middle course, has led to faith, opinion alone remains. When inquiry concerns lower things, however—for example, the constitution of an animal, the cause and treatment of illness—they lack absolutely nothing except the effect of practical work, if that is desired.

The theorists indeed do everything that belongs to them; perhaps, out of affection for you, they will give even more freely. From them you will receive the causes and natures of individual things. They judge health, illness, and the neutral state. They bestow health in words and preserve it. They order the neutral state to turn in this direction. They foresee and teach the causes of illness; they assign to it its beginning, increase, crisis, and decline. Why say more? When I hear them, they seem to me able to raise the dead, and are thought not inferior to Aesculapius or Mercury [Col. 0476B].

Yet I am greatly divided and disturbed by astonishment of mind at the fact that they break apart and disagree among themselves through so great a conflict of words and collision of arguments. One thing I certainly know: contraries cannot both be true.

What shall I say of practical physicians? Far be it from me to say anything perverse of them. For through the exigencies of my sins, I fall into their hands far too often. They should not be exasperated by words, but rather soothed by service. I do not want them to treat me too harshly, nor do I even dare think what everyone cries aloud.

I will therefore say with holy Solomon: “Medicine is from the Lord God, and a wise man will not despise it.” For no one is more necessary or useful than a physician, provided he is faithful and prudent. Who could sufficiently proclaim the praises of one who, as an artisan of health and begetter of life, imitates the Lord in this respect and performs his office: the health which the Lord works and grants as Lord and prince, the physician, as steward and minister, procures and dispenses [Col. 0476C]?

Nor is it relevant that some sell a counterfeit grace, and, wishing to seem more righteous because they take nothing before the sick person recovers, are thereby more unjust: they ascribe to their own hands the benefit of time—indeed, the gift of God—when the man whom God raises up and the strength of recovering nature would have been raised without their assistance. Although this is now the practice of few, physicians persuade and repeat it to one another: “Take payment while he is in pain.”

Nor am I troubled if their treatments conflict with each other, since I know that contraries often have the same effect. But when someone has collapsed into death under their hands, then they will produce necessary arguments by which it will appear that his life could not have been prolonged further. And, as they say, for those whom prolonged hunger has afflicted, they prepare sips that are useless for men already dead, and delicate foods.

Perhaps you expect me to say what the people say: that these are those who kill people with the greatest conscientiousness. But in vain. Far be it from me to utter that insult. If you should nevertheless wish to hear it, go to Seneca, Pliny, and Sidonius, who will repeat it in your ears with a loud cry [Col. 0476D].

# Book Three

[Col. 0477]

## Prologue

[Col. 0477A]

I make many enemies by exposing the foolishness of triflers. For this reason I had resolved to be idle and silent; but the tumult of affairs shakes me out of the one, and the movements of my mind interrupt the other. For one who is placed under authority, if he is wise, obeys the command of the ruler. One whom the goads of passions prick cannot conceal that he is moved into the form of his passion.

Thus one whom a breeze of joy caresses exults; hope induces cheerfulness; fear trembles; the mind of one who suffers is confounded by sorrow. In each person these expressions of good or evil alternate. But the sense of evils is deeper and falls more often upon everyone. For who is not more often scorched by the harshness of evils than caressed by the comfort of good things? Rare [Col. 0477B] is the person who can ward off from his whole self the assault of all fortune. He who prevails by his own strength is tested in the person or fortune of a friend or intimate.

Although he is scarcely human whom the loss of strangers does not shake, he is not human enough whom others’ troubles do not move. But wiser men have already questioned whether anything human can rightly be foreign to another human being. The progress of virtue, however, resolves this knot of uncertainty: both the comic poet holds nothing human foreign to himself, and the heavenly Master teaches that one human being must love another as himself.

It is therefore clear that a disciple is unworthy of so great a Master if he does not rejoice with truth and does not burn with indignation against the enemies of public welfare. The purpose of the present little work touches them in part, and will cast down their trifles with such weapon as it can and is accustomed to use [Col. 0477C].

## Chapter I. What universal and public health is

Public health, then, is the soundness of life which sustains all and each individually. For nothing is more excellent for a human being than his life; and nothing is more salutary than soundness of life. Ancient sages defined a human being as consisting of a rational soul and corruptible flesh. Flesh lives from the soul, since life cannot otherwise belong to the body, which always rests in the torpor of its own inertness unless moved by the benefit of spiritual nature.

The soul too has its own life. For God is the life of the soul. One of the moderns expressed this thought gravely and truly, though in metrical lightness:

> God is the life of the soul; the soul, that of the body.  
> When she flees, this body is dissolved; she perishes when God abandons her.

Just as, therefore, for the body to live is to be animated and moved by the soul, to conform itself to the soul’s motions, and to harmonize with it by a certain necessity of obedience, so the soul lives insofar as in its own way it is animated, is truly moved by God, obeys him in devoted subjection, and rests in him in all things. To the extent that it falls short of this, it lives less. For the body too, in whatever part of itself it is not moved by the soul, already incurs in that part [Col. 0478A] the torpor of death.

Therefore, while the body lives as a whole, it is wholly ordered to that soul which does not infuse itself into its parts part by part, but is whole and works in all and in each. So too God wholly occupies and possesses the perfectly living soul; he reigns and is vigorous in its entirety. No corner of it is excepted for him.

But why do I speak of a corner or a part in the soul? It is without parts, of simple nature, and ignorant of all doubleness. Yet it has claimed for itself the parts it could from the distributor of good things. What parts, you ask? The virtues, certainly, by which it is vigorous and active and makes trial of itself. Thus, though it does not grow through a multiplicity of parts or a certain extension of quantity, it is nevertheless enlarged—while the nature of its simplicity remains—by reason and understanding, by desire for good and aversion from evil.

When the Spirit fills these parts—for God is Spirit—the life of the soul is solid and perfect. For when understanding grasps, with the keenness of its sight and insofar as it is able and permitted, God, who is supremely good; when an uncorrupted will desires the good which understanding sees; and when reason opens the way lest the person drawn toward the good by sound affection turn to the right or left, the soul has already attained a certain glory of immortality.

Perhaps he already perceived this who, in the sweetness of his conscience, said: “My heart and my flesh exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). Certainly one who walks in this way neither hopes for nor fears, neither grieves nor suffers with any of those things which fail by departing from the highest and true good. And perhaps prophetic speech invites faithful souls when it says: “Return to me with your whole heart” [Col. 0478C] (Joel 2), so that no angel of joy or sorrow, fear or hope, may turn away from my face or be displeasing to my will.

This life fills every creature, because without it no creature has substance. For everything that is, is what it is by participation in it. Yet though it is in all things by nature, it dwells only in rational beings by grace. They exist, therefore, because truth is in them. They are enlightened because wisdom is in them. They love good because in them is the source of goodness and charity. For every angelic and human virtue is a certain trace of divinity, impressed in some manner upon the rational creature.

The indwelling Holy Spirit imprints holiness upon the soul and scatters its streams in many ways, exercising the charisms of diverse graces. This appears to me to be the true and sole soundness of life: when the mind, enlivened by the Spirit, is enlightened to know things and kindled to love honourableness and cultivate virtue.

Knowledge therefore precedes the cultivation of virtue, because no one can faithfully desire what he does not know, and evil cannot usefully be avoided unless it is known. The treasury of knowledge is opened to us in two ways: either understanding discovers through the exercise of reason what may be known, or revealing grace makes manifest to our eyes what is hidden [Col. 0478D].

Thus, through nature or through grace, each person can attain the recognition of truth and knowledge of necessary things. And, more wonderfully still, each person bears in his heart, as it were, a book of things to be known, opened by the service of reason. In it are depicted not only the forms of visible things and the nature of all things, but even the invisible things of God, the maker of all, are written by God’s finger. Thus those to whom the course of actions is made known by the benefit of nature or grace cannot excuse themselves through ignorance. As it is written: “What is known of God is manifest in them, for God has revealed it to them” (Rom. 1).

Yet I do not raise splendid fringes or trappings for corrupted nature against grace, as though it possessed any good that it has not received, since it is certain that without grace we can do nothing. The recognition of truth and cultivation of virtue are the public and universal soundness, for each and all, of rational nature. Their opposite is ignorance and its hateful, hostile offspring, vice.

Ignorance is rightly the mother of vice, because it is never so barren that it does not unhappily bear the fruit of hateful things. The moralist says:

> You will offer sacrifice with no incense at all,  
> so that scarcely half an ounce of right may cling to fools.  
> (Persius, *Satires* 5.120)

Recognition possesses certainty and consists either in knowledge or in faith. But let the rule of faith be deferred for a little while, because its own time and place await it [Col. 0479C]. Knowledge, moreover, entails awareness of itself. This cannot happen if it does not measure its own powers and if it is ignorant of others’.

## Chapter II. What is the contemplation of a person aspiring to wisdom, and what is the fruit of this speculation

The first task, therefore, of a person aspiring to wisdom is to contemplate what he himself is: what is within him, outside him, below him, above him, opposed to him, before him, or after him. Perhaps this is why those who took care to hand down to posterity the first elements of all philosophy thought that one should investigate the substance of each thing, quantity, relation, quality, position, being-where, being-when, possession, action, and passion; and the properties belonging to all these, whether they admit increase, whether they can receive contraries, and whether anything opposed is found within them.

They did this wisely and diligently, though they showed themselves negligent in this: amid so much light of things, they did not attain knowledge of themselves, and they lost knowledge of inaccessible light, because they became vain in their thoughts; professing themselves wise, they became fools, and their foolish heart was darkened. This is proved by the fact that, delivered over to dishonourable passions, they did things fitting neither sex, age, nor condition, nor nature, and by the testimony of their deeds made all persons ugly [Col. 0480A].

They were indeed given over to a reprobate mind, as is plain to those who know the Apostle more fully. Yet the strongest argument for everything is that each person’s faithfulness and sincerity should be judged from his deeds. For the works that one does bear witness concerning him.

But what does one who does not know himself know usefully? “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “most beautiful among women, go forth after the footsteps of your companions and after the flocks.” The saying γνῶθι σεαυτόν—that is, “know yourself”—is an oracle of Apollo and is believed to have come down from heaven. Did not the pagan know this when he said:

> Learn, O wretched ones, and know the causes of things:  
> what we are, or for what end we are born;  
> what course is allotted, how gently and from where  
> the turning-point must be rounded; what limit there is to money;  
> what it is lawful to wish for; what stern usefulness money has;  
> how much ought to be bestowed upon children and dear relatives;  
> what God has commanded you to be,  
> and in what part of human affairs you have been placed.

This contemplation produces a fourfold fruit: usefulness to oneself, charity toward one’s neighbour, contempt for the world, and love of God. Is not a tree good that brings forth such sweetness and such usefulness of fruit? Certainly one does not become proud who is small in his own eyes. When each person considers the things present or absent among objects of desire, who does not blush at his own poverty? If anyone reviews the things about himself that ought not to be desired, he encounters constant material for modest grief and humility.

Wherever he turns, he is cast down within himself, as one who asks the Lord for strength, saying: “I have been humbled utterly; give me life according to your word” (Ps. 118). And again: “I am ready for scourges, and my pain is always before me” [Col. 0480C] (Ps. 37).

## Chapter III. That pride is the root of all evils, and desire a general leprosy infecting all

Pride is the root of all evils and the nourishment of death. Streams dry up if the vein of their source is cut off. Branches do not flourish when the root is cut down. Vices fail if arrogance is slain. But if dung is heaped upon the root, the branches grow fat and the barrenness of what was withered grows green again. If you pour liquid upon the spring, the added supply passes into the streams. If you add fire to a furnace, the blaze revives in the wood. So, if you nourish the inborn poison of arrogance in corrupted nature, you will be unable—even if you wish—to prevent the deadly venom from infecting the very vital parts.

For love of self is not so much related to all as innate in all. If it exceeds its limit, it tends toward fault. Every virtue is bounded by its own limits and consists in measure. If you go beyond them, you are off the road and not on the way. If this love gains strength, let no one hope for a cure. For it is a leprosy more incurable than every leprosy.

Do you not know that desire is leprosy? Consult Gehazi: if he blushes to confess what he feels, convict him by the stain on his body. But why do I say that Gehazi should be consulted, as if he alone were afflicted? Go round the world, for it is wholly infected. Question me myself, for I am one among the wretched. Certainly desire is a wretched and pitiable leprosy.

Perhaps you do not know what I mean. You, who do not desire, are ignorant of the plague of desire because you do not know weakness; you are thereby set above humanity. But my faithful witness in heaven asserts with me that “all have become corrupt and abominable; there is none who does good, not even one” [Col. 0481A] (Ps. 13). Whether you are that one, you must see for yourself. For I know that this is not Paul, who cries out and groans under the assault of this plague: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). I know that this is not he who drank streams of wisdom from the breast of truth, when he thunders that the world is infected with this stain, saying that whatever is in this world is the desire of the eyes, of the flesh, or the pride of life (1 John 2).

Whoever, then, does not restrain this love should fear leprosy and dread the blindness of the eyes that follows from it. If those who do not check desire, the source and fuel of evils, incur the loss of salvation, what will become of those who inflame it with the goads of flatterers and kindle, as it were, the fuel of vices? What will they do—or rather, what will they suffer—who turn their hearing from truth, do not close their eyes amid admiration for corruptible and corrupting things, spread out their hands, and exercise the liveliness of every sense?

Then, as though its own malice were not enough for the day, one deceit drives forward another’s deceit. I gladly use the Terentian expression when flatterers and informers, accusers and detractors, envious, ambitious, arrogant, factious, and superstitious persons, criminals, and betrayers of every duty assemble to kindle the furnace of desire. Since such persons are found almost everywhere on earth, they are easier to find than to count. Against them stands every law; all legal systems conspire against them; and at some time every creature will be armed against them as enemies of public welfare [Col. 0481C].

## Chapter IV. What a flatterer, an assenter, and a fawner are; and that nothing is more destructive than they

Every flatterer is an enemy of every virtue. He drives, as it were, a nail into the eye of the person with whom he converses; and he must be guarded against all the more because, beneath the appearance of a lover, he never ceases to harm until he blunts the edge of reason and extinguishes the little light that seemed to be present.

Moreover, he stops the ears of his hearers so that they do not hear truth; and I could scarcely say what might be more destructive than that. Laelius—or rather Cicero—well said: “The salvation of the man whose ears are closed to truth, so that he cannot hear what is true, is beyond hope.” What could be more faithless than to ensnare with verbal blandishments one to whom you owe loyalty; to drive one, blinded by mockery, alteration of dress and gesture, and every allurement of vanity, into the filth of vices and the abyss of ruin?

What is more hateful than fraud and deceit, by which wickedness of treachery and enmity is practised under the appearance of love and loyalty against one who is simple and trusting—and, more detestably, a friend? This is indeed the kind of people who speak everything for pleasure and nothing for truth. “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit”; even to friends who are going astray, they repeat, to bring about their ruin: “Well done, well done.”

To know them more fully, look at Gnatho in the comic poet and hear what he confesses concerning himself:

> If someone says no, I say no; if he says yes, I say yes.  
> In short, I myself ordered myself  
> to agree with everything.  
> (Terence, *Eunuchus* 2.2.21)

Indeed, the entire party of Gnathonians is comedy:

> [Lacuna]  
> You laugh: he is shaken with a louder roar of laughter.  
> He weeps if he sees his friend’s tears, though he feels no grief.  
> If you ask for a little fire in wintertime,  
> he puts on his woollen cloak; if you say, “I am hot,” he sweats.  
> (Juvenal, II, 100)

Hence Umbricius says:

> We are not equals. Better is he who always,  
> night and day, can assume another’s face,  
> throw up his hands before that face, ready to praise  
> if his friend has belched well, or has done something  
> which modest speech could not utter openly.  
> (Juvenal, II, 104) [Col. 0482B]

This is fitting not merely for a friend, but not even for a free person, since true and sole freedom consists in the form of virtue, while shamefulness subjects those whom it infects to the lowest slavery. To be an actor or mime brings disgrace upon those whom dignity of nature or rank seems to have exempted from the reproach of such degradation.

Furthermore, the person who puts on another’s face and alternates the various expressions of passions lays snares for the soundness of his own senses, and “gathers food from the filth of other people’s ears.” Even if he denies in words that he is an actor, he confesses it in manners and shamefulness. This is characteristic of the assenter, who lives according to another’s nod and, before giving his own judgment, awaits another’s opinion on every matter.

The fawner, however—who is also designated by the name of assenter or flatterer, since one thing is marked by many signs—explores people’s minds and tests their will beforehand, so that he may conform his sentiments to whatever matter you wish, fraudulently stealing the favour of the person with whom he deals [Col. 0482C]. For he knows that, from the concurrence of feelings and the union of wills, the streams of friendship spring forth. “The same things to will and not to will,” as the historian says, “are indeed firm friendship.” Why not?

> Whoever believes that you agree with his pursuits  
> as their supporter will praise your game with both thumbs.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.18.66)

When he has perceived a person’s will, he so fawns, so caresses, so anoints with such an abundance of sweet favour, that he puts virtue to sleep and overturns the whole form of moderation—without which one never lives rightly—by an outpouring of the river Lethe.

“Does Thais give me great thanks?” The comic poet is pleasant and well suited to mingle often with our trifles. “Enormous,” he says. It would indeed have been enough if he had answered “great.” But because a flatterer’s fraud exaggerates everything and adds something of its own in order to heap up favour for itself, he says “enormous.” Nor does he blush at falsehood. For one who could persuade himself, for any reason, to stain a person’s honour with the mark of so great a shamefulness will certainly persuade himself to do what he desires, “if possible honourably; if not, by whatever means, the thing.”

But the person properly called a flatterer whitens each person’s vices; lest the other see himself, he fills the eyes of his interlocutor with a certain cloud of vanity and refreshes his ears with false titles of praise [Col. 0483A]. The moralist says:

> What of the most skilful race of flatterers, who praises  
> an unlearned friend’s speech, an ugly friend’s face,  
> and compares a weak man’s long neck with the neck  
> of Hercules holding Antaeus far from the ground?  
> He admires a thin voice, worse than which  
> not even he sounds whose wife is pecked by a hen.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 3.86)

This, however, appears by no means surprising if utterly depraved people, fouled by this grave and filthy disease, can be driven to such shamefulness. I consider this rather astonishing: that they have people who believe them, and who acquiesce more in another’s tongue concerning themselves than in the judgment of their own conscience. Each person seeks himself outside himself and disdains to know how scant is his own household store [Col. 0483B].

For there is nothing which a person cannot believe about himself when he is praised—not merely power equal to that of the gods, but whatever the soul swollen by the leaven of pride may conceive.

## Chapter V. On the caution required against flatterers, their manifold deceit, the companions of flattery, and their consequences
There are, however, people who do not admit common, plebeian flatteries—like those who, when they seek the favor of friends or dinner-guests, do not wish to be anointed with cheap perfume or rancid oil that smells foul to everyone. For what is more shameful than to transform one’s face for an actor’s blandishments, alter one’s dress, assume his gait, and not so much watch another as play the actor oneself? What is more absurd than, when another, with a great [Col. 0483C] gaping of the mouth, breathes forth the spirit of vanity in order to infect you, for you to spread the sails of your ears and the breadth of your heart so as to conceive swelling pride? And because these things are apparent to everyone, such services of vanity are more readily despised by most people.

Yet those flatteries are more to be feared because they are more harmful: those which are more carefully concealed beneath a kind of veil of caution and creep in, as it were, under the appearance of rebuke, correction, some other service, or virtue. You will find that some people have done this while seeking favor too immoderately. For Laelius says—not the Laelius who laid down the law of friendship, but the advocate of civil war and inciter of madness, also called Lentulus by others:

> “We complain that such sluggish patience has held your strength:  
> Did you lack confidence in us?  
> While hot blood still stirs these breathing bodies,  
>   
> [Col. 0483D] And while strong arms can still hurl the spear,  
> Will you endure the degenerate toga and the Senate’s kingship?  
> Is victory in civil war truly so miserable?”  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.361.)

Likewise, in comedies masters are deceived by the cunning of slaves: after first reproaching them, they allow their plans to be weakened and at last pretend themselves defeated, both to confirm credulous people in error and to win favor through the treachery of betrayal. With great industry they labor to deceive in such a way that they can never be convicted of falsehood. Their truth, indeed, serves falsehood.

What of those hunters after novelties, who pile up little rumors and satisfy the same curious ears, in order by this route to approach more readily what they desire? They are also most diligent observers of the right moment [Col. 0484A], lest they introduce anything untimely: rather, while someone is dining, or has been made cheerful by wine, or is possessed by any pleasure whatever. Vergil recalls this caution when he says that Dido sent her sister to recall Aeneas, she alone knowing the soft approaches and favorable moments of the man.

But who would not laugh when a groom, worth not three farthings, is clothed in purple through bundles of titles and, not without the sneering and loud laughter of his hearers, Dama becomes Marcus? Marcus has said:

> “Good heavens! When Marcus vouches for them, do you refuse  
> To trust the coins? Do you turn pale with Marcus as judge?  
> So it is: enter them, Marcus, in the tablets.”  
> (Persius, *Satires* V.79.)

Certainly, the goodwill of all ought to be sought, since it is the spring of friendship and the first advance of charity; but with honor intact—through zeal in duties, the path of virtue, the fruit of service, and integrity of speech. Let faithfulness also be present: that is, constancy in word and deed, and truth, which is the foundation of duties and of all good things.

Virtue seeks the favor of good people—and, if possible, of everyone—but disdains to approach it through sordid means. It is surely a noble and delicate thing, rejecting everything unbecoming. Every appearance that does not shine from itself is also suspect to it. Does virtue then lie in order to please? Does it call evil good and good evil? Does it urge on a friend who is not quite sound of mind, so that he may become still madder?

Moreover, although all assent is shameful, it is more pernicious when the authority of a person, nature, or rank is added [Col. 0484C] to the abetting of vice. Philosophers call probable that which appears so to all, or to most, or to the wiser persons, or to an expert in his own field. If, therefore, Plato—or Socrates—should commend someone’s wisdom, Aristotle keenness of intellect, Cicero abundance of eloquence, Pythagoras devotion to mathematics, Horace varieties of metre, or Ovid facility in verse-making—why should he not believe it? For incentives to vice enter individual minds more swiftly and forcefully,

> “…when they enter great minds  
> With weighty authorities behind them.”

Yet a mind in possession of itself is not led astray by these things, certainly because no one knows what is in a human being except the human spirit that is within him. Thus, in Vergil, a shepherd in possession of himself—and wiser than the learned and great men of our age—says:

> “The shepherds call me too a poet;  
> But I do not trust them.”  
> (Vergil, *Eclogues* IX.34.)

> “You too, if you turn pale at the sight of money, you scoundrel,  
> If in love-affairs you do whatever comes into your penis.”  
> (Persius, *Satires* IV.47.)

Though your entire neighborhood call you modest and chaste, do not believe them even when they swear it. Keep firmly in mind what you learned as a little child:

> “Do not believe others about yourself more than you believe yourself.”

I would not readily say which is first in fault: the person who pollutes his tongue with flatteries, or the person whose heart dissolves into joy because of them. In the latter, the blindness of self-exaltation is condemned; in the former, the fraud of blinding another. Everywhere deceit is condemned; and blindness arising from pride is nowhere acquitted. Granted that the flatterer is more wicked: the other is no less contemptible. He would not be caught in the snares of another’s tongue if he did not flatter himself. Why, then, does one who flatters himself accuse another of flattery? In accusing another, he condemns himself. For he does the very things he judges.

“Woe,” says the Lord, “to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand, and place pillows beneath the head of every age” (Ezek. 13). They surely sew cushions who lay snares for ears; who heap up vain and soft words with which to caress the feelings; who commend people’s deeds, in order to induce them to rest through the proclamations of fame and a certain sweet pleasantness of favor. For the use of a cushion and pillow is the softness of rest. Thus a cushion is put beneath every elbow when not merely an action, but everything attached to it, is commended. The head of every age is placed upon a pillow when someone takes delight, through the words of flatterers, in the works of his whole life.

And elsewhere: “He was building a wall, and they were plastering it.” Whoever heaps up depraved deeds upon the vice of a hardened mind builds a wall, not a house.
