Whoever makes a door in a wall alone remains outside wherever he enters. Whoever lives in depravity of action with a hardened mind is separated from the society of the saints. Therefore, whoever flatteringly applauds another’s evil deeds plasters the wall that has been built.

But although flattering everyone is shameful, it is far more shameful if flattery falls upon men of eminent authority or rank [Col. 0485C]. Indeed, the ordinances of the sacred canons provide that clerics known to serve flatteries are to be deposed without appeal. And rightly so, because every flattery has as its companions deceit and fraud, betrayal and the mark of falsehood; and in its train, the disgrace of servitude, the blinding of one’s neighbor, and the destruction of all honor. Should such a person not be expelled not merely from the clergy, but from the whole company of the faithful?

## Chapter VI. That flatterers have multiplied beyond number, and drive honorable persons, unlike themselves, out of distinguished households

Yet this plague has now grown so strong, through the Lord’s indignation, that if it should come to a conflict, [Col. 0485D] I fear that they could more easily drive out modest and good men than be driven out themselves. For a foul infection and cancerous disease creep through everyone, so that there is none—or scarcely anyone—whom this contamination does not stain.

Everyone seeks the goodwill of those among whom one lives. This is not merely permitted, but honorable, being among all the things brought forth by nature, the parent of virtues and excellent guide of right living. But when this affection abandons the rule of moderation, it is borne headlong; running through everything to be done and not to be done, through disgrace and good repute, it becomes a hunter for favor and an unchaste pursuer of influence. Once it has first corrupted a friend by blandishments, it steals away his fortune in the manner of a prostitute, diminishes his resources, heaps others’ spoils upon itself, and turns everything to [Col. 0486A] its own profit.

Thus it comes about that no slavish compliance is burdensome to it and no service seems unbecoming. It puts on the roles of every duty while fraudulently snatching the rewards of all. For who are those who gleam in fine clothing, walk in lofty style, are surrounded by a retinue of high-stepping horses, are whitened, as it were, by the services of fellow-soldiers and tent-companions; who boast of receiving the first greetings in the forum, have the foremost places at dinner, whose ears are soothed by the fostering use of forenames, and to whom the soft ears of nobles are opened? Who are those whom Fortune, by the oar-strokes of her wings, carries and exalts to the heights, and from whom every great household borrows the model and manner of its arrangement? Plainly, flatterers: those who live at another’s beck and call while fraudulently draining them dry.

Truth is harsh and often causes offense because it disdains to stroke someone. Yet its bitterness is more useful and more pleasing to sound minds than the dripping honeycomb of a prostitute’s tongue. For, as holy Solomon testifies, “The blows of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of a flatterer” (Prov. 27). Why should they not be? Faithfulness is always preferred to faithlessness. Faith does not remain unharmed where one thing is done and another feigned, especially where the mind and will intend harm.

If we follow the Stoics, *fides* (“faithfulness”) is so called because what has been said is done. “My light, my salvation, my refuge, my heart, and my life; unconquered leader, wisest of living beings, most generous and kind of all, pattern of life, mirror of virtue”—and other such importunately [Col. 0486C] introduced expressions—are they not full not so much of the vice of flattery as of poison? Some people do not even avoid the appearance of a buffoon while professing friendship. “Poisons,” says the wise man, “are not given unless coated with honey.” And there are no more hidden snares than those concealed under a pretence of service or under some name of relationship. You think it service, suspect friendship, assess affection: they are snares.

Nor, as myths relate—for even poets’ falsehoods serve truth—would Juno have driven deceived Semele into the fire unless she had put on the appearance of her nurse and feigned affection. You think service is being rendered to you: you are subjected to the most extreme and wretched slavery. For

> “…when he gently distils into the ear  
> A little…”

From the poison of nature and vice, I would perish if he does not remove all who speak the truth, since they disdain to incur the charge of flattery. A person is removed from favor—and fortunate if he is not judged an enemy—who not only opposes but even refuses to consent to the pleasures, even the more shameful pleasures, of a powerful friend. Indeed, not even agreement suffices for winning favor: one must approve, commend, applaud; when he has done every evil deed, he must be praised as though he had performed a good one. For as identity of wills is a sign of love, so each person is charged with enmity from disagreement. Therefore the satirist says:

> “What am I to do at Rome? I cannot lie;  
> If a book is bad, I cannot praise it or ask for it; I do not know  
> The movements of the stars; to promise a father’s funeral  
>   
> [Col. 0487A] I neither wish nor can; I have never  
> Inspected a frog’s entrails; others know how to carry to a bride  
> What an adulterer sends, what he commands. No thief  
> Will have me as his agent; and therefore I go out as nobody’s companion, as though  
> I were maimed, a body useless through a withered right hand.”  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* III.41.)

I therefore flee the city, full of such obscenities; poisoned by the venom of flatterers, I leave it to its own flatterers.

> “…Let Artorius live there,  
> And Catulus; let those remain who turn black into white.”

Yet do not suppose that the vices of one city alone are depicted: they are now those of the whole world. In this respect, believe the world to be Rome. I remember hearing that the Roman pontiff used to mock the Lombards, saying that they doff their caps to everyone with whom they speak because, at the beginning of a speech, they seek goodwill and soothe with a certain oil of commendation the heads of those with whom they deal.

“My son,” says Solomon, “if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1). “For they lie in wait against their own blood and plot deceits against their own souls. Keep your foot from their paths. For their feet run to evil, and they hasten to shed blood.”

## Chapter VII. That the fraud of flatterers must be avoided at the outset; and that it advances most powerfully through gifts or through the difficulty of services

Behold, the wisest man, instructing all people in his son, makes the favor of flatterers suspect to everyone and frightens all away—and this at the very beginning, perhaps because the first encounter with flatterers attacks one who is walking rightly [Col. 0487C]. Perhaps this is the prostitute from whom he commands flight. “The lips of the prostitute,” he says, “are a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil. But her end is bitter as wormwood, and her tongue sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet go down to death, and her steps penetrate to hell; they do not walk the path of life; her steps are wandering and untraceable. Therefore now, my son, hear me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not come near the doors of her house” (Song 4).

Although these words are thought to refer principally to the sect of heretics, they are not alien to the fraud of flattery. If, therefore, it is not permitted even to approach the doors of her house, is she to be admitted into the innermost recesses of the heart?

Moreover, since the vice of flattering is manifold—some flatter by expression, others by word, others by deed or gift—the fraud of flattery is most effective when gifts confirm the pretence, or difficult service bears witness to it more emphatically. If you believe otherwise,

> “…your own times deceive you,  
> If, after taking a bribe, you think honey sweeter.”  
> (Ovid, *Fasti* I.189.)

In the corruption of this age, frequent giving is the proof of true affection. The art of arts, if you wish to please, is to give frequently.

> “…If you know how to serve hot sow’s udder,  
> If you know how to give a rough companion a worn cloak,”  
> (Persius, *Satires* I.53)

you will be another Mercury to him; and, if you wish for more, you are Apollo:

> “Fairer than Phoebus and Phoebus’ sister.”

[Col. 0488A] Nor need you despair of the support of one whom you feed with gifts. For little gifts are the nourishment of shadowy favor and a prostituted name; unless they are frequently bestowed, they destroy the name of friendship. It is useless to presume upon the size of a gift unless you moderate a soul inflamed with the fire of desire by the refreshment of frequent visits, and soothe the continual hunger of avarice by frequent installments of benefits.

It is said to be the nature of eagles that, when they have crammed their stomachs with a fuller meal, they suspend hunger until the fifteenth day—or, as others think, until the fortieth—and reject an abundance of food offered to them, content with one satiation. The condition of the rich, however—or rather of those who prostitute their favor for sale—is very different. In some respect they are more like human beings who must eat often because they are hungry often; they can scarcely prolong accumulated hunger to the fortieth day [Col. 0488B] without becoming angry with their friends if they have not filled avarice’s gaping mouth.

In antiquity, statues of the Graces used to be fashioned naked, because the solidity of friendship and the truth of faithfulness—without which even the name of grace cannot subsist—cannot be obscured by any cosmetic of pretence. But now, when we come among people who love not friends but themselves in each individual, the cosmetic of duplicity is necessary to please. For among such people favor, because it is not gratis, is no longer favor but a bait for gain. It has become the face of a prostitute and blushes at no vice whatever while it aims at profit.

It is the ancient complaint of a wise man grieving the unworthy decline of friendship:

> “That once-venerable name of friendship  
> Is for sale and sits in the marketplace as a prostitute.”  
> (Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* II.3.19.)

This is evident from the fact that, if usefulness ceases, rare indeed is the person—or none at all—who cultivates the virtue of friendship for its own sake. In so many cycles of ages, through such a lapse of time, amid such a multitude and diversity of persons, scarcely, as Laelius says, are three or four pairs found in love.

Our arbiter himself laments this, although he seems to have assumed another person’s role. He says:

> “If the name of friendship clings only so far as it is useful,  
> The movable counter makes its play upon the board.  
> While fortune remains, you preserve the face of a friend;  
>   
> [Col. 0488D] When it has fallen, you turn your faces in shameful flight.  
> A troupe performs a mime on the stage: one is called father,  
> Another son, another bears the name of a rich man.  
> Soon, when the page has enclosed the laughable roles,  
> The true face returns and what was feigned perishes.”  
> (Petronius, *Satyricon* 76.)

## Chapter VIII. On the comedy, or tragedy, of the world

He indeed employs an elegant comparison, because almost everything done in the crowd of the profane multitude resembles comedy more than an actual event. “The life of man upon earth is warfare,” says Job (Job 7). But if the prophetic spirit had conceived our times, it might excellently have been said that the life of man upon earth is comedy, where each person, forgetting himself, represents another’s role.

But perhaps the prophet uttered his oracle to teach those not yet swallowed up by earth to wage continual warfare. For those who, captive to the impulse of vices, are dragged to punishment—going after their own desires as an ox to be slaughtered for sacrifice—although they seem in body to inhabit the surface of the earth, are nevertheless swallowed up alive and descend alive into hell.

And if we follow another figure of speech, those utterly inhabit the earth whose citizenship is not in heaven, who do not know that anything exists for them in heaven, and whose minds desire only what is seen upon the earth. Continual warfare is likewise appointed for those who, to return to fables, lack neither Tantalus’ water, Tityus’ vulture, Ixion’s wheel, the jar of the Belides, nor Sisyphus’ stone, while a will entangled with the world cannot fulfil its purpose so long as it is absent [Col. 0489B] from the Lord. Their life is warfare—and certainly wickedness.

If this shocks you, another interpretation will teach you that the life of man upon earth is temptation, a word which, if we follow its proper meaning, more often bears the sense of evil. In this temptation—or wickedness—although the Lord has reserved for himself seven thousand men, nearly the entire world seems, in our author’s judgment, to be playing the mime, somehow looking toward its own comedy. And, what is worse, people persist in their comedy to such an extent that they cannot return to themselves when need arises.

I have seen boys imitate the defects of stammerers for so long that afterward they could not speak correctly even when they wished. “Practice,” as someone says, “is difficult to unlearn, and habit supports a second nature,” which, though

> “You drive it out with a fork, will still return,”  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.10.24.)

Thus the moral philosopher wisely and usefully says: “Choose the best habit of life from your earliest age; practice will make it pleasant to you.”

Accordingly, this worldly comedy assaults the minds of great men. The changing appearance of times is a kind of variety of actions. The roles serve those actions, while in them the sport of playful Fortune is performed. What else is it when she now clothes some newcomer and unknown person in the greatest power and raises him to the summit of kingship; now hurls another, clad in purple before he was born, from the height of a kingdom into enemy chains, and plunges him, enslaved, into the most extreme miseries [Col. 0489D]? Or, as frequently occurs, stains infamous swords with the blood not only of tyrants but also of princes—by the hands of the lowest men, even worthless slaves?

> “If Fortune wishes, a rhetorician will become consul;  
> If the same Fortune wishes, a consul will become a rhetorician.”

In this respect, human life seems more like tragedy than comedy, because the end of nearly all is sad: all the world’s sweetness, however great, turns bitter, and grief takes possession of the end of joy (Prov. 3). However much the wicked flourish in their ways and are gilded by the concurrence of prosperity; however readily Fortune serves them, she will overthrow their steps at the end and finally become bitter as wormwood.

“Why,” asks blessed Job, “do the wicked live, are lifted up, and strengthened by riches? Their offspring endure before them, a throng of kinsmen and descendants before their eyes; their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them. Their bull has conceived and has not miscarried; their cow has calved and has not been deprived of her offspring. Their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children leap in play. They take up tambourine and lyre and rejoice at the sound of the instrument. They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend to hell” (Job 21). What outcome of preceding joy can be more bitter, or what end of a fortunate course more unfortunate?

For this is the way of those “who are not in the toil of men, nor shall they be scourged with men” (Ps. 72). Surely the Lord’s counsel cast them down precisely while they were being raised up. These things are more rightly ascribed to him than [Col. 0490B] to Fortune, who either is from him or, as I am more inclined to think, does not exist at all.

For the moral philosopher says:

> “Do not call Fortune, who does not exist, blind.”

Homer too, in that work of most celebrated perfection, disdained to know Fortune, so much so that she is not named in any part of so great a poem. He preferred to commit the government of all things to God alone, whom he called Morphan, rather than ascribe anything to the rashness of Fortune. For it is as certain that she is no goddess as it is certain that she is called and painted blind. Her blindness, therefore, is vainly reproached, since she cannot be found in the nature of things.

Thus chance also is proved not to exist, if someone defines it as an unforeseen event, since nothing occurs whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason; and the faithful preacher teaches that nothing happens on earth without cause. Yet because certain things happen apart from the intention of those acting and some things contrary to expectation, they are enclosed under the name “chance,” although they are foreseen by the reason of the One who orders all things just as much as those things which seem bound by the constraints of the law of nature and necessity.

Therefore these contingencies themselves are demonstrably so joined to the first cause of all things that everything is referred to it; and, in my opinion, these very things necessarily follow from the establishment of all that exists. Perhaps wiser people will laugh at my foolishness, because I agree that God’s existence follows from the existence of all things; but the Peripatetics have taught me that a cause may be inferred, at least probably, from its effect. Teachers of the faith, moreover, necessarily infer that Cause from all things: the Cause from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, and without whom nothing can have been made or subsist [Col. 0490D].

That we appear to ascribe something to Fortune does not prejudice him in any way. But because our discourse concerns human beings, we use human language, treating each matter, as we said before, with a broad brush and offering a subtle account of none. If this is patiently admitted, what prevents us from hearing those things written by the philosophers of the Gentiles for public benefit? “Whatever things were written,” he says, “were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15).

Since peace is absent from the children of Adam—born for labor, conceived ready for scourging in sins, brought forth into toil, not so much going as running toward death, than which nothing is sadder—patience is necessary and consolation useful. Drawn from the oil of gladness in the conscience and from the immensity of God’s mercy, it cherishes and strengthens, with hope of future things, those predestined to life.

“O guardian of humankind,” says blessed Job, expressing in himself the calamities of the human race, “why have you set me as your adversary, and made me burdensome to myself?” (Job 7). For there is no one who, as his sins demand, does not find within himself the causes and material of pain, since even philosophy testifies that everyone encounters what he would not wish, or lacks what he would wish.

Thus also the faithful soul, whose joys of true blessedness are delayed, seeks the upper spring together with the lower spring. Therefore, to lend a devout hearing to the fictions of the Gentiles, the end of all things is tragic. Or, if the name “comedy” is more agreeable, I will not draw out the rope of contention, since it is agreed between us that nearly the whole world, according to Petronius, plays the actor.

A distinguished writer of our own time has also elegantly expressed this, though in the words of unbelievers:

> “Blind fate turns about the ridiculous labors of men;  
> Our age is a jest and a plaything for the gods.”

The theatre in which this immense, marvellous, and indescribable tragedy or comedy can be performed is wonderfully proportioned to it. Its arena is as great as the world itself. It is very difficult for anyone to be admitted while excluded, or sent out while enclosed, as long as he wears the muddy garment of flesh [Col. 0491C]. For one must put it off with such subtlety that one may pass through a needle’s eye without any friction. Otherwise no one departs whole—perhaps because “Styx, flowing nine times around, confines” this capacious arena.

“I have seen all things under the sun,” says Ecclesiastes, “and behold, at once all is vanity” (Eccl. 1), because all things that depart from the solid state of truth are subject to vanity, which befits our comedy. For creation has been subjected to vanity unwillingly. Although the whole habitation of our seats is enclosed by nine spheres—or rather globes—nevertheless all must someday depart, and that inexorable Charon will ferry all across in the ancient ship of his time.

Others will succeed all alike; and so a passing human being remains in appearance, just as a familiar river remains in its channel although water flows past. “Where,” says Baruch, “are the mighty men, who from the beginning knew war; or those who played with the birds of heaven and stored up gold for themselves, in which people trust; joining field to field, house to house, to the boundaries of a place, and there is no end of their possessions?” (Bar. 3). And he immediately adds what use and continual experience have now persuaded everyone: “They went down to hell, and others succeeded into their place” (ibid.).

Yet it goes well with those who depart without being transferred from this sport of Fortune in order to be cast into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8), and who do not pass from the waters of snow mentioned by holy Job (ch. 24) to excessive heat. It goes well with those who await their own Elysian fields, which the true sun of righteousness illuminates by his presence.

But why do I exclude the Elysian fields from the enclosures of mutable things by my words? Certainly, they are included in part, lying open in the breadth of good minds, to whom the Father of lights has granted that they may move in their entire activity in the knowledge and love of good. Thus the moral philosopher says to the restless person who foolishly seeks happiness outside himself:

> “What you seek is everywhere—  
> It is at Ulubrae, if an equitable mind does not fail you.”  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.11.29.)

## Chapter IX. That the world has its own Elysian fields; that the faith of our time and of the preceding Fathers is the same; and that cultivators of virtue are spectators of this theatre

The world, therefore, has its own [Col. 0492B] Elysian fields, and knows its own sun and stars. Virtue is a kind of solar ray, given for the use of all from the fountain of brightness; and it makes all things it touches outstanding through its own splendor. Hence even those whom the beauty of this ray seems to have breathed upon—as though by a reflected image of themselves—immediately shine in the sight of those subject to them and become, in a certain manner, glorious by the title of virtue.

Far be it that anyone should be truly glorious except one who glories in the Lord. “For it is not the person who commends himself, or whom a human being commends, who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10). This true and sole virtue merits; not every image of virtue whatsoever.

I think this is whatever philosophers promise themselves as excellent in morals through nature’s benefit and exercise of mind, without grace. For in this very thing they became vain in their thoughts, trusting in free will; and “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1), and appeared foolish. Hence the moral philosopher says:

> “…It is enough to pray to Jupiter, who gives and takes away,  
> That he give life and wealth; I myself will provide my own character.”

Another likewise says:

> “If prudence exists, you have no divinity; but we  
> Make you, Fortune, a goddess and place you in heaven.”

Cato also, although he did not know the true God and wandered amid the superstitions of the Gentiles, nevertheless in Libya despised the oracles of Jupiter whom he worshipped, thinking himself sufficient for the things he had to do.

Indeed, even the image of virtue itself possesses a certain brightness of beauty and comeliness, so that whatever is seen in it is believed beautiful and comely by reason of it. Yet what is obscured in the darkness of ignorance is not altogether comely; nor can anyone shine except in faith in him who is the true light and enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). From this it is plain that true virtue cannot exist except in knowledge and worship of the true God.

Ezekiel’s vision also did not leave this unspoken, asserting that those who preceded Christ and those who followed him possess the same confession. The faith of the saints of the Old and New Testaments differs in this: the latter rejoice that what the former awaited and desired to be fulfilled has now been fulfilled for them. Therefore let the image of virtue be venerable, since without faith and love [Col. 0493A] the substance of virtue cannot exist. And would that there might be found among us someone who possesses even the image of virtue!

For who embraces virtue itself? Who even puts on the shadows of the virtues in which we see the Gentiles to have flourished, although, Christ being withheld from them, they did not obtain the fruit of true blessedness? Who imitates the diligence of Themistocles, the gravity of Fronto, the self-control of Socrates, the faithfulness of Fabricius, the innocence of Numa, the chastity of Scipio, the endurance of Ulysses, the frugality of Cato, the dutifulness of Titus? Who does not venerate them with admiration?

> “For goodness is praised—and freezes.”  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* I.74.)

The men mentioned above, and great and praiseworthy men like them, shone as certain stars of their ages, illuminating their own times and leading their contemporaries forward into that measure of righteousness and truth which had shone upon them by divine ordering.

Likewise, in the successive generations of the faithful people, humanity has never lacked its own stars for driving away the darkness of its night and the troubles of its blindness: men noble by the title of virtue and shining with the badges of great deeds, through whose examples others are continually advanced toward the worship of righteousness.

Did not Abel teach innocence, Enoch purity of conduct? What did Noah lack in endurance of hope and work? What was lacking to Abraham in faithfully fulfilled obedience? Isaac instructs in marital chastity, and Jacob displays endurance of labor. Joseph rewards his fratricidal brothers with good recompense and thereby teaches that good things should be returned by good people for evils. Amid many thousands of an unbelieving, hardened people, ever provoking God, the gentleness of Moses is displayed, and the greatness of spirit of Joshua, confident amid impending adversities, is shown. Job offers an example of patience.

And the Baptist, the forerunner of the Savior’s grace, while preaching repentance and commanding flight from vices, draws out confession of truth and sharpens the tongues of all believers for rebuking injury and condemning wickedness. Why should I recount the Fathers of both Testaments, whose examples are instruction in morals and the most upright ordinances of life?

These are among the seven thousand men whom the Lord reserved for himself, so that they might not bend their knees before Baal or prostitute their precious souls to any vanity whatever [Col. 0493D]. These are those considered mad among the senseless because they refuse to share another’s madness. They are believed destined to an end without honor because they disdain to pollute the dignity of their nature with the costume of a worldly actor.

These are perhaps those who look down from the lofty summit of virtues upon the theatre of the world and, despising Fortune’s game, are driven by no enticements toward vanities and false madnesses. They already rejoice in their own Elysian fields; they see very many things for their benefit and turn everything they see toward it. For when a faithful soul is lifted from the earth, then at last it draws all things to itself.

They observe the worldly comedy with him who stands above, ceaselessly beholding people, their actions, and their wills. Since all play the actor, someone must necessarily be a spectator. Let no one complain that his movements are not seen by anyone, since he acts in the sight of God, his angels, and the few wise people who likewise are spectators of these circus-games. Rather, let anyone blush who behaves indecently in so great a light and makes his whole self ugly by mimetic performance.

## Chapter X. That roles are fitted to one another and languish when separated; concerning Cleopatra, Augustus, and Scipio; that the Romans are devoted to vanity; and what the end of flattery is

Moreover, in this mockery of Fortune, roles are fitted to one another [Col. 0494B]; and if they depart from each other in either direction, the appearance of the entire action is altered—as if you removed Glycerium or Pamphilus. For once either has been removed, the other’s name disappears; and if you remove the suspicious old man from lovers, Davus is either nonexistent or entirely useless. Hence this passage:

> “…Labienus, brave in Caesar’s arms,  
> Now, a worthless deserter,”

With a private commander, he surveys lands and seas. (Lucan, V.345.) For if Fortune’s decree separates persons who have grown accustomed to one another and mutually sustain one another, it commonly happens that each seems unfit for all its own activities and, as though excluded from the logic of its role, is disgraced. Cleopatra’s seductions were broken when she found neither Julius nor Antony. Indeed, she bent Caesar, conqueror of the world, with gifts; the unconquerable spirit of that invincible man was overcome by a courtesan’s beauty and an unveiled face. Thus the poet, expressing the anxious artifice of her seduction, adds:

> Her look supports her prayers, and her shameless beauty pleads.

But when Julius had been removed from human affairs, she who had gloried in marriage to the Roman emperor dared to seek the enslavement of the Roman prince. Nor without cause, since she found Antony ready for anything. She thought that nothing would be lacking to her glory in comparison with Caesar if she mounted the bed of one who, as successor to Pompey’s power—and, as he pretended, to Caesar’s lawful authority—trusted more in Fortune’s rashness than in consciousness of virtue.

When, moreover, she approached Augustus with the boldness of feminine shamelessness, and was disappointed in her hope, she counted his love of honour an injury, called chastity pride, and believed war must be declared upon one whom she had found stronger than Julius Caesar. She attempted every art of harm; and at last, when captured and cast at Augustus’ feet, she was still soliciting the commander’s eyes. But in vain: her beauty stood beneath the prince’s chastity. When, despairing, she learned that she was being kept for the victor’s triumph, she found her guard less vigilant, escaped, withdrew into the mausoleum of the kings, and there, dressed as custom required in her most splendid ornaments, amid rare perfumes and upon a throne heaped everywhere with riches, laid herself beside her Antony. Applying asps to her breasts and veins, she was thus released by death as if by sleep.

The Psylli—[Note: Paris edition: *Persilli*]—summoned by Augustus’ command, who are accustomed to draw out the poison’s malignity with their tongues, were unable to help because they had been called too late. It was fitting that this poisonous courtesan, born to corrupt morals and storm the chastity of noble men, should perish thus. Formerly she had ruled kings; afterwards, pitiable but not deserving pity in her lot, she made an end not tragic for herself but comic for the Roman Empire which she had tried to overthrow. Among Augustus’ more illustrious titles is counted the fact that, in his encounter with so great a plague, he remained unconquered.

Yet something no less remarkable is found in Scipio Africanus. After his extraordinary victory over Hannibal, he earned the signal praise of extraordinary self-restraint. Hannibal had cut down the Roman army until his enemies were glutted, and until he ordered his own soldier even to spare the sword. By the victor’s command a solid bridge was made from the corpses of the slain in the torrent Vergellus. Two bushels of rings were sent to Carthage, so that he might honour Mars, Libya’s protector, with a golden shield for the notable victory. And Rome would undoubtedly then have met her final day, had Hannibal known how to use victory as he knew how to conquer.

In vengeance for these disasters Scipio Africanus was sent by the senate. From the Pyrenees to the Pillars of Hercules and the Ocean, he recovered the lost province with such success that it is scarcely known whether he conquered more swiftly or more easily. He also restored to the barbarians captive boys and girls of outstanding beauty, and allowed none of them to come into his sight, lest he should seem to have sampled, even with his eyes, anything of virginal integrity. How Hannibal yielded to him, and how the laurel conspicuous upon the commander’s ship promised manifest victory, Titus Livy, historian of the Punic war, recounts.

But amid the glory of so great a triumph, what citizen was more modest than he? In such success he allowed himself to be addressed neither as lord nor as victor by anyone except Hannibal and a few accomplices who, after breaking the treaty, had deceitfully rejected equitable conditions of peace. He also ordered those removed from the army who, though reproved, did not obey his prohibitory command, as guilty of flattery and enemies of public welfare. Yet the race of Aeneas has not even now put off this softness of ear, so as not to take pleasure in flatteries. Though they were very grave from the beginning—in this chiefly denying the origin of Trojan frivolity—the famous testimony of histories is that they have continually suffered from this fault. Hence the saying: “Every Roman is corrupted by flattery, or corrupts.”

Certainly, if not by words, all can be overcome by deceitful gifts. Those whom little presents do not cast down are caught by honours. Romulus consecrated the auspices of the city to his gods by the sacrilege of parricide and the bloody crime of a brother’s blood. Then, troubled by ghosts, he appeased his slain brother by the vain honour of a pretended sharing of power. The Roman people also deified their emperors—whom, according to Roman custom, it had faithfully slaughtered—with even more faithful empty consolation, clothing manifest treachery in a pretext, as though it were serving draughts to the man it had killed. They lied that these men had passed into the lot of the gods, as though the hand of the Almighty were not sufficient for governing his heaven and world unless tyrants were added to it. Thus they became native gods (*divi indigetes*), or, as others prefer, heroes—men whom Roman treachery had not judged worthy even of the human condition.

From this was derived the term by which princes, conspicuous in titles of virtue and in the light of true faith, dare—indeed, rejoice—to be called “divine,” by an old custom still prevailing even in fault and against the Catholic faith. But if one comes to words, the Roman now surpasses Greek treachery in this respect: he taught the artifice of flattery so thoroughly that it most easily passes to a receptive people. This nation invented the forms of address by which we lie to rulers while adorning singularity with the honour of plurality, and transmitted them by the authority of its name to neighbouring peoples and descendants.

Whenever you inquire into this, let that time come to mind when Gaius Caesar, casting off—or perhaps completing—the dictator, became everything and seized everything. The image of that age often occurs to me whenever all the affairs of subjects are disposed according to a more powerful man’s nod, and, though their minds resist, they are ready to pronounce upon themselves a sentence of exile or death. Hence comes dreadful power; hence the goads of an oppressive and burning conscience shake fearful hearts and claim chief authority over all. So much so that priests conceal the precepts of divine law; elders do not know wisdom; the judge is ignorant of law; the superior knows nothing of authority; the subject rejects discipline; the free-born despise liberty; in short, the whole people reject quiet and peace. For while all are borne along by the will of one ruler, every one and all are deprived of their own judgment.

Was this not the appearance of the time when

> [lacuna] the fathers sat ready to vote,  
> should he seek kingship, the temples, the senate’s throat,  
> and daughters-in-law ready to suffer unspeakable things?  
> (Lucan, V.305.)

And was it well with the citizens in this alone: that Caesar was ashamed to command more than Rome could endure? Did not the idea of a tyrant pass to the successors of tyranny, while they suppose that he preferred laws to be abolished by himself rather than observed by humble men? And the shadow of liberty is preserved in this: each person pretends to have wished what is commanded and makes—indeed, seems to make—a virtue of necessity, joining consent to necessity and gladly embracing what is imposed upon him. Here, however, there is no part of true or free liberty, where flattery claims everything for itself, vanity everything, and nothing is left to truth or virtue.

Do not doubt that flattery is inseparable from deceit, since Gnatho, in the character of the flatterer, confesses of himself: “When I deceive most, then I triumph.” For as the end of an orator is to persuade by speech, and that of a physician to cure by medicine, so the end of a flatterer is to deceive by sweet talk. Thus:

> The pipe sings sweetly while the fowler deceives the bird;

and poisons are offered coated with honey, so that they may harm more quickly. Yet

> It is not always the physician’s task that the sick man be relieved.  
> (Ovid, *Pontics* I.iii.17)

Nor does the orator always attain his end, which lies in another person. Likewise, the flatterer does not always deceive or triumph over his friend; nevertheless, he does not fail of his purpose if he has omitted nothing within the circumstances available to him. Ulysses did not escape the Sirens’ voices because they lacked any sweetness to charm him, but because he opposed the solid strength of virtue to the spurs of pleasure and the prostituting enticements of vanity.

The Pharisaic tempter and the Herodian plotter likewise used every art of fraud in order to catch in deceitful speech him “in whose mouth no deceit was found” (1 Peter 2). “Master,” they say, “we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in truth; and you care for no one, for you do not regard the persons of men” (Matthew 22). What, I ask, could be more flattering? But the question that follows revealed whither their deceit tended and whither their envy was directed: “Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” (ibid.). Behold, a snare is laid at the innocent man’s feet, and wickedness vainly stretched out its traps for his overthrow. For if he judged tribute ought to be paid, he would subject to slavery the Lord’s peculiar people, the seed of the free, the Lord’s splendid inheritance, hitherto bound only by tithes, first-fruits, and legal ceremonies. But if he answered that taxes should be refused to those who fought for the welfare and peace of all, he could justly be seized by the tax-collectors as an instigator of sedition and guilty of offence against imperial majesty.

But because “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of the winged creatures,” all the snares of their calumny were undone when, after the tribute coin had been produced, he ruled that each person’s image should be restored to its owner: thus Caesar’s things were to be rendered to Caesar, without defrauding God of his own right. Not everyone, indeed, is granted such escape from the snares of blandishments: one person does not foresee them; another cannot avoid them even when he has foreseen them. Yet one thing is certain: those devoted to this vice are no more pleased by virtue than those who live in a kitchen smell sweet.

## Chapter XI. On Gift-Givers and Promisers; and Why It Is Not Expedient to Promise as a Matter of Virtue

A flatterer’s power consists greatly in appearing, after setting aside his own interests, to care for those of another: never or rarely speaking of your own advantage, but always or often of the advantage of the person you are seeking to catch. Moreover, keep your hand restrained, lest you accept anything even when it is thrust upon you against your will—though the Jordan should flow into the mouth of one who, because he desires everything, thinks that everything belongs to him by right.

The hungry belly of certain insatiable animals, until it is satisfied, begrudges others their common food; and wherever another’s want is relieved, it suspects itself of suffering fraud. Thus the fortunate man sometimes thinks that whatever is bestowed upon another, under any title whatever, has been taken from himself. Crassus bears witness: as the story goes, because he alone, or beyond all others, had thirsted for gold among the Parthians, and his soldier dissembled this fact, he drank gold. Jugurtha too often disarmed and broke Roman power and army, shaking even the majesty of the city itself, now by giving much, now by promising very much.

Such conduct, however, is permissible and often advantageous for those accustomed to make gifts. Otherwise, a promise does not advance the gaining of favour; rather, as a fraudulent deception, it commonly extinguishes even the favour which appears to exist. This is all the more true when one deals with a more prudent and serious man. Simplicity lies more open to the traps of deceivers and is more easily tripped up. Hence he who filled not a city but the world with wanton loves, instructing the seducer of girls and the shameless lover, says:

> Make promises: for what harm is there in promising?  
> Any man can be rich in promises.

But the philosopher declares that this is never, or very rarely, advantageous—and then only for a just cause. For if one lacks the means to fulfil a promise, it is rash to promise what one cannot perform. If one has the power to give, but the will to confer a benefit does not produce its effect, the promiser incurs not gratitude for the promise but the stain of lying. And if he fulfils his pledged word after an interval, the very splendour of generosity and appearance of beneficence are tarnished, because the delay made him seem in the meantime to have been unwilling. Hence the excellent versifier:

> Delay blackens the giver’s merit; gifts bestowed swiftly  
> win more praise and more favour.

Moreover, who is certain about the future, so as to know that he will at some time be able to fulfil what he postpones? Did not the counsellor of truth, defender of faith, vessel of election—I mean the Teacher of the Gentiles—disappoint the desire of the faithful whose minds he had kept in suspense by expectation of his coming? What else does his excuse accomplish, in which he says that with him there was not “yes and no,” but only “yes,” and protests that he has not acted lightly? If he could not do what he wished, because the Lord hindered him—for he wished what he promised—what wise person securely promises what depends on the ease of nature, when he can easily be prevented by very many causes?

Further, anyone may sometimes change his intention for a just reason. Someone appears worthy of a benefit at one time, but in the course of events is found unworthy of it. And sometimes one is unworthy who, turning to the fruit of a better life, extorts a benefit by his merits even from an outside hand, as the common saying has it. In such cases changing one’s plan is often not a fault but a virtue. For, to learn from fables, Theseus would not have been deprived of his only son had he wished to change his purpose. And Phoebus, driven by the goad of grief which he conceived at Phaethon’s fall, would not, as an exile from the region of heaven, have pastured Admetus’ herds, had he been permitted to change the vow by which he had bound himself, with the Styx as witness to his oath, to that ambitious son.

And lest you despise examples drawn from fables: the unbelieving king, from the Gospel history, would more salutarily have dissolved his rash and faithless oath than, in extinguishing the lamp of the Word, removing the forerunner of grace, and killing the herald of truth, he should pollute the table, defile the banquet, and overthrow the majesty of the palace, while all things serve incest and obey the dancing girl. The ethical rule is that promises need not always be kept, if perhaps they would be harmful to the recipient or ruinous to the promiser. And the law of friendship prevailed: from friends one may ask or do only honourable things. The law itself also provides that no promise which has a shameful or grievous outcome should be fulfilled.

Finally, a prior promise either destroys or diminishes the gratitude owed for a subsequent benefit. And as missiles that are foreseen strike less heavily, while those not anticipated at all wound more severely, so in benefits that which is conceived from a promise is received less gratefully, while that which comes unexpectedly is accepted with greater pleasure. Although a bare promise, as legal experts say, produces no action at law, every promiser has, before truth—as the saying goes—“fixed his thumb”: when civil law falls silent, he is bound by faith according to nature. But what plaintiff will act more harshly than faith if faith itself begins to accuse? If conscience brings the action, who will acquit?

> Whatever is committed as an evil example displeases its own author:  
> this is the first punishment, that with himself as judge  
> no guilty person is acquitted.  
> (Juvenal XIII.1)

But if conscience itself justifies, who will condemn? Undoubtedly he who is feared at that tribunal where the human day is despised and conscience finds nothing to allege in opposition. But if deeds accuse the soul, conscience stands by as witness against it, and truth examines the case by the standard of equity, what praetor, I ask, will punish more severely one charged and liable for serious falsehood? Certainly, though the praetor is called the living voice of the law, truth often reverses his sentence. But truth’s sentence remains incapable of reversal, because its righteousness is everlasting righteousness and its law is equity. By contrast, in the praetorium the strictest law is often the greatest injustice.

Therefore whoever promises is a debtor, and under the compelling sentence of truth is forced to fulfil the pledged faith of his undertaking. But what necessity extorts diminishes gratitude. Hence the philosophical saying cited above: “Do not hasten to promise, lest when you wish to do so you cannot; or, when you can, you may not wish to do so for a just reason; or, when you have done it, you may lose or diminish gratitude, because you have first ensnared yourself in the word of your mouth.” Yet it happens that it is not only permitted to promise, but advantageous. To pass over for the moment other examples: Christ himself both promised and sent the Paraclete to the disciples. To the same disciples, when they asked what would happen to those who had left everything for him, he promised seats in the regeneration and the judicial authority which they would possess with him. From these examples it is clear that the cause commends both intention and deed; and thus it is evident that the philosopher’s rule need not be invalidated.

## Chapter XII. On the Accountants and Secretaries of the Rich; That Friendship Exists Only among the Good; That a Rich Man Is More Apt to Have a Dependant Than a Friend; That Familiarity with the Rich, Though It Seems Useful, Is Often Dangerous; and That One Must Live Innocently

But if you persist in surpassing not only promisers but gift-givers in the favour of the person whose favour you seek, involve yourself in his accounts. Spare expenses, for one who knows his secrets and saves his money-chests cannot displease a diligent householder. The faults of the person who compensates for moral ugliness by economy of expense are welcome. “The best revenue, if you do not know it,” says Cicero, “is thrift.” A poor thrifty man is easily supplied; a rich spendthrift is very easily emptied.

Even the largest chest has a bottom; through a small outlet, however great the quantity of accumulated waters, it flows away; and the abundance of a spring disappears when the fruitfulness of its bubbling vein is removed. A jar usually pours out its enclosed liquid through a narrow passage. Thus, by very small yet frequent and continual expenditures, the greatest resources are exhausted; and by the subtraction of brief trifles, a vast inheritance is plundered—unless perhaps the spendthrift finds money restored to life.

> Luxury is the ravager of wealth, and poverty, miserable,  
> always clings to it, following with humble step.  
> (Claudian, *Against Rufinus* I.35)

Therefore one must spare things whose necessary use is imminent, and add something to a quantity diminished by the continual deduction of portions. Though the resources of an only heir flow away to his use, it pleases a diligent householder if they are at least kept by the reckoning of accounts; and what slips away without his knowledge is lost twice over. Moreover:

> … the smell of profit is good from any source whatever.

Let that saying of the poet, worthy of the gods and Jupiter himself, always be upon your lips:

> “No one asks where he gets it; but he must have it.”

To occupy yourself with such matters is to bind the rich man with the closer cords of favour, though he surpass Proteus in changeableness of mind. Or, if the favour of truth fails, you may at least secure the display of closer familiarity. But even if you cannot attain both a share in private affairs and the safeguards of account-keeping, force yourself into his secrets by any art. Do you not know that those who seek to rule emperors themselves

> wish to know the household’s secrets, and thereby to be feared?

The more carefully something is concealed, the more diligently it should be investigated. Indeed:

> He will be dear to Verres who can accuse Verres whenever he wishes.

If, however, charity or friendship can exist among the wicked—this was the question. At last it was decided that it cannot exist except among the good. There is certainly great agreement among effeminate and wicked people; but it differs from charity as much as light differs from darkness. And though the wicked, like the good, can sometimes will the same thing and reject the same thing, they do not attain the title of friendship. Thus Crispus, the foremost Latin historian, and Cicero himself, held that among the wicked there is faction, whereas among good men there is true friendship.

Yet though, prevented by his wickedness, a vicious person cannot be a friend, he who can inspire fear through his awareness of secrets is to be feared, even if he is not to be revered. The saying of the moralist is apt:

> He who has made you a partner in an honourable secret thinks that he owes you nothing, and will never confer anything upon you.

It has also long been questioned whether anyone among the rich and powerful ever comes to love. The accepted conclusion is that they never, or rarely, love—and especially in cases in which they seem to love themselves rather than others. Contraries cannot exist in the same thing. The more desire the rich possess, the less charity they have; for these are especially opposed to one another. As someone says: “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man; and it is exceedingly rare for wealth to abound unless it is consolidated by the glue of love and desire.” The vigilance and labour of a desiring mind acquire wealth; yet a more diseased anxiety retains and preserves it. The moralist says:

> It is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been gained than to seek it:  
> there is chance in the latter, but in the former there is the work of skill.

Since the one is reckoned under the name of skill, the other under that of chance, who preserves wealth long without intense application of mind? Certainly the old proverb says: “Where love is, there is the eye; and where there is vigilant attention of mind, there is a fixed placing of heart.” Therefore, though riches often come even to a reluctant and resisting mind, the faithful philosopher forbids one to set one’s heart upon them; and the Teacher of the Gentiles says that those who desire to become rich fall into the snare and temptation of the devil. He who is greater than both—the firstborn of the dead and prince of the kings of the earth—asserts that God and Mammon cannot be served together, because:

> Accumulated money rules or serves each man.

But money never, or rarely, serves the rich man. Hence it is clear that the rich are more often unjust than heirs of unjust men. How then does charity reign where injustice rules? Certainly a rich man knows how to have a dependant; he is never, or rarely, a friend. Yet this discourse concerns not the person who possesses riches, but the person who loves them. From this it is clear that, however great the favour of intimacy with a more powerful man may seem, it demands diligent caution from dependants. Otherwise all its enticement will have, at its end, “more aloes than honey.”

Yet to be aware of secrets is very advantageous for success. Why not? Respect increases, authority grows strong, inconveniences are kept away, advantages arise, the number of friends is enlarged, devotion is added among one’s adherents, and Fortune seems to breathe upon the happy man the breeze of all her favour and prosperity. But the final results of all these things are more bitter than any wormwood; and if they are not bitter in the meantime, they rightly give cause to suspect bitterness. It is dangerous to share the secrets of rich or powerful men. For if anything slips from them through carelessness, upon whom will it be laid except the confidant? Whatever chamberlains, ash-carriers, actors, or any other parasites—without whom the refined taste or frenzy of a rich man cannot exist—have scattered in brothel or tavern, or publicized among the people in order to avenge themselves upon intimacy with a powerful man, is turned into an accusation against the person who seemed to hold some place in the counsels.

If you desire to foresee public disturbances, investigate inns and inquire into the opinions of camp-following sutlers. Nothing is so hidden that it is not disclosed to them in some respect. If you do not believe me, lend your ears to our Aquinas. He says:

> O Corydon, Corydon, do you think any secret of a rich man exists?  
> Though his slaves keep silence, his beasts of burden will speak—  
> the dog, the doorposts, and the marble. Shut the windows;  
> let curtains cover their cracks; fasten the doors; remove  
> the light from the middle; let everyone be silent; let almost no one  
> recline nearby. Yet what he does by the second cockcrow,  
> the neighbouring innkeeper will know before daylight.

I proceed. If he buries his secret in the earth, even a reed growing up will bring it into public and, with a light breath, carry it into the air:

> Midas has ass’s ears.  
> (Persius I.121)

Pallas too could not conceal her Erichthonius without the babbling of a crow publishing what was already known. Therefore, because the crow was the informer and accomplice of another’s offence, she lost the beauty of her colour and incurred the mark of babbling.

Further, the secretaries of the rich are rather like pack-horses or baggage-bearers, burdened with their employers’ faults: whatever their employers do wrongly is stamped upon these men’s reputations. Unless, perhaps, the powerful man’s reputation is such that no counsel can corrupt him. For if his wickedness is habitual, if his reputation for fraud and deceit is widely known, the reputation of his whole household is cleared, just as a headache darkens the pain of suffering sides. Otherwise, if his rule is believed more kindly and civilized, his dependants carry all his absurdities upon their shoulders like baggage-bearers. Yet nothing well done is ascribed except to the kindness or civility of the powerful man. And whenever a more serious reckoning threatens, the rich man will give your life for his own reputation, as skin for skin; to turn his own blame upon you, he will not hesitate to expose your head to punishments deserved by crimes.

What is more remarkable, he will congratulate himself if his craftiness has rewarded your labours and cares with this recompense: making you infamous, and rendering you—or alleging that he has rendered you—liable for unheard-of crimes. For no evil occurs in a city which is not charged against the rich man’s counsellors, since the excuse is vain that every administrative office conforms itself to its ruler and that no wise man long wavers in the counsel of fools. He discerns and judges everything. Do you suppose he rests secure in his conscience, whose disgrace you can bring into the light and publish abroad? Certainly everyone who is evil hates the light. Every work appears to bear the image of its maker.

When the cosmetic of prostituting women fears to be exposed by light, it seeks shadows and fears that they may seem more ugly to those who behold them if they are exposed to the immediate light of seeing eyes. Their whole vigilance therefore aims at making sharp-sighted eyes see in them what is not there, and at making those who see blind. But things that trust in their native colour are very different:

> One loves the dark; the other wishes to be seen in the light,  
> because it does not fear the discerning sharpness of a judge.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry* 363)

Therefore, although sharing secrets seems to add something to good fortune, it greatly diminishes security. It is difficult—indeed, impossible—to recount those who, descending to hell by this path, have groaned that they were afflicted by their final punishments.

> Alas for me! Why did I see? Why did I make my eyes guilty?

So says one concerning whom it is uncertain whether he deserved exile because of awareness of another’s guilt or the guilt of his own deed. It is certain, however, that it is not expedient to know another’s evils. Yet whether they are known or unknown, nothing is safer than preserving one’s own conscience. The philosopher judged that one should live among enemies as among friends, and among friends as though one lived amid enemies. And the satirist says:

> One must live rightly for many reasons, but especially for this:  
> that you may despise the tongues of slaves;  
> for the tongue is the worst part of a bad slave.

But one must heed the satirist’s precept not only because of slaves’ tongues, but because of the swords and poisons of the powerful and the snares of all men.

## Chapter XIII. That What Is Acquired by Flattery May Be Reclaimed; On Procurers and the Effeminate, and Their Punishment; and That Chastity Cannot Be Taken Away by Violence Unless the Mind Itself Consents

Yet the flatterer cannot possibly be serviceable to one who seeks nothing but to please. If he can, he acts in his own person; if not, he seeks a substituted person—perhaps a wife or another person joined by law or affection. Affection, however, is more effective because it approaches nature more intimately; whatever is joined by the bond of affection is joined to the soul itself. No flattery is more destructive than that which proceeds by introducing affection. Thus husbands often embrace more closely, expose themselves more fully to their rivals, and more often invite corruptors of their marriage to dinner; for, as the proverb says, the incautious lover trusts his chaste wife more than unfaithful eyes.

Is not he sufficiently deceived who prefers a woman’s assertion to his own eyes—an assertion which deceives more often precisely because it is intercepted more rarely? For the pillow is a most effective magpie, and, as the saying goes, the nocturnal crow is more eloquent than any orator, clothing the appearance of every deed in whatever colour it pleases. The more cautious it is, therefore, the more suspect it should be held. If fraud gave cause for a contract, the contract is rescinded and everything which proceeded from or because of it is restored. The heirs of the deceased are also bound fully and perpetually in respect of what is shown to have reached them.

But what is more deceitful than a flatterer? You may perhaps object that I do not know them all. That is true; but I seem to have learned the character of all from many. Duellius, already an old man, decrepit in body and trembling in heart, was distressed because during an argument he had been reproached for having foul breath due to a defect of his mouth; he went home. Complaining bitterly to his wife that she had never warned him to seek a remedy for this fault, he received her answer: “I would have done so, had I not thought that all men’s mouths smelled like that.” You may praise the chastity of that marriage and prefer the woman’s patience, since she bore her husband’s defect with such patience that he learned of his bodily misfortune not from his wife’s disgust but from an enemy’s insult. I give a similar answer concerning flatterers: I think that all smell thus. All exhale deception and fraud; wherever they turn, they bring to chaste nostrils not an odour but a stench. Therefore whatever is acquired by that cause may justly be taken away even from an heir. Nor do I think that claimants can be prevented if they dare to reclaim what they bestowed upon flatterers.

But who is wise enough to understand these things? Who is equal to this task, when not only in every household or company of diners, but everywhere, there is such a multitude of flatterers that, if any modest person dares to murmur against them,

> Their numbers will defend them, and their phalanxes, shields joined.  
> (Juvenal II.46)

Certainly, while an honourable man, relying upon conscience and standing safely by his duties, hungers, thirsts, freezes, and endures the many injuries of indignant Fortune,

> The base flatterer lies drunk upon embroidered purple,

gorges himself on luxuries unto surfeit, burns with wine, is swollen with sumptuous food, and, as he pleases, tempers heaven for himself by various devices. He receives the foremost places at dinners, the foremost seats at gatherings; he is hailed by his chosen name, receives the first greetings, pronounces the first opinions in courts, judges most honourably in public displays and most usefully in deliberations. Whatever he says is pure salt; whatever he does is justice or generosity. Go on, then: dare to be wise among such people. Immediately “a great band of flatterers will come,” and, like the Jews, compel you to enter their crowd. They are safe through their multitude and through artifice, so that they can overcome kings and princes themselves. In a remarkable manner an unarmed people prevails over the armed, and softness powerfully conquers what is strongest.

I had intended, however, to be silent about the effeminate, who, as they are shameful, so they are and seem unnamable. Reverence for morals enjoins silence, and a modest mind, nature dictating, avoids the sight of them. Why say more?

> If nature refuses, indignation makes speech.

Among these men it is an art to prostitute their own chastity and to violate or assault that of others. Nor merely their own, since the rights of marriage are dishonoured and a husband himself arranges his wife’s adultery. When the bride leaves her chamber, do not think her spouse a husband but a procurer. He brings her forth, exposes her to the lustful, and, if the hope of deceitful money shines out, prostitutes his affections under a clever pretence. For a more attractive daughter, or anything else in the household that pleases a richer man, is merchandise publicly exposed if it finds a buyer.

Although righteous grief may in some degree torment those who admit or arrange participants in their marriage-bed, the sickness is softened by the profit of advantage, or at least conceals the torment of pain. For if the matter is seriously considered, if free judgment is granted to all, there is no pain like that by which someone sees his own body defiled by another’s lust. All other sins are outside the body; but the person who fornicates sins against his own body (1 Corinthians 6). “This,” he says, “is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” so that man and woman are now not two but one flesh. This is not divided without pain, nor shared without jealousy.

“Venus and kingdoms do not thrive well with partners” [Col. 0505B]; and, just as “there is no loyalty among partners in rule,” neither is there in the marriage-bed. Certainly it is easier to yield the riches of a kingdom to another than the affection of marriage. Yet these men are not husbands but pimps. They are thought finally to have offered everything up to the rich when violated fidelity gives assurance to fidelity. But why do I complain that daughters and wives are exposed or prostituted—though the laws forbid it, nature nonetheless permits it in some fashion? Like another race of Giants, waging a new war against God, they rise up against nature itself. They offer their sons to Venus, and compel those same sons, dressed as virgins, to go first in the offering of dolls (*puppae*). In the former, maturity of age is awaited; in the latter, it is enough that the pleasure of another’s shamelessness can be fulfilled.

It is shameful to say that men more advanced in age and understanding do not withdraw themselves from so great a disgrace [Col. 0505C]; though nature created them in the nobler sex, they descend, so far as lies in them, into the inferior one through innate wickedness, feminized by vice and the corruption of morals, although by nature’s gift they cannot be women. When the extravagance of some lustful rich man harnesses its wishes to desire, a little curled-haired attendant receives the feet of the reclining man. Envying the elegance of a prostitute, he adopts an actor’s dress, a lover’s finery, a virgin’s adornment, even the triumphal array of princes; before the eyes of others he handles feet, and, lest I say more, shins with delicate hands. For he has long gone about wearing gloves, so as to soften hands kept from the sun for the rich man’s use. Then, as licence advances a little further, roaming over the whole body with shameless touch, he scratches the itch which he has caused [Col. 0505D] and kindles the fires of languishing Venus.

Yet this abomination should be spat upon rather than displayed; and it would shame me to insert it among these trifles of ours, if the Apostle himself, writing to the Romans, had not expressed it more plainly, saying that “their women exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature; and the men likewise, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned in their desires toward one another, men committing shameful acts with men, so that they were given over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1), and did what was altogether unfitting, becoming subject to every vice and provoking against themselves God’s indignation and all the stings of punishments.

And indeed this apostolic trumpet was proclaiming this in Roman ears [Col. 0506A] when the most impious emperor Nero, in the frenzy of his luxury, attempted to transform the boy Sporus into a female nature by cutting off his testicles. From that time arose the proverb: “The use of handsome persons is abuse,” and this saying: “The grace of beauty is so much the less pleasing to the wise as corruption is more pleasing to the corrupter.” What more persons desire is guarded with greater difficulty by weak defenders. The deceitful man more easily steals it from the unwary, or the violent robber of chastity extorts it against the victim’s will.

Yet the Fathers long ago determined that chastity cannot be taken away unless corruption of mind comes first. For, as the great Augustine maintains, what the body suffers violently without preceding lust should be called an affliction rather than corruption. [Col. 0506B] Therefore chastity can be preserved where no corruption can occur except voluntarily: namely, in integrity of mind, where chastity can be preserved forever. It is no great thing for the flesh to remain intact where the mind is polluted with foul corruption.

But now, even where no deceiving lover or violent assailant is present, youths are trained so badly from their earliest age that, by lascivious eyes, a nod of the face, bodily gesture and outward dress, and by an enticement scarcely permitted even to prostitutes, they solicit corrupters. They have neither reverence nor fear for the many laws already enacted against them, although the emperor decreed that they should be punished with utmost severity. For he says:

> “When a man marries one who is to offer a woman’s powers, what does he desire? Where sex has lost its place, and where there is no crime that it is not possible to accomplish; where Venus is changed into another form; where love is sought and not found: we command laws to rise up and legal rights to be armed, so that with the avenging sword and carefully devised penalties the infamous persons who are, or will be, guilty may be brought low.” [Col. 0506C]

Nor does he spare those who consent, but imposes the capital penalty upon them, since both those who act and those who consent are punished equally under divine law. And, on the authority of the great bishop—consider Ambrose of Milan—he defined as consenting persons those who conceal a known wrongdoing, or neglect to correct it when they can. But why do we prolong shameful and hateful speech about them? To close their lot with its fitting conclusion: undoubtedly the Lord will rain snares upon them [Col. 0506D], fire and sulphur and a stormy wind, the portion of their cup; and with their authors, whom Sodom swallowed, they shall be through the ages an object of stench and everlasting reproach. What, I ask, will the favour of the rich then profit them? Or what use or pleasure can there be in temporal things which such pain and such shame do not consume?

## Chapter XIV. Flatterers must be punished as enemies of gods and men; truth must be gladly embraced and patience maintained, by both arguments and examples of the ancients.

But, as the common proverb says, “That god is believed to be worshipped above all others who gives help in the present.” Accordingly, they do not care how, provided only that they accomplish [Col. 0507A] what they seek. Caecilius Balbus spoke admirably:

> “Emperor Augustus, your prudence shines forth in many things, but most especially in this: those persons who applaud you have not yet made you wholly mad, though, in doing so, they wrong not only the gods but you yourself and the people. They diminish reverence for the gods insofar as they make you their equal. They charge you with folly when, against the nature that resists your condition, they presume to persuade you that you are equal to divinities. They brand the people with superstition, persuading them to worship mortal gods in place of immortal ones. You will indeed show that something divine is in you if you have all those who fraudulently applaud your divinity dragged off to torture. For which of the gods would spare a person by whom he understands himself to be deceived? [Col. 0507B] Who would not rush upon one who gouges out Jupiter’s golden eyes, or who, by removing the silver and gems, attempts to blind Vesta? Who could with impunity dig out with reckless nails the diamond light from Mars’s head? Clearly, to circumvent invisible and immortal gods and to lay snares of deceit for them is a graver offence, since the handiwork of visible gods is sustained and governed by these gods, and they repay the honour or contempt bestowed upon the former. Therefore, Augustus, if you are wise, rise against the enemies of the gods; and, if not God—which you certainly are not—you will show yourself at least a worshipper of the gods if you exterminate these deceivers, those who blind you, contemners of the gods, and punish the wrong done to both.”

So spoke Caecilius. Yet the party of flatterers prevailed, as the condition of present affairs shows. So much is this the case that, if anyone among the people, conscious of moderation, believes that he should refrain from the vice of flattery and buffoonery, he is judged an enemy of the fortunate or an envious man. Their ears are delicate and have already become deaf to truth; they do not admit a sterner tongue without the gravest offence. [Col. 0507C]

How far our age has declined from the virtue of the ancients is plain, since they taught by words and examples that, without patience, no work of virtue exists—or scarcely any. Thus Aristippus, walking away from a man who was abusing him, is reported to have said: “As you are master of your tongue, so I am master of my ears.” Antisthenes likewise, when someone said to him, “That man abused you,” replied: “Not me, but the person who recognizes in himself what that man censures. And even if he intends to abuse me, I do not care, because hearing ought to be stronger than speech: each person has one tongue, but two ears. Yet I care somewhat, because by this very act he admits that I am superior, since it is the role of the superior to endure detractions and of the inferior to inflict them. I would therefore rejoice, did not humanity compel me to pity the unhappy man.”

Likewise Titus Tatius said to Metellus, who abused him: “It is easy to speak against me, since I shall not answer.” What of Xenophon? He said to someone: “You have learned to abuse others, and I, with conscience as witness, have learned to despise abuse.” Diogenes too, when a friend announced to him, “All your friends criticize you,” said: “Wisdom must be struck by fools; for an evil tongue shows that the one it attacks is better.” [Col. 0508A] What of Plato? Patience is the strength of all philosophy. Socrates too maintains not merely in words that the wise person cannot be injured, but that, against every fortune, he remains unmoved by the strength of his virtue.

And lest you think patience pleased philosophers alone in this way, examples of emperors themselves unite in proclaiming it. Who in Greece was greater or more famous than Alexander? Antigonus, his tutor, broke and threw away his lyre, saying: “At your age it is already fitting to rule; you should be ashamed that, in the body of a kingdom, the pleasure of luxury should rule.” Alexander endured this most patiently, though he was generally most impatient and surpassed his father in vices as in virtues.

The pirate whom Alexander captured is likewise recorded to have answered him wittily and truthfully. [Col. 0508B] When Alexander asked why he kept the sea hostile, the pirate answered with free defiance: “Why do you keep the whole world hostile? But because I do it with one ship, I am called a robber; because you do it with a great fleet, you are called an emperor. If Alexander were alone and captured, he would be a robber. If peoples served Dionides at his command, Dionides would be emperor. For in their cause they differ in no respect, except that worse is the man who plunders more wickedly, abandons justice more basely, and attacks laws more openly. The laws from which I flee, you pursue; I honour them, however imperfectly, but you despise them. The unfairness of fortune and narrowness of means make me a thief; intolerable arrogance and insatiable greed make you one. If fortune became kinder, perhaps I would become better. But you, the more fortunate you are, the more wicked you will be.”

Alexander, admiring the constancy of the man who had justly rebuked him, said: “I shall test whether you will become better, and I shall change your fortune, so that henceforth what you have done wrong may be attributed not to it, but to your character.” [Col. 0508C] He therefore ordered him enrolled in military service, so that he might thereafter serve as a soldier without violating the laws.

But let us not borrow examples of virtue only from the Greeks. When someone accused Scipio Africanus of not being warlike enough, he replied: “My mother bore me a commander, not a fighter.” Likewise, when a Teuton challenged Marius to a combat, Marius answered that, if he desired death, he could have ended his life with a noose, and that a wise person seeks victory rather than combat.

Julius Caesar, the first emperor of the Romans, endured many things most patiently. For, though he bore his baldness most badly and combed his thinning hair from the back of his head to his forehead, an angry soldier said to him: “Caesar, it is easier for you not to be bald than for me to have done, or to be about to do, anything more timidly in the Roman army.” [Col. 0508D] Caesar himself wore a broad purple-striped tunic fringed down to the hands, and girded it rather loosely. Hence Sulla frequently warned the optimates to beware of the badly belted boy. Moreover, Caesar was extremely fond of pearls and sometimes distinguished them by comparing their weight in his hand. When, therefore, he commanded Caecilius—against his will and by the Senate’s authority—to do something which Caecilius considered unjust, Caecilius said: “You will be satisfied with pearls sooner.”

Perhaps these things may seem trivial or foreign, matters which the mind of a strong man would more honourably disregard. Yet notorious pamphlets were written against Caesar [Col. 0509A], and jesting verses publicly circulated against him, such as this, sung by soldiers in his Gallic triumph:

> Caesar subdued the Gauls; Nicomedes subdued Caesar.  
> Nicomedes, who subdued Caesar, does not triumph.  
> (*SUETONIUS, Caesar* 49.)

For Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, was said to have subjected Caesar to sexual violation after admitting him, when young, to closer intimacy. Cicero also mocked Caesar’s readiness to enlarge the Senate too sharply and publicly. When his host Publius Manlius asked him to procure a decurionate for his stepson, Cicero said, before a crowd standing by: “If he has influence at Rome, it is difficult at Pompeii.” And in a letter to Gaius Cassius, the assassin of the dictator, he wrote more mordantly: [Col. 0509B] “I wish you had invited me to dinner on the Ides of March: surely nothing would have been left over. Now your leftovers torment me.”

But Augustus, fortune’s favourite and the glory of the Roman empire, proved far more patient than his uncle Julius.
