When Antony, despising his maternal ancestry, called him African by race and by nature a baker, Augustus endured it laughing, and gave Antony his sister in marriage, admitting him into kinship for the sake of alliance. When Augustus himself grew too hotly angry against a private individual, the man said: “Speak, Augustus, whatever pleases you; for I have imposed attentiveness upon my ears, silence upon my tongue, stillness upon my hands. In all these matters accuse your power, because nothing else can be faulted in my patience.”

Augustus not only maintained patience in himself [Col. 0509C], but required it of others. Accordingly, when Tiberius complained in a letter that many spoke wrongly about him, Augustus replied: “My Tiberius, do not be too indignant that there is anyone who speaks ill of you. It is enough if we have this: that no one is able to harm us.” He received anyone who approached him with such courtesy that he jokingly rebuked a Roman for hesitating to present him with a petition, as though he were offering alms to an elephant. And as much as Nero was captivated by flatteries, so much was Augustus averse to them. Thus he always recoiled from the title “lord” as from abuse and reproach. Finally, as he was descending the Sacred Way, a desperate man said to him, “O tyrant!” “If I were one,” he replied, “you would not say it.” It was also observed [Col. 0509D] that whenever he entered the city, no punishment was inflicted upon anyone.

Curtius, a Roman knight living in luxury, took a lean thrush at Caesar’s banquet and asked whether he might send it away. The prince replied: “Why should that not be permitted?” Curtius immediately threw it out of the window. A soldier skilled in bird-catching captured an owl that had disturbed Caesar’s nights and brought it to Caesar in hope of a great reward. Caesar praised him and ordered a thousand coins to be given. But the soldier dared to say, “I prefer that it should live,” and released the bird. The soldier went away defiant, to the admiration of many; Caesar was not offended.

When a veteran was in danger because a day had been set for his trial, he publicly asked Caesar to appear for him. Caesar immediately provided the most distinguished advocate whom he had selected and commended the litigant to him. [Col. 0510A] But the veteran shouted aloud: “When you were in danger in the Actian war, Caesar, I did not seek a substitute, but fought for you myself,” and he uncovered the scars of his wounds. Caesar blushed and came to act as his advocate, fearing to seem not merely proud but ungrateful.

A young man extraordinarily like Caesar entered the city and was brought before Caesar. Augustus asked him: “Tell me, young man, was your mother ever in Rome?” He denied it, and, not content with that, added: “But my father often was.” By the sharpness of his urban jest he gained for himself the acquaintance of all and the emperor’s familiarity.

Augustus had written abusive Fescennine verses against Pollio. “But I,” Pollio said, “am silent. It is no light matter to write against one who can proscribe.” Just as Augustus did not readily conceive anger, so he did not readily admit persons to friendship; but anyone whom he admitted once he retained most steadfastly. [Col. 0510B] Amid various reproaches someone shamefully threw this at him: that he had earned adoption by his uncle through sexual violation, because Julius was said to have admitted him more closely, not without a rumour of violated chastity. Another angry man reproached him for allegedly being accustomed to burn his legs with a blazing torch so that softer hair might grow. And when he was playing a tambourine, as I remember having said in the first book, a plebeian remarked: “Do you see how that effeminate man governs the world with his finger?” When someone abusively called him a dwarf because of his short stature, Augustus replied that he ought to wear rather large shoes.

Tiberius also, though he is recorded to have been blameworthy in many respects, proved sufficiently firm and patient against insults, saying that in a free state the tongues and minds of human beings ought to be free. And, to pass to worse men, Domitian was quite patient with words. The orator Licinius is said to have joked about him thus: it was no wonder that he had a bronze beard, since he had an iron mouth and a leaden heart; for he spoke only harsh things, which proceeded from the fat of injustice that he had conceived in his heart. [Col. 0510C] For Injustice is described as sitting upon a talent of lead.

Vespasian too, whom we mentioned in the second book while describing the destruction of Jerusalem, patiently bore even the insults of inferiors. When an old ox-driver shouted in reproach that “a fox can change its coat but not its nature,” because Vespasian was by nature excessively greedy for money and advancing age did not lessen his avarice, Vespasian is said to have replied: “To persons of this kind we owe laughter; to ourselves, correction; but punishment to criminals.”

What shall I say of his son Titus? He cleansed his father’s avarice by such generosity that all called him “the love and delight of the human race.” He held most steadily to the practice that he would never send away, in any fashion, anyone who approached him to make a request without either the thing requested or hope of it. When members of his household asked why he promised more than he could perform, he replied: “No one ought to leave the speech of a prince saddened.” Once, at supper, recalling with grief and groaning that he had bestowed nothing on anyone that whole day, he said: “Friends, [Col. 0511A] I have lost this day.”

I have not yet read whom he offended after returning from the destruction of Jerusalem. Perhaps the Lord chose him as the avenger of innocence and of the crucified Redeemer, that he might oppress and destroy, with an uninjured conscience, the blinded people not only innocently but even religiously. When the hour came at which he was to die, he is said, while being carried in a litter, to have looked up to heaven and complained greatly that life was being taken from him though undeserving. For he said that no deed of his existed for which he ought to repent, except one alone. What that was he did not then reveal, nor was it known to anyone.

What shall I say of the patience of a man whose kindness was so great that, because he refrained from injuring his fellow citizens, he scarcely believed that anyone could be moved by his own injury? Such was his civility and humanity in rule that he sought to benefit all and punish no one. He dismissed unharmed persons convicted of conspiring against him and received them again into their former intimacy.

Domitian also, because after Nero he waged a most grievous war against God, sometimes granted something of this virtue to citizens, although he occasionally raged against them without cause: a man wholly worthless, who had nothing manly except the name of imperial power. [Col. 0511B] Yet, to conceal his cowardice of mind and bodily inactivity under the pretext of rule, he claimed daily for himself a period of private hours. Sometimes he was accustomed to do nothing except catch flies and pierce them with a sharply pointed stylus. Thus, when someone asked whether anyone was inside with Caesar, Metellus was not absurdly answered: “Not even a fly.” Although this became known to that most impious prince, he preferred to overlook it rather than punish it.

But why do I set forth examples of patience, when it is clear to all that nothing is firm and stable which is shaken by the light breath of a breeze? Who would believe that man strong whom the impact of words moves, shakes from him his tranquillity, and, tearing apart the structure of virtues, draws forth the very blood of his soul? Thus it has also been established by public law that no one be branded with the severity of punishments for frivolous words. For the emperor says, confirming the enactments of the divine Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius:

> “If anyone, ignorant of moderation and unaware of shame, believes our names should be assailed with wicked and wanton abuse, and, turbulent in drunkenness, becomes a reviler of the times, [Col. 0511D] we do not wish him to be subjected to punishment or to endure anything harsh or severe. For, if it proceeds from levity, it is to be despised; if from madness, it is most worthy of pity; if from injury, it is to be forgiven. Therefore, with everything remaining intact, let this be reported to our knowledge, so that we may weigh words according to the persons who utter them and determine whether they should be passed over or investigated.”

From this it is gathered that one who loves virtue, or obeys the constitution of the law, is not disturbed by human speech.

> Clever Flaccus touches every vice in his laughing friend,  
> and, once admitted, plays about the heart.  
> (HORACE.) [Col. 0512A]

For, as the great Augustine thinks, it is characteristic of the wise person to prefer rebuke from anyone to praise either from one in error or from a flatterer. No rebuker is to be feared by a lover of truth. The rebuker will be either enemy or friend. If an enemy insults, he must be endured; if a friend errs, he must be instructed; if he instructs, he must be heard. But a praiser who is mistaken confirms error, and a flatterer entices into error.

Therefore the faithful king, chosen in the Lord’s good pleasure, leaves to kings and princes, if they are wise, an example of justice, humility, and courage: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy [Col. 0512B] and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140). The moral philosopher agrees with him, saying:

> False honour pleases, or lying infamy terrifies—  
> whom, if not one who is faulty and deceitful?

## Chapter XV. Only the person whom one may kill may be flattered; and the tyrant is a public enemy.

But to whom is due that oil of the sinner which the forerunner of faithful kings rejects, and which the evangelical saying sends the excluded foolish virgins in their folly to buy? It is due, certainly, to the one who is in filth and, by the just judgment of God, becomes still filthier; who seeks rather to shine in popular opinion than to burn with the fire of charity and its works. Hence secular literature too warns that one must live differently with a friend and with a tyrant. Certainly one may not flatter a friend, but it is permitted to soothe a tyrant’s ears. For it is permitted to flatter the person whom it is permitted to kill.

Moreover, to kill a tyrant is not only permitted but just and right. For whoever takes up the sword is worthy to perish by the sword. Yet he is understood to take it up who usurps it by his own rashness, not one who receives from the Lord authority to use it. Certainly the one who receives authority from God serves the laws and is the servant of justice and right. But one who usurps it suppresses laws and subjects laws to his own will. Therefore the laws are rightly armed against one who disarms laws, and public authority rages against one who strives to nullify the public hand. Though there are many crimes against majesty, none is graver [Col. 0512D] than that committed against the very body of justice. Tyranny, therefore, is not merely a public crime, but, if that were possible, more than public. For if all persecutors commit the crime of violated majesty, how much more so does the crime that suppresses the laws which ought to command emperors themselves? Surely no one avenges a public enemy, and whoever does not pursue him sins against himself and against the whole body of the worldly commonwealth.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0513]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0513A]

The profession of truth is indeed a difficult matter, and one that is very frequently corrupted by the encroaching darkness of errors or by the negligence of its professor. For who rightly examines what is true in matters unknown? Yet knowledge of things, because it does not direct the paths of one who despises it, sharpens the stings of justice for the punishment of the offender. Thus the first stage of philosophizing is to examine the kinds and properties of things, so that one may prudently recognize whatever is true in each. The second is for each person faithfully to pursue that portion of truth which has shone upon him.

But this road of philosophers is passable only to one who passes from the kingdom of vanity into that freedom by which those whom truth has set free become free, and who, serving the Spirit, have withdrawn their necks from the yoke of inequity and injustice. [Col. 0513B] “Where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3); and servile fear, consenting to vices, drives out the Holy Spirit. Moreover, it is the Spirit who speaks equity, does not blush before princes, places or makes equal the poor in spirit to kings, and teaches those whom he has made cleave to himself to know, speak, and do the truth. But the one who does not wish to hear or speak truth is alien from the Spirit of truth. But enough of this. Let us now hear in what a tyrant differs from a prince.

## Chapter I. The difference between a prince and a tyrant, and what a prince is.

There is, then, this one difference between a tyrant and a prince: the latter obeys the law and governs the people by its judgment, believing himself its minister. In performing the offices and bearing the burdens of the commonwealth, he claims the first place for himself by benefit of the law; and he is preferred to the rest in this, that whereas individuals are bound to particular obligations, all burdens threaten the prince. Thus authority over all subjects is rightly entrusted to him, so that in seeking and accomplishing the advantage of each and of all he may suffice for himself, and the condition of the human commonwealth may be most suitably ordered, since its members belong one to another. [Col. 0513C]

In this we follow nature, the best guide to life. Nature placed all the senses of its *microcosm* (μικροκόσμου), that is, the lesser world—namely, the human being—in the head, and subjected all the members to it in such a way that all move rightly when they follow the judgment of a healthy head. Thus the pinnacle of princely office is raised and made splendid by as many and as great privileges as it judged necessary for itself. Rightly so, because nothing is more useful to a people than that the prince’s necessity be supplied, since his will is found to be opposed to no justice. Therefore, as many define him, the prince is public authority and on earth a kind of image of divine majesty.

Without doubt something great of divine power is shown to exist in princes when people submit their necks to their commands, often offer their necks confidently to be struck, and each person, by divine prompting, fears those to whom he himself is a cause of fear. [Col. 0513D] I do not think this could occur except by divine ordinance. For all power is from the Lord God, has always been with him, and is before all time. Therefore what the prince can do is from God in such a way that the power does not depart from the Lord, but he exercises it through a subordinate hand, in all things providing an instruction in his clemency or justice.

Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance (Rom. 13); authority belongs to him who grants it and, when he wills, takes it away or diminishes it. For it is not in the power of a ruler, when he wishes, to rage against subjects; rather, it belongs to divine dispensation, according to its good pleasure, to punish or test those who are subject. Hence, in the persecution by the Huns, when Attila was asked by the devout bishop of a certain city who he was, he answered: “I am Attila, the scourge of God.” The bishop, as is written, revered divine majesty in him and said: “Welcome, servant of God”; and, repeating, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117), he opened the doors of the church and admitted the persecutor, through whom he also attained the crown of martyrdom. [Col. 0514B] For he did not dare exclude the Lord’s scourge, knowing that the beloved son is scourged and that even the scourge itself has no power except from the Lord.

If authority is so worthy of reverence among the good even in the affliction of the elect, who would not revere the authority established by the Lord for punishing evildoers and praising the good, and which serves the laws with most ready devotion? “It is indeed a saying worthy,” as the emperor declares, “of the majesty of one who reigns for a prince to profess himself bound by the laws.” For the authority of law depends upon the prince’s authority; and indeed it is greater than imperial power to submit princely office to laws, so that a prince should think nothing permitted to him that conflicts with the equity of justice.

## Chapter II. What law is; and how the prince, though free from the bonds of the law, is nevertheless its servant and the servant of equity, bears a public person, and sheds blood innocently.

Nor should princes think themselves diminished in this if they do not believe the ordinances of their own justice ought to be preferred to the justice of God, whose justice is justice forever and whose law is equity. Equity, as jurists maintain, is the fitting correspondence of things, which equalizes all things by reason and requires equal laws in equal matters; it is equal toward all, giving to each what is his own. [Col. 0514D] Law is equity’s interpreter, because the will of equity and justice has been made known to it.

Thus Chrysippus declared law to possess knowledge of all things, divine and human; therefore to preside over all good and evil things, and to be ruler and guide alike of things and human beings. Papinian, a man indeed most experienced in law, and Demosthenes, a most powerful orator, seem to support him; they subject all human beings to obedience because every law is an invention and gift of God, the doctrine of wise men, correction of voluntary excesses, the ordering of a state, and the avoidance of every crime. According to it, all who participate in the whole political order ought to live. [Col. 0515A]

Therefore all are bound by the necessity of keeping the law, unless perhaps someone has been granted licence for wrongdoing. Yet the prince is said to be free from the bonds of law, not because unjust things are permitted to him, but because he ought to be the person who cultivates equity not from fear of punishment but from love of justice, attends to the commonwealth’s advantage, and in all things prefers the good of others to private will. But who would speak of the prince’s will in public affairs, when in them he may will nothing for himself except what law or equity persuades, or what the reasoning of common advantage commends? In these matters his will ought to have the force of judgment; and most rightly, what pleases him in such matters has the force of law, because his decision does not depart from the mind of equity.

“Let my judgment come forth from your countenance; let your eyes behold equity” (Ps. 16). [Col. 0515B] For an incorrupt judge is one whose judgment, from constant contemplation, is an image of equity. Therefore the prince is a minister of public advantage and a servant of equity; and he bears a public person in that, by the mediating equity, he punishes all wrongs and injuries, and every crime. His rod and staff likewise, when joined with the moderation of wisdom, bring back all deviation and error to the path of equity, so that the spirit may fittingly rejoice in authority, saying: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4).

His shield too is indeed strong, but it is the shield of the weak, and powerfully receives the missiles of evildoers on behalf of the innocent. His office benefits most those who have least power, and most strongly opposes those who desire to harm. Therefore he does not bear the sword without cause, by which he sheds blood innocently; yet he is not a man of blood, and though he often kills people, he does not incur the name or guilt of homicide. For, if great Augustine is to be believed, David was called a man of blood not because of wars but because of Uriah. Nor is Samuel anywhere written a man of blood or murderer, although he killed Agag, the very fat king of Amalek. [Col. 0515D]

This indeed is the sword of the dove, which contends without gall, strikes without anger, and in fighting conceives no bitterness whatsoever. For just as law prosecutes offences without hatred of persons, so the prince most rightly punishes offenders not by any movement of anger, but by the judgment of the gentle law. For although a prince seems to have his own lictors, he himself must be considered either the sole or the chief lictor, to whom it is permitted to strike through a subordinate hand. To turn to the Stoics, who investigate the causes of names more carefully: a *lictor* is so called as though a “striker of the law” (*legis ictor*), because it belongs to his office to strike the person whom the law judges should be struck.

Hence in ancient times, when the sword threatened the accused person at the hands of officials by whose hand the judge punishes offenders, he was told: “Obey the judgment of the law,” or “Fulfil the law”—whether to lessen the accused person’s grief or through the gentleness of the words.

## Chapter III. The prince is the servant of priests and their inferior; and what it is faithfully to perform the ministry of princely rule.

[Col. 0516A]

The prince, therefore, receives this sword from the hand of the Church, although the Church herself has no sword of blood whatsoever. Yet she has this sword too, but uses it through the hand of the prince, to whom she has entrusted authority to restrain bodies, while reserving to herself authority over spiritual matters in the persons of bishops. The prince, then, is indeed a minister of the priesthood, exercising that part of sacred office which seems unworthy of priestly hands. For every office of the sacred laws is religious and devout; yet that office is lower which is exercised in the punishment of crimes and seems to present a kind of image of an executioner.

[Col. 0516B] Thus Constantine, the most faithful emperor of the Romans, when he had summoned the council of priests to Nicaea, did not dare to occupy the first place or to mingle with the presbyters in their seats, but took the lowest seat. The decisions which he heard approved by them he so revered as though he believed them to have issued from the judgment of the divine Majesty. Likewise, he received the written accusations which they had drawn up against one another and presented to the emperor, containing the offences of priests; but he set them aside unopened in his bosom. When he had recalled them to charity and concord, he said that it was unlawful for him, being a man and subject to the judgment of priests, to examine the causes of gods, who can be judged only by God alone. And the documents he had received he gave to the flames without [Col. 0516C] inspecting them, fearing to publicize the crimes or reproaches of the fathers and to incur the curse of the reprobate son Ham, who did not cover what should have been veiled in his father.

Hence it is reported that he said the same in the writings of Nicholas, Roman pontiff: “Truly, if I saw with my own eyes a priest of God, or any of those clothed in the monastic habit, committing sin, I would spread out my cloak and cover him, lest he be seen by anyone.”

The great Emperor Theodosius also, for a fault he deservedly incurred—though not a fault so grave as that—was suspended by the priest of Milan from the use of imperial prerogatives and insignia; and he patiently and solemnly performed the penance for homicide imposed upon him. Certainly, to use the testimony of the Doctor of the Gentiles, greater is he who blesses than he who is blessed; and he in whose power lies the conferral of dignity precedes in the privilege of honour him upon whom the dignity itself is conferred. Moreover, by the principle of law, the one who has the right to will has the right to refuse; and the one who may lawfully confer has the right to take away. Did not Samuel pronounce against Saul the sentence of deposition because of his disobedience, and substitute in his place, at the summit of the kingdom, the humble son of Jesse?

But if the appointed prince faithfully performs the ministry he has undertaken, he is to be shown such honour and such reverence as the head surpasses all the members of the body. He performs this ministry faithfully when, mindful of his condition, he remembers that he bears the person of the whole body of those subject to him; when he recognizes that he owes his life not to himself but to others; and [Col. 0517A] when he distributes it among them in an ordered charity. Therefore he owes his whole self to God; very much to his country; much to his parents, kindred, and strangers—least to the latter, but still something. Thus he is a debtor to the wise and the foolish, to the lowly and the great.

This consideration belongs equally to all prelates: both those who have care of spiritual things and those who exercise secular jurisdiction. Hence Melchizedek, whom Scripture first introduces as both king and priest—to say nothing for the moment of the mystery by which he prefigures Christ, who was born without a mother in heaven and without a father on earth—is said to have had neither father nor mother. This does not mean that he lacked both, but that flesh and blood do not, by right, beget kingship and priesthood; for, in creating either one, regard for parents ought not to prevail over the merits of virtues and the salutary wishes of faithful subjects. And when anyone has ascended the summit of either dignity, he must forget the affection of the flesh and do only what the salvation of his subjects requires.

Let him therefore be a father and husband to his subjects; or, if he knows a tenderer affection, let him employ that. Let him strive rather to be loved than feared, and show himself such to them that out of devotion they prefer his life to their own and regard his safety as a kind of public life. Then all things will proceed well for him, and, though attended by the service of few, he will prevail, if need be, against countless enemies. For love is strong as death (Song of Songs 8), and a wedge bound fast by cords of love is not easily broken.

The Dorians, when about to fight the Athenians, [Col. 0517C] consulted oracles concerning the outcome of the battle. The reply was that they would be victorious unless they killed the king of the Athenians. When they came to battle, the soldiers were commanded above all things to guard the king. At that time Codrus was king of the Athenians. Having learned the god’s response and the enemy’s instructions, he changed his kingly attire, put brushwood around his neck, and entered the enemy camp. Amid a crowd of those resisting him, he was killed by a soldier whom he had struck with a sickle. When the king’s body was recognized, the Dorians departed without a battle. Thus the Athenians were freed from war through the courage of their leader, who offered himself to death for his country’s safety.

Likewise Lycurgus, when establishing decrees in his kingdom, confirmed the people in obedience to their rulers and rulers in justice toward the wicked. [Col. 0517D] He abolished the use of gold and silver, and the material of every crime. He entrusted to the senate the guardianship of the laws, and gave the people the power to select the senate. He ordained that a virgin should marry without a dowry, so that wives might be chosen rather than money. He decreed that the greatest honour should belong to the aged according to the rank of age; indeed, nowhere on earth does old age hold a more honourable place.

Then, in order to give his laws permanence, he bound the city by oath not to alter anything in his laws until he returned. He set out for Crete, spent there a perpetual exile, and at his death ordered his bones to be cast into the sea, lest, when they had been brought back to Lacedaemon, the Spartans should consider themselves released from the obligation of their oath and free to abolish the laws.

I use these examples all the more willingly because I find that the apostle Paul used the same examples when he preached to the Athenians. That outstanding preacher sought to impress Jesus Christ—and him crucified—upon their minds in such a way as to teach that through the disgrace of the cross the deliverance of many had arisen even among the Gentiles by the example of Gentiles. He also persuaded them that such deliverance was not ordinarily brought about except through the blood of righteous men and of those who held magistracy over the people. But for the deliverance of all, namely Jews and Gentiles, no one sufficient could be found except him to whom the nations were given as an inheritance and the whole earth appointed as his possession. He affirmed that this man could be none other than the Son of Almighty God, since, apart from God, no one had subdued the nations and all lands.

Thus, while he preached the disgrace of the cross so that the folly of the Gentiles might gradually be emptied away, he gradually raised the word of faith and the preacher’s speech to the Word of God, the wisdom of God, and indeed to the very throne of divine Majesty. [Col. 0518B] And lest the power of the Gospel should be despised beneath the weakness of the flesh, he set forth the works of the Crucified, which were confirmed even by public report, against the scandal of the Jews and the folly of the Gentiles; for everyone agreed that no one but God could perform them. But since rumour often lies greatly in either direction, the report itself was aided by the fact that his disciples did greater things: at the shadow of a disciple, the sick were healed from whatever infirmity afflicted them.

Why say more? The risen dead man refuted the subtleties of Aristotle, the acuteness of Chrysippus, and the snares of all philosophers. It is very well known that the Decii, Roman commanders, devoted themselves for their armies. Julius Caesar likewise said: [Col. 0518C] “A commander who does not labour to make himself dear to his soldiers does not know how to love a soldier.” He does not know that a commander’s humanity has a place in an army against enemies. Caesar himself never said to his soldiers, “Go here,” but, “Come.” For he said that labour shared with the commander seems lighter to soldiers.

Moreover, according to the same author, bodily pleasure must be avoided. He said that in war men’s bodies are wounded by swords, and in peace by pleasures. For the conqueror of nations had perceived that pleasure is never so easily overcome as by flight, since an unchaste woman bound in Venus’ chains even him who had subdued nations.

## Chapter IV. That by the authority of the divine law the prince is shown to be subject to the law of justice

[Col. 0518D] But why do I resort to borrowed examples from the Gentiles, though they are very numerous, when each person may more properly be compelled to action by laws than by examples? Yet lest you suppose that the prince himself is in every respect released from laws, hear what law the great King—terrible above all the earth and he who takes away the spirit of princes—imposes upon princes:

“When you have entered the land which the Lord your God will give you, and have possessed it and dwelt in it, and say, ‘I will set a king over myself, like all the nations round about have,’ you shall appoint him whom the Lord your God has chosen from among the number of your brothers. You may not make a man of another nation king, who is not your brother. And when he has been appointed, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor lead the people back [Col. 0519A] into Egypt, relying upon a multitude of cavalry; especially since the Lord has commanded you never again to return by that same way. He shall not have many wives, lest they turn his heart; nor immense weights of silver and gold. But after he has sat upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write out for himself the Deuteronomy of this law in a book, receiving a copy from the priests of the tribe of Levi. He shall have it with him and shall read it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to fear the Lord his God and keep his words and ceremonies which are commanded in the law. Let not his heart be raised in pride above his brothers, nor let him turn aside to the right or left, so that he and his son may reign for a long time over Israel” (Deut. 17).

Is he, I ask, bound by no law whom this law binds? This is indeed divine law, and it cannot be violated with impunity. If each of its words had understanding in the ears of princes, they would be thunderclaps. I pass over his election and the form required in the creation of a prince. Consider with me for a little while the rule of life prescribed to him.

“When he has been appointed,” the text says—he who professes himself brother of the whole people by religious worship and the affection of charity—“he shall not multiply horses for himself,” by whose abundance he may burden his subjects. To multiply horses is to accumulate more than necessity itself demands, for the sake of vain glory or another error. For “much” and “little,” if we follow the chief of the Peripatetics, signify in every class of things a falling short of, or an excess beyond, lawful quantity.

May he then multiply dogs, birds of prey, savage beasts, or any prodigies of nature, when the number of horses needed for military service and for the use of the whole household has been fixed by lawful quantity? As for actors and mimes, buffoons and prostitutes, pimps and such monstrosities of mankind—whom a prince ought rather to banish than foster—there was no need to mention them in the law. For it excludes all these abominations not only from the prince’s court but expels them from the people of God.

By “horses” is understood the necessary use of the entire household and all equipment. Its lawful quantity is that which the reason of necessity or usefulness requires—yet in such a way that usefulness and honourableness are held equal, and civic life is ordered by what is honourable. For philosophers have long held that no opinion is more pernicious than the opinion of those who separate the useful from the honourable; and that the truest and most beneficial proposition is that the honourable and the useful are in every respect interchangeable.

[Col. 0519D] Plato, as the histories of the Gentiles report, when he saw Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, guarded round about his person by guards, said: “What such great evil have you done that you must be guarded by so many?” This does not befit a prince, who should win the affections of all through his services so completely that each subject would, when dangers threaten him, offer his own head in his defence. For even under nature’s compulsion the members are accustomed to expose themselves for the head, to give skin for skin, and to lay down all that a man has for his life.

It follows: “Nor shall he lead the people back into Egypt, relying upon a multitude of cavalry.” Every person set in high position must take the greatest care not to corrupt those beneath him by his example and misuse of things, nor lead the people back through pride or luxury to the darkness of confusion. For it is common for subjects to imitate the vices of their superiors, because the people strive to conform to their magistrate, and everyone readily seeks what he sees make another illustrious.

That famous passage of the excellent poet, expressing the thought and words of the great Theodosius, says:

> If you command or decree that anything be observed by all,  
> first submit yourself to your own commands. Then the people  
> become more observant of justice, and do not refuse to bear it  
> when they see its author obeying it himself.  
> The world takes its form from the ruler’s example,  
> and edicts do not have such power to bend human minds  
> as does the life of the one who governs.

[Col. 0520B] The fickle crowd always changes with its prince. Yet the resources of individual persons are by no means equal to the wealth of all. Each person takes from his own purse, whereas authority draws from the public treasury or royal storehouse; and, if this should perhaps fail, recourse is had to the resources of individual persons. But each private person must be content with his own means. If those means are reduced, he who had once sought the splendour of the powerful becomes, in the squalor of poverty, ashamed of the darkness of his humiliation.

Accordingly, by a Spartan decree, frugality in the use of public goods was imposed upon those in authority, while it remained lawful by common right to use hereditary possessions and goods accruing from a more prosperous fortune.

## Chapter V. That a prince ought to be chaste and avoid avarice

[Col. 0520C] The law adds: “He shall not have many wives, lest they turn his soul” (Deut. 17). It was indeed once permitted among the people of God, for the sake of multiplying offspring and enlarging the faithful people, that a man should take several wives. The patriarchs furnish examples of this permission: Sarah exercised her right over Abraham’s body, receiving a son, Ishmael, by her husband in another’s womb through the service of a handmaid. Jacob likewise, in a double marriage with sisters, took to himself their fruitful handmaids.

But kings are held by the snare of a perpetual prohibition: they are barred from the embraces of several wives, and though it might be lawful in other persons for several women to belong to one man, in kings the rule perpetually obtains [Col. 0520D] that one woman belongs to one man. Is it then permissible to commit fornication, adultery, or sexual violation with several women, when it is not even permissible to have intercourse with wives for the purpose of multiplying one’s lineage or begetting heirs? How will an authority subject to the same crimes punish sexual violations, adulteries, or any fornications?

Let no one object to David’s wives, who perhaps in this, as in many other matters, enjoys a special privilege. I readily concede, however, that he too sinned in this respect. Certainly that marital passion drove him into adultery through treachery and homicide; nor do I labour to excuse one who, confronted and convicted by the prophet’s parable, declared himself to be a man worthy of death. You have, then, a king sinning with kings; and would that they might repent with the penitent, [Col. 0521A] acknowledge their guilt with the one confessing, and, by making satisfaction with him who makes satisfaction, return to life. Even Solomon’s wisdom was made foolish by the love of women.

It follows: “Nor shall he have immense weights of silver and gold” (ibid.). Let them now, though the Lord forbids it, heap up silver and gold for themselves, make profit from calumny, seek abundance from others’ poverty, riches from plunder, and place their own singular blessedness in the calamity of many. But someone objects with Solomon’s wealth. Very well: I do not forbid a prince to become rich, but to become avaricious. Did not gold and silver become cheap in Solomon’s time? They would surely not have become cheap if a covetous king had amassed for himself immense quantities exceeding their use. He might have buried them in the earth and withdrawn them from human use, so that they became more precious.

Petronius relates of Trimalchio that there was an artisan who made glass vessels so tough that they were no more readily broken than gold or silver vessels. Having made a bowl of this kind from pure glass, fit, as he thought, for Caesar alone, he approached Caesar with his gift and was admitted. The appearance of the gift was praised, the craftsman’s hand commended, and the giver’s devotion accepted. But the artisan, to turn the spectators’ admiration into astonishment and secure the emperor’s favour more fully, received back from Caesar’s hand the bowl he had requested and hurled it violently upon the pavement, with such force that not even the most solid and enduring substance of bronze would have remained uninjured.

[Col. 0521C] Caesar, however, was no less alarmed than astonished at this. The man lifted the bowl from the ground. It was not broken but dented, as though the substance of bronze had assumed the appearance of glass. Then, drawing a small hammer from his breast, he repaired the defect most skilfully and, with repeated blows, restored it as one might restore a dented bronze vessel. This done, he imagined himself to have reached Jupiter’s heaven, because he believed that he had earned Caesar’s friendship and everyone’s admiration. But the result was otherwise. Caesar asked whether anyone else knew this method of making glass. When he answered no, the emperor ordered him beheaded, saying: “For if this art became known, gold and silver would become cheap, like mud.”

Whether the account is true and reliable is uncertain, and different people judge Caesar’s action differently. For my own part, without prejudging the understanding of wiser persons, I consider the devotion of the powerful artisan to have been poorly rewarded and mankind to have been ill served. An excellent art was destroyed so that money—the tinder of avarice, the food of death, and the cause of disputes and wars—and the material of money might be kept precious, though it would have possessed value without human effort, since that which is the price of things cannot exist without it.

> Price itself is now held at a price; wealth grants honours,  
> wealth grants friendships; the poor man lies everywhere neglected.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti* I.217)

Far more usefully, certain persons have endeavoured to banish from their commonwealths every material cause of quarrels and ground of hatred, [Col. 0522A] so that, when the cause was removed, the effect of wickedness might vanish. Such was Lycurgus’ decree among the Spartans, and such was the teaching of Pythagoras of Samos in ancient Greece, which is now part of Italy; by the strength and efficacy of his institutions, he is said to have preserved all Italy.

Would that gold and silver might become cheap, while virtue alone and those things whose use Nature, the best guide of life, commends are held precious. Then the poor man will not lie neglected, nor will the rich be honoured merely for his money, while each person is esteemed or despised according to the dowry of his own self. Some things possess worth in themselves; others, through the opinion of others. Bread, indeed, and provisions consisting in necessary food or clothing are valued everywhere on earth by nature’s direction. Things that delight the senses are naturally pleasing to all. Why say more? Things belonging to nature are not only the same, but flourish among all peoples. Things that follow the judgment of opinion are uncertain: as they exist by pleasure, so by pleasure they disappear.

The emperor, therefore, need not have feared that the material of commerce would fail, since trade is still common even among those who do not know money. I know indeed that Solomon possessed wisdom so great that he never feared gold and silver would become cheap for his descendants, whose nature he saw to be hungry and, for the most part, to hunger after nothing but money. Therefore, through inspired wisdom, that outstanding king despised this rust, in order to invite posterity by his own example to despise money.

Moreover, it is advantageous for a king to be abundantly supplied, provided that he regards his wealth as belonging to the people. Thus he will possess no wealth under another’s name, nor will fiscal goods, which he acknowledges to be public, be private to himself. Nor is this surprising, since he himself belongs not to himself but to his subjects.

## Chapter VI. That he ought always to have the law of God before his mind and eyes, be learned in letters, and be guided by the counsel of learned men

“After he has sat upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write out for himself the Deuteronomy of this law in a book.” See that a prince ought not to be ignorant of law; although he enjoys many privileges, he is not permitted, on the pretext of military service, to be ignorant of the law of the Lord. He shall therefore write out the Deuteronomy of the law—that is, the second law—in the book of his heart. The first law is that which the letter sets before him; [Col. 0522D] the second is that which mystical understanding recognizes from it. The first could indeed be written on tablets of stone; but the second is not impressed except in the purer understanding of the mind.

And rightly is the Deuteronomy written in a book, because the prince thus turns over within himself the sense of the law, so that the letter does not depart from his eyes. He adheres to the letter in such a way that he does not at all depart from the purity of understanding. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life (2 Cor. 3); and in it there is an intermediate interpretation, necessary and universal, concerning human law and equity.

“Receiving a copy from the priests of the tribe of Levi” (Deut. 17). Very rightly. The judgment of all laws is empty if it does not bear the image of divine law; and a prince’s ordinance is useless if it is not conformed to ecclesiastical discipline. Nor was this unknown to a most Christian ruler, who commanded in his laws that they should not disdain to imitate the sacred canons. He commands not merely that copies be requested from priests, but sends the prince to the Levitical tribe in order to borrow one.

For legitimate priests must be heard in such a way that every righteous man closes his ears entirely to the reprobate and those who climb up by another way. But who are the priests of the tribe of Levi? Surely those whom the law introduced into the Church without the spur of avarice, the impulse of ambition, or the affection of flesh and blood. Not, however, the law of the letter, which kills, but that of the spirit, which gives life in holiness of mind, purity of body, sincerity of faith, and works of charity. For just as the shadowy law, bearing all things figuratively, chose priests beforehand on the basis of flesh and blood alone, so, after the shadows have ceased and truth has been revealed and righteousness has looked down from heaven, the Spirit joins to the Levitical tribe and establishes as legitimate priests those whom merit of life, the fragrance of good reputation, and the unity of the faithful or the diligent providence of prelates has set apart for the work of ministry.

[Col. 0523B] It is added: “He shall have it with him, and shall read it all the days of his life” (ibid.). Consider how great a prince’s diligence in keeping the law of the Lord ought to be, since he is commanded always to have it, read it, and turn it over—just as the King of kings, made of a woman and made under the law, fulfilled all the righteousness of the law, being subject to it not by necessity but by will. For his will is in the law, and he meditated on the law of the Lord by day and night.

But if he is not believed worthy of imitation in this respect—he who embraced not the glory of kings but the poverty of the faithful, and, clothed in the form of a servant, sought no resting-place for his head on earth; and, questioned by the judge, confessed that his kingdom was not of this world—let the examples of illustrious kings, whose memory is in blessing, at least advance. Let David, Hezekiah, Josiah, and the rest come forth from the camp of Israel: they believed the glory of their kingdom to consist in binding themselves and their subjects in the bonds of divine law, while seeking God’s glory.

And lest their examples seem remote, and therefore less to be followed because we appear to depart to some extent from their law, ritual practice, religious worship, and profession of faith—although ours and theirs is the same faith, provided that what they awaited as future we rejoice in and revere as, for the most part, fulfilled, casting away only the shadows of figures since truth sprang from the earth and was revealed before the nations—lest, I say, their examples be despised as foreign or profane, our Constantine, Theodosius, Justinian, Leo, and other most Christian rulers can instruct a Christian prince.

[Col. 0524A] For they made it their chief concern that the most sacred laws, which bind the lives of all, should be known and observed by everyone, and that no one should be ignorant of them, unless either public utility compensated for the loss caused by error, or mercy toward age or the weakness of sex spared a person the stings of lawful severity. Their deeds are incentives to virtue; as many words as they spoke, so many are instructions in conduct. Finally, having subdued and taken captive their vices, they raised up their life like a triumphal arch consecrated to posterity, inscribed with the titles of magnificent virtue, proclaiming in faithful confession in all things that not an exalted hand but the Lord had done all these things.

Constantine, who founded and endowed the Roman Church—to say nothing of his other outstanding deeds—is distinguished by perpetual blessing. Who Justinian and Leo were is clear from the fact that they strove to consecrate the whole world, elucidated by most sacred laws, as a kind of temple of justice. And what shall I say of Theodosius, whom these men regarded as a model of virtue, and whom the Church of God, because of his venerable reputation for religion and justice, and because even when angry with priests he was most patient and humble, revered not merely as emperor but as a bishop?

He who had promulgated laws bore patiently the judgment of the priest of Milan. And lest you suppose that it was the mild judgment of a yielding presbyter, flattering princes: the prince was suspended from the use of imperial prerogatives, excluded from the Church, and compelled to complete a solemn penance. But what had subjected him to such a necessity? A will subjected to the justice of God and obeying his law in every respect. And, unless you consider verses written with metrical lightness worthy of contempt, you will recognize briefly from those things with which he instructs his son in Claudian the man he himself was in the sanctuary of morals.

[Col. 0524C] But when I turn over the words of the foregoing law, each one seems to me weighty and to come before my mind as though made fruitful by the spirit of understanding. “He shall have,” it says, “the law with him,” taking care that, since he must have it, he does not have it against himself for his condemnation. For the powerful shall suffer powerful torments. And it adds: “He shall read it.” For it is of little use to have the law in one’s satchel unless it is faithfully kept in the soul. It must therefore be read all the days of his life. From this it is plainly evident how necessary skill in letters is for princes, who are commanded to turn over the law of the Lord in daily reading. Perhaps you will not often find that priests are commanded to read the law daily. But the prince reads daily, and on every day of his life. For the day on which he does not read the law is for him not a day of life but of death. An unlettered man cannot do this without difficulty.

Hence, in a letter which I recall having been sent by the king of the Romans to the king of the Franks, exhorting him to ensure that his sons were educated in the liberal disciplines, this elegant addition occurred among other things: “An unlettered king is like a crowned ass.” Yet if, by dispensation on account of outstanding merit of virtue, it should happen that a prince is unlettered, he must be guided by the counsel of learned men if his affairs are to proceed rightly. Let the prophet Nathan, the priest Zadok, and the faithful sons of the prophets stand beside him; since they will not allow him to turn aside from the law of the Lord, they will bring before him through their speech—[Col. 0525A] as through a kind of gateway of the ears—that law which he himself does not behold with his eyes and mind.

Let the prince’s mind therefore read in the priest’s speech, and whatever excellence it sees in conduct let it revere as the law of the Lord. For the life and speech of priests are like a certain book of life before the face of the peoples. Perhaps this is the point of the command that copies of the law be taken from the priests of the tribe of Levi: the authority of the office entrusted to him must guide its helm by their preaching. Nor is one wholly without reading who, though he does not read himself, faithfully listens to what others read. But how can one who does neither fulfil faithfully, rather than despise, what is commanded? For the gathering together of all desirable things is an increase of wisdom.

Did not Ptolemy believe that something was lacking to the fullness of his blessedness until, although a Gentile, he summoned the Seventy Translators and communicated the law of the Lord to the Greeks? For it makes no difference whether the translators consulted together enclosed in the same cell or prophesied separately, provided it is established that the king, diligent in the search for truth, conveyed the law of the Lord into Greece.

I remember reading in the *Attic Nights* [Note: [Col. 0525D] Paris edition, “volumes”] that, when the notable qualities of Philip of Macedon are recounted, among other things his devotion to letters adorned, as it were, his military enterprises and triumphs of victory, his generosity at table, his duty of humanity, and all the things finely and publicly said or done. Indeed, this very quality in which he knew himself superior to others, as the foundation of an inherited patrimony of goods, he took care to pass on to the only heir of kingdom and happiness whom he hoped to have.

For this reason, Philip’s letter to Aristotle, the expected teacher of the newly born Alexander, seemed worth writing here. Its sense is approximately as follows:

> Philip sends greetings to Aristotle. Know that a son has been born to me, for which I thank the gods—not so much because he has been born as because it has happened that he was born during your lifetime. For I hope that, educated and instructed by you, he will prove worthy both of us and of assuming these responsibilities.

I do not remember Roman emperors or commanders, while their commonwealth flourished, having been unlettered. And I do not know how it happened that, from the time learning’s virtue languished in rulers, the armed hand of military service also was weakened, [Col. 0525D] and the very root of rulership, as it were, cut off. Nor is this surprising, since no rulership can stand or exist without wisdom. For the Wisdom of God said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

Socrates was judged wisest by Apollo’s oracle; and, surpassing beyond comparison and without contradiction those seven who were called wise, not in the reputation of wisdom but in its actual possession, he maintained that commonwealths would finally be happy if philosophers ruled them, or if their rulers happened to pursue wisdom. And if Socrates’ authority seems contemptible to you, Wisdom says: “By me kings reign, and makers of laws decree what is just. By me princes rule, [Col. 0526A] and the powerful decree justice. I love those who love me, and those who watch for me in the morning shall find me. With me are riches and glory, abundant wealth and justice. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone; my offspring than choice silver. I walk in the ways of justice, in the midst of the paths of judgment, that I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasures” (Prov. 8). Likewise: “Mine are counsel and equity; mine is prudence; mine is strength” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Receive instruction, and not money; choose teaching rather than gold. For wisdom is better than all precious riches, and nothing desirable can be compared with it” (ibid.).

Although the Gentiles believed that nothing should be done without the nod of the gods, they nevertheless worshipped one being as the god of gods and ruler of all—namely Wisdom—because she presides over all things. Thus the ancient philosophers thought that an image of Wisdom should be painted before the doors of all temples and that these words should be written:

> Practice begot me; Memory bore me:  
> the Greeks call me *Sophia*, you call me Wisdom.

And these likewise: “I hate foolish men, idle works, and philosophical opinions.” They indeed invented these things elegantly, although they did not fully know truth itself. Yet they approached it to some extent when they regarded wisdom as the guide and ruler of all things rightly done; for Wisdom herself truly boasts that from the beginning she held primacy in every nation and people, trampling under her own power the necks of the proud and lofty.

Solomon likewise confesses that he loved her above health and every beautiful thing, and that with her all good things came to him.

## Chapter VII. That one ought to be taught the fear of God and be humble; that preserving humility does not diminish public authority; and that some commandments are mutable and others immutable.

It follows that he should learn to fear the Lord his God and to keep the words commanded in his law. The law itself adds the reason for lawful observance: “That he may learn,” it says. For the attentive reader is a disciple of the law, not its master; he does not twist the law, held captive, toward his own meaning, but adapts his own understanding to its mind and integrity. But what does this disciple learn? Certainly, to fear the Lord his God [Col. 0526D]. Rightly so, because wisdom begets and strengthens sovereignty. Yet “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). Therefore, one who is not initiated by the first step of fear strives in vain toward the summit of lawful rule. Lawful, I say, because it is written of certain persons, when they are raised up, after others have been cast down and are to be cast down still more miserably: “They have reigned, but not through me; they have become princes, and I did not know it” (Hos. 8); and elsewhere: “Those who held the law did not know wisdom” (Jer. 2). Let the prince therefore fear the Lord, and profess himself his servant through ready humility of mind and devout performance of deeds. For the Lord is the master of the servant. Thus the prince serves the Lord when he faithfully serves his fellow servants—that is, those subject to him [Col. 0527A]. Let him also acknowledge him to be Lord and God, to whom no greater fear is due because of majesty than love because of mercy. For he is a Father, and no creature, by his own doing, can deny him the affection of love. “If, therefore, I am a lord,” he says, “where is my fear? If I am a father, where is my love?” (Mal. 1).

The words of the law must also be kept; this proceeds from the first step of fear by a happy ascent, as it were, up a ladder of virtues. “Love of him,” it says, “is the keeping of laws” (Wis. 6), because all wisdom is fear of the Lord. Moreover, “he who fears God will do good; and he who holds fast to justice will lay hold of her, and she will meet him like an honoured mother.” But what words will such great diligence preserve? Certainly those commanded [Col. 0527B] in the law, so that with the prince not one iota or stroke of the law will fall to the ground without being taken up either by him personally or by the hands of his subjects.

Some commandments have a perpetual necessity: they are lawful among all nations and cannot in any way be set aside with impunity. Before the law, under the law, under grace, one light binds all: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4); and what you wish to be done to yourself, do that to others. Let the whitewashers of the powerful now come forward, whispering—or, if that is too little, publicly proclaiming—that the prince is not subject to the law, and that whatever pleases him has the force of law, not only when he enacts law according to the form of equity, but in whatever manner whatsoever. Let them, if they wish and dare, make lawless a king whom they withdraw from the bonds of law. I affirm, not only against their resistance but against the world’s outcry, that they themselves are bound by this law. For, says he who neither deceives nor is deceived, “With whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. 7) [Col. 0527C]. And certainly the most severe judgment will be upon those who rule, since a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be poured into their bosoms.

Yet I do not withdraw the administration of the law from the hands of authorities; but I do not think that matters involving a perpetual command or prohibition are to be subjected at all to their discretion. Accordingly, only in matters that are mutable is a dispensation of the wording admitted—provided nevertheless that, through an equivalent consideration of honour or utility, the law’s purpose is kept whole. “And let not his heart be lifted up in pride above his brothers” (Deut. 17) [Col. 0527D]. What is especially necessary Scripture repeats more frequently, because humility can never seem sufficiently commended to princes, and it is most difficult for a rank of honour not to produce swelling in the mind of the imprudent. “God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4). Therefore the king prays that the foot of pride may not come against him, because “there fell those who work iniquity; they were driven out and could not stand.” Let him certainly not be proud over his brothers; rather, remembering that they are brothers, let him extend brotherly affection to all his subjects.

And indeed, prudently, humility is prescribed to princes together with discernment and charity, because rule cannot subsist at all without these. Whoever, therefore, loves the height of his own station should most diligently maintain the practice of humility toward his inferiors [Col. 0528A]. For he who withdraws from humble acts falls from the summit of his dignity under the weight of pride. For it holds perpetually that whoever humbles himself shall be exalted, and conversely whoever exalts himself shall be brought low. Pride made Tarquinius the last king of the Romans, and in place of him magistracies more necessary to humility were established. Indeed, whom among the proud have you read of as reigning for long? History abounds in those who fell through pride.

Yet he should not avoid pride to the extent of falling into contempt, because abasement, no less than arrogance, must be avoided. Hence Roman law also provides that one who administers justice should make himself accessible to those who approach him, yet should not allow himself to be despised. It is further added to the commands that provincial governors should not admit provincials into too intimate familiarity [Col. 0528B], because contempt arises from equal intercourse. Therefore let him honour in public the majesty of the people, and at home likewise measure the condition of private life.

Recognize that this very principle is to be followed from the ancient teachings of philosophers. To the philosopher Taurus came, for the purpose of seeing and knowing him at Athens, both the governor of the province of Crete and his father, a private citizen. Taurus rose calmly at their arrival and, after mutual greetings, sat down again. One chair, which happened to be at hand, was immediately brought and placed there while others were being fetched. Taurus invited the governor’s father to sit. But he said: “Let this man rather sit, since he is a magistrate of the Roman people.” “Without prejudice,” Taurus said [Col. 0528C], “you meanwhile sit, while we consider and inquire what is fitting: should you rather remain seated because you are the father, or your son because he bears the magistracy of the Roman people?” When the father had sat down and another seat had been placed for the son, Taurus spoke to those assembled on the matter, weighing with the utmost care the good, the equitable, moral virtues, and duties. The sense of his speech was approximately this: in public places and offices, the rights of fathers, when compared with those of sons who hold magistracies or powers, should rest and, as it were, close their eyes for a little. But when people sit, walk, or recline at a friendly meal outside public business and in domestic and private life, then public honours cease between a son who is a magistrate and his private father [Col. 0528D], and natural and genuine honours arise.

“This too,” Taurus said, “that you have come to me, that we are now speaking, that we are discussing duties, is a private affair. Therefore you, father, should first enjoy those honours which it is fitting for you to enjoy before your son also in your household.” I therefore think that magistrates generally should be persuaded of this: amid the splendour of public dignity, let them remember their own condition; and let them attend to the state of their own condition in such a way that they do not diminish the beauty of public rank. Let them so preserve the integrity of the honour conferred upon them that they do not lessen the dignity of others; and let each flourish in private dignity in such a way that no injury is done to public authority.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the moderation of a prince’s justice and clemency, which must be harmonized in him for the advantage of the commonwealth

[Col. 0529A]

Let this therefore prevail in the prince, as it ought to prevail in all: let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to others. Yet the measure of that very affection by which he embraces his subjects as brothers in the arms of charity is enclosed within the limits of moderation. For he so loves his brothers that he corrects their errors medicinally; he so recognizes flesh and blood in them that he subjects these things to the dominion of the spirit.

It is the practice of physicians to cure with more severe remedies—fire or iron, for example—diseases which they cannot cure by fomentations and gentler means. Nor do they ever employ the severe remedies unless recovery has been judged hopeless by the benefit of the gentler ones [Col. 0529B]. So too, when authority cannot heal the lives of inferiors by a gentle hand, it rightly and sorrowfully applies the bitterness of punishments to their wounds; it rages with merciful cruelty against the wicked while securing the safety of the good. But who has ever been able to amputate the members of his own body without pain? Thus vengeance is painful when guilt requires it, though the unwilling right hand performs it. For the prince has no left hand; and, in the suffering of the bodily members of which he himself is the head, he serves the law sadly and with groaning.

When Philip heard that a certain Phytias, a good wrestler, had become alienated from him because, poor as he was, he could scarcely support three daughters and had received no help from the king, his friends advised him to beware of the man. “What?” Philip said. “If I had a diseased part of my body, should I cut it off rather than cure it?” Then, having privately and familiarly drawn Phytias out, he learned the difficulty of his domestic needs, supplied him sufficiently with money, and found him better and more faithful than he had been before he was thought offended [Col. 0529C].

For, as Lucius says, a prince ought to be an old man in character, following more moderate counsels and playing the part of physicians, who cure illnesses sometimes by reducing what is overfull, sometimes by restoring what is empty, and soothe pain now by cautery, now by fomentations. Moreover, let him be gracious in speech, generous in benefits, and of unimpaired authority; let him preserve dignity in his conduct. For good speech and a gracious tongue win a reputation for kindness. Benefits compel even the harder sort to the most faithful and steadfast love, and they cherish and strengthen the love they have created. Reverence from subjects is due to dignity of conduct.

Trajan, the best of the pagan emperors, answered excellently when his friends reproached him for being too approachable to everyone, beyond what befitted an emperor: “He wished to be such an emperor to private persons as, were he a private person, he would have wished emperors to be to him.” Accordingly, on the report of Pliny the Younger—who was then appointed, among other judges, as a persecutor of the Church—he withdrew the sword of persecution from the slaughter of martyrs and moderated the edict [Col. 0529D]. Perhaps he would have treated the faithful more mildly had he not been urged, by the laws and examples of his predecessors, by the counsel of men thought prudent, and by the authority of judges, to destroy the sect of men popularly regarded as superstitious and hostile to the true religion.

Yet I do not commend in every respect the justice of a man who did not know Christ; rather, I mitigate his fault, since he was carried beyond himself by the pressure of others and was moved to kindness and mercy by the impulse of his own piety—by nature merciful toward all, severe toward the few whom it was held sinful to spare. So much so that throughout the whole course of his reign only one member of the senatorial or noble order of the city was condemned, although very many are found to have grievously offended against him. This man, however, was condemned by the senate without Trajan’s knowledge. For Trajan said that a man who, having eyes afflicted with inflammation, preferred to gouge them out rather than cure them was mad. He also said that, if one’s nails are too sharp, they should be trimmed [Col. 0530A], not torn out.

For if a lyre-player and other musicians take great care to correct the defect of a string that has gone astray and restore it to harmony with the others, producing the sweetest concord from discordant notes—not by breaking strings, but by tightening them proportionately or loosening them—how greatly must a prince take care, now through the severity of justice, now through the relaxation of clemency, to make his subjects like persons of one mind in a house, and to make from those discordant in the service of works of peace and charity one perfect and very great harmony? It is certainly safer, however, for strings to be loosened too much than stretched too much. For the skill of the craftsman can restore the tension of loosened strings and return the due charm of sound; but a string once broken is repaired by no skill [Col. 0530B]. Indeed, if a sound is required which they do not possess, they are stretched in vain; and one often reaches no sound sooner than the sound demanded too greatly.

The pagan says:

> A ruler should be slow to punish, swift to reward,  
> And grieve whenever he is compelled to be severe.

The one quality belongs to justice, the other to mercy; both are so necessary to a prince that whoever claims not merely rule but any magistracy without them vainly makes a mockery of himself and also provokes in others laughter, contempt, and hatred toward himself. “Let not mercy and truth forsake you; bind them around your neck and write them upon the tablets of your heart, and you shall find favour and good instruction before God and men” (Prov. 3). For favour is due to mercy [Col. 0530C], and instruction to justice. Certainly the favour and love of subjects, produced by divine grace, is the best instrument for accomplishing everything. But love without discipline does not profit, because when the spur of justice is absent, the people abandon themselves to unlawful acts.

Therefore he continually meditates upon wisdom, and from it so practices justice that the law of clemency is always upon his tongue; and he so tempers clemency by the rigour of justice that his tongue speaks judgment. For by the requirement of his office justice becomes judgment, with such necessity that he cannot be free from it without forfeiting the honour conferred on him. For the honour of a king loves judgment, and he restrains the faults of offenders with the tranquil moderation of his mind.

Plutarch is said to have written a book on the moderation of magistrates, entitled *Archigrammaton*, and to have instructed the magistrate of his city in patience and the practice of justice by words and examples [Col. 0531A]. He had a slave, a wicked and obstinate man, but remarkably well educated in the liberal disciplines and sufficiently trained in philosophical disputations. It happened that, because of some offence I know not what, Plutarch ordered the slave’s tunic removed and that he be beaten. He had begun to be struck rather severely with a strap, although he denied the offence, saying that he had done nothing wrong, had committed no crime, and had earned by many services no such treatment as to be beaten. At last, when this availed nothing, he began to shout; and while being beaten, he hurled forth not complaints, groans, and cries, but serious and reproachful words. Plutarch, he said, was not behaving as befitted a philosopher: anger was shameful, especially in one who had often discoursed upon the evil of anger and had written a most beautiful book on patience [Col. 0531B]. He added that it was disgraceful for Plutarch to oppose his teaching by his conduct, since, falling away from soundness of mind, poured out and prostrate in anger, he was punishing an innocent man with many blows.

To this Plutarch replied slowly and gently, but with the utmost gravity: “Do I seem angry with you because you are being beaten? Is it anger on my part if you receive what is due from me? Do you perceive from my face, voice, complexion, or even words that I am corrupted or overcome by anger? I think my eyes are not fierce, my mouth is not disturbed, I do not shout idly, I do not boil over into foam and redness, I do not say shameful or regrettable things, nor am I at all trembling or excited with anger. All these, if you do not know, are usually signs of anger.” Then, turning to the man who was beating him, he said: “Meanwhile, while this man and I discuss the matter, do your work; and, without any anger of mine, break down his slavish obstinacy, and teach the wrongdoer rather to repent than to quarrel” [Col. 0531C]. Such was Plutarch. In this, some instruction has been left for all who are in high station.

## CHAPTER IX. What it means to turn to the right or the left, which is forbidden to a prince

It follows: “Neither shall he turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (Deut. 17). To turn to the right is to press too vehemently even upon virtues themselves. To turn to the right is, in works of virtue—which consist in measure—to exceed the measure. Every excess, indeed, is hostile to health, and every excess is blameworthy; excessive practice even of good things is very bad. Hence the moralist:

> The wise man will bear the name of madman, the just man that of unjust,  
> If he pursues virtue itself beyond what is sufficient.

And the philosopher says: “Beware of what is excessive, because if this very caution abandons moderation, by that very fact it heedlessly departs from the path of virtue.” Solomon also says: “Do not be too just” (Eccles. 7) [Col. 0531D]. What good, then, is excess, if justice, the queen of virtues, harms by its own excess? Elsewhere too: “Excessive humility is the greatest part of pride.”

To turn to the left is to turn aside or stray from the way of virtues along the precipices of vices. Likewise, one turns aside to the left who is too ready to inflict vengeance for the faults of subjects; and one bends his step to the right who, from gentleness, indulges offenders too greatly [Col. 0532A]. Both paths are aberrant, but the one tending to the left is more destructive.

## CHAPTER X. What advantage princes obtain from the cultivation of justice

But what will be the advantage of this lawful observance? The prophetic utterance immediately adds it: “That he himself and his son may reign for a long time over Israel” (Deut. 17). Behold what reward is to come from so great a difficulty: paternal kingdoms are extended to sons for a long time. For the succession of sons is prolonged by the virtue of their parents, while the happiness of successors is cut short by the wickedness of those who have gone before. For the testimony of the Holy Spirit is certain: “The unjust shall perish together, and the remnant of the wicked shall perish.” But “the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord,” who protects them in time of tribulation [Col. 0532B].

But since eternity, however great the whole of time may be, is exhausted through the tiniest moments and remains in that entirety for no more than a very brief instant, what can be long in it, when all such things, if gathered into one, compared with true eternity do not even occupy the place of a point, since there is absolutely no comparison between finite things and the infinite? Certainly there is, as many think, some proportion, however small, between a centre and a *peripheria*—that is, circumference—but none between eternity and time. What, then, will be long in that which is wholly brief? Or what happiness of time will seem lasting to the soul if that faithful and everlasting soul must lose it after however much time has elapsed?

Yet in this place, so that the statement may be understood without prejudice to a better or sounder interpretation, I think that a kingdom “of long time” means the age of the unfailing soul itself, which the glory of eternal blessedness will crown for a kingdom well administered. For since it is certain that God will reward the works of each and all with abundant mercy or fuller justice, whom will he regard with brighter light than those who bring all to the practice of justice or draw them with themselves away from death? Therefore, just as the powerful will suffer powerful torments, so they will enjoy more fully the rewards of justice if they have exercised power rightly; and they will have in the future so much greater glory than their subjects [Col. 0532C] as they surpassed them in virtue amid great freedom to sin. “He was able to transgress and did not transgress; to do evil and did not do it; therefore his good things have been established in the Lord” (Ecclus. 31).

For princes are credited with justice even when they refrain from injuries; and the capacity to offend is material for their merit. For them it is a great thing to turn aside from evil, even if they do not do great good, provided they do not destroy their subjects by indulgence toward evils. Is it not a great thing that continuance is promised to them, if they act rightly, of the blessedness which they seem to possess? Some say that it is impossible both to flourish here with the world and to rejoice eternally with Christ; and this statement is true if among the flowers of the world you count the enticements of vices. Yet kings too can flourish and gather forever the sweetest and most useful fruits of worldly flowers. What could be happier than that princes should be transferred from riches to riches, from delights to delights, from glory to glory—from temporal things to eternal?

## CHAPTER XI. What other reward belongs to princes
