Yet I do not exclude what the first surface of the letter promises: it promises fathers a kingdom lasting a long time and extends its succession to their sons, who will be heirs both of the temporal kingdom and of eternal blessedness. For I know that the law spoke to a carnal people, which still had a heart of stone, uncircumcised in mind rather than flesh, and for the most part did not know eternal life, considering it a great thing if earthly goods were given or promised to it for food [Col. 0533A]. Accordingly, a promise of flesh was made to one who thought carnally; duration of time was promised to one who had not yet conceived hope of eternal blessedness; and a temporal kingdom was extended in succession to sons for those who did not yet seek the eternal kingdom.

Thus a son succeeds his father temporally if he imitates his father’s justice. Solomon says: “Remove wickedness from the face of the king, and his throne shall be established by justice” (Prov. 25). For if wickedness withdraws from his face—that is, from his will—the acts of the whole kingdom are directed by the rod of equity and the practice of justice. Hence: “A king who sits upon the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze” (Prov. 20). See with what great privilege princes rejoice: to say nothing of eternal blessedness, the glory of their kingdom is perpetuated even in their flesh and blood.

The Lord glories that he has found a man according to his heart; and when he later raised him to the summit of kingship, he promises him an everlasting kingdom in the line of sons succeeding him: “From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne; and if your sons keep my commandments, which I have already given, and my testimonies, which I shall teach them through myself or through my vicars, they too and their sons shall sit upon your throne” (Ps. 131) [Col. 0533B]; “and I will establish his seat for age upon age, and his throne as the days of heaven. But if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my just ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. 88). Thus the kingdom is transferred from nation to nation, and these heirs—who appear to be heirs according to the flesh in the seed—are destroyed, so that succession may be transferred to those found to be heirs of faith and justice. In this the truth of the promise remains, and what has proceeded from the mouth of the Most High stands firm: for righteous kings, their seed continues forever through the succession of the faithful.

But even without speaking here of Christ, who was made from David’s seed according to the flesh and is King of kings and Lord of lords, I think that this holds perpetually even according to the letter: sons succeed their parents if they faithfully imitate them in the Lord’s commandments [Col. 0533C]. Indeed, so much is this the case that, even if all things seem rightly ordered and remaining in that order, so that no concern or duty of a ruler appears necessary, it is established for those who have once admitted a prince that succession from his seed will not fail—even if for no other reason than to preserve the distinction of blood. The examples of histories make this clear.

For it is reported that when Alexander the Great was exploring the furthest shore of Ocean, he was preparing to subdue the island of the Brahmans. They sent him a letter in these words: “We have heard, most invincible king, of your battles and of the success of victory that has followed you everywhere. But what satisfaction will there be in such things for one to whom the whole world is insufficient? We possess no riches for the desire of which you ought to conquer us; all goods belong in common to all. Food is our wealth; in place of finery and gold, our clothing is cheap and scanty [Col. 0534A]. Our women are not adorned in order to please; indeed, they count such attention to ornaments as a burden rather than an adornment. For they do not know how to seek, through increased beauty, anything beyond what they were born with. Caves serve us a double use: shelter in life and burial in death. We have a king, not for the sake of justice, but to preserve nobility. For what place would vengeance have where no injustice is committed?”

Moved by these words, Alexander judged that there would be no victory if he disturbed their perpetual peace, and left them in their quiet. And perhaps, had he attacked them in war, he would by no means have prevailed against the innocent, because innocence is not easily overcome and truth, steadfast in its own strength, triumphs over an army however armed. But because nothing is more desired by human beings than to have their children as successors in their goods, so that those who foresee their own death as the condition of their nature may perpetuate life in the offspring of their flesh, this is promised to princes, and by it they can especially be invited to the practice of justice [Col. 0534B]. For those secure about themselves are continually anxious concerning the condition of their children.

And an excessive order of affection is observed in this: the father transfers to his children the love which was owed especially to parents by their country, since filial affection alone drains the chamber of the fatherly breast. Children in turn respond worthily to their parents, imparting to their own children the same affection which they received from their parents—although ordered charity requires another order, which the most learned of poets expressed wisely. For when Troy was destroyed, he placed aged Anchises upon the shoulders of his dutiful son; Aeneas gave his father’s right hand to Ascanius, while his wife Creusa clung to her husband, following the tracks of those going before because of feminine weakness [Col. 0534C]. He gave all his fellow-countrymen as leader a man marked out by arms and piety. Otherwise a leader would be useless, since kingdoms cannot be acquired without strength or retained without justice.

But now the sole concern of everyone is to distinguish their children, whatever they may be like, with riches and honours rather than virtues. What burden is thereby imposed upon the commonwealth is neglected. After the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus, the last king to reign in the City, when Brutus, the first consul, learned that his sons were plotting to restore kings to the City, he brought them into the forum and, after they had been beaten with rods in the midst of the public assembly, finally ordered them struck with the axe, so that he seemed plainly, as the father of the public, to have adopted the people in place of his children [Col. 0535A].

For my part, although I shudder at parricide, I cannot but approve the loyalty of the consul, who preferred to endanger the safety of his children rather than that of the people. Whether he acted rightly, let the wise judge. For I know that this field lies widely open to rhetoricians, and that declaimers have often laboured over this ambiguous theme, since in acquitting the parricide loyalty is troubled, while parricidal impiety attempts to extinguish the merit of loyalty.

But if you press me for my judgment, I answer with what I find the Areopagites replied to Gnaeus Dolabella in the Smyrnaean case. When he was governing the province of Asia with proconsular authority, a woman of Smyrna was brought before him. She confessed that she had secretly killed her husband and son by administering poison, because they had wickedly murdered her own son, an excellent and wholly innocent young man from another marriage, after waylaying him. She asserted that, by indulgence of the laws, it was lawful for her both to disregard the law and to avenge so atrocious an injury to herself, her family, and her whole commonwealth [Col. 0535B]. The legal issue was external to the case, since the deed was established and the law was being asked about.

When Dolabella referred the matter to a council, there was no one who, in what seemed an ambiguous case, dared acquit the manifest poisoning and parricide, or condemn the vengeance that had been executed against the impious and parricidal men. He therefore referred the matter to the Areopagites of Athens, as judges more weighty and experienced. After hearing the case, they ordered the accusers and the defendant woman to appear in the hundredth year. Thus neither was the poisoning, which the law did not permit, acquitted, nor was the guilty woman punished, to whom, in the judgment of many, pardon might be granted. Valerius Maximus, Book 9 of his *Memorable Sayings and Deeds*, teaches that this occurred.

Moreover, I readily agree that both Brutus and the woman sinned, because the remedy exceeded its measure,

> [lacuna] and pursued too far  
> Where the diseases led her hand.

And although the crimes had been great, it would have been better to avenge them without the crime of the punisher. Hence even the poet who praises Brutus bears witness to his misfortune, for Virgil says in Book 6:

> …And the father summoned his sons, stirring up new wars,  
> To punishment for fair freedom’s sake—  
> Unhappy man, however later generations may bear his deeds.

But in the following verse he so excuses the misfortune of parricide that he indicts truth by empty glory, saying:

> Love of country shall prevail, and an immeasurable desire for praise.

But lest anyone henceforth imitate Brutus in preferring the people to his children, you will be troubled in vain, since even children’s vices are preferred to the safety of the commonwealth—although it is certain that the safety of the people ought to be preferred to all children. In the Book of Kings Saul is reproved because, after making a vow of a daytime fast under penalty against anyone who took food before night contrary to the vow, his son Jonathan tasted honey which he had touched with his sceptre—that is, his spear; moved by paternal affection, Saul spared his son contrary to the religious vow, through whose transgression the people of Israel appeared to have fallen that day [Col. 0536A]. Eli also, though he is read to have been holy in himself, because he spared the vices of his sons, fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died.

To say nothing of the rest, how greatly, I ask, did he love humanity and seek its salvation who “did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8), so that he, innocent and free from guilt, should endure the chains, scourges, and cross which we had deserved, and should be condemned to the most shameful death? Search the history of kings, and you will find that a king was sought from God for this purpose: that he should go before the people and fight their wars, and, in the likeness of the nations, bear the burdens of the whole people [Col. 0536B]. Yet he would not have been necessary unless Israel too had transgressed into likeness with the nations, so that it no longer seemed content to have God as its king. For if it had cultivated justice by itself, if it had walked faithfully in the Lord’s commandments, God would have humbled its enemies as nothing and laid his hand upon those troubling it, so that, with God’s customary help, one would pursue a thousand and two would put ten thousand to flight.

I recall my guest from Piacenza saying—certainly a man noble in birth, possessing the prudence of this world in the fear of the Lord—that it was most commonly and notably the case in the cities of Italy that, when they love peace, cultivate justice, and abstain from perjuries, they enjoy such gladness of liberty and peace that there is absolutely nothing [Col. 0536C] that disturbs their tranquility even in the least. But when they lapse into deceits and are divided among themselves through various paths of injustice, the Lord immediately brings upon them either Roman pride, German fury, or some other scourge; and his hand remains stretched out until they themselves return from wickedness through repentance. By this remedy alone does every storm among them cease.

He added also that the merits of the people either make every government void or make it very mild; while, conversely, it is certain that because of the sins of a people God permits a hypocrite to reign, and that it is impossible for one to enjoy rule for long who exults too proudly in the humiliation of the people and in his own exalted position. But he said that the rule of the man is prolonged who, from consciousness of humility, is always troubled within himself as though he ruled unwillingly [Col. 0536D]. These things my guest from Piacenza told me, and, I believe, they accord with the faith.

Something similar is found in the writings of the ancients. When Helius was carrying out the prefecture at Rome with particular distinction, he was made emperor from being a senator. When the senate begged him to call the son he had Caesar “Augustus,” he said: “It ought to be enough that I myself have ruled unwillingly, although I did not deserve it. Rule is owed not to blood but to merits; and he rules uselessly who is born a king rather than earns kingship. And undoubtedly a parent strips himself of affection who destroys his little children by laying upon them an unbearable burden. This is to suffocate children, not to advance them. They must first be nourished and trained in virtues [Col. 0537A]; and when they have progressed so far as to prove that they surpass in virtues those whom they ought to surpass in honour, let them ascend when invited, and not withdraw themselves from the wishes of their fellow citizens. For who doubts that those are to be preferred to others who, enlarged as it were by a natural privilege of virtue, are invited to virtue by the titles of their ancestors and by that same advantage give others confidence in their future goodness?” Thus he spoke. And indeed he elegantly expressed the privilege of a prince, whose sons succeed him undoubtedly by the ancient gift of God, unless wickedness overturns the rule.

## CHAPTER XII. From what causes principalities and kingdoms are transferred
It is a celebrated saying of Wisdom that “a kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, wrongs [Col. 0537B], insults, and diverse deceits” (Ecclus. 10). Do you not see how swiftly the throne of the first king among God’s people was overthrown? Saul and Jonathan, with the rest of his sons, fell upon the mountains because their faults demanded it, so that the throne of him who was chosen from behind the nursing ewes might be established. Run through the sequence of all histories, and you will see the successions of kings cut short in a brief span, as though at the very beginning of the web, with the Lord cutting the threads. And the more illustrious kings have been, the more swiftly, if they have swelled in pride against God, is their offspring trampled down.

There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord—certainly no strength either. If he rises up, if he pursues, one runs in vain to the borrowed aid of sacraments and to the defenses of fortifications, because there is no one who can snatch from his hand [Col. 0537C]. Who was greater than Alexander in Greece? Yet it is recorded that not his own son succeeded him, but the son of a dancing-girl. Who does not know the succession of the Caesarian house? Few or none of them left a son as heir; and all, after diverse dangers and very many slayings of themselves and their own people, were in a short time wiped out by different deaths, almost all disgraceful. Descending to the underworld, they had as successors either enemies or strangers.

“What, I ask, so quickly overthrew and transferred kingdoms so powerful?” Surely the indignation of God, which manifold injustice provoked against them. Injustice, as the Stoics hold, is a disposition of the mind that banishes equity from the domain of morals. For that justice is taken away from the soul is shown even by the privative particle in the name *injustice*. Justice consists chiefly in this [Col. 0537D]: that you do no harm, and that by the duty of humanity you restrain those who do harm. But when you harm another, you approach wrongdoing; when you do not prevent wrongdoers, you serve injustice.

An insult is present when an outward act of injury accompanies the swelling pride of the mind. Thus it serves iniquity, because it insolently rises against one to whom reverence is owed, whether by virtue of office or by fellowship of nature. Deceit, moreover, is, as Aquilius defines it, when one thing is done and another pretended. It is certainly evil whenever it is committed with the intention of harming. Deceit differs greatly from insult: the latter harms openly and arrogantly; the former fraudulently, as though from ambush.

These are the things which, when they occur, overthrow the seats of all powers [Col. 0538A], because the glory of rulers is perpetuated by their opposites. Deceit bears the mark of weakness under the appearance of timidity and is especially opposed to courage. Prudence represses insult, continually repeating: “Why does earth and ashes grow proud against earth and ashes?” Temperance admits no wrongdoing, unwilling to inflict on another what it would not wish another to inflict upon itself. Justice excludes injustice, always doing to another what it would wish done to itself.

These are the four virtues which philosophers call cardinal, because they are believed to flow, like first streams, from the primary fountain of moral goodness, and to send forth from themselves the rivers of all good things. Perhaps these are the four rivers which go forth from the paradise of God’s delights [Col. 0538B], to water the whole earth so that it may bring forth desirable fruit in its season. Would that streams of this fullness might pass also to me from the fountain of life—I mean divine grace—making drunk the land of my dryness, so that, as the fruit of good works grows, I may at least escape the blow of the threatening axe which, because my faults demand it, has been laid at my root as at the root of an unfruitful tree.

Every tree planted beside these waters does not wither. But whatever they do not moisten, even at the root, is dissolved and perishes dry, like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. I therefore think that neither leaders nor powerful men are excepted, since the glory of kings shall be transferred if they are found unjust, injurious, insulting, or deceitful. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken [Col. 0538C].

Nevertheless, without prejudice to the understanding of wiser men, I think it is not without reason that he set forth the names of these vices in the plural, and prudently inserted a certain diversity in that plurality itself. For he says, as stated above: “A kingdom shall be transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, wrongs, insults, and diverse deceits.” Since he added “diverse” at the end, I think it should be understood as applying generally to them all, and with so full a sense that it refers not merely to different kinds of vices but also embraces the various kinds of persons and all the ways in which these vices are committed by anyone whatever.

For the ruler is held responsible for all things and is regarded as the author of all, because, since he can correct everything, he rightly shares in those things which he has refused to amend [Col. 0538D]. For public power, as we said above, draws upon the strength of all; and, lest it fail in itself, it must procure the well-being of all its members. As many offices as exist in the administration of a principality, so many, as it were, are the members of the princely body. While it preserves the offices of individuals through integrity of virtue and the grace of reputation, it procures, as it were, health and beauty for the members. But when, through the negligence or connivance of power regarding offices, there is loss of virtue or reputation, diseases and blemishes fall, as it were, upon its members. Nor does the soundness of the head long endure where the weakness of the members gains strength.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0539]

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 0539A]

Great things are not usually examined completely and without delay, nor is it easy to traverse in a moment the length and breadth of provinces. Thus a great matter is indeed sometimes set forth concisely by a wise man, but is never perfectly explained within the excessive narrowness of speech. What in human affairs is greater than rulership, whose office in a manner encompasses, fills, and penetrates all things, and, by the strength of its virtue, bears the whole mass of the commonwealth?

Its consideration therefore has breadth and requires time, both because of its magnitude and because of the beauty which all find delightful to contemplate in the head of the commonwealth. Let us therefore linger with restrained brevity in examining its body, and hear what Plutarch [Col. 0539B] thinks on this subject. For, once the superstition of the Gentiles has been removed, he is trustworthy in his opinions, eloquent in expression, and so great an arbiter in the sanctuary of morals that you may readily recognize him as Trajan’s teacher. But if anything in him disagrees with faith or morals, let it be attributed rather to his age than to the man himself. For if Virgil was permitted to seek the gold of wisdom in the mud of Ennius, what envy is there in sharing with our own learning those writings of the Gentiles which are useful for it? Let us therefore omit these matters and proceed to what remains.

## CHAPTER I. Plutarch’s letter instructing Trajan

There survives a letter of Plutarch instructing Trajan, which expresses the tenor of a certain political constitution. It is said to be as follows:

“Plutarch sends greetings to Trajan [Col. 0539C]. I knew that your moderation did not seek the principate, though you always strove, by elegance of character, to deserve it. You are judged all the more worthy of it because you seem more remote from the fault of ambition. I therefore congratulate your virtue, and my own good fortune—provided, however, that you conduct yourself rightly—since you have honorably deserved it.

“Otherwise, I do not doubt that you will be exposed to dangers and I to the tongues of detractors, since Rome does not tolerate the indolence of emperors, and public speech commonly lays the faults of pupils upon their teachers. Thus Seneca is attacked by the tongues of those who deservedly disparage his Nero; the rashness of Quintilian’s young men is laid upon Quintilian; and Socrates is accused of having been too indulgent toward his ward.

“But you will manage everything most rightly if you do not depart from yourself. If you first order yourself, if you dispose all that is yours toward virtue, all things will proceed rightly for you. I have set before you the chief powers of political order: if you obey it, you have Plutarch as your authority for living. Otherwise, I call this present letter as witness that you are not proceeding to the ruin of the empire under Plutarch’s authority.” [Col. 0539D]

## CHAPTER II. What the commonwealth is according to Plutarch, and what holds within it the place of the soul or of the members

[Col. 0540A]

There follow chapters of this same political constitution in the little work entitled *The Instruction of Trajan*. I have taken care to insert them, insofar as concerns the present treatise, yet in such a way as to imitate rather the traces of the ideas than the steps of the words.

First of all, then, the ruler must measure his whole self and carefully observe what place he occupies in the whole body of the commonwealth. The commonwealth, according to Plutarch, is a kind of body, animated by the benefit of a divine gift, moved by the nod of highest equity, and governed by a certain moderation of reason. Those things which establish and shape religious worship among us, and which hand down the ceremonies of God—lest, following Plutarch, I say “of the gods”—hold the place of the soul in the body of the commonwealth [Col. 0540B]. Those who preside over religious worship ought therefore to be regarded and revered as the soul of the body. For who doubts that ministers of holiness are the vicars of God himself?

Further, just as the soul holds primacy over the whole body, so those whom he calls overseers of religion preside over the whole body. Augustus Caesar was subject to the pontiffs of sacred things until he himself, so as to be subject to no one at all, was made pontiff of Vesta; and shortly afterward, while still living, he was enrolled among the gods.

The ruler holds the place of the head in the commonwealth, subject to God alone and to those who act in his place on earth, since in the human body the head too is enlivened and governed by the soul [Col. 0540C]. The senate holds the place of the heart, from which arise the beginnings of good and evil actions. Judges and provincial governors claim for themselves the offices of eyes, ears, and tongue. Officials and soldiers are fitted to the hands. Those who always stand beside the ruler are likened to the sides. Quaestors and record-keepers—not those who preside over prisons, but the counts of the private treasury—are referred to the image of the belly and intestines. If these gather things together with boundless greed and retain what they have gathered too tenaciously, they produce innumerable and incurable diseases, so that through their fault the ruin of the whole body threatens.

Farmers are fitted to the feet, which constantly adhere to the ground [Col. 0540D]. The providence of the head is all the more necessary to them because they encounter more obstacles while walking upon the earth in the service of the body. And the aid of coverings is more justly owed to those who raise, sustain, and advance the burden of the whole body. Remove the supports of the feet from even the strongest body: it will not proceed by its own strength, but will either creep on its hands shamefully, uselessly, and painfully, or be moved by the aid of brute animals.

In this manner he sets forth, in his own fashion, a great many further matters, which he pursues more carefully in a fuller treatment for the formation of the commonwealth and the instruction of magistrates [Col. 0541A]. To go through all these syllable by syllable would be the work of a slavish translator, who is more concerned to imitate the author’s appearance than to convey his force. And because he discusses rather superstitiously many matters concerning ceremonies and the worship of gods which he thought ought to be impressed upon a religious ruler, let us omit what pertains to idolatrous worship and briefly set forth the meaning of the man, by which he instructed the ruler and the offices of the commonwealth in the worship of justice.

## CHAPTER III. What chiefly occupies Plutarch’s intention; and concerning reverence to be shown to God and sacred things

[Col. 0541B]

In sum, there are four things which he seeks to impress upon the rulers of the commonwealth: reverence toward God, self-cultivation, discipline of officials and authorities, and affection and protection for subjects. He maintains, therefore, that God must first be honored; then each person must cultivate himself, so that, in the Apostle’s sense—although Plutarch does not acknowledge the Apostle—each may possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor (1 Thess. 4). Next, the entire discipline of the household should reflect the teaching of its head; and finally the whole body of subjects should rejoice in the safety of the head set over them.

He also employs stratagems and military examples of great men, which would weary the reader if inserted individually and would in part depart from the purity of our faith. Yet [Col. 0541C] since the holy Fathers and the laws of rulers, after his impiety has been removed, seem to follow his traces, let us touch upon his teaching in brief and Catholic language, adding in part his military examples.

For him, the beginning is reverence for divine beings; for us, it is reverence for God, who must be loved universally by all and worshipped with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one’s strength. The proof of love is the offering of action. And although he can be loved in himself, because he pours himself into the one who loves without the help of an intermediary, nevertheless an intermediary is necessary for outward worship, because no one has ever seen God.

You must extend the term “seeing” to denote all the senses of both natures, because no human being can sense him immediately and purely and live [Col. 0541D]—unless perhaps through that part of the senses which knows none of the body’s limitations and feels no failure of time, but by its own vitality remains eternally through grace. I mean charity, which does not fail but increases as it approaches more familiarly the one whom it desires. Faith, indeed, has a veil; and hope, through the encouragement of grace and merit, soothing the conscience, stretches the joy of its desire into the future. Faith and hope therefore imitate sense, but remain short of it, acting meanwhile as through a mirror and in an enigma, until their form, with the substance of truth unchanged, shines forth fully.

But one who cannot be clearly seen by any sense cannot easily be known. And what is not known cannot be diligently worshipped [Col. 0542A], except through an intermediary. Thus we read that Numa Pompilius prescribed certain ceremonies and sacrifices for the Romans, so that under the pretext of the immortal gods he might more easily invite them to cultivate piety, religion, faith, and the other things which he wished to instill in them. The sacred shields and the Palladium, certain sacred pledges of empire; two-faced Janus, arbiter of war and peace; the hearth consecrated to the virgins of Vesta, in which the flame, guardian of the empire, kept continual watch in honor of the heavenly stars—all bear witness to this.

So too does the year extended into twelve months, marked by the variety of lawful and unlawful days; the pontiffs, augurs, and varied rites of priesthoods. By these he so occupied their barbarism that they refrained from injuries, rested from arms, cultivated justice, and bestowed civil affection upon one another [Col. 0542B]. Thus he reduced a fierce people so far that it happily governed, by the laws of justice and piety, the empire which, as is said, it had occupied by force and wrongdoing.

But why do I bring forward Numa, when even the fathers of our faith maintain that the sacrifices of the Old Law were instituted lest the people, occupied in the worship of demons, unlearn the worship of true religion, sacrificing their offerings to demons according to the rite of the Gentiles and not to God? God, therefore, is worshipped either by the affection of the mind or by the offering of action. But the affection of love reaches him directly, although, while it is away from the Lord and the mind is weighed down by the body’s burden, it cannot fully comprehend him through any sense of body or soul. And indeed he is loved more ardently and sought more diligently because the height and immensity of the riches of his power and wisdom surpass every understanding [Col. 0542C].

Yet by such power he encompasses, penetrates, fills, and protects every creature that no rational creature can possibly fail to perceive him. Irrational creatures also attest by many signs that he exists, and that he is such and so great. In a wondrous way, therefore, he so imparts understanding of himself that he withdraws it; and so withdraws it that he imparts it. According to the measure of his good pleasure, he works thus in individuals, so that, although one does not know the alternations of increase and diminution, he seems to be present through grace more or less, though not through essence, by which he uniformly fills every creature.

For by union he is faithfully demonstrated to be present in the Virgin’s only-begotten Son alone. Thus he is now, as it were, individually in each person, and will be, as it is written, all things in all the elect. And just as the nature of fire—though in an unequal comparison, since nothing can be compared to it equally—produces diverse effects from the sun according to the diversity of bodies, so that nature, if it is permitted to compare great things with the greatest, shines in many persons in manifold ways [Col. 0542D].

For if a ray of sunlight happens to strike a carbuncle, it goes forth or rebounds ruddy and makes the neighboring air gleam red. The same fire becomes green in an emerald, takes on the likeness of the purer sky in a sapphire, and is made like-colored in kinds of hyacinth. In topaz, which is more precious the rarer it is, it displays almost every color. If you set a rainbow before it, it will represent the image of Thaumas’s daughter. Cast upon water, it ripples upon the ceiling; and through beryl it sends heavenly fire into what is placed beneath it.

You see, therefore, how manifold is the nature of fire in many things [Col. 0543A]. So in some there is prudence, in others courage; in certain persons temperance, in others justice; in some faith, in others the long-suffering of hope. In these is the fervor of charity; here patience under labors, there consolation in sorrows, elsewhere perseverance in good works. Yet in each and every one of these is the one and same God.

But in the future, when through his grace we shall see him as he is with unveiled face, he will be all things in all, when no substance of any virtue will be lacking to anyone for blessedness, since he himself will be in all the fullness of virtue and the sum of blessedness. Indeed, according to the tradition of the Fathers, he will seem present to the elect with such fullness of his majesty that they will lack nothing in any grace, and he alone will almost seem to be in them [Col. 0543B] and they will be designated by his name—while the truth of their substance is preserved and their nature undergoes no change whatsoever.

Perhaps this is the meaning of the saying: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. 149), since then the hearts of the saints are believed to lie open to one another, and each person rejoices not only in his own conscience but also in that of all. For as fire, to remain with the foregoing comparison, penetrates and ignites the nature of iron so that nothing is seen in it but fire, and as a sunbeam illuminating the air is called by the name of sun or ray, so God will fill all the elect, so that, when all weakness and changeability have been swallowed up, when the mortal has put on immortality and the corruptible incorruption, God alone will almost be recognized in all.

Some refer to this sense the fact that angels, already partakers of future blessedness, when seen by human beings are adored, because a certain presence of Deity was seen in them, although a creature must by no means be adored by a creature [Col. 0543C]. Thus too something of Deity shone in the Savior’s face when, having made a whip of cords, he drove buyers and sellers from the temple, teaching that all commerce must be expelled from the house of prayer.

In others, however, although the presence of Divinity is there, its fullness is by no means present in this life; nevertheless it cannot be wholly concealed. He is therefore wonderful in majesty, venerable in wisdom, lovable in goodness; and a faithful creature can render him this worship without any intermediary. For what is needed in order that we may fear, revere, and love him? This perhaps [Col. 0543D] is the threefold cord between Creator and creature which cannot easily be broken. But the power of love is the most tenacious of all. For charity never fails; whoever clings to God is united to him and is one spirit with him. Certainly one who is united with him and is, as it were, one spirit is familiar with him and cannot be excluded from his service in the spirit.

But that worship which consists in the offering of outward action requires an intermediary, because bodily persons have no open access to spirit. This was plainly taught by him who, instructing the Church in the Samaritan woman, said: “God is spirit, and those who wish to worship must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4). Yet, so that the weakness of our humility may somehow ascend to his throne and possess some material for merits, he who gave sense, who will glorify both soul and flesh, willed to be worshipped sensibly [Col. 0544A], and he demands the faithful service of both. He also willed to be honored bodily, so that no degree of slowness arising from unbelief or negligence may have an excuse.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning reverence for persons and things, and the ways in which a person is venerable

Reverence rendered bodily, then, consists either in persons or in things. The basis for regarding persons is drawn from nature, office, morals, condition, or fortune. By nature we revere parents and children, and those whom flesh joins to us, such as a wife, relatives, and connections by marriage. Thus this has been received by the law of nations, because it is done alike among all nations [Col. 0544B]. We are also bound to it by divine law, since we know what is written: “Honor your father and mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth”; and: “Whoever curses father or mother shall die” (Matt. 15).

Children need not be commended at length, because no one has hated his own flesh (Eph. 5). Nor need one say much of a wife, for whose sake a man leaves father and mother, clinging to his wife, so that the two are one flesh (ibid.). Yet commands of divine law are not lacking in this matter. Although they are less often inserted because nature’s impulse presses strongly enough, they extend to relatives and connections by marriage, whom nature itself commends.

Office is the obligation of carrying out those things which, according to institutions or customs, each person ought to do [Col. 0544C]. From it appropriate actions belong to individual persons. Among things to be done in this way, some pertain to the public condition and some to the condition of each individual. Hence it is clear that some offices are properly called public and others private. The multiplicity of private offices is nearly as great as the diversity of persons. All public offices, however, are reduced to two kinds: they derive either from divine or from human law.

These matters are more fully set out in books on offices, but they concern the present topic insofar as reverence is to be rendered to public offices. For as much reverence is due to them as corresponds to the eminence of each magistracy. This eminence is either established or indicated by the proper jurisdiction of each office, since reverence for or contempt of magistrates [Col. 0544D] rebounds upon the honor or disgrace of subjects. Hence in the constitutions of rulers and in the edicts or promulgations of magistrates, a plurality of persons is conceived by anticipation, so that not so much the person as the entire constitution of the community seems to be speaking, or likewise any other promulgation. This is evident from daily use even to one ignorant of laws and canons.

Moreover, not only the ordinances of canons and laws but the precepts of all moral philosophers explain the rationale of offices. Custom is a disposition of the mind from which the habitual practice of individual actions flows. For something done once or several times is not immediately counted among customs unless continual doing turns it into a practice. This includes virtues and vices alike, although vices are said by many not to be morals but to oppose morals [Col. 0545A]. In this it is evident that virtues alone are designated by the name “morals,” since, although we speak of good or bad morals, we distinguish vices from virtues. Hence we name persons of good character, or compliant persons, from the good; but persons of bad character from vices. This seems also to be suggested by the very term denoting fullness, since no one in the flesh can attain a fullness of virtues, while many possess an excess of vices.

When, therefore, a person is said to derive reverence from morals, it is signified that the virtues for which honor should be given are present in him. For who would not venerate and respect one believed prudent, courageous, temperate, and just? Hence also comes the wise man’s counsel to one who desires to be feared, loved, honored, and preferred: that he fear, love, and revere God, and submit himself to him with complete devotion [Col. 0545B].

Some define condition as the accidental state of a person, by which he is either depressed by adversities or raised by prosperities and displays by his very appearance the nature of one or the other lot. Thus we revere some as freeborn; we heap servile insults upon others. We honor the riches of these people; we despise the poverty of those. Cicero maintains that it is difficult to define nature. I believe that it is still more difficult to define fortune, because nature has some substance whereas fortune has none. Nature gives things their origin; it could not do so unless it itself existed in truth. What does not exist at all cannot grant another thing existence. But fortune, since it does not exist, cannot be defined. For in that which is not, it cannot be established for anyone what it is.

Let the Epicureans bring forward their principal doctrines, which they call *kyriai doxai* [Col. 0545C]—“authoritative opinions”—and to which they think the whole progress of philosophy is subject, and let them, after their fashion, subject all things to fortune. In this, as in very many other matters, I think Plutarch should be heard. He denies that a blind goddess ought to be worshipped, asserting that she cannot be worshipped except by the blind. He also gives many examples by which it is clear that all worshippers of the blind goddess have been blinded and finally hurled into the pit of destruction.

Galba bears witness to this. Having advanced brilliantly through his whole lifetime into old age, he was swiftly elevated by intimacy with and worship of this goddess, and more swiftly hurled down. Seek in Suetonius how this occurred. Yet the aforesaid philosopher laments and groans tearfully into the ear of the ruler just mentioned that this disgraceful goddess—blameworthy for her blindness and rashness, and shameful among all divinities—has defiled the temples of all gods and stolen the worship of them all [Col. 0545D]. Besides the private shrines which she has everywhere throughout the world and the city, she has even occupied the Tarpeian Rock, made equal to Jupiter Most High; and the golden image of Public Fortune is publicly adored on the Capitol by foreigners, newcomers, and natives. She possesses such authority above all others that, in the whole ordering of mortal affairs, she alone, as the saying goes, appears to fill both pages.

There you may see her turning her revolving wheel; and, more astonishingly, by the impulse of that same wheel she casts down and tramples the sisters’ threads from Jupiter’s breast.

Whoever posits fortune casts down and overturns fate.

> “The Stoic says,” ‘The Fates rule men; fate is in those parts  
> which the bosom conceals.’”

Epicurus’s *kyria doxa*, or “authoritative opinion,” protests against this Stoic paradox:

> “Remove fated necessity, because  
> if Fortune wills, you will become consul from being a rhetor;  
> if that same Fortune wills, you will become rhetor from being consul.”

But, to speak more gently of fortune, let it be the form of unforeseen events. Although it seems very close to condition, because a concurrence of chance events produces the state which we have called condition, it differs greatly in this: condition is now from nature, now from office, now from morals, now from various forms of events; fortune always consists in things that arise unexpectedly [Col. 0546B].

Plutarch strives entirely to empty fortune of force, and believes that the origin of all reverence flows from the four preceding sources: nature, office, morals, and condition. Yet he pursues this too superstitiously, in the manner of unbelievers. Therefore I have taken care to include some of his opinions in a Catholic sense and language. He especially maintains that in the worship of gods those should be revered who approach them more familiarly and closely: either by nature, as Liber, tamer of the Indians, and Hercules, who testified that Jupiter was in him precisely by strangling serpents in his cradle; or by office, as pontiffs and overseers of sacred rites; or by morals, as philosophers, who display a draught of the divine mind by the investigation and ordering of wisdom; or by condition, as those whom divine favor has raised to preside over others, more from a private cause than from public office [Col. 0546C].

The language is indeed faithless and deserving of every condemnation, as is the meaning of the words, which does not befit a philosopher. But perhaps he did not dare to declare before the ears of a corrupt people what he thought about the nature of the gods. He had read that the books of the philosopher Pythagoras had been burned and that Pythagoras himself had been exiled by the Athenians because he had doubted whether what was commonly said about the gods was true. What contrary assertion, then, would one dare to make when he knew that even doubt concerning error went unpunished? It is therefore plausible that he accommodated himself to his hearers and, in order to recall them from unlawful acts, made some concession to error.

For in moral teaching he is most eloquent. I all the more readily assent to this view because the Apostle of the Gentiles, while preserving faith and religion intact, became all things to all people in order to gain all. But we [Col. 0546D], upon whom truth has shone from heaven, believe that great reverence must be shown not to ministers and friends of gods—which do not exist—but to the ministers and friends of the true God; and sometimes even to his enemies, because he himself commanded this, he who has often granted very great power to the worst people for the instruction of his own.

Thus: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake, whether to the king as preeminent, or to governors, as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (1 Pet. 2); and: “Servants, be subject to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh” (ibid.) [Col. 0547A].

People become God’s friends either by grace, when merits are absent—as Jeremiah and John were sanctified before birth, and Nicholas, the jewel of priests, who in the cradle nursed only once on Wednesday and Friday—or by merits arising from grace: those who merit the kingdom of heaven by the easy way of good works, like the repentant thief, or by a difficult and blessed passage, like the company of apostles and martyrs.

Maro indicates these three orders:

> “The descent to Avernus is easy.  
> Night and day the gate of gloomy Dis stands open;  
> but to retrace one’s steps and escape to the upper air—  
> that is the task, that is the toil. Few whom just  
> Jupiter loved, or whom ardent virtue raised to heaven,  
> sons of the gods, could accomplish it.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.126

[Col. 0547B] Those, therefore, whom we see conformed to divine goodness by the elegance of their morals, we ought to venerate as the truest and most faithful image of God. Ministers, however, are those whom divine dispensation has called to procure their own salvation and that of others by rebuking and correcting vices, or by implanting and propagating virtues. Those who minister to him in human law are as far inferior to those who minister in divine law as human things yield to divine.

## CHAPTER V. What punishment threatens those who inflict injuries upon ministers of the Church and venerable places; concerning the privileges of venerable places; and that absolution can neither be extorted by force nor stolen by fraud
In those, however, who administer divine law, God is honored or despised above all others, since He regards their honor or contempt as His own. Hence the saying: “I said: You are gods” (Ps. 81); and: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). Truth Himself also says: “He who hears you hears me; he who receives you receives me; and he who despises you despises Him who sent me” (Luke 10). And the prophet: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2).

The reverence consisting in the veneration of things is manifold. For things are either bodily, such as churches and sacred places, things assigned to pious uses, and sacrifices visibly performed; or incorporeal, such as the rights belonging to sacred things. To violate these is sacrilege, to be expiated by death or another most severe penalty, [Col. 0547D] according to the nature of the offense. But to overthrow the immunity of sacred things is to rise up against God and, as it were, to claim Him for slavery.

Indeed, much might be set forth on behalf of divine law itself; but lest boldness speak against a rival authority, in this matter the enactments of princes are more ample and generous. They venerate and approve the Christian faith and confirm in their entirety the privileges of churches, ministers, and all venerable places. For who has not heard the constitution of that prince whose memory is blessed—I mean Arcadius?

“If anyone has burst forth into this kind of sacrilege, so as, by rushing into Catholic churches, to inflict some injury upon priests or ministers, even in the very worship or place itself, let what has been done be punished by the governors of provinces; and [Col. 0548A] let the provincial governor know that the injury done to priests, ministers of the Church, the place itself, and divine worship is to be avenged by a capital sentence upon offenders convicted or confessing. Nor should he wait for the bishop to demand vengeance for a personal injury—for holiness has left him the glory of forgiving. And let it be praiseworthy for all to prosecute atrocious injuries committed against priests or ministers as a public crime, and to exact vengeance for such offenses.”

Likewise: “It pleases Our Clemency that clerics have nothing in common with public functions or those pertaining to the curia, to whose body they are not attached.”

And elsewhere: “If the privileges of a venerable church have been violated by anyone’s rashness or neglected through dissimulation, let the offense be punished by condemnation to five pounds of gold.”

The privileges of churches, venerable places, and ministers are well known by both divine and human law. For it is now clear from practice that they cannot be summoned except before ecclesiastical judges; and if anyone lays violent hands upon a member of the clergy, he is struck with anathema, so that he cannot be absolved except by the Roman pontiff. Pardon for this crime is sought elsewhere in vain, unless perhaps the hour of death is at hand, because absolution can neither be extorted by force nor stolen by fraud.

With Claudian as authority, Theodosius says:

> “[lacuna] You will not force others to love you;  
> Mutual trust and simple favor grant this.”

Nevertheless, it is true that you cannot compel yourself to be absolved, an absolution which contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and [Col. 0548C] satisfaction in deed alone merit. Certainly it is not force but grace alone that justifies the ungodly; nor does fraud benefit the sinner, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit and does not dwell in a body subject to sins.” Elsewhere I recall having said, on the testimony of the great Father Augustine, that feigned innocence is not innocence but a double wickedness, because it is both wickedness and pretence. Likewise feigned equity is not equity but double iniquity, because it is both iniquity and pretence.

Hence I am confounded by an excessive astonishment when I see very frequently—I do not know whether to call them believers or unbelievers—persons caught in such sacrilege striving with all their strength to press priests, by threats and terrors, to grant absolution: an absolution which the priests cannot faithfully give, nor the sacrilegious persons usefully receive while remaining obstinate. Certainly it is easier for both parties to become entangled than for either of them to be released. Yet whose fault is graver I would not easily say. These matters concern those things which, in Plutarch’s political constitution, hold the place of the soul.

## CHAPTER VI. On the prince, who is the head of the commonwealth; his election, privileges, and the reward of virtue and fault; on his obligation to imitate blessed Job; and on the virtues of blessed Job.

It remains for us, following his footsteps, to consider the members of the commonwealth. It has been said that the prince occupies the place of the head and is governed by the judgment of mind alone. Divine providence, therefore, as has already been said, has placed him upon the summit of the commonwealth; and now, by the secret mystery of its providence, sets him above the rest; now, as it were, by the judgment of his priests; now the wishes of the entire people concur in appointing him to rule.

Thus in the Old Testament we read that Moses, when he was to appoint the man who should preside over the people, called together the entire assembly, so that he might be chosen in the presence of the people and that afterward no one might object and no scruple remain. In the Book of Kings we read that Saul, who was to become king, standing before the people, towered over all the people from the shoulders upward. Why, I ask, except because one who ought to preside over others must stand out in breast and speech, so that, as it were, with the arms of good works he may embrace the whole breadth of the people and protect them as more learned, holier, more circumspect, and excelling in every virtue?

For the Lord says to Moses: [Col. 0549B] “Take to yourself Joshua, the son of Nun, a man who has the Spirit of God within himself; lay your hands upon him; set him before Eleazar the priest; give him commands in the sight of the whole assembly; command concerning him before them; and give your glory to him, that the children of Israel may hear him.”

You plainly hear the ordination of the prince of the people so clearly described that it scarcely needs exposition. Yet if you seek a clearer explanation, at the Lord’s prompting, when you command, I shall expound it for you in its proper place and time, adding the significance of the garments and certain sacraments. But here there is plainly no acclamation of the people, no consideration of blood relationship, no regard for kinship.

When Salphaad died, his daughters claimed their paternal inheritance before Moses. God Himself testifies that their petition is just. The inheritance of fields and estates—and, for the most part, of legal claims—is indeed to be left to relatives. But the government of the people is to be entrusted to the one whom God has chosen: namely, a man who has God’s Spirit in himself, before whose eyes are God’s commands, who is very well known and familiar to Moses—that is, one in whom are the brightness of the law and knowledge, so that the children of Israel may hear him.

Nevertheless, favor for innovations must not permit departure from the bloodline of princes, to whom succession by their children is due through the privilege of divine promise and the right of lineage, provided that, as prescribed above, they have walked in the righteousnesses of the Lord. [Col. 0549D] If, however, they have deviated a little from the way, they are not immediately cast down altogether, but are patiently corrected in justice until it becomes evident that they are obstinate in evil.

For Rehoboam was not immediately thrown from his father’s throne; but after, despising the counsel of the elders, he departed from Solomon’s way and wished to impose an unbearable burden upon the children of Israel. Yet his kingdom was divided: ten tribes withdrew after Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, and kingdoms were divided while Judah or Israel held the kingdom. Thus he felt punishment for obstinacy, but mercy because of God’s grace and the privilege of blood: he remained king indeed, but was maimed by the loss of a great part of his kingdom. Why did this happen to him? Because he had attached himself to the counsels of the young men, despising the ways and precepts of prudence.

For it is impossible that one who does not act by the counsel of the wise should govern beneficially. “Woe,” it says, “to the land whose king is a child and whose counselors eat in the morning. Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at their proper time, for refreshment and not for luxury” (Eccles. 10). For wisdom cannot be there. Hence holy Job:

> “Where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding?  
> Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly.  
> Nothing of the things that perish is equal to it, for wisdom is drawn forth from hidden things”  
> (Job 28).

It would have been far more profitable for him to reject the young men and acquiesce in the counsel of the elders, taking the life of blessed Job as a pattern for ruling. Hear, then, what Job confesses concerning himself:

> “When I washed my feet in butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil;  
> when I went forth to the gate of the city, and they prepared a seat for me in the square.  
> The young men saw me and hid themselves, and the elders rose and stood.  
> Princes ceased speaking and put their finger upon their mouth.  
> Leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.  
> The ear that heard me called me blessed, and the eye that saw me bore witness for me,  
> because I had delivered the crying poor man and the orphan who had no helper.  
> The blessing of him about to perish came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow.  
> I put on justice and clothed myself with it as with a garment, and judgment was my diadem.  
> I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.  
> I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the cause that I did not know.  
> I broke the jaws of the wicked man and snatched the prey from his teeth.  
> And I said: [Col. 0550C] ‘I shall die in my little nest, and, like the palm tree, shall multiply my days.  
> My root is open beside the waters, and dew will remain in my harvest.  
> My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.’  
> Those who heard me waited for my judgment and, attentive, were silent for my counsel.  
> They dared add nothing to my words, and my speech dropped upon them.  
> They waited for me as for rain, and opened their mouths as for the latter rain.  
> If ever I smiled upon them, they did not believe it, and the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground.  
> If I wished to go to them, I sat first; and though I sat as a king with an army surrounding him, yet I was a comforter of those who mourned”  
> (Job 29).

Behold: in great measure a pattern for ruling is set forth in this just man. If we should wish to pursue every point, the sequence of virtues inserted here alone would fill the size of an entire book. Let the diligent reader examine each word, because in all these things not an iota or a stroke is devoid of the mystery of salvation. Yet I shall briefly touch upon a few matters that stand out upon the very surface of the words.

“When,” he says, “I washed my feet in butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil, while I sat in a prepared chair in the public square, the young men hid themselves and the elders stood before me.” He signifies, then, that abundance of possessions and a concurrence of favors did not shake his prudence; rather, amid them all, his authority remained unshaken through the testimony of conscience and good works. He went out to the gate because he had no need of hiding places; and he who had merited the seat of teaching raised up the prudence of the elders while youthful frivolity hid itself.

Princes ceased speaking, and the tongues of leaders clung to their throats. They did not dare utter grand things or place unbearable burdens upon men’s shoulders, burdens which cannot be touched even with a finger-tip. For he taught that all praise of virtue consists in action and that brilliance of speech without the solidity of deed beneath it is empty. Solomon says: “In every work there shall be abundance; but where words are many, there is often want” (Prov. 14). The duty of princes and rich men is to precede others on the way of morals, not proudly thunder out to others what ought to be done.

“The ear that heard and the eye that saw called me blessed.” He elegantly identified the bodily instruments by which the perception of the soul is especially strengthened. For knowledge of external things passes most faithfully to the soul through the service of the eye and ear, while a careless tongue often scatters the treasures of the heart. In adding “hearing” and “seeing,” he expresses the judgment of the wise, according to the saying: “Blessed is he who speaks in the ear of one who hears.” He therefore does not say that he was called blessed by human tongues, which are often impelled in either direction by love or hatred. The testimony of conscience is sufficient for him, especially when it is strengthened by the judgment of the wise.

“Because,” he says, “I delivered the poor man, the orphan, and the perishing man, and consoled the heart of the widow.” In these things chiefly shines the authority of a ruler established by the Lord for repelling injuries. These are indeed works of mercy, and the name of the man performing them shall be blessed forever. [Col. 0551C] But do not suppose that by a more relaxed clemency he gave boldness to vices: “I put on justice,” he says, “and judgment was my diadem. I investigated most diligently the cause that I did not know.” A judge must examine everything, investigate the order of events through full inquiry, and not act against anyone before the case has been most completely defined by lawful reasons. For, as the moral philosopher says: “Whoever judges quickly hastens to repentance.”

“I broke the millstones of the wicked man.” Wicked is whoever in judgments follows not the case but the prey, who loves gifts so as to pursue recompense. Even if the decision he reaches for a price happens to be just, serving greed he proceeds toward death.

Hence follows: “And I snatched the prey from his teeth, and I said: ‘I shall die in my little nest.’” He had therefore composed his mind, being content with the abundance of his own possessions. He was not driven by the goad of avarice or ambition to join house to house and field to field, even to the boundaries of the place, as if he alone were to dwell upon the surface of the earth.

“And, like the palm tree, I shall multiply my days.” A remarkable fact! Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Problems*, and Plutarch, in the eighth book of the *Memorabilia*, say: “If, upon the wood of a palm tree, you place great weights and press and burden it so heavily that the weight cannot be borne, it does not yield downward or bend to the earth, but rises against the burden, strives upward, and bends back.” Therefore, says Plutarch, the palm was chosen as the sign of victory in contests, [Col. 0552A] because the nature of its wood is such that it does not yield to those pressing and crushing it.

It is also reported that the branch of that palm which is called in Greek *basileros* cannot be torn away if drawn downward, but yields if you draw it upward. It is established that the trunk or stem of the palm is narrowed from the root but broadens in its upper parts. The opposite is true of any other tree, which swells all the more as its trunk comes nearer the ground.

By the palm tree, therefore, invincible justice is signified: justice which knows no descent, but only progress toward higher things. Hence: “The just man shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91). “My root is open beside the waters”: namely, the waters of Scripture and virtues, concerning which it was said above. “And dew”—that is, grace—“will remain in my harvest”: understand, the harvest of good works, the sheaves of which the just Judge will store up for the elect with Himself on that day.

Hence follows: “My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored,” because:

> There is something toward which the just man aims and upon which he directs his bow,  
> and he does not wander everywhere after crows, potsherds, and mud.

“Those who heard me waited for my judgment,” and so forth. It has often been said that *judgment* (*sententia*) must always be understood in a good sense, according to: “The sluggard seems wiser to himself than seven men speaking judgments” (Prov. 26). You hear three things combined in a wise man: “They were attentive,” he says, “and silent for my counsel; they dared add nothing to my words; my speech dropped upon them.”

A difficult matter calls for attention, and it befits a serious man to ponder his counsels, so that whatever he does, whatever he says, may be done with counsel by one aspiring to wisdom. It is the mark of a restrained mouth to utter things from which nothing may be removed or to which nothing may be added. It is most disgraceful in a serious man if he continually entangles himself in tales and trifles, and clamors among babblers like a quarrelsome goose mingled with swans, believing every subject fit for disputes:

> “For men debate whether Castor knows more,  
> or whether the road to Brundisium leads Numicius better than Appius.”

Moreover, things that abound become cheap through their very abundance; and, since sin is not absent from much speaking, the speech of one who speaks little and prudently is precious. Thus Socrates, when asked how someone might acquire the best reputation, replied: “If he does the best things and says few things.” This is what the just man, fearing to sin in speech, means when he says that his utterance fell in drops. For “he who does not offend in word is a perfect man.”

“If ever I smiled upon them, they did not believe it.” Laughter is an indication of frivolity; and the more open it is, the more shameless and blameworthy it is. For it says: “A fool raises his voice in laughter” (Ecclus. 21); and the Savior wept, though indeed He is nowhere read to have laughed. Nor would I readily believe that one who speaks of laughter with such hesitation—that, even if he laughed, it was not believed—was prone to loud laughter. “And the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground.” Perhaps the just man smiled, but temporal foolishness did not dissolve him in merriment, and whatever was earthly in his behavior feared his stern countenance.

“If I wished to go to them, I sat first.” He was indeed worthy of the first seat, since he preceded others on the path of so many virtues. Though he sat as a king while others attended him, he wiped away the tears of the mourning. A pleasing conclusion indeed: when public power strives to preside in such a way that it does not permit anyone in its whole community to be sorrowful.

By what art this may be accomplished, the moral field set below explains—of such delightful beauty of flowers and abundance of fruits that anyone entering it may rejoice to share the delights of paradise. Perhaps you wonder and are struck with amazement that anyone in the exile of this flesh can partake of such sweetness and be a fellow-citizen of the citizens of heaven. But judge for yourself from the works of the just man whether this can be so:

> “If I denied the poor what they wanted and made the eyes of the widow wait;  
> if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat from it—because compassion grew up with me from childhood and came forth with me from my mother’s womb;  
> if I despised a passerby because he had no garment, or a poor man without covering;  
> if his sides have not blessed me, and he was not warmed with the fleeces of my sheep;  
> if I raised my hand against an orphan when I saw myself superior in the gate, let my shoulder fall from its joint and my arm be broken with its bones.  
> For I always feared God above me as swelling waves, and could not bear His weight.  
> If I considered gold my strength and said to refined gold: ‘You are my confidence’;  
> if I rejoiced over my many riches and because my hand had found very much;  
> if I saw the sun shining and the moon moving brightly, and my heart rejoiced secretly, and I kissed my hand with my mouth—which is the greatest iniquity and a denial against God Most High;  
> if I rejoiced at the downfall of him who hated me and exulted because evil had found him;  
> if the men of my tent did not say: ‘Who will give us of his flesh that we may be satisfied?’  
> The stranger did not remain outside; my door stood open to the traveler.  
> If I hid my sin like a man and concealed my iniquity in my bosom;  
> if I feared an excessive multitude and the contempt of my kinsmen terrified me, and I did not rather keep silent and go out of the door;  
> if the earth cries out against me and its furrows weep with it; if I ate its fruit without payment and afflicted the souls of its cultivators, let thistles grow for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley”  
> (Job 31).

Do you not believe that he walks in the spaciousness of God’s delights who, from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, makes these declarations concerning himself under so great an imprecation? Which of these words requires interpretation, or who does not see amid such light of virtues? Excessively dull indeed and of blunt understanding is one to whom these things do not shine by themselves.

Here very many things are gathered into one, any single one of which would suffice to illumine, as it were, an entire world. If princes are weary of reading or hearing more, let them at least read, hear, examine carefully, and imitate this small portion. For the same passage continues: “If kings hear and observe the voice of the Lord, [Col. 0554A] they shall complete their days in good things and their years in glory. But if they do not hear, they shall pass by the sword and be consumed in folly” (Job 36).

Do you see the twofold end of useless kings? Either they pass through the sword, or they are consumed by folly. They are rightly said to pass through the sword, not to end by it, because the sword is, as it were, a passage for them to the place where, according to the multitude of their iniquities, “the mighty are mightily punished.” Folly also consumes the impious, because in the oppression of the people the strength of the prince is enfeebled. For a crushed people either cannot or will not raise the prince’s strength.

## CHAPTER VII. What evils or goods accrue to subjects from the character of princes; confirmed also by examples of certain stratagems.

“It is as one who throws a stone upon Mercury’s heap, so is he who gives honor to a fool.” This is explained in different ways by different people. With the permission of wiser men, I believe the heap of Mercury to be that in which the method of calculation consists, because Mercury is the deity of those who conduct trade and diligently attend to their accounts. To throw a stone into the heap by which the method of calculation is governed is to throw the whole calculation into confusion; and to confer honor upon a fool is to overthrow the life of the commonwealth. It is impossible for one whose own error ruins him to govern others beneficially.

For it says: “Where there is no governor, the people shall fall” (Prov. 11). And elsewhere: “A foolish king shall destroy his people, and cities shall be inhabited through the understanding of the prudent. Every rule has a short life; a more prolonged sickness burdens the physician. The physician cuts short a brief sickness: so too a king exists today and dies tomorrow. For when a man dies, he shall inherit serpents, beasts, and worms” (Ecclus. 10).

I ask: are the poor oppressed by injuries, diminished by exactions, stripped by multiplied plunder, and peoples commanded to rush against one another and shake the world, so that these heirs may succeed the powerful? These heirs succeed to all things by their own right; no formality of a will is required: they arise as intestate heirs. Whether you wish it or not, these will be your heirs.

In secular writings Plato is reported to have said: “When a magistrate oppresses his subjects, it is as if the head of a body should swell so that it cannot be borne by the limbs at all, or not without pain. It is impossible for this affliction to be endured or cured without the most severe pain of the limbs. If the affliction is incurable, to live thus is more miserable than to die; and for the wretched nothing is more useful than to end their misery somehow.”

He is also read to have said: “When power rages against subjects, it is as if a guardian persecuted his ward or cut his throat with the very sword entrusted to him by that ward for his defense. For it is a widely known fact that the commonwealth enjoys the legal position of a ward; and it then proceeds rightly only when its head recognizes that it is of use only if it faithfully cleaves to the limbs.”

These things he said, elegantly and truly. But, in my view, a faithful and firm cohesion cannot exist where there is not a tenacious unity of wills and, as it were, a gluing together of souls themselves. If this is lacking, human works vainly correspond to one another, while deceit proceeds toward destruction without affection for advancement. Job says: “Dissemblers and crafty men provoke the anger of God; they will not cry out when they have been bound. Their soul shall die in the tempest, and their life among the effeminate” (Job 36).

For shame now supplies a motive for actions, and sometimes fear does. But that union is most solid which proceeds from the richness of faith and love and rests upon the foundation of virtue alone. Yet actions, since they are indications of character, produce favor, because nothing is more useful or effective for the stability and advancement of magistracies.

Hence that saying of the emperor—or, if you prefer, of an outstanding poet, though you cannot doubt that they thought the same:

> “Be merciful above all; for though we are surpassed in every  
> office, mercy alone makes us equal to the gods.  
> Do not act as doubtfully suspicious or false toward friends,  
> or greedy for rumors: whoever cares for such things  
> will dread empty noises, anxious at every hour.  
> Not sentries and surrounding spears protect one  
> as love protects; you will not force others to love you:  
> mutual trust and simple favor grant this.”

When Alexander, leading an army in winter, was seated by a fire, he began to inspect the troops passing by. Seeing a certain man nearly lifeless from cold, he ordered him to sit in his own place, saying: “If you had been born among the Persians, it would be a capital crime to sit upon the royal seat; but this is granted to one born in Macedonia.” [Col. 0555C]

Another story is told of the same man. When word was brought that a maiden of extraordinary beauty, betrothed to the prince of a neighboring people, was among the captives, he spared her with the utmost self-restraint, so that he did not even look upon her. Soon restoring her to her betrothed, he reconciled to himself the hearts of the entire people through this kindness. Thus, by humane treatment of his own people, he bound the minds of foreigners to himself by justice.

Similar is the deed which Scipio Africanus is reported to have done in Spain. When a noble maiden, drawing all eyes to herself in wonder at her beauty, was brought to him, he returned her to her betrothed, named Alicius, adding the gold which her parents had brought to ransom the captive, so that it might serve the maiden as a dowry or her husband as a wedding gift. Thus, conquered by manifold generosity, the entire nation—which perhaps otherwise would not have yielded—joined the Roman people’s empire.

When Camillus was besieging the Falisci, a schoolmaster led the children of the Falisci outside the walls under the pretext of taking a walk and handed them over to him, saying that, once the hostages were retained, the city would necessarily do whatever was commanded. Camillus not only rejected the treachery, but had the schoolmaster’s hands tied behind his back and handed him over to the boys to be beaten with rods back to their parents. He gained by kindness the victory which he had not desired by fraud. For the Falisci voluntarily surrendered because of this justice.

There is also a no less distinguished title of the same Camillus. After cities had been subdued and notable triumphs won, envy stirred up among the soldiers resulted in his condemnation and expulsion from the city, allegedly because common booty had been distributed too unfairly. [Col. 0556A] Then the Senonian Gauls invaded the city, and the Romans were defeated eleven miles away at the river Allia; nothing in the city itself could be preserved except the Capitol, and even this only by giving gold so that the Gauls might depart. Yet Camillus, having compassion even upon his ungrateful country, struck down those same Gauls, took back the gold, and recovered the Roman eagles. Hence, in the sixth book of Virgil, Anchises prophesies among the other descendants of Aeneas:

Camillus bringing back the standards. Thus recalled from exile, he entered the city in triumph for the third time and was called a second Romulus, as though another founder of his country. Julius Hyginus, in the sixth book *On the Life and Deeds of Illustrious Men*, relates the following concerning Fabricius. (For the preceding material is from Plutarch in the *Instruction of Trajan*, and from Julius Frontinus [Col. 0556B] in the book of *Stratagems*.)

The Samnites therefore sent envoys a second time to Gaius Fabricius. Recalling the many great things he had done generously and kindly for the Samnites after peace had been restored, they offered him a large sum of money as a gift and begged him to accept and use it, since it was evident that so great a man lacked many things necessary for subsistence and for the splendour of his household. Nothing, indeed, was luxurious or ready to hand in proportion to the man’s eminence and the dignity of his virtue.

Fabricius, however, ran his open hands from his ears to his eyes, then down to his nostrils, mouth, throat, stomach, and lower parts, and answered the envoys in these words: “So long as I can control and command all these limbs which I have touched, I shall lack absolutely nothing. Keep, therefore, this money [Col. 0556C] for uses necessary to yourselves, and do not press it upon those for whom it is neither necessary nor welcome. The Romans do not care to possess gold; they wish to rule those who possess gold.”

So Hyginus. Frontinus, however, reports that the physician of Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, came to Fabricius, the Roman commander, promising that he would give poison to Pyrrhus if a reward worth his while were fixed for him.
