Fabricius judged that his victory ought not to be won by such a deed, and disclosed the physician to the king. By this act of good faith he brought Pyrrhus to seek friendship with the Romans.

Let Valerius Maximus and Claudius Quadrigarius contend, so far as I am concerned, in this case over the traitor’s name and office. [Col. 0556D] Whether, according to Valerius, he was Timochares, the father of the man who served cups at the king’s banquet, or, according to Quadrigarius, Nicias the physician, matters little to me, provided it is agreed that the Roman consuls subdued Pyrrhus because they had rejected treachery. Quadrigarius reports that the consuls’ letter to Pyrrhus was as follows:

> “The Roman consuls send greetings to King Pyrrhus. Moved by your injuries against us, we are resolutely bent upon waging war against you as enemies; yet we are armed with the example of honour and good faith. We have therefore judged it right to desire your safety, so that there may be one whom we can conquer by arms. Nicias, one of your intimates, came to us, seeking a reward from us if he secretly killed you. We declared that we did not wish this, and that he should expect no advantage for that reason. [Col. 0557A] At the same time, we thought it right to make you aware of it, lest, if anything of this sort happened, nations should think it had been done on our advice; for they shall know that we do not approve of fighting by promises, price, or trickery. Unless you take care, you will fall.”

Why should I mention that, when Pyrrhus offered him half a kingdom if he would accept peace on fair terms, Fabricius treated the offer with contempt? Nor would he consent to receive even half the kingdom in return for promising friendship to the king. When the outstanding man Cineas, who had been sent to Rome, was asked on his return what Rome was like, he replied that he had seen a homeland of kings: almost all there were such men as Pyrrhus alone was in Epirus or in the rest of Greece. Hearing of Fabricius’ firmness, the king said: “This is certainly that Fabricius [Col. 0557B] whom it is harder to turn away from virtue than the sun from its course.”

The Emperor Caesar Augustus Germanicus, in the war in which, after defeating the enemy, he earned the surname Germanicus, when he established forts within the bounds of his army’s encampment, ordered payment to be made for the produce of the lands enclosed by the rampart. Thus, by the reputation of his justice, he bound all men to trust him.

What shall I say of self-restraint and contempt for possessions, since I promised some of Plutarch’s stratagems? Marcus Cato is said to have been content with the same wine as the oarsmen. Attilius Regulus, though he had held the highest offices, was so poor that he supported himself, his wife, and his children from a little farm cultivated by a single bailiff. On hearing of that bailiff’s death, he wrote to the senate asking that a successor be appointed for himself, since the slave’s death had left his affairs destitute and made his own presence necessary.

Gaius Scipio, after successful achievements in Spain, died in the utmost poverty, leaving not even enough money for his daughters’ dowries; because of their poverty the senate publicly provided their dowries. [Col. 0557C] The Athenians did the same for the sons of Aristides, who died in extreme poverty after administering the greatest affairs of state.

Hannibal, accustomed to rise during the night, did not rest before nightfall; only at twilight did he summon his companions to supper, and no more than two couches were used for dining with him. When he served under Hasdrubal as commander, he generally slept on bare ground, covered with a military cloak. Scipio Aemilianus is said to have eaten bread received while walking on a journey with friends. The same is also said of Alexander of Macedon.

Caesar Augustus ate very little and ate ordinary food. He particularly liked rather coarse bread, small fish, soft cheese pressed by hand, and twice-bearing figs, especially green ones. He ate before dinner at whatever time and place his stomach demanded. Hence he himself writes in a certain letter: “Not even a Jew, my Tiberius, observes the Sabbath as carefully as I observed it today: after the first hour of the night, in the bath, I ate two mouthfuls before beginning to be anointed.” [Col. 0557D]

He also very quickly let go of anger once he saw the mind of the offender changed—more quickly, as he himself said, than asparagus is cooked. By this expression he habitually conveyed [Col. 0558A] the speed of a hurried matter. He had, indeed, used this and certain other expressions nobly in conversation, as copies of his letters show. Whenever he believed something would never happen, he said that it would occur “at the Greek Kalends.”

We read that Masinissa, at the age of ninety, used to take food at midday while standing or walking in front of his tent. When, after defeating the Sabines, Gaius Curius had the allotment of land received by veteran soldiers enlarged for him by decree of the senate, he was content with a common soldier’s share, saying that a citizen was bad if what sufficed for the rest did not suffice for him.

The self-restraint of entire armies has often also been remarkable, as in the army which won conspicuous glory under Marcus Scaurus. Scaurus has left on record this instance of military self-restraint: [Col. 0558B] “A fruit-bearing tree enclosed within the boundary-marking of the camp remained unharmed, its fruit untouched, when on the final day the trumpeters sounded and we departed.”

“Under the imperial auspices of Caesar Domitian Augustus, in the German war stirred up in Gaul by Julius Civilis, the very wealthy city of the Lingones, which had revolted to Civilis, feared plundering by the army of Caesar as it approached. When, contrary to expectation, it had lost nothing of its possessions and remained unharmed, it was reduced to obedience and surrendered seventy thousand armed men to me.”

Lucilius Mummius, who after Corinth had been taken adorned not Italy alone but also the province with pictures and statues, turned so little of such great spoils [Col. 0558C] to his own use that the senate publicly provided a dowry for his impoverished daughter.

Constancy, too, though manifest in many stratagems, shines especially in Roman virtue. If the histories of all nations are reviewed, nothing shines more brightly than their magnificence and courage. This is demonstrated by the vast splendour of their empire, greater than which human memory can recall none since the beginning, nor one enlarged in unbroken progress by greater increases. For by the cultivation of justice in peaceful freedom, reverence for the laws, friendships with neighbouring peoples, mature deliberation, and gravity in word and deed, they gained the world’s submission to their dominion.

But since we began with their constancy, let one example from Julius Frontinus’ *Stratagems* stand in place of many. [Col. 0558D] While Hannibal sat before the city walls, the Romans, to display confidence, sent reinforcements through another gate to their armies in Spain. When the owner happened to die, they also put up for sale the land on which Hannibal’s camp stood, and bidding brought it to the price at which it had been sold before the war. While Hannibal besieged them and they themselves besieged Capua, they resolved not to recall their army from there unless Capua had been captured.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why Trajan seems to be preferable to all others

Now, to set a limit to Plutarch’s *Stratagems* in the case of Trajan: he possessed such courage and civic virtue [Col. 0559A] that he spread far and wide the borders of the Roman Empire, which after Augustus had been defended rather than nobly enlarged. Yet he surpassed military glory by moderation: at Rome and throughout the provinces he showed himself equal to all; he regularly visited friends to greet them, whether they were ill or, on feast days, held indiscriminate reciprocal banquets with them; he used their vehicles and clothing without distinction; he enriched all publicly and privately, granted immunities to cities, remitted provincial taxes, was burdensome to none and beloved by all. Thus even down to our own age, emperors are acclaimed in the senate in no other words: “May you be more fortunate than Augustus and better than Trajan!”

His memory was therefore so honoured, and the reputation of his goodness prevailed so greatly, [Col. 0559B] that he offers his friends who praise him—or flatter him—the occasion of a most magnificent example.

Greatness of spirit unconquered and effectiveness in action are rightly praised in Julius Caesar, since his mind and hand sufficed for enterprises almost impossible in themselves. How great he was in armed warfare is testified not only by the Gauls and Britons first subdued by him, but by the whole course of the civil war and the succession of the Caesarian house. In literary study he was so great that he dictated four letters at once. The ancient laws of the Romans show what he was in his mastery of civil law. The Bissextile day alone—his invention—proclaims and extols the strength of his powerful intellect, so constantly exercised in philosophy.

What is more marvellous than all is that he devoted himself simultaneously to love affairs and business, and in every undertaking [Col. 0559C] he was so great that one would believe him occupied with that alone: wholly present at once to each individual and to all. The whole world celebrates Augustus’ praises; and it reveres Titus, the love of the human race, its own delight, in joyful memory. Yet I do not hesitate to prefer Trajan to all these, since he established the majesty of kingship in the cultivation of virtue alone. The ethical writer judges that whoever acts rightly is a king.

Such is the passage in which Claudian, under the name of Theodosius, gives instruction:

> Though you rule widely over the remotest Indians,  
> Though the Mede, the soft Arab, and the Seres adore you,  
> If you are afraid, if you desire what is wrong, if anger leads you,  
> You will bear the yoke of slavery; you will endure unjust  
> Laws within. Then you will rightfully possess all things  
> When you can be king of yourself. The easier course  
> Is granted toward worse things, and licence urges luxury,  
>   
> [Col. 0559D] And favours unbridled desire with its allurements. Then it is harder  
> To live chastely when Venus is ready at hand; then anger  
> Is restrained with greater difficulty when punishment lies open. But check your impulses:  
> Let not what is permitted to you, but what it befits you to have done,  
> Occur to you; let regard for honour discipline your mind.

So that those who think others should be preferred to Trajan may more readily acquiesce in his praise, the most holy Pope Gregory is recorded to have commended his virtues and, by tears shed for him, to have restrained the fires of hell. The Lord rewarded with abundant mercy the justice Trajan had shown to a weeping widow.

For when that emperor, already mounted on his horse and setting out for war, was seized by the foot by a widow, who mourned pitifully and asked that justice be done for her against those who had unjustly killed her most excellent and entirely innocent son, [Col. 0560A] she said: “Augustus, you rule, and I endure so atrocious an injury?”

“I shall satisfy you when I return,” said the emperor.

“But what,” she said, “if you do not return?”

“My successor,” Trajan replied, “will satisfy you.”

“And what benefit will it be to you if another does good? You are my debtor, and you will receive your reward according to your deeds. It is surely fraud to refuse to pay what is owed. Your successor will be liable for himself to those who suffer wrong. Another’s justice will not free you. It will go well for your successor if he frees himself.”

Moved by these words, the emperor dismounted, investigated the case at once, and consoled the widow by due satisfaction. The most blessed Pope Gregory is said to have shed tears for him until it was announced to him in a revelation that Trajan had been delivered from the punishments of hell, on the condition, however, that he should no longer presume to solicit God for any unbeliever. [Col. 0560B] He is therefore deservedly preferred to others: his virtue pleased the saints so greatly above that of the rest that, by their merits, he alone was set free. These things have been said concerning the head of the commonwealth.

## CHAPTER IX. On those who hold the place of the heart in the commonwealth; why the wicked must be excluded from the counsels of rulers; and on the fear of God, wisdom, and philosophy

According to Plutarch, the senate holds the place of the heart. As the ancients determined, “senate” is a name of office [Col. 0560C] and bears the mark of age; for *senatus* is named from old age (*senectus*). The Athenians called it the Areopagus, because the virtue of the whole people resided in its members. Although the Athenians made very many brilliant discoveries, they instituted nothing more beneficial or more glorious than the senate.

For what is nobler than an assembly of old men who, discharged from common offices, pass to the duties of counsel and government and exert the powers of the mind in a decaying body? They are more suited to the business of wisdom precisely because they are less able in bodily exertions. Their honour was so great among the Greeks that leaders of the commonwealth went nowhere and no outstanding action was taken unless the appointed elders introduced or approved it; and, what is more, from the foundation of the city their names were written in golden letters. [Col. 0560D] They themselves were called “enrolled fathers” (*patres conscripti*), because they surpassed others in wisdom, age, and paternal effect. The authority for deliberation and for all public business lay with them.

Yet, although the name seems to derive from bodily age, I judge this age to belong to the mind as well as the body. The age of the mind is wisdom, in which lie the ordering of every duty and the art of the whole of life. For the art of living rightly, as the Stoics maintain, is the art of arts. To suppose that there is no art of the greatest matters, when no one is ignorant that even the least matters possess their art, is the opinion of men who speak with too little consideration, err in the greatest matters, and decide everything according to whim [Col. 0561A] rather than truth.

Wisdom, according to the ancient philosophers, is the mistress of divine and human things and the knowledge of what must be done and what must be left undone. To pursue it is to philosophize, because philosophy is the study of wisdom. Thus, as the ancients held, philosophy knocks at wisdom’s door; when it is opened, the soul, sweetly illuminated by the light of things, loses the name “philosophy.” Or, as more penetrating minds have thought, the appetite of the will is fulfilled when the flower of study turns into fruit. For wisdom is philosophy’s end.

Yet somehow we are now occupied with its end when we have not yet recognized its beginning, though that beginning is considered the most powerful part in all things. Nevertheless, one who knows the end cannot be ignorant of the beginning, since the root of the beginning, by the many paths of virtue, passes in the firmness of its life all the way to the crown of the end and the sweetness of its fruit.

“Behold,” says blessed Job, “the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28). [Col. 0561B] I find no other root of wisdom, since all agree that “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 105). Fear, therefore, is the beginning; progress is in fear; and the summit of all virtues—whether one calls it charity or wisdom—is not wholly separate from fear. Distinguish filial fear from servile fear: in the latter place the beginning, in the former the progress of wisdom and, from this, perfection.

Whatever verbal extravagance may assert, it is true that wisdom begins in fear and that “the holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever.” [Col. 0561C] The root therefore remains; strengthened by the increases of grace, it grows into the branches of virtues, and its power reaches to the fruit of perfect charity. Charity knows none of the stings of punishment, since there is no fear in charity that has punishment; and it is a sign of fear that a person continually performs good works and holds fast to justice.

Fear, then, seems to give place as grace advances into virtue. The man who is prompted by filial affection toward reverence and good works no longer fears servilely. “Always,” says blessed Job, “I feared God over me as swelling waves, and I could not bear his weight” (Job 31). [Col. 0561D] He plainly says not that he feared at some particular time but always; and you do not doubt that he was perfect, since by the Lord’s own testimony no man like him existed on earth. Nor is it credible that he abstained from evil through fear of punishment, apart from charity, when you do not doubt that he had been perfected in the fullness of justice.

Our discourse has now advanced in praise of fear, and still it has not made known what fear is. Would that it might abide in the heart, when its name turns so often on the tongue. If it touches the mind, the tongue will reason more effectively and more profitably for itself. For words roll vainly in the mouth if works of virtue are lacking.

The fear of God, as the most blessed Pope Gregory declares, is to omit none of the things that must be done. What is omitted is what is fulfilled neither in deed nor in will. For whatever you will but cannot do, God reckons as done, because a full will receives the reward of the entire deed. [Col. 0562A] It is certain, however, that one who fears God neglects nothing and does good. Whoever carefully investigates everything and, after learning what must be done, carries it out, is without doubt wise and most fit for the counsels of princes [or ought not to be excluded from prelacy, if distinguished by gravity of character].

Where such gravity of character is known, anyone pleads bodily age in vain. This is the old man whom the counsels of wisdom teach should be chosen before others for deliberations. For it says: “Venerable old age is not long-lived, nor measured by a number of years” (Wisdom 4). “Grey hair is the glory of old men” (Proverbs 20). “The senses of a man are grey hairs, and an unstained life is the age of old age” (Wisdom 4). Truly blessed is he who attains this age, so that he rejoices in the witness of his conscience to the innocence [Col. 0562B] of his life.

But perhaps you say: “Who is this man, that we may praise him?” (Ecclesiasticus 31 [printed: 30]). Certainly I do not think that, when counsel must be given, one ought to wait for a man who has committed no sin; rather, for one who takes no pleasure in sinning, hates sin, rejoices in virtue, and desires it with great longing—in other words, a man of good will.

Yet even this ought not to be trimmed to the quick; rather, as the saying is, it should be taken with a more kindly Minerva: that is, one should be considered innocent not simply, but by comparison with others. For who will boast that his heart is entirely pure, when even the stars are not clean in the sight of him who found perversity in his angels?

Therefore the wicked must be excluded: the proud, the avaricious, and every such plague of mankind. Nothing is more ruinous [Col. 0562C] than an unjust counsellor of a rich man. “Keep your heart with every guard,” it says, “for from it proceeds life” (Proverbs 4). A ruler must therefore take care that his counsellors lack nothing and do not desire others’ possessions too excessively.

This extends even to those who, in the body of the commonwealth, perform the role of its internal organs: the quaestors, record-keepers, and counts of the private estate, as we said before. All these must be maintained to sufficiency; and this must be understood according to necessity and use, with regard to the persons concerned. For if they are replenished too greedily and digest too little, they produce diseases either incurable or difficult to cure.

Indeed, it is impossible for anyone to pursue both justice and money. Each person will either cleave to one and despise the other, or be tormented by the other while deprived of the better. For, as Wisdom testifies, nothing is more wicked than the miser, and nothing more unjust than to love money. Such a person holds his own soul for sale and, while alive, has cast away his inmost parts. [Col. 0562D] Perhaps for this reason Nature, the most diligent mother, set about the intestines the grating of the breast, the firmness of the ribs, and the enclosure of the outer skin: that they might be safer against every outward violence, that what is necessary might be supplied to them, and that they might never be exposed outwardly without danger to their health. This image of Nature’s handiwork must be preserved in the commonwealth, and its necessary members must be supplied abundantly from public resources.

## CHAPTER X. On the sides of rulers, whose necessities must be supplied and whose wickedness must be restrained; [Note: The bracketed passage [Col. 0563D] is omitted in the Paris edition.] and on advocates, whose harmful tongue, unless it is bound with silver cords; on receivers of gifts; and on how a gift is judged by the hand, the cause, the time, the place, or the manner

[Col. 0563A]

The same pattern of nature must also be observed in the sides—that is, in those who ought to stand beside princes. It is certain that character is formed by companionship. “He who touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclesiasticus 13),

> And one grape, when touched by another, takes on its dark hue.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 2.81)

Do not believe that justice, truth, or piety exists in the household of men among whom you see that everything is for sale. Christ himself is shut out; and if he knocks at [Col. 0563B] the door, it is not opened to him. They flee from grace and drive it away, who put a price on everything and do nothing free of charge.

If a petition must be presented, a case examined, a judgment carried into execution, or a legal instrument drawn up, money accomplishes everything. Truth is blind and piety crippled, while:

> As much money as each man keeps in his own chest,  
> So much faith does he possess.  
>   
> The poor man is believed to despise  
> Thunderbolts and the gods—even with the gods’ own forgiveness.

Among such people, the more corrupt a man is in morals and the more corruptible by gifts, the happier he is thought. If you escape the hands of princes, a great road still remains before you—narrow and steep. Before you escape the final torturers, you must sweat. See: Cossus draws up your document. If you are allowed to greet him, count it a great favour. If you have not brought a written request, you approach in vain. But if you have brought one, it is useless, and he will not consent that his noble hand should be degraded by the fault of the parchment.

Why say more? You must buy his own parchment, since neither his labour, nor his pen, nor a little cuttlefish, nor the black juice of the squid, comes to you without purchase. [Col. 0563C] Unless you make him favourable to you, he will distort the very syllables and letters and set so many verbal traps for you that the instrument of a friend will seem to inscribe war instead of peace and litigation instead of tranquillity. If by chance your belt is rather handsome, your knife rather suitable, or anything in your small personal equipment rather attractive, count it among his possessions, unless you wish your labour and expense to be lost. Either it will be wrung out by entreaties, or you will anticipate them with generosity. At last, whatever sort of cap it may be, your friend will carry it away as a remembrance of you.

You leave Cossus now, but purgatorial fire threatens you: Veiento remains. You will assail him with much importunity, much skilful demeanour, many prayers and gifts, if you want him to look upon you without pursed lips. Then every single word is referred for consultation; time is set aside for deliberation; every letter is placed in the balance. Unless you coax him, you will encounter either a record not faithfully drafted from the transaction, or an uncultivated style will harm you, or the favour—or negligence—of a notary or archivist departing from the public form of record, or neglect of the law; and some knot will always require money as its avenger. Even if it does the least possible harm, you will be tortured by long waiting [Col. 0564A] while what cannot be refused is postponed.

Trust one who has experienced it: I have fallen into their hands a thousand times. And, to borrow something from fables, the harsh ferryman Charon, who never spared anyone, is far more merciful than these men. For he is accustomed to be content with a small coin, even a third of one; but these men demand whole asses multiplied for themselves. But why do I complain that everything among courtiers is for sale, when even things that do not exist—namely, privations of things—are plainly subject to sale? No service and no speech is free; they do not even remain silent except for payment. Silence, indeed, is a saleable thing.

Perhaps they learned this from Demosthenes. When he asked Aristodemus, an actor in dramatic performances, how much payment he had received to perform, and was told, “a talent,” Demosthenes said: “But I received more to [Col. 0564B] remain silent.” Advocates have a harmful tongue unless, as the saying goes, you bind it with silver cords. It is not enough to ensnare one man with gifts, unless perhaps he is extremely powerful, because in gaining the favour of one you arouse the envy of the others. They think what is bestowed on others has been taken from them. This attitude passes from the greatest to the least; unless they are soothed by services and refreshed by gifts, they suspect that an injury has been done them.

> Every great household is full of proud slaves  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 5.66),

and it is equally full of greedy and avaricious men. Yet the most ruinous among all the triflers of court are those who, under a pretence of honour and generosity, habitually colour the follies of their own wretchedness: those who walk more smartly, dine more splendidly, more often force strangers to come to their table, are more civil at home, more gracious abroad, more approachable in conversation, freer in their opinions, lavish in their attention to neighbours, and conspicuous in imitation of every virtue.

For, as the ethical writer says: “No injustice is more capital than that of those who, when they most deceive, act so as to appear good men.” [Col. 0564C] Such men are given licence even by the shadow of virtue, and win glory where pardon could scarcely have been hoped for. They can extort very much without penalty, since they cannot—or rather do not deign to—be content with little. It is well known, indeed, and proverbial, that:

> He who cannot use a little will be a slave for ever.

Yet do not suppose that I wage irreconcilable war against them: let courtiers freely accept gifts, so long as they do not shamelessly extort them. Shame is cast aside as soon as exactions begin. “Please,” it is said, is a modest word, to be spoken in a suppliant and subdued voice; and the man who received while asking did not receive for free. For he who asks buys twice: he has sold his modesty for the price of the thing—or of the hope—he seeks.

But a gift bears no mark of just reproach when devotion to generosity offers it and the shamelessness of the petitioner has not extorted it—provided, however, that one does not accept the gifts of the wicked. It belongs to an ungrateful person not to foster a benefit with good wishes, and it is impious, as the Lord says, to justify the wicked for gifts. [Col. 0565A] Certainly, to accept a benefit is to sell one’s freedom, and it is shameful that those who ought to rule others should be slaves.

Nonetheless, the nature of the case and the person must also be considered, so that what is accepted is neither from a base person nor accepted basely. This must be investigated more fully according to place, time, and manner. For gifts often shine or become sordid because of the hand from which they come, often because of the cause, sometimes because of time, sometimes because of place or manner. Yet the shamelessness of courtiers has become so notorious that no one can confidently rely, unless payment intervenes, upon the testimony of conscience, the grace of character, the fragrance of reputation, the sincerity of his case, or the torrent of his eloquence.

> Though you yourself come attended by the Muses, Homer,  
> If you bring nothing, Homer, you will go outside.  
> [Col. 0565B]

Orpheus is said not only to have tamed lions and tigers by the benefit of eloquence: even before Dis himself his sweeter voice pleaded, and his more favourable case entreated the three-headed dog, so that Eurydice, once admitted, might be permitted to leave contrary to the law of the underworld. But even if you are Orpheus, Arion, or the man who, as they say, softened stones by the sound of the lyre alone, you will accomplish nothing among courtiers unless you soften their leaden hearts with a golden or silver hammer upon the anvil of vanity or greed.

All shudder at Cerberus’ cruelty. I believe I have seen gatekeepers harder than Cerberus. Yet in the underworld Cerberus is only one; as many as are the byways of courtiers, so many Cerberuses there are. You will endure Cerberus-like hall-porters as well, and the whole household, which always either bites or barks. Every one of them has listened to the same physician, saying: “Take it while it hurts”—ready, if they believe it benefits them, even to make healthy things hurt.

Yet you will marvel at their great piety in one respect: they willingly listen to complaints, foster the causes of the lowly, and patronize the afflicted so far as to empty the purses of those who are more fully supplied. [Col. 0565C] For however a case proceeds, the same aim is always pursued: that purses be filled, though greed cannot be satisfied. Whoever falls into these men’s hands, if he is found repentant, may, I think, find these torments sufficient for forgiveness. Nothing is so grievous that it cannot be expiated here.

For what is more miserable than to sit beside proud thresholds, endure the arrogance of those passing by, be trodden down by the contempt of contemptible people, bear the vexations of those who have been thrown out, and suffer every indignity from the unworthy? When Alcibiades asked Socrates why he did not drive from his home his wife Xanthippe—excessively difficult and quarrelsome, and a woman who for a long time, day and night, overflowed with womanish vexations—he said: “By enduring such a woman at home, I become accustomed and trained to bear more easily the insolence and injury of others outside.”

An old proverb is celebrated: “An empty hand makes a rash petition, and certainly the petitioner who trusts that goods will be given in response to words is importunate.” In both places, that is, among courtiers and physicians, the following rule holds:

> In return for words alone, we use mountain herbs;  
> In return for costly things, perfumes and spices.  
> [Col. 0566A]

Among the rest, however, the kinder ones are those who have least power, although nearly all are inclined to harm, since this is far easier for anyone than to help. Let them then conduct their commerce, drain others’ purses, stuff their own, possess as much as Pacuvius, make gold equal to mountains, love no one and be loved by no one; let them be objects of admiration to strangers while they are hated or despised by their own households.

You will find something of this sort in writings concerning the ancient Romans. When Publius Gnaeus Graecinus—or, if he is more correctly called by another name—was criticized by friends for repudiating a beautiful, chaste, noble wife, he replied: “This shoe which you see is new, elegant, and pleasing to all who look at it; but no one except myself knows where it pinches me.”

We read in the Book of Numbers that, when Israel committed fornication with the Midianites and provoked the Lord’s indignation, Phinehas drew his sword and transfixed Zimri, son of Salu, together with the Midianite concubine; and with the destruction of the guilty, God’s anger ceased. [Col. 0566B] Then the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them upon gibbets before the sun” (Numbers 25).

The people had indeed sinned, and the fornication of the leaders is not expressly stated; yet the leaders are commanded to be seized for the gallows, and in their punishment rest is restored to the offending people. For the transgression of subjects very often arises from the negligence of those who govern. It therefore concerns the ruler to restrain these men’s wickedness and provide for them from public resources, so that every opportunity for predation may be removed. This too was anciently provided for in Roman law; otherwise, one who neglects his duty and refuses to correct wrongdoing will seem the author of the crime.

The more distinguished and powerful the court, the fuller and more ruinous it is with these scourges of humanity and terrors of the innocent. [Col. 0566C] For it often happens that a court either receives vicious men or makes them so; among them boldness in wrongdoing grows strong, since vices are indulged through intimacy with the powerful. It is also vain to form presumptions from anyone’s former life, since innocence can scarcely be preserved among courtiers. Who is there whose virtue is not shaken by courtiers’ follies? Who is so great, who so steadfast, that he cannot be corrupted? The best man is he who resists longer, more vigorously, and is corrupted less.

For virtue is to remain unharmed only if one turns aside from the life of courtiers. Take note: whoever said this expressed the nature of the court wisely:

> Let him leave the court,
Whoever wishes to be devout. (Lucan, VIII.394.) Hence the spring of Salmacis, notorious for its shameful softness, is aptly compared to it. For, as the fables tell, its water is beautiful in appearance, sweet in taste, pleasant to the touch, and most agreeable in the use of every sense; yet it so enfeebles those who enter it by its softness that it deprives emasculated men of the nobler sex. Nor does anyone emerge before he is astonished and grieves that he has been changed into a woman. Either the sex wholly yields and degenerates into the inferior one, or, with some trace of its former dignity remaining, it assumes the form of a hermaphrodite, who, by a certain mockery of a corrupted nature, so displays the image of both sexes that he retains the reality of neither.

By this poetic cloud of fiction is represented the image of the frivolities of the court, which soften men by stripping them of virtue, or pervert them while retaining virtue’s outward appearance. He who assumes courtly absurdities while professing the office of a philosopher or a good man is a Hermaphrodite: with a rough and shaggy face he disfigures feminine beauty, and pollutes and defiles the man with feminine things. For a courtly philosopher is indeed a monstrous thing; and while he desires to be both, he is neither, because the court excludes philosophy, and the philosopher in no way accepts courtly frivolities.

The comparison, however, does not extend to every court, but only to that which is disordered by the will of a fool. For he who is wise drives away trifles, orders his household, and subjects all things in it to reason. For, as Wisdom says: “What fellowship has a holy man with a dog, or light with darkness? Every animal loves its like, and every person his neighbour. All flesh associates with its like, and every person will associate with one like himself. If a wolf has ever had fellowship with a lamb, so has a sinner with a righteous man” (Ecclus. XIII).

## Chapter XI. On the eyes, ears, and tongue of authorities; on the office of a governor; on the fact that a judge ought to possess knowledge of law and equity, the will to do good, and power to execute it; and on the fact that he must be bound by oath to the laws and free from the filth of gifts

[Col. 0567C] There follows the comparison of eyes, ears, and tongue, which, it was said above, resides in provincial governors. A governor, then, is one who presides over provincials in the administration of justice. He ought to possess knowledge and capacity concerning what is equitable and inequitable, together with the disposition to carry out what is just. For just as a physician ought not to be blamed for an outcome of death, so, if any grievous event occurs through his incompetence, it is rightly imputed to him. But if he knows and does not will it, he is condemned not for ignorance but for malice. The end for both is condemnation, although the ignorant are punished more mildly—unless, perhaps, negligence has brought about their ignorance. For if ignorance is invincible, it does not bring death, but is excused by the inborn darkness.

[Col. 0567D] But if he knows and wishes to serve equity, yet cannot, the fault lies not so much with the governor as with the prince. Yet it is most certain that these same things belong to a judge’s religious duty, since he ought himself to have knowledge of the law, the will to do good, and the strength to carry it out; and he must be bound by oath to the laws, so that he knows it to be altogether unlawful for him to depart from their integrity.

For Wisdom teaches concerning his wisdom: “A wise judge shall judge his people, and the rule of a discerning man shall be stable. As is the judge of a people, so also are his ministers; and such as the ruler of a city is, such are those who dwell in it” (Ecclus. X). Nor does it pass over the necessity of strength, saying: “Do not seek to become a judge unless you have the strength to break through iniquities by force, lest perhaps you fear [Col. 0568A] the face of a powerful man and place a stumbling-block in your uprightness. Do not sin in a multitude of a city, and do not thrust yourself among the people; do not bind upon yourself double sins, for not even in one will you be immune. Do not be faint-hearted in your soul; do not despise praying and giving alms. Do not say: ‘God will regard the multitude of my gifts, and when I offer my gifts to God Most High, he will receive them.’ Do not mock a man in the bitterness of his soul; for God, who humbles and exalts, is watchful” (Ecclus. VII).

[Col. 0568B] From these passages the attentive reader will perceive that the will to do good is no less necessary to a judge than knowledge or power, since he is liable not only for his own offences but for those of others, and is burdened by the double weight of his own sins and those of others. Thus, even amid a multitude of gifts, he can have no confidence before God without purity of will.

Accordingly Plato excellently and eloquently—if only he is heard—asserts that those who contend for office in administering the commonwealth behave toward one another as sailors might contend in an adverse storm over which of them ought chiefly to steer. In this reckoning of fortune, either no one, or only a rare person—and he a reckless one—claims office without skill and strength. And certainly in my own time I have seen nothing more miserable than judges ignorant of legal knowledge, devoid of good will, convicted by their love of gifts and rewards, and employing whatever strength they possess in the service of greed, vanity, or flesh and blood, while released from the obligation of a lawful oath. From this it is plain [Col. 0568C] that the princes who granted them ordinary jurisdiction are either ignorant of the law or contemptuous of it.

But whatever we may say about knowledge of law or power to execute it, a judge must be most religious and must hate every iniquity more than death itself. Since governors possess ordinary jurisdiction, or the power of declaring the law, the same consideration applies to them and to other judges; and what is said of these is easily extended by consequence to the others.

This, then, is first imposed upon both by the necessity of their office: that justice must be obeyed in all things, and that none of the things which ought to be done should be done for a price. For what is unjust is never lawful, not even for the sake of temporal life. What is just, however, needs no intervention of reward, since it ought to be done for its own sake, and it is unjust to sell what is owed. To sell justice, therefore, is iniquity; to sell injustice is iniquitous madness. The latter is so condemned everywhere that it ought nowhere to exist; the former is owed everywhere, and therefore cannot be sold without crime.

[Col. 0568D] Balaam, indeed, is not blamed because he condemned the cause of God’s people or said anything other than what the Lord inspired; rather, blinded by greed, he devised, at malice’s prompting, how the cause of unbelievers might lead Israel into sin so as to provoke God’s wrath. He sought, then, how he might justly justify the cause of the ungodly and, as though deceiving God, withdraw His favour from the elect. Or, if the adverse cause could not be justified, he at least worked to make God depart from this people also. For when the wicked contend, the one who is stronger in resources is accustomed, as they say, to prevail.

[Col. 0569A] You may see many Balaamites who, although unwilling to pronounce an unjust sentence, are nevertheless corrupted by gifts and strive by every artifice to transfer the justice of one party to the other. I would not readily say which is more wicked, although the seller of equity colours his malice with a more deceptive disguise. Yet he may seem more wicked who hawks in the marketplace, as merchandise, the prince and queen of his office—justice, to whom fidelity owes service—as though an unfaithful slave were selling his master. For every magistrate is justice’s servant.

It is evident that equity is alienated from the seller, even if it does not pass to the buyer; and purchased iniquity passes to the buyer in such a way that it by no means departs from the seller. And, unlike what occurs in other contracts, he alone sells justice who does not possess it. For before the transaction it leaves its seller defiled. Is not he defiled who pollutes his conscience by accepted or offered filth, and has for sale not so much justice as his own soul?

[Col. 0569B] The Doctor of the Gentiles despises riches, honours, and the varied furnishings of the whole world as dung, in order that he may gain Christ alone, judging that everything which brings loss to salvation must be numbered among filth. This is right and faithful, because nothing clean, honourable, or fitting obstructs salvation, but only baseness, which, as it is disgraceful, so is it unclean and certainly useless—indeed, so harmful that no temporal advantage can compensate for it. “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss of his soul?” (Luke IX).

[Col. 0569C] Observe that he did not say that the world is useless only where salvation is lost, but also where glory is diminished. However brightly jewels gleam, gold shines, and the world smiles with all its allurements, whatever destroys a person’s purity is filthy; whatever extinguishes the beauty of the soul is base; whatever overturns honour is shameful.

Accordingly, among the ancients also, though ignorant of saving truth, everything which by the duty of office ought to be gratuitous, if done for a price, was counted among filthy gains. They likewise extend the meaning of “price” so that it includes not only money or a thing of value, but service and every labour not otherwise owed. For what comes from filth can be nothing but filthy. “A bad tree cannot bear good fruit,” since the power of nature consists in producing like from like.

Since, moreover, we have stated that governors and other judges are subject to a common scrutiny, they are servants of equity and public tranquillity. Therefore they ought to be more circumspect, cautious, and diligent in proportion as they are reserved for the judgment of Him whose wisdom cannot be deceived and whose justice cannot be corrupted. He has ordained that they shall be judged by the judgment with which they judged, and shall receive from the just Judge into their own bosoms “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.”

## Chapter XII. On the oath of judges; the comparison of Pythagoras and Alexander; the matters in which a judge may grant favour to parties; and captious questions

[Col. 0570A] Judges, indeed, are bound by oath to the laws, because they are sworn in every respect to order judgment in accordance with truth and observance of the laws. The law itself has also provided that the awe-inspiring writings of the holy Gospels be placed before the judicial seat, and remain there from the beginning of litigation to its end, not being removed until the judgment has been pronounced. Thus, the entire breadth of the court being filled by God’s own presence, all may be inspired with fear and reverence for the most holy Scriptures, and every iniquity may be driven away from the investigation of truth.

[Col. 0570B] Judicial religion also drives away every affection of flesh and blood, extinguishing anger and hatred, fear and friendship; because, as Julius Caesar says, the mind does not readily discern truth where such things prevail. Hence comes the proverb, most celebrated among the ancients, with Cicero as its author: “Whoever puts on the person of a friend puts off the person of a judge.” For equity, to which the judge owes obedience, recognizes neither the left hand of hatred nor the right hand of love. In judicial matters one may not depart from truth.

Yet, in order that friendship may be granted as much indulgence as possible, a judge sometimes grants a friend the favour of a postponement—though this very thing should be rare, and only after the cause has been examined. Moreover, while a case remains uncertain, postponement should be extended, if not of the dispute itself, at least of its decision. For hasty judgments breed repentance.

[Col. 0570C] Hence the Greeks, when pressed to pronounce judgment before the case is clear, reply that their fathers did not see the sun among the antipodes, but always waited until it rose for them also. For they say that a traveller is rash who, before the morning star rises, while thick darkness still prevails and light is absent, undertakes a journey.

Nor should a judge be intimidated by the authority of the powerful, since Pythagoras’s petition was postponed for a very long time, while Alexander of Macedon’s cause was condemned in a military court. Alexander accepted this, thanking the judges because he had proved their integrity in that they preferred justice to every power. In my judgment, I find nothing more illustrious in any history concerning that Alexander whom public opinion calls “the Great.”

[Col. 0570D] For my own part—though I say it with the permission of those who prefer recklessness to virtue—poor Pythagoras will always be greater to me than wealthy Alexander. That you may judge this with me, let us review the comparison of Philip and Alexander, with Trogus Pompeius, or, if you prefer, his abridger Justin, as authority. He says:

> “Philip was a king more devoted to arms than to banquets. His immense resources were instruments of war; he was more diligent in acquiring wealth than in guarding it. Thus, amid daily plundering, he was always poor. Mercy and treachery were loved by him with equal favour. With him no method of victory was shameful; in speech he was alike flattering and deceitful, promising more than he performed. He was skilful in serious matters and in jokes; he cultivated friendships for usefulness, not faithfulness. To feign favour toward those he hated, to sow hatreds among those who were united, and to seek favour from both sides, was his habitual practice. Amid these traits he possessed eloquence and distinguished speech, full of sharpness and skill, so that neither grace lacked ornament nor ornament the grace of invention.

> “His son Alexander succeeded him, greater than his father both in virtues and in vices. Their methods of victory, therefore, differed. Alexander waged open wars; Philip by stratagems. Philip rejoiced in enemies deceived; Alexander in enemies openly routed. Philip was more prudent in counsel; Alexander more magnificent in spirit. The father concealed anger, and often even conquered it; the son, once inflamed, allowed neither delay nor limit to vengeance. Both were excessively fond of wine, but the vices of their drunkenness differed. Philip’s custom was even to rush from a banquet against the enemy and rashly expose himself to dangers. Alexander raged not against enemies but against his own people.

[Col. 0571B] “Therefore battles often spared Philip when wounded; Alexander frequently left a banquet after killing his friends. Philip wished to rule with his friends; Alexander exercised kingship over his friends. The father preferred to be loved; the son, feared. Their cultivation of letters was alike. Philip surpassed in shrewdness; Alexander in fidelity. Philip was more moderate in words and speech; Alexander in deeds. The son was readier and more honourable in sparing the conquered. The father was more given to frugality, the son to luxury. By these qualities the father laid the foundations of world empire; the son completed the glory of so great an undertaking.

[Col. 0571C] “But in one respect Alexander surpassed the vices not only of his father but of all men of noble birth: he was possessed by the most unrestrained envy, so that even his father’s triumphs drew tears from him, as though his father’s virtue had snatched away from him the glory of every deed he was to perform. Those who proclaimed praises of his father’s virtue he either killed with his own hands or ordered to be carried off for punishment.”

Pythagoras, however, possessed such authority among philosophers that, for the decision of every question, it was enough if Pythagoras was believed to have taken one side. So great was the force of preconceived opinion that nothing could prevail against it when it was said that he himself had said it; and, by the customary usage of those who assented, the bare pronoun itself indicated Pythagoras. For when one simply said, “He himself said it,” Pythagoras was necessarily understood from his established authority, as Cicero testifies.

Yet he did not bend the judgment by the whole weight of his authority. Rather, while the postponement remained in force, the sentence was still suspended because of the case’s ambiguity.

[Col. 0571D] The subject was this. Euathlus, a wealthy young man, wished to learn eloquence and to plead cases. He placed himself under Pythagoras’s instruction, promising the sum Pythagoras had demanded: half paid before he began, and the other half to be paid on the first day when he had pleaded a case before judges and won. Afterwards, when he had long been Pythagoras’s pupil and follower, had developed eloquence through study, and, after a considerable passage of time, refused to undertake advocacy in cases—supposedly in order not to fulfil his teacher’s fee—Pythagoras, after deliberation, brought suit against him.

When they came before the judges to initiate and frame the case, Pythagoras began thus: “Learn, most foolish young man, that in either event you will pay what I demand, whether judgment is pronounced for you or against you. For if the suit is decided against you, the fee will be owed me under the judgment, because I shall have prevailed; but if judgment is given in your favour, the fee will be owed me under the agreement, because you will have prevailed.”

[Col. 0572A] Euathlus calmly replied: “I wish that someone had met this two-sided trap of yours, if I were not speaking for myself and using another advocate. But this victory is rather a preliminary exercise, since I shall defeat you not only in the case but also in this argument. Learn, therefore, most wise teacher, that in either event I shall not pay what you demand, whether judgment is pronounced against me or for me. For if the judges decide in favour of my cause, you will be owed nothing under the judgment, because I shall have prevailed; if judgment is pronounced against me, I owe you nothing under the agreement, because I shall not have prevailed.”

[Col. 0572B] Thus the famous master of eloquence was refuted in his own argument by his youthful pupil, and his cunning, devised trap was frustrated. Then the judges, to use the words of the ancient history, thought what was argued on both sides doubtful and inexplicable; and, lest their judgment, pronounced for either side, should itself undo itself, they left the case undecided, postponing it to a very distant day.

It matters little for the present purpose whether Pythagoras or Protagoras, as Quintilian and Aulus Gellius prefer, was the litigant. For the name has no force, provided it is established that the ambiguous matter cannot be decided without rashness.

[Col. 0572C] There are many captious questions which it is safer and more expedient, especially in judicial proceedings, to defer than to hurry. Hence among dialecticians this kind is called *Tractus* (“a dragging-on”), and by the Greeks **Ζήτησις** (*zētēsis*, “inquiry”), where whatever you determine to be true is found to be false. And although in such cases the matter can often be moderated through the defence of fraud, and equity itself can sometimes mitigate the rigour of law, nevertheless, unless the most urgent necessity of circumstances compels otherwise, it is expedient in such cases to defer a judgment rather than pronounce one.

You learned almost as a child that questions containing implicit propositions and secretly enclosing contradictions are laborious to resolve—unless perhaps you consider yourself wiser than the ancient Nestor. “Do not trust the dream,” Agamemnon was told in a dream, while Greece was suffering in the destruction of Troy. The wisest Greeks also judged that the interpretation of this dream should be reserved for Jupiter.

[Col. 0572D] I have seen very many people labouring over the question whether one who says, “I am lying,” speaks truly. But I have seen no one avoid Scylla and Charybdis unless he encountered an enemy who was weak or favourable. In contentious disputations and school declamations, however, such matters are handled without this danger. But when one comes to the forum, where empty display of intellect ceases and only serious matters are treated, no error is made in casting judgment without danger to the litigants or the judge.

In my opinion nothing is more useful than postponing danger, if it cannot altogether be avoided. Yet it is most unjust for disputes to be prolonged when the interest of one of the litigants is endangered and the difficulty of the matter does not require delay. Whatever, therefore, can be settled should be expedited; what needs more careful treatment should be deferred.

## Chapter XIII. How a judicial proceeding ought to be arranged; the formulation of the oath against vexatious litigation, which plaintiff and defendant must necessarily take; the consequences for one who refuses to take the oath; the oath of advocates; and the punishment of malicious accusers, colluders, and deserters of an accusation

That the truth of matters may appear more quickly, the judge shall not admit the litigants themselves—that is, the principal parties—to trial until, after taking an oath, they give assurance that they will pursue justice and keep every form of vexatious litigation far away.

[Col. 0573B] The plaintiff shall swear that he has not brought the suit with an intent to harass, but because he believes that he has a good cause; and that throughout the whole litigation he will do nothing vexatiously, so that he will demand neither proof nor delay merely to frustrate, but only what justice appears to require. The defendant, however, shall swear that, believing himself to have a good defence, he has come to resist; and that in no part of the whole litigation will he act vexatiously, demanding from the judge or adversary only what he believes truth and the necessity of justice require to be supplied.

The concluding clause of the oath of each shall include this: they shall swear that they have given nothing, promised nothing, and will give nothing—either personally or through an intermediary—to judges or to any other persons on account of that case, except what by legal indulgence may be provided to advocates and certain other specified persons.

[Col. 0573C] If the plaintiff refuses to swear in this manner, he is excluded from the suit and loses his action as a dishonest litigant. But a defendant who refuses to undergo the oath is held to have confessed and awaits a condemnatory judgment.

The advocates themselves, too, that the examination may be more trustworthy, are bound from the very joining of issue by an oath to truth and fidelity. They swear that, with all their ability and every resource, they will endeavour to present to their clients whatever they determine to be just and true, leaving no effort unexhausted insofar as it is possible for each; and that they will not deliberately prolong lawsuits. Judges ought to bring such suits to an end within two or three years.

The judge shall also assign advocates to the parties in equal distribution, whether they have requested them or not, so that the case may proceed on equal terms.

[Col. 0573D] This equality consists in merit of ability, vigour of intellect, depth of counsel, reputation for learning, and authority of name, so that, if possible, all these may be weighed for the parties in a kind of balance of equity. If one advocate’s reputation is more distinguished than the others’, the judge, so far as he can, shall compensate the opposing party in the exercise of his office.

Yet one who knows the secrets of either litigant shall not act for the adversary, unless, apart from any arrangement before the judge, he has separately undertaken matters with several others in such a way that the opportunity for an equal defence is not withdrawn from the other party. Nor may anyone, once warned by the judge, refuse advocacy to either party without a probable excuse, unless he wishes the forum to be closed to him, so that afterwards he is not heard in conducting cases.

[Col. 0574A] If an advocate acts collusively, a most severe penalty must be imposed upon the convicted man in accordance with the nature of his offence. The duty of advocacy must be discharged with the utmost fidelity and without injury to opponents. One must contend by arguments, not insults; and, by an imperial edict, anyone suffers a loss of reputation who, abandoning the matter in dispute, proceeds openly or covertly in insolent abuse of his adversary.

Although an advocate may be owed a fee by way of honorarium, he may not be an arranger or purchaser of lawsuits, bargaining for a fixed share of the proceeds to the grave injury of the litigant and under a kind of agreement (*deprecatio*). Whatever an advocate alleges in the presence of his client must be treated as if it had been put forward by the client himself, unless the client contradicts it immediately—that is, within the next three days.

[Col. 0574B] Although an advocate happens to lose, his reputation is not injured in any respect if he omitted nothing that was possible and faithfully supported his client’s just cause. For he is not compelled to advocate a falsehood. If the case brings any harm, it falls upon the litigants, whether the proceeding has been civil or criminal. Whatever that harm may be, it is declared by the final judgment, which condemns or acquits defendants and sometimes most wisely directs sharp penalties against the accusers themselves.

For, to say nothing of civil cases, though the same things may be found in them, the recklessness of accusers is disclosed in three ways and subjected to three penalties. They either bring malicious accusations, collude, or abandon the accusation. To bring a malicious accusation is to allege false crimes; to collude is to conceal true ones; but to desist altogether from an accusation is to abandon it.

[Col. 0574C] Under the Lex Remmia, similarity of punishment calls malicious accusers to retribution, provided that, after the defendant has been acquitted and the accuser’s counsel and intention have been established, the accuser is acquitted if he erred through justifiable mistake. But if he is caught in manifest calumny, he is condemned to the statutory penalty. This is made clear by the very wording of the pronouncement. If it is pronounced, “You have not proved it,” the plaintiff is spared; but if, “You have acted maliciously,” he is condemned. Even if the judgment adds nothing concerning the penalty of infamy, the force of the law will nevertheless be exercised against him, so that he incurs infamy.

## Chapter XIV. On the assessment of evidentiary instruments

[Col. 0574D] In the very examination of a case, both in civil and criminal causes, due account must be taken of evidentiary instruments in assessing proofs. All means by which a case may be supported are called instruments, whether they are testimonies or witnesses; nevertheless, the latter are superior to the former, because witnesses are preferred to written testimonies. Witnesses can be examined, whereas testimonies are always the same and the same for everyone.

In examining witnesses themselves, no rule can determine what the judge ought chiefly to follow. For if all witnesses are of equal honesty and standing, and the character of the matter and the judge’s own impression concur with them, all the testimonies are to be followed.

[Col. 0575A] But if some of them say otherwise, even though they are equal in number, that is to be believed which accords with the nature of the matter and is free from suspicion of hostility or favour. The judge shall confirm his own impression from arguments and testimonies which he finds more suited to the case and nearer the truth. For attention ought not to be paid to multitude, but to the uncorrupted faithfulness of witnesses and to the testimonies upon which the light of truth more fully rests.

He shall also very often stand by presumptions until the contrary is proved. Thus Solomon, when in the dispute of the harlots he commanded the infant to be divided, and one woman preferred to yield him alive to the other while the other cried, “Let him be neither mine nor yours, but be divided,” judged that the living child should be restored to the woman who would not consent to his dying alive (III Kings III). He was led by a probable argument to believe that she was the mother who loved him, since no contrary proof overthrew his opinion or conviction.

[Col. 0575B] Hence the Emperor Hadrian, enlarging the discretion of a judge in examining witnesses, issued this rescript; its words are as follows:

> “You can better know how much credit is to be given to witnesses: what their rank and reputation are; whether they appear to have spoken simply, whether they have brought one and the same rehearsed account, or whether, in response to what you have questioned, they have replied plausibly on the spot. By no fixed rule can it be adequately determined what arguments, and in what manner, suffice to prove each matter. At one time the number of witnesses, at another their rank and authority, at another something like a concordant reputation, confirms belief in the matter under inquiry. Therefore this alone can I answer you in summary: the assessment of proof ought certainly not to be attached at once to one particular kind; rather, according to the judgment of your own mind, you ought to decide what you believe or what seems to you insufficiently proved.”

[Col. 0575C] A judge has very great power, provided that in all things he serves truth. If he learns that truth is endangered—as is customary among the dishonest—he will summon those whose testimony is necessary to state their position, and compel unwilling persons to testify, excepting, however, those whom the laws do not compel to testify against particular persons.

## Chapter XV. Matters pertaining to the official integrity of proconsuls, governors, and ordinary judges; the extent to which *xenia* may be offered; and Cicero, Bernard, Martin, and Geoffrey of Chartres

[Col. 0575D] It belongs to a governor’s official integrity to ensure that more powerful men do not injure the humbler, and that their defenders do not harass the innocent with malicious accusations. He shall prohibit unlawful exactions imposed, acts of violence committed, sales extorted by fear, and securities exacted without payment of the price. He shall also take care that he himself does not burden the province by providing lodgings; in short, he shall prevent anyone from suffering unjust gain or loss.

It befits a good and serious governor to ensure that the province is peaceful and tranquil. He will readily accomplish this if he acts diligently to rid the province of bad men and to seek them out. For [Col. 0576A] he ought to seek out sacrilegious persons, robbers, thieves, kidnappers, and their harbourers—without whom a robber cannot remain concealed for long—and punish each according to his offence.

Everyone who administers justice must observe that, in granting access, he presents himself as approachable, yet does not permit himself to be despised. Hence official instructions add that governors should not admit provincials into excessive familiarity. For equal social intercourse gives rise to contempt for dignity. In brief, justice must be administered so that a man increases the authority of his rank by his own character.

Moreover, in investigating a case, he ought neither to become inflamed against those whom he considers wicked nor to weep at the entreaties of the distressed. That is not the conduct of a steadfast and upright judge, whose countenance reveals the movements of his mind. For what is more unbecoming in a dignified man [Col. 0576B] than for his cheeks to grow pale at a breath, his skin to be drawn into wrinkles, his eyes to flash, and his expression to be disturbed? Or for anger to kindle the blood in his face and thrust it, as it were, to the surface; for his foaming lips to twist, arms to flail, feet to leap, body to tremble, and his whole bearing to express not so much anger as madness?

Certainly, when I see such people, I pity them and fear for myself, remembering the people whom I learned from Pliny’s *Natural History* to exist in Africa. They are said to bewitch by voice and tongue, so that if perhaps they praise too extravagantly beautiful trees, especially lovely crops, flourishing children, outstanding horses, or livestock in excellent condition and pasture, these suddenly die or perish. The bewitching power of the eyes, too, is fatal.

[Col. 0576C] The same author reports that there are people among the Illyrians who kill by looking at those upon whom they have gazed for too long in anger. These men and women, whose sight is harmful, have two pupils in each eye. Apollonides also reports that women are born in Scythia who are called *Bithyae*, and that they likewise have two pupils in their eyes and kill anyone at whom they happen to look in anger.

I fear that angry judges are kin to these people. Physiognomists also maintain that those with spotted eyes are more inclined to wickedness.

What has been said concerning governors and other judges ought also to hold concerning proconsuls, whom our countrymen commonly call “wandering justices.” The name of wandering, although it does not suit their office, nevertheless suits the persons of those who, pursuing their own desires in their pursuit of greed and plundering of the people, stray from the path of equity.

[Col. 0576D] The offices of all should be gratuitous, so that nothing beyond what is fixed may be demanded or received. But perhaps you ask what has been fixed. A plebiscite provides that no governor may accept a present or gift except something edible or drinkable, and that this must indeed be consumed within the next few days. By an imperial mandate the same rule extends to proconsuls and other magistrates.

They ought not, however, wholly to abstain from *xenia*—gifts of hospitality—but should observe a limit. That they should neither abstain altogether nor greedily exceed the measure of such gifts, the deified Severus and Emperor Antoninus have most elegantly regulated by letter. The words of this letter are:

> “As regards *xenia*, hear our judgment. An old proverb says: ‘Not everything, not always, not from everyone.’ For to accept from no one is very inhuman; to accept indiscriminately is most contemptible; and to accept in every case is most greedy.”

[Col. 0577A] What the official instructions contain—that neither the proconsul himself nor one holding another office should accept a house or gift, or purchase anything except for the purpose of daily sustenance—no longer concerns *xenia*, but things exceeding the use of provisions. Nor should *xenia* be extended to the level of formal gifts.

Although an advocate may sell lawful advocacy, and a jurist sound legal advice, it is altogether unlawful to sell judgment. When Cicero wished to buy a house on the Palatine and did not have ready money, he secretly borrowed two million sesterces from Sulla, who was then a defendant. Before the house was bought, the affair was disclosed [Col. 0577B] and became public. He was charged with having accepted money from a defendant in order to buy a house. Cicero, shaken by the unexpected reproach, denied that he had received it, saying that he was not going to buy the house. “So far,” he said, “is what you allege from being true, that it will be true that I received the money if I buy the house.” But when he later did buy it, and his enemies reproached him in the senate with this lie, he laughed heartily and, laughing, said: “You are foolish men, since you do not know that it belongs to a prudent and cautious householder, when he wishes to buy something, to deny that he intends to buy it, because of rival purchasers.” Thus, by a witty and urbane saying, he glossed over what he could not deny, making the matter seem more fit for laughter than for accusation. For it was his habit [Col. 0577C] that, whenever he could not deny a disgraceful charge, he would evade it with a joking answer.

Pope Eugenius, of revered memory and exemplary sanctity, whom you have seen, accepted absolutely no gift from a litigant, or from anyone whom he believed to have litigation impending. Thus, when, at his arrival, a prior of modest means, whose case he had not yet heard, urgently and most devoutly offered him a mark of gold, he said: “You have not yet entered the house, and already you wish to corrupt its master?” For that holy man considered anything offered to a judge while a lawsuit was pending to be corruption.

Bernard, monk of Clairvaux and cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, dwelling at Rome in high office, lived in a singular manner [Col. 0577D], shaking his hands free from every gift; so that no man has yet been born whose gold or silver he accepted as a present. Why should I mention Martin, who, contrary to custom, returned poor from an embassy? Though he had accepted, under great pressure, from the bishop of Florence a horse necessary for his companion, he restored it to the donor when he learned that, from the very beginning of the gift, that donor had had a cause to be argued in the Roman Church. Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who knew him more thoroughly, recounts this more fully in the instructive book which he writes to Saint Eugenius, *On Contemplation* or *Consideration*.

I pass over the fact that the venerable Father Geoffrey of Chartres, legate in Aquitaine, accepted no gifts from provincials except food and drink, [Col. 0578A] and that with the greatest frugality; but he despised as dung everything offered under the designation of hospitality-gifts (*xenia*). Saint Bernard of Clairvaux testifies that he refused to accept freely from a certain devoted cleric of his legation a fish commonly called sturgeon; nor did he yield to the importunity of the giver until he had paid him its price for the hospitality-gift accepted.

## Chapter XVI. On the crime of extortion, by which governors and judges are liable when they receive anything whatever for matters which they are bound to perform by virtue of office; and on Samuel, who teaches that there ought to be a continual sacrifice in the house of a judge, which, through the offering of justice and good works, presents itself as God’s temple

But as vices increase, examples of such self-restraint are today exceedingly rare even among the clergy, although [Col. 0578B] the rigor of the laws enjoins the highest restraint upon all magistrates. Indeed, so strictly that one who has exercised ordinary authority is compelled, while still within the province, to pay from his own resources—at the cost of reputation and fortune, that is, honor and rank—whatever he has squandered under an old title of delegated authority.

He is also liable under the Julian law concerning extortion who, holding any authority, has received money for judging or not judging, decreeing or not decreeing, giving testimony or not giving it, or, in short, for doing more or less anything belonging to his office. Nor can that which has been received be acquired by prescription before it returns into the power of the person from whom it came, or of that person’s heir. This law also rescinds sales and leases made at too high or too low a price; and those convicted are prohibited from giving public testimony, serving as judges, or appearing as advocates. Although persons convicted are now punished extraordinarily, they are usually condemned to exile, or even more severely, according to their offence. Punishment is exacted also from their heirs.

Consider the words of the law, and observe with what indignation it pursues this crime:

> “That the punishment of one may be a warning to many, we command that the leader who has behaved wickedly be sent under suitable guard to the province which he stripped bare, so that he may unwillingly pay fourfold not only what he himself did—not merely what a member of his household, but what even a common soldier or servant received—but also what he himself seized or carried off from my provincials.”

And again:

> “Let all examiners and judges keep their hands from money and estates, and not think another’s lawsuit their own plunder. For an examiner in private suits who is also a trader shall be compelled to suffer the loss fixed by the laws.”

And this also:

> “We likewise command and exhort that, if any member of the honorable classes, decurion, landholder, or finally even tenant farmer, has been shaken down on any pretext by a judge of whatever rank; if anyone knows that a judgment concerning a right was for sale; if anyone knows that a penalty was remitted for a price, or imposed through the fault of greed; if, finally, anyone can prove a judge corrupt for any cause whatever: let him come forward publicly, whether that judge is still in office or has laid down his administration; let him bring the accusation, prove the charge brought, and, when he has proved it, carry off both victory [Col. 0579A] and glory.”

Would that our own people at least heard these things; for I scarcely dare hope that they might observe them! The more carefully I inspect them, the more I seem to see extortioners rather than judges, as though they had been appointed for this purpose alone: to despoil the province. The very laws and customs by which men now live are traps and snares for calumniators. Verbal nooses are set forth, and syllable-hunting tricks. Woe to the simple man who does not know how to parse syllables! “I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who calumniate me” (Ps. 118 [119]); as though he openly said: Let those who pervert judgment and abandon justice be handed over to the accuser who accuses the children of Adam before the Lord day and night.

In the Book of Kings Samuel is read to have said to all Israel: “Behold, I have listened [Col. 0579B] to your voice according to all that you said to me, and I have set a king over you. And now the king walks before you, but I have grown old and gray. Moreover, my sons are with you. Thus I have conducted myself before you from my youth until this day. Behold, I am here. Speak concerning me before the Lord and before his anointed: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or ass; whether I have calumniated anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have received a gift from anyone’s hand. I will despise it today and restore it to you” (1 Sam. 12).

O modest spirit! O restrained hand! O incorrupt judge, and voice magnificent, admirable, and worthy of imitation by all—a voice that thus speaks from a pure conscience! “Speak concerning me before the Lord and his anointed,” who judge judges in heaven and on earth. [Col. 0579C] Speak, I say, whether I have taken anyone’s ox or ass. Certainly he had not extorted estates and landed properties, or immense weights of gold and silver, or loads of costly household goods, if he thought it a grave matter for a judge to have accepted an offered ox or ass. “Whether I have calumniated anyone, whether I have oppressed anyone.” He had unjustly harassed no one, who excluded every calumny; nor did flesh or blood pervert his judgment, he who never oppressed anyone. For if anyone fell into his hands, it was not the judge but that person’s own iniquity that oppressed him. “Whether I have received a gift from anyone’s hand, I will despise it today and restore it to you.” What, I ask, could be said more plainly? To remove, in sum, every suspicion of avarice, he declares that he was conscious of no gift from anyone, ready to reject and restore it if anything at all could be demanded of him. [Col. 0579D] For he preferred to restore it now rather than repay it with interest in the future; and he judged it better to despise it today than to appear contemptible forever before God and all the elect on that account.

But what answer did his hearers give to this declaration? Listen. “And they said” (ibid.)—who? Surely all Israel, for he had addressed his speech to all: “You have not calumniated us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand” (ibid.). If any proconsul or governor, tribune, centurion, decurion, or indeed any magistrate whatsoever has deserved such testimony from provincials, let him, I pray, come to our province and teach [Col. 0580A] our magistrates.

For nothing of the sort is heard concerning sheriffs and justices—who, to use our common phrase, are rightly called “errant”—because they love gifts and pursue rewards; they do not free the poor from the powerful, they do not render judgment for the stranger and orphan, and the widow’s cause does not gain entry to them. Nor do ecclesiastical judges follow Samuel; rather, as is the people, so is the priest.
