Wisdom complains generally: “Those who hold the law did not know me; rulers arose, and I did not know” (Jer. 2). This is evident even from their inferiors: what are deans and archdeacons, unless they are those of whom our venerable Simon, a teacher in the law of the Lord, used to say: “In whose hands are iniquities, and whose right hand is filled with gifts” (Ps. 25 [26])?

Ask the most fortunate king of the English, and still unconquered duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, what he himself thinks even of those whom he thrusts into office, and he will say, I suppose: “There is no evil in the clergy that these men do not commit.” The name and office of bishops would be venerable if they were fulfilled with as much care as they are sometimes sought with ambition. Bishops would be loved as fathers, feared as lords, and revered as saints, if they spared men exactions, cast out of their hearts everything arising from calumny, and did not believe every gain to be godliness. But instead they withdraw both reverence and affection from themselves while they seek honors, desire money, and either make calumnies their own or foster those of others. Indeed, I do not know how those escape every mark and punishment who claim for themselves at least two-thirds [Col. 0580C] of the proceeds of all calumnious gain. For they either appropriate the whole as for themselves, or, at most, yield only a third to archdeacons and other officials—not to mention the servants of iniquity among the people.

Nor do legates of the Apostolic See shake their hands free from every gift. At times they rage so violently through the provinces as though Satan had gone forth from the presence of the Lord to scourge the Church. They shake the corners of the house in order to cast down its sons and daughters—of the house of him who healed the sicknesses and pains of souls on the cross. They disturb and convulse the land so as to appear to have something that needs healing. Yet this is not said of all, but of those who, despising the Father’s will, serve their own. For it is certain that in every office of the Lord’s house some are left behind so that others may be taken up.

I have myself seen, among all these—that is, deans, archdeacons, bishops, and legates—men laboring with such concern in the Lord’s harvest that, by the merit of their faith and virtue, the Father’s vineyard might rightly be thought prudently and profitably entrusted to their hands. But others conduct themselves as though Tisiphone or Megaera had been dispatched from the underworld to Thebes to stir it up to crime. For they have commonly attained public offices in the Church from the court, against all the wishes of the faithful. Among such men,

> … judgment is nothing but public merchandise,  
> and the knight who sits in a case approves what has been bought.

They justify the wicked for gifts; they exult in the worst things and rejoice when evils occur:

> And they can scarcely keep back their tears when they see nothing to weep for.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.796.)

[Col. 0581A] For they devour the sins of the people, clothe themselves with them, and indulge in them in many ways. They are respecters of persons and, as it were, hammers of good men; for this is what they learned from those by whom they were chosen.

Wisdom says: “The wild ass is the lion’s prey in the desert; so the poor are the pastures of the rich. And as humility is an abomination to the proud, so the poor man is an execration to the rich. When the rich man is shaken, he is supported by friends; but when the humble man falls, he is cast out even by acquaintances. When the rich man is deceived, many come to his aid; he has spoken proudly, and they have justified him. The humble man has been deceived and is moreover rebuked. He has spoken sensibly, and no place is given him. The rich man has spoken, and all are silent; they raise his words to the clouds. The poor man has spoken, and they say, ‘Who is this?’ And if he stumbles, they overthrow [Col. 0581B] him” (Ecclus. 13).

Such are indeed the judgments of those whom the court has taught—indeed, of all who prefer riches to justice and think nothing better than possessing riches, though scarcely anything is more useless. None of these rejoices when he sees Christ upon the earth; none wishes him to dwell among men; none sings for the good works of neighbors: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). This, indeed, is the song of faithful prelates, who walk with beautiful feet and are therefore blessed because they bring peace—and peace joined to holiness, without which no one shall see God.

These too say with Wisdom that “wealth is good when there is no sin in the conscience, and poverty in the mouth of the wicked is most evil” (Ecclus. 13). [Col. 0581C] They cry aloud in the streets that “blessed is the man who is found without blemish and who has not gone after gold” (Ecclus. 31); as though they openly said: Whoever seeks gold in the office of any magistracy finds the blemish without which it can neither be acquired nor remain with its greedy possessor. Who ever handled money for long without soiling his hands? Yet the hand is certainly less soiled by it than the soul.

I do not wish the thresholds of the wicked to grow cold to me, nor that this page should seem to bark from a dog’s snout. I do not set my mouth against heaven, in order to say anything concerning the fathers who judge the world and are judged by no one on earth, except what is full of faith, charity, and reverence. Yet I shall say what is true—so true that no believer dare oppose it; I shall say what they themselves preach. I shall say, indeed, that a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, and that things done before the eyes of nations cannot possibly escape public notice; for:

> Every vice of the mind bears within itself a crime so much more conspicuous  
> as the sinner is held to be greater.  
> (Juvenal VIII.140.)

[Col. 0581D] Salt that has lost its savor is good for nothing except to be cast out and trampled underfoot by men, like worthless refuse, useful not even for manuring fields. The sun also illuminates the world more fully because it is set on high. In short, each person’s works bear witness concerning that person. Thus Samuel was justified by the testimony of his works.

But lest the people seem to be flattering him, or, through fear or deceit, bearing testimony to a [Col. 0582A] false innocence and empty justice, he judged that the people ought to be bound by the religious force of an oath to a profession of truth, saying: “The Lord is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.” And the people said: “He is witness” (1 Sam. 12), as though they made the faith owed to God and their king a pledge of their solemn affirmation.

Whether he received food and drink, I have no certainty from Scripture. For it is written thus: “Samuel also judged Israel all the days of his life; and he went yearly, making a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and judged Israel in the places mentioned above; and he returned to Ramah. For there was his house, and there he judged Israel” (1 Sam. 7). What else [Col. 0582B] does the text appear to mean except that he traveled through the province by virtue of his office in order to discharge judgment, and returned home in order to meet his needs from his own resources? “He also built there an altar to the Lord” (ibid.). Rightly so, because there ought to be a continual sacrifice in the house of the judge: a house which, by the worship of justice, uprightness of conduct, and the light of good works, presents itself as God’s temple. There no longer is sacrificed the blood of goats and calves, nor does the ash of a heifer sanctify the defiled for cleansing of the flesh; but through the great high priest who passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, there must everywhere be offered:

> The well-ordered law and sacred right of the soul, the holy recesses  
> of the mind, and a breast imbued with noble uprightness.  
> (Persius II.73.)

[Col. 0582C] For true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and truth. Do you suppose that he received anything under the name of *sportulae*—customary small allowances? Under this pretext, not so much judges as tavern-keepers of judgments, who wish to cloak their wickedness in the seeming respectability of permission, seek to color their injustice. They look, that is, for some profit from the business whose burdens they partly bear. Or, if it may not be called profit, let it at least be compensation for expenses and losses. Yet these are rare. For who is ashamed to say, “What will you give me if I do justice for you?” For if justice is to be rendered for its own sake, you wait in vain. Is it not like saying, “What do you wish to give me for denying myself, betraying my office, and selling the Lord?” [Col. 0582D]

## Chapter XVII. Money ought to be despised in comparison with wisdom, as is also proved by examples of ancient philosophers

Many philosophers are recorded not merely to have despised riches but to have cast them away as an impediment to wisdom and virtue. Socrates did this, whom the schools of all philosophers revere as the unique fountain, as it were, of prudence and truth. Antisthenes likewise, after teaching rhetoric with distinction and hearing Socrates, is said to have told his disciples: “Go away; seek a master, for I have now found one.” At once he sold what he had and distributed it publicly, reserving for himself nothing more than a little cloak. That celebrated Diogenes [Col. 0583A] was his follower, more powerful than King Alexander and a conqueror of human nature.

Since Antisthenes accepted no disciples and could not dismiss the persistent Diogenes, he finally threatened him with a club unless he left. Diogenes is said then to have bowed his head and said: “No staff will be so hard that it can separate me from your company.” The satirist who writes histories of illustrious men relates that this Diogenes used a double cloak because of the cold, kept and carried a bag as his pantry, bore a staff because of the weakness of his little body—by which, now old, he was accustomed to support his limbs—and was commonly called an *emorathius* [reading uncertain], because he asked for and received food from anyone for the present hour.

He lived in gatehouses and in the porticoes of cities, [Col. 0583B] everywhere professing the truth and rebuking or censuring the vices of passers-by that defiled their morals. As he turned himself about in a jar, he jested that he possessed a movable house and changed with the seasons. In cold weather he turned the mouth of the jar southward; in summer, northward. Wherever the sun declined, Diogenes’ residence was turned with it.

On one occasion, while carrying a wooden cup for drinking, he saw a boy drink from his cupped hand; he smashed the cup upon the ground, saying: “I did not know that nature had a cup.” He never relaxed the sternness of his spirit, but maintained the same composure of countenance even when adversity assailed him. Thus, that you might recognize him as completely Socratic, he trampled underfoot the storms of chance and persisted [Col. 0583C] in a single resolve against every pain and misery. He always said that such things were alien to a philosopher, and that the mind was not master of itself if anything belonging to fortune had power over it.

His death too reveals his virtue and self-restraint. When, already old, he was traveling to the Olympic contest, celebrated with great crowds in Greece, he was seized by a fever on the journey and collapsed upon the edge of the road. Though his friends wished to place him upon a beast of burden or in a vehicle, he refused. Going instead to the shade of a tree, he said: “Go, I pray, and continue on to watch the contest. This night will prove me either victor or defeated. If I conquer the fever, I shall come to the contest; if it conquers me, I shall go down to the underworld.” There, during the night, having strangled himself, he said that he was not so much dying as [Col. 0583D] excluding the fever by death.

Misled by the opinion and example of brave men, at the extremity of difficulty, lest death be brought upon him from elsewhere, he thought voluntary death ought to be sought. For a preconceived opinion had commonly persuaded even wiser men that they should prefer to provoke death rather than endure anything shameful. Cato did this, and others did likewise, who, taking up the sword, hemlock, or another poison beforehand, fled every—and the only, as they thought—stain of disgrace. Ignorance of truth seems to plead for them; but it is gross and supine ignorance, which puts certainties behind uncertainties and casts away and rejects whatever is held best for an empty reason. Nor does it attain the name of courage in that wherein a deceptive opinion boasts that it has attained more than others. Certainly it boasts deceitfully and vainly, because, as that poet says:

> In adversity it is easy to despise life.  
> He acts more bravely who can endure being miserable.

[Col. 0584A] None of those who provoke death is excusable. More excusable are those who shrink from death when it is imminent. For who has known the counsel of the Lord, or whether one can by some means escape impending death?

Sandrococtus, ordered by King Alexander to be killed, sought safety in swiftness of foot. Exhausted from this exertion, he fell asleep. A lion of immense size approached the sleeper, licked away the streaming sweat with its tongue, and left him gently awakened. By this prodigy he was first moved, through the majesty of the omen, to hope for kingship. Later, when he was preparing war against Alexander’s governors, an elephant of [Col. 0584B] boundless size voluntarily presented itself and, as though tamed by gentleness, received him upon its back; thereafter he became a leader in war and a distinguished fighter.

Andronicus too, condemned to the beasts, was exposed to a lion which, by its enormous body, fierce onset, terrifying roar, resounding voice, and the flowing mane of its neck, drew all minds and eyes to itself. Yet he escaped unharmed. For when the lion saw him at a distance, it suddenly stopped as if in astonishment; then it approached the man slowly, as though playfully and gently. It moved its tail mildly and affectionately, in the manner and fashion of fawning dogs; pressing itself against the man’s body, it gently licked his legs and hands with its tongue, though the man was now almost dead from fear. Amid the caresses [Col. 0584C] of the savage beast he recovered his lost courage and only gradually, with difficulty, opened his eyes to look at the lion. Apion reports that he saw this in public spectacles at Rome; he adds that then, as though they recognized one another mutually, one could see the lion and man joyful and congratulating each other.

For this reason, amid the loudest cries of the people, the man was summoned by Caesar and carefully asked why that most savage lion had spared him alone. He related the marvelous event as follows: “When my master held the province of Africa with proconsular authority, I was compelled to flee because of his unjust and daily beatings. Seeking safer hiding-places from my master in that land, [Col. 0584D] I withdrew into the wildernesses of fields and sands. And, as though nothing else were lacking, I resolved somehow to seek death. Therefore, when the midday sun was swift and blazing, I found for the moment a shady cave and entered it, concealing myself there. Not long afterward this lion came to the same cavern, its foot weak, bloody, and grievously wounded; it uttered groans and murmurs, lamenting the pain and torment of its wound, so as to move any hearer present to pity.

“At first sight of the approaching lion I was terrified and wholly dismayed. But when the lion entered, as the event itself showed, that dwelling-place of its own, and saw me from afar, having entered and hidden there, it approached mild and gentle, and seemed to raise [Col. 0585A] its foot and stretch it out to me for help. Then,” he said, “I pulled out a great splinter lodged in the sole of its foot, pressed out the collected pus from the deep wound, and, now without great fear, carefully dried it thoroughly and wiped away all the blood. Relieved by my service and treatment, it then lay down, resting its foot in my hands, and went to sleep. From that day the lion and I lived for a full three years in the same cave and on the same food. For whatever beasts it hunted, it brought the choicer portions to the cave; and I, having no fire, ate them roasted in the midday sun.

“But when I had grown thoroughly weary of that beastlike life, I left the cave while the lion was away hunting. Having traveled about three days’ journey, I was seen and seized by soldiers and brought from Africa to my master at Rome. He immediately arranged for me to be condemned to death and given to the beasts. [Col. 0585B] I understand that this lion too, captured when I had then been separated from it, is now repaying the favor of my service and healing.”

Thus Andronicus was released from punishment, and the lion was given to him by the vote of the whole people. Thereafter, as man and lion lived amicably together and walked about and around the city, everyone said: “This is the lion who is the man’s guest; this is the man who is the lion’s physician.” Do you seek more familiar histories? Daniel came out from the lions’ den, and the youths escaped unharmed from the furnace of fire. Among every people, very many have unexpectedly been delivered by grace from evils that threatened them. Therefore none of those who have laid hands upon themselves [Col. 0585C] seems to me sufficiently excusable, although ecclesiastical history celebrates with great praises some who provoked death because they preferred their temporal life to perish rather than have their chastity endangered.

Yet bodily weakness, ignorance of the law, the fire of charity, and perhaps a special command of God excuse them in such a way that they may be saved in their simplicity, but what they simply presumed must by no means become a precedent. For what room is there for courage if one is so weary of one’s life that, as though overcome in patience and cutting off the path of merits, one either cannot or neglects to endure what is commanded? Among wise persons life is despised in such a way that even another lifetime seems foul as the price of disgrace; it is loved in such a way that, so long as it can be [Col. 0585D] maintained innocently, it is not cast away when any crisis of difficulty comes upon it. Thus life must be preserved so that it may be held in contempt; it must be despised so that it may advance salvation.

But who today despises life, when no one, or scarcely anyone, does not desire money with the whole gaping appetite of the mind? Why should they not?

> Since queenly money bestows rank and beauty,  
> and persuasive speech and Venus adorn the well-moneyed man.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.6.38.)

He who is rich, who prospers in his ways, is judged wise and happy. For this one man takes a wife, another buys five yoke of oxen or an estate, exchanging their souls for these things. They deem blind, lame, and feeble those upon whom the world does not smile, [Col. 0586A] though Wisdom, once the rich have been cast out, brings them into the wedding feast (Matt. 22), where they are intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and given drink from the torrent of eternal delight (Ps. 35 [36]).

Meanwhile, anyone without riches is a fool, an ass, a stump, a log, lead, or something still more senseless. Therefore, whoever is poor is foolish and miserable. Nor can anyone love a person whom bad fortune oppresses, because:

> No loyalty has ever chosen the wretched as friends.

And each person is justly believed to deserve the evils he suffers. So greatly has money’s kingdom prevailed that one despairs of the honesty of a judge who rejects an offered gift. If you refuse to bargain, you appear to hate the cause of the person making the offer. Perhaps you are thought to have been bribed beforehand by affection or a gift [Col. 0586B] if you wish to remain unbribed. The teaching or opinion of philosophers has altogether vanished, while everyone runs after riches as though rest from labors and solace for sorrows could be found nowhere else; as though shipwrecked persons could swim from the deep more easily if burdened with an excessively heavy load.

But who ever gathered thorns while ulcerated, in order to roll upon them and rest softly? Certainly, if people perfectly believed him who says that riches are thorns, the wise of our age would not seek them with such zeal. Therefore, as Publius Carpus says, the rich are more wretched than the poor because they stand farther from wisdom. Desire for riches excludes wisdom and flees the virtues; fruitful poverty in men follows nature, the best guide to good living, and is the [Col. 0586C] parent and guardian of virtues. It alone produces security, because it alone knows no incentives to wars. The person who knows no causes of strife has no quarrels. The world trembles, and only the poor man does not fear Caesar’s hand.

Certainly, even if riches were not to be fled or despised for any other reason than because they hedge the paths of wisdom with thorns, they ought not to be loved. Yet, lest the opinion of philosophers seem burdensome to those who blush at poverty’s lowliness, philosophy does not command flight from riches but restrains desire for them. It seeks a mind master of itself and sufficient to itself in every calculation of fortune—yet so that its sufficiency comes from God. Thus it uses gold as though it were pottery, and pottery as though it were gold. For as wealth is admitted for use, so the wise man despises its misuse. [Col. 0586D]

But perhaps cheap household goods will appear disgraceful to the great, and slender means dim the splendor of honor. Yet it is far better to shine in character than in possessions; nor will the person whom the stain of his own disgrace dishonors ever be made illustrious by the appearance of things.

> They say that King Agathocles dined from earthenware  
> and often loaded a Samian table with clay vessels.  
> When he set courses of gold in gem-studded dishes  
> and mingled wealth with poverty alike,  
> he answered one asking the reason: “I, who am king  
> of Sicily, was born to a potter as my father.  
> Reverence fortune, whoever you are, if suddenly  
> you rise rich from a humble house.”  
> (Ausonius, *Epigrams* VIII.)

[Col. 0587A] Things themselves, then, are not at fault, but their use is. And a noble fruit of the philosophic mind is a generous equanimity of spirit. For if one bears all things evenly from numbness, the sick mind degenerates from the virtue of soundness. But while there are many paths of philosophy, that one seems to me nobler and more praiseworthy than the rest,

> which patiently dines on vegetables, so as to use things—
…may know how to conduct itself in the use of things. (HORACE, *Epistles* I.17.13.) Thus it should be taught not to disdain vegetables and whatever gifts belong to the extremity of poverty. For this is an outstanding fruit of philosophy: that a person should know how to abound and how to endure want; that with a cheerful mind he should bear all things evenly [Col. 0587B]; that, placing the barrier of solid virtue before himself, he should disarm every stroke of fortune. Certainly, whoever has attained these things neither hopes nor fears, and every fortune always falls crippled against him. “What,” says some inquisitive investigator of philosophy, “has philosophy brought you?” And Aristippus replies: “That I may converse fearlessly with all men.” Indeed, if he were desirous of honour, money, or any other thing, he could by no means answer truthfully thus. Yet the safest road to salvation lies open to one unencumbered by riches and other possessions. For it is exceedingly difficult for possessions not to hinder their owner’s course.

Who does not know that Hippodamia ran ahead to the prize, when she was able to delay the course of her competing suitors by throwing down gold? Thus the maiden remained unconquered until she came to one who despised money [Col. 0587C]; by despising gold he overcame the maiden, won the gold, and from it—so the story goes—made waxen torches for the competing girl, since love of incorruptibility swallowed up love of money. Does not God’s judgment itself commend this, and render wealth contemptible, since the wicked abound in it amid the poverty of the good? Yet sometimes, by some means I cannot explain [Col. 0588A], riches press themselves upon the righteous for their overthrow; and the more carefully they are excluded, the more eagerly they knock at the despiser’s door. Because blessed Eugenius drove gifts away with especial caution, they flowed to him abundantly from every side. Almost everywhere, too, it happens that they flee while they are sought, but hasten while they are driven away. This, indeed, is a short and most honourable road to riches. For when riches are prudently excluded, eternal life is acquired and an increase of riches is added.

And if this seems too arduous for others, it must at least be fulfilled by judges, both ecclesiastical and secular, who are bound to justice by profession or oath. Samuel is the model for both: he so presided over sacrifices that he did not spare the blood of the ungodly; he so administered both jurisdictions that he oppressed no one and received nothing from any man’s hand [Col. 0588B]. Samuel’s conscience bears witness to this, and the people bear witness as well; yet that scrupulous conscience was not satisfied unless the people confirmed their testimony by an oath. For he says: “The Lord is witness against you, and his Christ is witness this day, that you have found nothing whatsoever in my hand.” And they said: “He is witness.” Let anyone to whom the provincials give such testimony approach confidently the judgment of almighty and all-knowing God. For he wisely prepares his case who produces his conscience at the examination, and before the human day has the one conscious of all things as his judge on high.

But those who, unlike Samuel, do not examine their judgments here, being ready with excuses for sins, cry out with Pilate as though their hands were washed [Col. 0588C]: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matt. 27), shall be condemned because they sinned against the law and shall be condemned through the law. Those also shall share their condemnation who can restrain them but will not. Of these the saying of the wise prophet has been spoken. Accordingly, let the pen pass on to the proportionality of the hands introduced by Plutarch.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0587]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0587C]

[Col. 0587D] That saying of the ethical poet is well known:

> A single craftsman will reproduce a fingernail  
> And imitate in bronze the soft hair of an Aemilius;  
> Unfortunate in the totality of his work, because he will not know  
> How to fashion the whole. If I should wish to compose anything,  
> I would no more wish to be such a man  
> Than to live with a crooked nose, conspicuous for black  
> Eyes and black hair.  
> —HORACE, *Art of Poetry* 32 ff.

While I follow more closely the footsteps of Plutarch in instructing Trajan, I think that I am addressed by this image of myself; and I shall be everyone’s laughing-stock unless I pursue more carefully what I have begun. For I have professed myself to be his client in this present work. I therefore follow him, and with him shall descend from the head of the commonwealth down to its feet—on this condition, however: if I appear rather sharp in this section to those who are permitted to be ignorant of the laws, they should ascribe it not to me but to Plutarch, [Col. 0588C] or rather to themselves, because they have refused to learn the rule which they profess and by which they ought to live. For what I have said about our own countrymen I added only in order that they might return, even unwillingly, to the path of virtue. For the examples of their ancestors and the greatness of the unconquered prince suffice to encourage them to action. I now gather his titles together before me into one heap, so that, while the trumpets and clarions of others and every kind of musicians loudly proclaim his praises all together, I, an unlearned commoner, may distribute his praises among men like myself through my shrill pipe. Who would expect a half-rustic to possess a brass-bound flute, rival to a great trumpet? Yet I shall be present and thrust myself into so great a celebration; what the vein of talent withholds, abundance of devotion shall supply.

[Col. 0589A]

> While the boar loves the mountain ridges, while the fish loves the rivers,  
> While bees feed on thyme, while cicadas on dew,  
> Your honour, name, and praises shall always endure.  
> —VIRGIL, *Eclogues* V.76 ff.

If commanders think that anything has been said to their injury, let them learn from the prince that bitter medicines are administered not for the destruction but for the health of the sick. With these matters prefaced, let the discourse proceed to what remains.

## Chapter I. That the hand of the commonwealth is either armed or unarmed; what the unarmed hand is, and its duty

The hand of the commonwealth, then, is either armed or unarmed. The armed hand is that which performs military service in camp and sheds blood. The unarmed hand administers justice and, without striking by arms, performs the service of legal warfare. [Col. 0589B] For those alone do not serve the commonwealth who, protected by helmets and breastplates, wield swords or every sort of missile against enemies; advocates also serve it, who, relying upon the protection of their glorious voice, raise up the fallen and restore the exhausted. Nor do they provide less for humankind than if they protected from enemies, by the defence of arms, the lives, hopes, and descendants of those who labour. Tax-collectors, court officers, and the officials of all judges also serve. For as the offices of peace differ from those of war, so the same tasks must necessarily be performed by different persons.

The armed hand is directed only against the enemy; the unarmed hand extends also to the citizen. The discipline of both is necessary, since conspicuous wickedness commonly belongs to both. The conduct of the hands also declares the image of their head, since, as Wisdom says: “An unjust king has all his ministers wicked; and as the ruler of a city is, so are its inhabitants” (Ecclus. 10). “A praetor,” Pericles said, rebuking his colleague Sophocles, “must have continent eyes as well as hands.” The praiseworthy continence of rulers consists in keeping their own hands from actions and injuries, and restraining the hands of others. Yet the hands of both kinds of service—the armed and the unarmed alike—are the prince’s hands; unless he restrains both, he is scarcely continent.

The unarmed hand must indeed be restrained more strictly, because, while armed men are ordered to abstain from exactions and plunder, the unarmed are also excluded from gifts [Col. 0589C]. Nevertheless, if a lawful penalty is imposed, or if what has been legally established or permitted is exacted or received, the official is in no way punished or blamed. Whatever this may be does not receive the name of exaction; nor does it fall under the category of a gift, which officials are forbidden to accept. But because officials have greater licence, since under the pretext of office they can despoil or harass private persons, what they presume to do against their office must be struck by a heavier penalty.

Blessed Lawrence, bishop of Milan, says: “What is a tax-collector? Is he not the head of robbery and the law of violence? What is a tax-collector? A shameless brigand, a physician of destruction. Is not the tax-collector more savage than thieves? For a thief steals even while afraid; this man sins confidently. A thief fears the snares of the law; this man thinks that whatever he does is law. The law deters a thief from unlawful acts; this man twists the law to the unjust advantage of his own wickedness. Who is more unjust than one who, with the words of justice, condemns justice and, with the weapons of innocence, strips, wounds, and kills the innocent? He destroys law by means of law; and while pressing others toward law, he himself is lawless.”

For just as a praetor, even when he decides unjustly, is said to declare the law—regard being had not to what he does but to what he ought to do—so also a tax-collector, even when he commits an offence, seems to perform law, regard being had to his office rather than to his wickedness [Col. 0590A]. But what is the office of a tax-collector? We have learned from Luke’s account that tax-collectors came to John to be baptized by him and said: “Master, what shall we do?” He answered them: “Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you” (Luke 3). Behold the tax-collector’s office: to exact and receive what has been established. Whatever is more than this proceeds from the evil of the exacter and receiver, not of the giver. This applies to the officials of every magistracy: nothing more is to be exacted by them.

Court officers may lawfully exact what is owed them from official fees (*sportulae*), and all ranks of attendants (*stratilati*) may justly receive their fixed salary. Yet it is not lawful to extort or harass people in order that gifts may be wrung from them. Blessed Job says: “Fire shall devour the tents of those who willingly receive gifts. Their assembly has conceived pain and brought forth iniquity, and its womb prepares deceits” (Job 15). The whole company of tax-collectors, from the greatest to the least, devotes itself now to extortion rather than justice [Col. 0590B], and rages so against the people that what one leaves behind, the others do not delay to take away—as though, according to the prophet’s complaint, they had been appointed for this purpose: that the caterpillar should consume what the locust left.

To give themselves greater freedom to injure, one man accumulates several offices in himself, so that what he does not receive through one office he may take through another. Natural philosophers relate that the *bruchus* is born from the locust; it is so called until it has wings. Then, as its wings grow, when it begins to fly, it is called an *athelebus*. When it can fly fully, it becomes a locust. The *bruchus*, moreover, is much more grievous than the locust or the *athelebus*, because it lacks wings and cannot quickly depart. Therefore, wherever it comes, it consumes the crops completely. The locust and the *athelebus*, wherever they arrive, also do harm—perhaps in many places—but less than the *bruchus*, which, once it settles, does not move until it has entirely exhausted human labours.

Among officials, however, you will find this same *bruchus*, *athelebus*, and locust: one who harms neighbours and distant persons alike, devours the fortune of the person upon whom he has once settled, and does not depart until he has taken away all his resources [Col. 0590C]. Who can count how many wards he has most officiously defrauded, how many estates he has made saleable through injustice, and how many among us, stripped of their goods through the licence of such men under the guise of religion or another pretext, he has made not so much pilgrims to Rome and travellers as exiles? These things now plainly occur; nor do governors or proconsuls restrain them, because, as the saying goes, the raven rejoices in the wolf’s deeds, and the wicked judge applauds the minister of iniquity.

All this is known by experience to rulers whose unfaithful companions are thieves: when they see them engaged in wrongdoing, they run with them, adding their own share of iniquity so that they may receive some portion of the profit. If you pity the poor, if you weep at the downfall of justice, if you resolve to give help, if you dare to keep silence so that you do not say “Well done, well done” to every word and deed of theirs, then, upon the accusation of the Herodians, you will answer before the governor for injured majesty. Unless you comply with them in all things, you will be contradicting Caesar; and whatever Caesar decrees—unless it proceeds thus, unless it stands thus—is treated as an attack upon the king’s person and against the crown.

The clamour of the officials will rise, redouble, and grow strong unto the clouds [Col. 0591A], as they cry loudly again and again: “We found this man subverting the people, forbidding tribute to be paid to Caesar, denying that Caesar is king and that all things are lawful to his ministers. We found him nullifying the laws of the fathers, introducing novelties, and despising most ancient custom. We are witnesses of this” (Luke 23). And if you seek to clear your innocence or establish anything for justice, if you say that Christ is king (John 19), whom one must obey rather than men (Acts 5), if you produce some privilege of his Church—since this is most hateful—they will immediately thunder out: “What further witnesses do you desire? Behold, you yourselves have heard the blasphemy. Whoever asserts such things contradicts Caesar” (Matt. 26).

But if the judge, seeing the innocence and reverencing justice, passes the matter over, they will cry out from all sides: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 12). “Let one man’s punishment be the liberation of many: take him away and destroy him, so that Barabbas may live and prosper.” For all are as one body, which, as their manifest deeds prove, is from the devil their father, and they are its members. Blessed Job speaks excellently of them: “His body is as shields cast in one piece and compacted with scales pressing upon one another. One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them. One shall cling to another, and, holding fast, they shall by no means be separated” (Job 41). They support one another because they have gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ [Col. 0591B]; and they flourish with such authority that whatever they say prevails as though it were found in the official records. Their testimony prejudges the truth. No one except the prince may oppose their judgments.

Unless the prince restrains them, even if all say that there is peace, there is in fact no peace—or rather there is only that peace in which lies the bitterest bitterness. For although otherwise, under the moderation of blameless self-defence, it is permissible to repel force by force, yet against these men when they extort, despoil, and torture, one may not utter a word. For they appear to be ministers of the law. A man who does something for the defence of his own body is excused; yet if he resists these men dragging him away with any injury whatsoever, he is judged deserving of any penalty. If one drags your disordered and dishonoured hair, pulls your beard, stretches out your ears as though they were too short [Col. 0592A], gives you a slap, or impiously strikes you with his fist; if he tears out one of your eyes, endure it patiently unless you prefer to lose both. For whatever they presume to do, they boast that it is done by Caesar’s right hand.

If you carry a weapon, if you refuse voluntarily to offer your neck, he bares his belly, displays his throat, stretches out his neck, and provokes you: “If you dare, pierce Caesar’s entrails with your weapon, and lay hands upon Caesar in whatever manner you please.” For they glory that they bear Caesar’s person. But if this is Caesar’s right hand, what then will his left be? Certainly this faction does not execute justice but mocks it; it does not fulfil the law but empties it of effect—although some men, by the cruel prerogative of words contrary to the mind of the law, fraudulently defend their own error. For they are wise in doing evil.

Yet though this plague is destructive to provincials, it can be destructive to no one more than to the prince. The property of provincials is the prince’s property. All that belongs to provincials is legally available for the prince’s necessity and use. The whole province is like the prince’s treasury; whoever empties it commits a most grave offence against the prince, whose resources he diminishes. For provincials are, as it were, holders of a surface-right, and whenever the need of authority requires it, they are not so much masters of their property as its guardians. But if no emergency presses, the provincials’ goods are their own goods, which not even the prince may use at will [Col. 0592B]. For if it benefits the commonwealth that no one should misuse his own property, it is utterly unlawful to misuse another’s.

But when a province has been exhausted by ministers of iniquity and crime, the satellites of Satan, the Herodian men, what will the prince use if necessity is at hand? Therefore, if he is wise, he will break their jaws with bit and bridle (Ps. 31 [32]), so that, in the manner of wolves driven by the shameless greed of their bellies, they may not ravage and tear apart the province and, to the prince’s injury, exhaust the strength of the whole commonwealth. Otherwise he himself will fall into poverty, rendered hateful to all provincials, and will have to render to his Judge an account in a strict examination of the works of his hands and of the injury done to provincials, whom he unjustly, and as if by fraud under the shadow of protection, despoiled and mangled with an unarmed hand.

## Chapter II. That military service requires selection, knowledge, and training

[Col. 0592D] There remains the armed hand, which, as has been said, performs military service in camp and sheds blood. In its regulation the prince’s wisdom and justice shine most clearly. For, as Vegetius Renatus says: “There is no one who ought to know more things, or better things, than the prince, whose learning ought to benefit all his subjects.” Since he must regulate the works of peace and likewise of war, he must possess knowledge of the laws and of military affairs. Something has indeed been said above concerning peaceful studies; now the armed hand is considered, which cannot be strong without selection, knowledge, and training. If any one of these is absent, the hand is useless and brings no benefit. Of these, knowledge and training are more useful.

For knowledge of military affairs nourishes courage in fighting. No one fears to do what he confidently believes he has learned well. In the contests of war, a trained few are more ready for victory than an unskilled and untaught multitude, always exposed to slaughter [Col. 0593A]. What made the Romans victors over all nations? Knowledge, certainly, and training, and the loyalty which the selected men rendered to the commonwealth by their oath. For what could Roman fewness have achieved against the multitude of the Gauls? What could short stature have dared against the tallness of the Germans? It is plain that the Spaniards exceeded the Romans not only in numbers but also in bodily strength. The Romans were always unequal to the cunning and riches of the Africans.

Against all these disadvantages it was useful to select the alert recruit and, so to speak, teach him the law of arms; to strengthen instruction by daily exercise; through field training to foresee whatever may occur in battle and combat; and to punish the idle by the severity of discipline. The author just mentioned testifies to this, adding in almost the same words that it is useless to keep soldiers who are delicately reared and accustomed to luxuries. He judges the rustic populace more suitable: men brought up in the open air and in labour, able to endure the sun, indifferent to shade, strangers to baths, ignorant of luxuries, simple in spirit, content with little food, their limbs hardened for every endurance of toil. For them, carrying iron, digging a trench, and bearing a burden are country habits. Will singers, gamblers, or bird-catchers be found fit for these tasks when the need arises? Certainly he rejects from military service not only such men [Col. 0593B], but fishermen, confectioners, linen-workers, and all who seem to have handled anything connected with women’s quarters (*gynaecea*); he considers that blacksmiths, carpenters, hunters of deer and boar should be selected for military use.

Moreover, leaving aside the mysteries of allegorical interpretation, Jerubbaal was forbidden by the Lord’s command to place confidence in a frightened and untrained multitude, and was instructed to lead against the Midianites only those whom strength of spirit and bodily training approved. When Gideon proclaimed in the hearing of all: “Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return,” twenty-two thousand men withdrew from the people, and only ten thousand remained. But from these ten thousand the judgment of the Lord selected in advance only those as more ready for war who, in their thirst, lapped hastily like dogs, throwing water to their mouths with their hands. He left behind those who drank with bent knee [Col. 0593C].

Thus by three hundred men the people were delivered, the enemies slain, the kings captured, and the leaders slain—not so much leaders of military service as of wickedness. Gideon struck Zebah and Zalmunna with the sword, took the ornaments and crescents with which the necks of royal camels are customarily adorned, as well as the ornaments, necklaces, and purple clothing which the kings of Midian commonly used. From so great a spoil he kept for himself only the golden earrings of the Ishmaelites, distributing the rest among the people according to equity. He therefore conquered innumerable enemy forces by means of a small but unencumbered company of brave men. I can scarcely believe that they learned in the luxuries of cities, royal banquets, and daily feasts to lap water—on account of which the Lord judged them more worthy than the others of selection.

Yet if necessity sometimes requires that city-bred and more delicate men be compelled to take up arms, from the moment they first give their names to military service, let them learn to labour, run, carry burdens, and endure sun and dust. Let them use scanty and rustic food; let them stay sometimes in the open air and sometimes beneath tents. Only then let them be trained in the use of weapons. If a longer expedition arises, they should be kept especially busy with transport duties (*angariae*) and held far from the enticements of the city, so that their bodies and minds alike may thereby acquire strength [Col. 0594A].

It cannot be denied that after the founding of the City the Romans always went out to war from the city; but at that time they enjoyed no luxuries. By running and field exercise, Roman youth gathered sweat and washed it off by swimming in the Tiber. The same man was soldier and farmer; he merely changed the kinds of his tools. This is so true that it is well established that the dictatorship was offered to Quintius Cincinnatus while he was ploughing:

> His trembling wife clothed him for dictatorship before his oxen,  
> And the lictor carried his ploughs home.

Therefore the strength of an army must chiefly be supplied from the fields. For, as someone says, by some means a man who has known fewer pleasures in life fears death less.

## Chapter III. On vainglorious soldiers who are useless for military service

Perhaps the glorious soldiers will blush—men who portray the comic Thraso more by life and character than by profession and name—at these duties of armed military service, which seem to them to smell not so much of military discipline as of the constraints of shameful slavery. They think military glory consists in shining in more elegant dress; in drawing tight and twisting their linen garments or silken clothes so that they make them cling to the flesh like skin whitened with ceruse or subjected to other cosmetics; in sitting more softly on pacing horses; in being curled and so carefully groomed that they yield nothing to Actaean Apollo; and in being distinguished more by luxury than virtue [Col. 0594B].

If you should perhaps draw up their battle-line, you would storm the camp of Thaïs more safely than that of Hannibal. Whoever among them is more boastful at court, when the danger of battle approaches will send Laconians, under the command of Sanga, in squadrons ahead to fight, himself following at the rear under pretext of providing support, together with slingers and others who prefer to hurl missiles from a distance at the enemy rather than join hand-to-hand combat. But when they return home without wound or scar—as happens more frequently—

> Then they sing of battles exhausted by grim Mars:  
> “There stood the descendant of Aeacus; there Achilles stretched himself;  
> And all Pergamum they paint in flowing wine.”

Each boasts that a thousand deaths have passed around his head. Thereafter you will be unable to bear their glory. The tale will be prolonged for a hundredth year. Sons who are born and arise will tell it to their sons. If diligent idleness has acquired some spears, fragile like hemp stalks, who broke them; if gold, vermilion, or another colour has been knocked or fallen from a shield—of this their chatterbox tongue, if allowed, will make an eternal memorial [Col. 0594C].

These men have the first places at dinners, and, whatever our Renatus has handed down concerning military affairs, feast splendidly every day if fortune permits. Every labour and exercise not imposed by invincible necessity they flee more eagerly than dog or snake; and every hardship that threatens they cast upon their subordinates. Meanwhile they gild their shields and adorn all the implements of their camp so that you would think any one of them not merely a worshipper but a governor of Mars. If the shield or helmet of one of these men is stripped away, his spoils could honour Mars himself.

## Chapter IV. What knowledge and training soldiers ought to possess; that they must not be idle; and Augustus, who had his daughters trained in wool-working

[Col. 0595B]

Scipio Africanus, as Julius Frontinus relates excellently in the book of *Stratagems*, once saw a certain man’s shield ornamented rather elegantly and said that he was not surprised the man had adorned with such care that in which he had more protection than in his sword. Nor could you endure the arrogance of these men unless you possessed greater patience. No degree of modesty can restrain you from laughing at their absurdities.

Who was happier or greater than Octavian Augustus? Although he did not beget sons, he adopted them. Though noble blood could have sufficed them for glory, and inherited property for abundance beyond use, they were nevertheless trained with such diligence as though neither their own possessions could be retained nor others’ acquired except by virtue [Col. 0595C]. He therefore had them trained in military marching, running, and jumping; taught them swimming, cutting and thrusting blows, throwing missiles, casting stones by hand or sling, and how every war ought either to be endured or waged. For the most prudent and diligent emperor knew that

> The vessel long retains the scent  
> With which it was once freshly steeped.  
> —HORACE, *Epistles* I.69

He knew also that things learned in childhood are absorbed not only more quickly but more perfectly. Military agility, jumping, and running must be acquired and trained before the body grows sluggish with age. For speed gained and strengthened by practice makes an energetic warrior. Nor does it matter much, provided the other marks of courage concur, whether they are tall or of shorter stature. It is more useful for soldiers to be brave than large. Pyrrhus is said to have told his recruiting officer: “You choose large men; I shall make them brave.”

When Greece celebrated solemn games at the tomb of Archemorus, Tydeus is famously said to have surpassed Capaneus because

> Greater valour reigned in his small body.

Sallust records concerning the training of Pompey the Great that he competed in jumping with the agile, running with the swift, and lifting a beam with the strong. For he could not otherwise have matched Sertorius unless he had prepared himself and his soldiers for battles by frequent exercises [Col. 0595D]. The art of retreating, assaulting, and leaping upon an opponent is no slight matter. It preserves the precaution that a soldier, in rising against an enemy to inflict a wound, does not expose himself to a blow from some quarter.

Training in swimming is very useful, since no one can foresee what necessity may produce in battle by land or sea, and no one can readily escape dangers by an art he has not learned. The use of missiles also is of the greatest importance: by them an enemy is wounded or frightened from afar; their practice strengthens the arms and acquires skill and experience in throwing. Constant practice in so great an exercise made soldiers fearless and effective in the tumult of war because they had been so diligently trained in peace [Col. 0596A].

We also read that the aforementioned Augustus had his daughters trained in wool-working, so that, if fortune beyond expectation should cast them into utter poverty, they could support life by a craft after their resources had been exhausted. For they possessed not merely knowledge but practice and habitual use of spinning, weaving, using the needle, and shaping, making, and arranging garments. The man who did not indulge idleness in maidens certainly did not allow soldiers to be idle, whose profession is ordained for labour. Nor do I believe he would have boasted of softer dress among soldiers when his own daughter did not dare approach him except with a sterner expression and more modest clothing.

Lucan commends Cato and Roman military service in a brief encomium, adding among other things that his costly manner of dress was to draw a rough toga over his limbs in the Roman fashion of a Quirite:

> A rough toga drawn over his limbs,  
> In the Roman fashion of a Quirite.  
> —LUCAN, II.386

He surely would not have said this unless the use of a rougher toga had derived from the custom of the Quirites. But now “those who are clothed in soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 9)—indeed, in camps—and proceed to war whitened as though to weddings [Col. 0596B]. They protect themselves by the great privileges of ancient military service, because in this they imitate it particularly well: they are ignorant of the laws. This would be tolerable if they did not equally despise divine and human laws, so that, whether you wish it or not, that line from the satirist frequently comes to mind:

> “I am Dinomachus; puff me up: I am radiant—so be it,  
> Provided Pannucia Baucis knows no worse  
> When she has sung basil to a loose-girt slave.”  
> —PERSIUS, IV.20 ff.

## Chapter V. The two chief things that make a soldier: selection and equipment

Do not suppose, however, that I am hostile to military service or turn the vices of persons against the office itself. I undertake its defence against anyone’s opposition and, with the Lord as its author, shall defend it most sufficiently. For the profession is as praiseworthy as it is necessary, and no one can condemn it without violating reverence for God, by whom it was instituted. Review the course of the Old Testament, and you will find it to be as I say. It makes no difference that these men transgress, since the law of military service has not been laid down for them and, properly speaking, none of them is a soldier.

Read both ecclesiastical and secular books that deal with military matters, and you will plainly find that two things make a soldier: selection and the oath [Col. 0596C]. These two are common to those who perform spiritual and bodily military service. The bishop’s voice calls the former to the ministry of the altar and worship of the Church; the commander’s voice selects the latter for the defence of the commonwealth. The writings of the ancients explain which persons and in what manner are to be selected for either office and station. But since secular military service is now in hand, let us hear Vegetius Renatus on the selection of soldiers. He says:

“In this the safety of the whole commonwealth turns: recruits of outstanding quality must be selected not only in body but also in spirit. The strength of the empire and the foundation of the Roman name rest upon the first examination of the levy. This duty must not be thought light, nor indiscriminately entrusted to anyone; among the ancients it is especially agreed to have been praised amid so many kinds of virtue. For the youth upon whom the defence of the provinces rests ought to excel both in character and strength. Honourable character makes a suitable soldier; modesty, by preventing flight, often makes him victorious. What good is it if an inferior man is trained and lingers in camp through many terms of service? An army whose selection limped in testing recruits never prospers in time of war.

“And, as we have learned from practice and experience, hence have come all the defeats inflicted by enemies everywhere: prolonged peace selects soldiers too carelessly; useless men pursue civil employments; and recruits demanded from landholders, through the favour or connivance of those examining them, are joined to the army who are the sort their masters disdain to keep [Col. 0596D]. Therefore suitable young men must be selected by eminent men and with great care. Once diligent selection has been approved by examination, those found fit for service must be marked and enrolled. Speed, strength, ability to learn the discipline of arms, and military confidence must all be sought. For many who do not appear unacceptable in appearance are nevertheless proved unworthy by trial. The less useful must therefore be rejected and the most vigorous substituted in their place. In every conflict, valour benefits more than numbers.”

In examining, forming, and advancing that valour lie both the work and the judgment of the commander. Once recruits have been enrolled, the instruction must be demonstrated by daily weapons-training, so that they may become vigorous soldiers, whether lightly or heavily armed, on land or sea, infantry or cavalry.

## Chapter VI. What evils arise among us from neglecting the selection of soldiers, and how Harald subdued the Welsh

But the practice of this discipline has fallen into disuse, whether through the indulgence of prolonged security, or through the onset of softness and luxury that breaks the spirits of men, or through the indolence of youth and the inertia of commanders in our time [Col. 0598A]. For whom will you find able vigorously to teach what he has not himself learned?

> Now we endure the evils of prolonged peace;  
> Luxury, more cruel than arms, has settled upon us  
> And takes vengeance upon a conquered world.  
> —JUVENAL, VI.291 ff.

Review ancient and modern histories and you will plainly find that the disturbance of peoples, clash of arms, slaughter of men, and terrible scourge always either accompany or follow luxury. To avoid seeking examples far away: the Snowdonians rush upon the Britons, already extend their borders, and, emerging from their caverns and forest hiding-places, occupy the plains; before the very eyes of noble lords they attack, capture [Col. 0598B], and destroy or retain for themselves fortifications, because our youth—
Which rejoices in shelter and shade, born to consume crops, sleeping by daylight, preferring prostitution to honorable duties, pursuing pleasure all day long, and recognizing the cithara, lyre, tambourine, and the sound of the organ more readily at banquets than the trumpet or bugle in camp. In such a force, either the selection of the commander was absent or mistaken, and discipline has either ceased or grown weak. For if there is need to join battle, they have little confidence in light equipment and the least eagerness in heavy armour. With the latter they are burdened so that they cannot pursue the enemy; by the former they are exhausted, so that, as men exposed to a wound, they cannot withstand him.

The enemy ravage our borders. While our youth [Col. 0598C] are being trained and our soldiers equipped, the enemy escapes; and, as the saying goes, while the dog grumbles, the wolf enters secure hiding-places. There is no one to seize him as he departs or pursue the enemy, because one encumbered can neither keep up with nor make progress against one unencumbered. Yet he does not seek the protection of walls or ditches, but ground that is accessible to his own soldier as well as mine—though it may not be equally familiar to both. He is certainly secure there, because my soldier trusts not in his own strength but in the protection of his weapons.

Recent English history relates that, when the Britons had made an incursion and were ravaging England, King Edward—a most devout king—sent against them the commander Harold: a man indeed vigorous in arms, resplendent with the marks of praiseworthy deeds, and one who might have enlarged among posterity both his own glory and that of his followers, had he not, imitating his father’s wickedness, stained the titles of his merits by treacherously usurping the kingdom. When, therefore, he understood the nimbleness of that people, he chose, as though selecting troops equally matched for combat, to engage them with an unencumbered force. Wearing light armour, splendidly arrayed, covered with bands and very hard leather, holding small shields in his left hand against their missiles, and hurling at them now javelins, now wielding the sword, he clung so closely to the tracks of those fleeing that he was pressed:

> Foot against foot, spear against spear, and shield-boss drove back shield-boss.

Having entered the Snowy Hill, he devastated everything; and, when the campaign had been prolonged for two years, [Col. 0599A] he captured the kings and presented their heads to the king who had sent him. Killing with the edge of the sword every male he could find, even to the arousing of compassion for little children, he pacified the province. He established a law that, if thereafter any Briton were found bearing a weapon on this side of the boundary prescribed to them—namely, Offa’s Dyke—officials of the kingdom should cut off his right hand. By the commander’s valor the Britons were then so thoroughly crushed that almost the entire people seemed likely to perish; and, through the indulgence of the aforesaid king, their women married Englishmen. Do you see how greatly the selection of a commander and the military training of youth contribute?

## CHAPTER VII. What the nature of the military oath is, and why it is unlawful to serve as a soldier without it

[Col. 0599B] Nevertheless, under the ancient law no one was invested with the military belt apart from the religious bond of the oath. For, as we read in Julius Frontinus, in the consulship of Lucius Flaccus and Gaius Varro soldiers were first made by an oath. Previously, oaths were merely administered by tribunes. Besides this, the soldiers themselves bound one another by oath that they would not leave their place through flight or fear, nor withdraw from the ranks, except to seek a missile, strike an enemy, or save a fellow citizen. This was called the military oath; it is confirmed both by the authority and by the practice of most Christian princes.

The wording of the oath, according to Vegetius, is as follows. Soldiers swear by God, by His Christ, by the Holy Spirit, and by the majesty of the prince, [Col. 0599C] which, after God, ought to be loved and revered by humankind. (For when someone has received lawful sovereignty, faithful devotion must be offered to him as to a God present in bodily form, and unceasing service rendered. For whether private person or soldier, one serves God when one faithfully loves him who reigns by God’s appointment.) They swear, I say, that they will vigorously carry out everything the prince commands, that they will never desert military service, and that they will not refuse death for the commonwealth in whose army they are enrolled.

Once they have taken this oath, they are invested with the military belt and its privileges. Thus it became established that selection and oath made the soldier: no one was enrolled or sworn without selection, and without the oath no one acquired the name or office of soldier.

In the *On Duties*, Marcus Tullius reports that the commander Pompilius held a province in whose army Cato’s son was serving as a recruit. When Pompilius decided to discharge one legion, he discharged Cato’s son also, because he served in that legion. But since, from a love of fighting, the young man remained in the army, Cato wrote to Pompilius asking that, if he permitted him to remain in the army, he should bind him by a second oath, because, having lost the first, he could not lawfully fight against the enemy.

There is also a letter of Marcus Cato the Elder to his son Marcus, in which he writes that he had heard that his son had been discharged by the consul while serving in Macedonia in the Persian war. He therefore warns him to take care not to enter battle; for, he says, it is not lawful for one who is not a soldier to fight an enemy. Behold: this exceedingly wise man did not consider anyone a soldier [Col. 0600A] unless he had been consecrated to military service by an oath.

## CHAPTER VIII. That armed service is necessarily bound to religion, just as is the service consecrated in the clergy to divine worship; and that “soldier” is a name both of honor and of labor

But consider the words of the oath itself, and you will find that armed service, no less than spiritual service, is necessarily bound by the duty of its office to religion and the worship of God, since faithful obedience according to God is owed to the prince, and watchful service to the commonwealth. Hence, as I said before, those who have neither been selected nor sworn, even if they are counted under the name of soldiers, are no more truly soldiers than are priests and clerics whom the Church has not called to orders.

For “soldier” is a name of labor as well as honor. No one takes honor to himself, but he who is called by the Lord (Hebrews 5) glories in the honor bestowed upon him. When enemies had to be attacked, Moses and the leaders of the faithful people chose strong men, most skilled for war. Such things precede selection. But whoever, not having been selected, thrusts himself into military service provokes the sword against himself, which he usurps through his own rashness. He therefore falls under the perpetual ordinance: “Whoever takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26).

If Cicero’s authority is accepted on this point, such a person is rightly called not a soldier but an assassin. For in ancient writings *sicarii* means both assassins and robbers: all who handle weapons without the law’s command. Weapons which the law does not employ attack the law. The sacred history of the Gospel testifies that two swords suffice for Christian rule; all other swords belong to those who come with swords and clubs to seize Christ captive, desiring to erase His name.

What, then, have those men of the soldier about them who, although summoned by oath, do not obey the law, but think that the glory of their military service consists in making the priesthood contemptible, diminishing the authority of the Church, enlarging the kingdom of man so that Christ’s dominion is contracted, trumpeting their praises, and soothing and exalting themselves with false proclamations, to the mockery of their hearers, like the boastful soldier? Their valor shines most brightly, they think, when they pierce clergy and the unarmed soldiery with either tongues or weapons.

But what is the purpose of ordered military service? To protect the Church, assail faithlessness, honor the priesthood, repel injuries done to the poor, pacify the province, shed blood for one’s brothers—as the wording of the oath teaches—and, if necessary, lay down one’s life.

> The praises of God are in their mouths,  
> and two-edged swords in their hands,  
> to execute vengeance among the nations  
> and rebukes among the peoples;  
> to bind their kings in fetters  
> and their nobles in iron shackles  
> (Psalm 149).

But to what end? That they may serve rage, vanity, greed, or their own will? By no means. Rather, “that they may execute upon them the judgment written” (ibid.), in which each person follows, in fairness and for the public good, not so much his own judgment as that of God, angels, and humankind. “That they may execute,” I say: for as it belongs to judges to pronounce judgment, so it belongs to these men, in executing it, to perform their office. “This honor have all His saints” (ibid.). For soldiers acting thus are saints; and they are more faithful to their prince insofar as they more zealously preserve faith toward God, and they promote the glory of their valor more profitably insofar as they seek in all things more faithfully the glory of their God.

## CHAPTER IX. That faith owed to God must be preferred to every human being, and is not preserved toward human beings unless it is preserved toward God

It makes no difference whether one serves a faithful or an unfaithful ruler, provided one serves with faith intact. The faithful are recorded to have served Diocletian, Julian, and other impious men, rendering them faithfulness and reverence as princes in defense of the commonwealth. For they fought [Col. 0601B] the enemies of the empire, but kept God’s commandments. Princes sat and accused them; they were exercised in the Lord’s ordinances, speaking steadfastly and carrying out His commands without shame and with complete confidence.

David too is recorded to have served Achish, fulfilling the faithfulness and reverence owed by one in military service. This rule must be prescribed and fulfilled for every army: first, faith owed to God must be preserved inviolate; then faith toward the prince and the commonwealth. Greater obligations must always take precedence over lesser ones, for neither loyalty to the commonwealth nor loyalty to the prince is to be kept against God, but according to God, as the very wording of the military oath provides.

I am therefore greatly astonished if any prince places trust in persons whom he sees failing to preserve the faith owed to their God—toward whom, to say nothing else, they are bound even by the military oath. What disease of reason afflicts a man who believes that someone will be faithful to him when he sees him corrupt and faithless toward the One to whom he owes most? “But he fears the prince.” Certainly, if someone stronger should arrive, he will fear that one still more. “Perhaps he loves the prince.” But if someone kinder and more generous appears, he will love that person more. The impious person who prefers a human being to God has no direction in which he will not turn; one who makes the first faith void will never keep the second.

## CHAPTER X. On the privileges of soldiers; that they are bound by oath to the Church; and why the sword is offered at the altar

[Col. 0601D] Soldiers rightly have many privileges, which are broadly established by ancient law. Their provisions are more generous, and they enjoy more exemptions. They are exempt from compulsory transport services, from the provision of post-horses, and from degrading public burdens. They may legally be ignorant of the laws; and though they are under paternal authority, they may make a will concerning their military property. Most importantly, public provision does not permit them to be needy. There are many further privileges of this kind, too lengthy to recount.

Although some may appear not to be bound to the Church by a solemn oath because, by custom, it is now commonly not performed, nevertheless no one is exempt from being bound to the Church by an implicit or explicit oath. Perhaps the solemnity of the oath has ceased because every necessity of the office and the sincerity of faith alike invite and compel one to this end.

Thus a solemn custom has now taken root: on the very day on which someone is adorned with the military belt, he solemnly enters a church and, placing and offering his sword upon the altar, as though making a public profession, devotes himself to the service of the altar and promises God perpetual service through the sword—that is, through his office. Nor need he profess this in words, since a lawful profession of military service is seen to be incorporated in the act itself. Who would demand a literary profession from an unlettered man, one who ought to know arms more than letters? Bishops and abbots appear to be bound to faith and obedience by a written or spoken profession. And they truly are bound, because one may not lie to God. Yet what soldiers do is either greater, or no less: they offer not a written document but a sword, [Col. 0602B] and as though redeeming from the altar the first-fruits of their office, so that they may serve the Church forever. For as much is permitted them on behalf of the Church, so nothing is permitted against the Church.

Luke relates that soldiers came to John in order to be baptized, asking, “Teacher, what shall we also do?” And he said to them, “Extort from no one, make no false accusation, and be content with your pay” (Luke 3). A faithful saying, worthy of every acceptance (1 Timothy 1), fitting for the forerunner of grace, herald of truth, and precursor of the Lord. For he knew that the hand of the soldier was ready for wrongdoing, accustomed to plunder, and that what soldiers possess never, or rarely, suffices them without their desiring another’s property. By forbidding extortion, therefore, he excluded injuries; by excluding false accusation, he eliminated plunder. He also condemned greed when he commanded each person to be content with his pay. For, as has been said, a soldier may not be needy: while serving, he receives military pay; and when he has completed his service, estates or maintenance are publicly provided, insofar as necessity requires.

## CHAPTER XI. That soldiers must be punished more severely if, despising military law, they abuse their privileges

If, contrary to John’s prohibition and lawful enactments, a soldier lapses into theft and robbery, he must be punished more severely, as one who has always handled iron and harsh things. His boldness must be restrained in such a way that he learns in himself how sternly those must be punished who attack the law which they undertook to defend.

[Col. 0602D] For as military service enjoys many immunities and higher privileges, so it must be subjected to harsher penalties if it is proved to have forfeited its privileges. Ignorance of the law does not benefit the soldier in this respect: although public laws may be permitted to be unknown, it is not permitted for him to be ignorant of his own office. A priest, for example, may be ignorant at his ordination of the difficulty of his order; yet, because he succeeds without objection to a burdensome office, he is obliged to bear the burdens of the priesthood he has undertaken. If he neglects them or acts maliciously, he will be rebuked more severely, because those to whom much honor is owed are worthy of greater punishment when they are found guilty, openly or secretly.

Crimes, however, are punished differently from transgressions: crimes generally incur the penalty of blood, whereas transgressions demand a remedial treatment proportionate to the offense. That treatment is sometimes simple, sometimes mixed with a certain severity. Yet although discipline is necessary in every profession, it is nowhere more necessary than in the clergy and in military affairs. Military affairs, being less exercised in the spirit, must be punished more harshly in the body.

Nothing attacks both more than luxury, because every form of intemperance is strongly opposed to order. Where there is no order, moreover, confusion takes its place; and unless it is restrained by the spur of correction, it undoubtedly brings disgrace as a necessary consequence. What can a man do bravely when luxury and intemperance have not merely disarmed him but drained his spirit?

The fourth book of Julius Frontinus’s *Strategems* [Col. 0603B] relates that Publius Scipio, sent to Numantia, reformed an army corrupted by the negligence of previous commanders. He dismissed a vast number of camp-followers and reduced the soldiers to their duty through daily exercise. Since he frequently ordered them to march, he commanded them to carry provisions for several days, so that the soldier might become accustomed to enduring cold and rain and crossing river-fords on foot. The commander repeatedly reproached them for cowardice and idleness, and destroyed vessels of more luxurious use and little necessity for a campaign.

This is said to have happened most notably to the tribune Gaius Numnius, to whom Scipio is reported to have said: “For a short time you will be worthless to me; forever you will be worthless to yourself and the commonwealth.”

Quintus Metellus likewise restored, in the Jugurthine War, military discipline that had fallen away, with equal severity; indeed, he forbade soldiers to eat any meat except roasted or boiled. When Philip first organized his army, he prohibited the use of wagons for all; he allowed cavalrymen no more than one *lacon* each, and infantrymen one for every ten, to carry mills and ropes. When they went out to summer quarters, he commanded them to carry thirty days’ flour around their necks.

Gaius Marius, in order to cut down the baggage that especially burdens an army’s march, fastened a soldier’s utensils and provisions, packed in bundles, to forked poles, under which there could be both a convenient load and easy rest. Hence arose the proverb, “Marius’ soldiers are mules.”

Lysander the Spartan punished a man who had left the line of march. When the man said that he had not left the column to plunder anything, Lysander replied: “I do not want you even to give the appearance of one about to plunder.”

Although there was no need for naval operations in winter quarters, Publius Nasica nevertheless began building ships, lest the soldiers be corrupted by idleness or, through the license of leisure, inflict injury upon allies.

Frontinus also relates, among many examples of constancy, that while Hannibal was besieging Casilinum, the inhabitants suffered such great want that a mouse is recorded to have been sold for one hundred denarii. Its seller died of hunger, but its purchaser lived; and amid such distress they kept faith with the Romans. The people of Petelia, besieged by the Carthaginians, expelled their parents and children because of the shortage. They themselves prolonged life on moistened and fire-dried hides, leaves of trees, and every kind of animal, and endured the siege for eleven months.

The Spanish Fabrenses endured all the same hardships, yet did not surrender their town to Herculeius. When Mithridates besieged Cyzicus, he brought forward captives from that city and showed them to those under siege, believing that pity for their own people would compel the townsfolk to surrender. But they encouraged the captives to meet death bravely and kept faith with the Romans.
