The people of Eglovina, when Juriacus offered them back their children and wives, preferred to watch the punishments of their own dear ones rather than defect from the Romans. The Numantines, lest they surrender, preferred to die of hunger after fastening shut the doors of their houses; and, according to Orosius, they would have defeated the Romans had those Romans not fought under Scipio.

## CHAPTER XII. That varying punishments were imposed on those who disobeyed their commander; how far obedience is due; and in what commands military judgment has a place, and in what commands it does not

[Col. 0604B]

Various punishments were imposed upon those who did not obey the commander’s or the law’s decision. Some were punished in property, others in reputation, and others in blood. Read Frontinus and you will find this everywhere to be so.

When the consul Aurelius Cotta, compelled by necessity, ordered cavalrymen to assist with labor and some of them rejected the command, he complained before the censors and obtained their branding by the fathers; he then secured an order that their past pay should not be issued. The tribunes of the plebs also brought the matter before the people, and discipline was established by everyone’s consent.

In Spain Quintus Metellus Macedonicus ordered five cohorts that had yielded ground to the enemy to make wills; he then sent them to recover the position, threatening that they would not be received back except after victory. When the soldiers of Publius Valerius had been disgracefully put to flight, the Senate decreed that no reinforcements should be sent to him until the enemy had been defeated. The legions that had refused service during the Punic War were banished, as it were, to Sicily, and for seven years were given barley by decree of the Senate.

By the decision of Appius Claudius and a decree of the Senate, all those captured by Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, and later released, were reduced from cavalry to infantry; all were ordered to encamp outside the rampart with light equipment until each had brought back two enemy spoils. These are Frontinus’s accounts.

But Pliny asserts that this too was once a military punishment: a soldier might, for disgrace, be ordered to have a vein opened and blood let. Although he could not find the reason for this in ancient writings, he nevertheless thinks it was first done to soldiers of stunned mind and departed from their natural condition, so that it seemed not so much a punishment as a remedy. Later, however, he believes that it came by custom to be done for many other offenses, as though all who sinned against their duty were regarded as less than sound.

For disgraceful punishment was not a light penalty, although even it, given the vigor of military discipline, left no place for indulgent disregard. It is widely reported that the ancient Greeks wore a ring on the finger of the left hand next to the smallest; the Romans too are said generally to have used rings in this manner. Apion, in his Egyptian books, gives the reason: through the dissection and opening of bodies, as was customary—what the Greeks call *anatomás* (ἀνατομάς)—it was discovered that a very fine nerve reaches and proceeds from that one finger of which we have spoken to the human heart. It was therefore thought that this finger especially should be adorned with such an honor, since it seemed attached and, as it were, connected with the heart’s governing power. Hence they thought that those who had sinned in military duty, being as it were out of their minds, should be treated or punished.

To return to Frontinus: Crassus, according to Sempronius Asellio and very many other writers of Roman history, possessed five greatest and foremost advantages: he was the richest, the noblest, the most eloquent, the most learned in law, and chief pontiff. While he held Asia as his province during his consulship and was preparing to surround and besiege Leucae, he needed a very large and tall beam for constructing a battering ram to strike the town’s walls. He wrote to Gaius Magnus, the chief man among the Athenians, allies and friends of the Roman people, asking him to arrange for the larger of two masts which he had seen among them to be sent.

Gaius Magnus, learning why Crassus wanted the mast, sent not the larger one, as ordered, but the smaller, which he judged more suitable and more convenient for making a ram and easier to carry. Crassus ordered him summoned; when he asked why he had not sent the one ordered, he rejected the reasons and arguments he gave, ordered his clothes stripped off, and had him severely beaten with rods. He believed that every duty of one giving commands would be destroyed and dissolved if, when someone was ordered to do something, he responded not with due obedience but with unsolicited advice.

What more, I ask, could a severe abbot have commanded of a monk under a stricter rule? For the man had sinned in this alone: he had not obeyed the command, even if perhaps what he did was in fact more useful. For just as those living in religion ought not to scrutinize but to fulfill the commands of their superiors, so long as those commands do not oppose a perpetual precept, so in military affairs there is no military examination of a commander’s commands, unless what is ordered is found expressly contrary to the safety of the commonwealth. [Col. 0605D] In such a matter only a faithless and impious soldier obeys.

For what is more unjust or more detestable than to undertake, without reverence for faith, whatever the commander may dictate? Is not this, among all people, a dreadful and cruel voice, full of treachery?

> If you order me to plunge a sword into my brother’s breast  
> or my father’s throat, and deep into the pregnant womb  
> of my wife, I shall nevertheless carry out everything with unwilling hand.  
>   
> If you order a camp pitched above the waters of Tuscan Tiber,  
> boldly I shall come to survey the western fields.  
> Whatever walls you wish thrown down upon the plain,  
> the battering ram, driven by these arms, shall scatter their stones.  
> Though the city you command to be utterly destroyed  
> be Rome itself.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* VI.810.)

What more wicked thing could be said? What should more deeply offend a Roman commander, if he were faithful? For in that very act the criminal soldier endeavors to prove the faithfulness of his allegiance, and thereby proves himself most faithless and treacherous.

Great reverence is indeed owed to a commander, but with the sacred obligation of faith preserved. Some things are so necessary that they do not await a command; others are so detestable that they admit no command at all. Intermediate matters, which are neither necessary goods nor detestable evils, depend upon the decision of the superior.

Whether the commander wills it or not, God must be loved by necessity of the good. Whether the commander wills it or not, adultery must be avoided by reason of the evil of iniquity. But serving as a soldier or not serving, setting out or not setting out, and other matters which philosophers call indifferent, belong to the diligence and reverence due to the superior. In such matters, to open one’s eyes without the superior’s command, or irreverently to stretch out one’s hand on one’s own initiative toward the result of any work, is equivalent to a crime.

Let the subordinate be blind in this respect, that he may live; for on whatever day he rashly reaches out, as by his own judgment, toward the tree of knowledge—which the Lord reserves for Himself and for superiors—he incurs the noose of death. For subordinates are not permitted to judge what is good or evil in such matters, while full reverence is shown to superiors and faithful obedience to their commands.

Therefore, in all matters belonging to the public order, a soldier is not permitted to attempt anything whatever unless what he has decided to do is confirmed by the commander’s order or permission. Hence those who, despising or not awaiting their commanders’ orders, entered battle with the enemy and won victory for the commonwealth, [Col. 0606C] often obtained not so much glory from victory as punishment for their rashness or negligence. What, then, will the deserter or abandoner of his post deserve, if a victor is rebuked with such severity under military discipline?

In Julius’s *Strategems*, Clearchus, commander of the Spartans, is said to have declared that an army ought to fear its commander more than the enemy, because those who feared the uncertain death of battle had a certain punishment awaiting them if they abandoned their station.

Lucius Papirius Cursor ordered Fabius Rullianus, master of the horse, to be scourged because he had fought against his orders, though successfully, and was about to strike him with an axe. He would not yield in imposing the punishment to the soldiers’ resistance or prayers, and pursued the fugitive all the way to Rome. Even there fear did not remit the punishment until Fabius and his father threw themselves at his knees and the Senate and people together pleaded.

Nor should you suppose that he did this out of prior hatred. Manlius, later surnamed Imperiosus, had his son—who had fought the enemy contrary to his father’s edict, though he was victorious—scourged in sight of the army and struck with an axe. Military discipline was as necessary to the commonwealth as it was welcome to everyone. Indeed, when the army was preparing a mutiny against Manlius the father on behalf of the son, the son denied that anyone was important enough for military discipline to be corrupted on his account, and obtained their consent for his own punishment.

Appius Claudius selected by lot every tenth soldier among those who had given ground and beat them with a staff. Fabius Rutilius, the consul, selected by lot twenty men from two legions that had given ground and struck them with an axe in sight of the soldiers. The same man condemned three from each century whose station had been broken through by the enemy to the axe. Quintus Fabius Maximus cut off the right hands of deserters. Marcus Cato handed down that the right hands of men caught stealing from fellow soldiers were cut off, or, if they wished to punish the accused more leniently, blood was let in the headquarters.

Mutiny, too, calls for the axe, though in accordance with the commander’s judgment, so that by the punishment of a few the security and peace of the commonwealth may be restored. When a mutiny of soldiers arose, Julius Caesar is recorded to have calmed the camp and restored the soldiers’ loyalty by striking down a few.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why soldiers are deprived of the belt; that one dismissed from service may have no dealings with sword or weapon; and why the sword is inserted in the belt

[Col. 0607B]

It sometimes happens that because of his offense a soldier is deprived of the military belt, especially where sacrileges are committed. For ancient law established—and new law has not abolished—that a person who, without preserving the military oath, attacks the religion he professes must be punished by loss of the belt. Julius is said to have restrained his soldiers by this edict when, upon entering a city, they were forbidden to plunder persons or the temples of the gods; later, as the mutiny intensified, this was thrown in his face. For those who had sworn allegiance to the Roman gods and citizens could not attack those whom, by the military oath, [Col. 0607C] they had undertaken to defend.

Likewise, during the Dardanian War near Dyrrhachium, when Gaius Curio saw one of his five legions in mutiny, he ordered it to come forward unarmed and without belts; before the armed army he compelled its members to cut straw. Finally, he made the soldiers, again without belts, dig a ditch; and no entreaties of the legion could obtain from him that he should not lower its standards and abolish its name. He distributed the soldiers as replacements among other legions. For those who had deserved deprivation of the belt were not restored before merits of valor distinguished them beyond the rest.

The soldiers who had been exiled to Sicily after retreating from the battle of Cannae petitioned the consul Marcus Marcellus to lead them into battle. He consulted the Senate, and the Senate declared that it did not approve entrusting the commonwealth to those who had abandoned it. Yet it permitted Marcellus to do what he thought fit, under the stated condition that none of them should be excused from duty, receive a reward or honor, or be brought back into Italy while the Carthaginians remained there.

While they are stripped of the belt, soldiers neither receive their pay nor enjoy military privileges, nor may they have any dealings with a sword or weapon. Thus, by the provident ordinance of the ancestors, the sword is inserted in the belt, so that, with the honor of the belt conferred, the authority of the sword itself may also be understood to have been conferred in some measure. And anyone who enters military service is rightly adorned with the belt, because the necessity of his office requires that he be unencumbered for the duties of the commonwealth. A person with tasks impending is customarily girded; one who is given leave may be ungirded.

Hence this saying in the Book of Kings: “Let not the one who is girded boast as the one who is ungirded” (3 Kings 20). For concern over impending labor does not permit freedom to boast, whereas the liberty of idleness and security of rest commonly produces arrogance. The belt, therefore, is a sign of labor, and labor is the merit of honor, so that all may understand that whoever refuses to undertake the labor imposed by military service bears the honor of the sword in the military belt in vain.

The belt’s own significance is likewise empty unless labor strengthens and confirms its faithfulness. You may see many swelling with the honor of the belt; but unless arduous merits fulfill that honor, it is as though someone claimed froth as a solid substance. Certainly he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses authority granted to him. A person abuses it either by failing to do what ought to be done or by doing what ought not to be done. Though each is evil, sin is usually said to be graver than fault. For one commits a fault who does not fulfill his duty; but plainly anyone who commits the opposite sins.

Black is more opposed to white than is non-white; sadness attacks happiness more than hope or fear, which neither fall under the category of happiness nor are most contrary to it. Accordingly, the person who fails to fulfill what he ought under the military oath abuses the belt, as does one who attacks the military oath. But one who attacks it sins more gravely, just as a true enemy is more hateful than a cowardly soldier.

Hence whoever attacks the commonwealth and an unarmed body of people with military arms is most justly dismissed from service, as one who has assumed the guise of an enemy. Yet above all others, by divine and human law, those who commit sacrilege and those who attack the Church of God with various disturbances are punished more severely; the law imposes upon them not the cutting off of right hands but capital punishment.

Even if Cicero and Demosthenes assumed their defense, even if Quintilian sharpened his tongue in their defense and exhausted all the powers of his genius, if the laws retain force, they could not protect their property and lives from lawful penalties—matters which, after God, are in the prince’s hand. If the prince does not draw his sword against such people, he undoubtedly provokes against himself the two-edged sword which the Son of Man bears in His mouth: the sword that is “living and effective” (Hebrews 4), which divides body and soul and casts into Gehenna. Before it every sword is blunt, and every armor frail, shifting, and weak, except that which grace alone constructs in the fabric of good merits.

There are many who, by the outcry of their evil works, when they offered at the altar the belt by which they were to be consecrated to military service, seem to declare that they then approached with the intention of declaring war upon the altar and its ministers, and also upon God, who is worshiped there. I would more readily believe that these men were accursed for wickedness than consecrated to lawful military service.

## CHAPTER XIV. That military discipline is highly beneficial, and what especially destroys military service

[Col. 0609A]

Therefore military discipline is necessary; how great its usefulness is I could not easily say. For, as has been stated, discipline profited the Romans so greatly that they subjected the world to their rule. Alexander of Macedon likewise received from his father a small body of soldiers, but a trained one; accustomed to warfare, with it he assailed the whole world and routed countless forces of enemies. Xerxes, harassed by three hundred Spartans at Thermopylae, when he had scarcely overcome them with an infinite host and at the loss of very many of his own men, said that he had been deceived in this: he possessed indeed many human beings, but no men steadfast in discipline. This he said truly, as that flight testifies in which, shamefully defeated at [Col. 0609B] Salamis, he who had drawn so many nations into war that their commanders could not readily be numbered, scarcely escaped in a single ship. For it is reported that, because of their multitude, he was accustomed to count the commanders of his army in no other way than by having each man receive a missile, so that the number of missiles might preserve the number of commanders.

A commander is altogether useless where discipline does not flourish; and he vainly hopes for victory who does not continually train the spirits and hands of his soldiers. A suddenly raised soldier suddenly deserts his commander, and cannot endure toil when continuous toil has not trained him. Confidence strengthened Caesar’s resolution because he had to deal with an unseasoned soldier and a commander grown old in service, who through the long repose of peace had unlearned how to command. [Col. 0609C] But even where victory is despaired of, the mind must be raised to hope for vengeance. For sometimes

> The one safety for the conquered is to hope for no safety,  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* II.364)

so that they may consider themselves victors if they do not die unavenged. For it counts as a great reward to be satisfied with vengeance, and the loss of life is compensated by the consolation of revenge. He readily accepts the necessity of fighting upon whom the difficulty of flight is imposed. Those who bring war are bolder; and often others, while wishing to die honourably and manfully, win happily.

> For Fortune helps the daring,  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* X.284)

and when the peril of battle hangs near,

> Fear exposes base spirits,  
> [Col. 0609D] (Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.13)

than which nothing is more disgraceful to those who profess the name and office of military service. For military law punishes the cowardly most severely.

A commander too must take the greatest care in military affairs

> Lest Venus and wine break fighting breasts.

For luxury always conquers—but only those whom it has first corrupted. It must therefore be avoided all the more diligently because it rages most fiercely in bringing men into its own bondage. Antiochus equipped his army with such luxury and superfluity that even common soldiers made themselves gold boots and trampled underfoot the material for whose love peoples fight. The nation of the Parthians too is very often defeated because it is exceedingly luxurious. For

> Whatever slopes toward the eastern regions and the warmth of the world,  
> [Col. 0610A] the mildness of the sky softens the nations.  
> (Lucan VIII.365)

They do not usually fight hand-to-hand in line of battle; rather, so far as they can, they wound the enemy from a distance. They do not know how to take besieged cities by delay and strength. They fight while their horses are charging forward or retreating; often they even feign flight. By ancient custom their signal is given not by trumpet but by drum. Nor can they fight long; for they would be intolerable if their perseverance equalled the greatness of their onset. By nature they are silent, readier to act than to speak. They are sparing in food; they have no fidelity to word or promise. They obey their rulers from fear, not shame or religion.

A principality corrupted by luxury cannot stand long. Or, if it does stand, [Col. 0610B] when God’s judgment presses upon it, it will vomit out all that luxury’s excess has swallowed. For it knows no measure of itself, nor checks intemperance before it slips, from more indulgent licence, into extreme shamefulness. Examine the regions of the Assyrians, and historical testimony will prove that their kingdoms were overthrown by the force of luxury. Among other things Trogus relates that Sardanapalus, the last king of the Assyrians, reigned—a man more corrupted than a woman. A prefect, having with great eagerness scarcely obtained admission to see him, a thing permitted to none before him, found him among troops of prostitutes, spinning purple thread, in woman’s dress; in bodily softness and wantonness of eye he surpassed all women, and he distributed tasks of wool among maidens. Outraged at the thought that so many men [Col. 0610C] were to be subject to such a woman, and that men handling iron and bearing arms should obey him, the prefect went out to his companions and reported what he had seen. He declared that he could not obey one who preferred to be a woman rather than a man. A conspiracy was therefore formed. Hearing of it, that king withdrew into the royal palace. There, having erected and set fire to a pyre, he cast both himself and his riches into the flames: in this alone imitating a man.

The strength of the preceding kings had indeed been softened by luxury; then, as softness grew by individual stages, it was at last made effeminate, broken, and crushed in him. The Roman Empire too was almost drained and torn apart under Nero’s rule: his gluttony devoured nearly everything, lust defiled it, greed exhausted it, cowardice broke it, and luxury together with pride emptied it. He did not wear any garment twice, that in at least one respect he might shine before others with singular glory. But while Rome allowed it, he made the whole world inglorious. What the industry of others had acquired, his idleness almost lost.

## Chapter XV. That the Romans excelled others in discipline, and that Julius Caesar flourished among them above all others

But when I review and reconsider the examples of all nations, the discipline of the Romans shines above the rest. Discipline is also recorded to have profited the Moesians greatly: having overcome their neighbours despite their small numbers, they dared contend with the Romans for dominion over nations. How fierce they were may be inferred from words spoken by one of their commanders to men about to fight the Romans. After demanding silence before the battle-line, he said: “Who are you [Col. 0611A]?” The answer was: “Romans, lords of nations.” And he replied: “That will be so, if you conquer us.” At last a severe battle was fought; the Romans won, being more numerous, stronger in force, and more practised by use, yet they lost many of their own because they had been grappling with a people trained in discipline.

Yet in all military affairs nothing is more useful or more brilliant than a learned commander. For a commander’s courage and skill, as the proverbial saying goes, counterbalance the effectiveness of an army as though in a second scale-pan. Antiquity attributed Caesar’s triumphs to the commander rather than to the army. For, as Solinus says, as Senicius or Sergius stood out among soldiers, so Caesar the dictator stood out among commanders—indeed, among all human beings. Under his command one million, one hundred and twenty-two thousand enemies were slain [for he did not wish it recorded how many he had overthrown in civil wars]. He fought fifty-two pitched battles. He alone surpassed M. Marcellus, who had fought in that fashion thirty-nine times. Moreover, no one wrote more swiftly, no one read more quickly; he is said even to have dictated four letters at once. He was so endowed with kindness that those whom he had subdued by arms he conquered still more by clemency.

## Chapter XVI. The evils that come upon our countrymen through lack of discipline

But why do I rehearse and reconsider the virtue of our ancestors? Our age has failed and has almost been reduced to nothing. It swells with honours, while not knowing the ranks of honour; it delights in the vanity of titles, despising the vanity and profit [Col. 0611C] of things themselves. Gamblers, fowlers, and—what is more astonishing—buffoons and men who have never handled manly affairs nor even known the duties involved, when, with hair growing thickly and skin hardened, they are rejected as unfit for the works of wantonness, put on the soldier’s garb, seek the rank of chief centurion and command, and promise that they will be leaders and instructors in a duty they have never learned.

No power was ever enlarged by any virtue so much that these men are not equal to contracting its borders or wholly draining its strength. If you do not believe me, believe at least their deeds. It is shameful to tell what is painful and disgraceful to endure. While our armed soldiery snores; while they storm the chastity of others and prostitute their own; while they go round noblemen’s houses and spy out banquets in order to feast magnificently every day; [Col. 0611D] while they throw about inflated and foot-and-a-half-long words, slaughtering Saracens and Parthians without bloodshed, and whatever else is reckoned by the name of enemy—while these glorious soldiers do this, untamed Nivicollinus grows insolent, unarmed Britons puff themselves up, and they almost compel even those called the Counts Palatine, who glory in royal blood, to surrender, making them as it were tributaries.

No one is willing to join battle with them, or to test on equal terms what they can do. Armed men challenge the unarmed to the open field; but no one of our men pursues them, unarmed, into the woods, because he distrusts his own courage. Would that they had remembered what Roman history relates about the Cisalpines, in these words: “The inhabitants of Cisalpine Gaul had the spirits of wild beasts and bodies more than human. But experience showed that their courage, as it is greater than a man’s in the first onset, is thereafter less than a woman’s. For Alpine bodies, reared under a moist sky, have something like their own snows: once they grow warm in battle, they immediately sweat, and at a slight movement melt away as though under the sun.” Elsewhere too the savagery of Alpine nations is readily shown even through their women, who, when weapons failed, cast their infants, dashed upon the ground, into the faces of the opposing soldiers.

If there were people to attack our Nivicollini, they would undoubtedly be conquered. But, as Amentius says, there is no one to do the things that almost self-moving Fortune compels to be accomplished. Unarmed and unwarlike barbarism attacks an armed province, [Col. 0612B] plunders and ravages it; and he who is hungry in his own home, our soldier giving way, fills himself from our goods and makes a feast-day of luxury in our country. Does not a soldier give way when he does not repel an enemy rushing upon him and threatening him?

But if neither love of country, nor the loss of possessions, nor the impending destruction of safety by the enemy, nor even the spur of shame ought to have stirred the courage of our military force—at which now the unarmed and insolent Welshman scoffs—then, as the proverb says, “Wretched is the land that a driver or muleteer lays waste.” If our soldiers cannot be urged to manly action by any manly exhortation, let the mothers and wives of those who yield press them toward courage. Something of this sort is found in ancient histories. When the Medes attacked and the Persian battle-line was driven into flight, wholly failing and not daring to look upon the victor, their mothers and wives ran everywhere to meet the fugitives and, massed in a womanly line, begged them to return to battle. When they would not, the women lifted their garments, showed the shameful parts of their bodies, and asked whether the men wished to flee back into the wombs of their mothers or wives. Reproved thus, they returned to battle; making an attack, they compelled those from whom they had fled to flee. Would that the wives and mothers of our Marchers would act likewise, so that by every means they might keep their country safe and remove the stain of shame.

## Chapter XVII. That we have among our own people examples of virtues, and what cities Brennus founded in Italy according to ancient histories

[Col. 0612D] But what we now seek from our own people has long passed away; and the virtue of our ancestors has flowed out to others so far that the abundance of the rich vein seems to have failed from its spring into streams. We have examples of virtue not only from Romans and Greeks, for we abound also in domestic ones.

Histories relate that Brennus, leader of the Senones, destroyed the Roman army at the river Allia, burst into and captured the city of Rome itself, and, after slaying the senators and subduing Italy, invaded Greece. Ravaging everything and terrifying all, he advanced as far as the temple of Delphic Apollo, situated on Mount Parnassus; desiring Apollo’s spoils, he jested scurrilously that rich gods ought to make gifts to men. This Brennus, I say, they relate to have been born in Greater Britain, which since the arrival of the Saxons on the island has been called England.

In the twentieth book of Trogus Pompeius it is found that the Gallic Senones, Brennus’s fellow-soldiers, when they came into Italy, drove the Tuscans from their seats and founded there noble cities: Milan, Como, Brescia, Verona, Bergamo, Trent, and Vicenza. As for their having built the city of Siena for their old men, sick people, and cattle-herds, this is affirmed not only by the authority of history but by widespread tradition—made stronger indeed by the fact that the Sienese, in the outlines of their bodies, beauty of face, charm of complexion, and even their customs, appear to approach the Gauls and Britons from whom they derived their origin, although antiquity of time, the region of the world, the situation of their country, and association with neighbouring peoples, with whom they have long been mixed in blood and custom, [Col. 0613B] have changed them in large part. Yet all these have not sufficed to eradicate, in likeness to their neighbours, the Gallic colour—that is, fairness.

For the Greeks call milk γάλα (*gala*), whence γαλαξίας (*galaxias*) means “milky”; and the Gauls are, as it were, milk-coloured, as are the Galatae, who were at one time called Gallo-Greeks, in the borders of Greece occupied by the military force of the Gauls.

That army, under Brennus as its leader, remained triumphant and always unconquered until it dared rise against the gods by attacking the very temple of Delphic Apollo. When the inhabitants were humbly imploring God’s help, they saw, upon the summit of the shrine, a young man of beauty remarkable beyond human measure. The creaking of a bow and the clash of weapons were also heard. Then, suddenly, an earthquake broke away part of the mountain and laid low the Gallic army. A storm followed, which destroyed the wounded with hail and cold. Brennus himself, unable to endure the pain of his wounds, ended his life with a dagger.

Nor should anyone be troubled that Apollo was said—as has been stated—to have been seen in the temple, to restrain the boldness of the unconquered commander and destroy the army which, God permitting it because of the sins of men, had destroyed many nations. For it is certain that aerial powers exercise much of their wickedness upon those lacking sound faith and ignorant of true religion. Grace is withdrawn from such people, and malignant spirits receive permission to harm them; yet, unless the Lord permits, they cannot harm at all, even if they wish to do so. And, as Gospel testimony teaches, without permission granted they do not dare, nor are they able, to rush even into a herd of swine.

## Chapter XVIII. Examples from recent histories, and how King Henry II calmed the tempest and storms of King Stephen and pacified the island

Since Brennus’s story may perhaps seem to someone too remote for displaying the virtue of a people to whom not nature but instruction, exercise, skill, and perhaps a leader are lacking, I come nearer and shall set out briefly matters almost universally known.

How greatly Enudus [reading uncertain], by the courage of the English, broke the Dacians or Danes and quelled the disturbances of the Noricans is clear even from this: because of the merit of the remarkable courage which our Kent there exercised powerfully and openly, it holds to this day in every battle the honour of the first cohort and the first encounters with the enemy. The province of Severiana, which in modern usage and name is called Wiltshire by its inhabitants, claims the supporting cohort for itself by the same right, with Devon and Cornwall joined to it.

I come down to our own times. The king of the English surnamed Rufus, energetic indeed in arms but not very religious, who through his persecution of saints—and especially Saint Anselm of Canterbury—seemed to have called down upon himself the dart of envy by which he was suffocated: this man, I say, captured Le Mans and took its count, yet did not deign to consign him to prison custody. Mount Barbatus will bear witness to that great deed forever; or, should one prefer to call it by another name, let it be called Mount Barbarus, or Mount of the Barbarians.

I pass to his successor, the renowned King Henry, called the Lion of Justice, whom, as is publicly known, not only cities but the towers of France feared. But since it is exceedingly well known how in a pitched battle he broke and put to flight the king of the French, and since very many witnesses to that victory survive in both kingdoms among those who were present in the public battle, I deliberately pass over the most familiar facts, lest it be tedious to repeat them.

How he captured the duke of Normandy—a warlike man, vigorous in arms, who had returned after Jerusalem was liberated—when he crossed the borders of another’s kingdom under cover of a name, I think needless to relate, since even younger men have seen him captive in public custody, though with due respect paid to his rank and blood. The Norman nobles bear witness to this to the present day: some captured, others imprisoned, others disinherited. And among us is the tomb of the captive duke.

Finally, that examples may not be sought from afar: his nephew is the best king in the British Isles of the whole age, if the merits of his virtues, once grace has been bestowed, endure together to the end; most fortunate duke of the Normans and Aquitanians; first alike in extent of dominion and brilliance of virtues. How valiant, magnificent, prudent, and moderate he has been from infancy itself, so to speak, not even Envy can be silent about or conceal, since his recent works are manifest, and from the borders of Britain to the limits of Spain he has stretched out and continued the titles of his courage.

> Indeed quick intelligence and practical wisdom come before the beard;  
> he knows what should be said and left unsaid,  
> and can set the black theta against vices.  
> (Persius IV.11)

For God, wishing to punish the wickedness of a transgressing people, allowed the favour of newcomers to rise, after the covenant had been broken which had been confirmed by the oath of the nobles with the daughter of the Lion of Justice. He allowed a man contemptuous of goodness and equity to reign in another’s kingdom—a man whose counsel was foolish from the beginning, whose cause was founded upon injustice and perfidy, and who neglected discipline. Thus, not so much reigning as shaking and dashing together [Col. 0615A] clergy and people, he provoked all men to every kind of deed. For force was the measure of law.

Invading the kingdom, he disinherited and expelled its lord, for whom indeed, if faith existed in man, one ought to have died both because of the merits of his forebears and because of the necessity of the oath. He sought to corrupt neighbouring nations, contracting marriages and alliances with their rulers, lest the little child, still crying in his cradle, might by any favour of God reach his claim to the inheritance. He devised very many schemes against innocence, but in all these things iniquity lied to itself. And it became known that God is true because he did not find among his subjects the fidelity which he had not kept toward his God and earthly lord. The same measure was measured out to him which he himself had measured to others, as though all had learned from Ennius:

> I neither gave nor give faith to any faithless man.

Although he did much badly and little well, he acted most wickedly in laying hands, in contempt of God, upon His anointed; and not without the mark of perfidy and treachery, which he deservedly incurred through that criminal act in the eyes of all. From then on no one could safely approach his court. Yet he seized not bishops alone, though they were the first, for his own destruction; against all whom he suspected he spread the snares of his treachery. The capture of the bishops was the beginning of his evils; from that day the sword never left his side, and the latter things of the man were always worse than the former.

Why say more? In his days evils multiplied in the land, so that anyone recounting them summarily might surpass the history of Josephus. Yet the courage of the boy opposed them, and, almost before reaching the age for or holding military office, he so broke the attack of the malicious that he was sometimes said not to be inferior to the younger Theodosius, whom histories compare with Alexander, and was never found inferior in offices [reading uncertain]. Without delay, in the first years of adolescence, still under age, he entered upon warfare; and with a fiercer countenance, a stronger hand, and divine aid, he shook and broke the hearts of his enemies.

Immediately the kings of the French and English rose against him with their forces gathered, and Eustace, brother-in-law of the king of the French, a foe fiercer than either, pursuing his own cause and striving to preserve the paternal crown not so much for his father as for himself. Our Neoptolemus not only withstood them manfully, but for the most part conquered them powerfully. Therefore Eustace, whom I have mentioned, wounded inwardly by grief of heart, departed human life in the one thing he did best while alive. Him, while the good rejoiced and congratulated the public fortune because another scourge of the country had been impending in this man, mourned

> the companies of flute-girls, drug-sellers,  
> beggars, actors, buffoons, and all that kind.  
> (Horace I.2.1)

Yet that his death might take nothing from our commander’s glory, he lived to endure and see the surrender of Craumersia [Crammersie; place-name uncertain], to whose aid he had come with his father, strongly armed, in a larger number, and supplied with an abundance of soldiers. The duke, warned by the counsel of one man, placed his own, much smaller army between the castle which the king had fortified and the king’s forces. Yet foreigners must not ascribe this to their own strength: he relied principally upon our soldiers.

At last, driven to it by his sins, the man who had occupied the kingdom was compelled to disinherit his son, yield to the duke the succession to the realm, and bind all the nobles and military force of the entire kingdom by an oath of fidelity. I pass over the siege of Chinon, since no one is ignorant that there the English and Normans, now united by manifold alliance, proved foremost and most valiant in taking the castle. For I say nothing of Nantes and the whole county of Lesser Brittany, though a large province: it would remain rebellious to this day if the strength of the English nation did not hold it in fear. Either fearing this or attracted by love and courage—it is uncertain which—the illustrious count of Blois and Chartres restored to the duchy of Normandy the castles which had been lost during the duke’s minority.

It would be long if I attempted to enumerate the renowned deeds of so great a prince; just as all must admire them, so it is impossible fully to describe them. Nor do I arrogate to my own powers the task in which, should prosperity long continue to attend him in accordance with the course of grace already bestowed, Orosius, Hegesippus, and Trogus might labour. Yet the outcome of his youth is suspected by some; and would that good men feared it in vain.

## Chapter XIX. On the honour to be shown soldiers and the restraint to be imposed upon them; those who handed down the art of war, and certain general precepts of theirs

[Col. 0616C] Why do I linger in praising a people which nature itself proves worthy of praise? Blessed Eugenius said that it was fit to be applied to whatever purpose one wished, and to be preferred to others unless inconstancy hindered it. But just as Hannibal declared that the Romans could not be conquered except in their own country, so this people too is unconquerable while abroad. In its own settlements, however, it is more readily overcome. Perhaps this is common to the inhabitants of Britain and Italy with other peoples.

If soldiers are rightly trained and confirm instruction by practice, let them walk honourably and be regarded as defenders of their country. Let them shine in attire, but attire suited to men; for more wanton adornment is not free from fault or reproach even in the female sex. It has often been found in war that the luxurious and splendid display of military equipment contributes victory to citizens not so much as it invites enemies to plunder.

Thus Hannibal, while staying with King Antiochus as an exile, very wittily mocked the king when he displayed an army glittering with gold and silver insignia, bringing forward chariots with scythes, elephants with chariots, and all the cavalry resplendent with bridles, saddles, necklaces, and decorations. As the king, glorying in the sight of such a great and richly adorned army, looked toward Hannibal, he asked: “Do you think all this sufficient for the Romans?” Then the Carthaginian, mocking the cowardice and unwarlike quality of soldiers so expensively armed, replied: “Certainly I think it sufficient, even though the Romans are very greedy.” A neat, brief, and bitter answer. For the king had asked about the number of the army and the calculation of equivalent strength; plainly, Hannibal answered about plunder.

Finally, if Naso excludes from military service youths unarmed and dressed like women, who will believe them fit to be admitted to vigorous warfare? Craftsmen in each art adorn above all those possessions by which they know themselves to be honoured above others. Hence it is clear that soldiers ought to shine more in arms than in clothing. Aeneas is said to have transferred jewels from his fingers to his sword; Virro, to his cups. It is also established that the Maccabees gilded their shields and that the brightness of them scattered the courage [Col. 0617B] of nations. Yet they should be believed to have been content with ordinary dress.

Nothing is less fitting for a soldier than soft attire and the refined luxuries of clothing—unless perhaps, with Thraso, he has devoted his military service to Venus for the storming of Thais’s fortification, despising Mars. Filth too is to be avoided, and one must constantly adhere to moderation, which travels the golden road. I wish, however, our countrymen to be convinced of this: if they are trained, courage will not be lacking, though it frequently perishes when discipline does not strengthen it.

The Spartans are said to have handed down the art of war. Hence Hannibal, intending to attack Italy, sought a Spartan as his military guide.

> Let him who desires peace prepare war.  
> Let him who desires victory train his soldier diligently.  
> Let him who seeks favourable outcomes fight by skill, not chance.  
> Let no one dare challenge or attack one whom he knows will be superior if battle occurs.

Ancient annals say that the Athenians especially gave soldiers this one command: “Let a soldier not yet discharged continually accustom himself to exercise and labour.” For these are wont to preserve health in camp and secure victory in conflict. They likewise taught that the strength of an army lies in infantry, and that he is scarcely fit for military service who cannot fight unless he is a horseman.

Nevertheless, he is neither exercised nor usefully called to battle if his pay does not come forth. For if you withdraw provisions, the soldier will deny you obedience or loyalty. Hunger, as the saying goes, fights within, [Col. 0617D] and alone takes by storm even things that seem safest. A hungry populace does not know how to fear. But if provisions have been supplied, let soldiers be urged to duty now by fear of punishment, now by hope of rewards. Let there everywhere be field-commanders and masters of military exercises; let these men themselves receive pay, and you will shortly see the nation restored to that degree of courage in which it flourished when Julius Caesar, greatest of commanders,

> showed terrified backs to the Britons after seeking them out.

Let mock military deliberations also be frequently conducted, so that the soldier trained in them may know, when need demands it, how to choose what is most expedient. But if the affair is serious, let it be concealed from the soldier, because it is a military precept: deliberate with many about what ought to be done, but with very few and the most trustworthy—or rather with yourself alone—about what you intend to do. For what comes to the knowledge of a multitude seldom remains hidden.

Military precepts and examples of valiant men should also often be related to younger men, so that the former may instruct them in knowledge and the latter kindle and animate them to courage. My purpose, however, is not here to hand down the art of war, which is indeed very great and most necessary, and without which, to use Plutarch’s words, every principate is understood to be maimed. Whoever wishes to learn it should consult Cato the Censor; let him read also what Cornelius Celsus, Julius Hyginus, and Vegetius Renatus wrote. Because Vegetius handed down the art of war most elegantly and carefully, though he touched upon examples only briefly, I have inserted more from him. Let him, I say, read what these men judged should be prescribed for posterity.

Yet the usefulness of every art depends upon this: practice must by no means be absent from precepts. For, as Cicero says, it is very easy to give precepts for anything, but most laborious to carry it out effectively. What he asserted in the rhetorical precepts addressed to Herennius concerning the art of speaking—namely, that it is ineffective and useless without practice and exercise in speaking—I think must be applied to every art, insofar as they are not confirmed by use nor strengthened by exercise. Indeed, if you separate art and practice, practice lacking art is more useful than art lacking its own practice.

Thus David, with sling and stone, whose skill and use he possessed, struck down the foreigner; and with his staff he dared attack a man terrible to all and a warrior from his youth. He rejected the royal coat of mail and weapons in which he had not been trained, judging that everything whose use is not secured by exercise is a hindrance to warfare. Yet as art is barren when ignorant of practice, so practice is incomplete when it does not spring from art. The beginning of each lies in nature; when nature resists, and, as the saying goes, when Minerva is unwilling, we undertake nothing rightly. Progress comes from practice; perfection from art, provided it has been made firm by continual exercise.

This holds true in liberal, manly, and mechanical arts, and in any others of which we have not yet heard mention: art is unfruitful without practice, and practice rash without art. Military service without art is idle; without practice, incapable of duty. Therefore whoever wishes to be a soldier must first learn the art and confirm it by use and exercise, so that when he has been chosen and enrolled under the military oath, he may live usefully for the commonwealth and himself, and may not be, as Plutarch says, a maimed hand. Plutarch used these very words at the end of his instruction of Trajan, when he descended from hands to feet. Let us therefore follow him and, as he himself says, make shoes as it were for the feet, that they may not stumble against a stone or another obstacle which manifold chance presents.

## Chapter XX. Who are the feet of the commonwealth, and the care to be bestowed upon them

The “feet” are those who perform the humbler offices, by whose service the members of the commonwealth walk upon the ground. Among them is the sphere of farmers, who always cling to the earth, whether occupied with sowing, planting, pastures, or flowers. To these are added many kinds of wool-working and mechanical arts, practised in wood, iron, bronze, and various metals; servile services also, and manifold means of gaining a livelihood, sustaining life, or enlarging household wealth. These do not belong to the authority of governing, yet they benefit the community of the commonwealth in every way.

They are so numerous that the commonwealth exceeds not merely eight-footed crabs but even centipedes in its multitude of feet. They cannot indeed be counted because of their multitude, though by nature they are not infinite; rather, their forms are so various that no writer on offices has ever laid down special precepts for every individual species. Yet provision is made for what is common to all and each: namely, that they do not exceed the bounds of law and that everything be referred to public benefit.

Inferior members ought to render service to their superiors; the latter in turn owe them all necessary support. Plutarch therefore says that in all things one must pursue what benefits the humbler persons, that is, the multitude. For the few always yield to the many. Magistracies were instituted for this reason: that injuries might be repelled from subjects and that the commonwealth itself might be shod, as it were, by their workmanship. For it is as though unshod when it is exposed to injuries, and nothing can be more disgraceful than this to those holding office. An afflicted people exposes and proves, as it were, the gout of its ruler.

The safety of the entire commonwealth will then be sound and distinguished if the higher members devote themselves to the lower, and the lower respond to the higher with equal right; so that each may be, as it were, a member of the others reciprocally, and each may believe himself most effectively provided for in that in which he knows provision has been made more usefully for others.

## Chapter XXI. That the commonwealth should be ordered in likeness to nature, and that its order should be borrowed from bees

Cicero and Plato wrote on the commonwealth, though in different ways: the one discussed what it ought to be, the other what had been instituted by the ancestors. Yet both prescribed this form both for a commonwealth instituted and one to be instituted: civil life should imitate nature, which we have very often called the best guide to living. Otherwise it will properly be judged not merely uncivil but rather beastly and brutish. Experience of reason itself sufficiently shows what nature’s ordering is.

Maro, the most learned of poets, to whom Plutarch sends his Trajan in order that he may borrow civil life from bees, sings of

> the marvellous spectacle of small creatures:  
> they alone, born for community, possess shared homes  
> of a city, and pass their life beneath great laws;  
> they alone know a country and fixed household gods;  
> mindful of the coming winter, they endure labour in summer  
> and lay up in common what they have acquired.
>
> For some watch over provisions and, bound by an agreed compact,  
> labour in the fields; some within the enclosure of their homes  
> lay first foundations for the combs—Narcissus’ tear  
> and sticky glue from bark—and then hang their clinging waxes.  
> Others rear the grown offspring, the hope of the race;  
> others pack the purest honey  
> [Col. 0620A] and swell the cells with liquid nectar.  
> To some the duty of guard at the gates has fallen by lot,  
> and in turn they watch the waters and the clouds of heaven.

They either receive the burdens of those arriving, or, formed into a column, drive the idle herd of drones away from the feeding-troughs.

The work seethes, and fragrant honey smells of thyme.

And just as, when the Cyclopes hasten to forge thunderbolts from yielding masses, some take in and give back the blasts with bull-hide bellows, while others plunge the hissing bronze into a pool, and Aetna groans beneath the anvils laid upon it; they, with great force, raise their arms in rhythm against one another and turn the iron with gripping tongs—

So, if it is permitted to compare small things with great, an inborn love of possession urges the Cecropian bees, each to her allotted task: the aged have charge of the city, to fortify the combs and fashion the Daedalian dwellings. But, wearied, the smaller bees return late in the night,

[Col. 0620B] their legs laden with thyme; and everywhere they feed upon strawberry-trees, gray-green willows, cassia, blushing saffron, rich linden, and iron-colored hyacinths. One repose from work belongs to all; one labor belongs to all. In the morning they rush forth from the gates: nowhere is there delay. Again, when evening has at last warned them to leave the same fields where they have fed, then they seek their homes, then tend their bodies. A sound arises; they hum about the thresholds and doorways. But when they have already settled themselves in their chambers, silence falls through the night, and their own sleep takes possession of their weary limbs.

Nor, when rain threatens, do they venture far from their stalls, nor do they entrust themselves to the sky when east winds approach. Instead, safe beneath the walls of their city, they range about nearby and make short excursions; and often they lift little stones, as unstable boats take ballast when tossed by the heaving wave: with these they balance themselves amid the empty clouds.

You will especially marvel that this practice has pleased the bees: they indulge in no mating, do not languidly surrender their bodies to Venus, nor bring forth offspring through the pangs of birth. Rather, they themselves gather their young from leaves and sweet herbs with their mouths; they themselves supply a king and little citizens, and restore their courts and waxen realms.

[Col. 0620C] Often too, while wandering among rough stones, they wear away their wings and freely give up their lives beneath their burden: so great is their love of flowers and the glory of producing honey.

Therefore, although the narrow limit of their lifetime receives them—for no more than a seventh summer is allotted them—the race remains immortal, and for many years the fortune of the house endures, while grandsires of grandsires are counted.

Moreover, neither Egypt nor vast Lydia, nor the peoples of Parthia nor the Median Hydaspes, observe their king in this manner. While the king is safe, all share one mind; when he is lost, they break faith, themselves plunder the honey they have constructed, and tear apart the comb-frames. He is the guardian of their labors; they admire him, and all surround him with a dense buzzing, crowding closely about him. Often they raise him upon their shoulders, expose their bodies to battle, and seek a beautiful death through wounds. (VIRGIL, *Georgics* IV.133 ff.)

[Col. 0620D] Survey all writers on the commonwealth; review the histories of states: nowhere will civil life meet you in a more correct and elegant form. And cities would beyond doubt be blessed if they prescribed for themselves this pattern of life.

## Chapter XXII. That no magistracy remains sound without prudence and care, nor does a commonwealth flourish when its head is weakened

Venerable places also, if they follow in the bees’ footsteps, proceed by a most direct and open road toward life. Look in Virgil at the foundations of Carthage, and by comparison you will be able to admire the beginnings of the blessed City. For you will recognize that everyone’s labor is shared and that no one is idle; and that the very queen, by whose aid the city’s fabric rises,

[Col. 0621A] although she by no means puts her own hands to the labor of those beneath her, nevertheless directs her eyes toward the work and exercises all the concern of her mind over it. For without prudence and concern not only does a commonwealth fail to advance, but even the smallest household cannot stand.

Thus, in commending Ulysses, Homer teaches that prudence was always his companion, calling it Minerva according to poetic custom. Virgil likewise, his imitator, when describing the man distinguished in arms and piety whom he judged worthy to make the father of the Romans, rightly associated Achates with him in every undertaking. For the concern belonging to prudence most correctly advances what must be done; and a watchful man’s affairs often proceed in such a way that no stratagems of plotters impede him and that, as though by an invisible, unpublished route of action,

[Col. 0621B] he reaches the appointed end of his intention. This is elegant indeed, since neither military affairs nor the work of piety can be carried out without concern and prudence. A trustworthy union surely exists when concern is joined to prudence: keen intelligence is blunted by idleness, while concern makes no progress unless it rests upon the foundation of a rich vein [of intelligence].

Thus one thing requires another’s aid and joins with it in friendly alliance. (HORACE, *Art of Poetry* 411.)

However sound the beginnings of any undertaking may be, they do not advance when Minerva departs. Let the Mantuan poet come before you, who beneath the image of fables expresses the truth of the whole of philosophy. Attend, then, to the industry of the new citizens:

As bees in early summer through flowering fields

[Col. 0621C] ply their labor beneath the sun, when they rear the mature offspring of the race, or pack the flowing honey and swell their cells with sweet nectar; or receive the burdens of those arriving, or, formed into a column, drive the idle herd of drones from the feeding-troughs. The work seethes, and fragrant honey smells of thyme. (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* I.432 ff.)

Thus the citizens are occupied in diverse tasks; and while each person’s duties are maintained so that provision is made for the whole community, while justice is cultivated, a honeyed sweetness bathes the boundaries of all. Yet no commonwealth enjoys lasting prosperity unless a sound head provides for the whole body. If you did not know this, let Dido’s example teach you.

For with what thoughtlessness is Aeneas admitted! How quickly does an unknown man—an exile, a fugitive, whose cause is unknown and whose person is suspect—find favor!

[Col. 0621D] With what curiosity do the ears of rulers receive the fabulous tales of a man excusing his own fault, seeking his own glory, and aiming at whatever might overthrow the minds of his listeners! Smooth speeches precede the man’s entrance; the allurements of praise win the favor of hospitality; everyone’s studied attentiveness furnishes the banquet with greater care; tales follow banquets; hunting and the frivolity of manifold luxury accompany incest. These produce conflagration, the desolation of citizens, and prolong the causes of perpetual hostility.

Such is the end of a womanish and effeminate kingdom, which, though it had a foundation of courage, could by no means find a successful course amid ensuing prosperity. He was lightly admitted—though, under the duty of piety, he ought not to have been excluded as a guest, yet it would have been more expedient for him to enter as a stranger, not as though a judge.

## Chapter XXIII. That thoughtlessness in listening, as in speaking, is to be avoided; and that repentance is the end of pleasure

“Do everything with counsel,” he says, “and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclus. XXXII). Moreover, just as it does not become a ruler to utter trivial things, so neither should he be readily disposed to hear trifles. For Wisdom says: “A ruler who gladly listens to lying words has all his ministers wicked” (Prov. XXIX).

Venus throws herself with all her strength into conversations and banquets. Whoever willingly admits her first missiles scarcely escapes being more grievously wounded by those that follow.

[Col. 0622B] Sight and conversation, touch and kisses, the deed: as they precede one another in sequence, so by necessity they bring forth the offspring of sorrow. For repentance is the end of pleasure.

If you do not believe me, believe at least Demosthenes, who is said to have made a sufficiently witty reply to Lais. This Lais of Corinth, because of the elegance and beauty of her form, demanded a great sum of money. Distinguished gatherings of noble men from all Greece came to her, and she admitted no one unless he paid what was demanded. But she demanded an excessive amount. Hence arose that common Greek proverb: “In vain does one journey to Corinth to Lais, unless one can—or wishes to—pay what is demanded.”

Demosthenes secretly approached her and requested access to her person. But Lais demanded a sum

[Col. 0622C] equivalent in our currency to one hundred thousand denarii, equal to half a greater talent, which contains twenty thousand of our denarii. Struck and alarmed by the woman’s impertinence and the magnitude of the sum, Demosthenes turned away; and as he departed said: “I do not buy repentance at so great a price.”

Would you like nearer examples? You know who said that every pleasure has this property:

It drives the mad with goads;
and, like a swarm of flying bees,
when it has poured forth its pleasing honey,
it flees, and, having struck,
wounds hearts with an all too clinging sting.
(BOETHIUS, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Metre VII.)

For the beginnings of desire are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, but its latter end is more bitter than any wormwood.

[Col. 0622D] For what is the end of conversations, banquets, and fulfilled lust, except the burning pyre and the fire of desolation that scatters itself among all citizens?

## Chapter XXIV. That the vices of rulers must be endured, because in them rest the auspices of public welfare; and that they are dispensers of welfare, as the stomach distributes nourishment in an animal’s body; and this according to the judgment of Pope Adrian

“Go,” says Solomon, “to the ant, you sluggard, so that you may acquire foresight” (Prov. VI). But the philosopher sends the political man to the bees, so that he may learn his own duty from them. Had the Tyrians complied, they would never have indulged in luxury and would have rejoiced in their nation’s perpetual security. But because vice took root in a woman ruler,

[Col. 0623A] the effeminate citizens withdrew their necks from courage.

Further, although rule may be somewhat lax in the office of the virtues, it must nevertheless be honored. And as bees raise their king on their shoulders, so subjects—whom we have said are the feet and members—should render him every service, provided that he is not ruinous through vices. For even if he labors under vices, he must be endured, as one in whom the auspices of welfare for the provinces reside:

While the king is safe, all share one mind;
when he is lost, they broke faith.
(VIRGIL, *Georgics* IV.212.)

The Illyrians and Thracians, hardened by daily exercise, used to terrify the neighboring Macedonians with the glory of their martial renown. The Macedonians, defeated in battle, brought out their king—the son of their dead king—in his cradle and placed him behind the battle line; then they renewed the contest more fiercely,

[Col. 0623B] as though they had been defeated because their king’s auspices had been absent from those fighting, and would be victors because, through superstition or faith, they had conceived the courage to conquer. For pity for the infant also held them, since if they were defeated they seemed likely to make a captive of their king. Accordingly, joining battle, they routed the Illyrians with great slaughter, showing their enemies that in the former war the Macedonians had lacked a king, not courage.

How greatly, then, should one already advanced in age and dignity be esteemed, if the one who is to be advanced in both is held in such esteem? Although he may seem to treat the people rather harshly, nevertheless the authority of his dignity and the usefulness of his office ought to soften the minds of provincials.

I remember that I went to Apulia in order to visit Lord Adrian IV, the pope, who had admitted me into closer familiarity, and I stayed with him at Benevento for nearly three months.

[Col. 0623C] Since, as usually happens among friends, we frequently discussed many matters, and he asked me rather confidentially and carefully what men thought of himself and the Roman Church, I exercised before him the freedom of the spirit and openly set forth the evils I had heard of in various provinces.

For, as many said, the Roman Church, mother of all churches, presents herself to others not so much as a mother as a stepmother. Scribes and Pharisees sit in her, laying unbearable burdens on men’s shoulders which they do not touch with a finger. They lord it over the clergy and do not become an example to the flock proceeding by the straight path toward life. They heap up costly furnishings, load their tables with gold and silver, and are themselves excessively stingy through avarice. For the poor person is either not admitted at all, or only rarely; and when admitted, is sometimes brought in not so much by Christ as by vain glory. They oppress churches, stir up lawsuits, set clergy and people against each other, do not at all sympathize with those afflicted by labors and miseries, rejoice in the spoliation of churches, and judge all gain to be godliness.

[Col. 0623D] They dispense justice more according to price than truth. For today everything comes with a price, and tomorrow you will obtain nothing without a price. They often do harm and imitate demons in this respect: they are thought to do good when they cease doing harm—except for a few who fulfill both the name and office of shepherd.

Even the Roman pontiff himself is burdensome and almost intolerable to all. Moreover, all complain that while churches built by the devotion of the Fathers are falling and collapsing, and their altars lie neglected, he builds palaces and proceeds not merely clothed in purple but gilded. The palaces of priests shine, while in their hands Christ’s Church is made filthy. They plunder the spoils of provinces as though they were striving to restore Croesus’s treasures.

Yet the Most High deals rightly with them, since they too are handed over to plunder by others, often by the meanest of men. And, in my opinion, while they wander thus off the path, the Lord’s scourge will never be lacking to them. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken: by the judgment with which they judge they shall be judged, and by their own measure it shall be measured back to them. The Ancient of Days does not know how to lie.

“This, Father,” I said, “is what the people say, since you wish me to convey their opinions to you.”

[Col. 0624B] “And what,” he said, “do you think?”

“Hardships,” I replied, “are on every side. I fear lest I incur the charge of lying or flattery if I alone contradict the people. But if I agree, I fear a charge of treason, lest, as one who has set my mouth in heaven, I seem to have deserved the cross.

“Yet, because Guy Clement, cardinal-priest of Saint Pudentiana, bears testimony to the people, I do not presume wholly to contradict him. For he maintains that in the Roman Church there is a certain root of duplicity and a foment of avarice, which is the head and root of all evils. And he publicly declared this not in a corner, but while the brethren were seated and Saint Eugenius presided, when they had gratuitously become enraged against my innocence at Ferentino.

[Col. 0624C] “Still, with conscience as my witness, I boldly profess one thing: nowhere have I seen clergy more honorable than in the Roman Church, nor men who detest avarice more. Who does not admire the continence and contempt for money of Bernard of Redon, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian? No one has yet been born from whom he has accepted a gift. Yet he was sometimes persuaded to accept what rightly came to him from the more sincere common fund of the brethren. Who would not be astonished by the bishop of Palestrina, who, fearing a scruple of conscience, even abstained from sharing in common goods? Many possess such moderation and gravity that they are found not inferior to Fabricius, whom, having recognized the way of salvation, they surpass in every respect.

[Col. 0624D] “Since, therefore, you press, urge, and command me—and since it is certain that one may not lie to the Holy Spirit—I confess that what you command must be done, although you are not all to be imitated in every action. For one who dissents from your teaching is either a heretic or a schismatic. But, by God’s favor, there are people who do not imitate the deeds of all of you. Thus the stain of a few brings a blemish upon the upright and infamy upon the universal Church. In my opinion, they die more frequently for this reason: lest they corrupt the whole Church. Yet the good too are sometimes taken away lest malice change them, and because corrupt Rome is found unworthy of them before God.

“You, therefore, whose office this is, seek out and introduce humble men, those who despise vain glory and money. But I fear that while you go seeking what you want, you may hear from an imprudent friend what you do not want.

[Col. 0625A] “Why is it, Father, that you scrutinize the lives of others but do not at all examine yourself? All applaud you; you are called father and lord of all; and every oil of the sinner is poured upon your head. If, then, you are a father, why do you expect gifts and payments from your children? If a lord, why do you not instill fear in your Romans and, repressing their recklessness, call them back to faith? Yet you wish to preserve the city and Church by your gifts. Did Sylvester acquire it by gifts in this way? You are off the path, Father, and not on the way. It must be preserved by the same gifts by which it was acquired. What you have received freely, give freely. Justice is the queen of virtues and blushes to be exchanged at any price. If it is to be gracious, let it be free. Let that which cannot be corrupted never be prostituted for a price. It is whole and always incorrupt. While you press others down, you yourself will be oppressed more grievously.”

The pontiff laughed and rejoiced at such freedom, ordering me to report to him without delay whenever anything unfavorable concerning him sounded in my ears. After he had replied at length, now for himself and now against himself, he offered me the following fable.

He said: “It happened that all the members of the whole body conspired against the stomach, as against one that exhausted the labor of all by its greed. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing; the hands persevere in labor, the feet grow calloused with walking, and even the tongue usefully regulates speech and silence.

[Col. 0625C] In short, all the members watch over the public good; and amid such concern and labor by all, the belly alone rests. And when all things which manifold labor has acquired are prepared, it alone devours and consumes everything. Why say more? They agreed to abstain from labor and to destroy by severe hunger that idle public enemy.

“One day was thus completed; a more wearisome second followed. The third was so ruinous that it seemed to foretell collapse for almost all. Pressed by necessity, the brethren assembled again to deliberate concerning their own welfare and the state of the public enemy. But though all were present, the eyes grew dim, the foot did not lift the body’s weight, the arms were numb, and even the tongue, inert and joined to the failing palate,

[Col. 0625D] did not presume to state the common case. So all returned to the counsel of the heart; and after deliberation there, reason disclosed that these evils were inflicted by the one who had previously been denounced as the public enemy. For after the revenues due to him had been withheld, he too, as the public dispenser, had withheld food from all. Since no one can serve as a soldier without pay, when pay does not come the soldier is weakened and broken. Yet blame could not be cast upon the dispenser, who could not distribute to others what he had not received. It is far safer to provide him with what he may distribute than, when he has been emptied, for all the members to hunger.

“And so it was done: at reason’s persuasion the belly was filled, the members were restored, and the peace of all was re-established. Thus the stomach was acquitted: although greedy and desirous of others’ goods, it seeks them not for itself but for others, who cannot be sustained once it has been emptied.

[Col. 0626A] Such, brother,” he said, “if you attend rightly, is the case in the body of the commonwealth, where, although a magistrate may seek very much, he accumulates it not so much for himself as for others. For if he is emptied, he has nothing to distribute to the members. The office of the stomach in the body and of the ruler in the commonwealth is the same, in accordance with these words of Quintus Serenus:

Those who contend that the stomach is king of the whole body
appear to rest on true reasoning;
for its vigorous condition strengthens all the members,
but, conversely, all are weakened by its pain.
Indeed, unless care brings aid, it is said
to corrupt the brain and from there to pervert the unimpaired senses.

Therefore do not measure either our severity or that of secular rulers, but attend to the welfare of all.”

## Chapter XXV. On the connection of the head and members of the commonwealth; that the ruler is in some sense an image of the Deity; on treason; and on matters that must be observed in fidelity

For my part, I am satisfied and persuaded to place devoted shoulders beneath authority. I not only endure it but welcome it, so long as it is subject to God and follows His order. But if it resists the divine commands and wishes me to share in its war against God, I answer freely: God must be preferred to every human being.

Thus let lower things adhere to higher, and all members submit themselves to the head, so that religion may remain unharmed. Socrates, we read, established political science and gave it precepts

[Col. 0626C] said to flow from the purity of wisdom as from a kind of natural spring. This is summed up in the principle that the lower elements in a commonwealth should be preserved with greater diligence through the office of the greater. Read more carefully the institution of Trajan, mentioned above, and you will find these matters set out more fully.

For the present, let it suffice that we have spoken of the unity of head and members, adding what we stated before: injury to the head, as we said, is referred to all the members, and a wound unjustly inflicted upon any member concerns an injury to the head. Furthermore, what anyone maliciously and fraudulently undertakes against the head or the whole body of members is a most grave crime, close to sacrilege,

[Col. 0626D] because, just as sacrilege assails God, so this assails the ruler, who is plainly on earth a certain image of the Deity. It is called the crime of *maiestas* because it persecutes the image of him who alone—as the illustrious Count Robert of Leicester, governing his proconsulship in Britain with moderation, used to say—retains the reality of true and native majesty.

This occurs whenever someone plots anything against the security of the ruler or the people, whether by himself or through another. In prosecuting this crime, everyone is on equal footing; and it often happens that even the benefit of death does not release those whom no one prosecuted in life. For when the dead are convicted, their memory is condemned and their goods are taken from their successors. From the moment a person has conceived this most criminal plan, he is in a sense punished by his own mind. Once someone has incurred such a crime, it is established that he can neither alienate property nor manumit a slave, nor can a debtor lawfully make payment to him.

[Col. 0627A] Persons of bad repute, who otherwise have no right to accuse, are unquestionably admitted here; and so too are soldiers, who cannot otherwise conduct legal causes. For those who keep watch for peace ought all the more to be admitted to this accusation. Slaves may freely inform against their masters, and freedmen against their patrons.

Yet judges must not treat this crime as an occasion [for prosecution] merely because of reverence for the ruler’s majesty, but according to truth. They must consider the person: whether he could have done it, whether he did it, whether he thought it, and whether, before he ventured upon this, he was of sound mind. Nor should a slip of the tongue easily be dragged to punishment. For although the reckless deserve punishment, they must nevertheless be spared if the offense is not such as follows from the written law or is to be punished by analogy with the law.

[Col. 0627B] Women also are heard in cases of injured majesty. For Julia, a woman, exposed the conspiracy of Sergius Catiline and furnished Marcus Tullius, the consul, with material for its prosecution. Those believed to be guilty in this matter together with persons at whose counsel and instigation they seem to have joined in the accusation are indeed to be subjected to torture, if the demands of necessity or usefulness require it, so that punishment may be exacted from all accomplices in every crime committed.

There are many acts that constitute the crime of *maiestas*: for example, plotting the death of the ruler or magistrates; taking arms against one’s country; deserting the ruler by fleeing from a public war; inciting to sedition a people stirred up against the commonwealth; aiding the enemies of the people and commonwealth with provisions, arms, weapons, money, or anything else; causing, by one’s act or fraudulent design, friends to become enemies of the commonwealth; causing, by one’s act or fraudulent design, hostages to be given money against the commonwealth, or a nation in a foreign land to obey the commonwealth less;
