[Col. 0627C] likewise, releasing a defendant who has confessed in court and has therefore been cast into chains, and countless other acts, which it would be lengthy or impossible to recount.

But since in this matter the rule of fidelity must be observed above all else, a few principles make it especially easy to infer what is forbidden. For the contrary of what is necessary is impossible, and only unlawful things oppose what ought to be done. The rule of fidelity requires that the things necessarily included in faithfulness—security, safety, honor, usefulness, ease, and possibility—be preserved. We must not harm the bodily security of one to whom we are bound by fidelity, nor remove or presume to surrender the fortifications by which he is safe, nor commit an act by which his honor or advantage is diminished. Nor may what is easy be made difficult, or what is possible impossible.

Further, one who holds a benefice from the person whose faithful man he is owes aid and counsel in that person’s undertakings. Hence, how much is owed to the Lord of all is clearer than the sun, if so much is owed to those to whom we are bound only by fidelity.

[Col. 0628A] The punishment for this crime is so great that I would hardly believe even the lords of islands, who more often assume tyranny, could devise anything more severe. And lest the severity of the punishment be thought to derive from tyrants’ cruelty, we have quoted in part the words of a most moderate man himself. He says:

“Whoever, whether with soldiers, private persons, or even barbarians, enters into a criminal faction, or takes or gives the oath of that faction; and whoever has plotted the death even of illustrious men who participate in our counsels and consistory, or of senators—for they too are part of our body—or finally of anyone who serves us (for the laws have willed that the intention of crime be punished with the same severity

[Col. 0628B] as its accomplishment): he himself, as guilty of *maiestas*, shall be struck with the sword, and all his goods assigned to our treasury.

“But his sons, to whom we specially grant life through imperial clemency—for they ought to perish by their father’s punishment, since in them examples of their father’s, that is hereditary, crime are feared—shall be excluded from every inheritance and succession from their mother, grandfather, and all relatives; let them receive nothing under the wills of strangers. Let them remain perpetually needy and poor, with their father’s infamy always accompanying them. Let them never attain any honors or any offices whatsoever. Finally, let them be such that, stained by perpetual poverty, death is a consolation to them and life a punishment.

[Col. 0628C] “Finally, we command that those who ever seek to intercede with us for such persons shall likewise be marked without pardon. But to their daughters, however many they may be, we wish the Falcidian portion to pass from their mother’s property, whether she dies testate or intestate, so that the daughters may have a moderate maintenance rather than the full profit and title of an heir. For the sentence ought to be milder toward them, since we trust that, because of the weakness of their sex, they will be less likely to venture such acts. Their wives, having recovered their dowries, if their condition is such that they are obliged to reserve for their sons what they received from their husbands by title of gift, shall know that, when the usufruct is consumed, they will leave to our treasury all that by law is due to the sons. The Falcidian portion

[Col. 0628D] from these goods likewise shall be assigned only to daughters, not to sons. What we have enacted concerning the aforesaid persons and their sons we decree with similar severity concerning their knowing attendants and servants, and their sons. But if any of these, at the beginning of the faction’s formation, moved by zeal for true praise, himself reveals the faction, he shall be rewarded by us with both reward and honor. And one who has participated in the faction, if he nevertheless discloses unknown secrets of these counsels, shall be deemed worthy of acquittal and pardon.”

> **Note:** “[Col. 0627]” This is, I believe, the fourth part of the property which the Falcidian law assigned, at minimum, to heirs. —Patrologia Latina editor.

## Chapter XXVI. That vices must either be endured or removed, and differ from crimes; certain general precepts concerning a ruler’s office; and a brief conclusion on the reverence to be shown him

These few things, selected from many out of the pure vein of law,

[Col. 0629A] I have taken care to insert into the present little work, both so that those ignorant of the law, upon inspecting them, may keep themselves farther from the crime of *maiestas*, and so that no one may accuse me of having ventured anything in any respect against princely authority.

It is commonly said that the strength cannot easily be removed from cork without injury to the nails; but much more justly and swiftly is anyone injured who separates the obedience of the members from the head. May the eminence of the head always flourish, because in it rests the safety of the whole body.

Varro, in the satire entitled *Menippean*, composed concerning the duty of marriage, says: “A spouse’s vice must either be removed or endured. He who removes the vice makes his spouse more agreeable; he who endures it makes himself better.” Thus the vices of ruler and subjects must either be endured

[Col. 0629B] or removed. For their union equals or surpasses the affection of spouses.

Varro’s very words, “endure” and “remove,” are indeed neatly matched. It is clear, however, that “removing” signifies correction. It is evident that he means that what cannot be removed should be endured. Yet faithful interpretation adds this qualification: the vice intended is one which can be endured honorably and without injury to religion. For vices are lighter than crimes, and there are some things that may not be endured, or cannot faithfully be endured.

A spouse may lawfully separate from a spouse because of fornication; and one who conceals his wife’s crime is often a patron of shameful conduct. Hence perhaps: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. XVIII). These principles apply in some measure equally to bodily and spiritual adultery, though the spiritual is worse and must be avoided more diligently.

Likewise, in the structure of the members, Varro’s rule of enduring or removing must be accepted. For no one doubts that members must be treated, whether the treatment proceeds through the soothing oil or the harsh wine which the Samaritan pours upon the wounded man.

[Col. 0629C] But that they must be removed is clear from what is written: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. And if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you” (Matt. XVIII).

I judge that this must be observed by a ruler with respect to all members: they must not only be plucked out, cut off, and cast far away if they become a scandal to faith or public safety, but so crushed that by the destruction of one the safety of all is secured. Whom, I ask, will he spare who is commanded even to act harshly against his own eyes? Certainly neither ear nor tongue, nor anything else existing in the body of the commonwealth, is safe if it rises against the soul, for whose sake even the eyes are plucked out.

But when God is offended by the practice of crimes, or the Church is trampled down, the salvation of the whole soul is endangered. This is so alien to the ruler’s office that whenever these things occur in a commonwealth, the ruler must be thought either not to perceive them at all, or to be asleep, or to be away at an inn. The sun stands above all things, that it may see all and judge all. I believe the ruler to be another sun. He acts rightly when he

[Col. 0630A] drives the idle herd of drones from the feeding-troughs (VIRGIL, *Georgics* IV.167): those who plunder the hives and drink up or carry away whatever is sweet. He acts rightly when he advances the dignity of the Church, extends religious worship, humbles the proud and exalts the humble; when he is generous to the needy and more frugal toward the wealthy; when he rewards virtues and vices according to the equal balance of punishments; when justice everywhere walks before him and sets his steps upon the path of prudence and the other virtues. Indeed,

Thus heaven is sought—not so that Ossa-bearing Olympus
and Pelion’s summit may touch the highest stars.
(OVID, *Fasti* I.307.)

Wisdom says: “Do not appear glorious before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men” (Prov. XXV).

[Col. 0630B] The wise man’s precept tends to this: whoever is not humbled in the ruler’s presence deserves, once covered with merited shame, to be stripped of the glory he has usurped. For the ruler is the distributor of honors; and while he administers rule rightly, the continual dispensation of rewards belongs to him. He administers it rightly when, under his presidency, peoples rejoice and the whole breadth of the earth exults in the reign of equity. It is continual, I say, because, as it is written, “the king who judges the poor in truth—his throne shall be established for ever” (Prov. XXIX).

Who, then, would take honor from one whom he hears to have been honored by the Lord with an everlasting gift? To commit any offense against even an insensible statue of the ruler was once the crime of *maiestas*, punishable, as the ancients held, with a most bitter death.

[Col. 0630C] Who then can with impunity maliciously offend against the image of God, which is the ruler? Therefore the counsel of the Wise Man is most prudent: “In your thought do not revile the king, and in the secrecy of your chamber do not curse the rich; for birds of the air will carry your voice, and those that have wings will report your utterance” (Eccl. X). Is anything then permitted in deed or word, when thought itself, the secrecy of one’s chamber, and the judgment of one’s heart are restrained, lest they devise or conceive anything against the ruler?

## Chapter XXVII. That Gnathonic flatterers pervert everything and do not permit the truth to be confessed; that, following Marsyas’s example, their skin should be flayed if the rich are wise; and that God Himself persecutes the slanderers of the poor
[Col. 0630D] But if Gnatho is believed, anyone who does not smile upon the rich, even when they have done wrong, or does not applaud them in their worst actions, is thought either to envy their fortune or to fail in duty. For among the Gnathonic sort, speaking the truth is a crime against majesty. Yet, having obtained leave, I shall insert one point on behalf of the members, within hearing of the head—not I, however, but the Spirit of wisdom, the Spirit of truth, the Holy Spirit: “He who stops his ear at the cry of the poor shall himself cry, and shall not be heard” (Prov. XXI).

He certainly shall not be heard by his head, since his head is Christ, and in Christ is God, and God is Christ: he who delivers the poor from the mighty and breaks in pieces all the swollen kingdoms of the earth—the stone cut out of the mountain [Col. 0631A] without hands—rescuing the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the indigent and poor man from those who plunder him. Therefore, if anyone at all rises against those whose protector—indeed, whose Father—is Christ, he unquestionably provokes against himself the stone whose assault shattered the statue seen by Nebuchadnezzar, which represented the succession of kingdoms differing in splendour and strength.

Nor does it avail, in the tormenting of the poor, to multiply vows and to attempt, by pretended rather than genuine alms given by an unrepentant man, to corrupt God as though he could be bribed by gifts; for Wisdom declares that “it is ruin to a man to devour holy things and afterward reconsider vows.” And: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord, because they are offered from wickedness” (Prov. XXI); and he who offers a sacrifice from the robbery of a poor man [Col. 0631B] is as one who sacrifices a son to his father.

Nor should it be imputed to me if fraternal blood is demanded from their hand, or if they receive the recompense of their deeds in the same measure that they themselves imposed; for it is not I, but the Most High, who says and does all these things. For my part, I judge that service is due, in all humility and reverence, not only to the good and modest but even to the difficult; yet God must faithfully be worshipped also in the honouring of the authority which he has established. Thus the Hebrews too are commanded to pray for the Babylonians, because in the peace of rulers lies the repose of peoples; and Christ himself judged that taxes should be paid to Caesar by the faithful.

Yet Gnatho perverts everything; and, in his judgment, a profession of truth is equated with the crime of majesty. He is plainly worthy [Col. 0631C] to have his skin stripped off by a disciple of Apollo—that is, a worshipper of wisdom—after the example of Marsyas, who, while striving

> To surpass Phoebus in song,  
> > (VIRGIL, *Eclogues* V.9)

was defeated and stripped of nature’s covering. The faction of flatterers imitates him and reproduces the wretched Satyr, while it strives, by empty praises as though with musical instruments, not so much to surpass as to blind its deities—I mean the fortunate men. It is ever young in vice, never ripened by the gravity of judgment: light, wanton, talkative, and stirred by every breeze more swiftly than any reed.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the authority of the Socratics: when a man is commended for what is his own, and when praise is another’s.

[Col. 0631D]

Although these pipers of vanity are always intent upon undermining others, they are seldom—or at least less—occupied in praising what is most truly each person’s own. For a man is most truly commended for his own qualities when the tongue of the speaker joins in praising wisdom. All else is another’s. What each person understands is his own. His own, I say—yet not from himself, but from him whose gift is whatever in a human being deserves praise.

This is not my own saying, but one celebrated by the whole company of wise men, and easily found in the book entitled *On the God of Socrates*. Because of the elegance of its thought and the pleasing grace of its style, I have taken care to insert its words, so that readier credit may be given to what is written here [Col. 0632A] when it is evident that the same teaching has flowed from the purest spring of the ancients. Apuleius therefore says:

> Nothing surprises me so much as this: although all men desire to live as well as possible, and know that life is lived by no other means than the mind, and that it cannot be otherwise than that, if one is to live as well as possible, the mind must be cultivated, yet men do not cultivate their own minds.  
>
> But if anyone wishes to see keenly, the eyes by which he sees must be cared for. If you wish to run swiftly, the feet by which one runs must be cared for. Likewise, if you wish to box powerfully, the arms by which one boxes must be strengthened. Similarly, in all the other limbs, each has its proper care according to its function. Since everyone readily sees this, I cannot sufficiently reflect within myself—and, as the matter deserves, marvel—why they do not likewise cultivate their own minds by reason.
>
> This art of living [Col. 0632B] is equally necessary to all; not the art of painting, nor the art of making music, which any worthy person may disregard without any reproach to the mind, without disgrace, and without loss. I do not know how to play the flute like Sibimenias, but I am not ashamed not to be a flute-player. I do not know how to paint in colours like Apelles, but I am not ashamed not to be a painter. The same is true of the other arts, if I were to enumerate them all: you may be ignorant of them, and there is no shame in it. But say, pray: “I do not know how to live well as Socrates, Plato, and Pythagoras lived, nor am I ashamed not to know how to live well.” You would never dare to say this.
>
> Yet it is especially remarkable that, while they least wish to be ignorant of these matters, they nevertheless neglect to learn them, and at once reject both instruction in and ignorance of the same art. Examine, then, their daily accounts, and [Col. 0632C] you will find in their reckonings much lavishly spent, but nothing on themselves—I mean, on the worship of their own daemon, which worship is nothing other than initiation into philosophy.
>
> Certainly they build country houses magnificently, adorn their homes most richly, and acquire very numerous households. Yet amid all these things, amid such abundance of possessions, there is nothing shameful except the master himself. Nor without reason. For they possess in heaps the things which they diligently cultivate; but they themselves go about dirty, unlearned, and uncultivated.
>
> Thus you will find most delightful and elaborately built displays into which they have poured their estates: villas constructed in rivalry with cities, houses adorned in the manner of temples, households exceedingly numerous and curled, sumptuous furniture—[Col. 0632D] everything abundant, everything adorned, except the master himself. He alone, like Tantalus, is needy, destitute, poor amid his wealth. He does not indeed seek to catch that fleeting flow and the deceptive water's thirst; rather, he thirsts and hungers for true blessedness—that is, for a prosperous life and most fortunate wisdom.
>
> For he does not understand that the rich are customarily examined in the same way in which we buy horses. When purchasing them, we do not consider their trappings, inspect the polished ornaments of their belts, or contemplate the wealth of their elaborately adorned necks. If necklaces of varied treasure hang from gold, silver, and jewels; if ornaments full of craftsmanship surround the head and neck; if the bridles are engraved, the saddle-cloths dyed, and the girdles gilded: once all these coverings have been removed and set aside, we look at the horse itself, naked, at its body alone [Col. 0633A] and its spirit, to see whether it is handsome in appearance, lively in running, and strong in carrying.

> Let it have a finely shaped head, a short belly, and a fat back,  
> > And let a courageous breast luxuriate in noble muscles.  
> > (VIRGIL)

> Moreover, let a double spine run along its loins. For I want it to carry me not only swiftly, but very smoothly as well.
>
> Likewise, then, in considering men, do not appraise those external things; consider the man himself thoroughly—consider him as you would my poor Socrates. By “external things” I mean what parents have begotten and what Fortune has bestowed; none of these do I mingle with the praises of my Socrates: no noble birth, no lineage, no long pedigree, no enviable riches. For all these things, as I say, are external. “There is glory in being descended from Prothaon,” provided he was such a man that his grandson need not be ashamed of him. Therefore you may count all such things alike as external.
>
> Is he well-born? You praise his parents. Is he rich? I do not trust Fortune. Let me enumerate further. Is he strong? He will be worn out by illness. Is he swift? He will pass into old age. Is he handsome? Wait a little, and he will not be. But he is trained in good arts, thoroughly educated, and, so far as a human being can be, wise and of sound judgment. At last, at last you praise the man himself. For this is neither inherited from his father, nor dependent on chance, nor an aid supplied by popular favour, nor perishable with the body, nor changeable with age. My Socrates had all these things, and therefore despised having the rest. [Col. 0633C]
>
> Why then do you not devote yourself to the pursuit of wisdom—or at least hasten—so that you may hear nothing external in your praises, but so that whoever wishes to ennoble you may praise you as Accius praises Ulysses in the *Philotheca*, at the very beginning of that tragedy:

> Illustrious one, endowed with a small fatherland;  
> > Mighty through a renowned name and a famous heart;  
> > Leader of the Achaean fleets,  
> > Grave avenger upon the Dardanian peoples,  
> > Son of Laertes.  
> > (Fragment, p. 327)

> He mentions the father last. But you have heard all that man’s praises. Laertes, Anticlea, and Acrisius claim none of it for themselves. All the possession of this praise, as you see, belongs properly to Ulysses. Nor does Homer teach you anything else in that same Ulysses, for he always wished prudence to be his companion, calling it Minerva according to poetic custom. Therefore, with this same companion, he endured every terror and overcame every adversity. With her aid, indeed, he entered the Cyclops’ cave, but came out again. He saw the cattle of the Sun, but abstained. He went down to the dead, but rose again. With that same wisdom as his companion, [Col. 0633D] he sailed past Scylla and was not snatched away; he was engulfed by Charybdis and was not carried off. He drank Circe’s potion and was not transformed. He came to the Lotus-Eaters and did not remain. He heard the Sirens and did not approach them.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the people are shaped according to the merit of their ruler, and the rulership according to the merit of the people; and that, when God is favourable, every creature grows gentle and serves humankind.

These things Apuleius states elegantly and splendidly; and would that he were heard. For if each person laboured at cultivating himself and regarded external things as belonging to another, the condition of individuals and of all alike would surely be excellent; virtue would flourish and reason prevail, while mutual charity reigned everywhere, so that the flesh might be subject to the spirit and the spirit might serve the Lord in complete devotion.

If these things came about, the members would not be burdened by the swelling of the head, nor would the head languish through the failure or idleness of the members. Such disorders arise from the infirmity of sin. For the offences of inferiors bring a good ruler into disfavour, while the sins of superiors provide subordinates both occasion and warrant for wrongdoing. Hence: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint; from the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I). [Col. 0634A]

Thus the ruler is made gentle by the innocence of the people, and popular disturbances are repressed by the innocence of the ruler. For when God is gracious, every creature is gentle and serves humankind; but when he is angry, every creature is armed for his vengeance. The raven fed Elijah. The bear rendered service to the prophet. In order to spare Daniel, the lion unlearns the ferocity of its nature and does not recognize its accumulated hunger. Water is trodden by the dry feet of the righteous. The fire kindled against the youths in the furnace does no harm. At faith’s command, the air withholds rain, the earth its fruit, and heaven itself vomits forth its fires upon the ungodly. [Col. 0634B]

## CHAPTER XXX. A brief epilogue against the Gnathonic sort.

But while we pursue these matters, the Gnathonic sort lie in wait for us, so that they may turn whatever has been said into an accusation of hostility toward the fortunate. In order to make us guilty of falsehood or rashness, they falsely claim that we have imposed a law upon rulers and burdened their necks with an unbearable yoke. Truth is their enemy; and they procure the enmity of the rich against lovers of truth, in order to gain their favour, being ashamed of nothing in word or deed.

At every point Gnatho cries out, whether things are good or bad: “Beautiful! Fine! Right!”

> He grows pale over them; even from his friendly eyes  
> > The dew will drip; he will leap and beat the ground with his foot—  
> > As hired mourners cry and act at a funeral  
> > Almost more extravagantly than those who grieve from the heart. Thus  
> > The true mocker is more moved than the flatterer.  
> > (HORACE, *Art of Poetry* 429)

And somehow they overcome even all worthy people; even those who detest the wickedness of flatterers, though they do not seek praise from them, nevertheless take pleasure in it when it is offered. While I hold fast to truth, I can by no means please such people; nor, for their favour, do I think myself worthy to refuse assent to truth. Yet they can object nothing to me except that I do not agree with them, and that I sometimes whisper in the ear of a friend when he slips into their hands:

> Let not spirits lurking beneath a fox deceive you.  
> > (ID., ibid. 437)

These men are the commanders of courtly triflers; if you offend one of them, you will be guilty before all the others. By the counsel of the Gnathonic sort, therefore, the ambitious, envious, superstitious, and their like have gathered together, telling one another that war is being prepared against them and that I wish—as the saying goes—to exercise “dog-like eloquence” upon them. Yet I have proposed nothing of the kind, [Col. 0635A] unless either their wrongs compel it, or the authority of a superior friend urging me to it drives this pen, blunt though it is.

Indeed, my mind is more inclined to yield to courtly trifles and leave room for those who enjoy them. For, not to mention others, I cannot endure the Roman Gnathos, who think nothing has been accomplished so long as anyone remains who has withstood them, whose eyes they have not veiled in darkness, the sinner's oil having been rejected. If anyone escapes them, he is regarded as an enemy not so much of Gnatho as of leading men. Farewell, then, to the court with its tolerable trifles, provided that the Gnathonic faction may go away—ever toward evil—and that its latter end may always be worse than its former.

For the remaining days, their own day and leisure await them, even though the constraint of an unproductive breast and the dryness of an unfruitful tongue possess nothing that they can impart to everyone. Whenever you wish the ambitious, envious, and others lurking in our house to come forth—if, indeed, the foregoing little books have pleased you—give notice to one who is waiting; and by the spurs of your words they will be driven to appear in public. For not all are to be attacked at once; nor could their compact wedge easily be broken, since even military cohorts do not lightly submit to enumeration.

> Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths  
> > Could I run through all the names of trifles.  
> > (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VI.626)

# BOOK VII

[Col. 0635]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0635B]

Having left the court of courtiers, I should have withdrawn from the company of triflers, had not the authority of your command detained me at the very threshold as I was departing. For when I laid bare to you the narrowness of my heart and complained of the waste of time and life, you commanded me to endure everything with a strong mind until God should reveal something else and reform my condition for the better. You advised me, in the manner of labourers who drive away or lessen the weariness of their labour with songs and the sweetness of voices, to compensate for the losses of things and time.

For a road seems easier and shorter to travellers if they are refreshed by the thought of pleasant narration or the sweetest melodies of a voice. Thus you command me to persist in the study of reading or some other task; and, if nothing else is allowed, to complain at least to myself and the Muses about myself and the various forms of Fortune. For it is great progress for one aspiring to philosophy to lament within oneself the lack of virtue.

What answer should I make to this? The comic poet suggests:

> When we are well, we all give sound advice to the sick.  
> > But if you were here, you would think otherwise.  
> > (TERENCE, *Andria* II.i.9)

Yes, yes: from captives whose instruments are hung upon the willows are demanded the words of songs which cannot at all be sung, or are not customarily sung, in a foreign land. For although virtue may be ignorant of the injuries of captivity, or may not be deprived of its own function, exceedingly rare is the person able to meet the demands of both philosophical and courtly duties, since these for the most part are strongly opposed to one another. [Col. 0635C]

You seem, therefore, to command something nearly impossible—especially since I am a man placed under authority and, through the necessity of obedience, do many things unwillingly; and in matters which should be performed by the prompting of my own will and wisdom, I am scarcely granted time for a few. Day and night are spent in necessary and other people’s occupations, so that I am not even permitted to devote care to my household; and yet you urge me to write? I am indeed a man unskilled in knowledge and speech: shall I distribute to others the one thing I have not received?

> If a booted ploughman, ignorant of the Morning Star,  
> > Should demand a ship for himself, Melicertes might cry out  
> > That all good sense had perished from human affairs.  
> > (PERSIUS V.102)

If, then, you wish me to write, give—or rather obtain from him who is Lord of learning—the knowledge from which I may write; give me unencumbered time, and exclude the troubles of domestic necessities.

> For if a boy and tolerable lodging were lacking to Virgil,  
> > All the snakes would fall from the Furies’ hair.  
> > (JUVENAL VII.70)

Moreover, I fear that, while I devote myself to obedience, at the cost of my modesty, I may provoke the tongues of rivals, who most readily criticize others’ faults and most reluctantly imitate their virtues. But as for your wish that, if nothing else is possible, I should complain to myself and the Muses about Fortune’s reckoning: this is certainly very easy, given the distress of my mind. Yet, as Gregory Nazianzen testifies, nothing seems sweeter to human beings than to speak of others’ affairs or attend to them; but this seems alien to the judgment of a composed mind. [Col. 0636C]

For it befits a wise person to compose the mind, so that, against every assault of Fortune, putting complaints aside, he may set the shield of reason—like the revolving shield of a philosophical combatant—before himself. Whoever quarrels with the quality of his condition, unless perhaps he groans in weakness over the corruption of sin, has not yet entered the path of the philosopher.

I may rightly complain about myself, for, as my sins require, I have been cast into such misery that I seem ready for scourges; my mouth is pierced with pains in the night, and those who consume me do not rest. Since my pain is always before my eyes, do you think it can be soothed by the sweetness of a pen or of a shrilling pipe? Yet, with the Lord as author, I shall do both things you urge: amid the varied riches and delights of nations in which you abound, I shall dedicate to your name such small offerings as I can from a fasting breast and a dry tongue.

For I make no claim to subtlety of thought or elegance of expression, but in the sincerity of my life’s devotion I shall contend with any orator, confident that you, as a disciple of him who preferred the widow’s two small coins to the pompous offerings of the rich, will accept it before the gold of the wise [Col. 0637A] and the silver of the eloquent. Simplicity too will deserve favour; and, as a faithful reader, you will attend not to the meaning which the words first appear to convey, but to the intention from which, or toward which, they are made.

For serious things are interwoven with trifles and false things with true, so that all may be directed deliberately toward the worship of the highest truth. Nor should it disturb you if some things written here are found differently elsewhere, since histories too are found mutually contradictory in differing accounts of events, yet contribute toward the one fruit of usefulness and honour. I do not undertake the risk of determining truth; rather, I have proposed to share without envy, for the benefit of readers, what I have read in different authors.

For the Apostle says not that everything written is true, but: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV), although the totality of the things of which he speaks may be restricted to those alone written in the Law and the Prophets, whose truth no one doubts unless he does not agree with the catholic faith. Some things, however, which I did not find in books by authors, I have excerpted from daily practice and experience of affairs, as though from a kind of history of customs.

If any matters seem to approach the exercise of more serious philosophy, let them be understood as proposed in the manner of the Academics, with a mind investigating rather than obstinately contending, so that in the examination of truth each person’s judgment may remain free and the authority of writers may be judged worthless wherever a stronger opinion contradicts it. [Col. 0637B]

My purpose, however, is chiefly to treat matters in which error does not bring ruin, and not rashly to rise to define those matters in which one cannot err without danger. Let no one take anything said as an injury to himself, since there is no detraction from persons, but only an attack upon vices that must be avoided. In this, I think I render a service both to the bad and to the good: in the latter, what they do is approved; while the former, their vices being identified, may improve so as to win approval.

But enough of this. A brief discussion will show why it pleases me to imitate the Academics in preference to the others.

## CHAPTER I. That the Academics were more modest than other philosophers, whom rashness blinded, so that they were given over to a reprobate mind.

[Col. 0637D]

That the ancient philosophers flourished in genius and advanced through study is no longer merely a celebrated opinion, but a judgment commonly accepted by all. For human genius, through study and practice, made a path for itself toward matters almost incomprehensible by nature; and through their benefit, very many discoveries have been published for posterity, in which we rejoice and which we admire. They measured the world, subjected heaven to their rules, investigated the various causes of nature, and in some degree contemplated the maker of the universe with clarified eyes.

Therefore, raised up as though by a giant’s mass and now strengthened beyond human powers, they became proud and declared war upon God’s grace, trusting in the free choice of vigorous reason—as though, according to the fables, they were about to lay hands upon heaven, made captive by the virtues through which they were exalted. Thus they were cast down while being raised up; and, professing themselves wise, they became fools. Their foolish heart was darkened, so that those who had learned almost everything might most ruinously err in the greatest matters; and, scattered among various opinions, might even fail to know the gods.

But if the instruments of fable seem worthless to anyone—although the wise mind does not refuse to be taught even by an enemy, since God’s peculiar people shines with the gold, silver, garments, and all the adornment of the Egyptians—if, I say, pagan fictions seem worthless, then consider this: while impiety laid the foundations of Babylon in the plain of Shinar, while the engine of a tower of pride and opposition was raised to heaven, God brought about from on high the division of tongues in the fall; and, communication by speech being withdrawn from the wicked, the separation of peoples necessarily followed. [Col. 0638A]

So too, when philosophers raised the engines of their own genius on high in a certain kind of warfare against God, the unity of immutable and unfailing truth was truly withdrawn from them. Wrapped in the mists of ignorance, they lost most of their knowledge of those things that are true from the one and singular Truth. Thus their deeds prove that they were given over to a reprobate mind; and, as though their leader—the Spirit of truth—had departed, they were scattered into various sects of error and false madness. They became all the more miserable because they did not at all recognize their own deficiency.

Hence, while the Stoic worships his own *Pronoē* [Providence], he binds all things under the law of necessity. Epicurus, on the contrary, while defending the freedom of things, empties providential ordering of meaning and maintains that all things fluctuate by chance. The adherents of each stand opposed to the other and contend over almost every article of things; and, as though bound by Pallas’s oath, they utter only paradoxes, or affirm that their *kyriai doxai* (κύριαι δόξαι, “principal doctrines”) are wholly true.

The Academics, however, avoiding the precipice of falsehood, are more modest in this respect: they do not deny their deficiency, and, situated in ignorance concerning things, doubt concerning almost every question. This is far safer than rashly defining what is uncertain. The position of the Academics is also supported by the fact that not only Heraclides of Pontus and our Cicero, both held in the highest esteem among men of genius, [Col. 0638D] eventually joined them, but also many others whom it would take too long to list. Should they not therefore be preferred to the rest, recommended both by modesty in assertion and by the authority of such great men?

## CHAPTER II. On the error of the Academics; whom among them one may imitate; and what matters are doubtful to a wise person.

Yet not all who are called Academics, I say, maintained this rule of modesty; for the school itself has been divided, and one part is as open to ridicule as to error. For what could be more foolish than to waver in every matter, have certainty of nothing, and profess the name of philosopher? Those who doubt everything because they have nothing certain are as alien from faith as from knowledge.

For although faith does not attain the prize of knowledge, while it beholds as in a mirror the truth of absent things, it nevertheless possesses certainty, ambiguity’s darkness being excluded. But if the Academic doubts each particular, he is certain of nothing—unless perhaps he is uncertain even of this, whether, when contraries exist in the same subject and respect, one could be both doubtful and certain. But whether he doubts, he holds uncertain, since he does not know even whether he does not know.

Since a human being surpasses other animals in possessing reason and understanding—for in the senses, which, though belonging to the soul, are said to be bodily, he is easily surpassed, nor can he equal the lynx in keenness of sight: the boar excels in hearing, the vulture or dog in smell, the ape in taste, the spider in touch—since, I say, a human being excels in the powers of discrimination and understanding, who would not judge inferior to beasts, or rather more brutish than a brute, the person in whom reason does not discriminate and understanding does not know? [Col. 0639B]

For even brute animals seem in some way to rise toward a certain image of reason. A dog distinguishes its affections, remembers benefits, and forms familiarity with human beings from experience and practice; displaying, beyond other animals, something like fidelity in friendship toward those close to it, it is ennobled by a certain capacity for reason and understanding. Memory of injuries persists tenaciously in the camel; and the rhinoceros, which is also the unicorn, recognizes a virgin’s chastity so that it is caught, almost exclusively, in her embrace. Other animals follow the scent of the panther; and, more marvellously, fish gather in pools at the appearance of gold. Hence Nero, emperor of raging luxury, is said to have fished with golden nets.

Why say more?

> The grim lioness follows the wolf; the wolf himself, the she-goat;  
> > The wanton she-goat follows the flowering clover.  
> > (VIRGIL, *Eclogues* II.62)

And in this way very many are drawn by their own pleasure—which, I think, could not happen if even brute animals doubted their own affections. With what rashness or shamelessness, then, do those who are ignorant in every particular seize upon the profession of philosophy? For just as *notio* (“knowledge”) is grammatically named from what is known, so *ratio* (“reason”) is named from what is *ratum*, that is, certain and firm.

Surely vain is the reason of the person to whom nothing can be made persuasive, who always and in everything wavers on the slippery ground of opinions. What does philosophy confer on someone who always fluctuates in opinions, and for whom, while showing the path to happiness, it extinguishes reason’s light and, as it were, puts out the eye by which it is to show the traveller the road, so that he may go more cautiously and rightly? Does it not rather greatly harm the person whom it blinds? What will the man so torn by contradiction follow? [Col. 0639D]

Certainly no one reaches the homeland unless he follows one road; and one who lends his ear to every utterance will never be at rest. Is not the person more like one lethargic, foolish, or insane than a philosopher, if, remembering a dream, he doubts whether he has slept; if, having been filled with food, he does not know whether he is fasting; and if he knows nothing even of those things which he has just done? Further, by what means will a man advance in philosophical inquiry if reason persuades him of nothing that he may hold or follow, but leaves him always uncertain about all things?

Such an Academic, since he cannot equal even brute animals, is worthy neither of the honour nor even of the name of a human being, much less of a philosopher. Against the absurdities of such men Augustine, the Church’s great and faithful teacher, and Cicero as well, argue at greater length with forceful reasoning and most elegant speech.

Nevertheless, Cicero himself testifies that he joined those who doubt concerning particular matters which raise questions for the wise; and our Augustine does not pursue them, since he too frequently employs an Academic restraint in his works and proposes under ambiguity many things which others, arguing more confidently but no less rashly, would not consider questionable. Yet no one seems to me to speak more safely than one who is so cautious in speech that he cannot slip into falsehood. [Col. 0640B]

Matters doubtful to the wise are those which the authority neither of faith, nor of sense, nor of evident reason establishes, and which have supports of their own on either side. Such are questions concerning providence; the substance, quantity, powers, efficacy, and origin of the soul; fate; natural facility; chance; and free choice; matter and motion; the principles of bodies; the progression of multitude and the division of magnitude—whether they have no limits at all, or whether they finally encounter limits that are only *alogoi* (ἀλόγους, “irrational” or incommensurable).

They include questions concerning time and place, number and speech, sameness and difference—where there is much difficulty—divisibility and indivisibility, the substance and form of spoken sound, the status of universals, the use, end, and origin of virtues and vices; whether one who has one virtue has them all; whether all sins are equal and equally punishable; likewise, the causes of things and their conjunction or opposition; the flow and ebb of Ocean; the source of the Nile; the increase and decrease of humours in animal bodies according to the moon’s motion; and the various secrets of hidden nature.

They include the duties and classifications of causes which arise in various ways in contracts, quasi-contracts, wrongs, quasi-wrongs, and other forms of affairs; nature and its operations; truth; and the first origins of things, in which human intelligence fails; whether angels have no bodies at all, or what sort of bodies they have; and reverent questions concerning God himself, who exceeds the investigation of all rational nature and is exalted above everything that can be conceived in the mind. [Col. 0640D]

Very many matters might be enumerated in this manner—matters which admit the wise person’s doubt, although the doubt itself escapes the common crowd. In these matters, therefore, I readily believe that the Academics doubted more modestly, in proportion as I find them more carefully avoiding the precipice of rashness. So much so that, when writers employ in passages not indiscriminately doubtful words that are in a sense ambiguous—such as *si forte*, “if perhaps,” *fortasse*, “perhaps,” and *forsitan*, “perhaps”—they are said to use Academic restraint, because the Academics were more restrained than others: they feared to incur any charge of rash definition and to fall into the precipice of falsehood. [Col. 0641A]

## CHAPTER III. Why they were called Academics; and what fear or passion of the mind, according to Aulus Gellius and the Stoics, may affect a wise person.

Academics were so called from the Academy, from which Plato came. By the practice of study there, the number of his disciples, and the renown of his achievements, he made the very place of his birth famous. He preferred that place to others because, for instilling the fear by which vices are restrained and, once one’s condition is recognized, modesty is more faithfully preserved, it seemed especially suitable on account of its frequent earthquakes, by which it is often shaken. For fear, as it is akin to modesty, is also familiar to the wise man. [Col. 0641B] Not, however, that fear which disturbs the mind and, as by a kind of whirlwind, dims the eye of reason and understanding; but that which composes the spirit and, as a kindling of humility, renders a person readier for every duty of virtue.

Hence Aulus Gellius, a man of elegant speech and extensive learning, writes in the *Attic Nights* that he once sailed with a philosopher eminent among the Stoics. The prevailing Stoic opinion was that fear has no place in the mind of a wise man, since all things occur by necessity and it is foolish to fear what cannot be avoided. On the contrary, the sole remedy was held to be that a prudent man should equip himself with the powers of courage and, with the strength of endurance as the invincible shield of a most steadfast mind, receive every missile of necessity.

When, therefore, the ship was being tossed most dangerously by the stormy sea, the violence of the winds, and a threatening sky, the philosopher grew pale through fear. Then, when the storm had passed and safety afforded an opportunity for conversation and chatter, as commonly happens, one of the fellow-passengers—a rich, luxurious Asiatic—began to address and mock the philosopher, because he had turned pale with fear contrary to his profession, whereas he himself, though no philosopher at all, had remained undaunted amid the destruction threatening them. The philosopher replied with the answer of Aristippus the Socratic. When, in a similar circumstance, he had likewise been reproached by such a person, Aristippus answered that the other man had rightly felt no concern for the soul of a worthless scoundrel, whereas he himself had had reason to fear for the soul of Aristippus.

After dismissing the rich man’s question, Aulus Gellius approached the philosopher, not to provoke him but to learn, asking in a friendly manner what was the cause of his fear, since Stoic teaching commands that one should not fear the coming of death, which is admittedly the certain limit of life. Seeing that Gellius was eagerly and earnestly inflamed with a desire to learn, the philosopher produced a book of the Stoic Epictetus concerning divination, in which were written matters consonant with the doctrines of Zeno and Chrysippus, said to have been the founders of Stoicism.

When Aulus Gellius held the book in his hands, he found that the Stoics had maintained that it is not within a person’s power that impressions, which they call *phantasiai*, should enter or depart from the mind. When they arise from fearful things, or conversely, they assert that even the wise person’s mind must be moved: for a little while it trembles in fear, contracts in sorrow, expands in joy, and is stirred by desires, as though these passions anticipate the operation of reason and mind. Yet this does not mean that consciousness of evil is active in the mind, or that such movements are approved, or that anyone gives them consenting indulgence. For they hold that this is within one’s power; and they judge this to be the distinction between the mind of the wise person and that of the fool: the fool yields to passions by the consent of his mind, but the wise person, though he suffers them by necessity, nevertheless retains, with an unshaken mind, a true and firm judgment concerning what ought rationally to be sought or avoided.

These things, on the authority of Aulus Gellius, are in part both elegantly and truly stated. Yet they err if they attribute to their own powers, apart from grace, the restraint and chastening of these necessary passions, [Col. 0642B] since it belongs to God alone in his mercy—not to the person who runs or wills—that these may be turned to the service of righteousness. Let this suffice to show that modesty is governed by fear, and that the first path of philosophizing is laid out and prepared by it. For it is written that the beginning of wisdom and the end of modesty is the fear of God.

## CHAPTER IV. Why it is called philosophy; and concerning Pythagoras of Samos and his teaching, who became the founder of the Italian school of philosophy

The very name *philosophy* was invented by Pythagoras the Italian. Among the ancients he possessed such authority that, by a prejudicial opinion, his judgments outweighed those of all others; and it was enough to strengthen any opinion if it were said that he himself had said it. Indeed, the very utterance of the pronoun “he,” through a kind of customary usage, performed the office of a proper name.

He was a Samian by birth, the son of a wealthy merchant named Maratus. Yet he was far richer than his father, because his father’s trade could not acquire as much as the son preferred to despise rather than possess. Having therefore received great advances in wisdom, he first went to Egypt and then to Babylon, in order to learn thoroughly the motions of the stars and to investigate the origin of the world; there he attained the highest knowledge. Returning from there, he travelled to Crete and Lacedaemon in order to acquaint himself with the celebrated laws, then in force, of Minos and Lycurgus.

Equipped with all these things, he arrived at the city of Croton, wholly dissolute and needing only the works of virtue. Angry at fortune, its inhabitants hated the weapons which they had unhappily taken up against the Locrians; and they would have exchanged their way of life for luxury, had Pythagoras the philosopher not opposed them. From this it is clear how much one person surpasses another: the authority of a single individual recalled to the fruit of a better life a people already fallen away.

Thus each day he praised virtue, exposed the vices of luxury, and declared the causes of the ruin of fallen cities. He inspired the multitude with such zeal for frugality that it seemed incredible that some of them had ever lived luxuriously. He also frequently conducted separate instruction for married women apart from their husbands, and for children apart from their parents. At one time he taught the former chastity and obedience toward their husbands; at another, the latter modesty and zeal for letters. Throughout all this he impressed frugality upon everyone as the mother of virtues.

By the constancy of his discussions he brought it about that the matrons laid aside their gold-embroidered garments and the other ornaments of their rank as instruments of luxury; they brought all these things to the temple of Juno and consecrated them to the goddess, declaring that the true ornaments of matrons are chastity, not clothing. How much disorder had prevailed among the young is shown by the obstinate dispositions of the men who were overcome by women.

But three hundred young men, bound by the oath of a fellowship and living separately from the other citizens, as though forming a secret conspiracy against Pythagoras, turned the city against themselves. When they had gathered in one house, the city attempted to burn them; in that tumult about sixty perished, and the rest went into exile. From him, then, arose both the Italian school of philosophers and the name *philosophy*.

He was so great in that branch of philosophy called speculative that scarcely any philosopher could be considered his equal. So great was his innocence that he is believed to have abstained from the food of every living creature. So devoted was he to the cultivation of justice that, even after his death, the authority of his name governed the peoples of that part of Italy which was anciently called Magna Graecia.

Whereas formerly those who seemed superior to others were called “wise,” when he was asked what he professed himself to be, he replied that he was a philosopher—that is, a student or lover of wisdom—because it seemed exceedingly arrogant to profess oneself wise. Finally, after spending twenty years at Croton in driving away moral corruption, he moved to Metapontum and died there. Such was the admiration for him that they made a temple from his house and worshipped him as a god, perhaps taking occasion from his saying that the house of one who philosophizes is a sanctuary of wisdom and the truest temple of God.

He is also reported to have persuaded people that souls are immortal and, after the dissolution of the body, will receive the rewards of the preceding life. Yet he is said impiously to have been the first to introduce the fable of a thousand years.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the Ionic school of philosophers, the authority of Socrates, Plato’s doctrine, and the opinion concerning him after his death

[Col. 0643D]

The other school of philosophers is called Ionic and derived its origin from the further Greeks. Its founder was Thales of Miletus, one of the seven called wise men. Having investigated the nature of things, he stood out among the rest, and was especially admirable because, having mastered astronomical calculations, he foretold eclipses of the sun and moon. He was succeeded by his pupil Anaximander, who left Anaximenes as his disciple and successor. Diogenes too was his pupil, as was Anaxagoras, who taught that the divine Mind is the maker of all the things we see. He was succeeded by his pupil Archelaus, whose disciple Socrates is said to have been—the teacher of Plato.

According to the testimony of Apuleius, Plato was first called Aristotle, but afterwards Plato, from the breadth of his chest. By vigor of intellect, exercise of study, every charm of character, and also sweetness and abundance of eloquence, he rose to such eminence in philosophy that, as though seated on wisdom’s throne, he seemed by a certain authority to command both the philosophers before him and those after him.

Socrates is remembered as the first to have directed the whole of philosophy toward correcting and ordering character, whereas all before him had devoted their chief labor to investigating physics—that is, natural things. This was rightly and wisely done, since all things ought to be turned to one’s own benefit; and it profits little to know the works of God, which are all very good and correspondingly like their Creator, unless one takes special care not to be evil oneself.

Accordingly, Socrates’ illustrious reputation in life and death left his philosophy many adherents, who divided his words into various schools, of which a few things will be said later. Plato, however, by the authority in which he excelled, restrained the dissension of so great a multitude, and for a long time drew and held the attention of all upon himself.

There are those who believe that Plato was not the son either of Ariston or Aristides, but was born by a more august conception, because an apparition of Apollo had united itself with his mother Perictione, who is known to have descended from Solon, the most wise founder of Athenian laws. He was born in the month called Thargelion among the Athenians, on the day when Latona is believed to have borne Apollo and Diana on Delos; and Socrates, they say, was born the day before.

Such a man, descended from such people, not only surpassed the virtues of heroes but was said to have equalled the powers of gods. For Speusippus, informed by family evidence, praises both the boy’s quickness of intellect in learning and his disposition to remarkable modesty; he recounts that the first blossoms of his youth were imbued with labor and love of study, and testifies that, in the mature man, the growth of these virtues was united. Glaucon and Adeimantus were his brothers by the same parents. His teachers in elementary letters included Dionysius; in the wrestling-school, Ariston of Argos. Exercise brought him such progress that he won wrestling contests at the Pythian games. He did not disdain the art of painting and fashioned himself also for tragedy and dithyramb.

Already elevated by confidence in his poetry, he wished to declare himself a competitor, had not Socrates expelled the baseness of this ambition from his mind and taken care to instill in him the glory of true praise.

Previously Plato had indeed been trained in the school of Heraclides. But when he devoted himself to Socrates, he not only surpassed the other Socratics in intellect and learning; by labor and elegance he also gave philosophy distinction, and by a sound vindication of the senses and majesty of language he added greatly to its dignity. When Socrates died, Plato turned himself to Pythagorean teaching. Although he saw it furnished with careful and splendid reasoning, he desired more especially to imitate its self-restraint and chastity.

Then he visited Theodorus of Cyrene to learn geometry. From there he sought Egypt in order to pursue astronomy; and many believed that there he learned the oracles of the prophets. He subsequently returned to Italy and followed Archytas of Tarentum, the Pythagorean. He would also have turned his attention toward the Indians, Medes, and Magi, had the Caletian wars not prevented his journey. Therefore, having examined more carefully the discoveries of Parmenides and Zeno—which had been objects of admiration separately among great philosophers—he assembled them all in his books. He was the first to teach that the studies of philosophy are not merely not opposed to one another but mutually necessary, because the whole is sustained by their reciprocal assistance.

Many of his hearers, of both sexes, flourished in philosophy. He left his estate in a small garden adjoining the Academy, two servants, and the bowl with which he made supplication to the gods. He had only as much gold as a boy wore in his ear as a badge of nobility. Different hostile accounts criticize his three visits to Sicily. But he went there first to observe the natural history of Etna and understand the cause of its fires; second, at Dionysius’s request, to assist the Syracusans and learn the civic laws of that province; third, to restore the exile Dion to his native country, having obtained Dionysius’s permission. Yet in all these matters he was so diligent that at no time was he diverted from the studies or duties of philosophy.

Since philosophical study is concerned partly with action and partly with contemplation, Socrates cultivated the active part, forming the morals by which life is faithfully guided toward blessedness; Pythagoras devoted himself to the contemplative part, through which the intellect is exercised and knowledge extended. Plato, therefore, is praised for perfecting philosophy by joining each to the other. He divided it into three parts: ethics, physics, and logic—that is, moral, natural, and rational philosophy. Logic distinguishes truth from falsehood, and without it matters belonging either to action or contemplation cannot be discussed.

Some suppose that, during his travels, Plato saw the prophet Jeremiah, heard him in Egypt, and read the prophetic Scriptures. But calculation of the chronology contained in the histories of the *Chronicles* teaches that they were by no means contemporaries. Plato’s birth scarcely reached that period, but came one hundred and seven intervening years after the time when Jeremiah prophesied; and the prophetic Scriptures entered Egypt roughly sixty years after Plato’s death, under the reign of Ptolemy, a lover of letters, who summoned seventy interpreters from Jerusalem.

Nevertheless, this opinion gained strength because many things in Plato’s books accord with the sayings of the prophets. For in the *Timaeus*, while he investigates more subtly the cause of the world, he seems plainly to set forth the Trinity—which is God—by locating the efficient cause in God’s power, the formal cause in wisdom, and the final cause in goodness. Goodness alone led him to make every creature a participant in his goodness, insofar as the nature of each can be capable of blessedness.

Yet he seems in these matters to have understood and taught one substance, when he asserted that the Maker and Fashioner of the universe is one God. On account of his outstanding goodness and tender affection, Plato called him the Father of all; because of the infinity of his majesty, power, wisdom, and goodness, Plato said that he is as difficult to find as it is impossible worthily to declare him when found.

He also seems to establish that God rewards those who hope in and worship him, saying that the philosopher is a wise worshipper of God, who approaches wisdom in mind and desire, and is a lover of God. As God is admirable as the cause of the established universe, so he is the one unique and unfailing fountain from which blessedness is to be drunk.

Moses declares that in the beginning God created heaven and earth, and placed water and air between them. Plato says that, from the beginning, in order that the world—which was to be solid and visible—might be seen and touched, God laid the two first foundations of the worldly body, fire and earth. Having joined these in harmonious proportion, he inserted between them an indissoluble bond—unless, indeed, the will of the Creator, which alone is the most faithful security of so great a firmness, permits them to be dissolved. For everything bound together is by nature dissoluble; yet it is not the will of God, who wills only good things, that the covenant of this good union should perish.

Moses says, “He Who Is sent me to you,” and by a singular expression and privileged signification he judged that One to be who always remains the same: to him neither does the past pass away nor the future draw near, and he is free from every motion. [Col. 0646C] For he disdained to designate by the verb “to be” those things which hasten, with time, toward non-being and in every moment advance toward death through their various motions. In the case of a human being this is obvious: one’s life is not a state that should be expressed by the substantive verb, but a passage from womb to tomb, and, as it were, a flight or shadow of existence.

Plato likewise says that this alone possesses true being which always remains the same and is not changed by motions. Things subject to motion do not truly exist, but merely appear to exist; they do not remain at all, but continually vanish and flee, and do not wait to be named.

Moreover, Platonists and ourselves have many things in common, so that they are altogether inexcusable while they hold the truth of God in falsehood. The great Father Augustine is the authority for the statement—if I faithfully recall what I have read composed under his name—that in the books of the Platonists there was found that which the blessed Evangelist John thundered forth higher than heaven and beyond what the human mind can grasp, even though the ear may somehow hear it. There was found, I say, what he says at the beginning of the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), and so on to the passage where he says, “And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (ibid.).

For my part, unless I had read it in the writings of the Fathers, I should never have believed that any unbeliever had been permitted to open his mouth upon the oracle of so great a light, which the worldly eye cannot sufficiently behold. Yet the privilege of the Apostles and their closest familiarity establishes this: they made the word of faith illustrious by perseverance in good work, whereas philosophers became vain not only in their thoughts but in their deeds.

Plato wrote very many books. The merits of the political person did not suppress his contemplations, nor did the necessity of action extinguish the keenness of contemplation. If the book concerning his doctrine is held in contempt, Origen, Jerome, and Augustine, supported by the testimonies of all philosophers, suffice for his praise.

Different writers have written different accounts of his death. But it is more probable that one who had lived innocently and followed the precepts of philosophy to the extent of his ability did not surrender his life to ridicule. For the report that he died from shame because he could not solve a question proposed by sailors is demonstrably fabricated through an error of names. Whatever Greek tales say concerning Plato, Valerius Maximus reports concerning Homer, not Plato.

From this, however, came the common report that some called Homer Plato’s namesake because of the excellence of his wisdom, elegance of speech, and breadth of chest. For it is certain that eminent men bore many names. Plato died at the completion of eighty-one years, held by all in such reverence and with his authority so wholly unimpaired that for a long time there was doubt whether he should be numbered among gods or rather among demigods. And when, as that age faded, the merits of his virtues seemed almost incredible and in some degree approached the fables of antiquity, Labeo writes that he should be revered among the demigods, so that he might be understood to have been something greater than a human being but less than God.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Aristotle, his opinions and studies; how his various disputations gave rise to Academic doubt; and their rule

The sun seemed to have fallen from heaven on the day when Plato, prince of philosophers, departed from human affairs. Those who considered their studies entitled to precedence at wisdom’s throne, over which he had long presided, mourned him as the extinguished lamp of the world. But when his disciple Aristotle succeeded him in the office of teaching—a man of outstanding intellect and Plato’s inferior in eloquence, though easily surpassing many others—he shone upon humankind like the morning star. By the precepts of his manifold philosophy, as by the varied rays of wisdom, he illuminated the world and, as though the dimness had been wiped from their eyes, restored human minds to behold the appearance of truth.

He founded the Peripatetic school, so called because he was accustomed to dispute while walking. Excelling in splendid reputation and the art of persuasion, he gathered very many disciples into his school even while his teacher still lived. He treated every part of philosophy and gave precepts for each; but above all he so claimed rational philosophy as his own possession that he seems to have excluded everyone else from possessing it. Yet he was so strong in other fields that he deserved to make the common name of all philosophers—by antonomasia, that is, by excellence—his own particular title. For just as the poet Maro uses “the City” for Rome, so, by the judgment of its users, the name “philosopher” was restricted to Aristotle.

He was eloquent in speech, but richer in ideas, and learned in confronting every opinion. He is said to have been the first to distinguish kinds of study into acroatic and exoteric. Friends and, as it were, members of the household were admitted to the acroatic studies; the exoteric studies stood open not only to strangers, but also to guests and travellers.

Some believed him to be the son of the demon Incubus because of his bodily agility, keenness of intellect, and hunger for glory, which by manifold industry he was accustomed to snatch before everyone else. Valerius Maximus testifies concerning him that, scarcely preserving the last remnants of life in aged and wrinkled limbs amid the greatest literary leisure, he nevertheless labored so vigorously for his country’s safety that, though lying in an Athenian bed, he rescued it from the hands of the Macedonians, to whom it had been exposed, when it had been levelled to the ground by hostile arms. Thus, though the city was laid waste and overthrown, its restoration through Alexander’s friendship is known to have been Aristotle’s work.

Although he is regarded as one who confuses names and words, he prevailed not only through the subtlety for which he is famous to all, but also through a remarkable sweetness of speech, so that he seems rightly to have been closest to Plato. That he was extraordinarily eager for praise is clear even from this: when he had permitted the books on rhetoric by his pupil Theodectes to be published, he later resented having ceded so great a title of praise and glory to another. In a work of his own, treating some of the same matters, he added a clearer exposition for himself of what had been said on them in Theodectes’ books.

Hence Valerius Maximus says: “If reverence for learning so broad and extensive did not restrain me, I would say that he was a philosopher worthy to have his character strengthened by a philosopher of loftier spirit.” Yet glory is not neglected even by those who try to introduce contempt for it; for they carefully attach their names to their books, in order that they may attain by appropriating remembrance what they diminish by profession.

It was through his disputations that the Academy was shaken more by the collision of arguments than by the collision of winds. Though he is counted a Peripatetic rather than an Academic, at his prompting the Platonists who remained began, concerning individual matters and almost all matters generally, to doubt.

For after Plato’s death Chrysippus [Note: [Col. 0647D] Paris edition: Speusippus!]—his sister’s son—and Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, succeeded him in the school called the Academy; and for this reason they and their successors were called Academics from the place, just as Platonists were named from their teacher. Among these Greeks of great renown were Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Porphyry, said to have been the worst opponent of Catholic truth.

In both languages, Greek and Latin, Apuleius of Africa was distinguished: a man pre-eminent in many respects, who, by charm of character and abundance of speech, readily suggests to even a moderately wise person the Socratic spring and Platonic torrent. From these many others also proceeded, who preferred to investigate doubtful questions in such a way as to prejudice no one, rather than to define them by rash boldness—especially because they believed the truth to be hidden in matters about which one may dispute plausibly on either side. Hence the most ancient rule of the Academics is that each person should defend, by his own right, whatever seems probable to him.

## CHAPTER VII. That some things are established by the authority of sense, others by reason, and others by religion; that faith in every discipline claims a stable first principle which ought not be proved; that some things become known in themselves to the more learned and others to the unlearned; how far one should doubt; and that obstinacy greatly hinders the search for truth

There are certain things which the authority of sense, reason, or religion persuades. Doubting them bears the mark of weakness, error, or guilt. To ask whether the sun shines, snow is white, or fire is hot is characteristic of one deficient in sense. But to ask whether three is greater than two and contains both the whole of two and its half, or whether four is double two, belongs to one without discernment, whose reason is idle or wholly lacking. One who calls into question whether God exists, or whether he is powerful, wise, and good, is not merely irreligious but faithless, and deserves to be instructed by punishment.

In every philosophical discipline there are certain first principles—primitive principles, so to speak, in Cratinus’s term—which, according to the same authority, may not be doubted except by those whose labor consists in ensuring that they know nothing. For just as certain things present themselves to bodily senses so as not to be hidden from those who possess sound senses, while others are subtler, so that they are not perceived unless they are more closely applied, carefully observed, and thoroughly examined: so there are some things so clear in their own light that they cannot escape the gaze of reason, but are commonly seen by everyone, more or less according to each person’s capacity and powers.

There are other things that require, as it were, a certain scrutiny; and because they follow from those first matters, they cannot escape one who investigates them diligently. Yet certain things seem prior to both these kinds, which philosophical reason establishes, as it were, upon a foundation of faith, requesting that they be granted freely for the hope of making progress.

Geometry likewise first lays down certain postulates as the foundations, as it were, of the whole art, then adds common conceptions of the mind; and thus, as though its battle-line were drawn up, proceeds to those matters that are to be demonstrated. The postulates themselves agree with reason so closely that whoever refuses to grant them even to an opponent appears obstinate.

This, however, is not being said concerning matters pertaining to religious worship. For there also certain things are in some sense postulated which, in order that faith may deserve more, surpass the experience of reason; but these very things, though reason does not compel them, are owed to piety. For Christ has earned faith, where reason fails, to be applied to the sacraments by many benefits and great miracles; not to believe him is impious, just as stubbornly dissenting from probable conclusions is perverse.

For who, unless mad or obstinate, would deny that a straight line can be drawn from every point to every opposite point? [Col. 0650A] As in buildings, something fixed and stable must exist upon which a rising structure may rest, so in every discipline the necessity of most prudent reason requires some stable starting-point from which to proceed. Otherwise, whatever the builder adds wavers, as if someone built upon slippery sand or bitumen, or wrote in the current of a river. For more certain things give assurance to uncertain ones.

If, then, nothing follows unless something else precedes it, and every motion proceeds from rest, what process of proof can there be for one which never rests anywhere or acquiesces in anything? For the person to whom all things are merely probable can prove nothing.

Of things that are clear, some are known to everyone, others only to the more learned, each according to his own capacity. That every number is either even or odd is so publicly known that it does not escape even children, to whom their age permits:

> To play at odd and even, ride a long reed,  
> Build little houses, and harness mice to a toy cart.  
> —Horace, *Satires* II.3

But the fact that every multiple exceeds the unit by as many places as it precedes superparticular numbers of its own kind is known only to those who have devoted themselves to numbers. A more learned mathematician knows that “what a thing is” and “the being of the thing” are different. Thus, in every discipline, certain matters become known to its own practitioners which remain hidden not only from the crowd but from other philosophers.

Every religion likewise has its own principles, persuaded either by common reason or by piety, through which it advances in the worship of God and the exercise of morals toward the attainment of blessedness. Yet there is one principle of all religions, which piety grants freely and without any proof: namely, that God is powerful, wise, good, worthy of reverence, and worthy of love. The doctrine of the Epicureans, who deny that God exists and subject all things to chance, has long since been rejected through God made man.

To oppose principles or things self-evident, or to doubt them, belongs to a senseless or foolish person—or, worse still, a guilty one. Nor may one doubt those things that follow from principles, provided it is clear that they do follow. Matters should be debated only so long as it becomes evident whether they cohere with those principles or with their consequences. For it is not useless to doubt each of these matters individually. Indeed, until they grasped the truth, the Academic debate concerning probabilities turned upon such questions.

For what does it matter, or whom does it concern, if there were people who always investigated all things, learning yet never arriving at the knowledge of truth, because they knew that they possessed nothing certain? Cicero therefore prescribes this rule for the Academics: one whose purpose is to philosophize should inquire while a matter is obscure, but should assent to truth when it shines forth with probability. For he says: “We who follow probabilities can proceed no further than what presents itself as probable; and we are prepared to refute without anger and to be refuted without obstinacy.”

For these two things greatly oppose the discovery of truth: either becoming angry with one who speaks truth, or laboring obstinately in defense of falsehood. For, as the moral philosopher says:

> Anger hinders the mind from being able to discern the truth.

And Truth itself incarnate departed from those who more obstinately resisted the Holy Spirit in Chorazin and Bethsaida. Obstinacy likewise blinded the Jews, so that the veil of the Temple—which was torn from top to bottom when the Lord suffered—still holds their eyes.

## CHAPTER VIII. That virtue is the sole way of philosophizing and of going to blessedness; and concerning the three grades of those who approach, and the three schools of philosophers
Yet because “not all can do all things,” and “the Spirit breathes where it wills” (John 3:8), and because it often happens that the many things put forward by teachers admit of manifold interpretation among the multitude, many schools flowed forth from the words of Socrates and Plato—yet all hastening toward one goal, as it were by different paths. But that toward which the intention of all rational beings tends is true blessedness. For there is no one who does not wish to be blessed; yet not all travel by one road toward what they desire. One way, however, is set before all; but, like a royal highway, it is divided into many paths. This is virtue. For unless through virtue, no one proceeds to blessedness. Perhaps someone may be drawn to blessedness apart from works of virtue, and certainly without works; but no one advances thither except by the steps of virtue.
