Virtue, therefore, is the merit of happiness; happiness, the reward of virtue. And these are the highest goods: the one of this life, the other of the homeland. [Col. 0651C] For nothing is more excellent than virtue while the exile is a pilgrim away from the Lord; nothing is better than happiness when the citizen reigns and rejoices with the Lord. These surpass all other things because virtue comprises everything that must be done, and happiness everything that must be desired. Yet happiness surpasses virtue, because in every case that for the sake of which something exists is more excellent than that which exists for the sake of something else. For a person is not happy in order to act rightly; rather, he acts rightly in order to live happily. Hence that saying of Socrates in the book of the *Saturnalia* is praised: many men wish to live in order that they may eat and drink; but he drank and ate in order that he might live.

Blessedness, then, is the one singular highest good of all; but something else is in a certain respect called highest by comparison with certain things, and is thereby higher than others because it comes more nearly to that which is truly, singularly, and uniquely highest. Moreover, human weakness cannot attain either without philosophy as its guide. For whoever sets out for the way of blessedness without it is like a blind man proceeding upon slippery ground: presumptuous in reaching upward, he falls. Therefore Chrysippus declared philosophy to be mistress of divine and human matters; nor could it ever be sufficiently praised, since it drives out vices, displays and bestows virtues, and in human weakness in some manner restores divine integrity. And, to express his view more plainly, he says that all who are not watchful by philosophy or toward philosophy—which vigilance, nevertheless, comes from philosophy—are like brute animals; indeed, that it is an astounding miracle contrary to [Col. 0652A] nature for brutish human beings to exist in human bodies.

There are, however, three classes of human beings who are truly human—for he asserted that some are brutes. Some already enjoy the delight of wisdom, and these are the wise; others approach in order to enjoy it, and these are philosophers; others aspire to approach it, namely those who are not yet philosophers but desire to become so. For it is evident that very many, though they do not yet practise philosophy, emulate the life of philosophers, if not in deed, at least in desire. I approve his opinion all the more confidently because I seem to see it supported by the authority of the Holy Spirit, when the Prophet says: “My soul has longed to desire thy righteous ordinances at all times” (Psalm 118). In this passage he seems to me plainly to have expressed the three orders just mentioned. For since Plato calls the wise man a worshipper of God, who else should be considered wise but the one who abides in the Lord’s righteous ordinances and, with conscience soothing him by good works, already tastes beforehand and feels, with the whole eagerness of his mind, the savor of true happiness? [Col. 0652B] Undoubtedly he is by no means without it for whom known blessedness becomes sweet; and the abundance of desirable things is present to him who, in this life, tastes and sees how sweet the Lord is.

The philosopher, however, whose purpose is directed toward becoming wise, is, according to the same authority, a lover of God; and, subduing vices, he applies his mind to knowing things, so that, once these are known, he may be able to approach true blessedness. For these make a human being blessed: that the bonds of vices be loosed and that he be granted, as if by certain steps of contemplation, to behold the bright and unfailing fountain of good. For:

> Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things.  
> —Virgil

And, as the poet says—for incentives to virtue please us, from whatever source they come—

> Happy the souls whose first concern it was  
> To know these things and climb into the heavenly homes.  
> It is credible that they alike raised their heads  
> Higher than human vices and amusements.  
> Neither Venus nor wine broke their exalted hearts,  
> Nor the duties of the forum or the toil of war.  
> Neither light ambition nor glory steeped in false color,  
> Nor the hunger for great wealth, troubled them.  
> They brought the distant stars close to our eyes  
> And placed the heavens beneath their intellect.  
>   
> [Col. 0652D] Thus heaven is sought—not that Olympus may bear Ossa,  
> And Pelion’s summit touch the highest stars.  
> —Ovid, *Fasti* I.297

Yet there is no duty, whether in military service or at home, which philosophy does not treat, since it alone excludes vices, and without it nothing can be done rightly among human beings. Now, just as abiding in the righteous ordinances—that is, fulfilling God’s commandments—makes one wise (for the prophet also says, “From thy commandments I have gained understanding,” Psalm 118), so fitting one’s mind to fulfil them is the truest philosophy. But there are some who do not yet fulfil them or fit themselves to fulfil them, yet approve what they admire in others and desire, with God as author, to be conformed to them. Thus the highest rank is that of those occupied with righteous ordinances; the middle rank [Col. 0653A] is of those whose mind is freed from vices, so as to be occupied with them through love; the lowest is of those who desire to be freed, so that they may be able even to desire this. Though they are not philosophers, they nevertheless desire to be philosophers. The prophet had assumed their person when he said: “My soul has longed to desire thy righteous ordinances at all times.”

For wisdom possesses such beauty that, if—as Plato says—it could be seen with the eyes of the body, it would wonderfully inflame human beings with love of wisdom, so much so that all would necessarily fall in love at first sight. The faithful soul loves and seeks it from its youth; its old age consists in gravity of character, and its childish age in ignorance and the slippery course of vices. “Above health,” he says, “and every beauty I loved wisdom, and I chose to possess her instead of light; all good things came to me together with her.” If, therefore, all goods are appendages of wisdom, and philosophy is the pursuit of wisdom, surely contempt for philosophy excludes all goods. It follows that the more diligently one applies oneself to philosophy, the more faithfully and rightly one proceeds toward blessedness. For it dispenses the virtues by which one advances in every duty.

But because the ancients, although they believed in some measure that souls were immortal, had not yet received instruction concerning the eternal life which is to come after this one, they located the highest good in virtue—than which clearly nothing is better, except to enjoy Him who is supremely good and the highest good. For the use of virtue is best, and God himself is the fruit of using it. Since virtue alone makes one blessed, they attempted, taking occasion from the traditions of the learned, to ascend to [Col. 0653C] its throne by various tracks. The Stoic, to teach contempt for things, busies himself with meditation on death; the Peripatetic turns himself over in inquiry into truth; Epicurus, in pleasures. Though they tend toward one end, they open before their hearers differing doctrines, as if they were roads to blessedness. It is permissible to doubt and inquire about these until truth shines forth from a comparison of the proposed views, as if from a collision of arguments. But these matters will be discussed more fully below. For the present, let it suffice to have shown in what respects one may imitate the wavering Academics.

## Chapter IX. The arrogance of the ignorant multitude; how works which can profit or harm ought to be read; and that wisdom is not attained by talent or exercise without grace

[Col. 0653D]

Few, however, deem themselves worthy to be imitators of the Academics, since each chooses what to follow according to inclination rather than reason. Some are drawn aside by their own opinions, some by the opinions of teachers, and some by association with the multitude. For what does the man doubt who, having sworn allegiance to the words of a master, attends not to what is said but by whom it is said? He barks out anything whatever vehemently, and whatever his childish age has absorbed he supposes to have been drawn from the deepest recesses of philosophy. Ready to dispute even about goat’s wool, he believes it incredible if anything unknown has sounded in his ears; and the man captivated by his teacher’s opinion does not yield to arguments. Whatever that teacher has put forward is authentic and inviolable.

Yet the man who has spent his life learning a small number of things contradicts more readily and resists more stubbornly. He is hemmed in by so great a narrowness of words that, if you remove one or two words, he becomes speechless and quieter than any statue. You would suppose him made of marble and to have learned, in the lecture-room of Pythagoras or the cloister of monks, not so much the practice as the necessity of silence. If by chance one of these falls into your hands to be educated, you will rightly do what Quintilian relates, in his book *On the Education of an Orator*, that Timothy, who excelled in the art of the flute, used to do. He demanded and received double fees from those who had been badly taught beforehand than from those who came wholly untrained. For error requires a double labor: the seeds of corrupt instruction must be removed, and those of good instruction more faithfully implanted.

Look at those whom the multitude of hearers loudly proclaims as the leaders of philosophy in our own time. Examine them attentively: you will find them occupied with one rule, or with two or a few words; or, at most, they have selected a few questions suited to wrangling, in which to exercise their talent and consume their lives. Yet they are unable to unravel these questions; rather, they hand down to posterity through their hearers the knot and the whole ambiguity together with its entanglement, to be dissolved. To this place they invite you to join battle: they press and demand a contest. If you delay in engaging, if you hesitate a little, they leap upon you. If you come forward, if at last you engage against your will, if you press them, they seek hiding places, change countenance, twist their words, and take on deceptive shapes. You will marvel that slippery and shifting Proteus has returned—except that he may more easily be held if you persist in understanding what they mean and think, wherever their words flow and turn amid such variety of expression. At last they will be bound by their own meaning and caught in the word of their mouth, if you grasp and firmly hold the substance of what they say. Yet the matters most hotly disputed are more useless and more trivial than others once they are laid open. If you proceed further, if you are ashamed and weary of lingering too long over trifles, he falls back upon the bypaths of the question proposed and, like Antaeus returning to his mother’s bosom, strives to regain strength from that in which he was begotten and nourished. [Col. 0654D] Thus he goes round and makes so many windings that he returns to familiar ground, as though a labyrinth must be traversed:

> The stork feeds her young on a snake;  
> And when she has found a lizard through the winding fields,  
> They seek the same creatures once they have taken wing.  
> The vulture, leaving pack-animal, dogs, and crosses,  
> Hastens to her young and brings a portion of carrion.  
> This, then, is even the food of the great vulture,  
> Who, when she now makes nests in her own tree, feeds herself.  
> But the handmaids of Jove and the noble birds hunt  
> Hare or roe-deer in the forest; then the prey  
> Is laid in the nest. But when the tawny brood  
> Raises itself, spurred by hunger it hastens to that prey  
> Which it had first tasted when the egg was broken.  
> —Juvenal XIV.75

If, therefore, you detach them from their own words, you will be able to pity their poverty in almost every field. There are those who seem to excel in individual branches; there are those who lay claim to every part of philosophy. Yet neither group is less destitute of abundance in the individual branches of philosophy. Some hope for perfection from one branch; others attend to them all, while impoverished in each one. Yet I should not readily say whom I consider more mistaken, since perfection is secured from no one branch, and no one can faithfully serve them all. But the person who seeks all things from one is more foolish; the one who professes them all is more arrogant. Indeed, to be occupied with everything is the mark of an idle man; to range over everything, of one who is fastidious and makes no progress. But the person who surveys many things so as to choose what deserves more particular attention is prudent and, once the others have been examined, adheres more faithfully to his preference.

Perhaps the precept of the moralist commanding the reading of books has this in view. In the little book by which children are initiated, so that instruction and practice of virtue, drunk in by tender minds, may not easily be erased—since “a vessel long retains the scent / With which, when new, it was once imbued”—Cato, or someone else, for the author is uncertain, says:

> Take care to read many things; having read them, read many things again.

I would scarcely believe anything more useful to one aspiring to knowledge, apart from observance of God’s commandments, in which alone and uniquely lies unquestionable progress in philosophy. Yet everything should be read in such a way that, once some things have been read, they are neglected; some are rejected; some are looked over in passing, lest they be wholly unknown. [Col. 0655C] But above all one must apply greater diligence to those works which either form civic life—whether in civil law or in other precepts of ethics—or promote health of body or soul. For when the discipline chief among the liberal arts, without which no one can rightly teach or be taught, is to be treated in passing and, as it were, greeted from the threshold, who would judge that one should linger over other matters which, difficult in understanding or useless and harmful in effect, do not make a person better? For even those things whose use is necessary are most harmful if they occupy a person without moderation.

Who doubts that poets, historians, orators, and the mathematicians of sound mathematics should be read, especially since without them men cannot be, or are not ordinarily, learned? Those ignorant of them are called unlettered, even though they know their letters. Yet when they lay claim, as it were, to the mind as their own domain, although they promise knowledge of things, they unteach and displace the cultivation of virtue. Thus Cicero, speaking of poets, cries out so that he may be heard more attentively: “The outcry and approval of the people, as though of some great and wise teacher—and one whose applause suffices for recommendation—make those whom they wish authoritative.” Yet those who are exalted by such praises—what darknesses do they spread! What fears do they introduce! What desires do they inflame! They promote sexual immorality and adultery, devise various arts of deceit, teach thefts, robberies, and arson, and set before the eyes of the ignorant multitude examples of evils that are, have been, or indeed may be imagined. What conflagration of a burning sky, inundation of the sea, or opening of the earth has produced such slaughter among peoples as these writers produce in morals?

The comic poet most pleasing above the rest recounts, in the *Eunuch*, a young man’s lust inflamed when he saw a painting depicting how the god who shakes the temples of heaven with thunder, having sent gold through the roof-opening, corrupted Danaë, shut up in a tower and surrounded by guards. The multitude sees, marvels at, and praises similar pictures everywhere. For few spectators attend to the incentives of virtue:

> A thing that has in itself neither counsel nor measure  
> You cannot govern by counsel.  
>   
> [Col. 0656B] In love all these vices exist: wrongs,  
> Suspicions, enmities, truces,  
> War, then peace again. If you ask  
> To make these uncertainties certain by reason, you will accomplish no more  
> Than if you endeavored to be mad with reason.  
>   
> And what you now ponder angrily by yourself:  
> “I? That woman? She, that man? She, me? Why not?”—leave it.  
> “I would rather die; she shall find out what kind of man I am.”  
> These words one little false tear, by Hercules,  
> Which she has scarcely forced from her eyes by rubbing them miserably,  
> Will extinguish; and you yourself will accuse yourself  
> And yourself render satisfaction to her.  
> —Terence, *Eunuch*, Book I, 12

The slave advances an evident argument for repelling the insults of courtesans; but everything they say on this side is received as though the slave were recalling a mad lover to his senses.

Nevertheless, Cicero himself highly commends them elsewhere, saying: “That man alone makes poets and the various writers on the arts or on deeds contemptible who is not afraid of being despised.” For they also have a use for virtue and furnish material for philosophical inquiry. They mark vices, rather than teach them; and they are pleasing either for usefulness or for delight. They pass through moral dangers in such a way as to make room for virtue. For through weapons, fires, the various storms of the sea, through so many commotions, seditions, and plots of peoples, through Scylla and Charybdis, Ulysses passed, that he might at least return to his homeland in old age. He lost companions through various accidents of exile; but violence of fortune, weakness of nature, or pleasure of mind consumed them. Yet the account of all these is delightful. For even a foreseen disaster to a friend, although bitter, helps one to be cautious. And the more intimate a person’s association with one falling has been, the more that person’s downfall terrifies him. [Col. 0656D] Indeed, one often gains more from examples than from precepts. Evils are more readily avoided in proportion as they have been more faithfully foreknown.

Ulysses scarcely escaped, and in a manner escaped alone; but fewer escape into the delight of philosophy and, as it were, its proper pleasures. If you deign to hear the Lyric poet when his lyre is silent, Flaccus—or Horace, if you prefer—agrees with him, rejoicing that he has found in the Maeonian poet more uprightness and usefulness than is expressed in the precepts of many Stoics. For he says:

> While you, greatest Lollius, declaim at Rome,  
> I have reread at Praeneste the writer of the Trojan war—  
> Who tells more nobly and better than Chrysippus and Crantor  
> What is honorable, what shameful, what useful, and what is not.  
>   
> [Why I have believed this, unless something detains you, listen.]  
>   
> The tale in which, because of Paris’ love,  
> Greece is said to have clashed with a barbarian adversary in a long war  
> Contains the passions of foolish kings and peoples.  
> Antenor advises cutting off the causes of war.  
> What of Paris? That he may reign safe and live happily,  
> He denies that he can be compelled.  
> Within and outside the Trojan walls there is sinning  
> By sedition, deceit, crime, lust, and anger.  
> Whatever madness kings commit, the Achaeans pay the penalty.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.1

I readily yield to the opinion of those who do not believe that a person can become learned without reading authors. Yet an abundance of letters does not at all make a philosopher. For grace alone leads to wisdom. Amid the greatest abundance of learning there is sometimes ignorance or neglect of truth, without which it is impossible for anyone to become wise. Hence Augustine, that teacher of the Church whom no one can remember sufficiently, rebukes Varro; yet, to show that he was most learned, Augustine says, after the other things by which Varro is commended in singular praise:

> Finally, Cicero himself gives him such testimony that in the *Academics* he says that the discussion occurring there was held by him with Marcus Varro, “a man,” he says, “easily the most acute of all, and without doubt the most learned.”

He does not say “most eloquent” or “most fluent,” because in truth Varro is greatly inferior in that capacity; but “easily the most acute of all, and undoubtedly the most learned.” But in the first book, when he praised the literary labors of the same Varro, he says:

> “We, wandering and straying in our own city as though strangers, were brought home by your books, so that we might at last be able to recognize who and where we were. You have revealed the age of our country, the divisions of times, the laws of sacred rites, and of priests; private and public discipline; the locations, regions, and places; the names, kinds, functions, and causes of all divine and human things.”

Thus this man of such remarkable and outstanding learning, who read so much that one marvels that he had leisure to write anything, wrote so much that we scarcely believe anyone could have read it all. This man, I say, so great in talent and learning, if he had been an assailant and destroyer of the things he writes about as divine, and had said that they belonged not to religion but to superstition, I do not know whether he would have written down so many things in them worthy of ridicule, contempt, and detestation. Therefore, when superstition is reproved by the writings of a man most acute and, by Cicero’s testimony, without any doubt most learned—writings which themselves convict it—and when it is clear that superstition is opposed, through the fault of falsehood, to virtue, which consists in truth alone, and that wisdom cannot exist without virtue, who could believe that a person can become wise by reading alone, unless grace is present, illuminating, creating, and giving life to the virtues?

## Chapter X. All writings are to be read; the blessing given to the first-created and to Noah’s sons; and the fact that the authority of no pagan prejudges reason

[Col. 0658A]

It is reasonable, nevertheless, that all writings should be read, unless they are reading matter to be rejected; for all things, not only those written but also those done, are believed to have been established for human benefit, although human beings sometimes misuse them. For even angels were in some manner established for the soul, and the bodily world, according to the teaching of the Fathers, for the use of the body.

At the beginning God blessed man, saying: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living creatures that move upon the earth” [Col. 0658B] (Genesis 1). Adding every herb bearing seed and all trees for their use—for they are believed to have abstained from eating flesh before the Flood—he granted them as food. He likewise blessed those whom the ark, a prefiguration of the Church, had delivered from the plague of the Flood, and gave them a law, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth; and let your fear and dread be upon every animal of the earth, and upon all birds of heaven, together with all things that move on the earth. All fish of the sea are delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you. Like green herbs I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood.”

Behold: to the first-created and to Noah’s sons alike was granted the same grace of blessing, the same authority of dignity, and almost the same permission regarding foods. For increase and multiplication signify the extension of grace; dominion over the earth and the fear of beasts, the privilege of power; the universality of provisions, an indication of freedom. For all things are clean to the clean. Nor do I recall that the privilege of this blessing was granted at any other time than when innocence was given through creation or restored through the remedy of sacrament or repentance. For perhaps this is why “Increase and multiply” was said to the former before sin and to the latter immediately after the Flood: that only such increase and multiplication may be acquired as God conferred upon man by nature or reformed by grace. And a person is commanded both to increase in himself and, in a certain manner, to multiply in offspring: in himself, for progress in merit; in offspring, by a certain numerous propagation of virtues. But when nature has been corrupted by fault, I do not recall that one is commanded to increase or multiply.

Although what has been said may stand in its literal sense—since all things serve the needs of human life, and even those which seem deadly by sight, smell, or hearing, much less by touch or taste, such as the more harmful poisons, are food for man or are turned into his food—a mystical investigator may nevertheless find another meaning. Yet the historical sense is supported by the fact that we see fish in the best health, and wild beasts whose flesh is most beneficial, frequently devour the most poisonous reptiles; and poisons themselves are introduced into medicines by which not only is human nature sustained, but infirmity also restored to strength. [Col. 0659A]

Since the historical sense must first be examined, that interpretation is more praiseworthy and plainly more useful which more strongly forms the mind either toward faith or toward the works of faith, which are good morals. For this must always be sought in reading: that a person may continually become better than himself. But although the preceding letter may usefully be referred to many things, I agree that it can be adapted to this: that free choice may be stirred up, through grace conferred by God’s blessing, to the growth and multiplication of virtue; and that, when virtues have been multiplied by grace, there may be added the subjection of the earth. When a person has subjected this earth within himself, he gains mastery over himself and others, so that, set above all living creatures, he instills fear and dread in all things moving on the earth.

Thus all things are food for him, because in all creatures the Lord speaks to him the words of his salvation. He is plainly fed by all things through which a human life advances toward the ordering of life or character. For it is certain that every edification of morals comes from the Lord; and whenever anyone is instructed toward virtue, whether by deed, word, or any manner whatsoever, he is beneficially fed by what the Lord has granted him. For every instruction in salvation is in some way the word of God; and wherever the truth of teaching is set forth, it must be accepted, because truth is always uncorrupted and incorruptible.

Before and after the Flood, provided that one abstains from blood, in which the soul has its seat, the use of all things is permitted; and before and after baptism, provided one avoids sin, no one is forbidden to receive instruction from any source whatsoever. If the apostle is to some “an odor of death unto death,” what prevents vessels of death also from benefiting someone unto life? Therefore, when it is said, “Eat whatever you wish, except blood,” it is as though one said figuratively: provided you flee vices, read whatever you wish.

Just as among bodily foods some are beneficially digested, some are changed into raw humors, others are completely expelled through expulsive force, some benefit the healthy if taken moderately but harm the sick, and some suit the weaker yet are less suitable for those who are healthy or recovering—these latter do not strengthen nature so greatly, for more delicate foods nourish less, while commoner foods are, so to speak, richer in nourishment—so also among books there are those that benefit everyone, provided they are read with the moderation that governs works containing nothing but edification of faith and morals. There are some suited to stronger minds and certainly to be kept away from the reading of the simple; some which the nature of a good mind wholly rejects; some which it digests for the use of morals or eloquence; and some which harden the soul and produce only indigestibility in faith and good works. [Col. 0659D] A writing will scarcely be found in which, if not in its meaning or words, there is not something that a prudent reader leaves out.

But Catholic books are read in their entirety and with greater caution; pagan books lie open more dangerously to the simple. Yet in both it is most useful for more trustworthy minds to exercise themselves. For a careful reading of individual works makes one very learned; a cautious choice of the better works makes one excellent. For, as we read in the book of the *Saturnalia* and in Seneca’s letters to Lucilius, we ought in some fashion to imitate bees: they wander about and gather flowers, then arrange whatever they have brought, divide it among their combs, and by a certain mixture and the property of their own spirit change diverse nectar into one flavor. We likewise should turn whatever we have sought in diverse reading to the use of virtue, so that all things may coalesce into an ordering of actions, with judgment of reason arranging them. For things kept distinct are more securely preserved in the mind; and this very distinction, not without a certain leaven by which the whole is seasoned, blends diverse tastings into the use of one flavor, so that, even though its source may appear, what has been taken may nevertheless appear to be something different from its source. This is what we see nature do in our body without any work of our own. Foods that we take in are burdens to a weak stomach as long as they remain in their own state and float about undigested; but when they have changed from what they were, then at last they pass into strength.

For blood is drawn off in accordance with the divine command when vices are avoided. The shepherd of the Church is commanded to slaughter and eat reptiles and unclean creatures. Although this properly refers to the calling of the Gentiles, by analogy it can teach that, once errors have been slain, we should not shrink from pagan doctrines. While Pythagoreans teach innocence, frugality, and contempt for the world, let them be heard; while they thrust souls, which they have raised to heaven, back into the bodies of beasts, let even Plato be slain. For in this he followed Pythagoras too closely: he taught that, just as the dead come from the living, so reciprocally the living arise from the dead, and that souls migrate through diverse bodies according to the quality of their morals. Hence:

> I myself—for I remember—in the time of the Trojan war  
> Was Euphorbus, son of Panthous; once the heavy spear  
> Of the younger son of Atreus lodged in my opposing breast.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.160

Thus they should be read in such a way that authority does not prejudice reason. For even while one reads of a rose, the nettle sometimes burns the hand that touches it. Wisdom is a kind of fountain from which flow rivers [Col. 0660D] watering the whole earth; they not only fill the garden of delights of the divine page, but also pass over to the nations, so that not even Ethiopians are wholly without them. Hence there are among the nations gardens blooming, fragrant, and fruitful. If a simple reader enters them by chance, let him always remember that poet’s saying:

> You who gather flowers and strawberries growing on the ground,  
> Flee from here, cold boys: a snake lies hidden in the grass.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* III.92

For no sluggard carries off the apples of the Hesperides, guarded by the ever-watchful dragon; nor does anyone who has read the Scriptures not as one awake but as one drowsily dreaming, as though he were hurrying with spurs toward the end of reading. It is certain that the faithful and prudent reader, who applies himself to letters out of love, always excludes vices and in all things approaches life. Hence the saying of Jerome, teacher of teachers: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.”

## Chapter XI. What it is truly to practise philosophy, and the end toward which the whole purpose of Scripture tends

This is truly to practise philosophy, and this is the most delightful and health-giving fruit of much reading. For it contains the discipline of all things and, as the ruler of all, itself establishes measure and limits for every action, word, and thought of human life. Yet there is one thing for which it does not know how to set a limit. There is one thing to which it prescribes this measure: that it should have no measure. Whatever it does or says tends to that which, among those who practise philosophy rightly, has no end. For its substance consists in this: that it should never be brought to an end. If, according to Plato, the philosopher is a lover of God, what else is philosophy but the love of divinity? This, assuredly, does not wish to be ended, lest philosophy itself also come to an end—which would not be fitting. For what is ended ceases to be; and if love of God is extinguished, the name of philosophy vanishes.

Thus too the incarnate Wisdom of God, while prescribing measure to many things, commands that God be loved without measure—except that this measure is prescribed for charity: that God should be loved without an end to love. For he who says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19), first said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Matthew 22). He likewise added: “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (ibid.). If, therefore, all that is written serves the prophets and the law—that is, if every teaching tends to this, that man should be subject to the law of God—who doubts that all things are to be referred to the kingdom of charity? Whoever, by practising philosophy, acquires or enlarges charity has attained the highest end of the philosopher.

This, then, is the true and unchangeable rule of philosophers: in everything read or learned, done or omitted, each person should conduct himself so as to advance in truth and charity. Charity is never empty or alone, but introduces into the very person whom it consecrates to piety, as into the Lord’s temple, uprightness, modesty, chastity with sobriety, and the company of other venerable virtues. Whatever tends elsewhere in the arts or in any writings whatever is not the teaching of philosophy, but empty tales and inventions of those whose impiety causes God’s wrath to be revealed from heaven. Whatever they prattle, it seems to the right philosopher foolish, tasteless, and insipid. Hear not me but the prophet speaking of such men: “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to thy law” (Psalm 118). Thus, to speak true and just things is common to philosophers and non-philosophers alike. To speak truth and falsehood, to teach good and evil, does not belong to philosophers. Even the empty imitator of a philosopher sometimes teaches what is right; but the one who follows the right things he teaches is a true philosopher.

## Chapter XII. The follies of perfumed fops who suppose wisdom to consist in words; and that divine books must be read differently from pagan books

[Col. 0662A]

They certainly err—and err shamelessly—who suppose that philosophy consists in words alone. They err who take virtue to be words, as they take a grove to be trees. For virtue is commended by action, and virtue accompanies wisdom inseparably. Hence it is clear that those who cling to words prefer to seem wise rather than to be wise. They go about the streets, wear out the thresholds of the more learned, raise little questions, entangle words so as to obscure both their own meaning and another’s, being readier to bandy them about than to examine them if any difficulty emerges. [Col. 0662B] Yet these braggarts of wisdom, not its lovers, fear to betray their ignorance; and, through a perverse shame, they prefer not to know what they do not know rather than to seek and learn it—especially if others are present whom they suppose know what they themselves do not know. Yet you could not endure their arrogance: they speak offhand on every subject, pass judgment on everyone, blame others, praise themselves, and boast that they have newly discovered what the ancients had long worn smooth and what the testimony of books has conveyed through many ages to our own time. They multiply words, so that they are often less understood through the burden and multitude of their language than through the difficulty of the matters themselves. When they have succeeded in making themselves unintelligible, they suppose that they have earned the reputation of philosopher above the rest. And often one who knows very little proposes a great many things which not even Pythagoras himself would suffice to explain. At times he repeats and turns over the same things. And because he has nowhere to turn aside, he labours wretchedly, [Col. 0662C] wearing out the same subject, “and tracing the same circles of air.” For while you hear him from afar, you will marvel that a third Cato has fallen from heaven: he will seem capable of producing any man whatever. If you ask his profession or art, he is:

> Grammarian, rhetorician, geometer, painter, masseur,  
> Augur, rope-walker, physician, magician: he knows everything.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* III.76)

And he is far superior to the hungry little Greek. For, should you order him, he will go to heaven; more skilled than Daedalus, he will carry even you unharmed through empty space wherever you wish.

Approach him to be taught; inquire carefully what the authors meant in their writings; scrutinize the letter—and immediately he will rebuke your stupidity and call you slower than the Arcadian ass. You are duller than lead because you ask what lies hidden [Col. 0662D] in the letter. The letter is useless, and one need not care what it says. If you persist, you will be warned to flee from it, because it is deadly and kills. Take care that you are not the serpent which eats earth all the days of its life. You must either play, tell stories, or dispute. For he who is more wordy seems more learned. Nor need one care whence, or what, or concerning what anyone thinks or puts forward, provided only that he speaks. Nor does it matter what argument anyone relies upon, so long as each can provide not a proof but its shadow. What is true or false, probable or improbable, is sought in vain, when the appearance of probability is preferred in every case.

Establish whatever proposition you please: immediately some resemblance [Col. 0663A] nullifies it. For what holds in one similar case will, whether you wish it or not, hold in another. Yet it is certain that what is like the truth is not at once true, and that what appears false is not always false. If you endeavour to expose the dissimilarity of the analogous cases proposed, you undertake an empty task. For he will either obstruct you by shouting, or laugh at your superfluous labour, since every set of similar things must contain some dissimilarity. Otherwise they would properly be called not so much similar as identical. To show why this is not so is judged not merely frivolous but thoroughly deserving of ridicule. At once he asks whether you wish to declaim. They say that they have assembled to hear a Peripatetic, not Hermagoras; though they imitate the Peripatetics more by walking about and roaming the streets than by a careful investigation of things.

[Col. 0663B] If, however, this disputation is practised for acquiring abundance of eloquence, and similarities and dissimilarities are sought out, it is indeed a praiseworthy exercise; and I would not easily say what could be more advantageous for the young, provided that they do not allow their eyes to be blinded by the thick cloud of fallacies. For nothing is more useful or more serviceable to young people in gaining glory or resources than eloquence, which is chiefly acquired when the mind has an abundance of matters and the mouth an abundance of words. To utter words about matters unknown is the mark of a fool rather than a teacher or learner. You will see many such men who hold the entire day in a long speech and say nothing at all, or very little. You are exhausted [Col. 0663C] by listening; and, unless he were more wordy, he might have been utterly wearied out by speaking. Yet you still do not understand where he is tending or what he wants. You await the end; he has not yet made a beginning. Endure, nevertheless, so that you may see how he will come out; gather up at last what he has woven together, and there will meet you:

> … like the dreams of a sick man,  
> Fashioning empty shapes, so that neither foot nor head  
> Is restored to a single form.

You would believe him a man of deranged brain, unable through failure of reason to restrain his tongue. You would suppose that he passes sleepless nights, and that, reason being asleep, melancholy alone has been awakened in him. If, moved perhaps by pity, you persuade him to moderation, he will be inflamed [Col. 0663D] and invent every kind of reproach against anyone; he will abuse alike those who pity and those who mock him. Neither friend nor enemy will depart from him except spat upon. If you have begun, you must endure to the end, or suffer the insults of his insolent tongue. Desist, therefore, unless you prefer to be polluted by a filthy tongue. For unclean things, the more they are stirred, the more they stink.

You will recognize the saying of the prudent man:

> The wise fear to touch and flee the mad poet;  
> Boys tease him, and the heedless follow.

Although among private persons or people living seriously a man of this kind rightly seems useless, he is nevertheless convenient in a crowd, which delights in material for merriment and playful amusement. He is an excellent instrument for provoking laughter, and more effective than any mime. [Col. 0664A] To escape his poison, show patience with your ears; humour the madman, who spares no one. And if you happen to wish to restrain him, beg him most courteously, when teaching or disputing, to add more substance to his meaning and balance it by an economy of words. For one who proportionates words to things, and things to the occasion, observes the most moderate rule of all eloquence. That abundance, however, produces praise which agrees with truth, virtue, and every duty as their friend. To speak much and falsely belongs to a babbler of trifles, one wholly careless of reputation and provoking in himself the hatred and contempt of serious men. For the Spirit is the author of wisdom, because one who speaks sophistically is hateful.

[Col. 0664B] Yet there is no slight usefulness in detecting sophistical irrelevancies. Without knowledge of these, anyone who proceeds to examine truth and discuss matters is like a useless soldier advancing unarmed against a trained and equipped enemy. It is therefore permissible, as an exercise, to deceive one’s interlocutor in return and, as though in the school of military instructors, to practise a playful warfare among fellow citizens. But where the intention of those conversing requires the sobriety of philosophy, sophistical irrelevancies must lie hidden. And if they emerge from either side, the wise rebuke them as, in a commonwealth, the fraud of malicious persons is restrained among contracting parties.

[Col. 0664C] Moreover, to proportion words to things and things to times, and prudently expose intervening fallacies, is not the work of a few days or of slight effort. Hence very many who approach turn back, and, displaying some small shred of philosophy’s clothing, boast before the unlearned as though philosophy in its entirety had fallen under their jurisdiction. For, as someone says—the words remain, but the name has slipped away—

> Once each man knows how to join two parts in a syllogism,  
> He stands and speaks as though he knew every art.

[Col. 0664D] On genera and species he brings forward a new opinion which escaped Boethius, which learned Plato did not know, and which this man has recently discovered by happy chance in Aristotle’s secrets. He is ready to resolve an ancient question, a question over which the struggling world has already grown old, on which more time has been spent than Caesar’s house spent in acquiring and governing the empire of the world, and more money poured out than Croesus possessed in all his riches. For these matters held many people so long that, though they sought this one thing throughout their lives, in the end they found neither it nor anything else. Perhaps this was because what alone could be found in them did not suffice for their curiosity. For just as one seeks in vain the substance of solidity in the shadow of any body, so in things which can only be conceived intelligibly and universally, but cannot exist universally, no substance of more solid existence is found. To spend one’s life on these is the act of one doing nothing and labouring in vain. They are indeed mists of fleeting things, and the more eagerly they are sought, the more quickly they vanish.

[Col. 0665A] Authors disentangle this matter in many ways and with various expressions; and, because they have employed words indifferently, they have seemed to hold various opinions and have left contentious men much material for disputation. Hence some, having apprehended sensible and other singular things, since these alone are said truly to exist, raise them into diverse statuses, according to which they establish in the singular things themselves the most specific and the most general. There are those who, after the manner of mathematicians, abstract forms and refer to them whatever is said about universals. Others analyse concepts and maintain that these are designated by the names of universals. There have also been those who said that the spoken words themselves are genera and species; but their opinion has now been rejected, and it readily vanished with its author. Yet there are still some caught in their tracks who, although ashamed to profess either the author or the opinion, cling to names alone, assigning to words what they withdraw from things and concepts.

[Col. 0665B] Each shelters himself behind some great authority and, from the words of authors who used names indifferently for things or things for names, asserts his own opinion—or error. Great seedbeds of quarrels arise from this, and each gathers whatever can confirm his own heresy. He never departs from genera and species, but applies them wherever his discourse may have begun. You will suddenly marvel that you have found in him that poetic painter who perhaps knows, for every need that requires it, “to paint a cypress.” Rufus is as mad over Naevia as necessity, according to Cook, diverted him from her. For:

> Whatever Rufus does, Naevia alone is everything to Rufus;  
> If he rejoices, if he weeps, if he is silent, he speaks of her.  
> He dines, gives a toast, asks, refuses, makes a sign: it is one  
> Naevia. If Naevia is absent, he will be mute.

[Col. 0665C] That subject seems more suited to philosophizing in which there is freer license to invent what one wishes, and less certainty arising either from the difficulty of the matter or the incompetence of disputants. Often, just as a cautious soldier observes rough ground and narrow passages more readily in order to impede an enemy’s advance, so someone raises difficult questions either from Scriptures or from arguments; or, if another subject is proposed, he deliberately slips into them as though incidentally. And if you cannot satisfy him—for there is no one sufficient to explain everything asked even by the unskilled—he at once signals with his eyes, twists his face, throws about his arm, shouts, leaps, and transforms himself with gestures which would seem foolish in any actor or mime. You will certainly not satisfy him unless you answer him in his own words and say only what he is accustomed to hear. Yet he himself, though he raises more difficulties, knows nothing of the whole solution. Perhaps, however, he has prudently provided for himself in one respect: he has stuffed into his purse everything with which he swells. Still, by easily piercing this bladder as it were with a needle, a single little word of a wise man sometimes silences all the loquacity that had resounded in the bellows of his ignorant throat.

[Col. 0665D] Nor would I judge more suited to philosophy those who append a long discourse to every small word, as though a public speech had to be delivered concerning everything asked. For it has been handed down as a rule that whoever answers more or less than he is asked does not know the line of correct disputation. But when someone must be taught, only those things should be said which provide assistance toward resolving the matters proposed. Hence it is evident that those who read everything into individual points, and, when one thing is asked, strive to settle everything, do not observe the pattern of sound teachers. Either they do not know the method of teaching, or perhaps they advertise their own talents by a pretence of performing their duty. And, as Cicero says, they display not what the proposed discipline requires, but what they themselves can do.

[Col. 0666A] Those, therefore, who fill the little *Porphyry* [*Porphyriolum*, i.e. Porphyry’s *Isagoge*] with every branch of philosophy dull the minds of beginners and confuse their memory. They shake a pupil under so great a weight that he considers the burden he has undertaken unbearable. I might perhaps grant that the books of Holy Scripture, every point of which is full of divine mysteries, should be read with such fullness, because the treasure of the Holy Spirit, by whose finger they were written, cannot possibly be exhausted. [Col. 0666B] For although the surface of the letter is adapted to only one meaning, a multiplicity of mysteries lies hidden within. From the same subject allegory often builds up faith in various ways, tropology morals, and anagogy also draws us upward in many ways, so that it instructs us not merely by words but by the things themselves. But in the liberal disciplines, where not things but words alone signify, whoever is not content with the sense of the letter seems to me either to stray from understanding the truth or to wish to lead his hearers away from it for a longer time. Indeed, I consider the little Porphyry foolish if it was written so that its meaning cannot be understood unless Aristotle, Plato, and Plotinus have first been read. [Col. 0666C] Farewell to anyone who proposes to introduce me to a discipline by such a shortcut. I shall follow the man who opens the letter and, as it were uncovering its surface, teaches what may be called the historical sense.

## Chapter XIII. What things are necessary and, as it were, the keys to philosophizing; that simplicity is a friend to truth; what it is to wrestle with or feed the angel; and what it is, or what advantage it has, to leave one’s native land for the calling of wisdom

What the keys of learning are, which open the way for philosophers tending toward the contemplation of the form of truth, the old man of Chartres expressed in a few words. Although I am not captivated by the sweetness of his metre, I approve its meaning and believe that it should be faithfully impressed on the minds of philosophers. He says, then:

[Col. 0666D]

> A humble mind, zeal for inquiry, a quiet life,  
> Silent investigation, poverty, a foreign land—  
> These are wont to unlock much that is obscure in reading.

For the Lord gives grace to the humble, and grants understanding of truth to those who, initiated by fear, faithfully cling to Him in the love of God and the performance of His commandments. For, according to the testimony of the wise man: “Those who trust in the Lord shall understand truth” (Ps. III); but “God resists the proud” (Jas. IV). Who will philosophize against His will? Or who, with Him resisting, will attain anything? Humility means that no one despises the person of a teacher or any branch of knowledge, unless perhaps it is one condemned by religion. If, as the saying goes, we undertake nothing rightly against Minerva’s will, who will attain knowledge without Him who is Lord of the sciences and in whom all treasures of wisdom are hidden? [Col. 0667A] To attempt this is therefore exceedingly arduous, more difficult and far greater than—to use the language of fables—to snatch a club from Hercules’ hand. Indeed it is certainly far less, because it is nothing—if, that is, what is wholly nothing can be greater or less than anything.

Whoever, therefore, enters upon the path of philosophy should humbly knock at the door of the grace of Him in whose hand is the book of all things to be known, which the Lamb alone opens—the Lamb who was slain in order to bring back the wandering servant to the way of wisdom and true happiness. In vain does one flatter oneself concerning one’s intellectual capacity, tenacity of memory, assiduity in study, or fluency of speech. For if these are off the path, the more effective they appear, the farther they will wander. A horse, too, the faster it goes astray, makes its rider return home the more slowly. [Col. 0667B]

Simplicity is joined to humility, and by it the understanding of learners is greatly assisted. Humility acquiesces in what doctors write; simplicity, if something seems to have been said otherwise than it ought, turns it to the better sense through an interpretation of faith. For he is foolish who seeks to rule the Scriptures from which he ought to be instructed, and who, having made their meaning captive, strives to drag them—even while they resist—into conformity with his own understanding. To seek in them what they do not contain is to obstruct one’s own understanding, not to learn another’s. [Col. 0667C] Were not the eyes of the disciples held back, so that they did not recognize, through their ardour, the wisdom that accompanied them? They were slow to understand what the prophets spoke, seeking what was absent from the prophets’ minds and failing to attend to Christ hidden in the letter. But because they sought with the ardent zeal of charity what was hidden, the wisdom they sought was present; it opened their eyes so that they understood the Scriptures and, seeing the Lord, reproved their own slowness.

Thus zeal in seeking is beneficial if that very eagerness for knowledge is referred to Christ. Yet He Himself is recognized only in the breaking, because the meaning of Scriptures is not seen at all unless nourishment of faith or morals is given to the soul. [Col. 0667D] Whoever assails the integrity of Scripture for his own pleasure, through the powers of intellect or study, remains, as though excluded from the sanctuary of philosophy, estranged from the understanding of truth. For when the Sodomites wished to corrupt the angels who reproved wickedness and were guests of the just man, they were struck with blindness; wandering around the wall and feeling their way at noon, they were overwhelmed with thick darkness by God’s just judgment. So, while the proud and malicious wander at the wall of Scriptures, they do not reach the faithful meaning which is in the house of the simple man, where God’s discourse is, and which sees the angel rebuking wickedness.

[Col. 0668A] For the angel is Scripture, which, sent by God, is known to have descended into the Sodom of the world to rebuke human wickedness. “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to my words, people of Gomorrah.” Scriptures, therefore, must be served, not ruled—unless someone believes himself worthy to rule angels. Surely just men are read to have worshipped them and provided them food; and does human presumption seek to be preferred to them? They are fed with the food of faith and good works. Thus the Samaritan woman fed the Angel of Great Counsel at the well. Perhaps worshipping them will not help if food is withheld.

Is not the patriarch recorded as having been strong in zeal for inquiry? Seeing a ladder whose summit touched the heavens, he saw angels ascending and descending, and the Lord Himself leaning upon the ladder; and with the angel he underwent the contest of wrestling until dawn shone. Nor, wearied by the angel, did he consent to yield until, weakened in one thigh, he received the desired grace of blessing as the angel came to him. These things happened to him in spirit or in figure; but, as the Apostle testifies, figurative things serve us. [Col. 0668B] Therefore, on the path of our pilgrimage, let us seize the angels of the Scriptures; wrestling tirelessly with them, let us not yield until the dawn of truth illuminates us. Nor is it enough merely to know truth, unless, as the thigh of love for temporal things withers, we more readily attain through the angelic blessing an entrance to true virtue, in proportion as, aroused by love for eternal things, we limp in our desire for temporal ones.

For this struggle leads to the point that, by the testimony of the triumphant man, God Himself, who is supreme truth, is seen face to face. Whatever good appears in faith or works is a certain image of the divine vision. And rightly the dawn does not send away the Angel without a blessing, because knowledge of truth without the grace of good action bears no fruit for a sound conscience.

[Col. 0668C] Moreover, not only domestic but foreign examples encourage us to zeal for inquiry. Solon, who had always burned with the highest ardour for wisdom, on his last day, while friends sat beside him and conversed, lifted his head when it was already almost submerged in death. Asked why he had done this, he replied: “So that, once I have grasped whatever this is that you are discussing, I may die.” Sloth would surely have departed from humankind if people entered life with the disposition in which Solon left it. Carneades, a laborious and long-serving soldier of wisdom, spent ninety years in study; for he had the same end in living and in philosophizing.

[Col. 0668D] Cato, in his eighty-sixth year, yet with a youthful spirit, manly strength, and the gravity of old age, was active in public affairs, so that no one noticed that his memory had grown slower, his sides weaker, his flesh shaken, his limbs numb, or his tongue impeded. He sought to be educated even in Greek letters, though he had learned Latin late and almost as an old man. When he had gained for himself the glory of eloquence, he also worked to be considered extremely skilled in civil law. His remarkable offspring, worthy of Cato as father, burned so ardently with desire for learning that he did not even restrain himself in the senate-house, where the senate assembled, from reading Greek books. By this diligence he showed that some lack time, while others have time to spare.

[Col. 0669A] That a quiet life is necessary is taught even by the moral philosopher, who judges the exertion of a student empty if a crowd of pressing tumults knocks at his door. For he says:

> What room is there for talent, unless they torment themselves with song alone,  
> And our hearts are borne to the lords of Cirrha and Nysa,  
> Admitting not two cares?  
> It is the work of a great mind, not to be procured from a blanket,  
> To behold the chariots and horses, the faces of gods,  
> And what manner of Erinys confounds the Rutulian.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* VII.62)

That a crowd impedes the light of truth is taught by the blind man in the Gospel, whom the crowds going before and following alike rebuked, telling him to be silent. For, in the Lord’s words, one who moves among crowds “is troubled about many things,” than which nothing is more harmful to studies or to the cultivation of good character. If study, as Cicero holds, is an intense application of the mind to doing something with great willingness, then surely a mind troubled and drawn apart to many things is by no means faithfully occupied in a single work of virtue. But the practice of study is then especially profitable when virtue is strengthened by a silent inquiry within oneself into true judgment regarding each thing a person reads or hears. There reason examines everything and weighs the fruit of all things in the balance.

[Col. 0669B] A quiet life, however, cannot exist if nature’s necessities are withheld; and conversely, if the mind luxuriates in pleasures, abundance of possessions extinguishes the light of speech. Hence fruitful poverty, guardian of true humility and companion of virtue, is added to the foregoing, so that this moderating force may restrain luxury and, by its goads, compel a person, mindful of himself, continually to persist in virtue’s duty. Cheerful poverty, as the wise man says, is an honourable thing; yet, if cheerful, it is not poverty but superior to Croesus’ riches.

[Col. 0669C] Thus Democritus, though he could have been counted among the rich—for his wealth was so great that his father could easily provide a banquet for Xerxes’ army—gave his inheritance to his native city, retaining only a very small sum, in order to be freer in mind for literary studies. Living at Athens for many years and devoting every moment of time to receiving and practising learning, he lived unknown in that city, as he himself testified in a certain book. Likewise Crates of Thebes, after throwing no small weight of gold into the sea, said: “Go to destruction, evil desires: I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.” And Anaxagoras, when he returned to his homeland after a long absence and saw his possessions ruined, said: “I would not be safe, unless these had perished.”

[Col. 0669D] A Socratic saying holds that no one becomes wealthy in order to teach unless he considers himself poor and needy for learning; for learners will always lack more things that are pleasant or necessary to know. Philosophy requires a foreign land, and sometimes makes one’s own land foreign; indeed, it makes a foreign land one’s own and is never burdened by any exile. This means that it drives away domestic and fleshly cares, so that a person, wholly in a manner turned toward spirit, counts alien everything that hinders progress in wisdom. Yet he is everywhere at home and everywhere in his native land, because everywhere he dwells with himself and everywhere with wisdom.

[Col. 0670A] Perhaps this is why the Lord invites the patriarch when He commands him to depart from his land and kindred: so that, advancing in pilgrimage, he may become a great nation and happily acquire the very land he leaves behind, while, for the calling of wisdom, he despises all worldly things. Virtue grows through the practice of modest poverty, and courage is more easily overcome by riches than by labours. But one who fixes the foot of his affection in the kindred of temporal things, to which he is in some manner born, serves and is diminished; and all things are rightly and happily acquired by a title of dominion when they are trodden underfoot, as it were by the foot of the mind, through the affection of a pure heart.

[Col. 0670B] But who is there who resolves even to enter this arduous path? Who perhaps attacks an angel, or who, if he attacks, perseveres? Yet the face of truth is not seen without the peril of wrestling; and unless the bitterness of poor exile comes first, the marriage of Rachel and Leah is not made sweet, nor does a numerous offspring increase unless one has crossed the solitude of the flowing Jordan with the staff of virtue. Then one who has long sweated in the labour of pure contemplation and right action, an exile even among kindred, returns rich to his native land in two companies of spiritual and bodily goods. Those who strive to philosophize by another road err, and, when hunger presses, will sell their birthright—if indeed they find a brother who will bestow even a lentil of wisdom as its price. For, as Aristippus is said to have declared, to indulge vices is to abstain from study.

[Col. 0670C]

## Chapter XIV. On the seventh key of learners

In Quintilian’s book *On the Education of the Orator*, the seventh key of learners is set down as love for teachers, by which instructors ought to be loved and honoured as parents. [Col. 0670D] For as the latter are indeed begetters of bodies, so the former are begetters of minds: not that they propagate from themselves the substance of wisdom, but that, by reforming nature for the better, they in a manner beget wisdom in the minds of their hearers. Such devotion contributes greatly to study. For students gladly hear those whom they love, believe what they say, desire to resemble them, and, under the influence of dutiful affection, come joyfully and eagerly to the very gatherings of scholars. When corrected they are not angry; when praised they do not blush; and they will deserve to become themselves most dear to study.

For as it is the office of teachers to teach, so it is the office of hearers to show themselves teachable. Otherwise neither is sufficient without the other. For just as a human birth is accomplished from both parents, and you would scatter seed in vain unless a softened furrow cherished it, so eloquence cannot grow unless the harmony of giver and receiver is joined together. Quintilian indeed says these things in his precepts on eloquence, but they are no less applicable to the formation of wisdom. Certainly eloquence is not acquired unless it is joined to the precepts of wisdom. And into the forum of those who have ears to hear, anyone whom philosophy has not trained to speak more carefully bursts not only ridiculously but, in some manner, madly.

[Col. 0671A] The book entitled *On Christian Doctrine* brings to light the other seven keys which Tyconius set down for understanding Scripture; yet they do not conflict with these, but all rather operate within one of them. For zeal in inquiry embraces them. The discussion, moreover, had been begun concerning the tradition of the Gentiles, but in such a way that it is intentionally referred to the instruction of believers. Yet there is one sole and singular key, as it were the key of keys: that key which opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens, and without which no one approaches the understanding of truth. Whoever has either not seized or not retained it, I would judge to be mad rather than to philosophize.

## Chapter XV. In what Epicurus and his followers place the highest good; and that pleasures are reached through many labours

[Col. 0671B]

Many things are indeed difficult, by which the virtue of those who pursue philosophy is proved, since there is no road to the highest point except through steep places. Yet in the hope of advancement all things become gentle; and when the usefulness of toil is weighed, the mind is strengthened for everything. All indeed tend toward the highest good, but by different paths. Yet no one, I think, reaches or even strives toward it without labor. For although there are three schools of philosophers, themselves divided into many paths, all labor, though differently, to attain the end that they set before themselves. Epicurus and the whole flock of his companions maintain that the happy life is that which continually rejoices in such great delight [Col. 0671C] that not even the slightest motion of sadness or disturbance intervenes. This is indeed a true definition, and none could be more perfect. Yet the common people who follow him have turned aside from it into pleasures, judging that through their enjoyment they will become most happy.

Yet I cannot be persuaded that anyone drew this from the Socratic fountainhead, which taught such purity of morals that Socrates was believed by later generations to have possessed not merely a human but a divine spirit. But because excellent sayings are easily corrupted by the ear or mouth of fools, teachings that ought to have been instruments of virtue have been diverted into a shortcut to impurity. For the flesh has imagined—for this is certainly not the feeling of a sensible person—that nothing is more pleasant than love and jesting, nothing sweeter than the life of a parasite, or of those who feast splendidly every day, burn with wine, and wear splendid clothes: in short, that to think, say, and do everything the mind, tongue, and hand desire, and in nothing to oppose oneself or restrain the movement of one’s own will, is the life of a person enjoying true and supreme happiness.

But does one arrive at this without labor? How many obstacles, interposed by the variability of the human lot, prevent such a life! For one must have wealth in order to use things at will. A needy person does not use them thus, because they are lacking, or he often spares them lest they should fail; but suppose them to be present. Among many competitors running with such greed, the stronger will carry them away. Strength is therefore needed to preserve them; power too is required. Are these acquired gratis—that is, without labor and anxiety? [Col. 0672A]

Yet amid these things, to be despised is hard indeed and intolerable, because love of advantage is innate in humanity; thus even one who does not act so as to be good wishes to seem good, and believes that others’ judgments err in their estimate of him. For love not of advantage but of justice would make him good. Therefore the respect of one’s fellow diners is sought; but this itself quickly evaporates unless it is extended by the benefit of reputation. That which produces and prolongs glory arises from many elements, but is strengthened above all by the exercise of virtues. It is clear, then, how laborious the passage to happiness through pleasures is.

Those who heap up riches for the sake of sufficiency seek greatness so that they may rely on power; they aspire to offices, in order to obtain respect, avoid contempt, and gain renown, and thus they seek glory. Yet by all these means one does not acquire the life Epicurus describes, a life ignorant of sorrow and every disturbance. Either these advantages do not all converge upon any one person, or they do not bring about the effects they promise. Indeed, very often, as though standing directly opposed, they produce results contrary to the wishes of those who seek them. If you do not believe me, read more attentively the book *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, and it will be plain that these things turn to their opposite.

Although that book does not expressly name the incarnate Word, it nevertheless possesses no slight authority among those who rely on reason, since it prepares remedies suited to each person for checking every pain of an ulcerated mind. Neither Jew nor Greek ought, under the pretext of religion, to refuse the use of medicine, since among the wise in faith and those foolish in unbelief, the skilfully compounded medicine of reason works so beneficially that no religion dares abhor what it mixes—unless it belongs to one devoid of reason. [Col. 0672C] Profound in thought without being difficult, distinguished in expression without frivolity, a forceful speaker and an effective demonstrator, it sometimes plausibly persuades toward what ought to be followed, and sometimes drives one onward as with the spur of necessity.

If, as you must, you assent to this book, you will see that these things are sought with excessive labor for the sake of something else, yet that the thing for whose sake they are sought does not arise from them at all. Nevertheless, that very thing for whose sake they are sought could more truly and more directly have been found, if it were sought from no source other than itself. But now, as wickedness has almost gained the upper hand, it is not sought; rather, even when it presents itself, it is neglected in favor of these things. For since all other goods are accessories of wisdom, and since wisdom itself is admittedly to be desired above health and every beauty, wisdom is made cheap by comparison with those other things, while its accessories alone are valued.

For who philosophizes in order to become wise? You will see many imitate philosophers, even without philosophizing, in order to abound in possessions or flourish temporally. Yet riches more easily impede the philosopher than contribute anything to philosophy. For one cannot faithfully serve both God and Mammon. Do not expect anyone to leave his homeland, embrace voluntary poverty, and devote himself to study: philosophy itself seems useless labor unless the reward of wealth follows. Curiosity excites some to know; vanity, urged by the goad of pride, drives others to seem knowledgeable; deadly greed inflames others for gain. Rare is the person who searches out the paths of wisdom with the foot of charity or humility, in order to be taught or to teach. [Col. 0673A] For everything is directed toward the follies of impure pleasure or empty advantage. In these lies the goal of the wandering soul. Meanwhile philosophy is a provision for the journey—but for few, because another path seems much more direct. For, as the saying goes, love of learning never made a person rich.

## Chapter XVI. On the Love of Riches, and That the Soul Finds No Rest in Them

Those who care only to amass riches wish nothing in life to be believed a better path than that which they have preferred above all others. [Col. 0673B] Different means are tried by different persons to satisfy their need for them. No grave danger seems too great if the hope of deceitful money shines before them. Love of money nearly conquers nature itself and reduces things almost impossible to the compass of possibility. To the miser nothing appears mean or shameful; while the crowd hisses, he consoles himself—indeed, applauds himself—as soon as he contemplates the coins in his chest.

You might think that Petronius’ saying had been impressed upon everyone:

> Whoever has money, let him sail with a favorable wind  
> and govern Fortune according to his own will.  
> Let him marry Danaë, and he may command Acrisius himself  
> to believe that she is Danaë.  
> Let him compose poems, declaim, make all resound,  
> plead cases, and be superior to Cato.  
> Let him be a jurist—whether he is one or not, possess him;  
> and be whatever Servius and Labeo were.  
>   
> I say much: desire anything when money is at hand,  
> and it will come; the closed chest possesses Jupiter.  
> (*Petronius, Satires* 131.)

So long as a man can make a profit, no part of the world appears inaccessible; and a greater fire of avarice surpasses even the heat of the torrid zone. Hence one man “exchanges merchandise from the rising of the sun to the region warmed by the evening.” Another rushes with all his force against the enemy:

> …they clash; in a moment of time  
> either swift death comes, or joyful victory.  
> (*Horace, Satires* I.1.8.)

Another delights to sit at proud thresholds, so that through intimacy with the great he may more easily attain the wealth he desires. If he can, he occupies some post of service; if not, it is enough even to be enrolled on the register of court officials. [Col. 0673D] Enrollment itself is profitable. At the least, it makes room for frugality, than which no revenue is more advantageous. For he saves most conveniently from his own resources whose purse is supplied by another’s. He serves in the court until gray-haired; indeed, the court consumes even those gray hairs. It is scarcely possible for one whom the court has brought to old age to return home even when dismissed. If they leave, they perish of hunger, because, as Sidonius says, they are fed less by good fare than by another’s bread. For it is sweeter, and has some inborn sweetness derived from being another’s. He who has always misused another’s property does not know how to use his own.

If honorable employment comes to an end, he is not ashamed to play the parasite, or even the mime. He will endure any indignity before he leaves. Think of Trebius reclining at Varro’s table. For this man too has the same purpose and always the same mind:

> To judge it the highest good to live at another’s table, and to endure with a patient mind  
>   
> …things which neither Sarmentus at Caesar’s unjust tables, nor base Galba, would have endured.

There are innumerable ways, open or secret, by which people hasten toward gain; and one whom love of money does not subdue is sometimes overcome by desire for fashionable possessions. Horses, clothing, hunting birds, hunting dogs, large herds of cattle and flocks, and the varied furnishings of the world—to run through each item exceeds human powers—many value above money and exhaust all their strength in acquiring or retaining them. [Col. 0674B] For the whole madness of avarice consists in these two points: it desires other people’s goods too immoderately, or guards its own too tenaciously.

Whoever demands what he lacks beyond the law of necessity and use desires too immoderately. Things withdrawn from use are likewise held too greedily. And who can doubt that things which slip away from their possessors without use are useless to them? Avarice is plainly not merely to be avoided but detested, because it removes and distances its followers from heavenly things, from fellowship with divinity, and from the enjoyment of heavenly blessedness. For all creatures nearer to heaven desire less and gather fewer things. The birds of heaven neither sow nor reap nor spin nor gather into barns, nor do they build storehouses; rather, they exclude all anxiety for tomorrow. [Col. 0674C] By contrast, mice and creeping things lay up stores for the future. There are said to be tribes for whom earth is food; they live sparingly, fearing lest the earth should one day fail them—though they will doubtless themselves be dissolved into that same earth.

Let each person think what he wishes; I do not believe that a miser can attain what he desires, unless Epicurus too allows that a starving, parched, and languishing person enjoys the delight of complete pleasure. For each is hungry; but the miser hungers more ruinously, since he is always in want and cannot be satisfied. The abyss of the mind is greater than that of the body; unless God pours himself into it, it cannot at all be filled. For since spiritual nature, by its own power, so comprehends bodily things that it is not expanded by any quantity, nor does one thing, by occupying a place, prevent another from being comprehended, and the more things it receives the more room there is for more, it is clearer than light that a bodily thing cannot fill the soul, which is spirit. The entire world is too narrow for the soul’s capacity. It follows that the soul finds no rest in that whole world—unless Epicurus thinks that a person enclosed in a narrow prison-cell, lying upon thorns placed beneath him, rests comfortably. [Col. 0674D]

## Chapter XVII. On Ambition; That Desire Is Accompanied by Folly; the Origin of Tyranny; and the Various Vices of the Ambitious

Some strive to avoid, if not the stain, at least the hateful label of avarice. They seem to abstain from others’ goods and to be ready, when occasion requires, freely to use their own. Yet from the fountainhead of evils there springs for them a vein of some vice that turns their paths aside from the course of true happiness.
