Just as in the garden of delights rivers spring from a single source to water the field of sweetest fragrance which the Lord has blessed, so in the place of horror and vast solitude—in the land, that is, of forgetfulness, inhabited by those who forget themselves in the world, like a fool captivated by the vanity of entertainments in the theatre—the heads of all vices spring up, as it were, from one fountain. [Col. 0675A] This well is desire.

The authority of the Fathers defines desire thus: desire is the love of things which a person may unwillingly lose. Folly is joined to it as its companion, persuading a person to love and seek what cannot be retained. Folly is culpable ignorance of things which ought to be known. Thus the great Augustine portrays it in his book *On Free Choice of the Will*. For if someone does not know what cannot be known, this does not at all fall under the name of folly. But when a person is held in ignorance of himself, he passes into the class of fools. If among goods he prefers plainly lesser things to greater, he judges foolishly. If, by following vices, he makes his worse part his own, he is condemned under the curse of folly.

Therefore, if error has been inflamed by desire, a manifold way to ruin lies open: for error causes a person not to know what ought to be followed, and the furnace of desire inflames him as he wanders into a trackless place. And indeed the words of the wicked still prevail, while a person ignorant of self-knowledge and rejecting the yoke of due subjection seeks a counterfeit freedom, so that he may live without fear, do with impunity whatever he wishes, and in some sense already be like God. [Col. 0675C] Yet he does not wish to imitate divine goodness; rather, by granting impunity to evils, he wishes God to be bent toward his own wickedness.

Thus ambition slips in from the root of pride—namely, the desire for power and honor—so that a person may thereby have strength not to be oppressed, and gain respect so as not to be held cheap. For there is no one who does not delight in liberty or who does not desire the strength to defend it. Nothing exists that he would not exchange for it, if the opportunity arose. For slavery is a kind of image of death, and liberty the security of life. Hence wealth is poured out to gain power; and the more eager a person is for power, the more readily he spends it. Once he has gained power, he rises into tyranny and, despising equity, does not hesitate, with God looking on, to crush those who share his nature and condition.

Although not all can seize principalities and kingdoms, nevertheless either no one or only a few are wholly free of tyranny. A tyrant, it is said, is one who oppresses a people by violent dominion; yet a person can exercise his own tyranny not only over a people but over any number, however small. For each rules, insofar as he can, even if not over a people. The present discussion does not concern those whose spirits are altogether refined and who rejoice in continual subjection, refusing to be set over anyone in life. [Col. 0676A] Rather, it is the life of political persons that must be examined. Whom among them can you give me who would not wish to surpass even one person in power? Who does not wish to have a right over someone? Who treats a subordinate as he would wish to be treated, were he himself subject?

Therefore, when ambition grows strong, injustice advances with equity trampled down; and, fostering the birth of tyranny, it carries out everything by which tyranny grows. One who cannot prevail through his own strength relies upon the strength of others. One may see very many hunters after power and suitors for offices attaching themselves to powerful people and involving themselves in the services of the state, attempting a means of raising themselves from the side, or from the opposite side, to a height from which they may be powerful above others—or at least seem powerful by reason of association. They pour out their inheritances, undertake and endure immense labors, eagerly press their services upon those whom they court, and are not ashamed to solicit them with flattery.

Thus no office is unpaid: neither duke nor judge, centurion nor dean, nor even herald or innkeeper, comes into being except for a price. These things are tolerable among secular affairs, so long as ambition does not corrupt what is public. For whatever is public ought to be consecrated to piety and fidelity. Yet these latter offices are more objects of ambition, and scarcely, if ever, fall to anyone gratis. But what has been said above concerning Trajan’s institution may suffice regarding these matters. [Col. 0676B]

I cannot lament without groaning and tears the domestic calamities: the bedchamber of wisdom exposed to fornicators, and the inner recess of the sanctuary transformed into a brothel. For, though the Lord forbade it, the house of prayer has become a house of trade, and the temple founded upon the stone of help has been turned into a den of thieves. The Church has been given over to plunder: some openly, others secretly, seize it. Indeed, it is conceded to the very person who seizes it, perhaps because it belongs to no one’s property. For scarcely anyone is found who girds the sword upon his thigh to restrain the presumption of ambition. It erects many engines of attack to storm the Church, while no one defends it.

One person, trusting in noble birth or the strength of powerful connections, violently rushes into holy things; and, if he happens to knock at the door, he does not hesitate to undermine the wall or threshold. For he will stir up sedition against Moses, bring strange fire into the Temple, and defile the vessels of the sanctuary. [Col. 0676D] Another, hoping in the multitude of his riches, enters under Simon’s guidance, finding no one there to bid both him and his money go to destruction. Another is afraid to approach Peter with gifts openly; nevertheless, secretly, through a shower of gold—as Jupiter, slipping through the roof-tiles, descended into Danaë’s lap—the incestuous suitor descends into the bosom of the Church. Another presents himself with service, as though ignorant that service is a gift, as though services did not count as gifts. Certainly no gift is greater than when one person dedicates himself to another’s servitude.

Another is forestalled by the seeming generosity of a person who invites him, by a kind of collusion; but afterward he will more fully repay the favor bestowed upon him to his own Gehazi. Another acts so that he need not himself knock, but may be compelled to enter against his will—like a fraud who obscures God’s lamp in order to mock it with impunity. For another has long pretended. He has shown his ambition by many signs and confessed that he wishes to become rich, powerful, and distinguished—but by another route, in another status, with less danger and greater freedom. He wished to be noble among laymen, or at least great among the clergy. For this reason he sought the favor of leading men, entered into intimacy with them, and accepted from them whatever offices he received. [Col. 0677A] Perhaps he was placed over the archives, undertook the duty of sealing documents, the custody of a treasury of valuables, the keys of the public treasury, the various safeguards of accounts, or, if he could obtain nothing else, secured appointment as overseer of baskets.

Yet this is not because he has any concern for the needy or cares for the poor, but because he is a thief and has purses, which avarice loosens for a time so that, under the appearance of piety, the sacrilegious man may stuff them, making private wealth for himself out of the beggary and death of the poor. If he were moved by true compassion, he would distribute his own resources to the poor more faithfully and usefully than he would approach, an impure merchant, the administration of another’s property.

Now everything is openly bought, unless the seller’s modesty prevents it. So profane a passion for avarice hangs over the sacred altars that all these things are bought up beforehand as though they were a kind of parody; and because they do not themselves enter commerce, they are believed to be lawfully and justly acquired if they have been pre-purchased or jointly purchased. For why not? Do not things come into the marketplace with the praetor’s approval when, by ancient law, laypeople hold them in such a way that they pass to heirs and may be alienated by them under title of gift or exchange? [Col. 0677C] What then prevents the right of advocacy or church patronage from being sold?

For they interpret blessed Ambrose’s statement that the Simoniac heresy is committed in such cases as a provincial decree, one which should apply only in Italy and among the Lombards. And they construe the apostolic constitution—which forbids admission to churches of those who, while seeking churches and in order more readily to gain entrance, seek the right of advocacy, where that right has been fraudulently obtained—as spoken merely for deterrence, not as a perpetual provision but one to be dispensed according to place and time. For, as blessed Cyril says in the letter of the Ephesian synod, the manner of dispensation has never displeased the wise.

If you ask what manner of dispensation they mean, it is apparently reasonable if the rigor of the canons is relaxed in favor of the rich, noble, powerful, royal, or courtly. For “the last mention will be made of morals,” and the rigor of the canons was certainly not established for such persons. They are free from justice, indeed, and are led by such a spirit that they need not be under law. Let the law establish what pleased its maker; for these men, enjoying the benefit of a princely privilege, suppose that whatever they seek by ambition belongs to them. They bind bishops to the foremost offices and do not hesitate to bargain concerning future succession. [Col. 0678A]

It remains, then, that the bargain be fulfilled with a grim outcome, and that each person be encouraged and armed for the death of the man whose succession he covets. If he delays in yielding, they oppose him, harass him, and shake him in many ways. Possession, after all, gives an adversary a real action. If one of the prelates, mindful of his own condition, does not comply with their wishes, “he immediately hears bitter stories,” because they regard it as altogether unworthy and insulting if a shameful and dishonorable request meets with refusal anywhere.

Meanwhile they are borne on the rowing of their wings; they build nests in every province, and scarcely do they themselves know how many nests they possess. Daily lodgings are prepared for them as they spread themselves through some regions of the world; and amid so great a number, a shabby companion is scarcely granted even one little lodging. For if anyone does this, he is considered remarkably generous. Certainly he is also of outstanding prudence if he obtains, by whatever means, so many that, as in the Memphis rite, he can daily offer sacrifices at new altars. [Col. 0678B]

Yet those who live from the altar do not wish to be burdened with the priesthood or serve at the altar—lest, as the people allege, I should say that they live in luxury—but they introduce certain masked men, by whose title burdens are assigned to one person and profits to another. And though the Apostle says, “Whoever does not work must not eat” (*2 Thessalonians* II), the one who earns least receives more, and the idle or vicious person enters into the labors of others. Who, then, could say that simony can be committed in this license of buying, since the thing is not sacred but profane? For here, as the popular saying goes, one crosses by a silver bridge from filth—filth which pursues the traveler even across a golden bridge.

## Chapter XVIII. That the Ambitious Pretend Not to Desire What They Most Eagerly Seek, and the Excuses by Which They Conceal Their Aim

[Col. 0678C]

But behold: in order to promote one of these persons, the Church is either compelled or deceived into saying to a domestic enemy, “Friend, go up higher” (*Luke* 14). The fools then feign astonishment, recoil from the name of dignity, flee the burden, and, that they may be pressed more eagerly, retreat—like, as they say, a ram withdrawing so as to strike harder—with sighs, groans, and sobs interrupting their counterfeit tears. For it is well known that this see drags and impels unwilling men, while ambition repels those whom it marks. They therefore strive by arguments and authorities to show why it is unfitting for them to be bishops. [Col. 0678D]

“I am not,” he says, “a physician; and in my house there is no bread, nor do I possess treasures from which, at a moment of need, I may bring forth things new and old for the needy. Thus I may use the prophet’s excuse: because I do not know how to speak, and because I am a child—not in age, indeed, but truly in knowledge and in the frivolity of my conduct. From the beginning I have been clothed in filthy garments, and I have never tried to whiten them by the blood of the Lamb or by garments. How then, being defiled, shall I handle holy things, or cleanse what is defiled—as a priest ought? For I have continually despised the law, and, as Ezekiel rebukes me, have not ceased to profane the Holy One of God. Therefore my promotion is the people’s downfall. Evil priests are the ruin of a people. For they have become a snare for the people, being on the watchtower, and like a net spread out to entangle souls.

“Haggai terrifies me, expressing by a mystical parable the peril of priesthood and plainly teaching that the people contract vices from priests’ conduct more easily than virtues. ‘Ask the priests concerning the law,’ he says, ‘and say to them: If a garment touches something most holy, or a holy vessel, will it be made holy by what it touches?’ And when the priests said that it would not make it holy, he said to them again: ‘If uncleanness touches a clean garment, will it defile it?’ And they said, ‘It will defile it.’ [Col. 0679A] It is therefore more tolerable that I alone should be consumed by my own vices than that I should spread the pestilence of vices among many.

“Moreover, even if my person were wholly commendable, even if I were not bound by the chains of the court, Micah most sternly bars my entrance, not allowing Zion to be built in blood and Jerusalem in the iniquity of her rulers. Here there is either no election, or one made under compulsion, or a pretended election.” He pursues this line too in an extended argument.

Finally, he says that he cannot be promoted without suspicion of Simoniac wickedness, since it appears that for this purpose he bought the right and authority associated with the seal, treasury, or archive—though with another intention: namely, to serve those in power. As the present day testifies, on which he refuses the honor offered to him, he came with his conscience as witness, desiring through this means to obtain honor without burden. He also repeats and turns over the apostolic enactments, long ago established to exclude from holy orders and every hope of promotion those who buy offices in any secular court, or render mean or servile compliance to princes, or whose election is not canonically celebrated by the clergy in the church and without the prior designation of any worldly power. If such persons are elected otherwise, the universal Church forbids their consecration under penalty of anathema. [Col. 0679C]

One of our princes—I have forgotten his name—was remembered to have performed a notable deed in a similar case. Whether it was Henry or Robert matters little. When a certain ambitious monk was called to an abbey which he had destroyed, and pretended modesty so that he might be sought more eagerly, fleeing the burden, refusing the honor, and openly confessing himself unworthy of so great a matter, the prince said: “Certainly you are unworthy, because you secretly bought it from me for so much money”—and he named the sum. “But since it does not rest with me to prevent the agreement from being fulfilled, it is right that I be held free, that you return home, and that the man who is worthy be put in charge of the abandoned church.”

But now matters turn out quite differently for the ambitious excuse-maker. He multiplies these and many other arguments in order to be believed unwilling to receive what he desires, and finally to receive gratis what he has bought in advance. Thus, regarded as a man of singular modesty, he is seized, dragged, and led, pressed by the crowd, to the chair amid the shouts of the throng and the singing of choirs. [Col. 0679D] It does not help that he has alleged the lowliness of his flesh or blood, because a successor is sought not for an emperor but for a fisherman; for the son of a craftsman, not for Augustus. His elaborate excuse reveals his learning, and he is proved religious because, when invited, he long refused to ascend; for the person who delayed seemed not to wish it.

The objections he raised for himself from the canons are dispensed with by a companion crowd of persons pursuing honors by the same route, after consideration of place, time, and person. If they cannot rely on present or past accomplishments, they prophesy future improvement. Thus the crafty horse-dealer, while he describes a horse that moves with difficulty, or a colt of unknown quality, as a future fine-paced mount, pushes it with lavish praise and faltering steps into the stable of an unwary buyer. [Col. 0680A]

## Chapter XIX. On Those Who Rush In More Shamelessly, Without Concealing Their Ambition, Whom Neither Reason nor Authority Can Restrain

Very many stand opposite, [Col. 0680B] not concealing their purpose at all, but proclaiming, as the saying goes, the insignia of their ambition. They deride the cowardice of those mentioned above, as though they were soldiers who dared not profess the titles of their own military service. Though they are impure and neither wish to reform their own life nor know how to instruct another’s, they rush in competition, as the phrase has it, with unclean feet into the Holy of Holies, intending to handle with hands not merely unwashed but, if the expression may be permitted, defiled, the loaves of the Lord’s presentation and the flesh of the spotless Lamb, roasted in the fire of his Passion upon the cross.

These are persons who, though judged unworthy even of the first entrance and the doors, nevertheless immediately aim at the priesthood and hurry to the tribunal; having repelled all others, they settle upon the sacred altars so that the order seems no longer instituted to furnish the people with a model and example, but rather to provide an opportunity for living in abundance and security. [Col. 0680C] Nor is the office thought liable to the strict judgment of God, but merely an administration that is safe and never subject to examination. You might suppose that the following poetic words had been proclaimed aloud by a herald to everyone:

Scabies may occupy the last place. Hence it comes about that all, as though in the contest of a stadium, struggle and pant, each striving that another may not receive the bishopric. Thus, in desire if not in fact, there are more rulers in number than those whom they rule. For very few wish to be ruled, since each seeks with all his strength to free himself from the yoke of his own ruler. By apostolic privilege or royal command, very many are protected from obeying their judges, from doing justice, from being subject to the law of God. [Col. 0680D] I do not blame the clemency of the Apostolic See, but I do not think that this indulgence of hers benefits the Church of God. We read of nothing of the kind in that glorious household of Christ, although contention also arose among them as to which of them should seem to be the greater. We remember no such emancipation granted by the apostles, although we have heard that Paul and Barnabas parted from one another. We believe that in that heavenly city above, which is our mother, there is no cause for discord; nor ought there to be one here, unless most urgent reason demands it.

Concerning these men, then—to speak with the leave of the multitude and of those who foster its iniquity—I shall say what I think, lest I withhold anything from truth or probability. I say, therefore, what I unhesitatingly believe: that those who, lifted up by pride, seek emancipations of this kind would shake off from their necks the yoke of Christ and of His Father, if they could. I say more: indeed, so far as lies in them, they do shake it off, and deceitfully resist the divine ordinance. Thus the Apostle’s saying has no place: “Are all prophets? are all teachers?” For all are prophets and teachers. So that, according to the old proverb, one may rightly say: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” And truly, as Gregory Nazianzen says, no history has recorded either so great a number of ministers in the Church or one so usefully assembled.

Hence there arises a grave reproach to Christian religion and teaching: priesthoods and ministries are conferred rather through ambition and favour than through an assessment of merits. All therefore run, but when the goal is reached, one receives the prize: the man who proved swifter than others in the race of ambition, who outran Peter and every disciple of Christ. For he immediately goes up and surpasses all the speed of a hasty calling. These are the men who repeatedly visit persons in authority, solicit their attendants and intimates, commend themselves to the leading men of churches, applaud everyone, and entreat not merely the officials but even the ash-carriers of great households, so that, when they see an opening, they may remember them. These are friends to everyone, and men who wish not themselves but their friends to be advanced in their persons. These scrutinize others’ lives and neglect their own; they count the years of mitred prelates, rejoice at their grey hairs, consult physicians and astrologers about the destinies of those in office, weigh their humours, and, as if in a balance, weigh the elements of living men. Those whom they see likely to survive longer they say have exceeded Nestor’s age and are now filling up the measure of the stag or the crow. [Col. 0681C]

They harass men weakened by age or illness, smear even the innocent with fabricated charges, and, like legacy-hunters, lie in wait for the seats of those who totter; and through shameful bargaining they often obtain unlawful possession of occupied sees. These are the men who enter into wicked pledges to assist and advance one another; yet when the matter comes to action, forgetful of their pledge, they obstruct and repel one another, contrary to the faith they gave, under the goads of ambition and envy.

Therefore, if, while the quarrel of rivals grows fierce, the wisdom of God by the hidden and righteous path of His providence introduces an unknown faithful man, of whom there had been no previous talk or thought, these men nevertheless omit nothing among the possible means—unless perhaps they omit moderation among those possibilities, since in their ambition they exceed all measure, if indeed there can be an excess of measure where there is no measure at all. Thus they knock upon and press the authorities. If services do not suffice, if intercessions do not profit, ambition puts forth its strength, displays the riches both of its own resources and of others’, now speaks openly, ascends the mountain of pride, and cries: “All these things will I give thee, if, falling from the foundation of faith, thou wilt promote me” (Matt. IV).

For this is indeed to fall: it is certain on the authority of the holy Fathers that whoever, in spiritual matters—that is, sacred and ecclesiastical things—commits the commerce of avarice falls from the sincerity of faith through the Simoniacal heresy. Nor does it matter whether money enters into the agreement before it, in it, or after it, since at every time the condemnation of Simoniacal perversity encompasses those who traffic in such things. Since it is perpetually forbidden, on this account, either to receive or to give anything, it can never be lawful to give or receive what is prohibited in every respect. For, as Patriarch Tarasius says, “to give is to give at any time, and to receive is to receive at any time.”

Something remarkable of this sort occurred in Apulia in my own time. While Roger the Sicilian was reigning, the church of Avellino in Campania, Apulia, and Calabria became vacant. Robert, chancellor of the aforesaid king, presided: a man vigorous in affairs and, without great abundance of letters, exceptionally acute. He was the most eloquent among the leading provincials, not inferior in speech to any of them; feared by all through the privilege of his power, venerable through the refinement of his manners, and all the more remarkable in those regions because, among the Lombards—who are known to be most sparing, not to say avaricious—he spent enormously and displayed the magnificence of his nation; for he was English by birth.

Three men accordingly approached him: an abbot, an archdeacon, and a lay provost of the king, pleading the cause of his clerical brother. Each secretly offered a large sum for the aforesaid bishopric. In short, having summoned his intimates, he separately agreed a price with each of them. [Col. 0682C] Thus purchase and sale were completed on every side; payment was most fully secured by pledges and sureties; and a day was fixed for the election to be solemnly celebrated.

When, therefore, on the appointed day the archbishops, bishops, and many venerable persons had assembled, the aforementioned chancellor set forth the cases of the competitors and what he had done with each of them, saying that he would proceed in accordance with the bishops’ judgment. The Simoniacal competitors were therefore condemned, while a poor monk, wholly ignorant of the entire matter, was canonically elected, approved, and installed. Nevertheless, the others were compelled to pay what they had bound themselves to pay, down to the last farthing.

Would that our own suitors were treated thus—those who scent out every see more attentively and curiously than the keen nose and sagacity of dogs detect the tracks of hares or the lairs of wild beasts! If I were believed, those also would be excluded who, while concealing their ambition, withdraw in order to force their way more strongly into the seat from which, as they themselves confess, they ought to have been rejected. For it was just that they should be believed about themselves against themselves. What lies hidden in them no one knows more faithfully. Yet more often they pursue office without restraint and shamelessly.

It is useless, when you would reject any one of them, to raise some objection, for it will be erased by the prevailing outcry of hired supporters, with examples and enactments of the Fathers pressed into service.

“He is low-born.” But Peter was not a patrician, nor does he glory anywhere in nobility of blood.

“He is too young.” He has Jeremiah and the Lord’s forerunner as precedents.

“He is a boy.” He points to the elders condemned by the boy Daniel.

“He is unlearned.” The apostles are not recorded to have attended schools.

“He is married.” Yet the Apostle commands that a husband of one wife be chosen.

“He abandoned his wife, to the injury of his marriage.” Yet John is reported to have been recalled from marriage to the Gospel.

“He is uncouth—or rather, inarticulate.” Yet Aaron is recorded to have performed the priestly office in the place of Moses, whose tongue was more impeded.

If more modern examples are wanted, Valerius was to Vincent a teacher of faith and morals, and an example of martyrdom.

“He pursued prostitutes.” Yet Hosea, by the Lord’s command, clung to the embraces of a harlot.

“He is foolish.” Yet God decreed to save believers through the foolishness of the world.

“He is violent.” Yet Peter drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant.

“He is timid.” Yet Jonah was afraid to go to the Ninevites, and Thomas to the Indians.

“He is bound by public duties.” Yet Matthew was taken from the tax office.

“He is drunken and devoted to gluttony.” Yet the Lord Himself was called a drinker of wine and a devourer of flesh.

“He does not submit to his superiors.” Yet Paul also withstood Peter to his face.

“He is quarrelsome.” Yet contention among Jesus’ disciples is recorded.

“He is garrulous and talkative.” Let him be regarded as eloquent, since the Apostle too was called a *seminiverbius* (“half-worded,” perhaps “wordy”) speaker.

“He has served in armed warfare.” Yet Martin is recorded to have served under Julian.

“He is a man of blood.” Yet Moses killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

“The homicide is manifest.” Yet Samuel killed the very fat king in the presence of the people.

“He is faithless and perjured.” Yet Peter added perjury to his faithlessness. [Col. 0683C]

“He is mute.” Yet this did not exclude Zechariah from the priesthood.

“He is blind.” Yet Paul could not see when Ananias consecrated him to the Lord.

“He was deposed on account of charges.” Yet many such men were restored and afterwards greatly benefited the Church of God.

“He is deaf.” Yet this does not prevent him from proclaiming God’s law. A preacher, not a hearer, is required.

“He is leprous.” Yet the Church remembers of the Shepherd of shepherds that He appeared without form or beauty, such that He might seem to be excluded as a leper and unworthy even of human sight.

“His appearance is contemptible.” Yet in a similar ground for rejection the Church did not listen to the accuser of Martin.

“He errs in faith.” Cyprian is said to have done this.

“He is infirm.” Yet Gregory, in extreme illness, governed the Roman Church most excellently.

“He is proud and vain.” Such was Brictius of Tours.

“He is weakened in body and limbs.” This is recorded to have happened to the excellent confessor Paphnutius.

“He has incurred condemnation for canvassing.” Yet the petition of the sons of Zebedee, seeking preeminence, was also rejected.

“He once taught heresy.” Yet Augustine confesses that he was a Manichaean.

“He worshipped idols.” Yet the distinguished martyr Marcellinus, while pope, was compelled to offer incense.

“Perhaps he is not yet a Christian.” Yet the election of blessed Ambrose, as is related, was celebrated while he was still a catechumen.

“He persecuted the Church of God.” Yet Paul became a preacher from being a persecutor.

“There is no election.” Yet the apostles were sent without the peoples asking for them.

“There is no vacant see into which he can be thrust.” Let him be added to the existing bishop. For Augustine is described as not so much having succeeded Valerius of Hippo as having been added to him.

“He is avaricious.” He will be able to gather together what has been scattered, and will not uselessly disperse what has been gathered.

To comprise everything in few words: he is unfit for all things; but Samson defeated the Philistines with an ass’s jawbone. He is powerful; and even now God can raise up children of Abraham from stones.

In addition to this, there must be no doubt that an episcopal chair receives saints—or makes them saints. For when Saul was anointed king, the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, he prophesied, and he was changed into another man. Caiaphas too, although sacrilegious and conspiring with the Jews for the Saviour’s death, prophesied because he was high priest that year, so that it may be clear that he received from the office of prophecy the grace which he had merited.

Since, therefore, the pleasant see and the sweet wood confer freely and without labour every desirable thing, is it not needless trouble to pass laborious days and sleepless nights in order to approach the sanctuary of philosophy?

> Sweeter it is to have lain upon a couch, to have held a girl,
>
> To have struck the Thracian lyre with one’s fingers.  
> > (Ovid, *Amores* II.11.31)

[Col. 0684C] Or, if even this seems too difficult, since touching the lyre to draw out its sound involves labour and requires skill, it is safer to exult at rest to the sound of the lyre and of the organ, and to open the gates of all the senses to pleasures. Meanwhile the studies of philosophers are mocked. If anything unfamiliar is heard, it is condemned as though profane; or, if it is of less consequence, it is despised. For you wait in vain for it to be rejected by reason or authority. If you rely upon reason or authority, they will object to the custom which they misuse and have established. And one noble says to another:

> “This is why he is pale; this is why someone does not lunch;
>
> And your teachers may be valued at a clipped hundred.”  
> > [Note: [Col. 0683D] In Persius, *Satires* V.191, one reads:
> >
> > “And a hundred Greeks may be valued at a clipped hundred,”
> >
> > [Col. 0684D] that is, at a small sum of money, which does not even amount to one hundred asses.]

And those who drink wine sing against the sober.

Yet it is not only episcopal dignity that is assailed by such great ambition, for now the same desire to dominate and preside possesses both the greatest and the least. Whoever does not dare to aspire to a bishop’s chair attacks prefectures, archdeaconries, and other dignities with equal greed and by the same devices. Indulge him a little, and he will dare greater things; he will advance gradually, remembering that

> Fortune favours the bold, and fear proves spirits to be base.

“No one became utterly wicked all at once.” If they succeed even a little, there is nothing which they do not hope can be achieved. At last, therefore, what is sought is obtained—but, as the saying goes, with God angry:

> Then they lamented that they had passed through fat days and marshy light,
>
> And that life had now been left behind them in misery.  
> > (Persius, *Satires* V.60)

They therefore conceive a new and belated anxiety, because the loss of time cannot be repaired. They ransack what is contained in the bookcases of cloistered men, plunder the desks of the learned, collect scraps of writing, read little flowers of words, hunt out little speeches, and labour by every means to seem to know what they do not know. For they are not yet concerned to know or to advance in virtue. They seek only virtue’s shadow, which they have always preferred to virtue itself.

[Col. 0685B] Certainly nothing is more wretched than to glory in another’s brilliance; and he is plainly a needy debtor who cannot celebrate repayment except by the favour of a new creditor. Yet they are eager to redeem time in such a manner that the satirist rightly seems to confront them with this reproach:

> You are moist and soft clay: now, now you must hasten,
>
> And be shaped without end on the swift wheel. You are being played with; madman, you run away.
>
> “To despise,” it rings out—a fault; maliciously
>
> The jar, not baked from green clay, answers when struck.  
> > (Persius, *Satires* III.23)

For truth’s freedom brings forth these words, as a spur to rouse sloth, not only against prelates of the Church but against all who have presumed upon the office of teaching before they have fulfilled the character of disciples. [Col. 0685C] Whence, then, will those bring forth things new and old who have always despised alike things new and old?

Nor should the error of those who flock together be excused under the pretext of their multitude, because the manner of life is drawn not from the likeness of one’s companions at table, but from the word of God; in its way the blessed walk, proceeding by a straight path toward the homeland of true happiness. What is sinned by many is not therefore no sin; rather, it is more grievous because it is committed by many. Nor does a crowd of fellow offenders lessen the offender’s guilt; it aggravates it, since it opposes correction by its own strength.

But lest the multitude of the ambitious prevail against God’s justice, not only divine but human laws are armed. The Law and the Prophets, the Gospel, and all the rules of the Fathers condemn their audacity. Nevertheless, they rise up against the Lord. “Be ashamed, O Sidon,” says the sea (Isa. XXIII); and you, cleric, what do you feel when a layman, almost ignorant of the law, rebukes and restrains your ambition? Be astonished, prophet, when the she-ass recalls you, her rider, and convicts you of your errors. A dumb animal—a stupid man—sees the angel holding the sword, that is, the spirit hidden in the letter; and do you, blind amid so great a light of Scripture, madly rush to death?

Be ashamed, therefore; be astonished; stop; withdraw from the curse toward which, driven by avarice, you hasten. And you who despise Moses and the Prophets, listen at least to the she-ass whom you drive with the spurs of your ambition. A miracle is needed: Balaam is not rebuked unless the she-ass speaks. Are you not ashamed that ambition, ignorant even of itself, has so blinded and overwhelmed you that you prefer the braying of a she-ass to prophetic and divine oracles? Perhaps you are terrified and tremble at the voice of the she-ass, but you are not pierced with compunction. For that is the gift of the divine word and of Him who alone kindles the fire of charity in the minds of the elect.

It is therefore plain that whoever despises the voice of God’s word hears the she-ass to no purpose. Yet listen also to the she-ass offering useful counsel, because in her too the Spirit speaks for your instruction. She foresees the angel restraining your unlawful steps and shows him to you. The canons teach by what path one ought to ascend to ecclesiastical honours and what path one ought to avoid. Yet you despise them, because on the path of God’s commandments you do not see the angel holding the sword to kill you.

[Col. 0686B] The same she-ass—a man duller and slower in comparison with you, who must be driven by the spurs of your word and example to obey the law—sees the angel, fears, stops, and declares God’s counsel to you. He speaks in this occurrence. Reverence the miracle; store up each of his words and engrave them upon the tablets of your heart.

## CHAPTER XX. On the laws of secular princes by which curials and officials are excluded from ecclesiastical honours; and by what examples the followers of Dathan and Abiram strive to obtain them.

Emperor Justinian therefore says:

> “The greatest gifts bestowed by the mercy from above upon all mankind are priesthood and empire: the former ministers in divine matters, the latter presides over human affairs and shows diligence. Proceeding from one and the same source, both adorn human life. Therefore nothing ought to be of such concern to emperors as the honourableness of priests, since they themselves always make supplication to God for emperors. For if this be without blame, there will be complete confidence before God from every side. And if the empire rightly and fittingly adorns the commonwealth entrusted to it, there will be a good harmony, bestowing every useful thing upon the human race.
>
> “We therefore have the greatest concern for the true doctrines of God and for the honourableness of priests. If these are maintained, we believe that the greatest gifts will be granted us by God: we shall keep firm the things that already exist, and acquire those which have not yet come. All things are managed well and suitably if a beginning worthy and pleasing to God is made. We believe that this will occur if the observance of the sacred rules is preserved—rules which the righteous, praiseworthy, venerable overseers and ministers of God’s word, the apostles, handed down, and which the holy Fathers preserved and explained.
>
> “We therefore decree, following the holy rules in every respect, that whenever anyone in time to come is advanced to ordination as bishop, his life shall first be considered according to the holy Apostle: whether it is honourable, blameless, and wholly irreproachable; whether he has good testimony; whether he is fit for a priest; and whether he comes neither from the condition of an official nor from that of a curial. [Col. 0687A] Nor shall one who was an uneducated layman immediately become a cleric and then, passing over some small interval, appear as bishop; rather, he must have lived from the beginning in virginity, or, if he has a wife, have received her as a virgin, and have no disreputable children.
>
> “Otherwise, whoever acts contrary to these provisions shall himself fall from the priesthood; and he who ordains him shall lose the episcopate for violating this law. Nor may one ignorant of the sacred doctrines approach the episcopate. He must first have professed the monastic life or have been established in the clergy for not less than six months, without cohabiting with his wife. Furthermore, from the enactment of this law onward, we permit no one who has a wife to receive such ordination.
>
> “As we seek good reputation and glory in the man to be ordained, so also we punish the accuser who brings a false accusation. If anyone says that he knows another to be guilty of any unlawful act, the latter shall not receive episcopal ordination before the accusation has been examined and he has appeared innocent on every side. But if, after such an objection, the man performing the ordination does not allow a lawful examination of the case and proceeds to ordination, let him know that what he does is null; the man ordained contrary to law shall fall from the priesthood, and he who imposes ordination without examination shall likewise fall from the episcopal seat.”

Likewise Leo:

> “If, by God’s authorship, anyone happens to be promoted to the rank of bishop, let him be brought forward by the pure minds of men, with the election openly known and by the sincere judgment of all. Let no one purchase the rank of priesthood through the venality of a price. Let a man be assessed by how he merits it, not by how much he can afford to give. For what place can be safe, or what cause excusable, if God’s venerable temples are stormed with money? What wall for integrity or rampart for faith shall we provide if the sacrilegious hunger for gold creeps into the venerable inner sanctuaries? Finally, what can be guarded or secure if incorrupt holiness is corrupted?
>
> “Let the profane ardour of avarice cease to threaten the altars, and let this sacrilegious abomination be driven from the sacred shrines. Therefore let a chaste and humble bishop be chosen in our times, so that wherever he goes, he may purify all things by the integrity of his own life. Let a bishop be ordained not by price but by prayers. He must be so far removed from canvassing that he is sought out only to be compelled, retreats when asked, and flees when invited. Necessity of excusing himself alone should support him. For he is certainly unworthy of the priesthood unless he is ordained unwillingly.
>
> “And indeed, whenever anyone is discovered to have entered this holy and venerable episcopal seat through the intervention of money, or whenever anyone is discovered to have received something in order to ordain or elect another, let him be removed from the priestly rank upon an accusation brought after the fashion of a public crime and of treason. We decree that he shall not only thereafter be deprived of honour, but also condemned to perpetual infamy, so that equal punishment may attend both men whom an equal crime defiles and makes equal.”

Likewise, a Novel of Justinian:

> “Before all else we decree that this be observed: no bishop shall be ordained through the patronage of any gift. If anything of this kind is done, the givers and receivers themselves, and their intermediaries, shall be subject to condemnation. Moreover, the giver, receiver, and intermediary shall be removed from the honour of priesthood or clergy. What was given on this account shall be claimed for that church whose priesthood he wished to purchase. If perhaps a lay intermediary has received anything on this account, he shall restore it twofold to the church.”

The same:

> “Nor shall it be permitted for any governor of a venerable house, or anyone performing any other ecclesiastical administration, to give anything to the person by whom he is appointed, or to any person, on account of the administration entrusted to him. Whoever gives, receives, or becomes an intermediary shall be stripped of the clergy, and the sums received shall be claimed for the venerable place. But if the receiver or intermediary is a layman, he shall pay double what was given to that same venerable place.” [Col. 0688B]

The same:

> “We decree that when it is necessary to ordain a bishop, the clerics shall immediately draw up decrees concerning three persons, with the most holy Gospels set before them, saying in those decrees that they have chosen these men neither on account of any gift, promise, nor friendship, but knowing them to be of right faith, honourable life, and literate; and that they have neither wife nor concubine nor children, and are neither curials nor officials.”

The same:

> “Nor do we permit a curial or official to become a cleric, lest injury thereby be done to this venerable clergy—unless one of them has completed the monastic life for not less than twenty-five years. We command such men to be ordained if, having retained a fourth part of their own substance for themselves and surrendered the remaining parts to the curia and fisc, once established in the clergy they live a life befitting a monk.”

The same:

> “We decree that bishops beloved of God shall, in accordance with the divine rules, ordain religious clerics only after much inquiry—men of good testimony, in every way literate and instructed. But among sacred ordinands we love none more than those living chastely or not cohabiting with wives.”

These are the utterances of secular princes. But although the doctors of the Church pursue these matters more fully, what they say is held cheap because it seems too difficult. Certainly whoever does not listen even to these is blinder than Hypsea and deafer than the Dulichian oarsman, and rightly deserves to be cast down, struck by the angel whom he despises, into the lowest hell.

You have heard that Nadab and Abihu were consumed by their own fire and carried outside the tabernacle at the Lord’s command; but these men strive to burst into the Lord’s temple and the Holy of Holies, while Moses resists—that is, while the law of God forbids. A numerous offspring has succeeded them; it fills the court of the Lord’s house and kindles alien fire. Though forbidden, they strive to burn incense; and, having joined company with the followers of Dathan and Abiram, they rush against Moses, tearing the Church, disturbing the priesthood, and stirring sedition among the people unless they are allowed access to the priesthood.

For when they have won the favour of the powerful, they assert that every right lies open to them, because, as they say, the prince is not subject to laws, and “what pleases the prince has the force of law.” [Col. 0689A] Since the people have transferred all their authority to and upon him, to oppose him is treason and manifest subversion of principate. Indeed, it is like sacrilege to doubt whether the man chosen by the prince is worthy. Nor does anyone who attempts, for any cause whatever, to frustrate the prince’s will escape the charge of rashness; and he is treated well if he suffers only punishment. They believe that no laws should be preferred to civil laws.

Anacharsis the Scythian compared these to spiders’ webs: they hold flies and gnats but allow larger winged creatures to pass through. Thus civil laws restrain the wills of the humbler, but certainly yield to the more powerful. For they inflict no lawful penalty on these men for transgression or contempt, but even when appealed to, cautiously pass them over. To this they add carefully sought examples of tyrants, by which they persuade the powerful that all things are permitted to them—especially wherever they live where an ancient custom prevails, even if it is contrary to reason and law.

They tell which tyrant thrust his dependent or intimate into some church without election; which compelled clergy by terror and losses to elect an unknown and unworthy man; which openly sold the Church of God; which forced a metropolitan to consecrate one who was unworthy; which drove religious bishops into exile, or compelled bishops driven out by them to go into exile; which burdened the Church and sacred property with disgraceful exactions; which tortured religious persons with unworthy punishments; which despised and crushed the clergy; which introduced deadly judgment into the provinces; which banished laws and canons from his territories; which silenced bishops in order to commit every wickedness with impunity and without any rebuke; which swelled for longest and most ruinously against the Roman Church; which governed everything by a law not so much his own as perverse; and finally, which was accustomed to make whatever he pleased lawful.

But whoever is more copious in recounting these things and more wicked in carrying out their malice is considered of more sincere faith and more effective industry. Whoever speaks from divine law concerning the truth of faith or integrity of morals is either superstitious, envious, or—what is capital—a foe of the prince.

If you say that the fire which lived under water through the seventy years of Babylonian captivity was at last extinguished when Antiochus sold the priesthood to Jason; or if you say, as blessed Gregory testifies, that plagues and famines, upheavals of peoples, collisions of kingdoms, and very many adversities befall lands because ecclesiastical honours are conferred for a price or human favour, rather than upon persons of merit; if you say that Uzzah was struck by the Lord because he presumed to steady the tottering Ark; if you say that Isaiah fell silent while King Uzziah the leper reigned and, after his death, saw the Lord seated upon a high throne; if you say that the burdens of the tabernacle rest only upon the shoulders and wagons of Levites [Col. 0690A]—and whatever like things there may be in God’s law—you will be treated well if you are not mutilated and thrown into prison or driven into exile.

They will cry out against you from every side, and both the ambitious and their supporters will not hesitate to pronounce upon your life the sentence of ultimate condemnation. Yet the Lord will provide you one remedy: the conscience of every wise man who fears God agrees with your words. Hence their judgment concerning you does not always prevail, God being its author. For if they had their way, you would be judged guilty as one accused of treason, a public enemy. You would be said to overturn public judgments; and, as a zealot for your own profession, while you uphold ecclesiastical liberty, you would be held to overthrow the wisdom of princes and contrive to make them appear foolish and contemptible.

It would be better, they say, for the diadem to be taken from a prince’s head than for the ordering of that chief and excellent part of the commonwealth which concerns religion to be withdrawn from his discretion.

> Whoever in the city of Rome seeks to surpass Pompey does not seek private things.

And perhaps one exceeds the wishes of private persons more arrogantly who, under the appearance of liberty, seeks to rule princes. For if any prince acquiesces in superstition of this kind, he is foolish and degenerates from the virtue of illustrious kings.

Yet David, as the history of Kings relates, and all Israel danced before the Lord with every kind of crafted wood, with harps, timbrels, lyres, sistrums, and cymbals; though he did not lack a rebuker of this kind. For the history just mentioned continues:

> Michal, daughter of Saul, came out to meet David and said: “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants and stripping himself naked, as one of the buffoons might strip himself!”
>
> And David said to Michal: “As the Lord lives, I will dance before the Lord, who chose me rather than thy father and all his house, and commanded me to be leader over the people of the Lord in Israel. I will dance and become more lowly than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes; and with the maidservants of whom thou hast spoken I shall appear more glorious.”
>
> Therefore no son was born to Michal, daughter of Saul, until the day of her death.  
> > (II Kings VI)

But David sat as king in his house, and the Lord gave him rest on every side from all his enemies. [Col. 0690D] Do you see how carefully this history teaches that contempt for religion joined with swelling arrogance is punished on the one hand, while devotion of faith and the worship of humility are rewarded on the other? For David obtained peace in his kingdom, while Michal, deservedly for her wicked rebuke, died barren and left no fruit of illustrious lineage or happy marriage.

This is fitting, since *Michol* is interpreted as “all water,” or “from all.” The counsel of an unlearned multitude, and that which follows popular judgment, has neither the fruit, the sweetness, nor the memory of good. Nevertheless, when you hear these counsellors of great men, you will not suppose that Michal died childless. You will marvel that all are Michal’s sons, and will think that, if not flesh, then spirit has descended from her stock. And to make this easier for you to believe, those who strive to invalidate divine authority in order to establish their own die without children or leave behind children degenerate and feeble. Without doubt, whoever suppresses ecclesiastical liberty is punished either in himself or in his offspring. Thus the sons lose even their own possessions along with those which paternal impiety had occupied through their favour.

## CHAPTER XXI. On hypocrites who strive to conceal the stain of ambition beneath a false appearance of religion.

Although the rashness of the people or the licence of the powerful may be restrained by lawful precepts and divine institution, ambition cannot be mastered. If it does not dare act openly, it creeps in secret [Col. 0691B] and enters deceitfully. If the doors of the Church do not open through gifts, and are opened neither by its own violence nor by another’s, it resorts to the arts of deception. With complete freedom of spirit it condemns everything which attacks liberty, overturns the ordinances of teachers, or is contrary to religion. You would marvel that Sinon had returned in order to deceive the simple and credulous. It feigns and dissembles, and…

He carries a crafty fox beneath his breast. (Persius, V.117.) He is freer than any Stoic, more rigid than Cato. At times he is even simpler than Paul, teacher of the Gentiles; more anxious and more fervent than Peter. For him too, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain”; he glories in nothing except [Col. 0691C] the cross of Christ, which he continually bears in his body, so that his spirit may be saved, desiring only to be dissolved and to be with Christ. He therefore mortifies the flesh with its vices and desires; and, unlike other people, though living among people, he leads an angelic life and has his conversation in heaven.

Such men fast continually and pray without ceasing—yet loudly, so that a guest may hear. They dress in rough and dirty clothes and rebuke the people. They censure the clergy, urge princes and powers to reform their morals, and acquire for themselves a reputation for righteousness if they disparage another person’s life. But so that deceit may gain strength under the appearance of honourability, they seek the communities of praiseworthy men, undertake arduous professions, display difficult practices, and carry out, more conveniently for themselves and more indulgently, such things as are possible and more humane. Thus they profess themselves successors of Basil, Benedict, Augustine, or, if that is too little, of the apostles and prophets. They put on the dress of Carthusians, Cistercians, and Cluniacs; and those who deign to be canons glory in woollen tunics and sheepskins. For “they come in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7); yet, as the Lord says, they are most plainly known by their fruits.

Nevertheless, the glory of true religion is not diminished by these men’s fraud. For it is unquestionably clear to all that the names they profess and the offices they promise are most honourable and most trustworthy. For religion is found among these bodies so true and so approved that it need fear no sting of reproach. Thus the Carthusians, [Col. 0692A] as conquerors, as it were, of avarice, shine pre-eminent everywhere. The Cistercians follow to the letter the precepts and footsteps of blessed Benedict, whom all acknowledge to have been filled with the spirit of every righteous person. The Cluniacs have handed down a pattern of religious life to many provinces. For canons, it ought to suffice for the fullest praise that all clergy ought to imitate their rule. Hermits likewise have as founders of their institution the Baptist of the Saviour and the sons of the prophets. The Knights of the Temple, after the example of the Maccabees, lay down their lives for their brethren. The xenodochi, that is, administrators of guest-houses or hospitals, follow the apostles’ footsteps; and, aspiring to the summit of perfection, faithfully obey Christ in this: that they live innocently and distribute all they possess [Col. 0692B] to the poor.

Yet in all these bodies both faithful persons and reprobates are found; and the truth of religion or profession is not thereby disfigured. For what profession is there, or what society has ever been known, into which a stain has not crept? We read of an apostate angel; of fratricide among the first brothers; of a reprobate prophet; of a traitorous apostle; and of faithless disciples of Christ. Yet the purity of the persevering angels is not corrupted; nor is the fellowship of brothers who love one another less holy; nor is the grace of prophecy blameworthy in the elect; nor is the apostolate contemptible in the faithful; nor is Christ’s discipline disgraced by the various errors of those who stray from it.

Therefore, just as the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, [Col. 0692C] and false apostles aspired rather to apostolic authority than to apostolic life, so hypocrites take refuge in the lofty bearing of the Pharisees, enlarging their phylacteries and magnifying their fringes. They will not touch with a finger what is written in God’s law, except in order to be seen by people, from whom they expect the reward of honour or some other recompense. Hence they display pallor of face, draw deep sighs from habitual practice, suddenly overflow with artful and compliant tears; with head inclined, eyes half closed, hair cut short, head almost shaved, voice subdued, lips moving in prayer, gait composed and quiet, as though their steps were ordered by a certain measured proportion, ragged and covered over, they claim the filth of their garments and their affected lowliness as their due—so that they may [Col. 0692D] rise more easily because they seem more zealously to have cast themselves down into the lowest place, and that those who voluntarily diminish themselves may be compelled to increase against their will.

These are the people who expose to public view whatever stain has adhered to the Church during her pilgrimage, so that they themselves may appear free of every stain. These are the people who proclaim that benefices not yet granted to saints ought to be taken away. These are the people who persuade the secular powers that, because of the vices of individuals, churches should be deprived of their rights. They withhold tithes and first-fruits from churches, and take churches themselves from the hands of laymen without consulting the bishops. These are the people who, depriving natives of their ancestral estates, reduce villages and hamlets to wilderness, turn all neighbouring places to their own uses, destroy churches, or restore them to [Col. 0693A] secular uses. What had been a house of prayer becomes either a cattle-stable, a shepherd’s shelter, or a workshop for wool-working.

Indeed, they do even greater things with impunity; and, as if with the horns of a twofold power, they do not cease to buffet the Church, in whose bosom they rest and beneath whose shadow they are protected. For they flee to the Roman Church, which, as mother of piety, has been accustomed to provide religious life with peace. They implore its aid and obtain the shield of its protection, so that they cannot be harassed by anyone’s malice; and so that they may display themselves more fully and fulfil the office of charity, they are fortified by apostolic privilege against paying tithes. They proceed further; and, so that more may be lawful for them with impunity, they exempt themselves from the jurisdiction of all churches and become spiritual sons of the Roman Church. Yet they do so in such a way that [Col. 0693B] they may be summoned anywhere before the court concerning a matter, while they themselves cannot be summoned except at Rome or Jerusalem.

Then they implore the aid of secular powers and promise them divine grace. They become mediators between God and humankind; they enroll in their societies those who need pardon, hear confessions, and, usurping the keys of the Church or stealing them from Peter, presume to bind and loose. Though the Lord forbids it, they put the sickle into another’s harvest. Yet they more readily relieve the more powerful and wealthy, having received favour or payment; placing their shoulders beneath the sins of others, they order all that those people lament having committed to depart into dark tunics and garments. They magnify the mercy of the Lord, who wills no one to perish, declaring that it is open and accessible to penitents and closed only to those who despair. Meanwhile, they permit those who are more ardently and tenaciously entangled in crimes to sin in hope, provided they grant them something toward their redemption; and they boldly promise pardon because, as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. Repentance, moreover, is never too late—provided it is genuine.

They therefore approve evil conduct and, stirring up popular feeling, stop people’s ears by flatteries so that they may not hear the rebukes of prelates. In addition, they hunt out rumours, delight in disturbances, investigate the secrets of parties at variance, and carry these now to friends, now to enemies: welcome to both, faithless to both, [Col. 0693D] but seemingly more suited to such business because they are less suspected under the appearance of religion. They alone are believed to know what is expedient in the palace, the law-court, the fields, and the camp, because they seem, above others, to concern themselves with all these matters, into which they continually intrude. If fathers meet in council, citizens in the forum, soldiers on campaign, or finally if a council or synod is convened, this shadowy religion will occupy the foremost portion of the seats. One would think the enclosures of monasteries had been broken open, the poorhouses or hospitals emptied, and swarms of diners had flown out from venerable places. So thoroughly does this appearance of religion thrust itself into crowds and public view.

They usurp the chief seats, the first places at table, and the first greetings; and if you delay granting them, they are most violently offended. If you speak against them, you are called an enemy of religion and an assailant of truth. Bear it patiently, therefore, if they inflict injuries and losses, since they appear to have obtained license for everything by apostolic and royal authority. For this too is believed to be owed to their merits. Certainly, “he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13). Nor do I think apostolic majesty or royal power should be resisted. Yet, to speak with the faithful’s leave, I wonder why they are not ashamed to usurp tithes and another’s rights. Perhaps they will say: “We are religious.” Certainly, paying tithes is part of religion, and only a religious people is required by God to pay them. But those who exact them are irreligious. Who appointed you judges over them? Or who are you to exercise judgment [Col. 0694B] over another’s servants? Each stands or falls to his own master. Yet they shall stand.

“But,” they say, “we are secure through apostolic privilege, by whose benefit we retain tithes from the increase of our animals and from our labours.” To be sure, everything is lawful to apostles; but by no means is it expedient for apostolic persons to do everything. Grant that they permissibly granted you this: see to it whether you rightly asked for it. For one who asks not to do what he owes does not obey righteousness voluntarily. Did not Abel have regard for the Lord in the increase of his animals? Cain offered crops—rightly indeed, because they were owed to the Lord—but his division was unjust, since he committed sin by withholding something from the division. The gifts of the man who shares the offspring of animals with the Lord are accepted before Cain’s. Perhaps returns from animals are more rightly made, because they arise without our cultivation and care. For greater labour is involved in sowing and reaping crops. They are not compelled to give from what is theirs. For who is to render an account for another person’s labour?

Why say more? By many lengthy arguments they seem to establish that they do not forbid others to give tithes, while they themselves are exempt from giving them because they are so religious that in this respect they can derogate from the divine ordinance, and are the less grateful to God’s grace in proportion as they experience it through greater benefits. For things which arise from grace alone—such as hay and spontaneously growing plants—are judged not liable to religious dues. At first, indeed, while religion rejoiced in poverty and poured out the resources of its want upon others’ necessities [Col. 0694D] or uses, privileges were granted to religious professions. Now that necessity has ceased and charity has grown cold, those privileges are thought to be instruments of avarice rather than religion. For behold: since all these privileged persons seek their own interests, Jesus, who is preached in public, is either entirely absent or lies hidden in secret places.

Hence, when blessed Adrian saw privileges being drawn toward the unjust profit of avarice, he wished to revoke them altogether, but restrained their license with this moderation: what they claim from their labours is to be understood only in respect of newly cultivated land (*novalia*). Thus they may enjoy their privileges without grave loss to another’s right. Yet there is one matter which so great a Father tolerated in some fashion; and since it conflicts with the canons of the Fathers, it is marvellous in our eyes. For the Knights of the Temple, by their own influence, claim authority over the ordering of churches; they seize *personatus* (ecclesiastical offices), and in some manner presume to administer Christ’s blood to the faithful—men whose profession is almost that of shedding human blood. I do not say that they are men of blood, since nearly alone among humankind they wage lawful wars; for David too was called a man of blood not on account of the wars he lawfully fought, but because of Uriah, whose blood he unjustly shed.

For, as the canons provide, no authority over ecclesiastical matters is recorded as having been granted to laypeople, however religious. It would surely be a sign of true religion if they restrained themselves from administering a matter which, the Lord forbidding, [Col. 0695B] they are not permitted to handle. Nor do I think the duty of hospitality should be fulfilled from plunder—not merely from plunder of churches, but even from that of any faithful person—because the Lord hates sacrilegious bread and rejects offerings made from blood. Whenever he is invoked by such people, he shuts his ears, so that they are not open to their prayers.

For the present, this discourse is not directed to those things which such people commit in fraud of God’s justice, although it is wholly wicked that, enticed by love of money, they open churches which bishops have closed. They celebrate divine offices while suspended; they bury the dead whom the Church rejects; and once a year they do what causes an erring people to be deaf to the Church’s voice for the entire year, so that one who cannot be restrained scorns correction. They therefore go round the churches, proclaim the merits of their communities, carry remissions of crimes, and at times preach a new Gospel, adulterating God’s word. They announce it not for grace but for a price; they live for pleasure, not for truth. At last, when late in the day they gather in hiding places, having talked of virtue by day, they move their buttocks in nocturnal error and toil. If this is the way to Christ, then the teaching of the Fathers, which showed the narrow and arduous road to one seeking life, is false and vain.

When the Church is indignant with such men, no one is more justly stirred than men who are truly religious, upon whom all these injuries recoil. The people are angered; but religious professions are more justly embittered against this stain of hypocrisy. For people do not say that hypocrites have done this, but Cistercians, Cluniacs, or others whose habit these windbags—or “belly-speakers” (*ventriloqui*)—wear and whose life they falsely represent. For cloistered people who are plainly and truly religious are free from this malice while serving their professions. No life is more faithful, simpler, or happier than that of those who dwell faithfully in cloisters: humbly rejoicing in their lowliness; obedient to their prelates in all submission and reverence; not seeking under obedience’s name either dominion or license to defraud, wander, or be idle; possessing their vessels in sanctification and honour; awaiting in silence and patience God’s salvation; avoiding another’s slander and [Col. 0696A] murmuring; receiving quietly from the Lord’s mouth the word that can save their souls; mingling grateful conversations with God; and, like earthly angels, ignorant of every worldly disturbance.

If anything seems to sadden them, it must be referred to brotherly love; for angels in heaven also in some fashion sympathize with our falls and rejoice together over one sinner who repents. And although in our own time, when virtue has been emptied of strength and Astraea is known to have left humankind and returned to heaven, it is difficult to imitate the philosophers, the life of cloistered people incomparably surpasses the philosophers’ virtue—or rather, as I would more gladly believe, they philosophize most rightly and safely.

Those, however, who humbly go out to provide for their necessities and faithfully conduct themselves in those affairs, if they do not follow a safer life, certainly follow a more useful one; and, though worthy of the greatest praise and reverence, they in no way join the faction of Epicureans or hypocrites. For you will most rightly class hypocrites with Epicureans: they profess philosophy and serve their own will. Since they foster lawsuits, abuse privileges, serve cupidity, do not perform the offices of charity, and seek their own glory, do they not walk according to the flesh, though they pretend to be spiritual? They rightly await the destruction of the flesh and will share that Gehenna whose spirit is evil and which, because he swelled with vain glory and wished to be conformed or preferred to the Most High, was cast down and hurled into the pit of eternal condemnation.

Indeed, mad are those who walk this road, and more wretched than all nations: they are deprived both of the goods of this present life and of eternal life. This is especially so because he who, for sinners, endured being made sin and showed himself friendly toward tax collectors and prostitutes could have no peace with hypocrites, who had no need of his righteousness. This is plain to those who attentively consider the disputes he carried on with the Pharisees. Yet they strive, after the Pharisees’ example, to hold the first place.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the same persons; and on Hezekiah, who lost the treasures which he displayed.

Wise men assert that it is most difficult, or impossible, to rejoice with the world in the present and rejoice eternally with Christ; and plainly it is most miserable to be tormented with the world and eternally scourged with the devil. Therefore, if hypocrites, who hope only in this life, are sad, disfiguring their faces so that they may appear righteous to people and proclaiming the works of their righteousness as if trumpets sounded before them, they vainly expect recompense from the Lord, because “they have received their reward” in the present life (Matt. 5). For concerning those who honour the Lord only in word and dress, his judgment makes it clear that he himself is far from them, because their heart is far from him. Their very works also bring the loss of salvation, and they serve Satan, prince of the Babylonians. For all things done for display result in death.

The history of Kings relates that [Col. 0697A] when Hezekiah, king of Jerusalem, received from the Lord through Isaiah son of Amoz a sign of preservation and salvation—the shadow on the sundial moving backward by ten degrees, contrary, it seems, to nature, since the shadow ordinarily advances with the sun and does not return—Berodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of the Babylonians, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, for he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill. Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival and showed them his house of spices, gold, silver, various pigments, ointments, the storehouse of his vessels, and everything that he could possess among his treasures. There was nothing in his house or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them. Then Isaiah the prophet came to the king and said to him: “What did these men say, and whence did they come [Col. 0697B] to you?” The king replied: “They came from a distant land, from Babylon.” He answered: “What did they see in your house?” Hezekiah said: “They saw everything that is in my house. There is nothing in my treasures that I did not show them.” And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: “Hear the word of the Lord. Behold, days shall come when everything in your house, and everything which your fathers have laid up to this day, will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing shall remain, says the Lord. And some of your sons who shall issue from you, whom you shall beget, shall be taken away and shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 20).

On the surface of the history, according to the Hebrews and on Jerome’s authority, the truth is clear when Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were taken captive with Daniel to Babylon and were there castrated, in order to serve in the king’s palace according to the custom of the nations. Unless perhaps it be objected that boys without blemish were ordered by the king to be brought in so that they might learn the Chaldean language, and that it is established that not only the king of Judah’s treasures were transferred to Babylon, but that a great part of the vessels of the Lord’s Temple at Jerusalem were carried off and profaned.

Yet it is elegantly said that, when the Lord had granted the king a miracle, Babylonian messengers came with gifts. For then a person is especially assailed by the messengers of confusion when, through God’s wonderful mercy, virtue becomes more clearly known. But then it is foolish to rejoice, because these men must not merely be held suspect but must be more carefully avoided as most destructive enemies, since they are to be feared even when they bring gifts. Therefore, whoever displays the spices of good works, the gold of virtue, the silver of eloquence, the pigments of thoughts, the ointments of mercy, the fitness and beauty of his vessels, and whatever good things have been more cautiously and usefully laid up in the treasuries of a good conscience, should hear the word of the Lord and know for certain that everything which seemed to serve glory is to receive the wages of confusion and death. Even the succession of his sons is castrated for the prince of the Babylonians, because things which otherwise possess the merit and fruit of virtue are useless to their author when done for the sake of vain glory.

For the righteous Rewarder despises hypocrites and accepts in good things only the worship of truth. His eyes can be deceived by no paint and no malice, because he sees in secret and searches the depths of hearts. He distinguishes appearances from realities,

> Lest some counterfeit ring beneath plated gold.  
> (Persius, V.106.)

Hence hypocrisy received its name; and it is undoubtedly a species of Epicureanism.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the Carthusians, by restraining avarice with the reins of moderation, and the new religious order of the Great Mountain, by despising everything worldly and rejecting everything without thought for tomorrow, exclude avarice and are far removed from the mark and name of hypocrites; who are secular and who religious; what are the royal attributes of the active and of the contemplative; and what is the end of hypocrisy.

The Carthusians and the new profession of the Great Mountain, established at the summit of ancient virtue with the Saviour as guide, most carefully and faithfully avoid the name and mark of hypocrites. For the Carthusians have set limits to their desire—or rather, to their necessity—and restrain every form of avarice with the reins of moderation. At times they even take something away from necessity itself, lest avarice contrive anything under necessity’s pretext. They are undoubtedly great men and should be numbered among the foremost, since not merely religious professions but, in this great multitude of declining ages now that the world is growing old, few people have arisen who have prescribed for themselves any limits of sufficiency. Something must always be lacking to a limited possession; and this very gap of desire, which continually longs for something further, is a sign of imperfection—indeed, I should rather call it a manifest defect [Col. 0698C] of conscience.

In a certain manner, then, and a glorious one, that person is perfect who foresees the means by which he can be satisfied. Although I believe no pagan—or very few—attained this, I know that some pursued this purpose, since even a heathen says: “Seek by your prayer a fixed end.” Without this, the striving of the human mind stretches into infinity and toward that which it can never attain.

But the inhabitants of the Great Mountain chose a most arduous life. Not only are they conquerors of avarice; in a sense they even conquer nature itself. They exclude every command of necessity, cast away concern for tomorrow, and regard contempt for all the world’s delights as too little. Whatever guise knocks at their gates is shut out and departs confounded; [Col. 0698D] for Christ alone enters them, on whose grace they rely.
