They cast their thought upon him who nourishes little children, gives food to beasts of burden and to the young of ravens (Ps. 146), clothes the lilies of the field, and provides necessities for all who hope in him or obey the law of his ordinance, so that nothing is lacking to those who have not withdrawn themselves from his will. They therefore cast their whole care and all their concern upon him, for he cares for the faithful. They avoid the straits of prudence so thoroughly that their entire life seems to some a temptation. For the holy Fathers define as a kind of temptation the case in which someone commits the reins of action solely to a divine miracle while he has not yet been deprived of human aid.

For my part, however, I judge a life pleasing to God to be one ignorant of cupidity, devoted to innocence, [Col. 0699A] and watchful in the work of charity. What, then, can cloaked hypocrisy claim for itself in these men or in the others when cupidity has been removed? For the truest rule is that evils do not arise from the root of charity, and good things never spring from the plant of cupidity. Nothing displeases God where the sacrifice of a sincere will is offered; and nothing fails to offend him if someone, in any rich offering, withholds from him his own will. Thus, the person who intends to do his own will provokes the Lord, while the person who puts aside his own will and subjects himself to God’s will appeases the Most High. In this alone consists the whole sum of true righteousness. Hence the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “My judgment is just, because I do not do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5).

Moses also says in Leviticus: “Every offering made to the Lord shall be made without leaven; neither shall anything of leaven or honey be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord” (Lev. 3). For leaven of pride and honey are offered when someone, neglecting humility and the bitterness of the commandments, offers something according to the inclination of his own will. But one who subjects his own will to lawful commandments, whatever he offers, excludes from sacrifice the swelling of leaven and that sweetness of honey which is forbidden. Therefore these men, forgetful of their own will and continually seeking how they may please him to whom they have devoted themselves, despising praise from people, neither possessing nor wishing to possess riches—how can they be said to have a portion with hypocrites?

Yet, astonishingly, someone is said already to have turned aside to the Carthusians in order to rise, drawn from the society of saints; and when afterward he turned back, he declared by the testimony of his works what he had sought. But he has his own judge; nevertheless, he could never bring it about that he should tarnish the glory of a most holy profession. I have not yet heard of anyone having been taken away from the Great Mountain; but would that no one were ever taken away, or that only such a person might be taken away as would not, by any act, discolour the beauty of a distinction singular among humankind. Others have Basil, others Benedict; these have Augustine; but those men have the Lord Jesus Christ himself as their unique master.

Although I have commended these two professions less than they deserve, I have said nothing, God being witness, in disparagement of others who walk rightly in their own professions. The Cistercians are holy; the Cluniacs are holy; monks and regular canons are holy. Among them, as star differs from star in glory, some are holier than others; and although one profession may surpass another, persons may perhaps be found in any of them who can equal superior saints. Plainly, the first rank and the title of singular glory belong to virgins; nevertheless, among the continent and married there may perhaps be some who are to be preferred to many virgins. The Catholic Church confesses that martyrs should be preferred to confessors; nevertheless, it will perhaps not fear to compare some confessors, in some respect though not absolutely, with certain martyrs.

Nor should any secular person—that is, one like myself—compare himself with the professions just named, [Col. 0700A] because it is scarcely possible for such a person to equal even a slothful cenobite. For if any one of us fasted every day from the Ides of September until Easter; attended the night vigils; continually abstained from meat; knew none of Venus’s impurity; was never absent, or only rarely and for a just cause, at the appointed hours; did not exceed the limits of sobriety; set a watch of prudent silence over his mouth; erased the day’s faults by daily satisfaction; fulfilled promptly and without delay what was commanded; and patiently endured not merely harsh words but harsh blows, so that he fell silent before the one shearing him—who would not admire and praise him reverently as a person of outstanding virtue and singular merit, as truly an apostolic man and an express imitator of Christ? Yet even slothful cenobites do these things, though from necessity. They differ from the zealous in this: the latter practise from love what the former are compelled to do by the spur of necessity, often unwillingly.

There are, nevertheless, persons in the common habit whom I do not dare call secular, since nothing in such people ought to be called secular except that they are bound to the world by an affection of wicked love. For just as circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments, so—to speak with the religious persons’ permission—monkhood is nothing and canonhood is nothing when observance of the commandments has been removed. These things, therefore, finally profit a person if he keeps the law. But if someone keeps the law without them, I would by no means call him secular. Still, let us accommodate religious persons: for the moment, let those be secular whom a dark garment does not distinguish from others. For there is no loss in the name unless the life is secular too.

Some are indignant that I, secular in habit and a sinner in conduct, make these pronouncements about religious persons; and, while I praise cenobites, they accuse me of disparaging others. Against such people I appeal not to Caesar but to Benedict, who, just as he rebukes Gyrovagues and Sarabaites, so openly praises cenobites.

Jerome is my authority, although some monks hear him less kindly because he seemed to prefer clergy in some respect. He is my authority, I say, that clothing makes no distinction of religion; rather, in every dress, one who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him. He also says: “Avoid dark clothing no less than white; adornment and dirt are equally to be avoided, because the one savours of luxury and the other of glory. For it is praiseworthy to go without a linen outer garment, provided one does not possess the price of linen garments.” He seems plainly to describe the sect of our own time—those, namely, who profess a certain irregular rule. Whether you can recognize them from his words, hear what he immediately adds: “Otherwise, it is ridiculous and full of disgrace to boast that you have no handkerchief or neck-cloth while your purse is full. There are people who give little to the poor in order to receive more, and who seek riches under the pretext of almsgiving; this ought rather to be called hunting than almsgiving. [Col. 0701A] Thus beasts, birds, and fish are caught. A small bait is put on the hook so that ladies’ purses may be drawn out by it. It is surely better not to have anything to give than to beg impudently in order to give.”

Let the hospitable brothers, or others, have no complaint here against me. The speaker of these words is a doctor of the Church, and perhaps Jerome did not have them in view. They know their own rule, although I know it as well. Yet I know the rule of truth, by which I know that religion pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction and to keep oneself unstained from this world. This belongs to all engaged in public affairs; and it goes well with such people if they keep it faithfully.

But with regard to those who dwell in God’s sacred leisure, the Prophet expresses their rule in himself, saying: “I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved; therefore my heart has rejoiced” (Ps. 15). So too Mary, withdrawn from crowds, sat at the Lord’s feet in the Gospel in order to hear his word.

But, to close the discourse on hypocrites, let us bring forward what blessed Job pronounces concerning them: “This I know from the beginning, since man was set upon the earth: that the praise of the wicked is brief, and the hypocrite’s joy is like a point. Though his pride should ascend even to heaven and his head touch the clouds, in the end he shall perish like dung” (Job 20).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the envious and slanderers.

Behold how wretched is the end of hypocrites, who, as sacred Scripture testifies, “shall perish like dung,” than which nothing is more unclean. In vain, therefore, did they affect the appearance of good works; for if those works were good, they certainly would not perish. In order to fulfil the desires of the flesh, which lusts against the spirit, they endured much in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and the like—by which the precious pearl of Christ might have been purchased. For the works of the flesh do not consist only in uncleanness or gluttony: the Apostle, speaking to the Galatians, proves that they are manifest in many vices, such as fornication, uncleanness, covetousness, shamelessness, wantonness, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and the like (Gal. V). Those who commit such things [Col. 0701D] shall not possess the kingdom of God. Whether, therefore, works are referred to the end of uncleanness and wantonness, or to the outcome of vain glory or covetousness, since they are deprived of their proper end, they incur death.

Hence the same Apostle says: “Do not become desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another” (Gal. V). Indeed, he wisely and elegantly expressed the vices through which false righteousness becomes known: for the swelling of arrogance readily provokes those from whom it supposes victory will come to itself; and envy begrudges those whom it considers superior or equal. I would believe that nothing is more miserable than this, though no misery moves pity less—and rightly so—than the calamity of those who have voluntarily cast away blessedness. For who could pity persons who would rather be miserable through the gall of malice [Col. 0702A] than blessed?

Long ago the Fathers held that blessedness consists in virtue, and that no virtue can exist without charity. Its fruit is most delightful, as the Apostle testifies; and he evidently sets these works of the Spirit, which lead to life, in opposition to the works of the flesh: charity, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, joy, gentleness, self-control, chastity (ibid.). Therefore, by what path do those proceed to blessedness who cut these branches of virtue from the soil of their own heart, and destroy the root of charity from which they spring? Plainly, nothing assails charity more than the poison of envy.

Envy, according to the philosophers, is a beginning of sorrow at another person’s apparent prosperity. For if someone grieves at the apparent prosperity of a tyrant or a depraved citizen, he is by no means stained with the blot of envy. Good men too are displeased when success, to the ruin of many, attends those thought more inclined to evil. If, therefore, envy is distressed by another’s good, it is plain that it is very far from charity, which does not seek its own things but those of its neighbours. Charity counts nothing good as its own and nothing evil as foreign: it sympathizes with the evils of others and pours out its own goods upon its neighbours. For it unites minds, so that they will the same things and refuse the same things.

The great Father Augustine says: “Take away envy: what is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine. And perhaps there will be nothing called mine or yours, but all things will be ours.” For envy is that which desires the neighbour to lack what it wishes absent from itself; and if it is not absent, it is miserably tormented, and is often tortured by that which it does not itself desire, when it sees that thing lacking to its neighbour [Col. 0702C]. Rightly so, since even the pagan says:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> Gnaws at its very author, tormenting his mind.

Do not think it a light torment, one than which the “Sicilian tyrants” could devise none more severe. Ovid, though beneath the cloud of poetic invention, has depicted this plague elegantly and truly:

> Pallor sits upon her face; emaciation over all her body.  
> Her gaze is never straight; her teeth are dark with rust;  
> Her breast is green with gall; her tongue is steeped in poison.  
> Laughter is absent, except such as another’s visible pain produces;  
> She can scarcely hold back tears, because she sees nothing tearful.  
> Nor does she enjoy sleep, roused as she is by wakeful cares.  
>   
> [Col. 0702D] But she sees men’s undeserved successes  
> And wastes away at seeing them; she tears, and is torn at once,  
> And is her own punishment.  
> *(Ovid, Metamorphoses II, 775.)*

The description is no less true because the author attributes a bodily constitution to a thing without a body; for the force of the figure called *sarcophagia* or *sarcography* consists precisely in its freely assigning bodily features to incorporeal things. What should rather be observed is that no force of kindness or of nature extinguishes envy’s flame. Thus Ovid describes envy stirred by Pallas’s strength and beauty; and a sister, goaded by envy, could not endure her sister’s happy marriage-bed, nor could she, to keep the faith pledged to the divinity or to her sister, be bent by any price:

> Often she wished to die, that she might see no such thing.

Envy incited the patriarchs to the crime of parricide against their brother, so that it was not even safe for him to disclose the grace which the Spirit showed the innocent youth in dreams. Thus the innocent brother is condemned to slavery, the father to bereavement; and, in order to frustrate the dispensation of God’s grace, wickedness obtained from the just Judge famine for itself, the yoke of servitude, the calamity of exile, the calumnies of the Egyptians, and Pharaoh’s cruelty. Joseph’s hands served in labours, and their descendants in mud and brick; even straw itself was considered unworthy of them.

You may see many driven by the goads of the same envy, so that they set whatever obstacles they can against grace and strive to hinder the ordinance of the Most High. If, as though dreaming, they surmise someone’s advancement, they oppose and resist, as though they would sell a brother to the Ishmaelites. If they do not kill him, [Col. 0703B] they besmear sincerity itself; and, in order to cloak their own crime, they display the innocent man’s bloodstained tunic. I see this description realized in many who burn at every moment of another’s happier fortune and would have fortune oppose themselves, if only others might be more grievously injured. And, if you believe Aesop or Avianus, you will see someone rejoice to have one of his own eyes torn out, provided his neighbour loses both. Nor is there any way to avoid envy except by becoming utterly wretched. For the ancient proverb is well known: misery alone knows no envy. And the most miserable fortune is that of the man whom nobody envies.

It is reported that Plato, when his fellow pupils envied him, asked Socrates how he might avoid human envy. Socrates answered him: “Be like Thersites.” Thus, while the envious are tortured, they wish others to share their misery, seeking everywhere to do harm; and they regard innocence itself as a kind of image of death. Hence Vergil—so that you may learn all from one—marking the envious man, says:

> And if you had harmed no one, you would be dead.

Nothing is less fitting for a philosopher, or for a man weighty in authority or character. Hence Socrates—not the ancient one, but he whom Cassiodorus praises in his *Tripartite History* as an author of deeds—said: “In expelling barbers and cooks from the palace, Julian performed the work not merely of an emperor, but of a philosopher.” But to slander and tear others to pieces was the act neither of philosopher nor prince. For when useful works cease for whatever reason, people run to the malice of detraction. This is indeed the undoubted offspring of envy, and it openly testifies that charity is absent. At one time it distorts another’s good qualities, at another it diminishes them; it invents evils that do not exist, or magnifies and exalts those that do.

Charity does not behave perversely; but detraction alone rejoices in perversity. When the Apostle enumerates many vices of the Gentiles, he places slanderers last, as though at the summit of evils—or rather, one might say, in their depths—and, marking them with a singular brand as enemies of divine goodness, declares them, as it were, uniquely hateful to God. Yet I would judge those most hateful to God among them who, with concealed hatred, so that they may do greater harm and be trusted more readily, proclaim another’s praises and feign friendship, while adding at the end of their speech something slight which contradicts the preceding encomiums:

> Proteus was blessed in his son, blessed in his wife;  
> And all things had befallen him, if you take away  
> The crime of murdering Phocus.

Does not the stain of such a parricide blot out all the gifts not only of fortune but even the greatest titles of virtue? Such is the orator’s saying: “I admit that Julius Fortunatus is a brave man, and one who is known to have performed very many deeds vigorously. Yet I should wonder how he escaped a trial for extortion before just judges, if the force of his eloquence were unknown to me.” Is this not poison, and does it not in some fashion extinguish the hope of good works and, so to speak, the life of virtue?

Much has indeed been said above concerning Gnathonics—that is, flatterers. But which should I call worse, Gnathonics or slanderers? It is not entirely clear. Yet I find that both vices were punished with death among the ancients. The Athenians imposed capital punishment on Timagoras because, in the course of greeting King Darius, he flattered him in the custom of that nation. The senate of the Lacedaemonians ordered Caristolus to be put to death because he preferred to carp at the deeds of great men rather than openly to criticize them with manly firmness. For among well-ordered people it has always been permitted for each person to use his own judgment and openly reprove what seemed not to have been rightly done. Liberty approves such freedom of criticism when supported by charity [Col. 0704C]; only tyrannical frenzy shudders at and obstructs it.

But you will see slanderers and the envious so abound in a court as though they had flowed into it as into the sewer of the whole world. There is no gathering of diners, however religious, which the goad of envy does not reach. Yet everywhere those who shine with more distinguished merits are more fiercely gnawed by envy’s poisoned tooth.

> For he who surpasses the arts set beneath him burns by his own brilliance;  
> When extinguished, that same man will be loved.  
> *(Horace, Epistles II.1.13.)*

But above all, slaves pursue their masters, and subjects their prelates. For, like slaves, the class of subjects is for the most part complaining; it alleges either that it is unjustly oppressed, that its efforts are unworthily rewarded, or that offices are badly administered. You will rarely find someone who does not slander his superior in some respect, even if everything is at times conducted rightly. Read again the comic poets, turn over the tragedians: you will see the household almost always ungrateful to the head of the household.

Yet you will be astonished to find this custom prevailing not only in court but in the school, the cloister, and the Capitol—if, indeed, domestic vices ought to be counted among habits. The venerable Father Gilbert, bishop of Hereford, used to tell me of a habit of cloistered men which he confessed he had experienced in himself. When he entered the monastery, still burning with the fire newly kindled within him, he censured the laziness of his superiors. Without delay, when promoted to a small office, he was moved to pity for his companions. Yet he did not spare the greater superiors. Soon afterward he rose to be prior; sympathizing with priors, he did not cease to criticize abbots. He himself became abbot; kindly toward his fellow abbots, he began to observe the vices of bishops. At last he himself became bishop and spared his fellow bishops. I do not, however, think that he suffered from the vice of envy; rather, being a prudent man, he elegantly expressed what is in some measure inborn in humankind. Perhaps that Father had imposed this task upon himself, so that, voluntarily joined to the crowd of such sufferers, he might be heard more kindly.

Julius Caesar, on hearing of Cato’s death, at last felt compassion for the labours and afflictions that had destroyed him, and mourned the removal of a distinguished citizen from human affairs. Yet he publicly confessed both that Cato had envied his virtue and that he himself envied Cato’s glory. The old man in the *Andria* teaches what is the most direct path to favour without envy, when he says that his son was obliging to everyone and injured no one. Augustine too, the father of the blessed life, says that either most cautious humility will avoid the dog’s tooth, or most solid truth will blunt it. By no other virtue does one escape the stings of detraction; nevertheless, a sound mind does not at all reject the healing of frank rebuke.

Though insults and defamatory writings are rightly punished. For:

> If anyone has composed evil verses against another, there is law  
> And judgment; and long ago against abusive speakers a “law was received, and the chorus”  
> Of those presuming upon foolish licence and abusing it  
> Fell shamefully silent, when the right to harm was removed.  
> [Col. 0705C] *(Horace, Art of Poetry, 284.)*

## CHAPTER XXV. On the love and favour of liberty; on those great men who bore free speech with a patient mind; and on the difference between abuse and a jest (*scomma*).

Liberty judges each matter according to its own discretion, and does not fear to reprove whatever it sees opposed to sound morals. Nothing is more glorious than liberty, except virtue—if indeed liberty can rightly be separated from virtue. For it is clear to all who think rightly that true liberty comes from no other source. Therefore, because virtue is agreed to be the highest good in life, and because it alone shakes off the grievous and hateful yoke of slavery, philosophers have held that, if necessity presses, one ought to die for virtue, which is the sole reason for living. But virtue does not arise perfectly without liberty [Col. 0705D], and the loss of liberty proves that perfect virtue is absent. Thus, each person is free according to the possession of virtues; and insofar as he is free, so far does he possess virtue.

Conversely, vices alone bring in slavery and subject a person to persons and things in an improper servitude. Although personal slavery sometimes appears more pitiable, slavery to vices is always far more pitiable. What, then, is more lovable than liberty? What is more deserving of favour in one who has any reverence for virtue? We read that all excellent rulers have promoted it, and that none has ever trampled upon liberty except manifest enemies of virtue. Jurists know what institutions have been introduced through favour for liberty; and historians’ testimony makes famous the splendid deeds performed out of love for it.

Cato drank poison and took up the sword; and lest any delay prolong a dishonourable life, he put in his hand, widened the wound, and shed his noble blood rather than see Caesar reigning. Brutus raised civil arms in order to free the City from slavery. The very seat of empire preferred always to be afflicted by wretched war rather than endure a master, however mild.

I pass to the weaker sex. The wives of the Teutons, for love of chastity, asked the victorious Marius to send them as a gift to the virgin priestesses of Vesta, promising that they too would remain free from intercourse. When they were not heard, on the following night they took their own lives with nooses, crushing their throats, lest they should be enslaved or suffer loss of chastity. If I wished to recount every example of this kind, time would fail before the examples did.

The use of liberty, therefore, is excellent, and it displeases only one who lives by slavish habits. Things freely said or done are free alike from fear and from rashness; and, while the straight path is followed, they merit praise and favour. But when, under the image of liberty, rashness pours forth the violence of its own spirit, it incurs rebuke. To the ears of the crowd it is indeed more pleasing than it is approved by the mind of any very wise person, since it more often enjoys the secure indulgence of others than its own foresight.

Yet it belongs to the best and wisest man to loosen the reins for liberty and to receive all its utterances patiently. Nor does he oppose its deeds, so long as he does not suffer loss of virtue. For although every virtue shines by itself, the title of patience gleams with a more glorious brightness.

When a man of Privernum was asked what sort of peace the captive Privernates would keep if impunity were granted them, he answered the Roman consul: “If you grant a good peace, it will be lasting; if a bad one, it will not last long.” By this word of liberty the Privernates obtained not only pardon for their rebellion but also the benefit of Roman citizenship, because a Privernate had dared to speak so in the senate.

A certain Philippus exercised free speech against the order of senators. Reproaching their idleness before the rostra, he said that he needed another senate; yet the senatorial dignity could not be moved. Nor could the prudence of the consul Philippus be moved when a defendant, upon whom he had ordered the lictor to lay hands, said: “My Philippus, you are not consul to me, because neither am I senator to you.”

Among all others Pompey the Great’s virtue shone brightly in this respect. When Gnaeus Piso was prosecuting Mallius Crispus, and saw that the accused, though manifestly guilty, was being rescued by Pompey’s influence, he was carried by youthful spirit and zeal into the prosecution and brought many grave charges against the powerful defender. Pompey then asked him why he did not prosecute the presiding magistrate too. “Give assurance,” Piso said, “that you too, if called to account as president of the state, will not stir up civil war; and I will send the judges to deliberate upon your case before that of Mallius.” Thus, in one judgment he sustained two defendants: Mallius by the accusation, Pompey by his free speech; and he dealt with the one by law, the other by a declaration of principle, as alone he could.

When the consul Gnaeus Lentulus Marcellinus complained during a debate of Pompey the Great’s excessive power, and the people loudly assented, he said: “Shout, Quirites, shout while you may; for, once Pompey has grown great, you will no longer be allowed to do it.” Yet the power of so great a citizen was assailed with impunity: here by an envious complaint, there by lamentation mingled with pity.

When Pompey had a white bandage bound around his leg, Favonius said: “It makes no difference on what part of the body the diadem is.” By this jest over a slight scrap of cloth he reproached him with kingly ambitions. But Pompey, without changing his expression in either case, guarded against appearing either gladly to acknowledge power by a cheerful face, or to profess anger by a sad one.

The same Pompey reproached Helvius Formianus, the son of a freedman, for having returned from the underworld in order to accuse Lucius Libo, Pompey’s friend. Helvius said: “I come from the underworld as an accuser against Libo; but while I stayed there I saw very many innocent persons, of different ages and sexes, making most grave complaints against you there—persons whom you had wickedly condemned through this power of yours, intolerable to good men”; and before all who heard, he set forth every perverse and blameworthy act of Pompey. Thus, at the same time, it was both bravest and safest to speak ill of Pompey.

Hence the tragic actor Deiphilus, while performing before the people, pointed his hand at Pompey and said: “Your misery is the Great One.” Likewise, when Gaius Carbo, as consul, ordered hostages to be given by the people of Placentia, Marcus Castutius, fired by liberty, yielded neither to threats nor to force. Indeed, when the consul said that he had swords, Castutius answered: “And I have years.”

Servius Galba, bound as surety for Pompey, when summoned in the forum, said: “Gaius Caesar, I stood surety for Pompey, once your son-in-law, during his third consulship; on that account I am now summoned. What am I to do? Shall I pay?” By openly and plainly reproaching Caesar with the sale of Pompey’s goods, he deserved to be removed from the tribunal; but Caesar’s heart, made gentler by its own mildness, ordered Pompey’s debt to be paid from his own treasury.

Pisistratus, tyrant of the Athenians, was urged by his wife to impose capital punishment upon a young man who, inflamed by love for their daughter, had met and kissed her in a public street. He answered: “If we kill those who love us, what shall we do to those who hate us?” This was a saying more worthy of a citizen than of a tyrant; he laudably bore the injury done to his daughter, and more laudably his own.

The same Pisistratus was torn without end by the insults of his friend Thrasippus at dinner, yet restrained both his spirit and his voice from anger. Although Thrasippus, in a drunken rush, spat in his face, Pisistratus held his sons and household back from revenge; and on the following day, when Thrasippus came as a suppliant and demanded voluntary death at Pisistratus’s hands, he gave him assurance and restored him to the former rank of friendship.

The province of Spain was being assigned by the senate to two very noble citizens, though of unequal fortunes. Servius Sulpicius, a man of humble station but most independent spirit, heard this. When the people too had given their assent to the senate, Sulpicius said: “I think neither should be sent, since one has nothing and the other is never satisfied.” He judged poverty and greed equally bad teachers of an unrestrained command.

A legate of the Cinnii, who had taken up arms against Roman rule, might have moved Brutus, the Roman consul and commander in Lusitania, by the weight of his words, had he not been a Roman; for moderation was always dear to that people above others. When the Cinnii were invited to ransom their freedom, the legate replied that their ancestors had left them iron with which to defend their city, not gold with which to buy freedom from a greedy commander.

Paschelius Junius, a man of the highest independence and extensive learning, renowned at home and abroad, but devoted solely to the study of philosophy, was asked what gave him such freedom to say whatever he wished. He answered: two things which men dread—old age and childlessness. For what can an old man without children fear?

Pyrrhus asked certain Tarentines who, at a banquet, had spoken of him with insufficient respect whether what he had heard was true. One of them answered: “Had our wine not failed us, what has been reported to you would have been mere sport and jest compared with what we were going to say.” So urbane an excuse for drunkenness, and so frank a confession of truth, turned the tyrant’s anger into laughter.

A woman of barbarian blood, but free spirit, joins these men. Having been condemned by King Philip while he was drunk, she cried amid the uproar: “I would appeal to Philip—but to Philip sober.” Thus she shook off the drowsy man’s drunkenness and compelled the man drunk with his present state of mind to recover his senses; after the case was more carefully examined, he gave a juster judgment.

A certain Syracusan woman alone, every morning at the time of prayer, most devoutly besought the gods for the safety of Dionysius, a tyrant most grievous and intolerable. When he learned this, astonished at goodwill not owed to him, he summoned her and asked why, or by what merit of his, she acted so. She answered: “My purpose has a certain reason. When I was a girl and we had a harsh tyrant, I desired to be rid of him. After he was killed, one somewhat more terrible seized the citadel; I greatly desired the end of his rule as well. We then came to have you as a third ruler, more troublesome than those before you. Therefore, fearing that, if you too were taken away, someone worse might succeed you, I devote my life to preserving yours.” Dionysius, though utterly vile, was ashamed to punish such witty boldness. For what will be secure if even virtues, among which liberty almost holds the chief place, are punished?

The Romans, therefore, as they were superior to others in other respects, so they proved more patient under criticism. Indeed, provided that care was taken in banquets and places less sober, whoever recoiled from and shunned criticism, though it was just, seemed ignorant of sobriety. For even when criticism contains open or hidden affront, patient endurance of criticism is far more glorious among the wise than punishment.

Hence the practice of abusive attacks and jests, even against men endowed with the highest power, is more licentious than lawful. Abuse (*loedoria*), as Eustachius teaches in the book of the *Saturnalia*, contains reproach and direct insult [Col. 0709A]. A jest (*scomma*) is a figurative bite, since it is often concealed by deception or wit, so that it sounds one thing and you understand another. Yet it does not always proceed to bitterness; sometimes it is even pleasant to those at whom it is aimed. This kind is exercised especially by a wise or witty person, chiefly at table and over drinks, where anger is easily provoked. For as a person standing at a precipice can be pushed by even a light touch, so a man steeped or sprinkled with wine is stirred to fury by even a slight pain.

Therefore, one should more cautiously abstain from jesting at a banquet, because it contains a concealed injury within itself. Such sayings cling all the more tightly than direct abuse, just as barbed hooks stick more firmly than straight points. Especially because words of this sort raise laughter among those present, whereby the injuries are confirmed as by a kind of assent.

An example of abuse is: “Have you forgotten that you used to sell salted fish?” A jest—which, as was said, is an indirect insult—is: “We remember when you blew your nose with your arm.” Although the same matter is stated in both cases, the former is abuse because it is openly cast up and reproached; the latter is a jest because it is expressed figuratively.

There are gentler jests, bites like those of a toothless beast. Thus Cicero said of a consul who held the consulship for only one day: “There are usually priests of Jupiter for a day; now we have consuls for a day.” And of the same man: “Our consul Camus is exceedingly watchful: in his consulship he has not seen sleep.” And when that consul reproached Cicero for not having come to him: “I was coming,” he said, “but night overtook me.”

But the use of abuse or jest, and urbanity, will be discussed later. For now, it is enough to have shown that it is lawful to criticize what it is right to correct. I shall attach only one of Alexander’s jests, as though at the end of this little book, to what has preceded. When King Darius, having tested Alexander’s courage in one battle and then another, offered him part of his kingdom as far as Mount Taurus, his daughter in marriage, and a hundred thousand talents, Parmenion—a great man among the Macedonians—said that, if he were Alexander, he would accept the offer. Alexander replied: “And I would do the same, if I were Parmenion.” Silently he reproached his adviser’s timidity; with words answering two victories, and worthy to be granted a third, as in fact occurred.

It was therefore free, and always lawful for liberty, while sparing persons, to speak about vices. For there is a legal right by which true words may be uttered; and December itself grants freedom even to slaves against their masters, provided they speak the truth. Then, therefore, without seeking pardon—which belongs to them by right itself—they sharpen their tongues and with impunity rebuke whatever has burned them throughout the year, openly exposing crimes. Yet after the Saturnalia have ended, without leave they must by no means spring to accuse their masters or patrons.

I therefore make use of December’s liberty. Obeying your commands, I confidently criticize, by the benefit of a common legal right, what burns both you and me. I do not think it necessary to seek pardon in matters that serve public advantage and accord with your approved will.

# BOOK VIII

[Col. 0709]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0709C]

Those who sail the sea customarily feel gratitude toward, and repay, those through whose aid they have escaped dangers. Fires are lit, cries raised, and signals erected, by which sailors may safely avoid the Scyllaean whirlpool, stormy Charybdis, hidden rocks, and the shallows and clinging sands of the Syrtes. So too, those who warn people of dangers threatening human safety most rightly deserve gratitude; and whoever does not render it to those who deserve it is ungrateful for the benefit and worthy to suffer the loss of safety.

No one fails to know that safety is impeded by vices, and that it is in the public interest that they should be marked out, from love of one’s neighbours, in order to be avoided. Human life is more stormy than any sea, and dangers cannot be avoided unless they are announced by their signs.

I am driven to this work by the goads of public benefit and your command, though I recognize nothing in myself to command the attention of hearers: a man on every side unprotected and diminished, who possesses neither a life fit for conscientious reflection, nor learning fit for instruction, nor works fit for an example. Hence many voices cry out concerning me that I should be silent, saying that even the fair praise of virtue is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner [Col. 0710C].

Only those to whom vices are pleasing do this: men running toward death with no one recalling them, or men saved against their will. Those, however, to whom good things are pleasing attend not to who speaks but to what is said; weighing sayings by the reasons of the speaker, they receive gladly whatever, drawn forth from whatever source, advances virtue. Therefore let the diligent reader attend not to who I am, but to what and for what reason I write. Where he finds me to have spoken badly, let him, as a sincere judge shaken by no movement of envy, hatred, or other affection, bear witness to the evil; and where I have spoken well, let him not strike me.

Yet it is a small matter to me if perverse persons gratuitously slander my innocence—persons whom I would wish to be corrected—provided the favour of your kindness receives me. Whatever I may suffer from the present generation, I hope, God being its author, and the charity that impels me to write giving me confidence, that grace will not be lacking to my labour among posterity. For the judgments of contemporaries commonly slip to one side or the other through hatred or love.

Nothing will intentionally be inserted into this work which is not supported by reason or by the authority of earlier writers [Col. 0711A]. Yet the decision what should be followed is left to the reader’s discretion, so that I may keep the vice and charge of lying far from my name. But enough of this. Now let us pass into the camp of the Epicureans and bring forth what has been established there as certain. For those who serve their own will in all things are known undoubtedly to belong to their sect.

## CHAPTER I. That Gnathonic dependence is subject to Thrasonian arrogance; on the seven principal vices and their consequences according to Blessed Gregory; and that vain glory has a noble origin.

In the whole household of the Epicureans, Thraso is conspicuous; and although he did not come forth first, he must be considered either the first of all or not the least among the foremost. For, though he is foolish, the whole faction of Gnathonics serves him. Perhaps the comic poet introduced Gnatho as the servant of the boastful soldier in order elegantly to indicate that, both in human life and in the analysis of character, Gnathonic dependence is subject to Thrasonian arrogance. Yet each depends upon the other, so much so that they cannot exist without one another. Gnatho’s service is useless if there is no boastful soldier; and perhaps Thraso’s arrogance would subside if Gnatho’s deceit did not sustain it.

Perhaps you despise the eunuch of the comic play, but in that eunuch the poet has portrayed the life of nearly everyone. He criticized all the more freely and elegantly because, by the cautious device of a fictitious plot, he laid vices bare without injuring individuals. If you seek a more distinguished authority, many opponents of *cenodoxia* come forward. *Cenodoxia*, as the Fathers held, is vain glory: it inflates the mind and ears, and brings mortals no other profit from the solidity of virtue.

Since pride is the beginning of all sin, it first begets this offspring from itself. From this poisonous root of pride arise the seven principal vices, so called in relation to lesser vices, which spring in many ways from them as from the heads of a hydra. If you have leisure, attend briefly to how the most blessed Pope Gregory depicts this deadly tree in the *Moralia*, so that its names and forms may be retained more faithfully. He distinguishes the chief branches of this plant as follows: the first is vain glory; the second, envy; the third, anger; the fourth, sorrow; the fifth, avarice; the sixth, gluttony; and the seventh, lust.

Therefore the Saviour, because he grieved that we were held captive by these vices of pride, came, filled with the sevenfold Spirit of grace, to the spiritual battle of liberation. Since five of these vices are spiritual and two carnal, each is joined to the others in such kinship that one is generated only from another. Each branch also has twigs proceeding from itself, spread to such vast extent that they almost cover the whole world, which lies in wickedness.

From vain glory arise disobedience, boastfulness, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in a neighbour’s adversities, and distress at his prosperity. From anger proceed quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sorrow come malice, rancour, faint-heartedness, despair, sluggishness concerning commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things. From avarice go forth betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, violence, and hardenings of heart against mercy. From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding. From lust are generated blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present world, and dread or despair concerning the world to come.

[Col. 0712B] But how the principal vices arise one from another, the same teacher explains. For the first offspring of pride, once it has corrupted the oppressed mind, immediately begets envy; since, clearly, while it craves the power of an empty name, it wastes away lest anyone else should be able to attain it. Envy in turn generates anger, because the more the mind is wounded by the inward injury of jealousy, the more it loses the gentleness of tranquillity. And because it is touched like an aching limb, the hand performing the contrary action is felt as though more heavily pressed.

Anger also gives rise to sadness, because the more disorderly the disturbed mind agitates itself, the more it takes refuge in speaking evils; and, once it has lost the sweetness of tranquillity, nothing feeds it except the sorrow that follows from disturbance. Sadness in turn is carried over into avarice, [Col. 0712C] because, when the heart has lost within itself the good counsel by which it should be consoled, it seeks outside itself the means of consolation. And it desires to acquire external goods all the more because it has no joy to which it may return inwardly.

Indeed, each of these bears the fruit of its own destruction: vain glory takes away God; envy, one’s neighbour; anger, itself. Sadness is ignorant of consolation; avarice, while it wanders among external things, is worn down by a fast imposed by its own greed. To fill the lack caused by its emaciation, it slips into the two following vices of the flesh. In these it is clear that lust is born from gluttony of the belly, since in the very arrangement of the limbs the genitals appear to be attached beneath the belly. Hence, when one is inordinately refreshed, [Col. 0712D] the other is without doubt stirred up to shameful acts.

These things are Gregory’s—indeed, the Holy Spirit’s through Gregory. From this it is clear that one who tends toward salvation must extinguish pride’s first offspring. If it grows even a little, it produces from itself, as has been said, thickets of every vice. For although it may sometimes be predominant in someone, it can by no means be alone. If vain glory spurs anyone on, that person must necessarily fall headlong down the precipices of vices.

This vice is considered noble, and so flatters the disposition of human frailty that it is scarcely absent even from distinguished minds. For it has a noble origin, and does not recognize the progress of its own ruin until it falls from the height it sought. Vices also arise mutually from one another, [Col. 0713A] and vain glory takes root even in virtue at its very origin. For whatever field a person excels in above others, there, unless governing grace is present, he more easily becomes swollen with pride.

## CHAPTER II. That the Contemner of Glory Is Rare; on the Three Sources from Which Matter for Praise Is Drawn; on Praise That Is True, Perfect, or Neither; and on Moderation in Giving

Yet scarcely anyone does not pursue vain glory and desire the praise that comes from men. Some attain it through virtue, others through the appearance of virtue, others through a benefit of nature or fortune. For orators have held that the material of praise is drawn from these three sources: it must be sought from the mind, the body, or external circumstances.

The goods of mind and body are either naturally implanted, acquired by study, or have accrued causally and accidentally. In these there are definite ranks corresponding to the worth of the things in which they consist and by which they are sought. The first rank of commendation proceeds from an endowment of the mind. The second and middle rank approves bodily health and beauty. The third and last contains the praise of external things. I have reported above that Apuleius taught this as well.

Praise of the mind is indeed true, and often perfect, provided that the good qualities commended in it adhere firmly enough to be inseparable. For it is certain that they cannot be taken away against one’s will. Otherwise praise may perhaps be true, but it cannot be perfect. [Col. 0713C] Commendation of the body is plausible, but never perfect, for its goods can always be taken away against one’s will. Its nature can continually be weakened and corrupted.

The grace of external acquisitions is transient: they possess neither true nor perfect praise—indeed, not even plausible praise. Let it suffice if they imitate what is merely probable. For they are easily turned in either direction. Unless they are aided by the use made of them by their possessors, they are more inclined to blame than praise. Riches, power, and influence, because they confer great strength, provide the surest test of character in either direction; and their possessor is sometimes made better, sometimes worse, in character by them.

Furthermore, the works of mind or body themselves, although simply good or absolutely evil, sometimes incur blame or praise according to the judgment of the evaluator. Therefore Aristotle considers it very important where a thing is praised or blamed. For the character of the audience and the persuasion publicly accepted among them matter greatly. In his rhetorical writings he teaches that hearers should especially believe that the qualities publicly approved are present in the person to be praised, or, in the person against whom one speaks, those qualities which all hate; and that, whenever possible, the advantage of each individual must be demonstrated. For everyone approves what is expedient, although different things appear honourable to different people.

Literary studies win less honour at Sparta than at Athens; perhaps endurance and courage win more. Among the former, living by plunder is honourable; among the latter, devotion to law. Frugality might perhaps have been hated among the Sybarites. [Col. 0714A] To the ancient Romans luxury was the supreme crime. Account must also be taken of the person who is praised, since necessary works surpass gratuitously good deeds in praise, and according to the status of persons an action is commonly considered either honourable or shameful.

If, then, someone wins praise for himself by the straight road—that is, through virtue—he rests upon his own foundation of praise. But if he seeks glory from elsewhere, he is plainly foolish and will not reach that which he seems to pursue. Among the works of virtue, however, those thought worthy of ampler glory are those flowing from the fountain of liberality or magnanimity. For popular favour exalts these more conspicuously, and those acts seem especially eminent which are more difficult or benefit more people.

Yet among these liberality greatly excels: it softens resentment of mind, blunts the tongues of detractors, restrains hostile hands, and covers a multitude of sins from the sight of men. [Col. 0714B] Therefore those who either court or fear human tongues pour out their patrimonies, scatter gifts among the crowd, lay out banquets, flatter great and small, and many—serving a pig rather than a human being—devote themselves to feasts and drunkenness. They patronize mimes and actors, reward the most worthless arts, admit scoundrels, and stir up the tongues of slanderers to fulfill the malice of their own insolence, while the slanderers’ silence or venomous wit is rewarded with an ill-earned payment.

There are some who consider this the greatest, indeed the only true, use of riches: that they multiply pots of meat, hold daily feasts of entrails, know neither the limit of a banquet nor the number of guests, and have no plan for governing a household. If you happened to see such a gathering, you would think the forum had been summoned, not a crowd dining at noon or at supper. This occurs among the very rich; though the lesser hand, too, among the powerful imitates the footsteps of those above it in proportion to its means.

For whoever seeks reputation exceeds his resources: he considers not what he can do, but what will please others, and hastens to accomplish that. But grant that someone practices liberality for reputation rather than conscience, since the way to no virtue ought to be closed: still, it is unlawful and disgraceful to support mimes and obscene professions with benefactions.

Valerius relates that the city of Massilia [Col. 0714D] was so vigilant a guardian of seriousness that it allowed mimes no entrance onto the stage, because their plots for the most part contained acts of sexual immorality, lest the habit of watching such things create licence to imitate them as well. Is it, then, honourable that those whom pagans would not hear in the theatre should be heard at dinner by Christians—indeed, by clerics?

The Lacedaemonians ordered the books of Archilochus to be removed from their city because they judged their reading insufficiently modest and chaste. They did not wish their children’s minds to be imbued with them, lest they harm morals more than they benefited talent. Accordingly they punished with exile a poet of the first rank, or certainly next to the first, because he had torn apart with obscene abuse in verse a household hostile to him. By nearly the same judgment, the wantonness of Naso’s poems was condemned. Is it permissible to hear over cups what fasting sobriety did not dare to hear?

The same city kept its gates closed to all who sought sustenance for idleness through some pretence of religion, judging that deceitful and counterfeit superstition ought to be driven away. Yet those conscious of superstition in themselves claim the chief place among persons wasted by the love of praise.

Moreover, just as the miser was judged to differ from the generous person, so the prodigal was judged to differ from the generous person by a certain opposition. They held these two to be opposites of one and the same thing: one by quantity, the other by quality. Thus cowardice is opposed to magnanimity by the quality of its evil, because it fears what should be dared; and rashness by quantity, because it ventures beyond what should be dared. Prodigality [Col. 0715B] pours out what ought and what ought not to be spent upon things that will leave no memory at all, or only a brief one.

Theophrastus, on Cicero’s authority, is said to have commended this extravagance in the book he wrote on wealth. In it he wrote many excellent things, but one absurd thing: he held that the chief fruit of riches lay in lavish magnificence, the provision of public entertainments, and the ability to meet expenses of that kind. How much more seriously and truly Aristotle criticizes these expenditures of money, especially since they neither relieve necessity nor increase dignity, and the very pleasure of the pampered crowd is for a brief and trivial time and is shared even by the most frivolous. In this very pleasure, however, memory dies along with satiety.

[Col. 0715C] He rightly concludes also that such things please children, little women, slaves, and free persons most like slaves, but cannot in any way be approved by a serious man who weighs what is done with sound judgment.

Valerius Maximus, and Cicero as well, relate that Philip rebuked this squandering of money in Alexander, who sought the goodwill of the Macedonians by largesse. The words of the letter are these:

> “What evil reasoning led you into this hope, that you should think loyal to you those whom you had corrupted with money? Or do you act so that the Macedonians may regard you not as their king, but as their servant and supplier?”

You do not doubt that this is disgraceful in a king, and that it ought rather to be called corruption than generosity. For the recipient becomes worse and more ready always to expect the same thing. What is more foolish than willingly taking care that what you do cannot be done for long? Unlimited largesses will be followed by plunder; for when, by giving, you begin to lack resources, you will be compelled to lay hands upon other people’s goods. Thus, though you are prodigal in order to gain goodwill, you will not obtain from those to whom you have given as much devotion as you will hatred from those from whom you have taken.

Therefore one’s estate should neither be so shut up that generosity cannot open it, nor so thrown open that it lies exposed to all; moderation must be applied from both sides, and it must correspond to one’s means. Either a philosopher or another popular figure elegantly restrained the immoderation of this expenditure, which appears to bring glory but, in the manner of a prostitute, vanishes [Col. 0716A] when resources fail. For affection secured not by virtue but by fortune is most rightly compared to the love of a prostitute.

## CHAPTER III. That Every Profession Has Its Thrasones; on Persons among the Vainly Glorious Who Resemble the Eunuch in Terence; and That Vain Glory, Like a Prostitute, Follows Moneybags

As we have said, in every profession one may find a boastful soldier who, by services and gifts, courts his Thaïs—that is, a celebrated name and, as it were, the favour of reputation. But he does not lack a Gnatho to deceive him, a Phaedria to rob him of praise, a young man to corrupt his gifts, or the slave Parmeno to mock his folly. Listen to Gnatho in the comic poet’s *Eunuch*, and observe carefully whether you see him in the household of the vainglorious.

> “There is a class of men who wish to be thought first in all matters,  
> Yet are not. I pursue these. I do not contrive to make them laugh at me,  
> But I smile at them unsolicited, and at the same time admire their talents.  
> Whatever they say, I praise; if they then deny it, I praise that too.  
> Does someone deny? I deny. Does he affirm? I affirm. In short, I have ordered myself  
> To agree with everything: this trade is now by far the most profitable.”  
> (*Terence, Eunuchus* II.ii.18)

Have you seen such a man anywhere? Indeed, you have not known any of those who appear fortunate without such a dependant; and everywhere you will find a clever fellow “who will make men, out of fools, as Parmeno says, utterly mad.” [Col. 0716C] See also what Thraso thinks of himself:

> “This surely is granted me:  
> That everything I do pleases men.  
> Even the king always showed me the greatest gratitude  
> For whatever I had done; not so to others.  
> He always kept me before his eyes, entrusted his whole army  
> And his plans to me; and whenever weariness  
> Of men, or at any time disgust with business, seized him,  
> He would rest where he wished;  
> When he wished to spit that misery from his mind,  
> Then he would take me alone as his dinner-companion.  
> All envied me,  
> Bit secretly; I valued it at nothing.  
> They envied me miserably.”  
> (*Ibid.* III.i.11)

“I openly criticized some, and mordantly ridiculed others, so that

> ‘All who were present died of laughter.  
> At last everyone feared me.’”  
> (*Ibid.* II.42)

Certainly this man is great in his own eyes, and has no equal in the whole comedy. He is therefore worthy to be admitted to Thaïs, while Phaedria—who is no less mad over her—is shut out. Shut out, he grieves; a sober slave advises him to withdraw from the prostitute and to take courage: if he approaches the fire, he will grow too warm; nor should he endure the insults of prostitutes, who, with a single little false tear, scarcely squeezed out by miserably rubbing their eyes, will check a lover’s anger and, accusing first, will make him render an unsolicited punishment.

For no one can love wisely more easily than he can be mad with reason. Phaedria's dealings with Thaïs, then, are on this condition: whatever word he hears, he must keep silent and keep it in well; but if it is false, vain, or feigned, he immediately pours it forth openly:

> “He is full of cracks; he leaks out here and there.”  
> (*Ibid.* I.ii.25)

He accuses both and mocks both, seeing one deceived and the other irretrievably mad. Thus Phaedria, shut out and groaning in pain, says:

> “O Thaïs, would that I had  
> An equal share of love with you, and that it might happen alike  
> Either that this hurt you, or that I should count as nothing this deed done to me by you!”  
> (*Ibid.* I.ii.14)

To this Thaïs replies:

> “Do not torment yourself, I beg you, my dear Phaedria.  
> By Pollux, I love or cherish no one more;  
> Yet I did it—it was the situation; it had to be done.”  
> (*Ibid.* I.ii.15)

“Clearly,” says Parmeno, “poor thing, in her love she has shut him outside.” (*Ibid.* I.ii.18.)

In short, the deceit of the prostitute works so that one lover yields precedence to another for some days, while, once admitted, the latter is more thoroughly squeezed dry after losing his property. For one must accommodate Thaïs, who admits those who are more lavish and more ruined. Meanwhile the excluded men deliberate what they can give or send. For he has most influence with her who sends the latest gift. But when she has squeezed out the first, the other returns; and, having excluded the former, she assigns him the sorrowful charge of his own pain.

The soldier is mad, and in the rush of his grief resolves that he ought rather to die than suffer so notable an insult against himself. He summons his household, arrays a battle, and determines with collected forces to storm the brothel. He advances, turns the injury over in mind and speech, speaks grandly, and burns with threats. But when he comes to the conflict, remembering his former love, he recalls the military maxim which, on Scipio’s authority, declares that it becomes a wise person to “try everything first by counsel rather than arms.” Thus he meets his Thaïs according to agreement, proceeding by right rather than force. First:

> “Thaïs, answer me this: when I give you that girl, did you say that you would give yourself to me alone for these days?”  
> (*Ibid.*)

Thaïs replies:

> “What then, afterward?”

She seems to concede because she does not deny it. Thraso says:

> “Yet before my very eyes you brought your lover.”

And she answers:

> “Why do you quarrel with him?”

See how, under the protection of a mistress, it is not even permitted to exchange words with a rival:

> “You secretly slipped away from me with him.”  
> And she replies: “I pleased myself.” Thraso says: “Then give Pamphila back here, unless you would rather have her taken away.”  
> (*Ibid.*)

His request seems fair and just, since what has been given for a reason can be demanded back if the result for which it was given has not followed. In short, at the prostitute’s cry her fellow-tribesmen and neighbours gather; a crowd arises; the soldier shouts abuse; force and law are resisted when he makes his demand. The most foolish gallows-bird of them all is warned to restrain tongue and hands, because if he does anything to the crowd, or attempts any scheme, he is threatened with an enduring remembrance of the place, the day, and the executioner, branded upon him with marks.

Thaïs orders him, when he asks, to seek someone who will answer him. The soldier is compelled to return inglorious, his effort and property lost. Such is the fruit these wretched lovers carry away; with the addition that another abuses the possessions they have lost. And, to increase the pain, the man who has stolen them for the prostitute does not think himself successful unless he proclaims and publicizes before all people the folly and misfortunes of the lovers and his own success.

Listen to Chaerea, Pamphila’s hidden corrupter, speaking as he comes out after deceiving the prostitute:

> “Is anyone here? No one. Is anyone following me? Not a soul.  
> May I now burst forth with this joy? O Jupiter!  
> Surely now I could bear even to be killed,  
> So that life may not contaminate this joy with some sorrow.  
> But let no curious person now come near me,  
> To follow me and, by questioning, batter, torture, and kill me:  
> Why am I so excited? Why am I happy? Where am I going? Whence have I emerged? Where was I  
> When I obtained this clothing? What am I to seek? Am I sane, or mad?”  
> (*Terence, Eunuchus* III.v.1)

Asked all these things, he says: “Indeed, Antipho, I beg you to hear everything: hear of a festival day, a delightful event, a sweet fortune, a story to be remembered by all forever.” He also added the stratagems of his own madness.

To sum up, I think that the whole present argument may be reduced to this: it must certainly be established that trust ought not be placed in prostituted friendship. For what comes from sincerity of mind is faithful, sure, and fixed; what comes from a money-chest or moneybags is fluid, uncertain, deceptive, and withers when its provision fails.

> “While fortune remains, friends preserve their countenance;  
> When it has fallen, they turn their faces in shameful flight.”

For every thing that enters commerce passes from one person [Col. 0718D] to another and accompanies the richer and more eager buyer. Yet no market is more unjust than this: having bought the thing once will not profit you unless you always buy it; and wherever one claims a thing another has sold, he can do so only if he too satisfies the price.

Who has sold popular favour? If it is to be possessed publicly, it must be bought by everyone together. Individuals are not permitted to dispose of public goods. The saying, too, has become proverbial: “Careless generosity has no bottom.” Moreover, if popular favour has raised someone to public office, and he happens, after the manner of Thraso, to demand his purchased celebrity, then another Thaïs—reputation, less faithful than any Thaïs—subjects him to insults, strips him of honour, bars him from the rank of honour that has been pre-bought, casts him down, and drives him away. A rival mocks him; a sober critic rejoices; Gnatho scarcely murmurs while there remains hope, but is wholly silent if he despairs, and goes over to others, for his policy is always to attach himself to those more fortunate.

## CHAPTER IV. That No Vice Is Worse than Avarice, and That One Suspected of Avarice Cannot Be Loved; on the Twofold Source of Liberality and Which Is Superior; and on Considius and Gellias

Nevertheless, although prodigality seems blameworthy, I do not think room should be left for avarice. No vice is worse, none more detestable, especially in those who exercise leadership or any magistracy in the commonwealth. Not merely the thing itself but even its reputation must be avoided; and it is altogether impossible that one who has deservedly incurred suspicion of avarice among serious and prudent men should appear faithful to anyone or worthy of love.

Since human praise and favour come, as it were, from a twofold source—service and money—the latter is easier, especially for a wealthy person. But the former is more splendid, more illustrious, and more worthy of a brave and distinguished man. For those who are liberal in works and exertions of virtue will, the more people they benefit, have the more helpers in doing good. Then, through the habit of beneficence, they will be readier and, as it were, better trained to deserve well of many.

If, however, one’s treasury were sufficient, nothing is more glorious than that liberality consisting in gifts—especially because Socrates, it is said, when asked what constituted the substance of happiness, answered: “Giving to the worthy.” [Col. 0719C] I think the Socratic definition should be interpreted so that worthiness is understood to lie in the need or merits of the recipients. It is just to give to those who have deserved it; it is pious to assist those in need—provided, however, that in each case one considers what can be exposed without shame or reproach in the sight of a wise person.

For we must imitate him who makes his sun rise upon the good and evil and rains upon the just and unjust (Matthew 5). If we see a poor actor or mime, we should certainly not encourage wickedness; but, when corrected and, if possible, reformed, human nature must be supported by the claim of fraternal charity. It is fitting to offer every petitioner either a kindly intention or the consolation of charity. Yet sometimes it is more salutary to rebuke an idler or put a prostitute or actor to shame than to give what they demand.

Why delay? Whatever charity bestows is repaid by the Lord. What vanity distributes vanishes. Valerius records the very wholesome example of liberality in Quintus Considius, not without a small benefit to Considius himself. When Catiline’s madness had so disturbed the republic that, because of the turmoil and the reduced price of landed possessions, not even wealthy persons could pay money owed to creditors, Considius had one hundred and fifty *sestertia* out at interest. Yet he allowed none of his debtors to be sued by his own agents, whether for principal or interest; and, so far as lay in him, he mitigated the bitterness of public confusion by private tranquillity.

At an opportune time [Col. 0720A] and in a remarkable way he testified that he lent his money, not civil blood. Those who now take particular pleasure in trafficking, when they have carried bloody money home, will learn how disgracefully they exult in joy if they do not disdain to read carefully the decree of the senate by which thanks were given to Considius.

Valerius adds to him Gellias of Agrigentum, who is known to have possessed, as it were, the very heart of liberality itself. He was outstanding in wealth, but richer far more in spirit than in riches. Always occupied in spending money rather than hoarding it, he made his house seem a workshop of munificence. From it were constructed monuments suited to public uses; from it were provided spectacles pleasing to the public eye; from it came magnificent arrangements for feasts and aid for the failing grain supply.

While these things were distributed to all, food was also given privately to those suffering want, dowries to maidens, assistance to people burdened by poverty, and consolation to those shaken by the onset of losses. Guests too were most kindly received, both in his urban household and beneath his country roofs, and were sent away adorned with varied gifts. On one occasion he fed and clothed five hundred horsemen of Gela at once, driven by a storm onto his estates. In short, you would call him not a mortal man but the kindly bosom of propitious Fortune.

Thus what Gellias possessed was, as it were, the common patrimony of all; for his safety and prosperity both the city of Agrigentum [Col. 0720C] and neighbouring regions kept watch in prayer. Set on the opposite side coffers secured by inexorable locks: would you not sometimes judge that expenditure superior to such guardianship? In conclusion, whatever wisdom arranges is approved; what rashness presumes never obtains the fruit of true praise.

## CHAPTER V. On the Two Natural Affections, Namely Love of What Is Just and Love of What Is Advantageous; on Their Consequences, Namely Love of Liberty and Love of Dominion; on the Comparison of Caesar and Cato; on Alexander, Aristotle, Augustus, and Plato; and on Those Who Pursue Glory by a Devious Road

The authority of Sacred Scripture indicates that these dispositions have existed in human beings from the beginning: the desire for what is just and the desire for what is advantageous. One consists in the will, the other in necessity; and the more the desire for justice, which resides in the will, increases, the better it is and the more worthy of greater blessedness. For no one can desire what is just too much—unless perhaps someone can be too just or too blessed.

But if the desire for what is advantageous exceeds the measure of necessity, it inclines toward fault; conscious of covetousness, it produces in itself the origin of vices. One of these desires, because it serves charity, seeks the things of God; the other is occupied with private advantage, setting aside the things of God or of one’s neighbours.

From this twofold fountain dispositions arise: upright ones, if a person does to another what he wishes done to himself, and refrains from inflicting upon another what he would not wish inflicted upon himself; distorted ones, if he injures another or does not benefit him when he can. Both occur in many ways.

From the former come love of liberty, love of country, and finally love of strangers. For one who loves himself and his country cannot fail to love liberty; and whoever loves his neighbour with sincere charity loves the stranger in his proper degree. Ordered charity consists in this. From the latter proceeds the desire for dominion, praise, and glory; and it grows so strong that, in the opinion of many—though of people who examine matters too little—it is counted among the virtues. Those who think rightly add it to the greater vices, though the ignorant, who nevertheless are reckoned among the wise, seem to find virtues beneath it.

Therefore the ancient and earliest Romans, as their history teaches and commends them, were eager for praise and liberal with money. They desired immense glory while despising riches, and preferred honour to advantage of whatever magnitude. They loved this glory most ardently, relating their whole life and death to it. While the desire for this one thing flourished, they suppressed their other desires. Finally, because to serve seemed dishonourable but to rule and command glorious, they desired their native country first to be free through every effort, and afterwards to be mistress. First they fought for liberty, afterwards for dominion.

Yet there were some for whom justice, so far as it was granted to a pagan, sufficed, once desire had been laid aside. For others nothing was enough; but, under the appearance of magnanimity, presuming even impossibilities, they attained the highest praise and glory. Thus Cato’s virtue seems far closer to truth than Caesar’s. This will readily become clear from his own statement:

> “Do not suppose that our ancestors made the republic great from small beginnings by arms. If that were so, we should possess it now in far more splendid condition. For we have a greater abundance of allies and citizens, and besides of arms and horses, than they had. But other things made those men great—things that we do not possess at all: industry at home; just rule abroad; a mind free in deliberation and subject neither to wrongdoing nor to appetite. In place of these we have luxury and avarice, public poverty and private opulence. We praise riches; we follow idleness. Between good and bad there is no distinction. Ambition possesses all the rewards of virtue. Nor is this surprising, when each of you separately forms plans for himself, when at home you are slaves to pleasures, and here to money or favour. Thus an assault is made upon an empty republic.”

The virtue of the few who strove for glory, honour, and rule by the true road—that is, by virtue itself—was therefore praised even by Cato. This was the industry at home which Cato recalls: that the treasury should be rich and private estates modest. Hence, when morals had been corrupted, he set in opposition the vice of public poverty and private opulence.

Tully himself could not conceal this in the same books which he wrote *On the Republic*, where he speaks of establishing the leading citizen and says that he must be nourished by glory. He accordingly recalls that his ancestors did many wonderful and illustrious deeds from the desire for glory. Therefore they not only did not resist this vice, but even judged that it ought to be stirred up and kindled, believing this beneficial to the republic.

In his philosophical writings Cicero likewise advanced this universal and general maxim: “Honour nourishes the arts, and glory kindles all men to their pursuits; and those things always lie neglected which are disapproved among any people.” It is therefore unquestionably better to resist this desire than to yield to it. For, as blessed Augustine says in *The City of God*: “The more like God a man is, the cleaner he is from this impurity.” Although in this life it is not uprooted altogether from the heart, since it never ceases to tempt even blessed and advancing minds, nevertheless [Col. 0722B] the desire for glory should at least be overcome by the love of justice. For he sees more soundly who recognizes that even the love of praise is a fault.

Nor is this Augustine’s judgment alone; the pagans too held that this glory is nothing other than a swelling, as it were, of a windy spirit, very like smoke. For smoke dulls the sharpness of the eyes; the higher it rises, the sooner it vanishes; and the more it is driven downward, the more densely it gathers. When it reaches the heights, it disappears. And rightly so, because it derives its origin from the prince of all vanity. Those are excessively captivated by self-love who, while they “pursue clouds and empty things” and strive to grasp I know not what solid thing in their hands, forget themselves, though they behold nothing but themselves with unrighteous eyes. For they are unwilling to apprehend what they are, and [Col. 0722C] to consider it with true judgment for their correction; they merely pursue the imaginary shadows of vain opinion. Thus they despise others in comparison with themselves and aspire to impossibilities, presuming upon a deceptive appearance of things.

So Narcissus in the fables, seized by a vain image of himself, becomes a flower; and while he imprudently gazes upon himself, the boyish flower, without fruit, fades away. It was also the opinion of many, including those who flourished above others in ancient philosophy, that Alexander and Aristotle were begotten by divinities, because in all things they sought their own glory. They likewise maintained that Plato, on account of the almost divine wisdom in which he excelled, and Augustus, on account of his power and tranquil good fortune, derived their origin from gods. Yet they would more rightly have concluded the contrary: either that these men were not of divine stock, or that, if they were sons of gods, they were degenerate sons—were it not that the gods of the Gentiles are demons, and incubus-demons leave certain indications of their vanity and malice in their offspring, if indeed they beget anyone.

For the true Son of God, God and man, does not seek his own glory in all the glorious things done by him, but the Father’s; and he is thereby adorned with greater grace because he refers to him, from whom are all things, the glory of his good works. So too every truly wise, truly powerful, and truly good person refers all that is praiseworthy in himself to the one fountain of all good things: namely, the supreme creating and indivisible Trinity.

Alexander’s breast was insatiable for praise. When his companion Anacharsis, on the authority of his teacher Democritus, reported that there were innumerable worlds, Alexander said: “Alas, unhappy me, because I have not yet possessed even one!” [Col. 0723A] Certainly he was wretched, and worthy of wretchedness, since the one unsated and insatiable hunger for praise had swallowed up all his virtues. The tragedies of the ancients mock him because a possession narrow for a man was sufficient for the dwelling-place of all the gods.

Yet although the appetite for glory always seems blameworthy, the error of those who considered it a great thing to become known even by crimes is more destructive. Pausanias asked Hermocleas how he might suddenly become famous; Hermocleas replied that, if he killed some distinguished man, the deed itself would redound to his glory. Pausanias immediately killed Philip, and indeed [Col. 0723B] obtained what he sought.
