For he made himself known to posterity by parricide; and the golden crown which Myrtalis—also called Olympias—placed hanging upon his head when he was affixed to the conspicuous punishment of the gibbet afforded no consolation.

Nevertheless, in vengeance for violated chastity—for Philip, instead of punishing the outrage, mocked it—the charge of sacrilege may to some extent be excused, on the authority of Trogus. There was a man who wished to burn the temple of Diana at Ephesus, so that, once that most beautiful work had been consumed, his name might be spread throughout the whole world. Put upon the rack, he revealed his madness. And unless the richly eloquent talent of Theopompus had included him in his histories, the Ephesians had acted wisely [Col. 0723C] in decreeing by common resolution that the memory of that utterly vile man should be erased by silence.

Those who, in a similar pursuit of glory—or rather with greater madness—devastate by the fires of lust not Diana’s Ephesian temple, which religious custom bids one destroy, but the temple of the Holy Spirit, namely whole human beings, souls and bodies, in order to become known among men by this means, seem to act similarly. For they seek praise, and often obtain honour, from that for which it would have been more just to suffer disgrace and punishment.

## Chapter VI. On luxury and lust; the fivefold entrance of death; which senses’ pleasure is more destructive; the threefold class of diners according to Portunianus; the ruin wrought by gluttony; and the banquets of Dido and Evander in Virgil

The discussion has now proceeded to the point that we must, as it were, assail either virtue or public opinion. For the struggle against flesh and blood now threatens; and we seem to close the doors against generosity and to take pleasantness from life when, despite the objections of the Epicureans, we narrow the twin paths of luxury. “Luxury,” as Valerius says, “is an enticing evil, easier by some measure to condemn than to avoid.”

For the scroll which the prophet is commanded to devour is sweet as honey in his mouth; yet the belly is made bitter when that sweetness of words must be digested into the use of deeds. Lust is akin to and joined with luxury; its consequence is impurity and its certain end is shame. Therefore let that which is prior in origin and cause come first in the discussion.

Although the enticements of luxury enter equally through the five gates of the senses, the pleasure of hearing seems nearer to decency; that which comes from taste or touch is more foul; while the delight of smelling and seeing occupies an intermediate place. For it sometimes has insufficient decency, yet does not sink all the way into the most destructive filth. Indeed, conduct enters through the windows of the eyes when someone delights in circus spectacles, athletic contests, the movements of actors, women’s beauty, the brilliance of gems, garments, metals, and other things by which the soul’s freedom is enslaved. [Col. 0724A]

Again, if hearing is soothed by the various music of instruments and modulations of voices—by poets’ songs, performances of comedies and tragedies, the witticisms of mimes, strophes, and whatever else enters through the ear—it effeminates the mind’s manliness. The sweetness of scent, varied perfumes, balsam, musk—the skin of a foreign little mouse—produce moral dissolution; none but a dissolute person denies it. For comic poet and cook teach that foreign scents suit only the dissolute and lovers.

Moreover, greed for food is the mother of avarice and holds the mind, as though weighed down by certain shackles, upon the earth. Thus for the brief pleasure of gluttony, lands and seas are searched; and, so that honeyed wine, wine, and costly food may pass through the throat, men sweat through the labour of their whole lives. Even Jerusalem’s walls, though they seemed founded solidly upon rock, finally fall and are levelled with the ground when Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks, holds command. [Col. 0724B]

But the touch of other bodies and the more burning desire for women are close to madness. Whatever any other sense may contrive is mere sport and jest compared with the things brought by this frenzy, to use the words of the comic poet. For from it come desire, anger, exultation, rivalry, and anxiety; and, once pleasure has been satisfied, a kind of repentance inflames us again. We seek to do what, once done, we repent of yet again.

Therefore, when through these gates, like wedges of disturbance, such things have entered the citadel of our mind, as blessed Jerome says, where will its freedom be? Where its strength? Where thought of God? Especially since the memory of touch depicts even past pleasures to itself and, by recollection of vices, compels the soul to suffer—and in a fashion to perform—what it is not doing. [Col. 0724C]

Perhaps this is why, though the Apostle judged that every vice must be resisted, against fornication he prescribed not combat but flight: “Flee fornication,” he says (1 Cor. 6). For while it is practised, it is commonly forgetful of the Lord; and, when it returns to memory, it arouses destructive pleasures from the past.

To say nothing of others whom simplicity led into fault: Origen, a most acute philosopher, a most learned Christian, and most fervent in faith, as ecclesiastical history relates, castrated himself, fleeing fornication very effectively—or rather, taking every possible precaution against even a fabricated suspicion, so that thereafter he might live with virgins without reproach. More remarkable still: some philosophers are said even to have gouged out their own eyes, lest they be captured by outward enticements. Certainly they burned with an admirable zeal for goodness and honour, though they lacked knowledge of what was right.

Aristotle’s saying is apt and worthy of knowing: he declared that the beginnings of pleasures should be consigned to oblivion and their endings alone remembered. For the mind sets before itself their weariness and repentance, so that they may not be eagerly repeated; and it orders what is pleasant in them to be hidden, lest they return. [Col. 0725A]

Let the Apostle say what he will: to flee fornication while serving gluttony is either wholly impossible or exceedingly difficult. For even that form of gluttony which removes the body’s strength is by no means free from adultery. Bacchus commonly conquers Venus; yet in the shrine of pleasure they meet with none protesting. If Bacchus prevails, he does not extinguish Venus, but pleasure. Either let there be no drunkenness, or let it be so great that it takes your strength away; whatever lies between the two harms. In either case one departs from God; but I would not easily say in which one departs more far.

Yet gluttony is no longer counted under the name of error, because it repels the stigma of avarice and seems to bear an image of inborn generosity. Now, since the effect of generosity is praised sometimes from place, sometimes from time, sometimes from quantity, sometimes from persons, sometimes from use and frequency of practice, that generosity is held especially commendable which shines out more clearly in food and in the things nature requires or civil life adorns.

Therefore he who admits everyone to his table possesses the most exact generosity. Certainly; and he is the more generous the more persons he admits. But by this reckoning very few qualify. Next comes the man who, though he does not admit all, feeds and gives drink to those whom he introduces, supports them in dining-rooms, and seats them reclining on couches, so that nothing more sumptuous could even be imagined. Courses are multiplied; some foods are stuffed with others, these are seasoned with those; and, in violence to nature, they are forced to abandon their native flavour and acquire an alien one. Preserved foods too are prepared. Nothing is cheaper than garum, unless it promises the effects and distinguishing marks of many ingredients. [Col. 0725B]

Yet what is excellent in such matters is what pleases mimes, actors, and tale-bearers. For all these things are done not for truth but for reputation. The cook’s solicitude seethes with manifold art: sauces are devised; the household dictator deliberates day and night what ought to be done on each day and served at the daily banquets. From every quarter he gathers provocatives of gluttony and means of stirring the strength of a dulled palate, reckoning nothing accomplished unless intemperance has been satisfied.

There are also those who wash down their courses with cups and, as though by Homeric decree, think wine a stimulus to talent, a fuel of virtue, and a sort of fountain of cheerfulness—provided they thoroughly drench themselves with unmixed wine or *sicera* [strong drink]. Accordingly they rise in Phaeacian fashion, and the more abandoned a man is in draining cups, the more eminent he is judged. It is commonly said that the more skilled a gambler is at his art, the worse a man he is; and certainly the more bibulous a man is, the more he surpasses others in malice and wickedness. [Col. 0725C]

Israel, apostatizing from its Saviour, sacrificed its sons and daughters to demons; and these men, while by a flood of wine or *sicera* they depress the spirit, extinguish the little spark of reason, prostitute themselves wholly to impurity, and devote themselves to the spirit of bacchants—what could they sacrifice more fittingly?

But there are people who despise such things, because this seems to be the practice of vulgar and, so to speak, plebeian banquets. For some banquets are called philosophical, others civil, and others plebeian. In the latter, it is commonly considered praiseworthy if you squander your own goods so utterly at once that, for an entire three-month period, a shameless hungry guest goes around other people’s tables. This is often a mark of prodigality, sometimes also of avarice. For, as the saying goes, when a miser begins, he exceeds all measure.

You may see very many who devote nearly the whole year to frugality and, in order to cleanse away the stain of avarice, summon gourmands, parasites, and a college of triflers—men captivated by the smell of another’s kitchen. Those whom they wish to honour more highly, they overwhelm and distend with larger quantities from smaller cups; and until they have shaken off their ravening appetite, they think something has been withheld from friendship or festivity. [Col. 0726A]

But this is so far from all civility that it belongs more closely to the vices of barbarism than to civil life. The principle of civil banquets is a mean: they should cheer even sobriety and, amid fullness, let abundance avoid drunken surfeit. For such a banquet has an abundance of food and drink and, dispensing everything like a horn of plenty, so spares as to pour forth and so pours forth as to spare. Nor does it neglect the reckoning it keeps; yet, as Portunianus says, “good faith does not display the account of its expenditure.”

For nothing is more tiresome than when the president of a dining-room seems to sit at a banquet with his tally. Hence certain men who vainly glory in generosity do not seem sufficiently civilized to me: every night they settle accounts with their slaves and mourn, as though with nocturnal tears, what they spent in the day’s use or abuse. Quarrels arise, threats are added, slaves are charged with theft or folly, and, as though the household had been badly managed, they are dismissed and sometimes tortured; at times they are compelled to repay what they were ordered to spend. Everyone privy to this is disturbed while the master follows with sighs and grief the money that escaped him. [Col. 0726B]

It often even happens that men who have gone to answer nature’s demands, there—where modesty flees the gaze of humankind—keep the most exact account of expenses with their attendants. And rightly so, since no place seems to them more suitable for handling filth. Certainly, I do not call it filthy if a diligent householder acts so that his expenditure may be accounted for, provided his rank or station does not forbid it. But to spend one’s life on it, to dwell upon it with one’s whole mind, and to do so in such a way that one person is present and another appears—this, I judge, is by no means removed from filth.

And indeed, according to Portunianus, the rule of civil banquets is that those gathered together should be allowed much in accordance with their custom, but with cheerful sobriety not abandoned. One ought so to accommodate the diners that freer merriment does not plunge into the disgrace of luxury. For luxury, that most vile and bitter enemy, as it were, of all nations, must be avoided. [Col. 0726C]

Diogenes maintains that tyrants, destroyers of cities, and wars, whether foreign or civil, are aroused not by the simple fare of vegetables and fruits but by meats and the delicacies of banquets. He would have spoken more accurately had he named luxury—the mother and nurse of foreign and civil wars—which consists not merely in gratifying gluttony. But he understood the whole through a part when he reduced to the form of gluttony that luxury which consists in food, drink, Venus, and splendid adornment.

For luxury especially flourishes, and harms more destructively, among those whose continual thought and daily practice are to feast splendidly. This intemperance overturns good morals, prejudices the welfare of the entire person, and, unless restrained, utterly dissolves the structure of the human body. Hippocrates is authority that persons thick and obese in body, when they have reached the limit of growth, require bloodletting in order to have room to grow again. Otherwise the surfeit of distended fullness breaks out into paralysis and the worst kinds of illnesses. For nature cannot remain in one state of bodies; by its motion it must either increase or decrease; and if a living creature is incapable of growth, it cannot continue in existence at all. [Col. 0727A]

They say that Galen always prescribed abstinence on every tenth day as a most effective and healthful medical treatment; and that one who abstains from all food every tenth day, or lives on the simplest diet, cannot easily be subject to grave illnesses unless his nature is more corrupted. There are still people who spend the sixth day in fasting without food, or consume only the least amount; this, as those who have experienced it say, serves both religion and health with the greatest certainty.

Pompeius Trogus relates that Dionysius, the most vile tyrant of Sicily, lost the light of his eyes while given over to gluttony and voracious eating. Nothing brings on blindness more surely or rapidly than continual gorging, because, as Portunianus says, “voracity grinds food, but devours the eyes.” Galen, according to Jerome, that most learned interpreter of Hippocrates, says in his *Exhortation to Medicine* that athletes, whose life and profession is fattening, can neither live nor remain healthy for long; their souls, wrapped as it were in mud by excessive blood and fat, think of nothing refined, nothing heavenly, but always of meat, belching, and the gorging of the belly. [Col. 0727B]

We also read that certain sufferers from joint disease and the humours of gout, reduced by confiscation of their property to a simple table and poor foods, recovered their health. For they had been relieved of the care of administering a household and of the lavishness of banquets, which break both body and soul. Horace mocks the craving for foods which, when consumed, leave repentance:

> Spurn pleasures: pleasure bought with pain does harm.  
> *(HORACE, Epistles I.2.55.)*

And when, on his most pleasant estate, he described himself as fat and plump in mockery of voluptuous people, he jested in these verses:

> [Col. 0728A] You will see me fat and sleek, with skin well cared for,  
> whenever you wish to laugh at a pig from Epicurus’ herd.  
> *(Id., ibid., IV, at the end.)*

But surfeit must be avoided even with the cheapest foods. Nothing so overwhelms the mind as a full and boiling belly, turning itself this way and that, and finding relief in belches or the discharge of wind. What sort of fast is that, or what sort of breaking of a fast, when we are distended by the previous day’s feasting and our throat becomes a passageway for latrines? While we wish to feel the hunger of a longer abstinence, we devour as much as scarcely the night of another day can digest. Thus it should be called not fasting so much as drunken surfeit, foul and burdensome digestion. So Jerome indeed says.

And although he mentions fasting, even apart from religion he commends the greatest and most healthful benefits of frugality. Portunianus says elegantly and truly that no one dines in a civilized fashion unless, in food and drink, he prescribes for himself the measure of frugality and moderation. Excess in food and drink drives away temperance, the steward of all duties. Under its compulsion a person becomes slow to hear, quick to speak, and quick to anger; he becomes prone to lust and headlong toward every disgrace. Whoever abandons moderation easily slips from civilized to plebeian habits of dining. [Col. 0728B]

Maro, the most faithful imitator of Homeric perfection, suggests this when, recalling Ulysses received by the king of the Phaeacians, he introduces shipwrecked Aeneas to Dido’s banquet and elegantly portrays, in a single feast, the luxury both of the Phaeacians and of the Africans:

> When first repose from feasting came, and tables were removed,  
> they set up great mixing-bowls and wreathe the wines.  
> Noise fills the house; voices roll through the spacious halls;  
> lamps, suspended from the gilded ceiling, blaze,  
> and torches overcome the night with flames.  
> Here the queen called for a heavy bowl of gems and gold,  
> filled it with unmixed wine—a bowl which Belus and all  
> descended from Belus had been accustomed to use. Then silence fell through the house:  
>   
> “Jupiter—for men say that you give laws to guests—  
> grant that this day may be joyful for Tyrians  
> and for those who set out from Troy, and that our descendants may remember it.  
> May Bacchus, giver of joy, be present, and gracious Juno.  
> And you, O Tyrians, celebrate the gathering with favour.”  
>   
> She spoke, and poured a libation of liquid honour upon the table,  
> then, after the libation, first touched it lightly with her lips.  
> Then, urging him on, she gave it to Bitias; he eagerly drained  
> the foaming bowl and washed himself in the full gold.  
> Then the other princes followed. Long-haired Iopas  
> makes music on his gilded lyre, as mighty Atlas taught him.  
> He sings of the wandering moon and the labours of the sun;  
> whence humankind and beasts arise, whence rain and fire;  
> of Arcturus, the Pleiades, the Hyades, and the twin Bears;  
> why winter suns hasten so greatly to dip themselves in Ocean,  
> or what delay holds back the lingering nights.  
> The Tyrians redouble their applause, and the Trojans follow.  
> Nor did unhappy Dido fail to prolong the night with varied conversation,  
> and drank deeply of a long love.  
> *(VIRGIL, Aeneid I.727.)* [Col. 0728C–D]

Do you see the arrangement, course, and end of a luxurious banquet? That superfluities had gone before, and that the extravagance of the feast had been oppressive, he indicates by prefacing it:

> [Col. 0729A] When first repose from feasting came.

Elsewhere, observing the sobriety of a more frugal table, content with necessities alone, he says:

> When hunger had been removed by food.  
> *(Id., ibid. 220.)*

But because food makes people silent and drink talkative, he prudently adds noise and the other marks of luxury which arise from license in drinking. Even in the practice of these banquet-companions it is plain to find a superstition by which divine favour is solicited and, as it were, invited by religious prayers—though the divinity is driven far away by luxury and impurity, enemies of devout minds. For either God is not sober, or drunkenness displeases him.

They drink without measure “to measure,” and the man prevails over the rest who has laid his fellow-drinkers low or defeated them, whether by gluttony or trickery.

> There you will find someone who drinks up Nestor’s years,  
> another who makes the Sibyl old through the number of cups.

Drink indeed releases the mind from cares, loosens it, and cannot conceal the joy conceived within. It bursts forth into songs and from songs inclines toward lust. Long-haired Iopas does not sound frivolous or pastoral love-songs, but things suited to the grace of a civil gathering and the dignity of philosophy. Would that Christian assemblies recalled those themes which dishevelled and disorderly Iopas sounded at Dido’s luxurious feast! Would that pastoral songs or the silly music of lovers fell silent in the house of the wise, [Col. 0729B] and that in everyone’s hearing resounded things which either profit or delight without shame and corruption!

Indeed, in the lyre-player’s song the most learned poet elegantly suggests the gravity of the ancients: in a civil assembly they admitted nothing except what possessed the power to instruct nature or morals. Varied conversation follows the applause of the banquet; and, while it procures Venus’ offices, the drunken mind drinks a long, indissoluble, and destructive love, which the philosopher defined as the desire for sexual union.

It is famous from historians’ testimony that Campanian luxury was highly advantageous to the city. For, embracing Hannibal, unconquered by arms, in its enticements, it delivered him over to be conquered by the Roman soldier.

That luxury summoned the most watchful general and the keenest army to sleep and pleasures by abundant banquets, plentiful wine, the fragrance of perfumes, and freer sexual indulgence. And only then was Punic ferocity broken and crushed, when Seplasia and Albania began to be chaste. What, then, is fouler or more ruinous than these vices, through which virtue is worn down, victories languish, sleeping glory turns into disgrace, and the powers alike of soul and body are so overcome that one cannot tell whether it is more destructive to be captured by enemies or by them? [Col. 0729C]

The city of the Volumnii, wealthy in riches, adorned with morals, and ordered by laws, was held to be the head of the council. But after it fell into luxury, it descended into the abyss of wrongs and shamefulness to such an extent that it subjected itself to the most insolent domination of slaves. At first only a very few slaves dared enter the senatorial order; soon they seized the whole commonwealth. They ordered wills to be written at their pleasure, forbade banquets and gatherings of freeborn people, and took the daughters of their masters in marriage. Finally they enacted a law that their sexual violations of widows or married women should go unpunished, and that no maiden should marry a freeborn man unless someone from their number had first tasted her chastity.

The tragedian Aesop portrays a young man of mad luxury who, it is well known, used to dissolve pearls of immense value in vinegar and sprinkle them over his drinks, so that he might swallow an exceedingly great inheritance in one draught. Writers of memorable events reproach Metellus Pius because he allowed enemies to receive him with altars and incense; he watched with pleasure as walls were covered, at his arrival, with Attalid tapestries; he allowed the most elaborate games to be interspersed with enormous banquets; and, wearing a palm-decorated robe, celebrated feasts and received crowns lowered from ceilings, as though from a heavenly summit. [Col. 0730A]

And where did this happen? Not in Greece or Asia, whose luxury commonly corrupts even severity itself, but in a harsh and warlike province, accustomed to dazzle Roman armies’ eyes with Lusitanian weapons. Xerxes took such delight in the extraordinary display of royal wealth that he offered a reward by edict to anyone who discovered a new kind of pleasure. While he was excessively captivated by indulgence, he barely escaped at Salamis in a single ship amid the vast ruin of his empire.

But since you have received from Maro the luxurious banquet of feminine intemperance, you will find the sobriety of a more frugal table and a more restrained gathering when Aeneas is received with the courtesy of hospitality by Evander. For the men make a treaty; the king of peace gives his right hand; and the most dutiful host first speaks the words of hospitality:

> When this had been said, he ordered food and the lifted cups to be set down again,  
> and himself placed the men upon seats of grass.  
> He received Aeneas with special honour upon a couch  
> covered with the shaggy hide of a lion, and invited him to a maple throne.  
> Then chosen youths, emulously, and the priest of the altar  
> brought roasted flesh of bulls, loaded baskets  
> with gifts of toiling Ceres, and served Bacchus.  
> Aeneas and the Trojan youth ate alike  
> of the back of an unbroken ox and the sacrificial entrails.  
> *(VIRGIL, Aeneid VIII.175.)* [Col. 0730B–C]

There everything is golden and all shines with its own brilliance. Here there is a seat of grass, a maple throne, and the shaggy hide of a vanquished lion, as befits a brave man. Here chosen youths serve necessities; there maidservants serve superfluities and destructive things. There repose is scarcely at last granted from feasting; here hunger is removed and the appetite for eating is restrained by frugal food. There long-haired Iopas delights the gathering of the luxurious; here the altar’s priest consecrates sober refreshment to religion. Here serious matters are considered after the table, and manly strength is demanded for raising up the commonwealth; there, to favour luxury, even divinities are invited by poured-out prayers.

Therefore, as is read in the book of the *Saturnalia*, many laws were enacted to repress luxury. It will be neither tedious nor wholly useless to set down a passing account of them at the end of the discussion of civil banqueting.

## Chapter VII. On the ancient food and sumptuary laws for restraining intemperance; their distinction according to Portunianus; Antony’s intemperance and Julius Caesar’s frugality; Augustus, Nero, Gaius Caligula, Vitellius, and Metellus

[Col. 0731A]

The first law of all proposed to the people was the Orchian law, which prescribed the maximum number of guests; nevertheless, it did not restrain immoderate expenditure, since everyone was permitted to consume his own goods at will among a few people. The Fannian law followed, which set a limit on expenses and was written for all, so that not only citizens of Rome but everyone throughout Italy should be bound by the sumptuary law. For this is the force of the Didian law.

To these was added the Licinian law, which prescribed a rule for the number of guests, the amount of expenditure, and the observance of places, days, and times, defining particular days on which people were permitted to dine, lest they might revel in daily banquets. Thus even amid the sobriety of that age the expense of dinners was restrained by legal prescription. For from the beginning the root of luxury had begun to sprout. Hence the old saying: “Good laws are produced from bad morals.”

The Cornelian sumptuary law was also added to the earlier laws. In it neither the magnificence of diners was prohibited nor a limit imposed on gluttony; rather, lower prices were fixed for goods. But for what goods? For what exquisite and almost unknown kinds of delicacies! What fish and what choice morsels it names there, and yet sets lower prices for them. I would venture to say that cheapness of food encouraged people to procure ample supplies of provisions, so that even those of small means might serve gluttony. [Col. 0731B]

Therefore, the man for whom such great things are provided at banquets even free of cost may appear especially luxurious and prodigal. Moreover, Lucius Sulla, Lepidus the consul, and Annius Restio are said to have enacted food laws; for Cato calls sumptuary laws by that name. Yet they differ in that food laws cut the throat of gluttony, while sumptuary laws, as Portunianus says, restrain luxury of a certain kind (*alcrimodam*, reading uncertain).

He praises as a mark of great liberty the fact that, though many laws concerning dinners and expenditure were proposed to the people, for a long time the rigorous force of one law prevailed—a law containing nothing indecent because it approved nothing hidden. For it commanded that people should breakfast and dine with doors standing open, so that, with the eyes of the citizens made witnesses, a limit might be imposed upon luxury.

Portunianus safely approves this because among a disciplined people, mindful of later hearers, frugality was a credit and poverty could not be an object of contempt or shame. Nor was it decent for anyone invited to another’s dinner to rush in shamelessly. Indeed, to join a conversation uninvited is not, I think, considered shameful. But to force one’s way unbidden into a banquet prepared for others is not mentioned without censure even by Homer, in the case of a brother. [Col. 0731C]

But those open-door—or door-breaking—laws, though in Portunianus’ judgment excellent, were rendered ineffective without formal repeal by the stubbornness of luxury and the invincible alliance of vices.

Although Antony was subject to no sumptuary law, he nevertheless proposed a law for restraining expenditure. He was certainly rash, but weak in hand and wholly given over to luxury; and by reason of expenditure he succeeded Pompey the Great by decree of Gaius Caesar. That vile flatterer and man defiled by vices triumphed over the conqueror of the world. Caesar, however, was captivated by an appearance of virtue, because Antony seemed popularly magnificent through lavish expenditure of money, public distributions of meat, and entourages of bandits and actors.

Thus it goes well with popular leaders who are compelled by necessity, for the preservation of their reputation, to flatter the meanest scoundrels. For among tyrants none came nearer to being a prince than Caesar. Although he had crushed the commonwealth, nevertheless the Roman people approved all that he had decreed—perhaps through fear of sedition and a renewed experience of civil war. Yet the prevailing opinion was that, because he had been endowed with the highest virtue, namely clemency, the people approved his enactments as for the most part more benign. Hence Cicero said in his praise: “Of your virtues none is either more admirable or more weighty than mercy.” [Col. 0731D]

Antony therefore easily deceived a pious mind by the appearance of outstanding virtue. For he, believing that whatever sea, land, or even heaven produced was born to satisfy his own gorging, subjected it to his throat and teeth; and, captivated by such things, wished to make of the Roman empire an Egyptian kingdom. His wife Cleopatra, who considered herself unworthy to be surpassed by Romans even in luxury, challenged him with a wager that she could spend one hundred million sesterces upon one dinner. This seemed astonishing to Antony, and he immediately entered the wager.

Numacius Plancus was a judge worthy of the kitchen, chosen as arbiter of so honourable a contest. On the following day Cleopatra, testing Antony, prepared a sumptuous dinner indeed, but not one at which Antony marvelled, since he recognized everything served as coming from their daily resources. Then the queen, smiling, called for a cup into which she poured a little sharp vinegar. Hastily she dropped into it a pearl removed from one ear; when it had quickly dissolved, as is the nature of that stone, she swallowed it. [Col. 0732A]

Though by this act she had won the wager—for the pearl itself was unquestionably worth one hundred million sesterces—she nevertheless moved her hand similarly toward the pearl in her other ear, had not Numacius Plancus, that most severe judge, promptly declared Antony defeated. The size of that pearl may be inferred from the fact that the one remaining was later, after the queen’s defeat and Egypt’s capture, brought to Rome and cut in two, and two pearls made from one. These were placed upon the statue of Venus, as objects of monstrous size, in the temple called the Pantheon.

But by these and similar acts that most intemperate and shameful man—the public enemy not of the Roman people but of the virtues—earned the result that the edict which he issued on expenses in the time of the triumvirate should possess neither the name nor the force of a law. [Col. 0732B]

That food laws had both occasion and necessity is evident even from the fact that luxury devised rules for selecting foodstuffs.

Marcus Varro attests this. After listing the regions of Italy that produce the best provisions for food, he awards the palm to the fish of the Tiber, in the eleventh book of *Human Affairs*: “For sustenance, the Campanian district produces the best grain; Falernum, wine; Cassinum, oil; Tusculum, figs; Tarentum, honey; and the Tiber, fish.” So Varro.

But among these fish the foremost place was held by the wolf-fish—especially one caught between the two bridges. This is shown by many others, and also by Gaius Titius, a man of Lucinian’s age, in the speech in which he advocated the Fannian law. His words should be set down, because they testify not only concerning the wolf-fish caught between the bridges [Col. 0733B], but also readily reveal the manners by which most people then lived.

For, describing extravagant men who came drunk to the forum to give judgment, and the sort of conversation they customarily held among themselves, he says:

> “They gamble eagerly, drenched in perfumes and surrounded by prostitutes. When it is the tenth hour, they order a slave to be summoned, to go to the assembly-place and inquire what has happened in the forum: who spoke in favour, who against; how many tribes voted for it, how many came. Then they go to the assembly-place, lest they conduct their lawsuit sober. As they go, there is no jar in any alley that they do not fill, for their bladders are full of wine. They arrive at the assembly-place sad; they order those whose business it is to speak. They state their case. The judge asks for witnesses; he himself goes off to urinate. When he returns, he says that he has heard everything. He asks for the documents, examines the writing, and can scarcely keep his eyelids raised because of the wine. As he goes to the council, this is his speech: ‘What business have I with these triflers? Let us rather drink mulled wine mixed with Greek wine. Let us eat a fat thrush and a good fish: a true wolf-fish, caught between the bridges.’”

So Titius. Pliny too elegantly touched upon the gluttony of his own day. Writing about the fish called *acipenser* [sturgeon], whose price, although it was rare, had fallen, he added after what he had said before: “It is now held in no esteem, which indeed surprises me, since it is difficult to find.”

But this frugality did not last long. For in the time of the emperor Severus, Sammonicus Serenus, a learned man of his age, after citing Pliny’s words, says:

> “There is no doubt that in Trajan’s time this fish enjoyed no esteem; yet he says that among the ancients it was valuable. But I make this manifest by testimonies—especially because I see its favour, as if restored from exile, returning to banquets. Indeed, to your indignation, when I am present at a sacred banquet, I observe this fish being brought in by garlanded servants accompanied by a flute-player.”

It would take long to recount everything that introduced food laws, or was produced by food laws; for neither can the extravagance of manners be comprehended in speech, nor are many things known to our age which the ancients could either express in words or practise in their customs. For just as

[Col. 0734A]

> Captive Greece captured her fierce conqueror  
> And brought the arts into rustic Latium.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* II.1.156

so the good and bad customs of all nations pursued the Roman conqueror. For they invoked the divinities—or rather demons—of the nations more superstitiously than religiously; and they thought they had attained great religious devotion because they had rejected no falsehood. They withdrew guardian gods from all peoples, not in pious but impious worship, so that, gathered in one city, all might keep continual watch under its protection. Thus they also transferred into the city whatever had pleased them anywhere, so that they might thereby attract to themselves the favour and glory of all.

King William the First of the English seems to have done something similar; Normandy, Maine [Cenomannis], and finally greater Britain yielded to his prowess [Col. 0734B]. Having taken up the royal diadem and established peace, he sent envoys to foreign nations, directing them to bring back from every illustrious household whatever seemed magnificent or marvellous. Thus there flowed into an affluent island—an island almost alone in the world content with its own riches—everything that could be found of magnificence, or rather luxury.

The purpose of this great man, who wished to pour the virtues of all peoples into his own realm, was indeed praiseworthy. Yet it would have been more praiseworthy had he proclaimed a law of temperance to the nation he had conquered by arms and overmastered by the greatness of its luxury. Certainly it would have been more beneficial to strengthen temperance by word and deed than, through the authority of many great men, to propagate boldness in self-indulgence.

Portunianus reports that Gaius Caesar acted otherwise, after peace had been restored to the city [Col. 0734C]. Following the precedent of a sumptuary law, he decreed that a household befitting a citizen rather than an emperor should be content, at the first course, with three customary dishes or courses—provided that supplementary dishes (*tellaria parenthetica*) might, for the necessity or rank of persons, for the exercise of generosity, or for a feast-day, be added to the first course.

The customary dishes are those served to everyone, and called by the Greeks “Catholic,” that is, universal. The supplementary dishes are those which, owing to necessity or courtesy, for some reason enter the prescribed portion; they are so called because they are customarily inserted in a particular way among the customary—that is, universal—dishes.

Nor is it certain that dishes consist only of vegetables or legumes: this is clear from many instances, and also because the patriarch Isaac ordered a dish to be made for him from his son’s game [Col. 0734D]. *Bellaria* signifies every kind of second-course delicacy, because the more beautiful and refined items are customarily placed there. Marcus Varro uses the word: “The most honeyed sweetmeats,” he says, “are those which are not honeyed.” This may perhaps mean that what necessity requires is more pleasing to the person who uses it than what the provocation of gluttony invents.

But perhaps he seems small-minded who restrains the luxury of the first course in this fashion, or who mentions a sumptuary law in such matters. Yet no one who exercises gluttony at the expense of morals and property is greater or more magnificent than Caesar [Col. 0735A]. They comply with luxury, serve vanity, and endeavour to console their wickedness or negligence under the appearance of generosity.

Who was more frugal than Caesar Augustus? At the summit of power, he was content with coarse bread and little fish, commonly called asparagus-fish, spinach-fish, or river-fish [*asparagos, spinaticos, ripileones*]; and he ate only under necessity or with a friend. Who was more gluttonous or lavish than Nero? Yet he will never be considered great or praised by any wise person, any more than Gaius Caligula or Vitellius—indeed, less so. For he too indulged excessively in lunches, dinners, and revels.

Most famous among the rest was the dinner to which he was invited by his brother, containing two thousand of the choicest fish and seven thousand birds. He himself surpassed this at the dedication of the “Fatherland,” which, because of its immense size, he called Minerva’s Shield [Col. 0735B]. In it he mixed brains of pheasants and peacocks, tongues of flamingos, and the milts of moray eels sought from particular parts of the sea.

Is luxurious Metellus the pontiff greater than Julius or Augustus? His dinner is easier to report than to understand. For he too made a famous—indeed, infamous—dinner, and arranged before the dinner an *anticoenium*, or, as Portunianus calls it, a *paracoenium*, with such luxury that it exceeded not only the splendour of a civic dinner but even Egyptian extravagance. Before the dinner he served: sea urchins; raw oysters in whatever quantity one wished; pelorides; spondyli; thrush; asparagus; beneath these, fattened hen; a dish of oysters; black acorns; white acorns; again spondyli; glycomarides; sea-nettles; fig-peckers; *bumbi*; goat-flesh dishes; boars’ trotters; fattened fowls wrapped in flour; fig-peckers; purple shellfish and murex-shellfish. At the principal dinner: boar’s head; a dish of fish; a dish of sow’s udder; ducks; boiled wood-pigeons; fattened hares; roasted fattened fowls; starch; fish-shaped breads [Col. 0735C].

Who then would accuse the luxury of others, when the dinner of the pontiffs was made of so many things? Indeed, the very kinds of delicacies are shameful even to name, and are in part unheard of among our people, though they pride themselves excessively on the splendour of luxury. Whoever wishes to know them should review the *Saturnalia* and run through Portunianus’s *Civil Institutions*.

Yet, lest examples of vices be sought far away, our age has added its own to the errors of its forebears. I remember that I myself attended a certain rich man’s dinner in Apulia [Col. 0735D], extended from about the ninth hour of day until the twelfth hour of night, and this during the equinoctial season. Into it the host from Canusium amassed Constantinopolitan, Babylonian, Alexandrian, Palestinian, Tripolitanian, barbarian, Syrian, and Phoenician luxuries—as though Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and Campania could not furnish a refined banquet.

A man of singular eloquence, surpassing everyone I have seen in the grace of three languages, can report more fully and better the abundance of provisions, the discipline of service, the diligence of attendance, and the host’s urbanity. That man is John, treasurer of York, for he too was present.

But, as Macrobius testifies [Col. 0736A], something that cannot be said or heard without shame among the faithful seemed more disgraceful and extravagant to unbelievers than it does to our age; yet, under luxury’s rule, it is called magnificent. Thus Titius, while advocating the Fannian law, reproaches his age because they bring a Trojan pig to their tables. They called it this because, like the Trojan horse pregnant with armed men, it was stuffed with other animals. If you can, enter Trimalchio’s dinner in Petronius, and you will marvel that a pig can thus be made pregnant—unless the multitude of unknown and unheard-of extravagances removes your capacity for wonder.

Many things which we, taught by use or misuse, do not marvel at seemed wonderful, indeed astonishing, to our ancestors. We now call the pig not Trojan but domestic; and by preparing it in this way we make very many things Trojan. Hence Marcus Varro, in the third book of *Agriculture*:

> “This too has lately been instituted: hares are fattened after being taken from the hare-park and confined in cages, where they are made fat in an enclosed place. Luxury has likewise brought it about that snails are fattened.”

So Varro. But luxury now carries no stigma in any of these things; whatever stimulates gluttony is a badge of refinement [Col. 0736B].

## Chapter VIII. On the Philosophical Banquet, and Its Connection with the Civic Banquet; and on Its Sumptuary Laws

Let us pass from the civic banquet to the philosophical. To those who see more keenly into the substance of things, civic matters appear connected with philosophical ones. For philosophy, the ruler of all things, cannot be absent from civic banquets, since there is nothing at all dutiful or civic that it does not treat [Col. 0736C]. It prescribes measure to all; and, while ordering duties, it deigns to concern itself even with common and ordinary matters. Otherwise nothing proceeds rightly unless philosophy itself confirms in actions what it teaches in words.

For what benefit is there in turning over in schools the duties of virtue in empty words, if they are not made firm in acts and life? Things are nevertheless called common which come less near to moderation and, as though released from the laws of philosophy, bring in either disorder through lack of discipline, hunger through parsimony, or madness through luxury and greed.

If guests gather at Nasidienus’s house, the shabby fare displeases; the disordered house is encrusted with whispers; and the avarice of him who presides over the dining rooms provokes the guests’ mockingly voracious appetite, so that, after overturning all the wine-jars of Aliphae [Col. 0736D], they mutter to one another Horace’s line:

> Unless we drink to our own loss, we shall die unavenged.  
> —Horace, *Satires* II.8.34

For every effort is made that the master of the household, whose expenditure and labour are wasted, should suffer loss. But if people recline at Cepheus’s house, abundance and lack of reason verge upon madness, and passage from Bacchus to Mars is very easy. This is what those banquets of the Centaurs signify in fable: Bacchus’s gifts do not cease until they draw blood. Such are the dealings of common banquets, which are not regulated by philosophy’s judgment. If you see such people gathering without moderation, believe them to be not fabulous but real Centaurs. They are half-beasts, puffed up emptily by the breath of their own spirit or the spirit of Bacchus.

For banquets celebrated by ordinary—that is, poorer—people are sometimes civic and sometimes philosophical, unless you think the banquets of Socrates, Alcibiades, Epictetus, and other philosophers uncivic [Col. 0737A]. Yet, according to our own practice, civic banquets are those conducted with a somewhat less exacting wisdom: not disorderly, certainly, but of freer licence, more abundant, and approaching common cheerfulness, with moderation preserved, more than philosophical strictness.

From these, therefore, the followers of Nasidienus are excluded, as is anyone who offends the cheerfulness of those admitted by severity of brow and a joyless expression. For whatever boils in the pot, is prepared in the kitchen, amassed in the pantry, or glitters on the table, is tasteless and insipid unless a cheerful countenance imparts the flavour of charity [Col. 0737B].

Jupiter himself, as the fables say, accepted a poor host’s banquet and deemed great luxuries the food supplied by Philemon’s devout poverty. And it was said of him, but applies to all:

> Above all, kindly faces were added,  
> And a willing spirit, neither sluggish nor poor.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII.79

Thus it is to dine civically: to brighten the banquet with a cheerful face, a generous hand, and attentive service; and, considering persons, place, and time, to distribute to each what is available for use—not from sadness or compulsion, since God too loves a cheerful giver.

For these purposes Catius may also

> Set forth standards by new precepts, able to surpass  
> Pythagoras, Anytus’s defendant, and learned Plato.  
> —Horace, *Satires* II.4.2

Philosophical banquets, however, are entirely disciplined and bounded by their own rules, so that those who take part in them may serve their duties without the troublesome impediment of food and drink [Col. 0737C]. They are sober and corrected of every luxury. They do not prevent Socrates from carrying out positive justice; they do not draw Plato back from natural inquiry; they do not shake from Critias the memory of past events. Timaeus is not prevented from explaining the causes of all things, nor is anyone delayed from any duty of virtue.

Here neither sadness nor a clouded face is considered good; nor is great admiration bestowed on that Crassus whom Cicero, following Lucilius, writes to have laughed once in his life [Col. 0737D]. Pleasures are present, certainly, but pleasures free from wantonness. Seriousness is present, but a seriousness that does not exclude joy.

These banquets also have their own sumptuary or food laws, though not to spare things but persons. They do not fear to expend goods so far as usefulness or honour requires; for in them nothing is dear to the wise person except use. Blessed Jerome seems to have established an excellent food law for guarding sobriety, a most pleasant and useful delight. He says:

> “Reason ought to be present, so that we take such foods, and in such quantities, that the body is not burdened nor the soul’s freedom weighed down. For one must eat, walk, sleep, digest, and afterwards withstand the incentives of lust when the veins are swollen [Col. 0738A]. Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness an affront; anyone who associates with them will not be wise. Nor should we take foods that are either difficult to digest or that, once eaten, make us grieve over the great labour by which they were acquired and lost.
>
> “Vegetables, fruit, and legumes are easier to prepare; they need neither the skill nor expenditure of cooks, and they sustain humankind without anxiety. Their expense too is moderate; since what has no stimulants to gluttony is not greedily devoured, but is digested more easily. No one burdens himself to the point of a swollen stomach with one or two cheap foods. Such swelling is conceived from a diversity of meats and the pleasure of flavours, when dishes steam with various odours and, after hunger has been filled, draw people as captives to eat them.
>
> “Hence diseases too are stirred up by excessive satiety, and many remedy gluttony’s impatience by vomiting: what they shamefully took in, they more shamefully cast out.” [Col. 0738B]

But perhaps Jerome seems too austere, and his edict exceptionally difficult to obey. Very well: let Jerome be disregarded; let the authority of the Stoics be despised; let the Peripatetics be excluded—provided that at least Epicurus, champion of pleasure, is heard. For, to say nothing of our own authorities, Seneca and many others distinguished among philosophers testify that Epicurus filled all his books with vegetables, fruit, and cheap foods. He said that people ought to live on these because meats and elaborate dishes are prepared with immense trouble and misery, and exact a greater penalty in seeking than yield pleasure in consuming.

Our bodies need only food and drink. Where there is water and bread, and other like things, nature has been satisfied [Col. 0738C]. Whatever exceeds this belongs not to life’s necessity but to the vice of pleasure. Drinking and eating should restrain not the fever of luxury but thirst and hunger. Those who eat meat need things that are not meat; but those who live simply do not require meat. Nor can we devote ourselves to wisdom if we consider the abundance of a table, which requires excessive labour and care. Nature’s need is quickly supplied: cold and hunger may be expelled by simple clothing and food.

This is Epicurus’s teaching, though he acquired a mark of infamy from the shameful mob of his followers. Aristotle, moreover, teaches which pleasures must especially be avoided:

> “Since pleasure arises from the fivefold source of the senses, he says that the pleasure of taste and touch—that is, of food and the belly—is alone common to humans and beasts. Therefore, whoever is engrossed by this brutish pleasure is reckoned among cattle and wild animals. The other pleasures, proceeding from the remaining three senses, belong only to human beings. What person possessing any human shame, then, would congratulate himself on these two pleasures, sexual union and eating, which humanity shares with the pig and the ass?” [Col. 0738D]

So Aristotle. Socrates said that many people wish to live in order to eat and drink; he ate and drank in order to live. Hence the satirist:

> Believe it the greatest crime to prefer life to honour,  
> And, for the sake of life, to lose the reasons for living.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VIII.83

Valerius reports that Roman women of old were unfamiliar with the use of wine, lest they slide into disgrace; for the next step from Liber Pater [Bacchus], by way of intemperance, commonly leads to forbidden Venus. The ancestors also instituted a formal banquet called *charistia*, to which no one besides relatives and connections was admitted, so that, if any complaint had arisen between persons bound to one another, it might be removed at the sacred rites of the table, amid cheerful hearts and with supporters of concord present [Col. 0739A].

Youth paid old age such abundant and considerate honour as though elders were the common fathers of the young. Thus young men escorted old men by day to the senate-house, just as they would a senator, kinsman, or paternal friend, and stood fast by the doors waiting until they could perform the service of escorting them back [Col. 0739B]. By this voluntary watch they strengthened both bodies and minds for energetic endurance of public duties. Before long, through their modest practice of labour, they themselves became wiser and emerged into the light of their virtues.

When invited to dinner, they carefully asked who would be present, lest they precede an elder’s arrival by reclining at table. When the table had been removed, they allowed their elders to rise and depart first. From this it is apparent how restrained and modest was the conversation that those of greater age customarily used at banquets when such persons were present [Col. 0739C]. To the flute they sang of the outstanding deeds of their ancestors, composed in verse, so that virtue might become readier to undertake such admirable acts.

What contest was more splendid, or even more useful? Young manhood rendered its due honour to grey hair; the age that had finished the course of manhood accompanied those entering active life with the nourishment of its favour. What Athens, what school, what foreign studies would I prefer to this domestic discipline? From it sprang the Camilli, Scipios, Fabricii, Fabii, and Marcelli. And, not to make myself too long by reviewing individually the lights of the Roman empire, from it shone forth the divine Caesars, the brightest part of the higher heaven. So Valerius.

Plato himself, although rich, nevertheless, as his time and circumstances permitted, and while Diogenes trampled his couches with muddy feet so that he might be free for philosophy, chose the Academy—a country estate far from the city—not merely deserted but even unhealthy [Col. 0739D], so that concern and continual illness might break the assaults of lust, and so that his pupils might feel no pleasure other than that of the subjects they learned. Indeed, every path to learning is barred if sobriety, wisdom’s companion, is removed. Those cannot possess sobriety who cry among fools: “Everything difficult has been set before us while sober.”

I myself know a man far inferior to Plato—except that he is a Christian, and I do not consider it permissible to prefer even Plato to a Christian. I know, I say, a sickly man, continually visited by illness, who nevertheless rejoices, provided his sufferings do not exceed what he can bear [Col. 0740A], so that the wantonness of the flesh may be worn down and the spirit raised and strengthened in the knowledge of God, contempt for the world, and exercise of virtue. He desires only that the faculties of soul and body remain unharmed, that he not be withdrawn by the violence of illness from what he must do, and that he may await and embrace some chastisement—light, however, and tolerable for one who is weak—from the Lord’s hand.

The Platonists and Stoics frequented the open courts and porticoes of temples, so that, warned by the sanctity of a more august dwelling-place, they might think of nothing but virtues. But those people have no such meditation whose god is their belly (Philippians III), whose expectation is confusion, and whose glory is dung, fire, and worm.

The Apostle too seems to prescribe a sumptuary law for those whom he trains in true philosophy [Col. 0740B], saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy VI). Yet, to deal more gently with people like myself, using a somewhat less exacting wisdom, let everything which the use of necessity or of genuine honour, in oneself or one’s dependents, reasonably requires—after the licence of abuse has been removed—fall under the category of food and clothing. Philosophy grants this also to its dependents, while restraining only the intemperance of immoderation.

## Chapter IX. That Holy Scripture Also Contains Excellent Rules of Civility; That Nothing Is More Civic Than Virtue; What Rules of Civility Must Be Observed at Banquets; and On Modesty

It has been said that philosophy is the teacher of all civility and of everything to be done, and that it assigns the duties to be performed at banquets. Since, then, there are many precepts of civility, the civic rule of him who surpasses all philosophers and sages, and who is more civic than any philosopher, rightly seems to be preferred to those that follow [Col. 0740C]. He says:

> “When you are invited to a wedding, do not take the first place, lest someone more honourable than you has been invited, and the one who invited you say, ‘Give this man your place’; and then you begin, with shame, to occupy the lowest place. But recline in the lowest place, so that, when the one who invited you sees you, he may say, ‘Friend, move up higher’; and you will have glory before those reclining with you” (Luke XIV).

Then, confirming this point as a general principle, he says: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (ibid.). Although this seems an ordinance of religion rather than civility, I do not separate the form of religion from civility, since nothing is more civic than devotion to the cultivation of virtue.

Moreover, he does not permit a law that breaks down doors, nor does he exclude joy, nor reject a more sumptuous provision; yet he does not seek stimulants to gluttony [Col. 0740D]. For he says: “My oxen and fattened beasts have been slaughtered” (Matthew XXII). And when the compassionate father prepared a joyful banquet for the returning prodigal, he admitted music and dancing in order to foster joy. The fattened calf was killed; and lest shabby clothing disfigure the banquet, a ring and robe are brought from the inner chamber through the servants’ service, for the naked man’s use and adornment.

But just as the doors of generosity stand open to the worthy, so they must be shut to the shameful. For even the foolish virgins, though they knock at the door, suffer rejection because of the mark of their folly, lest, if admitted, they be expelled. For it is established that:

> It is more shameful to be expelled than not admitted as a guest.  
> —Ovid

Yet one is expelled without disgrace if one’s own shamefulness disfigures the banquet. Thus the man who lacked a wedding garment was expelled. Although these things have a mystical meaning, they nevertheless set forth the rudiments of civility on their literal surface. For the Apostle’s command is certainly true in its literal sense: “If anyone called a brother is sexually immoral, or greedy, or serves idols, do not even take food with such a one” (1 Corinthians IV) [Col. 0741A].

The door of a generous house therefore exists to exclude the wanton, criminal, and notorious. It has a doorkeeper or porter so that no uncouth person may rush in, and so that someone may receive the worthy and admissible reverently, address them honourably, comfort strangers, instruct those unfamiliar with the place, and, when the opportunity arises, introduce them to the master.

There is also abundance of things without luxury; enjoyment without wantonness; and a free—indeed liberal—use of things, with virtue unharmed [Col. 0741B]. For Herod’s or Pharaoh’s banquet, when it conceives unrestrained delight from a dancing girl’s motions or the heat of wine, ends tragically and is stained by homicide.

Even pagan seriousness does not approve this. Valerius says that Porcius Cato removed Lucius Flaminius from the rank of senators because he wickedly struck with an axe a condemned man—at the proper time for execution, certainly, but at the whim and for the spectacle of a little woman dining with him, whose love had captivated him.

Lucius Flaccus and his colleague, the censors, likewise expelled Duronius from the senate because, as tribune of the people, he had repealed a law enacted to restrain the expenses of banquets. The reason for the censure was remarkable. For how shamelessly Duronius mounted the rostra to say this:

> “Bridles have been imposed upon you, Quirites, which you must by no means endure. You are tied and bound with the bitter chain of slavery. For a law has been given which commands us to be frugal. Let us therefore repeal that authority, encrusted with the rust of dreadful antiquity. What need is there for liberty, if people who wish to perish through luxury are not permitted to do so?” [Col. 0741C]

There is another mark of civility in the sacred writings: acts of thanksgiving should come first. For it is well known that the most generous, civilized, and witty master of the household, who satisfied five thousand guests with five loaves, customarily blessed the bread before breaking it [Col. 0741D].

There is also that celebrated saying of the wise man: philosophy—which is the gods’ unique gift and the discipline of disciplines—must be honoured by being spoken of first. It is likewise civic, and consonant with sacred Scripture, either to be entirely silent at table, in order to listen for one’s improvement, or to offer learned conversation from which others may benefit or enjoy themselves without fault. For the Lord himself frequently mingles parables or words of life with his hearers while they are eating.

But those occasions are exceedingly gloomy and almost ignorant of civility where, without the pleasure of hearing, the belly alone is filled, or where banquets resound with goose-like clamour and foolish tales. Nor should anyone ban music, since it is an innocent art—so much so that Socrates took care to learn it in old age.

> Damoetas and Lycian Aegon will sing to me;  
> Alphesiboeus will imitate dancing Satyrs.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* V.71 [Col. 0742A]

This is civic; it passes into the common. Therefore one should offer words that are more fitting and more hostile to vices—words that slay luxury, while removing even the slightest suspicion of avarice.

For although the vein of talent is dormant in the intemperate, it is not utterly extinguished: Polemo, once reformed, bears witness. He was a young Athenian of abandoned luxury, delighting not only in its allurements but also in its very infamy. Rising from a banquet not after sunset but after sunrise, he was returning home when he saw the open door of the philosopher Xenocrates [Col. 0742B]. Heavy with wine, drenched in perfumes, crowned with garlands, and dressed in a transparent garment, he entered Xenocrates’s school, which was full of learned men.

Not content with so disgraceful an entrance, he sat down and sought to ridicule, through the wantonness of drunkenness, that most distinguished eloquence and those most prudent teachings. When, as was fitting, universal indignation arose, Xenocrates kept his expression unchanged. Leaving aside the subject which he had been discussing, he began to speak about modesty and temperance. Compelled to come to his senses by the seriousness of his discourse, Polemo first tore the crown from his head and threw it away; shortly afterward he drew his arm back inside his cloak. As time went on, he laid aside the festive cheerfulness of his face. Finally he stripped off all luxury; healed by the most salutary medicine of a single speech [Col. 0742C], he became from an infamous reveler a very great philosopher.

His mind had therefore wandered in wickedness, but did not dwell there; it turned aside briefly, but did not fix its home there. Finally, the one aim toward which the whole philosophical company directs its attention is an honourable end, a cheerful and pleasant conclusion. This plainly cannot occur unless philosophy appoints modesty as guardian over all workshops and all ministers of duties—modesty which, as Cassian says, is the mother of every honourable counsel, the safeguard of customary duties, the teacher of innocence; beloved by neighbours, welcome to strangers; neglectful of private resources so that it may increase common ones; bearing before itself, in every place and at every time, a countenance that wins favour. Indeed, it is said to be welcome even to the immodest.

At Athens, a man of extreme old age came to the theatre to watch the games [Col. 0742D]. No citizen gave him a place to sit. At length he came by chance to the Spartan ambassadors, who revered the man’s age, grey hair, and years by rising, and gave him a seat among themselves in the most honourable position. When the people saw this, they loudly applauded the modesty of the foreign city. One of the Spartans is then said to have remarked: “So the Athenians know what is right, but neglect to do it.”

## Chapter X. A Rule for Dining, Taken in Sense and Almost in Words from Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*; On Jests; On Avoiding Drunkenness; On the Regard Owed by Banqueters; and On Gaius Claudius Caesar’s Saying That, as Sailors Avoid a Rock, So One Must Avoid an Uncommon and Unfamiliar Word
They may perhaps seem insufficiently civil, and excessively superstitious, [Col. 0743A] these things that are drawn from sacred writings. But, that we may deal more gently with ourselves, let us bring forward the rule for dining given by the philosophers of the Gentiles. Several, indeed, have supplied precepts on this branch of conduct; but for the present a few will suffice. Among others, the first book of the *Saturnalia* presents itself—a work, rightly examined, of such a kind and magnitude that there is no need to borrow anything elsewhere. In this chapter, therefore, we have resolved to imitate it not so much in its footsteps as in its stride, and, from the abundance of its store-room, to supply the narrowness of our own little cell. For it is weighty in its opinions, elegant in expression, and so overflowing with gracefulness of manners that, in its instruction and ordering of a banquet, it seems to pour out Socratic sweetness.

It says, therefore: “I know that philosophy, the ruler of all things, [Col. 0743B] will first observe this: that she should consider within herself the capacities of the guests present; and, if she finds in the company at dinner several persons skilled in her, or at least lovers of her, she will allow discourse concerning herself to be conducted. For just as a few mute letters, scattered among many vowels, readily soften into a partnership of sound, so the fewer unlearned persons, delighted by the company of the learned, either join in harmony as far as they can, or are captivated by hearing such subjects discussed. But if more persons are strangers to the training of her discipline, she will wound the wiser persons present, who are fewer, by concealing herself, and will allow the loquacity more pleasing to the larger party to bring healing, lest rare nobility be disturbed by a more tumultuous crowd. And this is one of philosophy’s virtues. For, whereas an orator is approved only by speaking, a philosopher philosophizes no less by keeping silence at the proper time [Col. 0743C] than by speaking.

“Thus the few more learned persons who are present will shift, while preserving discussion among themselves, into agreement with their untrained company, so that every suspicion of discord may vanish. Nor is it strange if a learned man does what Pisistratus, tyrant of Athens, once did. When he had failed to obtain his sons’ assent while giving them sound advice, and was therefore at odds with his children, he discovered that this had given joy to his rivals, who hoped that unrest might arise in the ruler’s house from that discord. He summoned the whole body of citizens and said that he had indeed been angered by his sons because they had not yielded to their father’s will; but that afterwards he had judged it more fitting for paternal affection that he himself should yield to the opinion [Col. 0743D] of his children. Thus the city might know that the king’s offspring were in harmony with their father. By this device he took away hope from those plotting against the tranquillity of the ruling house.

“So in every condition of life, and especially in the cheerfulness of a banquet, everything that seems discordant must, without injury to innocence, be brought into the single harmony of concord. Thus Agathon’s banquet, because it had Socrates, Phaedrus, Pausanias, and Eryximachus, heard no speech but philosophical speech. But the table of Alcinous, or of Dido, being suited as it were to pleasures alone, had—this one Iopas, that one Polyphemus—singing to the lyre. Nor were male dancers lacking at Alcinous’ house; and at Dido’s was Bitias, swallowing unmixed wine in such a way as to wash himself wholly in its excessive flood. Would not anyone who mixed discourses drawn from wisdom with the banquet tales among either the Phaeacians or the Carthaginians [Col. 0744A] both lose the favour congenial to those gatherings and incur entirely deserved laughter? Therefore philosophy’s first observance will be to assess the guests.

“Then, when she sees room has been made for her, she will not speak over the cups of the secrets of her own profundity, nor raise knotted and anxious questions, but questions that are useful indeed and yet easy. For just as, among those whose exercise consists in dancing in the midst of banquets, someone who, to train himself more strenuously, challenged his companions either to running or to boxing would be excluded from the banquet’s cheerfulness as an unsuitable person, so one should sometimes philosophize at table in such a way that the mixing-bowl of liquor, born for merriment, may be tempered by an admixture not only of the Nymphs but of the Muses as well.

“For if, as must be admitted, in every [Col. 0744B] gathering one must either be silent or speak, let us ask whether silence is suitable to banquets, or fitting conversation. If, as the Areopagites at Athens judge in silence, so one ought to remain silent among feasts, then there is no further need to ask whether one ought to philosophize at table or not. But if banquets are not to be mute, why, where speech is allowed, is honourable speech forbidden? Especially since words cheer a banquet no less than the sweetness of wine.

‘What,’ you ask, ‘has this to do with philosophy?’ On the contrary, nothing is more akin to wisdom than adapting speech to places and times, after considering the persons present. Reports of examples of virtue have stirred some; others, examples of benefactions; others, again, examples of moderation—so that even those who acted otherwise might, through frequently hearing such things, come to amendment. Thus philosophy will strike persons entangled in vices without their perceiving it, if the order of conversation at banquets requires even this; just as Father Liber struck with his thyrsus, by the hidden point [Col. 0744C] beneath the winding ivy; for philosophy will not proclaim herself at a banquet as a censor in order openly to chastise vices. Otherwise those liable to rebuke will resist, and there will be such tumult at the banquet that its guests may seem invited under this proclamation:

> “For what remains, men, cheer your bodies after deeds well done,  
> and look forward, armed, to battle.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.158

“Therefore, should an occasion for necessary rebuke arise, it will proceed from the philosopher in such a manner as to be both veiled and effective. What wonder if the wise person strikes, as I say, those who do not perceive it, when sometimes he reproves in such a way that even the reproved person is delighted? Nor will he show the power of philosophy, which says nothing unsuitable, only by his stories, but by questions as well. Therefore let no honourable action, place, or gathering exclude it; it adapts itself so that everywhere it appears necessary, as though its absence were a sin.”

And shortly afterwards he distinguishes invective from witty raillery, which are sometimes uttered by a wise person so as not only to lack bitterness but to bring timely sweetness. He next teaches courtesy, or wit, in questioning. Therefore, whoever wishes to be a pleasant questioner should ask things that the person questioned can readily answer, and which he knows that person has learned by diligent practice. Everyone delights [Col. 0745A] in being invited to bring his learning before the company; for he does not wish what he has learned to remain concealed, especially if the knowledge acquired through labour is familiar to him together with only a few others, and unknown to most—for example, astronomy, dialectic, and similar subjects. For then people seem to gain the fruit of their labour when they obtain an opportunity to make known what they have learned without the reproach of ostentation. This reproach does not attach to one who does not thrust himself forward but is invited to speak.

Conversely, it is very bitter if you ask someone before many people about something he has not acquired through abundant learning. He is compelled either to deny that he knows it—which they regard as the most extreme injury to modesty—or, in answering rashly, to entrust himself to the outcome, whether true or false. Hence there often results a disclosure of ignorance, and he attributes all this misfortune of his shame [Col. 0745B] to the person questioning him.

Likewise, those who have traversed seas and lands delight in being asked about something unknown to many people—the situation of countries or the recesses of the sea. They gladly answer and describe places, now in words, now with a pointer, thinking it glorious to place before others’ eyes what they themselves have seen. What of commanders or soldiers, always ready to recount what they have done bravely, yet silent through fear of seeming arrogant? If they are invited to relate these things, do they not regard it as payment rendered for their labours, counting it a reward to tell willingly what they have done? Indeed, this sort of narrative has such a flavour of glory that, if envious persons or rivals happen to be present, they interrupt such questions with clamour and introduce other stories, [Col. 0745C] preventing the narration of those things that commonly create praise for the narrator.

One who has escaped dangers already past, or hardships wholly ended, is most gladly invited to tell of them. For one who is still detained, even a little, in the midst of such things shudders at the reminder and fears the telling of it, as Virgil says:

> “Perhaps one day even to remember these things will be pleasant.”  
> —*Aeneid* I.207

It is welcome if you direct someone to tell of a friend’s sudden good fortune, which he did not dare spontaneously either to mention or to keep silent about, fearing now the appearance of boasting, now that of malice. Ask one who delights in hunting about the extent of the forest, the winding courses of the hunting-grounds, and the outcome of the hunt. If a religious person is present, give him an opportunity to recount by what observances [Col. 0745D] he has deserved the gods’ aid, and how great has been the fruit of religious rites there; for they consider it itself a kind of religious duty not to keep silent about divine benefits. Add that they wish to be regarded as friends of the gods. If an old man is present, you have an opportunity to seem to have bestowed a great favour on him if you question him—even about matters wholly irrelevant to him. For talkativeness is familiar to that age.

But, to return to railleries: those which contain more urbanity and less bitterness should be introduced into banquets—such as remarks upon certain bodily defects that cause little or no pain, for instance, if one jokes about someone’s baldness, nose, or a hooked prominence, or Socratic flatness. For the slighter the misfortune, the more pleasantly such things wound. By contrast, the loss of an eye is not reproached without arousing indignation. Thus King Antigonus killed Theocritus of Chios, though he had sworn that he would spare him, because of a jest made about him by the same man. When Theocritus was being dragged before Antigonus as though to punishment, and his friends comforted him and promised him hope that, when he came before the king’s eyes, he would assuredly experience the king’s clemency, he replied: “Then you speak to me of an impossible hope of safety.” Antigonus had lost one eye, and untimely wit deprived the slanderer of light.

Nor would I deny that philosophers too have encountered indignation through this kind of jest. For when a king’s freedman, newly elevated to wealth, had gathered philosophers at a banquet and, mocking their petty questions, said that he wished to know why a dish made from both black and white beans should have one colour, the philosopher Aridices, indignantly, said: “You explain to us why similar marks are produced by both white and black straps.” [Col. 0746B]

The condition of the speaker also commends a jest, if he is in the same case; for example, if a poor man mocks another for poverty, or one obscurely born mocks another of obscure birth. Thus Amphias of Tarsus, who had grown rich from being a market gardener, after saying some things against a friend as though he were of inferior stock, immediately added: “But we too are from the same seeds, and they have made us all equally glad.” Yet those jests directly infuse happiness into the person against whom they are spoken—for instance, if you blame a brave man as though he were prodigal of his own safety and willing to die for others; [Col. 0746C] or reproach a generous man because he pours out his property, providing less for himself than for others. In this way Antisthenes the Cynic used, as if blaming him, to praise his teacher: “He made me,” he said, “a beggar from a rich man, and, instead of a large house, made me live in a tub.” He said this better than if he had said: “I am grateful to him because he made me a philosopher and a man of perfected virtue.”

Thus, though “jest” is one name, diverse effects are contained within it. Therefore, among the other institutions of their strict life, Lycurgus established this form of exercise among the Spartans also: young men were to make jests without a sting and learn to endure such things said about themselves by others. But if any of them fell into indignation [Col. 0746D] at such a remark, he was no longer permitted to make remarks against another.
