Yet because anger often lies in wait for merriment at banquets, one must refrain from such remarks, and questions for the banquet must be proposed to everyone, or resolved by everyone. The ancients did not consider this subject so frivolous that Aristotle did not write something about it, and Plutarch, and Apuleius with Fronto. That which received the care of so many philosophers must not be despised.

But in the exercise of rhetoricians, or in the forum of orators, jests have a far more advantageous place. For there an opponent’s irritation often contributes to victory. Hence this practice too is said to have been very familiar to Cicero. Even invectives themselves often have a place in forensic disputes, provided they do not proceed to disgraceful abuse; and although they may not cease through the litigant’s favour, they should nevertheless cease out of reverence for the judge and the audience. For the person is offended

> “…who has a horse, a father, and property, if anyone rushes into abuse without the most evident reason.”

But one who bears such things patiently is seen to have earned everyone’s favour by his self-command. Therefore banquets exclude invectives, lest the gall of them make all banquet sweetness bitter. One must seek from every side whatever promotes cheerfulness while remaining conscious of propriety. For a kindly joke and the graceful laughter of guests are more pleasant than every parenthetical aside. For, elegantly, though in the person of a mocker, the moral writer says: “But, as with a general, adverse circumstances tend to reveal a diner’s character, prosperous circumstances to conceal it.”

Wine too, though it is commonly said that “to the dry, God has made all things hard,” has its limit, although there have been those who, on Plato’s authority, believed it should be drunk freely everywhere.

> Wine-soaked Homer is reproved for his praises of wine.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.19.6

And Plato too is shown by those same persons to have been a wine-drinker. It is certain that both praised the use of wine, because it strengthens nature, sharpens intellect, and kindles the relaxed spirit for action. But Plato is more faithfully reported to have approved a pleasanter and more liberal entertainment conducted with small and moderate cups, under certain persons who were, as it were, arbiters and sober masters of the feast. This is what [Col. 0747C] he decides in the first and second books of the *Laws* to be not useless for men. For he thought that minds were refreshed and restored by moderate and respectable relaxations in drinking, so as to renew the duties of sobriety; and that, gradually rendered more cheerful, they became more able again to undertake serious applications. At the same time, any deeply seated errors of passions and desires, which reverent shame concealed from others, might, without grave danger, be disclosed by the freedom afforded through wine and become more amenable to correction and cure.

And Plato says in the same place: exercises of this kind should not be avoided, in order to repel the violence of wine. No one, he says, has ever appeared entirely trustworthy as self-controlled or temperate if his life has not been tested amid the very dangers of error [Col. 0747D] and in the midst of the enticements of pleasures. For he to whom licence and all the attractions of banquets are unknown, and who is wholly without experience of them, if either desire carries him to share such pleasures, or chance brings him into them, or necessity impels him, is immediately softened and captured, and his mind and spirit cannot stand firm. Therefore one must engage and, as it were, in a certain battle-line fight hand to hand with pleasurable things and with this licence of wine, so that we may be secure against them not through flight or absence, but preserve temperance and self-restraint through vigour of spirit, steadfast presence, and moderate use; and, with the mind at once warmed and refreshed, wash away whatever cold sadness or torpid modesty it may contain.

Plato’s authority may move many people; but such an encounter with Bacchus—or indeed with any pleasure—seems to me too arduous and rash for weaker minds. If Lot, a just man and worthy to be rescued from the fire of the Sodomites, fell into incest under wine’s impulse; if Noah, saved from the flood by faith and steadfast goodness, the second father of humankind and author of its salvation, exposed his thighs—who can engage safely, unless perhaps he considers himself superior to such great fathers? Yet, that we may not resist Plato’s decree, it may be braver to engage pleasure, provided it is safer to flee and avoid its conflict. Nor do I remember finding anyone among challengers of pleasures whom I have not read to have fallen. Perhaps the poetic fictions point to this: they do not recount orgies conducted without frenzy, and they do not blush to stain Bacchus’ rites with blood, parricides, and manifold crimes.

Moreover, at banquets care for arranging the household, managing the house, and regulating servants’ attendance should be entrusted to some one person, so that nothing unsuitable or unprepared may appear, nothing surprising or shameful arise, and the master need not call back to himself the concern for matters to be done and, as the saying goes, carry the guests on his shoulders. Let him too who wishes to be an agreeable guest avoid the habit of taking counsel and the practice of holding private conversation, since at banquets—that is, in the pleasant gathering of friends dining together—everything should be open, and in love and trust [Col. 0748C] nothing should be concealed. If it were possible, they should exchange their eyes for mutual sight into one another’s breasts. No place is less suitable, or scarcely any place, for conducting deliberations. For private words generally trouble those who sit nearby but are excluded. Exclusion itself bears the image of distrust.

And even in things said openly, one must faithfully observe what Gaius Claudius Caesar, a man of outstanding genius and great prudence, wrote in the first book *On Analogy*. He says: “Just as sailors avoid a reef, so one must avoid an uncommon and unfamiliar word.” The ancients also specified the number of dinner guests: they should be no fewer than the Graces, who are enclosed in the number three, and no more than the Muses—that is, nine—or, at the utmost, should complete the combined number of Graces and Muses, ascending to twelve. Yet among those who judge more rightly, the principle prevailed that in such matters the host’s duty has the widest scope.

## Chapter XI. On the troubles and burdens of marriage, according to Jerome and other philosophers; on the ruinousness of lust; and on the fidelity of the Ephesian woman and similar women

Just as sobriety is necessary at banquets, so modesty must be present in all things. For from satiety arises lust; from lust, impurity and manifold ruin. From these follows nothing but the pain of repentance; and it goes well with those who grieve if their repentance is fruitful. Thus an opinion seems to arise from a dull heart which declares that pleasure is not perfect without the satisfaction [Col. 0749A] of lust. Epicurus is reported to have held this view. But whatever the swine of that herd may grunt, I do not think so filthy and ruinous a saying pleased any philosopher, much less Epicurus, who was so great that he established his own school among philosophers. According to Seneca, he has many excellent sayings, which can be found scattered among philosophers and are partly set forth and gathered in the book entitled *On the Traces*, or *On the Doctrines, of the Philosophers*.

This is the madness of an aged Silenus rather than the judgment of a philosopher; indeed, it is more brutish than the ass he rode, to whom wickedness could persuade such a thing. Perhaps the fictions of the Gentiles hint at this very point: they report that the mad old man, burning with wine, while others obeyed nature and refreshed bodies wearied by repose, was especially captivated by Lotis; and that at last, amid everyone’s laughter, he—whom neither age nor shame restrained—was recalled by the braying of his ass. Therefore every pleasure of lust is shameful, except that which is excused by the covenant of marriage and, by the benefit of permitted licence, conceals whatever might contain shamefulness.

Hence the ancients taught that *nuptiae* (“marriage”) is named from *nubere* (“to veil”), because the law’s indulgence veils—that is, conceals—the shameful parts of human frailty, as Nonius Marcellus says. A custom has also grown up that those whom the Church’s authority joins in carnal union are covered with the cloth of the altar, or with another covering ordained by the Church, so that the marriage-bed, built under Christ’s reconciling agency, may in the faith [Col. 0749C] of chastity cover the stains of its frailty and remain unaware of every disgrace or shame. Torches are carried and lamps and lights kindled, because the honour of good marriage illumines the twofold marriage-bed, made openly and laid not under compulsion of one’s own lust but by the honourable mutual consent of those who agree. For Hymenaeus loves the light; but the lively boy Cupid with his quiver, bringing on a stealthy flame, seeks hiding places and corners.

Although marital union is honourable and useful, it is more fruitful in distress than in joy. It even bears children in pain; nor does it produce any fruit not preceded or followed by bitterness. Thus, according to Valerius, Socrates, a kind of earthly oracle of human wisdom, when consulted by a young man whether he should take a wife or abstain from all marriage, replied that he would repent whichever course he took. “Here,” he said, “solitude awaits you; here childlessness; here the extinction of your line; here an alien heir. There, perpetual anxiety; a web of complaints; reproach concerning the dowry; the grave scowl of in-laws; a garrulous mother-in-law; the cutting tongue of another marriage; the uncertain outcome of children.” He did not permit the young man, amid this array of harsh matters, to choose as though it were a subject of delight.

The whole chorus of sound philosophers sings in this manner, so that those who recoil from the strictness of Christian religion may learn chastity even from pagans. Yet I do not say this in order to detract from marital chastity; but although the hundredfold or sixtyfold fruit arises from the root of the thirtyfold, I by no means judge it comparable with the thirtyfold. Zeno, Epictetus, Aristotle, Critolaus, and very many Epicureans are reported to have transmitted this opinion to posterity.

A little book by Theophrastus *On Marriage*, golden in worth, is reported by Jerome. In it he asks whether a wise man should take a wife. Having decided that, if she were beautiful, well-behaved, born of honourable parents, and if he himself were healthy and rich, wisdom might sometimes enter marriage, he immediately adds: “But all these conditions rarely agree together in marriages. Therefore a wife should not be taken by a wise man. First, philosophical studies are impeded, and no one can serve books and a wife alike. There are many things necessary for married women’s use: costly clothes, gold, jewels, [Col. 0750B] expenses, maidservants, various furnishings, litters, and a gilded reception-room. Then there are garrulous complaints throughout the nights: ‘She goes out in public more finely dressed; she is honoured by everyone; I, poor creature, am scorned in women’s gatherings. Why did you look at the neighbour? Why were you speaking with the little maid? What did you bring back from the forum? We cannot have a friend or companion.’ She suspects another’s love and her own hatred.

“If there is a most learned teacher in any city, we cannot either leave our wife or travel with baggage. It is difficult to support a poor wife; it is torture to endure a rich one. Add that there is no choice of a wife: whatever woman falls to one’s lot must be accepted. Whether she is angry, foolish, ugly, proud, foul-smelling—whatever fault she has, we discover after the marriage. A horse, ass, ox, dog, and even the cheapest slaves; clothing also and kettles, a wooden seat, a cup and an earthenware jug, are inspected first and then bought. A wife alone is not shown beforehand, lest she displease before she is taken. One must always attend to her face and praise her beauty, lest, if you look at another woman, she think herself displeasing.

“She must be called ‘mistress’; her birthday must be celebrated; one must swear by her health and pray that she may survive; her nurse and bearer must be honoured. Her father’s slave and fosterling, her handsome attendant, her curled-haired steward, and the eunuch castrated for a long and safe indulgence of lust—under such names adulterers lie concealed. Whoever she loves, even though ungrateful, must also be loved. If you entrust the management of the whole house to her, you must be her slave. If you reserve anything [Col. 0750D] for your own judgment, she will think you do not trust her, and it will turn into hatred and quarrels; and unless you quickly take precautions, she will prepare poisons. If you admit old women, goldsmiths, fortune-tellers, dealers in gems and silk garments, chastity is endangered; if you forbid them, it is the wrong of suspicion.

“But what good is even diligent guarding, when an unchaste wife cannot be guarded and a chaste one ought not to be? Necessity is an untrustworthy guardian of chastity, and she alone ought truly to be called chaste who had the opportunity to sin but did not wish to. A beautiful woman is quickly loved; an ugly one most readily desires to be loved. What many people love is difficult to guard; what no one deigns to possess is burdensome to possess. Yet an ugly wife is kept with less misery than a beautiful one is guarded. Nothing is safe when the desires of the whole populace sigh after it: one assails by beauty, another by charm, another by intellect, another by generosity. What is attacked from every side is somehow conquered.

“If wives are taken for the management of the household, the relief of illness, and escape from solitude, a faithful servant, obedient to his master’s authority and compliant with his administration, manages much better than a wife, who thinks herself mistress precisely when she acts contrary to her husband’s will—that is, when she does what pleases her rather than what she is commanded. Friends and household-born servants, bound by benefits received, can attend a sick man more than she can—she who charges us with her tears, sells her squalor for the expectation of our inheritance, and, boasting of her solicitude, disturbs the sick man’s mind with despair. If she herself becomes ill, one must be ill with her and never leave her bedside. Or if she is a good and pleasant wife—which is nevertheless a rare bird—we groan with her in childbirth and are tortured when she is in danger.

“A wise man, however, can never be alone. He has with him all who are good, both those who are and those who ever were, and he transfers his free mind wherever he wishes. What he cannot embrace bodily, he embraces in thought. And if he lacks human company, he will speak with God. He is never less alone than when he is alone. Furthermore, to take a wife for the sake of children—so that our name may not perish, or that we may have supports in old age and use assured heirs—is most foolish. For what does it matter to us when we depart [Col. 0751C] from the world if another is not called by our name, when a son does not immediately bear his father’s name and countless persons are called by the same name? Or what aid to old age is it to rear at home one who may perhaps die before you, or be of utterly depraved character, or, when he has reached maturity, think that you die too slowly? Better and more certain heirs are friends and relatives whom you choose by judgment than those whom, whether you wish it or not, you are compelled to have. Even if an inheritance is assured, it is preferable, while you live, to use your property well than to leave what your labour has acquired for uncertain uses.”

These and similar things are Theophrastus’ words, which by themselves suffice to set forth the straits and calamities of marriages of exquisite sweetness. Thus Publius Clodius is reported to have said that a man improperly accuses Neptune who suffers shipwreck a second time. But it would be no less elegant to say that a man improperly accuses Venus of being adverse who takes a second wife. For who will pity one who, once released from chains, flies back to fetters? He is plainly unworthy of the honour and peace of freedom who returns to the yoke of slavery he has cast off.

Hence it is monstrous that those who claim for themselves the name not only of philosophy but also of religion cannot be kept away from women’s embraces. Often a man who, before professing either name—if indeed religion and philosophy make two categories, since no one can philosophize rightly without religion—lived most continentally, once promoted to some rank and having obtained ease, employs the keenness of his first and highest deliberation in selecting or taking a wife; or, what is more wicked, does not fear to solicit and corrupt the marriages of neighbours. At times the shameless intemperance of women breaks out, because, as Herodotus writes, a woman lays aside her modesty together with her garment. It breaks out, I say, brazenly, and before the faces of a blushing populace uncovers and lays bare the secrets of the marriage-bed. A woman complains of her husband’s frigidity, alleging as a sufficient and evident cause for repudiation or divorce that he is half a man and unfit for marriage because he is not ready for intercourse.

Geoffrey of La Ville, my associate, elegantly confounded the audacity of one such woman in a case of this kind. A legal advocate had been appointed for her by the judge, who was expected to pronounce a divorce. The noblewoman, with friends and supporters hearing, set out the merits of her case to the advocate with the greater care customary in such circumstances. The prudent man asked her whether she had ever had another husband. When she denied it, he asked again whether she was still a virgin, saying that this was most necessary for him to inquire and know, lest, in speaking, he should be caught by some opportunity by a discerning judge. She nevertheless asserted that she was, though modestly, because she was not believed readily. He then asked: “Did your husband and you customarily sleep together at night, kiss and embrace each other?” [Col. 0752C] When she admitted all this, the advocate said: “How then do you know, most chaste, most prudent, most modest virgin, that your husband did not consummate with you effectively and discharge all the duties of marriage? Who taught you what intercourse is, so that you deny that he had intercourse with you amid so many kisses and embraces, when by marital licence he handled you as he pleased and as often as he wished? For it is certain that certain animals couple by kissing each other; others conceive by touching lightly; and there are creatures which, impregnated by their own heat through temperate air, conceive and bear offspring.”

At last she blushed, saying only that she had nothing with which to answer such traps. But it goes well with philosophers—that is, clerics—because none of them is frigid or, in court, stained by a blemish of this sort.

Cicero, asked after divorcing Terentia to marry Hirtius’ sister, wholly declined to do so, saying that he could not give attention alike to a wife and to philosophy. Philip, king of the Macedonians, against whom Demosthenes’ *Philippics* thunder, entered his bedroom according to custom and was angrily shut out by his wife. Excluded, he kept silent and consoled his injury with a tragic verse. The rhetorician Gorgias recited at Olympia a most beautiful book on concord, when the Greeks were then divided among themselves. His enemy Melanthius said: “This man teaches us concord, though he could not make himself, his wife, and his little maid—three persons in one house—live in concord.” For his wife was jealous of the little maid’s beauty and harassed her most chaste husband with daily quarrels. Hence, in order that jealousy might cease and peace be restored to marriages, it became customary among the richer people [Col. 0753A] not to have any woman more beautiful in the house.

When Socrates wished to restrain the quarrels of his two wives, they finally turned their attack upon him. After punishing him severely, they pursued him for a long time as he fled, and afterwards drenched him with urine from the upper storey where they lived. Many things are everywhere written by authors about women’s fickleness. Perhaps very many are sometimes falsely invented; nevertheless, nothing prevents one from “speaking the truth with laughter” and, through fabulous narratives—which philosophy does not reject—expressing what can be harmful in character. From these things it is clear how easily women fall in love, with how much fickleness they hate, how swiftly they forget affections, and how, forgetful of nature, they are sometimes armed against their children and sometimes against their own flesh. Some women are most chaste, though the satirist says:

> “because” [Col. 0753B]

Rare is the woman of perfect chastity upon earth, and she is very like a black swan. (Horace.) And the tragedian says that no woman is so chaste that a stranger’s desire does not inflame her even to madness. A certain matron at Ephesus, Petronius relates, was so renowned for chastity that she drew women even from neighbouring peoples to gaze upon her. When she had therefore carried out her husband, she was not content, in the ordinary fashion, to follow the funeral with loosened, disordered hair or to beat her bared breast before the crowd; she followed the dead man even into the tomb and, after the body had been laid in the underground chamber according to Greek custom, began to keep watch over it and to weep [Col. 0753C] throughout nights and days.

As she thus afflicted herself and pursued death by starvation, neither parents nor kinsfolk could draw her away. At last the magistrates too were repulsed and departed. Mourned by all as a woman of singular example, she was now dragging out a fifth day without food. Her most faithful maid attended the sufferer, at once commending her tears to the mourner and, whenever the lamp placed in the tomb went out, renewing it. Thus throughout the city there was but one topic: people of every rank declared that this alone had shone forth as a true example of chastity and love.

Meanwhile the governor of the province ordered robbers to be fastened to crosses beside the little hut in which the matron bewailed the fresh corpse. The following night, therefore, the soldier guarding the crosses, lest anyone remove a body for burial, noticed both a brighter lamp shining among the tombs and the sound of a mourner’s groaning. By the common failing of humankind, he desired to know who it was and what she was doing. He therefore descended into the tomb; and, seeing the exceedingly beautiful woman, he first halted, troubled as though by some prodigy and by infernal apparitions. Then, when he saw the body lying there, considered her tears, and her face torn by her nails, supposing—as indeed was the case—that the woman could not bear longing for the dead man, he brought his little supper into the tomb and began to urge the mourner not to persist in useless grief or tear her breast with unavailing lamentation. The same dwelling, he said, awaits all alike, and the rest of those commonplaces by which wounded minds are recalled to health. But she, struck by this unfamiliar consolation, tore her breast more violently and laid the hair she had torn out upon the breast of the corpse.

The soldier nevertheless did not depart, but with the same exhortations tried to give the poor woman food, until the maid—overcome, I am certain, by the smell of the food—first herself held out her hand, conquered by the humanity of the inviter. Then, restored by drink and food, she began to assail her mistress’s obstinacy: “What will this profit you,” she said, “if you perish by starvation, if you bury yourself alive, if, before the Fates demand it, you pour out your uncondemned spirit?

> Do you think the ashes or the spirits of the buried care for this?” (Virgil.)

“Do you wish the dead man to return to life, though the Fates resist? [Col. 0754B] Do you wish, once womanly error has been cast off, to enjoy the benefits of daylight as long as it is permitted? The very body of the man lying here ought to admonish you to live.” No one listens unwillingly when compelled to live or to take food. Thus the woman, dried up by abstinence for several days, allowed her obstinacy to be broken. Nor did she fill herself with food less eagerly than the maid who had first been conquered.

But you know what human satiety commonly attempts. By the same blandishments through which the soldier had obtained the matron’s consent to live, he also attacked her chastity. The young man did not seem unattractive or ineloquent to the chaste woman, while the maid promoted his suit and repeatedly said:

> “Will you still contend against a love that pleases you?  
> And does it not come to mind in whose lands you have settled?” (Virgil.) [Col. 0754C]

Why delay longer? The woman did not withhold even this part of her body. The victorious soldier persuaded her in both matters. They lay together, not only on that night upon which they celebrated their wedding, but also on the next and the third day, the doors of the tomb of course having been shut, so that anyone known or unknown who came to the monument would have thought that the most chaste wife had expired over her husband’s body.

The soldier, delighted by the woman’s beauty and by their secrecy, bought whatever good things his means allowed and carried them to the tomb on the very first night. Accordingly, when the relatives of one crucified man saw that the guard had relaxed, they took down the hanging body by night and performed the final rites [Col. 0754D] for it. The soldier, deceived while he sat idle, saw the next day one cross without a corpse. Fearing punishment, he explained to the woman what had happened. He said that he would not await a judge’s sentence, but would pronounce judgment upon his own negligence by the sword; he asked only that she provide a place for one about to perish and make the fatal tomb serve both lover and husband.

The woman, no less merciful than chaste, replied: “May the gods never permit that at the same time I should behold the two funerals of the two men dearest to me. I prefer to hang up a dead man rather than kill a living one.” Accordingly, she ordered her husband’s body to be taken from the coffin and fastened to the vacant cross. The soldier made use of the ingenuity of this most prudent woman. On the next day the people marvelled how the dead man had gone up upon the cross. [Col. 0755A]

You may call this narrative or fable, as Petronius relates it in these words, according to your pleasure. Yet Flavianus too is an authority that it happened in this manner at Ephesus; and he relates that the woman paid the penalties for her impiety, parricidal crime, and adultery.

Petronius is not alone in ridiculing or portraying women’s follies. Blessed Jerome writes that all Euripides’ tragedies are invectives against women; and that Epicurus, although his disciple Metrodorus had Leontion as a wife, seldom says that a wise man should marry, because many inconveniences attend marriage. As riches, honours, bodily health, and the other things which we call indifferent are neither goods nor evils, but, as it were, placed in the middle, becoming good or evil through their use and outcome, so wives too are situated upon the boundary between good and evil. It is therefore a serious matter for a wise man to face the uncertainty whether he will marry a good wife or a bad one.

If, then, marriage—which is undoubtedly good and instituted by the Lord—is attended by such great inconvenience that a wise man dreads it, who except a madman would approve that pleasure which is unlawful and wholly occupied with filth, which men condemn and God will without doubt condemn? For these two pleasures, namely of gluttony and Venus, are in a sense those of brute beasts: the one seems to possess the uncleanness of the pig, the other the stink of the he-goat. As chastity stands out among virtues, so wantonness is the basest of vices; and although chastity befits both sexes, it adorns the female sex more especially. For, as a most learned man has said, chastity must above all be retained, since once it is lost every virtue falls. [Col. 0755C]

In chastity lies the pre-eminence of women’s virtues. It commends a poor woman, exalts a rich one, redeems an ugly woman, and adorns a beautiful one. It serves ancestors well, since it does not taint their blood with stolen offspring; it serves children well, since they need neither blush for their mother nor doubt their father; above all, it serves the woman herself, whom it protects from the insult of another’s body. No calamity of captivity is greater than to be drawn to another’s lust. Eloquence distinguishes men of consular rank; military glory conveys them into an everlasting name and consecrates triumphs over new peoples. Many things ennoble naturally brilliant minds; chastity is the distinctive virtue of women.

Jerome testifies that, before the Christian religion shone in the world, matrons who had only one husband always possessed honour; that rites to the goddess Fortuna were customarily performed through them; that no priest was twice married and no flamen had two wives. He says also that the hierophants of Athens were for a very long time emasculated by drinking hemlock and, once admitted to the pontificate, ceased to be men; there was no priest married twice and no flamen married twice. This page would stretch to an immense length if I were to touch upon everything handed down on this subject by tragedians, orators, comic poets, satirists, and poets—not to mention philosophers, moralists, and theologians. Yet I do not think that all of them sufficed, not merely to eradicate or restrain this wickedness, but even to describe it. If I say, as many have experienced, that:

> “She who strikes the black paving-stone with her feet is no better  
> than she who is borne upon the necks of her own slaves.”  
> (Juvenal, VI.349.) [Col. 0756A]

malice will slander this as spoken to women’s injury. For nothing is better, nothing more useful, than a chaste woman; and nothing that can be imagined is more delightful for those who cannot, or will not, remain continent. Yet it is foolish to seek praise from acts that more properly deserve pardon than glory—if indeed they have been moderated by the good of restraint. Otherwise punishment rather than pardon, disgrace rather than honour, will follow the stain of either lust—unless perhaps one ought to count as handsome the man transformed into a goat or a pig.

## Chapter XII. How some desire to conform themselves to brute and insentient things; how humanely one must live with slaves; and the pleasure of the remaining three senses

[Col. 0756B]

Those who place life’s highest good in the pleasure of taste and touch—not to say, luxury—certainly conform themselves most fittingly to no class of living beings. But this does not excuse the luxury of the other senses, since it is a manifest abandonment of human dignity if a person strives to make himself equal, not to goat or pig, but to lion or leopard, panther or satyr, peacock, nightingale, or parrot—indeed, to any brute or insentient thing. Rather, one who was created with such dignity of origin should aspire to angelic purity, so as to be able, in the fullness of true and eternal blessedness, to conform to angelic perfection. [Col. 0756C]

The unshaken authority of the Fathers has also established that the Lord alone is worthier than the nature of the human mind; and that all these things which human error admires were made by Him who made man, in order that they might serve man, whom He made a participant in His eternity and blessedness. Who, therefore, does not despise the judgment of the presiding Lord if he seeks a servile and abject condition?

Yet I do not say that slaves are to be held in contempt, unless they live by servile vices. For as the true and sole freedom is to serve virtue and perform its offices, so the one and singular slavery is to be subjected to vices. Whoever thinks that either condition comes about from another source is plainly mistaken. For the whole human race rises on earth from a similar birth, consists of and is nourished by the same elements, draws the same spirit from the same source, enjoys the same heaven, dies alike, and lives alike.

Hence Praetextatus, rebuking Evangelus in the *Saturnalia*, uses these arguments: “They are slaves—indeed, human beings. They are slaves—indeed, fellow-slaves. If you consider that Fortune has equal power over both of you, you may see him free as readily as he may see you a slave. Do you know at what age Hecuba began to be a slave, Croesus, Darius’ mother, Diogenes, or Plato himself? Finally, why do we shudder at the name of slavery? He is indeed a slave, but by necessity; perhaps he is a slave with a free spirit. Will this harm him? Show me who is not a slave. One man serves lust, another avarice, another ambition; all serve hope, all [Col. 0757A] fear. And certainly no slavery is more shameful than voluntary slavery. Yet we trample upon one bowed beneath Fortune’s imposed yoke as though he were miserable and worthless. What we ourselves put upon our own necks, we do not permit to be criticized. You will find among slaves one stronger in wealth; you will find a master who, in hope of profit, presses kisses upon the hands of other men’s slaves. Therefore I shall not assess human beings by Fortune, but by character. Each gives himself his character; chance assigns his condition. Just as he is foolish who, intending to buy a horse, does not inspect the horse itself but its trappings and bridle, so he is most foolish who thinks a person should be judged by condition or clothing.

“There is no reason, my Evangelus, why you should seek a friend only in the forum and the senate-house. If you pay careful attention, you will find one at home as well. Only live with your slave gently, and also courteously; admit him to conversation, and sometimes to confidential counsel. For our ancestors, removing every occasion of envy toward masters and every insult to slaves, called the master *paterfamilias*, ‘father of the household,’ and the slaves *familiares*, ‘members of the household.’ Let your slaves therefore respect you rather than fear you, believe me; and do not think too little of what is enough for the gods. For one who is respected is also loved, and love cannot be mingled with fear. Whence, do you suppose, came that most arrogant proverb, so proudly repeated, that we have as many enemies as slaves? Those people are not our enemies, but we make them so, when we are most arrogant, insulting, and cruel toward them; and luxury drives us to such madness that whatever does not answer our will provokes anger and rage. [Col. 0757C]

“For at home we assume the temper of tyrants and wish to exercise over slaves, not as much as is fitting, but as much as is permitted. To pass over the other kinds of cruelty: some, while stuffing themselves with the abundance and greediness of the table, do not permit the slaves standing around them even to move their lips—not even to speak. Every murmur is suppressed by the rod, and not even accidental sounds are exempt from blows. A cough, a sneeze, a hiccup is paid for at great cost. Thus those are made to speak about their master who are not permitted to speak before their master. But those who were allowed conversation not only in their masters’ presence but with their masters themselves, whose mouths were not sewn shut, were ready to offer their necks for their master and turn the threatening danger upon their own heads. They spoke at banquets, but were silent under torture.”

This is Praetextatus; and he adds many splendid things concerning slaves’ fidelity, things glorious in persons of however great nobility of blood and worthy of imitation by all. Nothing is honourable that does not flow from virtue; shamefulness and vice mutually enclose one another in an unhappy circle. Yet under the impulse of vices alone does anyone fall so far as to cast and devote himself to the slavery of those over whom he was born to rule.

Those who flock to spectacles, summon shameful spectacles to themselves, or wish to make themselves a spectacle to fools by affected trifles—because such enticements of vanity cannot rightly please a wise man—are captivated by the charms of the eyes. Though their fall is gentler, they nevertheless fall from the dignity of their condition and relapse into the servile state which they deny. What else, then, do mimes, actors, parasites, and such human monsters do except prove the foolish slavery of the prosperous? [Col. 0758A]

Those too who are captured by little sounds, although the sense of hearing is the purest and most refined, are slaves indeed, though they are pressed under a gentler yoke, if other vices do not prevail. Hardly anyone at all is captivated through smell, unless perhaps he lives as a Lotus-eater. I am not constructing an argument against singers or musicians, since Quintilian, Valerius, Flavianus, and many others testify that Socrates too learned music in old age, believing that if music were lacking, he would lack the crown of wisdom. Yet to be too much occupied with it is beneath philosophical seriousness. Would it, indeed, befit a wise man, especially when it does not escape the stigma of shame even in the female sex? Sallust reproves Sempronia, not because she knew how to dance and play the lyre, but because she knew these things exceedingly well. He says that she played and danced more elegantly than was necessary for a respectable woman.

Yet to sing exceedingly well, if it could be possessed without frivolity, is plainly desirable. In all things simply desirable, the more intense they are in the quality of good, the more desirable they are. But certain accompanying circumstances may make them suspect. Lucius Sulla, a man of such great name, is said to have sung exceedingly well; but he added the stigma of lust and cruelty to this gift. [Col. 0758C] Cato too thought that singing well was not the mark of a serious man. Hence he calls Marcus, a senator of no mean rank, “Caecilius the stroller” and “Fescennius,” and says that he “gives little poses”:

> “He gets down from his mule; then begins striking poses and pouring out ridiculous things.”

And elsewhere:

> “Moreover, he sings whenever he pleases; sometimes he performs Greek verses, makes jokes, imitates voices, and strikes poses.”

Now the pleasure of the ears is agreeable to honour when it is a friend of virtue or is unaware of shamefulness. But the pleasure of the eyes introduced actors and mimes—a matter Scipio Africanus Aemilianus reproved with no little force in his speech against Tiberius Gracchus’ judicial law:

> “They are taught shameful tricks; together with effeminate boys, sambuca, [Col. 0758D] and psaltery, they go to the actors’ school. They learn to sing—things which our ancestors wished to count as disgraceful for freeborn persons. They go, I say, to the dancing-school among effeminate men, freeborn girls, and boys. Whenever anyone told me this, I could not bring myself to believe that noblemen taught such things to their children. But when I was taken to a dancing-school, by Hercules, I saw in that school more than two hundred boys and girls. Among them—what made me feel most pity for the commonwealth—I saw the son of a candidate, a boy wearing the freeborn child’s bulla, less than twelve years old, dancing with crotala.”

*Κρότος* (*krotos*) is Greek for “a striking,” and cymbals are so called from it; or *crotalus* denotes a musical instrument whose sound imitates a stork’s cry, for the stork itself is called *crotalus* among the Egyptians. *Crotala* are also sounding little balls which, with certain grains enclosed within them, produce varied sounds according to their size and the kind of metal. [Col. 0759A] “A shameless little slave could not have danced that dance respectably.”

It is therefore clear with what feeling Africanus groaned at seeing the son of a petitioner—that is, a candidate—dancing with crotala. Not even the hope and prospect of obtaining office, when he ought to have protected himself and his family from every disgrace, could restrain him from doing what, of course, was not held shameful. For even at the time when the City lived by the best morals—namely, between the two Punic Wars—the freeborn sons of senators attended dancing-school and learned there to dance while carrying crotala. Indeed, dancing was by no means excluded from heroic banquets. The Socratic *Symposium* is renowned for the authority of the philosophers gathered there; yet there was one who, in the presence of their grave faces, asked that a female lyre-player be brought in, so that a girl softer than nature permits might, by the sweetness of song and the allure of dancing, entice the philosophers.

Cicero is authority that actors were not counted among the disgraceful; as Furius Albinus relates, he was on intimate terms with Roscius and Aesop, so much so that he defended their property and business interests by his own skill. This is shown not only by many other sources but also by his letters. For that speech became famous in which he rebukes the Roman people because they had raised a disturbance while Roscius was acting. It is also established that he used to compete with the actor himself over whether Roscius more often conveyed the same thought by varying gestures, or Cicero delivered it in varied language through his abundance of eloquence. This led Roscius to such confidence in his art that he wrote a book comparing eloquence with acting. This is the Roscius who was also especially dear to Sulla and received a gold ring from that dictator. Such was his favour and fame that he alone received from the public a daily payment of a thousand denarii, without the rest of the troupe. It is also established that Aesop left two hundred times one hundred thousand sesterces from the same art. [Col. 0759D]

But if actors are to be admitted to the company of the wise on the authority of Cicero and the heroes just mentioned, would that men like Roscius and Aesop might be chosen—men who, even if they cannot do what those men knew, at least know how to understand books and are lovers rather than enemies of letters, which no wise or good person has ever hated. Valerius reports that Cicero despised letters and was, in that very contempt, an abundant fountain of letters—perhaps because he placed study after public business. For he persisted in letters even while despising them, and Cicero’s very “contempt” was more devoted to study than the study of many.

Yet I would not easily believe that any educated person could be driven to profess acting, although very many may readily be found who are not ashamed to act and to play the vile actor to the full. For they portray gestures once the usefulness of the actions is removed.

[Col. 0760A]

Blessed Jerome is said to have excluded three clerics from his table because he saw them behaving without composure, thinking it shameful for an honourable and serious man to find anyone ill-composed in his company. This was indeed more worthy of praise than if, in order to be praised by them, he had admitted them. Although there may be some pleasure of the eyes in such things, it can scarcely be practised or admitted without shamefulness.

There is also that pleasure which is notable in a serious man because of luxury: he thinks his adornment lies in the value of his clothes, their colour, form, or novelty of use. For, as the moralist says:

> “Malthinus walks in a tunic hanging low; another man  
> is witty because his garments hang down all the way to his obscene groin.”  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.2.25.) [Col. 0760B]

One man excludes the horrors of winter with linen alone, and while everything is stiff with freezing cold, sweats in a thin *cyclas*; even a silk garment burns or oppresses his delicacy. Another, more tunic-clad than an onion, piles up skins and outer garments, draws a hooded travelling-cloak over his mantle, and, as if rolled into a ball, is better fitted to roll than walk. Another now wears a travelling-cloak, now a short open garment, doing nothing but making himself unlike others. Another seeks such exquisite refinement of dress that, through the excessive brilliance of elaborate attire, he seems to approach filth.

For whatever disfigures and in some measure soils—or rather expels—honourableness is filthy and must be reckoned among filth. Yet a thing introduced by necessity is not censured, because not everyone can do everything, and one person’s nature requires what burdens another or what another cannot bear at all. But philosophy commands this to be observed: that everyone in all things avoid notoriety, imposing rectitude upon action lest it be blameworthy; caution upon speech lest it be contemptible; modesty upon dress lest it attract notice. For notoriety exposes intemperance.

To this day Hortensius’ excess is censured. From him these white-powdered persons are still called Hortensians—not because he was the first, but because he was the chief of such people, so much so that he was enough to mark his age. He was certainly soft both in speech and by profession, placing all his distinction in his girding. He was fastidious in dress even to refinement, and, in order to go out well clothed, sought his face in a mirror. Gazing at himself, he arranged the toga upon his body so that an artful knot tightened wrinkles placed not by chance but deliberately, and the fold, falling in studied fashion, traced the line of his side. [Col. 0760D]

Once, as he was walking elaborately dressed for display, he brought an action for injury against his colleague because the latter, meeting him in a narrow passage and accidentally jostling him, had disarranged the structure of his toga. He judged it a capital matter that, upon his shoulder, a wrinkle had changed its place. Nothing of this sort befits a wise or honourable man. Indeed, respectable matrons and maidens about to marry blush more readily and more happily, despite the dowries of beauty, at so much concern for their own adornment. It is therefore remarkable with what shamelessness men of our age

> “wear splendid finery—men scarcely snatched from their brides.”  
> (Lucan, I.164.) [Col. 0761A]

What then of soldiers? What of clerics? For all these imitate the deceitful cosmetic paint and wickedness of a prostitute. What has a man to do with a mirror, except in the case in which Flavianus testifies that Plato carried one: so that in it he might see how much travel, zeal for study, the sharpness of weather, and advancing age had altered his natural condition, as indicated by the face, which bears most faithful witness to good and evil? He did this in order to preserve or restore nature, lest it be impaired by labour and an unfamiliar regimen.

But, to pass to other matters, which of those who seek the endowments of brute beasts would deign to be a brute? Or to whom would reason not seem to outweigh them, if he compares the reason granted him with theirs? Would a lover of strength wish to be a lion or leopard? Natural philosophers say that other animals follow the scent of the lynx or panther; yet I do not think that those who delight and stimulate their sense of smell with musk and exotic spices would wish, if they could, to be changed into a panther or lynx. I certainly do not believe that he who wears a satyr’s costume wishes to be a satyr; nor can those who polish themselves transform peacock colours into themselves. Let these men sing and exert their powers to perform the melodies of all music: none of them will equal a nightingale or parrot. [Col. 0761B]

Is it not, then, unbecoming and disgraceful to human loftiness, after setting aside its own endowment, in which it excels, to aspire to the endowments of others, in which it is surpassed? Yet if moderation is applied, I do not think it unbecoming for a wise person occasionally to take pleasure in these matters of the senses. As has often been said, nothing is honourable without measure. For leisure too is sometimes natural to a wise person, but not so that the exercise of virtue should disappear; rather, so that it may be more vigorous and in some manner restored. Laelius and Scipio, that notable pair of friends, read together; and, as Scaevola, the most certain witness of their relaxation, reports, wearied by civic business, they played ball. Scaevola himself too is said sometimes to have devoted time to dice and counters after he had well and long arranged the laws of citizens and the rites of the gods. For in serious affairs he acted Scaevola, but in games he acted the human being whom nature does not permit to endure uninterrupted labour.

Socrates, who is said to have left no part of wisdom unknown, saw this; and so he was not ashamed when Alcibiades laughed at him because, with a reed placed between his legs, he was playing with his little sons. Homer too, the heavenly poet of genius, intends nothing else when he gives Achilles’ mighty hands a tuneful lyre than to relax their military vigour by the light pursuit of peace. [Col. 0761D]

In short, to practise acting, dancing, and such enticements belongs to frivolity or shamefulness. But to take pleasure in them tends sometimes toward leisure, sometimes toward vice. If it is done modestly for recreation, it is excused under the permission of leisure; if it is for the enjoyment of a wantonly disposed mind, it falls into guilt. This is most easily distinguished by the distinction, mentioned above, of place, time, manner, person, and cause. A more wordy tongue might perhaps turn this over too much; but a cautious mind cannot turn it over too much or retain it too firmly. For this is the fountain and origin of all modesty, without which nothing is rightly performed in duties. From it it is certain that different things become fitting or unfitting for different people.

> “For what is shameful for the good Seius and Titius will be fitting for Crispinus.”

It is therefore an error of obvious plainness to consume one’s life, for the foundation of reputation and glory, upon such things as are either idle occupations or shameful businesses. Certainly, he who provides their wantonness is a participant in the wrongdoing; and he appears the author of another’s luxury who prefers to support it by expenditure or favour rather than pursue it with rebuke and denial of funds. Ambrose indeed is authority that one who gives to such people commits a great sin. [Col. 0762B] For he fosters in them that in which they are most wicked.

## Chapter XIII. In praise of frugality; Quintilian’s criticism of Seneca; and how suspicion of avarice may be avoided by living frugally

I seem to be attacking luxury in praise of frugality, and the ignorant—who live foolishly and speak without discrimination—tauntingly throw at me that saying of Publius Clodius, that frugality is attached to a good reputation. These are the people who, because they do not wish or cannot avoid luxury, regard whatever is said for virtue as a defence of avarice. But it is otherwise. No one doubts that luxury is shameful in itself; and although frugality is praiseworthy as though the origin of virtues and good works, it does not please everyone. Nor do they believe that avarice, the fuel of wickedness, can be avoided unless frugality too is avoided. This is plainly the opinion of the unlearned. For, as the moralist says:

“While fools avoid vices, they rush into their opposites” (Horace, *Satires* I.2.24), departing from the mean between vices, which is the realm of virtue. Yet there are people in whom frugality must be restrained—those, that is, whose nature is more inclined to avarice. There are also those upon whom it must be imposed more firmly: those who squander their possessions and, scorning reason, pour them out without distinguishing use from abuse. Horace relates that Servius Opidius of Canusium employed precisely this moderation in his final injunction, when he saw his sons seized by opposite maladies.

Yet it is simply established that frugality must be counted among goods [Col. 0762D], since it was she who, under Saturn’s reign, governed the golden kingdoms and administered all their functions. She kept Astraea and chastity upon earth longer, until, as luxury gained strength under Jupiter’s reign, they were able to fly away to the gods above. This fable concerns us, that we may know that justice and chastity cannot be preserved without frugality. For the necessity of practising luxury excludes justice, and the pleasure of its practice drives chastity away. For Scripture says: “He who hastens to become rich shall not be innocent.”

Yet Clodius’s saying in no way darkens the honour of frugality, but seems rather to commend its grace. For it is clear that what is taken up in defence and excuse of an unfavourable report is by no means evil. [Col. 0763A] Thus a dark complexion softens blackness; and what is swollen is honoured with the name of fullness. Frugality, moreover, is the virtue that regulates use and is ignorant of abuse. It provides nothing coldly or timidly, yet its expenditure is governed by reason. It spares resources indeed, but spares itself still more. It takes nothing—or very little—away from necessity, but grants absolutely nothing to luxury. For it is exceedingly diligent.

What Zeno, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and the whole chorus of philosophers have handed down concerning the preservation of frugality may suffice to commend it. But since these names are very ancient, or their precepts are not celebrated, let our Seneca at least be heard. He extols it with such great praise that anyone attempting to add anything at all would seem more properly to be idling than accomplishing anything [Col. 0763B].

There are, however, those who dare to despise him, relying upon Quintilian’s authority. By disparaging one who pleases very many, they seek to ennoble their own judgment, so that among the unlearned they may seem to surpass in glory those whose virtue they cannot imitate. Yet they seem to me to be foolish, whoever they may follow, if they do not venerate one who is known both to have deserved the Apostles’ friendship and to have been placed by the most learned Father Jerome in the catalogue of saints.

So that you may also judge Quintilian’s judgment, here are his own words, which, after listing writers, he set down to disparage Seneca:

> I have intentionally postponed Seneca, who exercised himself in every kind of eloquence, because of the widespread but false opinion about me, by which I was believed to condemn him and even to regard him with dislike. This happened to me while I was striving to call back to stricter standards a style of speaking that had been corrupted and broken by every vice, at a time when he was almost the only author in the hands of young men. I was not indeed trying to thrust him away altogether, but I did not allow him to be preferred to better writers—whom he himself had not ceased to attack, since, conscious that his own style was different, he distrusted his ability to please in the manner in which they pleased. They loved him more than they imitated him; and they fell away from him by as much as he had fallen away from the ancients. It would indeed have been desirable for them to become equal to, or at least close to, that man. But he pleased on account of his faults alone, and each person applied himself to reproducing those faults which he could reproduce. Then, when a man boasted that he spoke in the same manner, he was bringing Seneca into disrepute.
>
> Yet Seneca had many and great virtues besides: an easy and copious talent, very great industry, and much knowledge of subjects—in which, nevertheless, he was sometimes deceived by those to whom he entrusted the investigation of certain matters. He also treated almost the whole range of every branch of learning. For his speeches, poems, letters, and dialogues are extant. In philosophy he was insufficiently careful; yet he was an outstanding assailant of vices. There are in him many brilliant maxims and much that should be read for the formation of character; but in expression almost everything is corrupt, and all the more pernicious because it abounds in pleasing faults. One would wish that he had spoken with his own talent but another’s judgment. For if he had not despised the achievements of his contemporaries, if he had not coveted, if he had not loved everything of his own, if he had not broken down the weight of subjects into the tiniest maxims [Col. 0764A], he would be approved by the agreement of the learned rather than by the affection of boys. Yet even as he is, he should be read by those already strengthened and firmly established in a more severe style, if only because he can exercise both kinds of judgment. For, as I have said, much in him is to be approved and much also admired. But one must take care in choosing—which I wish he himself had done. For that nature was worthy to desire better things; what it desired, it accomplished.

Such is Quintilian on Seneca; but whether he judged rightly I leave to wiser persons. Yet I do not think that what he attributes to him—namely, great elegance in matters of conduct, even though corrupt in expression—should in any way be detracted from him. Let his moral precepts, then, be admitted; and let each person speak in the style he prefers to others. It will then be clear that the streams of virtues arise from the most pure fountain of frugality [Col. 0764B].

Let his letters be read; his books *On Benefits* and *On Clemency*; those also which he adorned with the opinions of ten orators under the guise of school declamations; those which he published on natural questions; and those in philosophy for which Quintilian reproached him as insufficiently careful. Everywhere he is encountered as a faithful guardian of virtue, everywhere as an enemy of vices—so great, indeed, that Fronto, according to some Plutarch’s grandson, whom Juvenal mentions in the opening of his first satire:

> “Fronto’s plane-trees and the shattered marbles cry aloud”  
> (Juvenal I.12),

always, I say, maintained that Seneca uprooted all errors so completely that he seemed to restore the golden ages and, by his work [Col. 0764C], to bring back among humankind the gods who had gone into exile from the human race, joining them with men in fellowship.

I readily agree that Quintilian was more learned and surpassed him in sharpness and weight of expression. But Seneca is more diligent; and by as much as he is defeated in rhetoric, by so much does he conquer in ethics. Quintilian himself also counts frugality among the great and chief goods, and is so great in commending it that he alone could suffice. Yet who does not praise it? Who does not regard it as necessary?

But lest luxurious persons accuse me, a praiser of frugality, of avarice, I believe and acknowledge that it is joined with liberality. Cicero, Julius Caesar, and others are my witnesses—men whom no one would dare accuse of stinginess. Much has been said above against avarice, and the duties of liberality will readily become known from the books *On Duties* [Col. 0764D]. Yet, if the genuine face of liberality is to be uncovered, the nobler, more praiseworthy, and unquestionably best manner of giving is that which excludes hope of recompense. For giving in expectation of return is foreign to liberality and akin to avarice. A moneylender, to receive more, sometimes gives something lavishly beforehand. Hence the poet:

> Because you send great gifts to old men and widows,  
> Gargilianus, you wish to be called generous.  
>
> Nothing is more sordid; nothing is fouler than you,  
> who can call your snares gifts.  
>
> Thus the deceitful hook indulges greedy fishes;  
> thus clever bait deceives foolish beasts.  
>
> I shall teach you what giving freely is, what donating is:  
> if you do not know, give gifts, Gargilianus, to me.  
> (Martial IV.54)

[Col. 0765A] Do you wish to see a liberal man? Do you wish to hear of true and fruitful generosity? Turn your eyes toward the man who, swarming with worms, lies upon a dunghill and scrapes with a potsherd the discharge flowing from his body. Hear what that just man says, who feared God and departed from evil.

He certainly does not say: “There were harp, lyre, psaltery, sambuca, and every kind of musician at my banquets.” He does not say: “I feasted splendidly every day, seeking flavours through every element, taking great pains to discover from what material excrement might be produced or how a distended belly might easily foam over into lust.” He does not say: “I clothed myself in purple and fine linen, or embroidered work, desiring that which, by the interlacing of needle and comb in silken places, has covered empty life with false images; and I glittered in gilded garments, surrounded by variegation.”

[Col. 0765B] He did not say:

> Beggars, actors, buffoons, all that whole tribe,  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.2.2)

noisy hunters, lying confectioners, vain performers, gluttonous parasites, deceitful prostitutes, tale-bearers, liars and informers, or singers together of empty stories, flocked to me from every side. He does not say: “I fed lions, bears, monkeys, and monsters of this kind, or disgraceful products of nature.”

What then? Are these not the things by which the liberality of our age is made illustrious? Can generosity almost exist without them? “Let my shoulder,” he says, “fall from its joint, and let my arm be broken from its bones, if I denied to the poor what they desired; if I made the eyes of a widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat of it; if the stranger remained outside [Col. 0765C] and my door was not open to the traveller; if I despised one passing by because he had no clothing, or the poor man without a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was not warmed by the fleece of my sheep” (Job 31).

Which seems to you more liberal: this man, or Antony, who believed that liberality could not be satisfied unless he supplied the belly and every vice of utter luxury? Do you see how the suspicion of avarice may be avoided frugally in many ways?

The Apostle commends the good of hospitality; through it, hosts so attentive to God were pleasing to Him that they deserved even to receive angels as guests. Abraham meets the men coming down the road, desiring the grace of exercising liberality; having overcome them with humility and entreaties, he brings the angels into his lodging [Col. 0765D]. Yet he does not set before them incentives to gluttony, nor does he make the calf that he takes from the herd into a Trojan dish by lavish outlay and the art of cooks.

Lot also, compelled by devotion, brought into his house the angels who punished luxury. Though he did not serve them for gluttony or any other luxury, nothing was lacking in charity—so much so that he preferred to expose his virgin daughters to the fury of the Sodomites rather than his guests.

When a feast-day was being observed in Tobit’s house, he said: “Go and bring some of our tribe who fear God” (Tobit 2); for he thought that a feast-day could not be celebrated unless charity had added someone to the household gathering. But in all these cases there is the same ordered administration of charity. For Abraham, seeing those who came down the road [Col. 0766A], gives greater authority to those who walk in the way of conduct—that is, according to the law of the Lord. And they are rightly described as descending, because grace had sent them down to the sight of the faithful householder for visitation and to furnish him an occasion for deserving reward.

Likewise, Tobit first recognizes his own tribe, which specially acknowledged the Lord; and within that tribe he prefers, not those commended by blood or the enticements of an emptied world, but those made illustrious by divine fear. The holy man certainly did not bring in ventriloquists and idle talkers, but those who bore before them the image of the God whom he worshipped.

But did the festivity of the day, the gathering of brethren, or an abundance of food delay this holy man from performing what custom required? Indeed, while the guests were rejoicing, he was reproached by his brethren, but went out after sunset—because earlier it was not permitted—to bury a Hebrew whom he had heard had been struck down by the impious [Col. 0766B]. Nor did he fear offending the ruler while performing the duty of charity. In this he was plainly like the man who preferred to expose himself and his offspring to a grave outrage from his luxurious fellow citizens rather than expose his guests.

The disciples too used persuasion to detain in lodging the Lord when he wished to go farther; and, prescribing for us by example the pattern of hospitality, they constrained him. They seemed to him to have yielded first place, though afterwards they recognized him as Lord in the breaking of bread. For we do not read that any other delicacies, except perhaps those required by necessity, were set before him.

Our Britain also produced Alban, distinguished in the duty of hospitality, who preferred to expose himself to the weapons of tyrants rather than the Christian guest whom he had received. Why do I speak of believers, when even unbelievers have been accustomed, even against enemies and at their own risk, to protect those whom they had received in hospitality for less than four days? For anyone who denied the protection of humanity to an enemy—that is, a stranger—before the fifth day incurred the charge of wrongdoing. As Cicero testifies, because hospitality had to be shown fairly, *hostis*—“enemy”—was anciently the term for the person whom we now call a stranger. Whoever is inhumane toward such a person is unjust by ancient law. The tablets of the laws and the legal title “the appointed day with a *hostis*” make this clear [Col. 0766C].

But one who shows humanity to a guest and fulfils charity withholds none of those things which reason permits to be offered. He indeed pours out his heart upon guests; but mindful of duty, if he is discerning, he does not incite them to shameful acts, nor urge anyone toward what he himself would not wish to be urged toward. Therefore every humanity and sober liberality must be exercised toward a stranger who is a guest; and the native host ought to receive fuller gratitude from the stranger, who should have a tenacious memory of benefits.

Nor does the fact of an opposing religion or of earlier enmity destroy this gratitude. For blessed Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, when constrained by a storm and the urgency of the moment and detained in the Alps, turned aside into a sanctuary of Apollo, worshipped there by the inhabitants. He was received with very attentive hospitality by the priest of the place, though that priest was pagan. Mindful of duty and hospitality [Col. 0767A], Gregory granted at the priest’s request release to Apollo, whom he had suspended from giving oracles and deceiving souls.

These matters may be found more fully in Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History*. According to his account, the priest pursued blessed Gregory with complaints, accusing him of ingratitude and reproaching him that his humanity had been repaid with an unjust measure. He brought back from the holy man this letter to his Apollo:

> Gregory to Apollo: “I permit you to return to your place and do what you were accustomed to do.”

When the priest delivered the letter to the idol, the demon was released and began, in his usual fashion, to deceive by oracles. Astonished at the majesty of the one whose humble servants could thus command even the gods of the nations, suspending and tormenting them by a word, the priest despised his Apollo, followed Gregory, and attached himself to him. He who had been Apollo’s priest became Christ’s disciple; and he advanced so greatly in faith and religion that he is believed to have succeeded blessed Gregory in the governance of the Church of Neocaesarea [Col. 0767B]. Thus the host’s attentiveness was rewarded first humanely and then beneficially.

Finally, even if the ethical philosophers had no rule concerning the civility to be exercised toward guests, blessed Benedict, in his chapter on guests, seems to express frugal humanity not only religiously but also courteously and politely. Yet what is read and observed by many in the book of Cistercian customs, concerning two points in establishing hospitality, is alien from every form of civility—indeed, I should say, from humanity itself—if it is true that these customs of such great perfection contain the rule that no meat is set before guests and nothing is bought for their sake. For perfection itself relaxes fasts on account of a guest and in many respects grants much indulgence to charity, departing from its own strictness.

Even the pagan seems in this matter to adhere more faithfully and familiarly to virtue, when he ordains that what is within should be set before guests with cheerful moderation:

> “And what is not at home but is possessed by a neighbour should be bought.”

I would judge it better and more perfect that virtue itself should relax a little and be moderately foolish. For, as the moralist says, it is sometimes pleasant to be foolish in the proper place; and this is as consonant with virtue as with humanity [Col. 0767D].

Augustine and Jerome likewise offer many things relevant to this subject. Blessed Gregory too reproves the election of a certain man as though he were avaricious, because he had heard that the man had invited no one to practise charity in his house. Yet I would not suppose that so great a father wished a luxurious banquet to be prepared for the invited guests.

Who then doubts that avarice can be avoided by frugality? Or who would dare stain Abraham, Lot, Tobit, and Job with the mark of avarice? You have heard the description of blessed Job. Now, if you wish, hear how M. Caelius describes Antony:

> “Those who entered came upon him overcome by drunken sleep, snoring from the depth of his whole chest, doubling his belching breaths; and his distinguished female companions lay stretched crosswise on every couch [Col. 0768A], while the rest lay scattered about everywhere. Terrified at the enemy’s arrival, they tried to awaken Antony: they cried his name, raised his neck in vain; some called more gently in his ear, others more forcefully, and some even struck him. Though he recognized the voice and touch of all of them, he sought the neck of whichever was nearest in an embrace. Awakened, he could neither cease sleeping nor, drunk, become awake; but, in a half-sleeping stupor, he was tossed about among the hands of centurions and concubines.”

These things were either true or plausible. Nothing more credible could have been invented, more forcefully reproached, or more plainly displayed. In short, one must either pursue virtue or despair of glory; for glory arises from nowhere else.

## CHAPTER XIV. That nothing is more fruitful for glory than the praise and favour of good persons, especially writers; that familiarity with the disgraceful harms more than it profits; and that glory is spread by a single good deed or saying.

[Col. 0768B]

There is indeed a difference between the desire for human glory and the ardour of desire. For although those who delight excessively in human glory are inclined even to desire condemnation ardently, those who desire true glory—even if it consists in human praises—take pains not to displease persons of sound judgment. It matters greatly who is pleased by you, whom you please, and by what means. Nor is it glorious to be praised by someone whose familiarity smells of disgrace.

The praise of one learned person has profited many and sufficed for glory; and the commendation of many has often produced infamy [Col. 0768C]. In rhetoric there is a celebrated topic drawn from companionship: it indicates similarity of character, and it is often taught that friendship and commendation derive from this source.

“The wise man says: ‘I do not wish to be praised by those whose praise is blame, nor do I fear blame from those whose accusation is praise.’” Therefore, when actors, mimics, parasites, and such human absurdities show, by the evidence of their lives, nothing praiseworthy, is it not manifest folly for a man, in order to shine, to hunt after the favour of those who are covered with filth and whose favour cannot be acquired except through disgraceful means?

Marcus Antony bestowed Pompey’s vast estate and almost the wealth of the entire world upon such monstrous people; yet he is not made illustrious by their praises, but appears to posterity all the more sordid for them [Col. 0768D]. Had he earned the favour of one wise man or eminent writer, something celebrated from him would have flowed down to posterity.

Virgil perpetuated Marcellus’s glory without great merits of virtue; and, distorting historical truth by poetic licence, he persuaded posterity that Dido—though she was most chaste—had been seized by an incestuous love for a guest whom, by the chronology, she could not have seen. Nisus and Euryalus would not have reached our age had the divine poems of Maro not rescued them from oblivion. He still fulfils the promise and does not allow their names to be obliterated by time:

> Live happily, if my songs have any power:  
> no day shall ever remove you from remembering time.  
> (Virgil)

Why then do those who purchase, at such expense, the favour of buffoons and contemptible slaves in their disgrace not seek to please honourable and learned men, especially writers? Do they not wish their absurdities to be handed down to posterity? Lucilius would be unknown if Seneca’s letters had not made him illustrious. Virgil, Varius, and Lucan added more to Caesar’s glory by their praises than that immense treasury by which he despoiled city and world. No one would recognize the wisdom of the Ithacan or the strength of Peleus’s son unless Homer had published them with divine genius. Therefore nothing seems to me wiser for a man hastening toward glory than the favour of faithful writers. Nothing is more foolish than to court Tigellius, who is unable to redeem even his own reputation [Col. 0769A].

There are many good qualities of character [Col. 0769B] which many judge well, although many do not possess them; and the rarer they are, the more distinguished they are. By these, therefore, some strive for glory, authority, and dominion. But whoever desires to rule and command without the desire for glory by which a person fears displeasing those who judge rightly, often seeks through the most open crimes to obtain what he loves. Accordingly, the person who desires glory either strives by the true road or at least contends by frauds and deceits, wishing to appear good when he is not.

And therefore, for one who possesses virtues, it is a great virtue to despise glory, because contempt for it is before the sight of God, but is not disclosed to human judgment. Yet although he makes little of the fact that his admirers praise him, he does not make little of the fact that they love him. Nor does he wish to deceive those who praise him, lest he deceive those who love him [Col. 0769C]. Therefore he earnestly strives that the One from whom a person receives whatever is rightly praised in him should rather be praised.

But a contemptuous despiser of glory who is greedy for dominion surpasses beasts either in the vices of credulity or of luxury. Such, as the great Father Augustine testifies, were the Romans. For when their vices are surveyed, no people is worse; when their virtues are surveyed, none is found better. Yet they subdued other peoples not by cruel domination but by gentle rule. And what moderation acquired, cruelty or luxury destroyed. For, though they had lost their reputation, they did not lack the desire for dominion.

But Nero Caesar first attained the summit, as it were the citadel, of this vice. His luxury was so great [Col. 0769D] that nothing manly was thought to be feared from him; his cruelty so great that, were he unknown, he would not be believed to possess anything soft. No one was more gluttonous; no one delighted more in the company of singers, actors, and the like; no one was more luxurious. Indeed, to make a display of elegance and liberality, he never wore the same garment twice. Yet who is so ruined as to praise him?

Before the power of Demosthenes’ eloquence became known, he is said to have sought the brilliance of elaborate dress, knowing that purple sells an advocate. But after he gained recognition and fame through eloquence, he was content with a toga, saying that he wished his glory to rest upon himself rather than upon the splendour of clothing or elaborate attire.

[Col. 0770A]

> Every colour, station, and circumstance suited Aristippus;  
> clothed however he pleased, he went through the most celebrated places.  
> (Horace)

For a man whom his own honour raises is not brought low by another’s poverty. Praise that depends on external things seems to be a solicited vote. Surely a person shines more brightly by the title of one outstanding virtue than by the most splendid instrument of luxury and every allurement of vanity. Since every virtue is strong through itself, justice shines most brightly.

Themistocles provides both testimony and example of this. After he had compelled the Athenians, by a most salutary counsel, to take to their ships, had expelled King Xerxes and his forces from Greece, restored the ruins of his country to their former condition, and was secretly gathering resources to obtain the leadership [Col. 0770B] of Greece, he said in the assembly that he had provided a measure through his deliberation which, if it attained its effect, would be nothing greater or more advantageous for the Athenian people; but he declared that it should not be made public, asking that someone be appointed to whom it might be explained privately.

Aristides—or, as others prefer, Aristotle—was therefore appointed, although a calculation of dates shows that Themistocles and Aristotle were not contemporaries. When he learned that Themistocles wished to burn the Lacedaemonians’ fleet, which had been drawn ashore at Gytheum, so that, once it had been destroyed, maritime dominion might pass to the Athenians, he went out before the citizens and reported that Themistocles was considering a plan as advantageous as it was utterly unjust. Immediately the entire assembly cried out that what was not just was utterly inexpedient [Col. 0770C], and ordered him to abandon the undertaking. Thus, by the people’s decree, justice was preferred to prudence—or rather, that which justice opposes was judged to be not prudence but cunning.
