Zaleucus, having secured the city of the Locrians by laws most salutary and useful, saw his son convicted of adultery. Under the law he had established, the youth should have been deprived of both eyes; but the whole city, in honour of the father, wished to remit the necessity of this punishment. For a while Zaleucus resisted. At last overcome by the people’s entreaties, he first had one of his own eyes removed and then one of his son’s, leaving to each the use of sight. Thus, through an admirable balance of equity, dividing himself between the merciful father and the just lawgiver, he rendered to the law the punishment due in measure.

Does not the memory of such persons cling more faithfully to the minds of hearers than if they had fed an army of rogues or thrust a succession of changes of clothing before the eyes of an untrained crowd?

Come, what did Solon’s wisdom achieve? “The last day,” he says, “is the judge of happiness, and the funeral pyre confirms the honour of the title ‘wise.’ For the beginnings of affairs belong to fortune; the end alone consecrates philosophy. Likewise, a person has nothing to fear except lest the end exclude philosophy.”

Thus, when he saw one of his friends grievously mourning, he led him up to the citadel and urged him to cast his eyes over every part of the buildings beneath. Then he said: “Consider now with yourself how many griefs there have been beneath these roofs in former times, how many now occur, and how many shall come in succeeding ages; and cease to bewail human misfortunes as though they were your own. For, if you attend rightly, cities are nothing but pitiable enclosures of human disasters” [Col. 0771A].

That king also, of subtle judgment, is said by Valerius to have examined for a long time the fresh diadem handed to him before placing it on his head, and to have said: “O cloth more noble than fortunate! If anyone fully understood how many cares, dangers, and miseries it contains, he would not take it up even as it lay on the ground.”

Aristophanes also says that one ought not to rear a lion in a city; but, if it has been reared, one must comply with it. He warns that young men of exceptional nobility and impetuous talent should be restrained; but that, once power has been obtained through excessive favour and lavish indulgence [Col. 0771B], one should not even hinder them—because it is foolish and useless to oppose the strength which one has oneself nourished.

Aristotle, sending his pupil Callisthenes to Alexander, urged him either never to speak with him or to speak most pleasantly, so that at royal ears he might be safer by silence or more welcome in speech. But Callisthenes, while rebuking Alexander for delighting in Persian obeisance and striving to reform his manners, was deprived of life.

The same Aristotle said that one ought not to speak about oneself in either direction, since to praise oneself is vanity and to blame oneself is folly. When Agesilaus learned by night of a revolt arising against the Lacedaemonian state, he immediately suspended Lycurgus’s laws, which forbade punishment to be imposed upon the uncondemned [Col. 0771C]. After the guilty had been seized and killed, he immediately restored the same laws, providing at once that the salutary punishment might neither be unjust nor be hindered by law.

Hannibal, defeated in a naval battle and fearing to pay the penalty for the loss of the fleet, diverted the blame by cunning. Before news of the disaster reached home from that unhappy battle, he sent one of his friends to Carthage. Entering the senate house, the man immediately asked whether it was necessary to fight the Roman forces which had arrived. When the senate shouted, “It is necessary!” the messenger said: “The battle was fought, and it was lost,” leaving them no freedom to condemn the act which they themselves had judged should be done.

Gorgias of Leontini, teacher of Isocrates [Col. 0771D] and many men of great talent, lived with such innocence that, when questioned in his one hundred and seventh year why he wished to remain in life for so long, he answered: “Because I have nothing with which to accuse my old age.” I believe this resulted from grace and his great mastery of letters, in which he excelled in his age, so much so that he was the first to dare ask in a public gathering what subject each person wished to hear discussed. Hence all Greece set up for him in the temple of Delphic Apollo a statue of solid gold, whereas it had previously set up only gilded statues of others.

Many such examples will occur which can furnish matter for true praise, if anyone recounts the cunning sayings or deeds of the ancients—their *strategemata* and also their strategic acts. But because *strategemata* have often been mentioned and the matter is not everywhere known by its name [Col. 0772A], Valerius Maximus defines *strategema* thus: it is an outstanding part of cunning, remote from every reproach, whose operations, because they can scarcely be expressed fittingly by a Latin term, are called *strategemata* by the Greek word.

Properly speaking, however, *strategemata* are things belonging to military affairs; indeed, military commanders are called *stratilatae* from this. But matters which, contrary to the force of the proper term, belong to other subjects are, according to the testimony of Julius Frontinus, called *strategematica*. For a *strategematicum* differs from a *strategema* as genus differs from species.

Publius Clodius returns again; I shall append a few of his sayings, for to have said even the least of them is greater and more fruitful for glory than to have done what those do who disembowel themselves for the empty love of praise [Col. 0772B]. He says, therefore:

> He who gives to one worthy receives a benefit by giving.  
>
> Endure; do not blame what cannot be changed.  
>
> He to whom more is permitted than is right wants more than is permitted.  
>
> An eloquent companion on the road is a vehicle.  
>
> Frugality is the misery of a good reputation.  
>
> An heir’s tears are laughter beneath a mask.  
>
> Patience, when injured, more often becomes rage.  
>
> He wrongly accuses Neptune who is shipwrecked a second time.  
>
> By excessive wrangling, truth is lost.  
>
> If you quickly refuse what is requested, that is part of the benefit.  
>
> Treat a friend as though you thought he could become an enemy.  
>
> By bearing an old injury, you invite a new one.  
>
> No danger is ever overcome without danger.  
>
> The man whom many fear must fear many.  
> (Publilius Syrus, in Gellius XVII.6)

Finally, even from a slight indication of virtue, whether in word or deed, reputation is extended; but when virtue is absent, however great the expenditure, it produces not glory so much as disgrace [Col. 0772C].

## CHAPTER XV. That honourableness is either the sole object of pursuit, or should be pursued above all else; that within it liberality has an altogether chief place; and, conversely, that avarice is greatly opposed to glory.

Just as glory—which, as Cicero held, is widespread reputation accompanied by praise—arises from the root of virtue and is made illustrious solely by its light, so disgrace, confusion, and every other dishonour derive their origin and growth from vice. Whether honourableness alone is good, as some Stoics hold, or whether it is the chief good and should be pursued above all others, as the Peripatetics maintain, this is altogether beyond doubt: nothing desirable is opposed to honourableness [Col. 0772D].

Other things are praised and not foolishly desired: good health, distinguished birth, abundance of possessions. But none of these makes a base or dishonourable person praiseworthy. From sound health comes strength; from strength, rashness; from rashness, violence; from violence, the spur of revenge, kindled like a torch of hatred and wars. Then follows contempt for justice, violation of laws, and the restless shaking of public order.

Distinguished birth produces arrogance, seeks power, tramples inferiors, despises equals, disdains to have superiors, speaks grandly, and swells entirely with lofty and great blood, as though it had itself done something for which it ought to be noble. Forgetful of itself, it forgets the things that lie behind and, without the cultivation of virtue, stretches itself toward what lies ahead—a ridiculous imitator of Thraso. The moralist says:

> I would rather Thersites were your father, provided that you were like Achilles,  
> son of Aeacus, and took up Vulcan’s arms,  
> than that Achilles should produce you like Thersites.  
> (Juvenal VIII.269)

Yet I do not wish our Simonides to suppose that this was said to injure him. He was indeed born from royal ancestors, nobler than the Capitoline families, the Marcelli, and all who look down upon the arena; and, as though he had burst forth from purer and more fortunate sheep, he is far nobler than his full brothers and uterine brothers, as they themselves testify. I would readily believe that whatever in the mass of his lineage had from the beginning been more pure and of more refined nature flowed together into him, so that he might shine as the star of his people; while whatever was more dreg-like and obscure settled in his full and uterine brothers [Col. 0773B].

Yet they rejoice as much in his distinction as in their own lowliness, lest, when circumstances require it, nobility of lineage should prevent them, on the ground of kinship, from being joined in marriage with neighbouring peoples. Thus Simonides’ kings, governors, princes, tribunes, centurions, and foremost provincials yielded place. Content with their modest estate, they strive through their own virtue; they account nothing in lawful duties base or disgraceful, and, if need requires, do not disdain to remember the kitchen or to practise its skill. They remember that no one judges dumb animals noble unless they are strong:

> “[lacuna] namely, the bird …”

[Col. 0773C] Thus we praise the horse whose abundant palm of victory readily burns hot and exults in the roaring Circus.

Noble is he from whatever pasture he comes, whose flight is conspicuous before the others, and whose dust is first upon the course.

But the offspring of Corythus and of the Hirpini, if rare victory has not rested upon the yoke,

[lacuna] are compelled to change masters for trifling prices, and draw post-carriages with necks worn raw. For nobility is virtue alone, and the only virtue. (JUVENAL, *Satires* VIII, 110.)

Therefore high birth and the splendor of distinguished blood, although Simonides may boast that they are in themselves something great, are nothing other than a manifestation of character: glorious indeed if the persons are good, disgraceful if they are bad. Yet, in my judgment—whatever he may think—high birth has this one good quality: it imposes the necessity of uprightness. [Col. 0773D] But abundance of possessions now kindles greed, now equips luxury for one’s own ruin and destruction. Of this:

Its appetite is ingenious; it turns votes toward plunder and the clamour of gain, (PETRONIUS),

so that

The people are for sale, the senate-house of the fathers for sale.

It dissolves strength and breaks both sexes into sexual indulgence; it resists the rule of law and nature. It abrogates, extinguishes, and buries the latter; it makes it foolish, weakens, and overturns it. Thus law is no law for it, and nature is for it almost idle and drunk.

[Col. 0774A]

Nature seeks itself and does not find itself. Therefore all are pleased by prostitutes, by steps made effeminate through bodily weakness, by loose hair, by so many novel names of clothing, and by whatever seeks a man.

Yet would that, under this dominion of luxury, men might be found—or at least men like women—who nevertheless obey nature or law. From these things it is clear that the chief praise belongs neither to health, nor to high birth, nor to abundance, but to virtue, whose instruments these are and for whose sake they are therefore to be desired. For it does not befit nature, which has made virtue either the sole thing to be sought or the thing to be sought above all others, to have made its instruments not worth seeking.

And in this the Peripatetics appear to hold the sounder view: while they acknowledge that virtue needs instruments for the exercise of deeds, they also acknowledge that the instruments themselves, though for the sake of something else, are to be sought. [Col. 0774B] The Stoics, however, maintain that virtue suffices by itself for happiness. I do not accuse them of error, but say that virtue is more readily effective through instruments.

Moreover, as I remember having said elsewhere, although every virtue is pleasing, generosity is most pleasing, because it benefits the greatest number. Certainly, if means are lacking, it pours out its inward parts—that is, it bestows its own affection. Otherwise, how, according to the Apostle, does charity remain in one who, when his neighbour’s need knocks at the door, closes the inward parts of his heart? (1 John 3.) Conversely, the most ungrateful and hateful vice is that which benefits others neither in deed nor in affection. This is avarice: an investigator of hidden gains, a most greedy abyss for manifest plunder, happy neither in the fruit of possessing nor—most wretched—in the desire to acquire.

What do you not compel mortal hearts to do, accursed hunger for gold? (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* III, 56.)

Eriphyle sold her husband’s life for gold. Greece sold its liberty to Philip. Valerius Maximus also inveighs against avarice itself through these examples:

> “When someone in Greece had forged a false will in the case of the very wealthy Lucius Muni­tius Basilus, and, in order to secure its confirmation, had entered in the tablets as heirs Marcus Crassus and Quintus Hortensius, the most powerful men of our state, though Munit(i)us was unknown to them, each of them nevertheless, greedy for money, did not reject the profit of another’s crime, although the fraud was evident. How great a fault—and how lightly I have described it! The lights of the senate-house, the ornaments of the forum, covered with their own authority the crime which they ought to have punished, enticed by the prospect of shameful gain. Yet avarice displayed considerably greater power in Quintus Cassius: in Spain, having caught Silius and Publius Albinus with daggers, intending to kill him, he agreed with the former for fifty times one hundred thousand sesterces and with the latter for sixty times one hundred thousand, and let them go. Would you doubt that, if twice as much had been offered, he would calmly have presented them with his own throat as well?  
>   
> “But before all others avarice took possession of the heart of Vettius Septimuleius. Being an intimate of Gaius Gracchus, he endured to cut off his head and carry it through the city fixed upon a spear, because the consul Opimius had proclaimed that he would pay him its weight in gold. Some relate that he filled the hollowed portion of the head with molten lead, so that it might weigh more. Let Gracchus have been seditious; let him have perished as a salutary example: nevertheless, the criminal hunger of his client ought not to have hungered after insults even upon the fallen man.  
>   
> “The avarice of Septimuleius deserves hatred; that of King Ptolemy of Cyprus deserves to be pursued with laughter. For when, through anxious miserliness, he had corrupted great wealth, and saw that he would perish because of it, he put all his money aboard ships and put out to sea, intending, after boring holes in the fleet, that they should perish at his discretion and his enemies be deprived of the spoil. Yet he could not bear to sink his gold and silver, but brought home the future reward of his own death. Beyond doubt, this man did not possess riches; he was possessed by riches: king of an island in title, but in spirit the pitiable slave of money.”

So Valerius. But even worse examples of avarice may be found. [Col. 0775B] For greed blinded the eyes of a prophet, and the Apostle, corrupted by money, delivered the innocent Lord to the hands of the ungodly to be crucified. It can indeed be defiled by words, but not sufficiently, because it is more ugly and shameful than human speech can express.

Avarice must therefore be avoided with greater diligence because it clings more tenaciously through the appearance of usefulness, and harms more ruinously through the destruction of charity. Hence it has formed a ridiculous and pitiable intimacy with old men: the less they need, the more greedily they covet; and the sooner they must part with their possessions, the more sparingly they employ them for use. For the hand extended in youth to give is drawn back in old age; and the hand drawn in during youth is either never or rarely opened in old men.

[Col. 0775C] Yet, when through nature’s kindness freedom is near at hand for them, they subject themselves, through empty fear, to most wretched slavery. Diogenes says: “Nature’s need does not fear fortune.” Blessed Jerome also says:

> “It is a great exultation of the soul, when you are content with little, to have the world beneath your feet and to exchange all its power, luxurious feasts, and the things for which riches are acquired, for cheap food and a coarser tunic.”

These things are praiseworthy, certainly, if they are done not for reputation but for conscience, which bears all things with equanimity. For, as Xenophon says: “The conscience of the righteous knows how to despise curses.” The use of things, then, is praiseworthy or blameworthy; the distinction lies only in things themselves. Hence for Diaspenis money is an honour when lavishly spent, a punishment when hoarded.

Macrobius says: “By every means, and by cutting with fire and sword, and by the whole art of healing, there must be removed languor from the body, ignorance from the mind, luxury from the belly, sedition from the state, discord from the household, and, in general, intemperance from all things.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On the four rivers which arise from the Epicurean fountain of lust and make a flood by which the world is almost overwhelmed; and on the contrary waters and Esau’s garments

All these matters converge to show that a condition of tranquillity in public or private affairs cannot arise except from the fountain of wisdom, whatever Epicurus may think. It was said above that wisdom is the most fertile garden of delights, from which the rivers of the four virtues arise. [Col. 0776A] Conversely, the garden of the Epicureans has its own fountain, lust, which likewise gives birth to rivers watering this entire valley of tears and misery, into which the exile was cast who chose to do what pleased him and what he was permitted to do.

One stream, as it were, is the love of possession, through which abundance is sought for sufficiency of goods; in it avarice labours to possess, or to know, beyond what is lawful. Another pours forth luxury’s enticements and flows into various pleasures, as it strives toward the delights of tranquillity and joy. A third gathers powers by which it may defend nature’s freedom and repel the injuries of every trouble; and, when it has overflowed in strength, it bursts out into the hateful vein of tyranny. The fourth swells deceitfully from the desire for renown and reverence, while it seeks pre-eminence.

[Col. 0776B] These are the four rivers that pour forth and encompass the world, gushing from the fountain of perverse will. They have their seat in the depths and draw their origin from the mud of vanity. When they have risen, they produce diverse streams from themselves and, like the swelling waters of a flood, overwhelm the world, destroy living creatures, and erase everything so completely that the earth might seem destined to be reduced to wilderness—were it not that the ark, the house of the Lord, preserves a few, that is, eight souls, namely the sons of resurrection. These are surely those whom the Lord chose beforehand from all flesh. Yet those who are in the flood of many waters shall not come near him.

And the love of advantage, of which we have spoken, pours these waters as it were into a deep sea; and, as wickedness gains strength, the Lord, as though the floodgates of heaven had been opened, rains down various occasions of sin to increase the flood, permitting, once grace has been withdrawn, him who is filthy to become filthier still (Revelation 22), and striking, as though in vengeance, the person whom he abandons to his own choice.

[Col. 0776C] Not that I would say that the desire for advantage, if moderate, is blameworthy, or that a sufficient abundance of possessions, joy of mind, the natural love of freedom, or the merit of pre-eminence is criminal. But none of these brings about what it promises; sought in that manner, it instead produces the contrary result.

Yet all these are good if the son who, taught by grace, wrestles rightly against flesh and blood and is to be blessed by the Father of joy and exultation, makes use of them; he is then clothed in them as in a flowery, fruitful, and delightful garment. [Col. 0776D] But if the man of blood, the carnal brother, despising the intimate fellowship of mother grace, usurps all these garments of character, they neither give fragrance, nor adorn, nor restore by feeding. Perhaps this is what is meant when Esau’s garments are written to have pleased in Jacob, while Esau himself is not written either to have used them or to have given their sweet fragrance to his father. For while he abuses good things, he cannot be pleasing to one whose senses are sound.

Therefore the empty appearance of good neither satisfies, nor gladdens, nor frees, nor exalts. Some things have already been said above against luxury, avarice, and vainglory. The craving for power has thus far in some fashion remained untouched. Although it seems to support freedom and eminence, it more ruinously leads the erring person away from the truth of both.

[Col. 0777A] For this is what introduces the most destructive plague and, bringing about the birth of tyranny, labours to extinguish the fabric of tranquillity and peace, than which nothing is more healthful. For these rivers extinguish charity in those to whom life is denied. In them Tantalus suffers in the fables without satiety, and the prophetic word reproves the thirst of those dwelling in these waters. Therefore it invites the thirsty to waters set before them, waters flowing from the Spirit without exchange, that they may freely receive from grace wine and milk. “Why,” it says, “do you weigh out silver for what is not bread, and your labour for what does not satisfy? Hearken diligently to me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight itself in fatness” (Isaiah 55).

Not surely in that fatness in which the soul has no delight but the flesh does; in which the beloved one kicked—grown fat, thick, and bloated—but in that in which the son is blessed so that, in the dew of grace coming upon him and in the richness of free choice, he may wisely understand God’s will, powerfully fulfil it, and patiently endure it.

[Col. 0777B] These, then, are fattening and sweet waters, and waters that temper all others, because by them the wood of the cross has absorbed the saltness of those other waters, sweetened them, and, through the infusion of heavenly wisdom, made them drinkable for the salvation and satisfaction of souls. These waters also set free: they prevent, restrain, or punish every assault of tyranny. Thus it is not empty power but truth, established in equity, that frees. Although vanity promises liberation, those are in no way truly free except those whom the Son has made free.

Distinguish the freedom of nature, grace, and glory, and you will find that none of them comes from vanity; nor will you encounter any condition more servile than that of a tyrant. For if “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3), then the person driven by an evil spirit is certainly crushed under most miserable slavery.

## CHAPTER XVII. How the tyrant differs from the prince; on the tyranny of priests; and how shepherd, thief, and hireling differ from one another

How the prince differs from the tyrant was said above when, with Plutarch as author, Trajan’s instruction was considered; and the duties of the prince and the members of the commonwealth were carefully explained. It will therefore be easier and require fewer words to make known what must be said in contrast concerning the tyrant.

[Col. 0777D] A tyrant, then, as philosophers have portrayed him, is one who oppresses the people by violent domination, just as one who governs by laws is a prince. Law, moreover, is the gift of God: the form of equity, the norm of justice, the image of the divine will, the safeguard of salvation, the union and strengthening of peoples, the rule of duties, the exclusion and destruction of vices, and the punishment of violence and of every injury.

Law is attacked either by violence or by deceit; it is laid waste, as it were, by the savage ferocity of a lion or undermined by the snares of a dragon. However this occurs, it is plain that grace is attacked and that God is in some fashion provoked to battle. The prince fights for the laws and the people’s freedom; the tyrant considers nothing accomplished unless he empties the laws of force and calls the people down into slavery.

[Col. 0778A] The prince is a certain image of divinity; the tyrant is an image of hostile power and Luciferian perversity. For he imitates the one who desired to set his throne in the north and to be like the Most High, yet with goodness removed. If he sought to be conformed to goodness, he would by no means strive to seize the glory of power or wisdom. Perhaps, however, he aspired to equality in the authority to reward.

As an image of divinity, the prince is to be loved, revered, and honoured; as an image of perversity, the tyrant must often even be killed. Iniquity is the origin of the tyrant; from a poisoned root a malignant and pestilential tree springs up and puts forth shoots, a tree to be cut down by whatever axe may be at hand. For unless iniquity and injustice, the destroyer of charity, had brought about tyranny, secure peace and perpetual tranquillity would have possessed peoples forever, and no one would think of extending boundaries.

[Col. 0778B] Indeed, as the great Father Augustine testifies, kingdoms would be tranquil and enjoy friendly peace, as different households do in a well-ordered city, or different persons in the same household. Or perhaps, what is more credible, there would be no kingdoms at all, which, as ancient histories make clear, iniquity either presumed to claim for itself or extorted from the Lord.

Nor do kings alone exercise tyranny: very many private persons are tyrants when they employ whatever power they have for what is forbidden. Nor should it disturb you that I seem to have associated kings with tyrants. Although *king* (*rex*) is derived from *right* (*rectum*), which befits a prince, the title may by misuse be applied to a tyrant. Hence:

What free people could raise any man higher? I have ascended, and above me I left nothing but kingdoms. (VIRGIL.)

And:

My hope of peace will be to have touched the tyrant’s right hand. (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VII, 166.)

And, if one may speak of a duty opposed to duty and to the rule of right living, the judgment of one man reveals all the duties—or rather the vices—of tyrants. Photinus is the first among the monsters of the Pellaean house—that is, among the other prodigies of Egypt—distinguished by foulness and cruelty. He dared to condemn Pompey to death, or rather, in the habitual presumption of tyrants’ character, expressed their ways:

[Col. 0778D]

Ptolemy, many guilty men make what is lawful and right. Praised loyalty pays the penalty when it supports, he says, those whom fortune crushes. Yield to fate and the gods; honour the fortunate; flee the wretched. As the stars differ from earth, as flame from sea, so expedience differs from right. The whole force of sceptres perishes if it begins to depend upon justice; regard for honour overturns the battle-line. Freedom for crimes and the removal of every limit from the sword preserve hated kingdoms. It is not permitted to do all things cruelly with impunity unless whoever wishes to be pious leaves the court. Virtue and supreme power do not coincide; he whom cruel deeds would shame will always be afraid. (LUCAN, VIII, 403.)

Therefore regard for what is honourable and just is minimal, or nonexistent, in tyrants’ eyes. Whether they are ecclesiastical or secular, they wish to be able to do everything, disregarding what precedes or follows from that power.

[Col. 0779A] Yet I would have both kinds persuaded of this: the divine judgment inflicted upon the first-created and their seed has not yet expired. Because they did not will justice when they could, it was inflicted upon them that they might be unable to obey justice even when they wish to do so. For the proverb says: “He who does not will when he can will surely not be able when he wishes.” Great Basil too is the source of this saying.

Asked by a poor little woman to intercede for her with the ruler, he took her written petition and wrote thus to the ruler: “This poor woman has come to me, saying that I can prevail with you. If therefore I can, show it.” He gave the document to the woman, who went and gave the letter to the ruler. Reading it, the ruler wrote back: “For your sake, holy Father, I wished to have mercy on the poor woman, but I could not, because she is liable for taxes.”

[Col. 0779B] The saint wrote back to him: “If, though willing, you could not, then matters stand well enough; but if, though able, you would not, Christ will lead you into the company of the needy, so that when you wish, you may not be able.” Nor did truth, which is always present to the chosen in its instrument, fail its instrument. For shortly afterwards this same ruler, attacked by imperial displeasure, was led bound among captives, either making satisfaction by his punishment to those whom he had unjustly oppressed. Yet through Basil’s prayer he was released on the sixth day after his removal, when the imperial standard came down, as the holy man had wished.

Accordingly, a king is sometimes called a tyrant, and conversely a tyrant sometimes a prince, as in: “Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves” (Isaiah 1). And elsewhere: “The chief priests and elders of the people took counsel together, that they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” (Matthew 26)—although he, of course, ought to have been set free by the just judgment of the law.

[Col. 0779C] For among the priesthood there are also many who, through sheer ambition and by all its arts, labour to exercise their own tyranny under the pretext of office. The commonwealth of the ungodly has its head and its members too, and, as though by civic institutions, strives to conform to the lawful commonwealth.

Its head, then, is the tyrant, the image of the devil; its soul is heretical, schismatic, sacrilegious priests and, to use Plutarch’s phrase, governors of provinces who attack the law of the Lord. Its heart is the wicked counsellors, like a senate of iniquity. Its eyes, ears, tongue, and unarmed hand are unjust judges, laws, and officials. Its armed hand is violent soldiers, whom Cicero calls robbers. Its feet are those who, in the lowest business, oppose the Lord’s commands and lawful institutions.

All these matters can quite easily be understood from what has been said above. Priests, however, ought not to be angry with me if I confess that tyrants may be found among them as well. Otherwise, to what purpose is that prophetic utterance:

[Col. 0779D] “Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds of Israel; prophesy and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves! Do not shepherds feed flocks? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves in the wool, and killed what was fat; but you did not feed my flock. What was weak you did not strengthen; what was sick you did not heal; what was broken you did not bind up; what was cast away you did not bring back; what was lost you did not seek; but you ruled them with harshness and with power. My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for every beast of the field, and they were scattered” (Ezekiel 34).

What else does this imprecation and rebuke of Ezekiel teach to be present, except that what ought to have been present was absent from the shepherds, and what ought to have been absent was present? Therefore the Lord says: “Behold, I myself am against the shepherds; I will demand my flock from their hand and make them cease from feeding my flock. The shepherds shall no longer feed themselves; I will deliver my flock from their mouth, and it shall no longer be food for them” (ibid.).

[Col. 0780B] Does this not seem plainly to portray the tyranny of the priesthood and to depict the life of those who seek in everything what is their own and cast behind their backs what belongs to Jesus Christ? (Philippians 2.) For this is not my utterance but that of another; indeed, it is the oracle of uncorrupted truth, setting forth a manifest distinction, in the presence of the intimate of the Most High, between the hireling, the shepherd, and the thief.

“For the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10). If you ask his duty, you will find it in the prophet already quoted:

> “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep. I will bring them out from the cloud and gather them from the darkness; I will bring them into their own land and feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the streams and in every habitation of the land. In the richest pastures, upon high mountains, shall their pastures be. They shall rest in green grass and feed in rich pastures upon the mountains of Israel. I will feed them and make them lie down. What was lost I will seek; what was cast away I will bring back; what was broken I will bind up; what was weak I will strengthen; and what was fat and strong I will preserve” (Ezekiel 34).

[Col. 0780C] Such is the care with which shepherds ought to watch over their flocks. But what follows, “And I will feed them in judgment and justice” (ibid.), plainly answers what preceded: “You ruled them with harshness and with power.” For it is written that “a weight and a weight, a measure and a measure, both are an abomination before God” (Proverbs 20).

Among people who conduct trade, however, the cleverness and deception by which they sell their own goods by one weight or measure and purchase those of others by another seems a great, though unlawful, prudence. But equity requires of a prelate that he himself should bear the burden he lays upon others and endeavour to fulfil in deed what he wishes to teach. This is to feed in judgment and justice, rather than to rule in harshness and penance. This is what those do who bind heavy and unbearable burdens upon people’s shoulders and refuse to touch them with one finger.

Hence it follows:

[Col. 0780D] “Although you drank the purest water, you muddied the rest with your feet; and my sheep fed upon what your feet had trampled, and drank what your feet had muddied. Therefore behold, I myself judge between fat cattle and lean, because you pushed with side and shoulder and tossed all weak cattle with your horns until they were scattered abroad” (Ezekiel 34).

But the hireling feeds the sheep, indeed, even if only in appearance; yet because he does everything for payment, if he sees the wolf rushing upon them, he leaves the sheep and flees, because he is not a shepherd but a hireling, and he cares not even for the sheep but for gain (John 10). He is certainly a mute dog, unable to bark (Isaiah 56), so as to frighten away the approaching wolf even by clamour and noise. For he fears the person who plunders temporal property and pays no attention to the one who will torment the soul in Gehenna. He is blind to great things and trembles at what is of no account.

[Col. 0781A] Of these it is said: “Woe to foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing. Your prophets, Israel, shall be like foxes in deserts. You have not gone up against the enemy, nor placed a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13).

For there is no freedom in them to speak against the powers of the world, no courage to defend truth in danger. In every matter they seek gain; in none, or in few, do they seek the salvation of souls. So long as they attain their own ends, so long as their desire for ambition or avarice succeeds, the loss of what belongs to Christ is despised. Let there be peace in their days; let the sheep be fertile, the cattle fat, the storehouses full (Psalm CXLIII); let a table laden with foods and vessels shine in the admiration of onlookers; let the laborious adornment of varied and costly furnishings abound; let them be honoured and revered by crowds, enriched and visited by their subjects with gifts; finally, let it be free, unpunished, and without reproach to do whatever lust dictates.

[Col. 0781B] At each point let them say, “Good! Good!” (Psalm 34), so that, according to the prophetic rebuke, they may seem to have plastered the hardened wall of sin with mud without straw (Ezekiel 13), though, by the Lord’s command, it was to be dug through and made to fall, so that the foulest abominations might perish from the house of the Lord. These are those who sew cushions beneath the head of every age (ibid.), placing pillows so that they may capture souls, eat the milk, and clothe themselves in the wool of sheep whom they have brought, as it were, into the sleep of negligence or audacity.

But the thief is convicted by his works, because “he comes only to steal, kill, slaughter, and destroy” (John 10). He is surely a destructive and open enemy, who has neither the possession nor even the appearance of a shepherd, and does not feed even for gain, but counts it as his own gain even when he kills. Love, then, is owed to the shepherd because he loves; patience is owed to the hireling because he seems to imitate one who loves.

[Col. 0781D] But the Church owes the thief nothing but punishment. If the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. The sheep hear the shepherd’s voice and follow him (ibid.). They sometimes hear the hireling’s voice, but disdain to follow him because he does not go toward life. They reject, dread, and flee the thief’s voice, because in his hand they see and from his mouth they hear works of death.

For he is not merely a thief and robber, but a ravening wolf, a follower in the lion’s tracks, who goes about roaring and seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5). Who, then, would not drive him away, or at least flee from him, when he enters the sheepfold in order to slaughter and kill?

The Apostle says: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (1 Timothy 3). Yet somehow matters have been turned to the opposite: although almost everyone desires to be made bishop, once they have obtained what they seek, they languish in idleness or, what is more shameful, busy themselves in works of vanity.

[Col. 0782A] I wished above to explain how eagerly ambition is pursued, but, as the matter stands, I could not explain it fully; and I shall find it even harder to relate how uselessly many occupy the rank they desired. Yet I know one thing: those who refuse to distribute to brothers in need fortune’s little gifts—or rather, as I should more rightly say, God’s temporal gifts of grace, granted for this purpose, that they may gain eternal gifts—do not run with such eagerness as to lay down their souls for others.

The chief shepherd showed, both by example and word, that this is the pattern of pastoral office. Therefore men who run after it with such great ambition hasten to become hirelings or thieves. Still, it goes well with sheep entrusted to the care of one who feeds them even for payment. For among the hirelings themselves there are ranks and distinctions. All cast nets for a catch; but some fish for the catch of souls and goods, while others fish only for goods, disregarding danger to souls. And they often disturb everything so that a more abundant opportunity for fishing to their desire may arise.

[Col. 0782B] You will marvel at the varied furnishings and the wealth of Croesus, as the saying goes, among those who preach a poor Christ and who, because they are not compelled to serve at their own expense, preach the Gospel in order to eat and abuse the support due to evangelists.

They roll about in the mouth of their sack the cup in which Joseph was accustomed to divine, but it does not come down into their hands. For the tongue of the priest is the cup of him who is truth and who, in the prefiguration of his name, is interpreted as Saviour of the world. It was established to prophesy hidden things and, by that Spirit with which the disciples were filled when, uttering the word of faith and salvation, they were considered drunk in Judaea, to dispense the grain of wheat that had fallen into the soil of their hearts and now bore abundant fruit for the Lord in the chastity of their speech.

[Col. 0782C] Some indeed live from the Gospel without the Gospel; and it is well if they merely live, rather than also live luxuriously. But I would call those hirelings who do not labour in order to eat, but desire not merely to eat without labour, which necessity requires, but to be idle and indulge in luxury.

Grace and reverence are due to all who exercise the shepherd’s office; and those who proclaim Christ for whatever reason and make profit, though they attach themselves to the shepherds of souls and dispensers of salvation for their own purposes and benefit, should be friends, should be venerated, and should rejoice in the honour of the Fathers. Although they are hirelings, they will never, by my authority, be deprived of their pay. Would that among them there were someone who might speak God’s word, someone who might build up God’s Church, even for gain! I do not begrudge the gain, if the works come first.

[Col. 0783A] But those who so gape after profits that they despise all that belongs to Christ, and yet neither teach heresy nor divide the Church by contentions, deserve neither the honour nor the name of shepherd or hireling.

I do not speak of legates. I leave untouched the Roman Church, which by God’s authorship is the mother and nurse of faith and morals, and which, fortified by heavenly privilege, cannot be judged or accused by man. For it is not credible that its members would presume or deign to commit acts which, by the law of the nations, are known to be unlawful for provincial governors and proconsuls—that is, Caesar’s legates.

With what audacity, then, could the disciple of the Crucified One, Peter’s vicar, the shepherd of souls, dare attempt what, while the discipline of unbelievers was still in force, the emperor’s deputy, the ruler of bodies under the office of consul, did not dare presume? The penalty for extortion is clear from what has been said above; both the enactments of laws and examples from histories have made known in our own age that, except in the matter of food and drink, a judge might not receive anything from provincials, and even what was received could by no means count as a gift.

Who, then, would believe that the Fathers of the Church—the judges of the world and, so to speak, its brightest lights—love gifts, pursue payments, shake down provinces in order to shake coins from purses, empty others’ coffers to fill their own; preach poverty in words while hastening toward riches by their crimes; condemn traffic in spiritual goods so that it may be lawful to trade in such things only with themselves; acting so as to terrify everyone and be loved by no one; teach peace in order to create quarrels; commend and feign humility in order to claim arrogance for themselves; strike at another’s greed while fostering their own; dictate generosity while persisting in stinginess? And, to embrace in a few words the winding passages and broad expanses of this subject: would anyone believe them to assign themselves a share with all the wicked and depraved, or to avenge every crime in full, so that they appear to be a council of vanity, a synagogue of those who do iniquity, a church of evildoers—in whose hands are iniquities and whose right hand is full of gifts? [Col. 0783C]

Far be it that anyone should dare to suspect this! Let so great a crime never befall anyone—that he should set his mouth against heaven and expose what is not shameful in the Fathers. All their things are white and beautiful; there is nothing in them exposed to a dog’s bite or, as the satirist says, afraid of a sneering grin behind its back. Yet if anyone should presume this, he will be answered with one most powerful argument, which none of our adversaries will dare resist or contradict. What argument? you ask. Their works, I say—the works they themselves perform—bear witness concerning them. If you seek the text: attend to the effect, by which the sincerity of the cause is made clear; for he whose work is good is himself also good. If you seek the author: it is he who says, “By their fruits you shall know them. For a bad tree cannot bear good fruits, nor conversely a good tree bad fruits” (Matt. 7). Many things could be advanced on their behalf, if indeed anyone considers them liable to detraction; but for their defense this one point is enough. For it is agreed that the footsteps of the apostles must be revered, and that those who occupy their seat and imitate their life are to be honored as Fathers and venerated as lords.

Rather, this page concerns those who are borne along on suspended feathers, dispute about fasting amid abundance, and destroy by their deeds what they establish by words. In the chariot of the Ethiopian queen’s eunuch, with eyes shut, they talk about and read the Scriptures; yet they disdain—or are unable—to look upon him who “was led like a sheep to the slaughter and did not open his mouth before the one shearing him” (Isa. 53), nor do they deem worthy to receive the disciple of truth as their interpreter until they descend to the waters by which they may be cleansed from dead works. [Col. 0784A]

Although they sit upon the wheels of Scripture and are carried along by the force of the winged creatures, when their tongue has discoursed upon things above, it licks the earth. Nor do they understand the Scriptures, because the Lord of knowledge does not open their hearts—the Lord who, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 16), opened the heart of Lydia the seller of purple, so that she might heed what Paul said. These things become known more reliably to those who fear God through humble obedience to the commandments than through wordy disputation.

Moreover, who is a thief is established in two ways. For the man who, from an earthly manner of life, climbs into the sheepfold by the ladder of pride, resting upon the steps of ambition and vices, despising Christ—that is, neglecting the straight and level way—undermines the thresholds by winding passages, breaks through the joints of the walls, or pours himself in through the tiles, is certainly a thief and robber. But he who enters when Christ opens the door—that is, when the Church calls him—and afterward, under the shepherd’s shadow, becomes a persecutor—that is, despoils, slaughters, kills, and destroys—is unquestionably a thief. [Col. 0784B]

Consider in what rank those ought to be placed for whom permission under divine law to shear and devour the flock is insufficient, unless they invoke the aid of secular laws and, made officers of princes, do without shame what any ordinary tax collector would readily blush to do. Meanwhile they serve pleasure or greed; and they ravage and oppress those who chose them or admitted them to the keeping of themselves, and they desire the death of those whom they ought to have cherished in flesh and spirit. Certainly they remember by heart that prophetic saying: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and to destroy and to ruin and to scatter, and to build and to plant” (Jer. 1). But what they find planted they endeavor to uproot, in order to build for themselves the house of the Lord by gifts of hand, tongue, or service; or in order to put in place of those uprooted persons whom fleshly affection has chosen—that is, either those begotten by themselves or those carnally begotten for them by others. [Col. 0784C]

Here an immense work opens before us, and the road stretches out before the pen; but I stop, sparing the particulars that are thrust before the public gaze. If anyone here complains that something is said too harshly, he will readily pardon me if he has read what has been said by the Fathers. For if a secular tyrant is put to death by divine and human law, who would judge a tyrant in the priesthood to be worthy of love or veneration? And if this seems harsh, I call in defense the blessed Gregory, who spoke only truths and sweetness, yet pursued these matters more severely. And, to pass over the rest, this is known to all: prelates ought to know that, whenever they sin, they deserve as many deaths as they transmit examples of destruction to their subjects. [Col. 0784D–0785A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. That ministers of God are tyrants; what a tyrant is; and the character of Gaius Caligula and Nero his nephew, and the end of each.

Yet I do not deny that ministers of God are tyrants, whom, in each primacy—that is, over souls and bodies—he willed by his just judgment to exist, through whom the wicked might be punished, and the good corrected and tested. For the sins of the people cause a hypocrite to reign; and, as the history of Kings testifies, the failings of priests introduced tyrants among God’s people.

Indeed, the first fathers and patriarchs followed excellent Nature as their guide of life. Leaders succeeded them, beginning with Moses, following the Law; then judges, who governed the people by the authority of the Law, and whom we read were likewise priests. At length, in the Lord’s anger, kings were given—some good, others evil. For Samuel had grown old; and, since his sons did not walk in his ways but followed greed and impurity, the people—who perhaps themselves deserved to have such priests set over them—extorted for themselves from the God whom they had despised a king. [Col. 0785B]

Saul, therefore, was chosen, but with the previously proclaimed right of a king: namely, that he should take their sons to make them charioteers, their daughters to become bakers and cooks, and their fields and estates to distribute at will among his servants, and should oppress the entire people beneath the yoke of servitude. Yet he was called the Lord’s Christ, and, though exercising tyranny, did not lose royal honor. For God struck all with fear, so that they might venerate him as a minister of the Lord, whose image he in some sense bore.

I shall add something stronger still: even the tyrants of the nations, reprobated from eternity unto death, are ministers of God and are called Christs of the Lord. Thus the prophet says: “The leaders will enter the gates of Babylon,” namely Cyrus and Darius. “For I have commanded my sanctified ones, and called my mighty men in my wrath, those exulting in my glory” (Isa. 13). See: he calls the Medes and Persians “sanctified,” not because they were holy, but because they were carrying out the Lord’s will against Babylon. [Col. 0785C–D]

Elsewhere again he says: “Behold, I will bring Nebuchadnezzar, my servant”; and, “because he served me well at Tyre, I will give him Egypt” (Ezek. 29). Every authority is good, because it is from him from whom alone all things, and only good things, come. Yet it is sometimes not good to the one using it, or to the one suffering under it, but evil, although in relation to the whole it is good—he who makes good use of our evils bringing this about.

For just as, in a painting, a dark or black color, or some other color considered in itself, is unbecoming, yet suits the entire picture, so certain things, considered in themselves, appear unseemly and evil, but, when referred to the whole, good and beautiful—since he whose works are all very good adapts all things to himself. Therefore the power of a tyrant is indeed good, though nothing is worse than tyranny. Tyranny is the abuse of power granted by God to a human being. Yet in this evil there is much and great usefulness for the good. It is clear, therefore, that tyranny is not found only in princes, but that all are tyrants who abuse, against their subjects, power granted from above. [Col. 0786A]

But if power comes to a wise person, who knows and possesses the proper use of all things, it is welcome to all good people and useful to all. If, however, it falls to a fool, although it cannot be evil for those good persons for whom all things work together for good, it is nevertheless burdensome for a short time. For it is manifest that authority falls to both kinds of people; though, because the wickedness of our age continually provokes the Lord’s scourge against us, it is more often granted to the wicked—that is, to fools.

For what in human affairs can any memory recall as more powerful than the Roman Empire? If the succession of times from the founding of the City is reviewed, wicked men are found to have governed it more frequently. For who was more foul or savage than Gaius Caligula, third successor of Augustus, except Nero, who surpassed all predecessors and successors alike in baseness of life and unheard-of crimes? [Col. 0786B]

This Caligula, though most depraved of all men, nevertheless governed—or rather tortured—the empire, with such perverse sentiment that, envying his own good fortune, he complained about the condition of his times because they were marked by no public disasters. For he whose birth had brought peace to the world had come to destroy the dominion of discord and death. Although this vast peace was attributed to Augustus, it ought rather to be attributed to Christ, who, when Augustus reigned, was enrolled as a Roman citizen in the census assessment. For the truthful report of the Gospels and histories establishes that under him was born the sole author of peace: Christ, God and man, son of the Virgin. His eternal dispensation enrolled the elect for true peace and the blessedness of a most happy kingdom; his coming had been foretold by many and revealed by signs. [Col. 0786C]

For, as Orosius relates, when Caesar, after Julius had been killed, was returning from Apollonia and entered the city, at about the third hour, suddenly, in a clear and pure sky, a circle in the appearance of a heavenly rainbow surrounded the disk of the sun. This is believed to have occurred on the eighth day before the Ides of January, the day called Epiphany, on which Caesar first shut the gates of Janus, after civil wars had been stilled and ended, and obtained the name Augustus—thus declaring the summit of empire, so that it might be known that the highest authority in affairs and powers belonged to one man, which the Greeks call *monarchia*, “monarchy.”

The same historian reports that, when returning from Sicily, having recovered the legions from Pompey and Lepidus, Caesar restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters and decreed that all former debts owed to the people should be forgiven, even having the written records abolished. In those same days a very abundant fountain of oil flowed for an entire day from a tavern of hire, manifestly announcing that he was present in the empire who had come to subject the slaves of the devil—that is, sinners—to God’s just lordship and to have mercy on the poor. [Col. 0786D–0787A]

Therefore, while all things were silent before Christ’s face and the world stood astonished at such mercies of the Most High, the supreme authority in affairs and powers passed, as the third from Augustus, to Caligula. To make his savagery clear in brief, he is said to have cried: “Would that the Roman people had but one neck!” Since he lacked an enemy, he set out in great and incredible pomp to seek one. Roaming through Germany and Gaul with idle forces, he stopped on the shore of Ocean opposite Britain; then returned to Rome, war lacking material and no undertaking accomplished, except that he accepted into surrender Belinus, son of the king of the Britons, whom his father had expelled, with a few followers. [Col. 0787A–B]

He proved most hostile to the Jews, ordering the holy places of Jerusalem profaned and filled with statues, and himself worshipped as God. He reduced Pilate, governor of Judaea, to such anguish that Pilate, piercing himself with his own hand, sought a swift death as a short end to his evils. Caligula first polluted his sisters by sexual violation, condemned them to exile, and afterward ordered all the exiles killed together. He himself was killed by his own guards. In his private rooms two lists were found containing the names of distinguished citizens whom he had marked for death: one bore the title “Sword,” the other “Dagger.” A huge chest of various poisons was also found; when these were sunk by order of the Emperor Claudius, the seas themselves are reported to have been infected, as the great destruction of fish attested. [Col. 0787B–C]

After Caligula’s uncle Claudius had intervened, Nero Caesar succeeded him: heir to his affairs and vices—indeed, their surpasser. He exercised wantonness, lust, luxury, greed, and cruelty in every sort of crime. For, Orosius testifies, driven by wantonness, he visited almost all the theatres of Italy and Greece and, putting on the disgrace of varied dress, was often seen to outdo heralds—that is, trumpeters—lyre-players, tragic actors, and charioteers. He was likewise so driven by lust that he is reported not to have abstained even from his mother, sister, or any reverence due to kinship; he took a man as wife, and was himself received by a man as a wife. [Col. 0787C–D]

His luxury was so unrestrained that he fished with golden nets drawn out by purple cords; bathed in cold and hot perfumes; never wore any garment twice; and is reported never to have travelled with fewer than a thousand carriages. Finally, he made the burning of Rome a spectacle for his pleasure: the city burned for six days and seven nights and fed the emperor’s gaze. Granaries built of squared stone, and those great ancient apartment-blocks which a racing flame could not reach, were shaken and set on fire by great engines once prepared for foreign wars; the wretched populace was driven to the lodgings of dependants and the shelters of tombs. [Col. 0787D]

Watching this from the highest tower of Maecenas, and delighted, as he said, by the beauty of the flame, he sang in tragic costume the *heliofeles odam sonat sacerdotates nymnos* [OCR-corrupt; meaning uncertain] of the city in which the splendor of the sun is worshipped. His greed, moreover, was so precipitous that after the burning of that city which Augustus had boasted of making marble though he found it brick, he allowed no one to approach the remnants of his property. He himself took everything that had survived the flames in any way. He ordered the Senate to grant him ten million sesterces annually; deprived very many senators of their property without any stated cause; and in a single day extorted from all merchants their entire wealth, even using torture. [Col. 0788A]

He was so unrestrained in his frenzy of cruelty that he killed a great part of the Senate and nearly emptied the equestrian order. Nor did he refrain from parricides: he destroyed without hesitation his mother, brother, sister, wife, and all other relatives and kin. The audacity of impiety against God increased this mass of his crimes. For he was the first at Rome to subject Christians to punishments and deaths, and ordered them tortured in every province by an equal persecution. Seeking to extirpate the very name, he killed Christ’s most blessed apostles Peter by the cross and Paul by the sword.

Soon afterward, most bitter disasters arising on every side crushed the miserable city. For in the following autumn such a pestilence fell upon the city that thirty thousand funerals were entered in Libitina’s register. Then immediately came the British disaster, in which two principal towns were plundered, with great slaughter and loss of citizens and allies. [Col. 0788B–C]

Moreover, in the East, after great provinces of Armenia had been lost, Roman legions were sent beneath the Parthian yoke, and Syria was retained only with difficulty. In Asia three cities—Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae—collapsed in an earthquake. Orosius reports these things; and I use his words and sense the more willingly because I know that he was a Christian and a great disciple of Augustine, and therefore pursued the truth more diligently on account of the religion of our faith.

These matters can be found more fully in other historians as well, who write more extensively about the atrocities of tyrants and their miserable ends. Whoever wishes to review them more carefully should read what Trogus Pompeius, Josephus, Hegesippus, Suetonius, Quintus Curtius, Cornelius Tacitus, Titus Livius, Serenus, Tranquillus, and other historians too numerous to list have included in their histories. [Col. 0788C–D]

From these it will readily become clear that it has always been permissible to flatter a tyrant, permissible to deceive him, and honorable to kill him—if, nevertheless, he could not be restrained otherwise. For the subject is not private tyrants, but those who oppress the commonwealth. Private persons are easily restrained by public laws, which bind human lives. Yet it is not lawful to use the material sword against a priest, even if he assumes tyranny, because of reverence for the sacrament—unless perhaps, after being deposed from office, he stretches forth a bloody hand against the Church of God; while this proviso always remains in force: for the same cause a double punishment must not rise up against him. It does not seem irrelevant, however, to support what has been said with some examples.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the death of Julius Caesar and other pagan tyrants.

[Col. 0789A]

First, then, comes the house of Caesar, than which the world remembers nothing more powerful or glorious in any age. Julius Caesar was the first to acquire the world by the strength of his prudence and military capacity. He was a man with very few equals, and Nature has not yet produced any mortal expressly like him. Although Cicero somewhere accuses him of taking delight in wrongs without any appearance of utility or honor, so much so that it pleased him to commit wrong against Cicero himself, Cicero nonetheless exalts the same man with such praises that he judges him a gift of the gods, compounded from virtues and bestowed upon the Roman Empire: one who knew neither to be puffed up by prosperity nor broken by adversity, magnificent without cruelty, high-minded without rashness. [Col. 0789A–B]

Though, if another man had been such, he might seem rash, Caesar ought not to seem bold, since his will, by the favoring aid of the gods, was always within his power. No one experienced Caesar as savage unless he rebelled in pride. Provoked by injuries, he was inclined to pardon. Those whom he conquered by force he surpassed in prudence. His excesses seemed to hope for and aspire to justice. This may be inferred from the fact that he wished no time of his to be without philosophy. Orosius seems in part to agree with this.

For when in Egypt a great part of Caesar’s soldiers had fallen and he himself, as Lucan mentions, was compelled to look back to Scaeva, who stood out in singular courage among Caesar’s followers and besieged

> “[lacuna] Magnus, treading the walls with his feet,”

Caesar, hard pressed by the force of the Egyptians attacking him, embarked in a skiff. When it was soon weighed down and sunk by the weight of those following, he swam two hundred paces to a ship, holding aloft in one hand the papers he carried. [Col. 0789B–C]

Yet because he had seized the commonwealth by arms, he was reckoned a tyrant and, with a great part of the Senate consenting, was killed in the Capitol by drawn daggers. But even there he showed regard for decency. For when he perceived that he was being attacked with drawn daggers, he covered his head with his toga and at the same time drew down its fold to the lower parts with his left hand, so that he might fall more decently.

His successor Augustus, the happiest of all, was forbidden under threat of punishment to call himself lord; acting as a citizen, he avoided both the reality and the stigma of tyranny. Tiberius, third from Julius, died by poison. The people rejoiced so greatly at his death that they prayed Earth the mother and the gods of the dead to grant him no resting place after death except among the impious. Although poisoning has always been detestable, the poison by which he was destroyed was judged life-giving by the world. A certain sign of poison was held to be that his heart was found incorrupt among the bones after cremation; for such is the nature attributed to things poisoned, that fire cannot consume them. [Col. 0789C–D]

The third tyrant, Gaius Caligula, was killed by his own household. Tiberius Claudius, fifth from Julius, although he avoided tyranny, was destroyed by evident signs of poison, like the other Tiberius. But Nero, sixth from Julius, most savage and contemptible of all, met the following end.

After he had burned the city, as has been said, offended by the ugliness of its old buildings and the narrowness and windings of its streets, he was deserted by all the people, as Suetonius relates. Entering his chamber, he looked for someone to kill him but found no one, since all had departed. “Then,” he said, “I have neither friend nor enemy?” A little before he stabbed himself, he ordered a grave dug before him to fit the measure of his body; ordered any pieces of marble that might be found arranged in it; and ordered water and wood brought together for tending to his corpse. He wept at each detail and repeatedly said: “What an artist dies in me!” [Col. 0790A]

When he heard that the Senate had condemned him to punishment, he asked what that punishment was. On learning that a fork was to be placed around the naked man’s neck and his body beaten with rods until death, terrified, he seized the two daggers he had brought out with him and, testing the edge of each, put them away again, claiming that the fatal hour had not yet come. Now he urged Sporus to begin lamenting; now he begged someone to encourage him toward death by example. At times he rebuked his own slowness in these verses:

> “I live shamefully; more shamefully I die.”

And now the horsemen were approaching, who had been ordered to drag him out alive. When he realized this, he drove the blade into his throat. With him the entire family of the Caesars came to an end. [Col. 0790B]

Lest anyone suppose that the laws permit such action against tyranny only in that one family: Vitellius, ninth from Julius—Galba and Otho being inserted between Nero and Vitellius—was most shamefully dragged from the little chamber into which he had shut himself. Naked, he was led along the Sacred Way, while some threw dung into his mouth from all sides; then, torn to pieces by countless blows at the Gemonian Stairs by the Roman people, he was dragged with a hook into the Tiber. Domitian, twelfth, with Vespasian and Titus inserted, was cruelly killed by his own men after a long and bloody tyranny. [Col. 0790B–C]

I shall briefly explain, on the authority of Eusebius of Caesarea, why he thereafter treated Christians more gently. His words are these, in Book Three, Chapter Eighteen:

> Domitian himself commanded that all who were descended from the family of David and the royal line should be killed. As ancient tradition records, certain persons were denounced as being descendants of Jude, whom they say was the Savior’s brother according to the flesh. They were pressed by a twofold suspicion, as persons descended both from David’s family and from Christ’s own kindred. Hegesippus relates the matter in order in these words:
>
> Some members of the fleshly family of our Lord still lived: the grandsons of Jude, who is called the Lord’s brother according to the flesh. They were denounced as descended from David’s stock. A certain man named Revocatus, who had been sent for this purpose, brought them before Domitian Caesar. For he too feared Christ’s coming, just as Herod had at the beginning. Asked by Domitian whether they belonged to David’s family, they confessed that they did. He then asked what possessions or resources they had. They replied that in both kinds of property they had no more than nine thousand denarii, of which, by apportionment, each had one half. They said this did not consist for them in cash, but in the valuation of land—thirty-nine *iugera*—which they cultivated with their own hands, thereby supporting themselves and paying taxes. [Col. 0790C–0791A]
>
> They also produced evidence of their rural daily labor: hands stiff from work and hardened with calluses. Asked about Christ—what his kingdom was like, who he was, whence he came, and when he would come—they answered that his kingdom was not of this world and that dominion over this earth was not appointed to him, but a heavenly kingdom was prepared for him through the ministry of angels. There he would come in glory, judge the living and the dead, and repay each person according to his deeds and merits. When Domitian found no crime in them and held their lowliness in the utmost contempt, he ordered them released as free men.

Thus far that author.

From this it is clear that Domitian restrained the rage of his cruelty against some of the faithful not from the gentleness becoming a prince, but from impious arrogance. Therefore, if the royal family was reduced to such scant numbers and poverty that, while Domitian reigned, scarcely two persons could be found from David’s line, who can be confident of perpetuity in descendants propagated through flesh and blood? And because Domitian tore apart the Church of God—indeed, the whole empire—God employed the same judgment against him, and he too was torn apart. His corpse was carried out in a common bier by corpse-bearers and buried most disgracefully. [Col. 0791B–C]

His successor Nerva annulled all his acts; numbered among princes rather than tyrants, he died of illness, having adopted Trajan to the throne. Trajan succeeded with such moderation that, just as Augustus had long been called “most fortunate,” so Trajan was long considered “best emperor.” As they report, he died at the city of Seleucia in Isauria from flux of the belly. He was succeeded by Aelius Hadrian, father of the fatherland, who ordered the commonwealth by most just laws. He completely subdued the Jews, driven into disorder by their crimes so as to invade Palestine, with extreme slaughter; took vengeance for the Christians whom they had tortured; ordered that no Jew should be permitted to enter Jerusalem; allowed the city only to Christians; restored it to an excellent condition by constructing walls; and ordered it to be called Aelia after his own forename. [Col. 0791C–D]

Antoninus, surnamed Pius, succeeding Hadrian with his sons, governed the empire peacefully and devoutly; he was deservedly called Pius and Father of the Fatherland, and, through the intervention of Justin the philosopher, showed himself kindly disposed toward Christians. Marcus Antonius Verus, successor of Pius, assumed the empire with his brother Aurelius Commodus. Aurelius died, suffocated in an attack of the illness which the Greeks call *apoplexia*, “apoplexy.” When he died, his brother ruled the commonwealth alone, a man whom, if Eutropius is to be believed, it is easier to admire than to praise.

From the beginning of his life he was calm and steadfast, so that from infancy he changed his expression neither in joy nor sorrow. He was trained in Stoic philosophy and devoted to it: a philosopher alike in life and learning. He was instructed in philosophy by Apollonius of Chalcedon, and in Greek letters by Chaeronensis, Plutarch’s grandson. In Latin letters he was taught by the most distinguished orator Fronto, who, according to some, was Plutarch’s grandson. [Col. 0792A]

Among other things he conducted a war comparable in magnitude to the Punic wars. Although, by the prayers of Christian soldiers—as this emperor himself is said to have attested in his letters—he brought great wars to an end, a severe persecution of them flared up, and many holy martyrs were crowned. Finally, having associated his son Lucius Commodus with him in the throne, he died in Pannonia of a sudden illness.

Lucius Antonius Commodus, fifteenth from Augustus, corrupted by every disgrace of cruelty, luxury, and obscenity, fought very often in gladiatorial arms and frequently exposed himself to wild beasts in the amphitheatre. He also killed very many senators, especially those whom he saw excel in nobility and ability. The punishment of the city followed the king’s crimes: the Capitol was struck by lightning, and the resulting conflagration consumed in a devouring blaze that library assembled through the care and zeal of the ancients, together with other adjacent buildings. [Col. 0792A–B]

Yet blessed Gregory is said to have burned the pagan library, so that the divine page might have a more honored place, greater authority, and more diligent study. These accounts are by no means inconsistent, since they could have occurred at different times. Commodus, harmful to all, was strangled in the house of Vestilianus, having while alive been pronounced an enemy of the human race.

This, then, is a description of the tyrant, explaining the reality concealed in the name. Therefore, just as it is lawful to kill a condemned enemy, so it is lawful to kill a tyrant. This reckoning, however, must not obstruct historical truth, since the cases of Galba, Otho, and similar figures have here been omitted. Nor is attention paid to which number each holds among the emperors, but to how God’s clemency subdued or restrained the tyranny of all, he who by the decree of justice, when he wills, brings in the scourge as punishment for sinners, and when he wills admits to pardon those whom he has made penitent. [Col. 0792B–C]

I had decided to stop here and pass from Roman to other histories; but because Severus occurs in the catalogue of emperors—the man from whom my people takes its name, who exercised a grievous tyranny against Christ’s name—I shall add this one alone, lest I seem to spare our Severia or Salisbury (*Saresberia*). Yet heavenly vengeance immediately followed this profane persecution of Christians and the Church. Civil wars at once broke out, in which a vast amount of Roman blood was shed.

Severus was African by origin, a Tripolitanian from the town of Leptis, savage by nature and often challenged by many wars. He governed the commonwealth very bravely, but with great labor. He fought with many peoples in order to triumph over many. He defeated and killed Pescennius Niger, who aspired to tyranny; he suppressed with the sword the Jews and Samaritans when they rebelled; and he overcame the Parthians, Arabs, and Adiabenians. [Col. 0792D]

This is Severus, conqueror of nations, who, drawn into Britain by the revolt of almost all its allies, often fought there great and grievous battles. He judged that the recovered part of the island should be separated from the remaining unconquered peoples by a wall. Accordingly, he carried a very great ditch and a most secure rampart, strengthened in addition with frequent towers, for one hundred and twenty-two thousand paces from sea to sea. There, as Orosius and other historians report, he died of illness near the town of Eboracum [York].

For Britain has always abhorred poisons and does not recognize their use against rulers, but knows how to wield unconquered swords for its rulers. In the course of time, perhaps by the burial of so great an emperor, the aforesaid town grew to such strength and boldness that it dares compare itself with ancient cities. [Col. 0793A]

Yet it is certain that Severus, according to the rite of pagans and the perversity of unbelievers, exercised tyranny against Christians and paid the penalties of his crime. For no one since the beginning of the world has acted out the image of the apostate angel without sharing in his condemnation and confusion.

## CHAPTER XX. That by the authority of the divine page it is lawful and glorious to kill public tyrants, provided that the killer is not bound to the tyrant by fealty, or does not otherwise lose justice or honor.

It would be lengthy if I wished to carry the succession of pagan tyrants down to our own times; but one man of this age will not be mentioned. For the matter escapes the mind and overcomes the tongue. Yet the little book entitled *On the Deaths of the Tyrants* will be able more fully to disclose what I think concerning tyrants—though in a careful [Col. 0793C] abridgment, so that prolixity may not breed weariness nor brevity obscurity. But lest the authority of Roman history, which has for the most part been written by unbelievers and about unbelievers, should be undervalued, let this be demonstrated by examples from sacred and faithful history.

For it is apparent on every side that, as Valerius says, only that power is secure which imposes limits upon its own strength. And indeed nothing is so excellent or so magnificent that it does not need to be tempered by moderation. Sacred Scripture first sets before us as a tyrant Nimrod, “a mighty hunter against the Lord,” whom certain histories also attest to have been called Ninus, although chronological reasoning does not agree; and above it was said that he was reprobate. For he wished [Col. 0793D] to rule, and not from the Lord; and under him blind mortal humanity, destined for dispersal and confusion, attempted to raise a tower to heaven.

Let us proceed to him whom divine election set over the people, but whom it abandoned to a reprobate will of domination rather than kingship, and afflicted so severely that, pressed by the anguish of sorrow, he was compelled to inflict death upon himself. For a sound beginning is of little or no use if the life that follows disagrees with it; nor do the beginnings of affairs prevail before the Judge whose sentence depends upon the end.

There is the celebrated history of Kings and the Books of Days, in which, according to Jerome, Israel is taught to have suffered under tyrants from the beginning. And Judah is shown to have had, apart from David, Josiah, and Hezekiah, only reprobate kings. Yet I would readily believe that Solomon, and perhaps [Col. 0794A] some others in Judah, recovered their strength when the Lord recalled them. And I shall readily be persuaded that a stiff-necked people, of unconquerable heart, which always resisted the Holy Spirit and provoked to wrath not only Moses, servant of the Law, but God, Lord of the Law, by the abominations of the nations, deserved tyrants for its rulers. For tyrants, whom sins obtain, introduce, and raise up, repentance destroys, excludes, and slays.
