Indeed, before they had kings, as the history of Judges relates, the children of Israel often served under many and various tyrants, afflicted in accordance with divine dispensation; and, crying frequently to the Lord, they were delivered. When the time of that dispensation was ended, they were permitted to cast from their necks the yoke by killing tyrants; [Col. 0794B] nor is any of those by whose courage a penitent and humbled people was delivered blamed. Rather, he is remembered with the glad memory of posterity as a servant of the Lord. This is clear from the examples set below.

Therefore the children of Israel served Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years. Afterwards they cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a saviour named Ehud, the renowned son of Gera, son of Benjamin, who used either hand as his right hand. The children of Israel sent gifts through him to Eglon, king of Moab. He made himself a two-edged sword, having a handle in the middle, a palm’s length long; he girded it beneath his garment on his right thigh, and presented the gifts to Eglon king of Moab. Eglon was exceedingly fat. When Ehud had presented the gifts, he sent away the companions who [Col. 0794C] had come with him. Returning from Gilgal, where the idols were, he said to the king: “I have a secret word for you, O king.” And he commanded silence. When all who were around him had gone out, Ehud entered to him. Now he was sitting alone in a summer upper chamber. Ehud said to him: “I have a word of God for you.” He immediately rose from his throne. Ehud stretched out his left hand, took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly so forcefully that the handle followed the blade into the wound and was enclosed by the very thick fat. He did not draw out the sword, but left it in the body as he had struck. Immediately the excrement of his belly burst forth through the secret parts of nature. Ehud, having very carefully shut the doors of the upper chamber and secured them with the bar, [Col. 0794D] went out by the rear way (Judges 3).

And elsewhere: Sisera, fleeing, came to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. For there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. Therefore Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him: “Come in to me, my lord; come in, do not fear.” He entered her tent, and she covered him with a cloak. He said to her: “Give me, I beg you, a little water, for I am very thirsty.” She opened a skin of milk, gave him drink, and covered him. Sisera said to her: “Stand at the entrance of the tent; and if anyone comes questioning you and says, ‘Is anyone here?’ you shall answer, ‘No one.’” Therefore Jael, wife of Heber, took a tent-peg and also a hammer. Entering secretly and silently, [Col. 0795A] she placed the peg upon the side of his head and, striking it with the hammer, drove it through his brain into the ground. Joining sleep to death, he collapsed and died (Judges 4).

Did she then receive praise or blame from posterity? “Jael,” Scripture says, “wife of Heber the Kenite, is blessed among women; let her be blessed in her tent. To one asking water she gave milk, and in a bowl for princes she offered butter. She put her left hand to the peg and her right hand to the workmen’s hammers. And she struck Sisera, seeking a place for the wound in his head and forcefully piercing his temple” (Judges 5).

Moreover, that another history also may establish that it is just for public tyrants to be killed and for the people to be liberated into obedience to God, the priests of the Lord themselves [Col. 0795B] also count their death as an act of piety; and, if anything seems to bear the appearance of deceit, they say that it is consecrated to the Lord by the holiness of the mystery. Thus Holofernes fell not by hostile strength but by his own vices beneath a woman’s sword; and he who had been terrifying to men, overcome by lust and drunkenness, was killed by a woman. Nor could the woman have gained access to the tyrant unless she had concealed her hostile purpose beneath a pious pretense. For deceit is not deceit when it serves faith and fights for charity.

It belonged to faith that she rebuked the priests who had set a time limit upon divine mercy, having agreed to surrender themselves and the city to the enemy unless the Lord came to their aid within five days. It belonged to charity that she feared no dangers while delivering her brothers and the people of the Lord from their enemies. For [Col. 0795C] these are also the words of her departure for salvation: “Make it so, Lord, that his pride may be cut off by his own sword; let him be caught in the snare of his eyes in me, and strike him by the lips of my charity. Give steadfastness to my mind, that I may despise him, and strength, that I may overthrow him. For it will be a memorial of your name when the hand of a woman has cast him down” (Judith 9).

Then she summoned her maidservant, went down into her house, removed her sackcloth, took off the garments of her widowhood, washed her body, anointed herself with the finest myrrh, arranged the hair of her head, placed a tiara upon her head, and clothed herself in her festive garments. She put sandals on her feet and took bracelets, [Col. 0795D] lilies, earrings, and rings, adorning herself with all her ornaments. And the Lord bestowed radiance upon her, because all this adornment depended not upon lust but upon virtue. Therefore the Lord increased this beauty in her, so that she appeared to the eyes of all with incomparable loveliness (Judith 10).

Having come there and seeking to entrap the public enemy, Judith said to Holofernes: “Receive the words of your handmaid; for if you follow them, God will accomplish a perfect matter through you. For Nebuchadnezzar, king of the earth, lives, and your strength, which is in you for the correction of all souls that wander, lives; for not only men but also the beasts of the field serve him through you and obey him. For the strength and skill of your mind [Col. 0796A] are reported among all nations, and it has been announced to every age that you alone are mighty and good throughout all his kingdom, and your discipline is proclaimed among all nations” (Judith 11).

And adding, she said: “When I come, I shall tell you everything, so that I may lead you through the midst of Jerusalem; and you shall have all the people of Israel like sheep without a shepherd, and not even one dog shall bark against you, because these things have been told to me by the providence of God” (ibid.). What, I ask, could be devised more treacherously, what said more deceptively, than this counsel of mystical dispensation? Therefore Holofernes said: “There is no such woman on earth in appearance, beauty, and wisdom of speech” (ibid.). For his heart burned, shaken by desire for her. And he said: “Drink now, and recline in pleasure, for you have found favour before me” (Judith 12).

But she, who had not come to indulge in luxury, used another’s lust as an instrument of her faith and courage. And the cruelty which she had once lulled asleep with blandishments she killed, for the people’s liberation, with the weapons of charity. Therefore she struck Holofernes in the neck, cut off his head, and gave it to her maidservant to place in a bag (Judith 12), to carry back to the city which had received salvation at the hand of a woman.

Yet the histories teach that this must be guarded against: no one should plot the death of a person to whom he is bound by the sacred obligation of faith or oath. For Zedekiah too is said to have been taken captive because he neglected the sacred obligation of faith; and, as I do not recall in the case of another king of Judah, [Col. 0796C] his eyes were put out because, while cautiously avoiding a tyrant even for a just cause, he fell into faithlessness and did not set before his eyes God, by whom an oath is sworn. Nor, although I see that poison has sometimes been employed by unbelievers, do I ever read that permission to use it has been granted by any law. Not because I think tyrants ought not to be removed, but because this must occur without loss of religious integrity and honour.

For David too, the best of the kings whom I have read of, and one who, except in the affair of Uriah the Hittite, conducted himself blamelessly in all things, although he endured a most grievous tyrant and often had opportunity to destroy him, nevertheless preferred to spare him, trusting in the mercy of God, who could deliver him without sin. [Col. 0796D] He therefore resolved to wait patiently, until Saul should be visited by the Lord through restored charity, or should fall in battle, or otherwise die by the just judgment of God. Indeed, his patience may be marked even from this: when he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak in the cave, and elsewhere had entered the camp at night and rebuked the guards’ negligence, he compelled the king himself to confess that David’s cause was the more just.

This manner of eliminating tyrants is indeed the most useful and safest: that those who are oppressed should humbly flee for refuge to the protection of God’s mercy and, lifting pure hands to the Lord, should by devoted prayers avert the scourge by which they are afflicted. For the sins of wrongdoers are the strength of tyrants. Hence Achior, commander of all the children of Ammon, gave Holofernes this most salutary counsel: [Col. 0797A] “Search now, my lord, whether there is any iniquity of this people before their God; and let us go up against them, because their God will surely deliver them to you, and they will be subjected beneath the yoke of your power. But if there is no offense of this people before their God, we shall not be able to resist them, because their God will defend them, and we shall become a reproach to the whole earth” (Judith 5).

## Chapter XXI. That misery is the end of all tyrants; and that God exacts vengeance upon them if the human hand refrains, as is evident in Julian the Apostate and in many examples from Holy Scripture.

For the end of tyrants is confusion: unto destruction, indeed, if they persevere in wickedness; but unto pardon if they are recalled. For even for the scourge itself a conflagration is prepared, [Col. 0797B] once the Father has used it for the correction of his children. “And Ahab,” he says, “has reverenced my face; I shall not bring this evil in his days” (3 Kings 21). But Jezebel, persisting in cruelty, furnished her blood for dogs to lick by an end worthy of her cruelty, in the place where dogs had licked the blood of innocent Naboth. If the blood of innocent Naboth is thus required, shall the blood of so many innocents go unrequired?

Wickedness desired the vineyard of the righteous man and, in exchange for it, lost the rights of the whole kingdom. Wickedness is always punished by the Lord; but sometimes he uses his own weapon, sometimes, as it were, a human weapon, for the punishment of the impious. Pharaoh afflicted the people of God, and was himself chastised by the same God with the most severe plagues, as Exodus relates (chapter 13). I have taken care to insert these plagues briefly, comprehended in verse so that they may be remembered more faithfully:

> First: the reddened water; second: frogs and corruption.  
> Then grievous gnats; after them, the more harmful fly.  
> The fifth struck down cattle; the sixth produced blisters.  
> Next comes hail; afterwards the locust with its dreadful bite.  
> The ninth hides the sun; the last kills the firstborn offspring.

I do not care who made these verses, attending only to this: they summarize sufficiently concisely the plagues of Egypt under Pharaoh. Yet in all these things his wrath against the people of God was not turned away; rather, pursuing them as they departed, with his chariots and horsemen, he was drowned in the sea. Thus the Lord used waters as a wall for the people’s defense and as a weapon for the tyrant’s overthrow.

Shalmaneser also, while [Col. 0797D] Hezekiah was reigning, oppressed the people of the Lord; and the king, turning in prayer against the tyrant’s threats, set the shield of divine protection before himself. Therefore the Lord strengthened him through the prophet, saying: “He shall not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow into it; no shield shall occupy it, nor shall a siege-work surround it. By the way by which he came he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord. I shall protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.” Therefore it came to pass in that night that the angel of the Lord came and struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. When he rose early in the morning, he saw all the bodies of the dead; and he departed and went away. Sennacherib king of the Assyrians returned and stayed in Nineveh. While he was worshipping his god Nesrach in [Col. 0798A] the temple, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him with the sword and fled into the land of the Armenians; and his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place (4 Kings 19).

Nor should it trouble us if he is designated by one name in one history and another in another; for, according to Hebrew tradition, as Jerome attests, he was the same man with five names. He was called Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Sargon. Unless he is held to have many names, the authority of historians who seem sometimes to disagree through a certain contradiction will waver. Thus the Lord first used an angelic sword against the army, then the hands of sons against the impious man.

Nature itself at times marvels at the vengeance of the Most High and, when human wickedness provokes it, wonderfully submits [Col. 0798B] to the laws of its Creator. Hence Nebuchadnezzar, swelling up against the Lord, lived as a beast when seven years had elapsed; and, repenting, he returned again to humanity, restored to his possessions and kingdom, although afterwards he deserved to be stripped of them by a wretched end.

I pass to Christian times, because in every nation and people the wickedness of tyrants and their manifest punishment are evident. Julian, a base apostate and foul emperor, persecuted Christ by deceit rather than strength—yet he did not restrain his power. For under him there arose a most grievous persecution of Christians, while he impiously attempted to extinguish the name of the “Galilean,” as he called him. But [Col. 0798C] while conducting an ill-fated expedition against the Parthians and vowing, upon his return, a slaughter of Christians to the idols as a sacrifice, God, moved by the prayers of Basil the Great and other saints, sent the martyr Mercurius, who by command of the blessed Virgin pierced the tyrant in the camp with a lance, and compelled the dying impious man to confess that the Galilean—that is, Christ, whom he persecuted—was victorious and had triumphed over him.

For when the aforesaid bishop had gathered the faithful of Caesarea in the church of the perpetual Virgin, Mother of God, to spend the night in prayers, the saint recognized the blessed Virgin in a vision that same night and received this consolation: “Call Mercurius to me,” she said, “and he will go to kill Julian, who blasphemes my Son and God with arrogant pride.” [Col. 0798D] But the saint came with his armour and swiftly departed; and she who had appeared, summoning Basil the Great, gave him a book containing, in an illustration, the whole creation of the world, and on the right a man formed by God. At the beginning of the book the inscription was “Speak”; at the end, when the man had already been formed, “Spare.” Receiving the book, he read from the beginning as far as “Spare.”

The quaestor of Julian, Libanius, saw a similar vision on that same night during the expedition. Returning that night to the martyr-shrine of Saint Mercurius, Basil did not find Mercurius’s weapons; but on the following day he found them, and the lance stained with fresh blood. Orosius, however, makes no mention of the martyr Mercurius, but reports that in the Parthian expedition the tyrant was killed [Col. 0799A] by the weapon of a soldier who met him. Eutropius also, who describes Roman history in elegant abridgment, admits that he was killed in camp but names no author of the killing. Yet it is agreed that the persecution which, according to the same author, he carried on against Christians beyond measure did him very great harm.

But the *Tripartite History* more carefully pursues Julian’s crimes and, throughout its entire sixth book, recounts with what savagery he persecuted Christ, whom he called “the Galilean.” From it I have inserted some things in praise of the Galilean, briefly extracted from what Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen, on Cassiodorus’s testimony, handed down concerning him.

Julian, then, descended from royal blood and a nephew of Constantine the Great through Constantius—Constantine who named Byzantium [Col. 0799B] Constantinople after himself—was at first a Christian. Growing up in the schools of the city of Constantinople, he was trained in the basilica where the teachers were, appearing in private dress. He had a tutor named Marconius and a Laconian grammarian named Nidocles. He studied rhetoric under the sophist Ebolius, already a Christian through the work and diligence of Basil the Great.

> [Note: [Col. 0799D] Paris edition: “Melodem.”]

For the emperor took precautions that, by studying under a pagan sophist, he should not turn aside toward doctrines of impiety. He advanced so far that his ability to govern the empire was widely reported. Therefore he fell under the emperor’s suspicion, was ordered to keep away from the imperial city, and was sent to Nicomedia. He was forbidden to associate with Libanius, the Syrian and pagan sophist, who was staying there after being expelled by the teachers of Constantinople [Col. 0799C]. Yet Julian used the reading of Libanius’s books; and, advancing in rhetoric, he became intimate with Maximus, the Ephesian philosopher, whom the emperor Valentinian later caused to be executed as one practising magical arts. Having tasted philosophical doctrines from him, Julian began to imitate his religion, increasingly inflamed by desire for imperial power.

But, fearing the emperor and guarding against suspicion, he had his hair cut and pretended to a monastic life. Acting the traitor beneath Christian dress, and ordained reader in the church of Nicomedia, he thus escaped the emperor’s wrath. Openly, however, he read the sacred books of the Christians, while secretly he pursued philosophy, his ambition for the empire continually growing stronger. [Col. 0799D] Thus he used to tell his friends that happy times would come when he himself possessed imperial power. And indeed he would not have escaped the emperor’s hand unless the empress Eusebia found him in hiding, interceded for him, and obtained leave for him to be sent to Athens to study philosophy.

Theodoret relates that thereafter, travelling throughout all Greece, he sought out soothsayers and consulted them about whether he would attain the empire. Having found a man who claimed to be most powerful in magic, he was led by him into a place of idols, so that, present in secret, he might consult demons summoned by the magician. When they appeared according to the solemn rite, Julian was compelled [Col. 0800A] to fortify his forehead with the sign of the cross. When this was done, the demons suddenly vanished. The magician then began to blame Julian. But Julian, pleading fear, said that he was astonished at the cross’s power because, at that sign, the demons had fled. “Do not suppose this, good sir,” said the magician, “because they feared it, as you say; rather, they withdrew because they abhorred this sign.” Thus, ensnaring the wretched man, he filled Julian with hatred of the Christian sign.

After this, as Socrates reports, the emperor summoned Julian, appointed him Caesar, gave him his sister Constantia as wife, and sent him into Gaul against the barbarians. Julian succeeded there and began conquering the barbarians by winning the affection of the soldiers.

[Col. 0800B] It is also reported that, while he had entered a certain city, a laurel crown, by which cities are usually adorned, was hanging between columns; its cord broke, and it fell upon his head, crowning him most fittingly. When this occurred, all cried out that it would be a sign of imperial rule for him. Then, engaging the enemy, he prospered with such good fortune that the soldiers hailed him Augustus. Since an imperial crown was lacking, one of the standard-bearers placed around Julian’s head the neck-ring which he wore; and in this manner Julian became emperor.

Let those who hear judge what that philosopher afterwards did. For at the very beginning he arranged everything as he pleased, cast off the fiction of Christian religion, opened the temples in every city, offered sacrifices to idols, and said [Col. 0800C] that he himself was high priest of the pagans. He would also have torn the empire apart by civil war had news not reached him, while he was in Thrace, of the death of the emperor Constantius.

But to win the favour of the multitude, he granted everyone the right to prefer whatever religion he wished. For this reason he sought to become all things to all people: here lavish through desire for empty glory, there frugal through an affected imitation of the philosopher; here gracious through counterfeit civility, there imposing through the weight of empire; and, above all, lest he be thought cruel, he feigned gentleness. But what he truly was, he showed in religion. Thus he ordered bishops who had been sent into exile to be recalled, and their confiscated property to be restored to them. He also ordered the temples of the pagans quickly to be opened to their adherents, and decreed that what had been taken from them should be restored without delay.

[Col. 0800D] He expelled eunuchs, barbers, and cooks from the palace: eunuchs because his wife had died and he had not married another; cooks because, in the manner of a philosopher, he ate simple foods; barbers because, “as he himself said, one is enough for many.” He greatly honoured writers and devotees of learning, especially philosophers. Therefore men of this sort from every quarter were gathered by reputation around the palaces, wrapped in cloaks and distinguished more by dress than by teaching. They were serious deceivers of all Christians and were always favourable to the emperor’s religion [Col. 0801A].

Staying awake at night, he composed books which he publicly recited in the senate. Alone among the emperors since Julius Caesar, he recited speeches in the senate-house. He abolished the public post of mules and horses, ordering them to serve public needs. A few praise these actions of his, but most blame them, because, with the pomp of the palace removed, the empire seemed contemptible.

[Col. 0801B] Sozomen reports that, immediately at the beginning, Julian so openly and shamelessly denied the Christian faith that he sought, by certain sacrifices and invocations which pagans call *expeditions*, and by sacrificial blood, to wash away our baptism and renounce the Church’s confession. From that time onward pagans freely celebrated sacrifices both secretly and publicly, and in the temples.

It is reported that, while he was once sacrificing, a sign of the cross encircled by a crown appeared to him in the entrails of the victim. At this sight some were terrified and understood the power of the true religion and the eternity of Christian doctrine, because the crown is an indication of victory and the circular enclosure, returning into itself, knows no end. But the ruler encouraged them, declaring that favourable things were being shown to him: the sign of Christian doctrine, he said, was being restrained so that it might not be permitted to spread, enclosed within the boundary of a circle.

When Gallus and Julian were still boys, they competed in building a basilica at the burial-place of their mother Mammaea, having divided the work between themselves. An event remarkable to tell and perhaps hard to believe is said to have occurred. [Col. 0801C] The portion belonging to Gallus increased and grew usefully; but Julian’s works were partly dug up and partly filled with rubble as the earth itself vomited it forth. Several times foundations laid in the earth could not be joined together, as though some violent force, striking them from below, drove them away. The event seemed prodigious to everyone, who thought that this man would not prove sound in Christian religion. Nor wrongly, as was evident from what followed.

For he stripped churches and their ministers of possessions and privileges; and, what was especially grave and plainly unjust, he ordered clerics to be enrolled among soldiers, to serve the provincial governor, and handed many of them over to the municipal council. He ordered the Christian people, with their wives and children, to be registered and to pay taxes like villagers; and he decreed that all Galileans were subject to the unhappy penalty of loss of civil status [Col. 0801D].

At first, while sparing Christians, he appeared milder, knowing that earlier persecutors had gained nothing by Christians’ punishment, since Christians had thereby increased all the more and had become glorious by dying for the true doctrine. Therefore, envying their glory, he abstained from tortures, judging it necessary rather to persuade the people by speech and exhortation to cultivate paganism, hoping also in this way to display himself as merciful.

For it is said that, while he was sacrificing to the Fortune of the city at Constantinople, Maris, bishop of Chalcedon, approached him and publicly called him an impious and godless apostate. Julian reproached him only for blindness, because the old blind man was led by another’s hand, [Col. 0802A] and added: “Nor can your Galilean God heal you.” Maris answered: “I give thanks to God, who has done this, so that I might not see you stripped of piety.” The emperor silently withdrew, pretending to be a philosopher, so that by a display of patience he might strengthen paganism.

By law he forbade the sons of Galileans to study the disciplines of poets, rhetoricians, and philosophers. “We are wounded,” he said, “by our own weapons, according to the proverb. For armed from our own authors, they undertake wars against us.” He enacted another law, ordering Galileans to be expelled from military service. He added another, that the property of Galileans should be taken away, because their Christ had commanded them to be poor.

Apollinaris, a learned and gifted man, wrote the Hebrew antiquities in heroic [Col. 0802B] verse in place of Homer’s poem; and in another work he imitated the comedies of Menander, removing their fabulous character. He also followed the tragedies of Euripides and the lyre of Pindar; indeed, to state it plainly, by taking subjects from the divine Scriptures he composed in a short time all the instructional readings, very closely comparable to those of the Greeks in metre, excellence, morals, composition, style, and arrangement. He also produced a notable book addressed to the emperor himself, or rather against the philosophers, in which, without expressly citing the testimonies of holy Scripture, he proved by unanswerable reasoning that they were irrational and that his own views concerning God were true. When the emperor had read it, he wrote to the distinguished bishops of the time: “I have read it, and I have condemned it.” The bishops replied: [Col. 0802C] “Though you have read it, you have not understood it; for if you had understood it, you would never have condemned it.” This letter is believed to have been Basil of Cappadocia’s.

When the emperor came to Antioch, he was mocked because his beard was extremely long. The people of Antioch said: “Let it be shorn, so that his beard may be useful for ropes.” Since he habitually sacrificed a bull, he ordered a bull and an altar to be fashioned for him upon his throne. Mocking him, they said: “This bull has overthrown the world; and unless Libanius had called him back, he would have grievously afflicted the Antiochenes,” against whom he then wrote a rather witty book.

Moreover, in order to encourage and arm the Jews anew against Christ, he ordered them to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem. Those whom he had summoned from all over the world assembled, and he supplied very many resources [Col. 0802D] and sent a governor, a most worthy executor of his impious commands. They say that they had silver hooks, baskets, and spades for clearing the site. When they had begun to dig, this very great multitude worked on the appointed day; but at night earth rose of its own accord from the valley. When the remnants of the former foundation had been removed, they prepared everything anew. After they had gathered many thousands of measures of gypsum and lime, a great force of winds suddenly blew forth, storms and squalls abruptly arose, and scattered all that had been collected. Yet while they still raved and were in no way corrected by divine forbearance, there first came a great earthquake, and everyone not initiated into the divine mysteries was violently [Col. 0803A] struck down. When they were not frightened even by this sign, fire issued from the foundations being undermined, burning many of the diggers to death and mangling the limbs of others. At night, while many slept in a nearby portico, the portico itself suddenly fell with its roof and crushed the sleepers. On the following day a shining sign of the saving cross appeared in heaven; moreover, the Jews’ garments were filled with the mark of the cross—not marked in a brilliant colour, however, but in black. Seeing these things and trembling at the divine scourges, those who had rebelled against God returned to their own homes, confessing that he was God whom their forefathers were shown to have hung upon the wood.

Yet amid all this the rage of the impious man did not turn away. With hardened heart he commanded that whoever refused to sacrifice should not enter the palace [Col. 0803B] and should share neither in a guild nor in the forum, neither in arbitration nor in rank nor in any public administration. When Christians were tortured or despoiled, he urged patience upon them, because, he said, their Galilean had taught his followers this by the explicit word of the law and by the example of his deeds. Thus many Christians turned back, either laid low by fear or caught by deceit; and the cruelty of the pagans grew stronger.

To accustom soldiers more easily to idolatry, he endeavoured to restore to its ancient pattern that most exalted Roman standard which Constantine had altered into the form of a cross. On public images, however, he depicted Jupiter as though bringing him a crown and purple robe from heaven; likewise Mercury and Mars looking upon him, as testimony, as it were, that he was wise and strong. By these images he sought to have the gods secretly worshipped under the pretext of imperial authority, so that subjects might be covertly deceived and, once so ensnared, more readily do what he wished. If they refused, they were tortured as despisers of the imperial power.

He approved Christians’ studies, although he persecuted the faith and the practice of virtues, in order to strengthen the pagans’ error: among the Galileans, he falsely asserted, these things were not true but fabricated. He therefore resolved to strip them of their virtues and wished pagans, without faith, morals, or instruction, to be practitioners of philosophy in imitation of Christians—as a letter written by him to Arsacius, high priest of Galatia, teaches in these words:

“The pagan cult is not yet being conducted in accordance with [Col. 0803D] our intention, because its adherents have fallen into negligence. For the splendour, greatness, and sublimity of the gods surpass every utterance and every hope. Yet may the gods be gracious to us despite our negligence, since by their providence in a short time so great a change has occurred as no one had previously dared even to pray for. Although we think this may suffice, we do not consider how the superstition of the Christians has been increased by their care for strangers, by their concern for burials and the dead, and by the many supports and practices of honourable conduct which are not genuine but feigned. I judge that such things ought to be done among us in truth.

“It is therefore not enough that you yourself should be such a man; all the priests throughout Galatia must likewise be so. Entreat them, bend them by argument, or else quickly [Col. 0804A] remove them from priestly ministry unless, with their wives, children, and servants, they bow their necks to the gods; and unless they cease tolerating their servants or children when these scorn to do this, or the Galileans when they act impiously against the gods and prefer impieties to acts of piety. Then admonish them all that a priest must neither attend spectacles nor drink in taverns nor preside over any trade or disgraceful or shameless occupation. Let those who obey be honoured; expel the disobedient.

“Establish hostels in every city, so that strangers may enjoy our kindness—not only our own people, but also foreigners lacking money. That you may have means for this, I have meanwhile decreed that each year thirty thousand modii of grain and sixty thousand sextarii of wine be distributed throughout Galatia. [Col. 0804B] One fifth of these is to be spent on the poor who attend the temples; the remainder is to be distributed to strangers and persons in need. For it is shameful that the impious Galileans do not cast off the Jews but rather feed them, along with their own people and even ours, while our people are abandoned by their own without support from their own. Therefore teach the pagans also to make contributions for such services and to offer the first fruits of their produce from pagan villages. Train them in benefits of this kind, teaching them that this was formerly the practice of our people. Homer proves it, introducing Eumaeus as doing such things. Yet we do not imitate the good practices of our own people; instead we abandon them to others, not ashamed of our negligence but rather rejecting reverence for the gods.

“If I learn that you are doing these things, I shall be full of joy. Receive provincial governors at home only rarely; write to them frequently. When they enter a city, let none of the priests go out to meet them. When they come to the temples of the gods, let no soldier or officer of the preceding retinue proceed within the doors; but whoever wishes may follow. Once he has reached the very threshold of the temple, let him be a private person. For you, as you know, are judge within. This, indeed, seems to be required even by sacred ordinance. Those who obey are therefore pious in truth; those who resist are shown to be devoted to vain glory. For what punishment ought they to suffer, or what aid do they deserve, who refuse to have the Mother of the Gods favourable to them? Those, then, who neglect her will not merely be without blame: they will also endure the onset of our indignation. [Col. 0804D] For it is not right that one who has the gods as enemies should be spared. Persuade them, therefore, that if they wish to enjoy my protection, all must diligently offer worship to the Mother of the Gods.”

He wrote these things and, in imitation of the Church, established temples of demons and appointed ministers in various ranks after the pattern of the clergy, so that there might be persons to teach others the worship of perfidy and to restore penitents after sin by a moderate correction, following Christian tradition. Nothing done by pagans against Christ seemed monstrous to him. So far was this the case that not even raging against the dead appeared inhuman or cruel to pagans. Thus in the city of Sebaste they opened the tomb of John the Baptist and consigned it to fire; [Col. 0805A] they scattered his bones and ashes.

If I wished to recount either the chief crimes of this man or even briefly the things done through him against the Church throughout the world, such an extensive subject would require many large volumes. But let us proceed to the end which the pious Galilean, the Son of the undefiled Virgin, powerfully inflicted upon his impious persecutor, for the consolation of his Church and for the glory of that majesty by which he is equal and consubstantial with the Father.

Accordingly, as he advanced upon the Persian expedition, he sent, according to custom, to Delphi, Delos, and Dodona, inquiring whether it was expedient to go to war. All the oracles promised victory; among their responses was one which encouraged him and which I do not hesitate to insert as an example of falsehood and deception. It was as follows:

> Now all the gods advance, bearing trophies of victory by the river Thire.  
> I, Mars the warrior, shall be their leader.

Whoever believes the Pythian god to be the leader of the Muses and lord of reason may interpret the force and meaning of this verse. Encouraged by it, the wretched man dreamed of complete victory and was preparing even to destroy the Galileans. Yet, as was fitting, he was scorned as a base apostate by very many.

For at Antioch there lived a most worthy man, an instructor of youths. There too was the very famous sophist Libanius, awaiting Julian’s victory and having his threats before his eyes. Mocking the true religion, he said: “What do you suppose the carpenter’s son [Col. 0805C] is doing now?” The teacher, filled with grace, replied: “O sophist, the Creator of all things, whom you call the carpenter’s son, is preparing Julian’s burial chamber.” A few days later Julian’s death was announced. He was brought in his bier, and the fear inspired by his threats vanished.

At the same time the exceedingly devout man Julian, surnamed Saba, when his attendants asked the cause of his sudden cheerfulness, replied: “The savage devastator of the sacred vineyard has paid the penalty for his devastation; he lies dead, his terrors and threats brought to nothing.” But the manner in which the impious persecutor died must be set forth.

After he had afflicted both citizens and enemies in many ways with the hardships and famine of the Persian war, he came to the city of Ctesiphon and pressed the king so severely that the latter repeatedly offered him by embassies a part of his kingdom if he would depart and end the war. The emperor, in his pride, despised this offer, failing to consider that victory is good, but excessive victory is exceedingly odious. He trusted in magical arts and, holding the Pythagorean belief that souls pass through diverse bodies, thought himself possessed of Alexander’s soul—or rather, that in another body he was another Alexander. The Romans complained of a prince who refused to end the war, but they resisted the advancing Persians, so that now one side, now the other, was often put to flight.

Julian, seated on horseback, encouraged the army. He was unarmed, presumptuously trusting in his own good fortune, when a missile suddenly hurled against him passed through his arm and lodged in his side. [Col. 0806A] From this wound he received the end of his life. Who inflicted this most just wound remains unknown to this day. Some say that one of the invisible beings struck him; others, an Ishmaelite shepherd; others, a soldier exhausted by hunger and travel. But whether it was a man or an angel, it is clear that he acted in service of divine commands. For they say that when he was wounded, he immediately filled his hand with his own blood and cast it into the air, saying: “You have conquered, Galilean; you have conquered.” In that very act, though blasphemous, he confessed the victory.

He died in the third year of his reign and the thirty-first year of his life; yet to good people he seemed to have lived far too long, for the victory of the Galilean was proclaimed not only in churches but even in theatres. All cried: “Great fool, where are your prophecies? God and his Christ have conquered.” When the impious man had died, astonishing images of the emperor were found in temples, and marvellous tokens of his loudly proclaimed wisdom and very famous piety. At Carrhae, when a temple which he had ordered to remain shut until his return was opened, a woman was found hanging by her hair, her hands stretched out, her womb opened, in whose liver he had examined the outcome of the Persian war. At Antioch also they found many chests in the palace full of human heads, and innumerable dead bodies submerged in wells. The Tripartite History relates more fully his monstrous and criminal deeds—deeds befitting neither emperor nor philosopher, but an impious magician, enemy of God and humankind.

Among the British people also, as a certain history of our country testifies, the hand of the most glorious martyr and king Edmund was exercised to restrain and punish the frenzy of tyranny. When Sweyn was ravaging and despoiling the island of Britain, much of which he had occupied, and was afflicting Christ’s members with many persecutions, he burdened the province with the levy called in the English tongue Danegeld and ordered that the possessions of the aforementioned martyr be included in the assessment. Entreaty was made to him, but he despised the prayers. A religious brother sent by the martyr forbade the tyrant under threat to oppress by unjust servitude the Church of Christ, the martyr’s house, and its free household. But impiety was deaf to prayers, swelled at prohibition, hardened at threats; and, abusing the humble messenger with insults and injuries, it hastened God’s avenging hand, provoked the scourge, and, despising God’s patience, blindly rushed by rashness into death. Nor was there delay. The tyrant immediately expired. For while he was among the soldiers in camp, alone—as he himself confessed—he saw blessed Edmund approaching with a weapon, fiercely rebuking him and striking him to death. From that day, although the island has had grievous tyrants, the Church of Saint Edmund has remained exempt from the aforesaid fiscal levy. None of them dared provoke the martyr or endanger himself by oppressing his church.

In our own times Eustace, son of Stephen, had resolved to rage against the Church [Col. 0807A] of God. When he had devastated everything to the limit of his powers and saw that the land of blessed Edmund, to which all plunderers had deferred, was wealthy, while he himself, having exhausted the resources of the kingdom, had no means of paying money to his soldiers even once or twice—for the customary gifts had already failed—he despoiled the estates of the aforesaid church. Yet he had not digested the food which he had received from the resources of the place before, on that very day and before he could return to his own home, which was very near, he was struck by the martyr’s hand and smitten with a deadly illness; about the eighth day he surrendered both possessions and life.

Why linger over a few examples? To speak of our own country: where are Geoffrey, Milo, Ranulf, Alan, Simon, Gilbert—not so much earls of the realm as public enemies? Where is William of Salisbury? [Col. 0807B] Where is Marimo, who, driven on by the blessed Virgin, fell into the pit he had prepared? Where are the others whose names alone would fill a book? Their malice is surely conspicuous, their infamy well known, their end unhappy, and one which the present age cannot fail to know. Therefore, if anyone does not know the ancient histories, if he does not know how Cyrus, before whom kings turned their backs in flight, was overthrown by Tamyris, queen of the Scythians; if he does not recall the falls and downfalls of earlier tyrants, let him at least attend to what is forced upon unwilling eyes, and he will see more clearly than daylight that all tyrants are wretched.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Gideon, who is a pattern for rulers, and on Antiochus

What, then, do those intend who strive to oppress the commonwealth—that is, God’s people—with an undue yoke of servitude? I cannot see, unless perhaps they seek power in order that they may powerfully endure the torments of misery. For if they desired only to govern and not to dominate, measuring the burden of office, they would not pursue it with such avidity. The will of a ruler depends upon God’s law and does not prejudice liberty. But the will of a tyrant serves desire and, resisting the law that fosters liberty, strives to impose a yoke of servitude upon fellow servants. Scripture teaches this, and it may not be contradicted.

“All the men of Israel said to Gideon: ‘Rule over us, you and your son and your son’s son, because you delivered us from the hand of Midian.’ To them he said: ‘I shall not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule.’ And he said to them: [Col. 0807D] ‘I ask one request of you: give me earrings from your spoil’” (Judges 8).

I seem to myself to see, on the face of this text, what I have said. For Gideon, whose name is interpreted as “one going about what is useless,” or “the testing of their wickedness,” seems by his name and words to indicate the office of a ruler. It is his task to go about what is useless and either destroy it or restore it to usefulness; and whatever he finds unjust, to exclude it from his borders, so that victory may advance with him against his enemies. The honour of dominion is offered to him, and he refuses it; yet he subjects to law those whom he has freed from the yoke of servitude. The honour which would pass from father to son is offered, but he prefers that God be honoured.

Who among those who confuse right and wrong and toil amid labours and miseries in order that they may leave their sons heirs not so much of honour [Col. 0808A] as of plunder and injustice can rightly be compared to him? Who is there that places the law of God and its justice, which consists solely in charity, before his children? “He who loves father or mother or children more than me,” he says, “is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). And certainly those who set transient things before Christ pass away more swiftly with those transient things; nor is glory perpetuated among those with whom, all else being preferred, Christ remains without glory.

Therefore let the ruler fear a fall who, through affection for children or the impulses of the flesh, diminishes divine honour, forgetful of charity. Yet no one admits to rising up against God; nevertheless very many do rise up, and these things now occur openly. Antiochus entered the sanctuary in pride, and many do this. Uzziah, whom the authoritative writings record as just in many respects, after the death of the priest Zechariah, surnamed “the Understanding One,” seized the priestly office not so much piously as boldly. When the Levites cried out, “Are you not Uzziah the king, and not a priest?” he scorned to listen. Immediately leprosy attacked that part of his body which the priest, by the law, covered with a plate of gold, so that, in accordance with the prophetic imprecation, his face might be filled with disgrace. This king is known both from contemporary kings and especially because Romulus, from whom the Romans derive their race, was born in the year of his death.

Many imitate Uzziah by presuming upon priestly things, but very few are ashamed of his leprosy. Yet more follow Antiochus, who enters holy things not devoutly, to offer in the priest’s place, but in order to destroy whatever is holy in the Temple of the Lord. For after Antiochus had fashioned the idol of desolation and abomination, he burned the books of God’s law with fire and tore them up; and wherever books of the Lord’s covenant were found, anyone found observing God’s law was killed according to King Antiochus’s edict.

In my time I have seen some men thrusting themselves into priestly office and rashly setting their shoulders to take the ark from the shoulders of the Levites, forgetful of the place which to this day is called “the striking of the flank.” I have seen others who devote books of law to the fire, and who would not shrink from tearing up laws or canons if they came into their hands. In King Stephen’s time Roman laws were banished from the realm, [Col. 0808D] though the household of the venerable Father Theobald, primate of the Britains, had introduced them into Britain. A royal edict also prohibited anyone from keeping the books, and silence was imposed upon our Vacarius. Yet by God’s action the force of the law grew stronger in proportion as impiety strove more fiercely to weaken it.

But who among so many thousands desiring to reign wishes to resemble Gideon? Or who wishes the law to rule both himself and the people? Yet that one thing which Gideon asks of his subjects ought to suffice for all rulers: namely, that he should receive only earrings from the spoil. For if he takes care to declare what the law says, and the people obediently submit to it, so that there may be neither injustice nor contradiction in the city and among the people over whom he presides, that should surely suffice for the ruler.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Brutus’s counsel should be used against those who contend, indeed fight schismatically, for the supreme pontificate; and that nothing is tranquil under tyranny

[Col. 0809A]

But suppose that those who are carnal may contend twice over precedence: I judge this utterly unlawful for ecclesiastical men. Yet by the example of carnal persons impiety creeps in under the appearance of religion, and now men not only contend for the priesthood but fight for it. Formerly men were dragged unwillingly yet readily toward martyrdom; they fled the highest sees as something worse than prison and cross. By contrast, priests now speak openly, and do not even state the proverbial formula: “We do not wish,” they say, “to be martyrs, but we do not give the glory of our sees to another.”

Wretched indeed and pitiable is this voice in the mouth of a priest, who thus acknowledges Christ while openly confessing that he does not wish to follow him. Can there be doubt whether he dies a true confessor who, if need be, does not await the persecutor? For Cyprian says: “If a bishop is afraid, it is all over with him.” Let him indeed be allowed to fear; but it is unlawful not to stand firm in necessity. A fugitive is useless and dishonoured. Yet there is one respect in which they seem to imitate the steadfastness of martyrs: if, that is, a contest must be fought for a see. Some report—and it is true—that ambitious men have at times, indeed often, disputed over the Roman pontificate, and that the pontiff has entered the Holy of Holies not without the blood of brethren.

Wars more than civil were again stirred up between Caesar and Pompey; and whatever was attempted at Philippi, Leucas, Mutina, Egypt, or Spain, whatever was wickedly done, a priestly contest has surpassed it. Do they procure the shedding of Christian blood so that they may have pre-eminently the right to lay down their lives for the flock, which is the shepherd’s duty? Do they demolish the Church and profane holy things so that there may be something needing to be built and sanctified? They shake peoples, disturb kingdoms, plunder the Church’s resources—perhaps in order to provide themselves material for earning merit, to set everything in order, to pity and provide for the poor, and, while others compete, to forestall their need.

For if they do these things so that more may be permitted them with impunity, so that they may amass money, cherish, enlarge, and corrupt flesh and blood, ennoble their household, or finally seek their own glory by ruling over the clergy—not becoming from the heart an example to the flock, although with their lips and by pretence of office they put on the shepherd—they approach tyranny more readily than princely rule.

The philosophers say—and I judge it true—that among human things nothing is more useful to a human being than another human being; and among human beings none is more useful than a ruler, ecclesiastical or secular. Conversely, nothing is more harmful to a human being than another human being; and among such persons a secular or ecclesiastical tyrant is more harmful still. Yet certainly, in either class, the ecclesiastical tyrant surpasses the secular. Salt that has become foolish is good for nothing at all but to be cast out and trampled by men. Further:

> So utterly does love of gold,  
> ignorant only of fear of steel and death,  
> overthrow laws without any distinction. But wealth,  
> the most worthless part of things, has stirred up your conflict.  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia* II

[Col. 0810A] Therefore let unity be divided, wholeness torn apart, sincerity corrupted, and holiness stained; let a new judgment of the world be celebrated, and let its prince—who was cast out by Christ’s passion—return and scatter scandals, so that blessed is he who is not caught in his snares:

> … Is it for so vast  
> an outpouring of new crimes that they ask which of the two shall rule the world?  
> It was scarcely worth stirring up civil wars  
> merely that neither should rule.  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia* II.59

Christ taught the most upright way to eminence. He did not wish his disciples to resemble the kings of the Gentiles, who lord it over their subjects and whose wielders of authority are called benefactors. Rather, he who is greater should voluntarily become lesser and, beyond the others, claim for himself only the office of serving—by right, peaceably, through strength, [Col. 0810B] and with contention removed. But these men have preferred another path: rising up against their brethren and rejecting the humility of service, they desire to dominate even above the kings of the Gentiles. Nor is there any doubt that, as charity grows cold—indeed, is extinguished—they too set their seat in the north. For “those brought forth hate their equals.”

Would that those who saw those times had followed Brutus’s counsel, from which Cato’s authority turned him aside when civil war was imminent. For Brutus had resolved to keep his hands from civil arms; and the more willingly and vigorously anyone engages in them, the more unjust and savage he is. Thus he says:

> You have Brutus now neither as Pompey’s nor as Caesar’s enemy,  
> but as the enemy of war’s victor.

If, therefore, those for whose lordship schismatics contend are wise, let them permit only the contenders themselves to meet; let them fear to offer aid to either side, uncertain who will be victorious but certain how great and grievous a ruin threatens the defeated.

> No hand is clean when war has a judge mutually borrowed.

For:

> The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.128

Let the world certainly rejoice if one alone has conquered; but let it rejoice with yet greater gladness if both, or neither, prevail. Let them meet, then, if they wish, on the island of Lycaonia, or elsewhere—if any place is more suited to war or single combat. For the ancients, Quintilian testifies, called *belli* what we now call *duelli*. And without danger to world or city, let whichever combatant God approves, or permits to be victor, overcome the other in single combat. The defeated man also, if it pleases the victor, should be drowned in the Tiber; or, if he seems to require gentler treatment, confined in a cage. When the abbot of the place opens the cloister—or rather, the prison—to him, let him declare that he prepared it not for the man now condemned, but for the defeated man. For:

> No loyalty ever chose the wretched as friends.

But the man who has won—that is, the more violent man—should be transported into perpetual exile to Lipara or another island, to cut marble, or be condemned to the mines. For the crime of schism makes equal all whom it stains, except that usually the stronger—indeed, the fiercer—man is also [Col. 0811A] the more unjust.

What is more destructive or hateful than civil war? Nothing at all, except the rage of schismatics or the pest of heretics. Which of the two is more destructive I could not easily say, if indeed there is a number among them such that one may be separated from the other. Civil wars will certainly cease if presumption lacks the helper of recklessness. Nor is there anyone who can drive fellow citizens into frenzy unless they take some pleasure in madness itself. The necessity of raging is either nonexistent altogether or, at most, imaginary. This too lies open to very many and very great dangers, whose outcome no one sufficiently avoids unless he forestalls the possibility.

This the most weighty poet suggests—or, if you prefer, following Quintilian, to call him more rightly an orator, I do not object—provided it be agreed that dangers even capable of occurring must be guarded against, and that the whole community cannot be compelled by any one person to comply unwillingly with wickedness. For he says:

> And though a soldier be stained by no blood,  
> he fears what he was able to have done. Why beat your breast?  
> Why do you groan madly? Why pour out empty tears?  
> Do you not confess that you obey wickedness of your own will?  
> Do you so greatly fear the man whom you yourself make fearful?  
> Let him sound the trumpet for war; you disregard its dreadful notes.  
> Let him carry the standards; stand still. Soon, soon civil Fury  
> will fall, and Caesar, deprived of his son-in-law, will love.

Yes, indeed—if only the Church of God be raised into the liberty of the Spirit. If it refuses to undertake the service of wickedness, either schisms will be wholly stilled, or, with the fabric of unity remaining, schismatics alone will fight among themselves. Meanwhile let the Church restrain her hands, because Peter’s sword, which thirsted for blood through carnal affection, is at the Lord’s command presently sheathed; and disciples hurrying to root out the tares are instructed to await the angels, the harvesters.

Let the integrity of unity pray that the cut stone, upon which the Church is founded and which the schismatics reject, may gather the dissenters into itself: he who made both one, and preferred that his garment pass whole by lot to the faithful rather than be cut apart. Let it pray, I say, that faith may not fail, and that Satan, demanding to sift, may not destroy and trample down even the wheat. Let it pray for peace, seek peace, and pursue it even when it flees. Let it remember him who, though he could have brought forth more than twelve legions of angels, acquired all things when lifted up upon the cross. For this very self-emptying deserved so greatly to be exalted that every knee bends to his glory. Priestly wars regard schismatics as guilty, but make guilty even those who assent, though they are righteous. Therefore let them remain still, standing at a distance with Peter, to see the end. Let them recall that pagan saying:

> … If fury had given arms to the dwellers in heaven,  
> or if the earth-born Giants had sought to assail the stars,  
> yet human piety would not dare, either by arms  
> or prayers, to aid Jupiter.

This, indeed, seems to be observed in cases where it is uncertain who has taken up arms more justly. For if a heretic or schismatic attacks a Catholic, it is pious to stand with truth and to serve the Roman pontiff with the deepest devotion. But this must first be known, for a schismatic often falsely claims to be Catholic. [Col. 0812A] Who indeed would presume to judge the supreme pontiff, whose cause is reserved for the examination of God alone? Whoever attempts this can certainly labour, but can by no means succeed. Nor do I distinguish the title of pontiff with excessive nicety: let that man be regarded here as pontiff whose canonical election came first.

Jonah caused a shipwreck in order to avert shipwreck, and preferred to perish alone rather than involve others in his own dangers, though he had not undertaken the charge of steering the ship. Solomon recognized maternal love because the woman preferred that the child claimed by the prostitute should remain whole rather than be divided. But these men prefer that the Church be endangered and divided rather than refrain from usurping honour and refrain from bringing a false charge against the innocent mother Church. “This,” he says, “is his mother, because out of love she recoils from division.” [Col. 0812B] Conversely, this man is a stepson who

> Probes his mother’s entrails with the sword.

How many and how great were the tumults and slaughter caused by that clash when the son of Peter Leonis tried to ascend from the north against Innocent V of blessed memory, predecessor of Lord Adrian—may the Lord extend his life and prosperity in himself for ever! Did not that man’s downfall also draw a portion of the stars down with it? Who does not know Giles of Tusculum? Who does not know Peter of Pisa, to whom no other in the curia was equal, or scarcely equal? Who could enumerate the bishops who fell throughout almost all Italy? Surely, while the memory of that downfall stood in our age, it is incredible that anyone should be so wretchedly ambitious as not to fear dividing the Church. I believe no one is so stupid that he would not prefer to be destroyed himself rather than have such a disturbance arise on his account.

If, through the demands of our sins, one of these executioners should ascend Peter’s see and, with the Lord angered, approach the helm of his ship, he will certainly make shipwreck, and not undeservedly. For Peter himself, though called by the Lord, began to sink when frightened by a stronger gust; and the ship which had the Lord as passenger despaired of safety until the sleeping Christ was awakened by prayers. He who ascends wretchedly is whirled about more wretchedly and will be cast down most wretchedly. Nor do undertakings begun from an evil principle have happy endings. Discord is the surest sign of injustice and failure. For:

> … Discord troubles the least of things;  
> the greatest preserve peace.

Phaethon in the fables, desiring his father’s chariot, set the world on fire; and at last, through the god’s pity, he too, set ablaze, fell headlong when the chariot was shattered. Then
[lacuna] They say that the day passed without the sun: (OVID, *Tristia* V.8.31); and while the Church blazes, set aflame by schism, Christ seems absent. Icarus too, while in the youthful recklessness of his exaltation he is borne into heaven, is drowned in the waves of the sea. He was cast down while he was being raised up. The elevation of the wicked is indeed preparation for a graver fall. For who is more wicked than the man who turns the ministry of peace, the office of sacrifice, into quarrels and slaughter?

[Col. 0813A] To what end, I ask, such savagery? Is it for life? But “their end is destruction” (Phil. 3). For glory? But “their glory is in their shame” (ibid.). For pleasure? Then “their god is their belly” (ibid.). Or that they may be ennobled in flesh and blood? But “flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). For against carnal persons it is not I, but this—and harsher words besides—that the apostolic trumpet sounds: “Whose end,” he says, “is destruction; whose god is their belly; and whose glory is in their shame, because they mind earthly things” (Phil. 3). If they seek to fulfil their own will by ruling others—which is tyranny—nothing could turn out less advantageously for them. Nothing, indeed, is safe or peaceful for a tyrant. Ask Damocles, and he will acknowledge that he learned this from the tyrant of Sicily: when ruin threatened him on every side in burning [Col. 0813B] coals, a sword, hanging at the slightest movement, as though from the thread of a weaver, rushed upon his neck amid royal delights, like one striking him.

Theodosius affirms this in Claudian. For he says:

> He who inspires more terror himself fears more: such is the lot  
> Of tyrants. Let them envy the illustrious and slaughter the brave;  
> Let them live armed with swords and surrounded by poisons;  
> Let them devise double-edged schemes and utter trembling threats.  
> But do you act as citizen and father; provide for all.  
> Let not your own wishes move you, but the public good.

“Blush, Sidon,” says the sea (Isa. 23), because she now speaks carnally—she whom a spiritual man cannot hear. For if priests heard this voice, they would by no means run through weapons and enemies in order to seize the foremost seats. Yet although all bear [Col. 0813C] the summit of the supreme pontificate, I judge that, so far as religion may safely permit, a wise man should flee it rather than accept it.

For, to speak truthfully from my own knowledge, its condition seems most laborious and, as concerns the state of this present age, most miserable. If he serves avarice, it is death to him; but if not, he will not escape the hands and tongues of the Romans. Unless he has means to stop their mouths and restrain their hands, he must harden his ears, eyes, and mind against the insults, disgraceful acts, and sacrileges which they carry out. Three things especially overthrow every judgment, even that of prudent persons: love of gifts, respect of persons, and readiness to believe. No one at all can be moved by these and dispense justice. Therefore [Col. 0813D] the Roman pontiff, whose duty it is to restrain the excesses of all, must be free from them.

If he hates gifts, who will confer benefits upon an unwilling recipient? What will he give who receives nothing? Or, if he gives nothing, how will he appease the Romans? If he does not respect their persons, how will he stand before them? For he can scarcely weigh a priestly case in the consistory without being compelled to admit them to every counsel. What of the fact that he is compelled to condemn simony, gifts, and payments? If he follows these practices, does he not condemn himself by his own pronouncement? If, at the height of power, freedom is slight, then surely the man set over laws is subject to no one, yet is more narrowly restrained from what is unlawful. Thus the Roman pontiff has least freedom precisely because he has most power.

What is weightier [Col. 0814A] than concern for all the Churches? The apostolic prerogative passes to his successors; indeed, part of that prerogative is what the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11). If you do not wish to review the whole matter, let whoever disputes for primacy claim even this, and, I think, he will quickly yield his place.

Moreover, whoever is Roman pontiff must, given the Church’s present condition, be the servant of servants. I do not mean this merely as a title of honour, as some suppose, but substantively: he must serve the servants of God even against his will. Every person serves God and is the steward of His mercy or justice. The angel serves; man serves; the good serve; the evil serve; and the prince [Col. 0814B] of this world himself, the devil, serves. Therefore Romans serve God, and tyrants too, whom the Roman pontiff must serve. So much so that, unless he serves, he must be either no pontiff or no Roman.

Who, then, doubts that he is the servant of servants? I call Lord Adrian—may God make his times happy—as witness to this: no one is more wretched than the Roman pontiff; no condition is more wretched than his. Even if nothing else harms him, he must soon fail from labour alone. He confesses that he found such miseries in that see that, by comparison with the present, all his preceding bitterness was delight and a most happy life. He says that the chair of the Roman pontiff is thorny, everywhere set with exceedingly sharp prickles, and of such weight that it presses, wears down, and crushes the strongest [Col. 0814C] shoulders. The crown and tiara rightly seem splendid, he says, because they are fiery; yet he would rather never have left his native soil of England, or have remained hidden forever in the cloister of blessed Rufus, than have entered such straits—were it not that he dares not resist divine providence.

Ask him while he is still alive, and believe one who has experienced it. He also added this very frequently to me: though he had risen, step by step, from a cloistered cleric through every office to become supreme pontiff, the ascent had added nothing whatever of happiness or tranquil rest to his earlier life. And, to use his own words—for when I am present he wishes nothing concerning himself to be concealed from my eyes—“The Lord,” he says, “has always stretched me upon the anvil and beneath the hammer; but now, if it please Him, let Him place His right hand beneath the burden which He has laid upon my weakness, because it is unbearable for me.”

Is he not therefore most worthy of pity who struggles for so great a misery? Let the man chosen be ever so rich: on the next day he will be poor and bound to almost innumerable creditors. What then will become of him whom no election calls, but whom blind and bloody ambition, with Christ resisting in His members and not without fraternal bloodshed, thrusts in? This is to succeed Romulus in acts of parricide, not Peter in the stewardship of the flock entrusted to him.

## Chapter XXIV. That Epicureans never attain their end

Unless the contentious man conceals what reason nevertheless does not permit to be concealed, it is clearer than light from the foregoing [Col. 0815A] that Epicureans never attain their end. For while they aspire to a tranquil life, withdraw themselves to fulfil desire, and philosophize—or rather behave foolishly, for no one can wisely fulfil what he perversely desires—no one attains this through the streams of Babylon.

I also think those should be classed under the name of Epicureans who wish in all things to fulfil their own will. For when things serve desire, affection passes into pleasure. If inclination does not obey inclination, the more strongly you will, the more you are tormented—provided desire lies within the will. Otherwise, it is sometimes pleasant and fruitful to will what you cannot have, if perhaps you hunger and thirst after righteousness—though it is laborious.

The world, then, is full of Epicureans, because among so great a multitude of human beings few [Col. 0815B] do not serve desire—that is, corrupt pleasure—while those who are not entangled in the toils of a laborious will are either none or very few. Man was excluded from the place of pleasure when desire gained mastery, because one over whom desire has begun to rule cannot enjoy a pleasant and tranquil life. He preferred doing what pleased him to doing what he was commanded; cast into a place of misery, he was sent into the land of toil, so that the earth might bring forth thorns and thistles for him and for his seed, and that he might eat bread in the sweat of his face (Gen. 3)—he who, obedient in uprightness of will, could have had full pleasure without difficulty and labour. For he found all things ready for necessity and pleasure alike.

Now *vultus* (“countenance”), according to those who investigate word-origins more curiously, is said to derive from *velle* (“to will”); [Col. 0815C] and its sweat signifies the toil and anguish of corrupt pleasure. If, therefore, one sweats over that which strengthens the human heart, and even in taking what makes glad, what is there which mortal nature may think has been granted to it without labour? The soul recalls what was said to the sinful mother of us all, whom the Creator’s sentence struck.

She therefore bears in pain the sons of virtues, whereas she bears the offspring of vices without labour. For sinful nature, inclined to evil and corrupted from its youth—which age lies near its origin—can slip without labour or difficulty; yet it cannot rise to good without labour, and, having risen, cannot stand without difficulty and grace. Thus it bears vices—daughters, indeed, not sons—without pain, but [Col. 0815D] certainly for pain; while it bears sons in pain, but plainly for joy, not pain.

Therefore Epicurus lives in pain, whose life bears sons or daughters, and who always groans at present or future anxieties. For, to pass over other matters, he does not rejoice in what is present; or, if he is not blind, while measuring the ends of things, he laments them as passing away and fleeing. Joyous things are forbidden to stand still unless one rejoices in those things that make one blessed or advance one toward everlasting life. For this world passes away, and all its desirable things. However much it flatters the unwary and offers the sweet enticements of its deception, its last things are more bitter than any wormwood.

And because reason convincingly proves in every respect that its present state is incomplete, it [Col. 0816A] always promises something solid in the future, though it has never from the beginning brought even one of its lovers and followers to perfection or made him attain his wish. Hence the miser hungers amid his wealth; the powerful ruler, at the highest pinnacle, serves in the depths of luxury; lack of joy afflicts the pleasure-seeker; and the suitor of fame and favour becomes worthless amid the whole swelling of vain glory. Whoever does not see these things is exceedingly blind, since every one of those engaged in them admits that he lacks the very thing he seeks.

Yet there are those whose eyes wickedness has so blinded that they cannot behold what shines by itself. Thus moles, deprived of sight, do not recognize the benefit of light; rejoicing in their inborn darkness, they hate the purer air and cannot live if they are kept too long from earth and their hiding-places. Do not those [Col. 0816B] bear the image of moles who always dwell in the earth, whose whole way of life is pressed down upon the ground, so that they savour nothing lofty or divine? Indeed, they savour not even what is human: whereas it belongs to man, though other animals bend down toward earth, to contemplate heaven and heavenly things with the erect dignity of body and mind. These people, however, are depressed by their own fault—yet by a fault in some respect like that of a mole’s nature. Certainly one stained by guilt is worse than one suffering under the compulsion of nature. Do not suppose that one thinks highly who wishes to surpass his companions in nature, not by virtue but by vices.

But why do I rebuke blindness in this herd of moles, except because it seems to be the source of all other evils? From it streams flow forth, as it were, of vices, so that you might see gathered together in a single body the rapacity of the lion, the savagery [Col. 0816C] of the tiger, the gluttony of the wolf, the changefulness of the leopard, the deceit of the fox, the graspingness of the harpy, the filthiness of the pig, the wantonness of the goat, the pride of the horse, the stupidity of the ass, the obstinacy of the mule, the venom of the hydra, the blackness of the raven, and whatever else of perversity that most foul creature could infuse into man.

For all these evils flowed from him when, by robbery, he promised knowledge of good and evil and likeness to God. From that point human nature was bent toward evil; before this there had preceded, as it were, a certain innocent infancy, while it abstained from perverting and perverse conversation. Man was silent and remained innocent; put to sleep, he slept innocently; awakened and recognizing the like help which God had made for him, he innocently [Col. 0816D] spoke the mighty works of God.

But once he had become more talkative, drawn out through the gate of curiosity, and carried on commerce of words with the tempter, he swelled with the heat conceived, like one passing from childhood into adolescence. Having transgressed the command, whose observance would have profited him unto glory, he was corrupted; so that thenceforth, by the wondrous and invincible law of his imposed condition, the union of flesh and spirit should resist itself and could by no means be reconciled unless the grace of Him intervened who made both one, and who at the end of the elect will cause flesh to be swallowed up by spirit.

If a Christian may use the words of pagans—one who believes that divine and God-pleasing genius belongs, through indwelling grace, to the elect alone—although I think neither the words nor the thoughts of pagans should be avoided, provided their errors are avoided, divine wisdom itself seems to have intimated this under the veil of a fictitious tale [Col. 0817A] in its own *Aeneid*, when Maro wisely set forth the six stages of life through the divisions of six books. In imitating the *Odyssey*, he seems in these books to have expressed the origin and development of the human condition; and he brings down to the shades the very person whom he introduces, advances, leads forward, and guides.

For Aeneas, who is there imagined as the soul, is so called because he is the inhabitant of the body: *ennaios* (ἔνναιος), according to the Greeks, means “inhabitant,” and *demas* (δέμας), “body”; and Aeneas is composed from these, to signify a soul dwelling, as it were, in the hut of flesh. Thus Neptune too is called *Ennosigaeus*, because he inhabits Sigaeum.

The first book of the *Aeneid*, under the image of a shipwreck, sets forth the evident buffetings of infancy, which is tossed by its own storms; and at its end, grown up amid an abundance of food and drink, it springs into banqueting joy. At the border of adolescence, therefore, commerce of conversation appears, and its excess either tells stories or mixes falsehood with truth, because sins cannot be absent from much speaking.

The third book, moreover, sings of the various errors peculiar to youth, since that age knows almost nothing but errors. For, as the moralist says:

> At last the beardless youth, once his guardian is removed,  
> Delights in horses, dogs, and the grass of the sunny field;  
> Wax to be bent toward vice, harsh toward advisers,  
> Slow to provide what is useful, lavish with money.  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, 161.)

The first age, then, has a nurse; the second, a guardian; [Col. 0817C] the third, the freer it is, errs the more easily, though it does not yet proceed to crimes. The fourth contracts illicit loves and brings the fire rashly conceived in the breast to the unhappy pyre of the lover. For reason, under the figure of Mercury, persuades us that fated blessedness does not lie in forbidden things, and teaches him who, while a little child, thought as a child, spoke as a child, and acted as a child, to put away the things of a child once he has inexorably taken flight.

Hence, to return to the moralist just mentioned:

> With altered pursuits, the age and manly spirit  
> Seek wealth and friendships, serve honour,  
> And fear to commit what they would soon labour to change.  
> (ID., ibid.)

Thus manhood blushes for childish and youthful things; [Col. 0817D] and if it cannot loosen the anchor of its voyage from perverse pleasure and impure love, it cuts the cable too. Thus the chaste son of the patriarchs left his garment to the adulteress, lest he be entangled in the crime of adultery.

The fifth book promises civil maturity and portrays an age near old age—indeed, already entering old age. For it recalls the honours of the Fathers, reveres the memory of ancestors, and, as if celebrating solemn games at Anchises’ tomb, recognizes in those very games the misery of its own exile.
