But when it departs from there, it passes to the sixth age; and, having lost Palinurus and Misenus—that is, the sleeping guide of the ship and the instigator of rash battle—when affection is already cooling and strength failing, it feels not so much old age as decrepitude, and, as if descending [Col. 0818A] to the underworld, there reviews the errors of its entire preceding life, as though its affairs had been uselessly conducted. It learns that those who wish to reach Lavinia’s sweet embraces and the fated kingdom of Italy, as though a citadel of blessedness, must walk by another path.

Those who examine the author’s mind more carefully agree that Maro displayed the strength of a twofold teaching by wrapping the mysteries of philosophical truth in the vanity of poetic fiction. Though this was said especially of the first corruption, it can also be shown by clear reasoning of each individual that human nature is inclined to evil from its youth. From the time it begins to use free, though depressed, choice, it falls of itself willingly into guilt, and then by its own deserts plunges headlong into punishment; [Col. 0818B] yet it can by no means be raised to good unless the grace of God puts its hand beneath it.

Broad, therefore, is the way of the Epicureans, and it leads without doubt to death, through dangers, errors, bitterness, and every kind of vanity, so that no one finds in it the joyous and peaceful condition of a tranquil life, or at last arrives at it under that way’s guidance. For if true blessedness is to be possessed, one must hold fast not to empty but to true goods. Empty goods drive their worshipper into outer darkness—to weeping of eyes, gnashing of teeth, ringing of ears, various oppressions, and the punishments of hell—where no order exists, but everlasting horror dwells.

## Chapter XXV. What is the most trustworthy way of attaining what Epicureans seek or promise

[Col. 0818C]

I do not, however, bring a charge against the proposition that defines blessedness as a perpetually joyous and peaceful condition of tranquil life; rather, I think it has been discredited by a perverse interpretation and a faulty execution. So much so that, although very many are Epicureans—that is, vain followers of pleasure—few profess that name. For they are ashamed to be called what they are, and strive to conceal their own disgrace under another name, desiring not so much to be good as to seem good.

But if the definition receives a faithful interpreter and the proposition a fitting executor, one who puts hand to mouth—that is, one who does what he says—you will prove that nothing is truer or more correct among the Stoic and the Peripatetic. When you command, I shall introduce these to you by the pleasant short-cut of a great road. Yet lest you suppose that there is any path toward the goal intended by the Epicurean definition, [Col. 0818D] I shall attempt to open for you, at the end of the book, as it were at the end of the road, that path itself.

It is arduous and narrow, yet smooth and straight for those who love God; under His leading, teaching, and support, no one strikes his foot against a stone. For He Himself is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” (1 Pet. 2); those who walk upon Him He receives, raises, and strengthens, so that, humbled in Him and glorying in Him, they may boldly and freely proclaim: “We can do all things in Him who strengthens us.” This way, indeed, is virtue, set between and confined by two bounds: namely, knowledge and practice of the good. To know the good and not do it is a ground for condemnation, not the path of blessedness.

“Whence,” you ask, [Col. 0819A] “shall I enter this path, when I am in a trackless place and not upon the road? A stranger and pilgrim amid such a diversity of unknown roads, whose eyes have grown weak through want and are almost failing—by what signs shall I discern it, so as to reach the tranquillity and joy which you promise?”

“There is,” I say,

> A lofty road, clear in the serene heaven;  
> It bears the name Milky Way.

Make your heaven serene, so that the eye of your soul is not troubled by indignation, and you will readily recognize this Milky Way. Return to yourself; look upon the memorials of the Fathers; and there carefully observe where you turned your step from the way and where you fell into error.

I recall that we first went astray where man was driven and overthrown so as to fall through transgression of the command: when [Col. 0819B], at the devil’s persuasion, he rashly and heedlessly stretched out his hand to the forbidden tree of knowledge. For from that point sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and by it killed me. The commandment itself worked in me every desire, because always

> We strive for what is forbidden;  
> What is not allowed burns more fiercely.  
> (OVID, *Amores* III.4.17.)

He stretched out his hand to the tree of knowledge, filled his appetite, and—contrary to the promise of the deceitful enemy and according to the prohibition of the truthful God—man was darkened and cast down into hunger, striking a covenant with death and making a pact with hell. Yet he became knowing of good [Col. 0819C] and evil by experience and made room in himself for manifold misery.

Therefore, when forbidden the tree of knowledge, man climbed it and fell away from and wandered from truth, virtue, and life. Nor will he return to life unless he returns to the tree of knowledge, and from it draws truth in knowledge, virtue in action, and life in joy. Let him therefore exercise the sharpness of reason so that he may distinguish good from evil and recognize, among good and evil things themselves, what outweighs what. Then let him take continual care not to make his part the worse, but with the whole effort of mind and body serve the things to be preferred.

Let labour itself become sweet to him, and let him temper the whole bitterness of present things, as blessed Gregory says, by hope of things to come. For the prophet feeds day and night upon tears while awaiting [Col. 0819D] his God; and to mourners in this way Truth itself, which neither deceives nor is deceived, has promised true blessedness. Nor should anyone fear to stretch out his hand to the tree of knowledge of good and evil because of the example of the first prohibition, since He who teaches man knowledge invited the exile and wanderer to that tree, and, according to the prophetic promise, reveals to the ignorant what is good.

Upon the tree of knowledge, therefore, a branch of virtue springs up, as it were, from which the whole life of the advancing person is consecrated. For no one returns otherwise to God, the begetter of life, unless he displays the branch of virtue cut from the tree of knowledge. But who will quickly pluck the branch when very few know even the tree itself—that is, what ought to be done? Will the branch readily become known [Col. 0820A] where the tree itself is hidden by the multitude of fools and evildoers?

Perhaps this is what Maro too perceived. Although ignorant of truth and walking in the darkness of the gentiles, he did not believe Aeneas could be admitted to the Elysian fields of the blessed and the sight of his dear father unless, taught by the Sibyl—who is interpreted as *siou boulē* (σιοῦ βουλή), “the counsel of Jupiter,” or as the wisdom of God—he consecrated to Proserpina this branch. Proserpina signifies the life which creeps forward and raises itself from vices. Thus he says:

> Receive first what must be done: hidden in a shadowy tree  
> Is a branch, golden in leaves and pliant stem,  
> Said to be sacred to infernal Juno. The whole grove conceals it,  
> And shadows shut it in among dark valleys.  
> Yet none is permitted to enter the hidden places of earth  
> Before he plucks from the tree its golden-haired fruit.  
> [Col. 0820B] Fair Proserpina has decreed that this be brought as her own gift;  
> When the first is plucked, another golden branch does not fail,  
> And a shoot of like metal puts forth leaves.  
> (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VI.136 ff.)

Plainly, only he recognizes what punishments lie hidden in earthly things, or what one may deserve in them, who plucks from the tree of knowledge the branch of good action. Once this has been plucked, another does not fail; because the more knowledge and virtues are exercised, the more they grow and advance.

Yet I do not follow the footsteps of Maro or the gentiles so far as to believe that anyone reaches knowledge or virtue through the powers of his own free choice. I confess that grace works both willing and accomplishing in the elect. I venerate grace as the way—or rather, as truly the Way—which alone leads to life and makes each person attain his good [Col. 0820C] desire. This is the Milky Way: manifest in the whiteness of innocence, it fulfils the office of a nurse through the diligent provision of nourishment and alone prepares one for progress. Without it no one advances.

It cries out in the voice of a trumpet to transgressors, that they may return to their heart; and, with the turning and flaming sword removed, it promises them guidance and entry into their homeland through the ardour of knowledge. I shall say more: it has drawn forth the very tree of knowledge and the tree of life—in which all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, and in which the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2)—without its substance being cut away. It has brought it into the land of our pilgrimage and planted it in the midst of the Church, that from it she may be enlightened through knowledge, strengthened through virtue, rejoice in abundant mercy, and have joy [Col. 0820D] full: joy from God and in God, joy which no one shall take from her.

Let him therefore approach the tree under grace’s guidance who, led away by desire, sinned at the tree; for our salvation was wrought through the same wood because death first proceeded from wood. But let him approach with contrary steps, because contraries ought fittingly to be healed by contraries. And because the tempter would not have cast man down unless pride had first preceded in his mind, let him begin from fear, so that he may humble himself under the mighty hand of God, he who desires to be exalted in the day of visitation. Let him abstain from lawful things who presumed upon unlawful ones, and let ordered charity mitigate the fire of desire.

Let him delight in these things; let him see even now that the tree is beautiful to behold and sweet to eat, and that it will give in its season the fruit of true [Col. 0821A] blessedness and the ever-joyful condition of a tranquil life. Moreover, the pleasant fear which passes into the reverence of love does not know how to be idle or to transgress the law appointed for it. It casts the stings of fear outside and, from love, does good: of its own accord it cleaves to justice and, with the strength of obedience and grace, strives in a sense violently to gain life—the one who through the levity of disobedient choice rushed into death.

Fear begets innocence; the obedience that does good advances justice; and by the straight path the righteous person is brought to true blessedness. For this is the one whom the Lord led through right ways, giving him knowledge of the saints, honouring him in his labours, and fulfilling in him in all things the blessedness for which he labours [Col. 0821B] faithfully and profitably (Wis. 10).

I could say that the whole Law and the Prophets, and all canonical Scripture, tend toward this because they tend toward the Son. Nor is this doubtful, since even the teachings of unbelievers have no usefulness unless they contribute something to blessedness. But passing these by—or rather, having placed them first—I say that these alone are the things

> Which alone can make and preserve a person blessed,

since from one branch of justice comes the principle that no one should be harmed, and from the other that each person should benefit himself and others.

Do you wish to establish for yourself that what I say is true? Do you wish to be blessed? “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. 111). Do you desire power? “Not only he himself, but his seed shall be mighty upon earth” (ibid.). Do you pursue favour and the praises [Col. 0821C] of men? “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (ibid.). Do you aspire to renown and spread your bosom toward abundance? “Glory and riches shall be in his house” (ibid.). Do you seek permanence for your works? “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (ibid.). Do you wish to be secure? “He shall not fear an evil report,” but shall despise all his enemies (ibid.). Do you desire grace of speech? “The lips of the righteous distil grace.” Likewise: “The memory of the righteous is with praises, but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Prov. 10). Do you wish the future to become known to you? “The expectation of the righteous is joy” (ibid.). Do you desire joy to be prolonged for you forever? “The righteous shall live forever” (Wis. 5), and “they are in peace,” though to the foolish they seem to die.

Behold, you have the truest and most trustworthy way to pursue the condition desired by Epicurus. [Col. 0821D] And if you hold it, “you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127). This alone can suffice for living well and blessedly; so much so that all things outside it add either nothing or very little to perfection.

Nor do I forbid you to shine in golden garments surrounded by variety, to feast splendidly every day, or to possess the highest honours; nor, to embrace much in few words, do I forbid you, while remaining upright [Col. 0822A] as you are, to conform in all things to the age—even to its perverse customs—and to mock the world as it mocks through its own allurements. For you are too great either to owe yourself to, or to be able to be taken by, its snares—although it has already taken many here.

Henry II, illustrious king of the English and greatest of the kings of Britain, if the outcome of his deeds matches their beginnings, thunders around the Garonne, and, as is said, with you as author and leader. Happily surrounding Toulouse by siege, he terrifies not only the provincials as far as the Rhône and the Alps, but, after breaking fortifications and subduing peoples, he shakes Spanish and French princes with fear, as though he stood threatening them all in person.

Amid such tumults of affairs, I pray you, preserve innocence; see, speak, and preach justice; and do not turn from the straight way through love or hatred, fear or hope. For “the righteous shall inherit [Col. 0822B] the earth,” and, as the authority of the Most High assures us, “the seed of the wicked shall perish” (Ps. 36).

If in so great a tumult you have no leisure to read what I have taken care to write to you in sincere devotion, or if it displeases because it is insipid in thought and unpolished in language, may the devotion itself at least not displease you—the devotion which strove to serve your honour. If you approve my intention, you will protect the work. But if not, let it be condemned as you wish. For what have others to do with judging another’s servant? This book, like any person belonging to his own master, stands or falls for you, its lord.

I do not fear the judgments of the ignorant multitude, but I ask them to spare my little works; and especially any courtiers, because I have never disparaged their books in any respect. If they refuse to heed my prayers, they will be liable to the charge of malice, because, as Martial says, [Col. 0822C] “he acts maliciously who displays cleverness in another man’s book.”

Whatever has been said concerning courtly trifles has been detected in none of them, but perhaps in myself or persons like me; and surely I am bound by too narrow a law if I may not chastise and correct myself and my friends. Certainly whoever wrinkles his nose at these matters, knits his brow, clothes his face with blushes or confuses it with pallor, whose lips contract or leap, whose tongue is poisoned, whose knees tremble, and whose hands behave insolently—such a person will convict himself of being liable to our trifles. For our purpose in them was always to pass from trifles to serious good things and to train life toward what is fitting or profitable.

But whoever sees a just occasion for criticism, let him freely make use of it in charity, and through my [Col. 0822D] correction acquire and possess for himself the reward of life. For I know that sin is not absent from much speaking; nevertheless, I exhort the reader, though unwillingly, in the charity of God, that, remembering me in his prayers, he may obtain that the Son of the living God and of the undefiled Virgin, God and man, may reveal Himself and make manifest the path by which we must walk in His good pleasure, and direct our steps upon it.

[Col. 0823]

# The *Metalogicus* of John of Salisbury

(*I have newly collated the *Metalogicum*, following the text of the Lug. Bat. Svomin. edition of 1639, with the manuscript preserved in the public library at Cambridge, Ii.2.31.* — GILES.)

## Prologue

[Col. 0823A] In human affairs I think that almost nothing is so polished that it is not exposed in some respect to detraction; for evils are attacked on their merits, but good things from envy. Hence I have persuaded myself to bear the stings of detractors more calmly, especially since, by divine arrangement, mother Nature brought us forth in an age and region and fortune placed us, once brought forth, in a condition and company of fellow-livers who prefer to criticize what belongs to others rather than look to, order, or correct their own affairs.

> Thus no one attempts to descend into himself; no one;  
> But everyone looks at the wallet on the back of the man before him.  
> (PERSIUS IV.23.)

I might in some measure have avoided in silence the bites of scholars and of those who profess the names of philosophy, [Col. 0823B] but I cannot at all escape the teeth of my fellow courtiers. To oblige everyone and injure no one once served to gain favour; so that, according to the comic poet, “You will find praise without envy and acquire equal friends.” But now, even in this way, one rarely succeeds in repressing the envy of one’s comrades in arms.

The habit of compliance is branded as a mark of abasement; innocence seems a profession of weakness. The unlearned man accuses the silent; the eloquent is counted among babblers. A serious man is said to sit in ambush; a less serious man is blamed as incompetent through frivolity. Whoever follows moderation in speech and conduct is considered factious. Finally, if there is no quarrel, envy can scarcely fail to arise from neglect.

Yet if I had spent my whole lifetime among my comrades at dice, hunting, and the other trifles of courtiers, they would not gnaw at my writings—just as I do not criticize theirs. For my part, it matters very little to me to be judged as a writer by men who set great store by the judgments of mimes and actors, and who, like the lowliest slaves, dread lest Thais or Thraso, Callirrhoe [Col. 0823D] or Bathyllus should speak or think wrongly of them.

But if professors of philosophy persecute one who loves philosophers, they are plainly unjust and repay charity badly. For it is my purpose, though I may be unable to imitate them, at least to love, honour, and cultivate them. [Col. 0824A] I ought, indeed, to have deserved the favour of scholars, whom, whether because they are what they are or because they were what they were, I defend by such advocacy as I can provide. If I have done so usefully, favour and reward are owed to the outcome; if less successfully, to the intention. Hence comes that saying:

> “You have done nothing,” you say, “and the case has been lost through you:”

All the more do you owe, Sextus, because I blushed. For I do not exclude my betters from the office of advocacy, though I declare the devotion of my own affection. Let those more eminent put the finishing touch to the work, and, in delivering judgment for the logicians, incline the office of judge. For when the work of logicians was being ridiculed more violently, as useless, and my rival provoked me—resentful and resisting as I was—to almost daily disputes, at last I undertook the lawsuit, and endeavoured to answer, as they arose, the slanders which he had contrived [Col. 0824B]. Hence it became necessary to follow the order in which he pressed his attack, and for the most part to pass over more important matters in silence while the objections were being disposed of. For he himself arranged the points upon which he wished the discussion to proceed.

It therefore pleased my companions that I should dictate this very work in a hasty, unpolished discourse, since neither zeal nor leisure remained for examining the arguments with precision or polishing the words. Indeed, amidst necessary occupations, scarcely any more time was available than the hour of refreshment or of sleep; since, by command of my lord, whom I cannot fail, the care of all Britain, so far as ecclesiastical causes are concerned, rests upon me. Besides this, concern for my household affairs and courtly trifles [Col. 0824C] excluded study; the interruption of friends had almost wholly absorbed me. I therefore think it just that more ready pardon be granted me for whatever has been said rashly; but if anything has come forth more suitably, thanks should be returned to him without whom human weakness can do nothing. For my intellect is dull, and my memory less trustworthy than would be needed for me to grasp the subtleties of the ancients [Col. 0824D], or retain for long what I have at some time grasped. The style itself proves that my language is unpolished.

And because I have undertaken the advocacy of logic, the book is entitled *Metalogicon*. For the reader’s recreation, I have taken care to divide it into four books [Col. 0825A]. Following the custom of writers, I have included various matters, which each person will approve or disapprove according to his own judgment.

> There are good things, some indifferent things, and more bad things  
> in what you read here: otherwise, Avitus, no book comes into being.  
> (Martial, I.17)

So Martial, and so I: preferring to trifle in this way rather than, in the guise of Ganymede, hunt hares, or

> Stink of wine drunk by night, stink of wine drunk by day.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.19.11)

Nor have I disdained to put forward the opinions of modern writers, whom I do not hesitate in many respects to prefer to the ancients. I certainly hope that posterity will celebrate the glory of those now living, since I admire the noble talents of many: their subtlety in investigation, diligence in study [Col. 0825B], felicity of memory, fertility of mind, capacity of speech, and abundance of expression. I have also deliberately inserted some remarks on morals, judging that all things read or written are useless unless they bring some aid to life. For every profession of philosophy is useless and false which does not disclose itself in the cultivation of virtue and the conduct of life.

As an Academic, in matters doubtful to the Wise Man, I do not swear that what I say is true; but whether it is true or false, I am content with probability alone. You, as you please, will examine everything [Col. 0826A] and each thing individually, because I have dedicated my little works to you as their judge, so that I may understand that neither my labour nor my expenditure has been wasted. But if—far be it!—it should happen that

> If this Alexis disdains me, I shall find another.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* II.73)

if you prefer any actor to a philosopher: there are indeed three things—to inform you more fully of my purpose—which bring not merely fear to me, but danger to salvation or loss of merit to most writers: ignorance of truth; deceptive or obstinate assertion of falsehood; and swollen profession of truth. For I know who said: “It is safer for truth to be heard than to be spoken.” In hearing, humility is preserved; but in speaking, pride very often steals in.

Yet in all these respects [Col. 0826B] I acknowledge my own error: I suffer from ignorance of things; I defend falsehood more often, and more strongly, than is fitting; and, for the most part, I proclaim truth itself proudly and with self-exaltation, until God rebukes and corrects me. Therefore I earnestly beseech reader and hearer, with all the supplication I can make, to remember me before the Most High in their prayers, seeking for me pardon for past offences, caution against future ones, knowledge of truth, love of good, worship of God, and that those things pleasing to the divine will may be practised by us in heart, speech, and deed.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0825]

## CHAPTER I. The calumny which compelled a reply to his Cornificius

A shameless litigant revives against the eminent gift of nature our mother and of grace an ancient calumny, condemned by the judgment of our forefathers. Seeking everywhere consolations for his own incompetence, he hopes to advance his glory if he sees many like himself—that is, many unskilled persons. For this swelling is characteristic of arrogance: it measures itself by others, exalting its own goods, if it has any, and debasing those of others; and it regards its neighbour’s deficiency as its own advancement.

But to all who think rightly it is beyond doubt that nature, the most gracious mother of all and most orderly governor, among the other living creatures she has produced, raised man by the privilege of reason and distinguished him by the use of speech [Col. 0825D]. She did so by her serviceable diligence and most orderly law, so that man, weighed down by the heaviness of a more turbid nature and dragged towards the depths by the slowness of his bodily mass, might, as though borne on these wings, ascend to the heights and, in attaining the prize of true blessedness, outstrip all else by a fortunate short path.

Therefore, while grace makes nature fruitful, reason attends to perceiving and examining things; it searches nature’s recesses and measures the fruits and efficacy of each thing. And the inborn love of good, urged on by its natural appetite, follows this alone—or this before all else [Col. 0826C]—which seems most suited to the attainment of blessedness. But blessedness is ignorant of communion: what it may be, or of what kind, outside society cannot even be imagined. Whoever attacks those things which conduce to establishing and fostering the right of human society—society which is, in a sense, the one unique brotherhood of the children of nature—seems to block for all persons the road to happiness. By closing the entrance of peace, he rouses nature’s inmost parts so that they may rush together to the destruction of the world.

This indeed is to sow discord among brothers; this is to supply weapons to those once at peace; this finally is to establish a new and vast chaos between God and humankind. For the creating Trinity, the one true God, ordered the parts of the universe for the cohesion of a firmer bond and the preservation of charity [Col. 0826D], so that one thing should need the help of another and one should supply the deficiency of another, while individual things are, as it were, members of individual things. Thus all things are half-complete if they are severed from one another, but made complete by association with others, because all things subsist through mutual assistance.

What is more trustworthy or more useful for attaining blessedness than virtue? What is more direct? For this is almost the single and only way which grace has prepared for blessedness. Those who become blessed without the merit of virtue do not so much reach that state by going there as are drawn there.

I therefore wonder—though not sufficiently, since I cannot—what the man means who denies that eloquence should be studied, and asserts that it comes freely from nature to anyone who is not mute, just as sight comes to one who is not blind and hearing to one who is not deaf [Col. 0827A]; although it comes more fully if nature’s gift is strengthened by practice. Yet he maintains that art confers no benefit, or at least none equal to the labour which art requires. For just as eloquence which reason does not illuminate is not only reckless but blind, so wisdom which is not advanced by the use of speech is not only weak but in a manner maimed. For though speechless wisdom may sometimes be of some benefit to itself, as comfort to conscience, it rarely and only slightly contributes to the use of human society.

For reason—the mother, nurse, and guardian of knowledge and virtues [Col. 0827B]—which conceives more frequently through speech and brings forth more abundantly and fruitfully through speech, would either remain entirely barren or at least unfruitful if it did not bring the fruit of conception into the light through eloquence, and make public to people what the prudent activity of the mind perceives. This is that sweet and fruitful marriage of reason and speech which has produced so many distinguished cities, reconciled and allied so many kingdoms, united so many peoples, and bound them in charity. Rightly, therefore, whoever strives to separate what God has joined for the good of all is judged a public enemy of all.

He begrudges Mercury Philology and tears Mercury from Philology’s embrace who banishes instruction in eloquence from philosophical studies. And although he appears to persecute eloquence alone [Col. 0827C], he undermines every liberal study, attacks the whole labour of all philosophy, tears apart the bond of human society, and leaves no place for charity or reciprocal services. Human beings will become brutish if deprived of the granted endowment of speech; cities themselves will seem rather like pens for cattle than gatherings of men bound in some social compact, living under one law through sharing duties and friendly reciprocal exchange.

For what contract will be duly concluded? What discipline of faith or morals will flourish? What obedience or mutual sharing of wills will exist once the intercourse of speech has been removed? Thus our Cornificius, an ignorant student of eloquence and a shameless assailant of it, attacks not one city, nor a few, but all cities together and the whole political life [Col. 0827D].

## CHAPTER II. Description of the person, with his name suppressed

I would indeed identify him publicly by name, and expose before public eyes the swelling of his belly and mind, the shamelessness of his mouth, the rapacity of his hands, the frivolity of his movements, the foulness of his morals—which the whole neighbourhood despises—the obscenity of his lust, the deformity of his body, the baseness of his life, and the stain upon his reputation, were I not restrained by reverence for the Christian name. Mindful of my profession and of the brotherly communion which is in the Lord, I judged that the person should be spared, provided that the error is not spared.

I therefore defer to God, sparing nature, which is from him, and attacking vice, which is against him, since it corrupts the nature which he created [Col. 0828A]. Certainly it is right to challenge an opinion without disparaging the person; and nothing is more shameful than, when one dislikes an argument or opinion, gnawing at the author’s name. It is much more reasonable sometimes to spare a false opinion, so far as its error is tolerable, for the person’s sake, than to attack a person for the sake of an opinion. Each matter must be examined by its own evidence, and rewards proportionate to merit must be assigned, yet in such a way that the gentleness of mercy overcomes severity.

With this consideration, therefore, I suppressed the mark of his publicly known name, lest I seem to have sought not so much to cure the error as to disfigure an enemy’s person. Yet, to confess the truth, nothing is less true, because, so far as is lawful for a Christian, I despise person and opinion alike [Col. 0828B]. Let him then, as he wishes, snore on until midday, gorge himself to drunkenness with daily devourings, and wallow and lie immersed in such filth as would not become even Epicurus’s pig.

But I resist the opinion which has ruined many, because it has a populace that believes in it. And although this new Cornificius is more foolish than the ancient one, a crowd of fools nevertheless acquiesces in him—especially those who, being idle and slothful, desire to seem wise rather than to be wise.

## CHAPTER III. When, how, and by whom was he educated?

I certainly do not wonder at all if, after receiving large pay and beating the air for a long time, he taught his credulous hearers that they know nothing, since he himself was so taught by his masters [Col. 0828C]. For he is not eloquent but wordy; without any fruit of meaning, he continually scatters leaves of words to the wind.

Yet this is the man’s precaution: though he criticizes everyone’s sayings equally, he never joins battle either to establish his own view or destroy another’s; never relies upon reason; never endures to engage in the field of the Scriptures. He has conceived, in the bellows of his inflated windy lungs, something lofty and unknown to all wise people; therefore he disdains to answer anyone or patiently listen to anyone. For if you propose anything whatsoever, he will abuse you or laugh. If you wait for him to prove his proposal, delay is necessary, so that when the day has passed, you are cheated of the fruit of your waiting, because, as he says, he does not wish his pearls to be common property with other people’s swine [Col. 0828D].

Meanwhile, however, he feeds his hearers with little tales and trifles; and, without art’s assistance, if what he promises is true, he will make them eloquent and philosophers by a short road and without labour. For he too received from his teachers what he now hands down to his disciples, and educates them just as he himself was educated. He will therefore make his disciples his equals in philosophy. Why say more? Will they not thus be perfect, according to that saying of the Gospel: “Every disciple is perfect if he is like his master”? (Luke VI.)

Cornificius learned at that time the things which he now reserves for teaching—things indeed fit to be heard by the fortunate and, as the saying goes, by Jupiter’s ears—when, in liberal studies, the letter counted for nothing and the spirit was sought everywhere, the spirit which, as they say, lies hidden in the letter [Col. 0829A]. To teach that Hylas was from Hercules was considered a powerful argument—namely, that from a strong and robust arguer come the powers of vowels, the five rights of kingdoms—and to teach everything in this manner was the pursuit of that age.

At that time, in that school of philosophers, the insoluble question was held to be whether the pig being led to market was held by the man or by the rope. Likewise, whether the man who bought an entire cloak had bought the hood.

A discourse was altogether unsuitable unless the words “suitable,” “unsuitable argument,” and “reason” clattered throughout it, with negative particles multiplied and placed across *to be* and *not to be*, so that an abacus was required whenever disputation took place. Otherwise, the force of affirmation and negation was unknown [Col. 0829B]. For a doubled negation often has affirmative force; likewise, negative force is strengthened by an odd number. Indeed, a negation repeated often destroys itself and is equivalent to a contradiction, as has regularly been handed down.

Therefore, so that it could be discovered whether it stood in an even or odd position, those who were to debate were customarily required, by prudent counsel, to bring collected beans and peas—provided, that is, they gave attention to the understanding of the things apparently at issue. Wordy shouting sufficed for victory, and whoever introduced something from anywhere reached the goal he had proposed.

Poets and historians were considered infamous; anyone who laboured over the works of the ancients was branded and made a laughing-stock to all, not merely as slower than an Arcadian donkey but as duller than lead or stone [Col. 0829C]. For each man laboured over his own inventions or those of his master. Yet even this was not permitted for long, since the very hearers were soon pressed by the impetuous rush of their companions to forge and establish new sects themselves, despising what they had heard from their teachers.

Thus they suddenly became supreme philosophers. For one who entered illiterate ordinarily remained in the schools no longer than the period in which fledglings grow feathers. Accordingly, new masters from the schools and young birds from nests, just as they remained for an equal time, flew away together. But what did these new teachers teach—men who had spent more dreams than waking hours in the investigation of philosophy [Col. 0829D], and had been trained more easily than those whom fabulous tales describe as suddenly emerging as poets after dreaming on Parnassus; or more quickly than those who drew from the Castalian Fountain the Muses’ gift of poetry; or than those who, upon seeing Phoebus, deserved to be enrolled in the company of the Muses, not merely of musicians?

Anything crude or uncultivated? Anything old or obsolete? Behold, all things became new: grammar was remade, dialectic altered, rhetoric despised; and, once the rules of earlier writers had been emptied out, they produced new paths for the whole quadrivium from philosophy’s very sanctuaries. They spoke only of “suitability” or “reason”; “argument” sounded in every mouth. To name a donkey, a human being, or any work of nature was regarded as almost criminal—too foolish, too crude, and alien to a philosopher [Col. 0830A]. It was thought impossible to say or do anything suitably and according to reason’s rule unless explicit mention of “suitability” and “reason” was inserted. Nor was it lawful for an argument to be made unless the word *argument* had first been uttered.

To speak in terms of art and to speak about art were the same thing. These people will perhaps teach that a poet can say nothing in verse unless he calls it verse, and that a carpenter cannot make a bench unless he keeps “bench” or “wood” turning on his lips. This, then, is that jumble of speaking in which the foolish old man exults, insulting those who honour the founders of the arts because, while pretending to devote himself to them, he found no usefulness in them.

## CHAPTER IV. How the companions of this error turned out

After loss of time and waste of resources, after disappointed hopes and a purpose left without consolation, the members of this sect found various outlets [Col. 0830B]. Some entered the cloister of monks or clerics, and most corrected their error, discovering in themselves and preaching to others that whatever they had learned was vanity of vanities and vanity above all things. I say “most,” because some, persisting in their madness and puffed up by their old perversity, preferred to be foolish rather than be faithfully instructed by the humble, to whom God gives grace. For those who had presumed upon the pride of mastery were ashamed to take the form of disciples.

If you do not believe me, enter the cloisters, examine the brethren’s conduct, and you will find there the pride of Moab, exceedingly intense, so that arrogance consumes his strength [Col. 0830C]. Benedict marvels and complains that, with himself in some sense as author, a wolf lies hidden in sheep’s skins; he certainly complains that tonsure and dark clothing are far removed from haughtiness. Or, more correctly, he rebukes haughtiness because it does not accord with tonsure and clothing. The customary rule of observances is despised, and under the appearance of a philosopher the spirit of deceitful pride creeps in. These things are well known and common in every dress and profession.

Others, seeing their failure in philosophy, went to Salerno or Montpellier, became medical attendants, and suddenly emerged as physicians in an instant just as they had been philosophers. Filled with deceptive experiments, they soon return and diligently practise what they have learned. They parade Hippocrates or Galen; they utter unheard-of words; on every subject they recite their aphorisms; and by unfamiliar names they strike human minds as if thunderstruck [Col. 0830D]. They are believed capable of everything because they boast of everything and promise everything.

Yet I have found that they retained two sayings more faithfully in memory and employ them more often in their practice. One is Hippocrates’—though it there tends to another meaning—“Where there is want, one ought not to labour.” And in truth they judge it improper and contrary to duty to devote attention to those in need, and to those unwilling or unable, even in words alone, to render them the full return of their fee. The other certainly is, so far as I remember, not Hippocrates’, but a saying of those devoted to physicians: “While he hurts, take.” For the most suitable opportunity for demanding payment is when pain tortures the sick man: the sufferer’s ulceration and the healer’s avarice work together.

If the patient recovers, it is attributed to the physician who took pains; if he declines, the authority of the man who previously revealed this outcome to his intimates is strengthened [Col. 0831A]. For what he has deliberately foretold cannot fail to happen, once he has announced recovery for this patient and an unfavourable end for that one. If the patient is going to recover, he is easily treated—except insofar as the incompetent physician obstructs his recovery. But if not, then, as Sollius Sidonius says, “he is killed with the greatest attentiveness.”

Why should this not happen? Can a man wholly ignorant of philosophy discover nature’s secret and hidden channels? And can one who knows neither how to speak correctly nor how to understand correctly things written [Col. 0831B] or spoken, when there are almost as many languages as disciplines, and when even among the authors themselves the variety in their use of languages is usually no less great than the difference of faces in bodily composition?

For one human resembles another; yet not even twins express one another entirely. One voice sometimes resembles another; yet even sisters—and, if you wish, not even the Muses—have the same agility of voice. Voices harmonize, but they are unlike; and their very unlikeness, proportioned by its proper ratios, suits harmony and is in some manner more pleasing than if likeness produced identity. Languages therefore have their own idioms, and each person his own manner of speaking. Whoever does not know this will no more conveniently practise philosophy than if he wished to equate a magpie attempting human words with a human being [Col. 0831C].

Others, indeed, like myself, devoted themselves to courtly trifles, so that, relying upon the patronage of great men, they might aspire to riches—for which they saw themselves unworthy and, by the judgment of conscience, confessed themselves unworthy, whatever their tongue might disguise. I pass over their ways, because our *Policraticus* relates them diligently, even though it cannot fully investigate them all; for that exceeds human powers.

Others, like Cornificius, relapsed into popular and profane professions, caring little what philosophy teaches or declares should be sought or avoided, provided that:

> They make money, if they can, honourably; if not, by whatever means.

They practise usury; they make their round sums by alternating dealings. They think nothing base, nothing foolish, except the straits of poverty, and regard riches alone as the fruit of wisdom [Col. 0831D]. For celebrated in their hearts is what the moralist says, though they may not know that he said it because it is scorned:

> Queen Money bestows both birth and beauty,  
> and persuasive Eloquence and Venus adorn the well-moneyed man.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.6.38)

By these four roads, then, necessarily as it were, those sudden philosophers escaped, together with Cornificius, despiser not only of our trivium but of the whole quadrivium. For, as has been said, they either sank into cloisters under the pretext of religion; or under the appearance of philosophizing and public usefulness fled to natural science [Col. 0832A]; or, under the veil of honourability, thrust themselves into distinguished households in order to shine and rise; or, under the pretence of necessity and the exercise of an office, while thirsting for profit, were swallowed by the abyss of manifold avarice. So much so that, by comparison with such advancing philosophers—or, more truly, failing ones—any person amid the crowd of the profane multitude seemed a novice in wickedness.

## CHAPTER V. What great men that school dares to disparage, and why

Master Gilbert, then chancellor of Chartres and later the venerable bishop of Poitiers, used to promise them the baker’s art when he saw them flying off to the studies mentioned above, whether laughing or grieving at the madness of his time I do not know [Col. 0832B]. For, he said, in his country it was the one trade accustomed to receive all who lacked other occupations or crafts. The trade is very easily practised and serves as a fallback for other trades, especially among those who seek bread rather than a craft.

Other men also, lovers of letters—namely Master Theodoric, a most zealous investigator of the arts; likewise William of Conches, a grammarian, the richest man after Bernard of Chartres, and a courtly Peripatetic, who carried off from all his contemporaries the reputation for logic, so that he alone was believed to hold converse with Aristotle—set themselves wholly against the error. Yet not even all of them could resist the madmen. Thus they were made fools while resisting folly, and were long considered erring while striving to oppose error [Col. 0832C].

Nevertheless, that smoke quickly vanished. Through the work and diligence of the aforesaid masters, the arts returned, and, as if by right of return from exile, recovered their former honour and, after exile, attained greater favour and glory. Cornificius envied this, and, thinking it shameful that an old man should be sent to school and appear a boy in understanding, began in his old age to condemn what he despaired of being able to attain. He criticized everyone’s opinions because everyone thought differently from him. Thus the fox, from despair, disparages cherries; and, as the rustic proverb says, whatever is denied is judged useless.

Hence the anger, hence the tears, hence the indignation which Cornificius’s household conceived against the disciples of the wise men mentioned. It exercises its teeth against them on every side, but breaks its jaw upon their solidity, as the saying has it [Col. 0832D]. It even shamelessly—though in hiding, because it cannot do so openly—strives to obscure the brightest lights of Gaul, the glory of Laon, the theological brothers Anselm and Ralph, whose memory is in joy and blessing. No one has torn them to pieces with impunity; only heretics or persons shrouded in the shame of heinous crimes have found them displeasing.

For they speak openly about Alberic of Reims and Simon of Paris, and utter no proverb; their followers they not only deny to be philosophers but do not even allow to be clergy. They scarcely allow them to be human, but call them only Abraham’s oxen or Balaam’s asses; indeed, they mock them, or say against them whatever can be said more scoffingly or abusively. William of Champeaux is convicted of error by his own writings [Col. 0833A]. Master Hugh of Saint Victor is scarcely spared, and this more on account of his religious habit than from reverence for his knowledge or teaching. In him they defer to God, not to the man.

Robert Pullen, whose memory is pleasant to all good people, would be called the son of a yoked beast unless deference were paid to the Apostolic See, which made him chancellor from a scholastic teacher. But in order that this household might more freely disparage others, its head put on outward religion—for the Lord will know and judge concerning the inward—and seeks the familiarity of the Cistercians, Cluniacs, Premonstratensians, and others whose reputation is more cheerful, in order to gain distinction from their authority.

For my part, I bear the disparagement of his household with equanimity, and I acknowledge that some of those mentioned were my teachers; likewise, that I heard disciples of others and learned from them the small amount that I know [Col. 0833B]. For unlike Cornificius, I did not teach myself. Nor do I care greatly what foolish thing he crows into the ears of his own people. Ungrateful and perversely minded is the person who denies the author of his own advancement. But enough of this. Now, setting aside the follies of the person, let us refute the error of his opinion itself.

## CHAPTER VI. The arguments on which he relies

It is not, then, according to his opinion—if indeed a false opinion ought to be called an opinion—that instruction in the precepts of eloquence should be pursued, because nature either supplies it to all or denies it [Col. 0833C]. If nature supplies it freely or of its own accord, work and diligence are superfluous; but if it denies it, they are ineffective and futile. For this proposition commonly supports his strongest claims: “Each person can do only as much as nature permits.”

So much is this so that the reliable historical record establishes that Daedalus did not fly, because nature had denied him wings, but escaped the tyrant’s rage suddenly by ship. Further, the system of precepts does not accomplish what it promises; and it is altogether impossible for anyone to become eloquent even by the most diligent study of rules. The use of speech and intercourse in speaking with those who live together are sufficient; and the person who frequently exercises the function of any language possesses its chief capacity.

This is clear among Greeks [Col. 0833D] and Latins. The Gauls and Britons bear the same witness for us. Among Scythians and Arabs—indeed, everywhere—it is true that practice makes the master:

> Persistent labour conquers all things.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* I.145)

And constancy in work makes the most excellent worker in every art. Moreover, even if the precepts of eloquence were useful, they involve more labour than benefit, and the loss of effort would never be equally compensated by the return of its reward. Greek and Hebrew common folk use their own languages with ease, without the difficulty of precepts; and Gauls, Britons, and other nations likewise receive the intercourse of speech from their nurses’ breasts before they receive it from teachers’ chairs [Col. 0834A]. Adult life for the most part retains the flavour of the nurse’s tongue, nor can a person sometimes be educated away, by teachers’ diligence, from what his more tender age had drunk in.

How correctly and fluently each people speaks in the languages which the ordering of the divine decree assigned to them! Do they wait for the art of speaking or the precepts of eloquence? Finally, what has eloquence to do with philosophy? The one consists in words; the other seeks, investigates, and ranges about the paths of wisdom, and sometimes effectively grasps wisdom through study. Clearly, the precepts of eloquence do not convey wisdom, nor even love of it, and very often do not contribute to obtaining it. For philosophy seeks things, or its end, wisdom—not words. Thus from these considerations it is clear that philosophy excludes the precepts of eloquence from its own works [Col. 0834B].

## CHAPTER VII. In praise of eloquence

This foolish school crows these things—in its own words—although it is plain that it has despised all precepts of eloquence. For, as it testifies concerning itself, it cannot at the same time attend to the connection and construction of weighty periods and give attention to the meaning. Let it speak falsely, provided it thinks truly; but it plainly will not assent to this, because the person false in speech both speaks falsely and thinks falsely in spirit.

For it says: “The precepts of eloquence are superfluous, because it is naturally either present or absent.” What, I ask, is more false? Eloquence is the capacity of expressing suitably what the mind wishes to set forth. What lies hidden in the heart, it brings in some fashion into the light and produces publicly [Col. 0834C]. For not everyone who speaks, or who speaks however he pleases whatever he pleases, is eloquent; but only the person who suitably expresses the decision of his own mind.

That very suitability requires capacity—called *facultas* from *facilitas*, ease—so that we may follow our own practice, which finds it agreeable in this respect to imitate the Stoics, who investigate the origin even of things more carefully in order to understand words more easily. Therefore, whoever possesses the ease of suitably expressing in words what he thinks is eloquent. The capacity to do this is most correctly called eloquence. What could be more excellent for practical life, more direct towards resources, more dependable for favour, or more advantageous for glory, I do not easily see.

Nothing surpasses or is rarer than this endowment of nature [Col. 0834D] and grace. For whereas virtue and wisdom—which perhaps, as Victorinus holds, differ more in words than in substance—hold the first place among things to be sought, eloquence claims the second for itself; the third place falls to bodily goods, and fourth place belongs to the favour of those living with us and abundance of things as material for actions.

The moralist followed this order and elegantly expressed the sequence of objects to be desired:

> What greater prayer can a kind mother make for her foster-child  
> than that he may be able to think wisely and speak what he feels, and that  
> favour, reputation, and health may come to him in abundance,  
> together with decent livelihood and a purse that does not fail?  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.4.8)

If, therefore, human dignity surpasses the nature of other animals through the use of speech and reason [Col. 0835A], what is more conducive to all things, what is more powerful for winning distinction, than to surpass one’s fellows in nature and race precisely in that whereby humanity alone conquers all else? Since eloquence teaches and adorns every age, it makes youth more distinguished, because tender age is in some fashion enhanced by grace so as to assert its natural talent.

For who flourish among their fellow citizens? Who are powerful in wealth? Who prevail in strength and carry every undertaking through, unless the eloquent? For, as Cicero testifies, nothing is so unbelievable that it cannot be made probable by speaking; nothing is so horrible and uncultivated that it does not shine through speech and, as it were, become gentle when cultivated. Whoever therefore despises so great a good is manifestly foolish [Col. 0835B]. But one who loves it—or pretends to love it—and does not cultivate it is excessively negligent and close to folly.

## CHAPTER VIII. That nature must be aided by use and exercise
Moreover, nature freely bestows this upon some who will one day possess it; upon those who will not possess it, she denies and permanently withholds it, so that it may be plainly evident that further effort is either vain or superfluous. Why then, most learned Cornificians, do you not possess mastery of every language? Why do you not know at least Hebrew—the language which, they say, mother Nature handed down to the first human beings and preserved for the human race, until impiety shattered unity and the arrogance that sought to ascend to heaven, not by merit but by strength, through the building of a tower, was overthrown by the confusion of languages? [Col. 0835C] Why do you not speak this language, which is, so to speak, more natural than the rest, Nature herself being your teacher?

Nature, according to some—although it is difficult to define—is a certain generative power inherent in all things, through which they are able to act or be acted upon. It is called generative because every thing derives it from the cause of its generation and from that which is the principle of its existence. For each thing derives from its constituent elements that by which it is fitted for this or that purpose: whether matter and form enter into its origin, as in simple things which admit no aggregation of parts; or whether the principle of composition is added by the decree of divine goodness alone. For this too is primary nature, according to Plato, who, as Victorinus [Col. 0835D] and many others attest, maintained that the divine will is the most certain nature of all things. Created nature flows from this source; and whatever it accomplishes has God as the author of its operation—unless it be an operation of corruption and fault, in which nature degenerates from its author.

The power originally implanted in each thing, from which its operation or capacity proceeds, is indeed nature, but created nature. Other definitions, scattered among different authors, should, I think, generally be interpreted as descriptions of created nature. Thus the “craftsman fire,” which proceeds by invisible paths to generate visible things, is certainly created; yet, with all respect to Aristotle and Chalcidius, some deny that it is nature. Likewise, I believe that no one would deny that the principle of motion existing in itself received its beginning from God. I am certain of Boethius: he will not deny that what can act or be acted upon is created. Moreover, the specific difference which informs every individual thing is either from Him through whom all things were made, or it is nothing at all. Nature is also described in other ways; but whatever is posited otherwise than in the Platonic account must either be removed from the number of things or ascribed to divine works.

But for the present let us use the first definition, which seems more closely suited to the present question. Let that generative power, originally implanted in things, be powerful and effective; still, just as it may be corrupted or impeded by a defect, so it may be repaired or assisted by various supports. Even children commonly chatter that a person has a natural aptitude for doing something when he has been denied the use of that aptitude. For what is capable of walking is sometimes unable to walk; and one who is by nature two-footed often lacks, in actuality, both feet or one of them. Care, therefore, is not superfluous: it assists nature and makes easier what perhaps might in some fashion have occurred even without it.

Socrates too, as tradition has it, was by nature unruly and womanizing—to use the word employed by the historical account—yet by philosophical correction and the exercise of virtue he restrained and subdued the intemperance of his nature. Scaurus Rufus, they relate, had a rather dull intellect; but through the diligence of practice he gained such strength that he called Cicero himself an Allobrogian. If examples are required, it will be apparent from every quarter that diligence is not fruitless where natural ability is dull; nor is care excessive and superfluous where nature is more generous for some undertaking. For although nature usually predominates and inclines more readily toward one side or another, still, just as it is easily corrupted by negligence, so it is very often tamed by cultivation and care.

> Whether a praiseworthy poem comes from nature or from art  
> Has been asked. I see that neither effort without a rich vein,  
> Nor can raw talent accomplish anything; thus each thing  
> Requires the aid of the other and joins with it in friendly alliance.  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, 409.)

Nature is certainly useful; but it only rarely, if ever, attains the summit without study. Nothing is so strong or robust that diligence cannot weaken it; nothing so upright that it cannot cast it down. Conversely, diligent care raises and preserves even the lowest rank. Therefore, if nature is favourable, it must not be despised but cultivated, so that it may be readily useful; if it is adverse, it demands more diligent cultivation, so that, with the help of virtue, it may grow stronger more happily and gloriously.

## CHAPTER IX. That he who attacks logic strives to make men inarticulate.

But who has acquired from the aid of nature such a distinction that, without study, he was considered most eloquent in every matter—or even in one language? Certainly, if it is good to be eloquent, it is better to be most eloquent. For the comparative degrees here do not grow into the opposite of the good proposed. This is not like the case of one called “eloquent” or “more eloquent,” where, while the positive degree retains the sense of wisdom, as the comparison increases the amount of eloquence, wisdom diminishes, and the stream of speech grows stronger. Thus some grammarians have held.

Yet although certain arts, which deal with contingencies and teach virtue, touch upon the nature of eloquence, that which depends largely on convention cannot be known naturally, because it is not natural; for it is not the same among all people. Consequently, that which is especially owed by man is imprudently demanded from nature without human assistance. But this school does not condemn eloquence, which is necessary to all and commended by all; it maintains rather that the arts which promise eloquence are useless. Thus its purpose tends not to make everyone mute—something neither possible nor desirable—but to remove logic from the midst. Logic, it says, is deceptive, a profession of wordy men; it has consumed many minds and has not merely blocked the path to philosophical study, but has prevented rational conduct and success in every undertaking.

## CHAPTER X. What the name “logic” signifies, and that all arts should be cultivated unless they are condemned.

Behold: the purpose of its proposal is clearer. It attacks logic in order to overthrow it, while pursuing the paths of all philosophy with equal fury. Yet one had to begin somewhere. It chose to set this art before the others because it seemed more familiar than the rest and more closely allied with this heresy. Let us therefore engage with it and bring forward for examination what is meant by the name “logic.”

Logic, in the broadest sense of the word, is the method of speaking or reasoning. Sometimes, however, the force of the term is restricted only to methods of reasoning. Whether, then, it teaches the ways of inference or supplies the rule of all discourse, those who call it useless are surely foolish; for the clearest reasoning shows that each function is altogether necessary. The name acquires this twofold meaning from its Greek origin, because there *logos* (λόγος) signifies now speech, now reason. But so that its significance may here be extended as widely as possible, let us for the present assign to it mastery over every kind of discourse. Then it cannot be convicted of uselessness, since even in this more general sense it will plainly appear wholly useful and necessary.

For if, as has often been said, the use of speech is necessary—a point no one denies—then the more efficiently it is taught, the more useful and certainly the more reliable is the instruction. It is foolish to spend longer, with labour and difficulty, on something that may otherwise be accomplished easily and quickly. This commonly happens to negligent persons, who regard the loss of time as of no importance. Thus the arts of all things to be done must be embraced and cultivated—indeed, with greater zeal in proportion as they derive their origin from Nature, the best of mothers, and attest the nobility of their stock by the easy and successful accomplishment of actions.

I say “the arts of things to be done” in order to distinguish them from arts occupied with wrongdoing, such as the arts of diviners and the other condemned forms of *mathesis*—occult or astrological learning. Since these are alien to duty, they ought, by the judgment of all rightly philosophizing persons, to be expelled from the entire human community. But these matters have been discussed more fully in the *Policraticus*.

## CHAPTER XI. What art is; the kinds of natural ability; and that natural ability must be cultivated by the arts.

Art is a method which, by its own economy, makes readily available a capacity for things naturally possible. It neither furnishes nor promises an effect in impossible things; rather, in matters that can be done, it provides a short route in place of nature’s circuitous and, as it were, costly course, and produces the capacity for difficult things. Hence the Greeks call it *methodos* (μέθοδος), as though it were a shortcutting method, which avoids nature’s expenditure and straightens its winding circuit, so that what ought to be done may be done more correctly and easily.

For nature, however vigorous, does not attain the ease of art unless it is instructed; nevertheless, nature is the mother of all arts and gives them Reason as a nurse, by which they may advance and be perfected. First it awakens natural ability to apprehend certain things; after it has apprehended them, it deposits them as it were in the keeping-house and treasury of memory. Reason then diligently examines what has been apprehended and ought to be entrusted—or has already been entrusted—to memory, and from the nature of individual things gives a true and uncorrupted judgment concerning each, unless perhaps it goes astray in some point. Nature supplies these three as the foundations and instruments, as it were, of all arts.

Natural ability (*ingenium*), according to Isidore, is a certain power naturally implanted in the mind and effective through itself. This description seems to express that Nature has implanted in the mind a certain power which is either the mind’s original motion, or which arouses that original motion exercised by the mind in investigating things. It is therefore said to be effective “through itself,” because it awaits the assistance of nothing preceding it; it goes before all things and assists what follows. Investigation precedes the comprehension, examination, and preservation of everything that is to be known.

Thus natural ability proceeds from nature and is assisted by study and practice, so that what was difficult in its first exercise becomes easier through habitual use; and, once it has discovered the rules for doing this, it becomes very easy—unless the torpor of disuse and negligence intervenes. This is the origin of all arts: nature, lying latent, produces use and the exercise of study; use and exercise produce art; and art produces the capacity now under discussion. [Col. 0838D] Natural ability is therefore effective through itself; practice is effective through use; memory through both; and Reason itself is strengthened by these, produces the arts, and does so according to the capacity of individual talents.

There are three kinds of such talents, as Bernard, the aged master of Chartres, used to teach his hearers in frequent conversation. One is flighty, another low, and another moderate. The flighty talent departs from what it has apprehended with the same ease with which it apprehends it, and finds rest in no settled seat. The low talent cannot be raised upward and therefore knows nothing perfect. But the moderate talent, because it has somewhere to rest and can be elevated, neither despairs of progress nor lacks suitability for the practice of philosophy. In this kind, I think, Nature has established the foundations of the arts, for its use is strengthened by study.

Study, according to Cicero, is a constant and vigorous application of the mind to doing something, with great willingness. Memory is, as it were, the mind’s storehouse and the firm, faithful custody of things apprehended. Reason is the mind’s power of examining what comes before the senses or the mind, and the faithful judge of what is more important. Weighing the similarities and dissimilarities of things, it finally establishes art as a certain finite knowledge of infinite matters.

For while the names in an art terminate an infinity, all are defined by the feminine article, excluding those things which it has distinguished by a determinate assignment of their own property. Species are infinite; yet art has established this finite rule concerning them: wherever a species is present, a genus is present also. Numbers are infinite; nevertheless, it has defined every number as either even or odd. To prove the point by a clear example: circumstance first introduced dispute; practice increased the habit of disputing; Reason discovered the form of disputation, which is the art of that activity; cultivated art conferred capacity.

Since Nature is the mother of the arts, contempt for them rightly rebounds as an injury to their parent. Natural ability must therefore be cultivated diligently by a balance of both study and relaxation: by the former it grows strong; by the latter it is refreshed. Hence a certain distinguished wise man—to whom I acknowledge a debt for the saying—said: “Natural ability proceeds from nature, is helped by use, is blunted by immoderate labour, and is sharpened by moderate exercise.” If it is properly ordered and lawfully exercised, it will not merely suffice for mastery of the arts; it will find a direct and ready path even to matters in some sense naturally inaccessible, and will be most reliable for quickly learning or teaching whatever needs to be made clear.

## CHAPTER XII. Why the arts are called liberal.

Although there are many kinds of arts, the liberal arts are the first to present themselves to the natural ability of the philosophizing mind. All of them are contained under the scheme of either the Trivium or the Quadrivium. The ancients who diligently devoted themselves to them are said to have found them so effective that they opened every text, raised the understanding to all things, and sufficed to unravel every difficulty in questions capable of proof. Those to whom either the system of the Trivium disclosed the nature of all discourse, or the law of the Quadrivium revealed the secrets of all nature, needed no teacher to explain books or resolve questions.

Thus, just as they are called “arts” either because they constrain by rules and precepts; or from virtue, which in Greek is called *aretē* (ἀρετή) and strengthens minds to apprehend the paths of wisdom; or from Reason, for which they provide nourishment and growth, and which the Greeks call *arses*—so they are called “liberal” either because the ancients had their children educated in them, or because they seek human freedom: that a man, free from cares, may devote himself to wisdom, and may often be liberated by them from cares whose origin wisdom does not admit. They also often exclude necessary concerns, so that the mind may have a freer path toward philosophy.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why grammar is so called.

[Col. 0840A]

The first of all these is logic, considered in that part of itself which concerns the initial formation of speech—so that the name “logic,” as has already been said, may have the widest possible scope and not be restricted merely to the science of reasoning. Grammar is the knowledge of speaking and writing correctly, and the origin of all liberal disciplines. It is likewise the cradle of the whole of philosophy and, so to speak, the first nurse of all literary study. It receives from the bosom of Nature the tender young of all things being born, nourishes their infancy, advances the growth appropriate to every stage in philosophy, and with maternal diligence brings forth and guards every age of the philosopher. Therefore it is called grammar from the first principles both of writing and of speaking.

For *grammatica* means a letter or a line; hence it is “literal,” because it teaches letters. By “letters” are understood both the shapes of simple sounds and the elements—that is, the sounds represented by those shapes. Or it is “linear,” because just as, in the growth of magnitude, the dimension of a line comes first and is, as it were, a material basis of a surface or body, so this discipline first assists those aspiring to progress in wisdom: it instructs the tongue and introduces wisdom through the ears as well as the eyes, so that discourse may advance in this manner. Words entering through the ear strike and awaken the intellect, which, as Augustine says, is a kind of hand of the soul, capable of grasping and apprehending its objects.

Letters—that is, visible shapes—are first signs of sounds, then of things. They set things before the soul through the windows of the eyes, and often make the utterances of absent people speak without a voice. This art therefore teaches the first elements of speech and trains the judgment of eyes and ears, so that a person can no more philosophize without it than someone who has always been blind and deaf can excel among philosophers.

## CHAPTER XIV. That grammar, although not natural, imitates nature.

But since grammar depends on convention, it does not appear to arise from nature. Natural things are the same among all people, whereas grammar is not the same among all. Yet it has been established above that Nature is the mother of the arts. Although grammar has proceeded to some extent—indeed, for the most part—from human institution, it nevertheless imitates Nature, partly derives its origin from her, and in every respect strives, as far as it can, to conform to her.

Thus, at Nature’s prompting, grammar has restricted the number of vowels, so far as the elements are concerned, among all nations to five; among most peoples, however, the number of written characters is larger. Yet our Teuredus, a grammarian more powerful in learning than in reputation, demonstrated a greater number even among elementary sounds. For, he says, if the distinctions of sounds are considered, there are seven. Nature has likewise fashioned among consonants diverse kinds of semivowels and mutes, and likewise simple and double consonants. Anyone who observes mouths modulating sounds according to Nature’s marvellous law, and carefully examines their powers, will clearly perceive their distinctions.

The imposition of names and of other words, although it proceeds from human choice, is in some measure subject to Nature, which it plausibly imitates within its own limits. For, in order to carry out the effect of divine ordering and establish among men the exchange of speech, human beings first assigned names to things already lying before them, formed by Nature’s hand. Nature had compounded and distinguished them either from the four elements or from matter and form, so that they might be presented to the senses of a rational creature and their diversity marked both by properties and by names. Hence, as Boethius says, “this is called a man, that a piece of wood, and another thing a stone”; and thus, as it were, their own names were impressed upon all substances.

But because substances have many differences—some derived from quantity, others from quality, others from various forms of accidents, and others again from those features which are more characteristic and contribute to being—names were invented which could be added to substantives and in some fashion portray their force and nature, just as the aforementioned differences of substances are expressed by their respective properties. For as accidents clothe and inform a substance, so substantives are informed, by a certain proportion of Reason, by adjectives.

And so that the institution of Reason may cohere more closely with Nature: just as the substance of each thing knows no increase or decrease, so substantives do not admit degrees of comparison; nor do the names of substantial differences, even though they are adjectives, because they indicate a certain quality of substance. Likewise, terms added to substances from quantity are not compared, because quantity itself does not admit more and less. In short, just as only an accident is capable of comparison—and not every accident—so only accidental adjectives, and not all of them, are comparable.

This imitation of Nature is apparent not only in nouns, but in all the other parts of speech as well, if one considers them carefully. Because a substance presented to sense or reason cannot exist without the movement by which it is moved in time through acting or being acted upon, verbs were devised to designate the bodily motions of agent or patient. Therefore, because motion does not exist without time, neither could a verb exist without a co-signification of time. And because such motion is not always uniform but, so to speak, many-coloured—acting or suffering differently, or at different times—adverbs arose, after the manner of adjectival nouns, to express its differences.

Again, certain verbs lack some tenses, as meditative and inchoative verbs lack the past: deliberation about things to be done is not at once completed, nor do the beginnings of things reach their own perfection. Is this not a trace of Nature expressed in human Reason?

## CHAPTER XV. That adjectives of second imposition are not fittingly joined to substantives of first imposition, as in “a patronymic horse.”

[Col. 0842A]

Let Reason proceed to the origin of second imposition, where the authority of governing Nature is apparent, though not so clearly. When names had first been imposed upon things, as was said, the mind of the name-giver turned back upon itself and assigned terms to the names themselves, through which the teaching of discourse might proceed, so that by their assistance one person might convey his thought into another’s mind.

Thus, a word that is declined by cases and lacks time is called a noun: a substantive if it signifies a substance, or ‘substantive’ when used substantively. An adjective is that which inheres, if one may so speak, formally in a substance, or something after its likeness. What signifies its temporal movement—yet does so temporally—is called a verb: active, if it signifies that movement as in an agent; passive, if as in a patient.

The words that arose secondarily were instituted in imitation of words of first imposition. Thus, just as among the latter, both substantives and adjectives, some are proper to individual things and others common by their own character to several things, so among the former some terms are found used singly and others used generally. What is called a noun or an assertion corresponds to the nature of substantives. What is called appellative or categorical, when attached to the preceding terms, performs the office of adjectival force, which determines the quality of substantives.

Nevertheless, just as in the works of Nature the investigation of what inheres in simple things is subtler than that of what composition presents to the senses or intellect, so adjectives of second imposition are more difficult to understand unless they are attached to the things to which they are naturally assigned. The nature of a substance is more solid than that of words and their accidents, more familiar to sense or intellect. Indeed, those who apply adjectives of second imposition to substantives of first institution either say nothing whatsoever or talk nonsense.
