For if a horse is called “patronymic,” or hypotheticals are called “secular,” the combination is unsuitable—not because of any discordance in their accidents, but because the principal meanings of the words obstruct understanding. In gender, number, and case, the adjective is sufficiently consistent with the substantive. But to join their principal meanings is not merely to speak falsely but also to speak nonsense.

Virgil is charged with *acyrologia*—improper expression—for saying “in a grassy field” (*gramineo in campo*), when he ought to have said “in a field full of grass” (*graminoso in campo*). Yet he would plainly be more blameworthy, and undoubtedly far more nonsensical, if he had said “in a categorical field” or “in a patronymic field.”

He also answers the objection of those who seek to prove, from the mere similarity of mutually compatible accidents, that not every consonant joined to a vowel makes a syllable. For consonantal *I* and *V* when joined do no more to make a syllable than adjectives of second imposition, placed with first-imposition substantives, do toward correct and proportionate speech.

It is agreed that speakers commit two faults: one is the fault of one who speaks falsely; the other, of one who transgresses established usage. At the least, these persons commit the latter. Pronouns of the first and second person are improperly joined with verbs unless there is a reason of distinction or emphasis, though the grammatical accidents of the words accord well enough.

I do not here restrict the notion of nonsensical speech so narrowly as to mean merely saying the same thing repeatedly—for example, when someone adds to a substantive an adjective already understood in it, as in “the rational man walks.” Rather, I extend it to every form of expression in which the combination of words is useless and, as it were, ineffective for carrying out its own law. Yet a combination is not useless merely because it bears the mark of falsehood and at one point explains, at another obscures. Grammar does not prohibit falsehood, even if words are joined from which no understanding arises for one skilled in the language.

It is clearer from this that a fitting adjective cannot be added from second imposition to first-imposition substantives: if adjectives are resolved into equivalent expressions—for instance, if a definition is given in place of names—the mind will not shrink from the addition of the equivalent term, though it will dread hearing the adjective of second imposition itself.

For example, “a categorical proposition” seems equivalently to assert either that it states something simply—that is, without any condition—or that it has a predicate term. Say, therefore, “a tunic is categorical,” and the intellect will halt because the addition is inappropriate; perhaps it will sooner complain of an inept combination of words than accuse the speaker of falsehood. But if he says, “a tunic states something simply, that is, without condition, or has a predicate term,” the listener will immediately charge him with falsehood, yet will not quickly leap to complain of the impropriety of the combination.

Certainly, when one says “a categorical proposition,” one understands “having a predicate term and a subject”; but when one says “a categorical syllogism,” one signifies that it consists of categorical propositions. What “a categorical horse” might signify, I do not know; but for the moment I believe it signifies nothing. For I think that what is found nowhere exists nowhere.

There is a similar misuse if someone says, “a horse ends in S,” and similar expressions. Likewise: “Cato, sitting between the Janiculum and the Kalends of March, repairs the garments of the Roman people by fours or by sixes.” Such a statement either is not discourse at all or is more corrupted than any nonsensical discourse whatever.

Speech of this sort is called *stichiologus* (στιχιόλογος), that is, inverted speech, because words are joined contrary to the laws of speaking. For *stichos* (στίχος) means a verse; hence a distich is a poem of two verses. Since I have heard many people discuss this topic and express varied opinions, I shall not hesitate to report—and perhaps it will not displease the reader to hear—what I learned while staying in Apulia from a Greek interpreter who also knew Latin well. I wish to acknowledge my obligation to him—not, perhaps, for usefulness, though there is some usefulness in these matters, but at least for the goodwill by which he wished to benefit his hearers.

[Col. 0844A] The first point of this judgment or opinion is the one I have already stated: the combination of adjectives of second imposition with substantives of first imposition is inconsistent even according to grammatical principles. This combination possesses, as it were, a hidden *aphōnia* (ἀφωνία), that is, lack of consonance; or, to use Quintilian’s term, *cacozugia* (κακοζυγία), that is, a bad coupling. Although we may not be able easily to condemn it by clear reasons, it is nevertheless displeasing in itself to the grammarian who hears it.

There are many such things which immediately offend, although the demonstration of their fault lies farther away. This perhaps occurs in cases whose merit or defect is evident. Where grammar is most indulgent, it detects *akyrologia* (ἀκυρολογία), improper usage. For grammar objects not only to disagreement of accidents in a combination of words; it also judges the addition of a term of secondary invention to a substantive of first imposition absurd. And it is absurd for this reason: the mind is deafened to such a combination. But who correctly examines by hearing things to which he is deaf? Is not a voice wasted when poured into a deaf ear? Therefore, since the intellect is, like a hand of the soul, also in a sense its ear, it has received nothing at all from a statement whose intelligibility absurdity has blocked.

Yet something is sometimes considered absurd merely because its use is, for the time being, unusual and infrequent; and it is not therefore wholly absurd. So an unattractive woman is indeed badly formed, but not altogether without form; and among letters some are called mute, not because they make absolutely no sound, but because they make the least sound in comparison with others. This addition, however, is utterly absurd: it does not merely sound false or bad in the hearer’s ear—for not everything false is absurd—even though an examiner of truth rejects and repels it.

Individual statements are also called absurd according to the judgment of the disciplines which examine the quality of words and deeds. Grammar regards an unsuitable combination of words as absurd, but does not aspire to judge truth. Caesar, in his book *On Analogy*, is indeed a grammarian, and declares that one must avoid whatever may seem absurd to a learned hearer: “Just as sailors avoid a reef,” he says, “so one must avoid an infrequent and unusual word.” Dialectic, however, accepts only what is true or probable, and considers absurd whatever departs too far from these. For it does not attend to the end of usefulness or honour.

Civic science, on the other hand, measures what is useful and is concerned with the end of what is just or honourable; it equally rejects things far removed from right, goodness, and equity, whether true or false. This will be clear in the remaining disciplines also. But let us now continue our Greek interpreter’s explanation.

“Man is rational”: given things as they now are, this is in some fashion necessary. “Man is capable of laughter”: this is probable. “Man is white”: this is possible indeed, but doubtful, because it may equally be true or false. “Man is capable of braying”: this is impossible, so that it cannot be true at all.

[Col. 0845A] The grammarian recoils from none of these statements, because everywhere he finds his own rule. He corrects none, changes none, and accepts them all gladly. The logician rebukes and refutes the fourth, because the examination of truth and falsehood has been entrusted to him. For this reason, he considers it absurd to lend it an ear. Now add to the foregoing examples a fifth: “Man is categorical.” The grammarian certainly condemns this as absurd, although he admitted statements that were doubtful, false, and even impossible. Why? Because, he says, it does not follow his rules: he had always maintained that these adjectives were forbidden to be joined to those subjects.

## CHAPTER XVI. That adjectives of first imposition are joined to first substantives.

Not, however, conversely, is it impossible or incongruous for adjectives of first imposition to be attached to names of second imposition. For nature is abundant, and makes the bounty of its richness available to human need. Hence the property of things overflows into words, while reason strives to make expressions akin to the things of which it speaks. Thus discourse is called hard or soft; a word harsh or light; a noun sweet or bitter—although these properly belong to bodies, not to discourse.

Very many expressions of this kind are found, and none of them is discordant or charged with falsity by an honest judge or hearer. For although trustworthiness is a virtue belonging only to a rational creature, nevertheless speech is called trustworthy, and likewise deceitful, although deceit is shown to reside not in speech itself but in the human being. For names belonging to natural things, if I may so put it, are customarily transferred to meet the need of rational things, whereas the transfer of names of rational things to natural things is by no means in such common use. Such transfer may be made now from necessity, now for ornament; but, as is well known among learned persons, what is not done for ornament is not free from equivocation.

Therefore, terms whose transfer is necessary are conveniently applied to many things and, according to the manner of those things which are said to be predicated accidentally, commonly change their sense in each particular case; yet no one reproves the incongruity of their combination. And although an improper sense—that is, a transferred sense—often prevails over the first signification of its word, that is, the signification it possessed from its original imposition, through an established usage [Col. 0845D], if such terms should happen to return to their native sense, there is either no absurdity at all, or not so great an absurdity as we allege when adjectives belonging to words are drawn over so as to signify the quality of things.

Behold, “convertible” obtains in usage among those things which are reciprocally circumscribed by predication, as in species and definition, or property. Likewise “finite” and “infinite” are attached, to indicate their qualities, both to noun and verb; but because these terms have been taken from things, it is by no means discordant if they return home, as it were, from travel, so that some thing is called convertible, finite, or infinite. Similarly, “universal” and “particular,” although their designation flourishes in words and has been borrowed from things—for they are not of second imposition—can be joined as adjectives to names of things without absurdity [Col. 0846A].

Indeed, what has been taken from things may return to things; but terms invented to indicate a quality of words are not called back with the same convenience or by the same usage to indicate a quality of things. They seem to have something in common with those classes of words called in Greek *syncategoremata* [co-signifying terms], because just as their signification arises from, or is determined through, the things joined to them, so these terms, when associated with the expressions from which they originate, conveniently awaken their proper meaning; but when transferred elsewhere, as though deprived of their natural force, they vanish or become discordant.

For if one says “a patronymic horse,” the grammarian hearing it will immediately either abuse the speaker so as to purge the fault in the word, or, if he wishes to show deference to one who talks too much, will use the comic slave’s proverb: [Col. 0846B] “I beg you, use good words.” Is not this entreaty, then, a kind of reproach for a fault? For one who asks for good words in place of these plainly does not allow that these are good. Otherwise he would say more elegantly: “I beg you, use better words.”

Certainly, if someone seeks mood or tense in a noun, or cause and comparison in a verb, the grammarian will rebuke him as a trifler. Therefore I do not think that he will extend patience to a pupil who calls a horse patronymic. So narrowly are adjectives of second imposition confined within the boundaries of their nature that they cannot merely not wander off to the names of things, but cannot even depart far from those terms to which they were assigned. For “proposition” is correctly called “hypothetical,” and “noun” “patronymic.” If you reverse this [Col. 0846C], so that you say “a hypothetical noun” or “a patronymic proposition,” then, in the grammarian’s judgment, you either say nothing at all or speak ineptly.

Moreover, usage possesses the highest authority in judging speech, and nothing which usage itself condemns will gain force unless usage restores it. Hence those lines:

> Many words shall be reborn that have already fallen away, and words now held in honor shall fall, if Usage wills it—Usage, in whose power lie the judgment, the law, and the norm of speech.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 70)

For just as in law custom is said to be the best interpreter of statutes, so the usage of correct speakers is the most powerful interpreter of rules. Hence I infer that what is read nowhere in writing, heard nowhere from correct speakers [Col. 0846D], and has no analogous class of usage, has long since been condemned, or at least has not yet been approved by grammarians.

Yet I do not think that all names of first invention can suitably be transferred to every kind of thing, although, as they are more general, so they are more suitable for transferred usage. But since something outside the rule is frequently found, perhaps something may somewhere be found otherwise than has been said, or the usage proposed may prevail. For that interchange by which things and expressions mutually attribute their own properties to one another, as though by reciprocal comparison, is expressed more frequently by transferred expressions than by those promulgated through secondary imposition. A particular case may perhaps derogate from the universality of a rule. But we are speaking of usage.

This power of transference [Col. 0847A], in ascribing to expressions what belongs to things and to things what belongs to expressions, produces a certain indifference in speech. Just as this benefits disciplined minds by its concision, so it confuses and overthrows undiscerning minds and closes to them the understanding of the whole truth. For one who aspires to knowledge of truth must carefully consider, with a disciplined mind, what even a stammerer intends to say; for he too very often speaks truth.

## Chapter XVII. That grammar also imitates nature in poetry

In other respects too grammar imitates nature; for the precepts of poetry plainly express the nature of human dispositions and require the craftsman of art to follow nature:

> For nature first shapes us inwardly for every condition of fortune:  
> she gladdens us, or drives us to anger,  
> or leads us down and oppresses us upon the ground with heavy grief;  
> then she brings forth the motions of the soul through the tongue as interpreter.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 78)

The point of this is that the poet should not depart from nature’s traces, but should strive with all his might to adhere to it in bearing, gesture, and speech.

> . . . If you wish me to weep,  
> you yourself must first grieve . . .  
> (Ibid.)

If you wish me to rejoice, you must first rejoice; otherwise:

> . . . if you utter your assigned part badly,  
> I shall either sleep or laugh . . .  
> (Ibid.)

In addition, account must be taken there not only of feet and quantities, but of ages, places, times, and other matters which it is not relevant to enumerate individually here, since all proceed from nature’s workshop [Col. 0847C].

Poetics adheres so closely to natural things that many have denied that it is a branch of grammar, maintaining that it is an art in itself and belongs no more to grammar than to rhetoric, although it is akin to both because it has precepts in common with them. Let whoever wishes rage over this—I am not prolonging that dispute—but, with everyone’s leave, I think it should be referred to grammar as to the mother and nurse of its study. Although neither of these arts is wholly natural, and each, in the greater part of its substance, acknowledges as its author the human being who discovered it, nature nevertheless claims some right for itself. Indeed, either grammar will retain poetics within itself, or poetics will be eliminated from the number of liberal disciplines [Col. 0847D].

## Chapter XVIII. What grammar teaches one to follow and what to avoid

Grammar is traditionally defined as the knowledge of writing correctly and speaking correctly. “Correctly” is rightly included in the definition, in order to exclude fault: namely, so that in writing one follows orthography, and in speaking the authority of art and usage. Orthography—that is, correct writing—consists in placing each letter in its proper position, neither usurping another’s office nor abandoning its own.

To speak is to express one’s own thought through an articulated and lettered voice. For the statement,

> “They speak by nods and signs”  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*)

[Col. 0848A] departs from the proper meaning of speech. To speak correctly is to avoid in speech the fault of solecism and barbarism.

A barbarism is the corruption of a non-barbarian word—that is, a Greek or Latin word. If, however, we use a barbarian word in our own speech, it is not a barbarism but a *barbarolexis* [the use of a foreign word]. A solecism, on the other hand, is corruption not of an individual word but of construction, when words are improperly joined contrary to the rule of construction. It arises in two ways: either through the parts of speech themselves or through the accidents of those parts.

It arises through the parts themselves when one substitutes one part for another—for instance, a preposition for an adverb or conversely—or when, within the same part, one employs one class of words for another; for example, a term of second imposition where one of first imposition ought to have been used [Col. 0848B]. It arises through accidents by means of qualities, genders, cases, numbers, and figures.

Likewise in metre there is *metaplasm*, which occurs in a single word through a license compelled by metrical law, just as barbarism occurs in a single word in ordinary prose speech. It is called *metaplasm*, as it were “transformation” or “deformation,” because it transforms or deforms a word, as though departing from its proper law. There are also *schemata*, translated as “figures,” in words or sentences; they arise through various forms of expression for the beauty of style.

Thus barbarism and metaplasm are detected in individual words; solecism and figures arise not in individual words but in the conjunction of several. Since there are three things—art, fault, and figure—the grammarian must necessarily know each of them. Otherwise he will neither be fortified by art [Col. 0848C], nor avoid fault, nor readily imitate the beauties of authors. If, ignorant of them, he writes or speaks correctly, this must not be attributed to his skill, because chance performs the work of virtue.

Art, therefore, is like a public paved road on which all have the right to go, walk, and conduct business without accusation or molestation. Fault is a byway for all, so that anyone who travels or acts upon it either encounters a precipice or suffers accusation and harassment from those who challenge him. Figure occupies the middle place: while it departs somewhat from both, it does not fall under the principle of either.

All therefore follow art, because it is prescribed; they avoid fault, because it is prohibited; but some employ figures, because they are permitted [Col. 0848D]. For between faults—namely barbarism and solecism—and art, which is the virtue and norm of expression, lie figures and schemata: metaplasm, when a word is faulted with justification; schema, when the deviation in the connection of words has a plausible cause.

For, as Isidore testifies, a figure is “a fault with justification.” Therefore this license is granted only to authors and those like authors—that is, to the most learned persons, who know the reasons for saying and for keeping silence. “They have attained,” as Cicero says, “and do attain, this license through great and divine goods.” The authority of persons is not slight: all their sayings or deeds either bring praise or remove blame—a status that one seeks in vain unless one shows oneself worthy of imitation through great goods.

Certainly, this authority arising from other virtues has made the faults of great persons sweet and pleasing to posterity. Hence Augustine, in the second book of *On Order*:

> “The solecisms and barbarisms which poets call—and have cherished—figures and metaplasms, they preferred to designate by altered names rather than avoid as manifest faults. Remove them, however, from poems, and I shall miss the sweetest seasonings. Transfer them to free and forensic speech: who would not command that it be shunned and hidden away in the theatres? Heap many of them into one place, and I shall be disgusted by the whole as affected and rancid.”

Therefore order, the governor of things, will allow them neither everywhere nor nowhere: when they are interposed, speech otherwise lowly and cheap is raised and made illustrious. So he says. From this authoritative precept it is clear how necessary is knowledge of those matters which, though granted to the more learned [Col. 0849B], occupy almost the whole expanse of writings; for those who have not learned what is said properly, figuratively, and faultily will rarely attain a trustworthy, and never an easy, understanding of what has been written.

## Chapter XIX. That knowledge of figures is highly useful

Grammar also sets out tropes—that is, modes of expression—when speech is drawn, for a plausible reason, from its proper meaning to an improper one. Such are metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, and similar figures, which would take too long to enumerate. These too are privileged in the manner of schemata, and their use is open only to the most learned; hence their law is stricter, by which they are not permitted to wander too far [Col. 0849C]. For it is regularly taught that figures must not be extended.

If anyone is a particularly zealous imitator of authors in transfers and figures, let him beware lest a figure be uncultivated through a harsh transfer. “For the highest virtue of speech is clarity and ease of understanding.” The cause of schemata is necessity or ornament. For speech was instituted to explain thought, and figures were admitted so that whatever in them departs from art might be compensated by some advantage.

Knowledge of these is especially necessary, because among all things that impede understanding, three are usually blamed above the rest: schemata joined with the tropes of orators; sophisms, which cover the minds of hearers with a cloud of deceptions; and the diversity of arguments, which lies beforehand in the speaker’s mind and, once understood, prepares a straight path for understanding [Col. 0849D]. For, as Hilary says: “Understanding must be taken from the causes of speaking.” Otherwise, even in the canonical Scriptures the Fathers will dispute, and even the Evangelists will be contrary to one another, if an incompetent judge attends only to the surface of statements and not to the minds of the speakers. Such conduct belongs to a perverse intellect that despises its own advancement.

Does not Solomon say, not merely in the same book and on the same page, but even in consecutive verses: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him”; and: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise in his own eyes”? (Prov. 26). Thus rules must be known, so that it may be clear by them what in speech is correct and what irregular; for unless you refer to a rule, you will not correct what is wrong [Col. 0850A], nor by any effort avoid an unknown precipice.

But among rules I would scarcely name anything more useful or concise than that part of the arts which, in marking the figures of authors, clearly displays the virtues and faults of expressions. I therefore wonder why it is so greatly neglected by our contemporaries, when it is most useful, most concise, and has been treated with the greatest care by almost all writers on this art. Donatus, Servius, Priscian, Isidore, our Bede, and many others each treat it, so that it cannot be unknown except through negligence. Quintilian too, in presenting it, extols it with such praises “that he says the grammarian’s professional title cannot stand without it, and that one aspires in vain to mastery of the art.”

The signification of words must be examined more carefully, and one must more diligently investigate what any expression can mean in itself and what it can mean from its adjuncts in context, so that one may dispel the shadows of sophisms which obscure the truth [Col. 0850B]. The method of speech must be weighed “from the circumstances of what is said, the character of the speaker, the character of the hearers, the place and time,” and other matters to be considered in various ways by a diligent investigator. Whoever applies himself carefully to these measures set forth against the three barriers to understanding will marvel at his own progress in understanding writings and utterances, and will appear venerable to others.

## Chapter XX. Matters with which the grammarian ought to be occupied

The study of grammar also concerns other matters. It considers not only the nature of letters, syllables, and words [Col. 0850C], and attends to feet in metres and accents in syllables, but also to the forms of accents, so that you may know on which syllable the grave, acute, or circumflex accent rests. It also distinguishes meanings by punctuation—that is, by marks indicating where a colon, comma, or period, that is, where a lesser division, a middle division, or a full division, should be made.

We may translate these terms more significantly as follows: *colon* is a limb; *comma*, a segment; *period*, a circuit which closes the sense of an utterance. But some, so that the matter may be clearer, say—whether they are correct, let them see—that a colon is what we commonly call a full stop, or a certain pause for breath; a comma is where we divide a verse as though by a middle division; and a period is that which concludes the sense of an utterance completely [Col. 0850D].

There are also signs which distinguish the kinds of writings, so that one may discern what in them is clear, what obscure, what certain, what doubtful; and there are very many more such matters. This part of the art, however, has now for the most part fallen into disuse—so much so that the most devoted students of letters rightly complain, indeed almost lament, that shorthand, an art of the greatest usefulness and effectiveness both for retaining and understanding matters, has perished through the envy or negligence of our forebears.

Nor should anyone wonder that such force lay in little marks, since musical singers indicate by a few characters many distinctions of high and low notes. For this reason they call those characters the keys of music. Yet if little marks were the key to so great a body of knowledge, it is astonishing that our people, though they knew more things, did not recognize their elders, or that the keys to so great a science were lost [Col. 0851A].

Seneca is reported to have readily promised that he would hand down an art for acquiring memory; I wish it had become known to me, but I do not recall at all that he handed it down. Cicero appears to have devoted attention to it in his rhetorical works, but it is of little use to people like me. Works exist which we scarcely have time to learn, yet care about still less.

The rules of analogies, etymologies, glosses, and distinctions would nevertheless be of very great benefit; as would those which point out the faults of barbarism, solecism, and other things to be avoided; teach the licensed and ornate principles of metaplasm, schemata, and tropes; elucidate prose; set forth the laws of metres; explain their causes; and explain how they ought to be employed in histories or fabulous narratives. Whoever desires the definitions and forms of these things should turn over the books of the earlier grammarians. If he cannot have all of them at hand, let him discover what worthy material he may glean from each.

For although not every author is found equally useful for every subject, Isidore is nevertheless useful for many things, is sufficiently common, and deserves praise for his diligent brevity. Even if one cannot possess his entire work, retaining even this portion of it by memory contributes greatly to the understanding of one’s reading [Col. 0851B].

## Chapter XXI. How great men have approved grammar, and that no one can engage in philosophy without it any more than if he were deaf or mute

From these matters it is evident that grammar is not occupied with one subject alone, but prepares the mind to receive everything that can be taught by speech. Let each person therefore consider how much all the other disciplines owe to it.

Some of our contemporaries think it contributes to their glory that they chatter without grammar. They believe it useless and openly blame it, boasting that they have devoted no effort to it. But Marcus Tullius did not hate his son, from whom, as is apparent in his letters, he demanded grammar with the greatest insistence. Gaius Caesar published books *On Analogy*, knowing that no one could attain either philosophy, in which he was most skilled, or eloquence, in which he was most powerful, without it.

Quintilian so highly recommends grammar that he says: “The practice of grammar and the love of reading are bounded not by the period of schooling but by the span of life” [Col. 0851D]. For it teaches both understanding and speaking; it governs accents and regulates throughout the instruments of the very voice we use according as they suit persons and things. For the rule of pronunciation is one thing in metre and another in prose. One pronunciation is melodic, another metrical, another significative. The melodic belongs to music.

Thus Caesar, while still wearing the *praetexta*, mocked someone with an excellent jest: “If you read, you sing; if you sing, you sing badly.” This is the point of Martianus’ presentation of Grammar in *The Marriage of Mercury and Philology*: he brings her in with a scalpel, a rod, and a physician’s ointment-box. With the scalpel she cleanses faults of the mouth and, while educating them, trims the tongues of children who, with her first suckling, feeding, and guiding them, will proceed to the art of philosophy [Col. 0852A]. She forms their speech so that they may not stammer with barbarism or solecism; she punishes offenders with the rod; and with the ointment of the honor and utility that proceed from her, she softens the punishment of those who endure it.

She also makes the hand fit for writing correctly, sharpens sight so that densely formed letters or an elaborately worked veil cannot obstruct it, and opens the ears, making them receptive to low and high, indeed to every kind of sound. If, then, she affords so much utility, is the key to all writings, and is the mother and arbiter of all speech, who will bar her from the threshold of philosophy except one who believes that understanding what is said or written is superfluous for philosophizing? Certainly, those who reject or despise her make the blind and deaf more suited to philosophical studies than those whose unimpaired senses nature’s grace has bestowed and preserves [Col. 0852B].

## Chapter XXII. That Cornificius defends his error by Seneca’s authority

Nevertheless, Cornificius defends himself with a great judge and praises Seneca as the author of his error. Seneca is deservedly commended by many for two reasons. He abounds in praise of virtue and moral instruction; and, using the sententious style of speaking, which gathers thoughts briefly and compactly, he shines in verbal ornament, so that he cannot displease those who love either virtue or eloquence.

For—to speak with Quintilian’s permission, though Quintilian praises the man’s talent in such a way as to censure his judgment, saying that he abounded in pleasing faults, pleased boys more than learned persons, and broke the chief matters into the tiniest maxims, whence one of the emperors called his books “sand without lime”—among the pagans there is no ethical writer, or scarcely one, whose words or sayings you can use more conveniently in every matter [Col. 0852C]. For he contributes something of his own to everything.

Seneca holds that the liberal disciplines do not make a good man. I agree with him, and judge the same of the other arts. “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1), but charity alone makes a person good. He disparages the arts, but does not reject them from philosophy; for good men are not philosophers alone. “The grammarian,” he says, “is occupied with the care of speech; if he wanders farther, with histories; if he proceeds farthest, with poems.” This is not a small matter, but is of great benefit to the formation of virtue, which makes a good man.

Horace boasts (*Epistles* I.2.3) that, for virtue’s sake, he reread Homer:

> He tells what is noble, what shameful, what useful, and what is not,  
> more fully and better than Chrysippus and Crantor.

That poets are the cradles of philosophers is a commonplace. Antiquity teaches that the liberal disciplines are of such great usefulness that whoever fully knows them can understand all books and whatever has been written even without a teacher. For, as Quintilian says, these disciplines harm not those who pass through them, but those who linger over them [Col. 0852D].

## Chapter XXIII. The principal requirements for the exercise of philosophy and virtue; and that grammar is their foundation

[Col. 0853A]

The principal things necessary for the exercise of all philosophy and virtue are reading, instruction, meditation, and constancy in work. Reading has written material set before it. Instruction commonly depends upon writings, and sometimes proceeds to unwritten matters, which nevertheless are stored in the hidden places of memory or stand out in the understanding of a present matter. Meditation extends even to unknown things and often raises itself to incomprehensible things; it investigates both things manifest and things hidden.

The fourth, namely constancy in work, although it is formed from pre-existing knowledge and requires knowledge, nevertheless prepares paths for understanding, because “good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Ps. 110 [Vulgate numbering]). And the heralds of truth, as it is written, “announced the works of God and understood his deeds” (Ps. 63 [Vulgate numbering]).

Moreover, knowledge naturally precedes the practice and cultivation of virtue. Virtue does not run uncertainly, nor, in the battle it wages against vices, does it beat the air,

> But sees where it aims and at what it directs its bow;  
> nor does it follow crows indiscriminately, nor potsherd and mud.

But reading, instruction, and meditation produce knowledge. Hence it is clear that grammar, which is the foundation and root of these, in a manner sows seed in the furrows of nature, grace nevertheless going before. If cooperating grace is also present, it grows together and increases in the strength of solid virtue [Col. 0853C], so as to produce the fruit of good work, from which good people both take their name and truly are such.

Yet grace alone, which works both the willing and the accomplishing of good, makes a person good. It bestows, above all other things, the ability to write correctly and speak correctly upon those to whom this ability has been given; it supplies various arts; and, while it kindly offers itself to those in need, it ought not to be despised. For if it is despised, it rightly withdraws, and no ground for complaint remains to the despiser.

## Chapter XXIV. On the practice of reading and lecturing; and the custom of Bernard of Chartres and his followers
Whoever, therefore, aspires to philosophy should lay hold of reading, instruction, and meditation, together with the practice [Col. 0853D] of good works, lest the Lord should at some time be angered and what he seemed to have be taken away from him. But since the word “reading” (*legendi*) is equivocal, applying both to the exercise of teacher and learner and to the occupation of one independently examining writings, let the former—that is, what is shared between teacher and pupil—be called “prelection” (*praelectio*), to use Quintilian’s term; while the latter, which belongs to the investigation of one who meditates, should simply be called “reading” (*lectio*).

Accordingly, on Quintilian’s authority, in prelecting the grammarian ought to perform even the lesser services: he should require that the parts of speech be identified for him when verse has been rendered into prose, and that the characteristics of metres, which ought to be recognized in poems, be explained. He should detect what is barbarous, improper, or otherwise composed contrary to the rules of speech. Yet he should not condemn poets, [Col. 0854A] who are so readily excused on account of metrical necessity that faults themselves in verse are reckoned under the name of virtues. For the offensiveness of necessity commonly usurps the praise of virtue; and assent cannot be withheld from it without loss. He should point out metaplasm, figures of expression, rhetorical tropes, multiplicity of wording where it occurs, and the various ways in which something may be said thus or otherwise; and by frequent reminders he should commit these matters to his hearers’ memory.

He should examine authors and, without provoking the laughter of his observers, strip them of the feathers which, like the little crow, they have inserted into their works from diverse disciplines in order to make their colour more attractive. The more abundantly anyone has been imbued with many disciplines, the more fully he will discern the elegance of authors and the more clearly teach it. For by *diacrisis*, which we may call illustration [Col. 0854B] or pictorial elaboration, when they had undertaken the raw material of history, an argument, a fable, or any other subject, they cultivated it with such an abundance of learning and such grace of composition and seasoning that the completed work seemed in some fashion an image of all the arts.

Indeed, grammar and poetry pour themselves wholly into it and occupy the entire surface of what is expounded. To this, as the saying goes, *campologia*, bringing the colours of proof, adds its arguments amid the glitter of gold; rhetoric, in its topics of persuasion and brilliance of eloquence, emulates silvery brightness. Mathematics proceeds upon the wheels of its quadrivium and, following the tracks of the other arts, weaves its colours and beauties into manifold variety. Natural philosophy, having explored the purposes of nature, [Col. 0854C] brings from its storehouse a manifold beauty of colours. But that discipline which surpasses the other parts of philosophy—I mean ethics—without which even the name of philosopher cannot stand, surpasses all the rest by the grace of its contributed ornament. Examine Virgil or Lucan, and there, whatever branch of philosophy you profess, you will find its seasoning.

Thus the fruit of prelecting authors depends upon the learner’s capacity and upon the teacher’s industry and diligence. Bernard of Chartres, the most overflowing fountain of letters in Gaul in modern times, followed this practice. In reading authors he showed what was simple and set forth according to the model of the rule; he presented openly the figures of grammar, rhetorical colours, sophistical quibbles, [Col. 0854D] and the point at which a section of the reading under consideration looked toward other disciplines. Yet he did not teach everything in every passage, but apportioned to his hearers the measure of instruction in due season according to their capacity.

And because the splendour of speech comes either from propriety—that is, when an adjective or verb is elegantly joined to a substantive—or from transference, that is, when a word is carried, for a plausible reason, over to an alien meaning, he impressed these things upon his hearers’ minds when occasion offered. And since memory is strengthened and talent sharpened by exercise, he urged some by exhortations and others by whippings and punishments to imitate what they heard. Each was compelled on the following day to recite something of what he had heard on the preceding one—[Col. 0855A] some more, some less; for among them the following day was the pupil of the preceding day.

The evening exercise, called *declinatio*, was filled with such abundance of grammar that, if anyone devoted an entire year to it, he would have at hand the method of speaking and writing, provided he were not unusually dull, and could not fail to understand the meanings of words current in common use. But because no school or day should be devoid of religion, a subject was set before them which built up faith and morals, and through which those assembled might, as it were by a mutual conference, be encouraged toward good. The final section of this *declinatio*—indeed, of this philosophical conference—bore the marks of piety and commended the souls of the departed to their Redeemer by the devout offering [Col. 0855B] of the sixth of the Penitential Psalms and the Lord’s Prayer.

For those to whom preliminary exercises of boys were assigned in the imitation of prose or poems, he set before them poets or orators and ordered them to imitate their traces, showing them combinations of words and elegant clausulae of speech. If anyone had sewn another’s cloth onto the splendour of his own work, he exposed and rebuked the detected theft; yet most often he did not impose punishment. But one thus rebuked—if his inept composition had deserved this—he instructed, with restrained indulgence, to rise to the expression of the authors’ image; and he made the imitator of greater men become one whom posterity should imitate.

Among the first rudiments he also taught and impressed upon their minds what virtue there is in arrangement (*oeconomia*), [Col. 0855C] what is praiseworthy in the decorum of things, and what in words; where there should be spareness and a kind of leanness of expression, where abundance is plausible, where it is excessive, and where there is moderation in all things. He urged that histories and poems should be read through carefully, even those which seemed to be driven to flight by no spurs; and from each he exacted, with diligent insistence, something stored in memory as a daily payment.

Yet he said that superfluous material should be avoided and that what had been written by distinguished authors was enough. For “to pursue what any of the most contemptible persons has ever said is either extreme wretchedness or empty vanity; it detains and overwhelms talents that might more profitably be employed elsewhere. But whatever takes away what is better is of no use to that extent,” and is not even reckoned worthy of the name of good. [Col. 0855D] To examine and turn over every scrap and every writing, even those unworthy of reading, is no more relevant than to devote oneself to old wives’ tales.

For, as Augustine says in *On Order*: “Who could endure a man being thought uneducated because he has not heard that Daedalus flew; a liar because he has said it; foolish because he has believed it; shameless because he has asked whether he is not thought so? Or in what respect should I not deeply pity our acquaintances, who, if they cannot answer what Euryalus’s mother was called, are accused of ignorance, though they do not dare call those who question them empty, foolish, and curious?”

Thus Augustine, elegantly and truly. Hence the ancients rightly counted it among the virtues of a grammarian to be ignorant of some things. And because, throughout the whole preliminary training [Col. 0856A] of pupils, nothing is more useful than becoming accustomed to what ought to be done according to art, they wrote prose and poems every day and practised together in mutual conferences. No exercise is more useful for eloquence, none more expeditious for knowledge, and it contributes greatly to life—provided that charity governs this diligence and humility is preserved in literary advancement. For “it does not belong to the same person to serve learning and carnal vices.”

My teachers in grammar, William of Conches and Richard, surnamed the Bishop—now archdeacon of Coutances, a good man in life and conduct—formed their pupils for some time according to the model of this master. But afterwards, once reputation had prejudiced truth, and men preferred to appear rather than to be [Col. 0856B] philosophers, while teachers of the arts promised that they would pour all philosophy into their hearers in less than three or two years, they yielded, overcome by the rush of an untrained multitude.

Thereafter less time and diligence was devoted to the study of grammar. Hence it has happened that those who profess all the arts, both liberal and mechanical, do not know even the first, without which one advances vainly to the rest. Although other disciplines also contribute to literacy, this one alone is said, by a special privilege, to make a person learned. Romulus calls it *litteratura*, Varro *litteratio*, and its teacher or defender is called *litteratus*, “a man of letters.” In antiquity, however, he was called *litterator*, according to Catullus:

[Col. 0856C]

> Sulla the schoolmaster gives you a present.  
> (CATULLUS XIV.9)

Hence it is plausible that a despiser of grammar is not merely no schoolmaster (*litterator*), but should not even be called learned (*litteratus*).

## CHAPTER XXV. Praise of grammar from Quintilian

But since these children of yesterday, masters of today—yesterday beaten with the rod, today teaching in robes from the chair—object, out of ignorance of the other disciplines, that grammar is commended, let them patiently hear what is found concerning its praise in the book *On the Education of the Orator*, and, if they please, spare innocent grammarians. Quintilian says:

“No one should despise the elements of grammar [Col. 0856D] as trifling, not because it is a great task to distinguish consonants from vowels and to divide the consonants themselves into semivowels and mutes, but because, to those entering the inner sanctuary, as it were, of this sacred art, much subtlety of subject matter will appear—subtlety able not merely to sharpen the minds of boys, but also to exercise the highest learning and knowledge. All the less tolerable, therefore, are those who mock this art as thin and barren. Unless it has faithfully laid foundations for the future orator, whatever you build upon them will collapse. It is therefore the first of the liberal arts: necessary for boys, pleasant for old men, a sweet companion in private life; and, alone among every kind of study, it has more work than display.”

# BOOK II

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857A] In the course of the preceding book, I think I have sufficiently established that grammar is not useless, and that without it not only is perfect eloquence unattainable, but no path is open to those striving toward the other professions of philosophy. It should also be interpreted more leniently because it is subject not only to nature’s constraint but acquiesces in human will. For even the laws of citizens generally draw their force from human enactment, and what is believed expedient for public advantage is equated with natural justice.

Yet logic has not been completed. Cornificius, though mutilated and destined to be mutilated further, like a blind man feeling his way along a solid wall, rashly attacks and even more rashly accuses it. Certainly quarrels do not please a lover of truth; and whoever embraces charity withdraws himself from contention unbidden, still less voluntarily. Whether grammar is or is not a part of logic, I do not dispute; for it is agreed that it is concerned with utterances and supplies them, although it does not examine every kind of relation among utterances. You, however, for whom the matter is established, will judge concerning the name, and either apply it to every form of discourse or restrict it solely to the examination of arguments. I do not fear your judgement, since I trust both the justice of the cause and the expertise and sincerity of the judge.

Let us therefore consider whether logic is rational and useful, and measure its powers despite the opposition of its adversary. In this matter my office entails so much less labour because the hearer more readily grants it favour even without persuasion. For all boast that they are logicians, [Col. 0857C] not only those who have made progress in learning through certain blandishments, but also those who have not yet even greeted it from the threshold.

## CHAPTER I. That logic, because it seeks truth, benefits the whole of philosophy

In order, then, to confine the meaning of the name, logic is the method of reasoning through which the activity of all prudence is made firm. Since wisdom is first among all desirable things, and its fruit consists in love of the good and cultivation of the virtues, the mind must be occupied in its investigation and examine things by a thorough inquiry, so that it may have a pure and incorrupt judgement concerning each matter. Its exercise therefore consists in the examination of truth, which, as Cicero states in *On Duties*, is the material of the primary virtue, [Col. 0857D] called prudence; for the benefits and necessities of the other three virtues are subordinate to it.

Prudence wholly consists in the perception of truth and a certain skill in examining it. Justice embraces truth; courage defends it; temperance regulates the exercises of the preceding virtues. Hence it is clear that prudence is the root of all virtues: if it is cut off, the rest, like branches deprived of nature’s nourishment, wither away in a kind of dry decay. [Col. 0858A] For who will embrace or cultivate what he does not know? But truth is the material of prudence and the fountain of virtues. Whoever fully knows it is wise; whoever loves it is good; and blessed is whoever possesses it.

Therefore the most learned of our poets, showing the origin of the blessed life, says:

> Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things,  
> and has trampled beneath his feet every fear, inexorable fate,  
> and the roar of greedy Acheron.  
> (VIRGIL, *Georgics* II.490)

And another, more eminent in faith and knowledge of truth: “Happy is he who has been able to behold the bright fountain of good; happy is he who has been able to loose the heavy bonds of earth”—as though they spoke in different words but with the same meaning: “Happy is he to whom understanding of things has been granted.” For the more familiarly things that are fluid and pass away in a moment become known, the more worthless the perishable becomes in a mind possessed of itself. Nor is one oppressed by the yoke of vices whom truth rescues and leads out from slavery into freedom. “For it is impossible for anyone who seeks and embraces truth with his whole heart to love and cultivate vanity.”

## CHAPTER II. On the Peripatetic school, the origin of logic, and its author

From this arose the school of the Peripatetics, which held that the knowledge of truth is the highest good of human life. They therefore investigated the natures of all things, that they might know what in all things should be avoided as evil, what should be despised as not good, what should be sought as simply good, what should be preferred as more good, and what receives the name of good or evil by accident. Thus arose the two parts of philosophy, natural and moral, which are called by other names physics and ethics.

But because through lack of skill in reasoning they drew many improper conclusions—as Epicurus, who held that the world was constituted from atoms and void without God as its author, and the Stoics, who imagined matter coeternal with God and all sins equal—it was necessary to investigate and publish a discipline that would distinguish words and concepts and scatter the clouds of fallacy. This, as Boethius states in his second commentary on Porphyry, was the origin of the discipline of logic. For there had to be a science that distinguished truth from falsehood and taught what reasoning keeps to the true path of disputation, what is plausible, what is fictitious, and what ought to be suspected; otherwise truth could not be found through the labour of the reasoner.

Although Parmenides the Egyptian lived upon a rock in order to discover the principles of logic, he had so many and such great successors in study that they almost wholly deprived him of the glory of his invention. Apuleius, Augustine, and Isidore accordingly report that Plato is praised for having perfected philosophy by adding logic to physics, fully taught by Pythagoras, and ethics, fully taught by Isocrates. Through logic he weighed the force of arguments after examining the causes of things and conduct. Yet he did not reduce it to the technical form of an art; practice and exercise nevertheless prevailed, and, here as elsewhere, preceded formal rules. Aristotle then discovered and transmitted the rules of the art.

He is the chief of the Peripatetics, whom this art praises as its principal author. He shares the other disciplines with their authors, but by claiming this one as his own right, he excluded all others from possession of it. Although I have written more fully about him elsewhere, I thought it by no means fitting to pass over what Quintilian says of him: “Why should I mention Aristotle, whom I hesitate to judge more distinguished for his knowledge of things, his abundance of writings, his practice in speaking, the charm of his eloquence, the sharpness of his inventions, or the variety of his works?” [Col. 0859B]

## CHAPTER III. That logic should be taught to students of philosophy; and on the difference between demonstrative, probable, and sophistical logic

Seeing that work can pass into use and use into art, the Peripatetics subjected what had been wandering and unrestrained to fixed rules: excluding falsehoods, supplying what was defective, cutting away superfluities, and prescribing suitable rules in every case. From this proceeded, and was thus perfected, the science of reasoning, which reveals modes of disputation and kinds of proof, prepares a path for those advancing, and makes known what in statements is true, false, [Col. 0859C] necessary, or impossible. It is later in time than the other philosophical disciplines, but first in order. For it must be taught to those beginning philosophy, because it interprets words and concepts, without which no branch of philosophy properly comes to light.

Whoever thinks philosophy can be taught without logic should banish from the pursuit of wisdom every mode of reasoning, because logic presides over them. To turn to fables, antiquity considered *phronēsis* (prudence), the sister of *alētheia* (truth), not barren but her distinguished offspring, and joined her in chaste embraces to Mercury. Prudence is indeed the sister of truth, and through eloquence she makes fruitful and illustrious the love of reason and knowledge. For this is what it is for philology to be joined to Mercury. Logic is so called because it is rational: that is, it ministers to and examines arguments.

Plato divided it into dialectic and rhetoric, but those who assess its power more profoundly assign more to it. For demonstrative, probable, and sophistical reasoning are subject to it. Demonstrative reasoning flourishes from disciplinary principles and advances to their consequences; it delights in necessity and pays little attention to what may seem so to anyone, provided that it must be so. This befits the majesty of philosophers who teach rightly, a majesty strengthened by its own judgement without requiring their hearers’ assent.

Probable reasoning concerns matters which seem so to all, or to most, or to the wise; and matters consequent upon things known and probable to all, or most, or especially to the wise. It includes dialectic and rhetoric, because the dialectician and the orator, striving to persuade—the former an opponent, the latter a judge—do not consider it greatly important whether their arguments are true or false, so long as they preserve the appearance of truth. Sophistical reasoning, however, which is apparent rather than genuine wisdom, affects an appearance of probability or necessity. It cares little what this or that may be, provided that it envelops the person with whom it debates in fantastic images and deceptive shadows. Of all branches, dialectic is certainly the one that everyone seeks most eagerly, though few, in my judgement, attain it: it neither aspires to the august manner of teachers, nor is submerged in the waves of civic affairs, nor deceives by fallacies, but examines truth with ready and moderate probability. [Col. 0860B]

## CHAPTER IV. What dialectic is, and why it is so called

Dialectic, as Augustine holds, is the science of disputing well. This must be understood so that force is given to the words: dialecticians must not be thought to be those whom chance assists despite their lack of art. Nor does one dispute well who does not truly and probably prove what he intends. With the demonstrator’s and sophist’s permission, I would say that neither proceeds well toward the dialectician’s purpose if the one lacks probability and the other abandons truth. Yet each proves well if he measures his own office and omits nothing belonging to the possibilities of his faculty.

To dispute is to prove or disprove, by means of an assumed argument, something that is doubtful, placed in contradiction, or proposed in one way or another. Whoever does this artistically and probably reaches the goal of a dialectician. Aristotle, its author, gave it this name because in it and through it statements are disputed. For, as Remigius testifies, grammar concerns words and operates in words; dialectic concerns statements and operates in statements. Grammar principally treats words as signs of meanings, whereas dialectic examines the meanings of words. For *lektón* (λεκτόν), Isidore says, is called a “statement” (*dictum*) in Greek.

Whether it is called from Greek *lexis* (λέξις), interpreted as “speech,” as Quintilian holds in the preliminary exercises, or from *lektón*, called “that which is said,” makes little difference. To examine the force of speech and the truth and sense of what is said are the same thing, or nearly so. The force of a word is its meaning; if deprived of meaning, speech is empty, useless, and, so to speak, dead. Just as a body is quickened to life by the soul, so a word advances to a kind of life through its meaning. Whoever utters speech without meaning does not speak at all, but beats the air. [Col. 0860D]

## CHAPTER V. On the parts of dialectic and the end of logicians

But to return from species to genus, since some things still seem to require discussion: authors have commonly divided logic into the science of discovery and the science of judgement, and taught that it is wholly concerned with divisions, definitions, and inferences. For it is the mistress of discovery and judgement, and has—indeed makes—an expert craftsman in dividing, defining, and arguing. Among the parts of philosophy it is thus distinguished by a double privilege: it is honoured as a principal member, and throughout the body of philosophy it performs the office of an effective instrument.

The natural philosopher and moral philosopher do not proceed in their assertions except by proofs borrowed from the logician. Neither rightly defines or divides unless the logician grants the favour of his art; otherwise their success is advanced not by knowledge but by chance. It is rational, as its name shows. What progress in philosophy can be made by one devoid of reason? Though someone may have acute reason—by which I mean a faculty of the soul—he nevertheless encounters many obstacles in philosophical business if he lacks the method for accomplishing his undertaking. This is method: a concise procedure that generates and facilitates the capacity to achieve one’s purpose. [Col. 0861B]

The disciplines mentioned as belonging to logic are occupied with these matters. Demonstrative, probable, and sophistical reasoning all consist in discovery and judgement and likewise employ their own methods of dividing, defining, and inferring, although they differ in subject matter, end, or mode of procedure. Since “reason” (*ratio*) is said in many senses, the office denoted by this name is very broad. It is not restricted only to that which is reason, but extends also to that which appears to be so.

To omit other meanings of the term, grammarians call a word “absolute” when it needs no addition in order to be understood, as “God”—unless some qualification is supplied for significance, as when “God almighty” is said, to distinguish him from idols, which can do nothing, or demons, which can do very little. So too, “necessary or true reason” distinguishes it from a reason that may be avoided by chance or falsehood. Here, in my judgement, a reason is anything that is brought forward or can be brought forward to establish an opinion or strengthen a judgement. Opinion commonly wavers, whereas judgement always adheres to truth—if, at least, we use terms correctly; but one is nevertheless used for the other.

Thus sophistry too is rational; and although it deceives, it claims a place among the parts of philosophy. It introduces its own arguments, sometimes pretending to be demonstrative reasoning and sometimes falsely presenting itself as dialectic. It never professes itself anywhere, but everywhere puts on another’s dress. For it is apparent wisdom and generally brings one to establish an opinion, not because one alternative or the other is true or probable, but because either seems so. Sometimes it even uses genuine truths and probabilities. It is a quibbler, and often advances from true and manifest things to doubtful and false ones by petty questions or other snares of its deceit. It transforms itself into a minister of light and, like Neptune, either leads the person whom it draws into byways into danger or exposes him to ridicule. [Col. 0861D]

The philosopher employing demonstrative reasoning works toward truth; the dialectician toward opinion, being content with probability. The sophist, however, is satisfied if something merely seems probable. I would therefore not readily say that sophistry is useless to know: it exercises minds not a little and, if unknown, harms those ignorant of things more effectively. Deceit is not imposed upon one who knows it; a person who refused to avoid a danger he foresaw must blame himself. But whoever does not embrace demonstrative and probable reasoning certainly does not love truth and does not seek knowledge even of probable matters. Plainly no one attains virtue without truth, and whoever despises probable matters is not approved. [Col. 0862A]

## CHAPTER VI. That all desire logic, but not all attain it

From what has been said, logic seems to promise something great. It furnishes abundance in discovery and judgement; supplies the capacity to divide, define, and refute; and is so notable a part of philosophy that it runs through all its members in the manner of a spirit. Every philosophy that is not ordered toward logic is inert. Hence there is such a rush of peoples toward it from every side that it alone keeps more persons occupied than all the other workshops of that philosophy which orders human actions, words, and certainly thoughts, if they have proceeded rightly. I mean philosophy, without which everything is tasteless and insipid, plainly erroneous, and displeasing to good morals.

All cry out to one another: “Let scabies occupy the farthest place, and let whoever does not approach logic wallow in continual and everlasting filth.” It is therefore shameful, disgraceful, and dangerous for me too to be left behind. [Col. 0862C] I should like to see the light that has been revealed to these preachers alone. I approach and humbly entreat them to teach me and, if possible, make me like themselves. They promise great things, but meanwhile impose upon me the silence of the Pythagoreans, claiming that the secrets of Minerva entrusted to them are at stake. Yet they permit—indeed command—me to chatter with them; for this, among such persons, is to dispute.

At length, once through long acquaintance I receive a kinder hearing, I press more earnestly, knock more vigorously, and ask more affectionately that the door of the art be opened to me. We begin, then, with definition. In a few words he teaches me to define whatever I wish: I am instructed to state first the genus of the thing in question and add its substantial differences until they are coextensive with the proposed object. The highest things, because they lack a genus, and the lowest, because they lack differences, cannot be defined. Yet description is applied to them, formed from properties whose combination is found nowhere else. For a substantial definition cannot exist without the genus of the thing proposed and some of its substantial differences.

See: I have thus been taught the art of defining, and he orders me to define appropriately, or at least describe, anything proposed. We proceed to the science of division. I am instructed to divide a genus sufficiently into species, either through differences or through affirmation and negation; to resolve an integral whole into the parts from which it is integrally constituted; and to divide a universal into its subjects and virtual powers. If a word is to be divided, either its meanings or its modes are to be enumerated. I am taught to divide an accident into subjects and instructed to indicate what things are capable of receiving it; likewise, to divide a subject into accidents when one must set out the diversity of what happens to it; and also to divide an accident into co-accidents when, according to the variety of subjects, they are shown to be exceeding or exceeded. Thus I have received a concise instruction in two parts of this exercise.

There remains a third, more necessary if it were possessed, and far more verbose if it were taught: namely, the art of inference. It serves to refute an opponent or, in philosophy, to demonstrate truth, whatever the hearers may think. A few rules for it are set forth, which I shall state more briefly for the sake of brevity. One must carefully observe that, to establish confidence in the matter at issue, we should first set forth something from which that matter can be inferred probably or necessarily—for example, genus for the positing of species; or, when one of two contraries is posited, the other is removed. [Col. 0863B]

I proceed, then, because I am a man of duller intellect, whose faith comes by hearing, and who can scarcely and rarely understand what he hears or reads. When the rules become known, I trouble the teachers—who deign to be ignorant of nothing—to teach me their use by giving examples drawn from books. For it is no great achievement for someone possessing the art of definition to recount, from definitions long written down, discoveries made by others. If logic is “definitive” because it has some definitions, then many disciplines, since they abound in more definitions, will be more definitive.

The pure philosophers are therefore indignant—those who disdain everything except logic, being as ignorant of grammar as of physics and ethics—and accuse me of being insolent, dull, a block of wood, or a stone. What has been said, they say, ought to have sufficed for the art’s threefold capacity. They also press for payment of the promised fee. If I object, according to that ethical saying, “You call it payment? What do I know?” they immediately reply, according to the same source: “Surely the teacher’s fault is being alleged when nothing stirs in the left side of the Arcadian youth’s breast.” Thus, they say, “all wish to know; no one wishes to pay.”

Since I fear the charge of ingratitude, I repay them instruction for instruction, necessary teaching for necessary teaching. I impart a compendium of rules, ordering them to acquire practice in their use; and because I have received three arts, and useful ones, I likewise teach three, but more useful. Let the first be military art, the second medicine, and the third civil law and decrees, completing the perfection of all ethics.

Whenever you must engage an enemy, carefully ensure that he does not harm you in any respect; then in the first encounter throw your whole strength against him and, unharmed, inflict wound upon wound, until he either acknowledges you victor or, lifeless, yields you the victory by public judgement. In natural philosophy, before all else foresee the cause of illness; cure and remove it; then raise and sustain the sick person by restorative and preservative means until he is fully recovered. In civil affairs, moreover, pursue justice everywhere; make yourself lovable to all; and, in accordance with the comic poet, find praise without envy and friends who are your equals. [Col. 0864A]

Why say more? In all things put on charity. For the use of these rules is as ready to hand for me as the exercise of the preceding ones is for them. They are therefore the more pitiable because they do not recognize their own misery: deceiving themselves, they pursue the study of truth so as to know nothing. Truth is sought only by the path of humility, which belongs to the faithful. Thus Pilate, hearing truth mentioned, asked what it was; but the unbelief of the inquirer caused the proud hearer to turn away from the teacher before he was instructed by the oracle of the sacred answer.

## CHAPTER VII. That the babbling “ventilators” must be unlearned in order that they may know

[Col. 0864B]

I do not, however, advance these points in order to attack logic (for it is a pleasant and fruitful science), but in order to make clear to those who shout in the crossroads and teach at the street-corners that it is not at their command—though in the one discipline which they alone profess they have spent not ten or twenty years, but their entire lives. For even when old age comes on, weakens the body, blunts the sharpness of the senses, and restrains their former pleasures, this alone is still turned over on their lips, handled in their hands, and takes precedence over every other pursuit. Thus they become old Academics in childish matters: they scrutinize every syllable—indeed every letter—of what has been said or written; doubting everything, always inquiring, but never arriving at knowledge; and at last they turn to empty talk. Not knowing what they are saying or what they are affirming, they devise new errors, and either do not know, or disdain to imitate, the opinions of the ancients. They compile everyone’s opinions; and, through poverty of judgment, they write down and repeat even things said or written by the most worthless persons. For they put forward everything, because they do not know how to prefer what is better. So great is the heap of opinions and counter-opinions that it can scarcely be known even by its own author. This happened to Didymus, than whom no one wrote more: when he disputed against a certain history as though it were frivolous, one of his own books was produced which contained it. But now you may find many Didymuses; commentaries are full—indeed crammed—with impediments of this kind of logic. [Col. 0864C]

They are rightly called “oppositions,” moreover, because they oppose better studies; for they obstruct progress. Yet not even Aristotle, whom these prattling hair-splitters deign alone to acknowledge, is heard when he says, faithfully, elegantly, and truly: “It is foolish to be troubled by anyone who advances views contrary to one’s opinions.” Quintilian relates that a certain Timotheus, famous in the art of the flute, used to demand double fees from pupils trained by someone else, compared with those handed over wholly untrained. For the labour is twofold: first, in washing away the faulty teaching they had received; second, in faithfully instilling what is true and right. Besides, one who already lays claim to the name of artist cannot easily be humbled so as to descend to lesser things, without which nevertheless he cannot advance. Timotheus certainly had good sense, because:

> The jar will long preserve the scent  
> With which, when new, it was once impregnated.

(Horace, *Epistles* I.2.69); and each person, once made his own master,

> … runs toward that thing  
> Which he first tasted as prey when the shell was broken.

## CHAPTER VIII. That Aristotle would have restrained them, if he were heard

Yet there is sometimes some use in this evil: namely, that those accustomed to such exercises, if they are nevertheless trained in moderation, acquire an abundance of words, fluency of tongue, and capacity of memory. For this frequent contestation about everything promotes these qualities; [Col. 0865A] it also adds a fourth, subtlety of intellect, since continual exercise indeed develops it. But if moderation is absent, all these turn to the opposite result; usefulness is taken away from subtlety. “Nothing,” says Seneca in the first book of the *Declamations*, “is more hateful than subtlety where there is nothing else but subtlety”; and, writing to Lucilius: “Nothing is sharper than an awn. But what use is it?” Such, certainly, is the intellect which frolics in subtlety alone and possesses no settled seriousness. This is what, in the book *On the Education of the Orator*, is called precocious, “and it does not readily come to fruit.”

It is praised in boys, but despised and censured in old men. For boys readily produce little things by its means, and, carried forward by boldness, immediately display whatever they can do; but what they can do is only what lies nearest at hand. They arrange and string together words, and utter them “with an unfrightened countenance,” delayed by no modesty. They accomplish little, though quickly; there is no true strength beneath, nor does it stand supported by roots driven deep. Just as seeds scattered only upon the surface of the ground shoot up more quickly, and little plants imitating ears of grain grow yellow with empty awns before harvest; so too intellects that seek subtlety or abundance, once seriousness has been removed, please when compared with their years, but afterward their progress stops and admiration declines. Thus too in Flavus, who, as Seneca reports, was declaiming before Arellius, something besides eloquence commended him: in a boy, namely, his age was an embellishment of talent. [Col. 0865B–C]

Nor does abundance of words retain praise forever. As Sidonius says: “There is no greater glory in saying what you know than in being silent about what you do not know.” Cicero likewise reproves words which, without usefulness or pleasure either to speaker or hearer, are uttered to no purpose. For that poetic saying holds good:

> Poets wish either to profit or to delight,  
> Or at once to speak what is pleasant and suited to life.  
> He has won every vote who has mingled the useful with the sweet.

(Horace, *Art of Poetry* 33.)

And sins accompany much speaking. Fluency of tongue is useful only when it is directed toward wisdom; for it stands on slippery ground and quickly slips. Although it is a small member, it sets on fire the wheel of human birth, throws life into confusion, and drives the whole person headlong unless it is checked by the bond of moderation. [Col. 0865D–0866A]

What advantage is there in storing up in the archives of memory things for which there is no use? For just as it is pointless to dispute about goat’s wool, so it is foolish and undiscriminating to commit to memory things that are uttered uselessly. Who has ever gathered and hoarded useless leaves and awns in order to abound in wealth? Aristotle ought to have restrained this intemperance of those who regard indiscriminate loquacity as the exercise of dialectic. And indeed he would have restrained it, if he were heard. “One ought not,” he says, “to consider every problem or every thesis, but only such as will cause doubt to someone who needs argument, rather than punishment or perception. For those who doubt whether the gods ought to be revered and parents honoured, or not, need punishment; but those who doubt whether snow is white, or not, need perception. Nor should one consider matters whose demonstration is immediate, nor those whose demonstration is very remote; for the former do not admit of doubt, while the latter involve difficulties greater than belong to exercise.” So he says. But these men, without consulting him—indeed, in defiance of his prohibition—dispute always, everywhere, and equally about everything; perhaps because they have equal knowledge of everything. [Col. 0866B]

## CHAPTER IX. That dialectic is ineffective if it lacks the aid of the other disciplines

That eloquence without wisdom is of no benefit is both well known and true; hence it is evident that, if it is to be beneficial, eloquence must draw from wisdom. Accordingly, eloquence benefits each person in proportion to the measure of wisdom he has acquired; for it harms when separated from wisdom. From this it is clear that dialectic, the most ready and prompt among the servants of eloquence, benefits each person according to the measure of his knowledge. It benefits most the person who knows very many things, and least the person who knows few. For just as Hercules’ sword is ineffective in the hand of a Pygmy or dwarf, but in the hand of Achilles or Hector strikes everything down like a thunderbolt, so dialectic, if deprived of the strength of the other disciplines, is in a sense maimed and almost useless. If it flourishes through their strength, it is able to destroy every falsehood; and, to ascribe the least to it, it suffices to argue plausibly about everything. [Col. 0866C]

For it is no great matter if, in the manner of our contemporaries, it continually turns upon itself, circles around itself, searches out its own secrets, and occupies itself only with things useful neither at home, nor in military service, nor in the law-court, nor in the cloister, nor at court, nor in the Church—indeed, nowhere except in the school. There, to a younger age, a number of things are allowed in limited measure which the fuller treatment of philosophy soon afterward, or at a later stage, eliminates.
