For when one comes here to a mature age in knowledge or life, philosophy rejects not only childish words and the indulgences of freer license, but often whole books.

This is what we are taught, beneath the cloud of a poetic fiction, in the marriage of Mercury and Philology, contracted under the auspices of all the gods and profitably to be embraced by humankind. There Philology, after she had ascended the temples of heaven and obtained the freedom of a purer state, is described as having vomited forth the multitude of books with which she was pregnant. [Col. 0866D–0867A]

It is very easy for every craftsman to speak about his own art; but to perform through the art what belongs to the art is very difficult. What physician does not often speak at length about elements, humours, complexions, diseases, and other matters pertaining to natural science? Yet one who becomes proficient at this is more capable of being ill than of curing illness. What moral philosopher, while moral rules are on his tongue, does not abound in them? Yet it is plainly far more difficult for them to be expressed in life. Mechanical craftsmen readily speak, each one, about their own arts; but none of them performs the work of an architect or a boxer with such slight effort. The same holds in the remaining fields. Thus it is very easy to speak about definition, arguments, genus, and similar matters; but to discover these same things, in each particular discipline, for the fulfilment of the art’s task, is much more difficult. Therefore one oppressed by poverty of disciplines will not possess the abundance that dialectic promises and supplies. [Col. 0867B]

## CHAPTER X. By whose authority the preceding and following matters are established

When first, still very young, I had migrated to Gaul for the sake of study, in the second year after the illustrious King Henry of England, the lion of justice, had departed from human affairs, I attached myself to the Palatine Peripatetic, who was then a renowned teacher on Mount Sainte-Geneviève and presided there, admirable in the eyes of all. At his feet I received the first rudiments of this art, and, according to the small measure of my ability, I received with the whole eagerness of my mind whatever fell from his lips. [Col. 0867C]

Then, after his departure—which seemed to me too hasty—I attached myself to Master Alberic, who shone out among the rest as a dialectician of the highest repute and was indeed the sharpest assailant of the nominalist school. Thus, for nearly the whole two-year period during which I lived on the Mount, I employed as teachers of this art Alberic and Master Robert of Melun—his surname indicating what he deserved in the governance of the schools, for he was English by birth. One of them, scrupulous about everything, found room for a question everywhere, so that even a polished plain was not without an obstacle and, as they say, no rush was without a knot for him. For even there he pointed out what ought to be untied. The other, most ready in response, never evaded a proposed point in order to escape, without either choosing one side of the contradiction or, after determining the ambiguity of the expression, teaching that there was not one single answer. [Col. 0867D]

The former was subtle and copious in questions; the latter perceptive, concise, and serviceable in answers. If these two qualities had together fallen to any one person in our age, certainly no equal disputant could have been found. For both possessed acute intellects and tenacious application; and, I think, they would have distinguished themselves as great and illustrious men in natural studies, if they had laboured from a great foundation of letters, if they had followed in the tracks of their elders as closely as they applauded their own discoveries. This was true at the time when I was attached to them. Later, however, one of them went to Bologna and unlearned what he had taught; indeed, on returning, he taught others to unlearn it. Whether this was for the better, let those judge who heard him before and afterward. The other, meanwhile, advanced in sacred letters and attained the glory of a loftier philosophy and a more celebrated name. [Col. 0868A]

Having trained under them for a whole two years, I became so accustomed to assigning loci, rules, and the other elementary rudiments by which youthful minds are instructed, and in which the aforesaid masters were exceptionally powerful and accomplished, that I seemed to myself to know all these things as well as my fingernails and fingers. For this, plainly, was what I had learned: in youthful frivolity, to value my knowledge more highly than it deserved. I seemed to myself a little scholar because I was ready in the things I had heard.

Then, returning to myself and measuring my strength, I transferred myself, by the good grace of my teachers and deliberately, to Bernard of Chartres, and heard him teach for three years. In the meantime I read many things, and I shall never regret that time. Later I followed Richard, surnamed “the Bishop,” a man almost unacquainted with no discipline, who had more heart than eloquence, more knowledge than fluency, more truth than vanity, more virtue than display. From him I reread everything that I had heard from others and learned certain things I had not heard before, belonging to the quadrivium, in which I had previously heard the German Hardewin to some extent. [Col. 0868B]

I also reread rhetoric, which I had previously heard only slightly from Master Theodoric along with certain other subjects and understood only a little. But afterward I received it more fully from Peter Helias. And because I had undertaken to educate the sons of nobles, who, when I was deprived of the support of friends and relatives, supplied food to my poverty through God’s consolation, I was compelled by the necessity of my office and the insistence of the young men to recall more frequently to memory what I had heard. Therefore I formed a closer friendship with Master Adam, a man of the keenest intellect and, whatever others may think, of extensive learning, who applied himself to Aristotle above all others. Although I did not have him as my teacher, he generously shared his learning with me and explained himself to me more openly—something he did either for no one or for few outsiders. For he was thought to suffer from envy. [Col. 0868C]

Meanwhile I taught William of Soissons, who later, as his followers say, constructed a machine for attacking the antiquity of logic, constructing unexpected consequences, and overthrowing the opinions of the ancients, the first elements of logic; and at last I placed him with the teacher just mentioned. There he perhaps learned that it is not the same thing, when Aristotle speaks against it, because when something both is and is not, it does not follow that it is the same thing; likewise, when something is, it does not follow that the same thing both is and is not. For nothing follows from a contradiction, and it is impossible for a contradiction to follow from anything. Hence I could not be forced, even by the pressure of my friend’s machine, to believe that from one impossibility all impossibilities follow. [Col. 0868D]

Financial straits, the request of companions, and the counsel of friends drew me away from there, so that I might undertake the office of teacher. I obeyed. Returning, therefore, at the end of three years, I found Master Gilbert and heard him in logic and theology; but he was taken away too soon. Robert Pullen succeeded him, a man commended alike by his life and learning. Then Simon of Poissy received me, a trustworthy lecturer but a rather dull disputant. Yet I had these latter two as teachers in theology alone. Thus nearly twelve years passed for me, occupied with varied studies.

It then seemed pleasant to revisit my former companions whom I had left behind and whom dialectic still held on the Mount, and to confer with them about our former ambiguities, so that through mutual comparison we might measure each other’s progress. They were found to be what they had been, and where they had been. They did not seem to have progressed a handbreadth toward resolving their old questions, nor had they added a single little proposition. They were themselves pressed by the same goads with which they pressed others. In one thing only had they advanced: they had unlearned moderation and knew no restraint, so completely that one might despair of their recovery. [Col. 0869A–B]

Thus I learned by experience what may clearly be inferred: just as dialectic expedites the other disciplines, so, if it stands alone, it lies bloodless and barren; nor does it make the mind fruitful unto the fruit of philosophy unless it conceives from elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XI. What dialectic alone can do

Yet, relying only on the aid of grammar, it promises and accomplishes something by itself: it resolves questions proposed about itself, but does not rise to other matters—for example, whether to affirm is to make an enunciation, and whether a contradiction can exist simultaneously. What this contributes to the use of life, if it does not assist another discipline, let each person judge. But whether pleasure is a good, whether virtue is to be preferred, whether good dispositions are among the highest goods, whether one must labour in want—these questions the pure and simple dialectician rarely examines. Yet the usefulness of living, whether for happiness or preservation, lies in these matters. For although logic resolves itself, it was discovered chiefly for the sake of other things. [Col. 0869C]

Almost as the animal spirit organizes and animates the animal, governs and sustains the humours for animal life, yet itself arises from the humours and by its subtlety and strength moves and orders a great mass, “so far as harmful bodies do not retard it,” so logic takes its origin from the other disciplines and orders and moves them, insofar as it is not delayed by the injury of sluggishness and ignorance. This is clear to those who know both the art of argument and the other disciplines. [Col. 0869D]

## CHAPTER XII. What its exercise consists in, and what instrument it uses

The exercise of dialectic is concerned with all disciplines, since it has the question as its subject-matter; but it leaves to the orator the question called a *hypothesis*, that is, one entangled in circumstances. The circumstances are those which Boethius enumerates in the fourth book of the *Topics*: “Who, what, where, by what means, why, how, when.” But dialectic claims for itself the *thesis*: that is, a question free from the connections of the circumstances mentioned above. It undertakes a more general inquiry and, by its proper right, does not descend to particulars. If this does happen sometimes, it enjoys another’s goods in the manner of a guest. [Col. 0870A]

The instrument used by either art in the service of its purpose is discourse. For the art which moves a judge other than the disputants uses continuous discourse and more frequently induction, because it addresses many persons and generally seeks to win over the people. Dialectic, however, uses broken discourse and more often syllogisms, because it depends on the judgment of an opponent and addresses one person; if it establishes credibility with him, it attains the end proposed. For it does not address the populace and does not await the decision of the law.

Reason itself, too, which discourse clothes and which enters the soul through the ear with the support of speech, thereby moving the soul, is likewise an instrument. Indeed, it is what makes discourse an instrument. For the power of discourse is mind and meaning; without these discourse can neither be vigorous nor move anyone. Therefore, since the question is its matter and reason or discourse its instrument, the work of the art is uniquely concerned with providing an abundance of this instrument and teaching its use. The other disciplines too furnish matter in common, since questions arise everywhere, though they are not resolved everywhere. [Col. 0870B]

## CHAPTER XIII. How useful the knowledge of probable matters is, and why things simply necessary are not easily known

The three disciplines—natural, moral, and rational—furnish subject-matter, since each sets forth its own questions. Ethics asks whether, if parents and laws happen to disagree, one ought to obey parents rather than laws. Natural science asks whether the world is eternal or everlasting, or whether it has had a beginning and will have an end in time, or whether it is none of these. Logic asks whether there is one and the same discipline of contraries, since their cognition is the same. Thus each discipline asks questions; and although they are fortified by their own principles, logic commonly supplies each with its methods—that is, abbreviated modes of reasoning. Hence it is most useful not only for exercise but for answering objections and for disciplines according to philosophy. [Col. 0870C]

For one who possesses a method concerning the subject in hand argues easily; one who knows many opinions and speaks from his own rather than foreign materials answers objections conveniently, changing whatever seems to have been badly said; and one who attends to the relevant reasons distinguishes more easily, in each case, the true from the false and becomes more capable of understanding and teaching, which the purpose and duty of the philosopher demand. Since dialectic is inquisitive, it has a route to the principles of all methods. For every art has its own methods, which we may figuratively interpret as approaches or entrances; discovery follows inquiry, and one does not gain the fruit of knowledge if one dislikes the labour of inquiry.

Demonstrative science, however, seeks necessary methods: methods which disclose that inherence of things which cannot be dissolved. For only that is necessary which cannot be otherwise. But because scarcely anyone investigates the powers of nature, or only a rare person does, and God alone knows the number of possibilities, judgment about necessary things is for the most part not merely uncertain but rash. For who knows completely what can or cannot be? For many ages people judged it necessary that, if a woman had given birth, she had had intercourse with someone or had been defiled. But at last, at the end of the ages, the birth of the most undefiled Virgin taught that this was not necessary. [Col. 0870D–0871A]

For what is necessary simply cannot in any way be otherwise; but what is necessary from a determination can be changed. Victorinus, in his *Rhetoric*, in explaining the necessary, teaches precisely this: that corruption follows childbirth not necessarily but probably. Augustine likewise asserts that necessary reasons are everlasting and can in no way be voided. It is evident that the reasons of probable matters can change, unless they are necessary. Hence it is clear how arduous is the task of the demonstrator, who always follows necessity and does not depart from the principles of the truth he professes. For if it is a great thing to apprehend truth—which, as our Academics say, lies hidden as though in the depths of a well—how great a keenness is required to penetrate not only the secrets of truth but those of necessity itself, since it is easier to determine what exists than what is possible? [Col. 0871B]

Thus demonstrative reasoning generally falters in natural matters—I mean bodily and changeable things—but is most effective in mathematics. Whatever it infers concerning numbers, proportions, figures, and similar matters is undoubtedly true and cannot be otherwise. Therefore no one should aspire to demonstrative knowledge who has not known probable matters. Demonstrative principles, then, are necessary; dialectical principles are probable. Therefore the dialectician will refrain from propositions which seem true to no one, lest he be thought mad; and from manifest propositions, lest he seem to grope in darkness; and he will confine himself to those matters known either to everyone, or to most people, or to the most eminent persons in each kind. [Col. 0871C]

## CHAPTER XIV. Further on the same subject

The principles of dialectic, therefore, are probable, just as those of demonstration are necessary. If anything is both probable and necessary, it can belong to both arts, though on a different ground in each case. For probability alone suffices for the dialectician. Hence Cicero says in the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “We who follow probable things, and can advance no further than what appears likely, are prepared both to refute without anger and to be refuted without obstinacy.” Elsewhere too he says: “Our Academy gives us this liberty: whatever probable thing presents itself, we may lawfully defend it as our own.”

A probable thing is one which becomes known even from its surface to a person capable of judgment, being so either in all cases and always, or otherwise only in very few cases and very rarely. For what is always or most frequently so either is probable or appears probable, even though it can be otherwise. It is more probable in proportion as it becomes known more readily and certainly to the person exercising judgment. Some things shine with so great a light of probability that they are even considered necessary. Others, because they are less familiar to opinion, are scarcely counted among probable things. For if opinion is weak, judgment wavers uncertainly; if it is strong, it passes into belief and tends toward certain judgment. If its strength grows still further, so that it can be extended little or not at all, then, although below knowledge, it is nevertheless equal to knowledge in respect of certainty of judgment. [Col. 0871D–0872A]

This is clear, according to Aristotle, in matters known by sense alone and capable of being otherwise. Once the sun has set, it will be unknown whether it is still moving above the earth or whether it is going to return to our hemisphere, because the perception through which there was knowledge of its movement then ceases. Yet belief in its movement and return is so strong that it seems in some measure to walk with knowledge in equal step. But if sense produces knowledge of something that cannot be otherwise—as when someone knows, through the teaching of sight, that a line is long or that a surface is coloured—then, when sight ceases, the knowledge does not vanish, because the thing must be so.

Therefore what is found separately in all or in most members of a certain kind must be established universally in all, unless an exception is produced in which it is not so. An exception is an opposing instance of some kind which prejudices the collected universality. Thus a plentiful knowledge of probable matters prepares a most ready route toward everything. [Col. 0872B]

## CHAPTER XV. What a dialectical proposition is, and what a problem is

A dialectical proposition is one against which, when it holds in this way in most cases, there is no exception—that is, no argument against the position. One who keeps such propositions in mind, together with any exceptions to positions, will be abundantly equipped for every kind of controversy, and, if he also exercises himself philosophically, will be by no means unsuccessful. For he can argue plausibly about every problem, ethical, physical, and logical.

A dialectical problem is an inquiry tending either toward choice and avoidance, or toward truth and knowledge—either in itself or as aiding something else of this kind—concerning which either most people hold no opinion, or most people hold an opinion contrary to that of the wise, or the wise hold one contrary to that of most people, or each of these groups is divided against itself. The style indicates the author of this definition, and the words make it clear that he is Aristotle. The sense of the words does so as well. For he did not reckon as a dialectical problem everything drawn between affirmation and negation, nor did he think that the practitioner of his art ought to be exercised in airing matters that benefit no one either in themselves or through any of the disciplines mentioned above. [Col. 0872C–D]

For the phrase “tending toward choice or avoidance,” although some think it should be referred only to ethical questions, I judge to concern physical questions as well; but logical questions either not at all or only minimally. For there virtue, vice, and similar things furnish matter for choice or avoidance; here, health, disease, causes, signs, and the circumstances of particular things. Questions tending toward knowledge and truth, however, are pursued equally by all three disciplines. Whether pleasure ought to be chosen or not is an ethical inquiry, useful for its own sake. Whether the world is eternal or not is indeed a physical inquiry, directed to knowledge and truth and perhaps useful for something else: namely, so that, once it is known to be created, we may revere the author of so great a work, and, together with transitory things, it may become cheap in the estimation of pious people, since it is wholly subject to vanity. Logic inquires whether one of two contradictory propositions is always true or not, and knowing this truth contributes to something else. [Col. 0873A]

Those, therefore, who continually dispute about goat’s wool do not exercise dialectical problems and are as remote from the material of the art as from its function. For its subject-matter is the thesis or position. A position is an opinion, foreign to the views recognized according to philosophy, concerning something known: for example, that everything is in motion, as Heraclitus held; or that being is one, as Melissus maintained. No one who possesses sense will turn into a question either what seems true to no one or what is manifest to everyone, or to those whose judgment prevails. For the latter matters admit no doubt, while the former no one will posit.

For this reason, I would judge no liberal discipline more useful than this one, from which progress into every part of philosophy is easy and successful. No one to whom probable matters become known is found deficient for any science. [Col. 0873B]

## CHAPTER XVI. That all other teachers of this discipline yield to Aristotle

It therefore seems plainly mad to disparage the discipline which instructs all the others and without whose benefit no one rightly proceeds in investigations of nature. Very many have written about it, and these philosophers were as keen as they were diligent; it is plainly these whom those who accuse this art reproach. For detraction from a discipline is an unquestionable accusation of its author.

I know one thing: posterity will by no means prefer Cornificius to them. For Aristotle, Apuleius, Cicero, Porphyry, Boethius, and Augustine—to say nothing of Eudemus, Alexander, Theophrastus, and the other commentators, whose glory is nevertheless celebrated—all raised the banner of this art, as though triumphant among the others, with great praise. But although each shines by his own merits, all glory in worshipping the footsteps of Aristotle, so much so that through a certain pre-eminence he made the common name of all philosophers his own. For by antonomasia—that is, pre-eminently—he is called “the Philosopher.” [Col. 0873C]

This man reduced the principles of probable matters to an art and, beginning as it were from the elements, carried them up to the completion of his purpose. This is clear to those who search and examine his works. Taking first from the grammarian’s hand significant vocal expressions—that is, uncombined utterances—he carefully explained their differences and powers, so that one might more easily proceed to the combination of propositions and to the science of discovery and judgment. But because Porphyry wrote a book in some manner more elementary for this elementary work, antiquity judged that it should be read before Aristotle. This is right, provided it is taught rightly: that is, provided it does not bring darkness upon learners or consume their lifetime. For it is unworthy that someone should wear out his life learning the five little words, [Col. 0873D–0874A] so that no time remains for advancing to those matters for whose sake these should have been learned beforehand. Hence, because it is introductory to other matters, it bears the title *Isagoge* (“Introduction”). Thus those who spend their time on it in such a way as to leave no place for the principal matters detract from its title; if those principal matters are unknown, there is no reason to be grateful for the work of an introduction.

## CHAPTER XVII. How perniciously it is taught, and what opinions modern thinkers have held concerning genera and species

Our contemporaries, to display their learning, instruct their hearers in such a way that they are not understood by them, and they imagine every individual point to be laden with Minerva’s secrets. They scrutinize everything ever said or done by anyone and thrust it into tender ears, so that, by the fault censured by Cicero, they are “often less understood because of the multitude of things” than because of their difficulty. It is indeed useful, as Aristotle says, to know the opinions of many, even of opponents, so that, from their mutual conflict, whatever appears ill said may be refuted or altered. “But this was not now the place for such things,” when a simple discourse, a brief subject, and as much ease as possible are owed to beginners. [Col. 0874B]

Indeed, even many things in difficult subjects are presented more freely and more easily than their nature requires, because in youthful years many things are learned which the later treatment of philosophy eliminates. Yet they all explain here the nature of universals, and they attempt, contrary to the author’s intention, to expound a matter of the highest difficulty and requiring a more extensive inquiry.

One man, then, locates universals in spoken words—although this opinion has now almost entirely vanished along with its Roscelin. Another considers utterances and twists toward them whatever he finds written anywhere concerning universals. Our own Palatine Peripatetic, Abelard, was found to hold this opinion; he left many followers and still has some adherents and witnesses of this profession. They are my friends, although they commonly twist the text, held captive in this way, so much that even a hard heart is moved with pity for it. [Col. 0874C]

They regard it as monstrous that one thing should be predicated of another thing, although Aristotle is the author of this monstrosity and very frequently affirms that a thing is predicated of a thing. This is evident to those familiar with his writings, unless they dissemble. Another man concerns himself with concepts and says that these alone are genera and species. They take their occasion from Cicero and Boethius, who praise Aristotle for having held that these should be believed and called *notiones* (“notions”). A notion, they say, is a cognition, requiring explanation, arising from a previously perceived form of each thing. Elsewhere: “A notion is a certain understanding and a simple conception of the mind.” Therefore everything written on the matter is bent toward the view that understanding or notion contains within itself the universality of universals. [Col. 0874D]

The opinions of those who adhere to things are many and diverse. One such thinker concludes, because everything that is one is one in number, that either a universal thing is one in number or does not exist at all. But because it is impossible for substantial things not to exist while the things of which they are substantial exist, they conclude again that universals must be united with singulars in respect of essence. Therefore, following Walter of Mortagne, they divide statuses: they call Plato, insofar as he is Plato, an individual; insofar as he is a human being, a species; insofar as he is an animal, a genus, though a subordinate genus; and insofar as he is substance, the most general genus. [Col. 0875A]

This opinion once had some defenders, but for a long time no one has professed it. One man posits Ideas, emulating Plato and imitating Bernard of Chartres, and says that nothing except these is genus or species. An Idea, as Seneca defines it, is “the eternal exemplar of those things which come to be by nature.” And because universals are not subject to corruption, nor altered by the motions through which singular things are moved and, as it were, in an instant, some pass away as others succeed them, universals are properly and truly said to be. [Col. 0875B] For individual things are thought unworthy of the appellation expressed by the substantive verb, since they do not stand still but flee, nor wait to be named; so greatly do they vary in qualities, times, places, and manifold properties that their whole being seems not a stable condition but a mutable passage.

“But we call those things beings,” says Boethius, “which neither increase by extension nor diminish by contraction, but always preserve themselves, supported by the resources of their own nature.” Such are quantities, qualities, relations, places, times, dispositions, and whatever is in some manner found united to bodies. These, indeed, seem to change when attached to bodies, but [Col. 0875C] in their own nature remain immutable. Thus too the species of things remain the same while individuals pass away, just as, when waves flow past, “the movement of the stream remains in the river”; for it too is called the same. Hence the saying in Seneca—though borrowed from elsewhere—“Twice we descend into the same river, and we do not descend.”

These Ideas, that is, exemplary forms, are the primordial rational principles of all things. They admit neither diminution nor increase; they are stable and perpetual, so that, even if the whole corporeal world should perish, they cannot perish. The number of all corporeal things consists in them; and, as Augustine seems to maintain in *On Free Will*, because these always exist, even should temporal things perish, the number of things is neither diminished nor increased.

[Col. 0875D] What these men promise is certainly great and well known to philosophers who contemplate higher matters; but, as Boethius and many other authors testify, it is wholly alien to Aristotle’s doctrine. Aristotle himself, as is evident from his books, frequently opposes this view. Bernard of Chartres and his followers laboured rather earnestly to reconcile Aristotle and Plato; but I think they came too late and laboured in vain to reconcile the dead, who disagreed as long as life allowed them.

Another, seeking to represent Aristotle, together with Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, attributes universality to native forms and works within their conformity. A native form is an original’s copy: it does not reside in the mind of God, but adheres to created things. [Col. 0876A] In Greek it is called εἶδος (*eidos*, “form” or “species”), standing in relation to an Idea as a copy to its exemplar. It is sensible in a sensible thing, but is conceived by the mind as insensible; singular in singulars, yet universal in all.

Another, with Gauslenus, bishop of Soissons, attributes universality to things gathered into one collection, and removes it from individuals. Thereafter, when he comes to interpret authorities, he labours in distress because in many places “he cannot endure the gaping mouth of the indignant letter.” There is someone who takes refuge in the aid of a new language because he lacks sufficient mastery of Latin; for now, when he hears “genus” or “species,” he says that universal things are meant, and now he interprets it as the matter of things. But in what author he has found this name [Col. 0876B] or this distinction, I do not know—unless perhaps in glosses or in the languages of modern learned men. Yet even there I do not see what it signifies, unless it means, with Gauslenus, a collection of things, or a universal thing—which nevertheless avoids calling it “matter.” For the name may, through interpretation, be referred to either, since “matter” may be called the number or condition of things in which such a thing endures. Nor is there lacking someone who attends to the conditions of things and calls them genera and species.

## Chapter XVIII. That Later Thinkers Always Alter the Opinions of Their Predecessors

It would be long, and altogether foreign to my purpose, if I set forth the opinions or errors of each individual; for, to use the comic poet’s phrase, [Col. 0876C] “There are almost as many opinions as there are men.” For among masters there is either none, or scarcely one, who wishes to adhere to the footsteps of his own teacher. To make a name for himself, each fashions an error of his own; and so it happens that, while he promises to correct his teacher, he offers himself to his disciples and posterity as one to be corrected or censured.

I myself do not doubt that this law hangs over me: while I dissent from others and profess my dissent in writing, I expose myself to the criticisms of many. He who speaks is judged by one person or a few; but he who writes receives the judgments of all and exposes himself to the judgment of the whole world and of every age. Yet, to deal more gently with the masters, very many appear to dispute more often about a word than about the thing itself. [Col. 0876D] Nothing, however, is less fitting for a professor of this art, since such a practice is most unsuitable for a serious man. For, as Aristotle says, dialecticians should altogether beware of disputing about a name, unless they cannot otherwise dispute about the matter at issue.

Indeed, on the points on which they seem most to disagree, each admits the other’s interpretation, although he insists that it is inept. Thus, in turn, they accuse the expression, not the other’s meaning.

## Chapter XIX. Wherein Such Teachers Must Not Be Spared

Let it be granted that I spare their opinions, in which they themselves, if one may suppose their interpretations reciprocally, do not disagree. Yet there are a few matters in which I do not think they should be excused.

First, they impose unbearable burdens [Col. 0877A] on the tender shoulders of their hearers. Secondly, having neglected the order of teaching, they take the greatest care that they may not observe:

> Let each thing hold its proper place, allotted fittingly.  
> > (Horace, *Art of Poetry* 92.)

For, so to speak, they read the end of the art in its title; and Porphyry teaches beforehand not only the force of the *Topics*, but also of the *Analytics* and the *Refutations*. Finally, as though beginning from the opposite side, they arrive contrary to the author’s meaning; and, in order that Aristotle may seem clearer, they teach Plato’s doctrine, or an erroneous opinion which strays with equal error from both Aristotle’s and Plato’s doctrine. For they all profess Aristotle.

## Chapter XX. Aristotle’s Doctrine Concerning Genera and Species, Surrounded by Many Arguments and the Testimony of Many Writings

[Col. 0877B]

Now Aristotle maintained that genera and species do not exist, but are only understood. What relevance, then, has asking what a genus is, if it has been established that it does not exist at all? For it is foolish to ask of that which is not what it is, how great it is, or what sort it is; for if you remove substance from anything, nothing else remains to it. Therefore, if Aristotle is right in taking being away from them, the labour of the preceding investigation—concerning substance, quantity, quality, or cause—is vain; since no substance, quantity, or quality can be assigned to that which is not, nor a cause why that which is not should be this [Col. 0877C] or that, so great or of such a kind.

Accordingly, one must either depart from Aristotle by conceding that universals exist, or oppose the opinions that identify them with words, expressions, sensible things, Ideas, forms, natures, or collections, since none doubts that each of these exists. But whoever establishes that universals exist opposes Aristotle.

Nor need one fear that the intellect which apprehends them separately from singular things is empty, even though they cannot exist separately from singular things. For the intellect sometimes regards a thing simply—for example, if it considers a human being or a stone in itself—and is therefore simple. Sometimes it proceeds step by step, as when it contemplates a human being’s being white or a horse’s running; and this is called composite.

Moreover, the simple intellect sometimes observes a thing as it is, as when it attends to Plato; sometimes in another way: now by combining things that are not combined, now by abstracting things that cannot exist apart. Whoever thinks of a goat-stag or a centaur supposes an unknown combination of human nature with beast, or of one beast with another. But he who considers a line or a surface without a body separates, before the eye of contemplation, the form from matter, although form cannot exist without matter. [Col. 0877D]

Yet the abstracting intellect does not conceive form as existing without matter—for then it would be composite—but simply regards one without the other, although it cannot exist without the other. This does not prejudice its simplicity; indeed, it is so much the simpler as it discerns simpler things individually, without an admixture of others. Nor is this contrary to the nature of things, which, for its own investigation, has conferred on intellect this power: to separate what is conjoined and join what is separate.

But the combining intellect, which joins what is separate, is empty; whereas the abstracting intellect is faithful, and is, as it were, a workshop of all arts. Things have one mode of existing, namely that bestowed by nature; but the same things have not one mode of being understood or signified. For although there cannot be a human being who is not this or another human being, he can nevertheless be understood and signified in such a way that neither this nor another human being is understood or signified. Therefore genera and species are conceived, for the signification of uncombined terms, by the abstracting intellect. Yet if anyone seeks them [Col. 0878B] in the nature of things, carefully removed from sensible particulars, he will accomplish nothing and labour in vain; for nature has produced nothing of the sort.

Reason discovers them by considering within itself the substantial likeness of differing things; and, as Boethius says, it brings its general conception, drawn from consideration of the conformity of human beings, to the formula: “a rational mortal animal.” This, certainly, cannot exist except in singulars. Therefore genera and species are not things actually and naturally separate from singulars, but certain images of natural and actual things presented to the intellect from their likeness—born, as it were, in the mirror of the soul’s native purity. The Greeks call these ἔννοιαι or εἰκονοφάνειαι (*ennoiai* or *eikonophaneiai*), that is, images of things appearing in the mind. [Col. 0878C]

For the soul, as though struck back by the ray of its own contemplation, discovers in itself what it defines; for its exemplar is within it, while the copy is in actual things. Thus, when grammar says, “Nouns ending thus are feminine or neuter,” it prescribes a general rule, which is as it were an exemplar of many declinable words; while examples are plainly present in all words with that ending. So certain exemplars are conceived in the mind, whose copies nature has formed and set before the senses. Those exemplars are indeed thinkable and are, according to Aristotle, like images and shadows of existing things; but if anyone tries to grasp them through an existence separated from singular things, [Col. 0878D] they slip away like dreams. For they are monsters and lie open only to intellect.

When universals are said to be substantial to singulars, this must be referred to the cause of knowledge and to the nature of singular things. For this is evident in individual cases: lower things can neither exist nor be understood without higher things. A human being is not, unless he is an animal. Nor is a human being understood without animal also being understood, since a human being is an animal of a certain kind. So too in Plato: he is and is understood as a human being because Plato is such, or this human being.

But for a human being to exist, animality is required; the converse does not hold, so that an animal cannot exist or be understood unless a human being exists or is understood. For animal is included in the account of human being, but human being is not included in the account of animal. Since, therefore, such a thing requires such another thing, and is not required by it, both for essence and for knowledge, the latter is called substantial to the former. The same holds for individuals, which require species and genera but are in no way required by them. For an individual will have neither substance nor enter into knowledge unless it is a species or a genus—that is, unless it is something, or becomes known as being of such or such a kind. [Col. 0879A]

Nevertheless, universals are called “things” and often simply said “to be”; but this does not mean that one should seek in them either the bulk of bodies, the subtlety of spirits, or the discrete essence of singular things. For even what lies under affirmation and negation is called a thing and is very often said truly to be; yet it is not classed with substances or accidents, nor does it receive the name of Creator or creature. For, as the venerable Ulgerius, bishop of Angers, says in *The Sale of the Disciplines*, “the interchange of words should be gracious between persons”; for goodness abounds in the forum of philosophers, and words are put up for sale as a favour.

Therefore let it be granted that universals are, or even that they are things, if this pleases the obstinate; nevertheless it will not thereby be true that the number of things is increased or diminished, because these are not among the number of things. If anyone counts universals separately, he will indeed find them subject to number, but not to a number to which the number of singular things is added. [Col. 0879B] For just as heads are not counted together with colleges or corporate bodies, nor bodies with their heads, so universals are not counted with singulars, nor do singulars increase universals by the addition of their number. Number embraces only things of the same account, which nature has distinguished among the individual kinds of things.

Nothing is universal except what is found in singulars. Many, however, have sought it separately; but in the end all found nothing in their hands, because apart from singulars there is nothing—unless perhaps things such as the true, or similar things, are the significata of complex expressions. Nor should it disturb us that singular and corporeal things are examples of universal and incorporeal things, since every principle of action, as Augustine says, is incorporeal and insensible, whereas that which is done, and the action by which it is done, is usually sensible.

Therefore, whatever the mind understands commonly and applies equally to many singular things, and whatever a word signifies commonly and is equally true of many, is undoubtedly universal. Yet this very phrase—namely, “what is understood” and “what is signified”—must be interpreted more generously, lest one descend into the straits of disputation and the subtleties of grammatical art. By its own nature, unless permission for latitude is obtained, grammar does not allow demonstrative expressions to be indefinite, nor relative expressions to be vague, without their signification being restricted by determination of person, action, or another’s actions. [Col. 0879D]

For a relative expression signifies a thing as that concerning which speech or thought has previously occurred. Thus when it is said, “He is wise and happy who knows good things and faithfully performs them,” the relative expressions—namely, “who” and “them”—although they do not express a person, are in some manner restricted from their indefiniteness by determination through the act of knowing. Yet it is necessary that one person underlie these expressions, who both knows and practises good things and is happy because of this.

For no relation can occur, without fault or figure, unless there is some certain and finite thing to which it applies. Hence, if a horse is promised generically and the stipulator says, “The horse promised to me is sound or unsound,” although every horse is sound or unsound, he is charged with speaking nonsense, because there is no horse promised to him. I do not say “there is no horse” because it does not exist; for even something nonexistent, such as the offspring of Arethusa, may be made the object of a most definite obligation. Rather, it is because a species—that is, a discrete thing—does not meet the obligation made in genus. [Col. 0880A]

When I say “what is promised,” “what is signified,” “what is understood,” and similar phrases, something discrete is subject to the promise or signification, provided the relation itself is proper. Yet relations occur at the level of genus which, while preserving the understanding of what is true, cannot be brought back to a species. For example: “The woman who saved condemned. The tree which gave the cause of death and life; and the mild west wind brings back the leaves which the north wind carries away.”

So too, in the cases mentioned above, I think relative expressions should be understood in such a way that they do not descend to species—that is, to some determinate thing which they distinguish—but remain at the level of genus. For instance, what is signified by the word “human being” is a species, since “human being” is signified and human being is a species of animals. What is signified by the word “animal” is a genus, since “animal” is signified and animal is a genus of things. For the signified of a word is that into which the word resolves, or what the mind rationally conceives from a word heard. [Col. 0880B]

Thus whoever hears the word “human being” neither runs through all human beings—for that is infinite and exceeds his powers—nor is confined to one, for that is imperfect and insufficient for instruction. Likewise, he who defines animal as “an animate and sentient substance” defines neither one thing, which would be imperfect, nor every thing, lest he labour endlessly. For none of these signifies or defines simply *what* something is, but rather *what sort of thing* it is: not simply this thing, but a thing of such a kind.

Similar is Galen’s statement in the *Technē* that medicine is “the knowledge of healthy persons, sick persons, and those in neither condition.” He does not say “of all,” because that is infinite; nor “of some,” because that would be imperfect for the art; but rather, “of persons of whatever kind.”

Likewise Aristotle says: “Genera and species determine concerning substance and quality; for they determine not simply what something is, but in a certain manner what sort of thing it is.” Likewise, in the *Refutations*: “Human being and every common term signify not this particular thing, but a thing of a certain sort, or in some manner something relative, or something of this kind.” And shortly afterward: “It is clear that one must not grant that what is predicated commonly of all signifies this particular thing, but rather a quality, a relation, a quantity, or some such thing.” [Col. 0880D]

Certainly, what is not this particular thing cannot have what it is explained by explicit signification. Things existing by nature have a determinate limit, and individual things are distinguished from one another by their own properties; but knowledge and conception of the same things are often less determinate and in some manner vague. Nor is this prejudiced by the common saying on nearly everyone’s lips: that what appellative words signify is one thing, and what they name another. Singulars are named, but universals are signified. Clearly, if one considers the simple relation made at the level of genus, nothing in the foregoing is harmed; but if one seeks a distinction, it may perhaps not be evident what distinguishes them.

It is regularly taught that demonstration produces first knowledge and relation second knowledge. Knowledge, insofar as it knows a thing, defines and circumscribes it for itself by a certain capacity of mind. Neither first nor second knowledge can proceed if the thing presents itself to the mind as wholly infinite. [Col. 0881B] For all knowledge or cognition of a creature is finite; God’s knowledge alone is infinite, because he is infinite. Yet by its own, that is, infinite limit, it most certainly defines things however infinite; and by the knowledge and wisdom of his immensity—whose number or end does not exist—he circumscribes them.

But we are pursuing the measure of humanity, which claims no glory of knowledge—not first, second, third, nor any knowledge—of an infinite thing, except insofar as it knows it to be unknown or infinite. Therefore every expression that signifies demonstratively or relatively either is not used quite properly or rests upon a subject that is certain and defined by its own account; otherwise such expressions will be deprived of their office, since the nature of knowledge seeks or possesses the limit of certainty. [Col. 0881C]

Yet common usage is frequent, and much use is often made, for convenience, of what is not permitted. It is admitted not merely to confound those for whom it is enough to chatter about any matter whatsoever, but also to establish in honest hearers an understanding of the truth: “Every human being loves himself.”

But if you examine this from the strict property of the relative expression, you may perhaps call the statement improper and false. For “not everyone loves everyone,” nor is there anyone loved by everyone; thus, whether “every” is taken collectively or distributively, the relative pronoun “himself” which follows cannot truthfully be fitted either to the totality of individuals or to any individual member of the totality. This is therefore a permissive relation, and, as though granted exemption from its own law, it establishes the truth of a universal by the truth of singulars. [Col. 0881D]

Because it is true in individual cases that each person loves himself, and is affirmed commonly of all by a certain distributive reasoning—“every human being loves himself”—the relation is understood more generously than grammatical strictness would allow, whether by gathering the totality or by extracting some individual from the totality one by one. Hence, in the view of those who always insist upon narrowness and subtleties and do not consider good faith in speech or reading, this is rather a form of enunciation than an enunciation of regular form.

They likewise maintain this whenever a pronoun is related to an appellative noun, because a pronoun, which is always demonstrative [Col. 0882A] or relative, performs the office of a proper name—provided it properly answers to the reason for its first imposition; though sometimes, by indulgence, it wanders more widely. Thus, when it is said, “If something is a human being, it is an animal,” this is not so much the consequence of a hypothetical statement as the form of consequence in hypothetical statements. For the “it” which is spoken neither refers to “human being” under the strictness of disputation, nor is any other certain thing evident to which it can refer.

From this come many annoyances from those who harass persons ignorant of things, or persons of a more generous disposition, while they themselves—restless scolders who persist in obstinate insistence—labour either from ignorance, obstinacy, or greed for advancement. Therefore, just as knowledge seeks certainty, so demonstrative and relative expressions, which make either first or second knowledge, rest upon a certain and determinate subject and, if properly used, indicate it to the mind as a singular. [Col. 0882B]

But grant that appellative nouns signify some general condition—for I take no delight in disputations, since I have long professed myself an Academic in matters doubtful to the wise: even if I could in some manner dream what that condition is in which singulars are united and which is none of the singulars, I still do not see how it can be fitted to Aristotle’s doctrine, since he maintains that universals do not exist.

Moreover, the names I mentioned above, “incorporeal” and “insensible,” are applied to universals only negatively, and attribute to them no properties by which the nature of universals is distinguished; for nothing incorporeal or insensible is universal. For whatever is incorporeal is either a spirit or a property of a body or spirit. If that does not apply to a universal thing, it does not rightly receive the name “incorporeal.” What, moreover, is incorporeal that is not a substance created by God, or conjoined with it? Thus, if universals are incorporeal, they are either substances—namely, bodies or spirits—or things conjoined with these; and, by reason of their existence and by a certain contact with substance, they are subject to their Creator. [Col. 0882C] Let universals depart—indeed, let them perish—if they are not subject to him.

“All things were made through him” (John 1): certainly both the subjects of forms and the forms of subjects, so that they are what they are called from their qualities or dispositions. Thus a substance is substance through him; it is quantified, qualified, relative, somewhere, sometime, possesses something, acts, or suffers, through the author by whom every substance exists, every property of substance, every part, and every joining together of parts. Both substantial and accidental forms likewise have from him that they exist and produce their effects in their subjects. Therefore, whatever is not subject to him is wholly nothing.

Although the Stoics posit matter as coeternal with God and say that forms had no beginning, establishing three principles—matter, form, and God, not indeed a creator but the uniter of the foregoing—and although certain others, philosophers in profession and disposition but by no means attaining full knowledge of the truth, feign a plurality of principles: there is one principle of all things, from whom whatever is truly called something derives its being. [Col. 0883A]

For, as Augustine says, God created formed matter; although it is somewhere called formless, it never existed altogether without forms. Thus reason serves investigation, not actuality: intellect pursues *hylē* (ὕλη, “matter”), which neither is nor can be formless, nor can even be fully understood, stripping away, as it were, its coverings until it reaches a certain nakedness of itself and its own deficiency. For the powers of reason in some manner vanish around the first principles of things.

Hence Boethius, defining nature in his book *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*, says that it is “of those things which, since they are, can in some manner be grasped by intellect.” Explaining the force of the phrase “in some manner,” he says this wording is added on account of God and matter, because human intellect fails in investigating them. Matter, moreover, God made from nothing; and form is conjoined to matter because it too was created from nothing at the same time, though such that, just as the form retains the function of distinguishing, so matter retains the privilege of existing. [Col. 0883B]

For in a certain manner form exists through matter, just as matter itself is distinguished through form. Form is not a thing existing through itself, nor is matter distinct without the benefit of form. There will be chaos—or rather, the sensible world will be nothing—unless nature composes the appearances of things by applying forms. This is the point of Boethius’s statement in the first book of *On the Trinity*: “All being is from form,” which he explains by the examples that follow.

“A statue,” he says, “is called a statue not from that which is its matter, but from the Hectorian or Achillean form impressed upon the bronze. Likewise bronze is called bronze not from the earth, which is its matter, but from the forms which it has received from nature. Earth itself is called earth not from ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης (*apo tēs hylēs*, ‘from matter’), which is its matter, but from dryness and heaviness, which are forms.” Thus, for each thing, its being what it is, or being of such a quality or quantity, is from form. But just as matter has from its creator the capacity to be this, so great, or such, so forms have from their Creator the capacity to make this or something else—for example, an animal, wood, something so great, or of such a kind. [Col. 0883C]

Moreover, although mathematics, which works doctrinally in abstractions and by its subtlety separates what is naturally conjoined, examines these things reciprocally and separately so that the nature of composites may be grasped more faithfully and clearly, nevertheless one cannot exist without the other: matter cannot be formless, nor can form be without a subject.

[lacuna]

[Of the other: thus.]

> One thing needs another’s help, and joins itself to it as a friend.  
> > (Horace, *Art of Poetry* 411.)

Hence heaven and earth are recorded as created in the beginning; then the adornment both of these and of the intermediate things between fire and water, which God set down as the first foundations, as it were, of the worldly body. In the very account of things, mention was made of species. I do not mean those species which logicians imagine not subject to the Creator, but the forms in which things first came forth into their essence [Col. 0884A] and finally into human intellect; for the very fact that something is called heaven or earth is an effect of form.

Likewise, “the earth brought forth green grass and a tree of this or that kind” (Genesis 1), in order to teach that forms are conjoined to matter and that God is author both of grass and of its greenness. For “without him nothing was made” (John 1). Yet certainly whatever derives from one principle is numerically one, and is itself good—indeed, very good—because it is from the highest good. For God willed all things to be made like himself, insofar as the nature of each, by decree of the divine disposition, could receive goodness; and so all things were made, and God, the maker of things, approved all that he had made as “very good” (Genesis 1).

Therefore, if genera and species are not from God, they are wholly nothing. But if each of them is from him, each is plainly one and the same good. And if something is numerically one, it is at once singular. For what some call “one thing,” not because it is one in itself but because it expresses many through the conformity of many, does not overturn the present argument: for such a thing is neither immediately nor sufficiently one, or else it is singular. [Col. 0884B]

However conformable God’s works may be, all are singular and mutually distinct, “by the ordering of him who created all things in number, for distinction; and in weight, for the dignity of their kind; and in measure, for the rule of determinate quantity,” while reserving for himself in all things infinite authority. For all other things are finite.

Every substance is subject to number through the plurality of accidents. Every accident and every form is likewise subject to number, not through participation in accidents or forms, but through the singularity of its subject. It likewise has its own weight: if it is a substance, according to the dignity of its form; if a form, according to the dignity of its effect. Hence we rank a human being above brute animals among substances, out of reverence for the form, because he is rational; and we rank rationality above colour because it makes rational.

Measure consists in this: every thing is bounded by a determinate law of quantity, so that neither an accident or form exceeds the measure of its subject thing, nor the subject thing the measure of its accident or form. Thus colour is diffused throughout the whole body and bounded by its limit; and the body is disposed in accordance with the quantity of its colour, neither exceeding nor falling short. [Col. 0884C] So every accident is wholly in its whole subject, but partially in the whole if it is in a part. And every subject is commensurate with the bounds of its accident.

I do not hesitate to affirm the same concerning genera and species. Though the world protest, I shall say: “They are from God,” or they are wholly nothing. Dionysius the Areopagite cries out with me and calls number, by which things are distinguished, weight, by which they are established, and measure, by which all things are defined, the image of God: “For God is number without number, weight without weight, measure without quantity. In him alone all things that have been made were created in number, weight, and measure.”

Hence Augustine: “The invisible differences of invisible things could be weighed by him alone who disposed all things in number, weight, [Col. 0885A] and measure—that is, in himself, who is measure, setting a limit to every thing; and number, giving every thing its species; and weight, drawing every thing toward stability”: that is, limiting, forming, and ordering all things.

In the works of the six days, individual things are said to have been created good “according to their kind,” yet no mention was made of a creation of universals. Nor indeed was this necessary, if they are essentially united with singulars, or if the Platonic doctrine prevails. Otherwise, where they have their being or when they began, I do not remember ever reading. Therefore, according to Aristotle, universals are only understood; in the actuality of things nothing is universal. For these names were given figuratively from a mode of understanding, and given freely and for instructional purposes.

For everything that is a human being is this or that human being—that is, a singular thing. But because a human being can be understood in such a way that neither this nor that human being, nor anything one by singularity of essence, is understood; and because, according to the intellect, it can be considered of the subject thing—that is, actually exemplified—on account of the commonness of understanding, the thing which can thus be understood, although understood by no one, is called common. For things are conformable to one another, and intellect considers that conformity after stripping away thought of individual things. [Col. 0885B]

For one human being is conformable to another in that both are human beings, though they differ in personal properties. Yet a human being has in common with a horse—though he differs from it in the whole species, that is, in the entire form of his nature and, so to speak, in his whole appearance—that they live and perceive, namely, that they are animals. Therefore, that in which human beings agree, alike in the form of their nature and differing only in number—that is, this one being one and that one another—is designated by the name of species. But that which is, as it were, the common image of diverse forms has received the name of genus. [Col. 0885C]

Therefore, according to Aristotle’s doctrine, genera and species are conceived not altogether as *what something is*, but in some manner as *what sort of thing it is*; and they are, as it were, certain fabrications of reason, which exercises itself more subtly in investigating and teaching about things. This is reliable because, whenever necessary, reason produces in things a manifest example of its activity.

Civil law likewise knows its own fictions, and no discipline is ashamed to devise the means by which its practice proceeds; indeed, each takes a certain delight in its own fictions. “Let species rejoice,” says Aristotle, “for they are monsters”; or, according to the new translation, “for they are chirpings of cicadas”; or, if they exist, they are irrelevant to reason.

Although this can be understood of Platonic Ideas, nevertheless, once account has been taken of the equivocation by which “being” or “to be” is distinguished according to the diversity of its subjects, species and genera are both, not without reason, said to be. For reason persuades us to call those things beings whose examples are seen in singulars, which no one doubts to exist. Yet genera and species are not called exemplars of singulars in such a way that, in the sense of Platonic doctrine, they are exemplary Forms existing intelligibly in the divine mind before they emerged into bodies; [Col. 0886A] rather, because if someone, on hearing the name “man,” asks for an example of what is conceived universally, or of what is defined when man is said to be a rational mortal animal, Plato—or some other individual man—is immediately pointed out to him, so that the account of the universally signifying or defining term may be made firm.

They may also be called “showings” or “monsters” (*monstra*), because they show individual things to one another and are shown by them; for things are now made manifest through what is prior, now through what is posterior. What is more universal is prior simply speaking, since it is also understood in other things; singulars, however, are posterior. But very often things naturally prior are less known to us simply speaking. Solid things are more familiar to the senses; [Col. 0886B] subtler things lie farther away. For, as Aristotle says, just as a point is prior to a line and more evident simply speaking, so a line is prior to a surface, a surface to a solid, unity to number—since it is its principle—and a letter to a syllable; and so in other cases.

For us, however, the opposite sometimes occurs. These latter things, that is, the posterior, are grasped more readily by anyone at all; the former, the prior, require a subtler and more abundant intellect. Hence, although an account of posterior things is better made through prior things, and it is more teachable to attempt this everywhere, yet necessity, owing to the weakness of the senses, often causes prior things to be explained through posterior ones: as when a point is said to be the limit of a line, a line of a surface, a surface of a solid; likewise unity the principle of number, an instant [Col. 0886C] of time, and an element of speech.

Genera and species, therefore, are exemplars of singulars; but this pertains rather to the rationale of teaching—if Aristotle is correct—than to the cause of being. This monstrous, if I may speak more freely, speculation of mental constructions proceeds even to the analysis of singulars. Since every substance consists of properties whose identical collection is not found in another thing, the activity of the abstracting intellect contemplates each thing by itself. For although Plato cannot be without form or devoid of place and time, reason, as it were stripping him naked and setting aside quantity, quality, and other accidents, contemplates him simply and calls him an individual. But [Col. 0886D] this too is certainly a construction of pedagogical effort and subtler inquiry. Nothing of this sort occurs among things; nevertheless such a thing is correctly understood.

Perhaps this explains the statement in the *Analytics*: “Aristomenes is always intelligible, but Aristomenes is not always,” because he is perishable. This is the individual in the singular sense, which some say alone can be predicated of something. For Plato, son of Aristeides, is individual—not by quantity, as an atom; nor by solidity, as a diamond; but by predication, as they say. I neither strongly attack nor defend this opinion. For I do not think it matters greatly, because I embrace that flexibility in the interchange of expressions without which I do not believe anyone can faithfully [Col. 0887A] attain the authors’ meaning. What harm is there if, just as “genus” is truly predicated of “species,” so this sensible Plato is truly predicated of the son of Aristeides, if Plato alone is his son? For just as man is an animal, so that man is Plato.

For Aristotle appears, in the *Analytics*, to have held this view according to the opinion of some, saying: “Of things that are, some are such that they are not truly and universally predicated of anything else”—such as Cleon and Callias, and the “singular and sensible”; “but other things are predicated of these, for both man and animal belong to each of them. Others, however, are themselves predicated of other things, but nothing prior is predicated of them. Still others are themselves predicated of other things, and other things are predicated of them: as man is predicated of Callias, and animal of man.”

Since, then, it is evident that some beings are naturally apt to be said of nothing else—for nearly every sensible thing is of this sort, so as not to be predicated of anything, except accidentally; for we sometimes say that that white thing is Socrates, and that the person coming is Callias—[Col. 0887B] this division seems altogether pointless unless the sensible thing can be predicated, though not of another thing except accidentally. For if it is predicated neither of itself nor of another, even accidentally, neither the truth of the statement nor the force of the example holds. But if a sensible thing cannot even be made a subject, no one can doubt that Aristotle spoke falsely or foolishly.

Accordingly, here as elsewhere, he performed what befits a teacher of the liberal arts, proceeding, as the saying is, with a “fatter Minerva,” so that he might be understood. He did not establish in genera and species a difficulty which the teachers themselves cannot understand, much less sufficiently explain to others. From this fullness of Minerva comes the statement in the *Topics*: “All differences will be either species or individuals, if they are animals; for each animal is either a species or an individual.” Likewise Boethius says: “Every species is its own genus.” For every man is an animal, and every whiteness a color. What, then, prevents sensible things, according to this principle of permissible usage, from either being predicated or being subjects? Nor do I suppose that authors imposed such force upon language that it must be tied, in every combination, to one meaning; rather, they spoke pedagogically, so that in every case they serve the understanding most suitable and demanded there above all others by reason. Thus [Col. 0887C] the very expression “to be predicated” acquires several modes of signifying from its adjuncts. Yet perhaps it can everywhere denote, in some manner, a certain fittingness or inherence.

For when a term is said to be predicated of a term, it indicates a certain joinability of the terms in a true affirmation; when a term is said to be predicated of a thing, it shows that such a designation is suitable to that thing. A thing’s being predicated of a thing sometimes means that this is this—for example, “Plato is a man”; sometimes that this participates in this, as a subject participates in an accident. Nor am I ashamed to confess that a thing is predicated of a thing in a proposition, even though a thing is not in a proposition; for I have in mind that the thing is signified by the predicate term of a true affirmation, whose subject concerns or signifies some thing.

Accordingly, I think that one should not oppose the letter, but make friends with it; one should accommodate oneself to it by accepting the flexibility of freer expression. Nor ought reader or hearer, at every metaphor or usage of a word thought difficult, exercise a dog’s tooth.

> What you bear badly, accustom yourself to bear: you will bear it.

Indeed, he is ungrateful, and of a disposition as impudent as it is imprudent, who takes offense at every word of his teacher [Col. 0888B] and refuses to comply with him in anything. Let us therefore follow the authors’ figures of speech and “weigh each statement according to the reasons for its utterance”; from these a faithful understanding must be drawn.

Let the word “thing” also extend more broadly, so that it may apply to universals, which, according to Aristotle, are understood as abstracted from singulars, yet have no being if singulars are removed. For, as he says, this is asserted by those who say that a genus is one in number. Those who posit Forms alone do this—namely Ideas—which, along with their author Plato, Aristotle vehemently attacks whenever occasion offers. Therefore, although Plato has a great company of philosophers, including Augustine and many others among our own writers, as defenders of the establishment of Ideas, [Col. 0888C] we by no means follow his doctrine in the investigation of universals, because here we profess Aristotle, prince of the Peripatetics, as the leader of this doctrine.

It is indeed a great task—and one which Boethius, in his second commentary on Porphyry, admits is not easy—to judge between the opinions of such great men. But one who approaches the books of the Peripatetics ought rather to follow Aristotle’s opinion: perhaps not because it is truer, but plainly because it is more suited to these disciplines. Far from this, however, seem to depart both those who maintain that genera and species are words or expressions, and others who, on the basis of the foregoing opinions concerning the investigation of things, are drawn in different directions. Indeed, all wander from Aristotle more childishly or foolishly than the Platonists, whose opinion [Col. 0888D] they disdain even to acknowledge.

I think this ought to suffice: those who rehearse all opinions concerning genera and species, oppose them all, and finally raise the banner of their own invention, deal neither faithfully with Porphyry nor usefully with beginners. This wholly departs from the author’s purpose, “blunts the minds of hearers,” and does not allow room for inquiry into other points equally necessary to know.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0889]

[Col. 0889A] Nearly twenty years have passed since financial necessity and the counsel of friends—whom I could not refuse to obey—tore me away from the workshops and training-ground of those who profess logic. Since then, to confess the truth as I sincerely think it, not even in passing have I once touched the writings of dialecticians that produce, preserve, or renew learning, whether in treatises, commentaries, or glosses. For meanwhile I have been distracted by occupations not merely different but almost contrary, so that I could scarcely philosophize even for an hour, and then somehow by stealth.

I crossed the Alpine passes ten times after leaving England; I travelled through Apulia a second time; I repeatedly conducted the affairs of lords and friends at the Roman Church; and, with various causes arising, I travelled many times not only around England but also through Gaul. In addition, concern for household affairs and the press of urgent business prevented me from devoting myself to letters. Hence I think the reader should be more indulgent toward those things which he finds expressed by me with less sharpness and polish. For the dryness of my language and sluggishness of my mind must be attributed partly to the aforesaid matters, partly to courtly trifles, and partly to the deceit and impudence of an adversary who, by obstinate pressure, provoked an unwary man and compelled him, however unwilling, to answer as best he could.

Accordingly, I am affected by that ethical reflection:

> Time carries all things away, even the mind. Often I remember,  
> when a boy, having spent long days in song.  
> Now so many songs are forgotten by me; even my voice itself  
> has already fled from Moeris.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* IX.51

[Col. 0889C] Is it not, then, unfairly dealt with me if youthful agility is demanded of me, the liveliness of a fervent intellect, the reliability of memory, amid so great a tumult of affairs and at an age occupied only with serious concerns—unless bodily weakness or spiritual negligence arising from these things, through the tinder of sin, diminishes or extinguishes seriousness through malice? Certainly, just as virtue which outruns years is accepted, so too is that virtue which does not desert a man as his powers fail.

A fierce lion struck down by a boy made Ascanius famous; and illustrious Dares, yielding in triumph to the veteran old man Entellus, added to Entellus’ honors. “For it is most glorious if nature seems to yield to virtue.” But I, already a veteran, and secure, if law prevailed, through the privilege both of my age and of my profession or rank, am somehow dragged into the arena and compelled to renew contests abandoned and long disused. A harsh and dreadful condition is set before me: either to enter a conflict which is inexpedient, or—what is utterly ruinous—to yield by confession and acquiesce in shameful falsehood. I chose, therefore, to avoid disgrace, which alone, or above all things, conflicts with the purpose of a philosopher.

And because I do not abound in weapons of my own, I use the missiles of all my friends without distinction. I do not, like men of our own age, neglect domestic resources; rather, I grasp them the more familiarly because I know more certainly that they are gifts of faithful friends. The truth of things remains incorrupt, and what is true in itself never vanishes through the testimony of a new author. Who but a tasteless or ungrateful person would reject a valid proposition because Coriscus, Briso, or Melissus—men equally unknown except insofar as Aristotle named them as examples—uttered it? And would he reject the same statement because it was advanced by Gilbert, Abelard, and our Adam? Certainly I am not among those who hate the good things of their own age and begrudge commending their contemporaries to posterity.

[Col. 0890B] No one of our own writers, so far as I know, has asserted that contradiction does not exist, or that motion cannot occur, or that a stadium cannot be traversed, or that the earth moves because, according to Heraclitus, all things are subject to motion—Heraclitus who, as Martianus says:

> … burns while he is wholly in fire,  
> because he maintained that all things were composed of it from the beginning.

And these opinions of the ancients are accepted precisely because they are ancient; while opinions of our own writers, far more probable and trustworthy precisely because they are our own, are rejected. Let each person say what he thinks. I believe this usually comes from envy, when each person thinks something has been detracted from his own reputation whenever praise is bestowed on another.

But I do not seek my own glory; I seek the glory of Him from whom comes whatever good is in me or others. I desire the honor of those who bestowed on me that little which I know or think I know, because I am an Academic; nor am I ashamed to praise the authors of my own advancement. For, as Pliny says: “It is a praiseworthy mark of a good intellect to acknowledge those through whom you have made progress.” Those who now criticize this in me will one day, God willing, be praised as authors of good things, because the glory of virtue awaits them and, with the passage of time, the envy of contemporaries will disappear.
