Let the discourse therefore proceed and briefly run through such recollections of youthful studies as occur—because that pleasant age returns to mind—reviewing with eager remembrance who above all should be read and how they should be read. What has been omitted or said faultily should be charged to forgetfulness, time, and occupations.

## CHAPTER I. How Porphyry and Other Authors Should Be Read

I sincerely think that every book ought to be read in such a way that knowledge of what is written may be acquired as easily as possible. For one should not seek occasions for introducing difficulty; rather, ease should everywhere be produced. I remember that the Palatine Peripatetic followed this practice. Hence, I suppose, he inclined toward the childish opinion concerning genera and species, if I may say so without offense to his followers: preferring to instruct and advance his pupils in elementary matters rather than be more obscure in the gravity of philosophers. For he most diligently did what Augustine directs to be done in all things: namely, “he served the understanding of things.”

[Col. 0891A] Porphyry should thus be read so that the meaning of the terms under discussion is retained and the sense of the words is gathered from their surface. In this way he will be sufficiently introductory and readily clear in his brevity. For a beginner, then, it is enough to know that the name “genus” has many meanings and, in its first institution, signifies the principle of generation: that is, the parent from whom, or the place in which, someone was born. Hence, when Polynices was asked by Adrastus about his lineage, he said, encompassing both:

> Cadmus is the origin of my fathers; Thebes, the land of Mars.  
> —Statius, *Thebaid* I

Then the word was transferred to signify that which is predicated, in answer to “what is it?”, of things differing in species. “Species” likewise is said in many ways. By its original institution it signifies the form that consists in the lineaments of limbs; hence *speciosus* means the same as “beautiful.” From this it was taken to signify that which, as Porphyry says, is predicated of things differing in number. It is consequently clear that these names are not of second imposition; rather, though they are of first imposition, they are called over to another signification by transfer. Because this occurs from necessity rather than ornament, it is compared to equivocation.

[Col. 0891C] Boethius adds a third signification of the same term, saying that the substantial form of a species—for example, humanity—is called the species of man. But he calls this a subtle species and deliberately maintains that Porphyry omitted it lest excessive difficulty impede the minds of beginners. What, then, do those intend who add not only this against the author’s purpose, but every other point that can be devised? I think they seek to appear to know and to have spoken much, when they have achieved only that they are less understood.

The same should be done with difference, property, and accident. Let the meanings of the terms simply be explained; let the one suited to the purpose be grasped through the clearest descriptions; then let the divisions of each follow. Finally, let the differences of each be assigned to each item, as they occur, on the surface of the text—and you have read Porphyry.

For the text should be gently examined, not harshly tortured like a captive until it gives back what it never received. He is too severe and harsh a teacher, taking what was not deposited and reaping what was not sown, who compels Porphyry to solve what all philosophers have received, and is not satisfied unless the little book teaches whatever is found written anywhere. Clearly truth is friendly to simplicity; and “he who exacts what is not owed, when he ought to receive what is owed, very often forfeits even that.”

Whatever the appearance of the text indicates, let the faithful and prudent reader meanwhile revere as sacred, [Col. 0892A] until truth becomes more fully and familiarly known to him through another’s teaching or the Lord’s revelation. For what one person faithfully and usefully teaches, another faithfully and usefully unteaches. The task of a correct teacher, according to the circumstances of time and person, is to dispense what he knows to be expedient for each person.

Thus Porphyry maintains that body is a genus of man because it is also a genus of animal. Aristotle, however, unteaches this and removes the error of those who think genus is predicated of species in a qualified sense; for it is not predicated of species in a qualified sense. Hence it is clear that visible or sensible is not a genus of animal; for they are predicated in a qualified sense, that is, with respect to body and not soul. Therefore, he says, body will not be the genus of animal, because it is a part. For a part is in no way predicated of the whole—if speech is proper, that is; for in figurative speech nothing prevents it.

Grammarians indeed teach that there is a trope of speech called synecdoche, which attributes the name of the whole to a part and likewise the name of a part to the whole. For a thing often takes the name of its more important or better-known part. Hence man, who consists of soul and body and, as Cicero, Apuleius, and—what is more important—Jerome, Augustine, and many others, both our own writers and pagans, testify, is no more body than soul, yet in common usage is in some manner, and in a diminished sense, designated by the name “body,” because that part is more evident and better known to the senses. Yet it is equally true, though accepted only by philosophers, that man is soul. Nor does it follow from this that he is incorporeal, because, as Abelard used to say, negation is stronger.

[Col. 0892C] Aristotle also restrained the extension of figurative speech because figures may not be extended; they themselves are admitted only when expedient. No genus is predicated of a species figuratively or metaphorically; it is always properly and universally true of everything of which it is genus. If anything more difficult to understand occurs, not merely in Porphyry but in any writings whatsoever, it should not immediately deter reader or hearer, but he should proceed; for authors interpret one another, and individual writings are in turn guides to others. Thus for one who reads much, either nothing or very little remains unknown.

## CHAPTER II. The Usefulness and Instruments of the Categories

[Col. 0892D]

Aristotle’s book of the *Categories* is elementary and receives, as it were, the infancy of one approaching logic. For it treats of uncombined terms insofar as they signify things, than which nothing is prior for the dialectician. It begins with equivocal, univocal, and denominative terms, because knowledge of them is very necessary to one who defines, divides, and reasons. Equivocation causes many errors if it remains unnoticed, and it hinders disputants if one does not know in what sense another directs his thought. But once it has been made clear, as Aristotle says, in how many ways a word is used and what it is directed toward, a questioner who does not make his statement with reference to that will appear ridiculous.

[Col. 0893A] It is useful both for avoiding fallacious reasoning and for committing it. For if we know how many senses a term has, we shall not be deceived; we shall know whether the questioner is not using the term in the same sense. And when we ourselves question, we shall be able to reason fallaciously whenever, among things said in many ways, some are true and some false—unless the respondent also knows how many ways the term is used.

Knowledge of univocal and denominative terms is likewise so necessary that Isidore calls these three—equivocal, univocal, and denominative—the instruments of the *Categories*. For whatever is predicated is applied to its subjects either equivocally, univocally, or denominatively: equivocally, if not in the same sense; univocally, if in the same sense; denominatively, if neither altogether in the same nor altogether in another sense, but with a certain neighboring relation in the understanding of the words, while the form of the words remains similar. Thus *bonus* (“good”) is said from *bonitas* (“goodness”), and *fortis* (“brave”) from *fortitudo* (“courage”), so that from the very form of the words a neighboring meaning may in some fashion be discerned.

[Col. 0893B] Hence, in the view of many, denominative terms and the things from which they are denominated principally signify the same thing; but Bernard of Chartres said that they differ in co-signification, because *albedo* (“whiteness”) signifies an incorrupt virgin; *albet* (“she is white”) the same woman entering the bridal chamber or lying in the bed; while *album* (“white”) signifies the same woman, but corrupted.

This was because, according to his assertion, *albedo*, simply and without any participation by a subject, signifies the quality itself—namely, a species of color that disperses sight. *Albet*, however, principally signifies the same quality, though it admits participation by a person. For if you examine what this verb signifies in respect of substance, the quality of whiteness appears; but among the accidents of the verb you find the person. *Album*, on the other hand, signifies the same quality, but infused and mingled with a substance, and thus already in some degree more corrupted. For the noun itself signifies, in respect of substance, a subject of whiteness; in respect of quality, the color of the whitening subject.

[Col. 0893C] Bernard also thought that he relied both on Aristotle and on the authority of many writers. For he says that “white” signifies nothing other than quality. He also advanced many examples, gathered from every side, by which he tried to persuade us that things are sometimes predicated purely and sometimes adjacently; and he maintained that knowledge of denominatives is very useful for this purpose. This opinion has defenders as well as opponents. To me it matters very little to dispute over a name in such matters, since I know that the meaning of utterances must be drawn from the reasons for their utterance. Nor do I think that the authorities mentioned from Aristotle or other authors should be interpreted so that everything found said anywhere is dragged into this view.

For Aristotle himself maintains that motion is predicated of animal and waking of biped, and so forth. Otherwise the examples in the *Analytics* would not work correctly; and Aristotle himself says: “If blindness and being blind were the same, they would be predicated of the same thing.” But now man is called blind, whereas blindness is not. Therefore one should not, on a slight occasion afforded by a word, prejudge the authors’ meaning; it must be weighed from the context of their discourse. Not every expression is always formed according to the same pattern.

[Col. 0894A] Clearly denominatives do not signify the same meaning as those things from which they are denominated. On hearing them the mind does not descend to the same thing; nor are they names of the same things. For they are often mutually exclusive, and contradiction follows from them. Yet sometimes they tolerate one another and denominatively are predicated at the same time of the same thing, or of one another. Thus goodness is called good, and unity one. But the regular rule is that contradiction follows from them; this, however, is said to occur more because of co-signification than signification. This is plausible; whether it is fully true, let the learned judge.

For contradiction follows, solely on the basis of signification, from things that signify the same thing. A singular number attached to the same noun excludes the plural: if something is “man,” it is not “men.” Yet it makes no difference to me whence this comes, since the entire concern of dialectic is directed to unveiling the force of words and, through their predication, acquiring the science of examining and establishing truth. This it does whether it divides, defines, reasons, or resolves what has been reasoned.

Denominatives, therefore, signify in some manner what things are like in virtue of something; whereas the things from which they are denominated indicate that by virtue of which they are such. Thus *fortitudo* signifies that by virtue of which someone is brave; *fortis*, what someone is like in virtue of courage. Hence *fortitudo* is said to be a name not of “whose,” but of “from what”: for it indicates a cause.

[Col. 0894C] Hence Gregory’s statement: “Angel is the name of an office, not of a nature”; for it is from an office, but it signifies a person and, as stated, indicates in some manner what sort of thing ministers in that office. There are many similar cases: *consul* is a name from rank; *studiosus* (“zealous”) from virtue; *Platonicus* and *Socraticus* are names from professions. They therefore signify the aforesaid things.

It follows that “to signify,” like “to predicate,” is said in many ways; but it is evident which mode is the most ordinary. Hence *justus* (“just”) and similar terms are commonly said by authors now to signify or predicate “the just,” now justice. But the usage is either not convertible at all, or is very rarely found—if indeed justice is anywhere said to signify or predicate “the just.” Boethius, however, says in *On the Trinity*: “When I say ‘God is just,’ I seem to predicate a quality; but I predicate substance—indeed, that which is above substance.” Why, I ask, does he seem to predicate a quality if the name “just” does not predicate a quality?

Aristotle’s statement is similar: they signify quality, as “white,” quantity, as “two-cubit.” Thus, just as they are given from quality or quantity, so they predicate the quality or quantity which their addition shows to be present in subjects. Sometimes they are said to signify what sort of things subjects are, because by their addition they disclose what the subjects are like. Yet these usages do not differ much, if the interpreter is charitable: upon hearing “white,” one understands that in which whiteness exists; but when “whiteness” is said, one does not understand that in which such color exists, but rather the color making a thing such. What the intellect conceives upon hearing a word is that word’s most ordinary signification.

## CHAPTER III. What the Conception of the Categories Is, and Within What Limits the Sobriety of Philosophers Is Contained

Because individual things are predicated either equivocally, univocally, or denominatively, in accordance with the principle of flexible usage; and because predication itself is a material of reasoning, the instruments of the *Categories* are prefixed. They impede, advance, or facilitate the efforts of those engaged in this art. For multivocal and diversivocal terms, which Boethius adds, belong more to grammar.

Multivocal terms are those in which several words concur in the understanding and naming of the same thing: for example, *ensis*, *mucro*, *gladius*—“sword,” “blade,” “sword.” [Col. 0895B] Diversivocal terms differ in both sense and sound: for example, “man” and “stone.”

This book especially commends, above others, the principle of flexibility which we always approve, though it is evident everywhere to a careful observer. For it treats now of signifying terms, now of things signified, and teaches about some things by means of the names of others. Some, because this book is elementary, call it almost useless; and they think it enough to persuade others that they are perfect in dialectical and demonstrative discipline if they despise or ignore those preliminary matters which Boethius teaches in his first commentary on Porphyry, before any part of the art is approached.

My view is very different. I do not see how anyone can be more a logician without this book than he can be literate without letters. From it we clearly learn what in things is singular, what universal, what substance, what accident; and what in words is said equivocally, univocally, or denominatively. From it the signification of uncombined terms becomes known; from it the right method of investigation is taught; from it the first and clear path to the perfection of knowledge lies open.

[Col. 0895C] For attaining perfect knowledge of any thing, these points appear sufficient, above all others, in the Peripatetic discipline which labors in the investigation of truth. First, one must know of a thing whether it is; then what it is, what sort it is, how great it is, in relation to what it is, where it is, when it is, how it is positioned, what it has, what it does, and what it suffers.

The final inquiry concerning each thing is why it is. This approaches no longer merely angelic perfection, but the prerogative of divine majesty. For to Him alone is the cause of all things known: His will is the primordial cause of all things, and He has willed to reveal to individual persons, insofar as He has willed, why each thing is as it is. “To know all things completely belongs to the divine; to err in nothing, to the angelic; to judge rightly in many things, to human perfection.”

[Col. 0895D] The sum of knowledge is therefore secured in this twelvefold number. Philosophical inquiry is content with the sobriety of eleven; if it goes further, it attributes its advance in large part to grace. For grace opens to those who knock, and the Lord reveals His will—which is the original cause of all things—to those who seek it with their whole heart.

The logician, however, knows the ten elements of his discipline; and when he has been fully trained in them, he proceeds, in the part concerning contradiction, to refute his opponent’s assertion more completely. These, then, are the questions called natural and in some fashion elementary, which lie before us: what, how great, what sort, and so forth.

Then, once the gymnosophists have been trained in these matters, they frame a contradiction; and, spreading it out, as the saying goes, upon a narrow field, they strive by the barbs of their reasoning to suppress the opposite side. For each endeavors to overthrow what has been established by another. But because inquiry into natural things comes first, it was in this field that the ten categories were first formed, and the expressions devised by which each of those things that first present themselves to sense or intellect—whether bodies or spirits—might be declared: what it is, how great it is, and of what quality it is, [Col. 0896B] or according to the other questions proceeding naturally.

Hence the categories are so called: whether in words or in things, they are ten classes of predicables, applied to individual and singular substances in such a way as to judge of them what they are, how great, of what quality, relative to what, where, when, in what position, what they possess, what they do, or what they undergo. The first category, therefore, concerns those things which indicate what some substance is. The second, those which indicate how great it is; the third, relation; the fourth, quality; the fifth, place; the sixth, time; the seventh, position; the eighth, possession; the ninth, action; the tenth, passion.

These were thus multiplied because among philosophers speculation concerning bodies was especially vigorous, whereas before Zeno either no one, [Col. 0896C] or very few indeed, held sound views concerning the soul or incorporeal spirits. For he, as Jerome attests, taught the immortality of souls. Certainly “being positioned,” and certain other predicates, can scarcely be fittingly applied to spirits, since these categories are in part especially attached to bodies.

The first contemplation, then—the contemplation, as it were, of philosophers of nature—turns upon the investigation of substances; the following one is mathematical and imitates nature. Hence the mathematician was called by the ancients “the ape of natural philosophers.” For just as the investigator of nature asks of Cleon or Callias what he is, or what sort he is, or how great he is, so the mathematician, once he has abstracted [Col. 0896D] the substance of the thing, asks of it what it is, or what sort it is, or how great it is, and thereafter proceeds further in the manner of natural philosophers.

But among those distinguished by a keener edge of purer philosophy, it has long been accepted that there is no place for a second mathematics, lest philosophical labor proceed to infinity and inquiry, which always tends toward an end, wander without end. Certainly, what has already been stripped entirely cannot be stripped further; and whether you abstract form from matter or remove matter from form, it will thereafter be superfluous labor either to clothe form in circumstances and properties which it does not admit, or to strip matter of qualities which it does not possess. Whatever is attempted beyond this, therefore, is not a constitution of nature but a fiction of a mind laboring in mathematical subtlety.

[Col. 0897A] For when the question is asked, “What is whiteness?” and the answer given, “A color of such-and-such a kind,” whatever is added to distinguish its subsistence either savors of effect, and is therefore dependent upon substance, or of a power whose operation perhaps does not yet exist. But if inquiry proceeds so far as to ask how great it is or where it is, recourse must be had to the byways of bodily things. Hence I believe that fewer philosophers have traversed those paths who make mathematics in every respect coequal with nature, imagining that in other things are found these classes of categories which are manifest in bodies and spirits.

Thus they place all genera and species of substances, qualities, and other things under the first category, because by adding the genus to the species the first question is answered—that is, it is declared of something what it is. Then [Col. 0897B] they arrange the succeeding categories according to the kinds of questions. This, indeed, seems foreign to Aristotle. For he says:

> It is plain that whatever is signifies at one time substance, at another quality, and at another something belonging to the other categories. For when, with a man given, one says that this man is a man or an animal, one says what he is and signifies substance. But when, with white color given, one says that what is given is a color, one says what it is and signifies quality. Likewise, with a cubit-long magnitude given, if one says that it is magnitude, one says what it is and signifies quantity. And similarly in the other cases. For each such expression, whether the same term is predicated of the same thing or a genus, signifies what it is; but when it is predicated of another thing, it signifies not what it is, but quantity, [Col. 0897C] or quality, or something belonging to the other categories.

The author does not, I think, here seem to state that all genera belong to the same category, even though they have the same mode of predication; or that the nine categories of accidental things are not predicated of substances; or that they are predicated in the same way of their subjects and of the things contained under them.

Isidore, Alcuin, and certain other wise men maintain that all the other predicates are predicated of primary substances, and they make a fully complete statement by employing all ten categories, as is clear from this example:

> “Augustine, a great orator, that man’s son, standing in the temple, today wearing a mitre, is wearied by disputation.”

For it is a complete statement, and it indicates the substance, quality, and quantity of the subject—that is, [Col. 0897D] of the person under discussion—together with the remaining categories, although perhaps it gives a less than proper example of quantity.

Certainly, just as nature, the parent of all things, created primary substance endowed with its accidents, so it created together with singular substances the singular accidents by which those substances are endowed. But the things understood as abstracted from singulars, such as secondary substances, are, as has been said, in some measure fictions of the mind based upon plausible reasoning. And just as, among substances, those are called primary which are substances in reality and, by the singularity of their essence, underlie accidents, while those are called secondary which are conceived, not without reason, from the conformity of singulars; so likewise, by proportional reasoning, quantities [Col. 0898A] and qualities which belong individually to primary things may be called primary quantities and qualities, and secondary quantities and qualities those abstracted from singulars by a certain rational recognition of likeness; and the same applies in other cases.

It is established, moreover, as Isidore says, that they are called *categories* because they cannot be known except from subjects. Hence they are rightly called *predicaments*, because they are dedicated—that is, attached—to present things which the constitution of nature displays. For *dicare*, “to dedicate,” is *addicere*, “to assign,” in accordance with Virgil’s line:

> “I shall join [her] in a lasting marriage and dedicate [her] as my own.”  
> (*Aeneid* I.73)

They are assigned to other things in such a way that they cannot be known without them. For, as stated above, if images of things merely turn over in the mind, the conception is empty if an instance of it cannot be found in an underlying thing. [Col. 0898B] Indeed, “the totality of singulars is the history of nature,” from which is excluded whatever is in no way actually found in things. And because categories are known from subjects, predicates are, as Boethius says, such as their subjects permit.

Thus the force of the categories, which is vigorous in the works of nature, vanishes in relation to divine excellence. Words transferred thither either change entirely or are false; and the labor, along with the error, of those who extend the force of the categories to all things is multiplied. In exceeding the bounds of natural things, they overthrow the integrity of the art, since they will not allow its rules to be limited to their proper kinds. Every rule and every universal is adapted to some kind; if it wantonly exceeds that sphere, it is immediately corrupted.

[Col. 0898C] Certainly, knowledge of categorical things and expressions, and Aristotle’s manifest teaching concerning them, is highly useful. He describes everything, divides it, and teaches which things admit comparison, which are receptive of contraries, which have contraries, and which are ignorant of all contrariety; thus leaving posterity an example of the shortest route to knowledge of truth. And because multiplicity of expressions often obstructs understanding, he teaches that one must ask in how many senses each thing is said. To this end belongs the fact that he filled a book with opposites, things said to be prior or simultaneous, species of motion, and modes of this kind. Nothing is more useful for knowledge or victory than distinguishing things expressed in many senses.

[Col. 0898D] It happens, however, with the passage of time and as users’ preference changes, that multiplicity of expressions comes into being and likewise dies away. For in Aristotle “a sharp knife” and “sharp angles” signified being sharp, whereas now it seems rather to indicate an edge that cuts easily. Thus one says, “a two-edged sword,” because it cuts readily on both sides. Yet to one considering the matter more keenly, this appears to arise from the sharpness of angles: a body is sharpest where its surfaces meet at a very sharp angle. For if the angle formed by the meeting surfaces is obtuse, the body is obtuse.

In some respect more things are said in various senses now than in Aristotle’s time; and words which then had some meaning may now perhaps have none. For:

> Many words that have now fallen shall be reborn, and words shall fall  
> Which now are held in honor, if Usage so wills—  
> Usage, in whose power are judgment, right, and the rule of speech.  
> (Horace, *Ars poetica* 70–72)

But those who read every possible thing into this little book, and do not allow it to be content with its brevity, plainly unteach more than they teach. They heap together here whatever can be said anywhere, regarding confession as more burdensome than ignorance of the truth. That English Peripatetic, Adam—whose footsteps many follow, though few, impeded by envy, acknowledge it—used to mock them. He said that he would have either no hearers or very few if he taught dialectic with the simplicity of expression and facility of meaning by which it ought to be taught.

[Col. 0899B] For I enjoyed close acquaintance with the man through frequent conversation, the sharing of books, and an almost daily practice of discussing newly arising questions. Yet I was not his pupil even for a single day. Nevertheless, I thank him because under his teaching I learned much; and, with his own judgment, I rejected much more of his teaching because, after deliberation, I had chosen another course of reasoning. Here, then, as everywhere, I think one should serve clarity. I have not offered all these preliminary remarks with the intention that they be said everywhere, but I have commended the book lest matters which are expedient to say somewhere be everywhere passed over in silence. Nor do I regret it, because it is truly commendable.

[Col. 0899C] But if excessive indulgence is granted to the affection which more zealously invites the untrained and reluctant to the first elements of the art,

> “Thus teachers of old, coaxing boys, give them little cakes  
> That they may be willing to learn their first elements.”  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.25–26)

—and because it is disparaged too much by many, it is commended all the more strongly. For, as Aristotle says, “one must oppose an utterly persistent man with utter persistence.”

## Chapter IV. The plan and usefulness of *Perihermeneias*, or more properly *Perihermeneias*

The book *Perihermeneias*, or rather *Perihermeneias*, is syllabic by proportional analogy, just as the *Categories* is elementary. For this work gathers the elements of reasoning which the former presents separately in uncompounded expressions, and produces them as though gathered into a syllable for signifying truth and falsity.

[Col. 0899D] The ancients regarded it as possessing such subtlety that Isidore relates in its praise that, when Aristotle was writing the *Perihermeneias*, “he dipped his pen in his mind.” Yet—to speak with everyone’s leave—whatever is taught in this book can be presented more concisely and clearly by any teacher, as many in fact do, without reverence for its exact words, in introductory manuals which they call *introductions*. There is scarcely anyone who does not teach these very matters, adding others no less necessary. This is so because knowledge of the art cannot be acquired without them.

Accordingly, they run through what a noun is, what a verb is, what speech is, its species, the powers of propositions, what propositions derive from quantity or quality, which are determinately true [Col. 0900A] or false, which are equivalent, which agree with one another, which disagree, which predicates are predicated separately, which jointly, which reciprocally, and which are not; likewise, what is the nature of modal propositions and what is the contradiction of singular propositions. The principal substance of this work lies in these topics; and just as its meanings are subtle, so its language is not without considerable difficulty.

Both are to be valued: the meanings educate the mind, and the words train expression. Moreover, reverence should be shown to the words of authors, both by cultivating and using them constantly, because they bear a certain majesty derived from the great names of antiquity, and because it is more disadvantageous to be ignorant of them, since they are most powerful for attack or resistance. [Col. 0900B] For they sweep the ignorant away like a whirlwind and, striking them with fear, agitate or overthrow them; unfamiliar philosophers’ words are thunderclaps. Thus, although modern and ancient writers have the same meanings, antiquity is more venerable.

I recall the Palatine Peripatetic saying—and I believe it true—that it would be easy for someone of our time to compose a book on this art inferior to none of the ancients in conception of truth or elegance of language, but that for it to acquire the favor of authority would be either impossible or extremely difficult. Yet he maintained that this very achievement must be ascribed to the ancients, whose intellects flourished and who, powerful in marvelous invention, left to posterity the fruit of their labor. Thus matters upon which many spent their lives, [Col. 0900C] sweating greatly in discovery, are now attained easily and quickly by one person. Our age nevertheless enjoys the benefit of the preceding age and often knows more—not because it surpasses it in native genius, but because it rests upon others’ strength and upon the abundant learning of the Fathers.

Bernard of Chartres used to say that we are like dwarfs seated upon the shoulders of giants, so that we can see more and farther than they—not, of course, through the sharpness of our own sight or the height of our bodies, but because we are lifted and raised on high by gigantic greatness.

I readily agree with this, because teachers of the arts hand down preparatory material and many points of truth, even in their introductions, as well as the ancients do and perhaps more conveniently. For who is content [Col. 0900D] with what Aristotle teaches in the *Perihermeneias*? Who does not add materials gathered elsewhere? All collect the whole sum of the art and hand it on in easy language. They clothe the authors’ meanings, as it were, in everyday dress, which in a certain fashion becomes more festive when it is more clearly marked with antiquity’s gravity.

The authors’ words should therefore be committed to memory, especially those which convey complete meanings and can suitably be transferred to many contexts. For they preserve the integrity of knowledge, and besides possess in themselves a great deal of force, both hidden and manifest. But many expressions, if torn from their proper setting, convey either nothing or very little to the hearer. Such are almost all the examples in the *Analytics*, where letters stand in place of terms; when treated in that context they contribute to instruction, but elsewhere they are useless.

[Col. 0901A] The rules themselves, too, have great force from the truth of their teaching but very little force in ordinary speech. For saying that one thing is wholly in another, or wholly not in it, and saying that something is universally predicated of something else or removed from it, amount to the same thing. Yet one expression is commonly used, while the other has almost disappeared except where it is occasionally admitted by convention. Perhaps both uses were more common in Aristotle’s time; but now one prevails over the other, because usage wills it so.

[Col. 0901B] Likewise, the term *contingent* has in some measure lost the sense it had in Aristotle. For now “contingent” is by no means identified with “possible,” although he seems to have understood it so in his treatment of modal propositions. Although it is possible for the Ethiopian people to become white and for the species of swans to become black, neither is contingent. If someone thinks these events are contingent because they are possible, let him proclaim this in public, relying on Aristotle’s authority; and, with common usage opposing the public assertion, he will plainly seem either to sit among madmen or at least to be insufficiently sober.

But let us turn to another meaning, in which “contingent” is not equivalent to “possible” but is bounded by it because it is narrower. Here too we shall see that the former usage has been displaced. For Aristotle says in the *Analytics*: “‘To be contingent,’ and ‘contingent,’ are that which, though not being necessary, if posited as being, will make nothing impossible on that account.” This meaning excludes the necessary from the contingent, but otherwise equates it with the possible. Yet this usage too no longer prevails.

[Col. 0901C] For it is not necessary that Hobinellus reign, nor will anything become impossible merely because he does; but if you were to say at Winchester that Hobinellus’s reigning is contingent, no one would readily agree with you. To make still clearer how far that usage has been abolished: the word no longer fully holds in any of the senses which Aristotle assigns to it. For Aristotle says that “to be contingent” is used in two ways: first, of what for the most part happens and fails to happen, and which is necessary—for example, a human being’s turning gray, growing, diminishing, or in general what is naturally apt to be. For this does not have a continuous necessity, since a human being does not always exist; but when a human being exists, this occurs either necessarily or for the most part. Second, it is used of the indefinite, which is possible both to be thus and not thus—for example, an animal’s walking, an earthquake occurring while it walks, or, generally, what happens by chance. For nothing is more naturally apt to occur thus than contrariwise.

[Col. 0901D] But now, following Usage,

> “In whose power are judgment, right, and the rule of speech,”  
> (Horace, *On the Art of Poetry* 72)

only what happens sometimes is called contingent. Otherwise, something will not be called contingent either because necessity has been removed or because possibility is present. It is plain, therefore, that usage is stronger than Aristotle in diminishing the force of words or abolishing words; but it cannot overthrow the truth of things, since man did not establish that truth.

[Col. 0902A] Thus, if possible, let the terms and meanings of the arts be retained. But if not, provided the meanings remain, let the terms fall away; for to know the arts is not to turn over the words of writers, but to know their force and meanings.

## Chapter V. What constitutes the body of the art, and the usefulness of the *Topics*

Preparatory studies precede the art; its maker and, as it were, legislator did not judge that the wholly untrained novice should be admitted to it irreverently and, as the saying goes, with unwashed hands. For just as, in military science, the preparation of the instruments by which military operations are equipped precedes the art itself, so certain elements are set before those approaching the worship of this sacred art, like the instruments of novices. By using them, they may approach the body of the art more expeditiously [Col. 0902B] and practice more conveniently what they profess.

These are indeed most useful; and even if they are not quite properly said to belong to the art, they are very truly said to be for the art. It matters little whether one says it one way or the other. Once the preliminaries have been set forth, the body of the art itself consists principally in the knowledge of the *Topics*, the *Analytics*, and the *Sophistical Refutations*. When these are perfectly known and their habit strengthened by use and exercise, abundance in invention and judgment will assist every discipline: the demonstrator, the dialectician, and the sophist alike.

[Col. 0902C] Among these, especially for those pursuing probability, the knowledge of the *Topics* is most necessary. Though it chiefly trains invention, it also provides no small assistance to judgment. And although, in many people’s view, it serves primarily the dialectician and the orator, I think it advances almost equally those concerned with the gravity of demonstrative reasoning or with sophistical deception and contest. For all these disciplines assist one another; and each person is more proficient in the proposed discipline to the extent that he has been better trained in a neighboring and connected one. Thus both analytics and sophistry contribute to the inventor, and topics likewise benefit the judge. Still, I readily grant that each discipline holds mastery in its own field and that the benefit of its connected discipline is accessory.

Since the usefulness of the *Topics* is so evident, I wonder why Aristotle’s book, together with others, was so long neglected by the ancients that it wholly, [Col. 0902D] or almost wholly, fell into disuse, until in our age, under the knocking zeal of a diligent intelligence, it was awakened as if from death or sleep, to recall the erring and open the way of truth to seekers. The difficulty of its language or subject matter is not so great that diligent students cannot understand it, while its usefulness is so great that it is advantageous above the rest to know it.

Among other works drawn from Greek under the very strict law of translation, it is sufficiently plain; yet it remains such that one can readily recognize its author’s style, and it is faithfully understood only by those who follow the principle of indifference. Without this, no one has ever understood Aristotle, either among us or among the Greeks, as the Greek interpreter of Severitan origin used to say. Certainly, by the very number of its books—an omen, as it were, of perfection—Aristotle commended the usefulness of the work, and gave, as it were, the seed of everything which antiquity spread out across many volumes.

[Col. 0903A] Each of its words, both in its rules and examples, benefits not only dialectic but almost all disciplines. It is enclosed in eight books, and the later books are always more important than the earlier. The first lays down, as it were, the material for all the rest and establishes certain foundations of the whole of logic. It teaches what a syllogism is; what demonstration is and from what it is composed; what are the principles of arts and of faith; what syllogism proceeds from the arts; what syllogism is dialectical and what contentious; what is probable, which the paralogist or false-writer does not follow; likewise what a proposition is and what a problem is.

[Col. 0903B] And because one must proceed to examine problems and prove positions, it adds from what things problems arise—that is, which propositions derived from the art are put into question—after distinguishing the categories, from whose nature the rationale of questions flows. For it does not apply its forms to every possible question, since it is not wise to inquire into everything, but to matters worthy of inquiry and such that, once known, contribute something. When anyone advances things contrary to received opinions, or merely contemptible matters, and investigates them contemptuously, it is not expedient to be troubled.

[Col. 0903C] Since the rationale of the categories predicates of subjects either greater things or equal things, Aristotle teaches that dialectical problems have a fourfold nature. He holds—although this, like his other points, may be disputed—that where the inquiry concerns what is greater and substantial, the inquiry is one of genus; where there is uncertainty about what is equal and substantial, the question concerns definition; if doubt concerns what is greater and accidental, it concerns accident; and where the inquiry concerns what is equal and accidental, it concerns property.

But since, when someone asks what something is, or how great it is, or of what quality it is, what is lesser than the subject is not properly said of it, neither is what is lesser predicated of it, nor is a question shown to concern the lesser. Accordingly, Aristotle teaches what genus, definition, accident, and property are much more conveniently than those who, in explaining Porphyry or the *Categories*, write many large volumes apiece. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor let any of my friends make use of such teachers.

[Col. 0903D] Further, he states what induction is, where it is expedient to use it, in how many ways “opposite” is said, and how things of multiple signification ought to be divided. Indeed, it is useful in many respects even to know that equivocation admits neither comparison nor a plural number that would gather together what is posited separately. For voice, angle, and knife are not said to be sharp collectively, nor is one sharper than another, although each is called sharp individually. This investigation into words used in many senses also helps one frequently to assess the force of contraries from their opposites. For if one of the two is said of many things either equivocally or univocally, the other is said similarly, at least in all or most cases.

[Col. 0904A] For because in the case of a voice the contrary of sharp is low, while in magnitude it is heavy, it is clear that “light” or “heavy” would be said equivocally in several senses. Whoever wishes to know what is being said must examine the force of an expression; if it is unknown, reliable understanding of words cannot stand. To this belongs Augustine’s observation—drawn from Aristotle, since all have drawn from this spring—that in every proposition three things must be considered: the expression (*dictio*), the thing said (*dicibile*), and the thing (*res*). The thing is that about which something is said; the thing said is what is said about something; the expression is that by which this is said of that.

[Col. 0904B] Sometimes, however, an expression may happen to be the thing, when the same expression is taken up for discourse about itself—as in what our teachers called, materially, imposed terms and things-said; for example: “*Homo* is a noun”; “*Currit* is a verb.” But things, for the most part, and things-said belong to nature; expression depends upon human choice. Thus, to test truth, it is necessary that the thing not be altogether removed from knowledge, that the thing-said fit the underlying thing—that is, the thing under discussion—and that the expression be cognate with both, so that every occasion for reproach may be removed.

## Chapter VI. The usefulness and plan of the three books of the *Topics*

[Col. 0904C] Just as the *Categories* is elementary and the *Perihermeneias* syllabic, so the book of the *Topics* is, as it were, lexical. For although the *Perihermeneias* treats the simple proposition, which is certainly an expression of truth or falsity, it does not yet attain the force of inference, nor does it reach the point upon which dialectic’s chief activity turns. This book is the first in explaining arguments: it supplies a teaching of topical argumentation and discloses the beginnings of subsequent combinations.

And just as, according to the ethical saying, “the later day is the pupil of the earlier,” so the first book is more instructive than those which follow. The first explains from what places problems arise. The following books expound from where and how they are proved, and why one proposition is more or less capable of argument than another.

[Col. 0904D] I do not, however, attribute so much to this work as to regard the labor of modern writers as empty. They are indeed born and strengthened from Aristotle, but add to his discoveries many arguments and rules no less firm than the earlier ones. Yet Aristotle deserves this credit: he taught that the whole may be proved from a part, and showed that an inference may be drawn from two parts, three parts, or more; and similarly in other cases. Therefore, we owe gratitude not only to Themistius, Cicero, Apuleius, and Boethius for their additions, but also to the Palatine Peripatetic and to our other teachers, who have labored for our advancement, whether in explaining the ancients or in discovering new things.

[Col. 0905A] I nevertheless wonder why the Palatine Peripatetic prescribed so strict a rule in judging hypothetical propositions that he thought only those should be admitted in which the consequent is contained in the antecedent, or in which, when the consequent is destroyed, the antecedent is destroyed. He readily accepted arguments but rejected hypothetical propositions unless an evident necessity compelled him. Perhaps this was because, as Boethius says, all wish to maintain a necessary consequence. They wish this, indeed, because they profess it by adding a condition; nevertheless, some consequences are admitted on account of an evident probability which commonly attends necessity.

For just as probable arguments suffice for dialecticians, so do probable consequences. But both lack compelling force if necessity is absent—as when you provide a counter-instance showing where the consequence does not hold. Aristotle, however, almost everywhere employs consequences, whether he teaches one to establish or overthrow what has been posited. And because many things follow upon one thing, one must consider the basis on which many results follow from establishing or destroying something. For, as Aristotle says, everyone who has said anything has in some sense said many things, because many things necessarily follow from each thing. Thus, whoever has said that something is a human being has also said that it is an animal, animate, bipedal, and capable of mind and learning.

[Col. 0905B] A rational problem is one for which arguments are both numerous and good. The whole second book, therefore, concerns accident. Since it elegantly teaches the nature of accidents, with both firmness of reasoning and attractiveness of examples, it is useful for many purposes. And because accident alone admits comparison, the third book discloses the force of comparable things. Persisting in its inquiry into the nature of accidents, it regularly shows the principle by which things are to be chosen or avoided, which things among those to be chosen are to be preferred, and which among those to be avoided are above all to be shunned. From this it is clear how greatly this discipline benefits physics and ethics.

[Col. 0905C] Since this part of the discipline is powerful in pursuing and avoiding things, and in all comparable matters generally, its commendation is plainly extensive. It was badly neglected by earlier teachers, although its usefulness is conspicuous, its language pleasing, and its benefit to both ethics and physics very great.

## Chapter VII. A brief account of the fourth and fifth books

[Col. 0905D] The fourth book treats problems derived from genus and thus teaches the interconnection of genus and species, both with one another and with other things. To make clear to everyone how much time has been wasted because our teachers neglected this inquiry, I do not think it necessary to linger longer, since much has already been said above about the genera of things, and it is not our purpose to write specialized commentaries upon this work.

Yet I think this must be added from Aristotle, because Porphyry, whom beginners follow, taught otherwise: genus is predicated univocally, not denominatively, and not *secundum quid*—in a qualified respect. Hence it is clear that body is not the genus of animal. For Aristotle says that one must consider whether a genus is participated in only in some respect in certain cases; for example, whether an animal is called sensible or visible. Animal—namely, body—is called sensible or visible only in one respect, but not according to the soul. Therefore sensible or visible will not be the genus of animal.

[Col. 0906A] But they sometimes conceal this by putting the whole in place of the part: “animal is a sensible body.” For a part is in no way predicated of a whole. Hence body will not be the genus of animal, because it is a part. Every genus, indeed, is truly predicated of its species and individuals without transference or figure. It is never predicated improperly, because no attribution is more familiar than that of substance, which is most correctly judged in genus and species. But body is said of man figuratively, by synecdoche.

[Col. 0906B] From this it is clear that one who is called body because of the manifestness of one part may likewise be called soul because of the dignity of the other. Yet lesser philosophers, together with Porphyry, follow popular opinion, which is accustomed to approve almost only what is evident to the senses. Plato, however, and the doctrine of both Stoics and Peripatetics declare that man is more properly called soul than body. Following this view, Marcus Tullius says in the *Republic*: “You are not that which your outward appearance designates; rather, each person is his mind.” The teachers of the Church, Augustine and the rest, also approved this same view. If anyone doubts it, let him read the Scriptures, which in some sense assign personal primacy to the soul and compare the body to a lodging or a garment.

Likewise, the fifth book teaches most fully in how many ways *property* is said; in these, it teaches when what is properly and multiply said has been correctly posited, and when it has been wrongly assigned. This inquiry is most useful for establishing and overthrowing arguments, because a property properly so called and that of which it is the property mutually entail one another through reciprocal predication.

## Chapter VIII. On the subject of definition treated in the sixth book

[Col. 0906C]

Moreover, the sixth book concerns definition, and sets forth the art of defining clearly, so that one who has fully mastered it ought not to hesitate in establishing or refuting definitions. It teaches a most exacting rule for defining, one which either no one, or very few, fully attain. Thus Aristotle would be distinguished above all others alike by the other methods of reasoning and by his treatment of definition, if he established what was his own as plainly as he refuted what belonged to others forcefully. Yet, as he proved a stronger assailant than defender, so most people affirm more strongly than they attack; for not everyone can do everything, and each, if one considers the efficacy of grace, is distinguished by his particular office. To say nothing of believers: Ovid successfully composes verse; Cicero pleads cases; Pythagoras investigates nature; Socrates prescribes a rule of morals; Plato persuades concerning everything; Aristotle produces subtleties.

Marius Victorinus and Boethius, together with Cicero, took the beginnings of their teaching from this source; each published books on definitions. They indeed extended the name “definition” to as many as fifteen species, placing modes of description under the term definition. Aristotle, however, is chiefly concerned with substantial definition, which must consist of genus and substantial differences in such a way as to be commensurate with the thing proposed. For a definition is correctly assigned when it is equal to the thing defined and employs a wholly plain explanation. Therefore, not only the imposture of equivocation must be removed,

[Col. 0907A]

but all obscurity arising from uncertainty must be avoided, since that which is given in order to make something else known ought itself to be evident. Therefore metaphors must be avoided, as must whatever is not said properly—for example, calling a law the measure or image of things naturally just.

Such expressions, Aristotle says, are worse than metaphor. For metaphor makes what is signified somewhat known through resemblance: everyone who speaks metaphorically does so according to some resemblance. But an expression of this kind does not make the matter known; for neither is there a resemblance according to which a law is a measure or an image, nor is it customarily so called. Hence, if one says properly that a law is a measure or image, one lies. For an image is that whose production is by imitation; but this does not belong to law. If, however, one does not speak properly, it is plain that one has spoken obscurely—and worse than in any of the expressions which are metaphorical.

Terms must be understood as “known” when they become known to persons whose understanding is properly disposed. But what is based neither on things more known simply nor on things more known to us does not serve for a definition. A definition must also be coextensive—that is, equal in members—with the thing defined. Thus, if one asks what speculative knowledge is, neither “speculative” nor “knowledge” should remain ambiguous.

Nor should anything tending toward an affection be included among the substantial elements of a definition. For, on Aristotle’s authority, every affection, when intensified, removes one further from substance. A difference, however, is not of this kind; for it seems rather to preserve more fully that of which it is the difference.

[Col. 0907B]

And it is simply impossible for an individual thing to exist without its proper difference. For when something is not capable of walking, it will not be a human being. In general, nothing according to which a possessor undergoes alteration is a difference of that thing. For all things of this kind, when they become more intense, remove one from substance. Therefore, if someone assigns such a thing as a difference, he errs. Strictly speaking, we are not altered according to differences.

Hence Plato too is criticized for including death in the definition of animals. For although it is not intensified—that is, although it is not predicated in greater or lesser degree, since things of this kind do not admit of more and less—it is nevertheless not a difference. Rather, perhaps it denotes more correctly a condition and a capacity for undergoing an affection, or, more especially, indicates a necessity imposed upon the sufferer.

[Col. 0907C]

This will be readily persuasive to a Christian who, expecting immortality, believes that the condition of life will be changed for the better, not that nature will be corrupted. For substance will be glorified and, without its own destruction, freed from the necessity of suffering. The very capacity for enduring affection will vanish when what is mortal puts on immortality and death is swallowed up; and what is now corruptible will possess incorruption.

Nor is it surprising that mortality should be ascribed to passibility, since immortality itself, according to Aristotle, must be called an affection. For he says: “Immortality seems to be an affection of life and an occurrence.” That this is true will become evident if someone grants that a mortal person becomes immortal. No one will say that he takes on another life, but rather that some occurrence or affection is added to this same person. Therefore life is not the genus of immortality.

[Col. 0907D]

From this too it follows that mortal and immortal are not species or differences of living things, but rather indicate modes of living or a condition of nature. Indeed, there is nothing bad in substance, for what is best in each thing belongs most fully to its substance.

Yet, unless one has extensive knowledge of things, it is difficult to define substance according to rule, because substantial features are often uncertain—either through the difficulty of the things and our ignorance, or through ambiguity of language. There are also many things which, through nature’s constraint, lack proper definitions: principles, because in ascending there are no genera above them; and individuals, because they are not separated from one another by substantial differences.

Here, however, descriptions take the place of definitions, and are more probable insofar as they approach more closely the form of definitions. Yet greater latitude is allowed to them. It is easier to have done anything whatsoever than to have done it well, because virtue is always difficult. But when a definition is secure, it is most effective for establishing or refuting the proposition, because it is weakened or strengthened together with the proposition itself.

## CHAPTER IX. On the problem of sameness and difference, treated in the seventh book; and certain general matters concerning the *Topics*

The seventh book likewise depends upon definitions and unfolds the problems concerning sameness and difference. Its discussion involves much wearisome effort, because a conflict of contrary arguments supplies matter for doubt. Yet, just as “different” is said in many ways in relation to something, so is “same”; for each is said with reference to genus, species, and number. But things different in genus are at once different in the subsequent respects also. Conversely, things the same in number are immediately united in all the other ways as well.

Most indisputably, that which is one in number and the same as something is held by everyone to be the same in every respect; for this is what it is to be simply the same. This too is commonly assigned in several ways. Properly and primarily, it is so when the same thing is designated by a name or a definition: for example, *vestis* (“garment”) and *tunica* (“tunic”); “a two-footed walking animal” and “human being”; and “what naturally moves upward” and “fire.” Thirdly, it is so by accident, as “the seated [man]” or “the musical [man]” is said of Socrates: for all these expressions intend to signify one thing in number.

[Col. 0908D]

That what has now been said is true may be learned from our changing names. For we often alter our form of address when instructing someone to call one of those sitting down, if perhaps the person to whom we give the order does not understand; then, using an accidental feature which he understands more readily, we order him to call the seated man or the man engaged in discussion to us. It is clear that we take the same person to be signified both by the name and by the accident. Therefore “same,” as has been said, is divided in three ways.

Thus, knowledge not only of definitions but also of genus, property, and accident is necessary both for establishing and for refuting problems concerning sameness and difference. Yet nothing is more useful for either task than definition, since nothing is more effective and nothing more familiar.

In those seven volumes, because of the abundance of “places,” the whole body of the *Topics* is most correctly said to consist. As Isidore says, they are called *Topics* because they contain τόπους (*topous*), that is, “places,” which are the seats of arguments, the sources of meanings, and the origins of expressions. The discipline itself is therefore called topical because it teaches the doctrine of places.

[Col. 0909A]

Whoever investigates this book more carefully will discover not only that the *Topics* of Cicero and Boethius were drawn from these seven volumes, but also that the book *On Divisions*, which, by its concision of language and elegance of thought, has acquired singular grace among Boethius’s logical works, derives from them. Yet I do not think that all the places were inserted into that work, since they could not have been; and I see that modern writers too, guided by the benefit of this work, explain equally necessary matters more plainly each day.

These matters concern invention, which William of Champeaux, of happy memory and later bishop of Châlons, defined—though not perfectly—as the knowledge of finding the middle term and thence drawing an argument. For when there is doubt about predication, one must seek some middle term through whose intervention the extremes may be joined. Whether any inquiry is more subtle or more effective for the matter at hand, I could not easily say.

A middle term is necessary where the force of inference rests in terms. But if it lies between whole propositions, so that it is subject rather to the combination of the parts than to the combined parts themselves, the connection of a middle term ceases. In matters which derive their compelling force from terms or parts of terms, the argumentative “place” arises from the relation

[Col. 0909B]

between what is removed from the conclusion and what succeeds when it has been removed; for successors are proved by their predecessors. What remains unmoved in both cases admits neither the force of the prover nor the assurance belonging to the thing proved.

Just as terms derive from signification their being called universal or singular, so their following from one another or their being repelled by one another results from the coherence or incompatibility of their meanings. Unless the things signified cohere or conflict with one another, there is no reason to seek friendship or hostility among the terms.

It is not easy, however, always to determine in individual cases how firm the connection of things is or how great their disagreement. Therefore it is sometimes difficult to judge what is necessary simply and what is more probable. But what happens most frequently is called probable; what never happens otherwise is called more probable; and what is believed unable to be otherwise receives the name necessary.

[Col. 0909C]

For the definition of necessary and possible things belongs to nature, which alone has recognized its own powers. The diamond was long believed uncuttable because it feared neither the edge of iron nor that of steel; but at last, when it was cut with lead and goat’s blood, what had previously seemed impossible was shown to be easy to do.

Therefore the customary course of things must be carefully observed, and nature’s recesses in a manner examined, so that the character of necessary and probable things may become clear. Nothing contributes more to knowledge of the places; nothing produces a fuller knowledge of truth; nothing advances more the tasks of teaching or persuading

[Col. 0909D]

and prepares a praiseworthy ability in all speaking.

## CHAPTER X. On the usefulness of the eighth book

It is customary with all skilled craftsmen to prepare the instruments of their art before they try their use, lest the effort of their own skill prove futile through lack of the tools belonging to it. Thus in military affairs a commander provides weapons and military equipment in advance. An architect seeks material together with tools upon which both he and they may be employed. A sailor prepares the helm, ropes, oars, anchors, and the other equipment of a ship, so that, relying on their assistance, he may more properly carry out the purpose of his art.

In the same way, the craftsman in rational matters and champion-teacher of those who profess logic had, in the preceding books, placed in the arena the instruments of disputation and, as it were, the weapons of his recruits, while he unfolded the meaning of simple expressions and likewise disclosed the nature of propositions and places.

[Col. 0910A]

He then teaches the exercise of the instruments and in some fashion imparts to his recruits the art of engagement. He shows the ways of proposing and answering, proving and escaping; he sets the limbs of the combatants, as it were, in motion; and by precepts he shapes the ability for which all the foregoing matters were presented.

To maintain the proportion of the foregoing comparison: just as the *Categories* are elementary books, the *On Interpretation* syllabic books, and the preceding *Topics* books concerning words, so the eighth book of the *Topics* is constructive of arguments, whose elements or places were shown in the preceding books.

It alone deals with the precepts from which the art is put together; and, if it is kept by heart and continually exercised in practice, it contributes more to the knowledge of disputation than nearly all the books of dialectic which our modern teachers were accustomed to read in the schools. Without it, one disputes not by art but by chance.

[Col. 0910B]

Yet, if it is to be of the greatest use, knowledge of the other books is necessary. Although they rarely abound in precepts, they provide the most useful teaching concerning things and language. Since the exercise of dialectic is directed toward another person, it teaches equals—whom it has produced and armed with arguments and places—to handle their weapons, to join battle with words rather than hands, and it imbues them with such caution that it is evident that the precepts of all eloquence, drawn principally from this source, flow as from the primitive fountain of their origin.

For it is unquestionably true, as Cicero and Quintilian acknowledge, that rhetoricians and writers on the arts took from here not only assistance but the very beginning of rhetoric; although it was later expanded by its own institutions.

Thus the entire activity of dialectic, because each person is the other’s judge, takes place between questioner and respondent. Each attains his end if he omits none of the relevant possibilities and presses his proposition in such a way as to free both himself and his argument from reproach. The occasion for reproach is not always the same: often the fault lies in the proposition, often in the proposer.

[Col. 0910C]

For, as Aristotle says, it is not equally within either party’s power to bring a common work to a good end. Both one who asks questions contentiously disputes badly, and one who, in answering, does not concede what appears evident or admit anything the questioner wishes to investigate. It is also evident that argument itself and the questioner are not to be reproached in the same manner.

For nothing prevents the argument from being bad while the questioner, as circumstances allow, disputes most effectively against the respondent. Indeed, against difficult people it may not be possible immediately to construct the syllogisms one wishes, but only such as circumstances permit. A bad partner is one who obstructs the common work.

Whether Aristotle teaches more usefully, more subtly, or more strictly how either party’s reproach should be made or avoided, I am uncertain. The work of a good questioner is to make the respondent assert highly improbable things, and other things besides those necessary because of the position. The respondent’s task is to ensure that impossibility, or something contrary to opinion, seems to follow not because of him but because of the position.

[Col. 0910D]

For it may be a different fault to posit first what ought not to be posited, and to fail afterwards to preserve what has been posited in the proper manner. The opponent, even if he sometimes labours to secure a universal through induction, or to lengthen the argument, or to make the argument clearer, regards concealment of the conclusion as the chief virtue in all things, so that, once the argument has been completed in its conclusion, the question may be asked: “Why?”

Thus, in *The Marriage of Mercury and Philology*, Dialectic carries a serpent in her hand and formulas of argument, so that the unwary and unlearned may be bitten by the serpent’s craftiness that conceals the proposition, or that the wicked may be instructed or convicted by formulas of reasoning.

This caution consists in the order and manner of carrying out the proposition, whether one must divide, define, or infer. It proceeds correctly from prior knowledge of places, arguments, and other forms of expression by which definitions and divisions are explained. For the places for arguing, dividing, and defining are for the most part common; but the power of the art is more vigorous in argumentation.

[Col. 0911A]

It is stronger in syllogisms themselves, whether the syllogism is complete in its own integrity or hastens to its conclusion, after removal of the middle proposition, in the manner of an enthymeme. Hence its use is more directed to another person.

Induction is gentler, whether it proceeds with a more deliberate pace from many cases to a universal or particular conclusion, or leaps with keener force from one introduced example to one conclusion by inference. This latter mode is more fitting for orators, though it is sometimes useful to the dialectician for ornament or explanation; for it is more persuasive than compelling. Hence, as Marcus Tullius testifies in his rhetorical works, Socrates used this kind of argument very frequently.

But when examples, whether many or single, are brought forward to prove something, they should be appropriate and drawn from things known to us: examples such as Homer’s, not such as Choerilus’s. If they are borrowed from authors, a Greek should use Homer, while a Latin writer should use Virgil and Lucan; for domestic examples move more strongly, and unknown ones do not establish doubtful matters.

[Col. 0911B]

Moreover, for concealing the proposition—or rather, so that each may more readily attain the aim of the contest—*idiotismus* and *orthonoismus* are very useful: each should so disguise his art that he is believed either not to possess it or, though possessing it, not to wish to use it. For display of art is always suspect, while, conversely, those who advance by a straightforward way are more readily admitted.

But above all it benefits both parties faithfully to know what the intention of those in conflict concerns. For unless it is made clear what has been posited, it is not easy to argue; from this arise disputes about a word, or often no dispute at all. Argument makes no progress unless the understanding of the disputants rests upon some common point. For opposition to occur, the same road must be travelled.

Therefore either there must be one question, or a multiplicity must be distinguished by its respective arguments. Hence Aristotle says that, since a respondent is permitted to say, “I do not understand,” when he does not understand, and, when a term is used in several senses, is not compelled to affirm or deny, it is plain that first, unless what is said is clear, one should not hesitate to say that one does not understand.

[Col. 0911C]

For a difficulty often arises because questioners do not state their question clearly. But if what is said is known yet has several senses, then, if it is true or false in every sense, it should simply be conceded or denied. If, however, it is false in one sense and true in another, one must indicate that it is spoken in several senses and that for this reason one sense is false and another true. For what is uncertain after division would have been doubtful from the beginning if one had perceived it then.

But if one did not foresee the ambiguity and, considering one sense, made a concession, one must tell the person who leads the discussion toward the other sense: “I made the concession not with this sense in view, but with the other.” For when several things fall under the same name or the same expression, ambiguity is easier.

But if what is asked is clear and simple, one must answer either yes or no. As Aulus Gellius says: “He who, in such matters, answers more or less than is asked of him does not know, or pretends not to know, the straight line of correct disputation.”

[Col. 0911D]

Indeed, one who obstructs his fellow disputant either by verbosity or by a distorted reply is not merely a bad partner but manifestly insolent—especially if, having no counter-instance, he contradicts a universal after particular cases have been admitted. For to obstruct an argument which is thus, or appears thus, without a counter-instance is insolence.

Therefore, if a universal is evident in many instances and one who has no counter-instance does not concede it universally, it is clear that he is insolent—unless perhaps he argues against it on the ground that the inference is untrue. For if the consequent is false, it is evident that it does not follow from true antecedents; since falsehood never follows from truth, “because the uncorrupted bosom of truth neither begets nor nourishes a lie.”

Yet it is not enough to argue the contrary, because many things contrary to opinions are often not readily resolved when arguments struggle on both sides. Thus Zeno maintains that motion and traversing a stadium cannot occur, while Empedocles argues conversely that all things move.

[Col. 0912A]

But the opinion of a few, especially one not supported by a most firm argument, does not invalidate an equally firm and more common opinion. Thus insolent is one who, in such matters, uses neither counter-instances nor contrary arguments. For in disputations insolence is a reply outside these modes which corrupts the syllogism.

This is so on the respondent’s side. Yet it is likewise present in the questioner if, once what has been conceded has been made clear, he proceeds to the contrary on the foolish pretext of petty words—refusing the faithful meaning, hunting syllables, and disputing vainly about a name. Insolence is the worse the more fiercely someone presses in this manner.

Yet either party may obstruct the other’s purpose without the fault of insolence if he properly resists or presses by the duties of his own role: for example, if someone presses a person slow by nature or habit through the use of speed; if someone restrains a person keen by intelligence or continual practice through the delay of deliberateness; if one conceals his purpose in order to deceive by art; or if the other reveals what has been concealed in order prudently to escape—and very many things in this manner.

[Col. 0912B]

But if something false appears to follow from something true, even if it is not clear where the fallacy lies, it is certain that the syllogism is sophistical, or that some other argument is deceptive and treacherous and ought not to be trusted. This belongs more to contentious disputes than to demonstration or dialectical exercise. For a sophism is a contentious syllogism; a *philosophema* is a demonstrative syllogism; an argument is a dialectical syllogism; but an aphorism is a dialectical syllogism of contradiction.

[Col. 0912C]

Knowledge of all these things is necessary, and practice in each of these capacities is highly useful. One must therefore become accustomed to disputation and rehearse the first principles by heart; one must distinguish necessary and probable things from their opposites and from one another; the meanings of words must be examined, so that a person possessing knowledge may easily turn one expression into several, or reduce several to one.

Greater diligence is required in establishing or rejecting universals, since in them progress or danger is more clearly apparent; for one cannot syllogize without a universal. Moreover, although brevity is the chief excellence in every discourse, it works more effectively in discourse directed toward another, is received more pleasingly, and shines forth more clearly; for prolixity causes the greatest loss in all things.

If the proposed argument cannot be hastened, delay must be relieved by novelty of matters which nevertheless do not appear irrelevant. For, as Aristotle says, whoever asks one argument over a long time inquires badly: for if the respondent answers what is asked, it is plain that the questioner asks many questions, or frequently the same ones. Therefore he either hunts for something or has no syllogism, since every syllogism proceeds from few premises. If the respondent does not answer, then he does not reproach him or withdraws.

[Col. 0912D]

Questions may be multiplied in order that an occasion for censure may be given and that grounds for justified reproach may be extracted from any side. This is often praiseworthy, but is sometimes a sign of deficiency, because the proposition is not fixed or the person who repeatedly traces the same circuits, circles through the same air, and continually moves without advancing has no open path toward progress.
