Heschelinus the smith [Note: [Col. 0913] The Cambridge manuscript reads “Heschelinus, smith of Conches”; but “Master William of Conches” would be preferable.], as Master William related, followed the practice of those who seek nothing definite in disputations, and conducted his smith’s craft as such people conduct dialectic.

For he awaited the end of his work not from art but from fortune. While he rolled a heated mass upon the anvil and shaped it beneath the blow of a hammer, if he were asked what he was making, he did not answer anything definite, but named many alternatives: a knife, perhaps, or a sickle, or a ploughshare, or anything else to which chance might bring the material.

[Col. 0913A]

For he produced not what he wished, but what he could. Nothing less befits a skilled craftsman than to follow chance rather than the judgment of reason. Therefore one must seek an abundance of arguments from every quarter for establishing or overthrowing a position, so that one may acquire the ability to press and to resist.

And if an adversary is lacking, each person should test with himself what arguments, how many, and how weighty, support or attack the issue of the question proposed. Thus everyone will easily become fit to compel and resist; and whether the task is to contend, persuade, or philosophize, one who has pressing arguments and counter-arguments will either prevail, escape with glory, or be overcome honourably and without disgrace.

Among the ancient Romans there was this military discipline: those to be trained in arms were accustomed from early youth to imaginary warfare, and young men continually practised it in play, so that later, in the necessities of the state, they might triumph successfully. Each learned the use of weapons and how one ought to attack cavalry or infantry, now to press, now to retreat, now to strike with a cutting blow, now with a thrust. These things were learned beforehand at home.

[Col. 0913B]

In the same way, dialectic must possess a ready command of its instruments: it must know its principles, abound in probable arguments, and have at hand every method of syllogizing and inducing. It must also measure the adversary’s strength, since the outcome of the undertaking often depends on this.

For it is not enough that only one party bring a common work to a good conclusion. Just as the incompetence of a questioner or teacher, so often the slowness of the hearer or the difficulty of the matter prevents one who proceeds by art from attaining his aim. As Palladius says, a great part of prudence is to estimate the person with whom one is dealing.

The law too provides that no one ought to be ignorant of the condition of the person with whom he contracts. Therefore one must proceed differently with an educated person and differently with one known to be uneducated: the educated person should be pressed by syllogistic arguments, the uneducated by inductive ones.

[Col. 0913C]

But for anyone to make progress, as zeal for exercise is necessary, so too there must be an underlying vein of praiseworthy natural ability. Good natural ability is that which readily assents to truth and rejects falsehood. It first arises from nature through the incentive of innate reason; then it becomes more vigorous through love of the good and through practice.

Practice indeed strengthens exercise and produces the ability to prove and test truth, though more easily and effectively if it is supported by the concise aid of art and precepts. Yet, though useful exercise with another person is possible, conversation seems more useful than solitary meditation. For as iron sharpens iron, so through another’s voice the mind of one engaged in conversation is stirred more keenly and effectively—especially when conversation is held with a wise or modest person.

Otherwise, the mouth of the fool, which bubbles over with folly, and the insolent person, who knows no moderation, do not so easily educate the minds of young people, who seek to conform themselves to others by imitation, as they corrupt them. They do not shape them for life or train them for knowledge, but make the soul foolish and poison the tongue.

[Col. 0913D]

Thus, although nothing is more beneficial than mutual discussion, one should not dispute with everyone or practise against just anyone. For, as Aristotle says, arguments must become bad against certain people. For against one who tries in every way to seem to escape, it is indeed right to try in every way to construct a syllogism; but it is not noble, because one ought not immediately to engage with everyone whatsoever. For a laborious conversation must result, since those trained in disputation cannot refrain from contentious debate.

Nor should one dispute everywhere, always, or about every matter. There are many things which do not admit disputation; some transcend human reasoning and are consecrated to faith alone. There are also matters which appear equally unworthy of questioner and respondent,

[Col. 0914A]

and prove that those who contend about them are either foolish or ignorant. These are matters which confer no benefit if known and cause no harm if unknown. To devote effort to them prepares not so much an approach to philosophy as a retreat from it; for it is an indication not of an advancing but of a failing mind.

Hence blessed Ambrose says elegantly: “I readily confess that I do not know what I do not know—indeed, what it profits nothing to know.”

The investigation of probable matters, from which human knowledge almost wholly proceeds, in a manner flows from the fountain of the *Topics*. Once discovered through the connections of things and expressions, they provide an abundance of arguments. Thus, if someone has been sufficiently trained in them, he will recognize the truth of the Pythagorean saying that concerning every matter one can argue plausibly on either side. But to apprehend truth itself as it is belongs to divine or angelic perfection. Each person approaches it more intimately insofar as he seeks truth more eagerly, loves it more ardently, tests it more faithfully, and delights more joyfully in contemplating it.

[Col. 0914B]

I have briefly set down these matters at the urging of the challenger, not because I have fully described the usefulness or purport of the preceding books—for that is beyond my powers and foreign to my purpose—but in order to show that the points proposed and accused of uselessness are serviceable. The same purpose obtains in what follows: namely, that we may meet the opponent rather than write commentaries on arts which everyone teaches or learns. Whoever does not like these things, let him teach better ones.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0915]

[Col. 0915C]

I am ashamed to return to the subject that I had interrupted and that should previously have been set before more serious studies. For the advance of age, the rank of my order, and the character of my position—to say nothing for the present of pressing causes and the burdens of household affairs—required a different occupation.

But since the opponent’s rashness does not rest, and you, whose wishes must be followed, seek my judgment of the matter, I shall run through, in the concise brevity permitted by the occasion, what I think. It would have been pleasant, to use Seneca’s words, to return to ancient times and look back upon better years, had not bitterness, arising partly from bodily illness and partly from another anxiety, weighed down my mind.

Yet because you thought fit to examine my conflict with Cornificius, I descend unwillingly and, as it were, dragged into the arena of this wrestling-school. But enough of this.

## CHAPTER I. That the book of the *Analytics* examines arguments

The champion-teacher of the Peripatetic discipline, which labours above all others in the investigation of truth, disdaining an incomplete work, composed the whole; confident that the perfection of every art proclaims the glory of its author. Therefore, having supplied the instruments and practice of invention, he sat, as it were, in a refining furnace and sought to forge a certain instrument of examination, by which arguments might be most carefully tested.

[Col. 0915D]

This is the book of the *Analytics*, which pertains chiefly to judgment, yet contributes in some degree to invention. For the branches of learning are interconnected, and each borrows its perfection from the others. Scarcely any, if indeed there is any at all, can rise to its height without another’s aid.

But that you may fully know the judgment of my opinion—what I think of this work—consider the following briefly.

## CHAPTER II. That this knowledge is useful for all things, and whence it received its name

The knowledge of the *Analytics* is indeed highly useful, and anyone who professes logic without it is ridiculous. To explain the reason for the name: what the Greeks call *Analyticē* (Ἀναλυτική), we may call “resolutory”; but we shall give a more familiar account if we call it “equivalent expression,” for they call *ana* “equal” and *lexim* “expression.”

[Col. 0916A]

When speech is insufficiently understood, it is common for us to wish that it be resolved into something more familiar in equivalent terms. Hence my interpreter, whenever he heard an unknown word, especially in compounds, would say, “Analyze this,” by which he meant: explain it equivalently. This resolution greatly assists the understanding toward knowledge.

Yet, although the teaching is necessary, the book is not necessary to the same degree; for whatever it contains is transmitted elsewhere more easily and reliably, though certainly nowhere more truly or more forcefully. Indeed, it compels assent even from an unwilling person, for it is forceful and, with something of Caesar’s impetuosity, “rejoices to have no roads except when the enemy has been overcome.” It assigns no importance to anyone’s friendship.

This is altogether fitting for the office of a judge, since affection for friend or enemy commonly perverts the integrity of judgment. Yet, through the confusion of examples and the transposition of letters—which Aristotle inserted partly deliberately, partly for brevity’s sake, and partly lest falsehood should somewhere be alleged in the examples—the work is so confused that one reaches with great labour what can be taught most easily.

[Col. 0916B]

And often, while avoiding falsehood, he is neither true nor false, or perhaps lies—if contentiousness gives rise to calumny.

## CHAPTER III. That the book is not equally useful for acquiring phraseology
[Col. 0917C] But just as rules are useful and necessary for knowledge, so the book is almost useless for forming style, which we may call the equipment of language. For style is a ready facility with words in any language. Knowledge, therefore, must be firmly fixed in the memory, and very many words must be excerpted; for such ought to be the caution of one engaged in philosophy: always to attend to the understanding of words, and besides this diligently to extract words that may conveniently be transferred elsewhere and may have more frequent use. The rest are like leaves without fruit, and for that reason are either trampled underfoot or left on their tree.

Hence those who follow Aristotle, amid a confusion of names and words and tangled subtlety, seem, in order to claim what is their own, to blunt the wits of others, and to have chosen for themselves the worst part. Our Englishman Adam seemed to me, beyond the rest, to have laboured under this fault in the book which he entitled *The Art of Disputation*. And, “Would that he had spoken well the good things which he said!” Although his intimates and supporters ascribe this to subtlety, very many have interpreted it as arising from the folly or envy of the vain man, as they call him. For he reproduced Aristotle’s entanglement of words so exactly that a sober hearer may rightly add:

> Is this not frothy, with its fat rind,  
> Like old brushwood cooked in a huge cork-bark?  
> (Persius, *Satires* I.97)

Nevertheless, gratitude must be shown to authors, because, by drawing from their spring, we are enriched through another’s labour.

## CHAPTER IV. The plan of the first book

[Col. 0918A]

But what must be known is presented most truly and most certainly. This includes: what a dialectical or demonstrative proposition is; what a universal, particular, or indefinite proposition is; what a term is, namely predicate or subject; what a perfect or imperfect syllogism is; what it is to be in the whole or not to be in the whole; which propositions can be converted for use in syllogizing and which cannot; and what obtains in those matters which, in modern usage, are said to concern natural, contingent, or remote matter.

After setting these things forth, he appends the principles of the three figures; and, having first defined both the extremes and the middle, he teaches how many modes there are in each figure and which they are, arising from the combination of the extremes. Thus the seed of the reasoning of those modes is given which, as Boethius states, Theophrastus and Eudemus added.

Then, after dealing with modal propositions, he passes to mixtures of necessary or contingent propositions with propositions of inherence, showing what follows from these in each figure. Yet I do not say that Aristotle himself, anywhere that I have read, did more than deal sufficiently, perhaps for his purpose, with modal propositions; but he supplied a most trustworthy method for proceeding in all matters. Expositors of Holy Scripture say that the consideration of modes is most necessary, and that great attention must be given to a mode, whether it is expressed or tacit. For in the phrase, “They have destroyed those whom you have perfected,” the mode is left unspoken and understood just as if the mode “by will,” that is, voluntarily, were added. Likewise here:

> He devours the tender lamb in hope.

For, as they say, mode is a sort of intermediate disposition of the terms. And indeed, although no one could suffice to enumerate individually all the modes from which propositions are called modal—nor does the art require this—yet schoolmasters dispute from them very conveniently and, if I may speak without offending the multitude, more conveniently, I think, than Aristotle himself. Certainly, whether they are called modal on account of a true mode or merely their form, knowledge of them is necessary in a great many passages of Scripture.

But in these matters I judge the authority of usage to be especially important: it increases, diminishes, alters, or empties the meanings of expressions. This is clear in the case of “contingent,” whose very broad usage, by which it was equivalent to “possible,” nowhere goes beyond the walls of the schools in common modern usage.

To this he adds the source of competence in syllogizing, since it is little to know the generation of syllogisms unless one also has the ability to make them. There follows the method of reducing syllogisms to the modes of the first figure; and thus the plan of the first book is concluded.

## CHAPTER V. The plan of the second book

The second book passes to the method of inference, which appears in the form of a conclusion, adding how a true conclusion may be syllogized from false premises in the second and third figures—a point perhaps missed by those who contend that nothing follows from falsehood. Then he proceeds to circular syllogisms [Col. 0919A] and treats them in all the figures; then to the conversions of syllogisms in every figure.

In order that imperfect syllogisms may be brought back to perfect ones and the validity of all alike may become clear, the matters which constitute the form of direct reasoning come first. The method of hypothesis is then added, which establishes the proposed point by the necessity of an impossible or improbable consequence. Its method is this: if the person drawing the conclusion is not accepted, take the contradictory of the conclusion and one of the conceded premises; arrange them in the first figure, and infer the opposite of one of the conceded premises. He shows how this is done in every figure and proves that all modes are valid through an impossible consequence.

Moreover, he clearly explains how, and in what figure, one syllogizes from opposed propositions. He also adds the rule concerning begging the question, an inquiry quite suitable both to the demonstrator and to the dialectician, although the latter delights in probability while the former embraces truth alone.

Further, if something that is not a cause is posited as a cause—for example, when someone claims that he has been led to an impossibility not by the compelling force of the inference but because some false proposition has been assumed—there follows a discussion of the cause of a false conclusion, of the *catasyllogism*, the *elenchus*, the fallacy according to opinion, and the conversion of the middle and extremes; though the whole usefulness of this could be taught much more conveniently.

The method of reducing induction is then added, which he calls a rhetorical syllogism, and likewise that of example and deduction. Then he explains what an objection is; what *eikos* (ἐίκος) is, which he calls a probable proposition, although it may admit an objection—that is, although it does not hold invariably—as “mothers love, stepmothers are envious.” He also explains what a sign is and how an enthymeme consists of probabilities and signs.

Finally, he treats the knowledge of natures. This is indeed a great chapter, and although it contributes something to the proposed subject, it by no means fulfils the promise made. One thing I know: by the benefit of this chapter I have seen no one made perfect in the knowledge of natures.

## CHAPTER VI. On the difficulty of the *Posterior Analytics* and its causes

The doctrine of the *Posterior Analytics* is subtle and accessible to few minds; and it is plainly so for several reasons. For it contains the art of demonstration, which is difficult beyond the other methods of reasoning. Moreover, because those who use it are rare, it has now almost passed out of use, since the practice of demonstration exists scarcely except among mathematicians, and among them nearly only among geometers. Even this discipline is not commonly practised among us, except perhaps in Iberia or on the borders of Africa. For these peoples practise geometry especially for astronomy’s sake; Egypt likewise does so, and certain peoples of Arabia.

Further, the book in which demonstrative doctrine is taught is far more confused than the others, owing to transposition of words, displacement of letters, and the unfamiliarity of examples borrowed from different disciplines. Finally—something which does not touch the author—it has been so corrupted by the fault of copyists [Col. 0920A] that it has almost as many obstacles as chapters; and it is well where the obstacles are not more numerous than the chapters. Hence many lay the blame for the difficulty upon the translator, maintaining that the book has not reached us correctly translated.

## CHAPTER VII. Why Aristotle deserved the name “philosopher” beyond others

Among the Peripatetics, the science of demonstration possessed such authority that Aristotle, who surpassed nearly all other philosophers and in nearly all matters, claimed the common name “philosopher” for himself by a certain right of ownership because he had transmitted demonstrative doctrine. Hence, they say, the title “philosopher” found its settled place in him. If I am not believed, let Burgundio of Pisa be heard, from whom I received this statement.

And because this science dispels the darkness of ignorance and makes a person knowledgeable through a certain prerogative of foreknowledge, it frequently brings the Academic school—which we profess in matters doubtful to the wise—from its gloom into the light. Just as Aristotle, first forging an instrument of examination, equipped a judge, so in these matters he raises his follower to the authority of a teacher. The order is elegant indeed: one who fulfils rightly the office of judge is deservedly elevated to the teacher’s chair.

## CHAPTER VIII. The function of demonstration; its materials and method; and why sense is the principle of knowledge

But who is qualified for this discipline? Certainly, even if someone attains it in one respect, no one attains it perfectly in many respects. One must know beforehand the principles of the disciplines and, from these, infer by linked arguments a necessary consequence of truths; one must, so to speak, press the matter more firmly, lest a gap seem to arise from a defect of necessity and prejudice demonstrative knowledge.

Not every knowledge is demonstrative, but only that which proceeds from truths that are primary and immediate. For just as not every syllogism is a demonstration, though every demonstration is a syllogism, so knowledge encompasses demonstrative knowledge non-convertibly. Common conceptions of the mind therefore come first, then things known through themselves; and from these demonstration arises.

It matters, however, whether the things known are more known by nature or more known to us. Things nearer to sense are more known to us; things more remote—universals, that is—are more known simply and by nature. From the principles of the disciplines, therefore, through immediate propositions, that is, propositions requiring no proof, the demonstrator has a path to the goal at which he aims.

And although this science is said to pertain especially to judgment, it contributes greatly to discovery as well. It teaches from what materials and in what way demonstration may occur, when it may occur, and how one should use proper or common principles; for sciences provide mutual aids to one another. Since not every topic is suitable for the demonstrator—for example, the topic from accident, because with regard to corruptible things there is neither demonstration nor knowledge simply speaking—he claims the necessary topics for himself and yields the rest to the dialectician and the orator. These are satisfied if the syllogism is made as probable as possible.

[Col. 0921A] Moreover, it explains which syllogisms and which propositions ought to be used, and what force the quantity or quality of a proposition, carefully considered, contributes in establishing a point. It discloses which syllogism suits which question and what figure is appropriate to a syllogism; and thus it establishes the science of demonstration, which reason proves to be so with certainty as though it were held by bodily sense.

For common conceptions receive their credibility through induction from particulars. It is impossible to contemplate universals except through induction, because, as Aristotle says, things spoken of by abstraction become known from being unknown through inductions. But induction is impossible for those without sense. For sense concerns particulars; nor can knowledge of particulars be obtained either from universals without induction or through induction without sense.

Thus memory arises from sense; experience from memory frequently repeated many times; and from experiences springs the principle of science or art. Further, from art, strengthened by use and practice, comes the capacity to carry out what art requires to be done. Thus bodily sense, which is the first power or first exercise of the soul, lays the foundations of all arts and forms a pre-existent cognition which not only opens a path to first principles but also produces them.

## CHAPTER IX. What sense is; and how every branch of philosophy is strengthened from it through imagination

[Col. 0921C]

This becomes clearer when each branch is considered more carefully. For since, according to Aristotle, sense is a natural power that indicates things, where sense fails there is either no knowledge at all or scarcely any. If someone investigates with the physicist the works of nature composed of elements, or of matter and form, he borrows his path of reasoning from the evidence of the senses. If he abstracts figures with the mathematician, or divides numbers of discrete multitude, or considers the magnitude of continuous bodies, he presents these to trustworthy eyes. The philosopher who practises the rational discipline, and who is a client of both the physicist and the mathematician, begins from what is established by the testimony of the senses and advances to knowledge of intelligible and incorporeal things.

Sense, according to Chalcidius, is an affection of the body arising from things placed outside it and variously striking the body, passing through to the soul. Unless this affection has some force, it neither reaches the soul nor brings its form within the range of sense. If the affection is pleasing, it produces pleasure by its gentleness; if it grows stronger, it is called joy. But if it wounds by its harshness, it produces pain.

Aristotle, however, holds that sense is rather a power of the soul than an affection of the body. Yet this same power is aroused by affections in order to form its judgment concerning things. Since it perceives things, it stores within itself their images. Thus, through retention and frequent recurrence, it forms for itself, as it were, the treasury of memory. When it turns over images of things, imagination arises. Imagination not only remembers precepts but, by its own liveliness, advances to fashion examples in conformity with them.

[Col. 0922A] Yet it has been asked whether imagination differs from sense by nature or only by its mode of perception. I recall philosophers who held that, just as the substance of the soul is incorporeal, simple, and indivisible, so there is one power which it exercises in many ways according to the diversity of things. In their view, then, the same power now senses, now remembers, now imagines; now distinguishes by investigating, now understands by grasping what it has investigated.

But more take the opposite view: that the soul is simple in quantity but composite in qualities, and that, as it is subject to many affections, so it uses many powers. And I would readily believe that there are more adherents of this view than their books make known, since the soul, while it is away from the Lord, is so ignorant of its origin that it scarcely recognizes its own powers.

## CHAPTER X. On imagination; and how affections arise from it, by which the soul is composed or, when disturbed, overthrown

Imagination therefore springs from the root of the senses through the kindling material of memory, and by a certain *symplasis*—which we may call “conformation”—it beholds not only presence but also absence, whether in place or time. Hence this:

> So she sat, so she was dressed, so she spun the thread;  
> So the hair thrown upon her neck became her.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti* II.771)

That imagination is abstracting is suggested by Maro, when Andromache confesses that in a certain act of recollection she has drawn forth for herself the image of Astyanax:

> O you, the one remaining image of my Astyanax!  
> Such were his eyes, such his hands, such his face;  
> And now he would be growing into youth of equal age with you.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* III.488)

And because, as Plato says in the *Republic*, it is easy to grasp the secrets of nature, imagination forms, from things that frequently occur, an image of things to come out of the quality of what it presently senses or has at some time sensed. Therefore, if it conceives a harsh affection concerning the future, fear arises; but hope if it conceives something pleasant through usefulness or delight.

From this also arises desire, a most destructive plague and one very hostile to the purpose of philosophy. For it is impossible for anyone to devote himself at once to desire and to philosophy. Desire is compounded of opposites: hope of enjoyment produces pleasure, but delay produces sadness and pain. If these grow strong enough to disorder and disturb the soul, anger arises from that agitation.

Thus, to restrain unlawful movements, imagination produces caution, which avoids what is harmful to it: the sources of pain, anger, desire, and their consequences, such as envy, hatred, detraction, lust, and vanity. Yet while it is too cautious, it approaches timidity; while insufficiently cautious, rashness. In this way the other affections arise from sense through imagination’s assistance, including love, which works greatly for the protection of the body, the preservation of useful things, or the procuring of offspring.

## CHAPTER XI. What imagination is; opinion, and the fallibility of opinion and sense; and the origin of *phronēsis*, which we call prudence

[Col. 0923A]

Imagination, then, is the first movement of a soul struck from without, by which the second judgment is exercised or the first returns through recollection. For the first judgment is active in sense when it declares something to be white or black, hot or cold. The second belongs to imagination: when, retaining an image, it declares something perceived to be such and such, judging concerning the future or what is distant. The judgment of either kind is called opinion.

Opinion is reliable if it judges things as they are; if otherwise, it is untrustworthy. Aristotle calls it an affection of the soul because, while it is exercised, images of things are impressed upon the soul. If one image is impressed in place of another, then, from the error by which it is deceived in judgment, the opinion is called deceptive or false.

For the senses are very often deceived, not only in little children, where reason is thought to be inactive, but also in mature age. Aristotle teaches this when he says that all infants take men for fathers and women for mothers because immature sense is deceived and cannot offer a firm judgment. A stick in water appears broken even to the most perceptive observers.

Because the soul detects the deceptiveness of the senses, it is stirred to hold onto something reliable upon which it may confidently rest without error. From this stirring arises the virtue which the Greeks call *phronēsis* (φρόνησις), and the Latins prudence.

## CHAPTER XII. What prudence is; its matter and parts; and how knowledge comes from sense

[Col. 0923C]

Prudence, as Cicero says, is a virtue of the soul exercised in inquiry, perception, and the skilful discovery of truth. The matter of this virtue, in which it is exercised, is truth; the matter of the other virtues is certain domestic necessities. Therefore, lest it be deceived from any direction, it directs its gaze toward future things and forms foresight; or, recalling the past to mind, it stores it in memory; or it is shrewd about present matters and produces a form of astuteness or craft; or it extends itself equally toward everything, and circumspection is born.

When it has attained truth, it passes into the form of knowledge. From these points it is clear that, since imagination arises from sense, opinion from these two, and prudence from opinion—prudence growing strong into knowledge—knowledge draws its origin from sense. For, as was said, many sensations, or even one sensation, produce one memory; many memories produce experience; many experiences yield a rule; many rules yield one art; and art yields capacity.

## CHAPTER XIII. The difference between knowledge and wisdom; and what faith is

Hence the ancients referred prudence or knowledge to the understanding of temporal and sensible things, but understanding or wisdom to spiritual things. For knowledge is commonly spoken of concerning human matters, wisdom concerning divine matters. Knowledge depends so greatly upon sense that, when things known by sense are withdrawn from sense, there is no knowledge of them. This is established by Aristotle.

There may nevertheless be reliable opinion, as when the sun is believed likely to return after night. Since human things are transitory, there can scarcely be a certain judgment of opinion concerning them. But if what is not wholly certain is held to be certain, there is an approach to faith, which Aristotle defines as strong opinion.

Faith is most necessary both in human and divine matters. Without it, contracts could not be made between people nor any exchanges conducted; indeed, even the exchange of merits and rewards among human beings could not exist if faith were removed. Faith has merit when it holds true articles concerning religion; and it is, as the Apostle says, “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11).

[Col. 0924B] It also stands between opinion and knowledge, because through its strength it makes certain what knowledge does not reach in its certainty. Hence Master Hugh: “Faith is the voluntary certainty of absent things, placed above opinion and below knowledge.” But here the term “knowledge” is extended and stretched to include comprehension of divine things.

## CHAPTER XIV. Knowledge of *phronēsis* and *alētheia*; the origin of prudence and its rationale

Because truth is the matter of prudence—for prudence labours to comprehend truth—the ancients imagined *phronēsis* and *alētheia* (ἀλήθεια, “truth”) to be sisters, since prudence has a certain divine kinship with truth. Therefore, when prudence is perfect, it cannot be shut out from the sight of truth. But because this does not belong to human beings, our frail condition eagerly seeks hidden truth.

[Col. 0924C] Indeed, because of the deceptions of sense and opinion, it scarcely proceeds reliably in the investigation of truth and is scarcely secure in apprehending it; for it remembers that it has been deceived and may be deceived again. It is therefore troubled in order to enjoy a firm perception and an undoubted judgment, which may be called reason; for the examination of reason is settled and firm.

Thus *phronēsis* gives birth to philology, when love of truth moves prudence toward knowledge of things concerning which it desires to render a sincere and firm judgment. Philology, like philosophy, is a moderated term: just as it is easier to seek than to possess wisdom, so it is easier to love reason than to exercise it. For reason—that is, the sincere firmness of judgment—belongs to few.

## CHAPTER XV. What reason is; the many meanings of “reason”; and eternal reasons

[Col. 0924D]

The soul, then, struck by the senses and more forcefully stirred by the concern of prudence, brings itself forth and, gathering its powers into one, studies more intently to avoid the deceptions of senses and opinions. By its own attention it sees more keenly, holds more firmly, and judges more sincerely. This is the power called reason.

For reason is a power of spiritual nature which distinguishes bodily and incorporeal things and seeks to examine things by a firm and sincere judgment. Its judgment itself is also designated by the name “reason.” Moreover, the things concerning which reason alone judges, and whose being is distinct from the nature of sensible and individual things, are called “reasons” (*rationes*). Father Augustine and many others assert that these are eternal.

These are the things in which, from the beginning and without beginning, the primordial Reason established the decree of eternal constitution and the order of its own disposition. If I call that primordial Reason the Wisdom of God, I shall certainly not be wrong. It is plainly possible to find infinitely many such things even among truths themselves: that God is God; that the Father has a Son; that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with both—these are indeed propositions, but true from eternity, firm by divine judgment.

This is clear not only in truths but also in other matters: the ratio of two to three, and likewise of three to two, and countless matters of this kind are eternal, according to Augustine. If this seems absurd to anyone, let him read Augustine’s book *On Free Choice of the Will*, and it will be clear that it is so.

## CHAPTER XVI. The distinction in the term’s multiplicity; irrational animals do not possess reason although they appear to discriminate; and how, according to the Hebrews, humanity received it

[Col. 0925B]

Cassiodorus, in his book *On the Soul*, uses this definition: “I call reason a probable movement of the mind which, through things conceded and known, leads to something unknown, arriving at the secret place of truth.” Thus both the power and the movement of the power are called reason.

Plato, in the *Republic*, says that this movement is the deliberative power of the soul. After weighing the kinds of things and their causes by reliable judgment, it examines what is honourable, useful, to be sought, or to be avoided. Brute animals also possess in some fashion a discriminating power: they distinguish foods, avoid traps, leap over precipices, and recognize kinship. Yet they do not exercise reason. They flourish by natural appetite and imagine many things, but cannot investigate the causes of things.

[Col. 0925C] The Hebrews say that this arises because, when at the beginning of creation the other creatures came together by the Lord’s ordering and, through the fostering warmth of heat and moisture, received a natural, animal, and sentient spirit—from which arise appetite and imagination, possessed by brute creatures—humanity alone received a power of reasoning more effectively and sincerely. For when God breathed life into humanity, he willed humanity to participate in divine reason.

The human spirit, because it is given by God and will return to God, alone meditates upon divine things and in this almost alone excels all other animals. For bodily things are apprehended not only by imagination but also by sense. Further, it knows in part the forms of bodily things and their actual coherence and incoherence. Sense sees a human being, certainly a bodily thing; it sees colours and movements, certainly forms of bodily things; it also sees a person move a hand, which is more than seeing a moving person—that is, one who moves a hand. If this seems surprising to anyone, let him defer to Augustine.

But reason transcends every sense and applies its judgment even to bodily and spiritual things. It contemplates all lower things and directs its gaze toward higher things.

Seneca’s definition agrees with that of the Hebrews, although he intended something else. He says: “Reason is a certain part of the divine Spirit immersed in human bodies.” This must either be accommodated to the error of the pagans, who supposed that the world-soul had been divided among individual souls and falsely asserted it to be the Holy Spirit, or interpreted more charitably: “part” should be understood as said not of quantity but of power. For, to express a figure of speech, he added “a certain.” Although reason is in some fashion a divine power, it is by no means a part of God, because God is of absolutely simple nature.

## CHAPTER XVII. The office of reason; why the senses are in the head, over which reason presides; and the handmaids of philology

Since reason is ennobled by divine origin and powerful through a divine activity, the decree of all philosophy has established that it should be cultivated above all else. It restrains disordered movements and brings all things into conformity with the rule of goodness, so that nothing may resist the divine ordering. Whoever obeys that ordering will pass through life with a happy course; whoever rejects it, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*, crawling through life’s lame and maimed path, is at last recalled to the underworld with his familiar folly.

Reason manages the care of body and soul and orders both. Whoever despises both is maimed and weak; whoever despises one is lame. Since reason examines the senses, which may be suspect because of their habit of deceiving, nature—the best parent of all—placed all the senses in the head, as a kind of senate in the soul’s Capitol. It established reason, like a mistress, in the citadel of the head, granting it a central seat between the imaginative cell and memory, so that, as though from a watchtower over senses and imaginations, [Col. 0926C] it might examine judgments.

Accordingly, because this power, though divine, is stirred as it were by a winnowing-fan of senses and imaginations, and because prudence, in investigating truth, seeks the sincere examination of reason and gives birth to philology, two handmaids continually accompany philology: *periergia* and *agrypnia* (ἀγρυπνία). *Periergia* is the effort that goes about the work; *agrypnia* is wakeful diligence, which moderates exertion so that there is nothing excessive, for love is not idle.

Philology has an earthly and mortal origin; but when it passes to divine things, it is made divine by a kind of immortality. For when prudence, which concerns earthly things, and love of reason rise to the mysteries of incorruptible truth and divine things, passing into wisdom, they are in some manner exempted from the condition of mortals.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The difference between reason and understanding; and what understanding is

By the same proportion by which reason transcends sense, understanding surpasses reason, as Plato attests in the *Republic*. For understanding attains what reason investigates: understanding enters into reason’s labours and stores up for itself in wisdom what preparatory reason has acquired.

Understanding, therefore, is the highest power of spiritual nature; it contains human reasons and has within itself the divine causes of all reasons naturally perceptible to it. There are divine reasons which surpass every sense, both human and angelic; and some become known more or less to different beings according to the decree of divine dispensation. Plato asserts that this belongs to God alone and to a very few chosen human beings.

## CHAPTER XIX. What wisdom is; and how it comes from sense through grace

Wisdom follows understanding, because the divine things which understanding has gathered from matters considered by reason have a sweet taste and kindle intelligent souls into love of themselves. I think it is called wisdom (*sapientia*) because in divine things it has a taste (*sapor*) of the good.

Hence the Fathers refer knowledge to the active life, but wisdom to the contemplative life. From these things it is clear that whoever reviews the foregoing stages will see that even wisdom flows from the wellspring of the senses, grace going before and assisting. So that we may enjoy prophetic testimony, fear itself—which is the beginning of wisdom (Psalm 110)—arises from sense or the imagination of punishment.

[Col. 0927B] When someone is troubled lest he be beaten, remembering the punisher, he avoids offending that punisher. He is also incited to obedience by sense or imagination of rewards, directed toward the one who has power to punish and to bless. Thus the person who avoids offence practises piety; but through experience of obedience he has gained knowledge. For this pertains to action.

If he becomes accustomed to experience, strength arises from habitual actions. In order to render rational obedience, which is most pleasing, counsel of deliberation concerning past or future acts arises. Understanding follows deliberation, retaining the better part in its bosom; for it concerns divine things, the taste, love, and attachment to which are finally true wisdom.

Nature, however, does not produce these stages, but grace. From the spring of the senses grace, according to its own will, draws forth diverse little shoots of knowledge and wisdom; it makes God’s invisible things manifest through the things that have been made, communicates what has been manifested in a certain unity of charity, and unites humanity to God.

## CHAPTER XX. On the knowledge, simplicity, and immortality of the soul, according to Cicero
Some minor philosophers therefore deny that there is any knowledge except of things perceived by the senses, on the ground that the passage to knowledge is from the senses. How contrary this is to the purpose of philosophy is plain. For the exercise of reason perishes—the exercise by which it seeks and retains within itself notions of things, which the Greeks call *ennoiai* [ἔννοιαι, “conceptions” or “notions”]—without which not even a name can be established.

It is therefore, as Cicero says in the *Tusculan Disputations*, the mark of great intellect to call the mind back from the senses and to draw thought away from habit. For God Himself, whom we understand, cannot be understood by us otherwise than when the mind is released, free, and separated from every mortal concretion. There is a certain singular nature and power of the soul, separated from these familiar and known natures: whatever it may be, it is surely divine. Yet the soul cannot fully see itself; rather, like the eye, the mind, not seeing itself, perceives other things. It does not see what is least—perhaps its own form. Although it sees that too; but let us leave this aside. It certainly sees its power, keenness, memory, movement, and swiftness. These are great, [Col. 0928A] divine, and everlasting. What its shape is, indeed, or where it dwells, ought not even to be asked.

Thus, although you do not see the human mind, just as you do not see God, nevertheless, as you recognize God from His works, so recognize the divine power of the mind from its memory of things, its invention, swiftness of movement, and every beauty of virtue. In the knowledge of the soul, moreover, unless we are altogether dullards in natural philosophy, we cannot doubt that nothing is mixed into souls, nothing concreted, joined, compounded, or double. Since this is so, it certainly cannot be separated, divided, torn apart, or pulled asunder; therefore it cannot perish.

These are Cicero’s words in the *Tusculan Disputations*, intended to teach both that the deliberative power—that is, reason—is divine, and that human souls are [Col. 0928B] immortal. These matters concerning sensory affection, and the powers and dignity of the soul, have been briefly sketched, so that it might be clear that, as Aristotle says, art or knowledge takes its origin from sense. If anyone wished to argue more fully about the powers of the soul, the subject would demand subtle intelligence, sharp ability, capacious memory, and unencumbered leisure; with diligent study, it would expand into the bulk of the greatest volumes. But those who wish to investigate the nature of the soul more carefully should reread not only the writings of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and the ancient philosophers, but also those of the Fathers, who have expressed the truth more faithfully. For doctors of the Church, and after them Claudianus, and other more recent authors, have written much about the soul [Col. 0928C]. Anyone unable to work through them may at least read the *Phrenouphysicon*, a book which discusses the soul most copiously. I do not, however, rank it above all the others. But enough of this: let us now return to our purpose.

## CHAPTER XXI. That Aristotle, though not sufficiently, supplied in what preceded a certain seedbed for hypotheticals.

The foregoing teaches dialectic and apodeictic, which we call demonstrative reasoning; yet in it hypothetical syllogisms have been treated little or not at all. Nevertheless Aristotle supplied a seedbed from which progress in this field could be made through the industry of others. For, when he showed the loci of both probable and necessary arguments, he showed [Col. 0928D] what follows from what, probably or necessarily. This, I think, bears especially upon the criterion of hypothetical propositions, so that the consequence may be established.

Moreover, Boethius says that Aristotle supplied this as a foundation for discovering such arguments, when he says in the *Analytics*: “The same thing, when it is and when it is not, need not be the same.” Therefore he himself and others have in some measure supplied Aristotle’s deficiency in this respect; yet, as it seems to me, imperfectly. Thus, in hypothetical syllogisms it is shown which syllogisms arise in the first form through affirming the antecedent, and which in the second through denying the consequent; what figures or valid moods arise from compound hypotheticals; what follows concerning propositions alike in mode and unlike in mode; and what is the nature of those that arise from disjunctives [Col. 0929A].

But perhaps Aristotle deliberately left this labour undone, because the book of the writer who treated it most carefully seems to contain more difficulty than usefulness. Certainly, if Aristotle had pursued this subject in his own manner, the book would probably have been so difficult that no one but the Sibyl could understand it. Yet even here I do not think the treatment of hypotheticals adequately complete; the supplements used in the schools are indeed very useful and necessary.

## CHAPTER XXII. On sophistry and its usefulness.

It has been said that sophistry is that which, by a false appearance, imitates both dialectic and demonstrative reasoning, and desires the semblance of wisdom rather than its virtue. Therefore, lest Aristotle’s adherent be overthrown by the snares of this mechanical art, he rightly appends it to what precedes [Col. 0929B]. It is a work worthy of Aristotle, and I could scarcely name another more advantageous for youth. For although youth cannot fully attain true wisdom in all things, it nevertheless seeks the reputation of wisdom and wishes that its own distinction should be celebrated by the judgment of others.

This, surely, is what sophistry promises: it is apparent wisdom, not real wisdom. Thus the sophist is “abundant in apparent wisdom, but not in real wisdom.” Sophistry imitates every discipline; under the appearance of each discipline it sets its snares for all and overthrows the unwary. Without it, anyone will vainly boast of being a philosopher if he cannot guard against falsehood or catch another in a lie. This is certainly the task of the knowledgeable person in every discipline. You may see people ignorant of this, when they are paralogized by others or by themselves, turned into Nicodemuses; once they have been caught out, they say in astonishment: “Lord, how can these things be?” (John 3).

Nothing, however, is less fitting for one who seeks either glory or victory. The contentious man seeks victory; the sophist seeks glory; and the end sought by each is especially pleasing in disputes and contests. Hence the exercise of sophistry is highly useful both for acquiring rhetorical expression and for investigations throughout philosophy—provided, however, that truth, not wordiness, is the fruit of this exercise. Thus it is the handmaid of truth and wisdom; otherwise it is an adulteress, betraying her lovers, whom, once blinded, she exposes to errors and leads over a precipice. [Col. 0929D] Wisdom says: “He who speaks sophistically is hateful” (Ecclus. 27); but plainly more hateful is one who lives sophistically, for an error of life is more destructive than an error of speech.

Yet scarcely anyone fails to imitate the sophist in life, when those who are not good wish to seem good and pursue this by every means; and when even those who are good often seek to deceive the judgments of others so as to appear better than they are. This is, indeed, to put on the sophist in one’s manner of life—provided the pretender seeks his own glory; for if he seeks divine glory, and does so knowingly, perhaps he may be excused.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Sophistical Refutations.

Aristotle accordingly introduces sophistry into the Peripatetic school and, having dispelled the cloud of fallacies, teaches how it should be admitted or avoided [Col. 0930A]. He sets forth all its powers and reveals the instrument it employs. For just as the dialectician uses the *elenchus*, which we call the refutative syllogism because it involves contradiction, so sophistry too employs an *elenchus*—an imaginary syllogism, certainly, since it does not involve contradiction but seems to do so. For it is a paralogism, that is, a shadowy syllogism.

He also sets forth the kinds of disputation, so that it may be apparent how the sophist imitates, now, the teacher who argues from principles; now, the dialectician who infers from probable premises; and now, the examiner who argues from premises that do not appear probable. The contestant, I say, who practises contentious disputation, adds the five aims of sophists, contriving how [Col. 0930B] an adversary may be brought into refutation, falsehood, paradox, solecism, or idle nonsense. It is enough for the caviller if he merely appears to accomplish any one of these.

He then adds the modes of argument that depend upon language: equivocation, amphiboly, composition, division, accent, and figure of speech; likewise those outside language: the fallacy according to accident; that arising from speaking simply or not simply; third, that arising from ignorance of refutation; fourth, according to consequent; fifth, taking what is at the beginning as given; sixth, positing as a cause what is not a cause; and seventh, making several questions into one. He carefully explains point by point how the opponent or respondent ought to conduct himself in these matters; and, like the finest commander in the field, he equips one man to bring on the battle and the other for caution [Col. 0930C].

Since, therefore, these things make clear what must be present and what absent; since the loci of probable arguments—which alone human weakness is sufficient to comprehend—have been disclosed; since the necessary combinations of arguments have been shown, the methods and paths of teaching explained, and the obstacles of fallacies removed: it is clearer than light that the art of reasoning has been completed in its proper limits and parts.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On those who criticize Aristotle’s works.

I cannot sufficiently wonder what sort of mind those people possess—if indeed they possess one at all—who criticize these works of Aristotle, works which my purpose was not to expound but to praise. Master Theodoric, as I recall, used to ridicule the *Topics*, not of Aristotle but of Drogo of Troyes. Yet he himself taught them on occasion. Some pupils of Master Robert of Melun allege that this book is almost useless. Others disparage the *Categories*. Therefore I have lingered longer in commending them; I did not think the remaining works required a laborious commendation, since they are commended by everyone’s judgment.

An objection is made to the *Refutations*, though foolishly, that they contain poetic verses; but it is evident that the idiom of languages cannot conveniently be brought into common exchange. In this respect, however, they seem to me preferable to the *Analytics*: they contribute no less to practice, while with easier understanding they promote eloquence.

## CHAPTER XXV. That Cornificius is baser than Bromius, the gods’ buffoon; and on the praise of logic according to Augustine and other philosophers.

[Col. 0931A]

Since logic possesses such power, whoever calls it foolish is himself most foolish. At the wedding of Philology, Pallas restrains Bromius, who ridiculed logic as Marsic or poisonous, and with abundant commendation associates logic with the gods. Now, as stories tell, Bromius, the buffoon of the gods, is despised; but our Cornificius, accuser of logic and buffoon of philosophers, will deservedly be despised even more. To say nothing of Plato, Aristotle, and Tully—by whom, as our elders attest, philosophy was begun and completed—Father Augustine, whom it is rash to oppose, extols logic with such great praises that it cannot be criticized except [Col. 0931B] by people possessing no prudence but much impudence.

Thus he says in Book II of *On Order*: “When grammar had been perfected and arranged, reason was admonished to seek out and attend to that very power which had produced the art. For by defining, dividing, and collecting, it had not only organized and ordered grammar, but had also defended it against every incursion of falsehood. When, then, could it proceed to construct other things unless it first distinguished, marked, arranged, and brought forth, as it were, its own mechanisms and instruments—the very discipline of disciplines which they call dialectic? This teaches how to teach; this teaches how to learn. In it reason itself shows and discloses what it is, what it wills, and what it is capable of; it alone knows that it knows. It not only wishes but is able to make men knowing.”

What has Cornificius to say to this? Surely what belongs to every deficient intellect and to idleness, which is accustomed to snore at exhortations to virtue: it condemns what it cannot attain.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What counsel should be employed against him, the insolent, and slanderers.

Let us therefore use against him, and against those who are becoming sluggish with him—for he now has companions in error—the counsel which Augustine says, in Book I of *Against the Academics*, that he learned from dialectic after much else that he learned through it. “It taught me,” he says, “that when the matter for which words are uttered is agreed upon, one ought not to dispute about words. Whoever does this, if he does it through ignorance, should be taught; if through malice, abandoned; if he cannot be taught, he should be warned to do something else rather than consume time and effort upon superfluities; if he does not comply, he should be disregarded. But concerning captious and deceptive little arguments, the brief rule is this: if conclusions are drawn by wrongly granting something, one must return to what was granted. If truth and falsehood conflict in a single conclusion, accept what is understood; leave aside what cannot be explained. But if, in some matters, their measure is wholly hidden from a person, knowledge of it is not to be sought.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Aristotle erred in many matters; that he excels in logic.

This is against Cornificius. But against those who, out of preference for the ancients, exclude Aristotle’s more important books, being nearly content with Boethius alone, very much [Col. 0932A] could be adduced. It need not be, however, because it is plain to everyone—to the point of pity—how incomplete are those who have spent their time and effort on Boethius alone, so that they know almost nothing.

Nevertheless, I do not declare that Aristotle everywhere thought or spoke rightly, as though whatever he wrote were sacrosanct. For in many things, reason and the authority of faith prevailing, he is shown to have erred. For he asserts that not only any student, but God Himself, can commit evil. Likewise, he denies that God’s providence extends as far as the region of the moon; and, in order to abolish divination and foreknowledge of future things, he asserts that lower things are not governed by the decrees of divine Providence, that the help of angels avails nothing in these matters, and that demons possess no discernment either concerning them or concerning future events.

There are also many other errors of his, which may be found in writings both pagan and Christian; yet it is not recorded that he had an equal in logic. He should therefore be received as a teacher for advancing young people toward the disciplines of weightier philosophy—not a teacher of morals, but of disputations.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How it should be used.

But although this art is useful for very many things, a person ignorant of the others is not helped toward philosophy as much by instruction in this one as he is hindered by acquiring from it wordiness and rashness. Logic alone is almost useless. It comes into prominence only when it shines with the excellence of associated disciplines. Yet greater indulgence should be granted to tender age, and, while it acquires abundance of eloquence, its wordiness must meanwhile be tolerated.

For just as youthful bodies, so youthful minds, must at first [Col. 0932C] be nourished lest they wither; they must be swollen with the fullness and abundance of nourishment, so as to conceive strength from their sap, and so that the flesh may luxuriate at that age through a certain fault of its own expansion. But exercise in labour, the weight of care, and diligent work will sufficiently digest and purge this in the following age. Therefore, as age and understanding advance, the licence of wordiness should be restrained, and the depravity of sophistry—called by Aristotle *dictitive*, and which we may call deceptive or cavilling—should subside.

This concern remains with anyone who claims the name and office of teacher. Instruction is useless unless it is strengthened by continual use and practice—unless, perhaps, the disposition has become a settled habit.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That youthful rashness must be restrained; why Mercury is joined to Philology; and what things should especially be sought.

[Col. 0932D]

The licence allowed to the exercises of the schools, which are conducted as a sort of game and wrestling-ground of philosophy in hope of improvement, must not be extended into more mature years or more serious studies. Buffoonish absurdities, tasteless and clamorous talkativeness, and childish frivolity must be laid aside with the first down of the beard. To practise such things is to renounce the philosopher and join the unsound of mind.

Therefore, that we may be instructed by fables, Mercury, the patron of eloquence, at his mother’s urging passes from earliest youth into marriage with Philology, because his cheeks, now growing bearded, did not permit him to go half-naked, clothed only in a small cloak [Col. 0933A] and with the summit of his shoulders veiled, without provoking great laughter from Cypris. Cypris, interpreted as “mixture,” flourishing in those who are seasoned by a mixture of wisdom and eloquence, mocks the absurdities of unarmed, naked, windy rhetoric.

But the most excellent and hidden nature of three things, which are especially to be sought, escapes human understanding, weighed down by its earthly habitation while it reflects on many earthly things. These are true goodness, sincere truth, and sound and certain reason. Yet human nature, as though scenting their sweetness—human nature to which God, as is read in the book of Sirach, “placed the eye above the heart, that He might show them the greatness of His works, that He might be praised in His goodness and glorified in His wonders” (Ecclus. 17)—feeling, I say, their sweetness [Col. 0933B], desires to know the true, to lay hold of the good, and to cling firmly to it so that it may suffer no loss. For this desire has been implanted naturally in human beings by God, although they cannot bring it to fulfillment through nature without grace.

Hence the fabulous antiquity of the nations invented three sisters, daughters of Phronesis: Philology, Philosophy, and Philocalia. Augustine explains the lineage of Philosophy and Philocalia; Martianus that of Philology; but Aesop indicates the kinship of all three. Therefore, because human weakness, although it does not dare arrogantly to promise itself true goodness, wisdom, and reason, nevertheless pursues them unceasingly, it occupies itself in love of these things until, through the exercise of love and by grace, it attains the realities themselves which it desires.

Phronesis gives birth to these affections because the taste which becomes sweet to human [Col. 0933C] nature provokes desire for the true and the good. For *phronō* [φρονῶ] in Greek means “I taste” or “I am wise”; here it expresses rather the savour of desire than wisdom, which consists in contemplation of divine things. For the latter is called not *phronēsis* [φρόνησις], but *sophia* [σοφία], “wisdom.”

## CHAPTER XXX. The same.

Of these, Philology is first, and she indicates the nature, power, and purposes of the others. For, since many plausible things meet us from every direction—because, as Pythagoras says, it is possible to argue on either side of almost every question—she seeks certainty concerning things and carefully avoids errors. And just as it is virtue to flee vice and the first wisdom to be free from folly, so that which guards against error naturally precedes those things which confer the virtues.

And, to use the words of Juno—or, more correctly, of Martianus—“Is there anyone who claims for himself the privileges earned by Philology and the reward of her night-long studies, yet does not know Pallor? She even compels the gods at rest to come to her by unheard-of entreaty; and a little earlier, she searches first through heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them; she,

> Ever wakeful, penetrating mysteries with modest labour,  
> Who by learned care can anticipate all  
> That it has been granted to the gods above to foreknow. Indeed, she more often  
> Holds power over us, urgently compelling the gods, though unbidden;  
> And she knows herself able, even against Jupiter’s will,  
> To do what no power of the gods above can attempt.”

And, as another writer, not inferior to Martianus, says:

[Col. 0934A]

> “Unrelenting labour conquers all things.”  
> —Virgil, *Georgics* I.144

From what has preceded it is clear that several things must concur for sensation to occur: there must be an external object against which the sentient spirit strikes; there must be the minister of sensation, the same spirit which conveys the quality of the external obstacle to the soul’s awareness; and there must be the soul. Thus there are three things: the soul which senses, the spirit by which it senses, and the obstacle which it senses externally.

By these, as was said, the deliberative power is stirred—what we above called reason—and exercises its judgment, which is likewise called reason. This judgment is sometimes true, sometimes probable. But reason is not true unless it is certain and firm, because *ratio* is a name of firmness. For nothing is called *ratum* [“settled,” “established”] unless it is firm. Therefore, as the great Augustine held: true reason belongs to God alone, and to those to whom He has granted certain knowledge and firm judgment concerning things.

Categorical examination is the first, or nearly the first, path of philosophizing: concerning any proposed matter, to consider what it is; likewise, by what properties it differs from other things and in what respects it resembles them; then, whether anything is contrary to it and whether it itself is receptive of contraries. When these points have become known, the matter, more familiarly identified, enters into knowledge. I have chosen to imitate this order in investigating so great a subject, even if I cannot express it as fully as I might wish, because it is most suitable.

Nor is there any place where one may more justly inquire into the substance of reason and truth than where the force of logic is examined—a force which professes itself, as Augustine affirms, to be the knowledge [Col. 0934C] of truth. Would that it might attain what it promises! It is, however, clear that it is highly useful and provides both method and abundant means for discovering and testing arguments.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That philology precedes the other two; and what categorical examination should be followed in discussing reason and truth.

Just as reason in creatures is a certain spiritual power, examining the nature of things and attaining knowledge of both bodily and intelligible things, so there is a certain primal reason which by its own power comprehends all things, bodily and intelligible alike, and examines fully and faithfully—that is, without any error—the nature and power of each. If I call this either the wisdom or the power of God, and the stability of all things, I shall undoubtedly not be mistaken.

Within it subsist the nature, progress, and end of all things. Indeed, this is the sphere which Martianus, veiling it in poetic fiction, says is composed of all the elements, so that nothing is absent which any nature is believed to contain. There are the whole heaven, air, seas, the diversity of earth, the barriers of Tartarus, cities and crossroads with their deeds and fortunes, and the species of all things, to be reckoned both individually and generically. This sphere appeared to be a kind of image and idea of the world.

Plato, however, raises the question whether the Idea is one or many. Certainly, if one considers the substance of knowledge or reason, it is one; if the plurality of things which reason contemplates within itself, the Ideas are infinite [Col. 0935A]. Beholding this, the Stoic venerates *pronoia* [προνοία], which we may call providence, and says that all things are constrained by its laws to necessity. Epicurus, on the contrary, observing the contingency of things, extinguishes *pronoia* and frees all things from the law of necessity.

But the Peripatetic, fearing the precipice of error on either side, is moved neither by the Stoic’s paradoxes nor by Epicurus’s *kyriai doxai* [κυριοδόξαι, “principal doctrines”]. Instead, he affirms *pronoia* with the Stoic in such a way as not to impose necessity upon things; and he regards things with Epicurus as free from necessity in such a way as not to take away the reality of providence. He therefore maintains that some things are necessary, while others are subject to natural contingency and free choice.

The Academic, however, wavers and does not dare determine what is true in particular cases. Yet this school is divided three ways. It includes those who profess that they know absolutely nothing and, through excessive caution, have forfeited the name of philosophers. It includes others who confess that they know only necessary things and things known through themselves—that is, things which cannot be unknown. The third degree consists of our own people, who do not hastily pronounce judgment on matters doubtful to the wise.

## CHAPTER XXXII. What primal reason is; and concerning the various schools of philosophers.

The first and true reason, therefore, is the divine reason of which we have spoken, and it admits absolutely no error. Nothing appears more opposed to reason than error: reason establishes and confirms, whereas error by its slipperiness casts down and trips up. And just as “sense” denotes sometimes the power and sometimes the act of sensing, and “imagination” likewise denotes both the power and the act of imagining, so “reasons” (*rationes*) denotes sometimes a power, sometimes the activity and movement of that power, and sometimes even those things in which reason exercises a movement of its power.

Such are the relations of implication in consequences, proportions in numbers, and the principles of demonstrations concerning things that are absolutely necessary. Augustine, in the books *On Order*, *On Free Choice*, and the *Hypognosticon*, as well as in many others, declares these to be immortal and everlasting. “The most true ratio of one to two and of two to four,” he says, “is so: that ratio was no truer yesterday than it is today, nor will it be truer tomorrow or a year from now. Even if this whole world should collapse, [Col. 0935D] that ratio could not fail to be, just as substance cannot fail to be if there is a body.”

The other things which the eye of divine reason contemplates are indeed true, but because of their mutability they are by no means called *rationes*. From this association of truth and reason, some philosophers have thought that whatever is once true is always true. The argument Augustine adduces to teach that our faith and that of the preceding fathers is the same seems to support them, although we rejoice in part that what they awaited has been fulfilled. For he says: “Faith has not changed, though the times have varied. We and they embrace the same truth, but proclaim it in different words.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What is contrary to reason; that “reason” is said in many ways; and which reasons are eternal.

[Col. 0936A]

The angelic nature, not slowed by a harmful body and more intimately attached to divine purity, flourishes in the sharpness of uncorrupted reason. Although it does not examine all things equally with God, it is nevertheless endowed with the prerogative of reason so that it is overthrown by no error. But human weakness, exposed to many errors both by the condition of nature and by the desert of sin—indeed, falling captive from its first and second purity—degenerates in its examination of things, that is, in the exercise of reason.

Because it wavers upon the slippery ground of uncertainty, it grasps what it can. Now, from a faithful resemblance of things, it forms true opinions; now, deceived [Col. 0936B] by vain images, false ones. For if a thing is apprehended as it is, the opinion is true; and if it is expressed in speech accordingly, the utterance is true. Hence some philosophers have plausibly held that truth, by which an opinion is called true or a statement true, is a kind of intermediate disposition of things examined externally in relation to reason. For if reason faithfully relies upon them in examining, it is certain and does not waver through any error.

Thus an utterance called true is termed *modal* from the manner it indicates; similarly, a true opinion is so called from the manner of perceiving; and true reason from the quality of its examination. Individual things also are called true: for example, a true human being or true whiteness, when opinion is not deceived in perceiving them by the phantasm of any image.

The reliability by which things are judged true is usually established from two sources: either from the form of the substance or from the effect of the form. A human being is true if true humanity is present in him—that is, consciousness of reason and capacity. True whiteness is that which makes white; true justice is that which makes one just. If you do not believe me—or rather, the great Hilary, who is exalted in Gallic buskin and far removed from the reading of the simple—lend an ear.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That human beings do not possess perfect reason, and that “true” is said in many ways.

In order, however, to comply with the Stoics, who busy themselves with the collection or analogy of words, *verum* [“true”] is said to derive from the Greek *hērōn* [ἥρων], which is interpreted “firm and stable,” or “certain and clear.” Hence *heroes* were so named, because they attained a firm and stable rank through association with divine beings, with whom fabulous antiquity joined them. These heroes were called *hēmitheoi* [ἡμίθεοι, “demigods”], as Martianus says, because the ancients called the earth *hēra* [ἥρα]. This explanation, indeed, derives from the certainty of their stability.

But we call no one either demigod—since there are none—or hero, because of the mark of unbelief; rather, by a Catholic word we signify the translation of the elect from worldly fluctuation and vanity into the glory of true certainty and firm stability. For from the confirmation which they have attained we call them saints: since *sancire* means “to confirm,” and a saint is one confirmed in virtue or glory. This indeed is to be removed from vanity and to dwell in truth.

Accordingly, *verum*, this word, is a mark of confirmation and signifies the stability of a thing upon which reason can faithfully rely. *Veritas* [truth] is a name of firmness and stability. Nor should it disturb us that Latin put the consonant *v* in place of Greek aspiration, since the Aeolic digamma has many affinities with this consonant.

Just as, for the power of sensation to exercise its movement usefully, there must be something upon which it may stably rest, so reason fails if it does not rest upon a stable object. For if you remove light, sight ceases; when sound ceases, there is no hearing; smell and taste rest through the absence of odour and flavour; touch is empty if it does not strike against some solid object. Yet people say that darkness is then seen, silence heard, and emptiness touched. More truly, however, one should say that nothing is then sensed by these senses. Augustine, both against the Manichees and in the *Hypognosticon*, as well as in many other books, teaches that not only these but any privations whatsoever are nothing. Aristotle, however, maintains that they are something, because they not only deprive but in some way dispose their subjects toward themselves.

Thus both sense and reason require something stable, lest their activity be empty and fail to comprehend something certain. For when reason acts in order to hold something and its aim is frustrated, it labours in vain and is deceived by its own error. Therefore, just as we have said that error is contrary to reason, so we declare vanity contrary to truth; for falsehood and vanity, although different words, approach in some way the same meaning. Vanity and falsehood, moreover, tend toward nothingness; for what is false is altogether nothing and does not fall under knowledge. For, as Augustine teaches in the *Soliloquies*, *Against the Academics*, and very many other works, all the ancients and even the Academics themselves agreed that no one can know false things. Indeed, as he likewise maintains in *Against the Academics*, there can be no knowledge of false things, because they do not exist at all.

Where some interpreters said that the earth at the beginning was “empty and void,” others translated that it was “nothing and unformed.” Therefore truth is opposed to vanity and falsehood—since these are the same—by the law of contrariety. Nor am I troubled if an existing thing is opposed to a non-existing thing, since this is plainly the case in propositions opposed contradictorily. For [Col. 0937D] Aristotle teaches that one of them always is, while the other necessarily is not. Is not an existing thing a sign of a non-existing thing, as a red sky is a sign of coming fair weather or storm? For:

> “A red sky in the morning foretells rain; in the evening, fair weather.”  
> —Virgil, *Georgics*

## CHAPTER XXXV. What is called true, what truth is, and what its contrary is.

All things that are vain, insofar as they are vain, deceive. And when they have mocked minds deluded by falsehood, they vanish like a phantom. Hence, because of this instability of evanescent things, Ecclesiastes proclaims in the assembly of all who dwell in the world that all things under the sun are vain (Eccles. II): with such majesty of expression and such persuasive force of thought [Col. 0938A] that the utterance passes through every nation and language and, penetrating them, shakes the hearts of all who have ears to hear.

Plato likewise, teaching the distinction between things which truly are and things which are not, though they seem to be, maintained that intelligible things truly exist: for they fear neither the assault or annoyance of passions, nor the injury of power, nor the wasting of time, but always remain the same in the strength of their condition. Hence, after the first Essence, being properly belongs to them—that is, a firm and certain state, which the substantive verb, when used properly, expresses. Temporal things, however, seem indeed to be, because they put forward an image of intelligible things. But they are not sufficiently worthy of the designation of the substantive verb, since they pass away with time, never remaining in [Col. 0938B] the same state, but vanishing like smoke: for, as he says in the *Timaeus*, they flee and do not await a name.

He divided this true existence into three things, which he established as the principles of reality: namely God, matter, and Idea, since these are immutable in their own nature.
