For God is altogether immutable; the other two are in some way unmoving, but differ from one another in their effects. For forms arriving upon matter arrange it and in some way make it subject to motion; and forms likewise, through contact with matter, are altered in a certain respect and, as Boethius says in his *Arithmetic*, pass into a changeable instability. Yet the Ideas, which he places after God as the first essences, he denies to be mingled in themselves with matter or to undergo any [Col. 0938C] motion; rather, innate forms proceed from them—namely, images of exemplars—which nature created together with individual things. Hence Boethius, in the book *On the Trinity*: “From those forms which are apart from matter came those forms which are in matter and make up body.”

Bernard of Chartres also, the most accomplished among the Platonists of our age, expressed nearly the same view in verse:

> I do not call that “being” which, compelled from a double part,  
> contains the form of matter folded within it;  
> but I call that “being” which consists of one of these.  
> The Achaean calls this *Idea*, that *hylē* [matter].

And although the Stoics believed matter and Idea to be coeternal with God, while others, along with Epicurus—who abolishes providence—removed Idea altogether, Bernard, with those [Col. 0938D] who philosophize, said that neither was coeternal with God. For he agreed with the Fathers, who, as Augustine testifies, prove that God made all things from nothing and created the matter of all things. Yet he agreed that Idea is eternal, admitting the eternity of providence, in which God made all things once and together, establishing within Himself all things that were to be in time or to endure in eternity.

But coeternity cannot exist except among those things which do not precede one another either by the nature of majesty, by the privilege of power, or by the authority of work. Thus he acknowledged only the three Persons—whose nature is one, whose power is singular, and whose operation is inseparable—to be coequal and coeternal; for in them there is complete equality. But Idea, because it does not rise to this equality [Col. 0939A] and is in some fashion posterior by nature, and like a certain effect abiding in the secrecy of counsel and requiring no external cause, he dared to call eternal but denied to be coeternal.

For, as he says in his exposition of Porphyry: “The work of the divine mind is twofold: one work creates from subject matter, or is created together with it; the other it makes from itself and contains within itself, needing no external assistance. Certainly it made the heavens in understanding from the beginning; in order to form them there, it sought neither matter nor form from outside.”

Elsewhere he says:

> What had divine will alone as its beginning,  
> age does not break, nor antiquity demolish.  
> Time dissolves whatever it brings forth into presence,  
> unless it stands as something that must at some time exist.  
> Therefore whoever grieves over such a condition  
> clearly possesses either no reason or very little.

[Col. 0939B] Some, however, although they grant that true things exist from eternity, deny that they are eternal, saying that nothing is eternal except what lives, since eternity, as Augustine testifies, is the state of unending life. From this it is clear that the Platonists, together with Solomon, held all subsolar things to be vain, and considered true only those things which do not vanish like phantoms, but are certain in the state of their substance and always the same.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Again concerning true things; and that things, utterances, and truths are said to “be” in different ways, and how.

Since the term “false” is applied alike to opinion, utterance, and thing, an opinion which suffers the deception of error is most properly called false, since it is itself what is deceived. An utterance, however, is false because [Col. 0939C] it signifies a false opinion. A thing is called false from its effect, because only an empty and vain intellect perceives it.

So also in natural science, now animals, now signs, now causes are called healthy or sick. But, to descend a little from Plato’s height to the Peripatetics, those things are called true or false which, where the signification of complex utterances is concerned, are perceived by a certain intellect or by a vain one. For these thinkers, philosophizing, as it were, more humanly, and not going beyond themselves and God in thought together with the Platonists, are moderate: they establish truth or falsehood for human beings in that in which, upon examination and comprehension, the intellect is faithful or erroneous. For if it grasps a thing to be as it is [Col. 0939D] or not to be as it is not, it has exercised a certain and faithful judgment. But if it supposes either that what is, is not, or that what is not, is, it is without doubt deceived and mistaken. The same is true also of utterances.

But a thing which presents itself to the intellect as it is, is true; one which presents itself otherwise is vain and false. Therefore truth or falsehood, both of opinions and of things, is demonstrated by the manner of perceiving—namely, the manner in which they are perceived or perceive; but in the case of utterances, by the manner of signifying. Hence, since it is impossible for God to be deceived, it is beyond doubt that the more faithful and certain knowledge is, the fewer false things it apprehends. Yet He knows false things to be false; and nothing can be hidden from Truth, which contemplates all things.

For in God’s essence is primitive [Col. 0940A] truth—that is, certainty, stability, or clarity—and from it is in some way derived whatever in things is faithfully called true. For to Him alone the coherence or incoherence of all things and utterances is known and certain. Any human being whatsoever indeed seeks to become more certain, because love of truth is akin and innate to reason; and, as Martianus says, with Philology prays with all its heart for truth that exists, and for truth from things that do not exist.

This comes from nowhere else than from some drop of divine wisdom pouring itself in through the filtering of grace and enlightening the mind which seeks and loves it. For this is the fountain-virgin from whom, according to Martianus, the aforesaid truth flows. Nothing is truly made known [Col. 0940B] except from the wellspring of this fountain. Nor does any falsehood flow from it, because that fountain-virgin, whom poetic invention wraps in a cloud, is a virgin ignorant of every corruption and falsehood.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. According to the Platonists, the differences between things which truly are and things which seem to be.

The eye of divine simplicity contemplates all things, so that neither future things are absent from it nor past things escape it. It weighs the coherence and incoherence of things, and exercises a certain and faithful judgment both concerning things which are and concerning things which are not. And those things which it saw from the beginning, because they do not vanish, are firm and are called true. These indeed are the thoughts of the Most High, whose depth no one is able to expound (Job XXIII). These are words spoken once, but which, in the course of time, according to the decree of divine disposition, come forth into act.

Who would call the mind of God idle, and deny that from the beginning it contemplated all things (II Chron. XVI)? If, therefore, true things are as it were certain thoughts of God, who but the presumptuous would affirm that they vanish? Or who would dare declare that they have not always existed in the mind of Him who disposed and knew all things from eternity? Does He too conceive new thoughts and undertake new counsels after our fashion? And although these things have been true from eternity, nothing is said to be coeternal with the Creator; for, as has been said, nothing whatever can rise to His equality, since it belongs to Him that these true things themselves are true or certain.

The totality of all things said to be either Creator [Col. 0940D] or creature is, by the authority of the Fathers, reduced to substances and to whatever inheres in substances in any manner; for the signification of propositions does not come under consideration unless some necessity of discourse compels it. Those who divided things thus had regard to the significations of non-complex terms. Therefore there are certain true things which subsist in the mind of God, yet they are not creatures, because they have existed from eternity. For that some things are everlasting admits of no question—unless perhaps the saying of Ecclesiasticus is referred to this: “He who lives for eternity created all things at once” (Ecclus. XVIII). Some refer this both to that work which the Trinity performed within itself by beholding and disposing, and to the creation of primordial matter, from which all things were created or are created together with things created in it.

[Col. 0941A] Moreover, for these things to be is to be referred to the primal knowledge of reason and thus to be, as it were, pronounced by a stable and unshaken judgment. Their being, therefore, is their becoming known. For the same is said of human words: to be uttered is to be; or to be retained in memory is to be. For Augustine says of the only-begotten: “This is the Word—not that which ceases once uttered, but that which remains once begotten.” This distinction seems in some way pointless unless words subsisted through utterance.

But since “being,” “one,” and “thing” are said in many senses, let each person determine how to interpret the meaning of the terms. Things, then—that is, natures or the works of nature—have their mode of existing; thoughts, utterances, truths, and reasons also have theirs. Each of these, I say, has its own mode of existing, [Col. 0941B] so that, according to its character, the interpretation must be received of those things which are faithfully enunciated, in order that, after the meanings of the words have been carefully examined, they may be said to be true or not to be true. I do not contend further, provided that true things are not utterly nothing, while false things are in every respect not, because they are altogether nothing. For thus both ancient philosophers and Catholic Fathers have defined the matter.

Moreover, for God, to remember and to speak is His knowing itself. For His memory, or Word, or Reason, is His wisdom. The Word by which omnipotence speaks, therefore, is one; but the words which it speaks are infinite. “The beginning of thy words is truth” (Ps. CXVIII), because from the inaccessible light which God inhabits (I Tim. VI) it has that all things become known to it. Yet I do not judge this light to be alien from His substance.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That a thing, an opinion, and an utterance are called true or false in different ways; and why such utterances are called of this kind and modal.

Let us now contemplate with every reverence the most delightful coherence of reason and truth, imploring the help of reason and truth; for without that help they can neither be faithfully apprehended nor even investigated. Reason, then, is a certain eye of the mind. And, to describe it more fully: reason is an instrument by which the mind exercises all its senses. Its proper function is to investigate and apprehend truth. The contrary of this power is weakness and inability to investigate and attain the true.

Error [Col. 0941D] is the contrary of that motion which investigates truth and which we above called reason. This power is simply perfect in God; perfect in the angel according to its nature; but in a human being it is either altogether imperfect or, for the most part, so—unless it is perhaps perfect in someone relative to time or by comparison with the more imperfect. Hence the human being claims for himself not reason but the desire for reason, which Philology expresses; for the philosophers’ modesty has tempered such names as *philology*, *philosophy*, and *philocalia*. Reason, however, is in no way capable of contraries, because divine Reason is immutable substance. But the reason of an angel or human being is not substance.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the coherence of reason and truth, and briefly what each is.

[Col. 0942A]

Truth is the light of the mind and the matter of reason. God beholds it universally; an angel, particularly; but a human being, even the most perfect, sees it only partially and slightly—yet the more perfect one is, the more one desires it. It is the solidity of certainty in which reason’s examination is active. Remove light and solidity, and sight and touch are frustrated, just as the other senses are frustrated if sound, smell, or taste is removed. In the same way, every sense of reason is frustrated when truth is withdrawn.

Its contrary, however, is falsehood or the void, which, as philosophy proves, is nothing among things. Hence some have held that *inane* (“void”) is so called, with one letter changed, as though *in-une*, namely, “not one.” But that which is not, is nothing. Primeval truth exists in the divine majesty. Another truth exists in the image of divinity, that is, in imitation. For every thing is so much the truer as it expresses the image of God more faithfully; and so much the more falsely does it vanish as it falls further short of that image. Thus: “Man has become like vanity, and his days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. CXLIII).

But there is no shadow unless the light of a body is impeded by some obstacle, and the absence of light introduces certain darknesses. Therefore, when the light of truth is removed, the darknesses of error grow strong; and error deceives. Hence falsehood is called the contrary of truth from deceiving, because “he who walks in darkness does not know where he is going” (John XII). It is truth’s proper office to foster [Col. 0942C] reason, enlighten it, and make it firm, just as it is reason’s office to seek, attain, and embrace truth. For external light too, as was said, supports sight; and a solid thing strengthens touch.

But in God these are one, because Reason and the eternal Word says of itself: “I am truth” (John XIV). For it needs no external help, because reason enlightens itself and truth finds itself. In creatures, however, truth is one thing and reason another; for truth is a certain image of Divinity, which reason seeks and finds in things. Reason is a power or movement of the mind occupied in discerning the true. Truth is not capable of contraries, for the same reason which we explained above concerning reason.

## CHAPTER XL. The same subject continued: that neither reason nor truth admits contraries.

[Col. 0942D]

If the purpose of the Peripatetics is to recognize the truth of things after rejecting all vanity, and with their whole reason to seek, revere, and worship the truth of God, their labor is not useless. Otherwise, both work and expenditure are wasted. But many things obstruct understanding: namely, invincible ignorance of matters which cannot be resolved by reason, such as the mysteries of the Holy Trinity; likewise the frailty of our condition, shortness of life, neglect of useful things, preoccupation with useless things, conflict of plausible opinions, sin which deserves the loss of light, and finally the number and immensity of things to be investigated. Thus the human heart is so veiled that it can rarely [Col. 0943A] approach knowledge of the truth.

Yet among these eight obstacles which have been set forth, in my opinion nothing impedes knowledge of what is useful as greatly as sin, which separates us from God and closes off the fountain of truth—though reason never ceases to thirst for it. “My heart,” says the mind conscious of its sins, “has forsaken me; and the light of my eyes, even it is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII). For unless a person directs to divine service the things he knows, his knowledge works not with him but rather against him. For it profits nothing to know many things if the one thing is absent which is necessary above all things and manifests itself through an understanding of creatures.

Holy Solomon says: “I set my mind to seek and investigate wisely all things done under the sun” (Eccles. I). “God gave this most grievous occupation to the children of men.” The philosophers of the nations were occupied with it; according to the Apostle, they held the truth of God in a lie and deservedly became vain in their thoughts (Rom. I). For because they did not render thanks for benefits to their Author, “claiming to be wise, they became fools” (ibid.).

Curiosity is a superfluous inquiry into useless matters, an inquiry in which not only the Peripatetics but almost the whole world is occupied. Lucan notes this vice when, as he brings forth the uncertain causes of the surging Ocean, he invites the curious to certainty regarding an inscrutable secret: “Seek, you whom the labor of the world agitates.” But when the mind is occupied more extensively with many things which do not much concern it, it wanders farther from itself and very often forgets [Col. 0943C] itself; and no error is more ruinous than this. For to know oneself, as Apollo says, is nearly the highest wisdom.

What profit is it to a human being to know the nature of the heavens or the elements, to inquire theoretically into the proportions of magnitude and multitude, to contemplate the conflict of virtues and vices, to attend to the combinations of arguments, and to dispute plausibly concerning everything, while remaining ignorant of oneself? Will not the man who surveys the dwellings of strangers but forgets where he himself must turn aside in need be thought foolish? He is indeed excessively curious and neglectful of himself who marvels at what belongs to others and does not attend to his own affairs.

But the person who turns external things to the use of life, so that he may know and revere their Author, measures his own imperfection—for he can scarcely comprehend a few things—and uses transitory things, along with which he himself passes away, only precariously and for the moment. He restrains, represses, or extinguishes desires; he strives by diligent effort to reform the image of God corrupted by vice; he cultivates and exercises with all his strength the duties of virtue: this person philosophizes most rightly.

His investigation is sober who first examines himself, carefully tests lower things, observes equals without negligence, and contemplates higher things with reverence, lest by rash daring he break into what is inscrutable. Such a person does not pride himself on himself; he does not at all covet the varied furnishings of the world except insofar as they are necessary or lawful; he bestows [Col. 0944A] charity upon his neighbor; reverence and love upon the heavenly beings who always stand before the face of God; and gratitude and praise for all good things upon the divine majesty. Its own immensity does not permit us fully to know that majesty; and, even if we were not oppressed by the weakness under which we labor, creatures would not permit us wholly to be ignorant of it, since all creatures proclaim the Creator’s glory as if by public testimony.

Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “Do not raise your eyes to riches which you cannot possess, because they will make wings for themselves like eagles and fly away into heaven” (Prov. XXIII). And Augustine says in the book *On Order*: “God is better known by not knowing Him.” If anyone ignorant of natures and morals, enslaved to arguments or desires, and longing after perishing things—or perhaps living chastely but unlearned in the disciplines—trusts that by the powers of his intellect, through seeking and disputing, he will find God, without doubt he will err as greatly as it is possible to err. Elsewhere likewise: “Ignorance of God is the truest wisdom concerning Him”; and again: “It is no small knowledge concerning God to know what God is not, because what He is cannot at all be known.”

## CHAPTER XLI. The end toward which the Peripatetics and all who philosophize rightly direct their purpose; and the eight obstacles to understanding.

Since some things cannot be known because of their preeminent dignity, some because of the multitude and magnitude of their quantity, and some because of their instability and slipperiness, Ecclesiasticus teaches [Col. 0944C] what should chiefly be pursued and what is most advantageous: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not search into things stronger than yourself” (Ecclus. III). Behold, he restrains the rashness of those who discuss with irreverent verbosity the mysteries of the divine Trinity and those things whose vision is promised in eternal life. Hence, even if knowledge seems to increase, devotion certainly diminishes.

“Do not investigate superfluous matters in many ways,” he says, “and do not be curious about the multitude of His works. For their suspicion has overthrown many, and has detained their minds in vanity” (ibid.). Here too he represses the audacity of those who trouble themselves about everything and wish to give an account of all things, although it is established by Solomon’s authority in Ecclesiasticus (Ecclus. I) that a human being cannot give a full account even of the least thing under heaven, much less of heavenly or supercelestial things.

But the son of Sirach teaches in what matters the intellect of a philosopher should be exercised: “Always consider those things which God has commanded, and you will not be curious about the multitude of His works” (Ecclus. III). Because knowledge flows from the root of senses which frequently deceive, and because deceived human weakness knows little of what is useful, the law was given through God’s mercy, to disclose knowledge of useful things and to indicate concerning God how much it is permissible to know or advantageous to seek. For it manifests divine power in creation, wisdom in ordering, and goodness in preserving things. But these are most eminently displayed in the restoration of redeemed humanity. It also plainly expounds the will of God, [Col. 0945A] so that each person may know what he ought to do. And because both human sense and human reason frequently err, it established faith as the first foundation for understanding truth. Hence Philo says in the book of Wisdom: “Those who trust in the Lord shall understand truth, and the faithful shall rest in love in Him” (Wis. III).

## CHAPTER XLII. What visible arguments prove that the world is subject to vanity; and why this book is here concluded.

But enough of these matters. For now it is more fitting to weep than to write; and by visible evidence I am taught that the whole world lies subject to vanity. For we awaited peace, and behold, disturbance and a storm descending upon Toulouse stir up the English and French on every side, and kings whom we had seen as close friends pursue one another without restraint.

Moreover, the death of Lord Adrian, supreme pontiff, although it has disturbed all the peoples and nations of the Christian religion, has moved our England, from which he sprang, with sharper grief and has drenched it with more abundant tears. He died lamented by all good people, but by none more lamented than by me. Although he had a mother and a brother by the same mother, he loved me with a closer affection than them. He acknowledged both publicly and privately that he loved me above all mortals. He had conceived such an opinion of me that, whenever the opportunity arose, he rejoiced to pour out his conscience before me. And when he was Roman pontiff, he rejoiced to have me as a guest at his own table; [Col. 0945C] and he wished and arranged, despite my resistance, that the same cup and dish should be shared by him and me.

At my request he granted and gave Ireland to the illustrious king of the English, Henry II, to possess by hereditary right, as his letters testify to this day. For all islands, by ancient law, are said to belong to the Roman Church through the donation of Constantine, who founded and endowed it. He also sent through me a golden ring adorned with an excellent emerald, by which investiture was to be made of the right to govern Ireland; and he ordered that this same ring be kept even now in the public curial archive. If I wished to recount his virtues, this single subject would grow into a book of great volume.

Yet what most wounds everyone’s minds is the schism of the Church, which, because our sins demanded it, occurred when so great a Father was taken away. Satan sought it in order to sift as wheat, and on every side, through the ministry of another traitor Judas, he scatters bitterness and scandals. Wars more than civil arise; for they are priestly and fraternal. Now is the judgment of the world, and it is to be feared that the fall of the ambitious traitor may drag with it a part of the stars. “Woe to him through whom this scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII); and plainly it would have been better if he had not been born.

I set forth the causes of public grief, though grief closer to home torments me from another quarter, and no less severely, in what concerns myself. For my father and lord—indeed yours also—the venerable Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, has fallen into illness, so that it is uncertain what we ought to hope and what fear. He cannot attend to business as usual, and he has entrusted to me a hard charge and imposed an unbearable burden: care for all ecclesiastical affairs. Therefore my spirit is anxious within me on every side, and I cannot recount the torments which I endure.

But amid all these things one counsel alone remains to me: to entreat the God-man, Son of the inviolate Virgin, who, as though sleeping in a ship, must be awakened by the prayers of the faithful, that He may calm the storm of the shipwrecked Church and mercifully deliver my lord, as He foreknew to be advantageous for him and for us, from every infirmity of mind and body. May He, I say—through whom [Col. 0946C] kings reign and princes rule (Prov. VIII)—set over the universal Church a shepherd fit for it and pleasing to Himself; may He defend our kings and princes from every adversity; and may He cause them, for the honor and glory of His name, to preserve the flock entrusted to them.

I also beseech reader and hearer by a devout supplication that they intercede for me, vain and wretched as I am, before the Son of the Virgin, who is the way, truth, and life (John XIV), that, once error, the darkness of ignorance, and the love of vanity have been driven away, He may pour into me the light of His knowledge and make me a dutiful seeker, lover, and worshipper of truth.

[Col. 0945]

# JOHN OF SALISBURY, ON THE SEVEN SETS OF SEVEN

Epistolary prologue to the little book *On the Seven Sets of Seven*, composed by John of Salisbury.

[Col. 0945D]

In writing on very difficult subjects to a man so distinguished and wise, I may perhaps appear presumptuous to some. Yet one is not presumptuous who has endeavored to interpret Pythagoras, who has learned to unlock obscurities with Minerva’s keys, who has persistently assailed a wise man with questions. Accius was presumptuous in writing to Caesar, before whom he refused to rise when Caesar came into the company of poets. Propertius, however, wrote to Augustus because in him there was both hope and discernment for learning. In the one case the Muse begged without virtue; in [Col. 0947A] the other, the begging Muse triumphed through humility. Yet learning without power was a punishment in both.

Learning alone puffed up Accius; virtue with learning more honorably shaped the character and mind in Propertius. Accordingly, the Muse of our smallness writes to the prerogative of your dignity—not feeble like Accius, nor thin like Propertius, whose talents were consumed upon the seven principles of things. But five considerations compel us to write to the firmness of your judgment: intimacy with a wise man, certainty amid ambiguity, the honor of the gift, the merit of the recipient, and the power of the giver.

In the giver’s power lies the restoration of distinction; in the recipient’s merit, the renewal of love; in the honor of the gift, true nobility of spirit; in intimacy with a wise man, [Col. 0947B] the strengthening of character together with knowledge; and in certainty amid ambiguity, the completion of knowledge. Therefore, since with you there is a place where gold is refined, we direct to your judgment this little book entitled *On the Seven Sets of Seven*, so that it may be tested by you as fine gold. In all these matters we know that you know: if any question or knotty dispute should arise before you, you know what ought or can be, in what respect, for what reason, and to what end.

We therefore consider it very honorable for you and most useful for us if, under your time and by the discerning skill of your judgment, the darkness of ignorance is turned into light, ambiguity into certainty, excessive transgression into an abundance of mercy, and enduring hatred into true love.

## SECTION I. The first set of seven: the seven modes of instruction.

[Col. 0947C]

The Chaldeans and Greeks seek wisdom; the Latins investigate truth. The former seek and find, because they unite character with knowledge; the latter investigate and do not find, because they apply themselves more to the cavilling of disputation than to the investigation of truth. Cavilling disputation stimulates the intellect by exercising it; but if it lingers there, it dulls and bewilders it. Thus, off the path and not on the way of truth, it wanders dull and groping. The investigation of truth, however, like a whetstone, makes the intellect bright and subtle: it directs the mind onto the royal road and raises the eyes of the mind toward lofty things.

And although by these eyes certain things formerly hidden are at times revealed, many things still remain hidden [Col. 0947D] which cannot be comprehended—either because of their subtlety, since they escape sense; or because of their obscurity, since they admit neither study nor intellect; or because of their immensity, since they exceed reason and understanding. Hence there are certain divine things which come into manifestation and offer themselves to knowledge. But because they are subtle, difficult, and lofty, almost everyone passes them by as though inscrutable. These are called the first principles of things, that is, the hidden causes and cognitions of things. To make truth more evident, the illustrious writings of the Chaldeans investigate these alone.

Other divine things, however, are so profound, so hidden, so inward, and altogether impenetrable that they can be examined by no reasoning, perceived by no understanding, and discovered by no wisdom. Hence the Apostle: “What is known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. I). When he says “what is known of God,” that is, what is knowable concerning God, he plainly shows that, among those things which are of God and in God, some are manifest and some hidden. But what is manifest may be reached through the sciences; what is utterly concealed can be penetrated by no reasoning. These are those secrets which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.

Accordingly, as it is written in the Apostle: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. XI). Wisdom is called Pallas, that is, “new,” because one who ascends to it is diminished; Minerva or Athena, that is, “immortal,” because one who follows it in word and deed is carried up to immortality. This Tritonian goddess, that is, the threefold notion, is so called because for the human mind enlightened by wisdom the *engerimion* [“book of rising”] is opened, in which it is instructed by seven sets of seven to rise from human to divine things and is more perfectly taught to ascend to a threefold knowledge: namely, that of human nature, angelic nature, and divine nature.

[Col. 0948B] There are seven modes in the first set of seven by which the human mind is led into perfect instruction. The first mode is to will instruction in all the arts; the second, to take delight in what one wills; the third, to apply oneself to what delights one; the fourth, to conceive what one applies oneself to; the fifth, to remember what one conceives; the sixth, to discover something similar; the seventh, from all these things to extract what is useful.

## SECTION II. The second set of seven: the ways of the soul.

To this first set of seven is joined a second, called the set of seven liberal arts, which are also called, by antonomasia, the seven ways of the soul. In them the human mind is educated freely and freed from servile cares. Of these seven arts grammar is placed first in instruction, because through it we are taught to speak correctly; through dialectic, rationally; through rhetoric, elegantly. Through arithmetic we are taught to divide things according to multitude; through music, to render discordant things harmonious; through geometry, to make equal things out of unequal ones; through astronomy, to distinguish signs, times, and temporal things, and from times and temporal things to foretell certain future events lying close at hand.

And it should be noted that in these sciences there is the greatest sweetness and usefulness, acquired in virtue through the sciences; moreover, it is adorned in six ways by the mixture of both: [Col. 0948D] the first mode is *idioma*, that is, originality of invention in discourse; the second, elegant composition in connected words; the third, *schema* in sense and thought, that is, pleasing ornament; the fourth, urbane charm in delivery, that is, a sweet and witty delivery, fitting to the sense and pleasant to hearers; the fifth, apologue, which is discourse introduced for the sake of delight, wholly ethical; the sixth, proverb, which is a concise, fixed ethical maxim that renders the mind teachable. Thus by these six modes—that is, by six forms of ornament—all Scriptures are colored with a certain sweetness, and the characters of those advancing through the arts are reformed.

These seven disciplines, to one who considers wisely, are seven paths of the soul in the uprightness of life and [Col. 0949A] morals. For the grammarian rightly enters and travels the path of grammar when, after correct speech, he follows equity in life and character. What good is it for a grammarian to pronounce according to rule and bear the monstrous hump of a disordered life? What does it benefit a dialectician to know the problems of propositions and yet possess ambiguous and deceitful morals? Therefore he follows the even path of dialectic, and argues truthfully in deed as well as speech, who reasons by distinguishing truth from falsehood and the straight from the crooked. What good is it for a rhetorician to glory in the pomp of eloquence and the urbanity of words, yet use a mercenary tongue? Therefore he walks in the straight path by rhetorical footsteps who, with a well-rounded censorial tongue, admonishes hearers by persuasion and instructs them by recalling them from strict law [Col. 0949B] to equity. Thus the *trivium* makes one eloquent and constructs paths to the virtues.

What good is it to count by arithmetic and devote one’s fingers and counters to avarice? Therefore he rightly enters the path of arithmetic—that is, the virtuous path of number—who approaches through the fivefold Pentateuch of Moses and its mystery, comprehends through the tenfold Decalogue, faithfully embraces through the twofold Old and New Testament; and who, through all numbers—by adding, fortifying, dividing, and multiplying—faithfully comprehends history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy. What does it avail a musician to make a discordant sound harmonious through low and high concords, while lacking harmony of character? Therefore he takes up the musical path who makes his life consonant [Col. 0949C] with his voice.

What does it matter to us to know how to divide manifold figures and areas by the *podismus*, radius, *lituus*, and *embados*, if we do not wish to share with a brother? What if we know how to find a circle by means of its diameter, a diameter by means of its circle, and the arc of a circle by means of both, yet do not govern the mind by any measure? Therefore he walks the geometrical path with equal paces of measure who preserves sobriety in himself and measure and proportion toward others in every respect.

What does it matter to consider the position of heaven and the configurations of the stars in an astrolabe, while taking no care for oneself? What if we know how to foreknow something through a horoscope, through the conjunction and opposition of sun and moon, yet refuse to know him who made these things? What good is it to admire the divinity [Col. 0949D] of the sun and not venerate the power of the Almighty? Therefore he strives to take up, pursue, and traverse the starry path who, setting temporal things aside, is carried from virtue to virtue and, ascending the steps of the virtues, contemplates God in Zion.

Thus the mind of the learner acquires eloquence and wisdom through these seven paths of the *trivium* and *quadrivium*; and the soul of every person, by these same paths and in the same ways described above, attains its own reformation and approach to God. Through these skillfully devised paths of the soul all the ways of the Lord are perceived: namely, mercy and truth. From mercy comes the law of the Lord, in which the blessed undefiled walk. In the law, moreover, are the way of the commandments, the way of testimonies, the way of justifications, and the elect way of truth, [Col. 0950A] concerning which the Lord says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14): the way in example, truth in promise, life in reward; or, the way to himself, truth from himself, life in himself.

## SECTION III. The third group of seven: the seven windows of the soul

The third group of seven is called that of the seven windows of the soul in the human head. Through them the mind of the soul goes out into, and returns from, the groups of seven mentioned above: it goes out by discerning all external things through reason; it returns by reporting those things inwardly to the soul. If they are evil, they make the mind sad; if good, joyful. From one’s own evils or those of others arises suffering; from others’ evils, compassion; from one’s own goods, *perpassio*; from others’ goods, envious detraction.

For if the mind is bent toward sorrow by adversities, suffering results: this harms the mind inwardly while afflicting the body outwardly. [Col. 0950B] But if the mind is moved by prosperity toward joy, there results *perpassio*, that is, a movement somehow remote from suffering. Concerning the seven windows or senses of the soul, which flourish in the head, one should know that the more powerfully each exercises its force, the greater the fiery power it is shown to contain within itself. From the first part of the brain the vital force of fire is distributed in service through the various senses: to the eyes through sight, to the ears through hearing, to the nostrils through smell, to the mouth through taste, and to the whole body through touch. The nearer these senses or windows are to the brain, the more powerful they are found to be. The eyes, being close to the brain, are mobile and powerful for contemplation; in a moment they fly across the spacious air, so that through their windows they send the sharpness of their sight to the heights of heaven.

[Col. 0950C] The ears, farther from the brain than the eyes, extend their power less far than sight; the nostrils less far than those, though they extend their sense farther than the others. Taste never proceeds outside the mouth, yet within it operates with greater subtlety than touch: it distinguishes light and rough, hot and cold, dry and moist, hard and soft, as touch does, but surpasses the other senses in flavors. Touch, however, being more hidden than the rest, perceives nothing except by feeling, and therefore the natural philosopher calls it not a window of the soul but a blind messenger.

Among these seven windows of the soul, the eyes, mouth, and ears are called the principal windows, as is read in the book of blessed Hilary: just as the mind in reading proceeds through sight to letters, through letters to [Col. 0950D] words, and thence to understanding, so in speech it proceeds through hearing to words, and thence to understanding, by which the mind conceives the qualities—that is, the natures—of things. Thus understanding falls short of nature, and speech of understanding, because neither does understanding fully grasp the thing nor speech fully grasp understanding. For we can speak less than we understand, and understand less than a thing is in accordance with its qualities. And it should be noted that we read with mouth and mind, by which we know that God speaks with us; we pray with mouth and mind, by which we believe that we are reconciled to God.

Therefore, if these windows are closed to the devil and opened to God, the soul wisely goes forth into the prescribed paths, lest it be detained by worldly vanities; it contemplates more carefully what belongs to God and what is from God, and thus proceeds into [Col. 0951A] a manifold knowledge and reformation of itself. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Take heed to yourself and see” (Deut. 26). Hence David: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end” (Ps. 28). Hence Jeremiah, concerning the unhappy soul ignorant of itself: “Her filthiness was upon her feet, and she did not remember her end” (Lam. 1). Again, under the figure of the happy soul knowing itself: “I am the man who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3). Hence Gregory, concerning the wandering soul: “A fool, beholding pleasant meadows on the road, forgets whither he is going.” Hence the steward in the Gospels: “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg,” etc. (Luke 16). Certainly, if he dug, he would not be a beggar but rich; for to dig is to search conscience and thoughts, and carefully contemplate speech and deeds. This digging, therefore, is humble [Col. 0951B] confession, health-giving compunction, and a perfect fortification of the windows against every ambush of the enemy.

## SECTION IV. The fourth group of seven: the seven powers of the soul

The fourth group of seven, the seven powers of the soul, follows. They are directed toward all external things, and through them knowledge of things is perceived more clearly. Although the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit, nevertheless, once the powers of the soul—exercised in the school of disciplines and virtues—are known, that person has a greater approach to such knowledge.

There are seven powers of the soul in a human being: *animus*, mind; *mens*, intellective mind; imagination; opinion; reason; understanding; and memory. *Animus* is the governing power of the soul, friendly to the operations of nature. *Mens* is a power of the *animus* [Col. 0951C] that rouses itself by the service of the senses and considers what passion or action of sensing is subject to each sense. This power first conceives the beginning of understanding and thus extends its movement toward knowledge of the thing. Hence elsewhere: “The *mens* is a power of the *animus*, forming understanding and establishing intelligence.”

Imagination is the power of the soul by which we perceive the shape and color of a thing absent yet previously seen. It arises from the senses, especially sight. Sense apprehends what is; imagination, however, perceives both what is and what is not. Imagination is necessary to a person lest he consign a thing to oblivion. Opinion sometimes arises from sense and sometimes from imagination. For when the soul uses the instrument of sight or imagination, and thinks a thing—or something else, or something otherwise, or in another manner—to be other than it is, this is called false [Col. 0951D] opinion. But if it wavers and does not know whether it is so or not, while nevertheless investigating the truth, it is called true opinion. Hence it is described thus: “Opinion is either a false judgment of the soul concerning things, or a true judgment that is wavering and uncertain.”

Reason arises from true opinion in this way: when uncertain truth wavers and is afterward confirmed by investigation, reason results. Reason is the discriminating insight of the mind, distinguishing what is true and certain from what is false and uncertain. Understanding, however, arises from reason in this way: reason grasps forms mixed with matter and therefore does not perceive the truth of things, but distinguishes and investigates. When, through the long labor of reason and great diligence, the truth of forms is sought out, intelligence arises from this; it abstracts form from matter and understands without any composition of parts. [Col. 0952A] Therefore . . . describes it thus: “Intelligence belongs to God alone, and is something other than this.” Understanding is a power of the mind, stirred by opinion, grasping incorporeal things concerning bodies; intelligence, proceeding from understanding, is a true and certain judgment concerning incorporeal things.

Memory follows, and arises from imagination, study, and practice. Imagination drives away forgetfulness of things and restores memory; study rouses memory through exercise of the mind; practice firmly remembers all things, both new and old. Memory is the power of the soul by which it firmly retains what it has known before. Thus by these seven active powers we can ascend, with intelligence, to knowledge of the soul. For these powers are so united in one substance that they are one soul.

To show this more clearly, [Col. 0952B] Mercury Hermes says: “Wisdom is called the mother of *psyche*; *Endelicheia*, as though *endon elicheia*, that is, daughter of eternity.” That is, wisdom created *psyche*, the soul, giving it from herself, not from her own substance, reason, intelligence, and immortality. Hence the soul is called from its office of animating—that is, giving life—and thus its powers are manifold and its mode of understanding multiple. Hence Plato, treating the composition of the soul, says that it consists of sameness and difference, of indivisible and divisible substance. He says “of sameness” with reference to that mode of understanding by which it grasps many things by uniting them generally; “of difference,” with reference to the mode of grasping singular things; “of indivisible [Col. 0952C] substance,” with reference to the mode of grasping a thing formally and immutably; “of divisible substance,” with reference to the mode of grasping, in the mode of a composite, a thing materially and changeably.

From such a composition Dorotheus describes it thus: “The soul is a certain virtual whole, composed from those powers of understanding.” Hence Plato in the *Phaedo*: “Although the soul is incorporeal, nevertheless it is in some way portrayed after the likeness of a body. Its head is immortality; its eyes are reason and intelligence.” Reason is a power innate to the *animus*, comprehending unity and difference in things; but discernment, acquired through use and experience of temporal things, is caution. Hence discernment is called the mixing of different things.

In the book of *Election* is found written concerning the manner of its sensory actions. Sometimes [Col. 0952D] the soul apprehends things through itself; sometimes through a bodily instrument. For it conforms itself so completely to its instruments that, whatever the instrument is like, it apprehends things themselves in a similar manner: as if you inspected letters with glass placed between; whatever color the glass might be, the letters would seem to you to be of that color.

The soul is united to an exceedingly subtle spirit diffused through the arteries, such that this spirit is the vehicle of the soul and blood is the vehicle of that spirit. A certain artery, full of that spirit, is directed and divided toward the eyes. This bodily spirit is the instrument of the soul through which it exercises the sense of sight; when it encounters some obstacle, it is driven back, and therefore the soul is aroused to discern what stands in its way. Likewise, that spirit diffused through two arteries directed to the ears [Col. 0953A] is the soul’s instrument of hearing; it is struck by a voice, and therefore the soul is aroused to distinguish sound. So too, the spirit diffused through arteries to the nostrils is the instrument of smelling; and just as hearing occurs in very thin air, so smelling occurs in dense air, smoky in itself. Therefore the spirit is slowed by its smokiness, and the soul is roused to apprehend the odor of that smoke.

Thus the soul uses the spirit diffused through arteries directed to the spongy palate. When moisture enters beneath the palate, the spirit is slowed and the soul is aroused to taste. The soul also uses as its instrument spirit diffused through the marrow; when some solid thing obstructs the body, the spirit is slowed and the soul is aroused to touch. Therefore about the eyes the soul employs fiery power; about the ears, airy power, but pure; about the nostrils, airy power, but dense and smoky; about the palate, watery power; and about the marrow, earthly power, according to the order of the four elements. Because the spirit directed toward the eyes is higher and more subtle, the power of sight is swifter and sharper than hearing; hence we see lightning before hearing thunder, though they occur together.

It is asked: since the spirit directed to the eyes is more subtle than that directed to the ears, why does sight apprehend only gross and earthly things, while hearing senses a voice constituted from the thinnest air? We answer that this is caused by the direction of the rays through the eyes: their ray is so subtle and sharp that the air yields to it, and nothing obstructs it except what is gross enough to set it a limit. The ears and the other senses, however, perceive nothing unless they encounter an obstacle close at hand.

HERMES MERCURY: In the first part of the head, in the chamber called the imaginative chamber, there is a spirit subtler and more agile than the spirit diffused through the arteries. When the soul uses this spirit as an instrument, it apprehends the form in matter while the thing is absent. This power of the soul is called imagination. It differs from sense because sense apprehends form in matter while the thing is present; imagination, while the thing is absent, and thus confusedly, because not distinctly.

In this same chamber that spirit becomes thinner and subtler; and when the soul uses it, it apprehends forms mixed with matter, yet does not perceive the truth of things, but distinguishes [Col. 0953D] and investigates. For matter confuses, so that the truth of forms cannot be apprehended in relation to it. This power of the soul is called reason, and then that chamber is the rational chamber.

In the middle part of the head, in the chamber called the intellectual chamber, the soul, being simple and immutable, returns also to its own immutability and considers the forms of things outside matter in their immutability. This power of the soul is called disciplined knowledge, because one arrives at this consideration of forms through discipline and instruction. In the same chamber, in which the soul considers the forms of things in their simplicity, it uses itself as its instrument: that is, it not only abstracts the form of a circle from matter, but also understands it without any composition of parts. [Col. 0954A] This power is called intelligence, which belongs to God alone and is something beyond this. It differs from disciplined knowledge because the latter considers the forms of things immutably as composed of parts, whereas intelligence comprehends them without any composition of parts.

## SECTION V. The fifth group of seven: the seven virtues on which the soul relies

The fifth group of seven, the seven grades of virtues, is joined to those already mentioned. Supported by them, the soul contemplates divine things more closely. There are seven virtues produced by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. These gifts are the first motions in the heart, like certain seeds of virtues cast upon the soil of our heart; the virtues, however, rise from them like crops. They are certain good effects of the gifts. Hence John in [Col. 0954B] the Apocalypse: “I saw seven spirits running before the throne of the Lord” (Rev. 5). They are called spirits—that is, inspirations—which precede virtues; they are gifts, nevertheless, and not merits. Virtues, however, are both gifts and merits. In the former God works without us; in the latter he works with us.

Thus the seven virtues are as it were grades of sevenfold grace, by ascending which the soul contemplates more divinely. The first grade is humility, arising from fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom and suppresses pride. The second grade, gentleness, arises from the spirit of piety and restrains envy. The third grade, patience, is born from the spirit of knowledge and conquers anger. The fourth grade, diligence in good works or perseverance, arises from the [Col. 0954C] spirit of fortitude and chokes sloth. The fifth grade, generosity or mercy, arises from the spirit of counsel and suppresses avarice. The sixth grade, frugality or abstinence, arises from the spirit of understanding and overcomes gluttony. The seventh grade, purity of heart, arises from the spirit of wisdom and destroys love of money.

And it should be noted that some virtues are natural and others meritorious. The latter are of greater merit than the natural virtues, because a natural virtue can coexist in a person with a vice of nature, as strength with frailty of the flesh, or chastity with desire. Therefore a patient or chaste person sins through a vice of nature, while repenting and praying with Paul: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but that which dwells in me” (Rom. 17). Through these seven meritorious virtues the seven powers of the soul are reformed. [Col. 0954D] By them, and as it were by the grades of sevenfold grace, they are raised up. Thus, with the Spirit of sevenfold grace as guide, the soul contemplates God more closely.

Accordingly, as is understood from blessed Gregory, the soul is reformed by ascending step by step, and by contemplation is led onward even to the ineffable approach of divine knowledge. In the first grade, that of humility, the spirit of the fear of the Lord humbles the *animus*, lest it be proud among those who presume, but strengthens it with the fare of eternal things hoped for. In the second, that of gentleness, the spirit of piety occupies the innermost parts of the *mens*, that it may fill it with works of mercy. In the third, that of patience, the spirit of knowledge reforms the imagination, that it may make the mind steadfast. In the fourth grade, that is, perseverance in good work, the spirit [Col. 0955A] of fortitude, while driving adversity from the *animus*, gives confidence of reason to the mind wavering through opinion. In the fifth, that of generosity, the spirit of counsel, while preventing reason from becoming rash, fills *animus* and *mens* with the firmness of consolation. In the sixth, that of frugality, the spirit of understanding penetrates the mind’s understanding by restoring it, and by penetrating illumines its darkness. In the seventh, that of purity of heart, the spirit of wisdom reforms memory in recalling good things and establishes it in contemplation and delight in eternal truth. Thus, if the soul relies upon the seven grades of virtues by ascending them, it is reformed in its seven powers by sevenfold grace.

## SECTION VI. The sixth group of seven: the seven kinds of contemplation

[Col. 0955B] The sixth group of seven, concerning the seven kinds of contemplation in which the resting soul dwells more delightfully, follows. There are seven kinds of contemplation: meditation, soliloquy, circumspection, ascent, revelation, emission, and inspiration.

Meditation is frequent thought in deliberation, prudently investigating the cause and origin, manner and usefulness, of each thing. Meditation takes its beginning from the examination of reading. It is bound by no rules or precepts of reading, for it delights to range through a certain open expanse, where it may fix free reason upon contemplating truth: now touching upon these causes of things, now those; now penetrating every depth; leaving nothing doubtful, nothing obscure. [Col. 0955C] Therefore the beginning of instruction is in reading, its consummation in the examination of reading, and contemplation in the meditation of examination.

There are three kinds of meditation: one consists in the consideration of morals, another in the examination of commandments, and the third in the investigation of divine works; and so the beginning of contemplation comes about. For when the *animus* passes from meditation on the Scriptures to prayer and from prayer to reading, it truly contemplates the misery of present things, the punishment of the condemned, and the rewards of the righteous. Then, drawn by love of rewards and touched by fear of punishments, it descends to remembrance of its own sins. When it knows its own fault, it forgives another’s; and therefore, after remembering sins, it descends to [Col. 0955D] compassion for neighbors. In meditation upon Scripture we often labor, fearing that we may lose the reward of the righteous; in remembering sins we groan, lest we be among the condemned; in compassion for neighbors, that we may love good work. Thus, when with the whole tranquility of the mind we pray or read in meditation, we rest in contemplation.

Soliloquy follows, which is the solitary discourse of someone to and about himself, producing contempt for that very person. It is called soliloquy because a man speaks with himself alone: that is, when the inward person is not disturbed by the outward, but searches the secrets of the heart, considers and examines mind and conscience in contempt of himself. Soliloquy occurs in three ways: from inspiring grace, from meditation, and from prayer. From [Col. 0956A] grace it arises into compunction; from meditation it is roused into devotion; from prayer it is formed into good will. Compunction bursts into mournful weeping; devotion raises the mind to heavenly things; good will hastens toward action. Mournful weeping seeks the merciful Lord. An uplifted mind runs ahead into the depths of the heart; the work of good will displays contempt for the person himself.

Concerning mournful weeping the Prophet says: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Ps. 6). This weeping—that is, the shedding of tears for sins—has a voice not for us but for God. Such weeping is useful and pious. Weeping for the death of parents is pious but useless; weeping for the loss of temporal goods is neither pious nor useful. Concerning the uplifted mind which investigates the depths of conscience, [Col. 0956B] wisdom is described thus in Apollo’s tripod:

> A word descended from heaven: “Know thyself” (*gnōthi seauton*).

Apollo’s tripod is the threefold understanding of wisdom: historical, mystical, and moral. Through the historical the outward person yields to the inward; through the mystical the inward person searches and examines the secrets of the heart—that is, mind and conscience; through the moral, one recognizes whence one is, what one is, and for what one is. Whence one is: from the material of the potter, that is, from the mud of earth. What one is: namely, an earthen vessel, yet one must fear lest it become a vessel of dishonor. For what one is: that one may return to the dust of the earth.

Hence Job says that he sits and sleeps in the dust (Job 42). One sits and sleeps in the dust who, lulled by the lightness of mutable things, cannot rise except through great [Col. 0956C] labor. Hence David says, “Let him flourish in the morning” (Ps. 89): in the morning—that is, in childhood and youth—one flourishes; but in the evening—that is, in death—one falls, stiffens into a corpse, and dries into dust. For after a human being comes a corpse; after a corpse, a worm; after a worm, ashes. Thus wisdom in the tripod makes known the human condition and mutability, and expresses self-contempt more clearly.

### The third kind of contemplation

Circumspection is a name with two meanings. Circumspection, as a species of prudence, is called provident caution in matters to be done or words to be spoken. But when circumspection is specified as contemplation, it is called examination of the *animus*, because the *animus* contemplates among worldly things by understanding, counsel, and choice. [Col. 0956D] For the *animus* ranges through worldly things by understanding; deliberates and investigates concerning worldly things by counsel; and distinguishes and chooses among them by choice. The movement of the *animus* apprehends worldly things as mutable, perishable, and transitory. The deliberating investigation of the *animus* perceives worldly things to be both good and evil, although transitory, and to be contrary both to goods and to evils. The discerning choice of counsel separates good things from evils; among good things chooses the better; among adversities, if they cannot be avoided, the less harmful. Hence Terence (*Adelphoe* IV.7.21):

> Thus is human life, as when you play at dice:  
> If that throw which is most needed does not fall,  
> Then by skill you must correct what chance has thrown.

Therefore let the *animus* employ these three powers, in order to contemplate more circumspectly among worldly things, [Col. 0957A] lest it be confused by an abundance of temporal goods, led astray by their variety, or deceived when crushed by the manifold adversity of evils. In such adversity, patience produces an eternal crown for those who endure patiently.

### The fourth kind

Ascent is the going forth of the *animus* toward immortal things on high. Hence the Prophet: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has disposed ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83). There are three ascents disposed in the heart. There are three ascents of Christ, and likewise three of ourselves. First Christ ascended the mountain, then the cross, and finally to the Father. On the mountain he taught the disciples; on the cross he redeemed captives; in heaven he glorified the elect. On the mountain he set forth the teaching of humility; on the cross he expressed [Col. 0957B] the form of charity; in heaven he offered the crown of blessedness. In the first he bestowed the light of knowledge; in the second, the summit of righteousness; in the third, the divine majesty of glory.

There are three ascents of ourselves: the first in action, the second in affection, the third in understanding. Actual ascent is threefold: first, in confession of sins; second, in the giving of alms; third, in contempt for riches. The first consists in works of repentance; the second, in works of mercy; the third, in works of consummate righteousness. The first merits pardon, the second grace, the third glory. Affective ascent is threefold: first, toward perfect humility; second, toward consummate charity; third, toward purity of contemplation. Intellectual ascent illuminates and commands; action is illuminated [Col. 0957C] and obeys; affection illuminates and is illuminated, obeys understanding, and commands action.

### The fifth kind

Revelation is divine instruction concerning hidden things through a created thing set before one. It is fourfold. The first was made to Peter through a sheet: “Kill,” he says, “slay, and eat; what God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10). The second was made to Dionysius, placed in prison: Christ says, “Receive this, dear one, which I shall shortly fulfill for you: together with my Father.” The third was made to Heraclius, to whom Christ showed the cross in heaven by night, saying: “Conquer by this.” The fourth was made, as Gregory relates, to a certain priest, to whom in the sacrament of the altar the truth of the Lord’s body and blood was revealed. The first mode of revelation occurred [Col. 0957D] for instruction, the second for consolation, the third for devotion, the fourth for thanksgiving.

### The sixth kind

Emission is a divinely instructed illumination of the mind, for its own benefit. There are seven emissions, as it were seven trees, concerning which it is read in the Book of Wisdom: “I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion. I was exalted like a palm in Cades, and like a planting of roses in Jericho; like an olive tree breathing fragrance in the plains, and like a plane tree beside water in the streets” (Ecclus. 24). The first is the fruit of repentance; the second, a work of mercy; the third, love of righteousness; the fourth, the rigor of mortification; the fifth, the sweetness of contemplation; the sixth, joy in future blessedness; the seventh, a tree of life to those who lay hold of [Col. 0958A] it; and blessed is the person who holds it.

There are seven trees and seven kinds of places. In the valley are penitents; on the plain, the merciful; in the city, those practicing discipline; on the mountain, those carrying Christ’s cross; upon the watchtower, contemplatives crucified to the world; in Lebanon, the perfect, who have attained the whiteness of innocence and been caught up to the third heaven. These are the seven women in Isaiah who will lay hold of one man on that day. The first produces tears and groans; the second, the most health-giving sufferings for the guilt of venial sins; the third, the sweetest affections of compassion; the fourth, hatreds of the world, flesh, and sin; the fifth, desires for virtues and for the kingdom of heaven; from the sixth arises the grace of ineffable action; from the seventh, understanding of heavenly mysteries and the incomparable [Col. 0958B] glory of a most pure mind.

### The Seventh Kind of Contemplation

But in the highest place is set the sublime kind of contemplation called inspiration: a health-giving infusion from above which affects the soul. This is fourfold: it arises either from fear of servitude, hope of reward, filial love, or conjugal affection. The first brings back the runaway slave; the second presses the hired laborer working in the vineyard; the third corrects and instructs the son; the fourth joins the bride to her bridegroom and places her in the marriage-bed.

Inspiration likewise arises from fear of eternal punishment, grief at present exile, fellow-feeling for one’s brethren, and the prompting of heavenly devotion. These are the four winds of heaven (Zech. 6), by which God’s elect are gathered: the first, the western wind, brings penitents out from the setting of their neighbors; the second, the northern wind, brings forth those mortifying their members from the coldness of wickedness; the third, the southern wind, brings those fervent in spirit from the warmth of righteousness; the fourth, the eastern wind, brings lovers of purity, who, as though from eastern brightness, behold through a mirror the light of wisdom. [Col. 0958C]

In this contemplation the knowledge of God consists in five ways: from the creation of the world; from the reason or nature of the soul; from knowledge of the divine utterance; from the ray of contemplation; and from the joy of the most blessed vision.

Of the first the Apostle writes: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made; even his everlasting power and divinity” (Rom. 1). In the second, reason plainly teaches that all things have descended from one first principle. In the third—that is, from knowledge of the divine utterance—the invisible things of God are known. Hence in Ezekiel: “The spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezek. 1); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “The words which I speak to you are spirit and life” (John 6). [Col. 0958D]

There are three invisible things of God: power, wisdom, and goodness. These the divine page especially teaches, commends, and urges us to seek, embrace, and love. In the fourth way—that is, from the ray of contemplation—the invisible things of divine contemplation are known. Hence the Apostle: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). Thus Manoah is said in the book of Judges to have told his wife: “We shall die, because we have seen God” (Judg. 13). Thus Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6).

There are three kinds of this contemplation, denoted by three expressions through three theologians: by Isaiah, as was said, through the throne (Isa. 6); by Elijah through the whisper, thus: “Behold, the spirit of the Lord passed by, overturning mountains and breaking rocks; the Lord was not in the spirit. And after the spirit, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, fire; the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19): there was the Lord. By Ezekiel, through the handbreadth: “Behold, a man, and in his hand a reed of six cubits and a handbreadth” (Ezek. 40). [Col. 0959A]

There are, moreover, three thrones. The first is low, when the mind is raised to the invisible things of the world; the second elevated, when it is raised to the invisible things of itself; the third lofty, when it is exalted to the invisible things of God. From this one ascends to the whisper, which is called the sweetness of divine grace. Gregory says of this whisper: “A whistle incites puppies and calms horses.” And the Lord, through Isaiah, speaks of the swift conversion of the sinner and the ascent from virtue to virtue: “The Lord shall raise a standard among nations far off, and shall whistle to them from the ends of the earth; and behold, he shall come swiftly and joyfully” (Isa. 11). [Col. 0959B]

By the six cubits the active life is signified, because God’s works are completed on the sixth day. The handbreadth, said to be beyond the six cubits, belongs already to the seventh [day], in which the repose of contemplation is understood. In the handbreadth contemplation is represented; in the hand, action; in the fingers, discernment. And as hand and fingers are extended in the handbreadth, so in contemplation good action and holy discernment are extended and governed.

The fifth mode of divine knowledge is called the joy of the most blessed vision. Very few happy persons enjoy this in the present life; carried away by the exceeding sweetness of divine savor, they contemplate God alone. This mode of divine knowledge differs from the fourth. In the fourth, the soul is illuminated by the ray of contemplation so that it may range in knowledge over the world and itself, and thus return to invisible things of greater knowledge. But in this fifth mode the soul, wholly illuminated by the splendor of eternal light, perfectly hates sin, puts the world aside, rejects itself, and wholly—alone, naked, and more nearly—tends toward the Lord: wholly, living wholly for the one God; alone, apart from matter but not from form; more nearly, apart from every circumscription. [Col. 0959C]

There are three kinds of this highest contemplation, indicated by three things through three persons: by Job through hanging, thus: “My soul chose hanging, and my bones death” (Job 7); by John through silence: “There was silence in heaven” (Rev. 8); by Solomon through sleep, as the bride says in the Song: “I sleep, but my heart wakes” (Song 5). The first kind is that of purity; the second, of charity; the third, of blessedness. In the first, the first step is that the soul gather itself into itself; in the second, the second step is that, once gathered, it see what it is like; in the third, the third step is that it rise above itself to invisible things, submit itself in purity to this pure contemplation, and so, purified and enlightened, direct itself wholly toward God.

There is a difference between revelation, emission, and inspiration. The first occurs with matter and form; the second without matter but with form; the third without matter and form. The first is real, the second spiritual, the third intellectual; or, the first is sensible, the second intelligible, the third intellectible; or, the first worldly, the second human, the third divine. Following our master, we have stated these things briefly, according to our ability; the rest, more loftily and more polishedly, we commit to Your Excellency. [Col. 0960A]

## Section VII. The Seventh Set of Seven: On the Seven Principles of Things

The final set of seven, that is, the seventh, is placed at the end and is entitled “On the Seven Principles of Things.” But in order that we may gain some knowledge of the seven principles of things—that is, of the hidden causes of things—a few preliminary matters should fittingly first be sampled, as Hermes Trismegistus says:

“The earliest sages, seeing the human race blinded by the darkness of this sort of ignorance, and perceiving it weak and infirm both in soul and body, first devised two principal sciences for the restoration of each: theology, namely, for the salvation of the soul; and physics for the health of the body. In order that these might be learned more suitably and easily, they set before them, as an introduction, the seven liberal arts which they afterward discovered.” [Col. 0960B]

Accordingly, they devised and wrote these nine sciences in order to have knowledge of things and to understand their causes and origin.

Although many read these sciences, they nevertheless remain ignorant of the causes and principles of things, for whose sake those sciences had been invented. A cause, according to Mercury, is “that which among first principles precedes its own effect by the rationale of substance, not of necessity.” This description applies to every primordial cause, that is, to every principle. It is called *causa* from *causon*, “burning,” because it kindles its effect so that it may pass into some substance. [Col. 0960C]

According to different authors, there are seven principles of things, called primordial causes. According to theologians, there is one principle: God, the creator of all. According to natural philosophers, there are three: matter, form, and created spirit—that is, nature. According to Mercury, there are four: the law of the stars, nature, the world, and the mechanism of the world.

Of the first principle Pope Clement says: “When we direct the sharpness of the mind to consider what God is, let ‘who,’ ‘what,’ and ‘where’ depart from the heart; for his essence is neither always nor everywhere.” Of the same principle Heraclitus the natural philosopher says: “God is essence joined to matter by the law of husbandhood, whose seed is nature.” And B[—]: “God is form without matter.” Dorotheus the astronomer says: “All things from eternity are joined in God as one; in actuality they are many; they are different from one another because the plurality of things which are common descends from that unity which is God.” [Col. 0960D]

Augustine, in the book *On the Five Heresies*, says that Hermes Mercury wrote a book called *Logostelios*. “A great name for the book, because it was written concerning the Great One. The Lord,” he says, “and maker of all gods made a second lord; he made him first, sole, and one. He seemed good to him, and most full of all goods.” John the Evangelist agrees with this when he says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1). Elsewhere in the same book Hermes says: “The son of the Blessed One and of good will, whom he loved as his only-begotten, whose name cannot be uttered by human speech.” [Col. 0961A]

Augustine says: “You cannot be narrated, you who are not a man but are judged by men to be God.” Where Hermes calls him “only-begotten,” he convicts the heretic who says: “If God delighted in the Son, he needed marriage; if he recoiled from marriage, he is alone without a Son.” Let us therefore seek the stone by which the stone may be struck: struck, it may be shattered; shattered, it may be crushed.

The Sibyl also rebukes him, saying: “Know that the Lord is the Son of God—he himself and no other; not Mars, not Jupiter, not Mercury, but he whom Mercury confesses and whom demons believe and tremble before, saying: ‘We know that you are the Son of God; why have you come before the time to torment us?’” (Matt. 8). Augustine says: “Why, Christian, do you marvel when you hear such testimony concerning Father and Son?”

Parmenides also says: “God is he for whom to be anything that is, is to be all that is.” Again, the same writer: “God is unity; from unity is begotten equality of unity; connection proceeds from unity and equality of unity.” [Col. 0961B]

Hence Augustine says: “To everyone who looks rightly it is clear why unity is assigned by the teachers of Holy Scripture to the Father, equality to the Son, and connection to the Holy Spirit; and although equality is begotten from unity and connection proceeds from both, nevertheless they are one and the same.” This is that unity of the three which Pythagoras taught should alone be worshipped. Of it Martianus says that, when Philosophy wished to worship it, she vomited forth circles and spheres. I suppose this is because whoever desires to contemplate that true unity must, leaving mathematical consideration behind, raise the mind to the simplicity of understanding. [Col. 0961C]

From this highest and eternal Trinity descends a certain trinity of everlasting things. From unity descends matter; from the equality of unity, form; and from the connection of both, created spirit—that is, nature. These are the three principles descending from the first principle.

Hence my master says: “The first principle is eternity, which, because it is immutable, is called necessity. The second principle is matter, which, because it is fit to receive all forms, is called possibility. The third principle is form, which, because it determines matter into some state, is called finality. The fourth principle is created spirit, which, because it is the universal motion of things, is called actuality.” [Col. 0961D]

According to Plato, necessity, which cannot be resisted, commands. Matter, because it yields like pliable wax, obeys necessity in order to receive forms. Created spirit—that is, universal and natural motion—joins the form, invisible in itself, to matter, invisible in itself, so that from them a composite may pass into some actual and invisible substance.

This spirit is natural and universal motion: it holds together the four elements as though they were *hyle*, that is, the bonds of matter; it is diffused through the firmament by means of the stars, and through the sublunary world by fire, air, water, earth, and all other things in the world which move naturally. This motion is called nature by Mercury, the soul of the world by Plato, fate by some, and divine disposition by theologians. [Col. 0962A]

Aristotle also says that matter is called possibility and privation: privation because, being formless in itself, it lacks forms of itself; possibility because it is fit to receive forms. From possibility comes generation; from privation, corruption. From possibility, life; from privation, destruction.
