Hermes Mercury describes the fifth principle of things thus: “The law of the stars is the just and perpetual ordering of their motions, which produces and governs the mechanism of the world; through it the world and worldly things are governed not by compulsion, but by the kindly peace of friendship.” Since “the law of the stars” has a double meaning, in one sense it is called motion moving all things; in another it is written “motion, without motion, moving all things.” This motion is called divine disposition by theologians; it regulates all things with highest peace, each thing with highest tranquility, and qualities with highest repose. [Col. 0962B]

The same writer describes nature, namely the fourth principle of things, thus: “Nature is a certain universal and spiritual vigor, born from cause and reason, first implanted in heaven, fourfold in all things and each thing, qualified and quantified, successively diffusing different qualities.”

Again, he describes the world, the sixth principle of things, thus: “The world is nature’s circular, harmonious, universal, temporal, and local motion, leaving nothing outside itself; proportionately abiding within in centered repose, and binding together the conflicting qualities of things in *syzygies* [conjunctions].” [Col. 0962C]

He likewise describes the seventh principle thus: “The mechanism of the world is a harmonious and measured motion of contrary motions, which *paragorizes*—that is, soothes—the world and worldly things by life-giving heat, tempers them by quality, and forms them by quantity.”

Thus the totality of things—that is, all things—are in eternity, that is, in God, immutably; all things are in matter suitably and potentially; all things are in form incorporeally and visibly—incorporeally in themselves, visibly when joined to matter; all things are in created spirit naturally and actually; all things are in the law of the stars orderly; all things are in the world movably; all things are in the mechanism of the world proportionately—that is, dissimilarly—and harmoniously. [Col. 0962D]

These, then, are the seven principles of things, in the inquiry into which the intellects of many philosophers have been consumed; for whose subtlety the studies of the Peripatetics have gone beyond bounds; by whose immensity all are swept away in a great abyss. For their sake every art and every discipline was invented.

To know them, the intellect alone, naked and pure, roused by the foregoing six sets of seven, can ascend more divinely: alone from matter, naked from form, pure from every stain. Toward these all things chiefly incline materially, look back formally, and tend spiritually—especially toward the first principle, which is the most causal cause of all. [Col. 0963A]

In theology this is called the divine nature, infinite in itself, invisible to us, and incomprehensible to us; and thus it is said not what it is, but what it is not. For one who calls it invisible does not say that it is what it is, but that it is not what it is not. Hence my master says:

“A great mystery! When it is asked what God is, this cannot be said, because it cannot be thought. Therefore God cannot be thought as any thing that is; for he is other, and otherwise, and far away, and remote, and dissimilar, and what he is cannot be said. For if any of these things is said, he is other; if, namely, any of these things is said, he is otherwise; if any of these things is understood through the suitability of tropology, he is far away and remote; if he is apprehended through some anagogical appearance of likeness, he is dissimilar. What, then, is God? This alone can be thought and said: that God is other and otherwise; and what he is cannot be said. For everything that we have, and everything that we can say, is other than God. Neither eye sees nor mind comprehends except this or that which is not God.” [Col. 0963B]

And as no one knows the things of a human being except the human spirit which is within that person, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God; and whoever has the Spirit of God knows, through the Spirit of God, the things of God.

But to consider this, I think we must go back a little higher. A person using reason sees with three eyes: with the eye of flesh, by which one sees the world outside oneself and the things that are in the world; with the eye of reason, one sees within oneself the soul and what is in the soul; with the eye of contemplation, one sees within oneself God and what is in God. Therefore those who have God’s Spirit within them have God and see God, because they have an illuminated eye by which God may be seen; and they perceive him not in something else or according to something else which he is not, but himself in himself, as he is, present. [Col. 0963C]

Yet he cannot be thought, because he is unthinkable; nor can he be spoken, because he is ineffable. He is seen and perceived, but not expressed. For whoever says anything says it according to something, thinks what is said, and knows what is said. You name God, form two syllables, and think that you have said the whole. What, then, do you think when you say “God,” or of what sort is that which you call God? If you interpret God under this name as one who sees all things, or as fear, who can explain how God sees or how God is fear? How can that be feared which cannot be seen, thought, or known? [Col. 0963D–0964A]

See, then, what you think or say when you say “God.” When you say “God,” you think that he made all things, but you do not think what he himself is who made them. All that you say is less than he is; and that whole which you say is not himself in his entirety, though you say it concerning him—not so that you may reach him, but so that you may draw near to him. For it is a great thing for a human being now to go toward him, even if it is not granted to arrive. But it will be granted later, when that which is perfect has come and a human being begins to see, not an image through a mirror, but truth face to face (1 Cor. 13).

For now, meanwhile, everything is an image, far from truth; yet it does what it can: it turns the soul, but does not bring it to its destination. Thus it is said that God is fire, and this is a manifest figure; yet God is not fire in its proper nature, because fire is a body and God is not a body. [Col. 0964B]

There is another incorporeal nature said to be nearer to God: that by which an exalted likeness of God is formed for us when it is said, “God is spirit,” wisdom, reason, and love. For the soul is spirit, and an angel is spirit, and in spirit itself there are reason, wisdom, and love. We know what spirit is insofar as we know the soul, and through the angel we know the soul. Therefore, when we hear that God is spirit, we think of soul and angel and conceive a likeness: that God is something such as a soul or angel, because he is spirit. Yet we do not know how far this is from truth, since his excellence is incomprehensible. [Col. 0964C]

In such a comparison, one is eternal and the other temporal; one immense and the other comprehensible; one always remaining the same and the other mutable. Yet because nothing else can be said, this is said, lest nothing be said, since we cannot yet attain truth itself—until the figure passes away and truth is openly revealed. Therefore figures now remain, to be accepted as signs of truth, almost in place of truth, until that which is perfect comes in truth itself.

For this reason all men seek this first principle and all the rest most diligently in the trivium, investigate them more keenly in the quadrivium, and examine them more subtly in the inquiry of theology and philosophy. All seek these things but do not find them, because their manner of inquiry and their ignorance of truth stand in their way. It should therefore be noted that there is a threefold inquiry into, and a threefold knowledge of, the truth of causes or principles. The first inquiry is mathematical, which contemplates—

[Lacking one leaf.]

## John of Salisbury’s *Entheticus on the Doctrines of the Philosophers*

[Col. 0965A]

You will examine the doctrines of the ancients and the fruit of their labor,  
which philosophy gathers from her studies.

May that good Spirit govern tongue and mind,  
who teaches good words and brings forth devout prayers;

may he direct your steps, support your works and deeds,  
so that grace, life, and salvation may be your companions.

The court delights in novelties and scorns its old friends;  
the sole cause that pleases it is pleasure and gain.

“Who are you? Why have you come? Whither do you tend, and whence?”  
perhaps it will ask. Little book, give a brief reply.

### On Aletheia and Phronesis

[Col. 0965B]

Aletheia is the sister of Phronesis, the source of virtue,  
pleasing in her own beauty and ever dear to God.

For she is disfigured whenever outward adornment attends her;  
the blessed virgin flees cosmetic artifices.

They turn their eyes and hearts upon each other in turn;  
the beauty of one is the beauty of the other.

Their race, their kind, and their work are shared;  
from them flows the holy rule and measure of life.

Let these be your companions; let them order your concerns and words,  
and seek to commend you to men of weight.

Let them show you the beginning, course, and end of speech,  
and what discourse is fitting for which persons.

[Col. 0965C]

From the trivium you will take your beginning in speaking;  
yet first observe what suits which circumstances.

### That Logic Makes Men Wise and Discerning

What logic can do, and why it pleases the wise man—  
if you are to speak of this, approach the countenance of the philosopher.

Who follows sound without understanding, who seizes words  
but not their meaning, cannot be an impartial judge.

Since it furnishes the force of words for the purpose of speaking,  
if this is unknown, what will words be but wind?

The good hearer weighs what proceeds from the speaker’s mind,  
not every meaning which the words may carry for themselves;

yet let the proper law of speech attend the words,  
without which they cannot have their proper weight.

[Col. 0965D]

Long ago Roman law ordered verbal quibbling excluded from court,  
but the unjust praetor loves it.

### On Triflers Who Make Logic a Lie

[Col. 0966A]

A lawsuit is unhappy unless the proper form of proceeding is sought—  
a form which, Justinian, you command to be kept far away.

Thus, unless you speak in a manner pleasing to boys,  
the chattering crowd will spit in your face.

If you are wise, if you review the writings of the ancients  
in order to establish anything you may wish to prove,

they will all cry out: “Where is this old ass going?  
Why does he report to us the sayings or deeds of the ancients?

“We are wise from ourselves; our own youth has taught itself;  
our company does not accept the doctrines of the ancients.

We do not take on the burden of following the words  
of authors whom Greece possesses and Rome honors.

I am an inhabitant of a little bridge, a new author in the art,  
[Col. 0966B] while I boast that what was discovered before is mine.

What the old men taught, and friendly youth does not know,  
I swear was an invention of my own mind.

A zealous crowd of young men surrounds me, and thinks  
that when I boast of great things I speak nothing but truth.”

### On the Men of Melun

This talkative and biting fellow scarcely smells of Melun;  
he is thought wiser than his own Alberic.

This verbose man corrects Abelard’s errors;  
worn coinage is expelled from our marketplace.

[Col. 0966C]

“The well-spoken sayings of the ancients pleased in their own times;  
in our age only new things please.

Since everything depends upon talent, do not concern yourself  
with what you learn first or read later.”

This school cares nothing for measure or order,  
or for the path teacher and pupil ought to keep.

“It is therefore more expedient to confuse various tongues  
than to be foolishly occupied with the studies of the ancients.

Grammarians inquire what numbers, cases, or tenses may agree;  
they guard against ungainly words.

They are tortured by study, tortured by consuming care;  
[Col. 0966D] no leisure and no rest are granted them.

Unhappy is labor from which no advantage follows;  
[Col. 0967A] he for whom wretchedness is sweet wishes to be miserable.

Whoever wishes to be miserable proves himself mad;  
clearly, then, miserable is he who wishes to be miserable.

He who matches numbers to numbers, cases to cases,  
and tenses to tenses is foolish and miserable.

For the labor is great, no shortcuts result;  
thus time perishes, and life altogether with it.

Without heavy labor you can be more wordy  
than those restrained by the ancient rule of the Fathers.

Whatever comes into your mouth, utter boldly; let arrogance be at hand:  
you possess the art that makes a man.

Fortune attends bold ventures. If grace deserts arrogance,  
[Col. 0967B] glory is more welcome to us.

For this alone our people seek above all things.  
If glory is lacking, what do you think knowledge is?

Chatter will provide it, every virtue abandoned;  
if you can chatter, glory surely remains.

To be able to chatter, do not run through books;  
be wordy and keep writings far away.

Books hinder these men, and the teachings of earlier writers hinder those;  
great labor prevents them from having success.

He disputes sluggishly who turns over writings and arts,  
for no supporter of the ancients can be a logician.

Whoever is about to dispute and follows ancient doctrines  
must be counted among the oxen of the patriarchs.

For the more you read, the more remains for you to read;  
[Col. 0967C] and the more they teach, the more they teach must be taught.

Read little so that you may know much. Let any author you encounter  
be so upon your lips

that whatever you say may be thought to have been said by the author,  
and his mind to be your spirit.

Do not merely appear to know what he wrote; boast that everything  
he intended is part of your own doctrine.

Promise that you can teach what he wrote and what he kept silent;  
no one forbids you to speak falsely.

For wealth is sought and glory rests upon falsehood;  
[Col. 0967D] shame makes truthful men say little.”

When childish error has persuaded others of these things—  
that a young man may learn very much by reading little—

he praises Aristotle alone, scorns Cicero,  
and all that conquered Greece gave to the Latins;

he spits upon the laws, physics becomes worthless, every branch  
of letters grows foul, and logic alone pleases.

Yet it does not please him so that anyone should labor to know it;  
if a man is believed to be a logician, that is enough.

You would think men mad rather than philosophizing:  
all serious things are far too burdensome.

Trifles become sweet, they recoil from a wise man’s face,  
and often the sight of a book is a kind of torture.

### On the Sertorians

[Col. 0968A]

Sertorius, we are told, once weaned his too-tender pupils  
by teaching them in this fashion:

for the teacher of youths, compelled by price and money,  
taught that to know nothing was a great reward.

This school wished its young men always to remain young,  
so that they might disdain either to know or to be old.

And although it is supported by the multitude of the Garamantes,  
whom frenzy teaches to dare both right and wrong,

whom gluttony and arrogance have captured and forced into slavery,  
whom Venus makes cross over into her camp,

yet you, armed with the shield and sword of virtue,  
will go forth to meet them, to destroy their madness.

### On the Rounders of Speech

[Col. 0968B]

The Sertorian thinks himself fettered  
if you bid him live or speak correctly.

“Look at this burden, this yoke,” which our youth avoids  
as it runs by a more favorable road to the heights.

It admits solecism, takes what the barbarian offers,  
inserts such things into speech, and neglects artful speaking.

By this practice the Norman dresses up his language  
when he desires to be considered polished and to imitate the Frenchman;

our puffed-up courtier, with his rounded speech,  
laughs at the rustic words of his native soil.

“Rounded speech” is speech restrained by no rule,  
which no people can properly claim as its own.

[Col. 0968C]

Among the ancients this manner of speaking had been worthless,  
for they were accustomed to live by good law and speak by law.

### On Hyrcanus

But because Hyrcanus once flourished in those times,  
to whom lust was more pleasing than God’s law,

who falsely believed that kings were held under no law  
and that whatever pleased them was holy,

this usage finds special favor: royal favor carried greater weight with him,  
and rounded speech has its price.

### On Mandrogerus

We see Mandrogerus flourishing by such a practice,  
under which not even a shameful cause can fail.

The trifles of Mandrogerus seem the highest wisdom,  
and the words of Mandrogerus will be the formula of law.

[Col. 0968D]

Thus it profits less to use Latin speech  
than, if one can, to utter rounded words.

One must sweat excessively to learn Latin;  
rounded speech will be yours without labor.

They persist in studies and seek the aid of art,  
by whose support elegant language pleases.

It is therefore better to confuse languages than to undergo together  
such losses of time and substance.

But they say these things; you, briefly state  
what are the elements of knowing and speaking well.

### What Contributes to Wisdom

A powerful natural ability soon masters every art,  
if this following company is present:

hearing speech, reading books, diligent  
[Col. 0969A] care, rest suited to study, and faithful love.

### What Contributes to Eloquence

If anyone desires to be held distinguished in eloquence,  
these things will unquestionably give him what he desires:

strong talent, the exercise of a retentive mind,  
the resources of art, organs of voice, and frequent speech.

### On Mercury and Philology

If anyone is strong in these accomplishments, both in mind and speech,  
he joins Mercury with Philology for you.

Let not Maurus, who writes *Philologia*, disturb you: in verse  
a long syllable is sometimes made short,

and a short syllable is sometimes lengthened by poetic art;  
yet in prose the sense remains the same in either case.

[Col. 0969B]

Since the matter rests upon sense, he errs childishly  
who makes a long dispute over goats’ wool.

You may utter either form, or both; but insist  
that Philology be Mercury’s companion,

not because reverence is offered to false deities,  
but because truths lie hidden beneath a covering of words.

Truths concerning various things lie hidden, covered in figures;  
for public laws forbid sacred things to be common.

The ancients therefore veiled such matters under their own figures  
so that faith might be able to win merit.

For hidden things please, while things known to the crowd grow cheap;  
what the vulgar can know, they think belongs to no one.

[Col. 0969C]

At times the false appearance of a word may conceal a true thing;  
provided the true thing lies beneath, the figure remains true.

Its verbal appearance is false, yet its meaning faithful,  
when it causes faith to adhere to hidden matters.

### On Furvus and Martianus

How a secret lies hidden beneath a false image  
is a question taught by Furvus and Capella.

They examine the causes of things and discuss alliances.  
Furvus, manners and histories please you more.

Furvus’ elevated style has fallen out of use  
and is seldom read because of its gravity;

yet he remains dear in the Ligurian town  
where his name derives from the budding of flowers.

My William of Conches often read him,  
and our Pontilianus also loves him.

[Col. 0969D]

He is shut up in the archives of Rheims; Belgica first produced him,  
and he holds first place at Orléans.

Furvus is more useful to the great, but Capella  
is fuller of milk, more suited to small understandings.

### On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury

Philology passes into the embraces of Stilbon [Mercury],  
and our Capella teaches that this occurs in a pious manner.

Mercury is the sign of speech, Philology of reason;  
Philosophy commands that they be joined.

If the talent for speech has the aid of rational practice,  
the husband will be illustrious through his wife’s dowry;

but if reason is absent, he is thought almost naked,  
scarcely able to cover his obscene buttocks.

The marriage is happy when virtue is joined with nature;  
the bridal chamber for this union will be the wise man’s mind.

### On Grace, the Reconciler of the Virtues

[Col. 0970A]

Neither Juno nor Hymenaeus can join these;  
grace alone, the bridesmaid of virtues, can do so.

Without it the talent for speech and reason are barren,  
or their fruit is born degenerate and bad.

Without it the powers of nature are frustrated  
and every effort toward good is vain.

For we are prone to evil and fit for destruction;  
if grace is absent, every work is evil.

If grace is absent, neither mind nor helpful hand  
will act; grace anticipates and governs the mind.

Grace moves affections and advances the practice of works;  
[Col. 0970B] it guards the tongue and does not allow it to become guilty.

It raises affection, directs reason, orders actions,  
unseals what is hidden, and teaches truth.

Those whom it cherishes it makes acceptable,  
makes them philosophize rightly, and enjoy desired prosperity.

Grace purifies, illumines, and fulfills nature,  
and draws noble work from the bosom of genius.

The Gentiles regarded Genius as a perishable deity,  
born subject to the fates of a dependent thing.

More truly, this will be called an innate good, adapting  
things subject to it so that they may be subject to gratuitous goods.

Grace enriches humankind with innumerable gifts  
and makes the human race flourish in angelic lot.

### That Philosophy Is Grace’s Chief Gift

[Col. 0970C]

Among all gifts philosophy excels,  
which the perishable mind guards and the noble mind seeks.

Always and everywhere it adorns, honors,  
and advances its followers, and always everywhere crushes opponents.

It bears and nourishes virtues and, a stepmother to vice,  
drives it away and allows no place for error.

### On Nursia and Her Jests

Adversity breaks the fool; prosperity raises him up.  
When blind Nursia wishes to make sport for the people,

what are her jests but the games of Fortune, the phantasms of the world?  
For by these jests she blinds their sight.

By empty illusion she fashions the wheel of Fortune  
and unteaches the weak whom she could have taught.

[Col. 0970D]

She displays false appearances and makes small things appear  
great—or, conversely, great things small.

She gives things contrary faces and assigns them  
false names at her own pleasure.

She feigns that false things are something and true things nothing,  
thereby shutting off the path of reason.

Though she may introduce a thousand masked figures,  
philosophy does not lose its judgment.

### On Freedom of Choice

[Col. 0971A]

True freedom of choice requires the assistance  
of two things, without which the guilty mind lies oppressed:

namely, that reason rightly discern, and that affection  
always love what devout laws approve.

Subjugated nature cannot provide this,  
for sin, its companion, presses it with an inflicted wound.

Sin, nursing punishment, confuses the sharpness of reason,  
throws the will headlong, and does not allow it to be devout.

Grace, restoring nature, purifies reason’s sharpness  
and tempers and governs the affections.

It frees the choice of those whom your devout mother,  
Philosophy, consecrates to your worship.

### What Philosophy Is

What is philosophy but the fountain, way, and guide of salvation,  
the soul’s light, life’s rule, and welcome rest?

It cannot indeed uproot troublesome motions,  
but restrains harmful ones and tames them by reason.

Nor does the assault of an enemy, soon to perish, greatly harm  
[Col. 0971B] one who remains, so that the savage beast may harm him less.

### That pride, a savage pest, takes away from a person the limb it takes possession of.

A savage beast always tears a member from the wounded body  
and marks the one whom it teaches to be its own;

[285] now by the foot, now by the eye, now by the tongue, now by a gesture  
of the shoulders, now by the expression of the face it marks each person;

sometimes by a movement of the head, or by the fashion of dress,  
or by deeds the savage beast reveals itself.

Enemies give instruction; but the savage beast makes one proud  
[290] and casts down and kills the exalted.

To have held one’s crown in battle contributes to merit,  
and, once the enemy has been overthrown, glory will be greater.

[Col. 0971C] A hard struggle will bear the fruit of a great reward,  
for a reward worthy of merits is given for labour.

Therefore labour is always in service and hastens to earn merit,  
[295] and brings about either the cause of death or of salvation.

That labour alone is shown to serve life  
which Philosophy, its companion, moves and governs;

that serves death which Philosophy abandons—  
and, without her, whatever the world can possess is of less account.

[300] If anyone attempts to utter praises worthy of her,  
his intellect fails and his conquered tongue falls silent.

Or, if it does not fall silent, it stammers and longs to say  
what it cannot express, and makes known its desires.

### That philosophy and charity are the same.

[Col. 0971D]

[305] If the true wisdom of humankind is the true God,  
then philosophy is love of the true God.

But if nothing in the world is greater than that love,  
and if divine love surpasses all things,

conclude that Philosophy transcends the world,  
[310] and that faith is present in her first principle.

True faith in Christ, full of sacraments, begets and nourishes virtue;  
deeds prove them both.

Without the sacraments this faith is not true, nor do they  
suffice unless the hand is ready for good works,

[315] ready for good works, if time is granted to an adult;  
[Col. 0972A] a shadow protects children, as does the Church’s faith.

Every pious doctrine owes its highest honour to the sacraments;  
the reprobate person thinks these to be nothing.

### That no one philosophizes without faith.

No one can philosophize sincerely without faith,  
[320] nor does merit arise without faith.

Therefore let the philosopher preserve faith and love  
the cultivation of virtue and the work of piety.

Vain faith, which no memorials of pious works testify to be alive,  
does not help; indeed, it harms.

### That philosophy requires order and measure in all things.

[Col. 0972B]

[325] Philosophy prescribes that all things be done in order  
and establishes that all things possess measure.

It teaches all things in order and hands down both the reason and method of reading;  
and order is pleasing in every art.

Under her leadership beginners approach the first elements of speech;  
[330] having advanced through the stages, they read every doctrine

in order, according to rule and measure; the prudent person dispenses doctrines thus.  
By contrast, rule, measure, and order perish in the babbler.

The foolish babbler pours forth speech at an unsuitable time;  
the words and deeds of the prudent have their proper time.

[335] [Col. 0972C] Do not concern yourself with what a fool invents or says,  
from whose speech no praise comes to you.

If you seek praise, let rule, measure, and order please you:  
without them glory does not exist, or exists only briefly.

All things flourish in order and rejoice in rule and measure;  
[340] whoever can despise these rightly perishes.

He deserves to be thrown into confusion whom no order restrains;  
and whoever knows no measure perishes without measure.

Whom rule does not restrain, fault dissolves when unbound,  
hurls him into evils, and kills him in his headlong fall.

[345] Therefore let there be order in good living and in speaking,  
[Col. 0972D] since rule, measure, and order govern the tongue and the mind.

Perhaps they will ask why he rejects the writings of the ancients.  
Hear what Pusio, or Tryphon, says:

### On the ancient practice of philosophers.

“Why the earlier school of our fathers is far from us  
[350] I shall explain briefly: it is excessively laborious.

They read much and teach much, and forbid their pupils to wander;  
they press them either to learn or to remain at home.

They weigh the powers of intellect, and the teacher gives everyone  
a measure suited to his own abilities.

[355] No teacher flatters; no one gives gifts  
so that you may wish to be his pupil.

[Col. 0973A] But among the ancients the order of reading is not confused,  
for each subject fittingly has its proper stage:

### On the order of learning.

Grammar is followed by *diasyrtica* [uncertain technical term], then by synthesis;  
[360] lexis follows it, and rhesis at the later stage.

Growing through these stages, eloquence takes possession of its summit  
and teaches the various arts without difficulty.

If anyone has perfectly learned the art of speaking,  
whatever doctrine you set before him, he will be skilled in it.

[365] At last industrious youth passes from these studies  
[Col. 0973B] and proceeds, philosophizing, into various paths,

which nevertheless tend harmoniously toward one end,  
for Philosophy has one head.

They investigate the natures of things, what is honourable,  
[370] and whence the blessed life comes to them;

they examine the powers of strict law and equity,  
and what medicine can do for the healthy or the sick.

### That sacred Scripture rules over all.

When someone skilled has learned all arts and all doctrines,  
the sacred page holds dominion.

### From what things praise arises.

[375] These four customarily bestow praise upon created things:  
the subject, the form, and the hand of the maker,

[Col. 0973C] likewise the end, which assigns names to all things;  
for all things are good or bad by their end.

God is its material, and the world’s equipment is the light  
from which truth is drawn and which adorns it.

### That truth is the form of the sacred page and the light of the soul.

Form indeed is that by which a thing is called true;  
[380] hence it follows that what sacred Scripture teaches is established.

It is the idea of the good, the source and origin of true things,  
whose cause shines in the mind of God.

A light kindled too greatly, and unkindled for mortal beings,  
makes itself smaller so that human beings may see.

[Col. 0973D] For no one could grasp it wholly; therefore it moderates itself  
so that the weak may be capable of it.

This same light, when participated in, gives the name “true,”  
[390] for its subjects can be called true.

It is the soul’s true light; without it the soul becomes brutish and, wandering,  
plunges from vice to vice and perishes.

The material is exceedingly precious, exceedingly suited to beauty,  
and the beautiful form proves its maker.

[395] The idea is the powerful substance of truth, which  
informs every thing and makes it be what it is.

Form or actuality establishes everything that is true;  
do not doubt that anything lacking both is false.

[Col. 0974A] Every form is held bound to its own kind  
[400] and always accomplishes whatever its origin commands.

Therefore whatever exists or acts in its native form,  
whatever enduring nature declares in accordance with reason,

is said to be true to its kind; and its effect indicates this,  
or its form proves it.

[405] Hence the connection of things displays another kind of truth,  
which no one can see without composite things.

The intellect is true because it conceives that truth itself;  
thus a threefold designation of truth belongs to things.

Speech is true whenever it signifies the same thing,  
[410] if things are as the words state that they are.

The sacred page distributes, by its doctrine, true things,  
true intellects, and true utterances as well.

The gracious Spirit testifies that he is the craftsman;  
[Col. 0974B] all good persons are his instruments.

If anyone sees something well done by mind, hand, or tongue,  
[415] let him know that it is the Spirit’s work.

Without him nothing is rightly accomplished; yet neither do guilty mind, tongue,  
or hand do anything evil without him as author.

### What is the end of philosophy?

The end is to love God, flee vice, cultivate honourable conduct,  
know oneself, know God, and keep measure;

knowledge of truth, contempt for the world, love of  
virtues, a happy life, and moderate repose;

sound faith, sure hope of good, and the earnest of everlasting life:  
[Col. 0974C] always to have God before one’s gaze.

[425] Although the human mind abounds in all the things  
which heaven displays and earth can give,

it is distracted by many great and anxious cares  
and endures perpetual hunger and thirst;

it is always tormented and nowhere finds rest,  
[430] except when true glory, God, reveals himself to it.

### On vain and true glory.

Vain glory makes people miserable, but true glory makes them blessed;  
the former swells with vice, the latter rejoices in God.

The sacred page bestows such an end upon its friends,  
and this precious stone is given to the pious worshipper:

[435] a stone to be desired, because it contains all the desires  
[Col. 0974D] of the mind and admits nothing that can harm;

whatever can harm it drives from itself and keeps at a distance,  
and it makes the ages run according to its own will.

No one can recount the goods which the sacred page confers  
[440] upon those who strive to keep God’s commands.

### That the divine page is queen of the others.

This is called queen of the Scriptures; it is called divine,  
for it makes gods.

It is sacred because it consecrates all persons and things;  
Philosophy acknowledges it as its head.

[445] All arts are its handmaids; every mechanical  
discipline which you see suited to various uses,

which law does not condemn but public practice approves,  
owes it its service and allegiance.

Practical philosophy serves it, and theoretical philosophy serves it;  
[450] Philosophy has given it the citadel of sacred dominion.

### On the doctrine of the Stoics.

The Stoic follows this when he always directs his gaze to final things  
and cuts down the shoots of vice with the sickle.

He establishes this as the cause of virtues and of the blessed life:  
that the mind may become accustomed prudently to fear death.

[455] This fear drives vain tumults from the heart,  
and worldly fear flees when it arrives;

pride is crushed, the impulse of hot anger dies,  
[Col. 0975B] and luxury, the devastator of wealth, ceases.

Reins are given to pleasure; seductive lust, terrified by its end,  
[460] lays aside its spurs.

He lightly despises all things who considers himself about to die  
and recalls that all things soon perish.

Yet if meditation upon death is without measure,  
so that numbness undermines hearts with excessive terror

[465] and hope, destroyed and shaken by diverse storms, falls,  
the image of death exceeds its lawful measure;

it exceeds the bounds which the law prescribed for its use,  
and the image of death produces true death.

### On moderating fear and avoiding despair.

The law commands you to fear, but does not permit one who fears  
[470] to despair; it considers this greater than every crime.

[Col. 0975C] Although pure confession releases every guilt  
and inner sorrow washes away every sin,

this crime excludes pardon and merits a punishment  
which no one can turn aside by prayer or price.

It heaps sins upon sins, neglects to confess evil deeds,  
[475] and fear swallows up vows and prayers.

It denies that God is merciful or ready to spare faults,  
but thinks him thirsty for blood.

No one thus softens the anger of an offended ruler,  
by saying that he always has a thirst for blood.

[480] The advocate is foolish who alleges the fierce dispositions  
of a judge in order that his severe anger may subside.

[Col. 0975D] It belongs to the Godhead always to have mercy;  
whoever removes this denies that God exists.

### That despair produces blasphemy.

Whoever denies that God exists plainly blasphemes,  
[485] kindles fires against himself, and prepares weapons and a cross.

He provokes eternal death, which no one can sufficiently avoid  
without God—whose existence madness denies.

Thus continual meditation upon death benefits good people,  
whereby the fool perishes who fears without measure.

### On approved fear.

[490] That measure of fear is pleasing to Majesty:  
it avoids every sin and nourishes hope;

it fears the just one, recalls his mercy, and thereby  
[495] [Col. 0976A] recognizes the name of Judge, and thereby the name of Father;

and it avoids the anger of Power in such a way as to strive  
to earn the Father through sweet acts of obedience.

### Definition of voice.

Voice is subtle air, formed by the throat and organs  
of the mouth, whose sound can be caught by the ear;

it reveals to one person what another thinks  
[500] and in turn makes hearts accessible to one another.

### That the Stoic introduces fateful necessity.

The Stoic, bound by fate, thinks that all things must proceed  
as the ages flow.

He calls fate the will of the Godhead, disposing all things—  
something which no one can annul.

[505] Hence the astrologer, with painstaking attention,  
[Col. 0976B] circles the stars and proudly turns over both poles.

Promising happy outcomes, he wrongly comforts his friends  
and, as a false prophet, often causes fear.

He gathers the motions of the stars in order to gather fates from the stars;  
with equal devotion he worships the Godhead and the stars.

### That he considers Providence the cause of necessity.

Because he does not admit an error in *pronoia* [Providence],  
[510] he draws from it a grave, time-worn error of doctrine.

In giving birth to fate, *pronoia* has pressed all things too hard  
and imperiously imposed harsh laws.

### What incongruities follow fateful necessity.

Freedom of choice perishes if the fates move minds, mouths, and hands  
by compelled obedience.

[515] Rewards are owed to no one according to merits;  
all crimes fall upon fate’s author.

[Col. 0976C] Many disadvantages follow these errors—  
it is pious to avoid them, but laborious to enumerate them.

The Stoic makes sins equal and equalizes them by the same punishment;  
the sacred page does the contrary.

[520] Therefore in many matters he agrees with the law,  
yet is accustomed in many matters to teach against the law.

Faith accepts a doctrine unless manifest law opposes it  
or a stronger reason can disprove it.

### On the doctrine of the Epicureans.

Another philosopher thinks that the highest good is joys of the mind  
[525] and teaches that all things are subject to pleasure.

This is indeed correct, if pleasure is pure,  
if reason understands the statement as true joys,

if the condition sought is that what the mind wishes may be present  
and what it does not wish may be absent, while it strives after pious desires;

[530] if labour aims at granting true repose,  
[Col. 0976D] and if the mind possesses the joys of tranquil peace.

Dutiful labour serves peace and seeks  
what can make its own joy perpetual.

Labour devoted to virtue becomes sweet, and within itself  
the mind, conscious of good deeds, flourishes joyfully.

### On the conflict of labour and repose.

[535] But labour and repose wage war within the body:  
the former distresses, the latter cherishes; the former flees, the latter remains.

Though the battle endures long, it ceases with time;  
yet time will grant no end to peace.

[Col. 0977A] True repose will come when the flesh, subject to the mind,  
has become spiritual through the triumph over death;

[545] when the flesh receives nothing except what reason approves,  
and God strengthens and moves the pure mind.

The subject flesh is united to the mind, and the mind is made blessed,  
full of God; this repose has no end.

### That the world does not possess true peace.

The world does not possess this repose: it produces lawsuits, wars, and plunder  
[550] and is continually drenched in human slaughter.

It produces, increases, and loves filth; it deceives lovers  
and is accustomed to defile its worshippers.

### That the grace of God grants true repose.

[Col. 0977B]

The sacred Scriptures teach this repose, but grace bestows it;  
without grace no delightful repose of peace is given.

[555] For we are commanded to rejoice once and again  
in the Lord, who gives double joys to his own.

Now rejoicing in hope, the mind will be glad; in reality,  
it will receive the full rewards of its warfare.

### On double and single joy.

Rewards are doubled when mind and flesh are glorified;  
[560] if glory belongs to one of the two, a single reward is given.

But whenever the glory of the soul comes first, it is certain  
that the flesh too will receive the same reward according to its merits.

### On the error of the Epicureans.

[Col. 0977C] Epicurus soberly hears the laws, yet when drunk  
he is subject to Venus and the belly.

[565] This craftsman fixes the anvil which he surrounds with emptiness  
in uncertainty; chance performs the rest.

Chance gathers tiny bodies into an immense heap  
so that this greatest globe of the world may arise,

and so that the elements may be fixed in their places under an everlasting law  
[570] and the seasons may carry out their appointed changes.

This school also teaches that the soul perishes with the body  
and that laws and justice are cultivated in vain.

It compares minds, subtle bodies, to breaths  
and falsely asserts that no rewards are given to the pious.

[575] [Col. 0977D] He does not know what is fitting; Venus, dice, sleep, perfumes,  
heavy cookery, jesting, leisure, and wine delight him.

Let applause, deceit, trifles,  
and whatever mime, actor, and buffoon approve be added to these.

### That Epicurus worships chance as God.

A slave of the belly does not care what is honourable  
[580] and considers Fortune to occupy the place of God.

He thinks that nothing is done by reason but all things by chance; pleasure is worshipped as a god—an evil thing, a greedy belly.

Epicurus loves nothing except what he sacrifices  
to belly and Venus; but the first victim falls to the belly.

[585] And the order of the limbs nourishes the seeds of vices;  
[Col. 0978A] gluttony gives seed to Venus and nourishes hope.

### What is the fruit of the Epicureans?

The victim slaughtered by the priest of belly and Venus  
always receives rewards fitting its merits.

The slaughterer’s rewards are fires, dung, and worms:  
[590] such a recompense suits such rites.

These are the joys of foolish pleasure; the final end is misery,  
the highest glory shame.

Gods are worthy of their rites, rites of their god,  
and the god of his worshipper, and the worshipper in turn of his god.

### On the doctrine of the Peripatetics.

[595] [Col. 0978B] Discussion of things stirs active philosophers  
so that they may see truth in its own source.

The source of truth—the idea of the good—makes individual things be  
what they are according to the condition of their kind.

The causes of things flow from this source, and all things  
[600] correspond to their causes by the law given them.

### On natural law and created nature.

Law is a series of causes; created nature produces effects  
by making them similar to their causes.

The highest power orders the series of causes  
in the form of number, weight, and measure;

[605] and whatever the reason of Power orders from eternity  
with its disposing hand sees fixed times.

### What is nature?

The series of causes is called nature; from it  
[Col. 0978C] this sensible world receives its being.

And if created forms agree with their proximate causes,  
[610] then mother nature fashions every work.

If a cause differs from its proximate outcome,  
the crowd thinks that it is contrary to nature;

and because the cause is hidden, it says that it lacks reason—  
but plainly there is nothing that lacks reason.

### That nothing is contrary to reason.

[615] Reason precedes the birth of all things  
and advances and moves them once born.

The same gives an end to perishable things,  
and the best cause governs all motions.

But among causes, that which goes before rules  
[620] and possesses all the powers of the inferior.

[Col. 0978D] Yet the inferior does not possess the right of the ruler,  
though it can proceed alongside it with equal steps.

Scripture teaches this, and creative nature commands it:  
inferior things must yield to those above them.

### What is the cause of all things?

[625] The one reason of causes is the divine will,  
which Plato often calls by the name of nature.

Created nature serves its command,  
and the whole order of causes adheres to it.

### What is human reason?

Human reason is an image of the highest Reason,  
[630] which inwardly apprehends truths while God teaches.

As light given to the eyes shows both itself and other things,  
[Col. 0979A] things evident beneath the light and hidden without it,

so a cloud becomes bright when it receives the light of the sun  
after it has driven away the waters suspended in vapours:

[635] thus subject reason, its stains expelled,  
puts on the form of the highest Reason and then shines.

Then the whole mind glitters, full of true light;  
it casts away false things and cultivates true goods.

### What enlightens reason?

Just as no one can see anything without light,  
[640] so human reason becomes blind without God.

God is true light and the author of that light  
by which alone each person can see himself.

### What are the uses of light?

That one may see oneself is a use of the highest light;  
[645] to love the gift bestowed is a use of the gift;

to distinguish all things powerfully is a use of the gift;  
worship and love of the good are a use of the gift;

to know the fruits of things is a use of the gift;  
to be drawn toward better things is a use of the gift;

to know the giver of the gift is a use of the gift;  
[650] the highest use of the gift is to love God.

### That the true philosopher cannot be without God.

If no power can separate those whom love unites,  
the true philosopher will not be without God.

Not even death can dissolve this bond;  
one who loves wisely will live forever.

### That reason is a mirror, eye, and hand for seeing and grasping things.

[655] Therefore reason is a mirror in which all things are seen,  
[Col. 0979C] and it performs the office both of eye and hand.

Conscious of nature, it investigates the true and the just;  
as arbiter of virtues, it alone dispenses their goods.

Reason is said to regard things in three ways,  
[660] nor has the mind been able to discover a fourth.

One combines things; another resolves composite things;  
a third compares and relates things to things.

The first attends upon nature, mathematics upon the middle one,  
and logic alone claims the last for itself.

[665] The mind is active in these and weighs every particular to the nail,  
so that it may cautiously see the powers of things,

lest dark error, deceived by a false image of virtue,  
drive it headlong into evil,

[Col. 0979D] and lest, instead of things, it hold phantasms of things;  
[670] the faithful seeker loves knowledge of truth.

### That knowledge of truth is the highest good according to Aristotle.

To know the causes of things is, he thinks, the highest good—  
as great Aristotle taught.

One whom an empty appearance deceives easily falls;  
a true appearance cannot deceive anyone.

[675] For a true thing is confirmed by truth, a good thing by blessedness,  
and a thing destined to endure by permanence;

but a false thing deceives, a perishing thing destroys, and a falling thing  
crushes: unhappy is whoever clings to it.

### What is the fruit of the Peripatetic school?

[Col. 0980A]

Contemplation of things produces contempt for the world,  
[680] because it proves that all things perish by their own contingency.

### On contempt for the world and its fruit.

True contempt for the world is the first way of salvation,  
for the world deceives and hurls down its own people.

For worldly love blinds the lights of the mind  
so that its blind follower falls into wretched death.

### Worldly love is contrary to love of God.

[685] No one can love both God and the world, because at the arrival  
of the one love the other is always driven out.

No lover of the world possesses the name of wise person;  
this love is opposed to God.

Whoever despises the world rules it; he weakens the enemy’s powers  
[690] and presses its neck beneath his foot.

Hope, grief, anger, fear, and blind desire for honours,  
joys, losses, and gain are like a light breeze.

The world gives tribulation, but wisdom peace;  
it banishes every evil and nourishes every good.

### Fear of God produces contempt for the world and deifies human beings.

[695] Contempt for the world, founded in heavenly love,  
draws into its own jurisdiction everything it despises.

Without this no one is wise; that blessed fear nurtures it,  
which gives you your beginning, Philosophy.

This implanted fear introduces holy love;  
[700] [Col. 0980C] by this a human being becomes wise, by this becomes a god through love.

### That one God is God by nature, but many are gods by grace.

God is one by nature, but many by gift,  
whom grace makes sharers in the Godhead.

God is one by nature, but by grace he willed  
many to be partners in his divinity.

### That three persons are one God, though distinct in their properties.

[705] For Father and Son, together with the Spirit, are one God,  
but each *prosopon* [person] retains its own property.

### That the three persons are of one nature, divinity, will, and operation.

Though they are of one nature, divinity, and action,  
[Col. 0980D] each *prosopon* is distinguished by its own properties.

The Son of the eternal Father and of the holy Virgin  
[710] is God by nature, made human by gift.

It is a gift that he is true man and likewise true God,  
weighing out rewards in an equal balance according to merits,

and that every creature worships him with bent knees  
and proclaims him equal to God the Father.

[715] And he who freely received such great gifts from the Father  
knows how to give the best gifts to his servants.

He disdains to keep the gift he has received for himself alone;  
he illumines those he loves and makes them gods;

he advances to the highest those whom mother grace adopts  
[720] [Col. 0981A] and makes them hold the highest place according to their degree of merit.

### On the threefold pride which prevents the deification of the human being: pride of reason, will, and life.

But pride of reason, friend of error, obstructs,  
and faith, stained by it, is emptied and perishes.

The worst companion of error is an exalted will,  
which bends shattered minds toward every evil.

A third pride, the pride of life, is joined to those already mentioned;  
[725] it overthrows and kills every virtue.

### On the doctrine of the Academics, whose leader is Arcesilaus.

Wretched Arcesilaus is distracted and, uncertain in all things,  
wavers and does not know where he wishes to stand.

[Col. 0981B] With sleepless effort he always seeks truths that flee,  
[730] and knows no measure in his studies.

He surveys all the doctrines of the wise; at last he teaches his followers  
that it is fitting to be ignorant of all truths.

For truths always lie hidden, if he is believed;  
mortal sense has no access to them.

### On Zeno.

[735] Zeno is praised for proving that nothing can be known,  
clinging to uncertainty in all matters and commanding doubt.

To know nothing is the end of his labour,  
and this gain is acquired at great expense through long labour.

### On Pythagoras and his doctrine.

No one rose to the name of the Samian;  
[740] as the ancients report, Sophia was complete in him.

Gentle Tarentum draws him toward the fruit of a better life,  
[Col. 0981C] as the greatest sower of morals in the world.

Five zones distinguish the heaven, five the air;  
the sea or land has the same division.

But the Samian teaches that there are three, and assigns the middle one  
[745] to settlers, while cold and heat prevail in the others.

He thinks it impious to hand down a doubtful matter to later ages  
and does not wish the wise person to be forbidden to be a poet.

Because certain knowledge of three is possible,  
he teaches three as true, and permits poetry in the rest.

[750] The extremes produce the temperateness of the middle zone, and he commands  
that one who wishes to be good should keep to the mean.

The pleasing temperateness nourishes animal bodies,  
as nature commands—these more, those less.

[Col. 0981D] Dense bodies are permeable to spirits, but a greater power,  
or the will of God, now restrains them.

Cold and heat do not harm the spiritual body;  
no force of the elements can injure it.

But animal life is tormented by these things and each receives  
[760] rewards suited to his own merits.

When the dregs have been boiled away, the origin of all is renewed  
purer, and the golden ages of the Fathers return.

He taught many things well and was very useful in that age;  
he was among the foremost, the greatest in the world.

[765] Yet he is criticized because he asserts that souls have fallen from the ether  
and that the body occupies the place of a prison,

[Col. 0982A] and because he thinks that souls, excluded from their own bodies, are sent  
into new bodies according to the character of their conduct,

and because he finally leads them back to their own bodily origins,  
[770] so that they may eagerly fall again to the depths.

Once these teachings have been accepted on his authority,  
reason proves that very many false consequences follow.

### On Socrates, his authority, and doctrine.

Humble pupils prostrate themselves at Socrates’ feet,  
and all Greece worships its needy god.

[775] To ask whether, though he surpassed all in teaching truth,  
he lived holyly is believed to be a crime.

Some investigate the numbers and weights of things,  
the rule and methods of measurement;

some search in the stars for the mind of the Fates,  
[780] [Col. 0982B] the motions of things, and the counsel of God;

some examine nature’s inner parts; others are held only by  
the nexus of causes and signs.

Thus they weary the mind’s sharpness and scatter it among external things,  
while their hearts remain deprived of their own light.

[785] But Socrates despises people’s vain concerns  
and instructs each person to see the heart’s hidden places.

He observes and contemplates all external things for use,  
and makes each of them only as important as he knows it to be.

### That Socrates considers the human mind to be God.

He draws the rays of the mind into itself; for him the mind  
[790] is God, the world a victim, the flesh a slave.

He abhors the unlawful motions of corrupted flesh  
and tames nature’s evil beneath reason.

He shapes morals and makes life serene; thus, in his judgment,  
to know how to suffer is the greatest of virtues.

### That the world is less than the mind in both reality and dignity.

[795] If it were possible to compare mind and world,  
the former would be greater, the latter lesser; the latter serves, the former rules.

For the world serves the flesh, and the flesh serves reason,  
which is a part of the mind sharing in God.

Thus all things serve cheerful Socrates; and the world attends  
[800] one whom no power can harm.

### On Socrates’ error.

This was a human doctrine; yet it contains an error:  
[Col. 0982D] he believed that every individual’s mind is God.

Hence he says that the human mind should be regarded as God,  
as one to whom divine honour must be given.

[805] Hardly anyone has been blessed by fate with so great an endowment  
that the evil of error cannot cast him down.

### On Anaxagoras and his doctrine.

Anaxagoras teaches that souls arise by propagation  
and that bone is given as the cause to tender bones:

that flesh flows from flesh and blood from blood,  
[810] and that the whole form of the fathers passes into their offspring.

The cutting of a portion diminishes the body, but no cutting reaches  
the simplicity of the soul.

As heat comes forth from heat, light from light,  
[Col. 0983A] so one spirit has its origin from another.

Pure faith forbids belief that souls arise by propagation;  
[815] God infuses them and continually makes them new.

They are made from nothing and are now enclosed in bodies,  
now, without bodies, carry out the commands of their Creator.

They do not perish, because everlasting reason and power  
make the image of God abide in them.

### On Aristotle and his doctrine.

[820] Great Aristotle possesses the arts of speech  
and has renown for the height of the virtues.

He composes books of judgment and of discovering truth;  
three faculties serve him:

he is a natural philosopher and teaches morals, but logic  
[825] always serves its author dutifully.

[Col. 0983B] This gives him the proper name that sacred Sophia formerly  
gave to her lover;

for whoever excels claims the honour of a common title.  
The poet Virgil is said to have done this by right.

### On Aristotle’s error.

Yet he erred when he believed sublunary things governed by chance  
[830] and things beyond governed by fate.

He says that created beings do not possess true freedom of choice,  
which God alone possesses fully.

Whatever lies beneath the moon consists of four elements,  
and he considers things beyond to be simpler.

[835] He defines the things which the high sphere above the sun possesses  
as flourishing in perpetual peace.

[Col. 0983C] There opposites wage no war against one another,  
for tranquil repose cherishes the higher regions.

### That souls are of the fifth essence.

A fifth substance is created so that souls may exist,  
from which the origin of the zodiacal sphere is constituted.

That is the seat of the blessed, this the court of the gods,  
[840] for things without weight are more suited to God.

He holds the world to be eternal and time coeval with it;  
and place too is said to be coeternal with them.

He teaches that nothing perishes, but all things revolve in a circle,  
and that every place is suited to its own times.

### That nature knows only singulars; universals are, as it were, certain fictions of reason.

[Col. 0983D] Everything that nature has created is individual,  
[850] and a corresponding state is a work of reason.

If anyone does not judge Aristotle worthy to be first,  
he does not render rewards worthy of his merits.

He is shown to have given a beginning or an end  
to every art; he masters whatever he wishes to possess.

[855] Whatever worldly reason could teach anyone,  
it gave to him, so that his doctrines became full of faith.

### That Aristotle was called son of Apollo.

For whatever he taught, Apollo is thought to have taught;  
Greek fable reports that Aristotle was Apollo’s offspring.

### That Aristotle tried to oppose everyone.

Although he teaches very many things correctly, he nevertheless errs in this:  
[860] he always seeks to go against the rest.

[Col. 0984A] For although he must be judged outstanding in the highest matters,  
he was an excessive seeker after praise.

Virtue makes a philosopher renowned, not vain glory;  
true honour is ruined by love of praise.

### What befits a philosopher.

[865] The philosopher strives that mind may answer to mouth,  
and that an upright life may agree with good words.

Not everyone who speaks correctly thereby philosophizes,  
but the one who lives so as always to do good.

For a lascivious girl may blame Venus,  
[870] a buffoon may praise virtue;

the unlearned may repeat the words of the wise,  
and an expert tongue sometimes sins in speaking.

### That Aristotle was conquered by glory, which he attacked in words.

[Col. 0984B] Aristotle conquers others; vain glory conquers him,  
though he attacks it and teaches that it is nothing.

### That philosophy flees vain glory after first conquering pleasure and avarice.

[875] This is the last thing to desert eminent minds,  
which Philosophy at length, victorious, puts to flight.

Lust first declares war upon virtue  
when flesh and blood burn with a new fire.

### What restrains lust.

Labour and a spare diet can calm it,  
[880] as can fear, a fleeting thing pleasing to the cautious.

### What represses avarice.

Restless love of possession raises a second war,  
kindling souls prone to every crime.

The eyes incite the mind when they behold individual things  
[Col. 0984C] so that it desires as its own what it judges good.

Careful contemplation of things crushes this vice,  
as do divine love and fear of punishment.

### That some vices arise from others, but pride also arises from virtue.

The origin of one vice from another is established,  
and many evils come from evil beginnings.

The heat of avarice commonly produces robberies;  
[890] luxurious Venus often makes one greedy.

Immoderate gluttony produces lust; fury gives boldness;  
devouring envy produces hatred; long-standing anger becomes rage.

Thus vice gives cause and sequel to vice,  
for a shameful thing cannot remain by itself.

### That neglect of small matters produces great vices.

[Col. 0984D]

[895] If you despise a small thing, great things will gradually follow,  
and grave ruin often comes from the least things.

The glory of nobles, flowing from the source of good things,  
claims distinction through the nobility of lineage.

For when virtue corrupted by leaven swells,  
[900] pride is born from wretched intercourse.

It puts itself above equals and despises inferiors,  
and foolishly does not know how to be subject to its creator.

Thus, arising from merits or distinguished blood,  
it is ungrateful to God, whose gifts it possesses.

### On the vice of ingratitude.

[905] The crime of the ungrateful person, with whom no grace is joined,  
forbids the ungrateful citizen to have a place.

### On vain glory.

[Col. 0985A]

It is ungrateful to God to seek the honours of a gift,  
to wish to retain the praises of a good work.

Whoever snatches from the author the titles of merits  
[910] calls avenging hands down upon his own ruin.

What is vain glory but smoke, shadow, and sound,  
which, at the very moment it begins, begins to be nothing?

Yet everyone seeks it because it always testifies  
to the presence of true virtue’s work.

[915] Glory, a sweet evil, softens great hearts,  
yet this same thing makes them weaker.

Those whom flesh does not bend, nor love of possession pervert,  
glory can easily hurl down.

### What represses vain glory.

Contemplation of things, contempt for the world,  
[920] fear of punishment, and love of God finally destroy it.

If one fully remembers one’s own evils and always  
considers another’s goods, how will one be proud?

If one weighs the merit of one’s life, considers the avenger’s anger  
and his power, how will one be proud?

[925] How will one be proud if one examines oneself to the nail:  
earth, ash, worm, dregs, vapour, shadow, mud?

### On the vice of self-exaltation.

The exalted person has no gifts of virtue;  
[Col. 0985C] both God and every human being are enemies to him.

The vice of the proud, than which none is considered greater,  
[930] does not allow the proud person to enjoy a brother’s love.

### On the virtue of humility.

The humble are worthy of virtue’s gift, worthy  
To know God; to the worthy, blessed life is given.  
Who teaches these things in words assumes the name  
Of philosopher; the philosopher does and teaches them.

[935] Aristotle too, it is said, taught these things in speech;  
Anyone teaches them more strongly by examples.

### On Plato and his doctrine

But Plato, initiate of truth, distinguishes among the very  
Knowable things what a created thing can know.  
For though at times he says things contrary to faith,

[940] [Col. 0985D] yet very many things of his are pleasing to the good.  
First he teaches that God exists, distinguishes time from eternity,  
And applies the Ideas, adapts *hyle*.

### On hyle

The mind discovers this while it analyzes and sets all things in motion,  
So that all created things may disclose their causes.

[945] If you contemplate *hyle*, at one moment it is every substance;  
At another, conversely, the same is believed to be nothing.  
While reason traces it out, it perceives it as dreams;  
And while you desire to hold it, it quickly hides, elusive.  
Thus the ear hears sound to be absent when it hears nothing.

[950] Thus see darkness with your eyes by seeing nothing.  
Thus by its own lack touch touches emptiness,  
Taste proves what is tasteless by tasting nothing,  
And, smelling nothing, it establishes odors to be far away,  
Though previously it was a keen judge of smell.

### On God, whose power is the efficient cause of the world

[955] God is eternal; the world began with time.  
He remains, but time moves all other things.  
Binding contrary elements together by numbers,  
He conquers them and makes them flourish in eternal peace.

### That number, weight, measure, place, and time are not commensurable with one another

The subjects of the primary genera are not symmetrical with one another,

[960] Nor do they fall under a similar, connatural principle.  
No known proportion exists between time and place;  
The relation of measure cannot be that of weight.  
Number is asymmetrical with the things mentioned before; and in these

[Col. 0986B] five philosophy performs its office.  
[965] To these is added the series of causes or reasons,  
Which intellect alone can perceive.  
The power of numbers does not know how to multiply limitation,  
Nor does any division set an end to magnitudes.  
Number grows without measure; it can divide without end

[970] Any continuum, yet only in reasoning.

### That human understanding fails concerning first and last things

Understanding fails when it reaches toward ultimate things; only  
He who makes and governs can see first things—  
He, fully known to himself and to blessed  
Spirits alone, insofar as grace favors each.

[975] Nor can anyone judge rightly concerning first principles  
[Col. 0986C] except him who gives all things their being.

### On the human soul

The human mind, a simple number fitted to move  
Itself, is said to be conformed to God.  
For as God rules, fills, and embraces the whole world,

[980] So the entire body is subject to its soul.  
A differing matter underlies the soul, and yet the same matter  
Is both individual and divisible.  
The bodily mass weighs down the power of souls,  
More here and less there, as the flesh joined to them permits.

### On rational and irrational motion

[985] There are two motions: an errant motion and one of reason;  
[Col. 0986D] the latter flourishes in the heights, the former draws downward.

### On the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of bodies

Souls are immortal, while the perishable body  
Dies; and at last its former life returns.

### On the great year

The former life returns when the completion of the great year

[990] Recalls all the stars to their first position.  
Then a new year renews all things; souls again  
Receive bodies, and times flow according to law.  
If the courses of sun and moon renew the world,  
All the stars together will do this more powerfully.

[995] Wandering Cynthia presides over moisture, and the sun over heat;  
Moisture, through heat joined to it, produces all things.

### On the rays of sun and moon, their offices and significations

[Col. 0987A]

The moon’s rays scorch and spoil flesh and fruits;  
The ray of the sun benefits both.  
Thus worldly wisdom perishes, while true wisdom profits

[1000] And cherishes nature, full of God’s warmth.  
Yet excessive heat breeds worms, that you may understand  
What an immoderate love of investigation contains.  
The sun both fosters and restrains sight, because sober  
He must be who strives to know God’s mysteries.

[1005] You see things subject to the sun; divine things created in light  
Stand open to you; no one fully sees both.  
[Col. 0987B] It is a heavenly good to see the sun and God;  
Mortals see lower things alone.  
Boundless light conceals the sun; so divine

[1010] Majesty is always hidden by its own light.  
In the body of the sun is a source of light and heat;  
God is the source of both for spirits.

### That no substance perishes

No substance can perish; form succeeding form  
Prevents what is moved from becoming nothing.

[1015] Renewed through these motions, the elements remain and flourish,  
While the old form departs and a new one is given.  
[Col. 0987C] A portion wearied by its condition recovers strength  
Through welcome newness and receives new being from forms.  
One species alters this; another makes that; and it is called a genus

[1020] And gives being to each thing.

### That God is formless and the form of forms

God is formless, the form and power of forms,  
In whom every thing endures perpetually.  
For divine reason always lives; all things live forever  
In God’s reason.

[1025] The Ideas remain unmoved; in them abides  
Whatever the wave of time carries toward decay.  
Reason, itself unmoved, dispenses the motions of things,  
And steadfast power moves all times.

[Col. 0987D] The gods whom creative nature causes  
[1030] To arise from diverse things are not formless—  
Gods whom reason circumscribes, and to whom created nature,  
Form, and genus are assigned through concrete things.  
God is formless because he is simple, neither  
Composed from elsewhere nor owing his being to several things.

### That a truly simple thing is absolute

[1035] Reason sets free the thing of true simplicity,  
And whatever no boundary can enclose.  
What is truly simple is changed by no motion,  
Is not made old by time, and is always the same.  
The world changes its appearances and cannot remain,

[1040] And time destroys whatever it calls into being.  
Thus all things return into themselves; thus, by the eternal law  
Of the everlasting Godhead, his work is perpetuated.

### That the earth is at the bottom, and that individual spheres have their inhabitants

[Col. 0988A]

The heavenly beings hold the heights; lowest earth lies in the middle,  
And a worthy inhabitant possesses the intermediate spheres.

[1045] There is a spirit in all the elements and in the stars,  
A spirit proper to each; one spirit moves the world.  
This one is greatest; all the rest are particular;  
This moves the whole, the others its individual members.  
For every region is full of its own inhabitants,

[1050] From whose motion the origin of things arises.

### That fire purges all things

Corrupted air is purified by fire alone;  
[Col. 0988B] it also purges the offenses of infected water’s motion.  
This water washes away earth’s filth; every higher thing  
Thus purges all that is subject to it by its own force.

[1055] The higher is sometimes defiled by the lower,  
But nothing can stain pure fire.  
Nothing is purer than it, which boils away every impurity.  
Hence the godlike thing has the highest place.

### That sublunary things are moved by higher motions

It is established that sublunary things are born through the motion of higher things,

[1060] And that God, himself unmoved, moves all things.

### What nature is

Nature is called the principle of the motion of things;  
In the name of nature there is a hidden cause—  
[Col. 0988C] a hidden cause which draws each thing toward its proper origin  
And makes streams resemble their fountains.

[1065] Many things are contrary to secondary nature;  
But what can be contrary to primary nature? Nothing!

### On the circle of the zodiac

The zodiac turns obliquely through twice six signs  
And does not allow the days to be equal to one another.  
The Arctic pole is the head of the middle axis known to us,

[1070] But the earth prevents us from seeing the other pole.

### That the globe of the earth is eccentric to the circles of the planets, and is the dregs of the elements

The earth lies eccentrically beneath the seven wandering stars,  
Though the greatest sphere has it as its center.  
[Col. 0988D] The lower globe always obeys the outer one;  
The earth lies beneath all the spheres, fitted to suffer.

[1075] It remains unmoved, but the rest run in a circle;  
All weights fall back toward the middle place.  
For dregs always rest sluggishly at the bottom  
And make everything foul by their contact.  
All things become foul when filled with ugly dregs,

[1080] Which, unless cleansed out, make vessels perish.  
Thus a mind long infected and overcome by the bitterness of dregs  
Hardly raises its head, weighed down with mire.  
For near the earth are smoke, winds, and clouds,  
Which trouble the eyes and the work of reason.

[1085] [Col. 0989A] Contrary to nature, the human face turns its gaze  
Toward earth, though born to see God.  
Yet earthly things are sometimes seen for use,  
And it is no sin if foul desire is far away.  
This is the doctrine of Plato, prince of sages,

[1090] From whom posterity receives true doctrines.  
Thus he taught what is knowable to whom, and what is not,  
So that all created things may retain their proper measure.

### That God alone knows all things, and every rational creature receives knowledge according to measure

Divine power knows things fully as they are;  
The attendant angel sees very many truths.

[1095] [Col. 0989B] The unclean spirit is powerful by nature and experience,  
And, taught even by the holy, is accustomed to see many things.  
Deprived of the use of light, it is mistaken in many matters;  
And the father of error always loves to deceive.  
Bodies imprison souls cast down in a dark prison,

[1100] And fault, by taking away light, prevents them from knowing.  
Fault and flesh bring in darkness, drive away lights,  
And do not allow wretched souls to see truth.

### That truth is the soul’s light, and reason its eye

Light nourishes the eyes; the vision of truth nourishes reason.  
The eyes flee darkness, and reason likewise avoids falsehood.

[1105] Reason is the eye of the mind; truth is its light.  
The eyes call the exercise of seeing knowledge.  
Let truth be sought by talent, studies, and skill;  
[Col. 0989C] beyond opinion no human being possesses it.

### That Plato’s teaching is in many respects useful

It does no harm for cautious persons to have heard the erring Plato,

[1110] Who teaches a few bad things and more good things than bad.  
The skilled hand avoids nettles and gathers wholesome herbs,  
And plucks unspoiled roses from thorns.  
Reason avoids errors, and the cautious person receives  
Chaste perceptions from madmen without madness.

[1115] The prudent man avoids heard-of dangers more effectively,  
For foreseen missiles usually do less harm.  
Hence the wise man wishes to hear whatever  
May do harm, that he may avoid whatever can injure him.

### On Endymion and his doctrine

[Col. 0989D] Whenever a true opinion concerning any matter is established,

[1120] Ancient Endymion held this to be faith.  
He asserts that error occurs if an opinion is false,  
And says that false things are not known, proving it by argument.  
The false is not known, because no knowledge deceives,  
Nor can light and darkness be mingled.

[1125] Sometimes empty people are deceived by an appearance of truth,  
And the sweet image of a desired thing holds them.  
There are those whom neither truth nor the image of truth delights;  
The appearance of vice and falsehood alone please them.

### That truth is likened to the sun, verisimilitude to the moon

The sun corresponds to truth, and Selene to falsehood,

[1130] She who imitates light and remains stained.  
For what lies beneath the moon is empty, mutable, and wavering;  
But things around the sun remain trustworthy and at rest.  
[Col. 0990A] Truth reigns in the heights; error thrives in the depths  
And deceives peoples oppressed by the wandering moon.

[1135] The bright dwelling of truth holds the heavenly beings above the moon;  
Cloudy error drives the lower world.

### On Arcesilaus, leader of the Academics, and his doctrine

The Old Academy follows Arcesilaus as teacher  
And makes humankind lack light.

### On Antisthenes, the Academic

The more learned Academic Antisthenes says that God alone

[1140] Knows all things, and proves it by reasoning.  
He also asserts that the heavenly beings know a great many things, but not all;  
He thinks mortals know few things.  
He hesitates concerning everything except what is proved  
[Col. 0990B] by living reason; he finds it astonishing not to have faith in this.

### What living reason is

[1145] Reason lives when it is clear through itself  
Or is always found together with self-evident things.  
He asserts that these things are known; the rest he presents doubtfully.  
In these, greater faith must be placed in experience.  
For the customary course of things makes those things probable

[1150] Which you always see under a similar principle.  
Yet because these sometimes happen otherwise,  
They are not sufficiently certain, though not without credibility.  
Therefore what he affirms to be true, he thinks necessarily so;  
Of the rest he says, “I believe,” or “I think it is so.”

[1155] And a modest mind is accustomed thus to restrain its speech,  
So that no one may accuse it of being guilty of falsehood.  
[Col. 0990C] Thus it qualifies all speech with adjectives,  
So that it ought always deservedly to have credit.

### Whence the Greeks received the Academic moderation in speech

Hence that manner of speaking also pleased the Greeks,

[1160] Which great and serious men praise:  
They restrain their words by condition, time, cause, and manner,  
And beware of speaking with excessive simplicity.  
But sometimes deceit is cloaked by the art of speaking,  
And feigned love gives fine words instead of realities.

### That the Romans imitate the Greeks in moderating words

[1165] The Roman citizen follows this custom: he gives words to friends;  
His greedy hand takes silver.  
[Col. 0990D] The cautious judge sells adverbs by weight,  
For a higher price will procure more useful ones.  
Adjectives will be given according to their prices;

[1170] A little paper or a rare pen will be had only at a price.  
Crassus seeks wealth in order to turn it into gold,  
And refines it again so that it may be pure.  
The city, corrupted by its own vices, corrupted the world,  
And the diseased head makes its members languish.

[1175] For every court imitates the Greeks, and the world, a lover of wealth,  
Has experienced the hunger of the city.

### On Varro and his doctrine

Varro is written to have been inferior to none of the Greeks;  
Rome is accustomed to call him Father.  
Certainly no one wrote more; no one could speak better,

[1180] Nor could anyone speak worse.

[Col. 0991A] He lays open the mysteries of nature, the rites of sacred things,  
The service of God, and the ancient deeds of the Fathers.  
He vainly worships the divinities of virtues which he invents,  
And thinks there are as many gods as there are plagues.

### On the one Pliny and the other
