[1185] Both Plinies follow him agreeably in many matters,  
Yet in many matters faith strikes at both.

### On Musaeus, who was thought to be Moses

Greece exalts ancient Musaeus with splendid praises,  
But Varro reports what he teaches.  
Therefore, for one wishing to know

[1190] What useful teaching either has, it is enough to read Varro.  
They think that Moses was called by the name Musaeus,  
He who first gave laws to humankind in the world.  
So be it; but the manifest calculation of their dates resists this,  
And their dissimilar lives prove them to be two persons.

[1195] Varro trained Romans, Musaeus Greeks, Moses Hebrews  
To live according to their respective custom.

### On Moses, that he himself is the fountain of the Scriptures

Musaeus errs greatly, and Varro errs with him,  
But the gracious Spirit moves the mind of Moses.  
Thus he writes five books full of mysteries,

[1200] So that in the history there is everywhere a threefold meaning;  
So that it may teach children, young men, and old men alike.  
The cautious letter teaches each according to what he can receive.  
It gives breasts to infants, applies lashes to servants,  
And makes their necks submit beneath the yoke.

[1205] And although it enfolds truth in mysterious figures,  
It nevertheless tears the veils, and the old shadow passes away.  
[Col. 0991C] Among philosophers the pagan calls this man uncultivated,  
Yet the greatest of them is less than he.  
He is the fountain and origin of the holy Scriptures,

[1210] From which sacred page takes its beginning.  
To some it is a spring; to others, a pool or deep well.  
From it you quench thirst, and from it thirst increases.  
All can draw what is enough, but no one  
Can wholly exhaust or diminish it.

### On Cicero and his doctrine

[1215] The Latin world had nothing greater than Cicero,  
Before whose eloquence Greece was mute.  
Rome sets him against, or exalts him above, all Greeks;  
Yet he is accustomed to approve uncertain doctrine.  
At last, when the nature of the gods troubled him,

[1220] He came to this point: to doubt what he should think God to be;  
How freedom of choice can coexist with fate—  
For if fate stands, that freedom perishes.  
How chance and conflicting fate agree with one another  
He does not know; therefore he advises the prophet to keep silence.

[1225] For ignorance of truth oppresses humankind  
And does not permit it to see truth in broad daylight.  
Even if truths happen to lie open, they appear beneath a dark cloud  
And are not wholly free from the suspicion of falsehood.  
He believes that God alone knows future things; but what God himself

[1230] Determines, Cicero does not know, though he proves that God exists.  
For he thinks God is a body, but greater than a body,  
[Col. 0992A] which neither a human being apprehends by sense nor brute flesh does.

### That bodily things are grasped by sense, incorporeal things by reason

The bodily sense clings only to bodily things;  
Incorporeal things lie under reason.

[1235] Faith alone and true love apprehend him;  
And to follow nature is the worship and love of God.  
For whoever strives to uphold the laws of reason  
Follows nature, serves, and loves God.  
Yet that service must not be considered servile:

[1240] Thus a daughter serves her mother, a bride her husband.  
And if Cicero’s life had corresponded to his words,  
He could have been the greatest among the greatest men.  
All admire the man’s mouth, not so his heart:  
His mastery of language matched it—or rather, fell short.

[1245] [Col. 0992B] Roman power is less than his eloquence;  
Citizen and enemy alike love his tongue.

### That virtue is preferred to eloquence

The man whom virtue has raised higher surpasses Cicero  
And makes a skilled tongue yield place to life:  
For though philosophy forms language and regulates conduct,

[1250] Its chief lesson is how to live.  
To live sincerely is the best part of philosophizing;  
Without it, what good is an eloquent tongue? None!  
For eloquence harms if it is deserted by the heavenly  
Gift which makes men wise.

[1255] But how much wise eloquence benefits, though the tongue  
Be eminent, no speech can tell.

### On Seneca and Quintilian

[Col. 0992C] Quintilian praises Seneca’s talent,  
Yet criticizes his words and style.  
He complains that great subjects are broken by loose discourse,

[1260] And charges his manner of speaking with diffuseness.  
He called his words, joined without a final close, sand without lime,  
Since every sentence completes its own thought.  
But although so great an author criticized his pen,  
His excellence prevailed, and the style itself is pleasing.

[1265] For the gravity of his life and the charm of his language conquered,  
And his novel manner of speech was agreeable.  
He is a keen Stoic, seeking abridgments of morals,  
And always has words suited to his meanings.

### That Christian faith surpasses all pagans

[Col. 0992D]

But why should I count pagans, whom error has led astray?

[1270] For every reasoning fails without faith.  
Christians alone are wise and truly philosophize—  
Those whom sacred page gives you as guides.  
I judge people to be Christians by worship, not by Christ’s name,  
A name which a chaste life and faith bestow upon a person.

[1275] True grace will be given to you if you follow  
Doctrines which excel in morals and faith.  
Yet you will not safely proclaim these things in that court  
Where grace is rare and faith is rare.  
Pure faith alone does not please everyone; it is deservedly

[1280] More pleasing when a good life sustains it.  
Pure faith is the fountain of true life, and the life of faith  
Is good morals: God grants both.

### That it is healthier to please a few good men than a multitude of fools

[Col. 0993A]

But because no one can please fools by reason,  
Let it suffice that you have pleased serious men.

[1285] One can scarcely endure the guffaws of the unlearned  
Unless one has a strong breast and sober mind.  
Wanton youth doubles its sneers and snorts  
When it hears unfamiliar words from a book unknown to it.  
You will not escape the snorts, the tongues, and the insolent hands;

[1290] You will scarcely escape unless you have a guide by whom to go safely.

### On Archbishop Theobald and Chancellor Thomas

He who bids you write is accustomed also to support what is written  
And to make famous the names which he has once received.  
That Theobald who presides over Christ’s court,  
Which our Kent reveres as mother of the faith,

[1295] Hopes that this man will succeed him, and prays that he may likewise  
Strengthen the office and place of bishop.  
This is the man who annuls the unjust law of executioners,  
Whom conquered England long endured as kings,  
Thinking them kings though she had suffered them as tyrants;

[1300] She reveres more highly those who harmed her more.

### On the character of Hyrcanus

For him who commanded the customs and laws of the ancients  
To be torn up, pleasure stood in place of reason.  
He surpassed Midas in greed, the lion in fierceness,  
The cunning fox in frauds and deceits,

[1305] He who oppressed the people, despised law and equity,  
Compared with whom every wolf and tiger was gentler;  
More defiled than a swine, more wanton than any goat,  
A seller of the Church, powerful through treachery,  
Greedy for human blood and an avenger of beasts,

[1310] Who, under the title of king, was a public enemy.  
He is set forward as an example of laws and governing a people,  
And as a sure model of good living.  
He favored the cultivation of peace, but in a tyrant’s manner,  
So that he might see all things subject beneath his feet.

[1315] Under this king a poor wolf feared the gallows,  
Though deserving acquittal if he could give a sheep—  
If he could give a sheep stolen or violently  
[Col. 0993D] Taken from a widow, then he was free from blame.  
The wolf who could shear the flock and knew how to give wool

[1320] Was innocent; he was worthy of a sheep.  
It did not harm the fox who wished to commit fraud  
To share his profit with the shepherd.  
This was a saying worthy to be heard from a convicted thief:  
“I shall speak of the king’s advantage.”

[1325] For the thief who considers the king a partner  
Does not perish, and often makes the righteous perish.  
But he deserves the cross who clings to theft alone  
And does not care to make the judge his accomplice.  
The greedy judge becomes partner in crimes for a price,

[1330] Acquits the guilty and kills the undeserving.

### That Hyrcanus gave modern depravity both its origin and its authority

[Col. 0994A]

These things flow from that fountain of law which Hyrcanus  
Once handed down, together with his office.  
The office conformed to the king, because an ingenious hand  
Follows the mind of its author.

[1335] The Julian law slept, buried with that king;  
Adultery was nothing but a game.  
Silvia yielded to Quartilla, Lauronia to Flora,  
And while Sulla flourished, there was no Sabine woman.  
Rejoicing to be feared, he scorned to be loved,

[1340] Subjugating neighbors by gifts, fraud, and deceit.

### On the peace of tyrants

That is the peace of tyrants: that no one may protest;  
Whatever they do, they may do everything, while laws are nothing.  
The laws are empty; abuse overturns the sacred laws;  
They decree that their own will has the place of law.

[1345] They say that a lion exercised justice in this fashion,  
When set over the other beasts to pronounce laws.  
This is the freedom of a people when a tyrant rules:  
Each person must wish precisely what is commanded.  
Whoever too eagerly seeks wealth or the favor of an unjust king

[1350] Rushes headlong into every crime, prone to every wickedness.  
Whoever upholds sacred laws is judged an enemy;  
Loyal love anticipates commands by its services.  
It is a kind of perfidy to distinguish any command,  
And it is a crime even to have feared some crime.

### How one may please the chancellor

[1355] [Col. 0994C] If virtue orders your soul, truth shapes  
Your tongue, and mother grace fosters your work,  
Then the champion of true liberty will love you  
And make you safe to go on every road.  
With this guide you will be safe in cloister, safe at court,

[1360] Safe amid ambushes, safe on every side.  
He is the one who, to defend the liberty of the clergy,  
Is grievous to Mandroger and his accomplices.

### On Mandroger

To Mandroger, who boasts that he alone preserves the crown  
And is the father of the laws of the realm,

[1365] Who—if liars are to be believed—keeps the laws  
Intact, so that through him the royal honor may stand;  
To Mandroger, whom the very name of liberty burns,  
If anyone wishes the Church to possess it.  
The liberty of a wealthy Church, destitute of nothing,

[1370] Is more heavily oppressed by the unjust hand of the king, her enemy.  
Public power rages under the honorable title of guardian,  
So that any robber would be milder than it.  
The unjust guardian ravages the property of his ward,  
And no enemy can be more wicked than a guardian appointed.

[1375] Mandroger’s faction makes lawful and pleasing equivalent,  
And proclaims good whatever has once pleased it.  
Under his influence the liberty of the Churches perishes,  
And Antipater’s hand takes up wicked arms.

### On Antipater, and why he is so called

The people revere priests as Fathers.

[1380] And it is part of faith to submit to a Father’s commands—  
[Col. 0995A] to submit to a Father’s commands, especially when he commands rightly,  
For obedience to them gives blessed life.  
But fierce Antipater persecutes them as enemies  
And, laying snares, everywhere stirs up wars.

[1385] Hence he is given the name Antipater, because he injures Fathers,  
Inflicts losses upon them, and prepares death.  
Diligently he heaps into a pierced sack all the wealth  
Taken from Christ which he wickedly seeks.  
He commands the Church to be enslaved and decrees

[1390] That clergy and people should by law hold the same rank.  
The clergy are oppressed, the priest is deprived of honor,  
But the name of informer thrives everywhere.  
The public tax-gatherer excels in the highest honor;  
Yet he is more pleasing who does more evil.

[1395] [Col. 0995B] If these men happen to wish to pervert anything, they say:  
“On one side the dishonor of the kingdom is being turned; on the other, its honor.”  
The ruler, not desirous of merit but greedy for praise,  
Has the chief name of honor without its reality.  
He does not care what honor is, but what appears honorable;

[1400] True goods do not please him, but the shadow of good delights him.  
Thus reason is blinded under the pretext of honor,  
And while vain glory is sought, true glory flees.

### On true and vain glory

Glory follows virtue, not love of praise,  
And is always joined to good merits.

[1405] [Col. 0995C] The upright man shines by praise rather than as a lover of praise;  
Conversely, the idle man is made foul by his polluted reputation.  
For the stench and horror of vice accompany its filth,  
And virtue fills good people with a pleasing fragrance.  
But the fragrance of virtue is destructive to those

[1410] Whom Antipater’s destructive hand drives.  
Lawless barbarism stinks; the ancient slaughterhouse stinks with a heavy odor.

### That the house of tyrants is a slaughterhouse

The court subdued by tyrants is an ancient slaughterhouse;  
Antipater’s house is an ancient slaughterhouse.  
Reverence for sacred law is removed from the midst;

[1415] Sacred laws give place to the decrees of executioners.  
Sporus demands little gifts from all; but if you give them,  
[Col. 0995D] you will lose; if you give nothing, you will be an enemy.  
If he is a friend, he harms; if he is not, he seeks to harm.  
Whatever you do will harm you, or he will wish to be harmful.

[1420] Perhaps you can preserve your property, but you cannot  
Recall his mind from its vices.  
A gift produces the appearance of friendship, but true virtue  
Produces friendship itself, and faith proves it.  
Yet it is increased by services and takes strength,

[1425] For uprightness returns rewards worthy of merits.  
Dinomaches and Polydamas rule at court;  
Cato counts for nothing, Curius for nothing; Photinus does all things.  
Photinus does all things with Labeo as his associate:  
Their life is crime; every word, deceit.

[1430] [Col. 0996A] It is painful to see Thraso’s pride and gestures,  
Whom Thaïs, won over by gifts, can scarcely endure.  
This man is grave, grave to behold, and a pleasing Sabinus,  
While he is a boy, tender and without sprouting beard.

### That the chancellor conforms himself to courtiers in order to recall them from error

[1435] The defender of law sees these things with sorrow and devises  
A method by which he may bring help, and forms a plan.  
That their madness may grow mild, he is accustomed to dissemble  
Many things; he pretends that he too is mad.  
He becomes all things to all; in outward appearance he puts on the enemy,

[1440] So that by like pursuits they may learn to love God.  
[Col. 0996B] That deceit is good which brings about usefulness,  
By which joys, life, and salvation are procured.  
The nurse stammers in order to form her pupil’s speech,  
And prudently avoids a real pain by a feigned one.

[1445] She restrains a wanton laugh by tears deliberately raised  
And deceives tender feelings through a holy art.  
A weeping face moves a friend to tears,  
And a cheerful face often produces joy.  
That a soldier may more strongly crush a combative enemy,

[1450] The commander arms himself while he wages fierce wars.  
The soldier presses enemies more fiercely through his commander’s example;  
If the commander flees, the soldier likewise turns his back in flight.  
The obliging teacher draws pupils by affection,  
So that his labor may achieve its result.

[1455] [Col. 0996C] No one willingly hears the words of a suspected teacher;  
Love makes them sweet, even though they be harsh.  
A way of life more quickly ensnares people and binds them more tightly  
Than a stern teacher does.  
Therefore by this method your patron’s sound mind

[1460] Strives to make the mad court bear him patiently.  
He strives to win the affection of the crowd  
That dines with him, lest drunkenly it pursue the path of death.

### That many successes have given boldness to error

The new court, drunk with fortune’s gifts,  
Believes under a boy king that everything is permitted.

[1465] You would think young and old alike mad;  
The judge is mad, and so is his office.  
[Col. 0996D] The court loves, hears, and honors only triflers;  
Every courtier has odious arts.  
Every courtier hates arts that serve virtue,

[1470] But every courtier loves those that serve the flesh.  
That rope-walker introduced these courtly customs,  
Who upholds by his grandfather’s law whatever he presumes.  
Those who are wise in trifles and crimes are called to the law;  
Those who think rightly, the law orders outside.

### That insinuation should be used in correction

[1475] Therefore those whom direct reason cannot recall  
From vices, the work of insinuation recalls.  
For as there is an insinuation of speech, so there is one of life,  
Which often draws the resistant to its desires.  
The persuasion of life is stronger than that of speech,

[1480] [Col. 0997A] for love is won by like pursuits.  
Love, once won, binds, commands, and urges minds,  
So that those whom holy love unites are not two.  
Thus holy love compels lovers toward every good,  
For the one accomplishes by wishes what the other accomplishes by hand.

[1485] But I fear the chancellor may labor in vain  
To change the proud court’s ways.  
For the world gapes after profit; an imperious hunger for gifts  
Defiles young and old alike,  
And blinds those to whom power has been entrusted,

[1490] So that every great house inclines toward filth.  
[Col. 0997B] The heat of avarice burns up the hearts of the wise,  
Defiles churches, and makes holy things profane.  
All lovers of the world suffer from this plague;  
Rare in the world is one who despises money.

[1495] Where, when, to whom, or in what manner these things should be insinuated—  
Take care that you do not perish through your own talkativeness.  
Speech that does not know how to sharpen its tongue is unlearned,  
Feeble speech that does not know how to keep measure in words.  
Triflers, tyrants,

[1500] The false philosopher, the glutton, and the buffoon are your enemies—  
Those driven by a compulsion to write or to talk,  
Those foul with vices, whom a light breeze favors.  
Snares are prepared by these people for one who speaks truth,  
[Col. 0997C] and unless you take precautions, you will be a public enemy.

[1505] The defender of truth does not know the role of friend;  
He grants no rewards to men according to their merits.  
He spares persons; as a judge he is fierce against crimes,  
And everywhere he always marks the stain of vice.  
Either be altogether silent, or speak little at court,

[1510] Or seek some country place in which you may hide.  
For if you do not spare words, no one will spare you,  
And an impious crowd will anticipate your days.  
If under the aforesaid leader you happen to leave the court,  
So that you may go safely and unharmed wherever you wish,

[1515] At last you will drop a few words into your patron’s ear,  
Which, recalling them, he cannot be unmindful of himself.  
The divine law is the sole teacher of good living,  
[Col. 0997D] not ancient rites, which lack reason.  
With sleepless care strive to observe it continually,

[1520] For it itself preserves its keepers.  
If human law is contrary to God’s law,  
It condemns its author, and perishes when he perishes.

### That civil laws are compared with spiders’ webs

The nets which a spider weaves are easily broken,  
Though its art makes the threads join wonderfully;

[1525] They hinder the small bodies of flies,  
But if large creatures come, they let them pass wherever they wish.  
Thus, Anacharsis says, civil laws restrain  
The weak, while the mighty may go wherever they wish.  
Not so the eternal law, powerful to torment the powerful

[1530] And to cherish the humble whom it sees to be devout.

### On the diversity of lodgings and hosts

[Col. 0998A]

Having said these things, depart and bid your patron farewell;  
When your native soil calls you back, return.  
Traveler, inquire how much trust exists in lodgings:  
For property is prized, while trust is cheap everywhere.

[1535] A host sits in ambush for traveling guests,  
And an evil listener marks every word.  
If your tongue utters a careless word or a joke,  
If your bag lies laden with a few possessions,  
The wicked host flies at either your possessions or your words,

[1540] Recounts them, and becomes a destructive interpreter.  
He calls in Bavius and empty Dolon as witnesses,  
So that you may perish in your possessions, or lose all that is yours.  
If a household possesses true faith and pure honor,  
Its face is cheerful and its hand obliging.

[1545] [Col. 0998B] By words and a pleasant expression, the care of host and good dependent  
Repairs the guest’s lack of resources.  
Not every house which displays the title of honor  
Possesses the reality, or deserves veneration through its merits.  
But whatever place you see consecrated in Christ’s praise,

[1550] Whoever occupies it, is a place worthy of honor.  
And since the members correspond harmoniously to the head,  
The house itself takes its color from its master.  
If a venerable house has received you as a guest  
Or perhaps gives you help,

[1555] Notice wisely who dispenses its goods; beneath him  
[Col. 0998C] stand the fortune of the house and the character of the place.  
For good reputation perishes if he is boorish or greedy;  
Reputation flourishes through the service of an urbane countenance.

### On Carinus

A house is hell when Carinus is its steward;

[1560] Guest and enemy fare alike.

### On Catius

Catius, with a serious face, feigns an honorable life,  
But his rear and belly reveal what he is.

### On the Corydonians

He who imitates Fabius in gesture and Cato in gravity of speech  
Has human wisdom with Corydon.

[1565] The clergy disgust them; they shrink from  
The names of common life; their proud sect approves itself alone.  
[Col. 0998D] Yet from where do both the people and these men seek their conveniences,  
Whom love of advantage equally deceives?  
They enjoy bread, wine, and clothing in the common manner,

[1570] And, just as for us, a lavish kitchen pleases them.  
They seek riches; pleasure without labor delights them,  
And sometimes alluring, hidden Venus takes them.  
Now they pursue serious affairs, then serious affairs yield to trifles,  
And a pleasing offering to the belly appeases the stomach.

[1575] The common market supplies food, the common tavern drink,  
One sheep supplies clothing;  
Yet they take clothing and food from the common stock  
Provided that the tailor and cook are common.  
For the name and honor of the house demand that clothes be made for them

[1580] And food prepared more lavishly.

### On the Bavian and Maevians

[Col. 0999A]

Bavius agrees with error; Maevius bites at what is blessed;  
They bark, and error is grave on both sides.  
Each of these gives his name to a sect, and is the authority  
For people whom you often see.

[1585] Let Maevius and Bavius always be avoided as enemies,  
And flee Catius with his Corydon.

### On the Carinians

Strive to appease Carinus, whom you cannot avoid,  
Since your fate often depends upon his judgment.  
For him it is enough to have earned the favor of a few,
[1590] Into whose bellies a lavish kitchen pours,

Whose care is wont to empty the pantry by drinking,

And public goods lie hidden in their private purses.

They dread expense and the face of a travelling friend;

[Col. 0999B] for a foreign prostitute pleases them more.

[1595] What, then, do you expect—that you should find an agreeable host,

For whom, unless she joins in his sport, no girl is pleasing?

### How one ought to behave among hosts

But since it is altogether shameful for a traveller to stir up a quarrel,

Let your hospitality, whatever it may say, keep moderation;

And, lest anyone be able to suspect you of severity,

[1600] let your tongue be full of pleasant jokes;

Let your wit be without a sting, your speech restrained,

Your bearing composed, and your life chaste.

Be a good hearer, patient and slow to anger;

And let him be a humble dependent who wishes to be yours.

[1605] Desiring to be welcome to hosts, moderate your expenditure,

[Col. 0999C] so that you may be able to return to each a worthy recompense.

And let full thanks be rendered to benefactors—

Thanks which a good interpreter makes every particular seem great.

A good and prudent man now preserves goods for use,

Now distributes them, and teaches them to be his own;

[1610] he seeks to spend when reason and occasion require,

And at the proper time scatters wealth long kept in store;

He rejoices to have incurred expense in the right place and manner.

The fool knows no measure in spending:

He is sparing with his own and lavish with another’s;

[1615] He lacks the praise which Chaerea alone seeks.

No one who is moderate is a burden in hospitality,

[Col. 0999D] if he can be content with modest expenses.

In short, see with whom you have dealings,

And, so far as you can, strive to be accommodating.

Always understand this saying, “so far as you can,”

So that the rule of honour may remain intact for you.

### That liars and drunkards are to be avoided

Likewise you will avoid liars and beware of drunkards,

And of those whose god is either their belly or Laverna.

### What sort of companion one ought to have

[1625] Let Venus be suspect; let the man whom you seek

As a companion for a long journey be sober and chaste.

Nothing is more useful than a faithful servant and companion;

No one is useful in service without faithfulness.

### What expenditure is necessary everywhere

[Col. 1000A]

Seek the resources for your journey; they will be supplied by

[1630] a reputation for good character, serious conduct, pleasing speech.

The more these are spent, the more they increase;

Money spent as an expense departs never to return.

These resources can bring you wherever you wish;

For this currency grows through its own use.

[1635] Therefore you will go securely wherever the road pleases you;

Yet it is sweeter to go to your own homeland.

### That Canterbury is the head of the kingdom, and who should and should not be avoided there

Canterbury, mother of pontiffs and kings, has reared you,

And prepares for you not merely hospitality, but a home.

She asks that you return and rest in that seat

[1640] [Col. 1000B] which is the head of the kingdom and the house of justice.

Obey your mother, especially when she gives right counsel

And strives to prolong your days.

You will enter the cloister—but, if you can, do so without the hood,

So that later, if you wish, you may leave still your own man.

[1645] There you will find those who labour always to know,

And for whom it is a great punishment to lack a book.

There are others who so bid for the writings of the wise

That they think all of them not worth a halfpenny.

Go to lovers of the law and those who cultivate writings;

[1650] beware, on the other hand, of triflers and worshippers of money.

The wise man admits to use the riches which he despises,

And sometimes seeks them, though never without moderation.

The miser seeks riches in vain, because he is never satisfied,

Though God himself should confer upon him whatever he possesses.

[1655] Money is god to the man who continually harasses his friends

And is accustomed to perpetuate an eternal hunger.

Grace, by its dew, restrains harmful desire,

But does not make the covetous mind free from hunger.

It is well enough known that God can do all things; yet he cannot,

[1660] though omnipotent, satisfy the miser.

[Col. 1000D] Nothing is more wicked than this, for it spares no one and acts

So that it too may always be miserable with the rest.

More wicked than others is the man who in words lives as Gillia,

In deeds as Demea, and behaves as Flaminius and Numa.

[1665] Tantalus is the exemplar of the covetous, the exemplar of misers;

He wastes away in perpetual thirst and hunger.

### On Brito

You will find Brito cheerful if cheese is present;

Yet at times he rejoices more that books are there.

For, insofar as Brito’s nature or station permits,

[1670] he gives himself to studies and devotes his leisure to poetry.

The administration of a household entrusted to him flourishes,

And the appearance of evil flees when he arrives.

[Col. 1001A] Balatro does not love him, nor does Davus; Pamphilus hates him,

For to each of them nothing is more burdensome than staying at home.

### On Odo

[1675] Odo is wholly devoted to books; yet greater grace resides in those

Which breathe of Christ.

He is grievous to the Eumolpi; Encolpius and Adonis—

While they beware of Giton—even Venus herself fears him.

Brito’s hand is cautious, Odo’s tongue golden,

[1680] when he speaks of Christ: each is full of faith.

Let these be your companions; disclose all that is yours to them,

For Brito approves what you play at, Odo what you understand.

### On Querolus

[Col. 1001B]

You marvel that Plautus’ *Querolus* is seen everywhere:

No household lacks such a slave.

[1685] Neither Fortune nor God can placate him

So that he does not always disparage the brave man and God.

You may see parasites standing by every rich man,

So that not even Gnatho can find a place.

If the greedy rich man suffers because a parasite despoils him,

[1690] who should grieve? Whatever the miser has is enough.

### On Zoilus

Zoilus reckons the servants’ expenses and reviews their deeds,

So that he may drip them into his master’s ear.

Is he therefore faithful because he weighs household expenses?

[Col. 1001C] No: by flattery he seeks and increases his wealth.

[1695] He is worse than a thief, since another’s property is in his heart;

He acts so as to deceive minds by means of their own light.

Nor does he spare possessions, which he more safely takes from a fool;

For the wise man keeps watch and guards against his own losses.

For, while he repels the deceitful and covetous flatterer, he says:

[1700] “Be gone, Zoilus the sycophant: I see you.”

### On Matho

You wonder that the servants of the court have yielded to Matho;

A mind full of guile and an evil tongue cause this;

So does the frivolity of listeners, so that a threepenny groom

Can drive anyone from an ungrateful house.

[1705] [Col. 1001D] The credulous hearer forgets his faithful old dependent

And always likes to have new ones.

For whenever the base fellow whispers easily into his ear,

He poisons within the workings of heart and speech.

Before the hearth the talker turns over and weighs

[1710] men’s ages, characters, fortunes, and conditions.

At his discretion, the master—unsound and senseless—

Either blesses or torments, hates or loves his own people.

Unhappy, therefore, and a punishment to good men is the house

Which, lacking a ruler, groans beneath a cinder-scullion;

[1715] indeed it is exceedingly unhappy, and the prey of parasites,

Which rejects the old, only to gain no benefit from the new.

Stellio has incurred an empty stain for theft,

And is no thief now that he has ceased to be accused.

### On the vice of envy and its cure

[Col. 1002A]

A happy lot lies beneath envy’s goad; the wretched man alone

[1720] is free from it and alone lacks an enemy.

While devouring envy longs to harm others and kindles fires,

It is first of all burned by its own fire;

It is pierced by its own goads, gnaws itself

With bloody tooth, and continually wastes away by its own impulse.

[1725] No one can avoid the bites and doglike maw of those

Whom school, cloister, or the harmful court nourishes.

Humble caution and tested virtue escape them,

Yet envy sometimes strikes both.

### On the Euphorbians

The talkative tongue was born not to speak but to lick filth,

[1730] [Col. 1002B] ever forward in uttering curses.

Euphorbus’ frenzy labours and acts through this plague,

Lest favour or faithful love should flourish,

Lest any household retain peace, any cloister quiet,

Or any court remain secure.

[1735] The harmful tongue befouls the *plani* (deceivers), continually profanes holy things,

And casts savage poisons against everyone.

### On Baccara

Whatever he has, whatever he can do, Baccara displays and offers,

And forbids you to lack his resources.

He promises great things, though intending to give not even small things; thus he so “enriches” his friends

[1740] [Col. 1002C] that no needy man receives any help.

If you ask assistance, he refuses it; if you seek counsel, he hesitates.

What, then, do you expect? Baccara will always be Baccara.

### On Davus

Disturbing everything by chatter and tricks, Davus

Mocks everyone and is himself the laughter of the household.

[1745] You see Sergiolus promising Scaeva by his gestures;

Wait a little: he will be Sardanapalus.

### On Thersites’ school

The court produces many men like Thersites—

Men whom school, cities, and empty law-courts produce;

Whom a village has reared, whom a barbarous land sends forth,

[1750] [Col. 1002D] whom Venus possesses in bedchambers and Mars’ camps;

Whom even the broken preserves of men send out,

When Venus drives them or Laverna draws them.

### That character must be observed

I have portrayed human characters so that you might be more cautious;

For each person must be treated according to his character.

[1755] Honour and respect must be given to proven character,

And love is won by deserving faithfulness.

For force can sometimes extort fear,

Overthrowing the unwilling and making them submit,

So that captive will serves others against its wishes,

[1760] frightened by blows and driven by threats.

[Col. 1003A] But perfect love drives this fear far away,

For chaste love makes everyone freeborn.

### That freedom befits a philosopher

The philosopher’s life is free, and his speech is free;

God is the author of freedom for both.

[1765] Therefore the philosopher cultivates those whom he believes to be friends,

Or whom he thinks may be brought back from vices.

Those whom the world possesses are not men, but men’s shadows,

When, brutish through vice, they lack reason.

What have you to do with phantoms, you who follow wisdom’s doctrine?

[1770] [Col. 1003B] Unless you flee quickly, they will say, “Go outside.”

### That place does not exclude vices

If a crowd full of haughtiness drives you away, depart;

And learn to despise those who despise you.

Do not care if you are despised by those

Whom the empty nets of the world hold captive.

[1775] He is taken in the cloister whom love of vices torments,

For the cloister wall stands open to them.

They storm strongholds; know that, once great evils rise,

No barrier can resist them.

No diamond bars vices, no iron rampart,

[1780] no water, no ditches, not even a hostile marsh.

### On the threefold obstacle to vices

[Col. 1003C]

By what art, then, can such savage enemies be repelled,

Or what compels them to take flight?

If fear guards the doors, shame the halls,

And chaste love holds the inner parts,

[1785] dutiful fear avoids punishment and everything

Which, unless it takes precautions, it thinks can do harm.

Noble shame wards off the stain upon one’s name

And scatters sweet odours everywhere, by which it may please.

Chaste love so constantly clings to honourable things

[1790] that no greater force can separate it;

It stations virtues in its camp and thus fortifies everything,

[Col. 1003D] so that the enemy can find no place at all.

But fear in a slave, once punishment can safely be avoided,

Will yield to easy gain and become harmful;

And shame, guardian of reputation, when fault can remain hidden,

[1795] consents to vices without blushing.

Not so true love, faithful in every circumstance,

Which rejoices that virtue alone dwells within it.

Other things are sought for various causes; virtue,

Content with itself, always has its own rewards.

All advantages allotted by fate yield to virtue;

[1800] virtue’s fruit lies in devout love.

Just as a chaste wife, desiring to preserve faith with her husband,

Avoids and diligently flees,

Lest any access to herself be open to a seducer—

Sight, laughter, gifts, words, or jests—

[1805] [Col. 1004A] despising them, and abhorring both the merit and the name of the adulterer:

So holy love abhors every fault.

### On grace and free choice

Grace alone produces and strengthens devout love,

Which fear and noble shame serve.

It alone does not declare that merit is nothing,

For the Spirit within nourishes the good things we do.

[1810] It alone teaches that, if grace is absent,

Nature’s effort toward good will be vain.

It alone teaches that grace is the one cause of salvation,

Grace which advances and produces merit.

The choice of the flesh is grace; it is the image of the mind;

[1815] the flesh lives by the mind, and choice by God.

[Col. 1004B] Fallen into ashes, the flesh returns to ashes if the spirit is absent;

The mind goes to earth when God abandons it.

Foul flesh, when the mind is gone, is given as food to worms;

[1820] the mind without God is foul food for worms.

No sect, if grace is lacking, is free from pride;

Every sect admits pride if grace is absent;

No small or great household excludes it.

[1825] A habit and the title of master do not make you wise,

Nor can a crowd of companions make you blessed;

Neither a shaven head, nor dark or white clothing

[Col. 1004C] draws you to life: grace alone draws you.

For fools can perish in any garment;

No rewards of life are rendered to a gown.

They hate truth; they shrink from what uprightness has ordained;

Thus it happens that they rush headlong in blindness.

Hell receives those who perish when their garment is stripped away,

Nor does its dark or white colour diminish their punishment.

### A traveller’s blessing

[1835] Often and at length I have warned you; now receive a few things

Which, if you keep them well, no matter will harm you.

Bend the knee, bow the head, and depart with a blessing:

This hand has often helped those mature in years.

Let the words of God shape your mind and restrain your tongue;

[1840] [Col. 1004D] let them likewise be the sure rule of your life.

Grace will direct your affections, order your tongue and actions,

If God is the single cause in these three things.

### What a book owes its author

To every author there are owed by perpetual right

Obedience, reverence, and dutiful love.

[1845] Since you are bound to these, strive to reconcile

The mind of a friendly reader to your author;

And continue to induce all the faithful whom you can

To be willing to entreat Christ on my behalf.

But why delay at length? You are hastening to depart. See to it

[1850] what you do; cautiously complete the journey you have begun.

That you may prosper, remember yourself; if you wish

To be held welcome, take care always to live by God’s law.

[Col. 1005]

# John of Salisbury’s Poem on the Conspiring Members

[Col. 1005A]

The limbs of the human body hold a council

Among themselves and exchange many words concerning themselves.

The discussion turns to the belly; they complain of the belly

Because that heavy master presses them too harshly.

At last, painting its words in rhetorical colours,

The proud tongue addresses its brothers:

“Citizens, what madness, what such licence of the belly is this,

That it should dare to impose a shameful yoke on us?

It is surely a shameful yoke when a slave rules

And a master serves: this one commands, that one performs.

Surely we are shameful slaves, worthy of the cross,

A spectacle to all, wretched and degenerate.

For have we chosen the belly as our master? We ourselves gather

Everything which it thinks pleasing to itself.

[Col. 1005B] We have no rest: it sets this one in motion, commands that one, calls another:

‘Rise, sluggard; shake off sleep; cease delaying.

Seek food, prepare feasts, and offer wine.

Set the table: the day passes, the hour flies.

Look: two enemies come and threaten death;

Hunger looms on one side, thirst on the other.

Therefore I shall fail unless you swiftly help me,

Anticipate hunger and anticipate thirst.’

Thus, thus the belly’s wantonness strikes me and the others,

And that swollen thing presses me more than the rest.

Like a herald of lawsuits, it often orders me

To pursue quarrels and seek small gifts.

Now as advocate, now as judge, now as witness,

I cry aloud, violate the laws of the Fathers, and speak falsehoods.

Under the appearance of truth, intent on introducing falsehood,

[Col. 1005C] I deceive, commit perjury, and betray faith.

Weighing right and wrong together in equal balance,

I range alike through what is lawful and unlawful.

If I stand at the side of a bishop or a prince,

Then, desiring to please, I prepare sweet ointments.

I anoint with flattery, so that the belly

May heap up pleasures for itself; and that harmful thing distracts me.

Do not our hands labour to serve the belly?

Do they not fear its threats and its commands?

They steal, snatch, toil—and the belly receives all things

And, a ravenous Scylla, gulps down everything.

The hunting eye serves it, running everywhere;

It reports to its master what it thinks best.

Alas, how many labours it has often imposed upon the feet,

Whom it afflicts excessively and oppresses without restraint.

[Col. 1005D] Hence pain consumes the bones of our body,

Shakes the limbs, drains strength, and ploughs the skin.

Our will is eager for service,

Yet there is no gratitude; for this I complain the more.

For when gratitude answers service, it greatly

Moderates—indeed, makes sweet—the burden of labour.

[Col. 1006A] But though we give it much, though we prepare much,

It does not cease complaining: ‘You give too little.’

If you give today, unless you give tomorrow, unless again

And again you give, you may lose what you first gave.

And if perhaps it says to its own people, ‘It is enough, that is enough,’

After a short time it begins to be too little.

Tell me: what can satisfy so great a Charybdis?

Tell me: who can give as much as it desires?

This creature also increases and heaps up our labours,

And that most evil gluttony often oppresses us too severely.

One serves as taste, another guards the gate, another is

A base pander, an impudent cook, a wandering buffoon.

These two roam through the elements of the world; they wish to know

What the air produces, what the earth, what the seas.

No bird escapes by wing, no beast by running,

[Col. 1006B] nor will a whale be safe in the whole abyss.

They know how to arrange varied flavours

So as the more to entice and allure with food.

Taste distinguishes; the throat transmits; the belly conceals:

The first approves, the second seizes, the third receives.

O belly, by what great crime you defile the world,

And make it unclean, stirring up every shameful thing!

Because of you come murders, thefts, plunderings,

Plots, massacres, quarrels, wars, and deceits.

The monk runs to church, the soldier bears arms,

The sailor pursues profits, the farmer ploughs.

From you come the fall of virtues and the ruin of the soul,

Diseases of the limbs and the contagion of luxury.

You are Nebuzaradan, prince and master of cooks,

For the kitchen resounds for you morning and evening.

[Col. 1006C] You are a swollen bellows, a vessel full of filth—nay,

A place full of dregs: not a place, rather a pool.

Therefore, brothers, discern with me what sort of master this is;

With me behold what kind of yoke it is.

I believe it a shameful yoke when a slave rules

And a master serves: this one commands, that one performs.

Truly it is a shameful yoke when, reason buried,

The belly commands within us and reason is silent.

We ought to live not for the belly but for reason;

The good man desires this, not that, as his guide.

Paul says: ‘The belly is for food, and food for the belly’;

The two are joined together; God will destroy both.

Let us therefore be ashamed to serve such a patron;

Through him our glory and nobility perish.

Rise, stand, I pray; fight with manly spirit:

[Col. 1006D] a brief struggle prepares great rewards for us.

Let him perish forever who continues to serve the belly;

Far from us be the man who bears his own kingdoms.

Let there be labour without end, shipwreck without harbour,

For him continual and everlasting toil.”

By these words the tongue’s eloquence encourages its companions,

[Col. 1007A] moves and arms them, and teaches them to be men.

Thus a single will allies those united together

And binds to itself those whom a single love chooses.

They declare war on the belly and swear

That they will dissolve its bonds and shake off its yoke.

So they decree and thus, a compact made, they confirm it:

They abandon the belly and do not serve it.

Now foot, tongue, hand, and the other limbs rest:

The foot refuses to go, the tongue to speak, the hand to help.

The first day runs its tranquil course for them;

The one asks nothing, and the others bring nothing.

The second day cannot restrain the fasting belly

Or quiet its barking throat.

The third scarcely supports the limbs consumed by emaciation,

For everywhere an all-too-malicious hunger presses them.

[Col. 1007B] The foot is numb, the hand sick, the head languishes, their faces

Grow pale, their breasts sigh, the tongue is silent.

Everything in the body is disturbed; there is no vigour in it:

There is sickly grief there, and pain everywhere.

Again, after long groans and with great effort,

The languid tongue scarcely stammers these sounds:

‘What are we doing? We accomplish nothing; more and more all of us

Fail, are crushed, and are consumed by hunger.

This injury comes upon us from the belly’s rage;

Its anger brings forth this evil for us.

I feel a great evil, but the cause of the evil is hidden from me:

What harms us is clear; why it harms us remains concealed.

Now, therefore, brothers, in your presence

I will approach it itself and inquire what is the origin of the evil.’

[Col. 1007C] Then the tongue, turning to the belly, says:

‘Why do you harm us so grievously? Whence this madness in you?

Look: do you not intend to destroy your fellow citizens?

When you see their fall, do you not prepare to raise them?

You are enemy and citizen: these things oppose each other plainly;

Joined together, they would be better: citizen and friend.

Whether empty or full, shall we always have you as an enemy?

Shall either condition always be grievous to us?

When you swell full, weighed down by excessive bulk,

Then you always make us heavy together with you.

Therefore I beg you, have mercy on yourself; have mercy on your own people;

Lest they perish with you, help yourself and yours.

Explain why you do not complain, or what you seek;

And, I pray, do not harm us, but teach us what must be done.’

[Col. 1007D] With these words the tongue ends its speech; and, answering in turn,

The belly begins to speak as follows:

‘I have heard the tongue’s clamour and wisely

Endured it; brothers, we are little harmed thereby.

The tongue is indeed a small limb, but soft, and quickly

[Col. 1008A] slips and too often speaks without measure;

For from a spark it feeds and stirs up a great fire,

And in its own furnace forges deceits.

Thus discord grievously agitates our fellow citizens,

For it disturbs peace and casts weapons at me.

It shows me to you as master and enemy,

But I know that I serve you and cultivate you.

When the nature of things called us forth from the mass

And gave us matter and form,

It joined us in one body, united us in a friendly

Covenant, so that one love might always unite us;

It commanded that all things be held in common by us all,

So that no one should wish to have anything as his own.

It distinguished duties among all: it did not appoint for you a servant

And make him a cook.

[Col. 1008B] Therefore, as your faithful servant, I provide you with pure food and nourishment;

I preserve life for my fellow servants and keep little for myself.

What you give I receive; what I receive I digest; once digested,

I distribute it to you and carry every dish.

What you put in, I digest; what harms, I expel;

What helps, this I convey to each one.

I am a poor servant: I can set nothing before you

If you contribute nothing, for my purse is empty.

I neither care excessively nor seek the least thing for myself.

Placed in the middle, I desire to keep moderation.

From excess come disgust, crimes, disease,

Drunkenness, the torch of luxury, and pain in the side.

From deficiency come the image of hostile death,

A sad brow, a pale face, and loose skin.

From moderation come a mind always sober, a body

[Col. 1008C] strong, a happy life, and tranquil rest.

Therefore let the rich man beware lest he devour more

Than is enough, and let the poor man take care to possess little.

And if you are wise, preserve moderation in what you give me;

I shall be a steward in proportion to what is given.

You will often give me, because you wish often to eat:

For through this life and health are given you.

Rise, lest idleness bring on death’s sleep:

I judge that men often die from the sleep of sloth.

He dies shamefully whom torpor wounds. Therefore

Rise: death hastens; I feel life fleeing.’

At these words of the belly, the throng of limbs recovers

Its strength, and returning vigour puts on its armour.

They rise, apply themselves to their duties, pay what is owed;

[Col. 1008D] each limb keeps watch over its own task.

Nature made them companions in life;

Mutual care makes them companions in labour and burden.

Thus concord buries their quarrel in a happy ending;

Here too the poem wishes to have its end.

[Col. 1009]

# The Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, by John of Salisbury

## Prologue

[Col. 1009A]

To drive away the darkness of unbelief and error, God works wonderfully; and thus, from the beginning of the world’s birth, he has always and everywhere dispensed his mercy so as to provide his Church with suitable ministers, through whom it may advance in virtue and, carried through the waves of this passing age, be brought onward to glory. For just as, in the darkness of night, when some stars set, others rise to illuminate the world, so sons succeed fathers for the continual illumination of the Church; through them the knowledge and worship of God are propagated without interruption from generation to generation. Holy men, indeed, are sons of the apostles and prophets: as they succeeded them in faith, so they attain the inheritance of virtue and miraculous works and the glory of eternal recompense.

Among them blessed Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, shone out like a most brilliant star. He not only illuminated the Latin order, but also cast the rays of his brightness into Greece at the Council of Bari, over which Pope Urban presided, refuting the Greeks’ detestable error concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. If anyone wishes to see how great this man was—as I do not doubt is beneficial to everyone—let him read more carefully the books which he wrote for various reasons, and his letters; let him examine the history written about him and the contemporary kings of England; likewise, let him read the two books which the venerable priest and monk Eadmer published, in an exceptionally lucid and wholly truthful style, on Anselm’s life and conduct—for he was a religious man who had been extremely intimate with him; and let him reverence the visitations of the Most High: the miracles which the Lord worked wonderfully after Anselm’s passing, and those which frequently occur in memory of him.

Certainly, I do not hesitate publicly to declare of this man what another said before me about Antony: that it is a great perfection to know who Anselm was. Approaching, therefore, the aforesaid memorials of books, by the mercy of the Lord, who does not always exclude sinners from proclaiming his glory, I have taken care to sketch certain matters concerning the life and conduct of so great a Father. I do so in concise brevity and sufficiently plain language, so that anyone unable to aspire to the abundance of all that was written by him or about him may at least taste from this drop of so great a river how good and sweet the Lord is, and how blessed and necessary was Father Anselm, who faithfully served him.

## Chapter I. On Anselm’s father, mother, childhood, and vision

[Col. 1010A]

Born in the city of Aosta, to his father Gundulf and his mother Ermenberga—who was one of the prudent women—he conceived from the beginning of his life the fear of the Lord. From it he subsequently bore the fruit of his salvation, from which the works of true righteousness later proceeded. He especially strove to express his mother’s character. For since, while his father was occupied with other matters, the care of the whole household rested on her, she wisely arranged everything. Applying herself with diligent zeal to works of mercy, she regularly attended church, praying and receiving God’s words with all the eagerness of her mind, and faithfully fulfilling the precepts of wisdom. What she had heard, she shared with others in delightful narration, encouraging both herself and them to obedience.

From her the boy heard that there is one God, creator of all, reigning in heaven and giver and rewarder of good things; he believed it, and even at that tender age aspired to knowledge of him. In his childish understanding, however, he supposed that heaven rested upon the neighbouring mountains, and that there was the palace of the God of whom he had heard, where God dwelt bodily with angels and saints. It seemed to him one night in a dream that he ascended there. On the slope of the mountain which he climbed he saw the Lord’s servants reaping wheat, though very negligently; inflamed by zeal for faith, he resolved to accuse them of this before God.

He ascended and found God sitting alone in the palace, except for a steward. Summoned through him, Anselm sat at the Lord’s feet and, at God’s command, received very white bread; there he ate it and was satisfied. He recounted the vision to his companions and boasted that he had been fed with divine bread, meanwhile supposing that these things had happened to him bodily. From that time he was so intoxicated with love of God that, despising the entire world, he even desired some serious illness, through which he might, as he greatly wished, be enrolled in the fellowship of monks. In accordance with his desire, as he prayed, he fell ill; but, as was then thought, his father prevented him from becoming a monk. In truth, however, the Lord was preserving him for something else.

He applied his mind only to letters and upright conduct; and, advancing beyond all his contemporaries in both, he achieved much in a short time. When he became somewhat older, after his mother’s death, he resolved to go to France, drawn by his eagerness for learning. He burned with an immense desire for it, and also wished, at least through the protection afforded by flight, to escape the hostility of his father, who treated him rather harshly. But when, as he left his homeland, he nearly failed from exertion and hunger while ascending a mountain and ate snow to restore his strength even in that way, the servant who was his sole companion on the journey took pity on him. He carefully searched whether there was any food in the bag carried by the donkey and immediately, contrary to expectation, found a most excellent loaf, though he did not know who had put it there. Thus refreshed for the road and its labour, Anselm gave thanks to God for his gift.

## Chapter II. Anselm’s deeds in Burgundy, France, and Normandy. Anselm follows the counsel of the Archbishop of Rouen and becomes a monk at Bec

[Col. 1011B]

After spending three years partly in Burgundy and partly in France, he went in Normandy to that Lanfranc whose memory is held in joy and blessing: a man distinguished alike in learning and virtues, wholly approved in manner of life, and one to whom all who desired progress in eloquence or wisdom flocked from different parts of the world. For by everyone’s judgment he was considered pre-eminent. Anselm therefore became more intimate with him than with the others, and in a sense drained his master’s spirit dry.

He devoted himself wholly to learning, incessantly either learning or teaching it. He persisted in his purpose through hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, with such obstinacy in study that the kingdom of heaven seemed purchasable at a lesser price. Returning to himself and prudently examining his ways, he perceived that one thing was necessary, and that the torrent of eloquence or philosophy of this world does not confer true blessedness. These often produce pride, but never, or only rarely, the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom. Learning sometimes represses certain vices and brings contempt for the world; but plainly contempt for the world is useless where love of God does not grow strong.

On hearing of his father’s death, he was moved still more; and, although he had wholly inclined his mind to God’s service, he hesitated in uncertainty over which path to choose. He did not know whether to seek the desert, a monastic cloister, or, constructing a house from his own patrimony, to minister according to his means to travellers and the poor. For his mind wavered among these three possibilities. Yet, lest rashness should precipitate a decision, followed as a familiar and constant attendant by repentance for deeds wrongly done, he disclosed his inward movement to Lanfranc. At Lanfranc’s counsel he came to the venerable Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, to seek his judgment on this matter, for Maurilius was believed to possess the Spirit of the Lord.

Accordingly, on his counsel, which preferred the monastic life above all others, Anselm became a monk at Bec in the twenty-seventh year of his life. The aforementioned Lanfranc was then prior of that place, under the holy abbot Herluin, who had built the church at Bec from its foundations out of his own patrimony. Receiving from them the first principles of monastic profession, forgetting the things behind and always stretching forward in accordance with the Apostle’s pattern (Phil. 3), Anselm strove to fulfil the role of monk. He devoted himself so diligently to emulation of the saints that he soon became an example for the more perfect to imitate. Within three years, indeed, he had advanced so far that he could deservedly appear to all as a most brilliant example of true holiness and monastic perfection.

## Chapter III. Lanfranc, prior of Bec, is appointed to govern the monastery of Caen. Anselm succeeds to the priorship of the monastery of Bec. On Walter Tyrell while dining with Anselm, and on the great sturgeon

[Col. 1012B]

When Lanfranc was appointed to govern the monastery of Caen, Anselm succeeded him in the priorship of the church of Bec. He strove that, as he had attained honour and rank, he too might advance in religious life and serve more faithfully the God to whom he had vowed his obedience. Already crucified to the world and its desires, he thought upon heavenly things and put into practice only those things which advance toward eternal life. He took not human conduct as the model of his life, but the word of God. Divine Scripture, as he himself was accustomed to say, is the best pattern for living well.

There were four sources from which streams of righteousness could spring for him: continuous meditation upon God’s law, careful performance of it, faithful proclamation, and devout prayer. For what is more perfect than to meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night; than to practise the commandments, from which the prophet rejoices that he gains understanding; than to proclaim God’s glory, by whose proclamation fishermen were made illustrious in teaching truth and confounded the philosophers of the nations? Occupied with these things, Anselm consecrated his service to the Lord in devout prayers, mortifying himself by such fasting that he restrained the allurement of gluttony. That is, from the beginning of his priorship he felt no pleasure at all in food or drink. Yet he did not suffer hunger through fasting, since he had already lost the pleasure of eating.

The prayers which he wrote show how great his devotion was; and anyone who examines his book of meditations will find it plainly. What was written of Martin is most certainly true of Anselm: Christ, or righteousness, or peace—nothing that pertains to true life—was ever absent from his mouth. He always had before his eyes the fear of the Lord and abhorred every appearance of sin above all things that can be said. Indeed, as he was accustomed to confess, if he saw bodily before him on one side the pain of hell and on the other the evil of sinning, and necessity required him to choose one, he would rather be cast into hell than be entangled in sins. He also said that he would prefer to be held innocent in Gehenna rather than to possess the kingdom of heaven stained by sins.

[The supplied source ends here.]

He gave this reason for his assertion: God loves the innocent and the good wherever they may be, and conversely hates and detests all wickedness. Supreme justice certainly does not make the wicked blessed, nor does supreme goodness make its friends miserable. [Col. 1013A] He was devout, so as to extend paternal affection to everyone. He investigated the paths of true knowledge in such a way that he read trustworthy writings, corrected the corruptions of books—which were then extremely numerous through custom—and ascribed such authority to the divine Scriptures that he confessed whatever they affirm to be wholly true. Nothing, moreover, turned the strength of his mind aside from the profession of truth and the worship of justice. The spirit of counsel flourished in him, so that the afflicted flocked to him in crowds from every side. The countenance of truth had shone upon him with such brightness and abundance that he prudently understood the riddles of Scripture, powerfully untied the knots of questions, frequently had manifest knowledge of the secrets of hearts, and, by a certain gift of prophecy, often foretold the hidden things of the future.

It happened that one night, [Col. 1013B] before the night-watch offices, while meditating to himself, he wondered how the prophets had seen past and future things alike, and things absent as though present, and had declared them faithfully and confidently. While he was wholly absorbed in these thoughts, he saw through the intervening walls of the oratory and dormitory how the church attendants prepared the altars and lights, and how one of them rang the bell to awaken the others. When they rose, he marvelled, inferring that it is most easy for God to reveal hidden things to his prophets and saints, since he had sent the rays of his eyes through the density of walls, while nature stood amazed.

Pressed by necessity, he turned aside to lodge with a poor monk, who complained bitterly of lacking fish to set before so great a guest; for he [Col. 1013C] had at home only bread and cheese. “Brother,” he said, “do not be troubled at the lack of food, which God will provide for us; rather, quickly cast your net into the nearby stream, and you will catch a fish sufficient for all of us.” His command was scarcely obeyed, since the thing appeared incredible and an evident testing of the divine majesty. But at length, to the immense astonishment of all, a fish of remarkable size was drawn out in accordance with the word of the man of God.

On another occasion, when a nobleman, Walter surnamed Tyrrel, detained him to dine with him and anxiously complained about a shortage of fish, Anselm, the true worshipper of God, said: “You comfort a man concerning a shortage of delicacies, yet complain—though a great sturgeon is being brought to you?” [Col. 1013D] Walter laughed, wholly disbelieving; immediately, in accordance with Anselm’s word, he saw a very large sturgeon brought to him by two men, who said that their shepherds had found it on the bank of the river Alcia and sent it to their lord. Thus, as it is famously reported of blessed Benedict, so this man too is believed to have possessed the spirit of prophecy.

## Chapter IV. Anselm obtained divine grace, so that he could profess to serve God with a pure heart and a good conscience. Concerning an old man of decrepit age. Concerning a young man [who, for no reason whatsoever, would] ever bring his hand to his private parts. Concerning Osbern the monk. Concerning a brother hostile to Anselm. Concerning the vision of the monk Riculf.

The Spirit of wisdom ruled him, so that nothing pleased him except God, to whom he referred all things: the origin, [Col. 1014A] development, and end of virtues and vices, discerning and explaining in each case how they may be attained or avoided. He fulfilled the Apostolic ideal, so that, had not the safeguard of humility restrained him, he could have declared with the Apostle: “With a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11.)

And as we know is written concerning the disciple whom Jesus loved—that whatever he says is aglow with the fire of charity—so Anselm too, although he does not rise to equality with so great an apostle, nevertheless imitated his footsteps with diligent zeal. His entire speech, his whole life, and all his writings seem to have been kindled by the fire of divine love which shines in them. You would have thought that he did not live for himself [Col. 1014B] but for others—indeed, all the more truly for himself, inasmuch as he lived more usefully for others and more faithfully for God.

While caring also for the advancement of others, he obtained divine grace for himself. Although he sought the salvation of all, he bestowed greater care upon those weak through age or sickness and upon the young. For charity comes more quickly to the aid of one in greater need, gives assistance more generously, and has deeper compassion for one who suffers more bitterly. Thus it more frequently succeeded according to his desire that the sick recovered, old people were strengthened, those who had strayed were recalled to the fruit of a better life, and young people advanced and became established in the cultivation of true virtue. For:

> The jar will long preserve the fragrance  
> With which, when new, it was once steeped.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.69

[Col. 1014C] And habits with which tender age is imbued are removed only with difficulty and not without a certain distress.

Let us explain these successes of his by a few examples. Herwald, a man decrepit with age and laid low by such illness that he retained control only of his tongue and could take neither food nor drink, was awaiting, as was thought, his imminent end in the infirmary. He recovered merely because Anselm gave him wine to drink with his own hand, wine which he had squeezed from grapes into his cupped palm.

A certain young man, in the heat of unconsidered zeal, had bound himself by a resolution never, on any occasion, to put his hand to his genital members. But because a more grievous temptation often follows ill-considered vows, such pain seized him in those parts [Col. 1014D] that a leaden weight seemed to be hanging there. Since he could not conceal it, Anselm advised him to test the extent of the trouble by touch; but the brother refused out of reverence for his vow. God’s servant, knowing that all things are clean to the clean, took the young man with an elderly brother to a more private place. The flesh was found entirely healthy; and from the moment it was seen by the holy man, every pain departed and troubled the young man no more.

A certain Osbern, a monk by profession, young in age, keen in intellect, and skilful with his hands at crafts, was of such perverse character that one could justly despair of his salvation. He showed canine teeth and pursued Anselm with insatiable hatred. But Anselm, pitying his error, captured the boyish mind by a kind of holy cunning: now softening its harshness with kindness, now tolerating such childish conduct as the strength of the rule allowed, and frequently employing prayer or exhortation but rarely commands. He did not so much tear away the perversity of his habits [Col. 1015A] as steal it away; and in a manner of which the young man was unaware, he bound him in the chains of divine law. First he restrained the hatred, then extinguished it; afterwards he elicited affection for himself; and little by little, in the breast now cultivated, he sowed and nourished the pure shoots of charity.

Thus, through kindness and goodwill, he secured from the young man a most ready obedience, so that one who previously would not accept even words from anyone now embraced even blows. He who had been the most perverse of all outstripped all his contemporaries as he progressed from virtue to virtue, and in a short time joined the more perfect. Others could easily behold in him, as in a mirror of divine grace, what they ought to imitate and by what means they should order their lives. But when the Church was hoping for very great fruit from him, the young man was overtaken by premature death, to the immense grief and tears of everyone.

When he had been carried into the church according to custom, Anselm withdrew to a more private place for prayer, while the others were occupied in prayers around the dead man. Overcome by grief and tears, he slightly let his eyes fall into sleep, as happens; [Col. 1015B] and he saw persons distinguished by the brightness of their faces and garments sit down to pronounce judgment upon his Osbern. Osbern too was present, resembling a man whom excessive bloodletting or illness had made bloodless. When Anselm anxiously asked what sentence he had received, Osbern replied: “Three times the ancient serpent rose up against me, and three times fell back upon himself; and at last the Lord’s Bear-keeper delivered me.”

It is indeed probable that he was assailed three times: he could be accused by the slander of the ancient enemy concerning original sin before baptism, actual sins afterwards committed before entering monastic life, and breach of his monastic profession. By the Lord’s “Bear-keeper,” I think a good angel is meant, one who restrains and punishes hostile powers, and who delivered him from the snare of the accuser because his faith and charity had endured and because of his final repentance. Anselm and Osbern had agreed, while Anselm sat constantly beside the sick young man and supplied what was necessary both for soul and body, eagerly anticipating the services of the others with great affection, that Osbern, if it pleased God, would make known to him after death the lot assigned to his condition. [Col. 1015C] The dead man also showed obedience to the living man, whose pattern he had received through zeal for the living.

Conceiving from the vision hope of salvation and that the departed Osbern could be aided by the intercessions of the saints, Anselm arranged that the sacrifice of the divine sacrament should be offered to God for him, either by himself or through another, on every day of the whole year. He also sent letters in every direction and obtained prayers, private and public, for his Osbern. The result was that all sought to succeed Osbern; and Anselm’s kindness gained more persons for the Lord than he would have done had he ruled with severity and power.

[Col. 1016A] Yet he relaxed nothing of the rigour of the rule; but he was more inclined to mercy than to harshness. For if he had to be condemned for one or the other, he said that he would prefer to be found by God too merciful rather than cruel. He knew that authority and severity produce fear rather than love. Nor is there order without love, because no religion is true without charity. Certainly, love cannot be extorted: mutual trust and unfeigned grace bestow it. Always devoted to works of charity and mercy, he gained much fruit for the Lord.

But because meanwhile he was greatly vexed by the tumult of affairs, he resolved to resign the priorship. Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, having been consulted, commanded him under the virtue of obedience to bear the imposed yoke a second time to the end, adding by the same authority that, when called to greater things, he should not resist the divine ordering. For Maurilius declared that he had seen many—and almost always—that those who declined pastoral care for the sake of their own quiet, and then walked in idleness, fell from bad to worse. [Col. 1016B] Anselm obeyed sadly and groaning; committing himself wholly to God, he devoted himself entirely to serving the welfare of the brethren. Although he was eager to comply with everyone and to harm no one, and was peaceful even with those who hated him, he could not avoid the envy which virtue, success, or the reputation of either always provokes. Those who had preceded him complained that a newcomer was preferred over them.

One of them, whom no service could soften, was brought to his last extremity. There he began to grow pale and tremble, and, hiding himself in a strange manner, to change his expression in various ways. Asked by the brethren the cause, he said that two enormous wolves were now strangling him with their teeth clenched. This was reported to the prior, who briefly withdrew to his usual oratory, returned to the infirmary, raised his hand, and made the sign of the holy cross, saying: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” When this was done, the sick man became calm, saying that at Anselm’s entrance and the raising of his hand, he had seen a fiery spear hurled from Anselm’s mouth at the wolves; terrified, they fled rapidly. The minister of that Spirit who was given to the Apostles in tongues of fire came to the sick man, led the brother to repentance and confession, [Col. 1016C] absolved him, and also foretold, by a certain prophetic gift, the hour at which he would die.

One night, a certain Riculf, acting as secretary, was passing before the chapter-house door on his way to the dormitory. Looking in, he saw a brother praying, encircled by a globe of fire. Astonished by this unprecedented sight, he withdrew; but he did not find Anselm in his bed when he looked for him. Returning, he found the servant of God praying, but the fiery globe had now disappeared. A globe of fire marked Martin while offering sacrifice, and encircled Anselm while praying. The Apostles received the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire, and Anselm’s tongue likewise flashes with fire. He also commands demons, drives out diseases, foretells the future, [Col. 1017A] practises and teaches God’s law, and is shown in many ways to be an apostolic man.

## Chapter V. At the monastery of Bec Anselm wrote six books: I, *On Truth*; II, *On Freedom of the Will*; III, *On the Fall of the Devil*; IV, *On the Grammarian*; V, called the *Monologion*; VI, the *Prosologion*. Anselm is seized by a severe illness, in which he was rapt in spirit. Concerning an abbot [who] came to Anselm seeking counsel. Concerning boys brought up in the cloister. Concerning a knight named Cadulus.

At this time Anselm wrote three books: one, *On Truth*; another, *On Freedom of the Will*; and a third, *On the Fall of the Devil*. He also wrote a dialogue entitled *On the Grammarian*, and another which he called the *Monologion* because in it he alone speaks. There, with all authority of divine Scripture kept silent, [Col. 1017B] what faith proclaims concerning God is proved by reason. He also wrote a sixth work entitled the *Prosologion*, in which he briefly demonstrates that the things said of God in himself—such as “almighty,” “good,” and all other such things—are one in him.

But while he was so troubled in seeking this proof that anxiety drove away not only sleep but also food and drink, he came in a kind of despair to attribute this investigation to temptation. Suddenly, during the night watches, what he sought shone upon him. He wrote down the argument on wax tablets and entrusted them to the keeper. But who stole them, since they could nowhere be found, has always remained uncertain. He restored it on other tablets; but when these were later demanded from the repository, they were found on the floor before the place where they had been deposited, [Col. 1017C] the wax torn off and ripped into pieces. Who did this is unknown to this day, unless, as is believable, it was the envy of the ancient enemy. Therefore the work was composed a third time on parchment, and so remained.

He was then seized by a grave illness, during which, rapt in the Spirit, he saw a great rushing river into which flowed the filth and every sort of impurity of all things needing purification. It swept away every article of the world that it could touch, together with men and women, old and young, poor and rich. When he felt compassion for those whom he heard were to be fed and given drink on such filth, his guide said: “Do not wonder, for [Col. 1017D] this torrent is clean, though it engulfs secular people.” The guide added: “Do you wish to see what a true monk is?” Willing, he was led into a cloister whose walls were covered with the purest silver; likewise, a silver meadow was clothed with green grasses of wonderful fragrance. Though the grasses bent softly beneath those resting upon them, when they rose the pressed grasses rose again. When Anselm was seized with desire to dwell there, the guide said: “Come, do you wish to see what true patience is?” As he asked this with immense longing, the guide disappeared, and Anselm returned to himself.

It is indeed probable that he was restored in this manner so that, in the tribulations which he was to suffer for the Lord, he might prove what true patience is. For thereafter he always more and more abhorred the world with its delights and embraced true monastic life more zealously and ardently. Thus people came to him from every side, even from distant regions, as to a fountain of religion, seeking fellowship, help, or counsel. Among them came a devout abbot. After speaking of many matters, he finally sought advice about the boys of his monastery.

“We make no progress,” he said, “though we beat them all day long; for they are wicked and incorrigible, always declining into worse things.”

“And what sort of men do they become when grown?” Anselm asked.

“Dull and beastly,” said the abbot.

“You have made laudable progress indeed,” said Anselm, “you who have deformed a human being, the image of God, into a beast! Do you not know that a plant which from the beginning is hemmed in on all sides by harder obstacles never grows into the height of branches? It neither sends down deep roots nor raises branches unless it possesses some freedom. Moisture must temper heat, if the shoots of seeds are to grow together; otherwise the latter consumes and the former dissolves.
