[Col. 1018A] “If you wish to shape a beautiful image from silver, you need not only a hammer and an anvil, but also a sculptor’s chisel, a chasing hammer, and other instruments by which the work of craftsmanship is done. It is not accomplished by cutting alone. Who introduces little children to solid food after withdrawing milk? That would be to strangle, not to feed. How can someone who begins with what is perfect make progress? Wax that is too hard does not receive the image of a seal; wax too soft and fluid does not retain it. Speak to one hardened excessively by worldly life about the subtleties of spiritual matters, and because of his hardness he does not receive your discourse. A little child does not understand what you say. Middle age, since it is tempered from these two, can do both. So adolescence, if it has a skilled craftsman, is easily formed and faithfully retains the image of instruction.

“Therefore one labours more usefully with such persons if, according to the Apostle, they are prepared with milk for solid food and proceed by appropriate stages in each case” (Heb. 5). [Col. 1018B] “But you demand from them that they rejoice in tribulations, love their persecutors, and do similar things which are assigned as the marks of the perfect. As charity casts out fear, so disordered fear casts out charity. The result is that they nourish crooked and thorny thoughts: suspicious, complaining, murmuring, envious, ambitious, faithless; and, since they have experienced no charity from their superiors, they return none to them or to others. And as they grow in the discord of the members within the body, vices increase by the same growth in the mind. Would you wish this to happen to yourselves? Your justice, not to put it otherwise, is openly evident.”

For he was accustomed to support his case with well-tested habits and common examples, and to communicate in a way intended not to make himself appear knowledgeable and eloquent, but to enable his hearers to make progress. He also gave great care to their education whenever he held any office, because their formation can either benefit or harm all those subject to them. On hearing this, the abbot groaned and openly confessed that he had strayed from the way of truth.

[Col. 1019A] Meanwhile Abbot Herlewin was worn down by grave illness, and entrusted the administration to Anselm. Horses and other things necessary for travellers were prepared especially for Anselm’s own use. But, hearing the word “private property,” he was alarmed and ordered that everything be shared with his companions. He wanted nothing to be called his own, but wished that these things should be common to himself and the brethren. Hence he rejected everything offered to him in this manner, even things procured by the devotion of those who came for the purpose of knowing the man.

One day, as he was turning toward his bed in the dormitory, he found a gold ring, whose owner and origin remain unknown. Yet it was believed to be a sign of his future episcopate. The devil, however, envied the salvation of many which the servant of God was bringing about. [Col. 1019B] As people flocked to him from every side, the devil laid his snares. To pass over others for the present, a certain knight named Cadulus, moved by devotion, was offering his whole self to the Lord in prayer when, outside the church, he heard what seemed to be the voice of his squire miserably lamenting that robbers were carrying off his horses and all he possessed. The knight nevertheless persisted in prayer, valuing devotion more highly than the loss of property.

The enemy, grieved at the steadfastness of the devout knight, took the shape of a bear and fell before him from the roof, hoping through the horror of the fall and the terrifying form to interrupt him as he prayed. But he persevered and fearlessly mocked the monster. At last, when he left the church, he heard as he walked a voice clearly saying to him: “Cadulus, where are you going? Where are you going, Cadulus? Why are you going to the hypocritical prior? In his customary fashion he will strip you of your goods and hurl you into the fountain of error. Then indeed you will repent. For his reputation differs greatly from his conduct.”

Hearing the voice but seeing no one, Cadulus fortified himself with the sign of the cross and prayers, came to Anselm, and at his counsel assumed the monastic habit at Marmoutier in the district of Tours. Anselm was accustomed to send each person to that place which, by the Lord’s inspiration, he had chosen beforehand. For those who move elsewhere are often accompanied by repentance.

## Chapter VI. Herlewin, abbot of Bec, dies. Anselm succeeds him as abbot of the monastery of Bec. Archbishop Lanfranc’s doubt whether Saint Ælfheah is a martyr or not. A question put to Anselm, abbot of Bec. Anselm’s answer to Lanfranc’s question on this matter.

[Col. 1019D]

As Abbot Herlewin died, Anselm succeeded him, unwilling and resisting, yet compelled by the brethren, and especially pressed by the command which Archbishop Maurilius of Rouen had imposed upon him. To be freer for prayer, reading, and the ministry of the word, he delegated lawsuits and external business to brethren qualified for this purpose. He commanded them always to choose to suffer fraud rather than commit it, and, as far as possible without excessive loss, to avoid disputes altogether. Litigation is scarcely, if ever, conducted without loss to charity.

When he was compelled to appear in legal matters, he spoke very rarely except about conduct or the word of life; often, disregarding the crafty twists of accusations, he fell asleep. [Col. 1020A] But when he awoke, he exposed the plots they had contrived as though he had received them from persons confessing them, or had in the meantime read them in the records. He showed such humility to guests that he often stripped the refectory bare for their sake. He had conceived such hope in God’s mercy that he never appeared to think about tomorrow. In accordance with his faith, it also came about that the monastery always abounded in every necessity. Like another Nicholas, jewel of priests, he so overflowed with tender mercy toward the poor that he seemed in some way to know this one thing alone: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6).

When he had crossed to England both on account of the monastery’s possessions and, above all, to see Archbishop Lanfranc, after many conversations on various subjects, Lanfranc at length spoke concerning blessed Ælfheah. “The English,” he said, “among whom we live, have established for themselves certain saints whose merits are uncertain. One of these rests in our church—Ælfheah, namely, our predecessor. He was certainly a good man, whom they venerate not only as a saint but also as a martyr. But when I examine his case, [Col. 1020B] I find that he was stoned by pagans and finally, after many injuries, insults, and beatings, killed with a sword because he refused to extort from his people the money demanded for ransoming his body. Since it is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr, I wish to hear your judgment whether they ought to be restrained or followed.”

For Lanfranc, as a recent inhabitant of England, did not yet fully know the history. Ælfheah had in fact suffered for Christ. Anselm, however, replied to what he had heard: “He seems an outstanding martyr, since he preferred to die rather than inflict injury, especially upon those whom he was bound to protect. And plainly, one who so greatly abhorred what appears a small matter would stand most faithfully if summoned to the confession of Christ. For one who avoids small things does not readily admit serious ones. Thus John suffered for truth, and thus Ælfheah for justice; each seems to me an eminent martyr. For both suffered for Christ, who is, just as he is truth, also justice.” [Col. 1020C]

Lanfranc assented, had the history read, and ordered the martyr’s feast to be solemnly celebrated every year.

Anselm, moreover, not only visited churches and holy places; invited and drawn here and there, he also went through cities, castles, and the houses of nobles, and, as a true follower in the footsteps of the Apostles, dispensed the word of faith and salvation to all. He became all things to all in order to gain all; indeed, he was even as one without law to those without law, though he devoted himself unceasingly and with all zeal to the law of Christ. Thus no one dreaded him; everyone venerated him; very many followed him. Every age, vocation, and rank heard him teaching profitably and acknowledged Anselm.

Even the king who had subdued the English, though feared by all, was subject to him. [Col. 1021A] For the Lord confirmed his word by the signs that followed. He healed the sick; and, nature yielding to the Creator, it is established that he healed a leper. A nobleman on the border of Flanders and Ponthieu, suffering from this disease, was instructed in a vision to drink water in which Anselm, abbot of Bec, had washed his hands while celebrating Mass. This was done, and he was immediately restored. Another member of the community at Bec was cured of a severe illness after being sprinkled with water that Anselm had purified. He had been instructed to do so in dreams while labouring almost at the point of death.

About these same days a man praiseworthy for learning and honourable conduct, named Boso, was joined by Anselm to the community of monks. But in a short time he was so tempted that, distracted by thoughts, [Col. 1021B] he had no rest at all. At last, after several days, he told Anselm what he was suffering. With the compassionate affection of one who pitied him, Anselm said: “May God provide for you.” From then on the entire temptation of his mind departed.

It would take too long to relate how many sick people he cured, especially those with fevers, whether by laying on hands, water from the washing of his hands, or blessed bread. For it is famously and truly reported that very many sick people recovered through remnants from his table.

## Chapter VII. Concerning the glorious King William I: he departs this world; his son William Rufus succeeds to the kingdom of England, a man little just or pious. Anselm writes the book *On the Incarnation of the Word* in England.

When the glorious King William died, [Col. 1021C] his son William, surnamed Rufus, succeeded him: a man indeed vigorous in arms, but little just or pious; lavish with his own resources, greedy for those of others; passionately fond of hunting, yet extremely negligent of souls; a patron of soldiery and wickedness, yet a most vehement assailant of the Church and innocence; a most ardent follower of pleasure. For in him love of the world and contempt for God flourished alike without limit or measure. What above all dishonours a ruler, he had no reverence for his body and defiled himself with every impurity. Not only the nobles, but even the afflicted common people, as far as they could, followed their ruler, as generally happens. For it is well known that as the ruler of a city is, so are its inhabitants:

> The world is shaped  
> By the example of its king. Edicts cannot so bend  
> Human minds as does the life of the ruler.  
> —Claudian, *On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*, 298

[Col. 1021D] Therefore, while the Church suffered on every side, the persecution was all the more grievous because there was no one to stand in the breach for the house of the Lord. In the fourth year of this persecution, when the venerable Father Lanfranc had passed from this world to the Lord, Anselm entered England, invited by the nobles and compelled by the Church.

Arriving at Canterbury on the day before the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, he departed very early in the morning, because people everywhere were crying out prophetically that he would be archbishop. He then proceeded to court, where the king who came out to meet him received him honourably and warmly. After a few matters had been discussed together, Anselm advised that everyone be sent away. Setting aside private concerns, he undertook the care of public affairs; speaking alone with the king, he laid before him matters spoken of both privately and publicly, and confronted the king to his face. For he had brought no “oil of the sinner,” with which hirelings flatter the heads of erring rulers. They parted; and a few days later the king fell gravely ill. Touched by sickness and moved by the counsel of wise men, he agreed that Anselm should be promoted to the archbishopric, declaring him most worthy of the highest honour and an illustrious preacher of truth.

Thus Anselm was carried off unwillingly in the year of grace 1093, on the day before the Nones of March, the first Sunday in Lent. At the following solemnity of Easter, while he was at Winchester, [Col. 1022A] the city suddenly began to burn in a great fire. Since the fire already seemed to be encircling his lodging, friends advised the mistress of the house to carry away her belongings. But she replied that she was not afraid, but safe in the presence of so great a guest. She would not in any way consent to anything being removed. The venerable men Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, and Baldwin, Anselm’s steward, were moved and compelled him at least to see the fire and oppose to it the saving sign of the cross. A wondrous thing: he extended his hand, the flame was cast down, and the fire left the house it had invaded half-burned, as though it did not dare proceed against Anselm’s prohibition.

After long resisting the election, he was finally compelled to consent; and on the day before the Nones of December he was consecrated at Canterbury by all the bishops of England. The following sentence of the Gospel was found over him: “He called many and sent his servant at the hour of supper to tell those invited to come, because all things are now ready; and they all alike began to make excuses” (Luke 14).

Then, proceeding to court, he spent the three days of the feast of the Lord’s Nativity in celebration. From that time the king conceived the gravest anger against him because Anselm refused to pay him a thousand pounds of silver, having wished to be promoted to the archbishopric without payment, service, or any intervention. Departing from there, he came to his estate called Herga and there dedicated the parish church. Now a certain clerk, accompanied from London by the bishop’s attendants, secretly stole the chrismatory during the service and fled. [Col. 1022B] But by God’s ordering, he wandered and returned so often, wholly ignorant of a road previously most familiar, that he was convicted by this evident sign of his error, confessed his fault, restored the vessel, and thereafter followed without error the road leading to London.

A few days later Anselm was summoned back to court in order to strengthen the king, who was about to cross the sea, with his blessing. While the wind delayed the departure, Anselm urged the king to secure peace for the churches, kindly warning him not to allow the law of God to be trampled down by royal authority. Angered by this, the king ordered him to leave and forbade him to wait there any longer for the crossing. From that day onward the Church of God was more grievously shaken; possessions were diminished and taken away; people were troubled with lawsuits and expenses; and “the latter things became worse than the former day by day” (2 Pet. 2). For every guilty person wished that evils should be openly manifest. For they rejoiced, like Sodom, in the public display of their sin. Whoever offended Anselm seemed to have rendered the king a most welcome service.

He had no rest except when he perhaps immersed himself in the cloister. He confessed this with tears, using the following comparison: “Thus an owl rejoices with its young in a cave, but when it goes out, crows and jackdaws tear and rend it. Keep yourselves within as far as you can, my dearest sons. It is enough that secular business and tumult consume me as their owl.” [Col. 1023A] Indeed, even a great part of his household opposed him.

He was so weak in worldly affairs that whenever necessity required him to engage for some time in secular business, he either failed in spirit or fell into some grave sickness. He could not take part in financial accounts; rather, all care rested upon Baldwin, of whom mention has been made. Therefore, whenever it was permitted, he sought a more secluded place; and neither by day nor by night, nor even while dining, did he cease from holy conversation and prayer.

Meanwhile he wrote the book *On the Incarnation of the Word*, composed in epistolary style; the Roman pontiff approved it for the Church. Urban also employed arguments drawn from it against the Greeks at the Council of Bari.

## Chapter VIII. How Anselm approaches the king, humbly asking leave to go to Rome for the pallium necessary to exercise his office. Concerning the dispute and its cause between the king, the archbishop, and the bishops of England.

[Col. 1023C]

Anselm approached the king as he returned from overseas, humbly asking permission, as the needs of his office and ecclesiastical custom required, to go to Pope Urban for the pallium, without which he could not exercise the fullness of his office. But at Urban’s name the king swelled with anger, maintaining that in his kingdom no one ought to name an apostolic pope without his own choice. A day and place were appointed for the archbishop to answer for this audacity. The parties were present, and all acclaimed the king’s will. The bishops especially argued more cunningly that the pope ought not to be received in the kingdom of England unless the king’s election had preceded it. [Col. 1023D]

When Anselm, wishing to render to Caesar what was Caesar’s and preferring to obey God rather than men, restrained them by canonical and plainly divine arguments, they cried out with one voice that he had offended against royal majesty by placing his own laws before the king’s will. For the wretches dared attribute nothing even to God unless the king had been consulted. Therefore, at a single word from the king, some renounced all obedience to their archbishop and forswore communion in brotherly fellowship; others did so in those matters which he might command on behalf of Urban, the Roman pontiff. All, except the bishop of Rochester alone, dissolved the bond of obedience and the faith of the promise they had made. Moreover, the king, taking away all security from the archbishop and his people, openly declared [Col. 1024A] his hostility unless Anselm publicly professed that thereafter he would not obey the Roman pontiff.

But Anselm, persevering in faith, asked the king for safe-conduct and permission to depart. At last, through the intervention of the nobles, he obtained a truce of some months, and the king promised peace to him and his followers in the meantime. Yet he soon departed from his pledged word: he expelled Baldwin from the kingdom and grievously harassed the archbishop in his men and lands. Meanwhile Lord Walter, bishop of Albano, bringing the archbishop’s pallium, arranged concord between the king and the pope; and he brought it about that Anselm was received into the king’s favor, at least outwardly. A little later, after the king had triumphed over the Welsh, he sought pretexts and began to renew the quarrels which had been put to sleep with the archbishop. [Col. 1024B] For he was excessively insolent and almost intolerable in matters of succession. Anselm returned and again requested permission to go to the lord pope. The king ordered him to abandon what he had undertaken, saying that the cause of this journey was either nonexistent or empty. For, he said, Anselm’s prudence had no need of counsel, nor his purity of absolution.

As the archbishop returned to his estate called Hersa, a hare pursued by dogs sought refuge beneath the feet of the horse upon which God’s servant was riding. The Father halted, and the pursuing dogs did not dare approach more closely. All marvelled and were astonished. The man of God pitied the unhappy little creature, saying that this represented the soul of a sinner departing from the body. Then, speaking aloud, he commanded the hare to go away, [Col. 1024C] and by the authority of his word alone restrained the dogs.

On another occasion, seeing a little bird with its foot caught in a thread, while a boy holding the thread alternately pulled the bird back and let it go, he wished that the bird might be freed when the thread broke. The wish was immediately fulfilled, and the boy wept as the bird flew away. Anselm rejoiced, rejoicing with the bird, and added that the devil likewise weeps when those whom he held entangled in the snare of sin escape. For he was accustomed to turn almost everything that he heard or saw toward the instruction of life.

Again summoned by the king, Anselm repeated for the third time, among other requests, his petition for leave. The king was disturbed and complained that he was being excessively troubled. In his rage he ordered through messengers that Anselm should immediately leave the kingdom without hope of return, or else abandon his undertaking and swear [Col. 1024D] never to appeal to blessed Peter or the Apostolic See in any matter whatsoever. He added that, should Anselm wish to remain, he must submit to the judgment of the court which he had sought from the king and in which he had not persevered.

To this Anselm replied: “The Lord is he: he says what he wills. But I go where necessity draws me. I must carry out that which I have professed and obey the commands of him whose ministry I bear.” The court was agitated by this, declared Anselm guilty of treason against majesty, uttered insults, and applauded its own resolution. But he patiently endured the council’s indignation, rejoicing that he too had been found worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). He entered the king’s presence with a calm face, offering him [Col. 1025A] his blessing before his departure, if the king did not reject it. When the king, quieting himself, replied that he did not reject it, the archbishop blessed his persecutor sincerely and departed. Those who feared God accompanied Anselm with affection and prayers and helped him, so far as they could, by petitions and commendations. But the king persisted in his savagery, so that God seemed justly to have departed from him.

## Chapter IX. Anselm is sent into exile. Coming to Canterbury, he explains to the community of the Church of the Saviour at Canterbury the reason for his journey; before Christ’s high altar, taking staff and wallet, he commends himself, with a blessing, to God and to the prayers of the faithful. The Roman pontiff’s commendation of Anselm.

[Col. 1025B]

The archbishop then came to Canterbury. First from his brethren, then from the holy places and from all the clergy and people, he received leave, having publicly explained the reason for his journey. Therefore, taking before Christ’s altar the wallet and staff customary for pilgrims, and commending his pilgrimage to God and to the prayers of the faithful, he set out for Dover, while nearly all followed him with inconsolable groaning and tears. There he found a certain clerk named William of Warewast, whom the king had sent to Anselm without God.

For fifteen days this man remained at Anselm’s table, as a member of the household, entering and leaving everywhere and in all circumstances; nor did he disclose to anyone the purpose for which he had been sent. But when the sailors urged them [Col. 1025C] to board the ship and the baggage was being brought out, behold, the same William, to the amazement and indignation of all, detained the archbishop on the shore as though he were a fugitive and guilty of some crime. He opened the bags and packs and, as an anxious investigator, carefully searched what the entire equipment contained. But the seeker’s diligence was disappointed, for no money was found. Then, when Anselm was at last allowed to depart, the surrounding multitude followed him with prayers and tears and hurled bitter reproaches and curses at the returning messenger.

The pilgrims had scarcely travelled some distance over the sea when, behold, the wind changed. At first the sailors murmured; then they openly declared and cried out that all must either die [Col. 1025D] or return. Hearing this, Anselm, filled with tears, groaned. Resorting to his customary aid of prayer, he said: “May God dispose of me, may the Lord dispose of me, as he wills, and thrust me back into my former miseries; or may he permit and cause me to proceed into his service, as I have purposed at his own inspiration. For I am not my own, but his.”

When he had spoken these words, one might at once have recognized the vicar of him who commands the winds and the sea: a favorable wind arose, and with immense joy it most swiftly carried the passengers to the desired shore. When the ship that had carried the archbishop was unloaded, a marvelous thing appeared: in one plank a hole nearly two feet wide was discovered; yet it had admitted no liquid element at all while the holy man [Col. 1026A] remained aboard. When the king heard of the archbishop’s crossing, the savage man ordered all his possessions confiscated and declared void everything Anselm had done.

But Anselm rejoiced at the exile imposed on him. He recognized it also as a pledge of future blessedness, because the Lord deemed him worthy to suffer for justice. He sympathized with the afflictions of the churches and the lot of his people; whoever faithfully remembers that tempest can scarcely recount their calamities without tears. Yet the faithful God, who does not forsake those who hope in him, accompanied the exile of his servant suffering for his sake, so that wherever among nations or places he came, he was received humanely, honored kindly, treated with respect, and heard by all because of the reverence due to him.

[Col. 1026B] For there shone in the very countenance of the man a certain grace of divine sweetness, so that he was loved by all; and the venerable gray hair of an old man fearing the Lord inspired in those who looked upon him both reverence and fear. Men of every age and sex, wherever report had announced his arrival, came out to meet him in crowds, that they might deserve to receive his holy blessing. Those who had deserved to see nothing of him in passing considered themselves fortunate. His words, seasoned with God, were pleasing to hearers and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to those who feared God (Psalm 18). The more he was honored, the more carefully he preserved the virtue of humility; and, as a true disciple of Christ, though greatest of all, he behaved among his companions as the younger, and as one who presides as a servant.

[Col. 1026C] Proceeding as far as Lyons, he waited there for the messengers whom he had sent to Rome, being prevented from travelling by bodily weakness and certain other causes. On their return, summoned by the Roman pontiff, he came to the Lateran and was received with the highest honor. The Roman Church gave him thanks; and the Roman pontiff himself, in the presence of the whole court and the noble peoples who had gathered because of so great an exile, delivered a long address. Among other things he said:

> “Although we ought to hold this man as a master, being most expert in all the liberal disciplines and trained and practised in religion, and though he ought rightly to be reverenced as an apostolic man and patriarch, as it were, of another world; yet such sincere faith and such outstanding humility preside in his mind that he has judged us, who stand more in need of his counsel, to be consulted by him, and that neither perils of land nor sea could deter him from reverence for blessed Peter, whom he has sought.”

These and other things were said by the Roman pontiff. But to all of them Anselm opposed his silence, through caution and divine fear. When the reason for his coming had been set forth, the Church marvelled and was astonished, promising the fullest assistance. Ordered to remain, he withdrew to the mountains, fleeing the unhealthiness of the Roman air. He was received with honor by the venerable John, formerly a monk of Bec and then abbot of Saint Saviour at Telese, and was conducted to an estate called Sclavia.

## Chapter X. Anselm completes in the province of Capua the work *Why God Became Man*. On the scarcity of water. On the well of water. On the duke of Apulia. On the count of Sicily, and friendship with Pope Urban. On the Council of Bari. On the confusion of the Greeks and their heresies. Anselm is called “the Holy Man” by the men of Rome. On the investitures of churches. On the council held at Rome.

[Col. 1027A]

Living there, on the summit of the mountain where the estate stood, delighted by the healthfulness of the air and by a kind of solitude, he said: “This is my resting-place; here will I dwell.” Giving himself to God and to himself, he completed there, in the province of Capua, the notable work which he had begun in England, entitled *Why God Became Man* (*Cur Deus homo*).

The inhabitants of the village suffered from lack of water, since springs, wells, and cisterns were almost wholly [Col. 1027B] lacking to them. A single well on the mountain’s slope gave them scant aid, for every day before the ninth hour it was so drained that it supplied no moisture until the following day. The monk who was in charge there, having learned from evident signs the holiness of his guest, explained the inconvenience and asked for help. He said that water must be sought on the mountain’s summit, though this seemed utter folly. Anselm praised the pious desire. He was therefore asked to choose the spot, first open the earth, and pray the Lord for living water. Like another Clement, he complied with his host’s request; and shortly an abundant vein of wholesome, ever-flowing water was found. For, as the inhabitants report, [Col. 1027C] sick persons are cured of adverse illnesses by drinking the water; and to this day that well, most abundant and of very little depth, is called the well of the archbishop of Canterbury.

In those days Roger, duke of Apulia, while besieging Capua, summoned the man of God to himself. Receiving him with the highest honor, he arranged suitable accommodation for him in a certain chapel, so that he might not suffer disturbance from the army at a distance, while the duke could have him near at hand very often each day. One night, when the others were resting, Anselm went out and fell into an old cistern of great depth. As he fell, he cried, “Holy Mary!” His companions ran up and saw the Father almost lifeless in the depths; but he made a sign indicating that he had suffered no injury, and [Col. 1027D] he was brought out wholly unharmed.

Urban, the Roman pontiff, came there; and in the city where they lodged they were so closely associated that almost everyone who approached Urban turned aside to Anselm. For majesty gave the former what holiness gave the latter: reverence. Even the pagans serving the duke in the same army showed greater deference to Anselm, wishing him prosperity and praying for him. Very many of them would have come to the faith through him, had not fear of the duke and count of Sicily restrained them. For they were not permitted to come to the faith.

When the siege had been lifted, the Council of Bari was held, where Anselm refuted the Greeks by Catholic reasoning and taught that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. From there he returned to Rome with the apostolic pontiff. At the pontiff’s command, he received Englishmen coming to Rome at his foot, in the manner of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 1028A] Anselm’s humility indeed rejected this, until the pope ordered him to moderate his humility in such a way that he would not hinder the devotion of anyone wishing to do good.

Moreover, the nobler citizens of Rome once laid snares for Anselm because of their loyalty to the emperor, who was persecuting the Church; they saw that Urban received very great authority from Anselm’s presence. Yet, that it might be clear that he was the anointed of the Lord and a true disciple of Christ, as soon as they saw him they cast down their arms and fell to the ground; and those who had come to do evil sought the gift of his holy blessing. His religious authority became so great throughout the whole city that he was called not “archbishop” nor “primate,” but “the Holy [Col. 1028B] Man” (*sanctus homo*) by antonomasia—that is, pre-eminently, as though it were his proper name.

Meanwhile, a council was held at Rome. Among its other decrees, it established that the sentence of excommunication should strike laymen who confer the investitures of churches, and those who receive them from the hand of laymen; the same sentence also struck those who presume to consecrate anyone to an office of honor thus obtained.

## Chapter XI. Archbishop Anselm comes to Lyons and is honorably received by the venerable Archbishop Hugh. King William of England sends messengers to Rome. Pope Urban postpones the case between the archbishop and the king. On the death of Pope Urban. Anselm is received by Guy, archbishop of Vienne. On two knights who petitioned him. On the crumbs from Anselm’s table. On the first, second, and third visions of the death of William, king of the English.

[Col. 1028C]

Anselm then returned to Lyons and was received by the venerable Hugh, bishop of the foremost see of Gaul, so that he was regarded as the lord of the place. Indeed, the archbishop and his fellow provincials deferred to him in all things as though they were suffragans of the Church of Canterbury. And truly, in those days the Church of Canterbury found more faith among strangers than among its own people. For sons persecuted their father, and a man’s household were his enemies.

By the counsel of his own people, that William mentioned at Anselm’s departure from England had been sent by the impious king to Rome while Anselm was still there. Among other things, William obtained from Urban a postponement of Anselm’s case [Col. 1028D] from the Easter solemnity until the feast day of Saint Michael. The archbishop therefore believed that, while the king lived, the way back to England was closed to him. But the guardian of Israel, who does not sleep, whatever human recklessness might dream, meanwhile executes the decision of his eternal counsel. He removed from human affairs Urban, who had postponed the cause of the man of God at the tyrant’s request, so that Urban did not see the appointed day. Yet Anselm prospered in exile; and God making him illustrious, he was celebrated by all not only in the Lyonnais but also in the neighboring provinces.

At the request of Guy, archbishop of noble Vienne, described as the greatest city of Gaul, he celebrated the feast of blessed Maurice, which was solemnly observed there because of the presence of Maurice’s head. [Col. 1029A] When the divine offices had been completed and they had sat down for bodily refreshment, two knights stood before him, with trembling voices and pale faces, weak and almost withered in their limbs. They begged him to deign to give them something from the crumbs of his bread. But he said: “As I see, you need not so much crumbs as solid bread. Food is plentiful and the place is spacious. Go, sit down with a blessing, and eat as much as you wish.” He added: “I shall do nothing else for you,” understanding their intention.

For he avoided doing anything that might be attributed to miracle, since he sought not his own glory but God’s, seeking in all things not what was his own but what belonged to Jesus Christ. Yet one seated at the right of the holy man, seeing their purpose and seeming overcome by the petitioners’ importunity, [Col. 1029B] took scraps and gave them to the petitioners, warning them to go away quickly lest they tire the man any longer. They tasted them and departed with the blessing of the man of God, immediately restored to health from quartan fevers, as became known from their own words.

A nobleman of that land, long afflicted by the same sickness, was brought in his servants’ arms into the Church of Saint Stephen, where Anselm was going to celebrate the divine mysteries. He heard Mass and went out well. A few days later he gave thanks to the Father, maintaining that he had been cured of quartan fevers by Anselm’s blessing. He also received counsels for salvation from him; instructed by these, he lived more worthily before God, more agreeably in the world, and more profitably for himself, as the conscience of many testified.

[Col. 1029C] At about this time, as Anselm was going to Cluny, a certain priest met him and asked that he would deign to look upon and bless his sister, who had become insane. But Anselm passed on as though deaf. The priest persisted, and the crowd gathering from every side persisted; he replied that God ought not to be tested in such matters. Yet he was not allowed to depart until, raising his right hand, he marked her with the sign of the saving cross. Having done this, he fled swiftly and, drawing his cowl over his head, wept for the afflictions of the unhappy woman. Before she had returned to the threshold of her house, she had been granted complete health, and in praise of the man of God the tongues of all were loosed.

Returning thence to Lyons, he passed through Mâcon. At the request of the bishop and clergy, while celebrating a solemn Mass in the Church of Saint Vincent, he publicly exhorted [Col. 1029D] the people to obtain by prayers from the Lord the rain of which the world stood in need. They replied that they had often done this and had often been disappointed, praying that by his prayer he would advance their necessities and petitions. The divine offices were celebrated, and through the ministry of their priests the people offered their prayers to the Lord. Without delay, rains came according to the desires of each and all; and the whole city poured itself out in praises of the holy man. Having arrived at Lyons, he wrote one book, *On the Virginal Conception and Original Sin*, and another entitled *Meditation on Human Redemption*.

While these things were taking place, Pope Urban died before the Kalends of August, and Anselm was exposed to God’s judgment alone. Though he suffered much and seemed greatly pressed by straits in his household [Col. 1030A] resources, nevertheless a joyful mind and episcopal authority flourished in him, because the origin of his words and works—he who in the beginning was the Word (John 1)—neither failed nor forsook him. Many things concerning the destruction of the impious king were also foretold by many, which became known as vengeance for Anselm through both evident signs and manifest visions. But he did not fix his mind on these things; daily he prayed to the Lord for the tyrant’s conversion and salvation.

In the third year of his exile, after a conference with blessed Hugh of Cluny at Martiniacum, mention happened to be made of the king of the English. The abbot, with religious assurance and publicly before many hearers, declared that he had seen, in a former vision, the same king accused before the throne [Col. 1030B] of God and receiving sentence of condemnation. The hearers marvelled; but considering the eminence of the speaker, they could not withhold belief from his words.

The next day he came to Lyons. On the Kalends of August, while all were asleep, behold, a young man of handsome appearance and venerable countenance appeared to a cleric lying before the chamber door, who still seemed to himself to be awake. Calling him by name, he said, “Adam, are you asleep?” He replied, “No.” The youth added, “Do you wish to hear news?” Adam said, “Gladly.” And he said: “Know for certain that the controversy which was being carried on between Archbishop Anselm and William, king of England, has been entirely decided.” At this, Adam lifted up his eyes and saw no one.

On the following night another man, standing with closed eyes during the morning vigils, was chanting psalms; and behold, someone showed him a small document on which was written: “King William has died.” Opening his eyes, he saw no one but his companions. The Lord had then indeed terribly executed his judgment upon the impious king; and he who had lived like a beast found a beastly end to life. Anselm was grieved; and, as Samuel mourned Saul cast down by the Lord, so, mourning and anxious, he lamented that this man had provoked the Lord’s anger against himself. For he would rather himself be in the body in the Lord’s favor than that the king should be dead in such a manner.

## Chapter XII. Anselm rests at the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu during his first exile. On lightning and thunderbolt. On the death of King William II. On King Henry. On the case argued before Pope Paschal. On the liberty of Christ’s Church of Canterbury.

[Col. 1030D]

Then, after three days, having been honorably invited and received at the venerable place called La Chaise-Dieu, he rested at night. Frequent flashes of lightning darted over the mountain during a storm, and a tremendous thunderbolt, with horrible terror, poured a great quantity of fire upon the building in which the monastery’s hay was stored. The neighboring structures caught fire; horror and noise, foul-smelling smoke, and bright flame terrified everyone and scattered them in different directions. Hearing that the blaze had gained strength, Father Anselm said: “Let us provide for you,

> For your own concern is at stake when the neighboring wall is on fire.”

(Horace, *Epistles* I.18.84.)

He hastened out to the fire and made upon it the sign [Col. 1031A] of the life-giving cross. The fire therefore collapsed and left the houses which it had invaded weakened; and, what is more marvelous, though some surrounding buildings were consumed, it caused no harm to the monks’ hay, since they had the man of God as their guest.

Without delay, upon returning to Lyons he received messengers from England announcing the king’s death and how the hand of the Lord had wrought that glorious vengeance for his Church. For on the second day of August, which dawned after the vision at Lyons, the same king went out early in the morning to hunt in the forest which the inhabitants call the New Forest. There, receiving an arrow in his side and wounded in the heart, he gave up his spirit.

Thus, thus, while Basil suffered, Julian was slain by a fatal weapon to the consolation of the Church; and when another Julian had been slain [Col. 1031B] in England, Anselm was recalled to the consolation of the Church. Who fired either arrow is indeed still uncertain. For Walter Tirel, who was said by very many to be guilty of the king’s killing, because he was familiar with him, was near him in the hunt, and was almost constantly at his side—even when the king lay dying—declared under invocation of God’s judgment upon his soul that he was innocent of the killing. Very many asserted that the king himself had shot the arrow by which he was killed; and Walter himself constantly asserted this, though he was not believed. And truly, whoever did this faithfully obeyed the providence of God, who sympathized with the calamities of his Church.

[Col. 1031C] First of all, the monks of Canterbury hastened to the Father with every speed. Then the messengers of great men, outstripping one another, expressed the devotion of the entire island. Moreover, the illustrious king of the English, Henry, who had succeeded his brother, earnestly arranged the return of the archbishop whom he had recalled. He promised that he himself and all the affairs of the kingdom would depend upon Anselm’s counsel. For at the beginning of his reign he sought to be regarded as pious and gentle, after the manner of rulers, who are gentle until their power is secured. Indeed, the lot of kingdoms is most mild under a new king.

But when Anselm had explained to the new king at Salisbury what had been done in the Roman council, the king was disturbed, and all things were changed to the contrary. How many and how great things Anselm suffered for the liberty of the churches during two [Col. 1031D] years would take too long to recount. When King Henry saw Anselm’s unconquered constancy, he asked him to go to Rome with his messengers and seek a remedy for the injury done to royal dignity in England. All the bishops, abbots, and nobles of England cried out that this could not lawfully be denied the king. To this Archbishop Anselm said: “I shall indeed go, since you wish it; but the Roman Church of God will do nothing at my counsel or prayer which prejudices the liberty of the churches, or which diminishes the majesty of the Apostolic See or the dignity proper to me.”

When the messengers came to Rome with the archbishop, they were kindly received by Lord Pope Paschal, Urban’s successor. In due course William, mentioned above, stated the king’s case and among other things asserted [Col. 1032A] that the king would not allow the investitures of churches to be taken from him, even at the loss of his kingdom. Pope Paschal replied: “If your king will not permit the donations of churches to be taken from him even at the loss of his kingdom, know this and faithfully report it to him: behold, I speak before God, that Paschal will not allow him to hold them unpunished even for the redemption of his own head.” The king’s case then stopped at those limits.

How greatly Paschal honored and aided Anselm in his time is clear from many things. He confirmed for him the primacy of Britain which his predecessors had held from the time of blessed Augustine. He also personally granted him the privilege that, for as long as he lived, he should be exempt from the jurisdiction of all legates. Moreover, after hearing the case, Paschal compelled Gerard of York, who refused to make a profession to Anselm, [Col. 1032B] to profess, although on one occasion, having been circumvented, he wrote the contrary. For Paschal followed the settlement of the case, solemnly made and reduced to writing in Lanfranc’s time by the Roman pontiff Alexander. His letters, still extant with their seals in the Church of Canterbury, testify to this. In short: we do not recall that Pope Paschal ever rejected Anselm’s petitions or deferred the requests made known to him.

## Chapter XIII. Anselm and his companions spend one night at Florence. On a certain man who lay in Saint Anselm’s bed and what happened to him. On Saint Anselm archbishop’s prohibition from entering the kingdom of England in the time of Henry I. On a certain blind man healed by Saint Anselm during the second exile. On the peace made between Henry, king of England, and Anselm.

[Col. 1032C]

On their return they came to Florence and spent one night there. After they departed, the master of the house lay down as usual in the bed in which Anselm had slept. While he slept, an unknown man appeared and warned him to rise from it quickly. He added that he was unworthy to occupy a bed in which so great a guest had rested. When he disregarded this, the vision was repeated on the second night more threateningly and terribly. Though the man was moved, he still did not yield; on the third night he was told to rise quickly and restrain himself from this, for he would discover that what he saw was not imaginary. Terrified by the dream, he went in the morning to the bishop of the city, and, having heard from him about Anselm’s holiness, thereafter kept the bed with every reverence. [Col. 1032D]

As they approached Lyons, the often-mentioned William, who was about to depart from the archbishop, prohibited him on behalf of the king of England from entering England unless, setting aside obedience to the Apostolic See, he promised faithfully to observe all the customs of both kings William. The archbishop marvelled, because he had left on different terms. He remained at Lyons, and King Henry ordered all his possessions confiscated when William returned.

Meanwhile a certain blind man came to Anselm in the oratory and obtained permission for him to trace the sign of the cross over his eyes with his thumb. He did this three times, saying: “May the power of Christ’s cross enlighten these eyes, drive every infirmity from them, and restore them to complete health.” When he had sprinkled them with [Col. 1033A] consecrated water, they were enlightened. The king’s anger continued for a year and a half.

Because certain ecclesiastical affairs required it, the man of God came into France. At King Henry’s request, he proceeded into Normandy and at last received from the king investiture of his possessions. When the king crossed into England, shortly afterwards that William, the royal messenger who had so often troubled the archbishop, returned to Bec. On the king’s behalf he earnestly begged him, since all former complaints had been entirely silenced, quickly to visit England. The bishop rejoiced in the liberty of the churches, which God’s mercy had now wrested from kings, and set out. He reached Jumièges, where adverse illness prevented him from proceeding; brought almost to his last extremity through failure of his natural powers, he caused all his companions [Col. 1033B] to despair, and swift, certain death seemed to stand at the doors.

Meanwhile the Father was urged, if only through love for his sons, to do violence to nature and allow some food to be given him. But, his speech failing and his breath labored, he confessed that he desired nothing at all and could not even take it. Bishops and abbots gathered from every side, that they might observe the passing of that blessed spirit and accompany his migration to heaven with psalms and hymns.

But a certain man more familiar with him—one of the monastery servants—was walking through the forest, thinking of none of this, when he saw a little animal called a marten carrying a partridge in its mouth. He cried out, and the fleeing animal dropped the partridge. When it was brought, the sick man tasted it and, recovering beyond expectation, became an object of wonder and brought joy to all. [Col. 1033C]

After those who had gathered had departed, one of the servants of Ralph of Sées began to speak much evil of him, asserting that he did not deserve pity, since he might have helped himself by taking nourishment had he given up his vainglorious pretension. The abbot enjoined silence upon his rashness, and the company of brethren rebuked him gently. But he, all the more zealously in the manner of fools who do not admit words of wisdom, did not cease to attack God’s saint.

Hastening on his journey as he spoke these words, he violently struck against a leafy oak in the forest through which the road passed. Falling from his horse, with one foot caught more firmly in the stirrup, and the horse terrified, he was dragged and shaken back and forth for so long that he seemed almost [Col. 1033D] to have breathed his last. At length, when his companions invoked the blessed Virgin, the horse was caught; and the miserable man, scarcely breathing, was taught to spare the friends of God, since it is great rashness even to pronounce judgment upon another’s servant.

## Chapter XIV. Henry, king of England, visited Archbishop Anselm amicably at the monastery of Bec on the day of the Assumption of Blessed Mary. On a clerk afflicted by mental derangement. On the war between Henry, king of England, and his brother Robert, count of Normandy. Anselm wrote in England the little work *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge, Predestination, and the Grace of God with Free Choice*. On Thomas, elected to York.

King Henry returned to Normandy; and on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary he paid a friendly visit to the archbishop at the monastery of Bec. At about that time Anselm, at the request of the abbot and with the favour of the archbishop of Rouen, dedicated the chapel of the court [Col. 1034A]; and at the very dedication, by his blessing alone, he restored to former health a cleric afflicted with mental derangement. He who, an exile for God’s sake and subjected to insults, had long gone about foreign sees, thereafter—as was just, God triumphing over men—returned to his own with honour and glory. There an Englishman, noble and wealthy, struck down by a severe bodily illness, sought through messengers a blessed loaf from him and received it; and, according to his faith, was healed.

Meanwhile the king, dwelling in Normandy, rejoiced in the peace; and he could no longer conceal his confidence that the Lord had thereby been reconciled to him, because he had received Anselm, His friend, into true and firm friendship. Hence he promised himself the whole of Normandy within a short time [Col. 1034B], and not without reason. For in a formal pitched battle he defeated and captured his brother and his brother’s supporters. Having won this victory, he communicated it to Anselm by letter, attributing it to the merits of the concord and peace restored between them.

When, moreover, on the Kalends of August [1 August] the king and archbishop had met, the Church’s triumph was evident to all: the king publicly relinquished investiture of churches and granted this concession to the archbishop, claiming in elections nothing except assent, such as the sacred canons do not exclude. For, claiming for himself neither the right to elect nor to invest with the pastoral staff according to ancient custom, he allowed canonical rulings to proceed in the ordering of churches.

Meanwhile the servant of God wrote one small work, *On the Harmony of God’s Foreknowledge, Predestination, and Grace with Free Choice* [Col. 1034C]. Contrary to his habit, he delayed over it because he had become physically infirm, so that thereafter he was always carried from place to place not on horseback but in a litter.

Since, then, his end was approaching, disputes between the Churches of Canterbury and York, which had ceased, began again to press forward. Thomas the Younger of York had already been elected and, at Anselm’s command, ordained priest by William, bishop of Winchester. But Anselm, though physically ill to the uttermost, was nevertheless clothed with strength from on high. He commanded every bishop throughout England, by virtue of obedience, not to communicate with Thomas until Thomas should abandon the rebellion he had begun. He further ordered that letters patent containing this command [Col. 1034D], duly sealed, be kept with the greatest care in every episcopal see. At this critical point he also sent Thomas a letter in these words:

## CHAPTER XV. Letter of Saint Anselm, lying sick in his bed, to Thomas, archbishop-elect of York, concerning the jurisdiction of Christ Church, Canterbury

> ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to THOMAS, archbishop-elect of York.
>
> To you, Thomas, in the sight of almighty God, I, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, speak, speaking on God’s own behalf. I forbid you the priestly office which, by my command, you received in my diocese through my suffragan; and I command that you by no means presume to involve yourself in any pastoral charge [Col. 1035A] until you withdraw from the rebellion which you have begun against the Church of Canterbury and profess submission to it—the submission which your predecessors, namely the archbishops Thomas and Gerard, professed in accordance with the ancient custom of their predecessors.
>
> But if you choose rather to persist in what you have begun than to desist from it, I forbid, under perpetual anathema, all bishops throughout Britain to lay hands upon you for promotion to the episcopate; or, should you be promoted by outsiders, to receive you as bishop or into any Christian communion.
>
> And I also forbid you, Thomas, under the same anathema and on God’s behalf, ever to receive the blessing of the bishopric of York unless you make the profession which your predecessors Thomas and Gerard made to the Church of Canterbury [Col. 1035B]. But if you entirely relinquish the bishopric of York, I permit you to exercise the priestly office which you have already received.

For, as he said when questioned, he feared to appear before the judgment-seat of God unless he had first punished so great a disobedience, arising in his own time within the jurisdiction entrusted to him. Accordingly, Thomas himself, terrified by the authority of the man and the severity of the sentence, came to his senses; and, even after Anselm’s death, made the profession in the presence of the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury acting in the primate’s stead.

## CHAPTER XVI. Anselm begins but does not complete the treatise *On the Origin of the Soul*, because death overtakes him. Of Anselm’s death on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, and of the year of his pontificate. Of the multiplication of balm, and of his miracles

[Col. 1035C]

In the third year after he had been recalled from his second exile by King Henry, he began to grow so weak that every kind of food became distasteful to him. Yet he compelled nature to receive it, because he knew that it could not continue without nourishment. His flesh indeed grew weaker and weaker; but that noble spirit, ennobled by love of God and of the Church, disdained to yield to infirmity. Indeed, he seemed stronger and more powerful because of it. He could not be hindered from divine meditations, conversations, and prayers; but continually occupied himself with his customary exercises pleasing to God.

Every day he attended the consecration of the Lord’s Body, either walking there or being carried in a chair [Col. 1035D]. Only on the fifth day before his death could he be kept away from it. Palm Sunday had dawned, and one of those present addressed him thus: “Father, from what we see, it seems likely that you will leave the world and pass to the Paschal solemnity of your Lord.” He answered: “As His will shall be, so let it be; and may the Lord’s good pleasure concerning me be fulfilled as He wills. Yet, if He preferred it, I should wish faithfully to complete before my death the question concerning the origin of the soul which I am considering in my mind.”

He felt no pain in his body; but because of the failure caused by an ailing stomach, he was truly wasting away. Then, as Tuesday evening drew on and he could scarcely form words, at the request of Ralph, bishop of Rochester, and those present, he blessed the king, queen, their children, and all their subjects; and, so far as lay within his power, absolved them [Col. 1036A].

The brothers of the Church of the Saviour were present at Matins, and one standing by him began the Lord’s Passion. When the words of the Lord Jesus were reached, “You are those who have remained with me in my trials; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22), he drew breath more slowly than usual; and, being now near his end, was laid upon ashes and haircloth. When the brethren had also gathered around him, he fell asleep in the Lord, insofar as grief and tears allowed them to attend him.

He passed away at dawn on the Wednesday preceding the Lord’s Supper, the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109 [Col. 1036B], the sixteenth year of his pontificate and the seventy-sixth of his life. The blessedness of his departure and the glory of his ascent were shown by signs of miracles; and the most holy merits of the confessor became publicly known through the signs then plainly visible.

The venerable men—the aforementioned bishop of Rochester and Baldwin, whom the holy man, as has been said, had made steward of his affairs—were endeavouring to anoint the sacred face with the small amount of balm available. The bishop, then, about to perform this office, had drawn from the bottom of the vessel only the very tip of a finger, scarcely dipped; and he saw that the balm had entirely failed, because the vessel had been kept carelessly. He was distressed, and all who were present were saddened.

Then the venerable Edmer, mentioned at the beginning, asked the bishop to shake the vessel more forcefully, upside down, into his hand [Col. 1036C]. The bishop agreed; and behold, liquid flowed in abundance from the nearly dry vessel and filled the outstretched hand. This was repeated a second and third time, and even more often; and the vessel always flowed abundantly. Thus, with tears bursting forth for joy and amazement, those present repeatedly anointed the entire body of the holy man. For why, amid such divine generosity, should they expose themselves to the charge of stinginess or avarice? While Elijah ministers, oil is multiplied; and balm, in order to serve Anselm, receives increase. It was indeed fitting that the flesh which, while he lived, he had striven to preserve uncorrupted from pleasures should not, when lifeless, suffer the injury of corruption.

[Col. 1036D] A certain man of Christ and true worshipper of the Church, who according to his means assisted the poor, was, when Father Anselm died, at Canterbury and had reached what seemed his final hour. For he had long been ill. When he had briefly fallen into a light sleep, a handsome young man stood by him and asked what he was suffering. He answered: “Behold, I am dying.” The young man said to him: “The father of his country, who is to live eternally, is now going to God—and are you dying? Rise quickly, and glorify God and His friend, Father Anselm, who has come to your aid.” On hearing this, the man rose, to the astonishment of all, hurried eagerly to the church to give thanks, and related what he had seen.

At the hour of the same departure, a brother in the monastery of Saint Augustine, anxious concerning the condition of the glorious Father, saw in a vision at the door of the archbishop’s chamber a most beautiful company of white-robed persons [Col. 1037A], eagerly awaiting, as though the coming departure of someone were expected. A bishop, distinguished by his dress and a certain majesty, went in and out at the head of this choir. At Anselm’s death he came out quickly and said: “Behold, he whom you await is here. Receive him, and bear him where the Lord has commanded, with a voice of praise and exultation.”

A few days earlier, moreover, a monk of the Church of Canterbury named Elias, innocent and proven in life, learned of Father Anselm’s passing through another vision. He saw the most blessed Dunstan and Archbishop Anselm conversing in Christ Church; and he heard Dunstan say to Anselm [Col. 1037B]: “Dearest friend, take this ring from my hand; would you like to receive it?” Drawing back his hand, blessed Dunstan said: “Not on this occasion; but on the Wednesday before Easter, while I keep it in the meantime, you shall receive it from the hand of the Lord.”

Thus Martin’s departure was made known beforehand to saints in a vision; and the Lord, whom they served in like manner, glorified Martin and Anselm alike.

## CHAPTER XVII. Of the miracles of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, after his death. Of the sarcophagus in which his body was enclosed. Of the chaplain of the bishop of Rochester, and of Count Arnulf troubled at sea

When the rites had been performed as custom requires, it remained for that precious treasure, his body, to be enclosed in a tomb. They therefore came to the sarcophagus and found it [Col. 1037C] too small to receive the body unless the limbs were broken and the upper stone removed. Since this seemed excessively harsh and intolerable to everyone, one of the brethren standing around took the bishop’s staff and set to work on the stone, manipulating and pressing it on every side, fitting it this way and that, until, to the amazement of all, it appeared entirely convenient and sufficiently large to receive the body. For the Saviour, at whose death rocks were split, did this for His glory: that stony nature might appear miraculously to yield to His confessor.

In those days a chaplain of the bishop of Rochester, a monk by profession and commendable in reputation for his character, named Robert, was crossing London Bridge [Col. 1037D] when he experienced and rejoiced in the protection of blessed Father Anselm. A horse carrying his servant and baggage fell into the river Thames—without the servant, indeed, but laden with baggage. Although a poor man might well be troubled at the loss of horse and possessions, nothing distressed him except one of Anselm’s books, which he believed had been in the bundles and mourned as lost. But the outcome was otherwise. For when, after repeatedly calling on Father Anselm, he reached the bank, he found the horse, the bag with its bundles, the book, and everything he had lost unharmed.

Furthermore, Count Arnulf, son of Roger de Montgommery, returned from Normandy to England. At first a favourable wind carried him midway across the passage. When it failed, the rowers were exhausted [Col. 1038A]; then, as provisions gave out over two full days, they suffered shipwreck through the instability and error of the winds. At length the count turned to blessed Anselm and asked his companions and sailors to entrust the entire ship to blessed Anselm, whom they knew and whose sanctity they did not doubt. For, he declared, the one who had always been merciful would not fail those who prayed to him merely because mortal remains had delayed him; now recently united to God and hindered by no obstacle, he burned with a fuller charity.

All agreed; and scarcely had they completed the Lord’s Prayer under this vow when, behold, the clouds were dispersed, a favourable wind arose, and they were carried to the place in England for which they had set out. Coming to the king’s court, they related to the king and others what had happened to them, and the mouths of all who heard were opened in praise of the outstanding confessor [Col. 1038B].

In addition, one of the brethren of Canterbury, very anxious about Father Anselm’s condition, entreated the Lord to make him more certain about it. Anselm therefore appeared to his friend in a vision, commanding him to be assured that, once he had been stripped of the burden of flesh, Jesus Christ—whom he had truly worshipped—had received him gloriously and clothed him with the robe of immortality.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Of the miracles of our holy Father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. Of a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, who came to the tomb of holy Father Anselm to pray—whether to Anselm or for Anselm; that it was fitting to pray to him as a saint because his name was written in the book of life; and of his other miracles

It would take long to recount all such things as happened then [Col. 1038C]. But let this book be closed with a few, since we have promised concise brevity; and those who wish to know more should return to the sources—great volumes, I mean—from which these things have been taken as so small an amount for the consolation and refreshment of travellers.

A novice monk of the Church of Canterbury, among the others who came in crowds to Father Anselm’s tomb to pray, went there prompted by devotion. Yet he hesitated as to what was more fitting to pray: namely, whether to Anselm or for Anselm. While he remained anxiously troubled in this uncertainty for a long time, he turned with all devotion to the Lord, asking to be instructed what he ought to do. Since he invoked the compassionate Lord frequently in truthfulness, while he prayed before the altar [Col. 1038D], a book was opened to him in a vision, in which was written in most fitting fashion: “Saint Anselm.” The devout man therefore understood that Anselm’s name was written in the book of life, and that by the merit of his former life he was worthy to be prayed to as a saint.

Another brother in the same church, seized by a grave illness, had long languished and did not know at all where to turn for help. At last he devoted himself wholly to the well-known compassion of blessed Anselm. He was led to Anselm’s tomb, prostrated himself on the ground, and prayed earnestly that the church might be relieved, either by his recovery or by his death. The Most High heard the desire of his heart, and the man who had invoked Anselm was restored to health.

A nobleman, a worthy and widely known knight named Humphrey, had fallen into dropsy and had been abandoned by all physicians as hopeless [Col. 1039A]. He had loved Anselm and could not let him escape from his memory. He therefore asked a monk of Canterbury named Haimo, an old acquaintance, to come to him so that provision might at least be made for his soul. Haimo came, and by chance brought with him blessed Anselm’s belt. After kissing it and first offering a prayer, the knight tried to wrap it around himself; but because of the swelling its ends could scarcely touch one another. Yet, in a marvellous way, his body gradually began to lose its swelling and return to its natural condition. When he perceived this, he wrapped the belt around every part of his body and, through the title of the most holy confessor, was restored to complete health.

At Lyons, at Saint Irenaeus, a very devout recluse saw herself one night brought before the throne of the perpetual Virgin [Col. 1039B]. Having heard and seen there many wondrous disclosures of the heavenly homeland, she asked, among other things, what was to be hoped concerning Hugh, archbishop of Lyons. The Virgin Mother replied: “Daughter, it will be well—well indeed—with him, through God’s grace.” The recluse added: “My lady queen, what am I to think concerning my lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury?” The Lady answered: “Be most certain concerning him: beyond any doubt he is in great glory with God.”

One of those who had been intimate with him saw a similar vision in England at about the same time. Seeing the Father clothed in white and adorned with episcopal insignia, and remembering that he had been taken from human affairs, he said: “Father, where do you dwell? How do you live? And what do you do?” Anselm answered: “There I live, where I see, rejoice, and am fulfilled.” On waking, the man reflected on these words and grieved that one of the four had escaped him [Col. 1039C]. In that same sadness, during a waking interval, he plainly heard a voice saying to him: “I rejoice”—for that was the word he had lost. Thus made still more certain of the Father’s glory, he rejoiced greatly and gave boundless thanks to the Creator.

And so that the glory of the blessed confessor might extend even to barbarian peoples, a certain matron in the regions of Scotland, born of noble English parents and approved everywhere in Christian devotion, named Estryldis, was reduced by severe sickness even to death. But at last, girded with blessed Anselm’s belt, of which we have already spoken, she recovered completely.

Edmer, worthy of happy remembrance, was present at these events, saw them, and brought them about [Col. 1040A]. In the Church of Canterbury a sick brother suffered from an acute fever. When every medical remedy had failed, the aforementioned belt was placed around his neck through Edmer’s care, and he was healed. It is needless to recount how many women in labour were aided in childbirth by that same belt, because it would be too long a matter and is known to many. By the same belt a brother was healed without any rupture, though beneath his navel an enormous swelling, like a large sphere, had formed. The Church of Canterbury knows this, because the event was famous there.

A certain Elphege, as is publicly known, had from birth been blind, deaf, mute, and lame. This too is publicly known. As the present day bears witness, he received complete health in all these respects at the tomb of blessed Anselm [Col. 1040B].

Fire seized a village of Saint Edmund and the house of a man who had been blessed Anselm’s fosterling and possessed nothing else. The devouring fire, which consumes everything, had already taken hold. The man had no comfort, when one brother advised him to remember Anselm, his foster-father, and entrust the house to him who was accustomed to extinguish flames. The man obeyed; and, before the Lord’s Prayer was finished, he marvelled and rejoiced to see his house delivered unharmed from the fire.

The venerable Elias, abbot of Holy Trinity on the hill of Rouen, publicly confessed that, through the prayers and merits of blessed Anselm, when he was ordained by him, he had been healed of swelling and pain in his knees, by which he had been so afflicted that he could scarcely walk.

But who am I, that I should recount the righteous acts of the Lord and presume to touch with presumptuous speech or pen the praises of so great a Father [Col. 1040C]? My powers and merits are indeed unequal to worthily describing so great a confessor; and to describe what is known inadequately is a mark of presumption and a matter rightly and deservedly liable to punishment. But may Father Anselm be gracious to me, and by his merits and prayers direct my mind to useful and honourable work pleasing to the divine majesty. I also beseech the hearer and reader; and I earnestly entreat them by every prayer permitted to us, that in this desire they may join with me and for me in beseeching holy Father Anselm, and may obtain for themselves and for me forgiveness of sins from Him who alone is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1039] Here ends the *Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury*, according to John, bishop of Chartres.

[Col. 1039]

# LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, BY JOHN OF SALISBURY

(See *Patrologia*, vol. 190, col. 193.)

## ABOUT THE YEAR 1180: JOHN OF CORNWALL

[Col. 1041]

# NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, IV, 67)

Master John of Cornwall, an English theologian about the year 1170, wrote, if we are to believe Possevino, an *Eulogy concerning the Assumed Man*. But the title of the book is *Eulogy*, written to Pope Alexander III, in which he disputes against Abelard and Peter Lombard [Note: Leland, *On British Writers*, p. 227: “The *Eulogy* written by John was the cause of great hostility between him and Peter Lombard, the distinguished theologian; and I still possess his apology, which answers the Cornishman’s *Eulogy* carefully, severely, and keenly, and, like a veteran soldier contending with an enemy, ambitiously strives for triumph.”] and teaches that Christ is some man, or, according to his human nature, is something—namely, a true man subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh. On this controversy it will be useful to consult Petavius, book V of *On the Incarnation of the Word*, chapters 6, 7, 8, and 9; Chancellor Pfaff of Württemberg, *On the Impersonality and Perpetuity of Christ’s Human Nature*, Tübingen, 1722, quarto; and Edmund Martène’s preliminary notice prefixed to John of Cornwall’s *Eulogy*, which he first published in volume V of the *Anecdota*, pp. 1657, 1702, Paris, 1717, folio.

In a manuscript codex in the library of Balliol College, Oxford, according to Cave, it is entitled: *Discussion concerning Philosophy and Heresies*. It is known, however, that our John wrote twice on this subject: once more briefly, in the work printed among the writings of Hugh of Saint Victor, vol. III, p. 68, under the title *Apology concerning the Incarnate Word*; and then at greater length, in the work published by Edmund, as I have already said.

His other writings are listed as follows: *Summa: How the Sacrament of the Altar Is Made through the Power of the Holy Cross, and on the Seven Canons or Orders of the Mass*, manuscript at Cambridge. This writing is also said to survive in print among Hugh of Saint Victor’s *Works*, vol. III, p. 399 ff. Commentaries on several books of Holy Scripture. Disputations. Letters to various persons. See Leland, chapter 200; Bale, III.6; Pits, p. 236 ff.

[Col. 1041]

# APOLOGY OF JOHN OF CORNWALL: ON THE INCARNATE WORD

Containing objections against those who say that Christ is not something insofar as he is man.

(It is found among the appendices to the works of Hugh of Saint Victor, *Patrologia*, vol. 177, col. 293.)

[Col. 1041]

# EULOGY OF THE SAME AUTHOR, ADDRESSED TO POPE ALEXANDER III, THAT CHRIST IS SOME MAN

(Dom Edmond Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, V, 1655.)

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

In the twelfth century many questions began to be debated among scholastic doctors. Since they contained more subtlety and curiosity than truth, they could lead not a few into error and even overthrow the principal foundations of the Christian religion. The chief promoters of these were Peter Abelard and Gilbert de la Porrée, bishop of Poitiers. The former underwent due censure for his errors, first at the council of Soissons and then at Sens; the latter at Rheims, especially through the efforts of Saint Bernard [Col. 1043].

Peter Lombard was not free from this blemish. He later became bishop of Paris and was easily foremost among the masters of his age, from which he has retained the title “the Master” to this day. Among the various errors he had taught while lecturing in the Parisian academy, he did not hesitate to proclaim that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not something, and that the divine Word was united to the human body and soul just as if it had been clothed in a garment—thereby overturning, through this perverse teaching, the Church’s faith in the personal union of the Word with human nature.

He had drawn this doctrine from reading the books of Peter Abelard, in which he took great pleasure, and afterwards almost imbued—or rather infected—countless persons with it. Yet he never taught it as his own opinion, but as an opinion which might be proposed in the schools and examined by disputation. But this opinion acquired so many and such influential defenders that councils of bishops had to be assembled to suppress it.

Such was the Council of Tours, convoked by Pope Alexander III in 1163. Very many bishops of both the Gallican and English Churches attended it. The same supreme pontiff also proscribed the same doctrine in letters sent to William, archbishop of Sens and afterwards of Rheims. By apostolic authority he ordered the masters of Paris to be assembled before the suffragan bishops, so that they might forbid anyone thereafter to teach that Christ is not something insofar as he is man; for, just as he is true God, so he is true man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.

Alexander’s letter is reported by Matthew Paris under the year 1179 in these terms:

> When you were formerly present before us, we charged you orally that, after summoning your suffragans to Paris, you should devote yourself entirely to abolishing the wicked teaching of Peter, formerly bishop of Paris, by which it is said that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not something, and should apply effective effort thereto. Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that you summon your suffragans to Paris, as we commanded you when you were present, and that, together with them and other religious and prudent men, you endeavour utterly to abolish the aforesaid teaching. You are to order that Christ be taught by the masters as perfect God and likewise as perfect man and true man, consisting of soul and body; firmly and strictly enjoining all that they shall in no way henceforth presume to teach that doctrine, but shall utterly detest it.

Among those infected by the poison of this doctrine, John of Cornwall did not disgorge it except with difficulty and after many years.
