But when he had at last recognized the truth, he not only renounced and condemned the error, but also wrote an outstanding work against it for Pope Alexander, which he entitled *Eulogy*. Who this John was is not entirely certain. Yet that he was a most learned man and well versed in reading the Fathers, especially Saint Augustine, can readily be inferred from this little work. Indeed, that he was honoured with a doctor’s degree is sufficiently indicated by the title “Master,” bestowed upon him in the inscription of this treatise.

He professes himself a disciple of Peter Lombard; he heard Maurice, who succeeded Peter on the throne of the Church of Paris, lecture more than once in the Parisian academy, as he did Robert of Melun. He wrote after 1175, when Archbishop William had already been transferred from the see of Sens to that of Rheims.

# EULOGY OF MASTER JOHN OF CORNWALL

[Col. 1043]

[Col. 1043A] At the Council of Tours, which was held some time ago by your authority and adorned by your presence, after most of the prelates of both the English and Gallican Churches had been summoned, the doctrine of certain persons maintaining that Christ is not some man and that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not a thing, began to be debated. I do not know which side of the disputants prevailed in this battle of words; but I believe that so unjust a falsehood, hostile to the Christian faith, was adorned in so great and such an assembly of Christ by no marks of truth or victory.

Yet the rich and abundant clemency of your gentleness did not at once strike that assertion with canonical censure, lest its authors and defenders—who perhaps had sinned through ignorance rather than obstinacy—be overwhelmed by the very condemnation of their error or branded with a permanent mark of infamy [Col. 1043B]. And from that same gentleness of yours, after a much longer interval of forbearance had elapsed, even in a certain decretal letter sent concerning the arrogation of that wicked doctrine to the venerable William, then archbishop of Sens and now of Rheims, it is by no means stated that those who should presume to hold or teach that error had been or ought to be struck with anathema.

Since, therefore, innumerable scholars, drunk from this cup and driven into frenzy, obstinately abuse your patience down to the present day [Col. 1044A]—persons who by no means praise the compassionate moderation of your mercy, but proclaim this impious doctrine as though it were Catholic—let what Prosper says in the Decretals at last be done:

> Those who, though long endured and beneficially reproved, refuse to be corrected, ought to be cut off like rotten members of a body by the sword of excommunication; lest, as flesh dead through disease, if it is not cut away, corrupts the health of the remaining flesh by the contagion of its rottenness, so these persons, who despise amendment and persist in their disease, infect others by the example of their own destruction.

Hence Pope Calixtus also says:

> It is just that those who despise divine commands and prove disobedient to paternal injunctions should be corrected by harsher punishments, so that others may beware of committing such acts [Col. 1044B], all may rejoice in brotherly concord, and all may take an example of severity and goodness.

Likewise Pope Pelagius:

> By the example of apostolic authority we declare that the spirits of those who err and lead others into error are to be delivered to Satan, that they may unlearn blasphemy.

Likewise Jerome:

> Rotten flesh must be cut away, and the scabrous sheep driven from the fold, lest the whole house, mass, body, and flock burn, be corrupted, rot, and perish.

## The Author’s Confession, with a Conciliatory Appeal

This, indeed, is the rigor of ecclesiastical mercy: it strikes in order to heal, destroys in order to build, uproots in order to plant [Col. 1045A]. Let not, I beseech you, the shepherd abandon the lambs, nor the father his children. And if the error of those who oppose cannot be corrected, let him at least not permit the tireless profession of sound faith to perish in me and persons like me.

If I, though dust and ashes, think rightly, may your authority strengthen my weakness; if I err anywhere, may it recall my simplicity to itself. For I believe that Christ is some man, and that he is something according to his humanity; that he who, according to divinity, is an incorporeal substance is, according to humanity, a corporeal substance; and that according to one nature he is a simple thing, but according to the other a composite thing.

I also believe that the very same one who according to deity is uncreated and unmade is according to humanity both created and made; and that he who according to one nature is Creator is according to the other a creature [Col. 1046A]. The following will show that these claims are fortified by the clearest testimonies of the saints.

But before all this, so that the individual matters may be easier to find, the chapter headings must first be set down according to custom. And then, so that what we are about to say may become clearer and stand more firmly, we judge that the three opinions which Master Peter Lombard left in writing ought briefly to be presented. For since all opposites placed beside one another appear more clearly, the truth of the first opinion will gain strength and shine more brightly through comparison with the second and third.

# CHAPTERS OF THE WHOLE TREATISE

[Col. 1045]

**Chapter I.** Three opinions concerning the assumed man, with their explanations.  
**Chapter II.** Authorities of the saints by which the second and third opinions seem to be supported.  
**Chapter III.** Authorities of the masters for those two opinions.  
**Chapter IV.** Authorities of the masters against those two opinions.  
**Chapter V.** Authorities of the saints proving that Christ is some man.  
**Chapter VI.** Arguments proving the same.  
**Chapter VII.** Authorities proving that Christ, insofar as he is man, is something.  
**Chapter VIII.** Arguments proving that Christ is essentially and substantially man.  
**Chapter IX.** Objections that may be raised are resolved, and the obscurity of John of Damascus is unravelled.  
**Chapter X.** Authorities proving that Christ is one thing and another.  
**Chapter XI.** Authorities that seem contrary.  
**Chapter XII.** Authorities proving that Christ is a living being and a body.  
**Chapter XIII.** Authorities that Christ is some whole or composite thing.  
**Chapter XIV.** Arguments proving this.  
**Chapter XV.** Authorities that Christ is called a whole.  
**Chapter XVI.** Authorities proving that Christ was made, created, and is a creature.  
**Chapter XVII.** Authorities that seem contrary, and useful resolutions, where, among other matters, it is asked whether that whole existed during the three days of burial or did not exist.  
**Chapter XVIII.** Authorities proving that Christ did not always exist.  
**Chapter XIX.** Authorities that seem contrary, fitting resolutions of the contradiction, and a repetition of what precedes, useful for many purposes. Conclusion from the foregoing, inferring the propositions set forth in the beginning.

## CHAPTER I. Three opinions concerning the assumed man, with explanations of these statements: “God is man,” “man is God,” “God was made man,” and “man was made God”

[Col. 1045B]

### First explanation.

The first is the explanation of those who say that, in the very incarnation of the Word, a certain man was constituted from a rational soul and human flesh—the two elements from which every true human being is constituted. That man began to be God, not indeed by the nature of God, but by the person of the Word; and God began to be that man. They also grant that this man was assumed by the Word and that he is only the Word. On this account they maintain that God is said to have become man, or to be man, because God became, or began to be, God; yet not through a migration of nature into nature. Rather, with the property of each nature preserved, it came about that God was that substance and that substance was God. Hence it is truly said: God became man, and man became God; the Son of God became the Son of Man, and conversely.

Second explanation.

[Col. 1046B]

The second explanation is that of those who say that this man consists not merely of a rational soul and flesh, but of human and divine nature, or of three substances: divinity, flesh, and soul. Accordingly, they confess that Christ was one person only before the incarnation, yet not merely simple, but through the incarnation became composite from divinity and humanity. Nor is he therefore a different person from what he was before; rather, whereas he had previously been the person of God alone, in the incarnation he became the person of a human being, so that there should not be two persons, but in one person there should be both God and man. Therefore the person which had previously been simple and existing in one nature only subsists in two natures and from two natures, because it began to be a certain substance subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; and that substance became the person which had been God alone. It also became a true human being, subsisting not merely from soul and body, but also from divinity. Yet that person ought not to be said to have become the person of a human being, just as the Word became—that is, began to be—the human Word, although it did not become, or begin to be, the Word.

Thus, as some of them hold, that person became a certain being subsisting from soul and flesh; but it did not become a person, substance, or nature. According to these writers, when it is said, “God became man,” it means that he began to be a being subsisting from two natures and three substances; and conversely, “man became God,” because the being subsisting in two natures began to be God, or afterwards man became God. And conversely this is said because God assumed man and man was assumed by God. Hence Augustine says in *On the Trinity*: “Such was that assumption as makes man God and God man.”

Third opinion.

[Col. 1047B]

The third opinion is that of those who, in the incarnation of the Word, deny not only a person composed from natures, but also that there is there any man or any substance composed or made from soul and flesh. They say instead that those two things, namely soul and flesh, are united to the person and nature of the Word in such a way that no substance or person is made or composed from those two or from the three; rather, the Word of God is clothed with those two as with a garment, so as suitably to appear to mortal eyes. He is therefore called a true man because he received the reality of flesh and soul. Scripture also says that he received these two into the singularity or unity of his person, not because those two, or some existing or composite thing, are one person with the Word and are the Word, but because, when those two were added to the Word, the number of persons was not increased so that there should be a quaternity in the Trinity; and because the very person of the Word, formerly without a garment, was neither divided nor changed by the assumption of the garment, but remained one and the same, unchanged.

Those who speak of God’s becoming man “according to clothing” say that God is called a true man by taking man, and man is called God because of the one who assumes him. For, they say, if God were man essentially, or man were understood to be God, then, if God had assumed a human being of the female sex, woman too would essentially be God, and conversely. But God could have assumed a human being of the female sex; therefore God could be woman, and conversely. In this opinion, then, he is called made man because he received man; he is called man because he has man, or because he is one having man; man became God because he was assumed by God; and man is God because the one having man is God. Therefore, when it is said “God is man,” either the clothing is predicated or the person. Cassiodorus seems to show that “the humanized one” and “the humanized person” are predicated when he says: “He became, so to speak, a humanized God, who does not cease to be God even in the assumption of flesh.”

Solution.

But what falsity, and indeed what impiety, lies in their argument—“For if God’s being man, or man’s being God, were understood essentially,” etc.—will be made clear by what follows. I called it false because it draws a false conclusion from true premises; I added impious because it opposes pious faith, while it labors to strip Christ, to whom it grants only the garment of man, of the true essence of man.

Note also that this third opinion has this in common with the second: Christ is not some substance consisting of flesh and soul, and Christ, as man, is not something. It differs in this: the person of Christ is not composed from two natures or three substances. Therefore authorities common to both opinions must first be introduced, so that, once suitable answers or reasons have followed, the same falsehood of both may be exposed. But with regard to that on which they disagree—whether Christ is some whole or composite thing—it will be discussed in its proper place when that question is reached.

## CHAPTER II.—Authorities of the saints by which the second and third opinions seem to be strengthened in what they agree upon

Discussing the Apostle’s words, “found in appearance as a man” (*Phil.* 2), Augustine says in the book *Eighty-Four Questions* that a habit or clothing is said to be in a thing when it comes to it so as to be possessed:

> “There is, however, this difference. Some things which come to produce a habit are not changed, but change the things to which they come, while themselves remaining whole and unmoved; as wisdom, coming to a man, is not itself changed, but changes the man, since it makes him wise from foolish. Other things come in such a way as both to change and to be changed: for example, food, which, losing its own form, is converted into the body, while we, refreshed by food, are changed from thinness and weakness into strength and vigor. A third kind occurs when the things which come neither change that to which they come nor are themselves changed by it; as a ring placed upon a finger—a kind very rarely found. A fourth kind occurs when the things which come are not changed from their own nature, but receive another appearance and form; as clothing, which when cast off and laid aside does not have the form which it has, or takes on, when worn. When it is put upon the limbs, it receives a form which it did not have when unworn. This kind suits the present comparison.

> “For the Son of God emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not changing his own form, nor converted or transformed into man through loss of stability; but, having been made in the likeness of men, he is the one who assumes, by assuming a true man; or he was found in appearance as a man—that is, by having man he was found as a man, not to himself, but to those among whom he appeared in man. And his saying ‘as a man’ expresses truth. Thus, by the name *habit*, the Apostle sufficiently indicated in what sense he said, ‘made in the likeness of men’: for he became man not through transformation into man, but through clothing, when he put on man, whom, by in some manner uniting and conforming him to himself, he associated with immortal and eternal life. Therefore the Word must not be understood to have been changed by the assumption of man, just as limbs clothed with a garment are not changed, although that assumption ineffably united the assumed to the one assuming.”

By these words Augustine seems to imply that God is said to have become man according to clothing. Seeking also to set forth the manner of the incarnation itself for those who inquire, he says in the fourth book of *On the Trinity*:

> “If it is asked how the incarnation itself came about, I say that the very Word of God became flesh—that is, became man—yet he was not converted and changed into that which he became, but was clothed with flesh so that he might appear suitably to fleshly persons. Thus he was made, so that there might be there not only the Word of God and human flesh, but also a rational human soul; and this whole is called both God because of God and man because of man. If this is difficult to understand, let the mind be cleansed by faith, abstaining from sins and doing good works; for these matters are difficult.”

The same author, in *On Faith to Peter*, says:

> “Although the Son of God is eternal and true God, for us he became true and complete man. He is true in that that God has true human nature; he is complete in that he assumed human flesh and a rational soul.”

Likewise:

> “That emptying of the supreme God was nothing other than the assumption of the form of a servant, that is, of human nature. Therefore both forms are in Christ, because in Christ both the divine and the human nature and substance are complete.”

Likewise, in *Against Maximinus*:

> “Though invisible in himself, he appeared visibly in the man whom he assumed from a woman, from whom he was born.”

And again in the same work:

> “We believe that Christ, true God, assumed a true man; that in him the invisible appeared visibly to men; that in him he lived among men; that in him he endured human things from men; and that in him he taught men.”

Hilary likewise says in *On the Trinity*:

> “How is the Son of God born of Mary, except because the Word is flesh? That is, we confess that the Son of God, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant—the one and the same—not through a falling away of God, but through the assumption of man; and that he was found both in the form of God through the divine nature and in the form of a servant, conceived by the Holy Spirit, according to the appearance of man. Yet that appearance was not of a man, but as of a man; nor was that flesh flesh of sin, but in the likeness of sinful flesh.”

### On Christ’s likeness to a worm

What is here said, “not of a man,” must be understood as “not of a sinner,” just as in the words, “I am a worm and not a man” (*Ps.* 21). He is a worm because he was born of the Virgin without male seed; and “not a man,” that is, not a sinner. Hence, by way of explanation, it is said: “nor was that flesh flesh of sin, but in the likeness of sinful flesh” (*Rom.* 8).

Add, if you please: “Over Idumea I will stretch out my shoe” (*Ps.* 59). Likewise: “Divinity came to us shod.” Likewise: “I clothed myself in sackcloth” (*Ps.* 34).

These and all authorities of this sort, they maintain, teach that Christ, as man, is not something, and that the one assuming is not the same thing as what is assumed. I wonder, however, why, among the testimonies of the saints set forth above in their support, they fail altogether to understand how even this one statement of Augustine utterly overturns this entire falsehood: “Therefore the Word must not be understood to have been changed by the assumption of man, just as limbs clothed with a garment are not changed, although that assumption ineffably united the assumed to the one assuming.”

### On the likeness of clothing

If they heed what is said regarding the likeness of clothing, why do they turn the mind’s gaze away from what follows concerning personal union? For what is this ineffable union except the personal union of God who assumes and man who is assumed? That union is nothing if man is not one person with God. But if man became one person with God, what became one person with God?

They also pay little attention to Augustine’s words, “These matters are difficult.” For what difficulty of understanding is there if God’s being man is nothing other than having the garment of human form and likeness? And if God’s becoming man means merely receiving such a garment, what is wonderful here, what ought to be called ineffable? Does not every person, whether human or angelic, who receives a garment remain the same person as before? It would rather be new and wonderful if taking or changing a garment changed the person.

If they would inspect more carefully what has been written concerning the appearance of man and similar matters, they would readily understand that neither by the words of the saints nor by the explanation of the words is it taught that Christ, as man, is not something; rather, it is taught that divinity received flesh. Therefore God is man not merely by clothing, but essentially, as will be shown in its place below.

But their supposed most forceful argument—that God is not essentially man because God could have assumed a human being of the female sex, and therefore woman could be God and conversely—is manifestly false. For it does not follow that, if God can do something, that thing can be. God can do many things which cannot come about, because they are impossible. Let them themselves answer whether God could have assumed human nature in the female sex. They cannot deny it; therefore their own premises conclude that God could be woman. Yet, according to their subtle judgment, they ought not to deny, “God could be woman,” but rather this: “God could be some woman,” just as he could be man, but could not be some man. They even burden us with the weight of great masters, whom their authors are accustomed to praise.

## CHAPTER III. Authorities of masters that seem to support them

Master Gilbert of Poitiers, as many assert, taught the matters set forth in the second opinion: namely, that Christ both is and became a composite person from two natures or three substances, and yet did not become some person, did not become some substance, and is not something as man. But because I have not read any writing of his on these points, and even his pupils disagree among themselves, I pass to others. By their writings the same falsehood, which he too is believed to have taught—namely, that Christ, as man, is not something—seems to be established and fortified.

Master Peter Abelard argues thus in his *Theology*:

> “What is it to say that God becomes man, except to unite to himself in one person the divine substance, which is spiritual, and the human, which is bodily? For what is spiritual cannot become bodily; but in that union of Christ’s person, in which the divinity of the Word, flesh, and soul come together, each of these substances retains its own nature, so that none of them is changed into another: neither flesh nor soul becomes divinity, just as flesh can never become soul, although in individual human beings soul and flesh are one person.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Change into another thing cannot occur unless that which was previously ceases to be. But the spiritual essence now remains spiritual as it was before, and has not become bodily. Therefore, since God is spirit, and that which is spirit never becomes bodily or receives parts, how can either the Word properly be said to become flesh or God to become man, since the Word himself is even now spirit, because he is God, just as he was before the incarnation? For man is a bodily thing, composed of members and liable to dissolution; God, however, is an incorporeal thing and does not consist of parts so as to be dissolved. Therefore God ought not properly to be called either flesh or man; otherwise man, conversely, would properly have to be called God, and one would have to grant that God is some created thing, or something which has not always existed, since man is admittedly a creature and has a beginning. But far be it from us to hold that any thing is God which has not always existed, or has not always been God! For this is to confess a new and recent God. Thus, when it is said that he becomes flesh or is man, it must be understood that divine and human substance are joined in one person. For the substance which was assumed is other, although the person is not other. For just as in one God there are three persons and one substance, so conversely in Christ the man there are two substances, but in the two substances or natures one person.

> “God has not been changed into something other than he was, although he joined something other to himself in personal union. For neither will our souls, when united with their bodies restored, become something other than they were merely because they are joined with them in one person; although they change the body by animating it, and advance it from inanimation to animation. Thus it is rather the body that must be said to be changed by the soul than the soul by the body. For it is the body which advances through the soul into a certain state, not the soul through the body, since the soul persists unmoved through itself. Much less, then, should God united with man be said thereby to become something other, to whom no creature can contribute anything. Hence we profess God wholly free from every changeability.”

### How these statements may properly be understood

If anyone inspects this argument more carefully, he will find that, first of all, it rejects the divine substance’s becoming human. Likewise, it says of the divine substance that it cannot become a composite thing, a bodily thing, or any creature. Likewise, the statement, “Far be it from us to hold that any thing is God which has not always existed,” if “God” is understood not as the divine person but as the substance—as he himself interpreted it at the beginning of the question—contains nothing erroneous.

That, before the solution, he mixes true and false statements after the manner of disputants ought not to trouble the reader. For the things said in the solution itself, beginning, “Thus it must be understood,” are Catholic for us, insofar as they do not oppose us, down to the words: “Much less, then, should God united with man be said thereby to become something other.” Even that which seems opposed to us, if understood of the essence, is not thereby contrary to us; or perhaps he understands “become something other” as equivalent to “be changed,” for he immediately adds: “We profess God wholly free from every changeability.”

Yet any Catholic may be disturbed by what he says: “Since God is always God, and that which is spirit never becomes bodily or receives parts, how can either the Word properly be said to become flesh or God to become man, since the Word himself is even now spirit,” etc. For he seems to mean that the Son of God is not properly, or essentially, man, but man only by clothing—unless one says that God is not properly called man, or the Word properly called man, because many names by which we speak of him are transferred from creatures to the Creator. But the question here was not what may or may not properly be said of him, but what it is for God to become man. Once this principle of transference has been admitted, he could equally say that the Word is not properly called Word, nor God properly called God.

Thus, if Master Peter Abelard’s doctrine is sound, it cannot support the false assertion; if it is unsound, it ought not prejudice the Catholic confession. I have the stronger suspicion that Master Peter Lombard received this opinion from Master Peter Abelard because he frequently had that book in his hands and perhaps did not investigate every point carefully enough. Since he possessed skill in disputation more from practice than from art, he could have been deceived. I have called it his opinion. For that this was his opinion is certain; but that it was not his assertion, he himself testifies in his own chapter.

### Why it is presumed that it was Master Peter’s assertion

“We have treated the question set forth above with sufficient care, according to the opinions of different persons, without assertion and without prejudice. Yet in so great a matter, difficult as it is to know, we do not wish the reader to think that this our disputation ought to suffice him; rather, let him read other works perhaps more carefully considered and handled, and let him examine with more watchful mind, if he can, the matters which may trouble him here. Let him firmly hold this: God assumed man; man passed into God—not through changeability of nature, but through God’s condescension—so that neither was God changed into human substance by assuming man, nor man, glorified, changed into divine substance in God; for such change or changeability of nature causes diminution and destruction of substance.”

### Another indication concerning the same matter

Moreover, a little before he was elected bishop of Paris, he declared before me and all his hearers then present that this was not his assertion but merely an opinion which he had received from a master. He added these words: “Never, God willing, shall it be my assertion except what is Catholic faith.” Afterwards, however, men more talkative than discerning proclaim from the rooftops, even to this day, things which ought not be heard even in private rooms.

Therefore, since our opponents boast of their masters, let us also bring forward some testimonies of masters on our own behalf, so that the lighter armament of doctors of this time may be put to flight by the mighty wedges of the saints.

## CHAPTER IV. Authorities of masters against that opinion

Master Anselm of Canterbury, in a letter to Pope Urban:

> “God assumed man in unity of person, so that there are two natures, namely divine and human, and one person. Some ask: how can we say that there are not two persons in Christ, as there are two natures? For God was a person before the assumption of man, and after assuming man did not cease to be a person; and the assumed man is a person, since every individual human being is known to be a person. Why, then, is there not one person of God, which existed before the incarnation, and another person of the assumed man? Therefore, just as Christ is God and man, so two persons appear to be in him. But it is not so. For just as in God one nature is several persons, and several persons are one nature, so in Christ one person is several natures, and several natures are one person. For in Christ God and man are not one person and another; although man is one thing and God another. Rather, the same one is God who is also man.”

And shortly afterward:

> “In the assumed man, or in the name Jesus, there is understood together with the nature—that is, together with the man—a collection of properties which is the same for the assumed man and the Word; hence they are the same person.”

Here, then, Christ is two natures or substances, and they are one thing and another, not one person and another.

Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, says in *On Consideration*:

> “It was fitting that the sacrament established for man should agree more intimately and more closely with the constitution of man. It was also fitting that it should correspond with the supreme unity which is in God and is God, so that, just as there are three persons and one essence there, so here, by a most fitting kind of contrast, there are three essences and one person.”

### On the three essences in the Godhead

By “three essences” he means the Word, soul, and flesh. Certainly, just as he understands divinity, so in flesh and soul he intended the whole man to be understood, following Augustine, who often customarily uses “flesh and soul” for the whole human being.

Master Hugh of Saint Victor says:

> “The Word was an eternal person; nor did he begin to be a person when he took soul and flesh into his person. He took soul and flesh so that they might be person in him, not so that they might make him a person. Therefore, since flesh and soul received being person in him when they began to be united to the person of the Word, they always remained one and the same person with the Word, because afterwards they never departed, separated either from the Word or from one another.”

### That by soul and flesh he understands the whole man

Here he plainly understands the whole man by soul and flesh—the man who began to be that person. Thus shortly afterward he adds:

> “Moreover, the parts of man are two, because there are two things in human nature: soul and flesh. Where these two are, there is the whole man; where one of them is, there is a part of man. Therefore the Word assumed the whole man because he assumed all that belonged to man: soul and flesh.”

If soul and flesh are parts of the man Christ, how is he not some whole? And if he has parts according to humanity, on what ground can it be denied that he is something according to humanity? Nor can these parts, soul and flesh, be parts except of some substance; therefore, according to Christ’s humanity, there is some substance.

Master Achard [Note: [Col. 1053] He was abbot of Saint Victor, then bishop of Avranches.] says in his book *On the Trinity*:

> “In Christ there are two natures, each of which can be called a person in itself; yet there are not two persons, but one in two natures: in God assuming man—that is, in the Word by his own nature; and in the man assumed, by the benefit and grace of the assuming Word.”

Likewise:

> “Although in the assuming Word and the assumed man one is from the other—namely, man from the Word—yet it does not follow that there are two persons there, or that one person proceeds from itself. For man has a nature other than the Word, according to which he can be from him. And therefore, because of the plurality of natures, plurality of persons is no longer required there. For if one were not from the other according to another person—but if there were not another nature there—then, since personal existence is admittedly there and each can be called a person in itself, there would necessarily be another person there; or neither would be from the other, or one person would previously be from itself.”

### What Master Robert of Melun and Master Maurice thought on these matters

[Col. 1055A]

I ought not to pass over in silence two venerable masters, whom it is most certain taught nothing heretical in theology: Robert of Melun and Maurice, now bishop of Paris. [Note: [Col. 1055D] He was elected bishop in the year 1164.] I have not read their writings on these disputations or questions. But I attended many of their lectures and disputations, in which they charged Master Peter Lombard’s teaching with falsehood—if I may not say error—both concerning the assumed man and concerning certain other matters.

Yet they could not easily or quickly tear away from me what I had long held. From that time my judgment began to waver, until at length the truth sought, through the testimonies of other doctors and also of saints, made itself known, as through a mirror and in an enigma.

### Master Achard’s assertion

This argument of Master Achard, at its beginning, asserts that there are two natures in Christ, each of which is a person—and certainly neither is other than Christ. The rest requires at least a slight explanation. Thus: “Each of which can be called a person in itself,” in this way: the assuming Word is a person; the assumed man is a person; hence there appears to be a plurality of persons. For in every other human being, these two natures, soul and flesh, are together called one man or one person, but neither by itself is man or person. Therefore no plurality of persons is required in any human being because of such plurality of natures.

But in Christ it is otherwise, because there are two natures, each of which is a person. Hence it might seem that, just as there are two natures, so there would also be two persons in him; and this is refuted by the words, “yet there are not two persons,” etc. What follows, “in the Word by his own nature,” etc., relies on this authority: “What the Son of God has by nature, the Son of Man has by grace.”

Likewise, “Although in the assuming Word,” etc. Here he attacks a twofold falsehood. Since the assuming Word is a person, and the assumed man is a person, and this latter is from the Word, it seems that one person would be from another, or the same person from itself. Thus, in the Trinity, the Father is a person, the Son is a person, and the Son is from the Father; consequently, since there are two persons, one is from the other. If they were one person, the same would be from itself. But the necessity is not alike in both cases. In Christ there are two natures, one of which is from the other. In Father and Son there is one and the same nature, but distinct personalities.

This is the meaning of “Although in the assuming Word,” etc. That this argument must be understood in this way, he subtly and briefly indicates where he says, “But if there were not another nature there,” etc. Since each is called a person in itself, if there were not another nature there, then either neither man would be from Word nor Word from man, or one person there would be from another, or the same from itself.

### Epilogue of the foregoing

Having briefly run through these matters, in order that fuller acquaintance might be had with what is to be said, it remains to establish by the strongest testimonies of the saints and by arguments consonant with faith the matters which we proposed to demonstrate at the beginning. Thus, after certain preliminaries, we may now proceed to serious matters.

## CHAPTER V. Authorities that Christ is a certain man

All these things are read concerning Christ in the Psalms: “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and assumed” (*Ps.* 64). Likewise: “What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man?” (*Ps.* 8). Likewise: “You will add days upon days to the king; his years” (*Ps.* 60). Likewise: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the Son of Man whom you have strengthened for yourself” (*Ps.* 79). Likewise: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (*Ps.* 33). Likewise: “I am needy and poor” (*Ps.* 39). Likewise: “You are a priest forever” (*Ps.* 109). Likewise: “What man is he who shall live and not see death, who shall rescue his soul from the hand of hell?” (*Ps.* 83).

### Recapitulation of the preceding points

If Christ is not some man, who is this blessed man? Who is this Son of Man? Who is this blessed king? Who is this man of the right hand? Who is this poor man? Who is this priest? Who is the man who will rescue his soul from the hand of hell? Certainly, no one. But if Christ is the man of whom these things are said, Christ is some man.

Likewise, on the Psalm this statement of Cassiodorus is read: “All these things do not belong to every blessed man, but to Christ alone.” It would have been better to say: they belong to no blessed man, for they belong to no other man. And is Christ, to whom alone they belong, not some man? Likewise it is read there: “This is the complete definition of the blessed man.” But how is it a definition of the blessed man if it belongs to no blessed man? For neither Christ nor anyone else is the blessed man to whom it belongs.

Likewise the Apostle: “For if many died through the trespass of one, much more did the grace and gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound unto many” (*Rom.* 5).

Likewise Augustine, in the book *On the Trinity*: “Just as [Col. 1056D] through one man sin,” etc. (ibid.), “the Apostle argues at greater length concerning two men: the one and the same first Adam, through whose sin and death his descendants are bound; and the other, the second Adam, who is not merely man but also God.”

Likewise Augustine on John: “The first man fell, and all who have been born from him have drawn from him the concupiscence of the flesh. Another man had to be born, who drew no concupiscence: man and man, man unto death and man unto life, as the Apostle says: ‘For since death is through a man, resurrection also is through a man’ (1 Cor. XV). Through which man death, and through which resurrection? [Col. 1057A] ‘For as all die in Adam, so all shall be justified in Christ’” (ibid.).

Likewise Augustine, in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*: “The most illustrious light of predestination and grace is the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus himself. What did that man merit, that, having been assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into unity of person, he should be the only Son of God? What good of his, of whatever kind, preceded this, so that he should attain to this ineffable excellence, and so that, by the Word of God making or assuming him, the man himself should, from the moment he began to be, begin to be the only Son of God?”

Likewise: “A man becomes a Christian by grace from the beginning of his faith, just as that man was made Christ by grace from the beginning.”

Likewise Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*: “He who made that man [Col. 1057B] without any preceding merits of his so that he might contract no sin to be forgiven, either by original descent or by committing it through will—he himself, without any preceding merits of theirs, makes believers in him, to whom he forgives every sin.”

Likewise: “Therefore both that one and those whom he predestined: for he foreknew, both in him, that he should be our head, and in us, that we should be his body, not our merits that would precede, but his works that would come to pass.”

Likewise Augustine, *On the Letter and the Spirit*: “God, humble, descended through mercy, commending clear and manifest grace in that very man whom he assumed with such surpassing love above his fellows. For he himself, joined to the Word of God so that by that very union he might become one Son of God and the same one [Col. 1057C] Son of Man, did not bring this about through preceding merits of his own will.”

Likewise: “The mountain in which God is well pleased,” etc. (Ps. LXVII). Augustine: “The Word dwelt in him—that is, in the man Christ—unto the end, because he is personally united to him in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily. Thus the Word was in the flesh, so that the Word alone was said to have become flesh; that is, the man was joined to the Word into the one person of Christ.”

Likewise Augustine on John: “The firstfruits: man and man, man unto life and man unto death. That man is not God; this one is God and man.”

Likewise: “A man says to Mother Sion.” Augustine: “Behold, there is a certain man, that is, Christ, who says: ‘Sion,’ that is, the Synagogue, ‘is my mother according to [Col. 1057D] the flesh.’ And who is that man? The man who was born in her,” etc.

Likewise Augustine, in the homily on the Creed: “This was the nature of the man who was made from the Virgin; the nature of the Virgin from whom Christ was formed and born is of the same nature as the Father according to divinity.”

Likewise Haimo: “Who was predestined,” etc. (Rom. I). “Here the Apostle does not speak of the Word, but of the man, who was not before he was made.”

Likewise John Chrysostom: “Let them worship him, the man who suffered and died. These words are not said of God, but of the assumed man: ‘Let all the angels of God worship him’” (Heb. I).

Likewise, in the Gospel Caiaphas says through the Holy Spirit: “It is expedient that one man die for the people and [Col. 1058A] that the whole nation not perish” (John XI). Likewise the officers answered the Pharisees: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John VII). The centurion also cries: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark XV).

If Christ, according to the Apostle, is one man; if, according to Augustine, he is the other of the two men concerning whom the Apostle argues; if he is a man other than the first Adam; if he is a certain man who says, “Sion is my mother”; if, as is read in the Gospel, he is one man who was to die for the people: it is clear that Christ is some man. Likewise, all those authorities in which one reads of Christ, “this man,” “that man,” or something of this sort, are incongruous if Christ neither was, nor is, nor had been some man; and, because of an incompetent [Col. 1058B] demonstration or reference, they yield either no sense or an empty sense—unless perhaps they say that “this man” and “that man” are said of Christ by the same trope by which “this god” and “that god” are said of an idol. But there the participation of nature is not regarded, but naming alone. Therefore, just as an idol is God by name alone, so Christ is man by name alone. Far be it! Behold, by these and countless other authorities we are taught that Christ is some man. The same may be proved by firm reasons.

## CHAPTER VI. Arguments proving that Christ is some man

For Christ is one of men; another is not Christ; therefore some man is not Christ. [Col. 1058C] Likewise, Christ is one of certain men; therefore he is a man. Likewise, Christ is one man alone, and there are many men; therefore Christ is one of men, and consequently Christ is some man.

Likewise, in such statements as “all have turned aside,” “all sinned in Adam,” “every man is a liar”—in these, I say, and similar statements, all Catholic expositors except Christ. But if by nature another man than Christ is to be excepted, and Christ is not some man who ought to be excepted, then no man is to be excepted. Therefore, statements uttered thus without every exception are true.

Likewise, Christ is the holiest of men, the most blessed of men. These and all similar statements are false if Christ is not some man. Likewise, whoever has human nature is a man; and whoever is some being having human nature is some man. Likewise, there is some being animated by a human soul; therefore there is some man.

Likewise, someone is a son of Abraham, to whom the promises were made; Christ is not some son of Abraham; therefore the promises were made to persons other than Christ, who is not Christ. Likewise, no man redeemed us, because no other could redeem, nor is or was Christ some man who redeemed us.

Likewise, two thieves were crucified with Christ. But those two men were crucified with Christ, and no other man was then crucified; therefore only the thieves were then crucified. Far be it! But if another man was then crucified, who is this other man, since Christ is not some man?

Likewise, where the twelve apostles were [Col. 1059A] with the Lord, there were twelve men; and not only twelve, because Christ was there. Therefore, if besides the twelve some man was there, and this was Christ, Christ was some man. But if no man besides the twelve was there, only twelve men were there.

Likewise, Christ was some male person; therefore he was some man.

But perhaps, by the reasoning through which they maintain that he was not some man, they will be found also to confess that he was not some infant, some boy, or some youth. For if, they say, Christ was some man, since he was not man from eternity, he became some man in time. But if he became some man in time, he became something in time. Therefore, by similar reasoning, let them concede that he was not [Col. 1059B] some infant, because, if he began to be something in time, this is what they call absurd and impossible.

Did not the Blessed Virgin then give birth to some infant? Did righteous Simeon, receiving Christ into his arms, neither see nor hold some infant? Did the apostles and others, seeing and hearing Christ, neither see nor hear some man?

I wonder that the defenders of this phantom do not observe how little they differ from the Manichaeans. The latter taught: Christ appeared to be a man and was not a man. These teach what compels them to confess: Christ appeared to be a man and was not some man. For if he was and appeared to be a man, he certainly appeared to be so, but [Col. 1059C] he was not some man; therefore he appeared to be a man and was not some man. In the same way, he appeared to be an infant and was not some infant; he appeared to be a boy and was not some boy; he appeared to be a living man and there was not some man who lived; he was seen as a dying man and there was not some man who died; later he was seen as a man raised from the dead and there was not some man raised from the dead; that man was seen to ascend into heaven, but there was not some man who ascended into heaven.

And because those who deny that Christ was anything according to his humanity fall into errors of this sort, let us demonstrate that the truth contrary to this falsehood is fortified by authorities and reasons.

## CHAPTER VII. That Christ, insofar as he is man, is something

[Col. 1059D]

Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “God is the head of Christ. If by ‘God’ all three are understood together, how then is God the head—that is, how is the Trinity the head of Christ, when Christ is in the Trinity? Or is that which the Father is with the Son and the Holy Spirit head to that which the Son alone is? For with the Father and the Holy Spirit the Son is God; but the Son alone became man.”

Likewise Augustine on John: “He is the man who is God, because God became man; becoming what he was not, without losing what he was.”

Likewise: “The Creator of man deigned to be man; he became what he had made, lest that which he had made should perish.”

Likewise: “The angel said to Mary the Virgin: ‘That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God’” (Luke I).

[Col. 1060A] Likewise, on that passage in the Gospel of John, “But now you seek to kill me, a man,” etc. (John I), this is read from Augustine: “He does not say, as he could have said, ‘the Lord of Abraham,’ lest there be an occasion for calumny; nor ‘the Son of God,’ but what they see, whom they can apprehend.”

Likewise Augustine: “Do not be silent from me; that is, do not separate the unity of your Word from that which I am, a man.”

Likewise Augustine, on the psalm “Lord, thou hast been our refuge” (Ps. LXXXIX): “He began to be what he was not; the property of the substances being preserved, what was created remained created, what was uncreated, uncreated.”

Likewise Augustine, *On the Trinity*, on “For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come unto you” (John XVI): “It was therefore necessary that the form of a servant be removed from their eyes, for in looking upon it they thought that Christ was only what they saw.”

Likewise Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “And what could be received more gratefully than flesh made the body of our sacrifice, [Col. 1060B] of our priest? For in every sacrifice they consider four things: for whom it is offered, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, and what is offered. The same one true mediator reconciled us to God through the sacrifice of peace: he remained one with him to whom it was offered; he made one in himself those for whom he offered; and he himself was both the one who offered and that which was offered.”

Likewise Augustine on John, on “Do not touch me” (John XX): “What is this? You suppose that I am only what you see here. Do not believe thus; that is, do not touch me.”

Likewise Ambrose: “Christ, the man—what is he? That is, how great [Col. 1060C] and worthy a thing! In that you are mindful of him, making him free from sin; or, that is, also the son of man—namely, this same Christ, man from man, as God from God. What is he? Namely, how exceedingly excellent a thing, in that you visit him by raising him again.”

## Recapitulation

Behold, according to his humanity the Son is something which the Father and the Holy Spirit are not. He is what he was not, and he became what he had made. According to that same nature, he is that which was born of the Virgin; that which the Jews saw and were able to kill; and that according to which he was man, that is, the one to whom the Word was united. He is that which was created; that which was offered; that which was seen; and, moreover, a great [Col. 1060D] and worthy thing, a certain most excellent thing. How, then, insofar as he was man, was he not something? From these and countless other authorities it shines forth that Christ, insofar as he was and is man, is something; and let this be more firmly established and demonstrated by reasons.

Likewise, other arguments.

Christ, insofar as he is man, has humanity; therefore, insofar as he is man, he has some substantial quality; therefore, insofar as he is man, he is something. Likewise, Christ according to humanity is man; but to be man is to be something. Likewise, Christ is of twofold substance according to two natures, and according to each nature he is of some substance; therefore according to each nature he is something.

Likewise, Christ, insofar as he is man, is *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial with his mother; therefore, insofar as he is man, he has something substantial in common with his mother; consequently, insofar as he is man, he is something. Likewise, according to humanity Christ is man or something else; therefore, according to humanity he is something.

Likewise, insofar as he is man, he is our head; therefore, insofar as he is man, he is something above us. Likewise, insofar as he is man, he is the price by which we were redeemed; therefore, insofar as he is man, he is some price, and consequently something. Likewise, insofar as he is man, he is the sacrifice by which we were expiated; therefore, insofar as he is man, he is some sacrifice, and consequently something.

Likewise, Christ, Enoch, and Elijah are three men; therefore they are three things; therefore [Col. 1061B] insofar as he is man, Christ is one of those three; therefore, insofar as he is man, he is one thing.

Likewise, Christ is man either by name alone or by name and reality. If he is man by name alone, he is not truly man; if by reality and name, he is man.

Likewise, another argument: the substance conferred according to this nature which belongs to every man belongs to Christ. But that is not a substantial definition which is convertible with the thing defined. Therefore, if, insofar as he is man, he has received some substantial definition, insofar as he is man he has some substantial properties; consequently, insofar as he is man, he is something.

Likewise, if humanity belongs non-substantially to that man but substantially to us, then he is not of the same nature [Col. 1061C] or substance with us by reason of humanity. For just as fire, substantially hot, and water, accidentally hot, are not of the same nature or substance, so neither are we, who are substantially men, of one nature or substance with him who is not substantially man, but either accidentally man or neither accidentally nor substantially man. But if he is substantially man, and the predicate “man” is predicated of him not in the category of quality but of substance, then insofar as he is man he is something.

Likewise, certain accidents were in the man Christ; therefore there was something in Christ in which those accidents existed. But there was not some being in which they existed; therefore there was something in which those accidents existed.

Likewise, Christ’s childhood was in some subject. Therefore, if that subject existed according to humanity, Christ according to humanity was something. But if body and soul were that subject, then body or soul was a boy or a girl; consequently body or soul was some man or some woman.

Likewise, if Christ, insofar as he is man, was not something, Christ’s crucifixion and sorrow were not in some subject. Therefore only the body was crucified and the soul alone was sorrowful; nor did anything composed of those two exist which was crucified and sorrowful, nor was any other thing crucified and sorrowful there; therefore nothing was sorrowful and crucified there.

By this reasoning nothing in Christ sat and knew anything; there was no being which uttered words and understood them; there was no being which died and consequently enjoyed. Therefore [Col. 1062A] sitting, uttering, and dying belong to the body; knowing, understanding, and enjoying belong to the soul. But Christ was neither those two nor anything composed of them, nor anything at all to which those things belonged.

Again, in this assertion of theirs they differ little from the Manichaeans. The latter said: Christ appeared to be a man and was not a man; he appeared to be crucified and was not crucified; he appeared to die and did not die. These say: Christ appeared to be a man and was not something which appeared; Christ spoke and was not something which spoke; he was crucified and was not something which was crucified.

Likewise, after the resurrection the apostles saw Christ, and did not see something which was Christ; they believed that they saw and heard Christ, but they neither saw nor heard something which [Col. 1062B] was Christ. When Christ ascended on high while the apostles watched, nothing which was Christ ascended on high. For the divine substance, which alone, as they maintain, is Christ, cannot ascend or descend locally.

But because my fellow-students and countless others deny that Christ is essentially or substantially man, let this be demonstrated here, and let the arguments customarily advanced against it be refuted.

## CHAPTER VIII. Arguments proving that Christ is essentially and substantially man

If Christ is man only by outward garb—that is, if he has man as a garment—and if it is not true that he is something which is man, then these statements are not true: “God is man,” “man is God,” “God became man,” and “man became God.” For if God merely has man and is not something which is man, God is not man. And if merely the one having man is God, and not something which is essentially man, then man is not God.

Likewise, if God became man and man became God, since neither earlier nor later did God become man, man insofar as he is man became God when God became man. Man became God. But this cannot stand if the doctrine of those against whom the argument is directed is true. For when God became man—that is, became one having human nature—neither he nor another having human nature became God.

For just as a man today becomes clothed in a tunic, yet the tunic-clad person [Col. 1062D] does not become man, so, according to their view, it would have to be said that then God became man, but man did not become God; that is, properly speaking, God having human nature became God existing as man. If they spoke truly, they would not toil in such forced and ridiculous interpretations.

Likewise, if it is said that Christ or God assumed man into unity of person because, remaining the one and same person that he had been before, he received for himself as a garment flesh and soul, which he had not had before, yet in such a way that neither those two nor anything composed of them became that person: by the same reasoning it can be said that he assumed a dove into unity of person. For the Holy Spirit himself, having assumed the dove in which he appeared, remained the one and same person he had been before.

By this reasoning the same must also be said of angels whenever they appeared in bodies assumed from whatever source: namely, that they assumed those bodies into unity of person. But if they say that the nature assumed by Christ is Christ’s nature, while the nature assumed by the Holy Spirit or an angel is not so assumed that it becomes the nature of God who assumes it or of the angel, let them know that this is so because the man assumed is one person with God who assumes him. Such a union between the Holy Spirit and the dove could not occur unless the Holy Spirit truly became a dove, and the dove itself truly became the Holy Spirit. The same must be understood concerning an angel and the creature assumed.

Likewise, if Christ’s body under the species of bread is essentially Christ’s body, how much more strongly is Christ himself, under his own species, essentially man. And indeed, because that species on the altar is merely as a veil, it is not of the nature of which the body itself is, nor is the body of the nature of which that species is. Therefore similarly, if God has man merely as a veil, then, insofar as he is man, he is nevertheless of the nature of which God is—and not conversely.

But if Christ is essentially man, since every man who is truly and properly called man is substantially man, Christ also is substantially man—or else he is not truly and properly called man. Yet, they say, Christ is not truly and properly called man; for he is called man by outward garb alone and not by essence. This, as has already been proved plainly, and will be proved still more fully by what follows, is false.

Likewise, Christ according to human nature is substantial to his mother, and human nature belongs substantially to his mother; therefore it belongs substantially to Christ also. Likewise, if Christ does not have humanity as substantial to himself, as the Blessed Virgin has it, then Christ according to humanity is not of the same substance or nature as the Blessed Virgin. He has it merely as a garment; she has it as a substantial form or nature.

Likewise, nothing which is substantial to the Blessed Virgin is substantial to Christ; therefore the Son is not *homoousios* with his mother; therefore son and mother are not of the same nature or substance.

But if they demand authorities, let them hear Jerome’s statement in the sermon *Cogitis me* (“You compel me”): “The one and same only-begotten Son, remaining inseparable, is beheld in both natures, and he naturally performed what belongs to either substance according to the essential quality implanted in each.” If Christ possessed the essential quality of human substance or nature, he was man in the general sense.

Dionysius indeed says to Timothy the bishop, concerning mystical theology: “The superessential Jesus became essence through human natural truths.” Augustine, in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “He who was conceived essentially was born of the Virgin.”

Likewise, that Greek and authoritative name *homoousios* plainly declares that Christ is essentially man, when Catholics call him *homoousios*, that is, essential or of one substance—that is, nature—with his mother. But if Christ is not essentially and substantially man, [Col. 1064A] then insofar as he is man he is neither an animal, nor a body, nor a substance. That Christ, insofar as he is man, is a substance, a body, and an animal, will be shown by what follows. Yet many arguments are advanced against our saying that Christ is essentially and substantially man.

## CHAPTER IX. Objections that can and commonly are made

It is substantial to Christ to be man; therefore, when the man is destroyed, Christ is destroyed. If a parallel is demanded from us, we reply: human nature is Christ’s nature; therefore, if it is destroyed, Christ too is destroyed. This does not follow. For Jesus alone is the giant of twofold substance and twofold nature; and therefore, just as he existed before the world was made and without assumed nature, so even today he could exist without it; nor would the whole Trinity be destroyed, whatever creature might cease to exist.

Likewise, even if all those things which are substantial to him insofar as he is man were destroyed, he would nevertheless exist; otherwise God would cease to be if certain creatures did not exist. But this seems to be said against that argument: a genus does not seem to be participated in in a qualified sense, for man is not an animal in a qualified sense, nor is grammar a discipline in a qualified sense; and elsewhere, to be present in a qualified sense and not simply occurs in accident alone. Hence it does not seem right to say that anything is substantial to Christ according to his human nature unless it is substantial simply. But if it is substantial simply, when destroyed it destroys.

To this we say that God makes foolish the wisdom [Col. 1064C] of this world (1 Cor. I). For all these are philosophical claims: “If she is a virgin, she never gave birth”; “if a man has once become blind, he never afterwards sees”; “if he is God, he is not man”; “if he is visible, he is not invisible”; “if he is eternal, he is not temporal”; and countless similar propositions which seemed most true to philosophers but which all Catholics agree are utterly false. Let philosophical teachings therefore have their place in matters that proceed according to nature, not in matters which occur and have occurred miraculously contrary to nature.

### Other objections

Likewise, it may be objected: the species “man” is substantial to Christ insofar as he is man, and the two are not equal; therefore there is something superior to Christ. But if this species, or any other universal, is superior to Christ, either not all universals are creatures, or some creature is something superior to Christ.

Likewise: if some predicate is superior to Christ, something that is not God but is personally united to God is superior to Christ.

A similar argument: the predicates “soul” and “body” are superior to Christ’s soul and body; therefore either these predicates are not creatures, or certain creatures are things superior to Christ’s soul and body.

Another similar argument: if these universals are superior to Christ’s body and soul, certain things which are neither Christ nor personally united to him are superior to Christ’s soul and body.

[Col. 1065A] Here I could distinguish the equivocation of the terms. For “superior” and “inferior” are said with respect to place, order, and dignity, and perhaps in other ways. In the order either of descending from the most general genera to individuals, or of ascending from individuals to the most general genera, the predicate “man” is superior to each of its singular instances, not in place but in dignity.

But I rather judge and say this: whenever there is disputation concerning Christ, or any person in the Trinity, or the divine essence itself, and whenever there is disputation concerning the sacraments and articles of faith, everything proper to logicians ought to be set aside. Or, if such things are at times admitted lest they be wholly absent, as soon as they begin to make a clamor, they should immediately be expelled: both because, as a rule, words which do not transcend the natural clothing of reason are not appropriate to divine majesties, and because most professors of logic are troublesome interpreters of words and hunters after syllogisms. But the waters of Siloam flow silently (Isa. VIII), and in the house of the Lord the sound of neither hammer nor axe is heard (3 Kings VI).

Moreover, this statement of John of Damascus is objected: “When we speak of one nature of men, it must be understood that we do not say this by considering the account of soul and body. For it is impossible to say that body and soul are of one nature in relation to one another. But because there are very many persons of men, and all receive the same account of nature—for all are composed of soul and body, all share the nature of soul, and possess the substance of body—we call the common species of many distinct persons one nature: namely, the nature of each person, who has two natures, namely soul and body, and exists perfectly in two natures. But in the Lord Jesus Christ one cannot take a common species; for no other Christ has been made, is, or ever will be; rather, Christ, from divinity and humanity and in divinity and humanity, is perfect God and the same perfect man.”

Here they suppose that John of Damascus says and thinks the same thing: that the species “man” does not belong to Christ. Hence they state more confidently that he was not substantially man, nor something insofar as he is man. But if they examined the whole sequence of this authority more carefully, they would clearly discover that it teaches only this: just as every species or one nature is in all men and in each individual man, because individual men also exist perfectly in two natures, namely soul and body, so in Christ one cannot take a common species or one nature. Rather, because he consists of divinity and humanity, it adds: “For no other Christ has been made,” etc.; by these words it rightly shows that Christ is God and man, and that he has nothing in common with others in this respect.

Otherwise, if it intended to say and prove that the species “man” does not belong to Christ, then by the reasoning by which it proves this, it could likewise be proved that divinity does not belong to Christ. For just as he is not man only, so neither is he God only; but he is perfect [Col. 1066A] man and perfect God.

But it seems rather to argue against heretics who said that in Christ there is one species or nature composed from two. Hence the same John says: “The natures are united to one another without conversion and without alteration: neither does the divine nature depart from its own simplicity, nor is the human nature converted into the nature of divinity or divided into non-existence, nor is one composite nature made from the two. For a composite nature cannot be *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial, with either of the natures from which it is composed, since it completes one from the other; just as a body composed of four elements is called neither fire nor earth nor air nor water, nor is it said to be *homoousios* with any of these.

“If therefore, according to the heretics, Christ became of one composite nature after the union, then he has been converted from a simple nature into a composite one; and he will be *homoousios* neither with the Father, who is of simple nature, nor with his mother; nor will he be called either God or man, but Christ only. And this nature, namely Christ, will be not his person’s nature but one composite nature according to them. But we do not teach that Christ is of one composite nature; rather, we say that “Christ” designates a person, not *monotropos*—that is, said in one way—but as signifying two natures, divinity and humanity. From divinity and humanity, we confess that he is and is called the same perfect God and perfect man, from two and in two natures.”

Behold, here he plainly shows that the nature “Christ” does not signify one composite nature, but two natures and one person of two natures.

Hence above he said: “In the Lord Jesus Christ one cannot take a common species,” namely, one composite nature from divinity and humanity. Or perhaps he said, “In Christ one cannot take a common species,” because a species is the whole being of individuals and common to all its individuals. But the species “man” is not the whole being of Christ, because he is God and man, which is not common to him with others. “For no other Christ has been made,” etc.

But Boethius, against Eutyches and Nestorius, says that there are two natures in Christ, two specific differences, as if he meant substantial differences. For God is not a species, nor is divinity a specific difference, nor even a proper difference, since it is a substance. Humanity, however, is much more properly a specific difference, or a substantial quality, by which it may be called a substance. Yet this is maintained by those who understand humanity in Christ not as a nature or property common to him with other men, but as either soul, flesh, or these two together. But these matters will be discussed in their proper place.

Behold, Boethius says that the specific difference, namely divinity, belongs to Christ. But if a specific difference belongs to him, the species itself also belongs to him. Therefore, since everything that seems to oppose the proposed truth is most easily refuted, it must confidently be maintained that Christ is essentially and substantially man, just as he is essentially [Col. 1067A] and substantially God; and thus, as he is something insofar as he is God, so he is something insofar as he is man. But that according to these two natures he is one thing and another rests upon sacred authorities and most solid foundations.

## CHAPTER X. That Christ is one thing and another
Augustine on John: “The Word of God is one thing, man another; but the Word was made flesh, that is, man. Therefore the person of the Word is not one and that of man another, since both are Christ and there is one person.”

The same, to Felicianus: “The Son of God is one thing, the son of man another, but not another.”

Likewise: “The Son of God is one thing from the Father, another from the mother.”

Likewise Pope Leo: “Although Christ remains one from eternity, nevertheless he began to be another in time; yet these meet in unity and can have neither separation nor end.” [Col. 1067B]

Likewise Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “The form of God received the form of a servant: both are God, both are man; but both are God because of the God who received, both are man because of the man received.”

The same, in *On the Trinity*: “When it is read, ‘the Word was made flesh’ (John 1), I understand the true Son of God; in the flesh I recognize the true son of man: both together, God and man, joined in one person by the bounty of ineffable grace.”

The same, on John: “We know both in Christ: that by which he is equal to the Father, and that by which the Father is greater than he. The one is the Word, the other flesh; the one is God, the other man; and Christ is one, God and man.”

The same, on John: “Whoever believes in me,” etc. (John 6): “Because he appeared as a man, God lay hidden in the man, lest they suppose that he was only what they saw. He wishes himself to be believed to be only such as the Father is and as great as the Father is.” [Col. 1067C]

The same, on the psalm, “I will exalt thee, O Lord, because thou hast upheld me” (Psalm 29): “Christ is neither only God nor only man, as various heretics have taught, but true God and true man; yet he is not two, but one Christ.”

Likewise Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “Christ Jesus is God from God, but man born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary; in both substances, namely divine and human, he is the only Son of God the almighty Father, from whom both proceed as one; but one thing on account of the Word, another on account of man—not two sons, God and man, but one Son of God: God without beginning, man from a definite beginning.” [Col. 1067D]

The same, on John: “Let us recognize the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and the human, by which the Father is greater; yet both together are not two, but one Christ.”

The same, in *On Faith to Peter*: “Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the Word of God, which was made flesh, remains in two natures without confusion: one divine, which he has in common with the Father; the other human, according to which he says, ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 14).”

Likewise, in *On the Trinity*: “Since the Son is God and man, God is one substance, man another.”

The same, on John: “Soul and body are two things, but one man; Word and man are two things, but one Christ.” [Col. 1068A]

Likewise Boethius, *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*: “If you understand Christ as man, he is both God and man: God by nature, man by assumption; and in him there are a double nature and a double substance, since man and God are one person, since he is the same man and God.”

But here those who oppose us rise up, because Boethius says: “God is God by nature, man by assumption,” as though this meant that Christ is God by nature, but man not by nature, rather by assumption—which is untrue. Therefore Boethius distinguished it thus: God is by nature and not by assumption; but man is by nature in such a way as also to be by assumption. Just as it is said: God is God by nature; the Savior is by grace. For being God belongs solely to nature; being Savior belongs to nature in such a way as also to grace. [Col. 1068B]

If they themselves answer: “How is Christ man by nature, but God by assumption?”—Christ is not man, that is, Christ possessing man, by possessing man through nature and God through assumption; rather, he is God by nature and man by assumption. How much truer, then, is what we hold with Boethius: that that man is man by his own nature, but God by assumption—that is, because he has been assumed by God into unity of person and is himself the same God. God is by his proper nature, but man by assumption—that is, because he assumed man.

Assumption does not exclude nature, but indicates the mode of possessing a nature. He who is God through eternal nature is man through a nature assumed in time. [Col. 1068C]

From the foregoing it is clearly demonstrated that Christ is one thing and another, and that one substance is one and another substance another. Hence it is plain that, insofar as he is man, he is one thing, and insofar as he is God, another. Likewise, insofar as he is man, he is one substance, and insofar as he is God, another substance.

Otherwise, if Christ is not one thing and another, Christ is not God and man. For if Christ is God and not another, Christ is only God; likewise, if Christ is man and not another, Christ is only man. Therefore, if Christ is God and not another, or man and not another, Christ is not God and man. If Christ is God and man, therefore Christ is God and another, and is man and another; consequently Christ is one thing and another. [Col. 1068D]

## CHAPTER XI. Certain statements which seem contrary to these

Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “What good will and what good works preceded, by which that man deserved to become one person with God? Was he previously a man, and was this singular benefit granted him, that he might singularly deserve God? Surely, from the time he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and that the only Son, and therefore the Word of God—because the flesh assumed by him was indeed made God; or, just as any man is one person, namely a rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, God and man?”

Likewise Hilary, in *On the Trinity*: “I ask whether the Son of Man is the same as the Son of God, and why the son of man is not another and the Son of God another, the Word made flesh. And I ask who was glorified in this son of man, who is also the Son of God.” [Col. 1069A]

We judge that this can be resolved without special pleading as follows: just as Augustine uses “three” for “three persons,” so here *aliud* (“another thing”) is used for *alius* (“another person”), as is evident from what follows.

Augustine also concludes his statement thus: “One person, God and man”; he does not say one substance or one nature. Hilary’s statement is understood similarly; or because Hilary does not simply say, “the son of man is not another, nor the Son of God another,” but immediately adds, “the Word was made flesh.” He does not deny that the son of man is one thing and the Son of God another; rather, he says that Christ the man is not one thing and God-man another. [Col. 1069B]

For when it is said, “God is one thing, man another,” the difference of natures is shown; but when it is said, “God-man,” or “the Word flesh,” the unity of person is expressed in such a way that both natures are designated. Therefore one must not say, “the son of man is one thing, the Son of God—the Word made flesh—another,” lest a third nature in Christ be understood in addition to the divine and human.

Or this is why it is said that the Son of God is not one thing and the Son of Man another: because there is nothing in the Son of God which is not in the son of man, nor conversely—although the Son of God is one thing and another, and the son of man is one thing and another. Just as the Son of God is not of a different nature from the son of man, although both the son of man and the Son of God are of one nature and another nature.

But where it is elsewhere said, “The Son of God is one thing, the son of man another,” it must be understood thus: the Son of God is one thing insofar as he is Son of God; the son of man is another insofar as he is son of man—not that anything is Son of God which is not son of man, or conversely.
