Or thus: “The Son of God is one thing, the son of man another,” that is, this nature is one and that nature another. For essential terms are often found used in place of personal terms, and personal terms in place of essential ones. [Col. 1069C]

Likewise Jerome, in the letter beginning, “You compel me, O Paula and Eustochium”: “Those who regarded two sons—or certainly another Christ than the Son of God—could not carefully understand and see the height of so great a mystery.”

Here Jerome seems to agree with those who said that Christ is nothing other than God, nothing other than the Son of God, [Col. 1069D] and thus that Christ is not one thing and another. Here too we may say that he used one grammatical gender for another; hence some books more plainly read *alium* (“another person”), not *aliud* (“another thing”). Or perhaps this authority strikes at two heresies: first, that of those who say that there are two persons in Christ, as though there were two natures, and therefore maintain that there are two sons, one the Son of God and the other the son of man; second, that of those who believe Christ to be merely a creature.

It seems that this should be understood thus: “They regarded Christ as altogether other than the Son of God,” that is, as something disparate, namely merely that which is not the Son of God. For they regarded him as only a creature and not the Son of God. Against them stands the familiar declaration: “The Son is from the Father alone, not made or created, but begotten.”

Likewise, in the same letter: “God thirsted and drank, and was mingled and united in the womb of the Virgin without corruption of himself, so that Christ might be one, God and man; so that there might be one person and one substance.” [Col. 1070A]

Here it should be noted that many today corruptly read *substantia* (“substance”) in place of *subsistentia* (“subsistence”), whereas Jerome himself uses *substantia* as the Greeks use *hypostasis*, but *substantia* or *essentia* as they use *ousia*. This is evident to anyone reading the entire letter itself.

Nevertheless, if anyone considers that the multitude of books should be believed, namely that Jerome wrote “one person and one substance,” let him without hesitation understand *substance* as *subsistence*, that is, as person, according to the idiom of Greek speech. Thus Augustine says in Book V of *On the Trinity*: “Most of our writers who treat in the Greek language are accustomed to say *μία οὐσία, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις*—one essence, three hypostases—which in Latin is ‘one essence, three substances.’ But since our usage of speech has now established that, when we say essence, the same is understood as when we say substance, we do not dare to say one essence and three substances, but one essence or substance and three persons.” [Col. 1070B]

Likewise, in Book VII: “For the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might in some way be able to speak, the Greeks said one essence and three substances, that is, one *ousia*, three *hypostases*. For Greeks understand substance differently from Latins. Latins have said one essence or substance, three persons, because in our speech, that is, in Latin, essence is not usually understood differently from substance.”

But if Jerome asserted one substance alone in Christ, that is, one nature or essence, he would be contrary not only to other Catholics but also to himself. For in the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith* he says: “Thus we confess that in Christ there is one person of the Son, while declaring that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely deity and humanity, which humanity consists of soul and body.”

I wonder that Master Peter Lombard subscribed to this authority.

See: here he openly shows that by “humanity” soul and body are understood. Therefore those are mistaken who contend that by the name “humanity” is signified not a substance but some property from which man receives his name. [Col. 1070D]

For if Jerome thought this, he would say not two but three substances. For if the humanity which he says consists of soul and body were not some nature—that is, a substantial property—but a substance, it would be either body or soul. Yet, as they say, nothing in Christ can consist of these; nor does body consist of body and soul, nor soul of body and soul.

Therefore we say that this authority should rather be understood thus: “We confess that in Christ there is one person of the Son, while declaring that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely deity and humanity”—that is, God and man, which man consists of soul and body. Or alternatively, “two substances,” that is, two natures, namely deity and humanity, understood intransitively—that is, which are deity and humanity. This humanity consists of soul and body, that is, of the nature of soul and the nature of body; for humanity is a nature composed of the nature of body and the nature of soul. [Col. 1071A]

But what is that substance which Master Peter says is signified by the name “humanity”? By what reasoning does it signify soul more than body, or body more than soul? Why is Christ’s humanity not something, but some things?

Likewise, when it is said, “Christ’s humanity is soul; Christ’s humanity is body; Christ’s humanity is body and soul,” body is the same as soul, and body is the same as body and soul. But these expressions are true, and the same subject is posited in them. Likewise soul is the same as body and soul.

But Christ’s humanity is numerically one. Therefore, if it is soul, it is not body; and if it is body, it is not soul. Likewise, Christ’s humanity is only one substance; therefore it is not soul and body. But if one thing is asserted here, “Christ’s humanity is body,” and another here, “Christ’s humanity is soul,” there is not one humanity nor one thing which is Christ’s body and soul, or which consists of them. It would be more proper to say that Christ is of three natures rather than two; for there are three natures: divine nature, the nature of soul, and the nature of body. And he would have to be called of three substances rather than two. [Col. 1071B]

Therefore those are rather mistaken who deny that the name “humanity” signifies the substantial property from which man receives his name. But, as we said before, Master Peter was thought to have maintained this either in his writings or in disputations; [Col. 1071C] afterward he left it to us not for assertion, but for more careful discussion or examination. Therefore Christ is one thing and another, and one substance and another; otherwise, if there were only divine substance, he would be neither animal nor body.

## CHAPTER XII. Authorities proving that Christ is an animal and a body

That Christ is an animal, Bede says on Mark: “I will build another [thing] not made with hands” (Mark 14): “The Lord said, ‘I will raise up a living animal,’ signifying a living and breathing temple.”

Likewise, that he is body—that is, corporeal substance—Jerome says on another Gospel passage in Matthew: “And Peter, descending from the boat,” etc. (Matthew 14): “Behold Peter walks upon the waters. Therefore do not doubt that Christ is one body, even though he walks upon the waters.” [Col. 1071D]

Likewise, Christ assumed sorrow by will, not necessity, just as he assumed flesh; for he was sorrowful, as the Gospel says. For if he was not sorrowful when the Gospel says, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26), then when it says, “Jesus slept” (Matthew 8), he did not sleep; or when he is said to have eaten (Mark 2), he did not eat. Thus nothing sound remains, so that it may even be said that Christ was not body.

Likewise, on Luke: “The body of Christ is a grain of mustard seed” (Luke 17), because Joseph received it and buried it in the garden, and it afterward grew in the resurrection and ascension, spreading out branches—that is, sending preachers throughout the whole world. But here Christ’s body does not seem to be understood as that part of man which, together with soul, constitutes man. For that part did not send preachers; rather, that whole being did, namely the corporeal substance which is a certain whole composite, which is Christ. [Col. 1072A]

Let no one insult the holy doctors because of Aristotle’s dictum: “They sometimes err by placing the whole among the parts, as when they call animal a sensible body.” For a part is in no way predicated of a whole; therefore body will not be the genus of animal, because it is a part.

Here many chatter that no man is a body, as though they understood these matters better than Porphyry, Boethius, and all the other interpreters or expositors of Aristotle. [Col. 1072B]

Nor do they notice that “body” is understood in many ways. Sometimes it signifies a certain continuous quantity; sometimes it means the same as corporeal substance; sometimes the part of an animal which, together with soul, constitutes the animal; sometimes a corpse; sometimes a collection, as when it is said, “the people are one body.”

Aristotle speaks against those who said that the part of an animal was the genus of animal. There were some who said that animal was nothing other than the body of an animal. Others said that animal was nothing other than the soul of an animal; hence, wherever there is no one to whom the contrary opinion belonged, “the body of each is this . . .” [the text is defective]. Certainly, as we have learned from scholars, among the Greeks it is evident that in that definition, “sensible body,” insofar as Aristotle criticizes it, “body” is understood in one expression not merely as all bodies, but as the part of an animal. [Col. 1072C]

But that Christ, according to his humanity, is a certain whole is proved both by authorities and by arguments.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Christ is a whole or composite being

Augustine on John: “The Lord Jesus Christ was the whole of what was seen, touched, and crucified. Is he this whole? He indeed is, but not wholly. What the Jews saw was not the whole Christ. And what is the whole Christ? ‘In the beginning was the Word’” (John 1).

The same, in the same work: “Because man consists of flesh and soul, and the whole man is in Christ—for he would not have assumed the inferior part and abandoned the superior. For the soul is the superior part of man, rather than the body. Therefore, because the whole man is in Christ, what is Christ, I ask? Word and man. What are Word and man? Word, soul, and flesh.” [Col. 1072D]

Likewise John Chrysostom: “Therefore, because children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same, that is, in the children, because he was made a child consisting of flesh and soul.”

Likewise Augustine on John: “The Word was made flesh—that is, God was made man in a rational soul and flesh. For it is the usage of Scripture sometimes to signify the whole man by soul alone, sometimes by flesh alone: by soul alone, as ‘Jacob went down into Egypt in seventy souls’ (Genesis 46); by flesh alone, as Isaiah says (chapter 52), ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God.’ Thus ‘the Word was made flesh’ was said as though it were said, ‘God was made man.’” [Col. 1073A]

The same: “Man is joined to God and becomes one person, so that he is not a demigod—God in part by reason of God and man in part by reason of man—but wholly God and wholly man.”

Likewise Hilary: “It was acquired for man that he might be God. Was it acquired for his divinity? Was it for soul or flesh? Certainly not; but for the man consisting of both.”

The same: “We do not doubt that Christ is God the Word; nor, again, do we fail to know that the son of man consists of soul and body.”

Jerome, in the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*: “But we confess that in Christ there is one person of the Son, while declaring that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely deity and humanity, which humanity consists of soul and body.” [Col. 1073B]

Likewise Anastasius [read: Athanasius]: “Cursed be anyone who does not confess that the whole man whom the Son of God assumed rose again from the dead on the third day, newly assumed and liberated. Amen, amen.”

The same: “Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Arguments proving the same

Christ has a human body; it consists of its parts; therefore those parts are parts of Christ, or of something which is Christ.

Likewise, Christ has human members—head, arms, and so forth. Those are members of Christ; therefore they are parts of Christ.

Likewise, since Christ is man, he is either man having parts or man having none. If he has no parts, then, since it is natural for man to have parts, Christ lacks parts. If he lacks all the parts of man, he lacks body and soul—which be far from us!

Likewise, Christ has a certain stature, which is not, nor can be, that of a simple thing; therefore Christ is a composite thing. [Col. 1073C]

Likewise, Christ is greater, according to the body’s three dimensions, than some composite thing; therefore either some simple thing is greater according to these three dimensions than some composite thing, or Christ is composite.

Likewise, if Christ did not grow without the increase of his members, neither did he grow without the increase of his parts. Therefore some part of him grew; therefore he was some whole, or composite being.

But astonishing is the dullness of men who do not notice that no man—not even a man’s finger—can exist without being composite; how much less can a whole and complete man exist without being composite. Nor does it escape us that Christ is called whole or composite in another sense. [Col. 1073D]

## CHAPTER XV. Arguments to the same effect

Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*: “Christ’s person consists and is constituted from God and man, since Christ himself is one God and true man.”

The same, in *On the Trinity*: “From both the substance of divinity and that of humanity there is one and the same God, Jesus Christ, Son of God and of man: as true God, so also true man.”

Likewise: “Human nature could be joined to God in such a way that from two substances one person might be made; and thereby he consists of three: God, soul, and flesh.” [Col. 1074A]

Likewise John Damascene: “In our Lord Jesus Christ we recognize two natures, but one hypostasis, composed from both. Therefore Christ was incarnate from the Virgin, assuming the first-fruits of our mass, so that the hypostasis of the flesh itself became the hypostasis of God the Word, and the hypostasis of the Word, previously simple, became composite—composite, moreover, from two perfect natures, deity and humanity.”

The same: “We confess that these two natures are united with one another in the one composite hypostasis of the Son of God.”

The same: “From deity and humanity we confess him both to be and to be called perfect God and perfect man, the same one from two and in two natures.”

Likewise Augustine: “Christ is truth in such a way that, when you take him as a whole, the Word is true, the soul true, the flesh true, God true, man true.”

The same: “Not only the Word of God and the flesh of man, but also the rational soul of man—and this whole—is God by reason of God and man by reason of man.” [Col. 1074B]

Likewise Boethius, in *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*: “If God and man are diverse substances, and yet the name Christ is one in both, we do not believe that a conjunction of diverse substances has produced one person; the name Christ is equivocal and cannot be confined by any definition. But in what Scriptures is the name Christ never generated? What new thing was effected through the Savior’s advent? For Catholics acknowledge both the truth of faith and the rarity of the miracle. For how great and how new is it—something that could happen once and in no other age—that he who alone is God by nature should unite with human nature, which was most unlike him, and that thus from natures far apart one person should be made by union.” [Col. 1074C]

But according to Nestorius’s opinion, what new thing occurred? “Divinity and humanity,” he says, “preserve their own persons. For when did divinity not have its own person, and humanity its own person? And when will they not?”

And shortly afterward: “But if no one person has been joined from man and God, then [the same applies to] all the saints, namely men.”

## Recapitulation of the preceding discussion

[Col. 1074D] In these passages, as I said, “whole” or “composite” is understood very differently from the sense above. There Christ is said to be a whole, to consist, and to be composite as from parts, and this according to humanity alone. Here, however, not as from parts but as from natures: this does not here signify the integral constitution of any thing, as it more often does, but only the personal union of diverse natures.

Augustine made this clear in the authority: “Christ’s person consists and is constituted from God and man.” For he immediately added: “Since Christ himself is true God and true man,” as though saying, “We say this because the one person of Christ is of two natures.”

Now because those against whom our argument is directed consider it impious and heretical for anyone, in whatever sense, to say that Christ was made, created, or is any creature, let them patiently hear the testimonies of the saints concerning these matters—testimonies greater than every exception and contradiction. [Col. 1075A]

## CHAPTER XVI. Authorities to the same effect

The Apostle: “Who was made for him from the seed of David” (Romans 1).

Likewise: “Made from a woman” (Galatians 4).

Likewise: “Put on the new man, who was created according to God” (Ephesians 4), which Haimo expounds concerning Christ.

Likewise Haimo: “The Apostle does not speak of the Word, but of the man who was not before he was made.”

Leo, in the sermon *Let Us Rejoice in the Lord*: “The birth of the child brought forth for the salvation of the human race.”

Augustine, against Maximianus: “Christ, the God of our Lord Jesus Christ according to his humanity, was born from a Virgin, so that he might not only be Father to him whom he begot, but also be God to him whom he created as man from his mother’s womb.” [Col. 1075B]

The same, on John: “As he created Mary and was created through Mary, so he gave baptism to John and was afterward baptized by John. In this is the great mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ: that he was made in time for our sake, through whom times were made; made among all things, through whom all things were made; made what he made. For he was made man, who had made man, lest what he had made should perish.”

Jerome, on Jeremiah, “God created a new thing upon the earth” (Jeremiah 31): “Note,” he says, “that the Savior’s birth and the conception of God are called a creation in the Book of Wisdom: ‘First of all she was created’ (Ecclesiasticus 1). This is expounded thus: ‘Created according to humanity in the counsel of God the Father,’ that is, it was predestined to be incarnate for the salvation of the human race.” [Col. 1075C]

Thereupon it is immediately added: “It should be noted, however, that on account of the unity of person Christ is sometimes called begotten and sometimes created.”

Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “Therefore God—that is, the divine essence or Trinity—is the head of Christ according to his humanity, because divinity, as creator, is the head of the assumed creature. By this interpretation the Son’s godliness is not diminished, but his mercy is proclaimed.”

Likewise, on the Apostle’s words, “See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Colossians 2), Augustine says: “The philosophers taught that God cannot become a creature, that a man cannot be born of a virgin, or that one who has died cannot come to life again.” [Col. 1075D]

Leo, in another homily: “O wondrous and exquisite offspring! O new and incredible union! God, who is and was Creator, becomes a creature; he who is immeasurable is contained; he who makes others rich becomes poor; he is clothed in a body.”

Likewise Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “The one through whom every creature was made, having been made a creature, had to have every creature as witness.”

Likewise, *On the Trinity*: “It belonged to the justice and goodness of the Creator that the devil should be overcome through the same rational creature whom he rejoiced to have overcome, and through one coming from the very race which, because of its corrupted origin, he held wholly under wrath.”

The same: “‘In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily’ (Colossians 2): ‘all,’ that is, in every mode of indwelling, so that it is also united personally, which is not so in any other creature.” [Col. 1076A]

The same: “‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 16). He set God the Father above not only his flesh but also the human mind which he bore; that whole [humanity] is without doubt recognized as the form of a servant, since every creature serves the Creator.”

The same, in *On the Trinity*, on “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me” (John 6): “How in him? How not in him? How can something so contrary and opposed to itself be understood? ‘Whoever believes in me’ believes not in this which he sees, lest our hope be in a creature, but in him who assumed the creature in which he might appear to human eyes.”

Jerome on Mark: “The Spirit remained upon him. This is the anointing of Christ according to the flesh, concerning which it is said, ‘God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness,’ etc. (Psalm 44). Oil cannot be beneath water, nor the Creator beneath the creature.” [Col. 1076B]

See: Jerome here compares the Spirit to oil, and Christ the man to water. Thus he wishes to show that it was fittingly said, “The Spirit remained upon him,” not beneath him; because, as oil cannot be beneath water, so the creating Spirit cannot be beneath Christ, a creature.

Likewise Augustine, in the sermon *On Physicists*: “Let it not offend you that he says ‘made,’ when we confess ‘born’; for we confess him to have been made only as man. But God is always making. He does not know how to be made so as to exist; rather, he is made to be something for someone, as it is said: ‘Lord, thou hast become a refuge to us’ (Psalm 89). When was he made who was never made? But the Lord Jesus Christ was made in order to be man; so that he who was always Creator might be creature. Remaining God, he was made man, that he might become what he was not, so that what he was might not perish. Therefore he says ‘made’ on account of the assumption of the creature.” [Col. 1076C]

The same, on John: “When he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father: to God, his Creator insofar as he is man, and to his Father insofar as he is God.”

Likewise Isaiah (chapter 45): “Drop down, ye heavens, from above,” etc., through “I, the Lord, created him.”

Likewise Augustine, on “God, thy God, hath anointed thee” (Psalm 44): “The Greek makes it clear, and it must be understood thus: ‘O God, thy God,’ that is, thy Creator.”

The same: “‘And for them I sanctify myself’ (John 16), that is, I sanctify myself as man in myself as Word, which is from the beginning of his creation, when the Word was made flesh.” [Col. 1076D]

## CHAPTER XVII. Authorities which appear contrary

All these authorities plainly declare that Christ was made, created, or is a creature, although certain scriptural testimonies, if considered merely on their surface, seem to present a certain contradiction.

Augustine: “He through whom every creature was made is not a creature.”

Likewise: “‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1), not ‘In the beginning he made the Word,’ as [he made] heaven and earth. See: therefore he is not a creature.”

Likewise, in Book I of *On the Trinity*: “‘All things were made through him’ (ibid.). It is plainly apparent that he through whom all things were made was not himself made; and if he was not made, he is not a creature,” etc. [Col. 1077A]

The same: “‘Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain’ (Exodus 20). His name must not be taken in vain, so that we suppose that he was made, through whom all things were made.”

Likewise Ambrose, in Book I of *On the Trinity*: “Let us prove,” he says, “that the Son of God was created. Where are those who call Christ a creature? For if he had been created, he would be subject to vanity. Therefore Christ is not a creature, because, as the Apostle attests, every creature is subject to vanity” (Romans 8).

Likewise Anastasius [read: Athanasius]: “Not made, not created, but begotten.”

But this apparent contradiction is easily resolved according to Augustine’s rule in *On the Trinity*: “Therefore,” he says, “having learned this rule for understanding the Scriptures concerning the Son of God, let us understand what in them is said according to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, and what according to the form of a servant which he received, in which he is less than the Father.” [Col. 1077B]

“We are not troubled as though the sayings of the holy books contradicted and opposed one another. For according to the form of God, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, because neither is a creature. But according to the form of a servant, he is less than the Father, because he himself said, ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 14). He is less than himself, because he emptied himself (Matthew 12); less than the Holy Spirit, because he himself said, ‘By the Spirit of God I cast out demons’ (Luke 3). And again, ‘The Spirit of the Lord,’ he says, ‘is upon me’ (ibid.). According to the form of God all things were made through him; according to the form of a servant he himself was made from a woman, made under the law,” etc. [Col. 1077C]

Therefore, [lacuna], following this as a useful rule, we say that all authorities which affirm that Christ was created or is a creature must be referred to his humanity; but wherever anything of this kind is denied, it must without doubt be referred to his divinity. Thus Augustine himself says in the same work: “What is said of him in respect of what, and what according to what, let the prudent, diligent, and devout reader understand, with the Lord’s help.”

Gregory likewise, on “He has risen; he is not here” (Mark 16): “‘He is not here,’” he says, “by the presence of the flesh, though he is nowhere absent by the presence of his majesty. See: there he was according to divinity, and there he was not according to humanity.”

[Col. 1077D] If, therefore, anyone examines this rule carefully, he will see that in such matters there is no contradiction or inconsistency. This applies especially to the authorities and arguments by which holy authors or doctors prove, against the Arians, that Christ or the Son of God is not a creature. For they say that Christ, the Son of God, is adopted, not begotten, but made and created. Master Hugh of St Victor gives this reason why Christ is not a creature:

> “To be a creature,” he says, “is to be something from nothing; that is, to be something that previously was from nothing. Yet not everyone who begins to be something begins to be because he begins to be something. Just as one who ceases to be something does not on that account cease because he ceases to be something. [Col. 1078A] He does not cease to be something in such a way as to become nothing, but only so that what he ceases to be is no longer. Likewise, not everyone who begins to be something begins, as it were, to be so that he may be something, but so that something which previously was not may begin to be and now exist. Thus, when Christ began to be, he did not nevertheless begin to be something in such a way that he had previously not been something; for before that which at some time began to be was what it was, there was something which always was and never began.”

Near the end of the chapter he adds:

> “Paul,” says Ambrose in the book *On the Trinity*, “forbids me to serve a creature and instructs me to serve Christ. For Christ was not a creature.”

And shortly afterward:

> “See, therefore, how he affirms that Christ was both made and created in one respect, although he denies that he is a creature.”

[Col. 1078B] In this chapter that venerable master testifies that Christ began in time to be something which he had not previously been, and that Christ was made and created. But he gives another reason than that which we set forth above why Christ ought not to be called a creature. Yet since Ambrose himself, upon whose authority he relies, as was shown above in the preceding discussion, elsewhere asserts that Christ was created, and Augustine and all other holy doctors agree in this assertion, the former solution according to Augustine’s Rule seems preferable.

But an objection still remains: if Christ is something created, then he is something later and less than the Father; and this is contrary to the saying: “In the Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less.” Again, if [Col. 1078C] Christ is something created, he is something different from the Father; but in the Trinity there is no difference, no diversity, but harmony and primordial unity. Likewise, Christ is of some created nature; therefore he is of a later and lesser nature than the Father. Again, he is of some created nature; therefore he is of another nature than the Father. Or thus: the nature of the Son is created, whereas that of the Father is not; therefore the nature of the Son differs from the nature of the Father.

All these points and others of the same sort are easily resolved according to the aforesaid rule of Augustine: because Christ is of a twofold nature, it matters what is said of God and in what respect it is said.

Again, Ambrose: If Christ was something personally united, then, once Christ had died, did that thing exist or not? [Col. 1078D] If it existed when Christ had died, then, since it was nothing other than a certain whole composed of soul and flesh, that whole or composite existed then. But if that single thing did not then exist, it lost the enjoyment of God and the personal union which it had possessed. Yet it could not merit such goods without sin; therefore either that united thing sinned, or God unjustly deprived it of so great and such a good.

Here I might say that that whole existed wonderfully in its separated parts, just as, even when locally separated, individual human beings are nonetheless one people; and when individual heads are scattered, they are nonetheless one flock; just as bread, when cut, does not perish but exists in its parts; and wine, when poured into different vessels, remains that same wine, though divided among different vessels. What wonder, then, if Christ, [Col. 1079A] though the parts of the human being were torn apart, was wholly human, since even when dead he lived, and in death, as before, was perfect God and perfect man?

It is nevertheless more probable that, in his integrity and totality, he temporarily ceased to exist, but rose again on the third day in a better state. This follows by the same justice according to which even the saints, in accordance with their good merits, after the bonds of body and soul have been dissolved, are nevertheless deferred from the glory of resurrection through long courses of time. Anastasius seems to have thought concerning Christ that some whole temporarily ceased to exist. He says: “Cursed be he who says that the whole human being whom the Son of God assumed was assumed anew”—that is, the one who in death was laid aside is said to have been assumed in the resurrection; for then the one whom he had assumed [Col. 1079B] into his person he assumed into glory. Hence comes the phrase concerning the “morning assumption,” that is, the resurrection accomplished in the morning.

There is also read, on the Gospel passage in John, chapter 10, “I lay down my life,” etc., this statement of Augustine:

> “The Word, from the time when he assumed the human being—that is, flesh and soul—never laid down the soul, so that the soul might be separated from the Word; rather, when he expired, the flesh laid down the soul, and when it returned, he rose. Death therefore temporarily separated flesh and soul, but neither from the Word of God.”

Perhaps this is why, after saying “he assumed the human being,” he explained it thus: “that is, flesh and soul,” but said that he separated neither from the Word of God. Perhaps, after saying “he assumed the human being,” he immediately added “that is, flesh [Col. 1079C] and soul,” lest the following phrase, namely, “he never laid down,” be understood of the composite of flesh and soul, which did not exist during those three days—unless it is said figuratively to have existed in its parts, because its parts, although separated from each other, were nevertheless on earth.

What in such matters may or ought properly or figuratively to be said, let the prudent and diligent reader understand.

It may also be understood more simply: “He assumed the human being,” that is, flesh and soul, so that by this explanation different heresies may be struck down. For some said that God received only a human soul; others, only human flesh. But beyond doubt, he who made the whole human being in order to restore the whole human being assumed the whole. Therefore, after saying that the Word assumed the human being, lest anyone who heard the name “human being” should understand merely a part of the human being, [Col. 1079D] he adds: “that is, flesh and soul”—not flesh without soul, nor soul without flesh. For, as Augustine says:

> “For our sake he became a true and complete human being: true because he possesses a true human nature; complete because he assumed human flesh and a rational soul.”

It therefore remains firm and indissoluble that Christ was made and created in time, and hence it is also read that Christ, or that human being, did not always exist.

## Chapter XVIII. Authorities proving that Christ did not always exist

On the psalm “May God hear thee” (Psalm 19), this authority is read:

> “When he says, ‘We shall rejoice, [Col. 1080A] we shall be magnified,’ the Prophet shows that he is one of the Church so long before Christ.”

Likewise, Augustine and other holy doctors unanimously teach that certain members preceded the head, that is, Christ, and others followed him, in accordance with the saying: “Those who went before and those who followed cried out: Hosanna to the Son of David” (Mark 11). If the ancient righteous preceded Christ in time, they existed before Christ.

Again, Augustine on John: “At some time the Son of God had . . . of human …” “The same Son of Man was not yet a human being; he was not always the Son of Man, and afterwards he began to have what the Son of God had. But from the time that he existed, he had wholly what the Son of God had; the Son of Man did not always have what the Son of God was.”

The same writer:

> “We are chosen in the same way as he was glorified, because before the world existed neither we existed nor he—the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.”

Again, Haimo:

> “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and King of all ages, namely past, present, and future. But the human being assumed by the Word is king of future ages from the time when he was assumed by the Word. For that human being, when he existed, was not king of past ages.”

Again, Augustine:

> “Christ, although perhaps he is naturally man, is recent; nevertheless, he is eternal God. If he is a recent man, he is a man who did not always exist.”

Again, Augustine:

> “From the time when he began to be man, from that time he is God.”

The same:

> “He created the Virgin, though he was to be created from the Virgin. [Col. 1080C] If he created, he existed; if he was to be created, he did not yet exist.”

The same:

> “From the beginning of his faith, every human being becomes a Christian by grace, just as that human being was made Christ by grace from his beginning. That human being was made Christ not from the beginning of time, not from the beginning of the world, but from his own beginning, namely, the beginning of the human being.”

Therefore that human being had an earthly beginning; hence that human being did not always exist.

## Chapter XIX. Authorities which seem contrary

Augustine on John:

> “How can he be from the world through whom the world was made? God and man were made from the world after the world, because the world was first, and thus the human being was from the world. But Christ was first, then the world, since Christ was before the world; before Christ there was nothing, because ‘in the beginning was the Word.’”

[Col. 1080D] Again, Isidore:

> “The Paulinians, descended from Paul of Samosata, say that Christ did not always exist, as though he had taken his beginning from Mary.”

Elsewhere also one reads: “That child created the stars.” And Christ himself says: “I am the beginning, who speak to you” (John 8).

### Solutions

The solution to these apparent contradictions is like that of the preceding ones, according to the rule of St Augustine: authorities saying that Christ, or that human being, did not always exist are to be referred to that person according to his humanity; those saying that he always existed are to be understood of that same person according to his divinity.

It may also be said that at times the name “Christ,” or the expression “that human being,” signifies the person; at times it signifies the substance or nature of that person. Therefore, when it is said that Christ or that human being did not always exist, that substance or nature is understood; but when it is said that Christ or that human being always existed, it is not human or divine nature, but the person, that is the subject.

For explaining also these expressions—“God is man,” “man is God,” “God is God and man,” “man is man and God,” “God became man,” and “man became God”—such a consideration will not be useless. For each of the two names, “God” and “man,” sometimes signifies a person and sometimes a nature or substance.

Thus, when it is said “God is man,” this means that the divine person is human substance. Conversely, when it is said “man is God,” this means that human substance is the divine person. [Col. 1081B] But when it is said “God is God and man,” two natures are attributed to one person. Similarly, when it is said “man is man and God,” the same two natures are attributed to the same person.

Again, when it is said “God became man,” this means that the divine person became human substance. But when it is said “man became God,” this means that human substance became the divine person. Yet I do not deny that these forms of speech frequently signify figuratively union, possession, or assumption. But, setting aside such figurative language for a while, let us distinguish their proper meanings.

For when God became man, either divine substance or nature became human substance or nature; or the divine person became a person which it itself had not formerly been; or divine nature or substance became a human person which had not always existed; or the divine person became human nature or substance. Similarly, when man became God, either a certain human person became the divine person, or human nature or substance became divine substance, or human nature or substance became the divine person.

[Col. 1081C] Since it is impossible for either, or both, of these natures to have become the other—for this could not occur without conversion or confusion of substance, contrary to the statement of Athanasius:

> “He is one, not by conversion of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity in God; altogether one, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person”—

and since it is likewise impossible for the divine person and a human person, or either of them, to become another, for this could in no way take place unless each passed by some mixture into the other and the other ceased to be; and since these things are also impossible, namely, that the divine nature in Christ should become some person, or that that person should become the divine nature—for this could not occur without Christ becoming one person and another person, contrary to Athanasius’s statement: “Although he is God and man, he is nevertheless not two, but one Christ”—[Col. 1081D] since, I say, all these things are impossible, these two propositions remain as true and catholic faith: the divine person became human nature, or human substance became the divine person. Thus one person is two substances, and two substances are one person. Otherwise neither did God become man nor man God, nor is the one Christ God and man.

That in this discussion we use “nature” and “substance” indifferently should disturb no one. For Boethius, in *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*, describes nature in four ways. The first description is stated thus: “Nature is of those things which, since they are, can in whatever way be grasped by the intellect.” He says that this includes all things that exist.

The second is this: “Nature is what can either act or suffer.” “You have,” he says, “a definition of that sense of ‘nature’ in which it is joined only to substances. In this matter, a definition of substance has also been supplied.”

[Col. 1082B] For if the name “nature” indicates substance, then when we have described nature, a description of substance has also been given.

The third definition is set forth in this manner: “Nature is a principle of motion in itself, not accidentally.” Here, as he himself says, the name of nature, leaving aside incorporeal substances, is restricted as far as bodily substances, so that only bodily substances seem to have nature.

A fourth is also added: “Nature is the specific difference informing each thing.” Since “nature” is used and defined in so many ways, both Catholics and Nestorius established that there are two natures in Christ according to the last definition. For they do not say that the same differences belong to God and to man.

Behold: on Boethius’s testimony, “substance” is sometimes understood by the name “nature.” Augustine, on the verse of the psalm, “I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance” (Psalm 68), says: “Substance is understood as that which we are from God.” Natures themselves are called substances, as human being, beast, earth, heaven, and all things of this kind. Thus, in the book *On the Trinity*, he says that the form—that is, the human nature—is the person of the Son:

> “That form of the assumed human being is the person of the Son, not also of the Father.”

Therefore the invisible Father, together with the Son invisible with him, is said to have sent the same Son by making him visible. [Col. 1082C] Clearly, he used “form” as though he had said “nature.” Hence the same writer says in the book *On Faith to Peter*:

> “When you hear concerning Christ that he was in the form of God, you must acknowledge and hold most firmly that, in the name ‘form,’ the natural fullness must be understood. Therefore he was in the form of God, from whom he was born.”

Likewise, the emptying of the supreme God was nothing other than the assumption of the servant’s form, that is, human nature. Therefore each form is in Christ, because each nature is in Christ; and divine and human substance alike are complete. Here too he has taken “form” and “nature or substance” as equivalent.

Hilary also says in the book *On the Trinity*:

> “Truly, in ‘form’ there is no understanding other than nature in the gift of God. But that Christ is divine nature, no Catholic denies.”

That he is human nature is demonstrated by the foregoing and many other authorities. Therefore Christ is two natures because he is two substances; and he is of two natures because, according to Boethius, he has two specific or substantial differences, divinity and humanity. According to nature, these always differ widely from each other, but contrary to nature they come inseparably together in unity of person.

Whether Boethius properly or improperly called them specific differences, we have said above. Moreover, Boethius’s statement that the same differences do not belong to God and man cannot stand if by both names, “God” and “man,” the person is signified. For everything which belongs to Christ belongs to the person of God and man. The person of God and man is one and the same and does not differ from itself. But here the two substances are signified by these names, and the same differences do not belong to them.

[Col. 1083B] Others, however, as we have already said—and it does not weary us to repeat it—understand each name to signify the person, not the nature. Thus, when it is said “God suffered,” and the like, nothing is said of the divinity, but of the divine person. And when it is said “man raised himself,” and the like, nothing is attributed to humanity, but to the person of the human being, namely Christ, who is not a different person from God. For the person of God and man is one, although the nature is one and another.

If anyone wonders that we maintain such a double signification in these names, what will he say in these cases: “God begot,” “God was begotten,” “God proceeds,” or “has proceeded”? Is not each statement about the person? Is it not about the substance? Yet these three properties are attributed by these three words only to the persons, as some infer from that authority of John Damascene:

> “The hypostases do not differ from one another according to characteristic idioms,”

that is, determining properties. “Characteristic” means “determining”; that is, they determine the hypostases.

Yet this does not mean that these properties do not belong to the divine nature. Rather, it means that they distinguish not nature from itself, but persons from one another. But this question—whether one substance or nature begot, was begotten, and proceeds—will not be regarded as perplexing by anyone who thinks that it is not one and the same God who begot, was begotten, and proceeds; or, conversely, by anyone who thinks that the one same thing is begetting in the Father, begotten in the Son, and proceeding in the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1083D] But these matters will be discussed elsewhere; for the present, let us return to our subject.

What, too, will they say of the following: “God is one,” “God is three,” “God is Trinity,” “God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit”? Is not the discourse about substance? Is it not about persons or person? Let them also hear something at which they may wonder more. Augustine, in his *Exposition of the Creed*, says:

> “If anyone should say and believe that the man Jesus Christ was not assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.”

Here, without doubt, “the man Jesus Christ” is understood not as person but as substance. Elsewhere, however, it signifies the person, as when it is said that the man Jesus is equal to God and coeternal with the Father, and created all things, and the like. No wise person can doubt that these things must be understood of the person whom he assumed, not of the [Col. 1084A] nature or substance which was assumed.

## Opinions of the heretics

My fellow disciples are not afraid, but I am afraid that this anathema may encompass them: “If anyone should say and believe,” etc., because they neither say nor believe that any human being was assumed by the Son of God. I do not doubt that all heretics either entirely failed to understand, or evaded at the peril of their error, this distinction of the twofold signification or use of each of these names, “God” and “man.” For they taught that Christ was either two persons or only one substance or nature.

Thus Nestorius, while confessing that Christ is God and man, thought that by these two names two persons in Christ must be understood. Eutyches, while confessing that God became man, did not believe that two natures remain in one person. He falsely thought that, if there were two rational natures in Christ, there must necessarily be two persons. It is miserable folly—and itself foolish and miserable—for so many crowds of scholars in these times, amid so great a light and glory of the Christian faith, stubbornly to imitate their wretched stupidity, whether from love of their teachers or from some other flattering cause.

But I do not fear being condemned either for ingratitude or for fickleness if, though I received or taught certain things when younger, I now alter them, older and sounder as I am, by a weightier and sounder judgment. This is not the fault of fickleness, unless all sinners who repent, even late, are to be judged fickle; nor is it ingratitude, unless this gratitude is owed to teachers: that we should follow their errors. For our one teacher is he who is in heaven, against whom it is not lawful either to think anything or to assent to anyone against him.

## Chapter XX. Conclusion from the foregoing matters proposed at the beginning

Since, therefore, what we proposed at the beginning has been strengthened by authorities and arguments, as far as the brevity of the work and the smallness of its maker allowed, following the holy Fathers and the established doctrines of faith, I venture to say, believe, and confess that Christ is a certain human being—and indeed the holiest and most blessed of human beings; that Christ according to his humanity is something, and indeed a true human being, a living and true body, a nature, a substance, one whole; and that he, according to the other nature, [Col. 1084D] is uncreated and creator, and according to the other is created and a creature.

I do not merely say simply, “The Son of God is a creature,” or even “Christ is a creature,” but add “according to his humanity,” as the Apostle says: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1). Hence Augustine says:

> “The Apostle says this lest he be thought merely man. For in saying that he was made according to the flesh, he indicates that there is another nature according to which he is unmade, namely the divine.”

Here the impiety of heretics is answered, for, understanding this passage with dull minds, they take Christ to be merely human and do not understand divinity to be in him. For by adding “according to the flesh,” while preserving for the divinity its dignity, by which Christ is the Word of God the Father through whom all things were made, [Col. 1085A] he was not made according to that by which he is the Word of God. Therefore, when the Apostle said that Christ was made, he added “according to the flesh,” in order to show that according to the Word, which is the Son of God, he was not made by God but born.

## When Christ is discussed, one must distinguish what is said of him and in what respect

But whenever the words of the saints or of the Lord himself lack such qualifications—for example: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14); “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 3); “From the beginning and before the ages I was created” (Ecclesiasticus 24); “I, God, created him” (Isaiah 45); “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8); and the like—then recourse must be had to the foregoing authority of Augustine, by which we are warned, when Christ is discussed, to distinguish [Col. 1085B] what is said of him and in what respect.

Therefore, as at the beginning, so also at the end of this *Eulogy*, which I have sent from my poverty to your grace, although I am the least in the Church, I address the chief of the whole Church: a father, yet a judge; a judge, yet a shepherd. This is my desire and this is my petition: that, as the height of the Roman pontificate befits, Your Sublimity may command by a general and perpetually valid decree that all of us think with one certainty concerning the assumed human being.

And that we believe more concerning the assumption of a human being than concerning the assumption of a garment: namely, that the God who assumed is the human being who was assumed, just as the God who created is the human being [Col. 1086A] who was created; the God who raised up is the human being [Col. 1086A] who was raised up; the God who glorified is the human being who was glorified.

By that same authority of yours, which no human being may despise, may we all, whether willingly or unwillingly, accept the necessity of an inviolable command, so that together and in the same manner we confess: against Eutyches, that the one person of Christ is two substances; against Nestorius, that the two substances are one person; against Apelles and Mani, that God did not appear as a human being in phantasy but truly and essentially existed as a human being; against Apollinaris, that he assumed not a body alone but body and soul together, in and from which a perfect human being is known; against the Aligians, that Christ is not merely human, but a human being who began in time, and the Word who was in the beginning; and against the Paulinians, that Christ the Son of God always existed and did not take his beginning from Mary, because he himself, according to his divinity, was creator before the Virgin was to be created.

These things, and whatever accords with them, are catholic; and unless they are believed in the Church, they may be not merely urged but commanded. For it is necessary to believe what no one can be saved without believing faithfully and firmly.

This conclusion is inserted into the petition, by which the writer’s intention is declared more fully than by the preface. Happily ended.

[Col. 1085]

# John of Cornwall’s Little Book on the Canon of the Mystical Libation and Its Orders

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXVII, col. 455, among the Appendices to the Works of Hugh of St Victor.)

# In the Year of the Lord 1180: Guichard, Archbishop of Lyons

[Col. 1085]

# Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IV, col. 126)

[Col. 1085C] Guichard, who is also called Wicard and Vicard, was first a monk of the Cistercian order, then abbot of Pontigny, where he received St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, clothed him in the monastic habit, and formed with him an intimate friendship. Finally he was elected Archbishop of Lyons against Drogo, indeed as early as 1164, if the letters of Drogo himself and of the canons of Lyons to King Louis are to be trusted.

Indeed, among the documents for Burgundian history collected by Perard (p. 135), this charter is reported:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord one thousand one hundred and fifty-nine [lacuna], the altar in the crypts of St Stephen was consecrated by Lord Guichard, Archbishop of Lyons. On the same day, the Ides of September, the cemetery was consecrated by the same archbishop,” etc.

But this cannot stand, for Heraclius had not yet entered upon the way of all flesh. Therefore there is an error either in the archbishop’s name or, more probably, in the date; 1159 was wrongly read instead of 1169.

He seems to have struggled with Drogo for some time. Each assumed the title of archbishop and performed such duties as he was able; at last Guichard prevailed, Drogo’s election having been declared invalid, and indeed not on a single occasion. Nor is this surprising, since in the end all votes converged upon Guichard, according to the testimony of St Thomas of Canterbury, who asserts that he was promoted to the archbishopric by the common assent of clergy and people. The justice of the cause, as it appears, and the favor of the magnates were on his side. The justice of the cause may be presumed from the pope’s decision and from the outcome; the magnates’ favor is shown by letters written on his behalf by St Thomas and the Abbot of Cluny, indeed also by King Louis, as may be seen in Humbert of Beaujeu’s letter [Note: [Col. 1087D] *Hist. Franc.*, vol. IV, p. 666.], in which he addresses the king as follows:

> “Wishing to obey your commands, we gladly receive, as is fitting, your request made concerning the Lord Archbishop of Lyons, that we should render him due obedience and reverence. [Col. 1087C] Yet we have not seen him, nor has he entered our land; but since we shall shortly have discussions with him, we shall comply with your wish.”

Finally, he was installed by the Roman pontiff himself, as we learn from the already cited letter of St Thomas:

> “Your faithful Abbot of Pontigny has been promoted by the common assent of clergy and people to the archbishopric of the Church of Lyons, and was consecrated by the lord pope at Montpellier, on the Sunday before the approaching feast of Blessed Lawrence. Concerning him we confidently hope [lacuna], as concerning our dearest friend, that, both for love of you and for ours, he will as long as he lives always be faithful to you, and will, as is just, subject his city and those regions to you and your kingdom to the extent of his power.”

But in what year he was anointed with the sacred unction, and to what point the beginning of his pontificate should be assigned, is not so easy to determine. Severtius and others assign the year 1165, both because Alexander was in the city in that year and because the following words are found in the charter of the Carthusian house of Constance reported by Severtius (ch. 85, § 4):

> “In the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year from his Incarnation one thousand one hundred and seventy-one, in the thirteenth year of the episcopate of Lord Pope Alexander III; in the seventh year of Lord Guichard, Archbishop of Lyons; in the fifth indiction, on the sixth Ides of November, by command of the same Roman pontiff, the delimitation of the wilderness of Portes was renewed [Col. 1088A] by the archbishop himself, legate of the Holy Roman Church.”

If 1171 was Guichard’s seventh year, he began in 1165. Not far from this reckoning is the ancient monk of Saint-Marien, who, according to Nicolas Camus as reported by Severtius, asserts that Guichard was raised to the archbishopric of Lyons in 1166. Nor is Guichenon far from it, for he records it in the same year in the fourth part of his *History of Bresse*, although in the second part he says that around 1165 Guichard was present at Stephen II of Villars’s donation to Utfrid, first abbot of Chassagne. This can easily be reconciled.

Giles likewise says: “In the year 1165, Guichard, Abbot of Pontigny, becomes Archbishop of Lyons.” The Chronicle of Auxerre, reported by Miraeus, agrees. Father Menestrier, however, assigns its beginning two years later, namely 1167, when no archbishop seems to have existed at Lyons. For in October an agreement concerning the rights of the archbishopric of Lyons and the Counts of Forez was made before the Archbishop of Tarentaise; Guigo, the count, and many members of the chapter are named in that agreement, but everywhere there is profound silence about the prelate. This could in no way have occurred unless the see was vacant or the bishop had not yet been admitted.

Certainly John of Salisbury, in Letter 225, written in 1167, says that Guichard suffered opposition and was excluded from entering the city for a full two years; but that at last, in that very year, “he received his Church and city with the honor and joy of all on the feast of St Martin.”

[Col. 1088C] He is mentioned in the year 1168 in a charter of agreement concerning the tithes of the church of Chaluas between Hugh, abbot of Île-Barbe, and his namesake, the archimandrite of Bonneval [Note: [Col. 1087D] Rud. Île-Barbe, p. 111.].

> “This was done,” it says, “in the year 1168 [lacuna]; the interposition of an alphabet divided through the middle makes this charter, written in duplicate, more certain; it was at the same time confirmed by the seals of the venerable G., Archbishop of Lyons, and of the chapter of that same place [lacuna].”

He also made the agreement and concord between the abbot of Saint-Martin of Autun and the church of Fontenay with Henry, Bishop of Autun [Note: [Col. 1088D] Perard, p. 399.], and Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, in 1169. Let no one be troubled that William is read instead of Guichard in this document: it is an error either of the printer [Col. 1088D] or of the copyist, as is clear from the following charter of the Abbot of Fontenay, which reports and confirms the same agreement; for Guichard is named in it:

> “It was done in the chapter of Saint-Martin through the hand of Guichard the archbishop, legate of the Apostolic See,” etc.

In 1170, by issuing a charter, he records that Stephen of Villars gave several things to the Abbey of Chassagne. In the same year he introduced the Duke of Burgundy into the general Cistercian chapter, in which the duke was admitted as an associate and participant in its prayers, and Guichard himself granted them a privilege. In the same year he procured peace and agreement between [Col. 1089A] Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, and the canons of Langres.

In the following year, by command of Pope Alexander, he renewed the delimitation of the wilderness of Portes; Severtius reports the charter, whose opening we transcribed above. In a charter issued in the same year, he makes known that Philip, abbot of Saint-Bénigne, granted to the Cistercian church the house called *Ducissae*, etc.

John Długosz, book V of the *History of Poland*, p. 462, notes that Walter, Bishop of Wrocław, who died in 1171, introduced into his own church the ceremonies, order, and chant of the Church of Lyons, the foremost church of the Gauls.

In the year 1173 a highly celebrated settlement was concluded between Guichard and the Church of Lyons, on the one hand, and Guy, Count of Forez, on the other. We have seen that the latter had contested [Col. 1089B] the county of Lyons; that, notwithstanding grants made or confirmed by the emperors, he had not yielded; that he had in fact possessed and exercised rights at Lyons; and that from this had arisen most serious disputes: the Church was harassed by war, the bishop and canons driven out, and the city plundered. At last, however, through Guichard’s diligence, piety, and generosity, peace was restored. The count’s rights—whatever they may ultimately have been—were redeemed, together with several castles which the Church held in the county of Forez, with the additional payment of 1,100 marks of silver. “This settlement,” says Pope Alexander in his charter, “being made by the common consent of the parties, we hold valid and firm; and, confirming it by apostolic authority, we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing.” Paradin records the settlement and the bull, and after him Père Menestrier, who maintains that by this agreement the canons of the Church of Lyons became Counts of Lyons, possessing the same rights, titles, and prerogatives by which the Counts of Forez had held that dignity: “for,” he says, “they acquired it by giving several estates and a considerable sum of silver in compensation.” Bernard, abbot of Savigny, acquired certain property at Arbravilla from Peter des Estolz, as the documents of that acquisition relate; they were written “at Saint-Leodegarius, in the reign of Louis, King of the Franks, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1173, while Guichard, Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, was residing at Lyons.”

[Col. 1089D] He was present at the dedication of the church of Clairvaux in 1174. He took part in the Council of Albi against the heretics named after that city; he refuted Oliver, the leader of the erring party, and in 1176 pronounced against them the sentence reported by Baronius. Baronius erred, however, in calling him Gillebert rather than Guichard. That he erred is clear both because catalogues of bishops and other ancient records contain no prelate of that name, and because Guichard held the crozier before and after that year. In 1178 he raised the body of St Bernard from the earth and displayed it for the veneration of the people; and in [Col. 1090A] 1179 he consecrated the abbey church of Belleville.

The same “Guichard, by the grace of God Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, wishes it to be known that Ulric of Villars, dean of Lyons, through his own hand gave . . . to the brothers of Chassagne the right of pasture throughout all his land of Meria, and through the land called Bresse . . . Done in the chamber at Cîteaux.” This grant indeed bears neither date nor consul. [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Bibl. Sebus.*, p. 350.] Yet, from comparison of the dates at which Guichard began to hold office, as also Peter of Tarentaise—“at whose prayers this grant was made”—and Utfred, to whom it was made, Dom Guichenon maintains that it was written in 1174, 1175, or the following year. Another document occurs in the *History of the Abbey of Trénor*, [Note: [Col. 1090D] *Instrum.*, p. 451.] by which Guichard again grants to Abbot Lebald the church of Moncelles, retaining a new rent, [Col. 1090B] but without any indication of time. He granted to his Church many movable and immovable goods, which Severtius enumerates. He died about 1180, on 28 July, the day on which his commemoration is celebrated in the Cistercian Menology. Others state that he died on 14 June, as the Martyrology of Pontigny reports. He ordered his body to be buried before the high altar of the castle of Retortorium (Riotier), situated on the River Saône, which he had acquired for his Church from John of Brienne, Count of Mâcon, for 16,000 pounds of silver. But the monks of Pontigny claimed it as their own with such ardour that they eventually obtained it and buried it before the principal altar of the monastery, on the epistle side, with this brief epitaph:

> Here lies Lord Guichard, [Col. 1090C] Archbishop of Lyons, second abbot of this monastery.

Chrysostom Henriquez, in the *Fascicle of the Saints of the Cistercian Order*, reports that Henry of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See, “in the year 1181, with vehement spirit, swiftly deposed two archbishops—namely, those of Lyons and Narbonne—because they appeared useless and blameworthy.” This is extremely difficult to reconcile with the histories of those Churches, since it can fit neither Guichard nor John of Bellesmains, who alone are recorded as having held the crozier at those times. Manriquez, in the *Cistercian Annals*, at 1182, chapter 2, no. 5, conjectures that another occupied the see of Lyons between Guichard and John; that he was deposed [Col. 1090D] by the legate Henry; that, being both unworthy and a bishop of brief tenure, he was not mentioned among the others; and that John was substituted in place of the deposed man. Baluze, however, in his notes concerning the bishops of Lyons, thinks that the first person to assert this transferred to the time of Henry’s legation an event of the preceding century, and that what he mistakenly said of the Archbishop of Lyons should be referred to the Archbishop of Arles. It is, moreover, established that the Archbishops of Arles and Narbonne were excommunicated and deposed in 1080, at the synod held at Avignon by Hugh of Die and Amatus of Oloron, legates of the Apostolic See. Those bishops were [Col. 1091A] Peter of Narbonne and Achard of Arles. Fiteriensis, in his notes on the *Exordium Magnum*, book II, chapter 31, assigns this act of Henry to 1188, when he was sent into Gaul by Pope Clement III. If that is true, it can be understood of no one but the John who follows, who was elected bishop of both Narbonne and Lyons in that same year. One might conjecture that not two, but only one bishop was removed from office by Henry, and that because he had presided over both Churches he was named from both. But these notions, devised at pleasure, rest on no foundation and are refuted by diverse and unanswerable arguments.

[Col. 1091]

# ANCIENT STATUTES OF THE CHURCH OF LYONS RENEWED BY ARCHBISHOP GUICHARD

(D. Edm. Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, III, 223, from a manuscript of the lord of Montevert, steward of the Church of Lyons.)

Here begin the Statutes of the Church of Lyons and the ordering of its Office.

[Col. 1091B] We, G., humble minister of the primatial Church of Lyons, and the entire chapter of the same Church, to all persons for ever.

With the passage of time, knowledge of events easily slips from human memory unless it is committed to written characters. For the folly or negligence of many, in calumniating, despising, and ridiculing all or most things, does not cease wickedly to burst forth from perverse hearts and most evil wills, and to put into most evil action its foolishness—or, so to speak, its ruinous character—of bad morals; nor does it cease shamelessly and incessantly to sow the most corrupt poison of its madness in the lax hearts of fools. Such persons maliciously strive and intend wholly to spurn and abandon the paternal custom instituted in the Church of Lyons, the approved order [Col. 1091C] of the most holy Fathers; indeed, they abandon the most holy order of the Church of Lyons and the rule issued by the most holy Fathers and established in the holy Church of Lyons, confirmed by an oath, as we find written in the book of canons. This book is so called by customary usage—a name which took its origin from the holy doctors of the same Church. The book is kept, produced, and read in all ecclesiastical assemblies and convents; and in our Church of Lyons too, by God’s favouring grace, it is honourably preserved and every year read during Lent, after the lesson at Prime, in the chapter of Lyons. Our predecessors, having carefully and fully examined this book, took common counsel to collect and set it in order, first invoking the Holy Spirit, so that all peaceable, prudent, most wise, and well-disposed sons of the Church of Lyons, into whose hands the form, ordering, and text drawn from this book may come, may most truly acknowledge and clearly know that the aforesaid Church of Lyons has always been governed and protected by the Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1092B] has never deviated from the right path of faith, and has faithfully preserved the paternal custom declared by ecclesiastical statutes. Nor does it by this depart from the ancient order of the Church, nor despise a different practice of order if it is shown to be worthy of approval; but, according to the Apostle, it follows what is more useful and more excellent (Rom. II).

## On observing the order

Therefore he himself says: “This is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge of the order and of the rule of the Church which must be observed, and in every understanding” (Phil. I), so that these may be retained in memory; “that you may approve the more excellent statutes of the order of the Church of Lyons, and may be sincere,” having firm hope and a sound conscience in preserving the statutes of the order and rules of the Church of Lyons, [Col. 1092C] and may remain without offence, courageously keeping the order, so that you may be found on the day of Christ, when you are to receive from him the reward of good will which you have shown by preserving perfectly and completely, to the end, the order of the Church of Lyons, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## On establishing the order

Accordingly, we wish both present and future persons to know that it was declared, established, and confirmed by oath in the chapter of Lyons that we wish the following practices, instituted and observed in ancient times in the Church of Lyons by the most holy Fathers, to be renewed, not changed. We wish them to be kept, as they have until now been observed, in our holy Church of Lyons, [Col. 1092D] which, as it has hitherto been distinguished among the Gallican Churches in dignity, has likewise been conspicuous in honourableness. For it has always, with God as author, avoided every mark of levity and inconstancy in work and action, and has observed and retained the vigour of its order, the rule of singing, the method of doubling each responsory chant, both at Matins and at Mass, and at Vespers [Col. 1093A] the rule of psalmody. Receiving manifold increase both spiritually and temporally, out of reverence for preserving the order and rule of the Church, it has always firmly advanced good men with ampler benefices, and has hitherto retained and observed without offence the order and rule, all other observances, and the statutes of the most holy Fathers, as they are established in that Church.

## On restraining those who despise the order of the Church

But it has restrained the wicked and rebellious, negligent and contemptuous of observing the order and rule of the Church, by stricter disciplines. Yet because in these days, as charity grows cold, there increases wickedness in sinning, transgressing the order, and wickedly despising the Church, [Col. 1093B] and [there are persons] wickedly opposing the statutes of the Churches (sic), after the manner of soothsayers, unwilling to obey God and despising to serve him, the licence of evil-doers has grown. Private love of impiety possesses the hearts of almost all who desire to act iniquitously and malignantly against the kindness of those who live piously, [lacuna] and because of most wicked misery, perverse malice, secret detraction, envy, and irreverence, we have judged it fitting, with so many and such great evils arising, to make provision and carefully apply a remedy, so that those who are continually present at the divine offices of the Church, without interruption, and preserve the order and ancient statutes, may appear to be assisted by daily diligence.

## On negligence in observing the order of the Church

[Col. 1093C] Since there are some among us who, attending to their nobility—or rather to their ignobility and baseness—despise and disdain to observe the Church’s order with discernment; and when they are instructed or reproved for acting wrongly, they scoff and ridicule.

## On renewing the order

But we, observing the pride—or rather the folly—of these persons, wish not to introduce new inventions, but to renew the institutions of the ancient Fathers, lest through the passage of time, forgetfulness, or the negligence of perverse persons, an occasion may be afforded for abandoning the statutes of the order. We begin with the greater matters.

## First statute

All canons swear to observe the order and institutions [Col. 1093D] of the Church, as is written in the charter which they read in chapter; they promise firmly to observe the canons of the most holy Fathers; they make and swear fealty to the Church; and they are to observe the other matters established in the Church of Lyons.

## On obedience

All, both greater and lesser, must obey the dean and the other officers of the Church in accordance with the form of the order and the institutions of the Church.

## On arranging the service of the Church

Our ancient Fathers established, ordained, and jointly confirmed by oath that throughout the year the canons should serve the high altar of St John and the altar of St Stephen, both at Masses and at the other hours, as will be indicated below. [Col. 1094A] On the Nativity of the Lord, all three Masses belong to the archbishop. The first Mass, at the high altar, is with two vested priests; the Gospel is [sung by] a canonical deacon with two other deacons; the Epistle by a canonical subdeacon with two subdeacons.

At the second Mass, at St Stephen’s, the archbishop is with two vested priests; the Gospel is [sung by] a canonical deacon with two other deacons; the Epistle by a canonical subdeacon with two other subdeacons. At the principal Mass, at the high altar, the archbishop is with six vested priests, two of whom are from our Church and four from the abbeys—namely St Just, St Paul, St Nicetius, and Plateries; the Gospel is [sung by] the archdeacon with six other deacons; the Epistle by the abbot of St Just [Col. 1094B] with six other subdeacons. All wear copes.

On the second day, the archbishop celebrates the principal Mass at St Stephen’s with two vested chaplains; the Gospel is [sung by] a canonical deacon with two other vested ministers; the Epistle by a canon with two vested ministers.

On the third day, the archbishop celebrates the principal Mass at the high altar with five vested ministers, as written in the table; likewise the Gospel with four vested ministers; likewise the Epistle with four vested ministers; with seven candle-bearers, as written in the table. The same is observed at Easter and Pentecost.

On all feast days when the great bells are rung, the canons sing Vespers, Matins, [Col. 1094C] and the principal Mass throughout the year. The Gospel and Epistles of principal Masses belong throughout the year to the canons, but their vicars provide the vested ministers. The morning Masses which occur throughout the year at the high altar must be sung by the sacristan, or another in his place. The morning Masses at St Stephen’s must be sung by the custodian of St Stephen; and if several occur there, or at the high altar, provision is made from the surplus ministers, as was ordained concerning vested ministers on feasts.

## Statute of the Church of Lyons, fortified by oath, concerning the celebration of Masses at the high altar, to which the archbishop and others are bound

The priest-canons and the two custodians of the Holy Cross must celebrate the principal and morning Masses at the altars of St Stephen and St John.

The aforesaid statute was explained as follows.

From the Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord to the Sunday before the Nativity of St John the Baptist, the dean, sacristan, custodian, master, and other priest-canons, and the two custodians of the Holy [Col. 1094D] Cross—excepting the four priest-canons assigned to St Stephen—are bound to celebrate principal or greater Masses at the high altar and to make holy water, as the order of the Church requires, except on the days written below, on which the archbishop is bound to celebrate Masses and sing the hours, as the order of the Church has ordained. The days on which the archbishop is bound to celebrate [Col. 1095A] and sing the hours are these: on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, he must celebrate Vespers and the antiphon at the *Magnificat*. Likewise, on the day itself, he must sing Matins and the seventh responsory, read the final lesson, celebrate the night Mass at the high altar, sing Matins Lauds, and intone the antiphon at the *Benedictus*. Likewise, he must celebrate the early principal Mass at the altar of St Stephen. Likewise, he must celebrate the principal Mass at the high altar. Likewise, he must sing Vespers on the day and the antiphon at the *Magnificat*. Likewise, on the feast of Blessed Stephen the Martyr, he must celebrate the principal Mass and sing Vespers. Likewise, on the feast of Blessed John the Evangelist, he must sing Matins and the first responsory in the greater church; if it falls on a Sunday, make holy water; and celebrate the principal Mass [Col. 1095B] at the high altar. Likewise, on the feast of All the Holy Innocents, [he must sing] Vespers and Compline, Matins and Prime. Likewise, at the beginning of the fast, he must give a sermon and expel the penitents from the Church. Likewise, on Palm Sunday, he must read the Passion at Matins; at the procession in the cemetery of St Irenaeus, say the prayer for the dead; bless the branches at St Just; preach at Forvenum; celebrate the principal Mass at the high altar; and sing Vespers and Compline. Likewise, on the following Monday, he must sing Matins and Prime. Likewise, at the Lord’s Supper, he must preach and reconcile the penitents, celebrate the principal Mass at the high altar, and bless the chrism and the oil [Col. 1095C] of catechumens and of the sick.
