Likewise, after dinner in chapter, at the Mandatum, he must wash the feet of twelve chaplains beneficed in the Church; in the refectory he must bless the supper bread and, kissing each one’s hand, give a portion of bread to each of the said twelve chaplains. Likewise, on the holy day of Preparation, he must perform the office at the Holy Cross. Likewise, on Holy Saturday, at the Vigil of Easter, he must perform the office there at the Holy Cross; likewise, at St Stephen’s, bless the fonts and celebrate Mass at the high altar. Likewise, he must sing Vespers and perform the antiphon at the *Magnificat*. Likewise, on Easter Day he must sing Matins, read the final lesson, and intone the antiphon at the *Benedictus*; celebrate the principal Mass at the high altar; sing Vespers; and intone the first [Col. 1095D] antiphon at the *Magnificat*. Likewise, on Easter Monday he must sing Matins, celebrate the principal Mass at the altar of St Stephen, and sing Vespers. Likewise, on the following Tuesday, he must sing Matins, celebrate the principal Mass at the Holy Cross, and sing Vespers and Compline. Likewise, on the following Wednesday, he must sing Matins and Prime. Likewise, on the Vigil of Pentecost and on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday [of Pentecost], [he must do] as on Easter Day and the following days, as expressed above.

Likewise, the four priest-canons assigned to St Stephen, and the treasurer and sacristan of St Stephen, are bound to celebrate the morning Masses at the altar of St Stephen from the aforesaid Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord until the aforesaid Sunday [Col. 1096A] before the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist. Likewise, conversely, the dean and the other aforesaid canons are bound to celebrate the morning Masses at the altar of St Stephen from the Sunday before the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist until the Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord. Except that, during those weeks when the order lapses, the two custodians of the Holy Cross must celebrate the morning Masses at the aforesaid altar of St Stephen.

It should be noted that during the said six weeks, on weekdays after the collect or collects of the day, the prayer of Blessed Stephen must be said, namely: “Almighty God, who [first-fruits].”

Likewise, conversely, from the Sunday before the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist until the Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, the aforesaid four priest-canons assigned [Col. 1096B] to St Stephen, and the treasurer and sacristan of St Stephen, are bound to celebrate the principal Masses at the high altar, or elsewhere wherever the community is to have the greater Mass; to perform the weekly duties of the hours; and to make holy water, as the order of the Church demands and requires. But during the six weeks in which the order of the Church lapses, or which precede the Sunday before the feast of All Saints—on which Sunday the order of the Church always begins again—they are not bound to sing the hours in choir or to make holy water, either themselves or through another; this belongs to the sacristan. They are nevertheless bound to celebrate the morning Mass at the high altar every day. But because on feasts when the greater bells are rung [Col. 1096C] the morning Mass is celebrated at St Speratus, in that case they are bound, in place of the morning Mass, to celebrate the principal Mass at the high altar. It should be known, moreover, that if the feast of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian falls on a Sunday during the said six weeks, the greater Mass shall be assigned by request, as the master shall direct. The same occurs on the feast of the dedication of the church of St Stephen, on whatever day it falls during the said six weeks. The same also occurs on the feast of Blessed Matthew the Apostle, if it falls in the September fasts or on a Sunday. Likewise, the same occurs on the feast of St Michael, on whatever day it falls. And the same occurs on the feast of Blessed Luke the Evangelist, if it falls on a Sunday: namely, all these greater Masses of the aforesaid feasts are assigned by request, if they occur on the aforesaid [Col. 1096D] days, as expressed above.

Likewise, concerning morning Masses which, because of a double or triple Office, are incumbent or occur during the year at the altars of Blessed John and Blessed Stephen, the following explanation was made. Throughout the year, excepting the six weeks in which the order lapses, on whatever day one, two, or three morning Masses occur at the high altar, the sacristan must celebrate the first Mass; the weekly minister of the preceding week, the second; and the weekly minister of the following week, the third, as is done with the vested ministers. If the said sacristan is the weekly minister of the greater Mass at the altar of St John, or of the morning Mass at the altar of St Stephen, then the weekly minister [Col. 1097A] of the preceding week must celebrate the first Mass, the weekly minister of the following week the second morning Mass, and the weekly minister of the second preceding week the third. Likewise, throughout the year, on whatever day one, two, or three Masses occur at the altar of Blessed Stephen, the weekly minister must celebrate the first Mass, the custodian the second, and the weekly minister of the preceding week the third. But if the said custodian is weekly minister of the greater Mass at the high altar or of the morning Mass at St Stephen, then the weekly minister of the preceding week must celebrate the second morning Mass and the weekly minister of the following week the third. The days of the Nativity of the Lord, the octave of the Nativity [Col. 1097B] of Blessed Mary if it falls on a Sunday or in the September fasts, and the feast of Blessed Michael if it falls on a Sunday, are excepted from this ordinance and statute. For on the day of the Nativity of the Lord the sacristan must celebrate the second Mass at the high altar, while the custodian must celebrate the third morning Mass at St Stephen. But on the octave-day of Blessed Mary and the feast of Blessed Michael, if they occur on the aforesaid days, [the custodian] must [celebrate] the second morning Mass at the altar of Blessed Stephen throughout the year, as expressed above.

## On the penalties and *sofrastis* [term uncertain] of canons who do not perform their offices

Likewise, it was established that every canon—priests as well as levites and subdeacons—should pay, as a penalty for failure in any of his offices, [Col. 1097C] three solidi of strong currency; that they should lose the food of the refectory until they paid the penalty imposed for the deficiency; and that all should be subject together to every penalty. This collected penalty was to be spent on the necessities of the Church and not on other things.

## How [lacuna] the church is to be served

When canons perform an office in church at Mass, Matins, or Vespers, the ancients ordained and commanded that they should carry out their service in due order, with the greatest reverence, trembling, and propriety, without offence or scruple, so that they may be an example, pattern, and mirror to the other clergy subject to them, and also to laypeople.

## On the obligations of the custodians of the Holy Cross

The most holy Fathers also established two custodians [Col. 1097D] in the Church of the Holy Cross. They were to be chosen from those beneficed in the church, whether of the seven or of the twelve; they were to undertake weekly duties at the high altar and at the altar of St Stephen, like the canons; and they were to serve the high altar and the altar of St Stephen during the six weeks, as expressed above. The most holy Fathers ordained this and confirmed it by oath, so that it might never be possible or lawful for any mortal to alter it or do otherwise. For in this ordinance the most holy Fathers exercised the greatest deliberation and reverent care, because the custodians of the Holy Cross, whom our lords had called to such excellence, glory, and honour, [Col. 1098A] and had made their equals in the service of the Church of Lyons, should sit and know that they were of lesser rank, subject to them, and prepared to obey them in all things.

This applies only to service during the six weeks in which the order lapses; and this is and was the reason why the custodians of the Holy Cross sing all morning Masses during those six weeks at the high altar of St Stephen.

## On succession among canons

It was also established that if any canon dies, of whatever order, the surviving canons succeed to his office and are bound without interruption to perform the deceased man’s weekly duty. Likewise, if one of the canons serving the altar of Blessed Stephen is removed from their midst, [Col. 1098B] the survivors continue the deceased man’s week without interruption.

## On succession among the chaplains of St Speratus

The ancients established twelve chaplains who serve the altar of Blessed Speratus and his companions: if any one of the twelve dies, the first [in order] shall perform the deceased man’s weekly duty.

## On alteration of the order

It was also established that no canon, church officer, or even any group of canons may add or remove anything, without the consent and will of the whole chapter, in the Office of Masses or in any other office of the Church of Lyons, in its order or in the rule of the same Church. If they seek to alter it, let them be struck by the sword of anathema.

## On the *vitatoria* [Note: [Col. 1097D] That is, invitatories.]

It was also established that all canons should say the invitatory on great solemnities, feast days, and during the weekly duty, when the invitatory is given on Saturday in Lent by the precentor from his side of the choir or by the cantor from the left side of the choir. But at the Nativity of the Lord and at Pentecost, the precentor and cantor, with two other canons, must say the invitatory. The antiphons at Matins and Vespers are said by the canons. At these feasts, they are sent to the canons by boys from the precentor and cantor, each from his own side; the precentor, however, brings the antiphon at [Col. 1098D] the *Benedictus* to the archbishop when he is present.

## That the altars shall not lose their Masses

It was also established and confirmed by oath that the high altar of St Stephen should never lose its appointed Masses, whether morning or principal. If, through some intervening cause, it should lose a morning Mass, the principal Mass must never be sung until that Mass has been restored. The lords should consider and provide for this before so great a failure of Masses could occur in the Church of Lyons, by sending for their nearest abbots to come and make up the deficiency of Masses before such great negligence or failure [Col. 1099A] of Masses occurs in the Church of Lyons, lest for this reason any hindrance, disturbance, or dissension arise in the chapter. It should be known that no one may celebrate at the high altar unless he is a priest-canon of Lyons, a bishop, a legate, an abbot of this diocese, a custodian of the Holy Cross, the treasurer, or the sacristan of St Stephen.

## On the manner of praying in choir

Likewise, it was established in the Church of Lyons that, whenever anyone enters the choir, whatever his rank, he must in the middle of the choir pray with all his heart and body, devoutly toward his place, and remain silent there until the hours begin.

## On maintaining silence in choir

[Col. 1099B] No one may speak in choir except in correcting or rebuking. Hence Ambrose: “By your words you will be condemned, if you have spoken in church without cause.” Again, Ambrose on this matter: “What need is there, then, for you to seek judgment and the danger of condemnation by speaking, when by keeping silent you can be safer?” Again: “I have seen very many fall into sin by speaking; scarcely anyone by silence. Therefore it is harder to know how to be silent than to speak. I know that most people can speak when they cannot, or do not know how to, be silent.” Again, the same author: “It is rare to be silent, although speaking brings no advantage; therefore the person who knows how to be silent, at least in choir, is considered wise.”

## Likewise, on silence in choir and in processions

It was forbidden and established that no one should speak or converse with another in a procession [Col. 1099C] in church or outside church; rather, they should proceed humbly in procession, with heads bowed, and should not look here and there, lest they set a bad example to laypeople and lest clerics, by their bad example, be corrupted by laypeople as though by swine, through their wicked disparagements. Therefore divine Wisdom said: “The Lord gave me a tongue of instruction when it was proper to speak” (Ecclus. L). A person is rightly wise, then, if he receives from the Lord the time when he ought to speak. Hence the same saying: “A wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclus. XX). For this reason holy lords loved silence, since they knew that the human voice is the beginning of human error.

## On those placed above the choir, or raised, and on the subformaries

[Col. 1099D]

We find it established in the annual books, written in the Church of Lyons, and confirmed by oath, that no man, however noble, is to be placed under the form in the Church of Lyons unless he is first a subdeacon. This was and is the reason: no one can or should perform the office of vested minister at Matins and Vespers on great feasts, or on other occasions, unless he is a subdeacon. What was established for lesser matters was also established for greater. Thus those who place anyone under the form contrary to the order and statutes of the Fathers sin by right and offend God. They also sin against God because the God of the Hebrews commanded Moses to ordain [Col. 1100A] Aaron and his sons to minister to him in the tabernacle of the covenant. Therefore those who change the order of the Church of Lyons and the statute of the ancients appear to sin, and do sin, against God and the law; they appear to sin, and do sin, against the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Hence: “Whoever has offended in one of the Lord’s commandments has become guilty of all” (James II). For nobles are more strictly and firmly bound than others to observe the statutes of the Church of Lyons, because, as subformaries, they possess and ought deservedly to possess the privilege of being called more quickly to the canonry. They should therefore eagerly and willingly aspire to the order of subdeacon, because no canon is to be raised above the choir unless he is a subdeacon.

The duties of the subformaries likewise include acting as vested thurifers at Vespers and Matins on feasts of the great bells; carrying the cross at the procession for holy water on the above-mentioned feasts from the Nativity of the Lord to the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany, and on all Sundays in Lent; [Col. 1100B] [from] the octave of Easter to the octave of Pentecost; saying the fifth lesson and singing the sixth responsory on feasts; saying the prologues; saying the fourth lesson in the Ember fasts and on Holy Saturday, and singing the tract *Laudate* (“Praise”); performing the weekly duties at the principal Mass from Septuagesima Sunday to the first Sunday of Lent; saying the lesson at Prime throughout Lent; going to the candle on the aforementioned feasts and on double feasts; carrying the large crosses in Rogationtide; carrying the brown chest on Ascension Day; making the seventh candlestick on the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, Pentecost, and on the feast of St John the Evangelist; and carrying staffs for the cantors when the procession is made to the cross. The said subformaries are appointed by the cantors for the *Benedictus* at Matins on double feasts.

## On the order of the diaconate

The order of deacon raises canons and four of the Church’s prebendaries—namely the steward, the bread-keeper, the refectory cupbearer, and the master of the schools—without permission of the chapter. The priestly order likewise raises all persons, both canons and others, without permission.

## When it is permitted to leave choir, and when it is not

[Col. 1100D] At Matins no one can or should leave according to the order without necessity, except during the last three lessons. If anyone leaves during the first or second lessons and then returns to choir, he cannot and should not meanwhile leave during the final lessons according to the order. No one who is on weekly duty, once he has entered Matins, whether he is from above the choir or from the floor, may leave without just cause, except during the third lesson. But if he leaves during the first lesson and afterwards returns to choir, he may not meanwhile leave during the third lesson according to the order.

## On missing Matins Lauds
No one from the floor may or can miss the morning praises (Matins) [Col. 1101A] except from necessity. If anyone misses them, he must be punished by the master, if he is a subdeacon or of lower rank. If he is a subformary or deacon, he is to be severely punished by the precentor or cantor.

### On missing Matins on two days

No one may miss Matins on two consecutive days. If he misses them on the second day, he may not enter the choir. If he is from the floor, he must be punished unless he alleges a just cause.

### On missing Matins on feast days

If anyone, whether from above the choir or from the floor, misses Matins on feast days through negligence, he may not leave his house for the whole day—not even for a meal, nor for any other cause or necessity. Nor may he [Col. 1101B] appear at the altar outside his lodging, nor let his neighbours know, so that it may be believed that he is not in the town. On the following day he may enter for Matins.

### On bloodletting on vigils

No one from above the choir, nor any cleric from the floor, may undergo bloodletting on the vigil of any feast, except from necessity; only the dignitaries are exempt.

### How and when they must enter the choir

All dignitaries and the weekly officiant must be the first to enter the choir for Matins and Vespers, and there they must keep silence until Vespers or Matins begins. Hence Saint David says: “I said, I will guard my ways,” etc. (Psalm 38). For he knew and had read that it belongs to divine protection [Col. 1101C] that a person should be hidden from the scourge of his tongue and from the testimony of his conscience. For we are struck by the silent reproach of our own thought, through the judgment of conscience; we are also struck by the lash of our voice when we speak things whose sound wounds our spirit and injures the mind. Therefore he saw that no holy person could keep his mouth in church free from the impurity of speech; he imposed upon himself the law of innocent silence, so that by keeping silent in church he might avoid a punishment which, speaking outside, he could scarcely escape.

Hence Ambrose: “But who has a heart clean from the filth of sins, or does not offend with his tongue?”

Likewise, no canon or cleric may enter the choir for Matins or [Col. 1101D] the other hours of the day after the fourth verse, except on the Epiphany of the Lord and its octave, and for three days at the Lord’s Supper. On those days he may enter throughout the first psalm and as far as the fourth verse of the second psalm at Matins, but not at the other hours.

### On lingering in the presbytery or before the choir

When there are two or three persons in the choir, no one may remain or enter in the presbytery while the final bell of the Hours is rung. Nor may anyone stand, remain, or linger before the choir. If, however, it happens that one passes before the choir, he must pass quickly and take care not to be seen by those who are in the choir. Likewise, all who are in the choir, if they leave, must take care not to remain before the choir, [Col. 1102A] not to linger, and not to converse there with one another. If they wish to speak with one another, they must go to such a place that they cannot be seen by those who are in the choir. All these rules must be observed by superiors as well as inferiors, because the former are bound to correct the latter.

### On how boys, or other clerics from the floor, must behave when they come to church

The boys must place themselves in a hidden place while the fourth bell is being rung, as must also the other clerics, so that they are not seen by the lords while the final bell is ringing or sounding. For formerly the boys, all the other clerics, the subformaries, and the deacons used to assemble in the chapel of Blessed Photinus. While that chapel remained, the boys went out first in [Col. 1102B] procession and proceeded to Vespers or Matins; the other clerics followed the boys; and thus, in ordered procession, they entered the choir. This arrangement ought to be maintained at all times.

### On rehearsal

Every day the master must hold rehearsal; and after they have rehearsed the antiphons and responsories, he must correct those who have not observed the rule and warn the others not to commit any fault for which they ought to be, and are, punished. He must urge them to keep and observe the order of the church, to enter church becomingly and walk becomingly, lest by their bad examples they corrupt anyone.

### On disorderly passage through the cloister

It was ordained by the ancients, and we wish to restore the same rule, [Col. 1102C] that no canon or cleric may go through the cloister improperly. From Matins until the sixth hour they must wear ecclesiastical clothing; from the sixth hour until the ninth they may wear secular clothing; and from then until Compline they may not go or pass through the cloister except in ecclesiastical clothing. If, however, canons or clerics have business in the town or outside it, they may pass through the town on horseback in other clothing; otherwise, not without offence. If any cleric is the agent of a canon and has business in town concerning his lord’s affairs, he must go in ecclesiastical clothing as far as the Brothers’ Gate, [Col. 1102D] have secular clothing carried with him, deposit his ecclesiastical clothing there in the house of some layperson, put on the other clothing, and thus may go about ecclesiastical business.

### On not wearing coifs

No canon or cleric may wear lay coifs by day beneath his hood through the cloister where anyone can see them, nor may they make garments of various kinds in the manner of laypeople.

### On clothing

Rather, they must make garments that are closed and decent to wear, and decent stockings—not white, red, or green, but preferably black or a similar colour.

### On correcting clerics, and on their proper conduct in cloister and church

[Col. 1103A]

Clerics must always be admonished by their superiors and masters to walk becomingly through the cloister, to observe the rule outside the church and inside it, and to avoid scandal. They must beware of entering church improperly; rather, they must walk humbly and enter the church and choir simply. When they perform God’s service, they must appear to stand becomingly in the choir. No one may presume to speak to another, nor turn to look toward the altar or to the left for any reason that arises; each must look before himself, perform God’s service with his whole heart and a pure mind, and chant with trembling.

### On conversations and antics not to be performed in choir

[Col. 1103B] No one may converse in the choir while chant is being sung, make antics, indecent gestures, or openly make shameful yawns, but only secretly. If anyone from above the choir happens to yawn, he must place some part of his clothing before his mouth, so that no one in or outside the choir sees him yawn. If anyone from the floor wishes to yawn, he must not improperly raise or lift his mouth upward while yawning, but put his mouth into his breast and yawn there discreetly, without fuss. Nor may anyone in the choir, while chant is being sung, make belchings, other most shameful gestures, empty laughter, or any bodily frivolities.

### That no one may linger in the street before the church

While the Hours are being rung, no cleric [Col. 1103C] may stand or remain for a long time before the church, or engage in conversation with anyone, whether dressed in secular or ecclesiastical clothing, in such a way that he may be seen by anyone from the church.

### On lingering at the Brothers’ Gate

Likewise, no noble or non-noble person may or ought to stand at the Brothers’ Gate in lay dress while the Hours or Vespers are being rung, nor hold conversations there with anyone from the church in such a way that one or more persons from the church can see them speaking together.

### On blowing the nose

If anyone from the floor needs to blow his nose in choir, he must not draw his hands outside his surplice [Col. 1103D] or bend down to the ground, but must blow his nose upright and secretly inside his surplice.

### On missing Matins

If anyone from the choir misses Matins two days in succession, he may not enter the choir on the second day, nor come even to Vespers, unless a great feast falls on the following day.

### On instructing clerics

The master and all the chaplains of the Twelve must always instruct the others, so that they may learn and observe the order of the Church, and walk simply and orderly through cloister and church in ecclesiastical clothing.

### On passage through the cloister

No canon, priest, or cleric may [Col. 1104A] go or pass through the cloister in secular clothing, unless he is passing on horseback, except from the sixth hour until the ninth.

### On admonishing clerics

At rehearsals clerics must always be admonished by the master, submasters, or sometimes by the precentor to observe the order and serve the church, for they are appointed especially for that purpose. They must not give offence by walking disorderly through the church or other places, but must walk simply and in order, carefully observing the rule.

### That no one may appear when they have left the Hours

No one from above the choir, nor any cleric or junior cleric—and indeed those who did not remain for the Hours even less than the others—may appear to those who [Col. 1104B] attended the Hours after they have left the choir. For neither junior clerics nor any others may show themselves, but must always avoid them as soon as they see them.

### On observing the statutes

If any from above the choir or from the floor have not attended Vespers, they may not after Vespers stand in the street before the churchyard, remain there, or linger there long, where the dignitaries and other canons customarily gather after supper, spend time together, exchange greetings, and converse. Those who were not at Vespers may pass through, but according to the rule they must not remain there long.

### On junior clerics

When a junior cleric passing through the cloister [Col. 1104C] sees a canon or chaplain, he must turn aside from them, withdraw out of sight, or hide himself if he can. If he cannot, he must at once place himself against the wall, put his hands before his eyes, and stand there until the canon or priest has passed. A canon who sees that the junior cleric is doing what he can ought to pass on without taking notice.

### How new clerics or priests ought to enter the choir of Holy Cross, and be formed

When a canon or another person calls a chaplain or cleric, who must have been born in lawful wedlock, must not have abandoned the religious life, and must have no other lawful impediment, he must send him [Col. 1104D] to his own table with one of his clerics, to one of the lords of Holy Cross, so that he may receive him into his choir and instruct him in the order of the Church. The cleric presenting that cleric or priest must say to the lord of Holy Cross or his vicar: “My lord commands you to let him know whether he comes well and regularly to church and continuously to all the Hours.” There he must serve for three months or longer.

### When he must go to Saint Stephen’s

After that period, he must send him to the sacristan of Saint Stephen’s and speak the same words that he spoke to the lord of Holy Cross. There he must serve for four months or longer. When that period has elapsed, he must send him to the precentor, who [Col. 1105A] must instruct the cleric or priest to observe the rule and serve the church continuously for a year, missing neither Matins nor any other Hour of the day except from necessity.

### When he must go into the greater church, and what must be done

Then he is sent to the cantor, who is bound to give him the same admonitions. Afterwards he must send him to the master, who must examine them, or him, in literacy and chant, to determine whether he can sing well according to the form of the Church of Lyons. If he cannot sing, and is a cleric, he must promise the master that he will chant and learn our use of the Church of Lyons. He must thus bind himself to know how to sing well and by heart, and take care to serve the church continuously [Col. 1105B] for a year without any interruption, so that he misses neither Matins nor any of the other Hours without cause, and does not dare to infringe the order of the Church at all. For he would be punished harshly and severely, since no one, without practice and the greatest exercise, can say what he has never learned.

### On clerics who do not have a master

Likewise, neither a cleric nor another person, such as a priest or one similarly situated, is received into the choir unless he has a master in whose household he is continually maintained.

### On expulsion

Nor may a lord expel him from his household without a just and lawful cause. Hence Ambrose: “For how can there be instruction without exercise, or progress without practice? He who wishes to acquire military discipline exercises daily from the beginning; though never placed in actual engagement, he nevertheless rehearses battle as though the enemy stood before him, tests the strength of his arms for skill, or avoids the blows of opponents. These things proceed from watchful observation.” [Col. 1105C]

Likewise, another comparison: one who strives to steer a ship on the sea by rudder or to propel it by oars first practises on a river. So clerics who wish to enter the choir of the Church of Lyons should first strive to train themselves constantly in other churches, and there first learn the order of the Church of Lyons, so that they may know how to serve on the sea—that is, in the Church of Lyons.

Likewise, those who seek sweetness of song and excellence of voice first gradually awaken their voice by singing; thus clerics [Col. 1105D] must strengthen themselves in the order in which they have been instructed for a long time.

Likewise, those who seek a crown through bodily strength and a long contest of wrestling, hardening themselves by the daily practice of the wrestling-school and exerting their limbs, grow accustomed through endurance to bear labour. Thus those who wish to serve God and live piously in God must and are bound naturally to accustom their whole body and soul to God’s service, because they are co-heirs of Jesus Christ and ought to be so if they are worthy.

Likewise Ambrose: “Nature herself teaches you this in little children: that they first practise the sounds of singing, retain them, and learn to sing … a certain exhalation and exercise of the voice.” Therefore, those who wish to learn the discipline of singing must not reject what comes from nature, but preserve and learn it, so that those who are [Col. 1106A] on watch may keep watch and not sleep; for everything is strengthened by its own proper and familiar exercises. Thus too clerics who wish to enter so great a Church as that of Lyons must for a long time attend diligently to the service of the church.

### How the guardians of Holy Cross and the sacristan of Saint Stephen’s must act if new clerics do not come to church

Likewise, the lords or vicars of Holy Cross are bound to make known, as is also the sacristan of Saint Stephen’s, to the lords who send them clerics … priests who ought to enter their choirs … the choir of Saint John … saying to those same lords: “Your clerics, whom you sent to us so that they might … serve our churches, have not come and do not come [Col. 1106B] to the office … as they should, to Matins and Vespers; rather, negligently and as far as … they have come and do come, and only seldom, for they scarcely come to Matins once in a week. Therefore take counsel concerning this, so that they may come better and more continuously to God’s service; otherwise, we shall expel them from our choir.”

The sacristan of Saint Stephen’s must say the same thing to the lords from whom he receives clerics.

### On the church service required of the clerics of Saint Stephen’s, Holy Cross, and the greater church

Likewise, clerics of Holy Cross and Saint Stephen’s, and the other clerics of the greater Church, must come on Sunday and especially on other feast days, when they are not occupied in the service of their own churches, to the procession of holy water, to the procession, to the Sunday Mass at Terce, and to Sext and None. [Col. 1106C] Likewise, all are bound to be at the procession of holy water, as stated above, until the end; then the master or submaster of the choir gives a cope to one of the lesser clerics, namely a subdeacon or someone similar. The same is to be observed also on feasts of the lesser class.

### On the third and sixth Hours, which they are bound to attend

Likewise, throughout the week they are similarly bound to come to Terce, to the Sunday Mass, and to Sext. The vicars of Holy Cross in particular are bound to sing Terce and Sext.

### On leaving the choir

No cleric, priest, or anyone else may or ought, according to the rule, to leave the choir [Col. 1106D] except from necessity, as has been said, or with his lord. If lords wish to leave the choir, their clerics may indeed leave with them. But when the lords are outside the choir, they must turn to their clerics and say, if the lords wish to enter the choir again: “You return; let this one alone come with me into the choir, or these two.”

### Likewise, on leaving the choir

All clerics who enter the choir at Matins may not leave it until the whole service is finished, whatever their rank. If they leave on their own authority and wish to return to the office, they act against the rule and sin. As soon as they return to the choir again, the master must punish and chastise them for disobedience. For [Col. 1107A] the lords received them into bodily maintenance for this very purpose: that they might serve the church and … [lacuna], being lukewarm in coming to the church’s service; but let the diligent lose the same [reading uncertain]; so that, God’s service having been abandoned, they may commend themselves worthily to God and people by serving, because to serve God is to reign.

### On entering the cloister

If a feast falls on the day after Sunday, no canon nor any other cleric who has been outside the town may or ought to come and enter the cloister during those two feast days, until the third day. If he should happen to arrive, he must remain outside the cloister; on the third day he may enter the cloister, if no feast occurs.

### On missing Matins

[Col. 1107B]

If anyone who is in the cloister misses Matins on any feast, knowingly or through negligence, he may not leave his lodging throughout that feast day, either for a meal or for any reason. If a “closed feast” falls on Monday after Sunday, no canon or other cleric may miss Matins; and if he misses them, he may not leave his house throughout that day, whatever cause may arise for him. If nevertheless he goes out, he acts against the rule and sins, and that day he may receive nothing in the refectory.

### To whom correction belongs

All the chaplains who are of the Twelve, and also the others who are of the Seven Knights, are bound to rebuke [Col. 1107C] and, when they rebuke, all those who act against the order of the Church; they must not flatter anyone. The master and submaster much … [lacuna].

### How they are to comport themselves in summer

All clerics, chaplains, and canons may enter the choir in summer without stockings for all the Hours of the day, from the feast of Saints Peter and Paul until the rule begins again after the feast of Saint Michael, if they wish to wear stockings. They must nevertheless have and wear long garments and a long surplice, so that the nakedness of their legs does not appear. But they may perform no service in church without stockings, nor go to the book or the candlesticks, nor [Col. 1107D] walk in the church.

### On correcting boys

If the weekly cleric responsible for the antiphons does not announce during the night to the weekly officiant of the vicars the *Benedictus* and the *Magnificat*, or the responsory for the second antiphon, the weekly officer of the *vitatorium* must beat the cleric at once before he returns to his place; and if he does not beat him, he acts wrongly.

### On rebuking clerics

No cleric from the floor may answer anyone from above the choir when he rebukes or reprimands him. If, however, he has done or said anything against the rule, then all clerics must patiently hear their superiors and humbly endure the reproofs of their superiors, making no response to them. If they have done or said … [Col. 1108A] anything, they must … excuse themselves without a clamour of words and without scandal.

### On correcting boys

When clerics and boys leave rehearsal, they must go out peacefully, without tumult, annoyance, or shouting. Nor may they push one another with their hands; rather, they must proceed without scandal and in order to their lodgings. They must not run here and there through church or cloister in ecclesiastical clothing, but must always remain in church and outside under rule and correction.

### On rehearsal

After the feast of Saints Peter and Paul rehearsal is not held except at the discretion of the master or submaster; but [Col. 1108B] it must always be held on Sundays, especially for the correction of clerics when they offend, appear likely to offend, or do anything contrary to the order of the Church. There clerics must be admonished and corrected by the masters, lest they appear to act against the order and so have cause for repentance or punishment.

### On a canon’s vicar

If a canon from the floor appoints a vicar in his office, he may not enter the choir while chant is being sung if the vicar is performing his office; nor may any other person from the floor stand in the choir while he has appointed a vicar in his office.

### On the vested: how and where they vest

A canon-chaplain must vest in the chapter house [Col. 1108C] on every Sunday and feast day in all priestly vestments. All other vested ministers must come adorned, each in his alb, when they enter the chapter house, and there must put on silk vestments. Canon-deacons and canon-subdeacons may not wash their hands in the chapter house or comb their hair; rather, they must be clean, well groomed, and dressed in their albs when they enter the chapter house to adorn themselves with silk vestments. Likewise, during the week, the junior cleric must serve the deacon, and the subdeacon the chaplain.

As soon as the junior cleric has served during the week, the deacon must put on his surplice and stand beside the entrances of the choir. When the introit of Mass begins, he must immediately [Col. 1108D] enter the choir and stand in the choir above the deacons, remaining there until the beginning of the prayer. Then he must ascend to the presbytery, remove his surplice, take the tablets, enter the choir, and stand opposite the subdeacon who reads the epistle. When the epistle has been read, the junior cleric must stand in the middle of the choir, at the place where the epistle was read, and sing the responsory and Alleluia there.

It should also be known that during the week, when no full feast or feast with a lesser *classicum* occurs, priest, deacon, and subdeacon must vest in the chapel of Saint Peter; the junior cleric must serve the deacon, and the subdeacon the priest, etc., as is set out above.

### On the arrangement of the junior cleric’s responsory and Alleluia

[Col. 1109A]

When the *retornus* for Terce begins to ring, the master or submaster must come to the place where rehearsal is held. The junior cleric must be there, rehearse the responsory and Alleluia, and establish that he knows how to sing them well and properly. The master is bound to show the Gospel to the deacon and the epistle to the subdeacon, lest anyone make an error or pronounce badly in the service of the Masses.

### On rehearsal of antiphons and responsories

When something must be changed in the offices—at Matins, Mass, or Vespers—the master of the choir, the sacristan of Saint Stephen’s, and the vicar of Holy Cross must come together after None, before the choir, and there discuss harmoniously those matters concerning which they have doubts. If [Col. 1109B] they act otherwise, they act wrongly.

### On entering Sunday Mass

No cleric from the floor may enter the choir by himself for Sunday Mass on feast days once the angelic hymn has begun, namely, “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*). But if he follows his lord, he may indeed enter. Those from above the choir may enter on feast days until the end of the epistle; afterwards not. The junior clerics, however, must all enter together at the third *Kyrie eleison*.

When the junior cleric commits the final responsory to the weekly officer of the *vitatorium* and has told him the responsory, he must sit in the choir before the person to whom he has given the responsory; shortly afterwards he may [Col. 1109C] leave the choir, if he wishes, or return to his place.

### On shaving the beard and tonsure

No canon, however great his authority, nor any other cleric—whether from the floor or from above the choir—may shave his beard without shaving his tonsure. Otherwise he may not enter the choir while chant is being sung with his head uncovered, nor perform any office in church while he appears so disgracefully ill-kept in his tonsure and the shaving of his crown. Likewise, weekly canons and all others must renew their tonsures at the beginning of their weeks; and all canons and others must do so at Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, All Saints, Rogationtide, [Col. 1109D] and the Ember fasts. On Maundy Thursday only the two who perform the office [must do so]; otherwise they perform … [lacuna] … must … minister the offices to others, nor be attached in the choir.

### Where clerics from the floor, of whatever authority, must assemble

It was decreed and ordained that clerics from the floor, for Matins and all the other Hours of the day, should assemble together in one place prepared for those clerics, namely the chapel of Blessed Photinus, while the *tabuscellus* sounds, or the *retornus* for whatever Hour, or the *classus* on feast days—whether they are subformaries, deacons, subdeacons, or junior clerics—so that they are not seen wandering idly through the church before the lords, dignitaries, or others who are above the choir, of whatever [Col. 1110A] rank they may be.

For it was ordained from ancient times that no cleric from the floor should linger, sit, or hold any conversation in or outside the church with anyone from above the choir, whether he be a canon or any other person. Nor should canons, chaplains, or those who are of the Seven permit any cleric from the floor to remain, sit, or linger in or outside the church, or speak with anyone from above the choir, where there is a subformary, or while Vespers or other Hours are being rung in the Church of Lyons. Rather, the clerics must hide themselves from the presence of the lords in the place prepared and assigned to them, remain and sit there in peace, without noise, clamour, or scandal, [Col. 1110B] until the *tabuscellus* or *classus* ceases. They must then immediately arrange themselves in procession: first the junior clerics, then the subdeacons, and third the deacons must enter the choir on feast days.

### On beginning Vespers

The weekly chaplain may not begin Vespers until the junior clerics and the other clerics, arranged in procession, enter the choir on Sundays and feast days. On other days the chaplain may begin Matins and the other Hours when he wishes, but first he must ring the signal so that the final bell of each Hour may cease.

### On admonishing clerics

Clerics must always be admonished, in the order of justice, [Col. 1110C] by those to whom mastery belongs, to walk orderly through the cloister and through the church with great reverence and humble devotion.

### How canons proceed to Mass

In Advent, Lent, and the Ember fasts, when the deacon proceeds at Mass to read the Gospel, the subdeacon must go before him as far as the entrance of the choir and stand there. If, however, … [lacuna] … thus the junior cleric goes to the candlestick, and the deacon must go before the cross to read the Gospel. When it has been read, the subdeacon must go opposite, as far as the descent of the cross, receive the book, and carry it open to the chaplain, so that he may kiss the Gospel.

Likewise, on Wednesday in Lent, when two [Col. 1110D] epistles occur, the candle-bearer reads; the subdeacon sings the first responsory; the weekly officiant sings the second responsory; and during the year the candle-bearer sings the second responsory.

### On the vested ministers

On the Sunday *Invocavit me*, Mid-Lent Sunday, and Palm Sunday, all vested ministers wear tunics and dalmatics at Sunday Masses. On Palm Sunday the Gospel-book is placed upon the altar at Mass, and candlesticks are carried.

### On responsories in Lent

It was also decreed in chapter and confirmed by oath, because of the pride and indignation of a powerful canon, nobler than the rest, who refused to sing the responsory in Lent [Col. 1111A] when it had been assigned and sent to him by the precentor. At length, after counsel had been taken with the lords and all the dignitaries, he was expelled from choir and chapter until he had made suitable satisfaction in chapter for that deprivation of the office, that insult to the office of Mass, and that contempt of the whole assembly.

Therefore it was decreed in chapter, and received and approved by all, that just as penalties are exacted from vested ministers, so they should likewise be exacted for all other offices assigned in the Church of Lyons by the precentor, cantor, or master: such as tracts, copes, responsories, *vitatoria*, and other offices which are assigned at some time during the year by the masters of the Church. Thus the Church might not be wholly deprived of its office and held in contempt by its servants, whom the populace calls noble. [Col. 1111B]

It afterwards came about that the greater and lesser nobles, including those of the highest rank among the dignitaries, performed for themselves the tasks entrusted to them by the masters of the Church [reading uncertain: *commissa*], in their assigned time, without objection or offence, and with the greatest humility, devotion, and reverence. Afterwards many nobles sought and caused the masters to know that they should assign them an office of singing, so that they might have an opportunity to perform the service of God in the church of God.

### On proceeding soberly through the choir, and on carrying the thurible or other things through the choir

Whoever carries the thurible or book on feast days at Matins, Mass, or Vespers must proceed soberly, humbly, [Col. 1111C] and becomingly through the choir while performing a canon’s office. Others also, when acting in the place of canons or bound to do so orderly, must attend to performing the same service without scandal to those who are in the choir or to themselves, so that God may be praised and honoured in all who serve him.

Likewise, during the six weeks when the order is deficient, the person carrying the thurible must wear only his surplice and incense the choir on both sides as at other times.

### On not laughing in choir

No one, whether above the choir or from the floor, may, while chant is being sung in the choir, display useless laughter or engage in empty conversation with those near him. Rather, all who are in the choir must keep silence while the *tabuscellus* or *retornus* [Col. 1111D] of the Hours is rung.

### On genuflection

During the week when there is a feria, those who go to the book and candle must kneel before the altar of Blessed Speratus while the psalm “Have mercy upon me, O God” (*Miserere mei Deus*) is said. At the end of the psalm they must rise; one goes to the book and the other to the candle. If they wish to return to the choir, they may enter from above the choir, but must wait until the psalm “I have lifted up” (*Levavi*) is said; afterwards they may enter. If they do not wish to enter the choir, they may go wherever they wish.

### On appointing the *matricularius*, and what belongs to his office
It was also enacted that the sacristan should appoint a **matricularius** [church caretaker], [Col. 1112A] a mature, honourable, trustworthy man, to guard the church by day and night, who knows and is able to arrange what must be arranged in the church, and faithfully to guard . . . He also keeps the key of one chest, in which are deposited the following priestly vestments for use at the Mass of the high altar and at votive Masses; two censers, one large for major feasts and one smaller for other feasts and daily Masses; two chalices, one for the high altar and the other for votive Masses; one cope for use on Sundays; a copper basin for washing hands; four hand-towels; one silver spoon for incense; priestly vestments; and the missal for the high altar, for use [Col. 1112B] at morning Masses . . . . . . . . on feast-days. He likewise has in his keeping the ornaments of the altar of St Peter, a priestly vestment . . . and another silk chasuble with a small . . . for adorning the altar on feast-days. He also guards the hangings and curtains for adorning the choir on major feasts, and the ornaments of the altar of St Photinus. For the matricularius must guard these things faithfully, wholly, and without diminution. He has custody of the entire treasure when it is placed upon the altar at solemnities, and of all the other ornaments which, in the presence of the treasurer, he brings and sets down, as needed to adorn the altar for the Mass, until the celebration of Mass has been completed and ended and all things have been replaced by the treasurer in the custody where they formerly were. The matricularius is likewise bound to guard [Col. 1112C] everything kept within the church and those things for which he has keys. He also keeps the key of the books necessary for the service of the church.

The office of the matricularius is to light and extinguish all lamps delivered by the treasurer for lighting the church, whether the remainder belongs to the church or to the sacristan; and he must faithfully preserve without any diminution the remainder belonging both to the church and to the sacristan. It must be understood that the matricularius has no right in the candles placed by the church on major feasts, nor may he strip them of their melting drippings. The matricularius is also bound to perform in his own person the duty pertaining [Col. 1112D] to him. He neither ought nor can appoint a substitute in his office—unless he is a deacon or priest—without a cause arising, namely illness or . . . . And he must always be ready to answer anyone who comes seeking him for some necessity. He is bound to be found in the church at every hour; if summoned by the senior official, if he is a deacon, he must not answer a subordinate when . . . . by the chaplains of the church. If he does anything or commits an offence contrary to the order or statutes of the Church, or if anyone in the church hears him speak against one who corrects him, he must be punished by the cantors or by the master; they must rebuke him sharply and severely, and no one ought to indulge him because of his folly, lest he think himself wise. A man who is obstinate ought not to be appointed to the office of matricularius, [Col. 1113A] but one who is patient and humble, who patiently endures correction and makes no reply, but amends himself when he has done wrong. He must also take care concerning the ringing of the bells: they are to be rung well and without fault, and he himself is bound to ring them if necessary; unless he does so, he must be punished most severely.

## How the servants of the church ought to conduct themselves, and their reward

Concerning the offices and servants of the Church of Lyons: how they ought to conduct and exercise themselves, and through such exercise attain eternal life. Thus Paul says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith, while I have earned the crown of righteousness, which he who is the just judge will render to me on [Col. 1113B] that day” (2 Tim. 4). “On that day,” he says, “he will render it,” not here . . . Thus one must contend and fight, like a good athlete, through labours and the perils of shipwreck; hence the saying: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Therefore no one can receive the prize unless he has competed lawfully. This is the glorious victory, where contests of labour are found. Hence the saying: “Is not he unjust who gives the prize before the contest has been completed?” Thus in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matt. 5); he did not say, “Blessed are the rich,” but “the poor.” Divine blessedness is received through a life in which misery is reckoned by human standards.

Why, then, do those serving the Church of Lyons, who are called servants yet do not serve, abound [Col. 1113C] in wealth, clothe themselves in purple garments, and feast splendidly without cease, with joy and without sorrow or mourning? But the righteous, who are always assiduous in church and in the service of God, lack assistants; they are despised by their superiors and suffer the wrongs of the powerful. The Gospel parable ought to satisfy them: “A rich man was clothed in fine linen and purple and gave sumptuous feasts every day; a poor man, covered with sores, gathered the remnants from the rich man’s table. But after the death of both, the poor man rested in Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man was in torments” (Luke 16). Is it not right that this should be a sign of their deserts: either rewards or punishment after death, since toil belongs to the contest? After the contest, victory belongs to some, disgrace to others. Is a palm awarded to anyone or a crown borne to him [Col. 1113D] before the race has been run?

Therefore I say to you who labour continually in God’s service in the Church of Lyons, who discharge the service of God wholly from beginning to end and carry it out perseveringly: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5:12). Thus Ambrose promised that a reward would be rendered in the future, not in the present, in heaven and on earth. Why do you seek what is owed to another? Why do you demand the crown before you conquer? Why do you desire to wipe away the dust, to rest, to feast, before the course is finished? . . .

But perhaps you say: Why do those who neglect to serve God and disdain to render God’s service in God’s church rejoice in the present and luxuriate in pleasures? Why do they too [Col. 1114A] not labour with me? [Col. 1114B] For those who have enlisted for the crown are not bound to the labour of the contest; those who have not entered the stadium do not anoint themselves with oil or cover themselves with the dust of the world’s lowliness. They are awaited and held by the vain glory of the world and by infernal sin; but when they endure him [uncertain reference], and serve with all the affection of their mind, and have fought manfully in God’s service against the impulses of the flesh, the vain glory of the world, and the pride of life, and . . . they shall eternally obtain the kingdom of glory. Ambrose likewise says: “Those grown fat and sleek in this world are accustomed to contend in sin, not yet to contend for [the good].” Therefore let Christ’s athletes say, while such men look on: “We would come to labour with you.” But sinners reply: “We are not judged here concerning ourselves; but you, if you conquer without us, will claim the crown of glory” (1 Thess. 2).

Those, therefore, who have devoted themselves here to pleasures, excess, robbery, gain, and honours are more sinners than combatants. They have the mourning due to their labour, but not the fruit of virtue. They foster idleness and, by cunning and wickedness, pile up heaps of riches; but they shall pay, though late, the penalty of their wickedness, because they have forsaken the fountain of living water, abandoning and neglecting the order and service of the holy Church of Lyons. Their rest is hell, but yours is in heaven; their house is in the grave, but yours in paradise. Thus Job aptly said of such persons that they desire rather to keep watch in the tomb of concupiscence and fleshly impurity, to rest [Col. 1114C] in the bed of sloth and perverse avarice, and to embrace the pride of the chair of diabolical deception, because they cannot possess the sleep of repose which our Lord Jesus Christ slept in the tomb and from which he rose.

## Concerning the rest of eternal blessedness, the other duties binding upon all servants, and the punishments of those who do not serve or perform their duty

You, therefore, who desire to sleep and rise again with Christ Jesus, keep the law of the Lord and observe his commandments. According to your ability, and insofar as God has granted and permitted you, do not cease until the end to preserve and fulfil the order and service of the Church of Lyons. Let not the judgments of powerful persons disturb you—those who have and exercise power over you, [Col. 1114D] and who . . . lay heavy and unbearable burdens upon you but refuse to move them with their own finger; who neglect and disdain even to incline their ear to God’s service and to keeping the order of the Church; who despise, reproach, and mock as vile and senseless anyone who says or announces anything concerning the keeping of the Church’s order; who laugh at him and hold him up to ridicule as a fool.

Thus Ambrose says: “Brother, do not think as a child, speak as a child, conceive as a child, or judge as a child; nor claim those things which belong to the later age, for the crown belongs to the perfect.” Await the coming of that which is perfect, when you shall know, not through a likeness and in a riddle, but face to face (1 Cor. 13), the very form [Col. 1115A] of truth, openly. Then it will be revealed why one man was rich though wicked and a robber; why another was powerful; why another was affluent; and why another was foolishly exalted in honours. And it will be said to the robber: “You were rich: why did you seize what belonged to others? Did I not make you rich before God, so that you might have no excuse? Poverty did not compel you; want did not force you. Why, then, did you take the goods of churches from innocent persons serving the church, and squander the alms of the dead, which they left to the Church of Lyons for the redemption of their souls—such as refectory endowments, anniversary endowments, and other benefices?”

[Col. 1115B] It will also be said to the powerful man: “Why did you not aid the widow, namely the holy mother Church of Lyons, and her orphans—servants of that Church suffering wrong when alms assigned to them were wickedly withheld and violently taken away? Were you weak? It was for that reason that I made you powerful: not that you should inflict violence, but that you should repel it. For that reason I exalted you and others in the Church of Lyons: that you might faithfully govern it in temporal matters, increase it in spiritual matters, and preserve the order established in that Church by the holy Fathers.” Despisers of the Church—was it not written to you and the other powerful persons in the Church of Lyons: “Rescue the one suffering injustice”? And in the Psalm: “Rescue the poor and needy; deliver him from the hand of the sinner” (Ps. 81), namely poor Christ, because you defraud him of his office in the Church of Lyons; and the needy Christ [Col. 1115C] in the prayers of those serving him, because “there is none who calls upon my name in the Church of Lyons” (Isa. 64), on account of the violence of the wicked who take from lesser servants the alms of the dead.

It will also be said to the man abounding in riches: “I heaped honours upon you and granted you bodily health, though you did not follow my commandments by strictly—and not slackly—observing the order of the Church of Lyons first ordained and established by the Lord. My servant, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you? Did I not give you children whom you begot to serve the holy Church of Lyons? Did I not also confer honour and grant health? Why did you deny me, as though what you did would not come to my knowledge? Why did you hold [Col. 1115D] my gifts and the goods of the church as if they were your own, scorning my commandments by wrongfully retaining the alms of the poor?”

Finally, all these lessons may be drawn from Judas the betrayer. He too was chosen as an apostle among the twelve, so that the money-bags containing funds to be distributed to the poor might be entrusted to him. He was not to seem to have betrayed the Lord out of need; and therefore the Lord conferred these things upon him, so that Judas might be justly condemned and become liable to a greater offence, not as one embittered by an injury, but as one who had violated grace (Acts 1).

## Concerning instruction and the duties of church servants: the instruction of juniors

Since it has been made sufficiently clear what punishment follows the wickedness of evil men and what reward the virtue [Col. 1116A] of good men attains, let us begin to say something about the instruction and duties of young men, so that as age advances, a corresponding progress in good character and learning may grow. We call persons “young” either by age or by knowledge. When a cleric wishes newly to enter the choir of Lyons, he is called young, because he does not know how to stand either in choir or outside it, until he has learned from the masters or seniors the instruction or manner of humbly praying and being on his guard, the time and hour for sitting or rising, and for leaving or entering the choir. He must learn and take care not to speak with his companion while in choir, nor make any improper sign or gesture with his body; but, as instructed by his teachers, he must observe the order of the Church. [Col. 1116B] In whatever matters he can learn, let him gladly learn from his seniors and humbly observe what he learns, so that no one may be able to rebuke him; thus he may grow with age and with instruction in the order of the Church.

Thus Ambrose says: “It belongs to the young to fear God, to defer to their elders, to honour seniors, preserve chastity, not disdain humility, and love gentleness and modesty; these are ornaments of younger age.” Yet seriousness belongs to old men and eagerness to the young; thus modesty is commended to youths as though it were a dowry. Hence the saying: “Isaac feared God, being Abraham’s offspring; he deferred to his father so far that, in obedience to his father’s will, he did not refuse death” (Gen. 31). Joseph, when he had dreamed that the sun, moon, and stars worshipped him, diligently . . . deferred to his father (Gen. 37).

Thus young and lesser servants of the Church of Lyons, remaining under the formative instruction of their elders, should persevere most kindly in the same rule of order, diligently and without offence submitting to the institutions of the holy Fathers, received from the instruction of their elders, and to the sanctions of the canons. Through the mercy of Jesus Christ the Son and the clemency of the Virgin Mary, they will be able to enter by the gate of the Church of Lyons and . . . [Col. 1116C] to prosper in age and grace. Ambrose: “Joseph was chaste . . . . . . .” So too let the servants of the Church of Lyons be chaste in body and pure in mind in the service of God and of all the other saints honoured in God’s Church; let them appear worthy . . . [Col. 1116D] A person virgin in flesh but not in mind will receive no reward in the promise. For as clerics ought to be chaste, so it is fitting that they should not be proud.

Caesarius says: “Integrity is not preserved where the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride. Joseph was humble even unto the servitude into which his brothers sold him to the Ishmaelites” (*ibid.*). “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things.” Gregory says: “He who gathers other virtues without humility is like one who carries dust against the wind.” It is necessary for those serving God to preserve humility in their minds and humbly perform God’s service in the Church, that they may become like him who says: “I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

Joseph was also modest even unto flight. His [Col. 1117A] modesty was so great that, when seized by the woman, he preferred, in fleeing, to leave his garment in her hands [rather] than lay aside his modesty (Gen. 39). Thus one who wishes to serve in God’s Church must preserve modesty in everything: in bodily movement, in the performance of work, in the gesture of every limb, in walking—so that he walks with composure—in looking at things not to be looked upon, in speech, in unbecoming laughter, and in vain disturbances. Rather, he must always be engaged in prayer while he is and remains in church.

Joseph was patient even unto prison; hence, “In your patience you shall possess,” etc. (Luke 21). He was also forgiving of injury even unto recompense (Gen. 45). Modesty, patience, and forgiveness of injuries are therefore beautiful virtues; and grace is sweet, because [Col. 1117B] it is observed not only towards brethren but in speech itself. Let no one exceed the proper measure in speaking in church, where he ought to preserve and maintain silence, lest your speech utter anything indecorous—you who have sworn to serve God and all his saints. For the mirror of the mind often shines in words. Modesty ought to regulate the very sound of one’s singing and speaking in choir or church, and an excessively free voice should nowhere offend the air in speech within the church or in song.

Finally, in the very manner of speaking or singing, modesty is the first discipline in choir: one should begin little by little to chant or sing in choir, or finally to speak in church; and the beginnings of modesty should commend one’s further progress. The silence itself which must be preserved and maintained in choir and [Col. 1117C] church, in which all the remaining virtues have their repose, is the greatest exercise in preserving and possessing modesty in church. Finally, if something be relaxed on account of childhood or pride in the chief man, let it be counted as praise of modesty, and let God be blessed. There is the modesty of the chaste . . . because chastity itself is safer in companionship. For a good companion is the first aid to preserving chastity. Shame does not allow chastity to be assailed by this modesty. In prayer itself, modesty is greatly pleasing to God and greatly reconciles one to grace before God.

Therefore all clerics appointed to serve God, St John the Baptist, St Stephen, and all other saints in the Church of Lyons must be well disciplined in modesty, laden with the shame of chastity and reverence, and suitably adorned in manners pleasing to God and to all the people. Did not this virtue—modesty—support and commend the publican, who did not dare lift his eyes to heaven? Therefore, in the Lord’s judgment, he was justified more than the Pharisee whom presumption deformed (Luke 18). For this reason all servants in the Church of Lyons established and customarily maintained a tranquil mind and modest conduct: devotion rich and abundant before God. As Peter says: “Modesty is a great virtue; although it is more yielding of its own right, claiming nothing for itself and asserting nothing, yet in a manner confined within the limits of its opposites, it is rich before God, before whom no one is rich” (1 Pet. 3). Modesty is rich [Col. 1118A] because it is preferred by God.

Therefore all serving in the Church of Lyons ought to be modest in church and in their actions, lest they do before clerics or laypeople anything shameful to do or base to accomplish. Paul also commands prayer to be offered with modesty and sobriety (1 Cor. 7). He wishes this to be the first, as it were the chief, element of the prayer to come: that the sinner’s prayer may not boast, but may, as it were, clothe itself with sorrow; and that, the more modesty arises from remembrance of sin, the more abundant grace it may deserve. Modesty must likewise be maintained in movement, gesture, and gait by all clerics, both senior and junior, who serve or wish to serve in church according to the order and statutes of the ancient Fathers, because the disposition of the mind is seen in the posture of the body.

[Col. 1118B] Hence the inward person of our heart, hidden among us, is either frivolous, boastful, or base within, and does not appear except through outward bearing. Bodily gesture, on the other hand, is often judged more serious, steadfast, pure, and composed. Bodily movement is therefore a kind of voice of the soul. For this reason the ancients ordained that all clerics . . . serving in the Church of Lyons should by no means display shameful movements and gestures, idle chatter, or indecent comportment. But anyone who happens to yawn while chanting in choir should put his mouth beneath his surplice and yawn there secretly, lest he be rebuked by others standing in choir.

## Other authorities

[Col. 1118C] “I offer you an example. You remember, sons and companions, a certain man chaste in body but not in mind. Although he seemed to commend himself by diligent duties, I did not receive him into the clergy for this one reason: his gestures were everywhere most unbecoming. I received another into the clergy, but commanded that he should never walk before me, because a certain insolence in his gait struck my eyes like a blow. When, after his offence, he was restored to office, I said this: ‘This alone I excepted. This alone I excepted.’ Nor did my judgment fail. For he withdrew from the church, so that, as he had been revealed by his gait, so was his treachery of mind displayed. One indeed abandoned the faith during the time of the Arian persecution; the other, from greed for money and to avoid being judged by a priestly tribunal, [Col. 1118D] denied that he was one of us. In that gait there mourned an image of frivolity, a certain likeness of roving buffoons.”

There are also some who, walking slowly, imitate theatrical steps and, as it were, the processional platforms and posed statues of pageants, so that whenever they take a step they appear to observe certain measured movements. Nor do I consider running in one’s walk honourable, unless some danger or just necessity requires it. All serving in the Church of Lyons ought to show approved steps, in which the spirit of composure, the weight of seriousness and authority, and the trace of tranquillity should appear humbly in all things.

If clerics serving in the Church of Lyons neglect to apply themselves to the ordered gait [Col. 1119A] of the Church of Lyons, how will they learn its order and serve worthily the church which they are bound to serve worthily and laudably? While remaining present in the cloister, they offend God and the saints, despise the statutes of the holy Fathers, incur the sin of disobedience, and may without doubt deservedly fear the sentence of the first parent, to whom it was said: “You shall die the death” [Col. 1120A] (Gen. 2), because you were not obedient to my commands. For this reason they are bound inviolably to observe the aforesaid holy statutes and ordinances issued by the holy Fathers, as good and true children of obedience.

## About the Year 1182. Peter, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, of the Title of St Chrysogonus

[Col. 1119]

## Notice from *Gallia Christiana*

(Vol. VIII, col. 1616, among the Bishops of Meaux)

Peter, fellow student of Stephen of Tournai [Note: [Col. 1119] See Stephen of Tournai’s Letter 46, to Peter (*Patrologia*, vol. CCXI): “I embrace the student, attend upon the archdeacon, kiss the abbot, rise before the bishop, and reverence the cardinal.” Henry of Clairvaux, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, praises Peter highly in a letter addressed to Pope Alexander III. See *Patrologia*, vol. CC, among the letters of various writers to Alexander. (EDITOR)], was first archdeacon, then abbot, and was elected bishop of Meaux, chiefly through the influence of William of Champagne, son of Count Theobald and archbishop of Sens. Some time afterward Pope Alexander III, because of his outstanding learning and immense merits, created him cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus and sent him as legate to France in 1173 to suppress the heresy of the Albigensians. He seems to have died around the year 1182.

[Col. 1119]

## Letters of Peter of St Chrysogonus

I. To Ervisius, Abbot of St Victor’s, Paris.

[Col. 1119B]

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXCVI, col. 1383.)

II. To Garinus, Abbot of the Same Monastery.

(See *ibid.*, col. 1392.)

III. To All the Faithful: On the Excommunication of the Albigensian Heretics. (1178.)

PETER, by the grace of God cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See, to all children of holy mother Church who keep the Catholic and apostolic faith: greeting in the Lord.

As the Apostle testifies (Eph. 4), just as God is one, [Col. 1119C] so too there is known to be one faith, from whose integrity no one can depart without danger. Its foundation—other than which no one can lay another—was so firmly and circumspectly laid by the apostles and apostolic men, their successors, under the inspiration and instruction of the Holy Spirit, through sound doctrines as though through living stones, that neither the blast of the sounding north wind [Col. 1120B] nor the engines of the impious, although it is attacked by repeated assaults, can move it from its firmness.

Therefore, although in these days certain false brethren—Raymund of Baimiac, Bernard Raymund, and certain other heresiarchs—transforming themselves into angels of light when they are servants of Satan, had previously preached doctrines contrary to the Christian and apostolic faith, deceived many souls by their poisonous preaching, and drawn them with themselves into ruin, yet at last he who reveals mysteries and gave Daniel the spirit to confute the elders of Israel (Dan. 13), looking upon souls deceived by diabolical fraud, did not wish their perfidy to remain veiled any longer, nor the purity of the Christian [Col. 1120C] faith to be corrupted by their preaching. Rather, by his wondrous power, before many hearers and witnesses, he exposed what had previously been hidden: the poison of their perfidy, for the increase and glory of the Christian faith.

[Col. 1121A] Accordingly, when the aforesaid Raymund and Bernard, together with others, had met our venerable brother Reginald, bishop of Bath, and the noblemen the viscount of Turenne and Raymund of Castronovo, who had come, by our counsel, into the land of Roger de Beders for the release of our venerable brother, the bishop of Albi [Albanensis in the text]; and when they complained that they were being unjustly treated by the noble Count of Toulouse and other barons who had abjured them forever; they declared that they would come into our presence to defend their faith if they had security for coming and returning.

[Col. 1121B] The said bishop and viscount, lest the hearts of simple people imbued with their dregs should suffer scandal, and lest it be imputed to our distrust if they were denied a hearing, granted on our behalf and on behalf of the aforesaid count that they should present themselves before us in complete security. They were to be heard under the examination of ourselves, our venerable brother the bishop of Poitiers, legate of the Apostolic See, other discerning men, and all the people; and, if they believed rightly and soundly, they were to be approved. After examination by us, they were nevertheless to return safely to their homes, so that they might not appear to have been induced by fear or any violence to confess the true faith. This was on the condition, however, that, after eight days had elapsed, in accordance with the edict that had been issued, unless they returned to our faith, they must be expelled from the lands of the princes who had abjured them.

[Col. 1121C] We therefore ratified the permission granted them by the bishop and viscount, although, as we have said, the aforesaid Count of Toulouse and other noblemen had issued an edict that they should be expelled from their lands. The bishop of Poitiers, the aforesaid Count of Toulouse, and about three hundred other clerics and laymen having assembled with us in the church of St Stephen, we enjoined them to set forth their faith to us and, returning to the truth of the Catholic faith, to remove by a saving confession of the true faith the infamy which both the whole region and they themselves had incurred through their damnable preaching.

Among other words exchanged back and forth, they produced in the midst of the assembly a certain document in which they had written the articles of their faith, and read it out as it had been composed at length. Since we noticed certain words in it [Col. 1121D] that seemed suspicious, and that, unless more fully explained, could conceal the heresy they had preached, we asked them to defend their faith by answering in Latin terms. We did so both because their language was not sufficiently known to us and because the Gospels and Epistles, by which alone they wished to confirm their faith, are known to have been written in the Latin tongue. Since they did not dare do this, being wholly ignorant of Latin, as appeared in the words of one of them—who, wishing to speak Latin, could scarcely join two words and failed altogether—it was necessary for us to accommodate ourselves to them and, concerning the ecclesiastical sacraments, to use the vernacular language because of their ignorance, though that was quite absurd.

[Col. 1122A] Denying, therefore, that there were two principles, they publicly confessed before us and the aforesaid men, and firmly asserted, that the one most high God had created all things visible and invisible; and they confirmed this from the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures, as is true. They also confessed that our priest, whether good or bad, just or unjust—even one whom they knew beyond doubt to be adulterous or otherwise criminal—could consecrate Christ’s body and blood; and that through the ministry of such a priest and the power of the divine words uttered by the Lord, bread and wine are truly transubstantiated into Christ’s body and blood.
