They likewise asserted that infants or adults baptized with our baptism are saved, and that [Col. 1122B] no one can be saved without that baptism, utterly denying that they possessed another baptism or an imposition of hands, as was alleged against them. They nevertheless affirmed that a husband and wife joined in marriage, provided no other sin hinders them, are saved and excused for the good of marriage even though they carnally render the marital debt to one another, and are never condemned on that account. They affirmed moreover that archbishops, bishops, priests, monks, canons, hermits, Templars, and Hospitallers are to be saved.

They also said it was fitting and just that churches founded in honour of God and the saints should be visited with the highest devotion; that honour [Col. 1122C] and reverence should be shown to priests and their other ministers; that first-fruits and tithes ought to be paid to them; and that all parochial dues ought to be rendered devoutly and faithfully. They further commendably asserted, among other things, that alms should be given both to churches and to the poor, and indeed to everyone who asks. Although they were previously said to have denied all these things, they asserted that they understood them according to our sound interpretation.

After they had thus been examined by us and had voluntarily confessed the things we have stated, we entered the church of St. James. There an innumerable multitude of people, who seemed to have assembled as though for a spectacle, gathered with us and heard, in the vernacular, their confession of faith, which had been written down in the aforesaid document. Then, after they had been heard by us and by all the people [Col. 1122D] assembled there, with complete patience and without any disturbance, and after they themselves had voluntarily finished speaking—since their exposition of faith seemed sufficiently commendable and Catholic—we again asked them, in the hearing of all the people, whether they believed in their hearts what they had confessed with their mouths, and whether they had ever preached the contrary, as had repeatedly been alleged against them.

When they replied that they did indeed so believe, and nevertheless denied ever having preached otherwise, the noble Count of Toulouse and many other clerics and laymen who had heard them preaching otherwise, deeply stirred with astonishment and inflamed with zeal for the Christian faith, rose up and most plainly convicted them of having lied outright. For some firmly asserted [Col. 1123A] that they had heard certain of them say that there were two gods, one good and the other evil: the good one made only invisible things and those unable to be changed or corrupted; the evil one created heaven, earth, humankind, and the other visible things. Others affirmed that they had heard in their preaching that Christ’s body is not consecrated through the ministry of an unworthy priest or one entangled in certain crimes. Many likewise testified that they had heard them utterly deny that a husband and wife can be saved if either renders the marital due to the other. Others directly charged them that they had heard from them that baptism does not benefit children, and that they had uttered many other blasphemies against God, the holy Church, and the Catholic faith—blasphemies which, because of the abominable enormity of them, we have preferred [Col. 1123B] to pass over rather than report.

Yet whatever they may have said in their earlier confession—which seemed sufficient for salvation if they so believed in their hearts unto righteousness and confessed it with their mouths—in the end, like men of twisted minds and perverse intention, they refused to abandon their heresy where the superficial appearance of some authority seemed to assist their gross and benumbed understanding. They took occasion from the saying which the Lord is recorded to have spoken in the Gospel: “Do not swear at all; but let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no’” (Matt. 5), saying that they ought not to swear, although the Lord himself is frequently read to have sworn, as it is written: “The Lord has sworn,” etc. (Ps. 109). And elsewhere: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord” (Isa. 19); and the Apostle: “An oath is the end of every dispute” (Heb. 6). And [Col. 1123C] many passages of this kind present themselves and occur to those reading the divine Scriptures, by which, because of the weakness of those whom we seek to persuade in some matter, we are permitted to swear.

But they, like unlearned men not understanding the Scriptures (Matt. 22), fell into the snare which they had hidden (Ps. 141). For although they had previously recoiled from an oath as an execrable thing forbidden by the Lord, they were convicted of having sworn in the very document of their confession when they said: “In the truth which is God, we thus believe and declare that this is our faith.” They did not know that to invoke the truth and word of God as testimony to a true assertion is beyond doubt to swear, as we read of the Apostle when he said: “For this we say to you [Col. 1123D] in the word of God” (1 Thess. 4); and elsewhere: “God is my witness” (Rom. 1). Other similar passages confirm this, and can more readily be found by those who understand and have read the divine Scriptures.

When they had been convicted by many sufficient witnesses, and when many more were preparing to testify against them, we admonished them more carefully—for the Church is accustomed not to deny the bosom of mercy to those who return—that, putting aside all heretical depravity, they should return to the unity of the faith. And because they had been excommunicated by the lord pope, by our venerable brothers the archbishops of Bourges and Narbonne, by the bishop of Toulouse, and by ourselves, on account of their perverse preaching and sect, [Col. 1124A] they should come to us to be reconciled according to the form of the Church.

When they, turned into a crooked bow and hardened in a ruined mind, refused to do this, we, in the presence of all the people—who continually shouted and raged against them with great ferocity—again, with lighted candles, together with the aforesaid bishop of Poitiers and the other religious men who stood by us in all things, pronounced them excommunicated and condemned them with their author, the devil. Therefore we admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that you carefully avoid the aforesaid Raymond and Bernard and their accomplices as excommunicated persons handed over to Satan. And if hereafter they presume to preach to you anything other than what, as we have written above, they confessed in [Col. 1124B] our hearing, reject their preaching as false and contrary to the Catholic and apostolic faith; and drive them far away, as heretics and forerunners of Antichrist, from fellowship with your sincerity and from your territories.

### IV. To Philip, dean, and the chapter of St. Martin of Tours

—He confirms the foundation for two candles to be kept continually burning before the tomb of St. Martin. (About the year 1180.)

*(Marten.,* Thesaurus Anecdotorum, *I, 592.)*

PETER, by the grace of God cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, [Col. 1124C] legate of the Apostolic See, to PH., dean, and to the chapter of St. Martin of Tours: greeting in the Lord.

Whenever things are established by the faithful for the honor and adornment of the house of the Lord, we ought to promote them with all the greater care because those who have undertaken them of their own free will ought all the more to be encouraged and induced by us to do so. Therefore, beloved brothers in the Lord, moved by your requests and more deeply rooted in devotion to the most blessed confessor who is known to rest among you, we ratify the institution made in your chapter with solemn devotion by you and by the burgesses of that place, your parishioners: namely, that two candles are to be lighted before the tomb of that confessor for all time, without any interruption whatsoever. And, as is more fully contained in the authentic document drawn up by you concerning this matter, we confirm it by the authority entrusted to us and strengthen it with the protection of this present writing. We decree and, under threat of anathema, strictly forbid anyone rashly to contravene this institution, or to diminish, defer, or in any way curtail the revenues assigned for this purpose. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the most blessed confessor, as well as the strict vengeance of the Last Judgment.

## ABOUT THE SAME YEAR: ROGER, ABBOT OF ST. EVURTIUS OF ORLÉANS

[Col. 1125]

### NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. VIII, col. 1575.)*

Roger, the first regular abbot, discovered the relics of St. Evurtius five years after his election. He reported their discovery in a letter to Abbot Freher of St. Ouen, printed by Martène. An error has crept into the assigned year in the bull by which Eugenius III confirms the possessions of St. Evurtius, issued to Roger: 1147 should be read instead of 1114. Following the pope’s example, King Louis honored Abbot Roger with a royal diploma, in which he recites the possessions of St. Evurtius in the same terms as the bull. In that same year Roger subscribed a charter of the same king for the people of Orléans; and two years later, in 1149, he subscribed letters of Simon of Baugency for Bourg-Moyen. He is found in the cartulary of Micy in the year 1150, when Bishop Manasses issued a charter at the request of Abbot Roger and the brothers of St. Evurtius. He obtained from Adrian IV and Alexander III bulls of the same tenor as the bull of Eugenius III. He is mentioned in charters of Pontlevoy in the year 1158. By an exchange he obtained from Louis VII, in 1163, Thoury [*Toarvilla*] in the parish of Souvigny [*Sebonvilla*] in the Beauce [*Belsia*]. Invited by the supreme pontiff to the Council of Tours, he consulted Ervisius, abbot of St. Victor, in 1164. He had a dispute with the prior of Pont-aux-Moines and Stephen, abbot of Cluny, which arbitrators settled in 1167: Bishop Manasses and Dean John. In this or the following year he yielded to the wishes of Stephen, the regular canon whose seventeenth letter is addressed to Roger, his abbot.

[Col. 1125]

### REVELATION

Which Lord Roger, abbot of the church of Blessed Evurtius of Orléans, sent to the monks of St. Ouen at Rouen concerning the discovery of that same most holy bishop Evurtius. (About 1150.)

*[Marten.,* Anecdota, *I, 413, from a manuscript of St. Ouen at Rouen.]*
  
[Col. 1125A] To the beloved lords and friends in Christ, F., [Note: [Col. 1125A] Freher, who governed the abbey of St. Ouen from approximately 1142 to 1157.] abbot of Blessed Ouen, and to that entire holy congregation: Brother ROGER, [Note: [Col. 1125A] The Sainte-Marthe brothers report that he was appointed first abbot of St. Evurtius in 1163, to which year they also refer the beginnings of regular life in the monastery [Col. 1126A] of St. Evurtius. Yet Freher, to whom Roger writes, had relinquished his abbatial office in 1157. Indeed, Abbot Suger of St. Denis, mentioned here, had already died in 1151.] called abbot of the monastery of Blessed Evurtius, and the entire community of the poor of that place: greeting and affection.

That you honor our blessed and glorious father and patron Evurtius with the due devotion of veneration, we indeed thank you to the extent of our ability; but that pious servant of God will, in his kindness, obtain worthy rewards for your devotion. Now, because you rejoice with us over his most sacred discovery and eagerly ask us about its manner and date, receive a brief account in a few suitable words.

Our predecessors, the secular canons [Col. 1126A] who served in the holy church of the blessed confessor nearly five years ago, frequently intended to enlarge the still narrow building of the church. They advanced so far in the project that they even made a kiln, from whose lime they would build the holy walls; and we still possess that very lime. But suddenly, by God’s prompting, they changed their plan, fearing, of course, that if by chance they found that holy treasure in their field, they would be expelled from the church and the place itself handed over to monks or regular canons who would render more devout worship to so great a Father.

But when it pleased divine mercy to place us, its servants living under a regular habit, in that holy church, we immediately [Col. 1127A] did not yield to flesh and blood—fearing, that is, where there was no fear—but trusting in God’s mercy. We frequently and long held this in our prayers, in our desires, in our fasts and afflictions: that the kindly mercy of God might reveal in our time the glorious body of the pious Father Evurtius to his servants. The Lord had mercy on us and heard the desire of his poor. For we received what we asked, found what we sought, and the place was opened to us where we knocked.

Indeed, almost all our lords and fathers, bishops as well as abbots, whenever they stopped among us for prayer or to visit us, as is customary, urged and incited our perversity, that we should seek without delay that singular joy of ours. Moreover, Lord Suger, abbot of St. [Col. 1127B] Denis, a man of lofty counsel and outstanding prudence, when he came to Orléans one day, was led by us into a certain sacristy of our church, which was enclosed from public access behind the altar of the glorious Father Evurtius by a partition wall. We showed him a certain large wooden chest, which from ancient times had been placed over the venerable tomb of the saint himself. At its bottom lay a long, somewhat black stone, called *achlesiam* [sic; uncertain], [Col. 1128A] apparently prepared for no other purpose than the sealing of a tomb; it supplied a striking indication, to one observing it, of a great hidden treasure. Then he said: “It is here; seek here, for here you will find it.” And he added: “Do not delay. Exalt God, and, when exalted, he will exalt you” (Ps. 98).

We took courage not only from the oracle of so great a father, but also from revelations granted to our brothers and from miracles openly performed before our eyes. And so, after a fast and a general prayer had preceded, on Friday of the third week of the Advent of the Lord, as night approached, we came with a few brothers to the place of holy repose. Then, digging, we found two sarcophagi, one above the other, not far apart; these themselves stood within four walls opposite one another, very beautiful [Col. 1128B] and constructed of painted little bricks, coated with excellent smooth red cement. We secretly opened the first sarcophagus after Mass on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, but found absolutely nothing in it. In the lower one, however, on the feast day of the Holy Innocents, after Matins, what we sought was found. We received prudent counsel from religious persons that the celebrated elevation of so holy a body, or its transfer from place to place, should be postponed until the arrival of the lord king.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1181: WALTER, PRIOR OF ST. VICTOR AT PARIS

[Col. 1127]

### NOTICE

*(Fabric.,* Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis, ed. Mansi, vol. III, p. 118.)*

Walter, prior of St. Victor at Paris, was the writer of four books containing many things worth knowing. Launoy testified in *On the Various Fortune of Aristotle*, ch. 3, p. 29, that he had seen two manuscript copies in the library of St. Victor at Paris:

> Against the manifest heresies, condemned even in councils, which the sophists Abelard, Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gilbert of Poitiers—the four labyrinths of France, inspired by one Aristotelian spirit—sharpen, polish, and reinforce in their books of Sentences.

He lived about the year 1180. See Bulaeus, vol. II of the *History of the University of Paris*, pp. 404–629. Mabillon, in the *Analecta*, p. 54 of the new edition, mentions this book of Walter [Note: [Col. 1127] *Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, under Abbaudo. See also the notes of Dom Mathoud on Robert Pullen, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, cols. 1047 and 1062.], whom he calls not prior but abbot; he says that he wrote four books against the four labyrinths of France, namely Abelard, Peter Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gilbert of Poitiers. He also reports there a fragment taken from the same book concerning Abelard. MANSI.

[Col. 1129]

## EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOKS OF WALTER OF ST. VICTOR AGAINST THE FOUR LABYRINTHS OF FRANCE

*(History of the University of Paris, by César Egasse du Boulay [Bulaeus]; Paris, 1665–1673, 6 folio volumes, vol. II, pp. 629–660.)*

### FROM BOOK ONE

[Col. 1129A] There exists in the library of St. Victor a manuscript codex of Master Walter of St. Victor, divided into four books against the four most celebrated masters of his age: Peter Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, Peter Lombard, and Peter of Poitiers. He calls them the four labyrinths of France and new heretics. He wrote about 1180, when one of the four, Peter of Poitiers, was still alive. He was a disciple of Lombard and also the master of the schools of that celebrated Peter Comestor. Because he treated scholastic theology more subtly and inquisitively than the rest, Walter especially undertakes to combat him in the fourth book, just as he bitterly attacks Abelard and Lombard, the leaders and chiefs of that sect, in the other books.

Accordingly, since that work has not yet come to light, it is useful to set forth what follows from it as a kind of picture of pseudo-scholastic theology, [Col. 1129B] so that posterity may recognize what change the method of teaching subsequently underwent in later times.

The first book contains these eighteen chapters:

1. On the new heretics and their phantom Christ: whence they arise.
2. That Christ is God and human: one without beginning, the other from a definite beginning.
3. On the new heretics who say that Christ is not anything in respect of his humanity.
4. How great is the rashness of denying that Christ is some human being or something composite.
5. On him who denied that Christ is something which is human.
6. On him who says that Christ is not something which existed from eternity.
7. On those who consider it unacceptable that God should be something which was not always.
8. That Christ is more worthy of belief than a heretic.
9. On him who says that Christ is not something from the Virgin, but that only his garment is in him; and why the human being assumed is said to have been assumed in the person, not in the nature.
10. On him who denies that there is in Christ anything composed of soul and body.
11. On those who concede with us that Christ is human, but in a heretical sense.
12. On him who says that the species “human being” does not apply to Christ.
13. On him who says that in Christ the Incarnation was like his garment, not his property.
14. On those who say: “Humanity is nothing.”
15. That it is established that a person is not united to a person, nor is one who has a human being united to himself.
16. On him who says that Christ is nothing except what he was from eternity.
17. That the assumed human being is assumed, and is most truly called: “a person, but not other than that of the Word.”
18. That, with a human being assumed, there is no “Quaternity.”

He prefaces the work with this title: “Here begins the book of Master Walter, prior of St. Victor at Paris, against the manifest heresies, condemned even in councils, which the aforesaid sophists set forth, sharpen, polish, and reinforce in their books of Sentences, under the following chapter heading: On the meaning of these expressions, ‘God [Col. 1130C] became human. God is human.’ Whether by these expressions God is said to have become something, to be something, or simply ‘is.’” He then adds the following:

> “A very difficult question arises here. For it is asked whether, in these expressions, ‘God became human’; ‘the Son of God became the son of man’; ‘God is human and a human being is God,’ God is said to have become something, or whether something is said to be God; or what their meaning is. In the resolution of this question great disagreement is found among teachers. Yet some say that the assumed human being is not God. He is not a person; he is not the Son of God; he is not the King of the ages; he is not the Lord of glory. Nor, according to the same persons, is the assumed human being a human being, or any human being, or son of man, or son of the Virgin, [Col. 1130C] or anything that is human or God. They say that the Son of God is nothing except what he was from eternity, but is God only. And when God became human, he did not become anything; for by the assumed human being they understand nothing but flesh and soul. The aforesaid persons also say that nothing is composed from Christ’s soul and flesh, neither that which is human nor anything else; but that the Word is clothed, as it were, with two things, soul and body, as with a garment. Therefore he is said to have become a true human being because he received the reality of flesh and soul. They also say that God became human only according to a state or habit; and thus, according to them, he is called human because he received a human being, and is human because he has a human being, or because he is one having a human being. And a human being became God because he was assumed by God; and a human being is God because the one having a human being is God.”

In chapter 2 he adduces authorities of St. Augustine and other holy Fathers, and of certain Catholic doctors, against the opinion stated above:

> “Augustine says in the book *On the Trinity*, when the words ‘The Word became flesh’ are read (John 1): ‘In the Word I understand the true Son of God; in the flesh I acknowledge the true son of man; and both together, by the ineffable bounty of grace, I recognize as one person, God and human.’ The same author in the *Enchiridion*: ‘Christ Jesus is God from God, but human, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. In each respect he is substance, divine and human respectively; he is the one Son of God the almighty Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds; in each respect one, but one thing because of the Word, another because of the human being—not two sons, God and human, but the one Son of God: God without beginning, human from a definite beginning.’ Likewise in the same work: ‘What did human nature in Christ the human being merit, that this singularity should be assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will? What good works preceded, by which that human being deserved to become one person with God? Was he perhaps a human being beforehand, and was this singular benefit bestowed upon him so that he should singularly merit God? Certainly, from the moment when the human being began to exist, he began to be the Son of God, this one and only Son, and did not begin to be anything other than human; and therefore the Word of God became flesh by assuming it.’ Etc.”

In chapter 3 he writes as follows:

> “I ask those who say that Christ is not anything in respect of his humanity what is signified by ‘me’ when it is said, ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 14): something which is Christ, or something which is not Christ? If something which is not Christ is said to be signified by ‘me’ in such a passage, it follows that Christ says he is something which he himself is not; and this does not accord with the truth. Likewise, if something which is not Christ is signified there by ‘me,’ it is either a created or an uncreated substance. But no uncreated substance is greater than the Father. If it is a created substance, it is either rational or irrational. It cannot be an irrational substance; therefore it is rational, and so either angelic or human. But it is not angelic; therefore it is human. Thus a created, rational, human substance must be signified there: that is, a human being constituted of soul and flesh. Hence Augustine says that the part, when it is said ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1), is put for the whole, namely for the human being. Necessarily, therefore, the human being is some whole, of which flesh is a part; and that whole is Christ. Hence the same author says: ‘God received the temporal substance of flesh into the eternal person of divinity.’ ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’ (John 20). If Christ is not some created substance, he does not have a God, because God belongs only to creatures. But he says that he has a God; therefore he is necessarily something that has God or a Creator. Elsewhere it is said that the whole is the union of human and God; that the whole is God, the whole human. For if ‘God is human’ is understood thus—‘God has a human being’—then it can similarly be said: ‘The soul is flesh,’ that is, ‘it has flesh.’ Augustine says on John: ‘The Word of God is one thing, and the human being another.’ What is signified here by ‘human being’? For if, as some suppose, soul and flesh are understood here by ‘human being,’ and not something composed of the two, he ought to say: ‘The Word of God is one thing, and human beings are another,’ since by ‘human being’ several things, and not one, are signified.”

In the following chapters of this book he adduces many other testimonies of holy doctors. To these he adds authorities from Anselm of Canterbury, Hugh of St. Victor, and Bernard of Clairvaux. Afterwards he proceeds to Book Two, in which he explains the aforesaid heresies more fully and proves more plainly that they had been condemned in councils in antiquity.

### FROM BOOK TWO

[Col. 1131]

[Col. 1131D] He sets before this book eight principal chapters:

1. On a certain book from which the aforesaid errors appear to spring.
2. On the errors of the new heretics, to be corrected by bishops, especially cardinals.
3. That not . . . the Catholic faith, and how many heresies have begun to spring from Abelard’s doctrine.
4. Why the third person in the Trinity is called Son by heretics.
5. That every human being, once human, cannot now be something else; and that a dead human being is human.
6. On the natural proofs from the Gospels that Jesus Christ is truly human.
7. On the natural proofs from the Gospels that Jesus Christ is truly God.
8. That the person who denies Christ’s true humanity betrays Christ as much as the person who does not believe him truly God.

[Col. 1132D] He therefore undertakes to treat against a certain heretical book bearing the following title, without the author’s name: “Here begin the Sentences of Divinity,” and beginning thus: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and drink, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved” (Isa. 55; Song 5). He says that this book, full of profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely so-called knowledge (1 Tim. 6), was commonly attributed to Peter Abelard, or at least extracted from his books. He says that it was condemned by Innocent II, who sent the following bull to the archbishops of Reims and Sens and their suffragans:

> “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops of Reims and Sens, S. and H., and their suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing. By these present letters we command your brotherhood to cause the books of error of P. Abelard, wherever they may be found, to be burned,” etc.

From that book he extracts certain heretical propositions, to which he opposes Catholic truth as follows:

> “HERESY: Some things are persons only and not personal. Persons and personal things are, for example, humanity and whiteness, which do not make a distinction from other things, because whatever is a white human being is a white human being through humanity and whiteness. Persons and personal things are, for example, Socrateity or Platonity: namely, the collection of all properties, compacted from all the accidents of parts both substantial and accidental; that is, the form of dissimilarity which makes him different from all others. For such a collection is never found so complete and full in any other. This is called a person, and is called a person through itself alone.

> “Now let us pass from natural matters to theology, similarly assigning certain properties. There is a person that is not personal, and a person that is personal. A person that is not personal is divinity, which is common to all persons. For just as the Father is God by divinity, so each personal person has its own property: paternity, filiation, and the connection of both. Again, let us truly and Catholicly say that God and human being are not parts of Christ, since nothing of Christ is God and nothing of Christ is human. For then some part would be its own whole. If it is objected: ‘Christ’s divinity is something of Christ, and it is God; therefore something of Christ is God,’ I reply: ‘Rather, we speak of God and divinity as one thing and another thing, and different.’ According to Augustine, Christ consists of God and human; this is understood not as consisting of that which is God and that which is human, but of divinity and humanity. Of these, certainly, he consists. Again, acting belongs not to nature but to person, just as begetting belongs not to nature but to person. Again, if we were to say that the nature common to the three persons was begotten, undoubtedly the Father is not that begotten nature; indeed, it is other than the Father’s nature, which is not begotten.”

> “CATHOLIC: Hilary: ‘Behold, the God who was born did not abandon the property of his nature, and he is in the Father by natural power, whose nature he holds in himself by natural birth.’ Augustine, against Felician: ‘You must confess that the Son came forth from the substance of the Father, if he is both born and God; or else deny equally the Son and God. For the Son, in that he is of undifferentiated nature, was truly brought forth; and, being born from him who is—that is, from the begetter—he was born not dissimilar, and by being born is seen to have incorruptible substance from the incorruptible Father. The Father’s substance is one, his person one. When this substance begot, that which came forth from it is known without doubt not to be different, but another—a thing taught to be nothing other than the first, since it is taught to be both common and proper: common, I say, in the unity of substance; proper, in the distinction of person.’

[Col. 1134A]

> “‘Therefore, when that which was born exists, not everything which happens to it necessarily passes to the begetter, just as everything which is shown to be proper and substantial to the begetter comes to the one born. For the Father’s divinity was not bestowed upon the Son by the very generation in the same way as the lowliness of offspring is referred back to the Father. This does not occur because, although the one begotten was similar, being from one substance, that is, the Father’s, yet because it now exists in itself, whatever is externally brought upon it is said to be not common but proper.’ Augustine, *On the Trinity*: ‘If the begetter is a principle with respect to what he begets, the Father is a principle with respect to the Son because he begot him. Therefore, since the one who is given has a principle from whom he is given, it must be confessed that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit—not two principles.’ The same author, on the Gospel [Col. 1134B] of John: ‘He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak’ (John 16). For him, hearing or knowing is being. Likewise, ‘whatever he sees the Father doing’ (John 5), the Son, etc.: the Son hears and the Son sees, and that very sight and hearing is the Son; and for him hearing is being, and seeing is being. He will “hear” from him from whom he proceeds. For him, hearing is knowing; knowing, indeed, is being: from whom he has essence, from that essence he has knowledge.

> “Bernard, to Eugenius: ‘God is one; if it may be said, he is most one. He is always the same and in one manner. He is not merely one for himself; he is one in himself. He has nothing in himself except himself: he has no alteration in time, no otherness in substance. Yet God is Trinity. What then? Do we destroy what has been said concerning unity because we introduce Trinity? No; rather, we establish unity. If there are three, how is there not number? If there is one, where is number? But, you say, I have something to count and something not to count. The substance is one; the persons are three. What is obscure in this? Nothing, if the persons are thought of separately from the substance. But now, since those three persons are that substance, and that one substance is those three persons, who can deny number? For they are truly three. Yet who can count them? For they are truly one. What have you counted? Natures, substances, or divinities? There is one. Many things are said to be in God, but the many are one,’ etc.

> “Likewise Bernard, sermon 80 on the *Song of Songs*: ‘Let those new men depart from us, beloved—not dialecticians but heretics—who dispute most impiously. “God is God by divinity,” they say, “but divinity is not God.” Accordingly, recently at the council which Lord Pope Eugenius held at Reims, that exposition in the book of Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, was judged perverse. For when Boethius says: “When ‘God’ is said, God pertains to substance,” our commentator inserted: “not that which God is, but that by which he is God.” Far be it from Catholic faith to assent to there being a substance, or indeed any thing whatsoever, by which God is and which is not God. But he condemned this and other things worthy of censure out of his own mouth in that same assembly. We say these things because those who are reported still to copy and read that book, published against the Apostolic See and forbidden there, remain among us.’

> “‘For these persons rave much about humanity. “A human being,” they say, [Col. 1135A] “is human by humanity, and owes it to humanity that he is human.” This is false. Indeed, he owes it not properly to humanity but to God, who made the whole—both matter and what comes from it; no matter acts or makes either itself or anything from itself. “Humanity,” they say, “is nothing.” The whole world sings: “Christ is equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.” (Pseudo-Athanasian Creed.) But if humanity is nothing, Christ is no longer less, but nothing according to humanity. Truth says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 4). Certainly this is according to humanity, as no one but a heretic doubts. But if he who speaks is nothing, he is nothing according to humanity—for example, it is properly his task to lead us from humanity into divinity, because after judgment we shall see in his divinity him whom before judgment we behold in humanity. Why say more? All Catholics establish by countless testimonies the assumption or reception of human nature, or humanity, in Christ. Apostolic authority also says: “The kindness, that is, the divinity, and humanity of the Savior appeared” (Titus 3). If humanity is nothing, no reception of human nature or humanity took place in Christ. But if no reception, no Incarnation; if no Incarnation, no religion of Christian faith; if no religion, no Christian. Who would not shudder? Therefore there is a humanity which is called accidental and not substantial; and there is one which is substantial, that is, natural. If it is nothing, no human being is human by humanity. O [Col. 1135C] madness! The dialectician proposes: “Every human being is human by humanity.” The heretic assumes: “But humanity is nothing.” The devil concludes: “Therefore every human being is nothing.” But if every human being is human by humanity and humanity is nothing, then no human being is human. O monstrosity! Behold how they mutually destroy one another, mutually concede, are nothing,” etc., etc.

> “HERESY: Concerning the sacrament of the Incarnation, inquiry must chiefly be made as to what is assuming, what is assumed, to whom the assumed things are united, and what the assumer became through assumption. And concerning the assumer, the faith of the Church holds that the third person in the Trinity, namely the Word of the Father, the Son of God, assumed flesh, so that he who was formerly *omousion*, that is, of one and the same substance with the Father, might by assumption become a giant [Col. 1135D] of twofold substance.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: What the Church holds ought to have sufficed; or at least those things which Pope Innocent, among other matters, wrote to the bishops of Gaul and to his son Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: Marcian, though a layman, was a most Christian emperor: “Let no cleric,” he says, “nor military man, nor anyone of any other condition, henceforth attempt to treat of the Christian faith, or strive to reopen and dispute again matters once decided and rightly settled. If he be a cleric, he shall be removed from the fellowship of clerics.” We grieve that in the pernicious doctrine of Peter Abelard the heresies of Arius, Mani, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus have begun to sprout. Therefore, together with its author, we condemn all the pernicious doctrines of that Peter, and impose perpetual silence upon him as upon a heretic. Thus far Innocent.

Master Peter Lombard, having set forth in his book of *Sentences* this chapter: “On the meaning of these expressions, ‘He was made man,’ ‘God is man’: whether by these expressions God is said to have become something, or to be something, or not,” says: “I have treated the question set forth above sufficiently carefully, according to differing opinions, without assertion or prejudice. Nevertheless, in so great a matter, and one difficult to discern, I do not wish the reader to think that this discussion of ours ought to suffice him. Rather, let him read other matters and whatever else may be raised; let him examine them, if he can, with a more intelligent mind,” etc.

I ask: where you and all the doctors, as it seems to you, are insufficient, what are disciples to do? Do you wish that the Catholic words, “God was made man; he remained what he was, and assumed what he was not,” and many others like them—hitherto everywhere sung with certain and exultant faith—should now, on account of your new frivolous disputations, either not be believed or be reconsidered? But by whom? The Catholic Fathers disagree among themselves. They even, as you suppose, lend support to heretics. But what Catholic will believe you in these matters? Yet let us hear this matter, as you call it difficult: a matter never to be reconsidered, but immediately to be rejected at its very hearing. For also in the council which Pope Alexander recently held at Tours, he condemned the heresy by which the most impious argue that Christ, according to his humanity, is nothing—indeed, neither God nor man.

«HERESY: The Son alone assumed flesh because man, by sinning, gave offense more particularly; and he alone and properly is called the image in the Trinity.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: How false and absurd this is, both Augustine in Book XII of *On the Trinity* and Scripture prove, which says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness”; and “God created man in his image and likeness. In the image of God he created him” (Gen. 1). First it says “our,” secondly “his,” thirdly “in the image of God.” This, Augustine says, amounts to the same thing as if it had said “his.” Why, then, does the Trinity say “our,” if the Son alone and properly is the image? But just as he imputes to Christ a false cause, so he imputes false flesh and false divinity; and likewise, by not believing and consequently not understanding the Scriptures and the authorities of Catholics, they falsely appropriate them.

[Col. 1136D] «HERESY: Augustine says: “He who assumes and that which is assumed are one person in the Trinity.” This authority seems to suggest that human nature together with the Word is one person in the Trinity. If so, then human nature together with the Word is God—though it of course never was God. Therefore not only the divine nature is God, but another nature also. But these things do not hang together. It ought by no reasoning to be said that the Son of God assumed any man.

And a little later: But it seems proved that not the person alone assumed, but nature also. For Augustine says: “The form of God received the form of man,” and “Divinity was incarnate.” But on the contrary it is proved that nature did not assume nature, just as person did not assume person.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: From the Council of Ephesus: “If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father is united to flesh according to substance, and that Christ is one with his own flesh—namely, the same true God and man—let him be anathema.”

Jerome, in *Cogitis me*: “The Catholic faith maintains the union of divinity and humanity as unconfused and undivided, so that one and the same Christ may be Son of God and son of man; because Scripture so joins and incorporates God and man in one and the same person that we worship and adore, in both natures, not a man separately—which would be impious—but that same and very Son of God as God.”

Pope Leo: “Although Jesus Christ is in the glory of the Father, we nevertheless unceasingly adore that saving birth from the Virgin herself; and we receive the indissoluble union of that Word and flesh no less when he lies in the manger than when he sits upon the throne of paternal majesty.”

Augustine: “The form of God received the form of a servant: both are God because of the God who received; both are man because of the man received.”

«HERESY: For if he assumed any man, either the one born of the Virgin or some other. But indeed the one born of the Virgin, according to the saying: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself established her” (Ps. 86 [87]). Thus authorities say, “The Son of God assumed man,” so that they make “man” a matter of quality, not substance. For names must thus be distinguished, especially in theological matters.

Again: It seems that he assumed man, that is, a thing which is man. For he assumed soul and body, not disjoined but conjoined. But these conjoined are man. Yet I say that these, whether conjoined or disjoined, are not man; if wall, roof, and foundation are joined, they are a house; soul and body are understood to be man—they are.

Again: He assumed an animated body; therefore he seems to have assumed an animal, that is, a thing which is man. To this I reply and say that different things are predicated. For in the first case a certain intermediate substantial disposition is predicated, which is also called animation; in the second, not nature but a thing is predicated, namely the attachment of a soul. For on this view entry into substance would already be corruption of substance, and departure from substance—contrary to Aristotle’s rule.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: Behold the false man, in quality and not in substance. For those things which exist in a subsisting body and in a subject—such as color, form, quantity, and quality—are not substance, but are in substance. For example: where there is no substance or no subject, there is no quality and no accidents.

Augustine: “You are told: man is a rational, immortal animal; or thus: man is a rational substance consisting of soul and body.” The same, *On the City [of God]*: “Soul and body, when both are joined together, at once have the name ‘man.’ Yet the individual parts do not lose [their names] when we speak of each separately. Scripture sometimes attests that even when these two are joined and man lives (Matt. 4), it nevertheless calls each separately by the name of man: the soul, the inward man; the body, the outward man; calling the soul [man] as though there were two men, though both together are one man.”

Jerome, in the sermon *Cogitis me*: “The same true God and true man is believed in one subsistence or person without division or confusion. Nevertheless, God is the Word and not flesh, although he assumed rationally animated flesh and united it to himself by a natural union and according to subsistence,” etc.

“It is contrary to Aristotle’s rules,” he says. Even if it is: “See to it,” says the Apostle, “that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2).

Pope Leo: “The whole divinity fills the whole body. The assumed man was received into the Son of God in such a way in the unity of Christ’s person from his very bodily beginnings that he was not brought forth without divinity. And in the nature of man he received from the Father what he himself also bestowed in the nature of divinity. Today the Word appeared clothed in flesh, and he who had never been visible to human eyes began also to be tangible by hands; and in the end of the ages there was fulfilled what had been ordained before eternal ages. God, the Son of God, begotten from the coeternal Father, was born man—that is, also by childbirth. The form of a servant was created without the condition of servitude, nor did the form of a servant violate the form of God. The supreme essence transferred us into his glory, but did not cease to be what he was; for the two natures did not so retain their properties that a distinction of persons could exist in them. Rather, both are God because of the power of the one assuming; both are man because of the humility of the one assumed.”

«HERESY: Behold, it has been shown who assumed—namely, the third person in the Trinity—and what was assumed, namely soul and flesh, or human nature. But it is proved to the contrary, by these arguments, that nature did not assume nature just as person did not assume person. Authorities say that the one assuming became something which it was not, because of the things assumed.

“Since, therefore, the divine nature became nothing which it was not, it neither itself is the one assuming nor anything assumed. Again: it assumed nothing of humanity except what was born of the Virgin. Since, therefore, divinity is not read to have been born of the Virgin, neither did it assume flesh. Again: if divinity assumed human nature, it ought not to have assumed its fullness and integrity. But if it assumed the fullness of humanity, then it could suffer and could die—which is contrary to all authorities.”

Contrary to this seems to be what Augustine says in the book *On Faith, to Peter*: “Nor is Christ’s humanity alien from the nature of his mother. For the eternal and divine nature could in no way be temporally conceived and born from a human being, unless, by assuming the truth of humanity, the ineffable divinity had received in itself a true conception and birth.” From this authority it appears that divine nature assumed human nature. But we are strongly troubled that he calls it naturally begotten of the Father and temporally born from a human being, unless perhaps he takes “nature” here for “person.” Otherwise, if we say that the nature common to the three persons is begotten, then without doubt the Father is not that begotten nature; indeed, he is other than the Father’s nature, which is not begotten.

[Col. 1139A] «CATHOLIC TEACHING: Behold one who goes beyond Arius, who denies that his third person is both God and man, by a horned syllogism, in order to mock Catholics: if you say it is the person that assumes, it will not be God, because divine nature is not the one assuming; if you deny it, this will not follow. Thus he excludes one alternative by the other, in order to deny both. If he assumed the fullness of humanity, as though he said: “If he had been truly man, then he could suffer and die”—which, he says, is contrary to all authorities. Therefore, according to all authorities, everything is false.

Jerome, in *Cogitis me*: “The Word of the Father deigned to become man. Since he assumed all that belongs to man, he is wholly man; and, receiving all that belongs to God, he could not be anything other than God, who was born of Mary. He knew and was able, without corruption of himself, to mingle and unite in the Virgin’s womb, so that Christ might be one: God and man, one person, one substance. Hence we truly confess her as *Theotokos*, ‘God-bearer’ or Mother of God, not *Christotokos*, Mother of Christ.”

Pope Leo: “The creature was not assumed into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that he was the dweller and it the dwelling; but so that neither nature was inserted into the other. Therefore, with the property of each nature preserved and remaining as they came together in one person, mortality was assumed by eternity, and the inviolable nature, remaining before time, began from time to be united to the passible. Human nature was assumed from the mother, and inviolable virginity supplied the substance.”

Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “If I am asked how the incarnation itself took place, I say that the very Word of God was made flesh, that is, was made man, so that there should be there not only the Word of God and the flesh of man, but also the rational soul of man; and this whole is called both God on account of God and man on account of man.”

«HERESY: Behold, it has been shown who assumed, namely the third person in the Trinity. Now one must see to whom the things assumed were united.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: Certainly to the assuming third person in the Trinity. Otherwise there will be no one assuming, and consequently no man. Although the Son is also called by some “the third person in the Trinity” in a Catholic sense, nevertheless, if we followed customary and rational speech—indeed, the authority of him who commands and says, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28)—we would always call the Father the first person, the Son the second, and the Holy Spirit the third. Although in this Trinity there is none earlier and none later, but all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another.

Here Peter Lombard, with devilish arguments, reasons that Christ, insofar as he is man, is the third person in the Trinity; therefore [he is] God. As though saying: If, insofar as man, [Christ is] person; and insofar as Word, person; and the Holy Spirit, person; and the Father, person; then, if insofar as man [he is] God, and insofar as Word [he is] God, and the Holy Spirit God, and the Father God—therefore there is a quaternity.

Still further, while piously expounding, he adds: “Because of these,” he says, “and other inconveniences, some say that Jesus Christ as man is neither a person nor anything”—understand: in the Trinity. I ask: are you a teacher in Israel and a bishop, though simoniacally intruded into the Church, and do you blaspheme thus? Christ, both insofar as man and insofar as God, is not two but always one person in the Trinity; no reasoning permits that person to be divided or cut apart. No Catholic at all doubts this. Had you believed it, you would never have written, for later generations to read, such subtle heretical arguments concerning the one and same person of God and man as though concerning two; rather, you would have condemned them.

So there are, as it seems to you, many inconveniences—indeed, many exceedingly fitting things: Christ, even insofar as man, is person in the Trinity, but not another person than the one assuming; and that same man is God in the Trinity, but not another God than God the Word. Consequently that same man is not nothing, as it seems to you; indeed, singularly and ineffably he is both person and God in the Trinity, he who lives and reigns with his Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Why do you impiously tear him apart? Behold: from your arguments a new heresy out of an old one introduces a fourth person into the Trinity, as is read in the body of canons from the Council of Ephesus: “If anyone adds ‘the crucified one’ to the *Trisagion* apart from the Son, to whom the holy voices in the midst sing the hymn, let him be anathema.”

«HERESY: It follows that one must see to whom the things assumed were united: not to the Word as person, but to nature in the person of the Word. That the Word did not unite flesh and soul to himself is proved by Boethius’s testimony against Nestorius. Again, if human nature were united to the Word, divine nature too would, by the same reasoning, be united to the Word. This seems quite absurd.

By these arguments it is proved that the Word, a person in the Trinity, would be united to no one; yet they are opposed by this. Augustine says: “The joining of God and man was made in Christ,” that is, of divinity and humanity; he does not say “to Christ,” but “in Christ.” Thus it appears that the person of the Son of God is not united to any things, nor are any things united to him; rather, three things are united to him, as Augustine says: “Three are in Christ: Word, flesh, and soul.”

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: Be astonished, all of you, not at dialectical art but plainly at devilish art: for example, one is not one; the same is not the same; he himself is not himself; Christ is not Christ; the same person is not the same person; the Son of God is not the Son of God! Who has ever heard such things? Truly, “the Athenians,” he says, “and all the strangers”—that is, heretics—“devote themselves to nothing else except to say or hear something new” (Acts 17). Behold, things altogether new and unheard of.

«HERESY: It follows that one must see what the one assuming became through the assumption of humanity. For he who was previously God, a person, eternal, became what he was not, namely a mortal creature. But you are told: “If God became something that he was not before, then God today is something which he was not from eternity”; and this must by no means be conceded. For then it could be inferred that he was a “recent God” (Ps. 80 [81]).

Behold, it is apparent who assumed: namely, the Son of God. What was assumed? Soul and flesh, or human nature. To whom were they united? Not to the Son of God, but soul to flesh and conversely; divinity to humanity and conversely.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: These are frivolous arguments, which are read almost word for word also in Peter Lombard’s book.

Augustine, on John: “For just as one man is rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man.” Accordingly Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these things and Christ in each individual one. Who, then, is he through whom the world was made? Jesus Christ, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Jesus Christ, but in the form of a servant. Who was not abandoned in hell? Jesus Christ, but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb and was to rise on the third day? Jesus Christ, but in the flesh alone. Therefore Christ is spoken of in each of these particulars. Yet all these are not two or three Christs, but one Christ.

The same, against Felicianus: “Therefore Mary bore, and did not bear, the Son of God. She bore him when Christ was born from her according to the flesh; she did not bear him when the Son existed from the Father without beginning. Thus Christ assumed an entire body from the entire body of his mother; he did not diminish his mother’s substance. And do we believe that he diminished the incorporeal substance of the Father, when he is said to have been begotten substantially from the very same Father? According to his humanity, I say, God was born of the Virgin in the manner in which the mind is taught to be born with the body: not because both have one substance, but because one person comes to be from both. Thus after birth there is not one Son of God and another son of man, but the same Christ, Son of God and son of man.”

Jerome on Jeremiah: “The Lord shall make, or ‘create,’ a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). Note that the Savior’s birth and conception is called a creation.

The same, in *Cogitis me*: “It is therefore clear that time did not prejudice the sacrament of the union of man and God, so that he who had not yet been born of the Virgin was already in him from the beginning of the world through unity of person. This is declared by many indications of Scripture: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who chose us before the foundation of the world’ (Eph. 1); ‘what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden in God from the ages’ (Eph. 3). Unless you believe thus, either Christ will not be God at all, or he will appear recent, contrary to the Prophet (Ps. 80 [81]): ‘Before Abraham came to be, I am’ (John 8).” By these words he certainly shows that the one speaking in him had always existed in the mystery of unity of person, because he always is. For “before Abraham came to be” declares the brevity of humanity, but “I am” declares eternity of nature. In that very eternity, the one speaking indicates that he was already present through the sacrament of his incarnation. Nor does he allow at all that one son of man and another Son of God be understood: he is neither bounded by time nor separated by suffering, but the whole of God passed into Christ and Christ into God.

Augustine on John: “One person indeed consists of two substances, divine and human.”

«HERESY: Finally, then, it remains to see whether God and man—that is, he who is God and the thing which is man—are parts of God composing Christ. This, deceived by the similarity of Athanasius, Nestorius intended to say. He thought that just as man is constituted from soul and body, and soul and body are the constitutive parts of man, so Christ consists of God, that is, the Word, the third person in the Trinity, and the assumed man born of the Virgin; and that these two would constitute some composite and complete thing, namely Christ.

But this must be understood as [the statement], “As rational soul and flesh are one man”; the wording must be rearranged, because otherwise there would be no grammar. One must say: just as one man has something from flesh and soul, because from flesh he is fleshly and colored, and from soul animated and rational, so one Christ is God and man and has something from divinity and humanity.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: May your grammar be with you unto destruction! For Athanasius did not say “has something,” but said, “Perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.” Certainly, those things which he says man has from soul or flesh are not substances but are in substance, as may be read above; and therefore man is nothing. Likewise, according to your heresy, this must be understood of Christ’s divinity and humanity.

«HERESY: Truly, then, and catholically, let us say that God and man are not parts of Christ, because God is nothing of Christ and man is nothing of Christ; for then some part would be its own whole. If it is objected: “Christ’s divinity is something of Christ, and it is God and not other than God,” I reply: it is not other than God; indeed, we speak of God and divinity as different and distinct things.

We say that during those three days Christ ceased to be man, and it could not be said, “God is man.” For what the conjunction of parts gave him, the disjunction of parts took away. He did not lose what Christ was by virtue of the parts, soul and flesh, but [he lost] what he was by virtue of the connection of the parts, namely the relation and bond between body and soul.

Again, if Christ, insofar as he is man, is an adopted son or a natural son, it seems possible to prove that he is an adopted son. Again, because Christ is mediator of God and men, but no middle term is either of the things between which it is a middle, the things which the middle mediates, namely the extremes. Therefore Christ seems to be neither God nor man.

[Col. 1142D] «CATHOLIC TEACHING: Whether the devil himself vomits forth things so impious, so contradictory, so unheard of, so horrible, in person or through one possessed, no one except a madman can doubt. Therefore let it suffice thus far to have marked an unheard-of heresy which surpasses the rest. We read in the *Conferences of the Fathers* that a demon confessed through Arius’s mouth that he had vomited blasphemy against Christ; this man, plainly inspired by a demon, admits Christ in no respect and nevertheless cuts him apart with insults, not understanding, as the Apostle says, either what he says or what he affirms (1 Tim. 1).

For, as Augustine says in the *Categories of Aristotle*, which he himself translated and from which he established his own dialectic: “Who,” he says, “would believe that Hortensius, a sensible, individual, numerically one, singular being, could be cut into parts? If this happened, Hortensius would no longer be.” This has been said so that heretics may know that Catholic doctors both understand dialectic and have always held the right faith.

Therefore Christ, who according to them both was and was not anything from the parts, in some way ceased to be man, or “God is man” could not be said, since God is nothing of Christ and man is nothing of Christ. For who would believe Christ could be cut into parts? If this happened, Christ would no longer be.

Augustine on John: “‘They have taken away my Lord’” (John 20). Calling the lifeless body “her Lord,” she designates a part from the whole of her Lord. Thus we all confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord—namely, Word, soul, and flesh together—yet crucified and buried, though only his flesh was buried, etc.

Pope Leo: “The strength of Christian faith, which does not fear the gates of death, confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, both true God and true man; believing him to be the son of the Virgin who is the author of his mother, the same one born at the end of the ages who is the creator of times, the same Lord of all powers and one from the stock of mortals. Catholic faith receives and defends both: according to the property of divine and human substance, it believes one Son of God, man, and Word.”

Bernard of Clairvaux, to Pope Eugenius: “I say that in Christ Word, soul, and flesh are one person without confusion of essences, and yet remain in their numerical distinctness without prejudice to personal unity. In the Virgin’s womb this mixing and leavening took place, as though that [woman] filled from the Gospel and leavened into one loaf (Matt. 13); and, according to the number of sacred [realities], [there are] most fitting degrees of devotion: new, eternal, ancient, eternal. ‘New’: the soul, which is believed then to have been infused as created from nothing. ‘Ancient’: the flesh, known to have been propagated from Adam. ‘Eternal’: the Word, coeternal with the Father. Let those be alien from us who attempt to make Christ’s flesh alien from us, impiously asserting that it was newly created in the Virgin and not taken from the Virgin. Therefore the flesh was taken from where the Virgin arose,” etc., etc.

Finally, after citing many passages of sacred Scripture by which he proves that Christ is true man and true God, he concludes thus in chapter 8: Since these things are so, it is clear that those who deny the true [Christ] lose Christ just as [do] these heretics who do not believe him true God—such as Arians, pagans, and Jews. For this reason they filled the whole world with prostitutes, because they believed and asserted that he was a living God at the very time when they believed him to be this most evident man, crucified and dead—indeed, what they reproached as the greatest mockery—[yet] shining with every kind of miracle, both in dying and, until today, now for more than eleven hundred years.

Let this great uncertainty of heretics at last be ended by an apostolic decree, and let the ancient, not new, undoubted faith of all the saints be confirmed at all times by so great and such a thunderclap, so that the truth of the Gospel may remain among Catholics. “I marvel,” he says, “that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you into the grace of Christ to another gospel—which is not another—except that there are some who trouble you and desire to pervert the Gospel of Christ. But even if we ourselves, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything besides what we have preached to you, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1). Repetition is confirmation.

[Col. 1144B] Pope Leo: “What is more unjust than to think impiously and not believe those wiser and more learned? But those fall into this folly who, when some obstacle impedes them in knowing the truth, do not turn to prophetic voices, apostolic letters, or evangelical authorities, but turn back to themselves. At least let them receive with attentive hearing that common and undiscriminating confession which the whole body of the faithful confesses: that they believe ‘in God the Father Almighty, in Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.’ By these three affirmations the engines of almost all heretics are destroyed, because it is equally perilous to believe our Lord Jesus Christ either merely Lord without man, or merely man without God.

Let these phantom Christians therefore say what substance of the Savior was fastened to the cross; what flesh rose on the third day; what sort of body Jesus presented to the disciples’ sight when he entered through closed doors, when, to drive away the unbelief of those seeing him, he demanded to be looked upon with eyes and handled with fingers, displaying the still-open marks of the nails and the fresh wound of his pierced side. But if heretical hardness does not leave its darkness in so great a light of truth, let it show whence it promises itself hope of eternal life, to which one cannot come except through the Mediator of God and men, Jesus Christ.

The eternal Only-Begotten of the eternal Begetter was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary; that temporal birth neither diminished nor added anything to that divine and eternal birth. And “every spirit which separates Jesus is not from God, and this is antichrist” (1 John 4). For what is it to separate Jesus except to separate human nature from him and, by most shameless fabrications, to empty the sacrament of faith through which we are saved?

## FROM THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1143]

[Col. 1143D] Book III follows, with these chapters:

1. On the three opinions held by all, and which is Catholic.
2. That heretics, through not understanding, corrupt the authorities of the saints and the divine Scriptures.
3. What blasphemies concerning Christ they committed to writing for posterity, deservedly to be burned.
4. Arguments concerning two persons in Christ condemned in councils.
5. On a new trick devised by new heretics.
6. That in the Catholic faith there is no question through which fools do not err.
7. That nothing is more foolish than wishing to comprehend what exceeds every creature.
8. On the truth of things and meanings in the Gospels, and the falsity of words and connections in scholastic writers.
9. That all the arguments of heretics are destroyed by the very things through which they impiously thought themselves strengthened.
10. That not only Peter’s doubts, but also many things which he affirms, are condemned by the faith of 830 bishops.
11. That he frivolously reconsiders many matters concerning the sacrament of the altar.
12. That absolutely no question ought to be entertained concerning the holy Mother of God whenever sins are under discussion.
13. That whoever says in any manner that the flesh of the Word is either liable [to sin] or cleansed accuses Christ of sin. And that the Greek Fathers confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, which heretics deny.
14. That the flesh of the Word is never read to have been formed from “bloods,” except among new heretics.
15. That Catholic doctors reconsider many matters and do not wish their books to be read as canonical.

“Let one be ashamed even to hear these fabrications, unless the two Peters had written them as though they were of great importance to be read by posterity, in this way: ‘On the meaning of these expressions, “He was made man,” “God is man”: whether by these expressions God is said to have become something, or to be something, or not.’

«CATHOLIC EXPOSITION, or rather the understanding of all the saints: God was made man; he remained what he was and assumed what he was not, suffering neither mixture nor division. God and man are one person, the only Son of the Father. What could be briefer or clearer? But the unbeliever babbles faithlessly.

«PETER: From what has been said there arises a question containing very great usefulness, but also excessive difficulty and perplexity: if by these expressions God is not said to have become something or to be something, what is the meaning of these expressions and similar ones? In the unfolding of this profundity and in the exposition of this thorny question, wise men are found to differ greatly.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: Certainly not the wise of God differ in this, but plainly the wise of this world—such as heretics and grammarians, who quarrel childishly and whose dispute is still before the judge. Their wisdom he made foolish, as it is written: “The foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1); and the authorities cited above prove this. Yet let us hear the ridiculous things.

«PETER: Others, he says, hold that in the very incarnation of the Word there was constituted a certain man from a rational soul and human flesh—the two things from which every ordinary man is constituted—and that this man began to be God, not indeed by the nature of God, but by the person of the Word; and God began to be that man. For they concede that this man was assumed by the Word and united to the Word, and yet is the Word. On this ground they teach that God is said to have been made man, or to be man, because God was made—that is, began to be—a certain substance subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh. And that substance was made—that is, began to be—God; not, however, by the migration of nature into nature, but, with the property of each nature preserved, it came about that God was that substance and that substance was God. Hence it is truly said, “God was made man,” “man was made God,” “God is man,” “man is God,” “the Son of God is son of man,” and conversely.

Although they say that this man subsists from rational soul and human flesh, they nevertheless do not confess that he is composed from two natures, divine and human, nor that the two natures are his parts; rather, [they say] that only soul and flesh are [his parts]. And lest they seem to speak only from their own opinion, they fortify this position with many authorities.

[Col. 1146B] «CATHOLIC TEACHING: This first opinion can be called neither that of heretics nor that of Catholics—like the man who propounds it.

«LOMBARD: There are others who agree in part, but say that this man consists not only of rational soul and flesh, but of human and divine nature—that is, of three substances: divinity, flesh, and soul. These confess that Christ is only one person: before the incarnation merely simple, but after the incarnation composite from divinity and humanity. Yet that person ought not to be called a person made, although it is called a person of man made. Therefore that person—or, as some prefer, a certain subsisting thing—was made from soul and flesh; but a personal substance or nature was not made. And insofar as it is that subsisting thing, it is composite; but insofar as it is the Word, it is simple. Those who say that the person of Christ was then made composite, whether consisting of two natures or of three substances, also fortify themselves with many authorities.

«CATHOLIC TEACHING: The second opinion is altogether Catholic.

«LOMBARD: There are also others who deny not only that, by the incarnation of the Word, a person composed of natures exists, but even that any man or any substance composed and made there from soul and flesh exists. Yet they say that those two things—namely, [Col. 1146D] soul and flesh—are united to the person of the Word, not to a nature, in such a way that no substance or person is made or composed from those two or from three things; rather, the Word of God is clothed with those two as though with a garment, so that he might fittingly appear to mortal eyes. He is therefore said to have become true man because he took on the reality of flesh and soul; and these two, it is read, he took into the singularity or unity of his person. Not because those two, or anything composed from them, is one person with the Word or is the Word; but because, when those two were added to the Word, the number of persons was not increased, so that a quaternity might arise within the Trinity; and because the very person of the Word, which previously existed without a garment, was not divided or changed by the assumption of the garment, but remained one and the same, unchanged [Col. 1147A]—that is, they say that the man made is the garment of God, etc.

“The third opinion is wholly that of heretics, condemned even in councils. Let the discerning reader recognize in Peter’s book itself that the testimonies were introduced with heretical intent, so that no one might dare oppose the heretics. Nor, as Augustine writes to Consentius, can not only the authorities of the Catholic Fathers but even the holy Scriptures themselves—which urge faith before the understanding of great matters—be useful to you unless you understand them rightly. For all heretics who receive these Scriptures as authoritative seem to themselves to follow them, while in fact following their own errors; and thus they are heretics not because they despise the Scriptures, but because they do not understand them.

[Col. 1147B] “CATHOLIC: It is also just that whoever proposes for others to read or believe not merely childish or foolish things about God, but blasphemies as well, should himself hear similar things said of him. They say, ‘God could have assumed a human being of the female sex,’ etc. In the same way God could have made Peter female, or even of asinine sex. Therefore Peter could have been a woman, an ass, or a dog, together with many similar things which are better left unspoken about any human being—how much more about God made man?

PETER OF POITIERS: ‘The Son of Man could have assumed Peter’s body; therefore Peter; therefore he could have made it so that he himself was Peter. It is also asked whether he could have assumed one human nature and another—that is, two bodies and souls. For by the name “human nature” [Col. 1147C] we understand nothing but soul and body in Christ; and therefore we rightly speak of one human nature and another. If this is so, then he could have been one man and another, and thus both of two men, and thus two men, and thus several. For if he had assumed two bodies and two souls, would it truly be said: “This man is that man”? It seems so to me, etc.’

“CATHOLIC: By reason and authority, therefore, we prove that none of these monstrous disguises ought to have happened, and consequently that what happened could not have happened; nor could God have been a woman, or conversely. God is truth; God is almighty; nevertheless, God can neither lie nor change. If he could, then he would truly be neither truth nor almighty. ‘Has he spoken, and shall he not do it? Has he declared, and shall he not fulfil it?’ [Col. 1147D] (Num. XXXIII). ‘In many and various ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets’ (Heb. I). But Paul, set apart for the Gospel of God, speaks ‘concerning his Son, who was made for him of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined, who is God over all, blessed for ever’ (Rom. I). ‘Who was predestined,’ he says—not at all a daughter in female sex, but the Son of God in power—as though saying to this heretic: ‘In no way in female sex, but in divine power, he is man in the manhood of God.’ Hence in the same place the Holy Spirit speaks through Isaiah: ‘Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, Emmanuel’ (Isa. VII), which is interpreted ‘God with us.’ He did not, therefore, say, ‘She shall bear a daughter, and she shall be called Woman-with-us.’ [Col. 1148A] Likewise Jeremiah: ‘The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man.’ Does he say, ‘A woman shall encompass a woman,’ etc.? Thus Pope Alexander rightly judged that these propositions should be condemned—propositions put forward as though profound by men barking such unspeakable things concerning the incarnation. Without doubt they ought rather to be silent; indeed, by a just judgment they ought to be burned by every Christian. For it is not teachers but pagans, not Christians finally but outright Jews and heretics, who vomit forth blasphemies of this kind. But you, universal Master, who compel both heretics and Catholic Fathers alike, as though before you, to play with their authorities according to your will—what do you believe? What do you confess? What do you determine?

“LOMBARD: ‘I have,’ he says, ‘treated the opinions of different persons sufficiently carefully [Col. 1148B] without assertion or prejudice.’

“CATHOLIC: Rather, condemn the blasphemies, lest you prove yourself a heretic; for you put forward not doubtful matters, but heresies already condemned.

“LOMBARD: ‘Nevertheless, I do not wish the reader to think that this discussion of ours ought to suffice for him.’

“CATHOLIC: Is this the great usefulness which you promised your readers: that all may drink in every error equally and all may doubt with you what the Catholic faith is? May God avert from the Church such doctrines—‘diverse and strange,’ as the Apostle says (Heb. XIII)—and such teachers, erring and leading into error (II Tim. III). For if these men had faithfully read the most firmly grounded and indubitable faith, and the Gospel testimonies alone written above, they would undoubtedly not have written down deliriums long ago condemned in councils. Thus also, with manifold rashness, he argues whether an assumed man ought to be worshipped with the Word as God is worshipped—as though he were either another or not the very same, the truest God, neither another nor any person other than the Word himself. Now one man, one person, is in no way double or multiple but simple, although consisting of many things; nevertheless, in many respects he may be worshipped with multiple, or at least twofold, veneration. For whatever injury or honor you inflict upon one man or one person, there is no doubt that you have rendered the whole of it to the whole man, the whole to the one person. [Col. 1148D] Therefore Christ, one person of God and man, cannot be divided either in person or in worship—though they most impiously strive to divide him.

“LOMBARD: ‘It is also customarily asked by some whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person, or even is something. Arguments arise on both sides of the question. That he is a person they set forth by these arguments: if, insofar as he is man, he is something, then he is either a person, a substance, or something else. But he is not something else. Therefore he is either a person or a substance, either rational or irrational; but he is not an irrational substance; therefore rational. If, insofar as he is man, he is truly a rational substance, then he is a person, because this is the definition of person: an individual substance of a rational nature.
