Therefore, if [Col. 1149A] insofar as he is man he is something, and insofar as he is man he is a person, and conversely: if, therefore, insofar as he is man he is a person, either a third person enters in, or another. But not another; therefore a third person enters in. But if, insofar as he is man, he is the third person in the Trinity, then he is God. Because of these absurdities and certain others, they say that Christ, insofar as man, does not exist and is not anything.’

“CATHOLIC: He argues this most foolishly concerning Christ. For if someone should say that one man, insofar as he is a body, is either a person or nothing, who would not laugh? For man is neither of these in himself. ‘Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves’ (Matt. X): against serpents [Col. 1149B] and scorpions indeed, who deceive the simple by the thorns and twists of arguments—as does this new man. For his arguments are not those of philosophers but of demons, speaking hypocritically about Christ through the mouths of heretics. From this the prudent reader should understand that no reason permits what he proposes concerning one person: that it is the same or another. That one man should be two—that is, that Christ should be one and another; that one God should be two; that one Son, Jesus Christ, God and man, should be two sons. For no individual, Aristotle himself testifying, can be divided; if it is divided, it will no longer be an individual. Hence this man too, proposing falsehoods concerning Christ and assuming absurdities, draws demonic conclusions: namely, two heresies long ago condemned in councils. The first says that Christ, [Col. 1149C] insofar as man, is a person and God—that is, two sons—and thereby introduces a quaternity into the Trisagion. But since he does not dare freely to assert this, this fantastical Manichaean fashions the other out of it as follows: if Christ, insofar as man, is neither a person nor God nor a quaternity, then it follows that he does not exist and is not anything. Behold the sort of novelties with which this teacher attacks the Church. Both are diabolical; both are the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps.

“This is as though Satan, transformed into an angel of light (II Cor. XI), were trying by every means in his Book of Sentences to persuade us, saying: ‘The man whom you worship and adore is not God; likewise, the God whom [Col. 1149D] you worship is not God. Therefore Christ whom you worship is nothing, because God is not man; and man indeed is not even anything.’ Thus, if the whole is not according to some respect, then the whole no longer exists, and consequently is not anything. Therefore, if Christ, God and man, does not exist according to some respect, Christ no longer exists. He will either be whole or not at all. Without doubt he who from the beginning did not stand in the truth, because he is a liar and its father, strikes such blows among Christians, etc. (John VIII). Likewise, by no reasoning can it happen—as Aristotle himself testifies—that the man who is should not be, and that the God who is should not be, God-man Truth himself testifying to men and saying: ‘Before Abraham came to be, I am’ (ibid.). This ‘I am’ can never on any grounds be cut apart; if it is, then ‘I am’ is no longer. But it is altogether impossible that non-being should be in him [Col. 1150A], because he alone is uniquely one, as the Apostle testifies: ‘For the Son of God was not in him Yes and No, but in him was Yes’ (II Cor. I). Therefore whoever says that something in him is not something denies the existence of both, as in the Decrees of Pope Eutychius: ‘He plainly does not know his own life who does not know Jesus Christ as true God and likewise as true man. And it is a matter of the same peril to doubt concerning the sacrament of that very Mediator between God and men, in whom, though each [nature] exists as one, he himself from the natures united into one is the same reality of each nature,’ etc. Likewise, from the Decrees of Pope and Martyr Gaius: ‘The impiety of heretics shows that it is engaged in great sacrilege when, under the appearance of honoring divinity, they deny the truth of human flesh in Christ and think it religious to believe that in our Savior that is not true which saves. And so the world is reconciled to God in Christ, according to the promise running through all ages, in such a way that, unless the Word deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved,’ etc. This too is from before the Council of Nicaea. These things also follow from the Council of Ephesus of two hundred bishops, confirmed by the Council of Chalcedon of six hundred and thirty bishops, which with one voice condemns the heresies set out above: ‘Thus we confess Christ and God as one, not worshipping a man together with the Word, lest some appearance of division be introduced, but worshipping one and the same, because his own body is not foreign to the Word, with which he himself also sits at the Father’s right hand,’ etc.

“Likewise, Nestorius says that God’s Word is called Christ separately [Col. 1150C], but has a continuous conjunction with Christ. Do you think, then, that he does not most openly assert two Christs and two sons? Likewise: ‘Those who proclaim either two sons or two persons, and do not proclaim one and the same Christ in one person, one Christ, one Son, one Lord, our Jesus Christ the Son of God, we anathematize and judge alien from the Church.’ We do not deny indeed one nature of God the Word, but incarnate; because our one and same Lord Jesus Christ belongs to both [natures]. It must be known that the whole man was created and simultaneously assumed by the Word; he cannot be called either a person, or an adjunct, or coupled, or deified, or an addition, or added to the Word or to the person of the Word [Col. 1150D], because he will never exist apart from the Word or outside the person of the Word. But from the point at which he began to exist, he properly existed as Word and as person with the Word. Athanasius: ‘What hell belched forth the saying of *homoousion*, that the body from Mary is of the Word of divinity?’

“The creed of the six hundred and thirty bishops, removing from the clergy heretics professing another faith: ‘Following the holy Fathers, with one harmonious voice we teach one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in divinity, God and true man; the same of a rational soul and body; according to divinity, of one nature with the Father; according to humanity, the same of one nature with us, like us in all things except sin; before the ages begotten of the Father according to divinity [Col. 1151A], but in these last days, for us and for our salvation, made man—namely, one and the same Christ, Son of God, only-begotten, to be acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation; the differences of the natures in no way abolished because of the unity; but rather,’ etc.

“CATHOLIC: Now then, men of Judah and Catholic Christians, judge between Catholic truth and diabolical falsehood. What is more magnificent, what clearer, what truer than this faith? ‘From this,’ Isaiah says, ‘there shall be for you a direct and plain way, so that fools do not err upon it’ (Isa. XXXV). Where, then, are the excessive perplexities and most scrupulous questions of faith in which this man says that Catholics differ—and, what is more wicked, makes even heretics differ? Why does he not name even one of those whose diabolical opinions he sets forth, except because he knows that they are condemned? Why then does he not condemn the heretical opinions themselves, except because by this he disavows himself as Catholic? The sole difference, indeed, between this man and the first Manichaean is that the latter called Christ a phantom man; this man calls him neither a person nor anything. Jerome: ‘Woe,’ says Isaiah, ‘to those who call good evil and evil good’ (Isa. V). Neither the honorable things which opponents possess nor the faults of friends are to be praised; each matter must be judged according to the weight not of persons but of things. Another says: ‘I cannot condemn what no one has condemned.’ Another: ‘Nothing concerning this was decreed by the Fathers in the Nicene synod.’ By this argument neither Valentinus nor Marcion nor Cataphriges nor Manichaeus [Col. 1151C] ought to be condemned, because the Nicene synod did not name them—though it is certain that they existed before the synod. Why, after four hundred years, do you strive to teach what we previously did not know, what Peter and Paul were unwilling to publish? Until this day the Christian world has existed without this doctrine. As an old man I shall hold the faith in which I was born. Likewise the same [writer]: ‘Know that in books of this sort very many things are to be detested; according to the Lord’s saying, one must walk among scorpions and serpents,’ etc.

“We know indeed that every art and wisdom is from the Lord God (Ecclus. I), and that divine Scripture—Truth itself—also proposes, assumes, and concludes in the Gospel (Luke XXI), but by the truth of things and judgments, not by contentiousness or facility in words [Col. 1151D] and logical connections. Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*: ‘There are many things called sophisms, false conclusions, often so imitative of true ones that they deceive not only the slow-minded but also clever persons who are insufficiently attentive. Someone proposed to the person with whom he was speaking, saying: “What I am, you are not.” The other agreed. For it was true in one respect, or simply because the one was deceitful and the other straightforward. Then the former added: “But I am a man.” When he had obtained this also from the other, he concluded: “Therefore you are not a man.” Scripture detests this sort of captious conclusion. Since, then, logical connections can be true not only for true but also for false propositions, the truth of logical connections can easily be learned even in those schools outside the Church; but the truth of propositions [Col. 1152A] must be sought in the holy ecclesiastical books,’ etc.

“Accordingly, let Catholics hear the clearest trumpet, which by the force of a single judgment laughs at, scatters, and utterly reduces to nothing all the inventions and heresies proposed above, as though they were an enemy camp: Jerome in *Cogitis me*: ‘Therefore what nature did not possess, custom did not know, reason did not comprehend; the human mind cannot grasp it; heaven trembles, earth is astonished, and every creature, heavenly and earthly, marvels. This whole matter is what is divinely announced to Mary through Gabriel and fulfilled through Christ. Hence it is clear that time did not prejudice the mystery of united God and man, so that he who was already in him from the beginning in the reality of person—that is, he who had not yet been born of the Virgin Mary—was present there, as many indications of Scripture declare: “He chose us,” he says, “before the foundation of the world in him” (Eph. I); because certainly whatever God did from the beginning, Christ did all through the unity of the mystery. Hence God is not “new” with us [Ps. LXXX]. Otherwise, if you look to human reason and senses, divinity and the human condition could in no way whatever have agreed with one another. Yet they came together in Christ, and in the one Emmanuel from both, who was not increased in himself by the man assumed, nor diminished or changed because the Word became flesh. If it seems new to you that he assumed man, know that this was always with him and in his counsel, that it should happen. And now, when “the fullness of time came” (Gal. IV), [Col. 1152C] what was always in Christ came to pass,’ etc.

“Nor is this scholastic to be guarded against only in these matters, but also in those which he commands us to believe. For he says: ‘I do not wish our discussion to be thought sufficient,’ firmly holding in ecclesiastical dogmas that God assumed man and that man passed into God, not by the visibility of nature. This indeed is Catholic. But let the prudent reader notice how the addition which he makes—‘but by God’s condescension’—has been condemned. From the Council of Ephesus of two hundred bishops, confirmed by Pope Leo and the Council of Chalcedon of six hundred and thirty bishops: ‘The heretic Nestorius in his expositions pretends to say, “One Son and one Lord,” but refers sonship to the Word of God alone. Again: he calls separately “another Lord,” the man who is from a woman, joined by dignity; he holds that this conjunction has equal honor with Christ. How is it not plain that he says there are two Christs, if Christ has a conjunction with Christ, one with another?’ Likewise, Nestorius, while confessing the divinity of the Son of God, believed that Christ was conceived and formed as a mere man and afterward advanced into God—that is, that the man was deified.

“CATHOLIC: It should be noted that heretics and Catholics employ the words ‘dignity,’ ‘conjunction,’ and similar terms in different senses. From the Council of six hundred and thirty bishops: ‘Confessing the Word of God according to subsistence, we worship one Son and our Lord Christ; we do not set apart and distinguish [Col. 1153A] man and God as though joined by dignity and authority, which are alien to one another. Therefore Christ, Son and Lord, is one, not as though a man had union with God by some conjunction in a unity of dignity and authority. For Peter and John are of equal dignity, yet the two are not one. Nor do we regard a comparison or connection as the mode of union. This is insufficient for natural unity; indeed, we avoid the names of conjunction as not being suitable to signify the mystery of unity, because a servant is not his own servant, nor a lord his own lord. For it is foolish—or rather impious—to think or say this. If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a conjunction according to dignity, authority, or [Col. 1153B] power, and not rather by the event which occurred through natural unity, let him be anathema.’ Likewise: ‘If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be worshipped together with God the Word, glorified together with him, and called God together with another—for the added syllable *con-* forces this meaning—rather than that Emmanuel is worshipped with one act of supplication and receives one glorification, according to “the Word became flesh,” let him be anathema. If anyone dares to call Christ the man *theophoros*, that is, “God-bearing,” rather than truly God, as Son by nature according to “the Word became flesh,” let him be anathema. If anyone divides between two persons or subsistences the expressions contained in apostolic and evangelical writings [Col. 1153C], or those spoken concerning Christ by the saints or by Christ himself, assigning some of them as though to a man understood separately from God the Word, while assigning others as worthy of God to the Word of God the Father alone, let him be anathema.’

“CATHOLIC: Behold, not only what he asserts—namely, that man passed into God by God’s condescension—but also his other arguments or many absurdities, by which he above testifies that he is troubled and at a loss, are openly struck down by the anathema of the Catholic Fathers. Their authorities seemed to support him where he himself thought impiously.

“It is a similar error to debate, as though more plausibly, by many opinions of heretics, whether the sacraments of the altar are saving by faith alone but ineffable to reason. May it be far from Catholics [Col. 1153D] to possess, as it were, many faiths rather than one certain faith in the sacrament of the altar! [lacuna] Concerning Berengar he adds the following: ‘This heretic asserted that everything occurred in figure and sacrament, nothing in reality. But afterward, corrected before Pope Nicholas and many bishops, he confessed and even swore that bread and wine after consecration are not only sacraments but also the true body and blood of Christ, and that they are sensibly handled and broken, not only sacramentally but in reality, by the hands of priests, and crushed by the teeth of the faithful.’ Behold the Catholic faith. But this scholastic explains it thus: ‘Truly indeed,’ he says, ‘but only in the sacrament.’ Again he says: ‘It may properly be said that that breaking and division occur not in the substance of the body but in the very form of sacramental bread [Col. 1154A], so that there is a true breaking and division there, which occurs not in the substance but in the sacrament—that is, in the species.’ Again: ‘There is there a true breaking and division which occurs in the bread, that is, in the form of bread.’ Again: ‘That breaking and those parts which are seen to occur there occur in the sacrament, that is, in the visible species. Therefore Berengar’s words must be distinguished in this way: the body is said to be sensibly broken by the hands of priests and crushed by teeth not merely in the sacrament but in reality—truly indeed, although only in the sacrament.’ Therefore the crushing and division are true.

“Behold, while he distinguishes by his customary arguments the Catholic faith, which needs no distinction at all, he proves himself another Berengar. For just as the latter asserted that everything occurred only in the sacrament, so does this man. But after being corrected, the former added to sacrament, breaking, and crushing at last the reality which he had denied. This man, on the contrary, removes reality in every respect while asserting that everything occurs not in substance but only in visible species, the form of bread, and sacrament. The former said: ‘sensibly, and not only in the sacrament, but also in reality.’ This man says: ‘only in the sacrament’; but, like a scorpion, he first puts forward a flattering head when he says ‘truly,’ then immediately introduces deadly poison with his tail: as if he said, ‘Truly indeed, but not in reality, because only in the sacrament.’ Thus he acts in everything, so that he may be proved neither heretic nor Catholic. For a man wholly given to human senses rather than faith fears, so far as can be understood, lest truth and life—which is Christ (John XIV)—be torn apart and die if it is received in Catholic reality. Yet he indisputably is [there], and one believes in him who, holding and breaking his own proper and true body in his own hands, while himself nevertheless remaining whole and living, then gave that same body; and today gives it throughout the whole world, not only sacramentally but also in reality, saying: ‘This is my body; divide it; eat’ (Luke XXII), because ‘unless you eat, you shall not have life; but there are some among you who do not believe’ (John VI); whereas Truth says, ‘Unless you believe, you shall die in your sins’ (John VIII).

“PETER LOMBARD. Again, when he most foolishly asked concerning this flesh whether it had ever been subject to sin, he determined thus: ‘Certainly,’ he says, [Col. 1154D] ‘it can be said, and must be believed, that the flesh of the Virgin Mother was subject to sin, like other flesh.’ We, on the contrary, say that this can be said only insanely and must by no means be believed. But first let us establish the case concerning the Mother, whom he says indeed lived without sin after the angel’s consent and the coming of the Holy Spirit, but before that was subject to sins. The celebrated feast-day of the most holy Nativity, whose glorious life illumines the whole Church, rejects this view throughout the whole world (*Office of the Church*). Concerning her Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, says (*On Virginal Conception*): ‘It was fitting that this Virgin should shine with that purity greater than which none can be conceived under God.’ The same author says (sermon on her Assumption): ‘The root of the human race was corrupted in the first parent; and it often happens [Col. 1155A] that shining gold is found in mud and a beautiful red rose springs from a prickly thorn. Thus, through the working of divine Providence, from a corrupted root came forth without a man a rod—by which is meant the most blessed Virgin Mary—as Isaiah testifies: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI).’ And Jerome (*Cogitis me*): ‘“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “shall come upon you” (Luke I). Before this, certainly, the Virgin’s womb was clean, undefiled, and free from the contagion of sin; no treacheries could break into it. The enemy’s deceit did not prevail; she remained holy in mind and body.’ Saint Bernard likewise wrote in these words to the canons of Lyons: ‘Without doubt the Mother of the Lord was holy before she was born; nor is holy Church at all mistaken in considering holy the very day of her nativity and receiving it with all devotion, in a vowed celebration, with the exultation of the whole earth. I think that a more abundant blessing of sanctification descended upon her, which not only sanctified her birth but also thereafter kept her life immune from every sin—a gift believed to have been granted to no other among those born of women. For it was fitting that the Queen of virgins, by the singular privilege of holiness, should live a life without every sin, she who, while giving birth to the Redeemer of sin and death, obtained for all the gift of life and righteousness.’ [lacuna] To these three suitable witnesses we shall add a fourth, one who permits neither the impious inquiry into nor even the hearing of the Mother’s sins. This is Augustine, who, while arguing with all his powers against those who asserted that any saints and perfect persons were without sin, and while they brought forward among others the holy Virgin against him, singled her out from all saints and affirmed her free from every sin, saying: ‘With the exception of this Virgin, when sins are being discussed, I wish no question whatever to be raised; we know that she entirely conquered sin.’ Peter, wishing to quote this authority, twists it according to his own view, as he does the others, first adding: ‘From that time,’ he says—that is, from the incarnation—‘she is to be understood to have lived without sin.’ Thus Augustine says, ‘With the exception of this Virgin,’ etc.

“It is certain, therefore, that Augustine determines not merely from that time but absolutely, whenever sins are being discussed, that she must be excepted in every respect and at every time—thereby defining most plainly against these scholastics, etc.

“It is therefore evident from what has been set forth that she who was

> First,
>
> nor was seen to have an equal or successor,

by singular merit lived her whole life without sin, not only after thirty-five years following the conception, but before it, as is read, for fifteen years: together these amount to about fifty years of her life. For, Jerome says, it was fitting that the Virgin should be endowed with such gifts—she who gave glory to heaven, the Lord to earth, faith to the nations, an end to vices, an order of life, and discipline to morals. Indeed, being uniquely filled with the Holy Spirit still from her mother’s womb, she not only filled Elizabeth from the abundance of her blessing, but also compelled John in Elizabeth’s womb to leap by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1156A] (Luke I)—John, of whom ‘among those born of women none greater has arisen’ (Matt. II [sic]). From this same fullness, as the angel revealed, it is read that after the assumption of her most holy soul, her most holy body also—remaining in the tomb untouched by corruption as by sin—was raised to heaven on the fortieth day, that is, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, now conformed to the glory of that body which God took from her (Acts I).

“If, therefore, on the necessary authority of so many and such great witnesses we believe that no question at all ought to be raised by Christians concerning such and so great a Mother whenever sins are discussed, is it not blasphemous and impious for any suspicion whatever to be admitted concerning the flesh of the Word, that is, her Son? If, I say, the Mother [Col. 1156B] came forth from the human race without fault, as Jerome testifies, and no question whatever ought to be raised concerning her, what do you say, what do you believe, O Christians, concerning Christ the Son, from whom, through whom, and in whom such a Mother came forth from the womb? On what grounds could the flesh of the Word have become subject to sin like the rest of the human race, when it could neither be tithed in the loins of Abraham and Levi, as the Apostle testifies (Heb. VII), nor sinned in Adam, as Augustine testifies in his commentary on Genesis: ‘Because,’ he says, ‘he was there in a different manner from the rest’? Augustine, *On the Trinity*: ‘So that what was born from the Virgin, though from the progeny of the first man, might derive an origin only of race, not also of guilt. For it was born not as a nature corrupted by the contagion of transgression, but as the sole remedy for all such faults,’ etc. What could be clearer? What can Peter Lombard, or I know not what John Damascene, scholastics, say against these authorities of the orthodox? Further: the apostolic distinction, by which God is said to have sent his Son not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that through sin—that is, through a sacrifice for sin—he might condemn sin (Rom. VIII), would have no truth at all if that flesh itself were subject to sin like the rest. This distinction, I say, clearly condemns the view of these men and of their like. Further: ‘The law, having a shadow,’ he says, ‘and not the very reality of things, appoints men as priests who have infirmity—that is, sin—and who first offer sacrifices for their own offenses, sacrifices which can never take away sins’ (Heb. X).

[Col. 1156D] “From these things it is plainly proved who is the true priest and the true victim. ‘Who is the Son of God,’ he says, ‘because he remains for ever, has an everlasting priesthood, without father, without mother, having neither beginning of days nor life.’ For such a high priest was fitting for us, namely, one separated from sinners, who has no need first to offer for his own offences. For by one offering of his body he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified (Heb. VII and VIII) [lacuna].

“Therefore, whoever, or in whatever way, says that the victim—that is, the flesh—of this High Priest, alone truly free among the dead, as the Prophet says (Ps. LXXXVII), was subject to sin so as to be abandoned, cannot by any reasoning defend himself from impiously charging the Word made flesh with sin; and for those so offending there no longer remains a victim for sins” [Col. 1157A] (Heb. X). “These are the Jews who say to Christ—casting that likeness in his teeth—‘Physician, heal yourself’ (Luke IV): namely, your own flesh, subject, infirm, captive under sin like the rest. For this is the distinction: ‘All have sinned and need the glory of God’ (Rom. III)—and, according to these people, the divine Word as well. But far be it from us to believe this! Far be it, I say, to think this concerning the flesh of the Word! For that great bishop Athanasius says: ‘The Word did not sin, he who delivered others from sins, so that, changed into flesh, he might offer himself for himself and, as a sacrifice, deliver himself. Far be it: it is not so. He offered his body for us.’ But divine Scripture itself, and Truth itself, contradict this and says: ‘Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do’ (Luke III). ‘They are justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood,’ in whom we have remission of sins, ‘that he himself may be just and the justifier’ (Rom. III): redemption and sanctification, medicine, deliverer and freedom, priest and victim, propitiator and propitiation, and other such things, variously and in many ways manifest in the divine pages, old and new.

“Otherwise, if God the physician needed a physician, or himself; if his medicine—his flesh and his blood—ever in any respect needed medicine, or itself; if the high priest needed a propitiator, or himself; if the victim, expiation, and freedom needed a deliverer, or itself; if the just one, the justifier, or justice itself ever needed justification, or itself—then all reason collapses, every [Col. 1157C] understanding likewise; and together all truth, all medicine, and truth itself perish, etc. The faith of the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, of eight hundred and thirty bishops, overturns the opinions set out above.

“We therefore ascribe the matters contained in the Gospel to one person, namely to the one substance of the incarnate Word, because ‘there is one Lord Jesus Christ,’ as it is written (I Cor. VIII). And when the Apostle calls him ‘Jesus, the high priest of our confession’ (Heb. III), we say that he is himself the only-begotten Son of God according to nature, and we assign the name and office of priesthood to no other man beside him. For he offered his own body, not for himself but for us. For he who needed an offering and sacrifice for himself is free from every sin, being God. But if ‘all have sinned and need the glory of God’ (Rom. III), this is because human nature was sick with sins; he himself, however, was not so. Therefore we need his glory. But those who say that he offered himself both for himself and for us cannot in any way escape the charge of impiety, since he committed no offence whatever.

“If, therefore, anyone says that the Word of God himself became our high priest and apostle when he became flesh, but posits as another beside him a mere man from a woman; or says that he offered himself as an offering for himself and not rather for us alone—for he who knew absolutely no sin had no need of an offering—let him be anathema. If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving and is the own flesh of the Word of God the Father, but regards it as belonging to another beside that Word, joined to him by dignity or as though possessing a divine indwelling, rather than as life-giving because it became the own flesh of the life-giving Word, let him be anathema.” [Col. 1158A]

“We have been taught to think this way by the holy apostles and evangelists, by all Scripture divinely inspired, and also by the truth-supported confessions of the blessed Fathers. The Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son as from God the Father. Why, then, do later Greeks deny the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son as from the Father, which the ancient Greeks affirmed so openly, unless because they are schismatics in unity, adherents of leavened bread in the sacrament of the altar, and heretics concerning the procession?

“If, therefore, the blood and flesh of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself to [Col. 1158B] God, cleansed our consciences from sins (Heb. IX)—without which no remission, cleansing, or liberation has ever been, or can ever be, accomplished—ought not, and could not, be offered for himself, it is certainly plain that the flesh of the Word could not and ought not ever have been cleansed, whether in his mother as they say or anywhere else, in order that it might be clean, or rather cleansed; or liberated, in order that it might be free, or liberated. Nothing of this sort could have occurred unless he offered himself for himself. This is truly anathema.

“(Chapter 14.) Again, this Athenian says that the Lord’s flesh was formed ‘from bloods’ (*de sanguinibus*), an expression sufficiently rustic and quite unsuitable; it is found neither in the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, Son of God, son of David, son of Abraham (Matt. I), nor is it read in the books of the Catholic Fathers as ‘conceived’ or ‘formed’ from blood, or even [Col. 1158C] from *bloods*. On the contrary, although in holy treatises they wrote hundreds and thousands of times ‘nature from nature,’ ‘body from body,’ ‘substance from substance,’ ‘man from man,’ ‘flesh from flesh,’ ‘flesh from blood,’ ‘flesh taken from a mother,’ they are shown to have avoided deliberately the strange and barbarous expression ‘formed’ or ‘conceived from bloods.’ Thus Ambrose, in a certain sermon, avoids saying ‘blood’ [singular]: ‘John is born from the cold blood of an elderly little woman; the Lord comes forth from the flowering vigor of a warm young woman. The one is the son of a corruptible womb; the other is begotten from the undefiled flower of the womb.’ O truly golden tongue, and truly an ecclesiastical teacher! For he had read in the Gospels: ‘who was born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh and of a man’ (John I)—that is, of male and female, in whom indeed the bloods coagulate during forty-six days in the case of other human beings—but he alone was born from God. Hence he says: ‘You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world’ (John VIII). Hence the Apostle: ‘The second man is heavenly, from heaven’ (I Cor. XV). Hence also the angel: ‘For that which is born in her is not from bloods, but from the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. I), and from the power of the Most High, as is written in the prophets: ‘The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man without a man’ (Jer. XXXI), because ‘the Lord himself will give you a sign, and the holy woman shall conceive and bear a son, Emmanuel’ (Isa. VII), from the blessings of the ancient mountains—of him who hangs the earth upon three fingers (Isa. XL)—from whom truth shall arise like the sun [Col. 1159A] (Ps. LXXXIV).

“And therefore, ‘that which shall be born from you’—here it is not said ‘from bloods,’ as the new teacher supposes; rather, he says, ‘the Holy of holies shall be born from you; by the blessing of God from heaven he shall be called the Son of God’ (Luke I). The angel, therefore, the prophets, apostles, evangelists, and Catholic teachers did not express the divine incarnation and conception in the prattling terms of scholastics, but exalted them uniquely, as has been said, in divine, reverent, and proper expressions.

“(Chapter 15.) Let the new teachers therefore cease—or rather, the new heretics drawn from the old, not dialecticians—from uttering these profane novelties of language, which divine Scripture has hitherto neither taught nor the Catholic faith believed. That truly Catholic Augustine, retracting certain things which he had rashly written, addresses Jerome, the chief of teachers, in these words: ‘Absolutely, my brother, I do not think you wish your books to be read as those of the prophets and apostles are read, concerning whose writings it is wicked to doubt that they are free from every error. But I read other writers in such a way that, however greatly they may excel in holiness and learning, I do not think something true merely because they thought it so, but because they have been able to persuade me, whether through canonical authors or by probable reasoning, that it does not depart from the truth. I want my own books to be read in the same way.’ If, therefore, men so great, whom the Church especially follows in the Catholic faith after the divine Scriptures, think so humbly of their own views and opinions, how much more should these scholastics correct their errors, which the Catholic faith [Col. 1160B] condemns.”

## From the Fourth Book

[Col. 1159]

[Col. 1159B] This book has eighteen chapters, in which he disputes especially against Peter of Poitiers, Lombard’s disciple:

1. On philosophers: how far they contradict themselves and the truth.
2. On Seneca’s pleasing, and therefore deadly, teaching.
3. On Socrates, master of all.
4. That a Christian ought not to drink the cup—that is, the teaching—of Christ and the cup of demons.
5. That Christian teaching ought to be defended against philosophers.
6. On compilers who compel Christians to plough with an ox and an ass together.
7. On Aristotle and dialecticians who offer probabilities to fools as truths.
8. That new heretics—or rather all heretics—are produced by philosophers and dialecticians.
9. That, just as there is an infinite conversion of things, so too of arguments; and what the rules of dialecticians are.
10. From this point the errors of those people will be set forth: that no living human being is a person, and on the heresies of John Damascene.
11. That in Christ nature is not person, but person is in nature; and that God, man, and humanity did not become some thing.
12. That the term *something* posits essence, not person; and that the term *man* predicates an accidental possession of Christ, but a subject of others—a rule observed neither by dialecticians nor theologians.
13. On another heresy of John Damascene.
14. The devilish solution of the heretics.
15. What their conclusion is.
16. On the false likeness with which the Word of God is clothed.
17. That Christ’s soul and body were neither man nor of a man.
18. Definition of the dialecticians’ phantom Christ.
19. That the heretics speak most truly when they say that their Christ is neither God nor man nor anything at all, just as is the Christ of the Manichees.
20. That these new heretics are wholly overthrown by the faithlessness of Jews and demons alone.
21. What the Christ of Christians is, as testified by the whole world.
22. What the name Christ signifies.
23. Recapitulation of the foregoing.
24. That the man assumed is, by supreme grace and fittingness, naturally both God and a person in the Trinity—a point which seems abuse and incongruity to both new and old heretics.
25. That not only of Christ’s divinity but also of his soul was it said: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John X); and that he who is Lord ought not to be called a “Lordly man.”
26. That by the final conclusion all the calumnies of the new heretics are most plainly blown away.

[Col. 1160C] It is now fitting to explain the more noteworthy matters in these chapters. In the first he has this:

“Peter of Poitiers: The Son of God assumed a soul; and a soul is a person, because it is an individual nature of rational essence; therefore the Son of God assumed a person. But they say that the soul, so long as it gives life to a body, is not a person—that is, is not one thing existing through itself, so that an allusion may be made to the origin of the word. John Damascene says: A common species—that is, man—is not to be taken of Christ, but is to be taken of Peter. Therefore, that Christ is a man is said in a different sense from that in which Peter is a man. Therefore, although Christ is a man and Peter is a man, one must not grant in a single utterance: ‘Christ and Peter is man,’ or ‘Christ and Peter are men.’

“Others say—my master is of their opinion—that uncreated power could lay aside the soul whenever it wished; which no one [else says]. Others say that those two things, namely soul and flesh, are united to the person of the Word, so that the divine Word is clothed with those two things as with a kind of garment. Nor is God said to have become man for any other reason than because he received the reality of flesh and blood, which he joined to himself in unity of person; not because those two things, or anything composed from them, are one person with the Word or are the Word, but because, according to them, this name *man* conjoins an accidental possession. The term *man* may also be used to designate a human person, so that it may denote something general, as it were. Note that when it is said, ‘Christ is man,’ this is the same as saying, ‘Christ is human nature,’ as will appear from what follows. For in the predicate it predicates an accidental possession. The Son of God is united to flesh through the mediation of the soul.

“(Chapter 2.) It is asked what this name *man* predicates when I say, ‘God became man’: person or accident. For if it predicates accident, it follows that God, not insofar as he is man, is something, but is of some kind; but if it predicates person, it is true that God, insofar as he is man, is a person, is a substance, is something. Therefore, according to different people, the meaning of this proposition differs: ‘Jesus’—which is almost constantly on everyone’s lips—‘remaining what he was, assumed what he was not,’ must be referred to nature, not person; and referred to nature in such a way that nature is not said to be person, but person to be in nature, etc.

“It is objected: Christ, insofar as he exists, is man; therefore, insofar as he is man, he is something. Or: someone has something; therefore he is something; and thus God or something else has something else. Therefore, insofar as he is man, he is God—which no one says. For humanity does not make him a *what*, except as though by force, if, as some say, we impose upon this word *something* a meaning other than substance: so that ‘insofar as he is man, he is something’ means that he is of some kind or of some nature.

“Again, there is the authority: ‘That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God’ (Luke I). Therefore, something born of the Virgin is God. Therefore God is something [Col. 1161C] born of the Virgin. Hence some have said that names fitting Christ according to his humanity, when masculine, are to be referred to the hypostasis, but when neuter, to the essence of God. Therefore they accept: ‘Christ is passible, mortal, temporal, visible,’ but not: ‘Christ is a passible thing, a mortal thing, or a temporal thing.’ Yet they do not accept: ‘Christ is nothing that is visible,’ because more is removed by the word *nothing* than is posited by the word *something*. For the word *something* posits essence, not person; the word *nothing* removes both person and essence. Hence they object to this inference: ‘Christ is not something that is visible; therefore Christ is nothing that is visible’; for this amounts to concluding: ‘There is no essence or person which is visible’—which is false of the person.

“Again, it is a rule of dialecticians that a name used equivocally of certain things makes false a proposition in which it is said of them in one utterance: for example, ‘a barking dog and a sea-monster are dogs.’ For one utterance cannot maintain two meanings. By the same reasoning, since *man* is said differently of Christ and Peter, it does not seem that one should grant, ‘Peter and Christ is man.’ For of Peter it predicates substance; of Christ, an accidental possession. Indeed, it seems that one should grant, ‘Christ alone is man,’ because the name *man* belongs to him alone in the sense in which it is said of him. But theologians do not always observe this reasoning, because dialecticians do not either. Thus Aristotle, in the book of the *Categories*, says that if someone calls them animals, speaking of a real animal and a painted animal—of which this name *animal* is said equivocally—yet there are some who say that the term *what* posits person as well as essence. Hence they accept: ‘Christ is something which is seen,’ that is, some person; and ‘something which is touched,’ and ‘something which dies.’

“(Chapter 13.) Since Christ died according to his human nature, it is asked whether, at his death, divinity was separated from flesh and soul. This appears to be so. For John Damascene says: ‘The divine nature is of such simplicity that it was not fitting for it to be united to a body formed from the clay of the earth except through the mediation of a rational creature.’ Therefore, since then the soul was separated from the flesh, it seems that divinity was separated from the flesh, since it was united to it through the soul; for when the middle is removed, the extremes are dissolved. Moreover, even while he lived, there was not anything composed from that soul and flesh. Indeed, if there had been something composed from them, it ceased to exist at death, because that death was nothing other than the separation of body from soul.

“(Chapter 14.) To solve the objections set out above, one must know in what sense Christ is called man and in what sense other human beings are called men, for there is a dissimilarity in the term. Peter or another is called man for two reasons: because he has soul and body, and because he has them united. For if they were separated, it would not truly be said, ‘Peter is man.’ But Christ is not called man on account of these two things, but solely on account of this one thing: that the Son is united to soul and body. Yet if an objection is raised concerning properties belonging by reason of the composition from soul and body—such as speech and the capacity for laughter, among which temporal death, life, and mortality appear to be numbered—it is difficult to see how they may be assigned to Christ. For when it is said, ‘Christ spoke,’ is this said according to something composed from soul and body, as in other human beings? No, because nothing was composed from that soul and body. Is it said according to the soul or according to the body? Both are plainly false, because neither was the subject of Christ’s speaking. Is it said according to the divine nature? No, because that was the subject of no accident. Therefore, since it is not said of Christ [Col. 1162D] that he spoke or wept, and the like, either according to the divine nature or according to the human nature, how is this said of him?

“Christ deigned to be born for us with as great charity as he deigned to suffer; therefore he merited as much for us by the former act as by the latter, or he merited for us by neither. Therefore he merited as much by being born as by suffering; therefore he merited nothing for himself or for us by any act which he did not merit by every other act. Let it suffice for me, then, to have supplied the beginning of a doubt, although it is not easy for me to provide its solution. To redeem is nothing other than to free from sin; he frees daily, therefore he redeems daily; therefore Christ was not a sufficient victim. Paul proves the same point likewise from the execration of fleshly victims. It is false that Christ redeemed insofar as he is man—that is, paid the price and freed from [Col. 1163A] sin. Christ is ‘the mediator of God and men’ (I Tim. II); therefore he is neither God nor man. The nature of a middle term is that it is neither of the extremes. Whatever that body had in itself cannot be said to have been possessed by the Son of God because of his union with it. Hence a continuity between the Son of God and the body is not admitted, although that body was neither God nor a part of God, but united to him; and thus Christ died, yet he is not dead according to either nature.

“Come then, prudent reader: gather the sum of their faith. Peter or another is called man for two reasons: because he has soul and body, and because he has them united. For if they were separated, it would not truly be said, ‘Peter is man.’ We grant this entirely, so much so that even in death it is no different, as has been proved and as the whole world sings: ‘All human beings shall rise in their own bodies.’ It does not say ‘all souls’ or ‘all dead persons,’ but ‘all human beings.’ Otherwise, at Christ’s coming, there is no one who will rise. Therefore everyone who is a man otherwise is not truly called man, and consequently is not man, because he is a false man.

“But Christ, he says, is called man not by this account or species of man, or because of these two things, but solely because the Son is united to soul and body. Nor is it required that soul be united to body; rather, the Word of God is clothed with those two things as with a garment, while soul and body are not united to one another. Therefore he is not man, nor does he have anything of a man, bearing only some soul that is not a man’s soul and some body that is not a man’s body. ‘By soul and body,’ he says, ‘we understand not a man but only the human nature with which Christ—that is, the Son of God—is clothed’: namely, by these names they posit, like Nestorius, not both natures but the divine alone, separately.

“For example, we read: ‘When Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded himself with his garment, for he was naked, and cast himself into the sea’ (John XXI). So, they say, ‘the Word became flesh’—that is, clothed, ‘found in appearance as a man’ (Phil. II)—‘and dwelt among us’ (John I), and cast himself into the great sea: there are animals there, arguments, of which there is neither number nor end. Thus Peter’s garment, although it adheres to, is joined, connected, and united with his nature in his person—so they say—nevertheless is neither Peter’s nature, nor a person, nor a part, nor absolutely anything of Peter; neither can it be called Peter, just as Peter cannot be called a garment. Although he wears it and in no way gives it life, he nevertheless gives form to it as clothed, while he himself is clothed by it. Just as the son of Joanna is truly called white by whiteness, which the garment cannot be in any way, nor can Peter be composed out of it and anything subsisting from it. ‘A likeness introduced is the mother of falsehood and the teacher of intelligible truth,’ says Augustine.

“Thus, they say, human nature united to Christ shows nothing more than one clothed—that is, incarnate. But it is itself nothing belonging to Christ, so that Christ, the Almighty, the King of the ages, the Lord, God, the Son of God, or the son of the Virgin cannot be said to be it any more than Peter’s garment can be called Peter or Joanna’s son; for it is merely an accident. Hence, they say, continuity between the Son of God and the body is not admitted, any more than between the coloured thing and colour, which is nothing of the coloured thing—just as the body is nothing, because it does not live through itself. Therefore nothing is composed from these two, soul and body, because, they say, they were never united to one another. ‘Humanity,’ they say, ‘does not make him a *what* except as though by force; nor is humanity itself a thing, but only of some kind.’ Therefore, by this reasoning, no virgin was ever mother of any son; rather, some unknown body without a soul merely conceived and miscarried. I shudder to pursue the remaining monstrosities. Even in death, they say, he was a true man because he always retained [Col. 1164B] that union of divinity with soul and body; while this remained, he could not truly be said not to be man.

“He could truly have been said not to be man if those two things had been united to one another or had been a man or belonged to a man. But since they were never united to each other, on this account they are neither man nor anything belonging to man; nor was divinity ever, as certain heresies said and were expelled by the Church, to body in place of soul or to soul in place of mind, reason, or will. It is plain that by that union of divinity with soul and body Christ could never be man, because those two distinct things were never man, nor anything of divinity or of man. Therefore, from what has been said, the following definition of this Christ is proved:

“Christ is not the Son—that is, the divine Word—clothed in a human fiction rather than in nature; possessing some body not of a man, which never lived or did anything with, or through, a soul; possessing some soul which never lived a human life or did anything with a body, nor did the body anything with it. Lest you think this a false definition, hear their confession. ‘Who,’ they say, ‘will assure us regarding those things read in the Gospels, how they are to be assigned to Christ, when he did nothing either according to soul, according to body, or according to something composed from soul and body, as in other human beings? Therefore, since it is not said of Christ that he spoke, wept, or did such things either according to the divine nature or according to the human nature, [Col. 1164D] how is this said of him?’ What more manifest question could be asked? By their own confession they show themselves deprived of all Gospel truth. Who, then, does not now see that they most truly say their Christ is not anything insofar as he is man? Indeed, as the heresy stated above truthfully asserts, he is neither God nor man, because he neither spoke nor did anything in the Gospel according to divine nature or according to human nature. I ask: who ever heard of such a Word of God, or who saw a monster like this? Did the Word made flesh in the beginning not have teeth, palate, arteries, tongue, feet, hands, and other limbs by which he could speak, move, and act? He certainly did. Why, then, did he do nothing? Hear their necessary reason: ‘Nothing,’ they say, ‘was composed from that soul and body, and neither was the subject of Christ’s speech and activity, because they were never united to one another.’

“But a body united to no soul is always dead, and cannot speak, walk, or do anything whatever. Likewise, a soul united to no body does not speak or perform anything humanly; and so neither is man nor anything of a man, and therefore neither can be called human nature. A rational soul belongs only to a human being, just as a human body does. ‘The death which Christ endured,’ he says, ‘was not in the soul, because human life had not been in it; nor was it in the body, because a body is not something which does not move. And then, when nothing is dead except Christ, and Christ is not body, he cannot be called dead. That death was not in the person of the Word, nor in anything composed from soul and body, because nothing there was composed. By soul and body we understand only human nature; for the divine nature, which is Christ, does not die. Nor does human human nature die, because human nature is not Christ.’ These are Peter’s words. What more is required? It is now evident that, just as the Manichees by their fables, so these people by their Aristotelian rules, with equal vanity have fashioned for themselves a phantom Christ, who is neither God nor man, who has neither acted nor done anything nor died according to divine nature or human nature.

“‘Sick about questions and battles of words’ [Col. 1165C] or fables, ‘understanding neither what they say nor whereof they affirm’ (I Tim. I). ‘I am not able,’ he says, ‘to explain such subtleties.’ Remove, I say, arguments from the sacred page; take them away where faith is. Indeed, by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we excommunicate such a Christ from the whole Church. Amen. And let him be cursed with every kind of curse. Let every Christian and Catholic people answer: Amen, let it be, let it be; because, both insofar as he is man and insofar as he is God, and in both respects altogether, he is nothing. And just as the name *nothing* signifies nothing, so the names which you use—Christ, soul, body—in the sense in which you understand, or rather imagine, them, signify nothing. Why do you not see the truth from yourself? If you had only a body, what would you be? If only a soul, what? But if neither, would you be anything, or anyone? Thus your Christ is neither God nor man, since you remove everything that is of God and of man.

“But you say: ‘Christ assumed and united to himself soul and body.’ Whoever hears this thinks that you are saying Christ assumed a true human being. But what do you say absolutely concerning the body? ‘Christ’s body is neither Christ, nor God, nor a part of him.’ And when you say this concerning both, ‘By Christ’s soul and body we understand only human nature,’ you immediately infer: ‘But human nature is not Christ.’ Without any doubt you remove from Christ the reality of the whole human being and of human nature. Therefore he is not man, because he has nothing of man. Thus you declare absolutely that he is Christ neither according to body, soul, nor both; and you state more explicitly that he did nothing according to divine nature or human nature, and assign to him nothing from the Gospel. Beyond doubt, by this you assert that he was nothing—that he had neither soul, body, both, divine nature, nor human nature. Therefore he is neither God, man, nor Christ, because you assert that he had or did nothing of God, nothing of man, nothing of Christ.

“Thus, when you say that Christ endured death, and immediately infer that this death was neither in soul, body, both, divine nature, nor human nature, you undoubtedly deny that he died, because he could die only in one of these. But just as, in the most evident combinations of your words, you assert that he neither was nor had any of these—that is, neither soul, body, both, divine nature, nor human nature—so consequently you find no death in him who is absolutely nothing.

“But because you dare not deny that Christ died, you evade the issue with the emptiest Manichean fables. Though dialectic is the science of arguing well, as Augustine began his own work: ‘For,’ he says, ‘one argues about words,’ in reality you deal only in bare terms; you deceive the unlearned, and are yourself deceived, a heretic deprived of all reality and alienated from the true Christ. Like a twisting serpent, a lurid and blind snake, as you slip horrifically this way and that through the slippery windings of the labyrinth of your opinions, nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, you openly betray yourself in your own words as fit to be condemned and trampled underfoot.

“With similar fables the Manichees say that their Christ—although they deny that the man was born from a woman, spoke, suffered, and died, because they do not dare and cannot deny these things—simulated them all by magic. But such teachers are overwhelmed by a thousand and a thousand authorities of Catholics and of the divine Scriptures.

“Concerning Peter Abelard, the most reverend Bernard says to Pope Innocent: ‘Indeed, he mocks the sacrament of the Incarnation just like the new evangelist whom we have in France.’ These people state outright: ‘Christ insofar as he is man is not something.’ That man too had his clerics in the Roman curia; perhaps these also have followers. [Col. 1166D] But Catholic truth presses us from every side, and Jewish faithlessness alone, together with demons, overwhelms us by saying: ‘You are Christ and the Holy One of God’ (Mark I); and: ‘You, being a man, make yourself God’ (John X). Behold, the Jews establish that he is man, while you say that he is nothing. Therefore, if they crucified nothing, you are truthful; but if, as not even a pagan denies, by crucifying they killed something and someone, a human being, then you are proved without doubt worse than Jew and demon, as is everyone who agrees with you. For no one is crucified by any arguments; therefore someone, and consequently something, was crucified. ‘For had they known it,’ says the Apostle, ‘they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (I Cor. II), because God and man are one person, Christ, life and invincible truth.

“‘Our mouth is open to you, O phantoms; our heart,’ the Apostle says, ‘is enlarged. You are not constrained in us, but are constrained in your own inward parts’ (II Cor. VI). ‘For we act as ambassadors, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God’ (II Cor. V).

“After Walter had thus for so long attacked Peter of Poitiers and the other theologians of his time, excessively devoted to Aristotelian and dialectical axioms and theorems, he finally adds the Catholic and Christian view of other masters concerning such mysteries, and prefixes this title: **Who the Christ of Christians Is.**
“I am,” he says, “the truth and the life” (John 14), not a phantom, but a man in that form, reality, and natural union by which the rest of men, including the first Adam, are men [Col. 1167B]. And I am a man, the son of that one. He had neither father nor mother. I myself, born of God the Father, am by nature God the Son; and, born of a human mother, am by nature man and son: subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh united to one another by a natural union. Yet I alone, born of a Virgin, lived a human life free from that corruption [the printed reading is uncertain], though in all respects according to the manner of others; yet I alone, without sin, truly died a human death, like others, my soul separated from my body; yet I alone did so by the power and mystery of the Redeemer. “Behold the man,” he says to the Jews: Why do you seek to divide and kill me, a man thus united and composed, who have spoken to you the truth which I heard from God? “Believe in God, and believe also in me” [Col. 1167C] (John 7, 8, and 14).

The reason and truth evident in the natural proofs and works in the Gospel demonstrate me most plainly; and indeed the whole world professes, saying: “As a rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ,” one person—not as Peter is his tunic, which is neither Peter’s nature, nor Peter, nor the son of Joanna. That comparison is more unlike than like the thing to which it is compared. Rather, it is as Peter’s soul with his flesh: a rationally animate soul, which is truly both Peter’s nature and Peter, one person with Peter, and the son of Joanna. So Christ, with his flesh properly united to a rational soul, is truly both Christ’s nature and property and Christ himself; and it is one person [Col. 1167D] naturally with Christ, and is and is called naturally the Son of God and the son of the Virgin. It possesses this and is one Son, not two; one Christ, not two; one person, not two.

Moreover, the name “Christ” signifies not the divine nature alone, as heretics think, but, as Jerome says, contains from eternity the individual mystery of both natures—divine and human, that is, of God and man. Hence Christ, insofar as he is man, cannot and ought not be understood apart from divinity; likewise, insofar as he is God, he cannot and ought not be conceived without humanity. Therefore, insofar as he is man, he is truly both something and a person and God; yet he is not other than Christ, nor another person than Christ, nor another thing than Christ.

[Col. 1168A] For just as man must always be understood as an individual of two natures, so Christ must be understood as an individual of three natures, as Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*: “The man himself assumed was God as soon as he was man; and from the moment he began to be man, from that moment he is God. For a creature was made, through whom every creature was made. For the Word was made flesh.” All creation must bear witness to this. Therefore let us say, as though we had not yet dealt at all with heretics: “How greatly are thy works magnified, O Lord! Thy thoughts are made exceedingly deep; a senseless man shall not know, neither shall a fool understand these things” (Ps. 91).

For just as every ordinary man is a son of man, his body first being formed from bloods over many days and then the spirit being infused, so man—an individual in and from two natures—is one person [Col. 1168B]. That person cannot by any means be divided or increased, either in the separation of death or in eternal death, so as not to remain one and the same person, although he is always changing.

But for the Word to be the Son of man, the reverse occurred. Nothing was first formed, then animated, and afterward assumed. Not so, heretics, not so. Here all your arguments are falsified, and your exceedingly hard foreheads are broken. It was not so, I say, as with the rest, but the opposite. That which was Christ’s, which first was “in the beginning,” “with God,” and “was God,” timelessly—“the Word was made flesh” (John 1), that is, was made a rational human substance on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], as the whole world testifies and celebrates today. And “what was made in him was life” [Col. 1168C] (ibid.), and that life was the Son of God himself, who was made the son of man.

He is one Emmanuel from both, who was not increased in himself by the assumed man, nor diminished or changed because the Word was made flesh, as Athanasius, Jerome, and Augustine said above. For what was made, or what he assumed, never existed as something alien outside his person, so that after the assumption one could properly speak of a rejection or alteration of person.

“But how did the whole man at once come to be and begin to exist? In that very respect he was not first someone other than the Word itself, while all the properties of Word and man remained whole and concurred in one person. Likewise, he who is without beginning and coeternal came to exist in time, as we have heard from the Law: ‘Christ remains [Col. 1168D] for ever’” (John 12).

Yet Peter calls God “man,” not because he is man, but because he merely has man; and conversely calls man “God,” not because he is God, but because he merely has God. And he declares that this is firmly to be believed in ecclesiastical matters: that God assumed man, and that man passed into God by God’s condescension. We have shown above that this was condemned by a council of eight hundred and thirty bishops.

For he considers it an abuse and a great absurdity that some created and simultaneously assumed man—namely, creature with Creator, thing made with maker, temporal with eternal, mutable with immutable, mortal with immortal, humanity with divinity, human nature with divine, son of man with Son [Col. 1169A] of God—should be believed and worshipped as one person in the Trinity, though not as a quaternity but as a Trinity; not because there are two sons, one distinct from the other, but because there is altogether one Son of God and of man, not two Christs but one, one thing indeed and another, yet with the properties of the three natures remaining; and that one God should be taught by Catholic faith.

Let the diabolical falsehood therefore be despised and condemned by Catholics—the falsehood which says that Christ the man is not someone or something. Even the prophet contradicts it, saying: “The earth,” that is, Christ the man, “is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges; if it is not he, who then is it?” (Job 9). This prophecy indeed rebukes the Jews, but above all throttles these new Manichees, when it says concerning Christ the man: “If it is not he, who then [Col. 1169B] is it?” Therefore he is someone and something. He is, I say, he is according to both natures; and he is uniquely so, as he says: “I am alone” (Ps. 140), because no other rational creature, no other man, except Christ the man alone, truly lives and reigns in the Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit—whence God for ever and ever.

Augustine: Simeon, an old man, was preserved until the infancy of the Word; he received in his hands the infant Word and said: “My eyes have seen thy salvation, O Lord” (Luke 2). But the Jews said: “How does this man know letters, since he has not learned?” (John 7). The Psalmist: “Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou disturb me? My soul is disturbed within me” (Ps. 41). Augustine: “My soul is sorrowful [Col. 1169C] unto death” (Matt. 26). “Jesus groaned in spirit and troubled himself” (John 11). For who could trouble him, unless he himself did so? Jesus hungered, slept, was troubled, and died—but because he himself willed it. It was in his own power to be affected thus or otherwise, or not to be affected.

For the Word assumed soul and flesh, adapting to himself in unity of person the nature of the whole man. The souls of apostles and holy prophets too were illuminated by the Word, but of none was it said: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1). Of none was it said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Christ’s soul and Christ’s flesh, with the Word of God, are one person, one Christ. Accordingly, when he troubled himself, it was truly the supreme power of Christ’s will at its command [*ad nutum*; the printed text reads “ad nutum”].

Likewise: “The mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2). When “Lord” is said properly, “Lord-man” cannot rightly be said. Likewise: We must beware lest we establish the divinity of the man in such a way as to deny the reality of his body.

Isaiah: “Therefore cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, because he himself is accounted exalted” (Isa. 2). Jerome: “The Jews, understanding therefore that the prophecy concerned Christ, interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that it might seem not to praise Christ but to hold him of no account. For what coherence of words, what order of speech and meaning, would there be if we said: Since these things stand thus and the day of the Lord is coming, on which the whole condition of Judaea must be overthrown and all things crushed, I warn and command you [Col. 1170A] to cease from the man who breathes and lives as we men do, because he is to be reckoned as nothing? Would anyone praise any man by saying: Beware lest you offend him who is wholly nothing? Therefore it must be understood in the contrary sense: Since all these things are to come upon you and are foretold by the prophetic Spirit, I warn and command you to cease from him who, according to the flesh, is indeed a man, has a soul, and breathes and draws air through his nostrils as we men breathe and live; but according to divine majesty is and is believed to be exalted.”

Reflecting silently within myself, I cannot discover why the Seventy [the Septuagint translators] wished to render into Greek so clear a prophecy concerning Christ; but the passage was added to Greek copies from Aquila’s edition under asterisks by Origen. The others who translated it, however, drew the ambiguous expression toward an impious meaning. That is no wonder, since they mistranslated it and would not say anything glorious concerning Christ, in whom they did not believe—being, plainly, Jews or half-Jews, that is, Ebionites, etc., etc. [Col. 1170B]

From this point William of Conches teaches that all things arise from the aggregation of atoms, that is, of exceedingly small bodies. And Peter says: “It is proved that Christ’s flesh was not in Abraham or Adam, because there were not in them as many atoms as there were men descending from them.” Therefore, if one atom, according to them, is a *what* or a *something*, because it is a body, and every body is a substance, while every substance is either rational or irrational—concerning which “what” and “something,” as has been said, the question is asked—how great a something is the whole [Col. 1170C] man, in whom there are almost innumerable atoms, and surely both spiritual and bodily substance.

Therefore, if every man—and hence Christ also, since he too is man—is something: insofar as his body is something, insofar as his soul is something, insofar as his divinity is something, insofar as his feet, hands, head, bones, and, to conclude briefly, insofar as the almost innumerable parts which he both has and is are something—how much more, insofar as he is whole, is he a great and, so to speak, ineffable something.

Let these dialecticians therefore choose one of two alternatives: either every man, and therefore Christ also, is not something insofar as he is man; or Christ is not man. Whatever they say, they are now condemned by their own judgment, not as dialecticians but as heretics. Yet we despise and excommunicate their atoms, the rules of philosophers, and their ridiculous “what” and “something” and the like, saying with the Apostle: “If anyone should preach anything other than what we have preached to you—even an angel, even Peter—let him be accursed” (Gal. 1). Such ravings are nowhere found in the divine Scriptures.

Therefore, although nothing is finer than spiders’ webs, nothing sharper than the points of ears of grain—such are the wits and arguments of demons through the mouths of heretics—yet, for Catholics, as Ambrose says in the *Hexaemeron*, they are to be blown away rather than read. For “everything born of God [Col. 1171A] conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5), by which we do not merely suppose, but without hesitation believe, hold, and worship the Father and the Son Jesus Christ—with skin and flesh, bones and sinews, soul and mind, and the reality of the whole man—and the Holy Spirit; whence God for ever and ever. Amen.

This is the faith which from the beginning to the present day has cast out demons, driven away sicknesses, and raised the dead, and by the dead raised others. This, therefore, is the one and universal limit, Alpha and Omega, beginning and end, for whose sake, through whom, and in whom are all things. To him be honor and glory [Col. 1172A], “who alone does wonders” (Ps. 135).

Walter said these things and many more against Peter of Poitiers and other theologians whom he regarded as pseudo-scholastics. From their school came disciples far more audacious, who, adding to their masters’ inventions, undertook to discuss so many ridiculous questions, while entangling serious and necessary ones in so many windings, distinctions, and arguments seemingly more probable that the Catholic faith—which rests upon the oracle of eternal truth, not upon the foundation of human reasoning—has wavered in the minds of many.

# Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury
## Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury

Prologue. 1009

CHAPTER I.—Concerning Anselm’s father and mother, his childhood, and his vision. 1010

CHAPTER II.—Concerning Anselm’s deeds in Burgundy, France, and Normandy. Anselm followed the counsel of the Archbishop of Rouen and became a monk at Bec. 1011

CHAPTER III.—Lanfranc, prior of Bec, was appointed to govern the monastery of Caen. Anselm succeeds to the priorship of the monastery of Bec. Concerning Walter Tyrell while dining with Anselm, and concerning a great sturgeon. 1012

CHAPTER IV.—Anselm obtained divine grace, so that he might profess to serve God with a pure heart and a good conscience. Concerning a certain old man of decrepit age. Concerning a certain young man [who on] no occasion whatsoever would put his hand to his private parts. Concerning Osbern the monk. Concerning a certain brother hostile toward Anselm. Concerning the vision of the monk Ryculf. 1013

CHAPTER V.—At the monastery of Bec Anselm wrote six books: [Col. 1194] I, *On Truth*; II, *On Freedom of Choice*; III, *On the Fall of the Devil*; IV, *On the Grammarian*; V, called the *Monologion*; VI, the *Proslogion*. Anselm is seized by a grave illness, during which he was rapt in spirit. Concerning a certain abbot [who] came to Anselm seeking counsel. Concerning boys brought up in the cloister. Concerning a certain knight named Cadulus. 1017

CHAPTER VI.—Herluin, abbot of Bec, dies. Anselm succeeds him as abbot of the monastery of Bec. Lanfranc the archbishop’s doubt whether Saint Ælfheah was a martyr or not. A question put to Anselm, abbot of Bec. Anselm’s answer to Lanfranc’s question on this matter. 1019

CHAPTER VII.—Concerning the glorious King William the First: he departs from this world; his son William Rufus succeeds him to the kingdom of England, a man little just or pious. Anselm wrote in England the book *On the Incarnation of the Word*. 1021

CHAPTER VIII.—How Anselm approaches the king, humbly asking to return to Rome for the pallium, in order to exercise his office. Concerning the disturbance and dispute between the king, the archbishop, and the bishops of England. 1023

CHAPTER IX.—Anselm is sent into exile. Arriving at Canterbury, he explains to his community of the church of the Saviour at Canterbury the reason for his journey; before Christ’s high altar, taking up purse and staff, he commends himself, with a blessing, to God and to the prayers of the faithful. The Roman pontiff’s commendation to Anselm. 1025

CHAPTER X.—In the region of Capua Anselm completed the volume *Why God Became Man*. Concerning the scarcity of water. Concerning a water-well. Concerning the duke of Apulia. Concerning the count of Sicily, and his friendship with Pope Urban. Concerning the Council of Bari. Concerning the confusion of the Greeks and their heresies. Anselm is called “Holy Man” by Roman men. Concerning the investitures of churches. Concerning the council held at Rome. 1027

CHAPTER XI.—Archbishop Anselm arrives at Lyons and is honourably received by the venerable Archbishop Hugh. William, king of England, sends envoys to Rome. The cause between the archbishop and the king is deferred by Pope Urban. Concerning the death of Pope Urban. Anselm is received by Guy, Archbishop of Vienne. Concerning two complaining knights. Concerning crumbs from Anselm’s table. Concerning the first, second, and third visions of the death of William, king of the English. 1028

CHAPTER XII.—Anselm rests at the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu during his first exile. Concerning lightning and the thunderbolt. Concerning the death of King William II. Concerning King Henry. Concerning the case argued before Pope Paschal. Concerning the liberty of Christ Church, Canterbury. 1030

CHAPTER XIII.—Anselm and his companions rest for one night at Florence. Concerning a certain man who had lain in Saint Anselm’s bed, and what befell him. Concerning Saint Anselm the archbishop’s prohibition from entering the kingdom of England in the time of Henry the First. Concerning a certain blind man illuminated by Saint Anselm during his second exile. Concerning the peace made between King Henry of England and Anselm. 1032

CHAPTER XIV.—Henry, king of England, amicably visited Archbishop Anselm on the day of the Assumption of Blessed Mary at the monastery of Bec. Concerning a cleric’s derangement of mind. Concerning the war between Henry, king of England, and his brother Robert, count of Normandy. In England Anselm wrote a little book *On the Harmony of God’s Foreknowledge, Predestination, and Grace with Free Choice*. Concerning Thomas, archbishop-elect of York. 1033

CHAPTER XV.—Letter of Saint Anselm to Thomas, archbishop-elect of York, written while Anselm lay sick in his bed, concerning the jurisdiction of the Church of Christ at Canterbury. 1034

CHAPTER XVI.—Anselm begins the little book *On the Origin of the Soul* and does not finish it, because death overtook him. Concerning Anselm’s death on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], and concerning the year of his pontificate. Concerning multiplied balsam, and its miracles. 1035

CHAPTER XVII.—Concerning the miracles of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, after his death. Concerning the sarcophagus in which his body is enclosed. Concerning the chaplain of the bishop of Rochester and Count Arnulf, troubled at sea. 1037

CHAPTER XVIII.—Concerning the miracles of our holy Father Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. Concerning a certain monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, who approached the tomb of holy Father Anselm to pray—namely, whether Anselm should be prayed to, or whether one should pray for Anselm; whether he was worthy to be invoked as a saint, because his name is written in the book of life—and concerning his other miracles. 1038
